Where do I even start? I’d have to say that the scariest thing about Resident Evil 7 is probably Capcom’s description of the game. They actually had the nerve to describe it as “photorealistic” with an “unprecedented level of immersion”.

Well, I can tell you now that’s absolute verbal diarrhoea, because the game looks terrible from a visual perspective. Bearing in mind I played this on a high-end PC on ultra settings and at times it looked like I was playing a PS2 game.

Not only are the graphics appalling, but it also lacks any real sense of immersion. The game tries to create horror with an overuse of gore and cheap jump scares, but none of it comes close to creating the kind of unsettling and scary environment you expect. I felt like I could run around each area without ever feeling worried, because nothing is scary once you realise it’s just the occasional jump scare and that’s it.

I’d have to say it’s one of the most scripted and predictable games I’ve ever played, which is disappointing because I was really looking forward to it and genuinely wanted to love it.

Playing as Ethan is a dampening experience as well, because if he’s not walking around whimpering with the same set of whimpers at timed intervals, he’s dropping one liners that feel completely out of place. The gameplay is frustrating too, because Ethan runs so slowly that I’d imagine his own shadow gets frustrated. At one point I actually had to check if I was using the correct button to sprint because it felt like I was walking, and it’s made even worse by the narrow field of view, which makes the game feel more like a colonoscopy simulator than a survival horror.

With all that said, I think the most frustrating thing is the gunplay. When you shoot an enemy in the head they often stagger, but while they’re in that stagger animation any other shots you fire don’t register, so they’re just wasted bullets. You have to wait for the stagger animation to end before firing again, which is ridiculous. The game takes away your ability to shoot when you want and instead decides when you can and can’t land shots.

I’ve played a lot of the Resident Evil games and I just expect this kind of stuff now. I’m actually convinced that Capcom’s creative department is so empty of ideas that if something original entered the building it would probably trigger the fire sprinklers just to wash away the confusion.

I could go on and on, but I don’t want to waste any more time on this game. If you’re looking for a great atmospheric horror, forget it, it’s garbage.

It isn’t that groundbreaking or scary as I hoped, but it isn’t that bad either. There wasn’t a time when I felt anything for our missing wife, in fact, I feel like the Bakers bear more emotional weigh for me than Mia keeping her bioterrorist secret from us (and how her involvement led up to the events of the story). The molded and enemies in general offer no real variety or real reason to fear them. Jack’s stalker AI is lame and I would argue remake Nemesis is scarier than him, Marguerite is meh and the boss fight isn’t as stressful as I hoped. Their crackhead son’s (I couldn’t be bothered to remember his name) section in the game is extremely underwhelming and I have heard from other people that his is one of the most challenging parts of it. Matter of fact, this whole game is underwhelming and disappointing after hearing the praises it receives. I feel like the horror and novelty ended after the first videotape of Clancy. Mia on the ship was a snoozefest, and I spent so much of time just walking in circles to the point I get annoyed and was just eager to finish this game and get it over with. The final boss fight was a whole nothingburger as well. I feel like my experience with this game could have been better if it was my first Resident Evil game, then again, this isn’t my first rodeo with survival horror. I think a big issue is how uneven the pacing feels throughout the game. It starts off strong but it doesn’t maintain that momentum. The game kinda plateaus and then dips with long periods where nothing interesting or tense is happening. The game leans heavily on that initial shock factor and atmosphere, but loses its novelty because there isn’t enough narrative depth to keep things engaging. Even the resource management and survival elements, which are usually a core part of what makes this genre compelling, feel a bit watered down. I never really felt that constant pressure of “I might not make it through this next encounter,” which is kind of essential for survival horror to work. I don’t think I’ve crafted a single ammo or item in this game besides anything that will help me get some of my health back. It honestly ends up feeling more like going through the motions rather than actually surviving something and the lack of pressure ties back into the enemy design too. Enemies aren’t that threatening or varied and the whole system starts to feel less meaningful when you could always just juke them and get them to walk towards the mines. The story presentation also doesn’t do it many favours. I’ll be honest I think there are interesting ideas there but they never fully come together satisfyingly. Ethan has no personality, Mia annoyed the ♥♥♥♥ out of me, and it completely disconnected me from actually caring or staying invested in the Winters. I also think part of the disappointment comes from expectations. With how much praise the game gets, I was expecting something that would really push the genre forward or at least leave a strong impression, but instead it felt more like a solid idea that wasn’t executed to its full potential. There are glimpses of what could have been a genuinely great horror experience. After finishing the game for the first time I just felt kind of indifferent and bored, which is probably the worst outcome for a horror game. It’s not terrible by any means but it never reaches the highs it seems like it’s aiming for, and that gap between expectation and reality makes the whole experience feel more disappointing than it probably would have otherwise.

The game that saved the series. I think Resident Evil 7 is a return to its roots. After the action-packed shooters RE5 and RE6, we got ourselves a survival horror at its finest. Mysterious story, an eerie setting, and a suspense atmosphere. 

The Bakers' house is full of key items and puzzles to solve. Once again you need to manage your inventory and resources carefully, since it's limited, you have to think twice about what you take and what you leave behind. 

The switch to first-person camera is a welcome change I'd say. Since RE7 leans more into horror, this perspective allows you to feel more immersed and tense. With smaller field of view, you ought to be more perceptive and vigilant. 

As for the gunplay and combat - it's very solid. The shooting is clean, the guns are responsive, and you need to collect chem fluid and gunpowder to craft ammo. Only flaw I would point out is the lack of enemy variety, but that's a minor issue. 

Overall, I really enjoyed the game. If you like survival horror, don't miss out on this one.

[h1]A Terrifying Return to Form — Survival Horror Done Right[/h1]

[b]29 HOURS PLAYED[/b] across two full playthroughs (Normal + Madhouse), and I’ve completed all DLCs. Even playing this for the first time in 2026, nearly a decade after release, this game holds up incredibly well both gameplay-wise and visually.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]
• Scariest Resident Evil game ever — genuinely terrifying
• Perfect return to survival horror roots
• Tight resource management + great level design
• First-person perspective adds immersion and tension
• Strong antagonists (Baker family are top-tier)
• Weak final section + underwhelming final boss
⭐️ 9 / 10
(RTX 5080 | Ryzen 7 7800X3D | 128GB DDR5 | 1440p 60FPS)

Full Review
[b]Gameplay:[/b]

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard completely resets the formula for the franchise. After the more action-heavy direction of RE5 and RE6, this brings things back to what made the series great: survival horror first, action second.

Resources are limited — ammo, healing, weapons — so every encounter matters. You actually have to think before engaging, which adds tension to every moment.

Gunplay feels solid and satisfying, and the game’s tight, interconnected environments make exploration feel meaningful. The puzzles are exactly what you’d expect from a strong Resident Evil title — nothing groundbreaking, but consistently well-designed.

The biggest change is the first-person perspective, which I was skeptical about at first, but it ended up being one of the best decisions. Everything feels more intense and claustrophobic since the horror is right in your face.

This game also plays a huge role in shaping modern Resident Evil:

Classic PS1 titles established survival horror foundations
RE7 refined it with immersion, crafting, and environmental storytelling
Later games and remakes clearly build off what this game introduced
Graphics:

For a 2017 game, this still looks great today. The environments — especially the Baker house — are detailed, grimy, and incredibly immersive.

Lighting and atmosphere carry a lot of the visual weight, making every hallway and room feel tense and unpredictable.

[b]Story / Characters (No Spoilers):[/b]

The story is engaging and expands Resident Evil lore in a meaningful way.

The Baker family are easily some of the best antagonists in the franchise. Each one feels distinct, memorable, and genuinely unsettling.

They aren’t just enemies — they carry the entire horror tone of the game.

[b]Lore & World-Building:[/b]

This game does a great job expanding the universe while still keeping things grounded and focused.

Environmental storytelling is strong, and the smaller-scale setting actually helps the immersion compared to larger, more action-heavy entries.

You can also jump into Resident Evil 7: Biohazard with no prior knowledge of the series and still fully understand and enjoy the story. It works really well as a standalone experience while still connecting to the broader Resident Evil universe.

[b]Music:[/b]

The soundtrack is solid. It’s not quite on the level of the classic PS1 trilogy or RE4 (2005), but it fits the atmosphere really well and enhances the tension when it matters.

[b]Performance:[/b]

Flawless on my system. No crashes, no frame drops.

Specs: RTX 5080 | Ryzen 7 7800X3D | 128GB DDR5 RAM | 1440p 60FPS | Installed on SSD

Pros ✅

• Genuinely terrifying — scariest in the series
• Strong return to survival horror roots
• Great level and map design
• Memorable antagonists (Baker family)
• Immersive first-person perspective
• Solid puzzles and resource management
• DLC adds meaningful closure and context

Cons ❌

• Final section (Wrecked Ship) loses a lot of the horror
• Becomes more action-focused toward the end
• Extremely underwhelming final boss

[b]Final Verdict:[/b]

A massive comeback for the franchise and one of the best modern survival horror games.

Even years later, it still feels fresh, terrifying, and incredibly well-designed. While it doesn’t fully stick the landing, the overall experience is so strong that it easily earns a place among the top-tier Resident Evil titles.

At the time of this review, I've played all the mainline RE games except for RE0, 1, and 6.

RE7 is definitely my flavor of horror game, leaning into more of the survival aspects instead of bombastic action, but some things were left to be desired for me by time I rolled credit on the game. I'll start with the positives though. In terms of atmosphere and setting, I absolutely adore this game, and I think its probably my favorite in those terms for the series. I loved the Baker family, and the twists in the story were pretty good with some nice hints of foreshadowing. Ethan I feel like gets an odd amount of hate from the community, but in RE7 I think his writing and dialogue were good.

My negatives is that, even with the amazing setting and atmosphere, I felt almost zero tension after the first few minutes. The enemy encounters were very sparse, didn't feel very threatening, and were very predictable after seeing they spawn from mold. What Grace's sections in RE9 do soooo well is that each enemy encounter feels deliberately placed there. The zombies have identity, fill the role where they stand, and does environmental storytelling so well. These are so so so important to a survival horror experience, and I think RE7 misses that. Granted, being mold monsters are hard to have identity, they just didn't feel compelling. It feels like the gaming is pointing at me saying "you should be scared because this thing is scary!" I felt more scared at times in RE8 despite the atmosphere/setting doing far less for these scary moments. RE7 and RE8 share this next problem, but the puzzles felt very on the rails, and the backtracking felt less meaningful and more like a chore. The best segment was definitely the birthday trap, as it felt like proper escape room where you had to think a little out of the box to finish. 

This game could have been my favorite in the series, but left me underwhelmed in more ways than one. I know I talked about a lot of negatives, but I actually did still really enjoy this game, and its DLCS were really fun and tied up loose ends. Just finished Resident Evil 7: Biohazard and yeah… what a ride.

This game genuinely pulled survival horror back to its roots. The shift to first-person was a risky move, but it paid off big time. It makes everything feel more personal and way more intense. You’re not just watching Ethan go through hell, you’re right there with him, every creak, every footstep hitting differently.

The Baker family is easily one of the most memorable parts. Jack especially is straight-up terrifying but also weirdly entertaining. The way the game blends horror with dark humor is something I didn’t expect, but it works. The atmosphere inside the house is insane, it constantly keeps you on edge without relying on cheap jumpscares.

Gameplay-wise, it’s tight. Limited resources actually matter, exploration feels rewarding, and the puzzles are simple enough to not get frustrating but still satisfying. Boss fights were solid too, each one feeling different instead of repetitive.

Story starts off mysterious and keeps you hooked, though towards the end it gets a bit more action-heavy and slightly loses that pure horror vibe. Still, it wraps up well and sets things up nicely for what comes next.

Overall, this is easily one of the best entries in the series. It’s scary, immersive, and just fun to play. If someone told me this was their favorite Resident Evil, I wouldn’t argue.

Rating: 9/10

I hate to say it, but respectfully this game is [i] very overrated [/i], most of its glazing rightfully coming from the fact that it revitalised the series and has some very good moments of tension, atmosphere, ambience and horror. You can however [b] very easily [/b] tell that this was their first attempt at making a new horror game with the new engine. The best way I can describe it is that it feels like a good horror game made by people who've never played a video game in their life, especially on PC, as there's almost no quality of life features like the ability to skip cutscenes for example. You can tell this was made with console as a priority. [b] Using a healing item is bound to control on a game with crouching. Diabolical. [/b]

The UI is probably the worst UI I've ever seen in a video game, compounded by the fact it's clunk to use [b] and [/b] doesn't pause the game. Either would be fine on it's own, but wrestling with a bad UI while the game doesn't pause is frustrating. The top four slots of your inventory are permanently bound as quick slots to D-Pad, even without a controller, or scroll wheel. This means items that can't be equipped (ammo, puzzle items, healing items.) will go in these slots and take up one of your four quick equip slots but will still put your weapon away and leave you defenceless if you select them. The problem with this is that, for example, if you have two weapons and two non weapons in your top slots, it means you have a 50:50 chance to equip a weapon or be unequipped and naked when you scroll your mouse wheel.

You're constantly grabbed, frozen, then turned 180 degrees around by Jack. This sounds fine on paper but in practice it's so frustrating and disorientating and annoying. There's plenty of time between the grab and his follow-up attacks making them a mostly non-threat, just an annoyance as you have to keep turning back every time. The healing animation is so slow and long, and you can't do anything else during it so gameplay is frozen and dragged to a standstill while you heal. 

The lighting in too many sections is way too dark, even with the slider turned up, looking good in most areas but a pitch black screen in far too many other places. The shadows are arguably broken. Google "Resident Evil 7 Shadow bug". There's so many steam and reddit posts about the shadows to the point I believe the game is just broken. The shadows work on other RE games so I don't believe it's the engine, I just think it's RE7. No matter what I did (Max setting, Min settings, any combination, RTX on or off, downgrade to Dx11), my shadows looked like a comic book.

There's no good characters in the game. Ethan is such a wet fart of a character who feels like he has no presence or impact in his own game, Mia is an easy to dislike character yet is supposed to be the player and Ethan's main motive. The Baker's start off good but never stop yapping and end up too cartoony before the first boss fight even begins.

There's one good dynamic and interesting boss fight in the game, the rest are bad. One of the first one's features buggy bodybags that you're supposed to kick (but it's a coinflip if they'll actually work) and equips the player with a chainsaw so all exploration and ammo you find/craft is meaningless.

Enemies are at a low-point for the franchise. There's almost no variation and only a few of them in the game anyway (like 40~ enemies in the game to fight on a playthrough?). Most enemies are a vague, black, humanoid blob that stumble towards you and poke or slap you. Visually bland stumbling blob, bland crawling blob that dies with one headshot from a pistol, slightly tougher blob man that tries to shield his head, insects in one section that can only be damaged by one certain weapon. That's it. The overwhelming majority of enemies are generic black blob men with no distinguishing features so they all feel copy and pasted.

The four VHS tapes just feel like padding, making you play the same area twice. Two of the VHS tapes are from the perspective of Mia who is alive in the present, so all tension is lost, and the two other two feature throw-away characters so you know they're doomed and you have zero investment.

Exploration is weak in a way, not so-much level design, but in terms of rewards and incentives to explore. There's only 3 items to buy in the 'shop'; a HP upgrade, a reload speed upgrade, and a Magnum. There's only two inventory upgrades, both places in well-lit areas, one placed by a save point so basically unmissable. The only real reason to explore is for ammo and healing items, but despite killing every enemy I came across and never running or avoiding fights, I had a mountain of ammo and healing items left in my inventory and storage after finishing the game.

It's the only RE game I regret my time playing and spent half of my playtime wishing I was playing something else or having to convince myself to not uninstall it but to try and keep playing instead of having an actual desire to play the game.

Resident Evil 7は素晴らしいゲームだ。子供のころRE4とRE5が大好きだった私は、近年のRE2、RE3、RE4のリメイクもとても気に入っていたが、本作を始めたとき、一人称視点のゲームプレイが魅力的かどうか少し疑問に思った。自分が好んでいたREのプレイスタイルから大きく離れていたため、最初は違和感があった。しかし、遊べば遊ぶほどRE7が紛れもなく見事なゲームであることに納得した。

アクション寄りだったRE4以降の作品と比べると、RE7はホラー面にしっかり焦点を当てた作品だ。ファーストパーソン視点は環境の圧迫感をより身近に感じさせ、最初のエリアであるベーカー家は小島監督のPTを連想させる雰囲気がある。開発元のカプコンは近年、ゲームプレイや環境デザインで立て続けに成功を収めているが、RE7のベーカー家や旧館のレベルデザインはまさに神クラスだと言える。

本作の銃撃はシリーズの他作と比べるとやや鈍く感じるが、エリア探索は相変わらず非常に楽しく満足できる。隅々まで探索し慎重に進むというプレイは、ダークソウル系のゲームでもREシリーズでも私が心から楽しめるスタイルであり、今回のRE7もその点で期待を裏切らない。

とはいえゲームが完璧というわけではない。序盤から中盤の四分の三ほどはベーカー家での展開だが、その後ストーリーの舞台が一変し、主人公が別のエリアへ移される。そこからのゲームプレイは残念ながら魅力に欠ける。前半があまりにも優れていただけに、後半のやや弱い締めくくりは惜しい。しかしそれでも本作を遊ぶ価値は十分にある。個人的にはRE2リメイクの三人称視点のほうが好みではあるが、それでもRE7は自信を持っておすすめできる。

Ethan is the slowest runner in all video games. After 8 hours of playtime so far the game consists of mostly cat and mouse scenarios with tons of locked doors and puzzles requiring an item blocking your progress. Gameplay loop consists of getting chased, fail, fail again until you do exactly as the game wants you to do to progress. Rinse and repeat. Some of the solutions don't feel like common sense and takes guessing with trial and error until you do the right sequence of actions to pass. The amount of items you're able to carry is abysmally small and you'll find yourself unable to carry new items, then forced to frequently run back to your storage chest to unload. 

Thankfully the locations are atmospheric and creepy, and you never know what you'll find around every corner. The enemies are out of their mind bonkers and all have totally unhinged personalities. The grandma appearing out of nowhere sitting in her wheelchair, her gaze following your every movement is totally unnerving, I love the sense of surprise and dread the game evokes when entering new locations, not knowing what you'll find around every corner.

I'm enjoying progressing and discovering new locations despite the somewhat frantic scenarios that usually lead to frustration due to Ethans clumsy and sluggish movements. The game looks great with some reshade touches. For some reason its been triggering motion sickness after an hour or two of play like I'm on some rickety boat stuck in a storm, but it's worth the ride and definitely worth a look for horror fans. There are genuine jump scares, a creepy claustrophobic location, and some completely bonkers inhabitants. Despite its flaws the world and scenario is engaging enough to provoke enough inspiration in me to continue this ride and discover the conclusion to all this mayhem.

[h1]This game is a masterpiece.[/h1]

After binging an unhealthy amount of hours into nearly every game with the title Resident Evil, across nearly every console they've come out on, this was something I was looking forward to with high hopes and honeyed memories from when I first got it in january 2017 on console. And I will say it now; this may still be the best resident evil to have been released, even when compared to how fantastic Requiem is.


The story is fantastic and in my first time playthrough left me guessing on so many things, leaning forward to what twists were coming, and jolting back when the scares came up as they do great to not overdo how often they happen, letting the tension build between story beats and letting the atmosphere build in a way most other games in the genre don't do well enough of. I will say a severe pain point for a few people will most likely be the replay value of the narrative tanks a bit due to how much this game relies on twist information, or big reveals/shocking moments, coupled with a short completion time even if you're aiming for finding collectables/all of the goodies to make your life easier.

Gameplay is tight for almost the entire way through the game, with only one or two 10 minute points I would say "Changes things up" in a way a good few people would hate in their own right; combat feels smooth and rewarding, but also not brainless and overly predictable, smaller molded enemies are able to be blocked and taken down pretty smoothly but as you fight more and more there either is more enemies, or more variety to everything you need to deal with in a way that feels like the PS1 titles and how they handled their combat - but obviously more polished and modernized to keep from restricting the player unnecessarily.

Characters and their personalities, how they talk, how they behave is honestly I'd say arguably the weakest point of the game; but there's also hardly any slacking here either, the game starts off with cliche horror tropes left, right, and center, right down to stupid people getting themselves killed/caught for fame and fortune trying to ghost hunt. But the further the game goes, the tropes melt away and soon you see something more genuine as the story progresses, and by the end of it some of these characters are nearly as enjoyable as the characters you've seen through several RE games by now.

OST and Soundscape, whoever worked on this did such a great job that I hope they got bonuses; providing probably one of my favorite videogame credit songs/intro songs that I can think of, a saferoom song that I think easily hits into the top-best ranges for the energy it gives and how comforting it is despite the distortion in certain notes that remind you that despite it being a safe room, everywhere around it is an immediate danger you have to walk into to get out alive. And away from the OST, you have very real sounds of what you'd expect walking through dilapidated Southern-USA buildings, from the constant creaking of every wood plank, the eerie silence when you get to rooms with more concrete/foundation level work, and so much more that kept me immersed almost every step of the way.


To add a lengthy sidenote to shill it further, Gold Edition/All DLC is what I'd recommend over just getting the base game. On the surface some of the content comes off as memes, but nearly everything except for two clearly labeled "pure distraction" modes adds something to the story, to several important characters that in some way come up during Ethan's struggle. The DLC is for the most part fun, I would say some of them are difficult without knowing the game well enough, and others are just puzzles waiting to be cracked with storytelling as the reward.


[h2]In short[/h2]
I cannot recommend this game enough, to anybody who enjoys horror games, survival horrors, or just good first person games with a goal for immersion with solid gameplay. Even at full price the first time experience is worth it.

Except twice the damage. No thermal scope needed but phew, that major damage increase threw me off. I even had the defense coin on me later and was still taking damage quick. Like, what the hell?!

Bosses is really where the damage gets to you. See, if you run into problems dodging their attacks, or bad parrying, or something, theyll kill you in 1 or 2 attacks. Sometimes just 1 attack, which really shocks you cause you were doing really well and BAM! Go back to the checkpoint/load and try again. Marguerite for instance does this. If she gets close enough she can go for a bite which will 1 shot you. Was doing great against her then: chomp. I was like WHAT THE HELL?!

"Resident Evil 7" has been such a refreshing and intense experience so far. Even with just 4–5 hours in, it’s already pulled me in completely. What makes it even more surprising for me is that this is actually my first Resident Evil game - and it was gifted to me by a friend, which made the experience feel even more special from the start. I usually just watch playthroughs on YouTube because I don’t really enjoy horror games myself, but this one made me want to try it firsthand - and I’m really glad I did. I actually watched a full playthrough of this game a long time ago, but I’m honestly glad I don’t remember much of it now, because it makes everything feel fresh and unpredictable.

The first-person perspective makes everything feel so much more personal and immersive—you’re not just watching the horror, you’re right there inside it. The atmosphere is easily one of the strongest parts of the game. From the creaking floors to the unsettling silence, it constantly keeps you on edge.

What I really appreciate is how it balances horror and exploration. It’s not just about cheap jump scares (though there are a few well-placed ones), but more about that slow, creeping tension that builds as you explore the house and uncover what’s going on. Every room feels like it has a story, and you’re always a little nervous about what’s waiting around the corner. There’s this constant feeling of vulnerability that makes every small victory feel earned. It’s the kind of game that’s hard to play for long stretches - not because it’s bad, but because it’s that intense.

Overall, it’s been an amazing experience so far, and I’m really excited (and slightly scared) to keep going.

The gameplay systems all work together to feed the tension of making it through encounter to encounter. My only complaint is that [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] follows the trend of Resident Evil games having a purely awful section. The Verdict: A Masterclass in Atmospheric Dread
Resident Evil 7 isn't just a game; it's a soft reboot that saved the entire franchise. It moves away from the global "super-soldier" action of the previous games and pulls the camera into a tight, terrifying first-person perspective. You aren't a trained hero with a machine gun; you are Ethan Winters, an ordinary man looking for his missing wife in a rotting Louisiana plantation.

The Atmosphere: Disgustingly Beautiful
The setting—the Baker family estate—is the real star of the show. Every room feels lived-in, filthy, and dangerous. Since you are moving games to your SSD, you will really appreciate the RE Engine’s detail here.

The Horror: It moves away from just "zombies" and leans into "Slasher" and "Body Horror" themes.

The Family: Each member of the Baker family provides a different type of fear: Jack is a relentless pursuer, Marguerite is stealth-focused and gross, and Lucas plays "Saw"-style mind games.

The Story: Simple but Emotional
For a series known for cheesy dialogue, RE7 is surprisingly mature. It feels intimate. The mystery of what happened to your wife, Mia, and the tragic secret behind why the Baker family became monsters is genuinely sad. By the end, you don't just feel scared; you feel a strange sense of sympathy for the people you were fighting.

The Downside
The final third of the game (the Salt Mines) loses some of the "horror" magic and turns into a bit of a generic shooter. It feels a bit rushed compared to the incredible beginning in the house.

Final Score: 9/10
If you want a game that makes you jump, makes you think, and—true to your taste—gives you a heavy emotional payoff at the end, Resident Evil 7 is a must-play.

Resident Evil 7 is where the series decided to trap you in a house, turn off the lights, and personally make sure you regret every life decision that brought you there. Switching to first-person was the best thing this game could’ve done—it’s way more immersive, and *way* more terrifying when everything is happening right in your face.

The Baker family? Absolutely unhinged in the best way. Jack casually strolling through walls like the Kool-Aid Man while saying “Welcome to the family, son” is the kind of energy that sticks with you. Marguerite is nightmare fuel, and honestly, the whole house feels alive in the worst possible way.

The vibe here is much more pure horror compared to RE4 and RE2. Ammo is scarce, resources matter, and sometimes the best strategy is just turning around and running for your life. The slower pacing works perfectly—it builds tension until you’re scared to even open a door.

Ethan as a protagonist is basically just a normal guy getting dragged through absolute chaos, which somehow makes everything feel even worse (in a good way). His reactions are low-key hilarious too:

* “Who builds this ♥♥♥♥?”
* “I guess this is it…”

The atmosphere carries the whole experience—dirty, claustrophobic, and constantly threatening. It feels less like a game and more like you’ve accidentally walked into a horror movie that doesn’t want you to leave.

Only downside? You will hesitate before opening *any* door ever again.

Overall: 10/10. Terrifying, intense, and a perfect reinvention of the series. Just… don’t play it alone in the dark unless you’re built different.

I'll be straight forward and say what needs to be said immediatly: while I enjoyed my time with this game overall, for me it doesn't really stand up to the other Resident Evils I've played till now.
The biggest culprit of this for me is the fact this game really felt like it was trying hard to be a more traditional horror game than the others in the series I've played, with quite a lot of jumpscares and such, which in general I'm not a fan of when it feels like it is the main focus of the game, hence why I enjoyed 2, 4 and now even Village quite a bit more than this. Add to that a combat system which while functional simply doesn't feel as good as the others and in certain sections way more enemies than I feel would be normal, and all this led to a very weird experience where I was having fun still and overall enjoying the game, but being dragged down by these things which were really annoying/tedious at times. Honestly, I think I had more fun with the 2 dlcs, Not a Hero and End of Zoe, than the base game, despite them being undeniably quite short simply because the actual gameplay moment to moment was more fun for me and they weren't so fixated on being more or less just traditional horror like the base game was.
I would still recommend this game to someone who is at least somewhat interested in the franchise especially on a sale since it is quite cheap, and especially if you are actually looking for that more horror oriented experience, for me personally though, it's just a pretty good game that I had a decent time with, but not much more.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a major turning point for the series, bringing the franchise back to true survival horror with a first-person perspective 👀

Story 🎭
You play as Ethan Winters, searching for your missing wife in a terrifying abandoned plantation home in Louisiana. The story starts simple but slowly turns into a dark, mysterious bio-horror plot with strong connections to the series lore.

Gameplay 🎮
This game focuses heavily on survival. Ammo is limited, healing items are scarce, and every encounter feels dangerous. Combat exists, but the game constantly encourages caution, exploration, and resource management.

Atmosphere 😨
This is where the game shines. The Baker family house is incredibly detailed, creepy, and unpredictable. Sound design and lighting create constant tension, making even quiet moments feel stressful.

Horror level 😈
One of the scariest modern Resident Evil games. It uses psychological tension more than constant jump scares, which makes the fear feel more real and lasting.

Pros 👍

Extremely immersive atmosphere
Strong survival horror mechanics
Great sound design and tension
Refreshing first-person perspective

Cons 👎

Some areas can feel repetitive
Puzzles are fairly simple
Story is relatively short

Verdict 💡
A top-tier survival horror game that successfully revived the franchise. If you like tension, fear, and resource management, this is a must-play 🔥

I went into Resident Evil 7 thinking “yeah yeah another horror game”… bro I was NOT ready.

This game doesn’t try to be cool. It just straight up messes with your head.

First thing — the vibe.
The house feels alive. Not in a fantasy way. In a dirty, real, uncomfortable way. Like you shouldn’t be there at all. Every room feels wrong. Every sound makes you stop.

Sometimes I just stood still listening… didn’t even wanna open the next door 😂

And Jack… bro this man is DIFFERENT.
He’s not just a boss. He walks around like he owns you. The way he talks, the way he chases… nah. Stress level 100.

But the hardest fight for me was his son.
That fight actually made me focus fr. No chill at all.

And that Eveline chasing sequence…
man that part hits different. It feels intense, like you just wanna get out asap.

But the BEST part for me was when the lift got stuck.
I had to find the switch, power cable, captain cabin key…and the transition between Ethan and Mia ...
that whole section felt so real. No hand holding. Just you figuring things out.

Gameplay is slow but that’s the point.
You don’t feel powerful. You feel hunted.
Ammo is limited. Healing is limited. Brain usage unlimited.

The puzzles are actually good. Not too easy. Not annoying.
You feel smart when you solve them.

Graphics still hold up.
Not flashy. But the lighting and shadows carry hard.

Story is simple but works.
Nothing too deep. But it keeps you hooked.

Now DLC — I’ve only played Jack’s 55th Birthday so far
and bro… getting S and SS is HARD.

But that’s what makes it addictive.
I kept going again and again just to optimize my run.
It’s not just playing, it’s like mastering the route.

That mode alone shows how deep the game actually is.

I haven’t completed all DLC yet, so I’m not giving it a perfect score.
Once I 100% everything, I’ll update this.

Only thing — some parts can feel slow
and if you don’t like tension-based gameplay, you might get bored

But if you like horror that actually makes you uncomfortable… this is it.

Overall:
Not the flashiest RE game
But probably the most intense one

9/10

Not perfect yet… but damn close.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is one of the best horror games that I have ever played. This game bring many inspiration from classic horror movies and mix them together in a very balance way. You can clearly see the influence from films like Texas Chainsaw Massacre or other old scary stories. For me, this is the first Resident Evil game I try, so my opinion is quite different from many fans who play the older parts before.

 Overall, the game is very strong in almost every area. The graphics is excellent and make the old house feel so real and creepy. Every room have its own detail that build the tension slowly. Sound design is one of the best part – the footsteps, the strange noises, and the sudden screams make you jump from your seat many times. Gameplay is mix between exploration, puzzle solving, and fighting, which keep the player busy without become too easy or too hard. The art and visual design create a dark, dirty atmosphere that stay with you even after you stop playing. The way the light and shadow work together help to make the environment feel alive and dangerous.

 However, there is some part that make me not fully immerse while playing. The main character, Ethan, his reactions and emotions sometimes not make sense. He see terrible things but respond in way that almost funny instead of scary. His goal to find his wife and stay in the dangerous place also feel not logical. This make the horror atmosphere become weaker than it should be. The story try to be serious but these small things break the tension and make some scenes less frightening. Because I have played many horror and thriller games before, I notice these problems more than other players.

 Even with this issue, I still think Resident Evil 7 is a very good game that successfully bring back the scary feeling to the series. It change the style from action to pure survival horror, and it work very well. The boss fights are intense and the enemies design is creative and disgusting in the right way. If you play for fun and enjoy the thrill and jump scares, you will have a great time. But if you start the series from this game and expect a deep, logical story, you might feel disappointed because the plot have some weak point.

 In conclusion, I recommend this game to anyone who love horror. It is not perfect but the good parts are much stronger than the small problems. Play it with lights off and good headphones for the best experience.

Another game where I wish I could leave a maybe recommendation. This doesn't feel like a Resident Evil game to me at all. It feels more like something akin to Amnesia, Outlast, or the PT demo which makes sense considering when this game came out in 2017, those style of games were doing the numbers. So Capcom likely sought to capitalize on that style of horror in an attempt to reignite interest in their otherwise dead IP at the time. 

 My issue with that is Capcom has been constantly chasing trends with this series in an attempt to keep it relevant. It's the reason we got games like Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6. Capcom has seemingly always been too afraid to embrace the identity of the games that made this series popular. Choosing instead to make Resident Evil something it isn't in hopes that it well sell well enough to justify the change. Now I'm not saying Resident Evil 7 is a bad game. It's not my style of horror, I don't like the jump scares and an enemy that constantly chases you to complicate puzzles or add tension. I'm not a fan of the first person perspective in a Resident Evil game and I think the design of the mold monsters is the weakest enemy design in the series.

 That being said I enjoy the setting and I think there is a lot here to like for fans of first person horror games like Outlast. This just doesn't feel like it was the reboot that Resident Evil needed. I feel like it started another bad trend for the series that people didn't notice at first because they were so starved for a new Resident Evil game that they got caught up in the hype. Although now almost a decade later they're starting to notice some of the bad habits Capcom picked up from this titles success in some of the more recent releases. 

All that being said, I don't think this game would fair well amongst fans after the success of the remasters. Though I do acknowledge that it's likely because of this games success that we even got them in the first place. Which is why I'm so undecided on recommending this game. It's put me in a weird place as someone who is a fan of the series but not a fan of where it's gone. This is a good game for someone who just wants a pretty formulaic survival horror game, but I don't think this is where Resident Evil shines as a series.

TLDR: If you like survival horror games like Outlast, Amnesia, or the PT demo from the PS4 days then you'll love this. It follows all of the design beats from those style of games and the setting really elevates it above them for me. Although if you're looking to get into the Resident Evil series in 2026 and looking for where to start, I would not start here. Start with the Resident Evil 1 or 2 remake and branch out from there depending on where you feel those games are lacking.

[h1] First person take on Resident Evil [/h1]

Straight from the get-go, Resident evil 7 is a great game, but i feel like its a bit overvalued by a lot of the fanbase since resident evil 6 left a bitter aftertaste to resident evil fans, so Re7 felt better than it actually is.

The story starts really simple, and thats how it usually is with resident evil games, but its very engaging and in my opinion it kinda reedeems itself towards the end of the game, since a lot of points start to connect and stuff makes more sense, mainly on why everyone was in that situation. it just clicks like a missing piece in a puzzle.
the characters are very well written in my opinion, every character felt different from the other, in terms of philosophy and in terms of how they try to kill you and stop you.
The gameplay loop is the classic and iconic survival horror of resident evil and here its done very well, so if you looking for that, you def gonna find it in this game, even tho i wished there were harder puzzles and different enemies, the enemies that you encounter for the first time are mostly what you gonna see for the rest of the game, excluding boss fights of course and some other exceptions, the main enemies feel a bit uninspiring and dull, but at the end the game kinda tells you why are the enemies like they are in the game, but it still felt like Re7 came short in enemy variety, it might be to allow the bosses to shine and make iconic, wich they have seemed to achieve.
The boss fight were intresting, except for the "Mom" boss, it didnt feel that intresting nor it felt rewarding to kill, idk its missing something.
The weapon selection is pretty restricted, but for how long is the game, they are enough, especiialy if you take into consideration the small enemy variety, since the game is very short they dont feel too redundant and you dont get bored of them.
Re7 sets, from the first 10min of gameplay, a very sinister mood, the devs did a great job with environmental story telling, the environment teases you towards whats gonna happen without leading you too much and spoiling it for you, from pictures of lost people. to the notes you might find around the map.
The setting and ambience are absolutely stunning, you are stressed constantly and the design of the map gives you this feeling of claustrophobia and powerlessness if you happen to encounter an enemy, since there isnt much room for you to escape or move left or right, just the tone of the game from the beggining makes you understand that you are in for a true horror experience.
The graphics are stunning, from how the light from the flashlight scatters on the different surfaces to the every single detail that the devs took time with, everything seems put there for a reason and objects dont feel out of place at all, its truly immersive.
Same goes for the audio and the music direction, its amazing how the devs managed to make everything click together and nothing felt lacking in that sense.
Even after all this i still think the game isnt as amazing as people make it to be, dont get me wrong its a great game, but i think i was spoiled by how good the remakes of Re2 and Re4 are, and honestly if i havent played those remakes and went to re7 straight from re7 i wouldve definelty valued re7 way better than currently do.
Overall the game is really good, i would highly advice anyone reading this to buy it and give it a try, its worth your money.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is one of the boldest shifts in the entire series, and it pays off in the best way possible. Moving to a first-person perspective completely changes how you experience horror. Everything feels closer, more personal.

The Baker estate is a masterclass in environmental design. It’s not just a location. It feels like a living, decaying nightmare. From the main house to the old house and beyond, every area has its own identity, yet all of them share that same suffocating atmosphere. The game constantly keeps you on edge with limited resources, tight spaces, and unpredictable enemy encounters.

The gameplay is focused on survival rather than action. Ammo is scarce, healing items are valuable, and every fight feels like a risk. Puzzles are well-integrated into the environment, and exploration is rewarding without ever feeling safe. It’s a true return to the roots of survival horror.

Now, Ethan Winters… this is where the game truly shines. Ethan isn’t a trained soldier or some action hero. He’s just a normal person thrown into an unimaginable situation. And yet, he keeps going because he has something to fight for. That makes him far more relatable. And honestly, more impressive than all of the protagonists in the series.

The story goes deeper than it first appears. On the surface, it’s about escaping a horrifying situation. But underneath, it explores themes like control, identity, and what it means to belong. The Baker family isn’t evil by choice. They’re just victims of something far beyond their control.

And that brings us to Eveline.

At first glance, it’s easy to hate her. She’s the cause of everything; the manipulation, the destruction, the suffering. But when you actually look deeper, that hatred starts to feel misplaced. Eveline isn’t just a villain. She’s a creation, designed and used as a weapon. She was never given a normal life, never understood real love, and never had a chance to grow up as a human. All she wanted was a family.

But the way she tries to create that “family” is through control, forcing people into roles they never chose. It’s disturbing, but also tragic. She doesn’t understand that what she’s doing isn’t real love. That lack of understanding is what makes her so dangerous… and at the same time, so pitiful.

So instead of pure hatred, what the game really builds is a mix of fear and sympathy. Eveline is both the cause of the horror and a victim of it.

That contrast is what gives Resident Evil 7 its emotional depth.

In the end, this isn’t just a horror game—it’s a story about a man trying to survive, a family that lost itself, and a “child” who never truly understood what family means.

And through all of that chaos, Ethan stands tall. Not as a hero, not as a soldier, as someone who simply refuses to give up.

That's why he surprass all of the Resident Evil cast.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard — Review
Score: 9.5/10

What Works
Resident Evil 7 is one of the best horror experiences in the series, and honestly one of the best in the genre. The shift to first-person was a bold move, and it paid off — the Baker house feels genuinely oppressive and claustrophobic. The first half of the game is near-perfect horror: limited resources, unsettling atmosphere, and the Baker family as unpredictable, terrifying stalkers. Jack Baker in particular is one of the most memorable enemies in modern horror games — relentless, brutal, and actually scary.
The sound design and visuals do a lot of heavy lifting. Every creak, every distant noise keeps you on edge. The game nails the feeling of being hunted.

Where It Falls Apart
The second half is a noticeable step down. Once you leave the main Baker house and head into the ship and salt mines, the tension drains fast. The environments become less interesting, the pacing slows, and the game starts to feel like it's just filling time.
The final boss is the biggest letdown — arguably the weakest in the entire series. After surviving Jack Baker and everything the house threw at you, the ending feels anticlimactic and almost laughably easy. It's the kind of finale that makes you wonder if the developers ran out of budget or time.

RE7 evokes lots of fantastic horror and retains the Resident Evil soul while working in new features and experiences for the series.  [u] Play it in the dark with headphones if conditions permit.  [/u] 

The in-your-face and desperate horror is paired with some of that good old campy RE cheesiness, sometimes in the form of a deadpan delivery, sometimes in the writing, but they all add a bit of a surreal feeling to the game, Resident Evil's own version of reality.  If you like Evil Dead (any or all of them), you should try this game out.

The visual presentation is nearly immaculate with the first person perspective really serving as a [i]camera[/i] into the world.  Our experience in RE7 is shown to us through thoughtfully composed scenes  in exquisitely detailed main locations which feature their own storytelling as well.  
Like with other darkly lit titles I advise calibrating brightness using the in game menu for each session.  Brightness should be set the lowest it can be. 

The soundscape is fantastic at flavoring levels of paranoia and alertness that bring new meaning to the physical environments.  Headphones are highly recommended, the dynamic range is really nice in this one.  You will have those moments where you really feel someone or something [b]right[/b] up on you next to your ear.  I will concede though that I think the guns can sound a bit underpowered.  The recorded sounds work great but just lack a bit of intensity and volume in the mix.  Minor impact for me but hey.
Just a few of many standouts in the audio for me: [list]
[*]"oh Ethan, [i]Ethan[/i], EEE[i]EEE[/i]THAN!"
[*] all the menu/UI sounds (endorphins released)
[*] the save room (dopamine and oxytocin administered)
[/list]
The only faults, small as they may be that I felt within the game were when it becomes a bit more explain-y in parts with the storytelling and things can be a bit on the nose and overt.  I think it could've said less in some places but overall I loved the story and presentation.  I'm a big fan of the tapes that you can find in the game, they're a really cool narrative tool and give a lot of insight.  The changeup focusing on a few main tormentors for most of the game is really fun and the voice actors did a great job.  I like the additions to the overarching RE story and feel like the additions from RE7 let you expand out quite a bit as well as reflect back on the game in a slightly different light.  Overall the story is really good with some bits that were not as good.  100% worth playing for the story.

[h1] A Horrifying Return to Form [/h1]

Resident Evil 7 puts the horror back into the survival horror that the series is known for after the deviation to a more action focused experience in entries 4-6. It is by far the scariest in the series and of the scariest games I've played, not just because of jumpscares, but because of the masterfully crafted and grotesque setting and atmosphere of the Baker estate. The first couple of hours of this game are so tense that it had me on the edge of my seat, scared to open every door and turn every corner. If you're a fan of horror games, and the classic Resident Evil games, this is an absolute must play.

The thing that truly separates 7 from the last couple entries in this series is it goes all in on horror. The color pallette is almost exlcusively gross greys, browns, and pale yellows. You're dropped into this disgusting, rotting, broken down mansion filled with creatures that want to do nothing but rip you apart. The sound design is amazing, and you never feel safe. The game is grotesque and disgusting, not afraid to show some truly horrifying things. If the atmosphere doesn't creep you out, the visuals certainly will. The Baker farm is definitely one of my favorite settings in the series, and it feels like your worst nightmare.

Gameplay wise, the switch to first person was a great choice. You feel more immersed in the horror, and combat is more tense. You can't see around corners at all, and have 0 visibility as to what could be creeping up behind you, or to your sides. The gunplay is great, and resources are scarce again, making exploring not only beneficial, but a requirement. There isn't a ton of enemy variety but it does the job, and the boss fights are pretty good. The series also brings back puzzles, and there's some great ones here. Some parts of the game actually challenged me mentally, and were a joy to figure them out. 

Overall, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is an incredible game, with one of the best settings in the series, and great gunplay. It brings the horror to 11, and while the narrative isn't crazy good, it kept me invested, and has some really good moments in it. The second half of the game falls off a little bit in terms of the setting, but as a whole I loved this game and beat it in a single day, in about 7 hours. I highly recommend checking it out. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard(2017)

СЮЖЕТ: Простенький, но при этом сразу цепляет. CapCom решили сделать ход конем после провала 5 и 6 частей, создав абсолютно новую сюжетную арку, которая практически никак не взаиможействует с оригинальными персонажи, и лишь происходит в той же вселенной. Это дало разрабам возможность разгуляться и развязало руки. И естественно это сработало! "Семерка" - это свежий глоток воздуха в давно проперженной вселенной Резака. Благодаря этому глотку у нас есть нетипичная история, абсолютно новая концепция и новые персонажи. Пускай и Итан мне нравится поменьше Леона, я не могу спорить, что именно арка Итана серию и спасла. Сюжетка легкоо воспринимается и сразу цепляет. Единственное, чтобы я отметил, так это хронометраж - я прошел игру за 9 часов. При этом, если бы я не втыкал в некоторых местах, то спокойно бы прошел за 7.5-8 часов. Естественно, что за такое время сложно эмоционально привязаться например к Зое. При том, что Зоя на самом деле хорошо вписана в сюжет - ей просто не хватает экранного времени. То же самое с Лукасом, которого раскрывают хорошо только в ДЛС, которые у резика по базе слабенькие. Чувствуется, что релизя "седьмой резак" CapCom очень хотел понравится, поэтому и все хотя бы минимально спорные решения или сюжетные ветки были вырезаны, чтобы не дай бог не отпугнуть хардкорных фанатов.

ГЕЙМПЛЕЙ: Дефолтный геймплей современных резаков, но с одним нюансом - этот ''современный геймплей'' именно в этой игре создавался. Поэтому в геймплее чувствуются шароховатости или ненужные куски. Yeah, Resident Evil 7 is still brilliant years later.
Coming off the heels of RE9 I was excited to see the game that brought the franchise back to it's survival horror roots and introduced first person perspective.

I did play this game briefly with friends well before I properly started playing horror games. 
Coming into the game seriously, you really get swept up in the absolutely stunning atmosphere. The lighting, the set design, the horrific intro - it all sets the mood for the game so well.
The intro segment is awesome. Just pure Resident Evil puzzle-box styled level design with different silly keys, creepy corridors and tight surroundings, and of course, a horrible entity stalking you.

I must say, the level design in this game is so effective for a few reasons, but primarily because of the use of space. The devs for this game decided to do something I rarely see in games - make everything life sized. The doorways are low, almost at head-level, the corridors are tight, too tight for two people. The fact that this house (minus the bugs and guts etc) could very well be a real place with the attention to scale and clutter- it just adds so much to the horror.

The stalkers are fantastic and the main one may honestly be my favorite in the series.
Jack is such an effective stalker and I think for me he is scarier than most because he is very vocal. Having a crazy southern man who will taunt you and gleefully announce he's spotted you is blood-curdling. The other stalker is also very cool and at some points was scarier than Jack. The boss fights are also super cool.

A lot of people will complain about the second to last segment, but I personally loved it. I think that part is great for it's natural way of explaining the story and also keeping to the tight exploration and terror.

Personally, I can't really fault RE7, other than the fact that it is probably the shortest RE game.
I have heard about some of the cut content and I really wish we got a bit more, especially exploring the Baker estate. Another complaint I suppose I could air is that the [spoiler] main house isn't returned to more than once. I would have loved to keep returning to the main house to uncover more rooms and segments. [/spoiler]. Although this gripe would potentially take away from how tight and replayable the game is, which is hugely important to RE.

Overall, the game is by far the best for atmosphere and horror in Resident Evil and (at least for me) is most likely going to stay as my favorite story in the franchise.

[h1]A Bold, Terrifying Reinvention[/h1]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Overview[/h2]
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is one of the most daring pivots a long-running franchise has ever made; and it mostly sticks the landing. After years of the series leaning heavily into action, Capcom stripped everything back to its roots and delivered something genuinely unsettling, tense, and memorable. It is not a perfect game, but it is absolutely worth your time.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Atmosphere & Horror[/h2]
This is where RE7 absolutely [i]shines[/i]. From the moment you step foot onto the Baker property, the game wraps you in a thick, suffocating dread that rarely lets up. The setting; a rotting, decrepit plantation deep in rural Louisiana; is masterfully crafted. Every hallway feels lived-in and wrong at the same time. The sound design deserves particular praise; creaking floorboards, distant moaning, and an oppressive ambient score work in perfect harmony to keep your nerves on edge throughout.
The first-person perspective was a controversial choice for longtime fans, but it was absolutely the right call. It pulls you into the horror in a way the older camera angles simply could not achieve. If you are playing this in the dark with headphones, expect to lose some sleep.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h2]
RE7 brings back the resource management and puzzle-solving that defined the classic entries in the series. Ammo is scarce; healing items are precious; and every encounter demands you think carefully rather than just blast your way through. This creates a constant undercurrent of tension that complements the horror atmosphere beautifully.
The crafting system is simple but effective; combining materials to create ammo or med kits feels rewarding without ever becoming overwhelming. Inventory management also returns, and while some may find it fiddly, it adds a layer of strategy that keeps you engaged.
[b]Now, here is where I have to be honest:[/b] the enemy AI is, frankly, embarrassing at times. Enemies have serious trouble detecting you even when you feel like you should have been caught ten times over. There are moments where you are practically standing in plain sight and the AI just wanders off unbothered. For a horror game that is supposed to make you feel hunted, this is a meaningful immersion-breaker. It does not ruin the experience; but it does take the edge off some encounters that should have been far more tense.
Boss encounters, on the other hand, are a different story entirely and are among the game's highlights.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Story & Characters[/h2]
Without spoiling a single thing; the story starts with a simple, gripping premise and slowly unravels into something far more layered than you might expect. The narrative is told in a way that keeps you asking questions and pushing forward, and the pacing is genuinely excellent for the most part.
The Baker family; your primary antagonists; are an absolute standout. They are terrifying, memorable, and surprisingly [i]human[/i] in ways that elevate them beyond simple monster roles. The voice acting across the board is strong, and the writing does a solid job of building tension without overstaying its welcome.
The protagonist is a bit of a blank slate, which can make emotional investment harder; but the supporting cast more than compensates.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Graphics & Sound[/h2]
Running on Capcom's RE Engine for the first time, RE7 is a stunning game. The environments are richly detailed and grotesque in the best possible way; the lighting in particular does extraordinary work in building dread. Character models hold up exceptionally well; and the overall visual fidelity gives the horror real weight.
The sound design, as mentioned, is a cut above. The music swells and retreats at exactly the right moments; and the environmental audio is among the best in the genre. Play this with a good headset and the difference is night and day.
[hr][/hr]

I completed the main game along with the Banned Footage, Not a Hero, and End of Zoe DLCs. Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic soft reboot of the series. This was the first game in the series that truly had me on the edge of my seat. The dynamic with the Baker family is something that will remain with me for quite some time. This is probably my favorite game in the series up to this point.
	The environments and character interactions feel well crafted and the pace of the game is excellent. The gameplay feels impactful, but I do think there is room for some combat improvements to feel more refined. The running and hiding aspect of the game is also tense, and has some great moments in the new first person design. The boss fights in the game also are probably the best in the series thus far, as you get to know them quite a bit before your ultimate conclusion with each of them.
	While the first half of the game feels like it is on a path to be an all time great in both the franchise and the horror genre as a whole, the second half of the game is where the major issues begin to show themselves. The environments are simply nowhere near as compelling as the beginning. The enemy variety is extremely limiting and leaves much to be desired. The conclusion of the game also feels a bit rushed, and leaves the DLC to do clean up. The first half of this game is my favorite in the series, but the second half is what keeps it from reaching the highs of a dense, compact game such as Resident Evil 4.

Resident Evil 7 is one of the best examples of a long-running series returning to its roots and doing it successfully. The game shifts to a first-person perspective and places you in the role of Ethan Winters, who is searching for his missing wife in a decaying, isolated house. What begins as a simple search quickly turns into a disturbing and deeply unsettling experience.

The game’s greatest strength is its atmosphere. It creates a constant sense of tension through dark, claustrophobic environments and excellent sound design. Instead of relying heavily on jumpscares, it builds slow, psychological horror that keeps you on edge for most of the game.

In terms of gameplay, Resident Evil 7 focuses on survival rather than action. You do have access to weapons, but ammunition is limited, which makes every encounter feel risky. Exploration and puzzle-solving are also important, adding variety and pacing to the experience. Resource management plays a key role, forcing you to think carefully about how to use your items.

The story is relatively simple but effective. Ethan is an ordinary character, which makes the situation feel more realistic, while the Baker family stands out as one of the most memorable and disturbing parts of the game. Their unpredictable behavior adds to the overall tension.

However, the game is not without flaws. Some sections feel slower than others, and the variety of enemies could be better. The story, while engaging, does not go very deep.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a highly immersive and genuinely frightening horror game. It focuses more on tension and atmosphere than constant jumpscares, making it a great choice for players who enjoy psychological horror. It strikes a strong balance between classic survival horror elements and modern gameplay design, earning it a solid 8.5 out of 10.

Full preface, I am not good at survival horror games. I planned to play this game when I was doing a marathon of Resident Evil in October. Unfortunately, I didn’t have enough time to finish them all in that month. Eventually it fell on my Next to Play list on Steam. 
The atmosphere of this game is amazing. The Baker house in the back of the bayou brings me back to how I felt watching the Skeleton Key. Ethan is a relatively flat character, but everyone else excels in their roles (they fix him in RE8 in my opinion). I don’t even think I wanted to kill Excella Gionne more than I wanted to kill Lucas. The mechanics are smooth and work perfectly to theme of the game. Whenever I play games, and especially in RE games I look for the moment when the game flips. When it goes from Leon skulking around, avoiding Mr. X, to when he’s just mowing through enemies after the sewer level. RE7 does not disappoint. Around the halfway point, Ethan’s arsenal builds up enough to where you stop surviving mostly, and you become the hunter. This is paired with good pacing, phenomenal DLCs, and an excellent set-up to RE8, which remains my 3rd favorite in the series (behind RE4, and RE: R). If you can get it on a sale (which these games tend to be on after a year) pick it up and give it a try. Shout-out to Joe Baker, the third toughest guy in the RE series.

Resident Evil 7 did not only reboot the franchise, it brought us the RE engine which is now a legendary powerhouse behind the REmake trilogy and the newer entries. One of the most impressive engines in modern gaming, in a sea of Unreal slop. 7 is a one of a kind entry and no other has tried to reclaim the same magic (although, FPS mods for RE2 remake come shockingly close and play a lot better than you'd think) but for all the right reasons. This entry deserves to stand on its own uniquely and now we have returned to the formula that many believe, caused 6 to 'fail' or 'not stick', but in all truth, Resident Evil has never been better.

How has 7 aged? Fairly well, it is still graphically extremely impressive, especially now with the ray tracing update and this genuinely was one of the few reasons to even have VR peripherals for some time. That being said, 7 has a lot of things that have been exercised out in more recent entries. The backtracking is truly nauseating in this one and some of it is because I am not a fan of extreme American rurality aesthetics. 

I love it when the games take us to urban centers in America, but even the first RE1 does not shine as much as 2 and 3 did to me, because I generally think the woods and creepy houses in them is a bit dull. This is incredibly ironic when you consider the fact I love the Friday the 13th movies, but I also generally enjoy the entries where Jason leaves the Lake the most. 

The game is incredibly gross, rather than truly scary. But I got really tired of seeing the same inner-wall sequence, crawling in centipedes, on the 7th time in a single run I had to go through it for the sake of ammo preservation and general completionism in the Baker's house. 

The game significantly gets more interesting after the house, at the cost of the gameplay. Everything after the Baker's estate feels rushed and at the same time, lasts far too long. The ship sequence has a lot going for it at first, but it overstays its welcome. Resident Evil tends to work best at RE4's pace or RE2's effective minimalism. All in all, backtracking is not fun in games and I distinctively remember this being the main reason why I did not want to return to this entry with as much enthusiasm as say, Village. 

But it is far from bad. 7 is an iconic horror, but lacks the iconic villains and set pieces in favour of having a more grounded and interesting story. The plot surely cooks and the lore implications, as well as being so separate from RE while also united with it in a subtle way, actually ties it all together. At least, that is what I thought until I played Chris' DLC, Not A Hero, which I think is a far superior ending (it is also canon) than the lackluster one we get in the main game. 

The mechanic of Chris having to advance through the mines via equipment for his gasmask is a great gameplay mechanic we sadly have never seen again, but its absolutely brilliant albeit the section overall being incredibly slow paced and sort of unfun. 7 is scary, has some teeth clenching moments, but the clumsy movement of Ethan translates to Chris and even if Chris can ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PUNCH BOWs in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ face, he still feels like a refrigerating trying to squeeze through a mouse-house door in every entry way. 

Many people enjoy the estate and I got to agree, everything with Jack and Mia in the beginning is fantastic to watch, but sort of unfun to play. The brief moment we play Mia near the end is a snorefest and the parts that are most interesting, specifically with Lucas, do not last long enough. Luckily, the Banned Footage DLC corrects this. 

The Saw-style 21 mini game is honestly worth playing this game over and over again. It is a huge inspirational for Buckshot Roulette and generally, has great dialogue, great stakes and some incredibly fun mechanics. RE7's torture-survival blackjack is so fun to put hours into, that its easy to just fall in love with the game all over again. 

All my complaints about 7 are rectified in Village, but can I recommend 7? Oh, definitely. 7 is a mandatory play and fans of Revelations will enjoy it the most. It actually has a lot more in common with Resident Evil than people realize and as a stand alone entry, its incredibly strong. It is the P.T demo but an actual game and with actual gameplay and a very unique identity. 

There is something about seeing Ethan's health deteriorate throughout the game. His wounds are visibly infected, he has bleeding wounds across his hands, painful hives from being attacked by bugs and sometimes burns from his own improvised weapons. There is a similar effect as Chris, where we see bleeding gashes through his tactical gloves. 

RE7 brings so many new things to the table and doesn't lose its own identity in homages to others. It knows just how much to borrow and just how much to make uniquely its own. Far from my favourite RE game, but this is a great entry into the Resident Evil series if you want something a little higher brow and with a large focus on character-driven plot. The game can terrify you, shock you, and it will definitely surprise the hell out of you, but it can also inspire some unique empathy in certain scenes. 

Other than that, Ethan is a functioning psychopath well before he arrives to the Baker estate. The guy doesn't question much of anything that is going on and has some clinical detachment to having to shoot his wife in the face with a gun or hack her to pieces with an ax in self defense. The early parts feel like Evil Dead at points and Jack even drops a "groovy" line when wielding a chainsaw. It is a madhouse but damn, its effective and one of the best starts to an RE game.

As someone who has played the Resident Evil franchise religiously since the old days of RE2, I can’t quite understand why the seventh installment gets so much praise. Don't get me wrong: from an environment and character design perspective, the game is gorgeous. It is pure eye candy for horror fans, and the setting in the rural deep south adds a masterfully unnerving atmosphere. The story starts out incredibly tense and enthralling.

But that magic is quickly ruined by the grueling gameplay. What I expected to be a tense, temporary segment of playing hide-and-seek with the "dad" character becomes the core experience of the game. You are trapped in a farmhouse, forced to solve escape-room puzzles while constantly dodging a stalking threat. It’s terrifying the first time; by the eighth, it’s just a tedious chore. You’ll be trying to figure out a door puzzle or combine items when you hear him stomping nearby, forcing you to drop everything and run. To make matters worse, the intense 1v1 boss fights with him feel like a sham when he just returns to stalk you anyway.

Then there's the basement. While classic RE titles give you weapons for self-defense, RE7 actively makes combat feel useless. Even with a handgun, you are funneled into tight hallways with bullet-sponge enemies where fighting quickly feels obsolete. I found myself constantly reloading saves, questioning my sanity as to why I was even playing.

I’ve played the newer titles, including RE Village (8), and none of them frustrated me like this one. If you love escape rooms and pure stealth, you might enjoy this. But as a long-time action-horror fan, I just can't recommend it.

The last Resident evil game that concludes my marathon.

Not gonna lie, this game feels like Resident Evil went through a full personality reset. The Bakers feel like a love letter to classic horror. The whole family dynamic screams The Texas Chain Saw Massacre—that grimy, disturbing “you’re not leaving this house” energy. Lucas? Dude is basically a walking Saw trap, turning everything into twisted games that mess with your head. And Marguerite… yeah, that’s straight-up "THE THING" or "THE FLY" body horror nightmare fuel. 

I actually played Resident Evil Village first before this. At the time, I understood the "what" but not really the "why". Playing RE7 after? Everything just clicked. Ethan as a character made way more sense, the whole situation hit harder, and suddenly Village felt less like a standalone wild ride and more like the continuation of something way darker and more grounded.

This might be the closest Resident Evil has ever come to capturing the psychological, suffocating horror that Silent Hill 2 perfected. It’s not exactly the same tbh, Silent Hill still owns that deep, symbolic, “what does it all mean” type horror, but RE7 gets surprisingly close with its atmosphere. The dread isn’t just jump scares; it’s that constant feeling that something is wrong and you’re not safe anywhere.

Gameplay-wise, it strips things back in a good way. Resources are tight, combat is clunky on purpose, and every bullet feels like a financial decision. 

Also worth mentioning: this game runs smooth as hell even on mid to high-end setups, and visually it still holds up.
