Resident Evil 7 has one of the strongest openings in the entire series, but it is also one of the most uneven modern Resident Evil games. For me, it is around a 7/10 overall.

The beginning is fantastic. The Mia sequence is brutal and memorable, and the Baker House delivers some of the best survival horror gameplay in modern Resident Evil. Resource management feels satisfying, Jack is a very effective stalker enemy, and the atmosphere is outstanding, especially in the lower parts of the house. It is probably the scariest Resident Evil game.

The biggest problem is the huge drop in quality in the final third. The tanker and the mines are much weaker than the earlier areas, and the final boss fight feels like a joke. The tanker is especially disappointing because the gameplay there is simply much less interesting than what came before, and repeating part of it through the videotape only makes it feel weaker. The final boss fight is also a letdown because it barely has any real mechanics.

Even with all that, I still recommend the game because the early and middle sections are so strong. Resident Evil 7 is absolutely worth playing, but for me it never maintains the quality of its opening.

After the bad impression Resident Evil 6 left on me, I went into Resident Evil 7 with a lot of skepticism. The move to first person only made me more unsure. Instead, it ended up being one of the most refreshing Resident Evil games I have played. It brought back a real sense of horror, tension, and vulnerability, and it felt like the game that pulled the series back in the right direction.

What surprised me most was how well the new approach still captured the core of Resident Evil. The Baker estate gave the campaign a strong escape-room quality that I really enjoyed, and the mix of puzzle-solving, exploration, resource management, and survival-focused combat made the experience consistently engaging. It felt like a proper return to horror, but in a way that still felt welcoming through its new perspective and structure.

The atmosphere was one of the game’s biggest strengths for me. Moving through the different areas kept a strong sense of curiosity and dread, and the way each location was presented made the campaign feel driven and interesting from start to finish. The environments, threats, and overall pacing all worked together to build suspense and add to the fear factor in a way that felt genuinely effective.

I also liked that the game was not relying on atmosphere alone. The story premise felt fresh, the enemies were memorable, and the character performances did a lot to sell the tension. There were several moments where the horror genuinely landed for me, not just through shock, but through the constant feeling of being trapped in a dangerous place with limited control.

Resident Evil 7 ended up being the exact kind of surprise I wanted from this series. I expected to be put off by the first-person change, but instead I got a game that reminded me how strong Resident Evil can be when it fully commits to horror. For me, it was a well-executed reinvention and an easy positive recommendation.

RE 7 looks to correct the mistakes of RE6 and leans full-tilt into the survival horror aspect of of the series, and we're better off for it. It's not perfect, but it is a [b] HUGE [/b] step in the right direction for the series.
The game looks and sounds incredible, and runs like a dream on Steam Deck.
The story, while a little threadbare at first, is much more fleshed out by the time the credits roll. If you're used to lore being sprinkled throughout the game like previous RE titles, you may be disappointed to learn that most of the blanks aren't really filled in until the final act. I was a bit put off by that, but the rest of the game is so strong, I didn't mind all that much. 
The game is much shorter, sweeter, and more streamlined than the bloated corpse of RE 6, clocking in at around 11 hours for the base game. I did a fair share of exploring as well, so if you sprint from one story beat to the next, it could reasonably take you 9 or 10 hours. 
If I had one complaint, it would be that your character often moves at a glacial pace. Even with the stimulant upgrades, Ethan takes 3 business days to reload a shotgun, and his "sprint" (holding shift) is a leisurely jog through the Baker house. The characters have absolutely no sense of urgency whatsoever. 
**MINOR EVENT SPOILERS PAST THIS POINT**
In the early game, there are several hints dropped that about 20 people have gone missing in the vicinity of the Baker house over the past 2 years. [spoiler] So naturally, a police officer comes out to the house [b] ALONE [/b] to investigate. He disregards your cries for help, and treats Ethan with suspicion before dying 5 minutes after you meet him. [/spoiler] This is just one example of some of the several more inane and baffling character moments in this game.
That being said, I love that the game doesn't rely on recycling the same cast of characters for the umpteenth time, as almost everyone here is brand new to the series (with the exception of [spoiler] Chris Redfield [/spoiler] who shows up at the very end before the credits roll.
I'm very excited for the new direction of the series. Resident Evil 4 is still my favorite in the series, but this scratched a horror itch that has been absent in the series for a very very long time.

[h2] The game that brought the franchise back to its roots [/h2]

After receiving a message from his wife, Mia Winters, who has been missing for years, Ethan Winters travels to an abandoned house in search of her. There, he finds Mia — and a disturbingly insane and violent family.

Resident Evil 7 features excellent antagonists in a story clearly inspired by classic horror films, particularly The Texas Chain Saw Massacre. We got a terrifying atmosphere, item backtracking, puzzles, and true survival horror with a gradual sense of progression as your arsenal expands. Unfortunately, the protagonist, Ethan, lacks charisma and personality, especially when compared to previous Resident Evil leads.

The Baker family is one of the game's strongest elements. Each member is memorable, charismatic, and works exceptionally well as a boss. They introduce new gameplay layers throughout the experience — from more direct, aggressive encounters with Jack Baker, to puzzle-focused, sadistic challenges from Lucas Baker, whose twisted games strongly evoke the Saw franchise.

The graphics are impressive, and the game is also well-optimized, running smoothly even on relatively low-end PCs.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 successfully revitalizes the survival horror formula while delivering one of the most intense and frightening experiences in the series.

Absolutely loved *Resident Evil 7: Biohazard*. This game brought the series back to its roots in the best way possible—pure survival horror with a fresh perspective. The first-person view makes everything way more intense, and the atmosphere is honestly one of the creepiest I’ve experienced in any game.

this game pulling up with a new main character and going full fps definitely threw some old fans off, and yeah, i get that. but from the moment i first played it, the fps perspective actually works in its favor. everything feels more immediate, more personal. and ethan not being some trained soldier, just a regular guy trying to get his wife back, thinking he’s walking into something normal, that adds a real layer of tension. the horror in this game genuinely hits.

that said, not everything lands the same. jack baker is easily the standout, best boss and presence in the game. but the other boss fights don’t quite hold up. the marguerite fight kinda feels like it’s there just to drain your resources, more than being memorable. lucas section leans a bit too much into that saw-like vibe, not bad, just a little out of place. still, up until that point, the tension and fear stay consistent, that constant feeling of being hunted never really drops.

the bigger issue comes after. up to a certain point, the game barely gives you story, then suddenly with the ship section it starts dumping everything on you. and the problem is, that part isn’t even fun to play. it creates this feeling of “just get on with it already”, like you just want the story and the final boss so it can wrap up. pacing there feels both rushed and dragged at the same time.

story-wise, the game leans heavily on flashbacks and documents, especially towards the end. and this is where a lot of players are split. if you don’t read the files, or just skim through them, it really feels like there’s barely any connection to previous games. but even if you do read them, the connection still feels a bit thin. so honestly, both sides got a point.

the link to older games feels a bit weak, probably because umbrella already collapsed before this. but what the game does show well is that even with umbrella gone, new organizations are stepping in, trying to do the same kind of bioweapon experiments. same cycle, different names.

then at the end, chris shows up working with blue umbrella, and now you have a company with the umbrella name actually fighting bioterror, which is kind of ironic. still, the game doesn’t fully build that connection on its own, so you can see why village steps in and ties everything together more clearly. i do respect capcom for expanding on that subtle storytelling in the next game.

overall, the gameplay and especially the tension and horror are solid. and after re6 leaned way too hard into action and made it feel like the series was losing its identity, seeing it come back to proper horror like this felt genuinely refreshing.

The bad:

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard — The Masterclass in Modern Survival Horror
I’ve been an RE fan for a long time, and hitting 100% on Resident Evil 7 felt like a homecoming. It’s the perfect bridge between the old-school "resource management" of the 90s and the high-fidelity horror of today. Achieving that 100% mark on Steam wasn't just a challenge; it was an obsession.

Atmosphere: The Baker Mansion Still Hits Hard
Even in 2026, the Baker estate is one of the most unsettling locations in gaming. The shift to first-person was a genius move—it makes the "stalker" mechanics with Jack feel incredibly personal.

The Sound Design: Every creak in the floorboards and every wet slap of a Molded’s footstep kept me on edge.

The Visuals: On PC, the lighting in the guest house and the "dinner scene" is still some of the most visceral, "sticky" body horror I've ever experienced. It’s gross, it’s icky, and it’s beautiful.

The Completionist’s Nightmare: Madhouse Difficulty
If you want that 100%, you have to conquer Madhouse Difficulty, and that is where the game separates the fans from the masters.

Old-School Stakes: I loved that Madhouse brought back Ink Ribbons (Cassettes) for saving. It added a layer of tension that Normal difficulty lacked.

The "Chainsaw Mia" Fight: This is the ultimate skill check. Without the late-game unlocks, this fight requires perfect timing and resource management.

Antique Coins: Hunting down all 33 coins on Madhouse (compared to the 18 on Normal) forced me to see parts of the house I completely missed on my first run.

The DLC Gauntlet
To 100% RE7, you have to survive the Banned Footage and the story expansions.

Ethan Must Die: This mode is absolute insanity. It’s a trial-and-error roguelike that demands perfection.

Not a Hero & End of Zoe: Playing as Chris Redfield and then Jack’s brother, Joe, provided the perfect "revenge" tour after hours of being a "victim" as Ethan. Punching Molded to death as Joe Baker is one of the most satisfying things in the entire series.

21: The high-stakes blackjack game with Lucas is a psychological thriller all on its own. Getting the "Survival+" achievements there was a test of nerves I wasn't expecting.

The Verdict
Resident Evil 7 is the foundation of the modern RE renaissance. It respects the "search for keys" and "manage your herbs" roots while pushing the horror to its absolute limit. To 100% it is to truly survive the worst night of Ethan Winters' life.

[h1]Resident Evil 7 Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 has to be one of my favorite Resident Evil games I’ve ever played.

I don’t have the biggest history with the series, but I’ve played enough to know what Resident Evil is about, and this game… this game is a banger. It mixes horror, survival, and action in a way that just works incredibly well.

It’s also probably the first Resident Evil game that truly stuck with me.

And yeah… if you want a game that makes you question every corner you walk into, this is it.

[hr]
[h1]What It Is[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 shifts the series into a first-person survival horror experience.

You play as Ethan Winters, a regular guy (not a super soldier, not a trained agent… just a dude having the worst day of his life) who travels to a remote house in Louisiana after receiving a message from his missing wife, Mia.

What follows is a nightmare involving the Baker family, a mysterious infection, and a whole lot of things that really don’t want you to leave alive.

The story unfolds through exploration, notes, and encounters, gradually revealing what actually happened in the house.

[hr]
[h1]World and Exploration[/h1]
Exploration in Resident Evil 7 is fantastic.

The game is mostly linear, but the way it handles exploration makes it feel very engaging. You constantly search for items, keys, puzzle pieces, and hidden secrets.

One of the coolest things is how the game encourages you to inspect items. Sometimes what looks like a useless object actually hides something important… if you bother to look closely.

The Baker house itself is incredibly detailed. It genuinely feels like a place that was lived in, and that makes everything even creepier.

You walk into rooms and think:
“Yeah… something very bad happened here.”

And you’re absolutely right.

[hr]
[h1]Atmosphere and Horror[/h1]
This is where the game truly shines.

The atmosphere is incredible. It’s tense, it’s uncomfortable, and it keeps you on edge the entire time.

The switch to first-person was a huge risk, but it paid off massively. Everything feels more personal, more intense, and a lot more terrifying.

And the Baker family? Absolutely iconic.

Jack, Margaret, and the rest of the family are some of the creepiest and most memorable villains in the series. They carry a huge part of the experience, especially in the early game.

[hr]
[h1]Combat and Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay is a mix of survival horror and action.

You manage your inventory, conserve ammo, solve puzzles, and fight enemies when needed. It’s not a full action game, and it’s not purely horror either, it sits right in the middle.

Weapons are somewhat limited, but they do the job. You get pistols, a shotgun, a flamethrower, and a few other tools, but nothing too crazy.

The focus is more on survival than domination.

That said, the enemy variety is pretty limited. Most of the time, you’re fighting the same mold creatures over and over again.

And yeah… by the 20th time you see them, you’re like:
“Alright guys, we get it… you’re mold.”

[hr]
[h1]Story and Pacing[/h1]
The story is good, but not amazing.

It’s easy to follow and has a solid concept, but it’s not particularly deep or emotional. There is a choice at one point in the game that seems important, but realistically… most people will pick the same option.

It doesn’t drastically change the experience.

The pacing, however, is where things dip a bit.

The beginning of the game is phenomenal. The Baker house section is easily the strongest part. But later on, especially in the ship and mine sections, the game slows down quite a bit.

These areas feel less interesting and drag the experience compared to the strong opening.

[hr]
[h1]DLCs[/h1]
The game includes several DLCs:

- End of Zoe: A more action-focused side story that is fun but less horror-driven.
- Banned Footage Vol. 1 & 2: These are smaller scenarios and challenge-based modes, including escape-room style puzzles, survival challenges, and extra story bits from different perspectives.
- Not a Hero (Free DLC): This is easily the best one. You play as Chris Redfield in a more action-heavy mission, and it’s a great addition for fans of the series.

Overall, the DLCs are a nice bonus, with Not a Hero being the standout.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]Fantastic atmosphere and horror design
[*]Memorable villains, especially the Baker family
[*]Strong exploration with clever item usage
[*]Great graphics and environmental detail
[*]Excellent intro and early-game pacing
[*]First-person perspective works incredibly well
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]Limited enemy variety
[*]Story is good but not very impactful
[*]Late-game sections (ship and mines) feel weaker
[*]Some pacing issues towards the end
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 is an outstanding survival horror game.

It successfully reinvents the series with a new perspective, delivers incredible atmosphere, and creates one of the most memorable horror experiences in modern gaming.

Even if you’re new to Resident Evil, this is a fantastic entry point.

Just… maybe don’t play it alone at night.

Or do.

Despite being produced in Japan, English is the base ("original") language like every other(?) resident evil game. The English acting / performances are very good for the most part but Ethan (the main character) is such a hit-or-miss. some lines are delivered really well but some make him seem bored or maybe just desensitised? Ethan's line delivery feels more consistent in the Japanese audio, although some of the other characters become less consistent. I ended up liking Ethan in the end but he might not be for everyone despite being the main character.

Some issues seem to exist when playing at high refresh rates although for the record I played the whole game through at 120fps and didn't notice anything wrong except a few messed up wall opening animations.

This is far in a way my favorite Resident Evil game. Capcom listened to all the criticism of 5 and the borderline irredeemable 6 and decided to make a straight-up survival horror game blending the tension of the old with the atmospheric sheen of the new. Out of all of the games in the series, it offers some of the most diversity of horror influences and experiences while also being consistent in the atmosphere that surrounds it.

The story is simple, but engaging and hooks you right away. You're not some ultra-cool guy with police training, you're a normal shlub. Your wife's been missing and you're going to find her- and unlike Silent Hill 2, there is legitimately an evil that awaits for you to confront to get her back. Meet the Bakers. On the surface, they're a mentally-unstable silly Southern family, but to horror fans at large, they are a variety of horror genres to experience in a bona fide monster mash. Jack is a slasher movie villain, Marguerite is a David Cronenberg body horror concoction, and Lucas is what would happen if Jigsaw just admitted he was having fun putting people through torment. Tonally, the whole game is akin to a Sam Raimi film- engrossed in its own camp while still having the temerity to take its characters seriously when appropriate.

The dialogue is gloriously overwritten in the best possible way and you can tell the writers had a blast when localizing the game. Characters are over-the-top vulgar in their speech in a way that's not cringe, but instead simply memorable for the audacity of what they're saying. You really feel like you're in a twisted version of a redneck household. (10/10 I grew up with these people.)

Gameplay-wise, this is real back-to-basics stuff for the Resident Evil franchise. Puzzles, locked doors, keys hidden behind exploration that forces you to confront horrifying situations using your own smarts. You get into the head of Ethan and make a game plan for how you're going to run around Jack to get to a door and outsmart him, or how much ammo you should pack for a trip into the basement. 

If you love the following movies: The Evil Dead 2, Saw, Friday the 13th, The Fly- play this game immediately. You'll have a blast.
If you love survival horror video games like Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Dino Crisis, or Clock Tower- play this game immediately. It was made for you.

Resident Evil 7 is one of the strongest horror games I’ve played. It hooked me almost immediately and never really let go. The first-person perspective does a ton for the tension, the atmosphere is nasty in exactly the right way, and the game is genuinely creepy in a way a lot of horror games aim for and miss. This felt more intense and effective to me than Resident Evil 2 Remake on the pure horror side.

What really carries it is the combination of pacing, environment, and presentation. The house is memorable, the visual design still holds up extremely well, and the enemy and boss designs are disgusting in the best possible way. The whole thing has that great Resident Evil quality where it’s tense, weird, a little campy, a little gross, and somehow still confident enough to make all of that work together. The story also does a better job than I expected. There’s a lot of environmental storytelling, notes, videotapes, and little discoveries that gradually reframe what’s going on, and I was way more invested in piecing it together than I expected.

I also liked that it felt different from other Resident Evil games I’ve played. It still has the series DNA, but the tone is tighter, meaner, and more intimate. The game is at its best when it lets the setting and sound design do the work. A lot of sections had me genuinely on edge, and several moments landed hard because the game understands buildup instead of just throwing noise at you.

It isn’t flawless. Some of the game logic is wonderfully stupid in that classic Resident Evil way. Inventory friction can be annoying. A few fights and puzzle solutions can feel a little gamey or trial-and-error-ish. Some of the healing and body-horror logic is completely absurd if you stop and think about it for more than two seconds. But honestly, that nonsense is part of the charm. The game knows when to be frightening and when to lean into its own ridiculousness.

The DLC is also worth mentioning. It gets much more over-the-top and action-heavy in places, sometimes to a hilarious degree, but I had a good time with it. It doesn’t all hit in exactly the same way as the main game, though the best parts still add a lot to the overall package.

If you want a horror game with great atmosphere, strong visual design, memorable villains, and a story that keeps unfolding in interesting ways, this is an easy recommendation. It’s nasty, tense, stylish, and surprisingly hard to put down.

The game that saved Capcom. We're familiar with this game now and what RE has become, but when this was announced it was a bold swing. Capcom needed a major shake up for not just this series, but their games as a whole. Switching to first person vs over the shoulder or tank controls was somewhat of a controversy at the time. I remember friends and online discourse comparing this to recent horror titles such as Amnesia and worrying this would be a "walking sim". Thankfully this delivered. Years later, we look back with a different perspective, because their titles since have been even better. It holds up, but it's clear they've learned a lot since this game.

It's strength is its compact setting and scope. RE at the time had recently escalated to world ending narrative subjects, but here it's about searching for your missing wife in the Louisiana bayou. Funnily enough, the setting still feels fresh, and the characters they developed for this locale feel authentic. The Baker family, the primary antagonists, feel grounded with their 80s-90s horror tropes, and their sprawling estate feels like something that could exist. Running through it the first time is a blast. 

RE7's main weakness is it's enemy variety and sometimes obtuse combat solutions. The Baker family as bosses feel amazing to fight, but other than that, there's very few different enemies that you actually fight. Most of them even look the same. Thankfully the game's length means that it doesn't drag on, but something that tends to be a strength of the series is missed here. The enemies also sort of shamble towards you in a way that makes it feel frustrating to hit headshots without aim assist. Their heads always seem to drift ever so slightly off the center of your crosshair as you take the shot. Overall this is an extremely minor complaint.

Without a doubt this is a recommend, especially for the common low low sale prices it's listed at. Definitely play RE8 as a follow up.

I tried, I really did, but I just can’t understand why everyone thinks this game is good, much less a “masterpiece” or “the scariest game they’ve ever played.” This game’s been getting hyped up for a while, I had some big expectations for this. Granted, I was getting a bit more skeptical of it the closer I was to getting my hands on it, but I was not at all prepared for just how intensely mediocre this game ended up being.

Before anyone reads this and starts going “Oh but the scariness is subjective!” I do not consider myself to be hard to scare. If you put me in a situation that I don’t immediately know how to deal with, I’m gonna freak out. But the game needs to be mechanically scary in order for those moments to occur and I don’t think this game has much mechanical horror. And the reviews for this game do little to persuade me otherwise. 

You see, when it comes to the other games, I can explain the actual mechanisms that make them scary. I can explain how tight inventory management in the PS1 trilogy and especially RE1R makes it easy for you to put yourself in tense and unfortunate situations of your own making. I can explain how RE2R expands on this by throwing Mr. X into the mix. I can explain how RE3’s ever changing enemy placement, combined with all the dynamic Nemesis encounters, makes it so that you’ll almost always be on your toes. Even with RE4, I can explain how the tank controls, and the shooting in place, and the sound design and unique enemy behaviors all come together to make each encounter tense because you never truly know what’s going on behind you. Similar things can’t be said about RE7.

I’ve tried going through a lot of reviews on YouTube and Steam and whatnot (again I really wanted to give this game a chance), and it’s always just ramblings about surface level details like the setting or the graphics or the jumpscares or the imposing personalities of the Bakers. If you’re lucky, maybe they’ll randomly throw out a “perfect modernization of the survival horror formula,” with little to no explanation, or they’ll just explain the concept of survival horror without giving details about how RE7 in particular uses the survival horror mechanics to create emergent gameplay. And I think there’s a good reason they don’t bring it up much, because it’s systems just are not that engaging.

The inventory management felt near nonexistent here. You already start the game with a whopping twelve inventory slots, and it’s not like you’ll be juggling tons of puzzle items at first, because the Baker Estate is quite minimal and short as it is (relatively speaking). But over time you get like double that, and then tense inventory management quickly becomes actually LITERALLY nonexistent. Sometimes it may feel like it’s tighter than it really is, because the huge inventory let’s you overcompensate quite a bit with the amount of resources you’ll realistically need to scrape by. But it’s all artificial.

Health is also not as scarce of a resource as it’s made out to be. You can easily block attacks from most enemies (even bosses) and take way less damage, and it’s not like their base damage is that much more than in any typical survival horror enemy. The crafting for health items is also way oversimplified. In previous games, you had to strategize around what kind of combinations would be best for you. You could just use two mixed greens when you’re in caution just for the sake of security in more tense situations, but if you don’t end up needing that security that’s just two greens flushed down the drain that could’ve been used to craft multiple better heals if you came across more reds later on. Inventory management also factored into this dilemma because you weren’t able to stack heal mixes or individual herbs. In RE7, you just need one green and one chem or enhanced chem, and you get what is basically a med spray handed to you for free. And just like with the inventory, you’ll get multiple max health upgrades across the game that only serve to further alleviate things.

In the Baker Estate, the only time you really have to deal with the molded is in the basement, they’re never upstairs roaming the halls with Jack like in RE2R. They don’t have much of a presence down there either because there’s hardly anything to do in the basement, and there’s even fewer situations where you NEED to deal with them. Even when I have to do the mad dash for the dissection room, the molded aren’t sitting there waiting to pounce. They have to slowly crawl out, and by the time I make it to the door all I have to do is block a hit or two and the instant I push through the door they immediately disappear. It’s not just the molded on their own that suffer from this seclusion though, it impacts Jack a lot as well.

Jack Baker is the closest this game gets to having emergent horror, and everyone loves to treat him like he’s the best thing the game has to offer. He’s not a true stalker like many try to paint him out to be, he’s still just a patroller type enemy, but his pathing isn’t completely linear. He can kind of just go wherever he wants and that makes him a bit less predictable, but I still don’t think he holds up to scrutiny that well. He seems a lot scarier than he really is at first especially because of how fast he comes at you. But once you realize you can just shut a door in his face, then run away a bit and see him immediately lose you, it takes out so much of the tension. Jack is functionally far less scary than you make him out to be in your head when you see him stomping around and taunting you.

This is why I find it so strange that they don’t have enemies scattered around the home upstairs. A lot of RE’s survival horror is built around there being a lot of enemies around basically the entire map, and every step of your pathing is strategized around the enemy placement. Ammo scarcity also comes into play here a lot with being able to create safer passage for yourself in case things go wrong down the line. I think taking that more into account and putting at least a few enemies upstairs would’ve done so much to make Jack a bigger threat. That’s not to say that the survival horror formula just can’t work with a single main enemy for most of the game, that actually works really well in other games like Amnesia: The Bunker. But that game has an actual good stalker enemy with an imposing mechanical presence. If you try to shut a door on the Beast in that game and just run away with no plan, he’s gonna instantly catch up to you and you’re dead.

You may notice that all my conversations about the mechanics are mostly limited to how they affect the first section of the game in the Baker Estate. That’s because, like most RE games, the first section of the game is usually the best, and that applies here too. I thought the Baker Estate was underwhelming at best and quite an embarrassing “return to form” at worst. But I’m gonna be honest, I think everything after the Baker Estate is just complete trash.

The old house is a mostly linear uninteresting slog with an even worse patroller enemy. The bugs weren’t an interesting replacement for conventional enemies either, they were just a nuisance that posed even less of a threat than the molded. By the time you get to Lucas’s section, the game entirely drops any notion of this game being survival horror. It’s just a big series of traps with barely any enemies and barely any exploration topped off with an admittedly neat escape room sequence that adds nothing to the overall experience. Everything after the Baker Estate just feels like a drawn out nothingburger intercut with mediocre boss fights. And yeah, the third act in the boat is horrifically dull, but I don’t have much left in my word count to even get into that.

So yeah, no idea why everyone hypes this game up to this day like it’s a top three RE game or one of the best horror games ever made. It’s just so painfully and shamelessly mediocre to me.

Resident Evil 7 is a product of its time. Resident Evil 2 may have introduced the "invincible baddie which chases you everywhere" but Resident Evil 7 turns that into a sub-genre. The entire game is a series of mini-boss encounters with some mould extermination in-between. And for that, RE7 is exhilarating and exhausting. Nearly its entire 10-12 hour game time will be spent with a high heart-rate, dodging "stalker enemies" whilst you scrape by. These enemies too, thrilling. Deeply-crafted, well-acted, unique characters that are so much more tense than your garden-variety shambling zombie.

Abandoning most of the Resident Evil series lore, RE7 offers a compelling new gameplay, setting, and atmosphere, that it cannot be understated how much of a surprise it was that this was a Resident Evil game. That is also its biggest weakness, it is largely un-replayable. Whilst an experience, it isn't always fun, and that make it far too stressful and repetitive to play through again.

If you haven't had your fill of this style of horror game, its well-worth the time.

Resident Evil's seventh entry is a lot of things, but it isn't [i]just[/i] an incredible return to form and fundamentals, or a great example of what can happen when a passionate team and company put enough care into something, or even an amazing achievement for a franchise willing to re-invent itself for the better again. RE 7 proves that things long thought dead and gone, whether it's bodies in a morgue or this very franchise, can still be absolutely terrifying when they suddenly start moving again.

Doubly so when that thing you thought was dead is now wearing a mile-wide grin, wildly swinging an axe, and taunting you in a southern accent that makes you equally afraid about the potential [i]slurs[/i] that an undead southerner would call you.


Seven's the title I'd recommend to someone wanting to give this series a try. What I love about classic Resident Evil's absurd architecture and puzzles are given a lovely re-imagining with a confident newfound tone in self-aware and self-indulgent grindhouse horror à la Evil Dead 2. It's ridiculous horror that's just as terrifying as it is oddly funny, only it's not happening to Bruce Campbell, noooo, it's happening to [i]you[/i] and it's laughing at you.

This is definitely the kind of game that you feel like is laughing at you, both loudly as the twisted inhabitants of this cursed parish gleefully prod at you, and silently, as the game's design makes you question if Capcom gave the job of "guy who makes sure there's enough resources for healing and ammo" to the world's most sadistic Turkish ice cream vendor. 

Which makes it all the more concerning when you start laughing back at the game, your face smeared in your own blood, and their blood, and more blood that you hope isn't Chris' blood, as you sharply exhale and slump against a nearby wall, upset that you're out of shotgun shells, but feeling very satisfied about the good use you put them to... 

...until the next boogeyman leaps out at you from around the corner and your breath jumps out of your throat like your lungs slammed on the brakes.

I am writing this as part of a broader playthrough of all games in the lead up to Resident Evil Requim with having completed:
- Resident Evil 2 
- Resident Evil 3
I state this because my experience thus far is going to be influenced by my exposure to those:

----Story----

8/10 - Follows Ethan Winters, who searches for his missing wife, Mia, at a derelict Louisiana home owned by the cannibalistic, mold-infected Baker family. This entry is by far the scariest to date with a deliberate focus on first-person horror. The story looks to expand on the Resident Evil lore by introducing a new variant of virus called the Mold. The story sees you facing off against all members of the Baker family each twisted by the Mold in ways that are genuinely terrifying. The first half of a game are near-perfect with this unfortunately taking a nose-dive towards the later end of the game where this becomes more of an action game. The DLCs do a really great fantastic job or reddeming the game, so if you can, try to pick up the Gold edition when it is on sale. 

----Performance----

9.5/10 - I had zero performance issues with the game. I was able to crank this up to 4K/60 (and then some) for the entirety of playthrough with the benefit of of Ray-Tracing and HDR selling the darkness and horror in ways that I would argue is needed for a full experience. The dark magic of the RE Engine shows its strength here with everything being detailed fairly meticulously for a game from 2017. My only complaint would be a slight grainy feel to the visuals that you forget about. I cannot tell if its an issue with my card/or as a result of FSR or if its just a design choice.

----Sound-------

I grew up playing the Resident Evil games, so going into Resident Evil 7 I honestly didn’t know what to expect. The series had gotten pretty action-heavy for a while, and I always liked the older games more when they focused on survival and horror instead of just shooting everything. After playing this though, it really feels like they brought the series back to what made it great in the first place.

Right away the game just feels tense. You’re not running around with tons of ammo blasting enemies like in some of the later titles. You actually have to think about your resources again. Ammo and healing items are limited, so every fight feels like it matters, and sometimes it’s honestly better to just avoid enemies if you can.

The atmosphere is probably the best part of the whole game. The Baker house is creepy as hell and the whole place just feels uncomfortable in the best way. The lighting, the sounds, and the way the rooms are designed all work together to make it feel like something bad is always about to happen. There were definitely a few moments where I jumped or just didn’t want to walk into the next room yet.

The Baker family are also great villains. They’re not just random monsters. Each one has their own personality, and Jack especially is terrifying when he’s stalking you through the halls. As the game goes on you start learning more about what happened to them, which makes things a bit more interesting than just fighting generic enemies.

One thing I wasn’t sure about at first was the first-person view since Resident Evil had always been third-person before. But after playing for a bit it actually works really well. Being in first person makes everything feel way more personal and intense. When something scary happens it feels like it’s happening right in front of you instead of watching it from a distance.

The level design is really solid too. The Baker estate is laid out in that classic Resident Evil style where areas connect back to each other and you slowly unlock new sections as you go. There are puzzles, locked doors, shortcuts, and secrets to find, which makes exploring the house actually rewarding.

It mixes exploring, puzzles, and combat in a way that keeps things interesting without just throwing enemies at you nonstop. The game builds tension really well instead of constantly relying on action.

For me, Resident Evil 7 feels like the game that brought the series back to its roots. It focuses on survival horror again, the atmosphere is incredible, and the Baker family are some of the most memorable villains the series has had in a long time.

[h1]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/h1]

[b]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/b] is the moment when the Resident Evil series looked at itself, realized it had become an action movie, and decided to go full nightmare mode again. You play as Ethan Winters, a regular guy searching for his missing wife… which somehow leads him straight into one of the most messed-up houses in gaming history.

The game switches to a first-person perspective and focuses heavily on survival horror. Resources are limited, the Baker family is absolutely terrifying, and the creepy Louisiana house feels like it’s constantly watching you. Instead of nonstop action, the game builds tension with exploration, puzzles, and sudden “oh no why is that guy chasing me again” moments.

[b]What works well:[/b]
• [b]Proper horror atmosphere:[/b] The Baker estate is one of the creepiest locations in the entire series.
• [b]Fresh perspective:[/b] First-person gameplay makes everything more intense and immersive.
• [b]Great pacing:[/b] The game balances puzzles, exploration, and terrifying encounters really well.
• [b]Memorable villains:[/b] The Baker family is disturbing, unpredictable, and honestly nightmare fuel.

[b]Some negatives:[/b]
• [b]Combat can feel clunky:[/b] Fighting enemies sometimes feels stiff compared to modern shooters.
• [b]Later sections lose some horror:[/b] The first half is scarier than the later parts of the game.
• [b]Inventory stress:[/b] Limited space means you’ll constantly play the “what item do I drop” game.

[u]Overall:[/u]
Resident Evil 7 successfully revived the survival horror roots of the series while introducing a new perspective and a terrifying new story. It’s tense, creepy, and one of the strongest modern entries in the franchise.

[b]Final verdict:[/b]
A terrifying return to classic Resident Evil horror — creepy atmosphere, intense moments, and a house you’ll definitely never want to visit again.

- I'm a bit iffy on the jumpscares in this one. Some of them were really well done, some of them felt cheap, and some were physically impossible without the characters straight-up teleporting. - I didn't like the videotape mechanic that much. It wasn't bad, I just wish it had a fast-forward option if you've already played it before (not for the DLC, obviously).

This game is CREEPY, you will constantly feel hopeless esp during the 1st half of the game. It feels like such fresh air, putting the player in the shoes of a Ethen Winters, an ordinary person, a complete juxtaposition to the rest of the franchise. There isn't that comfort barrier of being someone who feels like they can handle themselves already, no military/police background. Nothing. This allows the audience to feel that horror as that much more of a threat, with the added level of realness. 

The Bakers in their characters and performance are done really well, Each of them having a clear and distinct personality while maintaining a great mix of creepiness while also feeling human. Feeling crazy while also in control. You feel constantly on edge with the mix of enemies you encounter, having overwhelming pressure while also having to scrounge around for resources to defend yourself, makes the game that much more tense. 

Setting and atmosphere in the visuals and sound design is something the game excels at, you get a great feeling of not only the core locations but also the area that surrounds it. There is a constant feeling of a lack of cleanliness, which fits the core theme perfectly, you feel constantly grossed out by everything around you.

The diversifying of the different areas is done great, allowing a fresh feeling despite being confined to the same location. The variety of "Fears" they are able to make with the main theme of mould helps to keep the audience on edge as there are new threats which have their own set of attacks and weaknesses learn. 

However,

I'm not sure, if its just because I'm playing this after playing through the remakes of 2 through 4 or that I just didn't properly immerse myself within the game, but after playing all the way through I'm left feeling almost underwhelmed by the experience as a whole.

Ignoring the issues with it being the first game made with re engine causing issues with lighting and shadows with textures throughout the game. The core of the games direction isn't satisfying, instead of flowing seamlessly the narrative feels quite jolty. On top of this there was a numerous instances where I felt confused on what to do, I appreciate a good puzzle here and there but when it goes it the point of the audience not knowing what to do, it constantly breaks the emersion. 

Each of the boss-battles feel underwhelming, Clunky and unsatisfying. It doesn't feel like you've overcome this great challenge, rather its more so "guess that parts over". This is most apparent in the final sequence of the game, at no point is there a fear of dying more so just waiting for it to be over. The sequence split is unbalanced, the initial stage being a good bulid-up however in that it can be confusing to figure out where to go. The 2nd part then feels way too rushed, The "Twist" is so obvious throughout the game that it has no pay-off at this point.
 
Stealth is meant to be one of this games core mechanics, however even with 3d audio enabled, it can be rly difficult to judge exactly where sounds are coming from. Leading to the stealth feeling unfair at times, but also simultaneously feeling unsatisfying as the enemies don't react to the players sound ques and feel blind half the time.  

Another issue with the audio scape as a whole, is it feels unpolished. Explosions are missing a decent amount of base to them and there's not dynamic echo depending on where the bomb goes off. The final mix is also not complete well, as music will often be overcasting all else breaking emersion causing the player to have to manually adjust the levels within the games settings for a better experience.

Despite the game having a fresh feeling to it, it can at the same time feel very predictable to what is going to happen. When opponents are going to spawn in and from where, when the plot points are going to hit and where the story is going as a whole.

Overall, 6/10

A worthwhile game to experience, as a horror and also RE Fan. It without terrified me at times and without a doubt made me feel on edge, its not without its flaws though. Leading to my general summery being "Great Fundamentally but ultimately unpolished and incomplete". It has amazing intentions for what it wants to be, it makes me wish it was just finessed that little bit more to create proper immersion with the player.

As someone who hadn’t played RE7 or 8 before, I decided to jump in fresh after beating Requiem, as I just needed to play some more RE after that. But, after beating this game, I can honestly say I’m on the fence about how I feel about it.. On one hand there's aspects that I really liked about the game, but then on the other hand there’s something that started to really bug me about mid-way through which I’ll get into.. 

Ultimately I did enjoy my time with it, which is why I’ve resulted in giving it a positive, as it was enjoyable. But with that said, in my opinion there’s one or two things holding it back from its full potential.

I assume most are familiar with RE games by now, so I won’t waste time detailing everything this game does well. It’s an RE game, so you can expect horror/thriller, mystery, great puzzles and taking out infected etc.. The game nails this aspect! 

Now for what I disliked.. 

Main Characters: Basically this game is a perfect example of why character development is so important in story telling.. You play as Ethan Winters, and it’s entirely in first person. You don’t get to see Ethan’s face.. Which to me isn’t the problem, but even after beating the game, I still learned pretty much nothing about the guy.. Other than he’s Mia’s husband and he’s clearly lacking in personality. I don’t know about his background, profession, friends, or what he likes to do outside of chasing after his wife Mia, who he’s clearly obsessed with!

It seems this game was so fixated on making me discover things about Mia (who was also uninteresting) and every other character, that it forgot about Ethan himself. For me this is where it dropped the ball.. This game had me on the edge of my seat at times, and then other times I found myself losing interest.

Story: Now, don’t get me wrong, it’s not a bad game at all. In fact there’s a lot to love about it, but it’s definitely not perfect. Of course this is totally my opinion, and others will probably disagree! 

If you’re into horror games then this game will probably be right up your alley, as it genuinely has some of the most terrifying moments and characters that I’ve seen in a video game. The puzzles are challenging, which is what I loved about it. The story starts off interesting, but then like I said, it got quite boring about half way through.. I simply put this down to the main characters being uninteresting. That's my only real issue with the game, because other than that I thought it was great! 

Graphics: Considering this game is nearly 10 years old, the graphics hold up extremely well. Honestly it could probably pass for a newly released game, at least on PC! I did have to tweak the settings from its default to get it to look its best. 

Game Mechanics: The game mechanics have also aged very well, and I can imagine at the time of its release it was probably ahead of its time.  

Its worth noting that I played this game after requiem and RE 2 & 4 remakes. So with those characters being so great, it probably dampened my experience a little.. In hindsight I’d probably play this before those games. 

Judging by other reviews, a lot of people clearly rate this game highly. And I enjoyed the majority of my time with it, but also I can’t see me rushing back any time soon to play it again.

Score: If I have to give it an overall score, I’d give it a 7.5/10.. It’s pretty good, but if I compare it to the other RE games that I’ve played, it’s probably one of the weaker ones. 

I’ll be playing Village next to see how it compares!

Jack in particular stands out — being chased around the house while he’s talking to you like it’s just another normal day is pretty disturbing. Marguerite’s section is also one of the more uncomfortable parts of the game in a good horror way. They really carry the atmosphere for most of the game.

I also liked the story direction. It starts off pretty simple with Ethan looking for his missing wife, but as you explore the house and surrounding areas you slowly learn what actually happened to the Bakers and what’s going on with the infection. A lot of the background information comes from files and recordings you find around the house, which adds some interesting lore if you take the time to read them.

Gameplay-wise it leans more into survival horror again. Ammo and healing items are limited, and inventory management actually matters. Sometimes it’s better to avoid enemies rather than fight them, which keeps the tension high. It reminded me more of the older Resident Evil games in that sense.

The DLCs were also surprisingly fun. They add some extra story and different gameplay ideas, and they help wrap up parts of the story that the main game leaves open.

If I had a few complaints, enemy variety is a bit limited since you mostly fight the same molded enemies throughout the game. Also, the first half of the game inside the Baker house is easily the strongest part. Once you move past that area later on, the atmosphere isn’t quite as strong and the pacing slows down a little.

Overall though, I really enjoyed it. It feels like the moment where the Resident Evil series reset itself and went back to focusing on horror and tension again. The Baker family, the creepy house, and the first-person perspective make it one of the more memorable games in the series.

The best piece of found footage art is the television series Archive 81, which I will never forgive Netflix for cancelling after one season.
Resident Evil VII Biohazard may come in second place, but it comes very close.

Some might say that calling Resident Evil VII Biohazard a found footage video game is a stretch, but I think it’s reasonable. In a twist on the formula you don’t merely watch the footage you find, but rather you experience it as the camera person, having free control of movement, camera orientation and, to some extent, scene interaction like climbing a ladder.

The environment art, character art, atmospheric music, sound effects, voice acting and writing are wonderful and all come together to create a distinct and pleasing horror vibe that is distinct to a Resident Evil game, although I feel its style was greatly influenced by The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (1974). At time of writing, 9 years after release, the visuals still hold up, which I believe is a testament not only to the technical excellence in real-time rendering of the game at release but rather to what good art direction can do.

The narrow default camera field of view of 80 degrees combined with a dim flashlight with a tight beam and a short fallof makes exploring in the dark consistently feel very tense.
Resources such as ammunition and healing items are well measured out for the player, giving you just enough to survive your encounters. This keeps the combat desperate which maintains a feeling of vulnerability that reinforces an unyielding and persistent atmosphere of dread during quiet exploration and terror during combat encounters.

Resident Evil VII Biohazard is one of the best survival horror games ever made and has revitalised the Resident Evil series. If you’re new to the genre or series and looking for a place to start, or if you’re well experienced with the genre and have somehow missed this game, you will not be disappointed.

The Resident Evil franchise has swung back and forth on the scary vs action pendulum over the years. Some games stray to one or the other extreme while some sit firmly in the middle. Resident Evil 7 definitely swings more towards horror. In fact, this may very well be the scariest game in the franchise so far (I'm writing this after Requiem just came out). If you enjoy the tamer horror games, be warned that 7 may not be the game for you. If you're willing to venture into the Baker Plantation though, Resident Evil 7 may be the best the franchise has to offer.

For newbies to the Resident Evil franchise, 7 isn't entirely isolated from the rest of the series but it is a pretty great jumping on point. The main character, Ethan Winters, is new to the franchise and he serves as a good way to onboard people to what is going on in this universe. It's not fully a soft reboot but it's as close as Resident Evil has ever truly come so if you're new to the franchise, rest assured that RE7 won't give you any real trouble.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard - A Triumph of Survival Horror Reimagined
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was a gamble, a bold pivot for a franchise that had, arguably, lost its way. After years of leaning into action-heavy gameplay and elaborate narratives, Capcom decided to strip Resident Evil back to its terrifying roots, and the result was nothing short of a triumph. Biohazard didn't just revive the survival horror genre for a new generation; it redefined it, proving that sometimes the most effective way forward is to look back.

From the moment you step onto the crumbling, sun-baked grounds of the Baker plantation, Resident Evil 7 immerses you in a suffocating atmosphere of dread. The shift to a first-person perspective was a masterstroke. Gone are the cinematic vistas and distant threats; instead, you're plunged into the claustrophobic confines of a decaying, labyrinthine house, every creak of the floorboards, every whisper of wind, a harbinger of doom. This perspective amplifies the feeling of vulnerability, making you acutely aware of your surroundings and the unseen terrors lurking within them.

The Baker family themselves are the horrifying heart of the game. They are not just obstacles; they are characters etched in grotesque madness, their relentless pursuit and unnatural resilience creating an oppressive sense of being hunted. Ethan Winters, our protagonist, is a far cry from the muscled heroes of past entries. He's an ordinary man thrust into an unimaginable nightmare, his panic and desperation palpable. This grounded approach to the protagonist makes his struggle for survival all the more relatable and impactful.

Resident Evil 7 excels in its masterful pacing. While there are moments of intense, heart-pounding chase sequences and visceral combat, the game understands the power of quiet dread and psychological terror. The exploration of the Baker house is a slow burn, filled with environmental storytelling, unsettling notes, and disturbing discoveries that gradually unravel the horrific mystery. The limited resources – scarce ammunition, infrequent healing items – force you to make difficult choices, reinforcing the survival aspect that had been diluted in previous installments.

The game's visual and audio design are equally crucial to its success. The dilapidated environments are rendered with incredible detail, from the peeling wallpaper and stained floors to the unsettling taxidermy and the sheer oppressive darkness. The sound design is a character in itself, with disembodied screams, the guttural growls of the Bakers, and the constant, unnerving ambient noise creating a symphony of fear.

While the gameplay loop of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat is classic Resident Evil, Biohazard injects it with a fresh lease of life. The puzzles are well-integrated into the environment and the narrative, feeling like organic challenges rather than arbitrary roadblocks. The combat, while often frantic and desperate, is satisfyingly impactful. Every shot feels earned, and every enemy vanquished is a moment of hard-won respite.

Of course, no game is perfect. Some players might find the focus on a single, albeit terrifying, family to be a bit limiting in terms of enemy variety. Additionally, the shift in tone and gameplay might not resonate with everyone who grew up with the earlier, more action-oriented titles.

However, these are minor quibbles in the face of Resident Evil 7's overwhelming success. It was a bold, courageous step that paid off spectacularly. It proved that Resident Evil could still be truly terrifying, that survival horror could thrive in a modern gaming landscape, and that sometimes, the best way to reinvent a legend is to rediscover its core essence. For anyone seeking a genuinely frightening and deeply engaging survival horror experience, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is an absolute must-play. It's a chilling masterpiece that will linger in your nightmares long after the credits roll.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is one of the scariest entries in the entire franchise and the first to fully embrace a first-person perspective. Combined with spatial audio, a gritty atmosphere, and constant tension, it delivers fear in a way few entries have managed before. While it does mix in action, the focus remains on vulnerability. This time, you are not playing as a seasoned action hero like Leon, but as someone far more grounded and exposed.

[h1]Gameplay & Systems[/h1]
The game is built around first-person immersion, with a strong emphasis on exploration, puzzle-solving, and avoiding unnecessary combat. Exploration sits at the heart of the experience. You constantly search for keys, puzzle pieces, and tools while planning routes through tight corridors and interconnected areas. Often, you are being hunted while doing so, which adds a layer of tension to even the simplest objectives. Combat can quickly overwhelm you if you are careless, and that is exactly how it should be. It reinforces the feeling of being an ordinary man trapped inside a nightmare. Resources are fairly generous overall, but enemies are durable and can burn through your ammo faster than expected. That balance keeps encounters tense without feeling unfair. Boss fights are well designed and distinct from one another. Many of them include unexpected mechanics or phases that keep you alert. They remain memorable and enjoyable even on repeat playthroughs, which says a lot about their design.

[h1]Story & Characters[/h1]
Ethan Winters sets out to find his missing girlfriend Mia after receiving a mysterious message years after her disappearance. Despite the uncertainty surrounding the situation in Louisiana, he chooses to investigate. Ethan works well as a protagonist. He feels grounded, convincingly acted, and appropriately reactive to the horrors around him. The Baker family is one of the strongest aspects of the game. Each member has their own brand of madness, and from the first encounter, it is clear something is deeply wrong. Even Mia feels unsettling. The mystery behind the family’s condition keeps you engaged throughout most of the story. The pacing is generally solid, though it slows slightly in certain sections. The final act and reveal feel somewhat rushed, but the conclusion still lands effectively. Chris Redfield’s appearance feels slightly off compared to previous portrayals, though his limited role and separate DLC appearance make this a minor issue overall.

[h1]Presentation (Visuals, Sound & Atmosphere)[/h1]
For its age, the game still looks impressive. It achieves a grimy, decayed aesthetic that perfectly matches the setting. The environments feel dirty and oppressive, almost tangible in their discomfort. The atmosphere and sound design work seamlessly together to maintain constant tension. Even during quieter moments, you feel hunted. The audio design keeps you on edge, making every creak or distant sound unsettling. The soundtrack supports this perfectly, maintaining a steady sense of dread and anticipation, often making you brace for what might be waiting around the next corner.

[h1]Technical State[/h1]
The game runs exceptionally well across a wide range of hardware. Performance is stable, with no crashes or noticeable stutters during my playthrough. The controls are responsive and intuitive, and the camera feels tight and precise. The RE Engine once again proves why it is one of the most reliable engines in the industry.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 successfully brings the franchise back to its darker, more grounded survival horror roots. It keeps you tense even during simple exploration, forcing you to think carefully about resource usage and whether a fight is truly worth it. The slower movement, limited inventory space, and dangerous enemies elevate the stakes in every encounter. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it and can easily recommend it both to longtime fans of the franchise and to newcomers looking for a strong entry point.

[h1]Rating: 9/10[/h1]

When this just came out I was sort-of doubtful about the whole "darker, more sinister" vibe that the trailers gave off. But that is probably there for the first couple of hours or less. After which it quickly transforms into your standard RE game with you blasting monsters and doing some super simple "puzzles" which are basically fetch quests.


What's good:
[list]
	[*]First person view works reasonably well.
	[*]It is quite atmospheric. Graphics and sound are good.
	[*]There is a certain intrigue to the story (although it is more like "will there be a creepy underground laboratory complex somewhere under the house?" which was cranked to 11 in RE8). And some plot twists as well.
[/list]


At the same time it certainly lacks the variety of something like RE4 or even 5, 6, 8 in several ways:
[list]
	[*]There are about 3 types of base enemies with some stronger versions at times. The family members which are presented as these relentless stalkers are somewhat that, but very quickly become less threatening. I'm not exactly saying that it is a bad thing, but more than "something walking towards you" would have been nice.
	[*]Location variety is quite limited. No RE4 here once again. Now that I think of it dark corridors/rooms make about 80% of the game. With a very similar low saturation brown/grey look to it.
	[*]Weapons are quite limited as well, but then that's been a RE thing since birth.
	[*]There is 0 to gain from defeating most enemies. Perhaps RE8 was a little too arcadey, but something in-between wouldn't have hurt. Especially since the enemies are like slime-based. It would have been easy to make something useful stuck inside them.
[/list]


In general it's a good game, despite the negatives. Maybe because I got it as a part of a bundle. Say 8.5 with that discount, 7 without?  There is a decent amount of it (like I thought "ok, seems like they will end it here before the DLC" for it to just continue on for about three times). At the same time - if you want a sensible end to the whole thing you will want the DLC (which is well worth it). 


I'm just wondering how they manage to spend so much time and resources on certain elements (like the environments) and then be so mediocre on others (enemy variety, weapons). Also, 0 idea what they need human models for to scan etc. since the in-game results look 3D modelled AF anyways.

Bayou-Hazard.
There, I made the joke.

Resident Evil 7:BIOHAZARD is a lying title because its the 23rd game in the Resident Evil Series. Also known as BIOHAZARD: Resident Evil in Japan, which is really funny to me.

You play as Ethan Winters, the world’s dumbest man. After getting a message from his wife, Ethan travels to a shockingly large Louisiana plantation, sees the dead cow effigy and decides to go in anyway. After being beaten up by his wife and then beaten up by my actual dad, Ethan finds himself in a world of horror as he tries to find his wife and escape the Baker’s family home.

Seriously, are plantations actually this big? These guys have, like, 3 big-ass homes on their property.

A huge departure from the rest of the RE series, RE7 is actually entirely in first person, but still has more to do with the first two RE games than it does something like RE4 through 6, for the most part at least. There’s a lot of inspiration in 7 compared to other horror games of the time, down to having to hide from certain enemies who will chase you and say very rude things to you while trying to catch you.

There was this worry that RE7 was going to be this monster closet kind of game like the first Amnesia or it’s contemporaries, which hilariously, I can’t remember the names of at this time. This is where they kind of fluke you early game, because Ethan straight up squares up when he doesn’t have a choice. [s]There’s an actual chainsaw duel not even 3 hours into the game. [/s].

You get weapons and items just like you would any other Resident Evil game, so a huge part of the game actually is combat, or even just a deterrent for the Baker family. There’s something to be said about spinning around and ventilating Jack’s skull with a round while he’s threatening you.
Outside of the Baker family, you also have to deal with their weird goopy boys. The Mold Monsters are sort of a meme at this point in some circles, these weird, grotesque toothy ♥♥♥♥♥ that bleed a mix of blood and puss that grossed out a buddy of mine. They follow the usual Zombie formula of “Shoot them in the face to maximize damage.” so outside of the way they move and attack, they aren’t all that different from the things you’ve fought before in these games, they actually remind me of the monsters from RE: Revelations, for the most part.

I just think they’re kind of lame.

It is a quasi-open world kind of affair like the older games, the further you get through the game the more open the plantation becomes. You can revisit older areas and unlock doors or lock boxes you couldn’t before for extra stuff. Everything in the game is finite, but I never had a problem on regular mode staying stocked and ready for war.

Outside of the main campaign, you have a bunch of extra modes, entirely DLC of course, this was released in 2017. With the Season pass you get “Not a Hero”, a story DLC where you play as Chris “Ten Ton Punch” Redfield, as well as “End of Zoe”, a stand out DLC where you play as an old man who’s solution to big scary monsters is to punch the absolute mold ♥♥♥♥ out of them with his big meaty man mittens.

And also the Banned Footage volumes, which are sort of lame and I wasn’t having fun with them.

Mercenaries doesn’t make a comeback, which is super lame, especially after introducing a man who will headbutt Nemesis to pudding if given the chance. Also, the main goon force, the Mold Monsters, are probably my least favorite enemies in the series. They look like someone’s twitter OC horror monsters more than anything and they’re not really all that fun to fight.

Other than that, the big twist is basically revealed to you 30 minutes into the game, and the big bad guy makes more sense when you realize the lead writer was the dude that wrote the story for FEAR back in 2005.

That being said, its a very weird entry in the series, but still a lot of fun. One play through should take you around 8 hours or so give or take, longer if you’re a completionist, which is alright, a lot of the achievements are funsies to do. You can get RE7 and its DLCs for around $20 when it’s on sale, so its a pretty good deal.

Survival Reborn in the Bayou – A Review of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard

Overall Rating: 9/10

Resident Evil 7 represents a defining course correction for the franchise. After years of escalating scale and action-heavy spectacle, it returns survival horror to its roots—restraint, isolation, and vulnerability. Set within the decaying Baker estate in rural Louisiana, the game abandons global catastrophe in favor of intimate terror. The shift to first-person perspective intensifies immersion, grounding every encounter in discomfort and uncertainty. Resident Evil 7 doesn’t simply revisit survival horror—it rebuilds it from the inside out.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 10/10

The Baker estate is suffocating. Rotting wood, damp corridors, and flickering lights create a setting steeped in decay and dread. Unlike the explosive scale of previous entries, tension here is claustrophobic and personal. Hallways feel tight, doors feel unsafe, and even moments of quiet carry unease. Environmental storytelling is subtle but effective. Every room reflects abandonment, obsession, or corruption. Lighting design plays a critical role—darkness is not cosmetic; it conceals genuine danger. The house evolves as players progress, reinforcing the feeling of navigating a living nightmare.

Story and Narrative: 9/10

Resident Evil 7 narrows its focus to a personal search that spirals into biological horror. The narrative unfolds through discovery—videotapes, environmental clues, and carefully placed documents reveal the tragedy at the heart of the Baker family. By shifting away from long-running protagonists and global conspiracies, the story regains intimacy. The horror feels grounded, even when the bio-organic elements escalate. Themes of control, infection, and manipulation echo the franchise’s legacy while presenting a fresh perspective. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to breathe rather than rushing toward spectacle.

Gameplay and Survival Mechanics: 8.5/10

Survival mechanics return to prominence. Resources are scarce, inventory space is limited, and combat demands caution. Every bullet counts. Healing items are precious. Avoidance is often wiser than confrontation. The first-person perspective enhances vulnerability. Encounters feel immediate and physical, forcing players to react instinctively. Puzzle-solving is once again integral, blending naturally with exploration and combat. Item boxes reintroduce strategic planning, reinforcing the classic survival loop. Combat is slower and more deliberate than recent entries, prioritizing tension over empowerment. The result is an experience that feels disciplined and focused.

Sound Design and Music: 10/10

Sound design is masterful. Creaking floorboards, distant footsteps, and muffled voices create unease long before enemies appear. Silence is weaponized—moments without music are often the most terrifying. The save room theme provides rare comfort, offering brief emotional relief without fully dissolving tension. Audio direction reinforces immersion at every turn, making fear feel immediate and personal.

Replayability and Longevity: 9/10

Multiple difficulty modes, unlockables, and additional content extend replay value. Knowledge of the estate’s layout improves efficiency, but limited resources and enemy placement ensure tension remains intact. Speedruns, higher difficulties, and optional challenges reward mastery without diminishing the survival core.

Conclusion: 9/10

Resident Evil 7 restores identity to the franchise by embracing isolation, vulnerability, and restraint. It scales back the spectacle and rediscovers the power of intimate horror. Through disciplined design and immersive presentation, it proves that survival horror thrives not on size—but on tension.

Final Verdict:

Resident Evil 7 is a triumphant return to form. By stripping away excess and refocusing on atmosphere, scarcity, and personal terror, it redefines modern survival horror. It stands as one of the strongest entries in the series—not because it is the biggest, but because it remembers what survival truly means.

I genuinely believe this is the game that saved the Resident Evil IP.

The switch to first-person works perfectly for RE7 and RE8 Village. Earlier entries feel right in third person, but RE7’s claustrophobic, grounded horror absolutely benefits from the first-person perspective. It pulls you into the Baker estate in a way third-person never could.

------------------------
Horror & Replay Value
------------------------

My first playthrough was genuinely scary. The dinner scene, pulling the snake key from the body, and Jack stalking you around the house all stuck with me. Over time, though, the fear fades. Like most horror games, once you understand the mechanics and layouts, you desensitise.

Madhouse difficulty brought some of that tension back — not necessarily because it was scarier, but because it was harder. The early Mia chainsaw fight on Madhouse is brutal. Jack was actually less difficult for me on Madhouse because I had the circular saw unlocked from earlier achievements. Marguerite, however, was still tough on both Standard and Madhouse. The late-game cave section on Madhouse — with the double spitter bloaters and triple tripwires on the ladder — was one of the more frustrating sequences.

But overall, difficulty felt fair rather than cheap.

------------------------
Highlights & Low Points
------------------------

Favourite sections:

- The Lucas scenes and “Happy Birthday” room.

- The tension of early-game Jack.

Least favourite:

- The ship section.

- The cave escape sequence towards the end.

That said, I mostly enjoyed the experience from start to finish.

------------------------
The Baker Family
------------------------

The Bakers are fantastic villains — and tragic ones. It’s an unfortunate circumstance. That nuance makes them far more compelling than many past RE antagonists.

------------------------
DLC & Minigames
------------------------

I enjoyed Nightmare and Bedroom quite a bit. Some of the DLC felt slightly overemphasised and a bit excessive, but it’s not a major negative. The biggest positive is how they expand the story — showing what happened before the infection, Zoe’s scenario, and more context around the Baker family.

--------------------------------------------
One Criticism (Achievement Perspective)
--------------------------------------------

One thing I wish Capcom would rethink:

Beating Resident Evil on the hardest difficulty usually unlocks something powerful like unlimited ammo — but by that point I’ve already completed every difficulty and all story achievements.

There’s little incentive to replay again once you unlock the “fun” reward.

It would be great if they added an additional difficulty mode where you could actually use those endgame unlocks in a meaningful way.

------------------------
Final Thoughts
------------------------

Resident Evil 5 and 6 drifted too far into action territory. Resident Evil 7 brought the series back to its survival horror roots and restored faith in the franchise.

For me, RE7 and RE8 Village sit near the top of modern Resident Evil.

This wasn’t just another entry — it was a reset. And it worked.
