[h3]Resident Evil 7 Biohazard - Dinner with the Bakers Was a Mistake[/h3]
[hr][/hr]
Coming straight off [b]RE2 Remake[/b], which is a certified survival horror clinic, jumping straight into [b]RE7 Biohazard[/b] felt like Capcom switching cameras and saying, “[i]We’re going closer[/i].”

First person. New protagonist. No familiar hero safety net. Just [b]Ethan Winters[/b] and a house that would instantly fail any health and safety inspection.

[u][b]The Main Game: Baker Family Hospitality[/b][/u]

This was exhilarating. Not because it’s loud, but because it’s suffocating. Tight corridors. Chilling, claustrophobic environments. One of the most survival horror focused [b]RE[/b] entries I’ve played so far.

[b]The Baker family[/b] absolutely carries this game. [b]Jack[/b] is relentless. [b]Marguerite[/b] is pure nightmare fuel. And [b]Lucas[/b]? That chaotic gremlin energy made him genuinely entertaining, especially knowing what unfolds later.

The first person shift works brilliantly for immersion… though my inner ear had complaints. I did get bouts of dizziness and mild motion sickness, so I had to play in chunks instead of long stretches.

Two endings? I picked [b]Mia[/b]. Like any sane person.
Later realized that’s the canon route into the sequel, while [b]Zoe’s[/b] path mostly offers minor gameplay tweaks, altered cutscenes, and a bad ending. Not worth a redo just for a few fancy achievements. If it had [b]RE2[/b] style scenario depth, maybe. But here? I’m good for now.

Still, the ride was absolutely worth it.

[u][b]DLC Breakdown: Swamp Side Stories[/b][/u]

I didn’t dive into every single DLC and mostly stuck to the story based DLCs, so this is from that perspective.

[u][b]1. Banned Footage[/b][/u]

Mostly wave shooter modes, puzzles, and experimental mini game style content.

But [b]Daughters[/b] is the real story slice here. It shows how [b]the Baker family[/b] first got entangled with [b]Eveline[/b] after [b]Mia’s[/b] arrival, from [b]Zoe’s[/b] perspective. Two endings again, one canon and one bad. A strong prequel addition that adds context.

[u][b]2. Not A Hero - Action Dial Turned Up[/b][/u]

[b]Chris Redfield[/b] steps in post main campaign to clean up loose ends, with [b]Lucas[/b] as the central antagonist here. More ammo, more direct combat, and a clear shift from survival tension to tactical action. It works well as a change of pace.

[u][b]3. End of Zoe - Pure Swamp Chaos[/b][/u]

Uncle [b]Joe Baker[/b] shows up armed with nothing but fists and stubbornness. Punching all forms of molded. Impaling spears into mutated gators. Tracking down a mysterious Swamp Man who turns out to be… [b]Jack[/b] again.

Ridiculous? Yes.
Explained? Probably. The confusion is understandable, as the game doesn’t exactly spell it out unless you read most of the files for exposition.

It’s absurd, cathartic, and oddly emotional. Bittersweet ending with [b]Zoe[/b] finally freed thanks to [b]Ethan[/b]… I mean Uncle [b]Joe[/b] and his legendary left and right hooks.

Easily the most unhinged fun I had in the DLC lineup.

[u][b]Pros:[/b][/u]
[list]
[*]Heavy, oppressive horror atmosphere
[*]Exceptional sound design
[*]Strong visuals and lighting
[*]Tight, deliberate survival gameplay
[*]Fantastic antagonist focus, especially the Bakers
[*]Lucas is genuinely entertaining
[*]DLC variety adds meaningful context and tonal shifts
[/list]

[u][b]Cons:[/b][/u]
[list]
[*]Outside the Bakers, molded enemies get a bit repetitive
[*]Some plot links between base game and DLC can feel under-explained unless you read certain files carefully
[*]Ship section drags a bit with backtracking across multiple floors
[*]Sometimes the game caused me mild motion sickness. It happens with some FPS games for me, so could just be a “me” thing
[/list]

[u][b]Final Verdict:[/b][/u]

I understand [b]RE7[/b] was a massive tonal pivot for the franchise, especially after the more action heavy direction of [b]RE5[/b] and [b]RE6[/b]. It brought the series back toward focused, intimate survival horror.

But for me, coming right off the masterclass that is [b]RE2 Remake[/b], [b]RE7[/b] still holds its ground confidently. Different flavor, same quality ingredients. More intimate. More claustrophobic. More character driven.

Not perfect. Occasionally under explained. Sometimes repetitive with the molded. But undeniably gripping.

8.5 / 10 - Attending the Bakers’ family dinner: Would not recommend the food. Would recommend the experience.

[h1] Background [/h1]
[b] Resident Evil 6 [/b] was released in 2012 and received as a pretty, alright game, but it was the culmination of everything that [b] Resident Evil [/b] wasn’t at its conception. Fast paced action gameplay, massive theatrics, it was an, as GameInformer said in their review, “unhinged flaming rollercoaster ride.” After seeing this luke-warm response, CAPCOM said, “Okay, we got off-base there. Let’s take this back to square one.” 

Now, five years later, [b] Resident Evil 7: BIOHAZARD [/b] was released. In this game, the series went back to its roots in survival-horror. The lighting was much darker, the gameplay slower, and you had to make sure you made every bullet count. In addition to this, this was the first main-series [b] Resident Evil [/b] game to be completely in first-person (first ever award belongs to [b] Resident Evil Survivor [/b] on the PSX). But with the history lesson out of the way, let this random nobody tell you about his experience with the game. 

[h1] Story [/h1]
Ethan Winters just received an email from his wife, Mia Winters, who has been missing for three years. Mia urges Ethan to come find her in Dulvey, Louisiana, giving Ethan the address to some beat-up abandoned house in the bayou. Inside the house, Ethan does find Mia, but she is in a panic and wants to get out as soon as possible before “Daddy comes.” Ethan’s beautiful wife Mia then attacks him for taking so long to find her and he is forced to put her down. Afterwards, Ethan is welcomed to the family by Daddy and knocked out. 

The house is revealed to be owned by a perfectly average Louisiana family called the Bakers. In the family you have daddy Jack Baker, mommy Marguerite Baker, and big brother Lucas Baker. Ethan’s goal at this point is to politely refuse this good ol’ fashioned southern hospitality, find Mia, and get out of here before anymore crazy ♥♥♥♥ happens. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
As I mentioned earlier, this was the first mainline [b] Resident Evil [/b] game to be completely in the first-person. Ultimately though, this doesn’t really affect the gameplay. It still plays exactly like a [b] Resident Evil [/b] game would. You can find a multitude of weapons to defend yourself with, you pick up herbs to heal yourself, you can combine herbs with chem fluid to make stronger healing items (although this has its own dedicated menu now). Probably the only mechanic allowed by the first-person perspective is the ability to block. You press the button, Ethan raises his hands up, and you can prevent the full force of the enemy’s attack from hitting you. It’s a cool mechanic, but while playing the game, I often forgot it was there and ended up just running away from enemies to put some distance between us and attack.  

This game also introduces a new enemy bioweapon. You aren’t battling t-Virus zombies or people infected with las plagas anymore. The enemies in this game are The Molded, people infected with a fungal mold that has completely overtaken them and turned them into big black globs. For all intents and purposes though, these are still zombies. They’re slow like zombies, headshots hurt more like zombies, they’re zombies. There's even a licker variety of them! They can stretch their arms sometimes to hit you, which you’ll have to look out for. But just treat these guys like normal [b] Resident Evil [/b] zombies. 

Some aspects did annoy me during my playthrough of this game. First and foremost, Ethan moves like a slug. I try pressing the run button and Ethan gets as fast as a speed walk. Normally I wouldn’t mind this, I can take things slow, but almost everything in this game is faster than you. I can only assume the block mechanic was put in because the devs knew you wouldn’t be able to outrun enemies and wanted to give you something, so you don’t take a bunch of damage. Beyond this, the flamethrower you get feels completely pointless. Yeah, you use it to great advantage when taking care of Marguerite, but it has almost no use beyond this. Bugs don’t appear as an enemy after this point. You can still use the flamethrower on molded, but you’ll use half the clip on one enemy, it’s a waste. 

[h1] Gamefeel [/h1]
This game looks and sounds fantastic. The level of detail put into all the environments and models is staggering. You’ll get full close-ups of all the characters and it’s insane how gross and detailed the devs managed to make them. Marguerite will have bugs crawling through her teeth, you can see how mangled Jack’s mouth is, Lucas’s bloodshot eyes, etc.. The sound design is made to put you right on edge with everything going on around you. You’re surrounded by the ambiance of the house and creatures around you, listening carefully to make sure you aren’t about to run into any molded. When you’re trying to run away from them, it’s tense hearing their footsteps right behind you as you try to close the door. 

I’m not the biggest fan of the first-person perspective for this game. I’m a big fan of the fixed camera angles from the older games. I feel like that really added to the experience because you didn’t know what was beyond your view. You wouldn’t know a zombie is there until you walk to the next screen and see him, it was more tense. Now you have full camera control and can be fully aware of your surroundings. I know it feels better to play, but it lost some of that tension in the process. 

Ethan kind of stinks as a protagonist too. He’s meant to be a faceless blank slate for the player to insert themselves into. The problem is that Ethan still talks in this game and is given a character motive that the normal player can not relate to. All I know about this guy is that he wants to find his wife and that’s it. The whole time he’s in the Baker home, he’s reacting to everything like a normal Saturday. Obviously he’s bewildered by the Bakers but he isn’t shaken up or deterred, he just keeps making little quips. Don’t get me wrong, I like him for his unfunny quips, but he really should’ve had a character arc like Ash Williams from [b] Evil Dead [/b].

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Overall, I enjoyed my time with [b] Resident Evil 7: BIOHAZARD [/b]. I don’t think it was a standout game from the rest of the series, but it was enjoyable from start to finish. When I played [b] Resident Evil 2 [/b], I felt more engaged during that game to replay it over and over to try and get better completion times and I just didn’t feel that same compulsion with [b] Resident Evil 7 [/b]. This is a game I’d probably look forward to playing with my friends and seeing their reactions, but I’m not sure how much I’ll be replaying this one.

Setting aside the few times that enemies blatantly teleport in order to cheaply scare you and the annoying fact that you can't combine items in your backpack with items straight out of the environment (which leads to a bit too much backtracking for my liking), the first half of RE7 serves as a prime example of a borderline perfect first-person survival horror game. The Baker residence oozes its atmosphere through every pore it has. The sound design is amazingly creepy, with the creaks of a settling house, random thuds, and subtle random noises always keeping you on your toes and engaged with the mansion that you are exploring. With the addition of an ever-present looming threat that's searching for you immensely helping with the game's tension. Even if it many times steps a bit into the campy side of things, it's still a brilliant 3-4 hours of horror-filled gameplay.

On the other hand, the second half of the game derails pretty heavily. I don't hate it per se; I just find it to devolve into a mostly boring shooting gallery with enemies (especially in the mines) just lining up one by one to be shot in the head or slowly waddling into your remote-controlled explosive devices in the ship part of the game. The ship section has gained a lot of notoriety over the years for how bad it is, and while I'm not one of those staunch haters that thinks it's the worst thing ever or anything (from a storytelling perspective it is absolutely necessary for it to exist), it really does mark a noticeable step down from the beginning hours. These things on their own don't make me dislike the game, but as time goes on, they make Resident Evil 7 a pretty difficult game for me to return to and replay in its entirety.

I went into Resident Evil 7: Biohazard with a lot of love for the series, especially the classic era. I grew up on the style that Capcom perfected in Resident Evil, Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and Resident Evil 4. There was a certain balance in those games. Creepy, yes. Tense, absolutely. But also packed with memorable action moments and over the top showdowns that made you feel like a slightly underprepared action hero.

So when Resident Evil 7 shifted to a full first person perspective and leaned hard into pure horror, I definitely noticed the change.

Now, to be clear, this game is good. As a straight horror experience, it absolutely commits. The atmosphere is thick, the Baker family is unsettling in all the right ways, and the slower, more intimate perspective makes everything feel uncomfortably close. There were plenty of moments where I was cautiously creeping around corners thinking, “I do not like this. I do not like this at all.” Which, to be fair, means the horror is working.

But compared to the earlier titles, this entry feels much less action driven. The older games had a rhythm where tension would build, explode into a dramatic fight, then give you a moment to breathe before the next big set piece. Resident Evil 7 keeps the focus tight and heavy on fear. It is more about dread than spectacle. More “please let this hallway be empty” and less “bring it on.”

For fans like me who loved the blend of horror and cinematic action in the first four games, the shift can feel a bit limiting. It is not that the game lacks intensity. It just channels that intensity differently. Instead of feeling like you are gradually becoming a more capable survivor, you often feel small, vulnerable, and very aware that the house does not want you there.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a strong horror game. It is polished, tense, and clearly crafted with care. But if you are hoping for that classic blend of creepy atmosphere and bold action moments that defined the earlier Capcom era, this is not quite the same flavor. It is less explosive and more oppressive. Less action movie energy and more “why did I decide to play this at night?”

Still good. Just different. And maybe next time, I would not mind a few more dramatic one liners between the screaming.

Not a Hero and End of Zoe both felt like fun epilogues to the game and again gave it a more arcadey horror feel than the original base game, but the gamemode I believe to really shine out of all was Ethan Must Die, this gamemode with its RNG components really gives the mode more replayability and was honestly a lot of fun, despite my close to 50 failed runs.

This game has some insanely annoying achievements, but only one can really come to mind while typing this and that would be the Survival+ 21 achievement. [i]Resident Evil 7 Evil[/i] is terrifying, it's easily the scariest game I've ever played. Having played this after playing [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i], [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i], and [i]Resident Evil 4 Remake[/i], I was a little thrown off by how much clunkier the gameplay felt, but then I remembered this game is actually older than all of those games. The world design here is incredible, Jack, his insanity, and the glimpse of humanity left within him is terrifying in a way the other RE stalkers I've experienced are not. The use of video tapes as a way to shed light on the path forward, while creating condensed horror experiences is genius. I think [i]Resident Evil 7 Evil[/i] shows it's best pitch up front, as the initial Baker house is more memorable and built-out than the following two locations. Although, I personally felt the horror elevate again when [spoiler]playing as Mia on the boat section, and sneaking around without weapons for a while[/spoiler]. Major props to anyone who has played this in VR.

In terms of gameplay, the initial house certainly reminded me of [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i], but past that point it's more like [i]Resident Evil 4 Remake[/i] if the combat was much worse. I'm no professional at these games, but this is my 4th one, and I've done multiple playthroughs of some of the remakes, including S rank runs, and harder difficulties, but personally felt like [i]Resident Evil 7 Evil[/i] was a different beast. I died more times here than in the 3 remakes I've played combined. The boss fights in particular felt very bullet sponge, and are where most of my deaths took place. I was also confused about how to properly block attacks for a majority of the game, but I felt that could've been introduced more clearly. 

I love the more self-contained story here. In other RE games I've played, there is so much lore referencing countless prior entries that I'll never play because old game is old, but here each document I found I enjoyed reading, learning more about the Baker family, and getting a glance into what exactly transpired before all is revealed. Despite my few criticisms, [i]Resident Evil 7 Evil[/i] is a game I'd highly recommend, and it's easily one of the best "Show this to your non-gaming friends" games, of all time. 

[b]Highly Recommended[/b]

RE7, despite having reinvented the series, has an identity crisis. I'm not sure it escapes the shadow of PT, which it planted itself in with the "Beginning Hour" demo, but more importantly it doesn't escape any of the outwards genre trappings it dips into. Stalker enemies are nothing new for RE, but pseudo-stealth and crouching around corners feels like an advancement of those systems into something much more generic. The AI for these enemies was not properly developed either and I constantly faced inaccurate cues for detection, when I was detected there was so much confusion as to whether I was in actual danger that it brought no anxiety. In Thief (not that the comparison is particularly fair), enemies' states are clearly defined and there are no "false starts" wondering if I've been found or if the game is in error. The tension comes from the management of these states and the transitions between them. I know the guard is mildly alert, I know he's searching, I know he's looking right at me, I don't know if I'm hiding well enough to avoid detection and I don't know how to run 30 feet into a safe room and wait out his AI.

These don't need to function the same, a faster and less predictable stalker could be fun but it's just too sloppy, I should be frightened when Jack sees me, instead I'm confused because the animations are muddy and because there's so many times the game seems to think I've been caught while Jack is operating in a different time zone. The Stalkers are also much faster than the player, meaning chases have to start from a good distance away that isn't tense, my greatest relationship to these stalkers is voyeuristically watching them dawdle around and possibly running to an artificial safe zone.

Action is odd in RE7, I like the guns a lot. They're powerful and ammo is doled out smartly, at least for most of the game. The issue comes in the form of the enemies, the only good thing I can say about the molded are that they are satisfying to headshot. Their animations are markedly worse than the stalkers and I wasted way too much ammo shooting them after they had faded out into a death state because of the unclear animations. They remind of a Souls boss with a windup timed to make you mistime a dodge or parry, it feels inauthentic and ill considered for enemies that try their best to get close to you, further obfuscating information on them. Their visual design is horrible, they form an amorphous blob of an enemy pool that isn't dissimilar to their individual design. They don't inspire any feelings in me outside of momentary Rorschach tests.  The boss fights are also rough, Marguerite and the final boss had the only memorable designs though were only slight gameplay improvements from the other fights. Marguerite had an interesting idea for a fight, making you enter a compromised and confined space to hunt for her, but again I found the mechanics inconsistent and wasn't overly compelled to go out searching for her. It was a great idea executed poorly which is more than I can say for the others.

Chainsaw Jack might actually be THE low point for the series. I have played RE6, many RE games aside have more ridiculous moments or concepts, but it highlights the big issue with RE7. RE7 doesn't have a soul, it's your friend you quotes whichever Instagram reel had the most likes last time he opened the app. "Beginning Hour" was not wholly shameless in aping PT, but it becomes egregious considering it was for this game. I think PT is overrated, but it was saying and doing things that had meaning, RE7 expects the same gravitas between setpieces of giant monsters and one liners, sure it's lessened from prior entries, but at its peak this game expects you to take it deadly serious. It's funny how often I see it compared to Texas Chainsaw Massacre when it's greater filmic inspiration, at least for plot, is the Exorcist. A tragic perversion of normal people by an infestation that makes them crass, with a similar facial change to boot. Again, RE7 doesn't have any guiding identity so it rips this off and expects the care we place on Regan without caring enough to put in any of the additional work. It's borderline offensive in how haphazard it is. The Bakers having a dead child in their attic, pre-infection, aside even Mia is underwritten when she's the cause of this whole escapade, if you can't even try to make me care about her aside from generic lines at the beginning and end of the game then what do you expect me to care about?

I did care when this game showed originality, the Happy Birthday VHS, the early parts of the ship, the melee fight on the ending 2 path (no spoilers), even the gunplay doesn't quite play like most other games if only delineated by its first person perspective, but the former two points and similar wackiness feels horribly disconnected from the larger game, it just feels like the lack of soul in this game was a boon in those instances. 

The game is perhaps best described by its inclusion of VHS tapes in 2017, being recorded to directly from cameras that shouldn't be able to, by characters who shouldn't be recording and have two hands free. It was grabbed from other sources without consideration by developers who didn't bother to consider anything apart from its aesthetics in those sources.

RE7 Biohazard is the first game in years that made me consider installing a defibrillator next to my PC. Creeping through the Baker house felt so tense and oppressive that I started rationing my play sessions, because I was suffering almost like I was the one trapped inside.

🧟 Resident Evil 7: Biohazard | 👍 Yes, with minor caveats | ⏱ ~10h played

---

=== TL;DR ===
🧠 A tense, immersive return to survival-horror that masterfully blends exploration, puzzles, and first-person terror. The Baker Estate is a horrifyingly memorable setting. Minor late-game action bloat keeps it from perfection, but this is a true series revival.

---

=== What this game is ===
📖 Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a first-person survival-horror game where you play Ethan Winters, searching for your missing wife on a decrepit Louisiana farm. What starts as a desperate rescue mission quickly unravels into a nightmare: the deranged Baker family, grotesque Molded creatures, and sinister mysteries surrounding the house and the girl Eveline.
The game deliberately abandons the over-the-top action of RE6, focusing on dread, tension, and resource management. Fans of classic Resident Evil and horror films like *Texas Chainsaw Massacre* will feel instantly at home, while newcomers will be captivated by the palpable sense of danger.

---

=== Gameplay ===
🎮 Core loop: explore the Baker estate → gather items & ammo → solve environmental puzzles → survive encounters with the Bakers & Molded.
You search every room, craft healing items or ammo from scarce resources, and carefully approach enemies that cannot simply be shot down. The game mixes stealth, strategy, and panic-driven decision-making. The first-person perspective—and optional VR with mods — makes every creak, shadow, and sudden attack terrifyingly immediate.
Player freedom is moderate: you can explore rooms in different orders and tackle optional challenges, but major story events follow a linear path.

---

=== What it does well ===
✨ Atmosphere & world-building: The Baker Estate is a character unto itself—morbidly detailed, maze-like, and horrifyingly alive.
🎶 Sound design: Subtle audio cues—floor creaks, distant screams, sudden windows clattering—keep tension high.
🧩 Puzzles: Cleverly integrated into the environment, from key-based locks to shadow puzzles, balancing challenge without feeling frustrating.
🔫 Resource & combat tension: Limited ammo and invincible enemies force creative problem-solving rather than brute force.

---

=== Where it falls short ===
⚠ Late-game pacing: After the Baker Estate, gameplay leans more on combat than horror, and later Molded enemies feel less threatening.
⚠ Save points & checkpoints: Some automatic saves are poorly placed, occasionally forcing replay of cleared areas.
⚠ Choices have minimal impact: Narrative decisions affect only small cutscenes rather than branching the story.

---

=== Replayability ===
🔁 Moderate. Post-game unlocks (weapons, collectibles, higher difficulty) and hidden “Mr Everywhere” figurines encourage exploration and replay, while DLC content provide additional challenges.

---

=== Who should play ===
✅ Fans of survival-horror and classic Resident Evil
✅ Players seeking tense, atmospheric first-person horror
✅ VR enthusiasts craving immersion and terror (Only Mods)
🚫 Those expecting constant action or modern open-world design
🚫 Players who dislike jump scares or unsettling visuals

---

=== Technical & value ===
🛠 Performance: Stable with minor glitches (occasional clipping of Molded).
🎮 Controls/UI: Inventory management and crafting are intuitive; first-person controls are tight and responsive.
💰 Length: ~10 hours on normal difficulty; DLC & challenges extend replay value. Worth the price for horror fans.
🧩 Mods: Optional but not necessary; VR enhances immersion dramatically -> VR on PC requires third party mods

---

=== Final verdict ===
🏁 Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a terrifying, expertly crafted survival-horror experience. Capcom returns the series to its roots, combining puzzles, exploration, and first-person dread with one of the most memorable horror environments in gaming. The final act falters slightly with action-heavy sequences, but the journey through the Baker Estate is unforgettable. A must-play for horror fans and a new benchmark for the series.

Went into Resident Evil 7 years late and honestly don’t know why I put it off for so long. This game absolutely nails atmosphere. From the moment you step into the Baker house it’s just pure dread, no loud music, no constant jump scares, just that horrible feeling that something is very wrong.

First person was a risky move for Resident Evil but it works perfectly here. Makes everything feel way more personal and uncomfortable, especially in the early hours when you’re low on ammo and every noise has you second guessing yourself. The Bakers are genuinely unsettling without feeling cartoonish, and Jack in particular is an all time great horror antagonist.

Combat is simple but tense, puzzles are solid without being annoying, and the pacing is mostly spot on. The second half leans a bit more into action than I’d prefer, but it never completely loses the horror vibe.

The DLC is actually worth playing too, which isn’t always the case. Not a Hero adds some fun action and ties up loose ends, End of Zoe is weird in the best way and doesn’t take itself too seriously, and Bedroom/21 lean hard into puzzles and tension. They feel different enough to be interesting without overstaying their welcome.

If you like survival horror, this is an easy recommendation.

The inventory system actively works against you. Inventory full? Too bad. You can’t pick up the weapon you need. Jack rips your leg off? Sure, crawl over to it and heal. Inventory full? Tough luck. THE GOOD:
- It's in 1st-person view, making it more terrifying.
- The story is simple, but interesting.
- Animation work is top-class.

- Great OST and sound design.

- Graphics are beautiful and the visual style is great. It's hard to believe that this game is over 9 years old.
- Puzzles, while pretty simple, are well designed and fun.
- In my opinion the difficulty is almost perfect. It's not too hard to the point that it becomes unfair, but not too easy for the player to be able to beat this game while "brain turned off".
- Stealth and action is well balanced.

THE BAD:
- The menu and inventory navigation can be a bit "iffy" at times, because the UI was primarily designed to be navigated by using a controller. 
- Enemy variation is not that great (but not awful either).
- While RE7 has that signature inventory management which I enjoy, I found myself constantly battling with the inventory space. In my opinion RE7 has far too few inventory slots, which made me constantly dropping/destroying important items because I had no inventory space and I needed to pick story key items in order to proceed to next area. This seemed to be especially problematic in RE7 compared to other RE games I have played. You can store items to storage boxes, but these storage boxes are rare and in many situations very far away.
-  It's a very short game. You can beat this potentially under 5 hours if you know what you are doing. Took me bit under 6 hours to beat this game.

CONCLUSION:
It's an amazing horror game, one of the best Resident Evil games ever made in my opinion.

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. From the moment I decided to start playing every RE game before requiem as a certified pansy I was dreading the day it would be time to pick this one up. Not because I doubted the quality of the game mind you, quite the opposite in fact, I was sure I would be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bricks throughout my entire playthrough and at least for those first opening hours it did not disappoint. Jack’s far from the first stalker enemy I’ve played against so far and yet he was by far the most horrifying to me personally. Hell that goes for the whole game, I’d guess is a combination of the change of perspective, how intimate and tight the environment is, the fact that manipulating the map and menus no longer pauses the game and the whole aesthetic of the Baker Estate of being a place full of rotting things, bugs and mold everywhere feels like it was design in a lab to put me specifically on edge, its Brilliant.

This is my fifteenth RE game now and not since I’ve played the very first hone has the horror felt as intimate here, the tight spaces, puzzles galore and backtracking to older areas, scarce resources and the sheer amount of time you spent just, walking around taking every detail in without actually encountering any creatures but knowing full well they could be just around the corner so you’re constantly on edge. All of these things do this games name justice.

The story is one of the most restrained and grounded the franchise has to offer, it serves the tone of the game beautifully and it makes you take it seriously both to horrify you but also to make you feel the weight of the tragedy that befell to literally the entire cast of characters here.

Ethan is without a doubt the most uninteresting protagonist the series has had so far, there’s very few times where his personality shines through here and yet… I think that was exactly what the first RE game on first person needed, it allowed me to feel more involved in the horrible stuff that was happening in a way where I wouldn’t really connect if the protagonist was a legacy character because I know they have faced worse odds and come out on top.

The Baker Estate is what I pictured the Spencer Mansion would have been like if George Trevor wasn’t smoking crack and actually cared about designing livable spaces, of course the are several areas that are now broken down and covered in all sorts of traps but the overall layout, the furniture and assorted cluttered do start to give you the sense that things weren’t always this bad here.

This is the first game of the series in a while that actually considerably tone down it’s enemy variety it’s pretty much just 3 types of Molded, the bugs which last for just one area and the bakers, but they are eventually bosses so I’m not counting them. But it does work wonders here as part of the charm of the games is the length of time you encounter no enemies, having too much variety when they are already limited in number would have felt out of place.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard reminds me so much of the many first-person horror games that I've both seen and played throughout the years, and it does it in the best possible way by being head and shoulders above almost all of them.  This is my first "Resident Evil" game, and since finishing it, I feel like I chose a fantastic starting point.

Here's the number one thing with this game: it absolutely nails atmosphere. 

Every corner of every area has nearly perfect lighting and texturing that sells the tense, horrific, moody tone of the game.   You will be doing a lot of walking through hallways in this game, and because it does atmosphere so well, it rarely feels dull. 

Of course, the horror itself is fantastic.  Limited resources make the act of surviving enemies feel tense.  The chances of you dying are also very real, and it can happen with 2-3 attacks from an enemy.  (Take it from me, I ended up dying 25 times on my first playthrough with normal difficulty).  What I love so much about the combat in this game is that it almost never feels like it's on rails.  You can die at any moment, and seemingly anything can happen.

The puzzles were very chill in difficulty.  I only had to look up the solution for one, and that was only because I was stupid and missed something pretty obvious.  On a normal playthrough, you shouldn't struggle too much.

All in all, I ended up loving this game, even if I sucked at it, and I am very excited to play more games from this series!  Village is going to be the next most likely.

Resident Evil 7 is a return to the way Resident Evil was initially envisioned: a hardcore survival horror game where you never feel safe and danger lurks around every corner. While I appreciate that Capcom reverted back to my favorite type of Resident Evil, I have mixed feelings on the way the main campaign plays out.

One thing they got right was the atmosphere and tone of the game. The locale is incredibly eerie, set at the remote Baker farm where everything is decaying and oozing with grotesque substances. The baker family makes for iconic antagonists, each terrifying in different ways leaving you tense and afraid as you creep around hallways and rooms. The return to survival horror is also felt in the way that items are sparsely placed and success relies on intelligently using items and ammo. The actual combat gameplay is consistent with the game philosophy as well because it loses the dynamic action from RE 4-6 in favor of a simplified combat system that made older Resident evils scary. You’ll have extremely straightforward, limited ways of dealing with your enemies as opposed to the way you would roundhouse enemies in RE4. In tense situations you have to be very deliberate with movement and shooting, and you can take risks to preserve resources but at the cost of hard punishments if things go wrong. Its combat leans perfectly in the survival horror aspect of the game, but unfortunately after the first hour or so the enemy design undermines the experience.

There are only a few enemy types in the game, mainly just the two types of molded and the bugs. The molded individually are moderately more engaging to fight than the typical zombies from older Resident evils but are less visually striking and sadly rarely pose a threat the way old RE zombies did. They’re generally easy to avoid, exacerbated by the fact that you can abuse their AI including causing them to despawn when needed. Much of the tension in exploring the Baker estate is lost when it becomes apparent that these enemies are fairly easy to deal with. 
At the very least, the couple of boss fights in RE7 are some of the better ones I’ve experienced thus far in the series history. Quite a number of the bosses in the RE series are uninteresting, pure gimmick fights that are often plagued with large periods of inactivity while you wait for some mechanism to proc. The boss fights, relative to the game's systems, are much more interesting than many of the ones that have come before and remain tense through both gameplay and the taunting nature of the Baker antagonists.But boss fights are only a small aspect of the game and most of the time I felt underwhelmed navigating the farm when confronted with the basic enemy types.

Actual level design is also disappointingly simple. You’ll rarely find yourself getting lost in the house as most of the routes are designed linearly, with almost none of the puzzle design you’d find in older resident evils. The pacing is somewhat befuddling too because while many of the parts were memorable in a vacuum there’s a lingering feeling that the game is lacking as a whole. I wish that each area was a little larger, a little longer, a little more substance to the gimmicks that each area presents. The last third of the game is especially damning in that the areas lack both visual identity and design excellence, feeling they were just tossed in because they ran out of ideas after a stellar start.
Overall I think the campaign was fine, a preferred pace compared to the newer RE but nowhere close to the first Resident Evils that made the series so iconic.

But I’d be remiss not to mention that I think the DLCs in RE7 are incredibly good, some of them even fantastic. Each of them essentially addresses an issue I found with the core RE7 campaign then tweaks it to create a complete experience with each DLC. Not a Hero and End of Zoe each introduce more dynamic versions of the core RE7 combat experience that feel much better to play than Ethan’s adventure. Banned footage DLCs have episodes that have more clever puzzle solving aspects, or more interesting route planning aspects, or even more terrifying encounters than those found in the base game. I was initially feeling a little mixed after playing RE7 but the DLCs absolutely save the game and elevate the experience and I would consider them must plays for anyone getting into RE7.

If I could use one word to summarize how I feel about Resident Evil 7 it would be frustrating. I feel like this game could have been so much better but I feel that decisions in the later half of the game and in the dlcs really bring it down. When playing through it, I felt like this game would easily be my favorite Resident Evil game even having played a majority of them in the past. Despite that I felt like this game leaves you feeling hollow on how it struggles to move forward with the story after Marguerite’s boss fight.The setting and the circumstances that surround this game are very intriguing, like how a family lost their way of life due to an unexpected visitor. Playing as Ethan and discovering how things used to be in the house for the Baker family makes you want to dig deeper into uncovering everything. The game doesn’t really give you any of that in the main game, despite Mia trying to fight the infection no other character in the game ever does that. Which makes the Jack cutscene in the later part of the game so much more confusing that they tried to fight the infection, but there are no signs that point to that. Having scenes or moments where all these characters are seeming to struggle with this infection would have added so much depth and made that cutscene hit like a truck. Touching on all the characters, Lucas is basically a psycho but has so little screen time in the game that he doesn’t even matter especially during his little trap segment. Marguerite is just basically a bug lady, and it basically it, due to the same issue with Jack that there is no humanity for you to feel bad for her. Zoe is also a non-factor with just phone calls here and there until you meet her after Lucas’s section. Despite creating the cure she really doesn’t serve any purpose other than to be a ‘decision for Ethan. Mia is straight up a bio-terrorist and I know that Ethan wants to save her but she got everyone infected in this game while trying to kill Ethan as well. The decision to save her or Zoe is so dumb, Mia started all of this and despite that is still infected by Evie. If you choose Zoe the game says F you and kills Zoe shortly after and you have a short fight with Mia where you kill her a bit later on. Why even give people the choice of saving a person when you only intended for them to save Mia. The rest of the game just goes off the rails with a whole Mia section twice since you basically play the ship section twice. Regain control of Ethan and fight through a gauntlet of enemies and have a terrible boss fight with Evie and the game ends with someone pretending to be Chris Redfield saving you. Ethan as a character has to be one of most confusing people ever written, like he just doesn’t react to things normally. He has many weird emotions towards things or doesn’t react at all despite it being pretty horrific. One section that comes to mind is in the beginning with the mutilated symbol he has no reaction, but later on when you see another one being constructed he acts very disgusted by it. The other main positives I have for the game is that the gun play and menu feel pretty good over all, everything feels pretty fluent in that part of the game which makes it enjoyable to keep playing. Having the enemies move around the angle of your gun and tense it can feel when you miss a shot makes it very engaging. Other than that the main game offers a Madhouse difficulty which is basically twice as hard as the normal difficulty with nothing in between. Madhouse itself is not bad, the main house is quite different with the item placements and the enemy encounters. Once you unlock the front door to the house the changes basically stop. Everything else plays out the same as the other difficulties, despite some items changing locations. Overall I feel that the main game is very fun to play, but the story and the characters bring it down quite a bit. 

I would normally include any dlcs when talking about the base game, but since Re7 has so much in terms of dlc I figured it deserved its own section. The first one is called Bedroom, and basically it's an escape room with Marguerite coming in every so often. Which makes the player focus on making the room look the same every time she comes in, while also progressing towards finding a way out after she eventually notices. Which leads to another dlc being Nightmare which is like a wave based survival similar to Call of Duty Zombies. It is a neat idea with having to balance the scrap you generate to purchase new weapons to eventually survive 5 hours and beating Jack to escape. It offers many different unlocks based on how well you do along with a harder mode which just makes the enemies a bit tougher while reducing scrap. Which leads to a 3rd dlc called 21 which is making a game of Blackjack with 1 deck with cards ranging from 1 to 11. It's pretty intense to complete with 2 other modes pitting you against 5 and 10 opponents in a row with 5 or 10 lives depending on the mode. The added bonus is that there are trump cards that add effects to the game to change it up like increasing the bet or drawing specific cards. The next 2 dlcs are basically like some party additions in Ethan must die and Jack’s 55th birthday. Ethan Must Die is basically an RNG simulator where you run a course to kill Marguerite at the end of it. You get random drops from crates that change your experience every time while also dodging many traps laid out throughout and enemies which will kill you with 1 hit most of the time. Some crates are also filled with bombs along with crates spawning in different locations every time and of different rarity as well. Jack’s 55th Birthday is just trying to collect different types of food and drinks to feed to Jack to fill up his meter to complete the level within a time limit. There are 6 different maps that offer different ways to explore, kill enemies, and bring the food to Jack as quickly as you can. While I feel Ethan Must Die was a cool idea to experiment with how lucky or unlucky you can be, Jack’s 55th Birthday really does feel repetitive especially when trying to get a good time with how some of the layouts are designed for the maps. The next 3 dlcs are all story based and contain some answers and close some questions on how the game ended. Not a Hero is right after the main game where you play as Chris Redfield going after Lucas since he has been feeding information to a company about infection in Re7. While this is a very short story dlc there are some neat elements that could have been added to the base game. Especially the white molded since they need special ammo to bring them down. Besides that it is basically a shooting gallery as you go through 3 sections collecting upgrades and killing many molded till you get to Lucas’s bossfight at the end. Which feels like a letdown to the fact that he is meant to be very smart creating various traps and situations that Chris has to navigate. His fight just devolves into a giant mutated creature that is a bullet sponge until he just crumbles and the dlc ends. End of Zoe is easily the best dlc with having you play as Joe Baker shortly after the end of Re7 trying to save Zoe from the infection. Which implies that Ethan saving Mia is the canon choice despite how stupid that is given the circumstances in the base game. Joe encounters various molded and alligators infected by Evie as he tries to get a cure for Zoe while also encountering his brother Jack who is now a swamp man. Joe has this neat mechanic where he does use guns but his fists which makes for the combat to be pretty fun. As you are able to sneak attack and absolutely bash in each enemy's head as you try to find this cure. The final dlc is the most frustrating to me as it is called daughters and ‘shows’ how the Baker family was infected 3 years before the events of Re7. (1/2)

If you get a strange thrill from being terrified, this is a MUST PLAY. But you really do have to enjoy feeling scared.

--
It's brilliantly designed--the map layout feels labyrinthian, but actually subtly encourages a lot of forward momentum. No yellow paint or big arrows either. 

The game knows that tension and immersion are broken if you have to keep repeating sections over and over--so even though it makes you feel very vulnerable, it secretly wants you to succeed and to keep going and to keep feeling uncertain and scared. On "Normal," the autosaves felt very generous, so even if I died, I barely lost any time at all. It also features those famous Resident Evil save rooms, and the ones here are especially memorable.

--
The biggest obstacle I had to overcome to fully enjoy this game was the EXCESSIVE GORE. I actually left a negative review and almost quit playing because of it.

But eventually, I caught on that the game has the darkest, most pitch-black humor. It tries to make really horrible things funny, and it weirdly succeeds. There is a random stray note you find that says, "There is something really wrong with her." And it's the funniest thing ever.

The gore is strongest at the beginning to make you flip out and to make you terrified. But eventually, it's not like THAT anymore.
--

Finally, I was very excited to play this just because of that song, "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" from the OST. The build up at the end of that song is especially incredible to my ears.

In the first few hours, I was very disappointed because it didn't feel like that song belonged in this game at all. But by the end, I felt it was very fitting.

An original, realistic, inventive, mystery thriller, graphics, atmosphere, a first-person shooter with an incredible lack of banal character abilities and ease of control, good aim but very difficult to hit the mob, especially in the head. It features puzzles that reveal locations and return to previous locations, reminiscent of a Metroidvania, but with a realistic style and logic, inventive items (keys, guns to make defeating bosses easier) and action with a mysterious plot and even a touch of romance... in which you Ethan rescue your wife, who disappeared several years ago, and suddenly you receive a message from her. Saying she's alive and in such-and-such a place. It also evokes compassion when the villains are honest people, victims of the virus. That is, there aren't even any real culprits in the game (the creators of the virus), which gives the player constant compassion for everyone in the game. 
The hide-and-seek with Jack at the beginning and the fight with the saw are completely random on hard mode (Madhouse), and some other things will be discussed later. On easy mode, too, your victories often don't make sense; it's just random. These moments of the game are badly executed by the developers.

Revelation (in details)
It's clear why this game isn't as popular and replayable as TLOU 1 (2 is trash, even... calling it trash is insulting trash). Because there's no character here... you don't even see one in cutscenes. What immerses you in games and movies is the realistic character movement. Not what they see or the delays in controls. And in cutscenes, their realistic facial expressions, skin, etc. Plus, the cutscenes are short additions, not the main focus, like in all those new "inclusive" trash games that make you fall asleep on the spot. Capcom even tries to avoid depth at all costs and sometimes resorts to stupid Asian exaggerations in terms of believability. 
And then there's comfort... TLOU is comfortable and has perfect graphics; in battle, the character is fast, just like in real life. Just like in real life, you feel good moving, controlling yourself; you don't move like a rusty nag. Even disabled people feel good moving. These are basic actions that you don't think about, especially in games they feel good, like nice, adequate graphics, unlike God of War or Spider-Man graphics, and you want to play. In RE, the controls are awkward, sometimes stupid, and the decisions are tedious or illogical, and sometimes downright annoying, especially in combat, when the character moves as if he's just woken up. 
For example, there's no dodge, running stops if you turn even slightly. The slightest unevenness in the ground causes the character to stop, and mobs follow, forcing you to replay the game through no fault of your own. 
There are still some issues like this in TLOU, it's not perfect, but there are far fewer of them, for example, aiming is very slow compared to NPCs, movements are a bit like in water, etc. And there are so many intentional mistakes like this in the game that there's no room to tell you about them all. Some people might think that my reviews are long, but firstly, I write briefly about the game at the beginning if you haven't noticed, wise-guy, and then the details come, secondly, even with the details, it’s very short because there are many more details, both good and bad.

The problem is that these are deliberate inconveniences by the developers, which is what I strongly dislike in this company and find them strange – they don't understand basic common sense, don't distinguish between gameplay conventions ranging from idiotic to absurdly stupid and meticulous. Fortunately, there are easy and normal difficulties; it doesn't make the game any more enjoyable and as a result replayable , but at least you don't have to replay. 

The difficulty is also stupid. Besides the heavy damage taken on the highest difficulty and replaying through no fault of your own, it's also based not on the player's action skills, but on the skills of a professional and experienced cleaner. That is, you have to vacuum literally every corner of the locations with your eyes to find a coin for some weapon or some ammo, and you'll only notice them if you get really close to those corners. And the weapon purchasing is also half-joking, which ruins the immersion and logic. There's no line between immersion and reality. It's logical that a character can break a cage and retrieve a weapon without any coins (and who put it in cages? Jack? It's not plot), but the developers seem to be playing alongside you, letting you open a birdcage with coins, just like in real-money games, not based on the story. Or are the coins that improve your strength, speed, and so on not based on the story, are they magical?! No, this isn't fantasy, so these coins, as an out-of-game purchase, are purely like cheats and break immersion, even though, according to the game's balance, they're not cheats and are necessary on the highest difficulty. The problem is precisely in the experience, in that the illusion of the universe and immersion is broken, and it feels like real-life cheats. And action players want an action challenge if they've chosen the highest difficulty, even on lower difficulties, not just hoovering up locations. Even for an RPG, that's boring and dull. 

There's an easy difficulty setting, but it doesn't solve the believability issue. You're running around, you don't need special weapons from the cages, but getting hit like an autistic person, and you can't do anything about it, you just have a lot of HP. What's the point? There's no dodging, stupid squats rarely help, I just ran and still got hit—it's boring and the controls are awkward. How can the developer not understand this?! In Souls-like, the controls are pleasant and believable, as far as I remember, but there it's pointless because the mobs are even faster and have weird, otherworldly timings. There's also no point in the player, their skill, or experience, just learning ahead. Even an autistic person could get through it by replaying and simply memorizing but there is no game in this.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a claustrophobic, terrifying reinvention of the survival horror genre. By shifting to a first-person perspective, the game forces you to experience the rot and decay of the Baker estate through the eyes of Ethan Winters. It is a grueling, intimate journey that trades global bioterrorism for the visceral horror of a family dinner gone horribly wrong.

The sense of vulnerability is constant. Unlike the action-heavy entries that preceded it, ammo is scarce and every room feels like a potential trap. I spent my first hour creeping through the shadows of a dilapidated plantation house, jumping at the sound of floorboards creaking and the muffled footsteps of Jack Baker hunting me down. The combat is deliberate and heavy; every shot from your handgun feels like a desperate gamble for survival.

The puzzles return to the series' roots, requiring you to find strangely shaped keys and manipulate shadowed objects to progress. It creates a satisfying rhythm of high-intensity stealth and quiet, brain-teasing exploration. The atmosphere is thick with dread, aided by incredible sound design that makes the house feel like a living, breathing monster. 

Visually, the RE Engine delivers a photorealistic level of filth. From the mold growing on the walls to the unsettling detail of the food on the table, the game is a masterclass in environmental storytelling. It is a bold, successful attempt to make Resident Evil feel scary again, stripping away the superhuman powers and leaving you with nothing but your wits and a flashlight.

9.5/10. It is a nightmare you won't want to wake up from. It successfully bridges the gap between classic survival horror and modern immersion, proving that the most effective scares are the ones that happen right in front of your face.

Just when I think Capcom couldn’t possibly do anything dumber (RE6), you go and do something like this (RE7)…and totally redeem yourself!

I will admit, it is almost unfair how much RE6 ruined my interest in the series. Back in the day I had only dabbled in a few of the Resident Evil games so, though I really liked the games I played, I didn’t entirely follow the plot: I was just happy to plug along and shoot whatever zombies the game wanted me to. But RE6…RE6 was so painfully generic. Sure it played fine and had some production value behind it. But nothing about it was memorable, despite taking a much larger “plot” bite than most RE titles usually do. Generic co-op action shooter was just not the direction I wanted RE to go, and I thought the series would just be lost to me…

…until RE7. RE7 is a brilliant return to form with a surprising shake-up to the usual RE formula. Here we enter a first person mode and take on the role of a new character: Ethan Winters. I think swapping to a new character was a genius move by Capcom. If I were to speculate, plot progression-wise they must have felt like their hands were tied with the old cast. I LOVE the old cast, but they are zombie-fightin’, tyrant-killin’ pros by now. Seeing them enter a new game and having to learn how to shoot their pistol just wouldn’t make sense. But with a new character, they get to re-do the slow and satisfying build-ups that the originals were so well known for. Ethan is way out of his depth in this world, and that makes this entry terrifying again.

Very, very terrifying. RE7 earns my title of second scariest entry in the series. The setting of Louisiana and, more specifically, the Baker’s house works as perfect nightmare fuel. It almost has a Texas Chainsaw Massacre feel to it, and this mixture with the RE formula is just spectacular. The Baker family themselves are all excellently designed, and individually horrific in their own way. The bosses are all super fun, and there’s a healthy mix of old and new mechanics to fight with. Most importantly for me: RE7 is so memorable - the maps, the characters - everything feels so polished. And the way both gameplay and the narrative loop back in for the ending is very satisfying. 

I love Resident Evil 7. It’s a flawless return to survival horror that brings back what people love about the originals, while mixing in some refreshing gameplay updates in perfect balance. I know people consider there to be various golden ages for the RE series, but the one we are currently in absolutely started with RE7. You need to play this game.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is often described as a return to classic horror, but for me it misses the mark in many ways. While the first few hours do a good job building tension, the experience quickly starts to fall apart. The level design becomes repetitive, backtracking feels excessive, and enemy variety is extremely limited. After a while, every encounter feels the same, which completely kills the sense of fear.

Combat is one of the weakest parts of the main game. Shooting feels stiff and unreliable, enemies soak up damage, and resource management doesn’t feel strategic - it just feels annoying. Instead of smart survival decisions, you’re often forced into awkward fights with clunky weapons and unresponsive movement. The game relies too much on cheap scares and tight spaces rather than genuinely engaging gameplay.

The story also fails to stay interesting for long. The Baker family starts off intriguing, but the narrative loses focus as the game goes on, and the later sections feel rushed and poorly paced. By the end, the horror is gone, replaced with tedious action and uninspired level design.

The DLCs are where everything completely falls apart. Most of them feel shallow, boring, and pointless. Gameplay is stripped down to the absolute minimum, offering little challenge or enjoyment. Instead of meaningful expansions, they feel like low-effort side modes that exist just to pad out content.

End of Zoe is especially bad and feels completely disconnected from Resident Evil. It turns the game into a strange UFC-style fist-fighting simulator, where you punch enemies repeatedly with almost no depth or strategy. It’s goofy, immersion-breaking, and easily one of the most disappointing DLCs in the series. Rather than being a proper conclusion, it feels like a joke.

Final thoughts:
RE7 starts with potential but quickly becomes repetitive, clunky, and frustrating. The main game overstays its welcome, and the DLCs are extremely poor - with End of Zoe being a particularly embarrassing low point.

Not recommended - DLCs especially should be avoided.

[h1] Resident Evil 7 Biohazard [/h1]

This was my first game in the [b] Resident Evil[/b] series.
I chose it because the storyline with the Baker family was something I had seen very often on YouTube a long time ago — I have many memories of different YouTubers playing through it.

The game genuinely impressed me. It is a fully well-crafted product where every aspect is done right: the music, visual style, atmosphere, narrative presentation, gameplay, and game design all feel polished and cohesive. There is no deep philosophical message or overarching moral idea — the game exists purely to be a game, and it succeeds at that exceptionally well.

Enemy movement that makes it harder to land shots, limited ammunition that forces you to count every bullet, crafting items, and having to make sacrifices all add to the tension. Dark environments where you never know what to expect, truly frightening bosses that create real discomfort — especially the first encounter with Mia, when she suddenly rushes at you with a knife, which is genuinely terrifying.

This is a game you want to play and want to finish. It is extremely well optimized and offers a large amount of DLC content: some of it is fun and arcade-like, while other DLCs continue the story beyond the main events. Each DLC introduces different gameplay mechanics, unique ideas, and varied design.

However, in the base game without the DLCs, there is a noticeable issue: two major characters, Zoe and Lucas, are essentially written out of the story. They simply disappear, and nothing more is said about them — in Zoe’s case, you are even led to believe that she might be dead. Only the DLCs explain what actually happened to them.

There isn’t a strong emotional connection to most characters, and it can be difficult to truly sympathize with them. However, the vision scene involving Jack was genuinely touching, revealing that they were not truly at fault, but rather victims of horrific events.

One thing that remained unclear to me was where Lucas was sending the data in the Not a Hero DLC. In his final diary entry, he mentions wanting to cut ties with The Connections — so who exactly was he sending Eveline’s data to?

Overall, it’s not surprising that when the game originally released, it caused such a huge impact on the internet and generated countless memes centered around the Baker family.

So I just finished it and I am conflicted but overall I think it's pretty good and if you are a fan of the franchise then yes it is worth your time. It's a good survival horror experience and somewhat of a return to form for the series after previous entries dropped the ball.

They absolutely nailed the atmosphere in this game and I do think the 1st person POV suits this game particularly. It's a small location and feels claustrophobic which adds to the horror and I don't think 3rd person would have worked as well and that's coming from someone who loves the RE franchise for it's 3rd person perspective horror gameplay.

The narrative is driven at a steady pace and lore drops happen naturally as your explore with reveals occuring towards the end of the game as to what exactly has caused this place to turn into a swampy piece of Hell. Overall I enjoyed the story but have some gripes which I will get to.

The combat is decent here and gets progressively better as the game goes on. Crafting is solid and the game rewards you for exploring and using stimulants to better loot your surroundings. The game does a great job at not being overly difficult while still making you feel pretty helpless at times. There are several boss fights too and I found all of them to be quite well done and were all stand out moments in the game for me.

Now, lets discuss the cons.

I found Ethan to be quite a boring protagonist. He's not very interesting which is in stark contrast to all the other characters in this game. He has very little depth to his character and there's just not enough there to help you get attached to him, if that makes sense. I didn't dislike him, I just had no reason to really like him either and I feel this becomes more apparent towards the end of the game.

The game is very slow at times. The player also moves extremely slow too which is kind of annoying as you'll find yourself running back and forth a lot between places you've already visited and when you move like a slug it can be frustrating. 

I did not enjoy where the story started going towards the end of the game. Started to get a little too generic out of nowhere and while I can't say much without dropping spoilers, there are sections toward the end of the game that I found to be quite boring. It also felt like one particular aspect of the story did not get wrapped up with the ending whatsover but I later found out that there's a DLC that concludes that part of the story. I don't think a DLC should help to conclude the main story of your game. It leaves the player just feeling confused once they beat it.

The game has a mix of different kinds of puzzles which is standard for RE but I found a small number of the puzzles to be repetitive and some others to have maybe 1 or 2 more steps than was probably necessary but this is very much a nit pick to be fair.

Overall I think it's a solid survival horror game but not without it's flaws. I think for it's regular price it's a good deal and on sale it's kind of a steal as there is plenty of fun to be had with it and like with most RE main entries there's some replayability here too.

Just finished my first playthrough, and yeah, its peak. It is a perfect return to form for the series while still maintaining its own identity. 

RE7 is defined by slow placed exploration and combat. This isn't some grand world to explore, it is an old house. This is a good thing though, since it keeps everything feeling grounded. They make the map feel absolutely massive due to how they pack so much into the environment. Everything feels uneasy. Some things are just slightly off and it keeps me on my toes when I play. Combat keeps it simple. Point, shoot, click, and block. I will say that the simple "press space to block" mechanic is kinda meh, but I do not know how else they would have kept the slow paced combat while still giving you an option to avoid attacks.

I do have two major gripes though. Ethan is slow as hell and his eyes barely work. I tried playing on the intended brightness, but I could barely see anything. There is a strange effect where Ethan's eyes take time to adjust to new environments, which sounds cool, but in actuality it just made things really hard to see upon first glance. His walking and "running" speed also is terrible. I get that it is a small house he is going through, but he just does a brisk speed walk instead of actually running. It makes backtracking a bit troublesome.

Beyond that though, everything hits. A personal highlight of mine from this was the save rooms. I normally do not get too freaked out in combat heavy horror games, but this one got to me pretty good. Entering these safe rooms brought a tremendous feeling of relief whenever I entered. The music was the cherry on top for this.

At the end of the day, I feel RE7 is best described as a classic steak. It is simple, effective, and extremely solid. While there is room for expansion (hopefully RE8 and this games DLC does a bit with that), it completes what it needs to in the proper amount of time, expands on things just enough, and keeps you on your toes. 9/10, I look forward to the DLC.

I genuinely struggle to understand why Resident Evil 7 is so widely praised. This is not to say that the game lacks atmosphere or competent gameplay. On a technical level, it does a solid job of creating tension, and it is clear that Capcom was trying to return to what they originally envisioned for the franchise many years ago. That said, atmosphere alone is not enough to make a game great. While the title Resident Evil fits the setting and general themes, the game quickly fails to remain engaging. As I played, the experience became repetitive and increasingly tedious. Before long, I wasn’t immersed anymore. I just wanted the game to end. What begins with promise gradually turns into a chore, and the pacing does very little to sustain interest throughout the full experience. Ironically, players who are not familiar with the franchise may enjoy Resident Evil 7 more. Without any emotional investment in the series’ history, its narrative choices might come across as acceptable or even intriguing. However, from the perspective of a long-time fan, the game feels like a betrayal of the established lore.
!!!! SPOILER WARNING !!!!
Chris Redfield working for Umbrella is a narrative decision that borders on absurd. No amount of plot twists can convincingly justify it. It feels as if decades of character development and narrative continuity were simply thrown away in favor of shock value. The underlying message seems to be: “None of what came before really matters anymore.” 

Personally, I would rather replay Resident Evil 6, despite all its flaws, than revisit Resident Evil 7. At least RE6 respects the broader arc of the franchise. I’m only glad I finished RE7 so that I can say, with confidence, that for me it is a deeply disappointing entry and, frankly, a rather dull experience.

I've never been so torn on a game in my life. In retrospect I can appreciate a lot of elements of the game, but that I heavily disliked when I was playing through it. Most importantly, the story turns from a weird mish-mash of horror elements and concepts I've seen in movies, but then becomes a try-hard sci-fi plot regarding mold monsters that do not scare me in the slightest. The beginning of the game in the house is much more engaging than anything that comes after, with the dinner scene being the most memorable and creepy part of the story -- I love me a Texas Chainsaw Massacre parallel. I found Ethan to be an entertaining enough protagonist (even though I thought he was in the special forces or something), and Papa Baker was really cool, but every other character feels one-note and boring. Location wise, the game remains consistently interesting throughout, with every different environment feeling unique, fresh, and fun, offering its own creepy atmosphere different from the rest. Additionally, the VHS tape mechanic was really fun, almost like the Cyberpunk 2077 braindancing, except I actually want to do it, rather than being forced. Overall the story starts off interesting, but quickly loses steam, though there are good elements throughout the whole game.
What's more important -- to most at least, I personally put the story first -- is the gameplay. I want to preface this section by saying this is my first Resident Evil game, so my gripes could be rooted in a lack of familiarity with the established mechanics. First off, the combat, specifically the boss fights, are very boring. They can be summed up as "shoot the weak spot for 10 minutes." Very little variety in the fights, attacks are easily predictable, enemies are bullet sponges, and are generally uninteresting to fight at best, and downright boring and annoying at worst. Not to mention how lame the final 2 fights are, absolutely challengeless snoozefests. The best fights are clearly the garage fight, and the barn one, offering a variety of attacks, decent challenge, high stakes, and well designed environments. The worst fight is in the greenhouse, with the boss getting stuck in a wall in my playthrough, the player having 0 ammo going into it, the boss spending sometimes minutes at a time hiding from the player, and very annoying swarm attacks. Additionally, the enemies scattered across the game are generally uninteresting, with them being very slow they give no challenge other than draining your ammo. Worst of all were the bugs. ♥♥♥♥ the bugs I despised that whole section. Other than the combat, I found exploring to be a mixed bag. Sometimes I would find something and feel proud of myself, unlocking special gifts for myself and such, while other times the game is a wall hugging simulator, requiring me to do multiple laps of the same rooms dozens of times until I find whatever it is they want me to find. The most fun part of the game was most definitely the puzzles. While not very difficult, they were definitely enjoyable every time, and it gives me a sense of accomplishment with every small thing found.
Overall, the game is probably good enough for the average person, but I can't bring it in me to say it's good. It has fun elements, but I don't think I had a positive time with this game. Maybe I will check out RE8 one day, to see if they improved on any features. I also plan on RE2, but I am more drawn to 7 and 8 because of their first person viewpoint, and fps are by far my favourite genre of game.

Edit: I played through Resident Evil 8 and found it fixed most problems I had with this game. I recommend playing this game even if it is just to play Resident Evil 8, which is an amazing game

[i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a masterclass in modern survival horror, blending nerve-wracking tension, immersive first-person exploration, and deeply atmospheric storytelling into one unforgettable experience. Unlike many entries in the series, it takes a minimalist, grounded approach that puts fear, suspense, and dread at the forefront, creating an intense, personal horror journey that stays with you long after the game ends.

You step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, an ordinary man searching for his missing wife in a remote, decaying plantation. The game immediately establishes a sense of isolation and vulnerability: every creaking floorboard, every flickering light, and every shadow could conceal danger. Ethan isn’t a super-soldier or a trained fighter — he is human, fragile, and desperate — which makes every encounter with the grotesque Baker family and other horrific creatures feel genuinely threatening. The tension is constant, and the fear feels earned rather than artificial.

The true brilliance of [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] lies in its atmosphere. The derelict mansion, overgrown swamps, and dilapidated outbuildings are meticulously detailed, creating a world that feels both lived-in and haunted. Environmental storytelling is rich: discarded notes, bloodied rooms, cryptic recordings, and unsettling objects all contribute to the narrative while reinforcing the sense of dread. Lighting and sound design are perfectly tuned to heighten tension — the sound of footsteps, distant screams, or the subtle groan of the house itself can send shivers down your spine.

Gameplay balances exploration, puzzle-solving, and survival perfectly. Ammo and resources are scarce, forcing players to think strategically about every action. Stealth, improvisation, and careful planning are often more effective than direct confrontation, adding depth and realism to the horror. Combat feels weighty and consequential; each shot fired carries risk and importance. The game’s pacing ensures moments of quiet exploration and terrifying bursts of action alternate flawlessly, keeping players constantly engaged and on edge.

The story is gripping and tightly paced, combining mystery, psychological horror, and family tragedy. The narrative unfolds gradually, with twists and revelations that are both shocking and emotionally resonant. Characters are memorable, from the terrifyingly unhinged Bakers to Ethan’s own quiet resilience, making the story compelling as well as terrifying. The shift to a first-person perspective allows a level of immersion rarely achieved in horror games, placing players directly into the nightmare.

[i]Resident Evil 7[/i] also shines technically. The photorealistic visuals, detailed textures, and environmental effects — fog, water, mold, and decay — enhance the immersive horror. VR support elevates the experience further, transforming the mansion into a claustrophobic, life-sized nightmare that is simultaneously awe-inspiring and horrifying. The sound design and ambient music, haunting and subtle, reinforce tension and atmosphere throughout.

Ultimately, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] redefines modern survival horror. It is terrifying without relying on cheap jump scares, immersive without losing focus on gameplay, and emotionally engaging without sacrificing horror. It’s a game that challenges your nerves, rewards careful thinking, and immerses you in a world of dread, mystery, and terror.

A must-play for anyone who loves survival horror, atmospheric storytelling, and expertly crafted tension — [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a masterpiece that blends fear, immersion, and narrative in one unforgettable experience.
