Back in 2017, I got Resident Evil 7 gifted for my birthday. I came to the game with high expectations, especially after the return to form that was promised by Capcom. And long story short, [b]it delivered hard[/b].

I’m a sucker for horror and first-person shooters. RE4, RE5, and RE6 just weren’t my cup of tea back then (6 still is a turd-person shooter, IMO). But this game? It saved and redefined the whole franchise.

Even from the teaser, it was clear this was going to be something special. That teaser alone was a stroke of brilliance, clearly setting the tone for the experience yet to come without spoiling the story, by showing a different story (that is nonetheless [i]canon[/i])... 
Also, I feel like not enough people talk about [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3cR89qOunY8]the crazy development cycle[/url] behind this game.

Anyway, I played it an unholy amount of time on 3 different platforms and I might have bought it like 4 times because [b]it's that good[/b].

The first-person perspective and more intimate story/setting really immerse you by making every encounter feel personal and tense (which is a great way to adapt the tanky controls of the previous entries). It may be the scariest entry in the franchise.
The VR version is one of the most effective horror experiences imaginable. If you’ve played it, you probably remember the basement.

My only gripe is the third act, which, if you’ve played any previous entry, is always a bit more action-oriented.
I mean, once you have a Grenade launcher in an horror game, the tension somewhat drops compared to the earlier, scarier sections with a pocket knife or a glock.

[h3]TL;DR[/h3]
Without this game, the franchise would probably be dead, and we wouldn’t have the follow-ups we enjoy today. That says a lot, and I’m grateful for it.

Years after the controversial Resident Evil 6 dropped and split the entire fandom in half, this game was exactly what the series needed — a complete reset. A fresh start. A “let’s get our s*** together” moment for Capcom. It introduced a brand-new storyline, new main characters, new villains, a first-person perspective for the first time in the main series, and a completely reworked inventory system. It felt like a bold new direction, and honestly, it was the best move they could’ve made.

The opening section — both the beginning and everything in the main house was insanely good. Creepy atmosphere, tons of surprises, jump scares that actually hit, and enemies that feel kinda tanky at first… until you get the shotgun. Once you have that thing, the game becomes way more manageable and fun.

The boathouse section after leaving the main house wasn’t really “scary” to me, it was more disgusting, especially if you hate bugs. That whole area made my skin crawl.

After that, my least favorite parts were definitely the ship section and the mine section. The ship does give you important lore about Mia and Eveline, so I appreciate what it was trying to do, but the whole vibe felt a little out of place for a Resident Evil game at first. Same with the mines. But then I remembered that almost every classic RE game ends with some weird lab/mine/industrial area, so in that sense it actually fits the tradition. It’s just not as strong as the rest of the game.

The DLCs for this game also added a ton of important lore for Eveline, Lucas, Clancy, Zoe, and Mia, and honestly, they were pretty good. Each one filled in gaps that the main game didn’t have time to cover, and it made the whole story feel way more complete.

And I’ve gotta say, I really appreciate the fact that in the middle of all this chaos, gore, and pure stress, Capcom gave us Jack’s 55th Birthday. It might seem like a goofy, throwaway mode at first, but it’s actually such a nice break from all the intensity. It lets you chill out, mess around, and forget about the horrors of the main game for a while. Stuff like that makes me wish Capcom would lean into fun side modes like this more often in future Resident Evil games, because it adds so much personality to the overall experience. Overall, I give this game a solid 8/10.

[h1] Resident Evil 7: Biohazard — Survival Horror Resurrected [/h1]

After three action-packed titles in a row, Capcom decided to return to the roots of Resident Evil’s main genre — survival horror. This title was a make-or-break moment for the success of the RE franchise, considering the reception that Resident Evil 6 received.


The first major change you’ll notice right away is the use of a first-person camera (the second game in the franchise and the first mainline title to use it). To be honest, I was extremely skeptical at first, but it turned out that the first-person view was a great addition and improved the scare factor significantly. Even on my second or third playthrough, the game still managed to scare me with random enemy spawns that I had forgotten about.

Now, the thing that managed to hook me instantly was the moment I entered the first save room and heard the music — something we’d been missing since RE4. I immediately felt the same sensation I had when I was playing the original Resident Evil from 1996: the item box, the tape recorder for saving the game, and the melancholic tune of a RE save room. It felt like home.

The save room is not the only thing that brings the memories back – throughout the game you will be chased by the Baker family members, Jack and Marguerite, basically the same run and hide (or stay and fight) scenario from the RE2 and RE3 games with the Mr. X and Nemesis, but this time it gets much more personal in first-person view. This is where I will also point out the major flaw that this game has – apart from the Baker family, there isn’t really so much variety in enemies. You will be fighting the same molded monsters until the end of the game.

Two other things that I want to praise are gunplay and puzzles. Weapons mechanics is nice although the recoil is pretty bad, but that actually makes sense because you are playing Ethan, it’s his first appearance in the series which pretty much makes him a civilian. Puzzles were pretty interesting albeit not too complicated. The Happy Birthday puzzle was the clear winner, considering the fact that you could do it from 2 different perspectives, once over the VHs tapes and once as Ethan in the main storyline. 

One flaw that I often see people mention is the inconsistency between the first and second half of the game — and to that I say, they are absolutely right. The first half is much more interesting and intense than the second one. Sure, many of the questions about the game’s premise are answered later on, but the pacing becomes somewhat repetitive. The main issue here is, as I already mentioned, the lack of enemy variety. The game keeps throwing the same three variations of enemies at you over and over again until the final boss. Even with this in mind, I personally enjoyed the second half because it provided answers to many questions I had about the characters and the story in general.

The story doesn’t seem like a Resident Evil title at all during the first few hours, but once you read all of the files and connect the dots, the plot reveals the familiar RE pattern of storytelling — though I won’t spoil anything here. Also, the DLCs are something you must play if you want the full picture, both before and after the events of the main story.

The graphics are great. The new RE Engine did the game justice and absolutely nailed the atmosphere needed for this setting. I really liked the use of photorealism and the amount of time the devs put into delivering the ambience of a rural Louisiana region. The game’s visuals hold up remarkably well even to this day.

After 60 hours of playing this game, beating all the DLCs, and obtaining all of the achievements, I have nothing but praise for it. It’s probably the most time I’ve spent on a Resident Evil game since RE5. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a must-play title not only for old-school fans of the Resident Evil franchise, but also for modern survival horror fans. Capcom really did their fans (including me) justice with this revamp after more than a decade of action-packed third-person games.

Tier list update until I finish all the Resident Evil main titles:
RE2 (1998) > RE4 > RE7 > RE (2001) > RE (1996) > RE5 > RE3 (1999) > RE: Code Veronica > RE6 > RE0

The best section of the game involves going through the large Baker house - a dilapidated estate in Louisiana Bayou. The attention to detail is amazing, and it's the most memorable haunted house/house of horrors setting in any media that I've been exposed to. The story is excellent, and very intriguing, as you piece together why Ethan is there, what's really going on, and what happened to the Baker family. They're extremely memorable villains and very menacing as well. Also, even nearly 9 years after release, at the time of writing, the game looks incredible. Biohazard 7 truly broke the mould (no pun intended) of what everyone knew the franchise was about. Aesthetically, gameplay-wise, narratively, everything about this has been carefully crafted to be it's own independent story without too much reference to the other games. This is perfect, it's a breath of fresh air and grounds the player in the world that they're in through the eyes of Ethan Winters. We're not just playing as Ethan Winters, we feel like we are Ethan Winters weaving our way through a great story with just the right amount of exposition, tension, action, and emotion.

There are hardcore fans of the Resident Evil franchise who have been there since the beginning and express their discomfort with the new direction this game took. It's so different that it doesn't actually feel like a Resident Evil title, but instead an actual horror game like Silent Hill, Still Wakes the Deep, Find Yourself, etc etc. Whether you like the game or not depends. Do you want another heavily action packed resident evil with boulder-punching Chris Redfield with an ocean of bullets, or do you want something fresh, subtle, with amazing narrative and story?

I also loved how the characters operate in this game. Jack chasing you down the hallway like he owns the place, Marguerite with her creepy insect powers, Lucas being a psycho genius… and Ethan? That dude is HIM. The man takes more damage than any human should and still keeps going just to save Mia. Respect.

And bro — the guns feel AMAZING. The shotgun slaps, the pistol feels crisp, and every upgrade hits hard. When you finally get fully geared? You feel like a badass walking through hell to end everything.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 reminded me why this franchise is GOATED. It’s terrifying, emotional, intense, and unforgettable. If you love horror, story, and pure Resident Evil vibes, this is a masterpiece.

now for the main story, simply excellent. the main story single-handedly revived resident evil's horror after the period of time where resident evil was trying to be the next best call of duty like game. here we can see the big main thing Resident Evil 7 has to offer. Rot. rot is everywhere in resident evil 7, one of the most compelling horror elements it uses to scare the player. the molded are organisms made out of some hyper-evolved bacteria. the infamous dinner scene showcases the baker family for what they've become. monsters. they're all eating human parts and trash like it's just another Monday. they all act normal in such a dire situation. now that's peak horror if you ask me. Jack chases you around like a maniac and it's thrilling to see what he does next, like oh i don't know. runs through a wall? now that's pretty badass. it's quite cool to see such a game inspired off of many hit movies such as the Texas Chainsaw Massacre and the Blair Witch Project.

I really enjoy how the routing of the story takes you through each baker family member in order through a series of boss-fights where you progressively see each one get more and more.... moldified? Their certain end had me thrilled for more. Lucas had me the most excited to kill as he's well..... the black sheep of the family for sure.

his section also had me the most excited for what's to come as his portion of the game is pretty much 1:1 saw. with all the traps you have to go through, and not to mention the happy birthday sequence was very interesting and took a turn from the usual puzzles we get in resident evil games. not to mention the VHS tapes allowed us to see exactly what to do in that puzzle and the consequences following it. 

madhouse was genuinely so fun with the circular saw and the albert pistol. resources are tight but if you are resourceful then this isn't too difficult. madhouse also brings back cassette tapes from the older resident evil games and while an interesting concept I never felt like needing them was a problem as the game is pretty lenient with giving you them. but overall madhouse is super enjoyable and I personally think it was the greatest experience in this game. not to mention, there are way more antique coins in this mode, as well as the scorpion key being locked up (not needed, but allows you to get more resources) as well as the grenade launcher being available as soon as you access Zoe's Camper.

I think madhouse is a great difficulty, and spices up things such as item locations and enemy spawns to make the overall experience much more difficult but remains true to staying fair.

[h1] THE REAL SURVIVAL–HORROR? [/h1]
It's been one my favorite games for a while and i still think its quite impressive work in its genres terms for its time. Here are my drawbacks and upsides as of stuff which stands out:
[h3] Drawbacks [/h3]
There are really a few. Related to: unskipable cutscenes, blocked backdoors as in classic horror films, poor stealth mechanic for such a tight-spaced game, some overkill sci-fi ideas and maybe shooting. (I didn't apply critisizm to some non-realistic details and stuff since the other games aspects overwhelm them) [b] If you about to play on madhouse difficulty prep yourself heavily for the margaret greenhouse battle and watch out for bloody four-legged molded, they suck! [/b]
[h3] Upsides (Now here the game shines) [/h3]
[olist]
[*] Instantly sets up classic horror atmosphere with weird video message, arrival by car to abandoned territory, firstly silent atmosphere, stairs scene, then family introduction, that hopeful cop episode and more. It all screams classic (think texas chainsaw massacre, saw, maybe even jeepers creepers and outlast game).
[*] Story. It's not much relative to the previous games, but works perfecty or near-perfectly as a seperate. That's for i praise ethan winters installments of RE so much, because they work not as resident evil games. Toward the end it gets revealing and even dramatic with flashbacks, jack bakers confession, laboratory section, genious escape through mines to guest house, cinematic transition of eveline to its last form and finally that emotional epic ending. (Damn, even credits made me watch them and listen to that memorable tune "go tell aunt rhody")
[*] Quite gory and amoral scenes with severed leg/hand, gut eating iconic dinner, deputys body rip off, margarett spider mutation and much more.
[*] Bakers estate design. I do not care that much for the rest sections of the game, but the house design with all level content, secret/alter passages and details is a separate respect. Each location has something special and involving about it. One of my definite favorites is lucas' birthday quest, just brilliant.
[*] Graphics. Might be not objective, but this is one of my favorite looking games with that gritty, sometimes yellowish or greenish, dirtened sort of a visual style.
[*] DLCs. There are various and all nice i think. Some related to branches of story (end of zoe, not a hero, daughters, bedroom) and others are mini-game acrady gameplay alike (jacks's birthday, ethan must die, nightmare, and 21). My favs likely are original rather action branch of chris in not a hero, involving escape quest with margaret in bedroom and for sure addictive but deadly gambling of 21.
[*] I could carry on but here are mechanics or ideas i think made this game special: vhs tapes playthroughs, phone calls, authentic saferoom storage for item management, cassettes for saving game on madhouse, coins and bird cages, some puzzles, codex watch, choice between two endings with relatively different consequences and some more..
[/olist]
[h2] –VERDICT– [/h2]
Briefly, the game is full of proper horror design, nicely settled story and ain't cheap gameplay value. Maybe its sequel comes with freedom and better visuals, locations, characters and epic cinematic ideas, i think biohazard is doing its job in survival-horror genre much more better. My final word is:
[h1] 8/10 [/h1]

Resident Evil 7 is the course correction the series desperately needed. Instead of the bombastic action of the later games, this one drags you back into tight hallways, locked doors, scarce ammo, and the constant feeling that something awful is breathing just out of sight. The Baker house is a disgusting, beautifully crafted nightmare, and Jack is one of the best stalker enemies the series has ever had—equal parts terrifying and darkly funny.

Exploration, puzzles, item management, interconnected rooms… it all feels like classic RE, just rebuilt with a modern engine and a first-person perspective that makes every creak in the floor hit harder. Combat walks the line between empowering and panic-inducing; you think you have enough ammo until you definitely don’t.

A few rough edges exist—some weird character models, moments where the lighting is too dark for its own good, occasional flat textures—but none of it stops the game from being incredibly immersive and atmospheric.

This is survival horror reborn, and one of the best turns the franchise has made in years.

Finally playing the game, I now understand why this installment was/is divisive. "Resident Evil 7" (RE7) is a good horror game that has some solid connections to the rest of the greater REUniverse, even if the game itself doesn't benefit from (or perhaps suffers because of) connections to that same universe.

The opening portion of the game is brilliant (notwithstanding the intro, the travesty of which is addressed below). Not since "Alien: Isolation" have I played a game that elicited genuine feelings of dread, revulsion and apprehension. The emotional manipulation and psychological horror at play during the first hour or so with 'the family' is shockingly powerful. I did not anticipate how disturbing it would be to play through an experience that blended an abusive family with a haunted house. To this end, moving the player point of view to first person was the right call; that shift in perspective amplifies the dread and terror the player will feel in those 'up close and personal' moments of badness. 

It was scary to move through that dilapidated house while avoiding a single threat (i.e., an increasingly dangerous Jack), all while coming to terms with the fact that your wife, who you were meant to rescue from this sh*tshow, is every bit as dangerous to you as the rest of the family that you are now trapped with. Honestly, if the game had taken place entirely in the house(es), I would have been satisfied. It likely would have been an abbreviated experience but may also have been a much tighter experience for it.

Don't get me wrong; the ship and the mines weren't bad, per se. The ship had some neat stuff going for it, such as Mia's flashback and the revelation of some plot material. Those things could have been included elsewhere, though (such as in the mines) without requiring the player to suspend disbelief for something so logically inconsistent as how such a large ship made it so far inland. It's true that the bayou contains no small number of decent-sized vessels, but... that's a big ship. And it must have ended up there relatively recently, even if it's broken up in a way that suggests it's been there for a long while. Ships are a great setting for horror but that's usually because ships are confined spaces isolated from the rest of the world which makes true escape functionally impossible. That wasn't the case here and nothing about the changes to the ship, its location or situation were adjusted in a way that added impact to the contribution or purpose of that set-piece in the story or game. The ship felt shoe-horned in, while the mines... The mines didn't feel as unnecessary or illogical as the ship (as a location set-piece, not for what happens there as it relates to the plot) but it did seem odd. I appreciate Umbrella needed a place to monitor the site from a discrete distance... it just seems strange.

I wasn't sold on the mold monsters, either. I appreciate that you don't really have an RE game if you don't have some mindless monsters littered throughout the environment to either dodge past or destroy. If the game is intended to run more than a couple hours, you need some enemy variety, too. To me, though, their presence was a distraction from the horror of being trapped with Mia and her family. How the mold monsters were included made sense but I didn't find them to be a value add for the majority of my experience. At least not after the first few, notably in the basement and during a return to the second floor of the main house.

As far as straight-up bad goes, there's really only thing: the intro was terrible. It's a nigh-on unforgivable mix of lazy writing and bad voice acting that nearly put me off the game altogether. I wasn't looking for an inspired hook or a novel premise, but if you're going to use something as cliched as 'looking for missing spouse', you need better dialogue and an actor who can sell it. The actor for Ethan is good for most of what follows but those opening lines were not his finest hour. Since the premise for this introduction is distressingly close to the introduction of "Silent Hill 2", one of the best horror games ever made, RE7 would have benefited from more distinction or at least more refinement in this area. Introductions are important, after all.

Last bit of criticism: creepy kids with psychic powers were already an overused trope in 2017. I adore you as a franchise, Resident Evil, so know this comes from a place of love: you fumbled the attempt to put Alma into your game. Monster grandma was cool, tho. ;-)

One thumb up, 7/10. Bear in mind those ratings are offered 8 years after the game came out. I can see how the game would have scored higher when it was released and even in the year or so following. Recommended for: anyone seeking a genuine horror experience lasting an hour or two (play the beginning). Yes, it's that good. After the first couple hours, though... that's a tougher call. Fans of the franchise may dig it, provided they can move past the ways in which RE7 breaks from tradition (shift to first person, non-standard monsters and game play, inclusion of explicit psychic powers, etc). Fans of slower paced, more psychological horror may struggle with the RE weirdness that creeps in the longer the game runs on (creepy monsters that don't always make sense, repetitious boss fights, a growing reliance on combat, etc).

P.S. The DLC for this game is good. "Bedroom" continues the strong psychological horror vibes the base game implements so well in its first few hours. "21" is a lot of fun... in a gruesome, disturbing kind of way. A kind of bloody precursor to "Balatro" that uses blackjack rules rather than hold 'em. "End of Zoe" isn't just good DLC. It might be some of the best DLC released for the RE franchise and survival horror in general, full stop.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was the, expectedly, 7th entry in the beloved horror series Resident Evil. While the Resident Evil series used to be the golden child of horror, the 5th and, more specifically, 6th entries strayed from that path, being more like 3rd person action games. 7 was different. 
Resident Evil 7 is my first Resident Evil game, and my first horror game in general. For a while I had wanted to get into horror games, and through October I really thought I would; I bought this game on November 1st. Sigh. November’s scary because I feel like 2025 started yesterday but nah, it’s ending soon…
Let’s get into the review. Skip to the last paragraph if you want a shorter review.

Story
You play as a man named Ethan Winters. His wife went missing during a long-time babysitting job, but Ethan has an inkling to where she might be; a house in rural Louisiana. He checks it, and finds her; however, something's wrong. She seems paranoid, and keeps talking about the people who feed her. She then turns violent and starts to attack him. He fends her off, but is knocked out by a man he did not know was there.
He wakes up in a much larger house. A family of 3, the Baker family, is eating a revolting dinner. They don’t seem to get along. When Ethan refuses the food, they go nuts and just before Ethan is killed, something grabs the fathers, Jacks, attention. The Bakers seem immune to all the bullets Ethan throws at them. Your goal is to escape the Baker house and find out what the hell is going on here.
This story is actually really intriguing. The setting is a large departure from earlier Resident Evil titles, and there are a couple of twists and turns. There’s also secret lore like in Bioshock or a FromSoft game. The ending is very well done though, and you won’t have many questions about the actual story, maybe about the lore though.

Gameplay
Resident Evil 7 takes place in the first person, unlike every other game. It is a lot slower, and is much more horror-focused than its predecessors. Ammo is a lot more limited, and Ethan was the kid who thought that he didn’t have to go to the gym, because he is not as strong as prior protagonists. I have to say, the gunplay here is incredible. There’s only a handful of guns, but they all have an incredible punch and feel very powerful. Besides the Bakers, there are a handful of enemies who you can shoot who actually do die. Ammo is very limited, so you have to hit your shots and be smart. 
The game is focused around exploration of the Baker mansion, where you will fight these enemies and solve puzzles, some of which being pretty hard. There are very few places where you are truly safe in this game, but luckily there are some, where you can save and store items. You will need to store items because you have a limited inventory space, which is taken up by items for puzzles and guns. Heals take up this space, too. They’re hard to find, but you can find other items that you can craft into heals; however, these can be crafted into ammo as well.
I will say, I wish you could toggle the flashlight. This is an issue other Resident Evil games have suffered from; it’s dark, and only having the flashlight turn on when the game wants isn’t great.
The gameplay is very slow and methodical, which makes the game very tense. I have not played many horror games, but I can tell this is one of the good ones.

Presentation
For a 2017 game, this game looks incredible. Besides some visual jank (very few), the game has a very realistic look, adding to that atmosphere that I will be talking about. The game has a very consistent theme; Hollow Knight does something similar. The game keeps the same mood, the same atmosphere, throughout the whole game. Maybe for a Metroidvania this could be bad, but for a horror game? This is perfect. 
There are also a lot of smaller details. Each room is very detailed, with things like individual book names being visible. Depending on where you hit the enemy, their body will contort that way.
The game doesn’t have much for music (other than ambience), but the sound design is incredible. Some of the noises the monsters make rock my bones. Of course the guns sound really good. There are tons of small details like the creaking of the boards that you don’t notice, but add to the atmosphere. Also, the voice acting here is just incredible. The Bakers might be some of the best voice-acted video game characters, like, ever. 
As for actual scary stuff, there are lots of twisted, messed-up things in this game. Fortunately, it relies less on jumpscares to be scary (there still are some, but few) and it rather uses dark themes such as surgical violence. This is not a game to play around the family, and if you’re squeamish, you might want to sit this one out.
This is one of the most immersive games I’ve played. It creates an atmosphere that sucks you in and doesn’t spit you out until you have a big brown spot in your pants. This game is scary, simple as that.

Content
According to Howlongtobeat.com, the game is about 9 hours long. Mine was actually the same exact length, so good on you, Howlongtobeat. There are collectibles scattered throughout the game, although unfortunately you can’t return to some areas. However, you can make multiple saves, so if you do one before all of the gates (so to speak), you should be able to. You still will have to play through the rest of the game, though. There are also 2 endings, with it basically boiling down to the good ending and the bad ending. Bioshock did the same, but the difference here is that the endings don’t feel rushed. The game makes it very clear that the bad ending is not canon, so, you know… choose wisely.
There are two story expansions, with one being Not a Hero, and the other’s name spoils the story so I’m not going to name it. They both are after the story, so I can’t explain their plots. They also are both more action-focused than the main game, although at the end of the day, they still are more Resident Evil 7. According to Howlongtobeat.com, they are both 1 ½ hours long. They’re worthwhile expansions if you enjoyed the main game; if you get the season pass version (that’s a stupid name), you get all DLCs with it. There are some other DLCs, just being bonus challenges.

Closing thoughts
Positives:
-Incredible atmosphere
-Super tense gameplay
-Just plain scary (not in a cheap way)

Negatives:
-Certain areas become inaccessible after certain thresholds are met
-Flashlight is not toggleable

I have to say, Resident Evil 7 really surprised me. After playing all the older games, I noticed that after Resident Evil 4 the series went a bit too far into action and lost that sense of fear and tension that made it special. With RE7, though, Capcom truly brought the series back to its horror roots — and they did it perfectly.

The story isn’t bad at all: you play as Ethan Winters, a regular guy searching for his missing wife, which leads him to a creepy house deep in the Louisiana swamps. From there, the nightmare begins. The Baker family is just incredible — disturbing, crazy, and completely unpredictable. Every encounter with them keeps you on edge, and you never know what’s coming next.

The switch to first-person view was a brilliant move. It makes the experience so much more immersive and lets you really feel the fear through Ethan’s eyes. The atmosphere is always tense, and horror is literally around every corner. The jump scares are well-placed — not overdone, but always effective and perfectly timed.

The DLCs are also worth it:

Banned Footage Vol. 1 & Vol. 2 add some fun and creepy new experiences, including side stories and mini-games.

End of Zoe wraps up some plot points in a satisfying way.

Not a Hero, featuring Chris Redfield, connects the story back to the main series and adds a bit more action.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 7 brought back that feeling of fear and tension I hadn’t felt since the early games. It’s a true return to form, mixing old-school horror with a modern touch that works really well. If, like me, you missed the real horror in Resident Evil, this game will definitely make you feel that old fear again.

Resident Evil 7 is truly a masterpiece and an incredible turnaround for CAPCOM after the disappointment of Resident Evil 5 and 6. They made a bold move by shifting the game's focus back to true horror, and it really pays off. Instead of the usual zombies, we encounter some truly unsettling creatures that feel fresh yet familiar in the Resident Evil universe.

The switch from an over-the-shoulder perspective to a first-person view was a game-changer. It amplifies the tension and immerses you in the creepy atmosphere like never before. You feel every shiver and jump scare, making for a nail-biting experience that horror fans crave.

What I love most about Resident Evil 7 is that it embraces the darker, scarier elements of horror rather than leaning into action movie tropes. It’s about survival and fear, forcing you to think and make choices while constantly being on edge. This is exactly the direction we wanted for the series – something that truly captures the essence of horror. If you're a fan of the genre, or just looking for a gripping game, I can't recommend Resident Evil 7 enough. It's definitely a highlight in the series

Despite that, Resident Evil 7 is a brilliant game — terrifying, immersive, and one of the best survival horror experiences in years.

I've adored this game since I first played it in 2017 and championed it since as the greatest survival game on the market so I was looking forward to going back to the bayou and seeing how it held up in 2025.  It's still razor sharp and very strong despite some graphical muddiness and stiff gameplay.

(+)  I came fresh off the back of the RE4 Remake and it felt like a complete cold wash over as you dial right back into the electrifying atmosphere of a true survival horror experience.  The overall execution in its design is flawless, environments are still photo realistic and jaw dropping with fog swirling through cracks and clinging to the floor.  The sound design especially is incredible here as rotten wood creaks, water gently crashes and the wind howls through windows.  The first person perspective gives a refreshing new interpretation for this reboot and I think it joined nicely with placing you in the shoes of an every man only aiming to survive.  Exploration is given a good part of the stage which means you're paying that much more attention to the environment keeping you on edge as creatures can spill out of the walls and rise out of the mud.  With the new perspective, Resident Evil can now drive a more character focused narrative and with the Bakers as the core there are some really disturbing and emotionally charged scenes with my favourite moments in the series coming from RE7.  The Bakers are a wonderful homage to horror classics and this is a masterful execution of narrative and gameplay coming together to drive you through the game.  Every hour you're in a new part of the estate and the variety kept me engaged despite this being my sixth-ish playthrough.  The soundtrack is also phenomenal and has some of the best music I've heard from an OST.  It's perfect in its tone and I especially love 'Floating In-Between' and everytime I listen to it I think back to this game and how much I really do love it.

(-)  The combat is miserably clumsy and I always found it hard to hit the gyrating moulded as they stagger backwards and forwards.  There are three enemy types in the game in total and are all identical, the moulded were almost great but come across as wicked liquorice rather than twisted interpretations of the melted human form.  They weren't fun to fight and I never felt in any danger around them as you can mostly swerve past them.  Their presence was a popping sense of relief to the tension steadily building from the Bakers and the game shrugs its shoulders and gives up trying to scare you beyond the halfway point meaning the anaemic combat then has to carry you through for another two hours.  This is why the game is over generous with supplies, if you've played RE2R recently then you will find yourself shooting boxes just to free up inventory space.  Their swing at scaring you with Eveline as Mia was also laughable and way too cliche for my taste.  There are some hideous textures, even when playing on max settings, and the ray tracing gave a ghosting effect giving the impression of this being first and foremost a console port.

Overall, this is a near-perfect game that is still the front-runner in survival horror.  This and RE4 are the two sides of the horror coin and are some of the best games you can play. My first time playing a horror game, and Resident Evil 7 wasted no time proving what true terror feels like. You’re immediately thrown into the mystery and madness of the Baker house. You play as Ethan, searching for his missing wife, Mia, and from the moment you step inside, you know this rescue mission won’t be a peaceful stroll. The Baker family is beyond strange; they are nightmare fuel.

Throughout the game, you fight to survive, escape, and save Mia, while danger lurks around every corner. From the constant adrenaline of outrunning Jack, to Marguerite’s horrifying presence, and Lucas’s twisted puzzles, there’s always something testing your nerves. Then there are the Molded creatures, simple in design, yet terrifying enough to make you unload every bullet in panic.

One thing that might frustrate first-time survival-horror players is the scarcity of ammo and healing items. But instead of ruining the experience, it actually made me more strategic. Every shot mattered, and that added to the fear.

Visually, the game looks incredibly sharp. The environments ooze decay and dread, and the cinematic flow of the story keeps you fully immersed. It’s not just running and screaming; you explore, read notes, uncover secrets, and piece together the mystery of what really happened in that house.

I’ve always said the Japanese have a gift for horror storytelling. Now I can confidently say: they know how to make exceptional horror games, too. Resident Evil 7 didn’t just scare me, it made me curious to dive deeper into the entire Resident Evil franchise.

The gameplay mostly consists of environmental and escape-room style puzzles alongside the first-person shooting which I found really fun. It has several Dark Souls 1 exploration moments where you realize that you've looped back on yourself and that "Aha" feeling when you understand where you are and the mental map of the environment pieces itself together is very satisfying. The survival-horror elements of having very scarce resources and having to count each individual bullet (and agonizing over every missed shot) was very tense and added a lot of anxiety to the experience.

I would say the last 2 or 3 hours are kind of a slog, as the first 2 acts of the game are far stronger than the last act, but it only outstays it's welcome a bit. The resolution of the story is a bit meh in my opinion as well--leaving me with a bit of a "that's it?" feeling, but I wasn't too mad about it. There's very little enemy variety but the game is so short and combat only some of that already pretty lean experience that it doesn't matter much.

This is not Resident Evil. This does not even resemble Resident Evil. The tone is wrong, the feel is wrong, the design is wrong. This game is a generic first person action horror, with no personality of its own to set it apart from any other horror games or horror movies from which it liberally borrows and mashes up ideas.

Resident Evil 7 was the single most unpleasant experience I have had with this series and I own and have played and beaten Resident Evil Gaiden. I enjoy and still play RE Survivor on occasion and that game is objectively terrible but it is Resident Evil in tone, feel, and design.

The protagonist, Ethan Winters is a faceless, milktoast, nothing-burger. The player is given no reason to care about him or sympathize with him for even a second. Steve Burnside from Code: Veronica is a better character than Ethan. Joseph Frost from RE1 is a better character and left more of an impression than Ethan and Joseph dies in the opening cutscene of RE1.

The primary enemies, the molded, are lazy pallet swapped mashups of previous and better enemies from the series, namely the leach men in RE0, the regenerators in RE4, and the ooze in RE Revelations. The variety of molded is also minimal, they come covered in either black or white mold and skinny or fat, very lazy design. One variant does walk on all fours and jump but that just makes them a black licker without the tongue.

The Bakers are neither interesting nor developed enough to warrant any emotional response other than annoyance and boredom. Jack Baker is a stalker enemy but speaks far too much to be intimidating. Margarite Baker is so forgettable, I had to double check her name for this review as I could only remember her as the "insect woman". Lucas Baker is probably the weakest villain in the series and would fit nicely into the villain role in the later Saw films which are also terrible. Imagine Chop Top from Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2 with Jigsaw's engineeeing knowledge and that sums up Lucas pretty well. These particular enemies also swear at you like a 12 year old trying to shock their parents, apparently that is what makes modern media mature and edgy.

The remaining characters Zoe Baker and Mia Winters also have nothing to offer besides an ultimately unsatisfying choice. No matter which choice you make, you as the player lose because you played this game. One character is an innocent bystander deserving of salvation but choosing her nets the bad ending. The other is bio-terrorist but by saving her you net the "good" ending. Pretty stupid for a series about characters trying to stop bio-terrorist.

The story, is never good, but it only continues to decline in quality and entertainment after leaving the Baker estate.  The two final areas, the ship and the caves, are so generic and unmemorable that I struggle to recall anything about them other than the feeling that they would never end.

The final boss and surprise (not so suprise) main villain is unremarkable. All the boss fights are interchangeable due to the nature of the mold, they all look the same, black mold with a weak spot. Remeniscent of the Uroboros monsters from RE5.

The final cherry on top is a cameo from an imposter Chris Redfield, who also gets his own DLC. His character model must have been heavily criticized by the fans because the devs of RE8 put the real Chris in that game. This should be enough to tell any fan of the series how much Capcom thought of the fans that they could throw a completely random character in and call him Chris Redfield to loosely connect what should otherwise be a game in a new IP.

Full disclosure, I purchased this game but I did not play the game myself. I watched and commented as my friend put 20 hours into this game for YouTube recording purposes but I will never play or watch this game again. RE8 being a direct sequel to this is responsible for my decision to never purchase or play RE8 even for recording purposes. I have no desire to return to or support any new entries in this franchise until it returns to being Resident Evil. 

The remakes have been great but they are a distinctly different flavor than classic RE. Regardless, Capcom has been dropping the ball when it comes to new stories in this series since RE4, which is a great action game but a terrible Resident Evil game.

This game has been out for a while now, and I'll finally give my review of this masterpiece.

Originally, I played this the first time on Xbox. From there, I bought it on PC. Played it again, then played through Madhouse, and last, madhouse + VR mod via quest 3. Every time i played through, I enjoyed it every time, especially on VR, that was the ultimate game changer for me and this game. I will eventually play through again once i get a little rust from idle.

The setting where this game takes place is a pure 10/10. Nothing beats exploring a naturally abandoned house in the woods with a bunch of secret add on rooms put in. The aesthetic is PERFECT from inside the house, to the outside. I'm being greedy when I say I wish there was more house to explore. I just could'nt get enough of it. The wrecked ship is an excellent addition for that hunger for more when not full. 
The story line is amazing. It completely sparks your curiosity the moment you get out the car. Then you enter the house, and $h!7 hits the fan! Like, seriously, WTF!! I ended up craving for more in game dialogue and cut scene. The VHS tapes are so freaking awesome. Such a flex to throw those into full use and make it apart of the game. Follow the story line, and It ends with you making the decisions of all the decisions!  (Play through to get the reference)

The game play is 9/10. There are not very many games out these days that make it to where you start with nothing, and have to truly work for what you have and find. I like that if I miss my shots, I'll slowly be leading to a potential game over or slinging a knife around like a madman. The parry is awesome and saved me so much in those situations where I didn't know how to react. Inventory/expansion is perfect with the progression, very tight knitted, for me, anyways.. I have no problem taking the extra steps to back track if need be to micro manage inventory. Finding hidden treasures was one of my favorite parts of the game! The battles with all the variety of biohazards were pretty cool. I wish there maybe were a little more sprinkle of sub bosses, but that would involve making more changes to the linear of the overall game, so no biggie at all. I LOVED the ones that jump scared me! For me personally, it takes a lot for a video game to truly make me jump. They were very clever, and creative to find ways to make it happen. Such mad props. All that being said, you will be left greatly impressed after playing this super uniquely awesome first person shooter.

Graphics: 10/10. Even during initial release, these graphics will stand the test of time. Age like perfect fine wine even in 20 years. There are a few games that are a decade or two old we could all agree on without example to prove said point. I'd be mind blown if they ever top it with a remake of this game if they went that route similar to the previous RE years and years down the road.

Overall, this is one of my all time favorite games. Top 5, maybe top 3. The linear is so IMPORTANT to me. I love a game where I have to stick to a linear. Don't get me wrong, open world and sandbox is great. But I consider linear games kinda old school so it feels, and a luxury. Especially crafted at the beautiful level of this game. I hope they keep pumping these out and spoil me.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Resident Evil 7.

Now this is an interesting development. After years of bloated theatrics, muscle-bound heroics, and nonsensical viral gymnastics, Capcom decided to… start over.
Strip away the noise. Return to fear. To isolation. To the essence.

I must admit — when I first observed the events of the Baker Estate, I almost applauded. Almost.

The first-person perspective — a daring mutation. At last, the player is no longer an observer; they are the subject. Every creaking floorboard, every glint of light off rotting wallpaper, every grotesque breath of the infected Baker family crawls beneath the skin. It’s not merely horror — it’s infection through immersion.
This, I approve of. Fear made intimate. Personal. Inescapable.

And yet… the protagonist.
Ethan Winters.

Who is this man?
A nobody. A civilian. A blank slate with the charisma of a Petri dish. He’s not a soldier, not a spy, not even particularly bright — just an average man stumbling through hell in search of his missing wife.
And yet he survives.
Perhaps that’s what makes him fascinating. The virus of human stubbornness is, after all, the most persistent contagion of all.

Then there’s Mia, the lost wife, hiding secrets behind fragile smiles. A former operative tied to bioweapon research. I see a pattern emerging — the illusion of innocence masking a trail of scientific sin.
And the Bakers… delightful. Twisted. A perfect encapsulation of viral contamination breaking down the barriers of humanity. Jack’s resilience, Marguerite’s grotesque evolution — they’re art forms in decay.

But the real marvel here… is Eveline.
A bioweapon in the body of a child — the ultimate psychological vector. Why unleash a monster when you can make people love their captor?
A creature that infects through affection. Ingenious.
Were I still in power, I would have welcomed the opportunity to study her — or rather, refine her. But, alas, Umbrella had long since been “rebranded.”

Ah yes, Blue Umbrella.
The gall. The same corporation that poisoned the planet now parading itself as a savior.
New logo, new name, same rot beneath the surface.
They claim to fight bio-terrorism, to redeem themselves.
I can’t decide if it’s hypocrisy or performance art.

Chris Redfield even returns — leaner, colder, still clinging to his hero complex. “Umbrella’s helping us now,” he says.
How deliciously naïve. The man will trust anything wearing a badge and a vest.

As for the gameplay — tight, focused, brutal. Resource management, claustrophobic level design, and combat that feels visceral. It’s a revival of the old formula with modern precision. Every encounter feels earned, every shot precious.

Yet… despite its brilliance, something feels missing.
No grand design. No ambition for evolution. Just survival.
A fine return to horror, yes — but horror without purpose.
Without vision.
Without me.

My verdict:
An impressive mutation — stripped of excess, refined by fear, reborn in first-person terror. A bold rebirth for the franchise… but one that mistakes simplicity for transcendence.

8.5 out of 10.
A step in the right direction — but evolution demands more than survival. It demands dominion.

i'll start by giving props to capcom from stepping a bit outside of the box and attempting something new here.
that being said, the overall cosmetics of the game borrow a lot from PT but in a good way.
the game itself is quite short, there's even an achievement for finishing the game in under 4 hours.
what the devs rely on is how much valuable items blend in with the environment, combined with the fact that interaction prompts for them appear when you're pretty close to them. this *can* activate the "looter/completionist" in players and make them spend time going over every little corner of the house.
there are items (psychostimulants) that can help but on a blind/first time, normal or harder run, they are harder to come by and you may prioritize survival and craft ammo / heals instead. that in combination with the fact that, should you pop stims and encounter a cutscene.. your timer on those stims will keep ticking through the cutscene.
i took issue with the fact that keys and other key items do not indicate to you when they are no longer useful.. sure you can check the map to see if there are any doors you haven't unlocked but if you don't have the map for said area / haven't come across the door yet, you're SOL.
the lack of enemy variety was also a bit underwhelming, i believe i only saw 3-4 variants of the molded, with one just being a buff of the normal molded.
in terms of story and atmosphere, i feel like this is the HUGE highlight here.
the game excels in keeping you locked in and immersed. the sound design, the lighting and VHS like filter make the game feel like it's covered in a layer of dust and grime, just like the Baker house.
barring Ethan.. the voice acting is pretty damn solid with the family being the stars of the show. the southern drawl is done so well on the family that the game again immerses you and makes them feel even more believable. Jack, with his incessant parental teasing that quickly switches to abusive language and name calling. Marguerite with her scratchy high voice, yelling at you from behind her bright lamplight. Lucas with his erratic, high strung attitude, teen-like taunts and psychotic "games", surprised me and became one of my favorites behind the obvious, Jack. Lastly, poor Zoe. The only seemingly sane member of the family left. I made the choice I made because, well, I liked her more..
The cast was amazing and made this game memorably along with everything else said above. overall, the game is amazing and everyone should play it at least once. its quite the experience if you can look past my little nitpicks, the lightest being some corny voice acting

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 377:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

After years of bombastic action creeping further away from its roots, [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard [/i]brought the series crashing back into survival horror with a bold new perspective. Trading in over-the-shoulder gunplay for a haunting first-person viewpoint, Capcom created an experience that is intimate, terrifying, and refreshingly focused. It’s both a reinvention of[i] Resident Evil [/i]and a love letter to what made the series iconic in the first place.

⛓️[b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*]Terrifying atmosphere. From the opening moments in the Baker family farmhouse, RE7 never lets you feel safe. You start off in a dark guest house searching for your missing wife, and you are never safe. You'll be venturing into the deep, dark basement, exploring a huge mansion while being chased, and fighting the most disgusting bosses. The claustrophobic environments, grotesque enemies, and eerie sound design put you constantly on edge. There's creaks of the wooden floor, a shadow flickering, doors slamming shut a little too hard.

[*]Strong return to survival horror roots. Scarce resources, tense exploration, good puzzles, locked doors requiring keys, and inventory management—all classic RE elements—make a triumphant return. You’re not mowing down hordes of enemies with rocket launchers; you’re scraping by with limited ammo, counting your bullets, and praying you’ll make it through the next encounter. Many times I yelled at the screen: "why don't I have enough room for all this shir?!"

[*]The Baker family. Jack, Marguerite, Lucas, and Eveline are some of the most memorable antagonists in the series. Each encounter is unique—Jack’s relentless stalking, Marguerite’s grotesque insect horror, Lucas’s Saw-like traps, Eveline's powers—making them feel like distinct horror archetypes all wrapped in one game. They’re campy, terrifying, and unforgettable.

[*]First-person perspective. This was a controversial change at the time, but it works brilliantly. The shift makes every moment more intimate and immersive, whether you’re peeking around corners or being grabbed by Jack mid-combat. 

[*]Grotesque textures, realistic lighting, and smooth animations make the Baker estate feel alive (and gross). Add in the phenomenal audio design and a minimalist but effective soundtrack, and you have a sensory horror masterpiece.

[*]Pacing and structure. RE7 strikes a strong balance between exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. The Baker mansion sections are peak survival horror, while later areas gradually lean into action without overstaying their welcome. It feels like a complete package from start to finish.

[*]Replayability. Multiple difficulty modes, speedrunning potential, and unlockable weapons make RE7 fun to revisit even after the scares wear off. For hardcore fans, Madhouse mode is an entirely different beast.

[*] Terrific DLC content. There's DLCs for everyone, and the Season Pass is 100% worth it.
[/list]

⛓️‍💥[b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*]Weaker final act. After the brilliance of the Baker house sections, the game shifts into more conventional action-horror territory toward the end. The ship and salt mine segments aren’t bad, but they lack the same creativity and tension as the early game.

Honestly, it takes courage to play the Resident Evil series. RE 7 is the latest iteration of the Resident Evil franchise, bringing us back to the roots of the original games.

Resident Evil 7 tells the story of Ethan Winters, who is searching for his wife, missing for three years, and discovers a recording indicating she’s still alive. Ethan’s mission is to find Mia in a village filled with monsters and uncover the truth behind the anomalous events there. The story is incredibly complex and seamless, wrapped up neatly and smoothly, allowing us to understand the origins of the anomaly.

The gameplay mechanics have changed drastically. While the RE franchise was traditionally a third-person shooter (TPS), it has now shifted to a first-person shooter (FPS), making the game feel fresh and far more terrifying, as it immerses you closer to the game’s atmosphere. This change feels perfect, as Capcom successfully delivers an FPS experience in the Resident Evil franchise, making it feel like a brand-new series.

Regarding the horror aspect, this game truly embraces real survival horror compared to some of its predecessors, which leaned more toward horror action. Ethan’s survival feels authentic, with limited ammo forcing you to play hide-and-seek, navigating tight spaces with dark lighting that amplifies the horror atmosphere. As an ordinary human, not a soldier, Ethan faces numerous monsters in a dark setting, often engaging in close combat, which makes the game genuinely terrifying.

The graphics are stunning yet eerie. Despite being released almost eight years ago, the game still feels modern thanks to the excellent RE Engine. Everything feels real, from the environments to the zombies and monsters, with key elements of the RE world brought to life vividly. The performance is also highly stable, with no bugs or frame rate drops.

Puzzles, a staple of the RE franchise, remain a key feature. They require thought and precision to progress the story. The inclusion of tapes also helps clarify the narrative in RE 7.

Overall, I absolutely love the main story—it’s smooth, expands the RE universe, and has shocking plot twists. The unforgettable villains, the infected Baker family, tie into the main antagonist responsible for their condition. The FPS gameplay mechanics enhance the horror and atmosphere, making it more terrifying. The stunning yet creepy graphics, paired with smooth performance, make this game nearly perfect for the RE series, especially as it brings back the classic survival horror feel. It’s perfect for new Resident Evil fans like me.

DLC Review : 

The Not a Hero DLC continues the story, with players taking on the role of Chris to confront Lucas, the remaining villain and son of Jack Baker. The story is decent but leans less on horror and more on challenging puzzles. The DLC is brutal, with Chris’s teammates killed savagely, leaving him to hunt Lucas alone.

The End of Zoe DLC wraps up Zoe’s story, a character Ethan meets in the village. After Ethan saves Mia, Zoe is left without a cure. Here, you play as Joe Baker, Zoe’s uncle, a former soldier with impressive combat skills. Every fight feels satisfying, especially with the ability to perform stealth kills. In the endgame, you get a gauntlet that boosts damage, making gameplay even more enjoyable, though the gauntlet sequences feel too short.

RE7 is a great game in the Resident Evil series. It brings you back to a much more grounded survival horror experience than, say, RE4 -- and it does it very well.

My favourite part of RE7 is the tension. The first-person perspective, limited supplies, tight inventory, and deadly enemies all mix to create great tension during exploration. And then the combat is very satisfying and fun when it happens, and that gives you some needed release.

Tie it all up with fabulous visual and audio design and RE7 becomes an excellent game!

I don't want to say that it's perfect; I thought the characters were generally weak, there is little enemy variety, and the plot can't seem to resist going a bit off the rails by the end... but these are nitpicks in an extremely solid experience.

I would recommend RE7 to fans of survival horror provided you understand it is taking the pace way, way down from previous titles. It's not a shooting gallery, but it's a great game!

I enjoyed this game quite a bit, at the beginning it's probably the scariest game I've played. The game play is fun too. Recently replayed it and it holds up quite well. This is the game that revitalized the Resident Evil series and Capcom as a whole. I would also recommend RE2 Remake.

Make sure to play the RE7 demo first. It contains a story that is not present in the actual game, with multiple endings.

A solid Survival Horror game although very streamlined, almost to a fault. The last third of the game is also terrible past a first playthrough.

Beyond that simplicity, this game manages to feel extremely unique and immersive for RE, while staying perfectly on-brand for the series. The inspiration from Evil Dead and Texas Chainsaw Massacre becomes very obvious yet it combines perfectly with the VHS aesthetic. The villains are all charismatic, scary and memorable for different reasons, the story has a couple of fun twists, and the DLC also stretches the base game's mechanics to the absolute furthest. In particular, "End of Zoe" is a must play, as it turns the entire game into a first person beat 'em up where you play as a brainless hillbilly spouting hilarious one-liners before the game gives you an iron man fist and plays the most MCU-type music I've ever heard in a video game. When it comes to RE, 7 is peak comedy.

The only real distractions from the immersive and horrific world are the super low-res textures when examining objects up close, and the inability to skip cutscenes on subsequent playthroughs. If you plan on playing the game more than once, I urge you to create a save 10 minutes into the game and load it instead of starting a new playthrough when you can.

A decent addition to RE series, but with some awkward, unpolished parts.

Q: Would I recommend?
A: Yes. It's still a great game.

[+]
1) Good visuals
Though, some textures are low quality...
2) Crisp, but a little bit dull sound
3) First person perspective is a breath of fresh air
Though, it feels rushed and unpolished.
4) A sudden change of setting is very welcome
From old house to a wrecked ship and then mines... Intriguing.
5) Interesting, but bland story

[-]
1) Some graphical bugs here and there
2) Real photos
Why? This is such a bad decision that ruined the game's atmosphere.
3) Bugged reflections
With RT ON, some reflections flicker, which is really annoying and immersion-breaking.
Switching reflections to Variable or OFF fixes it, but you also lose reflections...
4) Unclear instructions during cinematic encounters
5) Bugged frame rate setting
It resets on every restart of the game.
6) Censored
Ethan supposedly gets his leg sawed off, but because the game is censored, the leg is fine.
By itself it would be OK, but Ethan's reaction ruins it. He gets surprised after grabbing a healing potion and pouring it on the chopped off leg to see it reattach (supposedly), but because in censored version the leg is intact, his surprised reaction doesn't make any sense.
7) Controller-oriented controls
Menu and inventory controls are clearly designed for the controller.
Devs, if you make a PC version or a PC port, please optimize the controls for PC as well, that is for keyboard and mouse, of course.
8) Unpolished facial animations

Unfortunately, this RE has lost its masterpiece position in my library.
Hopefully, devs will remake this someday.

Conclusion: 9/10

Imo, this is the best Resident Evil game ever made, even if it is just a spiritual remake of Resident Evil 1.

No other game in the franchise, not even RE2, gives you this constant feeling of dread, uneasiness, and claustrophobia like this game does, and the first person POV makes it infinitely scarier.

In terms of game-play, it's pretty simple, and there's not as much variety as the other RE games, but the story is absolutely fantastic and the replay value is high for me.

DLCs are okay, not the best tbh (End Of Zoe is hilarious and a blast but I wouldn't play it a second time, Not A Hero is fun but kinda generic, etc.).

Ultimately, this is a must play for any horror game enthusiast, though i would recommend picking it up on sale when possible, I got this and RE8 (both deluxe editions) for like $15 total.

The pacing in Resident Evil 7 is masterfully handled. Quiet, nerve-wracking exploration is constantly interrupted by sudden bursts of sheer terror, ensuring you never feel safe for long. Resource management plays a crucial role once again, pushing you to make tough decisions—do you use that precious ammo now, or save it for what might be lurking ahead? The puzzles and exploration feel like a love letter to the series’ roots, while modern polish ensures they never feel outdated or clunky. It’s a perfect balance of old-school design and fresh execution that keeps the tension alive from start to finish.

Genuinely, I am a huge Resident Evil fan. RE5 was my first R.E and I fell in love with the series. I went back and played all the mainline titles and even a few of the spin offs and I have to say...

Where I think RE7 excels, it also is EXTREMELY shallow in other areas. 
- The atmosphere and sound design are phenomenal! 10/10
- The story is arguably extremely dull and have some of the worst dialogue. I genuinely found myself cringing at many of the areas in the game that just DIDN'T MAKE ANY SENSE.
- The combat is extremely boring with little to no enemy variants or differences. They all feel out of place and just feel like "obstacles" at the end of the day. 
- The main protagonist: Ethan and Mia, are extremely awkward in their own regards with no real explanation as to why Ethan would even subject himself to finding his wife that's been missing for 3 years and COMPLETELY ignoring every little red flag and better decision that could've been made. Ethan is also EXTREMELY bland. He hardly ever reacts to the most insane and diabolical events (I.E Getting your hand sliced off and just pouring first aid over it and proceeding to use the gun and everything like normal then somehow getting it restitched back on like nothing ever happened.......) and has many areas that just make him feel like a 5th grader wrote his whole character. Mia is just extremely disappointing to deal with. With her always feeling like toxic towards the whole situation and never having real depth. Until the very end where the story takes a turn and just adds MORE questions to Mia with them never getting answered.
- The family/antagonist lacked any real depth in the main game and don't get any real love until the DLCs which provide a deeper look into the family before disaster struck.

Where I think the game does well it felt like many of the areas of execution just fell short... 

(SPOILERS)

Towards the end the game gives you so much ammo and health that you have no idea what to do with. Just to get to the final fight and its a genuine cut-scene that you don't get to take any part in, with an extremely disappointing ending and dialogue to top it off. Ethan getting grabbed by Evaline 40 feet into the air and getting dropped on his head with no reaction and then Chris Redfield popping up OUT OF NO WHERE almost like someone in the studio decided: "Hey, you know what would make them go crazy??? If we threw our first main protagonist into the game, wielding Albert Wesker's weapons. To save the day, after Ethan falls from a 3 story fall and getting impaled like nothing happened. ALL IN THE NAME OF: ⭐NOSTALGIA⭐."

The game is extremely vague and fails to commit on any of the actual things it set out to follow.
Game has so many holes in the dialogue and progression that I baffle as to how others don't see this.
The main protagonist are extremely bland and don't give us any reason to really give a crap about them.
The main antagonist are great! But they don't give us any reason to feel sympathetic towards them or their situation until playing in the DLC: Lost Tapes; Daughters. (NOT OF THE MAIN GAME THAT SOLD FOR $60)
The enemies are just pointless. They suck and make you wonder why they're even in the game at times. Just going through any door will reset them and going back into it they don't remain in the last area, as they respawn in their original spawn locations.

All to say, I enjoyed the game but I could not wait for it to be finished with everything it had to offer. relatively bad GAME. HORRIBLE Resident Evil game.

Verdict: 6/10

Biohazard was my first Resident evil game so I am probably a little more than just biased when I say its the best. It was a clean break from what the series had evolved into and a return to its roots while keeping up with the times. 

I think having it be first person is a huge advantage in setting the tone and controlling the player for the game. With 3rd person games unless the game takes control of your camera you are looking all over but when that autonomy is removed you feel more grounded and "stuck" in your situation forced to take in only what you can see with a turn of the controls and nothing more. 

The combat is simple, shoot good, shoot fast, and block. The best part of it is the survival elements (no figure) I really enjoyed being pushed to the edge of what I needed to use to get out of each encounter. While I said the combat was simple its no less enjoyable or satisfying, trust me blowing off a moldeds head with a shotgun never gets tired. The guns sound weighty and powerful making every new weapon you get really feel like you are geared up to the teeth. 

The best part of this game in my opinion is the story, I think its brilliant. Small in scale yet grand and still links back to the games of years past creating a way for future RE games to follow. The use of space and environments is mind blowing. Taking you from location to location without it feeling forced or unnatural and ramping it up as you go along. The ending and the tragic story of the Baker family keeps you so invested you will probably finish the game in 1 or 2 sittings and be left wanting for more. A criticism I do have is the weird unnecessary implementation of a choice system near the end between Zoey and Mia? It has no impact and there isn't another choice to be made in the entire game so why is it in here at all? Maybe it was left overs from the design process and they just decided to leave it in because it doesn't detract from the game? 

Anyhow, most of my play time is on the Playstation but I've easily played this game for over 100 hours I love it and this review kind of sucked ass but do give RE:7 a try, don't be turned off from it if you haven't played any other RE games before (I hadn't) this is it's own story mostly isolated (and in a game sense funnily enough) from the rest of RE

RE7 is a very solid game. It's far better than RE5&6, but not as good as 1-4. 

Pros: 
-Beautiful game with 10/10 atmosphere. 
-The Baker Family were great bad guys.
-I liked the 1st person mode for better immersion. 
-Exploration was fun, but the house did feel like a far smaller version of the RE1 mansion. 
-DLC is good.

Cons: 
-Shooting the guns sometimes felt like shooting wet noodles. 
-Enemy variety was laughably boring. The molded just weren't scary, so only fighting 2 types of them in the base game was just underwhelming. Luckily the boss fights are very fun. 
-The story was ok. It started off really great but just fell flat at the end for me. After about 1/4 of the game, it went from a spooky game to just a shooter for me. All the tension left after the initial gimmick was over. 
-Ethan is the most forgettable RE main character. I legit couldn't tell you one thing about him. His wife Mia was far more interesting and I cared a lot more about the back story we got for her than anything Ethan related. 

Neutral: 
-Short game. I beat it in like 7 hours with heavy exploration and getting nearly all the collectibles. Not necessarily a bad thing, but it did feel like a much shorter game that I would expect from a RE title. 

Overall: The game is a solid entry if you get it on super sale. I only paid $10 for this and the DLC, so it wasn't a big deal, but I don't see myself replaying this game like I would RE2 or RE4. I'd give it a 7/10.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumphant return to the franchise’s survival horror roots. Played years after its release and through multiple playthroughs, it remains a tense, atmospheric experience that strips away the action-heavy excess of its predecessors in favor of dread and isolation.

The shift to a first-person perspective heightens immersion, making every encounter with the grotesque Baker family feel immediate and personal. At the core of the horror is Eveline, a bioweapon whose ability to manipulate minds and mutate flesh through the Mold creates disturbing biological terrors. Her influence turns a once-normal family into monstrous reflections of themselves, embodying the game’s theme of corrupted domesticity.

Despite introducing new characters, RE7 smartly ties into the broader Resident Evil lore, offering subtle nods and late-game connections that reward longtime fans. Years later, it still stands as a bold reimagining of the series—one that redefined its identity while honoring its origins.

Resident Evil 7 went back to its roots with it being a survival-horror adventure - full of exploration and item hunting - compared to its early predecessors. The atmosphere was extremely frightening, eerie and hair-raising and kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the entire game. It takes place on the mysterious Dulvey plantation, in which Ethan desperately searches for his missing wife, Mia, after being summoned by a cryptic email by her. Compared to the cold, medieval interior of the Spencer mansion, which felt like a huge maze, the household of the Baker family feels like home, in which a normal middle class family could live in, which is a great change of scenery of something this series has never fully explored before.

Something this game has really failed are the far-to-simple and rare puzzles the players have to solve in order to progress further. Instead of resorting to have to find codes and passwords hidden in certain notes spread across the map or written on the side of various safes, the only thing you need to do is to find a certain item (which you only have to do once, as you don't have to pick up anything else the following times) and line it up to a certain form on a painting and press the "ok" button. That's already it. Not much exploring to do, which would immerse you even more in this game, no you just have to spin a weird looking object and align it with something shown on a painting and that's it. That's a huge shame. Proper exploring and thus discovering more about the history of the respective places, as in the predecessors or in the Last of Us games would've been million times more interesting and better.

Onto the good stuff: The Baker family, in whose home Ethan wake up in after being abducted by Jack Baker, are the first enemies you encounter and are, by a mile, the most interesting ones. The first fight with Jack forces you to have to make quick decisions in regards to whether you make use of your handgun with its limited ammo or find another way to fend him off. If you actually unload your gun on him, this will come back to haunt you. It was also a really threat and reminded you that you're not safe, even if you think you are. At one point, he burst through a wall just like Mr.X in RE 2.

RE 7 has no hiding or heavily stealth-focused gameplay, contrary to what its first-person horror style might lead one to believe. You need to shoot your enemies to kill or else they'll continue to road around the area, until they get the opportunity to unalive you. You can't really rely on the safety of load screen doors to keep your opponents out. Instead, you better not forget to close the doors behind you. All of which massively increases the tension, especially when your on low health or low ammo.

While the Bakers are the best enemies, the only other prominent and worth-to-be-remembered baddie are the hulking, oil-black creatures called the Molded. They come in a few varieties: The standard Molded; the ones with a giant, warped arm reminiscent of classic tyrant designs, ones that crawl around; ones who vomit acid. Although they're visually quite shocking, they very quickly lose their ability to scare the crap out of one, mainly because the scenarios you encounter them in are so similar (i.e. them tearing themselves out of a wall with a distinctly slimy sound and only in areas overtaken by mounds of black mold). That's the total opposite of the moments, during which you encountered Hunters and Crimson Head in past games.

Micromanagement is still a thing in this game, as in all other RE games obviously. Only this time, conserving your items and managing them was, for some reason, way to easy. Maybe it was the lack of various herbs and herb combinations compared to RE 4, in which you had so many different ones, which might've lead to someone losing his overview of them. Who knows. However, the introduction of psychostimulants, which helped the player in tracking down well-hidden items, was a welcome idea and brought something new to the table.

Thanks to compelling pace that ensured I always knew what to do next. Most of the times wandering hallways, searching rooms for possible useful items and unlocking secret passageways and shortcurts around the Dulvey property was very, very well-spent, especially as the story keep progressing with each file and phone call I received. The objectives are made extremely clear thanks to the great story direction. Albeit to obvious at times, which removed some of the confusion, tension and horror (which is something that makes such a game fantastic in the first place), it's almost impossible to hit a frustrating and time-consuming dead-end, which would take a bit of fun out.

Resident Evil 7 was just another fanastic sequel of this legendary series and the first modern original release of it giving it a new flair after RE 6, which came out in 2012 and was already extremely outdated compared to 2017 games. Admittedly, I absolutely hated it early on, just like the Resident Evil 4 remake, but as the time went on and I progressed further and further, this sequel just grew on me more and more. A purchase of this game is an absolutey must!
