after many years since a spiritual reboot of this franchise, i have finally played and completed this game and oh boy, what a beautiful journey it was!

let me first start off by saying what a lifesaver SteamDeck is. i bought this handheld a year ago and since then i have finished so many games in my library that i would have never have thought of playing on my PC or PlayStation. i would highly recommend everyone to give these new handhelds a shot if you are in the market of buying a new console.

Performance: i played RE7 completely on SD here and got constant 75+ fps on the highest settings with raytracing turned off. i know raytracing makes the game even more beautiful but thats the sacrifice you gotta make atleast for now with the handhelds as turning RT on even at lowest setting would drop your fps down to mid 20s.

Story [NO SPOILERS]: the game starts off with a new protagonist named Ethan. his wife Mia is lost somewhere and one he just receives a random email from her where she seems distraught. he quickly gets up and goes to find her only to unfold one of the sickest and true-to-the-art bioterrorism weapon RE universe has ever created, in the same ballpark as Mr. X and Nemesis. the chronological order of playing RE7 according to me is "Daughters" (dlc in Banned Footage Vol 2) then "Main Game" then "Not a Hero" dlc then "End of Zoe" dlc. you can essentially get all the dlcs with the gold edition which i highly highly recommend! imho, the game feels truly complete only after you finish all these 3 dlcs along with the main story. otherwise there's a void left which although you won't notice right away but you will definitely realise once you play the dlcs.

Gameplay: yes this game contains gore. but contrary to what most people say this is a survival horror game before a gore horror game. sad part is that you can never experience the true horror elements of this game if you never play it. if you have just watched someone stream this game or the full game on YouTube, i want you to trust me when i say this that the game is much much more spookier when you actually play it. there is a whole different level of immersion and spookiness when you are the one whos controlling the character rather than someone else on your screen. the game brings back the original resident evil mechanics but in a much more refined way with modern elements. now instead of collecting ink ribbons to save your progress you basically get an unlimited save state which is amazing! the level design is extremely claustrophobic so theres your heads up. a quick tip to the casual players - play this game on easy difficulty and then start on normal for your second playthrough where you will have a better gun from the get-go. this game is definitely worth playing twice. i completed all 4 parts of the game (mentioned above in Story section) within 15 hours but they surely felt like 30.

Sound and Visuals: i played this game both on headphones (Beyerdynamics DT990 Pro) and on speakers through SD. the sound feels immersive both ways but i highly recommend headphones if you want a true spooky gameplay. if you have a screen that is HDR compatible then its even great! turn HDR on within game settings and experience the darkness as its intended. if you are playing this game with RT or on PlayStation then even great!! the raytraced shadows and light seem soooo much better.

Multiplayer and Replayability: no multiplayer for this one but there are many arcade game modes with the gold edition dlcs. in terms of replayability, i would maybe give this game 2 more complete plays before putting it down for good. with how good the game is, i highly recommend getting it on steam sale where it goes for $5 - $10 depending upon where you live.

Final Thoughts: a perfect reboot to the franchise (although the story starts right after the events of RE6, i'd still consider this a reboot in terms of everything). get this game's gold edition on sale and enjoy it with headphones on, HDR on, RT on and doors locked!

There is a lot of debate surrounding this game, so here's my opinion that no one cares about: 

So we have an ongoing debate on ''What is a Resident Evil Game?'' and in my opinion, and as the game's tags suggest, it is a survival-horror game where you have to use your resources mindfully to survive in a harsh and scary environment where you are surrounded by danger. There is no place you can feel safe in, and the series gets more into the action genre as the RE series moves on. Every game until the 4th game is more on the side of the survival-horror, and the 4th game is the one that made the scale of Action and Survival-Horror tip to the other side. While RE4 had some horror elements, it was never the intention. However, after the 4th game's success, the series changed its perspective and shifted to an action game, as seen in the 5th and 6th games. Don't get me wrong, these games are not bad, even though how RE6 was harshly rejected and criticized by the most of the community, I liked it and it wasn't as bad as they said it was, if we don't count the bugs and unfinishedness of the whole game. 

To further disagree about how bad the Re5 and 6 are, think of them as a different type of game. A game that is inspired by the original Resident Evil but is actually not, do not expect the gaming experiences that you have carried with you from the 4 prior games.
Therefore, Re 5-6 are not actually Resident Evil games. In my opinion, 'cause they do not have a single element (other than inv management of the re5) that makes them a RE-Game. But that does not make them a bad game...
But what makes a game bad, especially a Resident Evil game [b] *cough* *cough*  REmake 3 [/b], is a game that doesn't have a vision of what it wants to be.

So after all this story about Resident Evil games, the last ''disappointments'' have been somewhat answered by the long-awaited game for the fans of the original RE Community. 

And this game is as perfect as a FP Resident Evil game would get. -Yes, devs could have done a better job, but after all those Resident Evil games. I have a tought that they are working on a tight schedule and a team that focuses on money instead of wellnes-, Because this game gives the initial Resident Evil game experience with tight corridors, scarce ammo and horrific creatures, enemies and unique boss fights with great storytelling that does not break the game's process with high replayibility values.

[h1]Resident Evil 7 Biohazard: Game that saved the series[/h1]
Resident Evil 4 was the game that introduced majority of players into the series, including me, and was more of an action shooter rather than survival horror, unlike previous installments. The game was a hit and spawned even more successful Resident Evil 5, which was even more of an third-person action shooter than its predecessor, and Resident Evil 6, that was a completely different game that was criticized for its lack of horror elements. Since then, there was no numbered Resident Evil game until 2017...

In 2017, Capcom announced Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, which was intended to bring the series back to its roots, and it was a success! Not only did Capcom returned to a survival-horror game with puzzles, but they also restored the dread that was lost back in Resident Evil 4 and brought a unique atmosphere to the game: it was inspired by the classic American horror movies, such as The Evil Dead, The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, SAW, The Blair Witch Project, etc. At the same time, the game was almost a standalone story, [spoiler]which still was somehow tied to the Umbrella Corp. with their bioweapons and viruses[/spoiler], and it introduced new charismatic main protagonist - Ethan Winters. The main antagonists in this story are Baker Family, who try to kill Ethan or decapitate him, in one way or another. The puzzles, even with their mediocrity, were still great and fun to solve. 

There were some parts that I didn't like in the game. [spoiler]For example the choice between Mia and Zoe was kind of...bizarre, due to the fact that Ethan came for Mia, his wife, and not some random woman named Zoe; the fact that game becomes a shooting range at the end, before the final boss fight with Evelyn; and that most of DLCs could be implemented as a part of narrative (e.g., Daughters DLC).[/spoiler]

Despite some flaws, the game is still terrific and a must-play, whether you are a horror-genre fan or a Resident Evil fan.

I also liked that the game doesn’t take the easy way out and forces you to think and plan — resources are limited, and every fight can be a challenge.

While I wouldn’t call it the best Resident Evil game, it’s definitely one that sticks in your memory and offers a lot of satisfaction.

After the atrocious Resident Evil 6, Capcom reinvents itself to offer a more horror oriented entry of Resident Evil from the perspective of a common civilian in search of his wife who went missing in Louisiana: Ethan Winters. Since you no longer control an action hero like Leon, Chris, Jill, or Ada, this game feels more personal, and the first person perspective increases the creepyness of the Baker's House. The intro itself already sets the tone of the game, although its very tedious to get through on subsequent playthroughs because its very linear and has a lot of cutscenes. This fact also impacts replayability in a negative way, but playing on harder difficulties also changes a few things like puzzles. items and enemy placement.

This changes once the game lets you explore the Baker's house, because it's reminiscent of the Spencer Mansion from RE1, where you have to solve intricate puzzles (which are canonically made by the same people who worked for Spencer, a fun detail) and you feel there is danger at every corner for the entire game except the endgame, which is more linear and the setting changes to a bit more action-oriented. 

Overall, I think Capcom did the right choice by returning to survival horror instead of action-horror, because this game literally revived the franchise, and just for that i'm gonna give it a 9/10. It also was the introduction of their new RE Engine which would be used for all subsequent games and remakes.

If you're accustomed to playing more modernly designed games, this will feel like you're trying to play while strapped into a straight jacket, lending nothing but annoyance to the experience.

While not as much of a polished action game as 8, RE7 absolutely stomps it in the horror department, and a lot of the comparatively basic gameplay is intentional in that regard.

For example, having a currency not earned by defeating enemies, but be a very finite collectable that can only buy a very small number of upgrades is amazing. Newer RE games, 8 included, will often have SOME way of replenishing a TON of ammo, but 7 is very stingy on higher difficulties and the ammo, or the means to craft it, will always be in the exact same place in the exact same quantity. This is not an oversight, this encourages (or forces on Madhouse) players to play smart with what they have, spend wisely, and avoid enemies instead of attacking all of them. 

Crafting items, using items, even swapping between weapons only being possible while the game is moving similarly is seen by some as some kind of shortsighted thing, but again, it has a purpose. You cannot simply stop in middle of a fight to craft 12 First Aid items and 200 rounds of ammo, you need to be ready at all times. You can still pause for a breather, but only a breather as the pause menu otherwise only has the games' options, a restart button, and a quit button. 

The atmosphere is immaculate, with each leg of the game being scary in its own unique way. 

Even the swap to mold instead of a virus really improves upon old RE. Mold is a product of decay, an inherent part of death, something that spreads disease not only through blood like the various Viruses of RE, but simply through proximity. It changes the environment itself, being a visual warning of "This place is dead and you will be too if you get close". It's inherently disgusting looking, instinctually you will never want to approach mold, while a virus is often invisible aside from its symptoms. 

Though to that end, I feel that is where RE7 falls short most: The connections to old RE. They feel a little shoehorned at times, and before RE8 elaborated (making it a little worse imo) it was as if the connections (heh) to the older games were just coincidence and only there to establish that this entirely new type of game with a new type of threat is indeed still Resident Evil. 

The only other qualm I have with the game is how easy it gets after the first half of the game. This game is the embodiment of anxiety. 

It's scary, it's very macabre, and there's plenty of gross-outs and creepy, sticky, nasty scenarios you'll just barely survive. You'll find relief in short bursts followed by longer stints of dread, paranoia, and feeling near-powerless to fight against this insane Louisiana family and the bioweapons they have as house guests. The drip-feeding of ammo, health, and weapon upgrades slowly builds your confidence that Ethan will prevail and rescue his girlfriend, but the swamp is as treacherous as it is wet. In these respects, RE7 is a fantastic survival horror madhouse. 

However, unlike some of the other RE games, I don't think this entry has the same replayability due to just how much of an ordeal the first 2/3rds or so of the game is. It feels very long and also a bit choppy in pacing. I want to admit that part of this is due to the first-person perspective. There's something about inhabiting a character through their own eyes that melds you the player with the game world. The sense of time and place are different, and with the game taking place almost entirely at night, there's this sense of being lost in a dark, nightmarish limbo. First-person was a unique and interesting risk taken in this series, though I wonder if it's too much--too up close and personal. Too anxiety-inducing... 

All said, having purchased the gold edition, the DLCs that come with it are fun and give some greater context and closure to this story, especially the two featuring Chris and Steve. They're definitely worth it and offer a chance to exist in this story a bit longer and with more robust skills and confidence.

Overall, RE7 offers a unique perspective, setting, and pacing. It might be a bit too strong up front, and feel a bit long and jerky compared to its more confident predecessors, but if you love this series you'll probably enjoy the endurance test it offers.

The fact that RE7 exists is in itself a miracle. 

A little bit of history! 
You have to understand that Capcom was doing alright at the time, and that Resident Evil 5 and 6 had at worst mixed reviews, and only the fans of the more classic games found them wanting. There were as many people that hated the direction the RE saga was taking as those that just embraced it, and you can still see it reflected in the reviews of those two titles.
 
Financially, RE6 was their best selling RE game ever, so even the people that hated it were paying for it. Capcom, as a company, had no real incentive to do things any other way, because *that* is what proved the most lucrative approach thus far. 

And yet, here we are. 
RE7 is the complete opposite of RE6. 
It's not a bombastic bollywood movie. 
It's not a cliche'd international drama. 
It's not a game that cares if you look at the action or not. 
It's not a game that is constantly taking control away from you.
It's not confused about what it wants to be and how it should play.

Some people will say that RE7 is a 'return to roots' - in part they are right, but don't take this as a dogma. More than a return to roots, it's a return to survival horror. Item management matters again, making every bullet count, dodging the fights you can't afford, or paying with your health. It's a return to all the things we had come to expect from the franchise, that slowly devolved in RE5 and completely disappeared in RE6. It's all the things I want from a Resident Evil game. 

And it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ miracle that it exists. 

RE7 is by no means perfect, but it's still a great game, and it served as the foundation to the even more spectacular RE8. 
More than anything, I will always be impressed by the RE7/8 we got, instead of the soulless cashgrab that could have been another high production dumpster fire following the frustratingly formula of the previous games. 
So more than a game, it's software made history, a turning point for a franchise that was spiralling out of control and that had no reason to get back on track.

But it did anyway, and that's why it's a game I will be ritualistically replaying every 5 years until I die.
Though I wouldn't mind to remove the boat segment entirely.

Over the years I've read comments about RE7 being a revival for Resident Evil and after completing the game I'm glad that those comments were entirely true. The game looks great, plays well, sounds good, and makes you finally feel like you're playing a Resident Evil game again. Once again you're in a dimly lit mansion, traversing the gloomy grounds that are filled with various types of mutated and dead people. This game dials up the horror elements and is arguably the first RE installment to be fully submersed in the horror genre. There's a heavy amount of puzzles like RE1 and a combat level more in line with RE2 Remake. The storage box makes a glorious return, allowing you to switch out your inventory freely, and you can more easily change which weapons are in which slots. You primarily play as a single character, only switching out once. The biggest change is the first person perspective, a change that makes the game more immersive and the horror more intense. Overall it basically feels like a modern day reskin of Resident Evil 1 that decided to lean more into the horror aspects of the game. The developers absolutely succeeded in getting the franchise back to its roots.

Even with how amazing this game is there are still small issues here and there. The first person perspective is a huge risk considering the franchise it's apart of. It works for getting the player immersed and scared, but problems arise with the combat. Similar to RE5, you can only sprint forward and not while strafing. This means if you want to dodge an attack you must turn and remove the enemy from your field of view. In third person you would still be able to see the attack and analyze where it will strike, but in first person you're basically blind to the attack's final location. You can see the wind up, but not the landing, unless you want to waste a couple of lives to discover this info.

Alongside the first person perspective, you move incredibly slow to the point where you will struggle to tell if you are actually sprinting or not. It seems everything outruns you in this game. You'll be sprinting and reloading during a boss fight, turn slightly to glance back, and see the boss's nose pressed directly into your cheekbone. This along with only being able to sprint forward can cause some frustrating hits to happen. Unable to keep an eye on the enemy while they attack, you can only sprint and hope that you get out of range, but you'll get hit more often than not.

A final, mostly minor frustration is that reading notes and opening your inventory does not pause the game. You'll want to sit down and soak in some of the lore, and the characters involved make it fun lore to read, but you can't because you're being stalked and will be attacked at any moment. Thankfully you can backtrack a number of times, but you won't know during your first playthrough. The lack of pausing with inventory is a bit of a bigger problem especially when combined with your slow movement speed not allowing you to create a gap from the enemy. There will be times during combat where you need to craft a health kit or assign a new weapon to a slot, but you can't get more than a split second to glance at your inventory before being attacked. It can be worked around, but it's still frustrating when it inevitably happens.

Overall, the game is really good. After the decline in quality of RE5 and RE6, and the lack of Resident Evil feeling in RE4 Remake, this game is a breath of fresh air. It still lacks the traditional zombies of RE0 through RE3, but at this point I think it's safe to say the zombie ship has sailed. At least you're back to getting those wonderfully creepy and gorey environments, ominous atmosphere, and limited resources that have been lacking in this series as of late. At this point we just have to hope RE7 sets the standard going forward and that the developers don't slip backwards into the FPS genre. Hopefully the success and praise of this game reminds the franchise that it's at its best when being a survival horror experience.

Cool game. I've never been a big Resident Evil fan, in fact, RE7 is the first entry I’ve actually played through in its entirety. I’d tried RE2 and RE4 before, but they never quite clicked with me.

That said, I really liked the Bakers. I normally hate the swampy, mould-and-rot aesthetic, but I have to admit it's incredibly effective, unsettling in a way that’s different from the usual gore-and-blood-soaked horror we’re used to. It gives RE7 a unique identity.

One thing I appreciated is how easy the story is to follow, even if you're coming in fresh. There are a few nods to the wider franchise, but nothing that alienates newcomers. It's quite self-contained.

Where I seem to differ from most other reviews is in the scare factor: I didn't find it particularly frightening. Silent Hill 2 Remake genuinely scared the hell out of me, but RE7 didn’t. Maybe it’s the setting. I’ve always found zombies (like those in RE1–3) more unnerving than the sort of horror on display here.

Next up is RE8, and after that, I think I’ll circle back and start from the beginning — RE1, 2, 3, and 4 — and see how it all ties together. I hope everything is done when 9 arrives.

Man, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is one of those games I used to see when I was younger, never played it, but I felt it. The name alone gave me chills, like some forbidden door I wasn’t old enough to open. I’d watch random clips on YouTube, pixelated as hell, volume low so my parents wouldn’t hear the screams, and something about it just stuck with me. But I never got the chance to actually dive in, life kept moving, new consoles came, trends changed. Then one day I finally said screw it, let’s see what this nightmare’s about…and bro, it grabbed me. That first walk through the Baker house? It’s not horror, it’s suffocation. It’s not monsters, it’s the fear of not knowing what the hell is coming around the corner. Everything felt dirty, alive, like the house hated me personally. And Ethan? He’s not a superhero, he’s just a guy, and somehow, that makes it worse, more real. There’s no safety net, no "cool moves" just survival and shaky breathing. Jack Baker? A demon in dad jeans. Mia? Sweetheart turned chainsaw psycho, and that moment when she says "I love you" after stabbing you? I actually paused the game and sat there like, "what the hell am I even in?" This wasn’t a game anymore, it was a damn fever dream I never wanted to wake up from. And the sound design, my God, it’s not even music, it’s presence. RE7 doesn’t care if you’re ready, it drags you through every room, every creak, and dares you to blink. It’s not just a return to form for the series, it’s a personal horror story dressed like a game, and for someone who grew up just imagining how terrifying it must be…now that I’ve lived it? It’s so much worse, and I loved every second of it

I haven't played nor enjoyed many if not any of the Resident Evil games, I got this as it was on offer at a big discount (thanks Gaben).

-The sound design is great
-The aesthetic is great
-The lighting is great however very dark at some times (It does get the whole idea of everything being dark across well however at some parts I couldn't see anything so turned the brightness up)
-I came across no Bug/Glitches when playing- it's a really well polished game
-The game captures moments of scaring the player, these do become less scary as you get used to being caught off guard (I know Mr Shakespeare here).
-The lore is also pretty straight forward and fun to read about, you can read pages with writing on them or other forms of reading across the map. This really kicks off inside the salt mines where you find out what E-001 really is and how she came to be.


Some complaints:
-The movement is VERY clunky, which is realistic in a sense however in fights this really angered me.
-Don't try to setup your graphics at the first part of the game, It looks VERY grainy no matter what you do but does get much better once you are inside the house.
-There are a lot of INSANELY HAIR RIPPING OUT MOMENTS IN THE GAME. One of the main culprits for this is the 2/3 of the fights with Jack, inside the garage and inside the basement. The fight in the basement was single-handedly one of the most amount of times I have actually rage quit in a game in over 2 years. This boss for being the first one you fight- was literally harder to fight than all of the other ones COMBINED.

One tip for the basement fight I found out, try to crouch to dodge Jack's attacks, I cheesed my way through the fight doing this.

Main complaint is how the fight is learning from your mistakes, but it's hard to do that as the game doesn't really let you know what you did wrong.

DLCs: A lot of people are spread wildly on this, it is not exactly fun to have to play for additions that should've been in the game when it launched, on another hand- if you can get them on the steam sale, you'll be able to pay under a fiver, which really in hindsight is not that much.

I personally haven't tried the DLCs yet.

Conclusion: If you enjoy a challenge and a scare, play this.

Unlocking infinite ammo by finishing it on the hardest difficulty (Madhouse) wasn't really worth the time in the end (it's like getting the strongest weapon in the game after completing everything), but I had fun with RE7 after frustration on my first playthrough. 
It had a learning curve and a somewhat early difficulty spike and I actually tapped out for quite a while because I couldn't make it through the basement. Never had to restart a single RE game ever because I backed myself into a corner, but RE7 I thought I may have to because of the difficulty spike at the basement. I didn't in the end but it did take quite a few tries. 
I actually still think that it was easier on Madhouse because, while the enemies are stronger and faster, there are fewer of them. Normal mode through the basement was like "You found 10 handgun bullets. Now you can go back and take out that enemy that was in your way. Right? Wrong! Here are 2 brand new enemies and each takes about 5 bullets to put down if you're lucky!" Once you get used to enemy movements and attack patterns, when to block, etc. the game is definitely less harsh. 
Coming off of 6 and Revelations 2, which are more action-focused, 7 was jarring at first and took some time for my opinion of it to change. It wasn't until after leaving the main house that I started to come around. 
+ pros +
+ looks good. 
+ sounds good. Ambient noise genuinely makes you question if something has dropped from a vent. 
+ I really enjoyed the Not A Hero DLC on Professional. Once you've got that parry down it's a lot of fun popping melons. Also enjoyed End of Zoe for being completely different but I've only done that on Normal. 
+ pretty good story. the Bakers are a highlight (even Ma's bug gunt) and there are unanswered questions for the next instalment, but...
- cons -
- but I don't like the latter chunk of the story as it feels more like Silent Hill than RE. 
- it wasn't until my second playthrough that I actually had fun. 
- I won't say who because of spoilers, but the reveal at the end would have actually worked if he didn't look like he picked up an extra chromosome along the way and looked as he should. Instead of "Oh, cool!", it was "Who tf is that?"
- definitely a learning curve and that difficulty spike at the basement put me off for a while. I can see it completely turning off newcomers to the series. 
- the tortoise from the story "The Tortoise and the Hare" would beat Ethan in a race. Seriously. Making him run slower when enemies are around is as dopey as RE5 how you can't shoot unless you're aiming, and you can't move while aiming. It's artificial danger. It feels manufactured and not genuine. The player hasn't gotten themselves into this pickle; the game forces you into it every time. It also makes revisiting areas for missed items a slog.
- too dark. I finished the main game 4 times, Not A Hero twice, and End of Zoe 3 times all with the brightness 2 notches below the brightest setting. On my Madhouse run I thought I'd go back to the default but it didn't take long to hate it. There are so many areas that are so dark you can't see obstacles in your way. Also, the whole "your eyes need to get used to the dark" thing isn't "cool"; it's just annoying. "bUt It'S rEaLiStIc". It has monsters made of mold and a spider-lady in it, dude. It's a game; not real life. If I want to see nothing I'll go bed. Why would I want to keep a setting active that makes it so every time I turn around I need to stop and do nothing for 3 seconds? Have fun with that.

My First Resident Evil 

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is the first RE game I’ve ever played. One of my best friends has been talking about the series for 20 years, and I never really gave it a chance—until now. I grabbed it on sale with all the DLCs on Steam, and honestly? I’m glad I did.

The game feels like a twisted mix of Saw and an escape room, in the best possible way. The horror is intense, the atmosphere is creepy, and the tension never really lets up.

The puzzles are enjoyable and not overly complicated. What I especially liked is that the game doesn’t rely too much on backtracking—you usually only need to revisit areas if you're going after collectibles, which is great because it keeps the pace moving without slowing down the story.

Speaking of the story—it’s actually easy to follow. No weird, overly cryptic stuff here. It starts off simple and slowly builds up in a way that makes sense. The more you play, the more the pieces come together, and it feels really satisfying as things start to click.

Combat is probably the weakest part—it’s a bit clunky, but honestly, it makes sense. You’re not a trained super soldier, you’re just some guy looking for his missing girlfriend. That vulnerability adds to the tension.
That said, the DLC combat is way better—you can really feel the difference in gameplay quality there, and it adds a ton of replayability.

With all the DLC content, Resident Evil 7 offers great value and feels like a complete package. I didn’t expect to enjoy it this much, but here I am, looking forward to more.

If you’re new to the series like I was, this is a fantastic place to start.

[h1]The Short Story[/h1]
Buy the Gold edition. Whether you should buy it on sale or not depends if you're new to games like this: if you know you like RE or survival horror in general, worth the full price. If you're on a less powerful rig, play the "dx11_non-rt" beta branch. Doesn't use RTX and file size is cut down considerably.

[h1]The Long Story[/h1]
RE7 is my biggest roller coaster ride of a game ever. It's amazing, then it's awful, then it's meh, then it's bloody fantastic again.
The Baker family are such a compelling, memorable and kooky group that are genuinely lovable humans twisted by higher powers. However, their charm - while plentiful and a major selling point - is not enough to justify the sometimes frustrating gameplay. Jack's part is fantastic (and the most horrifying part of the game due to how vulnerable you are), but after him the game turns more into an action game. Marguerite's section is frustrating, and I would've very much appreciated a warning for bugs ([b]seriously, if you hate crawlies this game has lots to go around[/b]) but it's bearable, and the plot really thickens here. Lucas...as much as I hate the bastard, his segment was really fun to go through.
[h3]But oh God the boat.[/h3]
After Lucas, I feel the game loses a lot. I won't talk much about it because spoilers, but it is a sluggish section that made me too angry to be scared.
Thankfully, the DLC makes up for it quite a bit! Banned Footage 1+2 is a goodie bag of prologue content that will most likely have at least something up your alley: wave-based survival, an escape room, a lethally twisted card game, a prologue and more. These pieces have their own fun intricacies that make them fun to mess around with and try to score high on. Meanwhile, Not a Hero is...middling, in my opinion, but if you want to be Chris "Big Balls" Redfield (not his canon name) and have a gun-fuelled power trip, it's fun.
End of Zoe will have a separate review saved just for it. It's the best part of the game. Seriously.
Although the game did push my patience at many times, it nails a mix of tense survival and atmospheric chills that always made me feel insecure, even if the horror did wane decently fast for me. I would give it...what, 7/10? 8/10 with the bonus links that the DLC provides?

I've always heard divisive thoughts regarding the direction the RE franchise took with 7 onwards, and honestly, this was quite the experience, the change to first person perspective was something I didn't expect, it's very alien to the RE franchise considering most games uses a third person perspective, however, I feel like this change made 7 a lot more immersive.

From a bunch of body horror reminiscent of games like Outlast, to a lot of horrifying "cat and mouse" game moments with scarce ammunition, where every bullet counts, as well as your health.

You need to choose your battles carefully, as you will be faced with a lot of stalker enemies and really tough enemies that early on will drive you insane until you finally figure them out. There aren't that many horror games that make me fight for my life as much as this one did, and for that, I quite appreciate it. 

I often found myself underestimating the game's difficulty at times, where I found myself at the verge of death due to underestimating enemies, often leading myself to boss fights with little to no heals, this game taught me resource management, the hard way. 

The overall story and characters were quite fun to get through, as well as horrifying given how much crap these characters went through, as well as the traumatizing experiences they lived through that madhouse, although I'd admit that the dialogue often felt really off (specially early on) with either weirdly placed dialogue, or very redundant stuff.

Another nitpick I have, is that some objectives are quite vague, and you can easily softlock if you don't plan carefully (I softlocked myself due to utilizing the pink sprays in the wrong order in a certain section of the game)

All in all, this was a solid experience.

Really enjoying so far, about 5 hours in

The game has an incredibly haunting atmosphere that really pulls you in and creates a lot of tension as you navigate through rooms and corridors. I'm liking the mysterious narrative so far, it still is essentially zombies, but there are lots of threads being presented here which I'm intrigued to learn more about. Rather than being a large-scale zombie apocalypse, the game feels much more insular, focusing on a single infected family in a remote location, which makes the story feel far more personal. I really like when Resident Evil embraces the horror rather than the action, and this game is doing just that.

My only criticism so far is that some of the level design is a bit lacking. There are a few "hide and seek" interactions you have with characters in the game, where you're hiding, and the layout of the floor you are on or the individual room doesn't really give you many ways to outmanoeuvre the person trying to find you. During one section, I just B-lined straight past them because there was just no way around and I lost patience. There aren't many mechanics tailored towards hiding either; the game is a bit basic in that regard. I think of games like Alien: Isolation which allow you to peek around corners or over desks you're hiding behind, and let you hide in lockers, etc. It would have been nice to see mechanics like that here but there aren't any

Overall, still really good so far

Edit:

Have now completed the game. Still a very solid 4 stars. I really liked the story and how things unfolded. I love how it slowly peeled back layers of what was really going on, and it all felt very satisfying. The horror elements definitely took more of a backseat towards the end and the game became more action-focused, but I think I'm okay with that, it feels quite good to have that sense that you have overcome the horror and now you're the one with the power.

Narratively, there was one character that I thought was underutilised. I won't go into too much detail for spoilers, but it felt like they were going to play a significant role early on, but they're just never really explored or have any impact on the story besides just existing. Seemed a bit of a waste and the game also gives you a choice involving them which I thought, based on what we knew of the main character and his motivations, didn't make any sense to include. I was thinking when it happened "Why would I make X choice over Y".

Another issue is that during boss fights the game didn't communicate very well what kind of scenario I was in. Was this a "kill-to-progress" section, or did I need to escape? Something as simple as a UI prompt that says "kill X" could have been enough.

Some of the design in this game was a bit lacking, and there was that one narrative issue, but overall, this game is really good and captures the horror brilliantly.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a game that earns a lot of praise, and to be honest, I can see why. It’s technically well-made, dripping with atmosphere, featuring tight level design and strong graphical fidelity that creates an immersive and grisly world. The first-person perspective was a smart shift, bringing players closer to the horror than ever before. The game runs smooth as butter, looks great, and has a cohesive, unsettling tone that clearly had thought behind it.

That said, it just wasn’t for me.

While the game is clearly immersive and artistically sound, I found the core experience more frustrating than frightening. The horror doesn’t land as deeply as I hoped, and what tension it builds is often undercut by the puzzle-heavy progression. To me, it felt more like a series of roadblocks than a scary or gripping narrative. It doesn’t help that some of the gameplay segments felt a bit repetitive or unintuitive, removing the dread and replacing it with irritation.

The Baker family are memorable characters, grotesque and full of personality, and they definitely elevate the experience. The first-person perspective does make the horror more intimate, but I wouldn't say it was a game that stuck with me emotionally or viscerally the way the best horror games do. I didn’t find it bad, just not my taste.

If you're into tense atmospheres, body horror, and escape-room-style puzzles with a narrative twist, this game might hit all the right notes for you. For me, it was a solid game I just didn't enjoy that much.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is an excellent survival horror game that brings the series back to its roots.

The story follows Ethan Winters, who travels to a remote house in Louisiana to search for his missing wife, Mia. This house belongs to the Baker family, and it slowly reveals many terrible secrets. The atmosphere becomes more intense step by step. Exploring the old house is very scary, especially in dark rooms and narrow corridors.

One of the biggest changes in this game is the first-person perspective. It makes the horror feel much more personal and realistic. Sounds, shadows, and small details create a strong feeling of danger. You never feel safe.

In many ways, the game feels similar to Outlast because of its strong atmosphere, dark locations, and constant tension. However, the big difference is that in Resident Evil 7 you can use weapons. You are not completely helpless. You can fight back, manage your resources. This makes the gameplay more balanced and gives the player more control.

The story is interesting and has some unexpected twists. Sometimes the pacing can feel a bit slow in the middle of the game, but overall it keeps a good balance between horror, puzzles, and action.

The game received very positive reviews from both critics and players. Many people consider it one of the best horror experiences in the Resident Evil series.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is the shot of adrenaline the series desperately needed—and it delivers in terrifying, claustrophobic, first-person glory. It ditches the action-heavy chaos of RE5 and RE6 and drags you kicking and screaming back to what Resident Evil does best: survival horror.

Pros:
🏚️ Creepy, unforgettable atmosphere – The Baker house feels like a living nightmare, filled with dread around every corner.

👁️ First-person perspective makes the horror feel personal. You’re not watching a guy scream—you are the guy screaming.

🧬 Solid story with just the right blend of mystery, madness, and classic RE weirdness.

👹 Fantastic enemies – From Jack Baker’s relentless pursuit to horrifying mold monsters, it never stops being unsettling.

🔫 Tight survival mechanics – Every bullet counts, healing is scarce, and inventory management is back in a big way.

🎧 Sound design is excellent – Play with headphones… if you dare.

Cons:
🔁 Some combat encounters can feel repetitive, especially near the end.

🎯 Shooting mechanics are a bit clunky, though it does add to the tension.

🗺️ Pacing dips slightly in the final chapters, but not enough to ruin the experience.

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 7 is both a love letter to the series' roots and a bold new direction. It’s terrifying, tense, and brilliantly crafted from start to finish. A must-play for horror fans—and a great place for newcomers to jump in (and scream a lot).

I’ll start with the positives — this really is a great Resident Evil. The atmosphere is fantastic, the Bakers are truly terrifying, and the sound design is amazing, which makes the game incredibly immersive. The puzzles are creative and well thought out. On Normal, the game isn’t too difficult — it’s actually a bit tougher than RE8, which was very easy. There are also lots of hidden items; you might think you grabbed everything, but when you use the pills that reveal nearby items, you realize there’s so much more to find, which is a nice touch. The mother and father are great bosses, and the garage fight was really original.


now the negatif 

The biggest downside of the game, in my opinion, is that the monsters are very repetitive. They lack variety and feel really redundant, which doesn’t make the game any scarier. I would have preferred classic zombies instead

The second biggest flaw — and one that’s often a problem in Resident Evil games — is that the further you progress, the weaker the levels become. The early sections are incredible, but as you go deeper and deeper, or further away from the house, the environments just get worse. The ship, wasn’t a great level, and the cave was even less impressive. but overall the later areas really drag the game down

the Bakers are far more terrifying when they’re still human rather than monsters — except for the mother


The intro of the game is a 9, the mid-game is a 7.8, and the late game is around a 5+. That’s why I’d give it an 

overall score of 7.5.

I had been avoiding Resident Evil 7: Biohazard for a long time. For some reason, I never felt too drawn to it, but I finally decided to grab it bundled with Resident Evil Village for collection purposes. To my surprise, there's a lot more content here than I expected.

The main story campaign tries to be scary, but honestly, it never really got under my skin. It’s definitely atmospheric, but fear-wise, it just didn’t land — at least not for me.

One thing that felt strange was how a game this linear still includes a choice that leads to two different endings, especially when one of them is clearly contradicted by the End of Zoe DLC. Thankfully, I picked the canon ending on my first run, so it worked out.

Speaking of DLCs:

Not a Hero was a nice surprise for bringing Chris Redfield back, but the DLC itself was pretty dull and forgettable overall.

The mini-game-style DLCs are fun in theory and offer a change of pace. They’re a decent way to mix up the 100% achievement grind — maybe one day I’ll actually go for them all.

End of Zoe was hands-down the best part of the whole experience for me. It’s chaotic, over-the-top, and doesn’t stop to explain anything — but it’s all the more awesome because of that.

If you’ve been sleeping on RE7 like I did, give it a shot.

[h2] RE7 Biohazard is a great example that some games age better than others, and some are better left alone as time passes.[/h2]

Is RE7 Biohazard a bad game? Certainly not. Would playing that game close to its release be a blast? Very likely. Would I recommend that game in 2025, especially to people who have played recent titles (RE8, RE4R, even RE2R) ? Unfortunatly not.

I found the story quite bland, the characters severely lacking, especially Ethan who's just a blank slate to allow player insertion onto him. If you're coming from Village, he was written much better there, and the comparison hurts this game. The Baker family is the highlight of the show, but they arent enough to carry the narrative. 

The graphical fidelity, in its own bubble, would be decent, but doesn't hold a candle to any recent game. Worse, the gameplay is also clumsy, fairly limited in your options. The loop of finding items, solving puzzles, unlocking door, managing your resources is still potent here, but the combat is very questionable. There are like 3 different enemies in the whole game, boss fights have wildly different quality, and there is also much less content in the main campaign that the other games. Sound mixing is also a mess, I frequently couldnt hear character voices well. Quite simply, this game has aged to standards I deem unsufficient anymore, though as always, your mileage may vary.

If like me, you're coming to this title after avoiding it for years, then playing one or some of RE2R, RE3R, RE4R or RE8, and considering finally jumping onto this one, I cannot recommend it now. That ship has sailed.

One of the best games I've ever played, I'm glad it got me into Resident Evil as a whole! Starts off with a really good opening story, even if simple. The beginning is a bit slow and can be annoying on second a playthrough with a lot of unskippable cutscenes and scripted events. You find your wife really soon and feel safe with her only for her to literally saw your arm off. And then you just easily attach it back? It was territying, awesome and insane. But once you get into the Baker's house the game really begins. The scene at the table is insane and introduces the whole family really well. Jack is a terrifying stalker enemy, the location itself is beautiful and the puzzles are fun, never frustrating. The metroidvania style of the main house really makes jack scary as you have to return for things many times. The garage scene, giving you a little hope before ripping it away, it's an absolute madhouse. The car bossfight was also amazing. What i really love about the game is how insane it all sounds. Jack gets blown up and just gets up again. The basement section introduces the Molded, a really fun enemy to go against and when you learn how to defeat it with the knife it is also really fun to do. Unfortunately the game only has 3 different molded variants as enemies and it's definitely not enough, I wish there was more variety. Each section is like it's own different type of horror. The chainsaw bossfight in the basement was just amazing, Jack's section is like slasher horror, Marguerite's is body horror and the fear of insects, then you have a short psychological horror section and a little disappointing "death game" horror section. In the last third of the game it kinda falls of a little bit, especially the mines. The boat section's puzzles, compared to the main house, are just tedious and annoying. Especially since you to through the boat TWICE because of the Mia tape. But i love the lore we get about Eveline in the boat section. Overall an amazing game that really makes me want to replay it, makes me want to collect everything and try the hardest difficulty. Even the collectible Antique coins are given a purpose, you can buy upgrades for them. One of the best games ever.

The Resident Evil circlejerk will suck this game off forever so I have no interest in arguing with it, it's so cheap now that you can just buy it and see for yourself. 

If you enjoy very short, easy, boring, repetitive, unbalanced, pointless games with near zero story (devolving into derivative, cliche cringe near the end) that are designed for the general public with no interest in evolving the series it is built upon then you'll love this game, along with thousands of other players that gave this game a thoroughly unwarranted "Overwhelmingly Popular" rating.

I finished this game recently (after 4 times restarting again over years due to being immediately reminded of the frustrating list of issues that I had previously experienced and me losing interest) so I could move on to Resident Evil Village, but after seeing reviews saying that Village is inferior to this, it makes me worried that it is even possible to get worse than RE7, especially if RE fanboys are saying it's worse. Maybe that's even an indicator that Village will be superior.

Overall it is a pretty tech demo for a pointless, unpleasant and annoying experience.

My take away is that I would have actually preferred it to be a tech demo/Short experience and only show off the start of the game, something like PT.

🎮 “Welcome to the family, son.”
I’ve played many horror games—but Resident Evil 7 didn’t just scare me. It stayed with me. Days after finishing it, I still found myself checking corners and hesitating to enter dark rooms. This isn't just a game. It’s a descent into madness, a masterclass in atmosphere, and the bold reinvention the franchise desperately needed.

🔥 What Makes It Great
🏚️ Atmosphere and Setting
The game swaps flashy bioweapons and global outbreaks for something more personal and terrifying: a decrepit plantation in Dulvey, Louisiana. The Baker estate is a masterpiece of level design—claustrophobic, decaying, and crawling with dread. Every creak of the floorboards, every flickering light, keeps you on edge.

From the mold-infested hallways to the grotesque “guest house,” the environments are dripping with tension and beautifully detailed. It feels lived in, and more importantly, died in.

👁️ First-Person Perspective
Gone are the over-the-shoulder camera angles. RE7 goes full first-person—and it works brilliantly. The immersive view amplifies the horror, especially in VR (if you’re brave enough). It puts you in protagonist Ethan’s shoes in a way no RE game has done before.

🧬 Story and Characters
You play as Ethan Winters, a civilian searching for his missing wife, Mia. What begins as a mysterious message quickly turns into a waking nightmare. The Baker family—Jack, Marguerite, and Lucas—are some of the most memorable and terrifying antagonists in the series.

The story is deceptively simple but unfolds with twists, secrets, and just the right amount of classic Resident Evil lore. It's not just about jump scares—there’s a deep unease that builds throughout, like something's always watching.

💉 Survival Horror, Reinvented
Inventory management returns. Ammo is scarce. Every bullet counts. Healing items are precious. It’s a refreshing step back from the action-heavy style of RE5 and RE6. You feel vulnerable—and that makes survival all the more rewarding.

Crafting is intuitive, puzzles are clever, and exploration is rewarding. The game encourages you to scour every drawer, every corpse, every shadow.

🧠 AI and Boss Fights
The Baker family are relentless. Jack stalks you like Mr. X on steroids. Marguerite's insect-infested madness will haunt your dreams. Lucas’s section is like Saw met Resident Evil, with psychological traps and deadly games.

These aren't generic bosses. They’re smart, scripted in ways that keep you guessing, and each confrontation feels unique.

📦 Extras and DLCs
The base game is solid on its own, but the DLCs like Not a Hero and End of Zoe add great post-story content. You even get to play as Chris Redfield, bridging the gap between RE7 and RE8.

👎 Minor Gripes
Some enemy variety is lacking (Molded can get repetitive).

The game slows down slightly in the final third.

VR is PS4-only (no native PC VR support officially), which is a missed opportunity.

💬 Final Verdict
Resident Evil 7 is a bold, brilliant return to form. It’s scary, smart, and stunningly atmospheric. It ditches over-the-top action in favor of raw, immersive horror—and nails it. Whether you're a long-time fan or completely new to the series, this is a must-play survival horror experience.

I laughed. I screamed. I panicked. I survived.

“If this is just the beginning of the new Resident Evil era, sign me up for the apocalypse.”

🧪 Highly Recommended. Play it in the dark—with headphones. If you dare.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard — A Revelatory Return to Pure Survival Horror

Resident Evil 7 reinvents the franchise by taking a bold detour into first-person perspective, plunging players into a claustrophobic, nightmarish experience that redefines what survival horror can be. The game dares to strip away familiar third-person angles, inviting players into an intimate, tenuous journey marked by paranoia, dread, and relentless tension.

Atmosphere and Immersion
From the moment you step into the crumbling, vine-entangled corridors of the Baker estate, the environment grips you with a palpable sense of isolation and imminent danger. Meticulously detailed environments—from the flickering lighting of abandoned hallways to the eerie creaks of floorboards—create a living, breathing nightmare. The clever use of shadows, sound, and space establishes an immersive atmosphere where every whisper and distant clatter potentially signals unspeakable horrors lurking just out of sight.

Gameplay and Mechanics
Resident Evil 7 reinvigorates the survival horror formula by introducing a first-person perspective that transforms the gameplay into a deeply personal struggle for survival. The combat feels raw and immediate, placing you face-to-face with grotesque adversaries. Resource management remains as critical as ever; every firearm, med-kit, and piece of ammunition feels hard-earned. The intimate perspective amplifies every jump-scare and stealth encounter, ensuring that even a brief moment of respite is fraught with tension.

Narrative and Character
The story takes a daring turn into psychological horror, moving past the familiar zombie outbreaks to consider the darker recesses of human depravity. As you unravel the mysteries of the Baker family, you confront unsettling secrets that blur the line between supernatural terror and human monstrosity. The narrative unfolds in a way that gradually intensifies the horror, pulling you deeper into the twisted psyche of a deranged family and their insidious hold over the estate. The game's decision to focus on a more personal, immersive storyline pays off, providing moments of raw emotion alongside gut-wrenching suspense.

Sound Design and Visuals
A cornerstone of Resident Evil 7's success lies in its exceptional sound design. The persistent hum of distant machinery, the whispered murmurs of unseen horrors, and the sudden, jarring auditory cues all blend seamlessly to heighten the nervous anticipation. Visual details are equally impressive—the textures, lighting, and environmental effects coalesce into a strikingly realistic yet fantastically haunting world that remains seared into your memory long after you’ve put down the controller.

Conclusion
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a masterclass in survival horror, skillfully melding innovative gameplay with an atmosphere so dense with dread, it feels almost tangible. The thing that sets the fear for this first part is the lack of resources, i played on normal and the resources were relatively scarce, either i had to pick between making ammo or first aid kits, i had to pick between looping around my enemies or killing them.
Unfortunately, after finishing the cerberus puzzle the game did lose a lot of it's fear factor for me, the enemies in the old house puzzle were pretty horrifying for me since i'm afraid of bugs but they were pretty avoidable, the main enemy however was not very menacing, atleast not until i've got to the greenhouse boss. The fight was pretty tense, i wouldn't say scary but i would say it was challenging, the greenhouse had abundant supplies but the boss was tankier and acctually made me waste all of my shotgun bullets on it. Overall it was pretty fun, challenging and in the end equally horrifying in the eyes of an entomophobic.
The Keycard puzzle and birthday puzzle, both sections were relatively short but also challenging. It was a nice change of scenery and pace to head back to the main house and explore it again, when i left from the greenhouse i was deserted of supplies so you can imagine my reaction when i found out that enemies spawned there, it wasn't awfully scary but it was somewhat tense, running around without ammo specially when they've just introduced a new type of enemy that can be quite tough to deal with. After doing some puzzles, unlocking doors and getting the keycards i got to the birthday puzzle, it was a nice change of pace from before, even the pre-puzzle section was calmer than before, despite the mini-boss at the end. The birthday puzzle itself wasn't tough, it's pretty intuitive and fun to solve. After the puzzle you're set for the next boss fight and then end game, which i'll only comment on the latter.
The... [b] ship puzzle [/b] and the endgame. After finishing the boss fight and making a choice you'll proceed through the game with a cutscene and end up at the ship section. Easily, that's where the game became stale and infuriating, the start wasn't all that bad and the ending wasn't bad either but the inbetween was. After entering through the 'playable' area of the ship you'll be tasked with routing around enemies with limited supplies and getting to the 'flashback' part, this part isn't exactly infuriating but it can be a bit long altough i took a bit of a liking to it. Afterwards you're set to look after some items to get through some locked doors which you can only get after finishing the mini-puzzle, while i'm unsure if i was just stupid or if it really was that hard but the puzzle took an infuriating amount of time to find, if i had to guess i'd easily shoot that it took me around one hour and thirty minutes to get through the entire section. After getting through the puzzle you're given the item you need to open the door and finish the entirety of the ship section.
Finally... the endgame, the game starts to become fun again and you're given back both your items and the items you got through the ship section. You'll go through some old mines and end back at the Baker's guest house, and after revisiting some memories you'll get to the last boss fight which is more of a cutscene than gameplay.

Overall, the game is pretty solid, has a good pacing, nice ambience and the setting matches well. The survival horror part of the game was [b] EXCEPTIONAL [/b], you'll be practically shivering through out the entire game when you have to decide how you manage your resources, you'll have to choose what you waste them on, save them for. [h1]Growing Pains[/h1]

Resident Evil 7 marks a return to survival horror after the action-focused RE5 and RE6, but I still think it could have been much better. As the first mainline FPS entry in the series, that shift is obvious from the start. The level and environmental design feels a bit too restrictive for my taste. I get that the game aims to create a claustrophobic, immersive experience by adopting a first-person perspective, but I believe it sacrifices some of the most beloved aspects of the Resident Evil formula.

The puzzles are among the simplest in the series. You never feel the fear of getting lost or find yourself scratching your head over a solution. It's all very straightforward and focused, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but in my view, good survival horror demands more from the player.

On a new save, the game offers just two difficulty options: easy and normal. Games that cap at normal difficulty are often challenging, finely tuned for that magical first playthrough. Unfortunately, I can't say the same for RE7. It quickly becomes too easy to navigate its shallow level and enemy design, and that’s my biggest criticism of the game by far.

Overall, RE7 is a very different experience from the holy trinity of RE2, RE3, and RE4, and not in a particularly good way. Many consider it the scariest entry in the series, but due to its lack of intricacy, challenge, and depth, it didn’t strike me the way those survival horror masterpieces did. For some, the first-person perspective and photorealism are enough to evoke fear, but for me, that effect is a fine line that only a few survival horror games have managed to walk in the last decade.

That said, RE7 is still a good game. Holding it to a high standard may make it seem underwhelming, but it manages to scratch the survival horror itch with passing grades. Maybe they fully realized the new formula with RE Village, and what we see here are just growing pains. I’ll be solving that puzzle very soon.

First playthrough review time.

Resident Evil 7 brings a strong and serious change in direction compared to earlier titles in the series. The game uses a different way of showing the world, which makes create a more direct horror experience. The setting is quiet, tense, and carefully built to keep the player alert. It focuses less on action and more on atmosphere, using darkness, silence, and slow pacing to create pressure. The style may not be the same as previous games, but the core idea of survival remains clear.

The visual design is detailed and supports the dark tone throughout. Even when played on basic settings, the game still shows strong use of shadows, space, and environment. The sound is placed carefully to add to the heavy feeling in each area. Some textures may not match modern high-end games, but the overall style and design remain consistent. I started playing this game after playing both the first and second spin-off games that is, Revelations 1 & 2. I usually play games in the order they are released, and in this series, many characters connect across different games at some point. I purchased the RE 7 and Village Gold Edition bundle for 22.3 dollars on Driffle, and there may still be a chance this offer is available. Buying during a sale like this can make the game much more affordable.

In Resident Evil 7, there are five DLCs in total. These are included in the season pass or gold edition if purchased. The Banned Footage DLC includes four chapters. One of them, Nightmare, is focused on survival. The other three chapters in that DLC are connected to the main story and provide little background related to the campaign. There are also Jack’s 55th Birthday and Ethan Must Die DLCs, which are survival-based. I have played the three campaign-related chapters from Banned Footage, as well as End of Zoe and Not a Hero DLCs. These are connected to the main storyline and are interesting additions.

It’s not a bad game, but it did leave me disappointed overall.

Early Impressions:
The first half of Resident Evil 7 is genuinely excellent. The gunplay feels tight, the puzzles are engaging, and there’s a great balance of resource conservation, stealth maneuvering, and tension. It blends horror and survival elements really well, and the pacing through the Baker house is top-tier.

Where It Falls Apart/Gameplay Decline
After you finish the Testing Area with Lucas, the game takes a sharp downturn. The story shifts in a way that makes everything you’ve done up to that point feel meaningless. Then comes the ship sequence, which just drags. After the ship, the Salt Mines just feels like enemy-spamming Hell. It becomes more of a shooter than a survival horror game. I ended up relying almost entirely on the pistol and shotgun because the more interesting weapons — like the Grenade Launcher, Burner, and Machine Gun — are either introduced too late or barely useful outside of a couple specific spots before you reach that point in the game.

Contrast Between 1st and 2nd Halves:
The first half of the game constantly keeps you on your toes — Jack’s unpredictable patrols, Marguerite’s creepy insect-infested ambushes, and Lucas’ twisted trap room (which feels like something right out of a Saw film) all contribute to a tense, but also creative survival horror experience. 

But after the Testing Area, that dynamic disappears. The ship sequence trades intensity for monotony: long, lifeless ship corridors filled with the same two Molded types — crawling or vomiting — over and over. Remote bombs are everywhere, but they can’t fix the lack of enemy variety or engagement. Climbing LONG elevator shafts and running up and down stairwells between floors feels like artificial padding. The survival horror tension is gone, it's replaced with bland repetition and empty space. 

Also, SAVE ROOM frequency changes too! The early game uses scarcity and spacing (of both saves and resources) to build dread, while the later game becomes more forgiving — almost like it’s prepping you for a faster-paced action ride, rather than it being a slow-burn horror in the beginning. It also makes the second half feel less risky and more like a guided corridor crawl.

Final Thoughts:
It really felt like there was supposed to be more here. Whether content was cut or they just ran out of steam, the second half feels rushed and diluted. I wanted to really like this game, it had some borderline Texas Chainsaw vibes with the Southern touch and haunting of a terrorizing, murderous family and for the first few hours, I really did. The ambience is done SOOO WELL. But in the end, it felt like more squeeze than juice.

Storytelling & Characters
The narrative is straightforward yet compelling. The Baker family is disturbingly memorable, each member bringing a unique form of horror. The game's pacing is impeccable, with twists and turns that keep you hooked until the very end. While the story ties into the larger Resident Evil universe, it's accessible to newcomers, making it a perfect entry point for those unfamiliar with the series.

Final Thoughts
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumph in survival horror. It combines atmospheric tension, innovative gameplay, and a gripping story to deliver an unforgettable experience. Comparing RE7 and RE8 directly:
-RE7 feels more like a traditional Resident Evil game. It's more condensed, more intense, and I like the story more. RE7 is more consistently horrifying and didn't need a [h1][b][u]THICC[/u][/b][/h1] momma to sell.


Considering this game also revived Resident Evil as a franchise and is a BIG reason for why we have every resident evil game and remake that came after it, I think that speaks for itself how well Capcom made RE7.

On an unrelated note, I had two nightmares over the past few months involving themes from this game and I developed an *irrational fear of Louisiana.






*completely rational: if you develop fear-like symptoms relating to Louisiana or any other states in the Southeastern US, this is normal.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is the jolt of adrenaline the franchise desperately needed. After a few action-heavy missteps, Capcom takes a bold pivot back to its horror roots—and it’s nothing short of brilliant.

Trading in global bioterrorism for claustrophobic dread, the game places you in the shoes of Ethan Winters, an everyman searching for his missing wife. His journey leads him to the decaying estate of the Baker family, deep in the Louisiana bayou, where something has gone horribly, unnaturally wrong. From the first creaking door to the final grotesque showdown, RE7 immerses you in an atmosphere dripping with menace.

The biggest change is the shift to first-person perspective. It's a gamble that pays off. Every hallway becomes a tunnel of anxiety, every sound a potential threat. The intimacy of the view heightens the horror—when Jack Baker bursts through a wall with a shovel, you don’t just see it. You feel it.

What sets Biohazard apart is its pacing. It knows when to dial up the terror and when to give you a moment to breathe. The puzzles are satisfyingly old-school, and the resource management is classic survival horror—limited ammo, tight inventory, and tense decision-making.

The Bakers themselves are unforgettable antagonists: grotesque, charismatic, and terrifying. They’re not just monsters; they’re characters. Each member of the family offers a distinct brand of horror—from Jack’s relentless pursuit to Marguerite’s insect-infested madness.

Graphically, the game is stunning in a disgusting sort of way. The RE Engine delivers uncanny realism, from mold-caked walls to glistening entrails. Sound design, too, deserves praise—groans, whispers, and footsteps constantly gnaw at your nerves.

If there’s a drawback, it’s in the final act, where the narrative takes a more conventional turn, slightly pulling you out of the suffocating tension that defined the earlier hours. Still, it's a minor blemish on an otherwise masterful experience.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumphant resurrection of the series’ core identity. It’s brutal, unnerving, and deeply atmospheric—everything survival horror fans crave. Not just a great Resident Evil game, but one of the best horror titles of the last decade.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is, in my opinion, the game that truly brought the Resident Evil franchise back to life, and quite frankly, saved it. Capcom took a bold step by switching to a first-person perspective, and that one change made the game feel deeply personal and immersive. 
Unlike earlier RE games, this one goes back to its survival horror roots in the purest sense. You constantly feel like you're being watched. There's always this heavy feeling of unease, as if something could go wrong at any second and most of the time, it does.
Whether it’s Jack Baker bursting through a wall when you least expect it, Marguerite creeping around the house while you're desperately searching for ingredients, or the molded monsters spawning out of the shadows, RE7 keeps you on your toes the entire time. Every bullet counts, every noise matters, and every corner you turn could be your last. Almost every moment in the game is fight or flight and often times more than I can count I made terrible decisions forcing me to either track back or move forward as if nothing happened.
What I also loved is how the game slowly connects back to the larger Resident Evil universe. But to be honest, I almost wish it didn’t. RE7 stands so strong on its own that I felt it could’ve been a completely separate horror experience. It doesn’t need Umbrella or the usual lore to be terrifying — it’s already a masterpiece in its own right.
Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a brilliant horror game. Genuinely scary, deeply atmospheric, and a reminder of what survival horror is supposed to feel like. I’ve loved every nerve-wracking moment of it.

The first half was nice. It was an interesting experience in which we fight off Venoms in Asmongold's house and solve puzzles inside an old-school RE level design. Apart from the ship sequence, the second half went towards the RE4 direction with its linearity and full action which is the main reason why the game dropped for me in the second half.

Overall, it is the easiest RE game I've ever played even on normal. The setting is decent. The gunplay is not bad but it's definitely a far cry from being the best out there. The enemy variety is literally non-existent. The story is just an average RE narrative. And lastly, seeing tons of RE clichés left a sour taste in my mouth.

I think the main problem of RE as a franchise is the clichés they contain: a mid narrative, an immortal creature stalking you throughout the game, an immortal main villain whom we fight as a boss 2-3 times at least, characters in a neverending recycle, an absurd weapon only used at the finale and so on.

And the thing is, Capcom has been looking for the solution in all the wrong places for 20 years. You want a better narrative? Let's put more cutscenes. Tired of puzzles and/or inventory management? Let's turn it into action. Not satisfied with the action? Let's pump it even more. Tired of the stalker or main villain cliché? Let's bring even a more absurd one. Tired of Leon? Don't worry, we've got you covered with Chris. Done with zombies? Let's give you vampires. etc. etc.

One of the things that this game accomplishes in making me feel that no other horror game I can recall has done is having to face an enemy that feels incredibly close, hard to kill, and with weapons that feel like toys. It's a game that mercilessly throws itself upon you as a good horror should but also helps you develop confidence to take on whatever is thrown your way. It's a lovely frightful game that feels layered not only in its gameplay, but also in its story. And for that I am thankfully for having played the game and hope that others can share the same way.

After eight Resident Evil games in a row that were okay at best and downright atrocious at worst (RE5 and the Revelations games were probably the highlights of that era, but that's not saying much) it's fairly satisfying to play a Resident Evil game that was not just good, but outstanding. Almost every single moment of this game had my heart pounding out of my chest. A return to not only survival horror game design but also what made Resident Evil as a franchise scary to begin with, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumph in horror gaming. Simply referring to RE7 as a return to form for the series, while true, is selling the game short, as it presents a plethora of original and unique concepts for the series as well.

On a gameplay level, RE7 feels exceptional to play. Resource management, fight or flight, and frequent puzzles are all back and in full swing, feeling almost exactly like the old-school games, just from a first-person perspective. The change in perspective proves beneficial too, as never before have you had to face your enemies so up close and personal. The weapon balance is absolutely perfect, with your pistols, shotguns, and more feeling powerful enough to be essential defense tools, yet weak enough to prove that you can't blast yourself out of every situation. Even in normal mode, the game provides a hearty challenge and oftentimes you will be running dry on ammo up until late game even if you're conservative with your resources. Although the game is admittedly somewhat short on enemy variety, I consider this a minimal issue considering the threat represented by the molded. Unlike the zombies of old, they don't just slowly shamble towards you, they make a mad dash and clobber you to death. This not only makes them highly dangerous but also necessitates mastery of the new block mechanic to survive. Player movement is another thing I'd like to praise, as I find Ethan's speed to be perfect for a horror game. It's not so slow as to ruin exploration but not fast enough to easily outrun enemies, and it's horrifying knowing that one is on your tail and you can't just easily sprint away. Item crafting actually feels like a core mechanic of the game, rather than tacked on like Revelations 2, with crafting itself requiring resources simply to perform the act rather than just the resources of whatever you needed to make.

Even the boat and mine sequences, areas that even fans of the game regularly criticize, I found to be much better than I anticipated. Although the boat sequence starts fairly slow, the moment you get a weapon it comes up to the pace of the rest of the game. The mine sequence turns into a molded blastfest, but that's just the structure of every Resident Evil game, so I find it hard to find fault in that.

If there's any complaint I have gameplay-wise, is that as cool and unique as the puzzles often are, the game too often seems to have little faith in the player and spells them out for you. The biggest example is the clock puzzle, where you have to find the correct time for a small, desktop clock by looking at the clock in the main hall. After some divisive action-oriented installments, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was a true revelation for fans of the series and newcomers alike. It's not just a reboot, but rather a return to the roots of survival horror with a completely new perspective and first-person gameplay.

What I Liked:

•   Atmosphere of Terror and Despair: The Baker mansion is a creepy and dangerous place where every corner holds a threat. The game keeps you on edge from beginning to end.

•   Excellent Gameplay: RE7 returns to the classic elements of survival horror: limited resources, puzzles, and a constant struggle for survival. The first-person perspective adds immersion and makes every encounter even scarier.
•   VR Support (Optional): If you have a VR headset, then RE7 is one of the scariest and most memorable VR experiences you can have.
•   Excellent Optimization: The game runs well on various PC configurations and has flexible graphics settings.

What You Might Not Like:

•   First-Person Perspective: Some fans may find it unfamiliar to play a Resident Evil game in first-person.
•   Storyline: In the second half of the game, the story loses some of its momentum and focus.
•   QTE Scenes: There are some slightly annoying QTE (Quick Time Events) scenes.

Conclusion:

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is an excellent game that not only revived the series but also set a new standard for survival horror. It's a must-have for all fans of the genre and a great entry point for those who have never played Resident Evil. If you are looking for a game that will truly scare you, then RE7 is your choice.
