I think Resident Evil 7 is an absolutely fantastic game, and I'm not 100% sure why, but I have a good idea of it. My only experience with the franchise before playing this game was RE2R and a little bit of RE4R, and both of those games are good but have their low points. 

RE2R has an absolutely impeccable first half and a serviceable enough second half that doesn't drag on too long, but that second half suffers from what I can only call "Writing Speedrun Any% Syndrome", something that RE7 doesn't really dodge either. Pretty much every modern game in the series tries to really up the ante with the reveals and the plot twists to the point that it all kind of blends together to form a vaguely interesting soup of half-executed ideas, but none of the games really falter for it. RE2R gets the point across and has a relatively complete and self-contained story. RE7 is an absolute mess of storytelling, but it somehow manages to not be dragged down due to the game's PRISTINE pacing.

I am a writer. I have been going to university for writing. I am like four months away from graduating with a degree in writing. It absolutely blows my mind that I'm not upset in the slightest at RE7 for its abject blunders in the writing department. The [spoiler]mold is never really explained, outside of the fact that it was created by Eveline. We never find out how to works, or how Ethan is entirely immune to it. (though we certainly do in RE8, but this isn't a review of RE8) The Bakers are randomly painted as the victims for no reason in the game's final act after they spend the the entire game trying to kill you. Marguerite Baker just kind of dies the first time you kill her, while Jack took three separate boss fights, one of which involving a CHAINSAW, to permanently put down. The game randomly gives you the choice to save either Zoe or Mia when Ethan, who is clearly a character in his own right, would obviously choose Mia and ends up with her regardless of the ending because RE8 happens[/spoiler] and I still absolutely adored RE7. 

Why? Because RE7 is a roller coaster like no other. In fact, the roller coaster analogy is bad, because this game has practically ZERO low points in its entire 8-10 runtime. The only part of the game that disappointed me in the slightest was the [spoiler]Old House and everything to do with Marguerite, who really isn't that intimidating in the slightest. Admittedly, the boss fight with her is really challenging and well designed, janky movement pathing aside, making great use of complex level design to put you on the ropes, but as a roaming enemy she just doesn't work. You can't take her down, she just stands there and throws bugs at you, and it's annoying. The bugs sucked. I didn't like the bugs. The Old House is so short though that it doesn't matter, and whenever the game was actively trying to engage with you as the player during this section it worked perfectly. The bug swarms just do not work in an RE game.[/spoiler] The reason I say practically zero is because this hiccup lasts for maybe a half-hour, probably closer to 15 minutes, and it serves to force you to slow down before the game finally decides to go full throttle and start taking cues from RE4 in how it gives out weapons and ammunition.

RE7 starts out as a very resource-scarce survival horror game, and that's very much on purpose. The opening level [spoiler]largely lacks enemies outside of Jack and a few molded in the basement, but to compensate it makes you work for your guns and resources. Jack is designed to soak up ammunition, much like RE3's Nemesis or 2's Mr. X, but he most notably does NOT drop any resources or upgrades in return. The only reward for taking him out is the peace of mind that he won't show up again for the next 30-or-so minutes.[/spoiler] Then, around the halfway mark, RE7 starts to change. You're forced to choose what weapons you want to bring with you, and you resources start being limited much less by what you're able to find, and much more by what you can carry. By the end of the game, you'll have more than enough ammo and healing to chew your way through hordes of enemies and [spoiler]yeah, the game expects you to.[/spoiler] It marks what I would call the perfect blend of survival horror and action in a game like this, and the first person perspective really helps make the pace of combat and exploration not detract from the horror. RE7 is a scary game, largely, and not necessarily in the same way the other RE games are. This game has jumpscares, several of them, but they're clearly telegraphed and I didn't really hate them as much as I expected. They don't feel cheap, and they're never a "you lose" sign clocking you in the face.

And that final stretch, pretty much everything that happens [spoiler]after you step foot on the boat is simply spectacular. I've heard that people don't like the last few chapters of the game, and I understand why, but I loved seeing just how different things are from Mia's perspective, and how much of a badass she was with a gun in her hands. Then, the mines serve as one final gauntlet before the final showdown, which takes place in the guest house from the game's opening. It was absolutely brilliant to turn the game's mechanics against the player and try to fool them into making a mistake by showing them taking damage in the traditional RE enemy "grab" animations, but letting the player check their HP and see that they're completely fine because it was all just a hallucination. Then, the final battle with Eveline is a RMB click simulator, which was a bit of a disappointment, but in traditional RE fashion an "old friend" tosses you down a decisive weapon for you to blast away at the big evil monster with, which was a fun nod to the game's ancestors, Chris showing up out of nowhere feels weird though, but I guess the game isn't too indulgent with its fanservice.[/spoiler]

So yeah, Resident Evil 7 is an amazing game and you should play it. I'd say probably an 8 or 9 out of 10. It goes on sale for 5-ish dollars pretty often, and if you're reading this while its on sale I suggest picking it up (if you're in a financial position to do so) and going in completely blind. You'll enjoy the ride.

Plot :

You set out to find your missing wife, only to discover she is trapped in a decaying house in the middle of a swamp. What begins as a search quickly turns into a nightmare of possession, violence, and psychological terror. The story captures the essence of survival horror while introducing a more intimate, personal narrative than previous entries.

Gameplay :

Resident Evil 7 shifts the series into first-person, heightening the sense of vulnerability and dread. Exploration is slow and tense, with limited resources that force careful decision-making. Combat is brutal and unforgiving, often leaving you scrambling for ammunition. The design evokes the feeling of being hunted in an environment that constantly shifts between eerie silence and sudden chaos.

Soundtrack :

The sound design is one of the game’s strongest elements. From subtle background noises to unsettling ambient tracks, the audio ensures players are never fully at ease. Silence itself becomes a tool of suspense, broken only by sudden, jarring sounds that signal danger.

Graphics :

The visuals are strikingly realistic, creating an atmosphere that feels oppressive and claustrophobic. The environments are grimy, decayed, and unsettlingly detailed, making even mundane locations like kitchens or hallways feel hostile.

Difficulty :

Survival depends on precision and restraint. Ammunition and healing items are scarce, and enemies are designed to absorb punishment, pushing players to use resources wisely. Boss encounters in particular are punishing, demanding both patience and adaptability.

Final Verdict :

Resident Evil 7 revitalizes the franchise with a bold shift in perspective and tone. It delivers a raw, terrifying experience that combines psychological horror with classic survival mechanics. A must-play for fans of the genre, best experienced in the dark with headphones for maximum immersion.

This is an excellent Resident Evil game. If you are looking for a horror, suspenseful, story-driven game, then this is absolutely the game for you. This is by far my favorite Resident Evil game that I have ever played. I first played the original Resident Evil 4 when I was a kid-I loved it so much and still do. Now, playing all of the resident evil games, I had to buy 7 on steam too because it was just that good to me. (I own all the other Resident Evil games on PlayStation). Ethan Winters is a great main character. I love the raw emotion he displays when he is put into dire situations. He is a complete normal guy that happened to be an engineer who sought out his missing wife. I love how he has genuine reactions to things that are scary or actions that hurt. I find that to be much more immersing and personal. Ethan Winters is my favorite Resident Evil mc, so well written. Ethan fought so hard to get his wife back and then his daughter too (Resident Evil Village). I find that so sweet and enduring for a main character.

Spoilers Ahead!

Now for the Baker family, they are such interesting people that I could talk about them all day. The fact that they were a normal, loving family (besides Lucas) is just gut-wrenching to me. All Jack and Marguerite wanted was to save a child AKA Eveline. Yet, that very child turns out to be evil and instead overtakes the Baker family controlling their mind and lives. This spirals into the Baker family being forced to kidnap and kill many people against their will. It is also even more sad to know that Jack Baker was a retired Marine which means he served his country to PROTECT people, not harm them. And then Marguerite was a house wife which is why she displayed such care and affection for children such as Eveline. The most emotional part is when Ethan sees Jack explaining that his family isn't evil and the fact that Jack never wanted to hurt or kill Ethan. I will forever love the Baker family (not Lucas) and despise Eveline.

Resident Evil 7 Review – ★★★★☆ (4/5)
A horror masterpiece that needs VR support everywhere

Resident Evil 7 is a return to terrifying form for the franchise. The first-person perspective, the oppressive atmosphere of the Baker house, and the constant feeling of dread make it one of the most intense horror experiences out there. The sound design is phenomenal, the visuals are gritty and immersive, and the storytelling is a creepy slow burn that keeps you on edge.

But here's the catch: if you're not playing it in VR (which is currently only available on select platforms), you’re missing out on what could be the ultimate survival horror experience. The idea of exploring those dark, narrow hallways in full 360° VR is both thrilling and horrifying—and it’s frustrating that this version of the game isn’t more widely accessible.

The fact that such a perfectly VR-suited game doesn't have universal VR support in 2025 is a missed opportunity. The immersion would take the already terrifying gameplay to a whole new level. Imagine actually peeking around corners, ducking under beams, or feeling like the Bakers are right behind you—it's the kind of heart-pounding realism horror fans crave.

Resident Evil 7 is still a brilliant game, but until full VR support is added across all platforms, it feels like there's an extra layer of fear and immersion that some of us just can’t tap into. I had to get a mod for VR gameplay

And speaking of that, 100% completing this game was really fun, I had to do 4 playthroughs in total and I didn't mind because it was honestly really fun, especially the madhouse mode! The only problem I really have with this game is the story, and to be more specific, how it handles Lucas and Zoe. NOW SPOILERS AHEAD: When it comes to Lucas i kind of get it, I did enjoy the stuff he did do in the game, and I do kind of get why they didn't continue his story here, as there were more pressing matters. But i do still kind of wish it didn't just end with him running away after his little puzzle game, and yes I do know he gets more screentime in the DLC, but when it comes to the base game I still wish we got a bit more without exactly defeating him. Now Zoe is a way bigger issue. This woman barely shows up in the game and then suddenly you're given a choice to cure either your literal wife, the one you came here to save, or this chick you've talked to on the phone like 4 times and are now for the first time meeting. I know her story gets a continuation too, but unlike Lucas I don't even care that much to find out about what happens to her, because the base game didn't make me care, and also side not the ending you get if you pick her is so bad but in the funniest way possible like both her and Mia die lmao, it genuinely didn't make the game worse for me as it was just extra stuff I got to experience in my other playthroughs which I would've had to do anyway, and the whole thing was just really funny to me. Resident Evil 7 completely revitalized the franchise and took it in a bold new direction. From the moment I stepped into the eerie Baker family estate, I felt a sense of dread that only built as the story unfolded. The shift to a first-person perspective was a game-changer, pulling me directly into the terrifying world and making every creak of the floorboards and distant scream feel personal. The atmosphere is thick with tension, and the survival horror elements are executed perfectly, forcing you to conserve resources while constantly being stalked by enemies that could appear at any moment.

The storytelling is gripping, with an engaging plot full of twists that keep you on edge, and the characters, particularly the Bakers, are wonderfully disturbing. The pace of the game is deliberate, letting the fear and isolation set in before any action takes place. The puzzles, combat, and exploration all come together to create a truly immersive horror experience.

However, the game’s difficulty curve can feel punishing at times, especially when you're low on ammo and trying to figure out how to deal with overwhelming threats. But that’s part of what makes Resident Evil 7 so rewarding: the sense of accomplishment when you manage to survive or solve a puzzle feels earned.

Resident Evil 7 is a return to form for survival horror, proving that less is more when it comes to creating an atmosphere that truly chills you to the bone. If you love being genuinely scared, this game is an absolute must-play.

Resident Evil 7 is one of the most important entries in the series, serving as both a major change and a return to form. The game's success reinstated the series as a staple in the industry and allowed Capcom to go forth with the modern era of Resident Evil. It's good, but unfortunately, it's as good as it had to be, not as good as it could have been.

After jumping the shark with RE6, RE7 reverts back to a true survival horror, benefitting greatly from a more isolated setting. The smaller scale makes the story feel plausible, allowing for an easier time to become immersed as part of the nightmare, accentuated by the switch to a first-person view. Ethan has the field of view of a cyclops, clambering around in the darkness of the Baker estate with a mortality that the veteran RE protagonists have left behind. His eyes adjust to the light every time you enter a new room, crafting a second of panic as you can't see if anything is waiting to jump you. The game crafts a very claustrophobic and gory experience akin to The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Evil Dead.

I had fun playing RE7, and you can argue that it's a very refined experience, but many of its issues stem from it being so short. The game doesn't allow any time for its concepts to breathe. The peaks of horror in RE7 are among the highest in the series, but it never lets it linger for long. Spurts of tenseness are over as quickly as they start as you're shooed off to the next setpiece. The 4 enemy types become stale even before the end of the short runtime, and puzzles and "Stalker" enemy segments are severely under-utilized. The final act of the game specifically feels rushed (in true Resident Evil fashion), causing me to finish the game with a sense of disappointment. [spoiler] And seriously, who the hell was that at the end? That is not Chris Redfield.[/spoiler]

Resident Evil 7 does a lot well, but a slower burn would've helped it burn twice as bright.

This is a terrifying throwback to what survival horror really is. Ammo conservation, sparingly used and smartly placed jumpscares, fun and perplexing puzzles. Nothing in this game is too difficult to find and all the puzzles are reasonable, but still new and intriguing. The black, sharp-toothed, and slimy amalgamation creatures called “The Molded” which take the place of zombies are hard to kill and disturbing to look at, plus their spawns are not only random but appear in unexpected ways. I had one drop through the ceiling, completely catching me off guard! The bosses of this game are no hidden object. Each one is shown clearly to you and through papers and notes it’s explained how they are just normal residents until they come into contact with a certain, inhuman substance. Since we are talking about the bosses I might as well talk about the boss battles. This game contains some of the most unique boss battles I’ve ever seen in video games. With multiple ways to play them, and mortifying character designs these have been the scariest, and the most creative boss fights I’ve EVER experienced. Except for the final boss battle. That one was a bit underwhelming. Still doesn’t detract from the rest of the game though. The map has a compact/claustrophobic feel, but is actually much bigger than it looks. There are so many routes and passageways that lead to many different areas plus some convenient shortcuts to help you get back to old areas faster. I truly applaud the level designers for their ingenuity when creating this amazing set! So to wrap up, this is a truly great throwback to the older start of the franchise with new and modern features to make it a more interesting play.

Resident Evil 7 ushers in a new era for the Resident Evil mainline series, featuring brand-new protagonist Ethan Winters and a brand-new first-person perspective to get truly immersed in the horror. Follow Ethan as he chases after his lost partner Mia in the backwoods of Louisiana, where a sinister mold has infected the residents and turned them...evil.

RE7 follows a pretty classic blend of two types of stories: a) the classic Resident Evil formula of "zombies" that have overrun a populace, their origin appearing to be a mysterious third-party organization, and b) what I dub "I miss my wife" horror, where your 30-year-old kinda depressed male protagonist will go through hell and back just to hold his wife one more time. The story was for the most part well laid-out, though I'd argue it gets a little muddled when introducing the mysterious origin of the virus. Despite this, the Baker family of whose property you're trespassing on is incredibly charismatic and makes for some great villains, I loved all interactions with them. The horror elements were pretty fun, definitely leaning into the gross/icky side and the paranormal side, and the first-person perspective while retaining the classic survival horror elements such as inventory management and puzzle solving was a very fun new take for the series. To round out my positives, RE7 has a pretty phenomenal selection of DLC, with End of Zoe being one of the most fun experiences in a DLC I've had in my whole life.

In terms of negatives, I only have a few. The first pertains to the horror; while it's enjoyable, I definitely was expecting it to be scarier, considering all the hype around it. Now don't get me wrong, it's in my opinion the scariest Resident Evil, but it still isn't super scary when you consider that you're regularly solving little puzzles and playing Tetris in your inventory and putting massive holes in zombies' heads. My second gripe is with the protagonist Ethan Winters, who I personally wasn't the hugest fan of. He's not the worst person in the world, but in the long line of iconic RE protagonists he doesn't match up great, often just appearing kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or corny (note, not cheesy like other protagonists are in that they're almost meta-aware of how cheesy they are, but corny in that Ethan sometimes thinks he's all that but isn't). He does have a very iconic death scream though, I will give him that.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a pretty solid and enjoyable RE experience. It reinvents the RE formula in some manners while still retaining the classic elements the series has come to be known for, and I'd definitely recommend it for both long-time RE fans and people new to the series.

After a short section where you find your wife, Mia, in the Guest House and things don’t go the way you planned, you end up stuck in the Main House with the Baker family. And this is the best part of the game. Exploring the house, finding items and weapons, and having constant battles against Jack. He has a really strong presence and won’t leave you alone.

After you finally manage to defeat him and get out of the house, the game slows down a lot. Then there’s a section where you explore the Old House and fight Marguerite, and after that, Lucas invites you to his place for a party. The next very long section of the game is, in my opinion, the worst part. Instead of a fun, unique, and engaging house, you explore a wrecked ship and find out what the hell really happened here. I won’t go into details to avoid spoilers, but sadly, the game never reaches the same heights as in the opening hours. Even the final boss fight pales in comparison to all of the Jack fights. Nonetheless, the campaign overall is very solid.

For the first playthrough, you can only choose between easy or normal, but after you beat the game once, you unlock the Madhouse difficulty. This should have been the one and only difficulty to play the game on. Or at the very least, it should have been unlocked from the start. Because to be honest, normal felt really easy to me. You get unlimited saves in addition to very frequent autosaves. In Madhouse, you need cassette tapes to save your game, making it another resource to manage and I like that a lot in survival horror games.

As is tradition in Resident Evil games, you get rewarded for your accomplishments in subsequent playthroughs, this time with new game+ items that become available in your item box. These range from coins that improve Ethan’s stats and extra weapons all the way up to infinite ammo, which you get for beating the game on Madhouse.

Where this game really shines is in its DLCs. First, there are two small campaigns. The first one is [i]Not a Hero[/i], where you play as series favorite Chris Redfield and go after Lucas in the mines after he escapes in the main story. The second one, titled [i]End of Zoe[/i], features a new protagonist: Joe Baker, Jack’s brother. He’s an absolute badass, taking enemies on with his bare hands as he tries to save his niece Zoe after the events of the main game.

Then you get a lot of fun minigames and game modes. You can play a sadistic version of blackjack, hold out against waves of enemies, escape from a bedroom, or even gather food to feed Jack on his birthday. An absolute highlight of these is the [i]Ethan Must Die[/i] mode - an extremely difficult challenge where you have to make it through the whole house and defeat Marguerite in the Greenhouse, all while dodging various traps and enemies that kill Ethan in just one or two hits. You get items from randomized boxes, and your inventory is very small, so you have to make constant decisions on what to do next. And let me tell you, after you finally make it, the taste of victory is very sweet.

[b]Overall, a very solid survival horror campaign with decent replay value and great DLCs, offering even more hours of fun and unique experiences.[/b]

I've played many of the Resident Evil games over the decades (not all of them, mind you, but many of them). Some were great, some were good, some were just okay, and some I just didn't like. Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is one of the great ones in my humble opinion.

The visuals are very good, and together with the sound effects and background music creates a nice tense atmosphere throughout, just like it's supposed to be.

The story-line is interesting, enjoyable and well thought out, and playing a Resident Evil game of this quality in first person view is a nice touch which I really enjoyed.

A few events in the game might be considered quite disturbing by some, which is exactly what you want from a good horror game. I mean, what good is a horror story/game that doesn't make you feel just a little bit uncomfortable at times?

Is the game worth replaying? Well, yes... You might want to replay the game to find all collectible items if you missed any on your first playthrough, or to complete the game on higher difficulty settings. You might also want to take a speed run through the game (which I would recommend... hint... hint...).

In some other Resident Evil installments it was possible to collect weapons, gear, and supplies which could then be used in subsequent playthroughs. Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is somewhat similar in this regard, but not exactly the same. Certain weapons and special items can be unlocked for use in all future playthroughs (once certain conditions have been met), but the regular weapons and items collected in game will not be carried over to future playthroughs. This is the one thing about the game that I don't really like... You might, for example, bend over backwards to obtain the powerful .44 Magnum in the game, but in a future playthrough you will have to obtain the .44 Magnum again from scratch. However, fear not... The special weapons and items which can be unlocked for all subsequent playthroughs are very good in their own right.

So, would I recommend this game? Yes. Absolutely. Both for Resident Evil fans, and fans of horror games in general.

Step right up, folks, and prepare to embark on a rollercoaster of terror, beauty, and... questionable protagonist choices in Resident Evil: Ethan "Should Have Stayed Quiet" Winters! As a first-time Resident Evil player, I strapped myself into this wild ride, and let me tell you, it was an adventure filled with stunning visuals, intriguing plot points, and the constant urge to facepalm every time Ethan opened his mouth.

Let’s start with the good stuff. This game? A visual masterpiece. It pulls you into its world with jaw-dropping graphics and a mood so immersive that you’ll almost forget you’re playing a game. The animations are mostly top-tier. The audio gets high marks too, with talented voice actors and great music.

Gameplay mechanics are as smooth as a zombie’s decayed scalp (which is surprisingly smooth). You’ll pick them up with ease and navigate the nightmare like a pro. They’re intuitive, engaging, and make the experience all the more satisfying. If only Ethan could apply the same level of competence to his own decision-making.

Ah, the story. For the most part, it had me hooked—like a moth to a spooky, flickering flame. Mysterious twists? Check. Gory thrills? Double check. Ethan Winters? Hard pass. Honestly, the guy is a walking paradox: half bumbling fool, half inexplicable military tactician. Is he secretly a genius or just incredibly lucky? Nobody knows, but what’s certain is that his grating dialogue and baffling motivations made me want to yeet him out of the game entirely.

By the time I reached the finish line, I was more determined to escape Ethan’s company than to complete the campaign. Sure, the story tried its best to keep me engaged, but Ethan’s personality was like a particularly persistent fly buzzing around my gaming experience. Swat it away all you want—it just keeps coming back.

In conclusion, Resident Evil: Ethan Blunders Through is an incredible game dragged down by one exceptionally mediocre protagonist. Visually and mechanically, it’s an absolute gem. Story-wise, it’s a gripping tale, so long as you learn to tune out Ethan’s quips and half-baked decisions. My advice? Pretend you’re controlling a mute side character and revel in the otherwise spectacular journey!

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is, without question, the scariest game in the Resident Evil franchise to me personally, and it completely revitalised the series for me. As someone who’s played through a lot of survival horror games, this one took me by surprise with just how intense, terrifying, and immersive it was.

From the moment you step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, a man searching for his missing wife, Mia, in a run-down, decrepit farmhouse, the game immediately sets a tone of dread. The first-person perspective is a game-changer in Resident Evil 7, making the horrors feel far more personal and inescapable.

The Baker family is one of the most unsettling and terrifying groups of villains in gaming. Their unpredictable behavior, twisted personalities, and brutal methods make them feel like real threats. There are moments in the game that feel so intimate, so personal, it makes everything that much scarier.

The setting is another huge part of what makes the game so terrifying. The derelict house, with its dark corners, narrow hallways, and disturbing imagery, is one of the best-designed locations in horror. You’re constantly exploring the house, solving puzzles, and trying to stay one step ahead of the terrifying family members chasing you, all while dealing with limited resources. 

The first-person view also lends itself to the intense, slow-burn horror. The encounters with the Bakers, particularly Jack Baker, are heart-pounding moments where you feel genuinely vulnerable.

What makes Resident Evil 7 stand out even more is the gradual escalation of the story. It starts with a relatively straightforward rescue mission but soon spirals into a horrifying nightmare full of mystery, terror, and grotesque imagery. The game pulls you into its world and keeps you guessing, with plot twists and surprises that keep you hooked until the very end.

In terms of scares, Resident Evil 7 is relentless, building tension throughout the entire game. The sound design is excellentfootsteps, creaks, whispers, the horrifying sound of the chainsaw, all these elements keep your nerves constantly on edge. There were times when I couldn’t breathe because I was so immersed in the atmosphere, afraid to move forward but knowing I had no choice. It’s a true horror experience from start to finish.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a masterpiece of survival horror. It’s terrifying, immersive, and filled with moments that will make your heart race. The first-person perspective, unsettling enemies, and incredible atmosphere make it the scariest entry in the Resident Evil franchise, and for me, it’s the perfect example of how to do horror right. 

All with the additional concept of purchasable DLC's to help provide more content of additional Horror and twists, this game is one of the better few in the Resident Evil Franchise.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard – A Terrifying Return to Survival Horror

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard marks a bold and thrilling return to the franchise’s survival horror roots. With its shift to a first-person perspective, intense atmosphere, and gripping storyline, RE7 delivers an unforgettable horror experience that stands out as one of the best entries in the series.

Story & Atmosphere

The game follows Ethan Winters, an ordinary man searching for his missing wife, Mia, in a seemingly abandoned plantation in Louisiana. What starts as a desperate rescue mission quickly turns into a nightmare as Ethan encounters the sadistic Baker family. The story is filled with mystery, tension, and unexpected twists, keeping players engaged from start to finish.

The atmosphere is one of the strongest aspects of RE7. The eerie, claustrophobic environment of the Baker estate, combined with outstanding sound design, creates an overwhelming sense of dread. Every creaking floorboard and distant whisper adds to the immersion, making players feel constantly on edge.

Gameplay & Survival Horror Elements

RE7 strips away the action-heavy gameplay of its predecessors and embraces true survival horror. Resources are scarce, ammunition is limited, and every encounter feels like a life-or-death struggle. The game encourages exploration and careful item management, reminiscent of classic Resident Evil titles.

The first-person perspective enhances the horror, making encounters with the terrifying Molded and the relentless Baker family even more intense. Jack Baker, in particular, is one of the most memorable antagonists in Resident Evil history, constantly hunting Ethan in a way that feels reminiscent of Nemesis or Mr. X but with a more personal and terrifying presence.

Graphics & Performance

Visually, RE7 is stunning. The RE Engine delivers highly detailed environments, realistic character models, and gruesome horror effects that enhance the game’s disturbing atmosphere. The lighting and shadows play a crucial role in creating a sense of unease, making every dark hallway a nerve-wracking experience.

Verdict

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard successfully reinvents the franchise while staying true to its survival horror roots. With its gripping story, terrifying atmosphere, and intense gameplay, it is a must-play for both longtime fans and newcomers to the series. Whether you're a veteran of the franchise or experiencing Resident Evil for the first time, RE7 is an unforgettable horror journey that will leave you on the edge of your seat.

Rating: 9/10 – A masterpiece of modern survival horror.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a remarkable departure from the series' traditional third-person perspective, embracing a first-person view that pulls players directly into its terrifying world. As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I can confidently say that this title successfully revitalizes the series while paying homage to its roots. The shift to a more immersive, survival-horror experience was a bold move, but it’s executed flawlessly, creating a sense of vulnerability that was often lacking in previous entries.

The game’s graphics are stunning for its time. The environments, lighting, and character models create a truly atmospheric world. The Baker family’s home, with its decaying, unsettling interiors, is a standout location that evokes the same claustrophobic dread that the series’ best entries are known for. The attention to detail in the textures, blood splatter effects, and lighting is a testament to the game’s commitment to realism and immersion.

In terms of gameplay, Resident Evil 7 retains the survival-horror formula, with limited resources and an emphasis on exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. The pacing is on point, slowly building tension with each encounter. The game also adds an extra layer of strategy with its inventory system, where players have to carefully manage what they carry—making every decision feel important. That being said, some might find the combat a bit clunky at times, particularly when trying to aim or when dealing with certain enemies. While it doesn't break the experience, these moments can occasionally pull you out of the otherwise tense atmosphere.

One of the most significant highlights is the game’s ability to deliver true horror. The eerie atmosphere, unsettling sound design, and relentless threats create a spine-chilling experience. The story, while straightforward in its quest to uncover the mysteries of the Baker family and their connection to the terrifying biohazard, is engaging and provides plenty of twists and turns to keep players hooked.

If I were to nitpick, the game does have a few small issues. The pacing of some sections might feel a little uneven, especially when the game transitions into action-heavy segments that might take away from the tense horror vibe. Additionally, certain characters could have had more development, especially considering how pivotal they are to the narrative.

Overall, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a worthy addition to the franchise. It embraces the horror roots that fans love while introducing new gameplay mechanics and innovations. It’s a must-play for Resident Evil veterans, but also accessible to newcomers, making it a great starting point for those looking to dive into the series.

Welcome to the Baker estate, where the mold grows thicker than the plot twists, and the hospitality involves chainsaws and dinner that would make Gordon Ramsay faint. In Resident Evil 7, you play as Ethan Winters, a guy so determined to find his missing wife that he ignores every single red flag screaming “turn around.” Ethan has the survival instincts of a cardboard box. This man watches his wife turn into a homicidal demon and still chooses to say, "Mia, what’s wrong?"
Pro tip: If a house smells like death and has VHS tapes scattered around, leave.

The shift to first-person isn’t just a change in perspective - it’s an invasion of your personal space. You’re not just playing Ethan - you are Ethan. Gameplay is a masterful blend of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. Supplies are scarce, forcing you to carefully manage resources while fending off terrifying enemies. The Baker family, each with their unique brand of menace, provides some of the most memorable and harrowing moments in the series.

The Baker mansion is one of the most terrifying settings in gaming history. Every creaky floorboard, flickering light, and blood-stained hallway feels lived in, but in the worst possible way. Footsteps behind you, whispers in the dark, and the ever-present feeling that someone is watching you. The game constantly builds tension, rarely giving you a moment to breathe before throwing something horrifying in your face.

While some may find the story’s conclusion slightly predictable, the journey is undeniably worth it. Enter the Baker estate if you dare, but don’t expect to leave unscathed.

[h2]Difficulty[/h2]

[b]Easy[/b] - Literally baby mode, you get heaps of ammo, first aid kits, etc. It's... fine for a 1st time play, but i'd much more recommend Normal mode. [b]By beating "Easy" you're awarded with the "Albert-01" Which is the best pistol in the game, and it will be your best friend in the "Madhouse"[/b]

[b]Normal[/b] - Yep, this is it, the perfect difficulty for a 1st time playthrough. Not much to say, harder than "Easy" But it's not too hard. [b]By beating 'Normal' you're awarded with "The Secrets of Defense" Which is... dissapointing to say the list, it's not really much, it boosts damage reduction when blocking attacks, but it's pretty weak.[/b]

[b]Madhouse[/b] - Oh boy... this is hard, it's actually really difficult to beat this, I personally had the most trouble beating 'Greenhouse Marguerite' that was a hell... in rest it's not that hard, especially if you decide to use the gear you got from beating the previous difficulties. [b]By beating 'Madhouse' You're awarded with "Infinite Ammo" Yeah xD literally infinite ammo, which makes it... really fun to be honest, I personally liked it, and it's clearly worth doing.[/b]

Oh God... we have a lot to talk here.

[h2][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/529930/Banned_Footage_Vol1/]Banned Footage Vol.1[/url][/h2]

Pretty challenging, not gonna lie. [b]2. Night Terror[/b] 

This is what I mean when I say it's hard. This is the harder mode of "Nightmare" And... it's quite frankly a night terror, it's hard, i actually had a pretty hard time trying to beat this, taking me many tries, but... by watching a few guides you can beat it.

Monster Hunter was going strong, but only published on handhelds and severely crippled by that choice. Dead Rising floundered, Dragon's Dogma laid ignored, and even Ace Attorney experienced bumps in the road. 

And Resident Evil? Christ, what a disaster. Resident Evil 6 is an embarrassment, a hackneyed and shoddy third person slugfest that looks terrible and plays worse. Raccoon City is a deeply weird game with terrible gameplay and a strange core premise, while Umbrella Corps can only be described as "uniquely atrocious". Only Revelations really stood it's ground, and even then that game was just "good", not great.

And so, delivered unto us was Resident Evil 7. Flawed, questionable in some areas, and not without its pockmarks... but easily the best game the franchise had seen in nearly a decade. 

Dragging itself back to the survival horror roots it once defined, Resident Evil 7 feels both old and new at the same time. The classic gameplay style of exploring a huge mansion is here, but with a major aesthetic departure. Ditching the sci-fi, zombie apocalypse looks of franchise past, this game instead took up a "hillbilly horror", Texas-Chainsaw-Massacre approach with influences from the found footage genre. This striking difference in look immediately set the game apart, as did its then-unique first person perspective. Being so willing to diverge from the established norms of the franchise was a great idea, as it meant that RE7 could build its new identity among rusty sawblades and flickering VHS effects. 

In terms of design, Resident Evil 7 doesn't add much new to the formula. You're still wandering around a spooky mansion, blasting monsters with a limited ammo supply. The gun combat is chunky and powerful, with enemies that respond well to your attacks and pose a solid threat. Puzzles are very easy, and some require you to look around the environment in fun ways. The biggest achievement that Resident Evil 7 earns is that it is genuinely scary at times. The intimidating Bakers act as strong roadblocks, and the game constantly uses them as a way to surprise the player. The game's strongest moment is easily it's opening three hours, which are so full of constant surprises that the average player won't know what to expect next.

Gameplay wise, Resident Evil 7 was also a return to form. Item boxes! Ammo management! Health vs. ammo decisionmaking! It's all here, though with a lot of the bite sanded off. You see, Resident Evil 7 is a true survival horror game... but it's also pretty easy. The game hands out resources like candy, and loves to pull you into scripted sequences. Puzzles are generally easy, the map is small and contained, and the gun combat isn't demanding in the slightest. Now, this would be a flaw in any other game... but beating RE7 once unlocks Madhouse mode, a bonus hardmode that is much tougher than the base experience. Madhouse mode easily saves this game, both helping out the short run time and giving franchise vets something to chew on. 

When RE7 came out, I was somewhat disappointed in it. I'm a huge Resident Evil fan, and have beaten almost every game in the franchise multiple times. To experience a game like this, with few of the elements I loved, and a difficulty that didn't seem to be taking me seriously, rubbed me the wrong way. With the release of the REmakes alongside Resident Evil 8, I can now look fondly back on this experience and appreciate it for what it did. In an era where Capcom seemed to be ignoring every request longtime fans were begging for, Resident Evil 7 stood tall as a horror experience that sloughed off all the baggage of triple AAA gaming at the time. No season passes, microtransactions or pointless multiplayer... just pure single player gameplay. The success of this game funded the creation of the REmakes and further games in the franchise, and that's something I'll always be thankful for. 

Resident Evil 7 might not be the best game in the series, but it is the one that took the most risks. A lot of those risks paid off in spades.

I've played RE:7 before I got this one, and gotta say, that one was better. But that does not mean Village is devoid of merit.

I find the weapon upgrade system to be a bit much. You'll always buy the best guns, so I found upgrading the weaker armaments to be useless.

The expanded crafting system is strange, but it is a welcome addition. You do not have to use precious inventory space to hoard crafting materials. This expansion leads to less complete loot, and more materials.

Enemies dropping loot is very much appreciated. you can either get money, ammunition or really useful materials.

This point leads to the shop. While very limited in consumables and ammo, weapon upgrades and new weapons are easily acceptable. And let's not forget about the (in my oppinion) best character: the Duke. Him being everywhere gives you some closure and relief when out of combat.

And this naturally leads to a big step up from the previous game: the characters. Side characters basically don't exist, but the villains are mostly an upgrade from Biohazard. Switching with Jack Baker, we get teh face of the game, Alicina Dimitrescu, who has a very charming personality, and her design is very tastefully horny, while nobly carrying herself. There isn't much to Beneviento and Moreau, other than their well made parts, they are not amazing characters. This is switched up by my second favourite character, Heisenberg, who, similar to Lucas, is a showman. His undeniable charisma is one of the main reason I was so invested in the game. Mother Miranda is one of the villains of all time. Her motivation is understandable, but she doesn't have enough presence to take seriously, unlike Evelin from the previous game, who was built up early enough to really set her role as the main antagonist.

Sadly the story is rather predictable, other than one twist I did not see coming. The horror at the beginning is very strong, but after Beneviento (which is the peak of terror in this game) it loses steam, like most action horror games. Exploration is very rewarding, but not getting any sort of indicator about a point of no return has always bothered me in most games.

Graphics wise this game rocks, a very big step up from the previous game, although the small and enclosed spaces in the Baker residence landed themselves much better even horror wise than the open air of the Romanian Carpathians.

Overall a worthy successor of the previous game, 8.5/10.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard – The "Why Did I Do This to Myself?" Experience

So, you’ve decided to play Resident Evil 7: Biohazard? First of all, I applaud your bravery. Get ready to embark on a terrifying journey where every corner holds the promise of death, weird hillbillies, and, of course, zombies. But unlike other Resident Evil games where you can at least try to kill your way through, this one has a lot of running away and hiding... and more screaming. Mostly your own.

You start off as Ethan Winters, a regular guy looking for his wife, Mia, who has mysteriously gone missing for three years. Naturally, you’ll end up in a decrepit house in the middle of nowhere, because that’s exactly what any sane person would do when searching for their loved one. What could go wrong, right? It’s not like it’s a horror game or anything. Oh wait, it is. As soon as you step into the mansion, you’re greeted by the weirdest, most unsettling family since... well, ever. Think The Texas Chainsaw Massacre meets Grandma’s House and you’ve got the general vibe.

The Baker family? Oh, they’re special. They’re like the family from your worst nightmares, but with an extra dose of creepy. There's Jack Baker, who’s like a creepy dad who wants to give you a hug, but only after trying to kill you in increasingly bizarre ways. Then there's Marguerite, who might just be the most terrifying mom of all time, especially when she’s talking about bugs... and I'm not talking about the ones in the kitchen.

And then there’s the Molded. These are the standard zombies in the game, but they’ve got a twist. Imagine if the zombies had a baby with something... much worse. These things crawl out of the walls, do creepy things, and come at you with a speed that suggests they’ve never heard of personal space. You’ll spend most of the game thinking, “Do I really want to go through this door? Maybe I can just stay in this safe room forever, thank you very much.”

But wait, there’s more! The survival elements in Resident Evil 7 really kick in when you realize that ammo is as scarce as common sense in a horror movie. You’ll shoot your last bullet in a fight, and just as you think “Finally, I can breathe,” you’ll walk into a room and find, you guessed it, more Molded, and you’ll be stuck in that endless loop of running and hiding while praying you find a box of ammo somewhere.

The first-person perspective adds a whole new level of immersion—or, if we’re being honest, panic. You’ll find yourself frantically glancing around corners, dreading the moment when something jumps out at you. And let’s not forget the jump scares. Every time you open a door, you’ll hold your breath, praying that it’s just a normal room and not another terrifying encounter with something that’s definitely not supposed to be in your world. At this point, your heart rate is on a permanent sprint, and you’ll probably end up hugging your controller a little tighter than you’d like to admit.

And of course, there’s Ethan’s reaction to everything that happens: “What the hell is going on here?!” Yeah, Ethan, I don’t know, but it’s probably time to call in some backup, because you’re in over your head. If only someone had told you that it’s never just a missing wife. It’s always going to be much, much worse than that.

The best part? By the end of it all, you’ll be utterly exhausted—emotionally and physically—but still somehow proud of yourself for surviving. You’ll look back on it and think, “That was a terrible idea... but I’m so glad I did it.”

In conclusion, Resident Evil 7 is like a perfect mix of fear, survival, and screaming internally. You’ll spend your time running from enemies, searching for scraps of ammo, and wondering why you didn’t just stay home and play something relaxing. But when it’s all over, you’ll have that feeling of accomplishment—and a strong desire to never go near an abandoned house again.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a masterclass in survival horror and one of the best reinventions of a classic franchise in gaming history. By shifting to a first-person perspective and returning to its terrifying, atmospheric roots, RE7 delivers a gripping, pulse-pounding experience that revitalizes Resident Evil in the best way possible.

From the moment you step into the decrepit Baker estate, the game immerses you in its unsettling, claustrophobic world. The level of detail in the environments is astounding, with every flickering light, creaking floorboard, and grotesque piece of decor adding to the overwhelming sense of dread. The sound design is phenomenal, making every distant noise and whisper a reason to stop and listen before proceeding.

The gameplay perfectly balances horror and action. Resource management is tight, keeping you on edge as you scavenge for ammo, healing items, and key resources. The combat is visceral and satisfying, but never excessive—every bullet counts, and every encounter feels meaningful. The game’s emphasis on exploration, puzzle-solving, and tense, scripted sequences keeps the pacing excellent from start to finish.

The Baker family is one of the best horror antagonists in gaming. Each member is terrifying in their own way, from Jack’s relentless pursuit to Marguerite’s unsettling transformations. Their presence turns RE7 into a constant game of cat and mouse, making even simple tasks feel like life-or-death situations.

The story, while self-contained, weaves in just enough Resident Evil lore to satisfy longtime fans while remaining accessible to newcomers. And once you finish the main campaign, the additional modes and DLCs add even more replayability.

Resident Evil 7 isn’t just a return to form for the franchise—it’s a bold new direction that proves Resident Evil is still the king of survival horror. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer looking for a genuinely terrifying experience, this game is an absolute must-play.

When RE7 first was announced, the hype for it was [i]huge;[/i] or at least mine was; a return to form for one of the biggest horror franchises in gaming history? Sign me right up! 

When it finally came out in January of 2017, I got it for Xbox fairly close to its' release and I was absolutely blown away; but it's just crossed its' 8th anniversary since release, so does it still hold up now? Yes, yes it does.

The graphics look beautiful, the atmosphere is top notch and the gameplay is as tight as ever, blending the classic RE formula of puzzle-solving and nail-bitingly tense combat to make an experience that still proves entertaining to this day, with this being easily the most disturbing entry in the series to date.

With that being said though, there are a few gripes I have; the inability to skip most cutscenes really hurts repeat playthroughs and Madhouse difficulty runs; some weak dialogue here and there and a lack of enemy variety are certainly downsides, but far from being dealbreaking.

All the above has been written about the main campaign which shipped with the game at launch; I'll review the DLCs separately, of which there are 4; Banned Footage Vol. 1 & 2, Not a Hero and End of Zoe.

Overall, I highly recommend this modern-day classic of the survival horror genre, though I'd highly suggest getting the Gold Edition as it contains all the DLC expansions which expand the game a lot; maybe even wait for a sale if you care about saving some extra change.

Before you read this, this is a long review and will go over a lot of points and frustrations with the game.

To begin I will say what I think the game did right. The premise is interesting, some unkillable man with god-like regeneration, and so is the story for how far I got. The puzzles seem fun and interesting to beat. The levels are very detailed and look gorgeous. So is the concept of “playable tapes” (where you play as the character in the tape.)

But now to the bad stuff. (I play on normal)

The gameplay is all-round boring. The following AI is either too simple to dodge or too bullet-spungy to kill. The intro sequence after the dinner was fun with Jack following you through the starting area, and the destructible environment just showing his raw power. So is the garage part with the part where the car explodes and he casually walks out of it. As I said I have no problem with the story part of the game. The part that drives me crazy is a common theme in the resident evil franchise:

COMBAT IS BORING. DIFFICULTIES ARE LAZILY DESIGNED AND BOSSFIGHTES DON'T MAKE ANY SENSE.  

Fistoff the combat is boring. I have experienced this while getting the third dog-head for the main hall door. I had to go through the ‘processing area’ as the game referred to it and I had to kill a total of 9 ish enemies. When they are individual this is no problem, but once there are 2 it’s impossible to manoeuvre around them, this is especially frustrating when the game also sets a trigger for the enemies to despawn. (so they respawn full health).

The difficulties are lazy because the only thing that changes is that the enemies take more headshots. I expect 2 headshots, maybe normal, so it's a somewhat relaxing experience. But on normal you have to plummet half a magazine in just the most basic enemy.

The boss fights are frustrating as ♥♥♥♥. It's not clear how to beat them, you are nearly instantly dead and you can sometimes go on for 6 attempts without progress. This doesn’t just make them incredibly frustrating, but also feels random. Like you just have to be lucky for the game RNG to throw you two sixes. Then the gameplay is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring again. Since the combat is not engaging at all even during the boss fights. You have to do the same thing again and again, hoping they will work.

TLDR: This game is terribly frustrating on the ‘recommended difficulty’ and it really drags down every other aspect of the game. If you want to play it either do it on easy or don't do it at all if you want a relaxing experience.

I'm suspicious that the whole reason you have a guard button is because you move slower than a snail. Every single encounter has me using all my supplies. I feel like you are not supposed to fight most of the enemies and be sneaky. But the enemies are much faster than you and trying to out run them to find a place to hide is annoying. I put 20 rounds into one of the enemies and it was still alive. Tried to finish it with about 10-15 knife strikes and it was still alive and killed me. I mean damn! Then it didn't auto save between rooms and sent me back about 15-20 minutes. Damn! I was underwhelmed with the bosses. It's a die repeatedly until you find the trigger to win. Almost like a Dragons Lair type thing going on here. 

One example. Spoilers ahead: The first boss encounter the boss is immortal. You don't know that though. Die a few times until you figure that out. Then you discover a key. Try to get into the car and you get pulled out within a second. I'm not sure if after that is a certain death or not but it seems to be. Resident Evil 7 is a triumphant return to form for a series that had lost its way! 
By embracing its survival horror roots and introducing a bold new perspective, Capcom has crafted a chilling and deeply atmospheric experience that revitalized the franchise.
The most striking change is the switch to a first-person perspective, a move that heightens the sense of immersion and dread. 
From the moment you step into the decrepit Baker estate, the game grips you with its oppressive atmosphere. 
The house feels alive with creaking floorboards, distant footsteps, and grotesque horrors lurking around every corner. 
It’s a masterclass in environmental storytelling and mood-setting.
The gameplay returns to the essentials of survival horror: limited resources, tense exploration, and nail-biting encounters!
Every bullet counts, every healing item is precious, and every room you enter could hold a horrifying surprise. 
The puzzles, while not overly complex, are satisfying and harken back to the series’ earlier entries.
The Baker family serves as some of the most memorable antagonists in the franchise. 
Each member is uniquely terrifying, with Jack’s relentless pursuit and Marguerite’s grotesque transformations standing out as highlights. 
Their twisted personalities and gruesome appearances make every encounter with them a harrowing experience.
While the story isn’t groundbreaking, it’s effective in its simplicity. 
The game’s focus on protagonist Ethan Winters’ desperate search for his wife Mia adds an emotional core that keeps the player invested. 
The ties to the larger Resident Evil lore are subtle but rewarding, providing satisfying connections for longtime fans.
Visually, the game is stunning, with its photorealistic graphics and meticulously detailed environments adding to the horror. 
The sound design is equally impressive, amplifying the tension with every creak, groan, and distant scream.
If there’s any downside, it’s that the game’s final act leans a bit more toward action, which slightly undermines the tension built earlier. 
However, this is a minor flaw in an otherwise exceptional experience.
Resident Evil 7 successfully reinvents the series while respecting its roots. 
It’s a terrifying journey into the unknown and a reminder of why this franchise is a cornerstone of survival horror.

Give it a try (maybe when the game is discounted). While not the most memorable Resident Evil game, RE7 offers satisfying gameplay mechanics and pacing, even if the mid-to-late game becomes grindy and monotonous and game has some annoying shortcomings.

Story & Setting
The story begins with a fresh take, drawing inspiration from redneck horror movies, which seems like a departure from the usual Resident Evil formula. However, as the game progresses, the narrative shifts back to the typical Resident Evil trope of human experiments and bioweapons. The first area doesn’t mesh as well with the traditional Resident Evil vibe, feeling forced at times. Eventually, the game moves the characters into more conventional Resident Evil locations, which are not actually better executed, but almost too generic.

Gameplay
The gameplay has some notable highs and lows. First-person mode works well for the most part, but close combat feels clunky and poorly implemented. It’s especially frustrating for new players to figure out how to evade enemies; turning your back often results in unavoidable hits due to the enemies’ long reach and the difficulty in gauging your character’s collider size. Melee combat, in particular, looks and feels messy.

Inventory management, a staple of the series, feels slightly inferior compared to other recent Resident Evil games. The UI design choices are questionable. Also, pickups are frustratingly hidden in noisy the environment. It seems like the developers anticipated this, as they included "radar pills" to help locate items, but relying on these pills diminishes the experience. Upgrades also feel underwhelming and don’t integrate well with the story, which weakens their impact.

Pacing & Tension
As mentioned earlier, the game starts off with a Wrong Turn-style horror vibe, full of surprises and shock value. However, the mid-to-late game loses much of its momentum. It transitions into what feels like an average walking simulator with formulaic mutant 
ambushes that lack creativity and fail to maintain tension.

Boss Fights
The boss fights are largely forgettable. Early on, there are at least two melee battles that feel poorly executed and unengaging. The later bosses, while more traditional, are almost too easy on normal difficulty. Kiting and shooting at the boss from a distance was often enough to succeed, offering little challenge or variety.

Graphics & Atmosphere
The game starts strong with its visuals and atmosphere, but later areas become graphically monotonous. Chris’ story, included in the standard edition, is visually drab with its overuse of dark and foggy environments. This expansion feels like a generic shooter and doesn’t stand out as a meaningful addition to the game.

Audio
The audio design in Resident Evil 7 feels oddly handled, similar to some of the recent remakes. The stereo effect is overly pronounced, making certain sounds feel disjointed or muffled. One late-game weapon lacked reload sounds entirely, which seemed like a bug and disrupted the immersion.

Extras & Replayability
The lack of unlockable extras, such as 3D character models or concept art, is disappointing. These collectibles have been a fun and rewarding feature in Resident Evil remake games. Without them, and given the game’s other shortcomings, I don’t see myself revisiting this title.

Resident Evil 7, release in 2017, finally has lived and earn its title and direction as "survival-action [b]horror[/b]"

Please keep in mind:
- I never played the classic RE games (RE 6 a slightly bit)
- I've played RE 2 & 3 Remake years ago before my bro christmas gift RE 7 to me (Thank you bro)
- I still vaguely remember watching pewdiepie's RE7 gameplay, so certain elements like the garage fight with Jack was swiftly dispatched less than a minute as I accidentally turned right, saw, snatched the key, and drove the car.


[h3]First Impression[/h3]
This is the most [i]Resident Evil game I've ever experience[/i]. What I mean is that the horror element is absolutely very center stage (for the most part) throughout the entire game, compliment with its disgusting antagonist, character, and enemies compare to any RE games I've touched so far.

Interestingly, the combat mechanics is designed [i]to be intentionally clunky[/i]. The weapon accuracy recovery rate is slow, combined with enemy's wobbly movement and a resources limited situation tells player to be careful with their shots, instead of blasting all over the enemy.

The story pacing is great, not too empty between gameplay to be consider boring. Upon second recall, [b]the story actually isn't that long;[/b] [spoiler]Ethan finds Mia by going to the designated address sent by a distressed, Ethan goes to the said address, leads to the Baker's family, Ethan found out they're disgusting as ♥♥♥♥, Ethan briefed by Zoe for possible solution, Ethan attempt escape the house, Ethan must find the item for Zoe to create a cure, Ethan gone through troubles just to finally had the items, Ethan rescue Mia and Zoe,  Ethan choose one of them to cure, Ethan escape with either cured person to attempt finding help, ended up stopped by Eveline, bunch of flashbacks on how the hell did Baker family ended up like this and what happened to Mia before the distress call, Ethan kills mind-controlled Mia out of self-defense, Ethan thirst of vengeance, Ethan gets the ultimate cure for plot reasons, Ethan fights bunch of disgusting enemies just to reach Eveline, And finally, the final form of Eveline is killed with weapon that was dropped by Chris Redfield to Ethan. (Cut some details out, but basically, it literally plays out like this)[/spoiler]


[h3]Quirks[/h3]
After some searching, the game engine was designed to run on the Xbox One & PlayStation 4, basically indicates the game will have issues on higher FPS. (especially they literally build the RE engine, ground up from scratch. Crazy devs, you earn my respect) Things like double-hit from the enemy is extremely common, making normal difficulty slightly harder.

Second of all, the [b]4th wall breaking puzzle from Lucas party house[/b]. Its a cool concept that you can "cheat death" by remembering the password and prevent Ethan's imminent death. But the only problem they never consider is that: games at the time have measures to prevent "this" kind of cheating. Ended up players keep killing themselves, hoping to search for an answer, or smart enough to make it. Hence almost 50% of the player never finish the entire of the game.



Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a pretty interesting game that "nail and balanced" horror and action-survival together. Albit clunky at time, but the thrill of uncertainty keeps the game being frustrating.

This is my [b] first and currently the only RE game I own [/b] so I can't tell you if this is a good RE game but I can tell you if this is a good horror game.

First off the atmosphere is really good, sound design does a lot of the heavy lifting here, your own footsteps that sound eerily similar to the enemies' footsteps, the occasional metal clank that sounds just like doors being shoved open by the stalker enemy, all work towards putting you on edge. The music that plays when you enter the save room reassures you that you are safe in there, which makes leaving all the more scary.

The weapons and shooting are fine, I dislike that they capped the fire rate on the pistols and don't let me magdump the scary monsters but if you are playing optimally (aka aiming) then that's not a problem. Both shotguns are great, the flame thrower less so, the grenade launcher is also ok, the smg you get towards the end of the game kind of suck, the rate of fire is too low compared to it's damage, I have't tried the magnum yet because I couldn't find all the coins to unlock it.

This brings me into the some what frustrating exploration, the game is generous enough with health and ammo and running past enemies is always an option, but getting all the coins to unlock all the bird cages is much more akin to a chore than something that happens naturally. For example the very first coin is locked inside a drawer and to unlock that drawer you need to unlock in a VHS tape and the lockpick to unlock it is literally on the floor [i] 20m away[/i] from the drawer, you'll never see the prompt to pick it up unless you know it's there.

The game gets more action oriented towards the end which is quite cathartic as you mow down the monsters that gave you so much trouble during the early game.

The free DLC is nice but I don't like the game locking the story of a fairly important character behind a 15$ DLC, and Banned Footage 1 and 2 are really expensive at 10 and 15 bucks each.

The writing is...[i] ok[/i], just ok you will end up questioning the decision making of some of the characters and how some items ended up where they were.

Lastly the game is quite linear and while it doesn't impact it's spookyness in the first playthrough it gets quite repetitive in later ones, mostly because you can't skip in-game cutscenes (you can skip pre rendered ones) and you run really slowly so getting to one place to another is tedious.

Overall RE7 is a good game, the first playthrough will be the most intense as the game will throw plenty of curve balls to shake up the gameplay loop even if the surprise factor takes a sharp nosedive after the first time. For this reason I can only recommend it when it goes on sale for like 8 bucks.

What makes Resident Evil 7 stand out to me is that it feels like a soft reboot of the franchise. It shifts away from the over-the-top, action-packed bioterror warfare of previous entries and instead delivers a genuinely terrifying experience—one that constantly keeps you on edge, questioning what you can trust. Unlike the more cinematic, Hollywood-esque approach of Resident Evil 5 and 6, RE7 feels raw, intimate, and disturbingly real… until the ending, that is.

The moment they shoehorned Chris Redfield into the finale and threw in an action-heavy sequence, it broke the immersion for me. Killing Eveline was, by far, the weakest part of the game. It would have been far more unsettling if we had simply escaped, left without closure—never truly knowing if the nightmare was over or if the infection was still lurking somewhere, waiting.

After End of Zoe, it’s clear that Resident Evil 7 strayed so deep into psychological horror that it almost felt more like Silent Hill than a typical Resident Evil title. The eerie, decayed Louisiana plantation house, the suffocating atmosphere, the sheer spook factor—10/10. No chance they’d ever make another Resident Evil this terrifying again.

Resident Evil 7 is very different from the other games in the series. Most Resident Evil games offer a good mix of both horror and action, while in RE7 they went all out on horror. Which means a lot of walking through dark and cramped environments, a lot of jump scares, various chase and stealth sections. It's a lot more like Silent Hill and P.T. The story and setting are very different as well, it's basically Texas Chain Saw Massacre meets J-horror, and the connections to Umbrella, bioweapons and other RE mainstays are minimal. And finally, it's a first person game, and the protagonist is very slow and sluggish, which does add to the horror factor, but can also be frustrating.

You do get weapons after a rather prolonged intro, but the combat mechanics are rather weak. Your movement speed is greatly reduced when strafing or moving backwards, so if you want to make some space between yourself and the enemy, you have to turn around first before you can start sprinting. And since it's a first person game, you now can't see what the enemy is doing. But that's when you have the room to maneuver, because a lot of the time you don't, so you just try to get off as many shots as you can before the enemy closes the gap, and then block. Blocking is rather overpowered, and reduces all sources of damage by 75%. There's no timing element to it either, you just hold down a button.

To be perfectly honest, this game took me some time to get used to, as I was expecting something more like the RE2 and RE4 remakes. But once I did, I was able to enjoy it on its own terms. The American South setting, the Baker family and their past and present, are all very fleshed out, and the game can be very immersive. There's a fair amount of puzzles and inventory management, similar to other RE games. So it's not that different in the end, once you get used to the new camera perspective and the redneck setting.

Cons wise, the game does eventually devolve into a corridor shooter in its later parts when you leave the Baker estate, and those parts are rather monotonous due to the weak combat mechanics and very low enemy variety. There's also a pointless Bioshock style "choice" about 2/3 in (don't pick Z, you'll get a bad non-canon ending hours later).

The DLC is all excellent, and each one features completely new mechanics, enemies and story content. I highly recommend them all. Just don't look up the store descriptions or promo materials, as there are spoilers.

[b]Resident Evil 7[/b] is a game that redefined the series, bringing it back to its survival horror roots while introducing a bold new perspective. As the first Resident Evil game to feature a first-person view, it completely changes how the scares hit you everything feels more immediate, personal, and far more terrifying.

The game's story is fantastic it's captivating, full of intrigue, and ties into the overall Resident Evil story in a super clever way. For longtime fans, the connections to past games in the series are super satisfying, blending the old and new elements together seamlessly. But even if you're new to the franchise, you'll still find the story compelling and the characters unforgettable.

The Baker family is at the heart of what makes this game so intense. Each member is more disturbing than the last, and every encounter with them leaves you on edge. The environment, from the dilapidated Baker estate to the creepy hidden areas, feels alive and oozes the atmosphere. It’s a masterclass in tension-building, with every creak and shadow keeping you on high alert.

[b]What’s amazing about Resident Evil 7[/b] is how it balances the horror vibe with excellent gameplay mechanics. Resource management, exploration, and combat all feel perfectly tuned, creating a true survival horror experience. The game doesn’t overwhelm you with action but instead makes every bullet and decision count, heightening the stakes at every turn.

[b]Overall[/b], Resident Evil 7 is a triumph. It takes the best elements of classic Resident Evil and evolves them into something fresh, terrifying, and unforgettable. For anyone who loves horror games, this game is highly recommended.

The graphics are exceptional, creating a hauntingly immersive environment that perfectly complements the gameplay. The level design is equally impressive, with each area presenting unique challenges and surprises that keep players engaged. The game still has the classic Resident Evil experience, with puzzle-solving remaining a core feature. The story is well crafted and compelling, packed with twists and turns that keep me hooked. The jump scares are great, blending seamlessly with the other horror elements rather than feeling cheap or overused. Overall, I can say that Resident Evil 7 is the scariest entry in the series I’ve played so far, offering a thrilling and unforgettable horror experience.

There's much to be said about in-your-face horror--jump scares and scary men chasing you with chainsaws--but where Resident Evil 7 truly shines is in the quiet dread it instills in you. 

You play as everyman protagonist Ethan Winters, who receives an email from his presumably dead wife to come find her three years after her disappearance. His search leads him to an abandoned property in Louisiana, where it's immediately obvious that something is terribly wrong. This simple premise kept me pushing through every closed door and rushing around every corner despite, or perhaps in spite of, my deep-rooted human reluctance to do so.

And yet, for every imposing door and corner, there is a promise of another weapon, another story crumb, another advantage over your tormentors. RE7 makes you work for it, of course, but it only makes those brief moments of power all the more satisfying. It incentivizes you to explore every nook and cranny of each new area, especially the ones your instincts tell you to avoid at all costs. 

Even with my newfound familiarity with the game, I'd still be just as unsettled and terrified if I were to play again. I played Resident Evil 7 after playing "Village" as my first RE game and had an absolute blast. Fans of Last of Us, Plague Tale Innocence & Requiem (especially if you like fungal horror) will have a good time with this game. 

We get thrown into the mix pretty quickly; you're a guy looking for your wife whose been missing for 3 years after she sent you a letter and go out into the middle of butt-♥♥♥♥ nowhere looking for her, and end up trapped in a crazy cannibal families house. 

I loved the constant tension created through the game play, the atmosphere was tense, and I always made sure to have my gun raised when looking around a corner. Gameplay wise, there were blessidly few moment that felt like a walking simulator, though there is a significant amount of backtracking especially if you don't want to miss any of those lockpick boxes that have tons of ammo and other valuable resources. 

The different areas and levels of the game felt very unique, and distinctly different from one another. Enemies were introduced at a consistent pace, and the progression with weapons felt really smooth. 

I also like how the game explains that one of the family members is an engineer, which explains some of the more intricate puzzles in the house. 

I also played the free DLC after the fact, which took about an hour and a half and was a solid ride the whole way through that I thoroughly enjoyed. 

Now for complaints. Some of the puzzles / boss fights were not intuitive enough to the point where I needed to look up guides. On more than one occasion, I found myself out of ammo for all my weapons during a fight; even after picking up every breakable ammo crate and pre-crafting ammo before a fight as well. I miss a short or two here or there, It's not like I'm hitting headshots every time but I don't have some IGN reviewer aim. The issue is there ARE certain boss fights where you can't do anything against them unless you DO a specific thing, and the game isn't clear if you need to run, or if you should just keep fighting, and you'll usually learn this after a death or two. 

Another issue I experienced, whether a bug, or just a feature NOT built into the game, was the lack of an ability to "equip" a weapon to one of your 4 weapon slots in anywhere other than a safe-area. 
For example, you have 4 weapon slots keyed to the D-pad if you're playing on controller, or 1-4 if you're playing on PC. When you open your inventory, your options are to examine, use, or combine, but there's no option to "equip / assign" to an open slot. This led to multiple occasions where I had 1-2 weapons out of ammo, or having thrown all the grenades I have in that slot... and despite having a different type of grenade or a 5th weapon availible, I can't switch to it. I feel this would be a really easy solution to implement in the game, and the lack of it left me frustrated, for having to restart 2-3 times because of dying. 

Overall though, this is a fantastic game and well worth the price on a sale.
