This is definitely the best game in the franchise and one of the best horror games ever, even if it has its flaws. It's exactly what a survival horror game (with guns) should be. It's actually scary.

The horror is just amazing. The atmosphere, the enemies, the sounds, the music, the gunplay, the inventory management (makes you feel less prepared for potential fights) and just how claustrophobic everything feels work together to make the perfect blend of horror and fun. I can't forgive whatever part of the fanbase thought that this game was too scary, because that's exactly what makes it so good. The small scale also makes everything feel so personal. Every encounter matters and isn't just a roadblock towards the next area, even the "peon" type enemies.

This game has so much content and variety. Even if you're not willing to spend any money on DLC you still get to partake in the full main story because the first DLC is free. Even if they don't contribute that much to the story and it's debatable if they're even canon (I'd love to believe that they are), the rest of the DLC is definitely worth picking up, at least end of zoe if you want more of the main game. The banned footage DLC is mostly just bonus modes in case you're expecting more content like the main game, but they're still fun and they're not all mercenaries or get from point A to point B modes unlike the other games in this franchise.

This game however has its flaws:
-You can tell that they ran into time constraints in the later stages of the game which is why that section feels somewhat undercooked. It's not terrible, but not good either. It had the potential to be good though. I just wish that game companies weren't so greedy.
-You can't skip any cutscenes which lowers the replayability. Probably because they aren't videos because you can interact with them to some extent. Fortunately there is a mod for it that allows you to skip the most of them, but it shouldn't be necessary in the first place.
-This is more of a personal nitpick, but the unlockables are all items rather than settings. Weapons of course make sense, but this makes walking shoes feel terrible since the loss of an inventory slot for faster walking (not running) speed is just such a horrible trade off. I wish they were accessories instead like in RE4 or preferably settings.

I'm extremely biased towards this game and I'm definitely glazing by every margin. I honestly wish that capcom would do another reboot just so that I could get more RE7. Buy it, at least on sale. It's definitely worth it if you can handle the horror.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard – Family Dinner Gone Horribly Wrong

Resident Evil 7 is like crashing a family BBQ, except instead of hot dogs, you’re served mutated meat, and instead of fun games, you’re running for your life from a chainsaw-wielding psycho dad.

Ethan’s just trying to find his wife, but instead, he stumbles into the Bakers—a family that’s way too into "togetherness." Jack, the dad, is like if Uncle Bob from every horror movie had a superpower: the ability to come back to life and chase you with a shovel. And then there’s Mama Baker, who’s got a serious thing for bug-infested stew.

The whole family’s like a mix of Texas Chainsaw Massacre and that one creepy family down the street you avoid. You’ll fight, run, and scream "Why is this happening?" while wishing you’d just stayed home and ordered pizza.

It’s horrifying, disgusting, and laughably fun. 10/10 would survive a chainsaw attack just to meet the Bakers again.

Positives:
- The start of the game through the entire house, i'd say is done perfectly where it's a mix of the usual Resident Evil puzzles and light combat that works perfectly with the house's design and layout making it feel fair yet easy to navigate to the point where it's the best part of the entire game. It's fantastic and captivating design with boss fights that are serve their purpose well.

Negatives:

Uhh... I enjoyed this game. This is one of those times I wish Steam really had a "soft recommend" option or a rating system.

First up, the good—this game is a pretty cool horror experience with some great thrills. I didn't think the story was anything particularly special, but the cutscenes and gameplay are genuinely terrifying. I came to really enjoy the game's video tape system, which (very mild gameplay spoiler) [spoiler]lets you to play through certain areas in a "flashback"; this gives your player character big hints for approaching the same situations in present day[/spoiler].

Playing in first-person not only adds a layer of immersion but also makes combat more complicated, with a decent chunk of the game taking place in dark and claustrophobic areas. Jump scares were pretty well executed. Visual and sound design is overall amazing, and the game is very atmospheric.

I finished RE2, RE3, and RE4 remake before playing this one, and my big gripe with this game was the just strictly worse map in this entry. There's a map and objectives screen, and even then I found myself lost on a few occasions. The game takes place through a few different set locations, all starting off as small and closed off, allowing you to unlock more areas. Even though the next objective to get to is pretty linear, once the map has been fully opened up it can get annoying to traverse especially if you missed a puzzle or a key item.

Combat was also not my favorite. At this point I'm familiar with RE's signature style of creating tension through ammo scarcity (mainly just at the start), and that you don't [i]have[/i] to kill every enemy, but several enemies quickly began to feel like bullet sponges. Crafting materials are fairly abundant, but I found myself hesitant to use them on regular "mob" enemies due to how many hits bosses can take. Thankfully, some enemies despawn if you leave a certain area, and you can outrun many kids of enemies.

Overall, I'd still recommend this game as an entertaining horror experience; but even among other RE titles, I find it harder to recommend over titles like RE2 or RE4. Might revisit at some point to play some of the side content though, it looks fun 🎈

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard : By Triple F

"Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" marked a pivotal shift in Capcom’s legendary survival horror series, bringing the franchise back to its terrifying roots after several action-oriented entries. Released in 2017, "Resident Evil 7" was a reimagining of the core survival horror experience, with a heavy emphasis on atmosphere, exploration, and psychological horror. The game introduces players to a new protagonist, Ethan Winters, who arrives at a derelict Louisiana plantation searching for his missing wife, Mia. This installment is unique not only for its change in perspective, offering a first-person view for the first time in a main Resident Evil game, but also for its approach to horror, abandoning the action-heavy style of its predecessors in favor of tension-building and claustrophobic encounters.

From the outset, "Resident Evil 7" establishes a deeply unsettling tone, transporting players into the decaying, oppressive world of the Baker family’s plantation. The first-person perspective brings the terror up close, making every creak, shadow, and noise feel personal and immersive. The game’s environments are meticulously crafted, with dim lighting, dilapidated furniture, and organic, foreboding sounds creating an atmosphere thick with dread. The narrow hallways and tightly confined spaces contribute to a sense of isolation that heightens the suspense, allowing the player to become absorbed in the haunted-house horror. Unlike previous Resident Evil games that leaned into larger-than-life creatures and bombastic action sequences, "Resident Evil 7" thrives in the quiet, horrifying tension of lurking dread.

The storyline revolves around Ethan’s search for Mia, but it quickly spirals into a nightmarish descent as he encounters the twisted, unhinged Baker family. Each family member represents a distinct horror trope, creating a terrifying dynamic. Jack Baker, the patriarch, is relentless in his pursuit of Ethan, and his presence evokes classic “stalker” mechanics reminiscent of Resident Evil 3’s Nemesis, forcing players to be constantly on guard. Marguerite, with her insect swarm and creepy demeanor, introduces a grotesque sense of body horror, while the son, Lucas, brings a sadistic, Saw-like psychological terror into the mix with elaborate traps and twisted games. This diverse cast of villains keeps the gameplay and horror fresh, adding depth to the narrative while allowing the game to explore different horror subgenres.

The gameplay mechanics in "Resident Evil 7" strike a satisfying balance between survival and exploration. Limited resources require careful management, bringing back the classic Resident Evil emphasis on conserving ammo, health items, and inventory space. Puzzles are cleverly integrated into the environment, often challenging players to solve mysteries or locate hidden items to progress. These elements contribute to a slower, more methodical pace that allows the horror to take center stage. Combat is minimalist but impactful, with a focus on precision shooting and evasion rather than brute force. Weapons are sparse, and ammo is scarce, intensifying the tension of each encounter, as every bullet matters. This scarcity and vulnerability return Resident Evil to its horror foundations, where survival feels truly challenging.

"Resident Evil 7’s" graphics and sound design are key to its success in delivering an intense horror experience. The RE Engine, used for the first time in this installment, provides impressive, photo-realistic graphics, especially in rendering the grotesque textures and environments that define the Baker estate. Every room is rich with detail, from decayed wallpaper to grotesque mold-covered surfaces, creating a visually disturbing experience that complements the horror. The sound design is equally impressive, with eerie ambient noises, distant footsteps, and haunting background sounds that add a layer of suspense. Every creak of the floor or whispering wind intensifies the immersive horror, creating a soundscape that makes players feel genuinely vulnerable and alone.

In terms of pacing and progression, "Resident Evil 7" strikes a delicate balance, gradually increasing the stakes without ever overwhelming the player with action. The game’s structure keeps players on edge, alternating between moments of exploration, suspenseful puzzle-solving, and shocking encounters. This pacing ensures that each encounter feels purposeful and horrifying, building tension organically without relying on jump scares or over-the-top sequences. The story unfolds through found documents, video tapes, and environmental clues, inviting players to piece together the macabre backstory of the Bakers and the mystery surrounding Mia’s disappearance. The game’s narrative structure, in many ways, feels like a throwback to the original Resident Evil’s mansion exploration, keeping the story grounded in suspenseful discovery rather than outright exposition.

Despite its strengths, "Resident Evil 7" is not without a few limitations. The first-person perspective may alienate some long-time fans, as it alters the familiar mechanics and shifts the feel of the game. Some players also find the latter portions of the game, particularly the sections involving the Molded enemies, repetitive as the grotesque black creatures lack the same memorable quality as the human-like enemies encountered earlier. Additionally, the final act’s action-heavy sequences lose some of the tension that defines the earlier parts of the game, though they are essential to concluding Ethan’s ordeal. Nevertheless, these are minor drawbacks in an otherwise skillfully crafted horror experience that revitalized the series.

In short, "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" succeeds as both a fresh start for the franchise and a love letter to survival horror. Its first-person perspective, coupled with immersive graphics, sound design, and an emphasis on atmospheric terror, sets it apart from prior entries while staying true to the series' roots. By abandoning the large-scale action in favor of intimate horror, "Resident Evil 7" captures the essence of survival horror, immersing players in a deeply disturbing experience that’s both terrifying and exhilarating. This entry not only revived interest in the series but also laid the groundwork for future titles, proving that Resident Evil can evolve while still delivering its signature fear.

This was scary.  Genuinely scary.  Not just a little jump-scare here and there, not just a general "atmosphere".  Pure terror.  The first person perspective has you locked in.  Every corner rounded, every door opened, is a scare waiting to happen.  Critters are shambling in the dark, clambering down the hallways, giggling in the rafters above your head.  You feel like they're crawling under your skin the entire time you're playing this game, there is almost never relief.  The sing-song delight of every member of the Baker family who stalks you through the rickety house on the bayou can switch to rabid cruelty in an instant, just as their languid, shuffling movements will become wild, furious flailing as soon as they've got their sights on you. 

This is resident evil with the gameplay elements streamlined to perfection.  There is almost no fluff here.  Save your ammo, slowly unveil the map, solving puzzles along the way.  Find collectables and trade them in for more weapons.  The first-person perspective is incorporated into non-linear gameplay elements in creative ways, like the VHS tapes hidden all around the map.  They provide crucial information for the player, such as the locations of weapons, or solutions to puzzles.  They allow you a "trial-run" through various stages of the game, with its most clever implementation being the Birthday Party Escape Room.

The characters and story are also fairly decent.  Ethan Winters is probably the most punished Resident Evil protagonist.  Man keeps getting hurt.  Stabbed, dismembered, called hurtful names.  Honestly, everyone in this game has just been subjected to the most cruel and unusual torture.  Mia, Zoe and the rest of the Bakers are all manage to be sympathetic characters, which is impressive given the fact you spend most of the game wishing they'd burn in hell forever.  The game doesn't linger on its characters too long, and most of the time you're too adrenalized to care too much about what they're saying or doing, but the presentation and performances are strong.  Story is that there's a biohazard in the bayou.  There's more too it, and a fun mini-twist at the end that I thoroughly enjoyed.  It's a suitable vehicle for the scares, and that's really what Resident Evil story's are about. 

I really loved this game, it was a great time.  Definitely check it out.

There were reasons for that, obviously. More realistic approach in portrayal of everything, first-person view, getting back to horror roots of the franchise - those things were talked a lot. And when the game came out it turned to be a true hit and an impressive comeback for the franchise. And so, for such important moment in the history of series Capcom even decided to play with names. Both names of the series, the name for domestic Japanese market and the name for international market, were used in the actual name of this title. So, the game is called "Biohazard 7: Resident Evil" in Japan and "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" in the world, which is kind of cool and interesting. Speaking of the game itself I can only confirm that it's indeed a very solid title. And yes, it's true that in its gameplay this game reminds of very first Resident Evil game from 1990s!.. With the release of this game Capcom basically divided all future games of the series into two categories - new main franchise entries and remakes. In the Resident Evil universe, a world of body horror, sinister environments, depraved scares and terrifying monsters, two games stand out as the scariest: the Resident Evil Remake, and this one. So let's recommend this one.

Resident Evil VII: Biohazard's name says it all: The mystique and fear factor of the originals are back, and the focus of the plot, setting and horror is on a new Biohazard. The eponymous Biohazard, the Mold, aka. Eveline (long story, play the game to find out why it has two names) can best be surmised as Las Plagas on Steroids, being able to corrupt anyone into a sinister puppet for the person using it whilst bestowing upon them various zombie-like strengths and replacing their personality with a new one, and also being able to be used to create horrifying, deadly monsters. The Mold has taken up Residence (seewotididthere?) in a Louisiana household, and both protagonist Ethan Winters and the Player are in for the longest night of their lives.

From that summary, Resident Evil VII succeeds as a horror game: the eponymous Baker household is a nice throwback to the Spencer mansion whilst also boasting its own tricks and claustrophobic style, The Mold itself is the scariest of the various Biohazards focused on in the RE series, the main monsters (The Baker Family and their Molded creations) are freaky as all hell, and the game does everything in its power to crawl up on you and whisper "boo". Trust me, after the seinen action anime tedium of 6, this was much needed and playing 6 (and its superior predecessor 5) only increased my respect for VII's darker, twisted tone.

And the "game" part of "horror game" isn't slacking: Resident Evil VII is a compelling experience that always finds ways to vary up the gameplay, be it environmental hazards, creative puzzles, optional flashback levels or even the flow of combat. Location-based damage is the name of the game for the combat as the game recommends going for the limbs of the Molded along with their heads, so the combat feels strategic, something that gets better thanks to this being the game where they introduced dynamic difficulty, meaning no two encounters go the same and the player has to think up new strategies on the fly. Finally, the puzzles are some of the most creative in the series' history, with some truly fun solutions.

So, yeah. Resident Evil VII is the game that saved everything, and I think only mad, raving 6 Apologists who think the series should be tedious Gears of War action on steroids and don't get the point of the series* can hate it. It's a genuinely lovable game that is beautiful in all its dark, depraved glory. Sure, they fumbled the sequel with Village, but VII still stands the test of time as an intense, gripping survival horror game.

*Look, if you enjoy RE6, good on you. I'm not talking about you. I'm talking about the idiots who genuinely think that the time the franchise sold out to capitalise on Gears of War's success was the pinnacle of its existence. if you play 6, are fully aware of its faults, and still say "I'm a fan of Resident Evil 6", you have my undying sympathies.

Most Overrated Resident Evil Game of All Time

People love "Glazing" this game as if it is one of the most revolutionary games to ever be created that supposedly "saved" Resident Evil. This could not be further from the truth and here is my take. This game succeeded "Resident Evil 6" which was heavily criticized due to its emphasis on action than horror. Of course, Capcom being a great studio understood their audience and delivered something that was something more opposite to "Resident Evil 6". This game (Resident Evil 7) is a slow atmospheric survival horror game that goes back to the "roots" of Resident Evil which is something the fans wanted. While I can assure you the game is well developed it honestly feels generic when you see how many game are on the market that have the same slow first-person survival approach with an atmospheric feel to the game. The only difference between this game and the various other first person survival horror games you can find on the steam market is that it slaps the "Resident Evil" Franchise logo at the beginning and with high quality graphics which is the only reason it got any attention. Otherwise, if this game was developed by another studio I seriously doubt it would have gotten the attention as the Resident Evil franchise does in the Horror scene given its reputation.

The game itself and why it is absolutely overrated.

The game takes place in Dulvey, Louisiana where its an overly used area for horror films and video games to select any region of the south. This is simply for the location's murkiness and run down nature with is very generic and overused which makes is very unoriginal. We are introduced to a new protagonist with no history in the resident evil franchise, ethan Winters. We follow him on a quest to find his wife Mia who has gone missing and is believed to be found in this (Baker) house. Before moving along further how many narratives do we have where a husband searches for a missing wife in an abandoned house? Literally the most boring and generic mission we could have. The game is also limited to a guest house, a main house, and bits of a swamp area which was very unimpressive considering how much the R.E universe could have expanded given the track record. Even Resident Evil 6 was more expansive in the areas and locations it progresses to. It feels like a step backward to Resident Evil 0 where you are simply on a train. the game is in a small area fighting one family that somehow has manages to get away with everything up until this point in time. The game ends as you would expect it, but the worst part is Chris Redfield (which if you could even tell that was Chris props to you because that character design of Chris Redfield was so far off from previous versions i'm surprised so many people were quick to turn a blind eye) coming in to "save the day" with a crew at the most convenient part once you have completed the game. Seriously? They had an idea that all these incident were happening and didnt move in until the very end? I guess we could not have had a game if it actually followed logical sense. Nevertheless, the RE storyline was hardly even impacted as a whole with the addition of this game other than the introduction of the "mold" and any supernatural powers that can be added that are disclosed later in the franchise. Literally, The entire RE franchise storyline could easily survive without this game as its inclusion to the story is minimal and could be summed up in a character conversation. 

Conclusion

The game is fine for what it is whether it is simply for Horror or Resident Evil. The game was a safe bet from Resident Evil 6 and promised a good immersive game for a few hours of the day but that's it! Ethan Winters will have hardly served as anyone's favorite main story character and with the most typical location for a horror setting...a spooky abandoned house! If you liked the game that's great, in fact that's wonderful! Capcom can use the money to keep building the RE franchise and i'm sure any RE enthusiast will welcome more well developed games in the franchise. I can't imagine a true RE enthusiast that would think otherwise! In the end, i'm simply grateful Resident Evil has continued thus far but I will be placing this game as the most overated Resident Evil game of all time with the most boring main character to receive not just one but two resident evil games and will never come close to Leon, Jill, or Chris that is simply a fact. Thank for reading, have a great day! <3

It's fair to say that I'm not a big survival horror guy. But, I am a Resident Evil fan. I went into this with fairly high expectations. How could I not given the reviews? I also went into it because I want to play Resident Evil 8, but thought I better play this first. Now that I have, completing the game in 8 hours and 20 minutes, I hope I'm more impressed with Village.

The game starts off strong. The atmosphere is oppressive, it's incredibly tense, the sound is perfect. It's genuinely scary, you have no idea what's going on, you don't know what you'll encounter. Was that noise ambient, or was it an enemy? But, as the game goes on, you start seeing the strings, the seams, the artificiality of it, and it's hard to ignore. Eventually, you have to make a decision: play along with the charade, or take advantage of what you've learned.

The enemy AI is absolutely terrible (referring to the Baker family). They will look you dead on but won't "spot" you for some inexplicable reason. They're slow and make plenty of noise. They very quickly stop being any kind of legitimate threat and turn into speed bumps in your path. What's worse, they become very goofy later on, to the point where I was laughing. And maybe that was the point, but I feel like it wasn't.

The standard enemies, which are few and far between and have very little variety, despawn when you leave their area and they never return. I learned this by accident, and it absolutely killed my incentive to even engage with them. Why bother? Maybe I'll need ammo later. And you will absolutely need ammo later because the game ends in a very linear shooting gallery, which was disappointing beyond belief. It not only fails to play to the strengths of the early game, but it's painfully boring and brightly lit. It just flat out sucks. This game's ending sequence should have been completely thrown out and rebuilt from the ground up.

The final boss is the easiest in the game, and isn't really a boss. It's like a cutscene that you shoot at. It's the lowest moment in a game that has a fairly steady decline in quality.

The puzzles are completely nonexistent. They require no thought and aren't very interesting.

The game is just too easy. Too easy to exploit, too easy to bypass challenges, too easy to win. The game really should allow you select something harder than normal from the beginning. You never have to make sacrifices, you never have to plan your route, you never have to leave items behind, you never have to manage an inventory, you never have to worry about ammo, you never have to worry about doing the right or wrong thing. This isn't a game I felt like I was surviving, I felt like I was flourishing. So many strong health potions, more bullets and shotgun shells than I would ever go through, tons of weapons and lots of crafting components on reserve.

It all makes a lot more sense to me when considering the game has a VR component, which perhaps guided a lot of the decisions around puzzle design, combat, movement, etc.

So, would I recommend this game? I don't know, not to anybody with my preferences. It seems like most people like it, but I really wasn't impressed. I thought it was slow, boring, easy, and the best parts are right at the beginning. This is another game with glowing reviews but low clear rates (according to Steam's global achievements).

So this is just an impression I had after 2 something hours in the game and watching a few videos / reviews. If I ever get back to it, I'll update my review, but right now I don't think I will.

First I want to say that it's not objectively a bad game and the reviews speak for it. I am sure it has its deserved place in the respective genre. But it feels terrible to me because I was expecting a Resident Evil game which this is just.. not.

My major pain points:
[list]
[*]The story and main character - the other Resident Evil games were Zombie games. The goals made sense, protecting people and fighting the baddies who caused it/try to profit from it. The setting was consistent, and so were the various characters: A more or less highly trained agent who is reasonably well equipped. Here you're just a dude walking into a house of perverted crazy people like the cliché horror stuff where you could just scream from a mile away [i]'don't do this, stupid'[/i]. In the other games it was actually your job to do this, which felt a lot better than being a poorly prepared dumbass.
[*]Interactive cut scenes - ugh.. I know that's part of the (body) horror experience, but I really don't enjoy how I feel barely in control of my character. How I can't fight or dodge in certain scenes and just have to watch. Someone said that the whole game feels like a tutorial and yeah.. it's oddly slow and feels very guided. There are still parts that are fun though. Some moments where you just run around and solve puzzles which reminded me of RE2R, but not enough to keep me attached. I rather go back to playing RE2R.
[*]Body horror - I'm not a fan of body horror in general and I am not a fan that Resident Evil took that turn. But not only that, I feel like the body horror doesn't even feel like a threat. Cutting off limbs and re-attaching them? Sorry but that killed all the fear and threat because nothing matters. I wouldn't even call it survival horror because it made me feel like I wouldn't die, but rather think the game would just come up with something new and ridiculous so I can keep going and get chopped up some more. The tension in a survival horror should be that you want to protect your main character from harm, but what's the point if I can just pop that limb back on? That's stupid. Actually worse than stupid, because [spoiler]it has the vibe of a fetish, some mutilation kink and that's just so gross I can't even put it in words[/spoiler].
[/list]

tl;dr
To me, it seems little bit like Resident Evil died the moment Albert Wesker died. It's just not the same. I'm happy for everyone who enjoys this, which seems to be the majority, but it's just not my cup of tea.

Resident Evil 7 returns the series to it's horror roots with a fresh presentation that will leave you feeling a little bit unsettled. Departing from the static and over the shoulder camera systems of the franchise's past, this entry introduces a first person perspective, for what can be an overwhelmingly intense experience at times. 

There is enough silence and stillness throughout the Baker Plantation to fill you with a strong sense of paranoia which will force you to walk down every hallway, open every door and take every corner very slowly and very carefully. For some, there are even some well executed moments that might trigger significant claustrophobia. Should you be easily spooked, disgusted or if you are afraid of the dark, consider yourself warned.

Featuring a simple story and controls to match, it's a satisfying amalgamation... a fitting love letter to various and certain elements of the genre's past and present, with strong ideas for it's potential future.

🎨 Graphics & Atmosphere
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard looks really good, especially for when it came out.

The environments carry the experience. Everything feels dirty, detailed, and uncomfortable in a way that actually works. The house alone does a lot of the heavy lifting.

It’s one of those games where the setting is the horror.

🎭 Ethan Winters (Yeah… Him)
Ethan Winters might be one of the most questionable protagonists I’ve played.

The guy just keeps going no matter what happens to him. It’s impressive, but also kind of ridiculous.

There were multiple times I wished he would just stop talking. Or at least say less.

🎮 Gameplay Loop
The gameplay is solid.

A lot of it comes down to:

Running when you need to
Conserving ammo
Picking your fights carefully

You’re not overpowered, and that helps the tension.

The game does a good job making you feel like every bullet matters.

🧩 Puzzles
Puzzles can get annoying.

Nothing new for this genre, but if you’re not paying attention, you’ll end up wandering around longer than you want to.

This is one of those games where having a guide nearby isn’t the worst idea.

👻 Enemies & Variety
Enemy variety is lacking.

You’ll see the same types over and over, which takes away from the fear over time.

That said, it’s still a nice change from the usual zombie focus the series is known for.

🔊 Horror & Jumpscares
The game does land its scares.

There were definitely moments that got me, especially with the volume up. It relies on tension and sudden moments more than constant pressure.

When it works, it works.

🎭 Story
The story is… fine.

It gets the job done, but nothing really stands out. It feels a bit generic, and I never fully bought into Ethan’s motivation.

Still, it’s enough to keep things moving.

🏆 Final Thoughts
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is solid, just not perfect.

Strong atmosphere, decent gameplay, and some genuinely good horror moments.

But the lack of enemy variety and a pretty average story hold it back.

6.5/10.
Worth playing if you’re into horror or the series, just don’t expect it to blow you away.

[h3]An intense horror adventure set in a remote and creepy location[/h3]

[i]Biohazard[/i] is the very first title of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] saga that I played, therefore I had no prior knowledge of the main storyline, and this for me was a great introduction to [i]RE[/i]. Set in the remote countryside of Louisiana, we will portray Ethan, a guy that is going to look for her wife Mia, after she went missing. The good thing is that you really do not need to play the previous chapters in order to understand the plot, as this is a self-contained story that is loosely connected to the previous chapters only at the very end. 

Capcom managed to create a creepy environment with plenty of claustrophobic spots. The sound design is amazing and very often we will hear strange noises that constantly put me on the verge, as I wondered if I was safe, or if there was someone else in the room. The puzzles are well done and not too tedious to complete. Most of the time you just need to find a key to open some doors or complete a certain combination in order to unlock a certain passage. However, the levels are designed in a way, where it is easy to miss certain details, even if the environments are small. It can get a bit tedious at times, however finding the solution of a certain enigma is rewarding.

[h3]Good combat and inventory system, that force you to manage wisely your resources[/h3]

Along the adventure we can collect resources such as medikits, weapons and ammo, but these are limited and not always easily accessible, therefore the game pushes to manage the items wisely. We cannot go in just blasting our guns. Wasting bullets can be very problematic. It is necessary to aim properly at the enemies and to make sure that our shots are successful. This can be challenging and at times we will find ourselves constantly swamped by enemies with not enough ammunition and need to rely on knives, which is not ideal.

[h3]Final verdict[/h3]

I definitely recommend this game to all the horror lovers that never approached the RE saga: you have the possibility to experience a prestigious franchise with modern and compelling mechanics, explicit graphics and good animation. I might give a chance to the other chapters in the future.

I think I actually got a little ill the first time I played it. And nothing makes me sick. My only complaint is that the game is too short. I wanted more to play. You can finish the game in eight hours. But you get more experience in those eight hours than 4, 5, and 6 combined.

I've been playing through the 'modern' RE games since RE8 was released: RE2R, RE3R and RE4R. I finally decided it was time for RE7. 

Serving as a soft-reboot after RE6 sent the franchise completely off the rails, RE7 is a smaller, more stripped-back survival horror experience that focuses on scares/atmosphere over action. 


Positives:
- The first half of the game is legitimately scary, it's like creeping your way through a series of virtual haunted houses. It gets sillier as it goes on, and as is (always?) the case with these games, the action is amplified in later chapters. 
- The story is pretty good imo. I hadn't been spoiled prior to playing and it more than held my interest.
- Loads of extra content, I haven't started looking at it yet, but there are a bunch of DLCs included with the version I bought.


Meh:
- I found RE2R more consistently scary, personally.
- Despite struggling early on, I had sooo much ammo saved up by the end of the game, which speaks to a resource/enemy balancing issue imo (played on Normal).
- Unlike RE2R, RE3R, and RE4R, I don't feel much desire to replay this one, even though I enjoyed it.
- Personally not a fan of the 'Psychostimulant' system, I prefer the rooms changing colour on the map to let you know if you've missed any collectables (you 100% will miss things without a guide imo). 
- Chris Redfield's re-design is so terrible that they hit CTRL+Z for RE8, lol


Negatives: 
- No 21:9 support. Kinda insane that this game was updated with Ray Tracing, but you still have to mod support in for a pretty basic PC feature.
- No DLSS. You get RT, but you're stuck with AMD's comparatively sh*tty upscaler to claw performance back (if you need to).
- Graphically this (2017) game is quite dated, despite the RTX update. I suspect the budget was quite small as it was something of a gamble after RE6 crashed and burned? The lighting is EXTREMELY dark in places, which is obviously partially in place for the creepy factor, but I think it also 'conveniently' covers some pretty shoddy textures and a general lack of high frequency detail. It looks overall 'good', but there are some very noticeable rough spots that I feel take you out of the experience. Compare it to other big studio games from this year and it has aged worse imo.
- To elaborate on the above, one of the things I found most jarring was the cruddy hair and facial animations/lip sync of certain characters that shove their faces RIGHT INTO THE CAMERA. It's obviously intended to be scary, but it just comes across funny in places. Mia's hair especially is so awful looking that it's distracting whenever she's on screen.


Overall I'd recommend this to fans of the franchise and survival horror, but I think I prefer RE2R, RE4R and RE8 over it.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard was born through a half-decade hiatus following Resident Evil 6. RE6 infamously went so off-the-rails that it fully dried the franchise out and necessitated a soft reboot with the creation of a new storyline with a new tone, protagonist, setting, and even game engine. It's safe to say Resident Evil 7, while being a very flawed game in many ways, unquestionably saved Resident Evil, and is easily the most important title in the franchise (Unless you want to argue the meta "RE wouldn't exist at all without the original 1996 game" nonsense. Either way, RE7 is the primary reason Resident Evil is what it is today). This review will be cut into four sections: Graphics & Audio, Gameplay, Story, and Final thoughts. Okay, time to complain.

[b]NOTE: Resident Evil 7 is a game very heavy on story, and I will include quite a bit of information pertaining to it. I won't be censoring anything this time, but I'll try to keep most spoilers contained in the Story section. You're still free to ignore this review for that reason, but know that I think that this is a absolute must-play for horror fans.[/b]

[h1]Graphics & Audio[/h1]

Environments in Resident Evil 7 appear desaturated, grimy, and a bit blurry at all times, which has caused a bit of contention among players as to whether it's intentional or not. The game is set in a dingy, mold-infested house in a Louisiana bayou in the middle of nowhere, and I think they intentionally went for a VCR-y, Texas Chainsaw Massacre-adjacent look to the game, which is fitting and very beneficial to the atmosphere they tried to go for. This is the first Resident Evil game to use photogrammetry, and also has the highest number of unique assets of any Resident Evil game ever, a feat made even more impressive when realizing this is the smallest Resident Evil team for a mainline game ever. For a team of only around 120, there has to be a few thousand fully unique objects in this game, which is insanely impressive. The models for the human characters, and the various Molded and bosses are well-made, deliberate, and greatly add to the fear and dread you'll feel playing this title. As for audio, I think it was handled very well. Voice acting is, for the most part, top-form, with the Bakers in particular very quickly becoming some of my favorite antagonists in this entire series primarily because of their voicework. You can tell immediately that the virus they're carrying drastically changes their behavior, NOT their mannerisms; they feel like the Bakers even when they're murderous sadists. Mia and Eveline are alright, but my only big issue is you: Ethan Winters. I don't inherently have an issue with Ethan, but his voice actor at the absolute least should have redone some lines. Ethan gets beaten and maimed by horrific monsters constantly in this game, something he has NEVER experienced, and yet seems oddly indifferent or silent at some points. The atmosphere and tone is hurt greatly when the protagonist's characterization is so weak compared to the brilliant villains in this game. I understand that Ethan is intentionally basic to act as a surrogate for the player to insert themselves into the world, but if he's going to be so integral to the story and lore, he needs SOME better characterization. I don't have any outstanding issues with this game's sound design, as I think most every little sound is at least beneficial to the game's atmosphere or fear factor. Overall, very solid graphics and audio.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Gameplay, and more specifically movement and combat, was greatly simplified from the previous RE, with only basic first-person shooting/aiming, walking, jogging, crouching, and the new block. I think the block is a cool, unique edge to the combat loop that reflects that Ethan is a completely normal person that can't dodge or parry, and I think the simple movement and combat helps to let you focus more on your surroundings and the level design of the Baker house. Speaking of, the Baker house is an incredible location for a RE game to take place, in a franchise KNOWN for its amazing locations. The Baker house has fantastic design, detail, and verticality, with intricate hiding spots and secret areas, but still to an extent feels like a realistic, huge house an extremely rural family like the Bakers would work hard to build. The ship seems to try to capture the same lightning in a bottle the Baker house did, but didn't do it as well. The pacing of the ship segment is already a mess, and the level design being frustrating and more linear in the ship didn't do it any favors. Enemy design is good, but limiting from there being so few regular enemy types in the base game. There are literally four [i]fully[/i] unique basic enemies. Bosses start phenomenal, and only slightly drop off in quality near the end. The only "bad" boss is Eveline, which is more of an epic, scripted finale than anything. Human Jack has created some of the best boss fights in the franchise, Marguerite is a harrowing endurance battle that'll keep you attentive and on your toes for a long time, and mutated Jack is the obligatory big hunk of meat boss that you'd expect in any RE game. Every difficulty is fair, especially Madhouse Mode, which is my favorite hard difficulty in any game I've played (For the record, I haven't played One Dangerous Zombie from RER, which I sometimes hear is better). The amount of changes to gameplay, level design, and strategy makes Madhouse a huge challenge, but an experience I think is FAR better than the default difficulty. I won't go into too much detail so you can discover the game yourself, but I think this game is extraordinarily fun and replayable (get the cutscene skipper on Nexus for repeat playthroughs, though).

[h1]Story[/h1]

RE7 is a much needed self-contained story that still ties itself into the Resident Evil canon in its final moments and DLC. To summarize, Ethan Winters is our protagonist who, after his wife, Mia, went missing several years prior, gets a sudden message from her to come and find her. He's led to a very rural area of Louisiana, to the property of the Baker family, who, unbeknownst to Ethan, has been afflicted with a mold virus that we later learn originated from a bioweapon named Eveline, developed by The Connections, a BOW company that we learn Mia worked for. Ethan, by luck and adrenaline, survives tons of encounters with the Bakers' victims, who have been contaminated with the same virus and turned into mold monsters, and, with help from Zoe Baker, the only still sane member of the family, ends up killing Jack and Marguerite and creating a vaccine for Mia, who has the same virus, as the story progresses. Ethan and Mia meet up again, canonically Ethan chooses to use the only remaining vaccine on Mia (Though there's a random choice system there for some reason where you can opt to give the vaccine to Zoe), and they are attacked by Eveline on a boat that they try to ride to safety, being left on shore at the base of the ship Mia and other employees of The Connections used to transport Eveline. This later third is a mess, with a huge flashback section that is out-of-place and not really necessary. Eveline isn't a very deep character, we don't need a (very boring) third of the game dedicated to her escape on the ship. The ending is epic, satisfying if you choose the canon route of curing Mia, and is left slightly open ended to hint at a sequel to Ethan's story and allows there to be story continuation DLCs in this game. I think this story is overall pretty solid, though not really close to the best story in the franchise, and is built on and improved in the sequel.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

RE7 is a paramount title in the RE franchise, and, though far from perfect, is still carried by incredible villains and atmosphere and a game absolutely worth your time if you like Resident Evil, horror, or even games in general. Overall, I give Resident Evil 7:

[h1]TLDR: RE7 is a return to form for the RE franchise. It's a fantastic Survival Horror experience. Great story, great atmosphere and setting with a well-polished gameplay. It surpassed my expectations, and I don't think we'll ever get another RE that's so close to its origins. Strongly recommended to any Survival Horror fan![/h1]

Resident Evil 7 is proof that sometimes, you have to fail to succeed. After the success of RE4, every new entry aside from the Revelations spin-offs were to be third person shooters with a strong emphasis on the “shooting” part.

Being a survival-horror fan, I had lost any interest about the series since RE4, and RE7’s demo did nothing to win me over. Was it a reboot, a sequel, a “re-quel” perhaps?
And then, I started hearing good things about it. Friends told me that I absolutely had to give it a shot, because I was missing out on a great survival horror. 

They were right. Resident Evil 7 is one hell of a survival horror game.
A lot of its core elements are pulled straight from the classic RE games: inventory management, few but strong enemies, puzzles, backtracking and a strong atmosphere to keep you on edge at all times, but there are also heavy actions sequences and intense set-pieces. 
Contrary to many horror games around that time you can fight back with a vengeance, though they managed to do that without compromising on the horror aspect. Getting that balance between tension and release is not an easy task – and to be fair, the game gets very shooting heavy towards the end – but they pulled it off for the most part.

Unlike previous entries in the series, RE7 has a great story. It’s immersive, mysterious and most of the characters are well written and well acted. There are ups and downs and contrivances, but it’s still a massive improvement over previous titles. 
One half of the DLCs is basically more of the same, but the other half is geared towards action-horror fans, and they’re all really good. I appreciate the fact that they kept the most insane stuff for the DLCs and not the main game.

With all of that said – yes, RE7 is a return to the survival-horror formula with a modern twist, but it’s not all sunshine and rainbows. I do have a few gripes with it.

The Standard difficulty gets way too easy due to the use of autosave. Hard mode aka Madhouse has manual & limited saves, with a tape recorder acting as the typewriter of old – the problem being that it is intended as a “Remix” mode of sorts. It changes enemy and key item placement, and assumes you know the ins-and-outs of combat. In other words, it’s meant for returning players and not for a first playthrough. There’s a pretty big gap in difficulty between Standard and Madhouse, a Standard difficulty mode with limited saves would’ve alleviated that significantly.

Then there’s a general lack of variety, which gets worse by the end of the game. There’s only 4 types of enemies and there’s that one type of puzzle repeated a dozen times throughout the game. 
The game offers a branching path at one point, but it’s really meaningless as it is a clear choice of good vs bad ending. 
And then there’s that one section of the game that’s just annoying and out of place, if you know, you know.

I really enjoyed RE7 and I’m glad I gave it a fair shake. It single-handedly revived my interest in the series and gave me high hopes for future titles. I haven’t played RE Village yet, but it doesn’t seem to be the sequel to 7 I expected it to be. But, at least, survival-horror fans of old got something new to play for a change, so there’s that – and there would be no RE2R as we know it without RE7.

I strongly recommend RE7 to any Survival Horror fan. It looks great, it runs great (Stick with the “DX11” version if your GPU can’t handle ray-tracing), it has a good story, great atmosphere and quite a bit of content. 

Oh and that save room theme? One of the best of the entire series. That has to count for something.

Absolute masterpiece of survival horror and one of the best in the franchise.
The atmosphere and setting are great, it was interesting to see the entire game take place in a (compared to other games in the series) small property in Louisiana. It was fun to see wehere the game took you and how they would expand the farm concept, very cool.
The gameplay is extremely fun, it gives off RE1 vibes with you going back and forth in a tight location. 
It´s very rewarding to get items to defend yourself against monsters like the shotgun, and also it´s very interesting to see the game hide useful resources in unconventional places. Normally they would be inside a closet or something, but in RE7 you can look under chairs, tables, beds or in small corners and find something, you feel like a mouse looking for small pieces of cheese and makes the place feel real and alive, you´ll be pressing E against walls while crouching ALL THE TIME to get something.
Resource management wise, i have to say, i was kind of dissapointed. Maybe it´s because im used to resource management games but during my 2 playthroughs of the game (one in standard difficulty and the other in madhouse) there wasn´t a single moment where i was actively looking for ammo, or had to flee enemy encounters because i was empty. AT LEAST IN THE HOUSE, because this game has another (smaller) section, the boat.
I hated this, in my first run it was fine and lore-wise it was very interesting, the plot twist of Mia working for this game´s evil company (the connections) was cool, however, gameplay wise it´s soooo boring, there´s nothing going on, it´s just you walking endlessly from one end to the other looking for the key item you need, it´s not an open section like the rest of the game, which makes it feel linear and boring.
The boat setting is boring too, it´s just the most nothing atmosphere ever, it´s just a generic dark metal ship and that´s it.

One time i had very few bullets left and i kept dying, and since i didn´t reach the next autosave, sometimes i would lose like 5 minutes of progress, so i´d have to repeat the section from the start, again, with the few bullets i had left.
Another complain i have with the game is the lack of enemy variety, there´s only 4 types of enemy (i don´t count the alligators from the dlc) ((the bugs don´t count either)) and while their designs are kinda cool, they sadly were a massive letdown.

It´s interesting, it´s tragic, the dialogue is fun and well written. Resident Evil 7 is simultaneously a return to the focus on horror and a big shift in how it’s presented. 

After three years of being missing Mia Winters writes to her husband Ethan to come pick her up from Dulvey, Louisiana. Despite the message being very suspicious, the man decides to investigate and falls into a trap set by the Baker family. What happened to this place and how does he make it alive out of it? 
I like the setup of the story. You delve into the rural outskirts of Dulvey in search of your lost wife. The place is falling apart and surrounded by swamps. Scenario in which you need to work hard to escape. The atmosphere, the setting, the story of the infected family – it all makes this game a more unique RE installment. 
RE7 is a shift from its predecessor that is visible from the beginning. The game is more atmospheric and realistic, you can see that the action has been toned down quite a bit – there are no fan kicks, no suplexing zombies. Ethan is just a helpless civilian with no actual combat training. The first-person perspective only amplifies the fear of turning every corner and restricts the awareness of everything around you. The first impression this game gives you, really does feel like a completely different franchise. 
Not for long though, with time stuff happens and you just go “oh, it’s Resident Evil alright”. Mia throws you around with supernatural strength, Ethan throws dry-ahh quips after defeating monsters. Then you have Chris and Joe in the DLCs, just punching s.hit around [b]and I’m pretty sure they aren’t mutated or anything like that.[/b] It’s not bad or something, I love it personally, it’s just kind of off with how realistic the game wanted to be. 
The worst thing about the plot however is Ethan. Not only the guy seems pretty unfazed by getting his hand cut off, the fact that he just murdered a guy with a chainsaw, the general situation of him having to fight for his life all the time, but he’s trying to be cool about it too. I don’t see any charisma in his “and stay dead” poorly delivered lines and it also doesn’t work with the “I’m just a random, terrified civilian” persona that they tried to go with. He even looks like typical a Greg in a shirt. It’s RE, it’s not that bad, but his reactions to stuff around him feel unnatural and he’s a very uninteresting protagonist. 
He’s in the middle of the Funny/Cool -------- Realistic/Helpless horror protagonist spectrum – not leaning into any direction it’s just bad man. I’m just going to tell myself that he’s weird because of the mold infection or smh. 
I also don’t understand the ending choice. [spoiler]I feel bad for Zoe, sure, but picking her is a non-canon, bad ending in which both girls die anyway and you get to fight Mia third time in the same exact way.[/spoiler] A completely unrewarding bad ending which just feels off when you choose it. Also, I’m getting grabbed and Zoe goes “use one of the ONLY TWO serums that we have on it to kill it” and then 20 seconds later she says “oMg, WhAt r wE gOnN dO” like it wasn’t her who suggested to waste one. 

As a survival horror gameplay goes, it’s really good. You move around the main location avoiding dangers or eliminating them if you have resources to do so. You explore looking for supplies and make decisions regarding inventory management. More weapons and ammo or heals and key items? You also solve cool puzzles placed around the house (Ethan’s “Who builds this shi.t?” is one of the few things that I’ve agreed upon with him). The item box makes a return and on harder difficulties you need cassettes to save your game, kind of like the original ink ribbons. The shooting feels good, but as always you need to get into the rhythm of enemies' headbob.
The whole “Mold Biohazard” situation is a good gust of fresh air, although the enemy types and their designs are not too diverse. Well, there is the fat guy, but we don’t talk about him, I hate him. 
The game has a fair share of replayability, the challenges not only give you achievements, but also unlock items for next playthroughs, like walking shoes, x-ray glasses, defense items, weapons or infinite ammo. 
RE7 features many DLCs with most of them being pretty cool. Banned Footage series are one-off adventures with their own twists, like trying to escape the bedroom, while simultaneously keeping everything how it was when Marge comes to check on you. We have Jack’s birthday which is an arcade parody mode. Not a Hero is about Chris hunting down Lucas, with more professional approach to combat. The best is probably End of Zoe which explains what happens after the main events and lets you just beat the s.hit out of molded with your bare fists. 

The game has realistic sound design, with the house making noises, cracking and stuff. However, the audio leveling is weird or at least I couldn’t get it to work properly. Some things are too quiet, some that are louder take you by surprise. Also, some dialogues just feel weirdly muffled. The music is great, [i]Main Menu[/i], [i]Saferoom[/i] and [i]Floating In-Between[/i] are all great tracks. 

The game looks great and realistic, but sometimes if you look closer at the backgrounds for example, you can see that there are a lot of extremely low poly/low-resolution objects, mostly in cutscenes or far-away. They tend to be kind of concealed in all these found footage-esque filters, but it’s still visible at times. Aesthetically, it’s a very atmospheric and climatic environment to be surviving in. 

Biohazard 7 turns its focus back on horror and is a refreshing formula for the series. While the voice lines and writing of some scenes could’ve been done better, it certainly got the franchise back on track. Also, it is [b]comical[/b] how many times Jack comes back to life.

While I never played the classic PS1 Resident Evil games, I was more invested in its universe's lore than playing those games. And I was not a fan of when RE went more and more into arcady action while horror took the furthest backseat, if even that.

And then Resident Evil 7 was released, and I found enjoyment (at long last) while playing RE game. It comes as no surprise that RE7 is my favorite in the series! Even though Village has my Big Titty Mommy waifu, and the Soldats... I cannot rate it higher than this. More so, because it leans towards action (and treasure hunting) like in RE4, forgetting the horror in the process but for a single section (which has no replay value). And also RE7 is a complete package, in regards to content.

[h1]Pros[/h1]

First-Person perspective, slower movement and tighter action, which makes defeating just one Molded or a few of them more rewarding. And just being patient with precise headshots is much more satisfying, unlike in some RE games where you unload all handgun bullets into basic enemies' noggin to no effect (looking at you, RE2 Remake). Knife is surprisingly effective in tactical instances when dealing with these super-organisms.

And being slower movement-wise, you find items where you may not be normally looking at while exploring the Baker House.

Speaking of items: Molded don't drop any of them. Which is more in keeping with the survival aspect. The game doesn't tell you that you can combine gunpowder with handgun ammo, so you can save Strong Chem Fluids for the Grenade Launcher.

Madhouse difficulty. Molded are more evasive, so accuracy and patience are all the more important. Items are mixed up, and it also includes enhancement coins to aid you in the struggle. Separating Agent becomes more useful when you're low on Strong Chem Fluid, and don't feel the need to use Strong First Aid anymore, for example. And the saves are limited to these Cassette Tapes.

The absolute best safe room theme! I listen to it even when I'm doing something else than playing games.

I also liked the Nightmare mode!

[h1]Mixed[/h1]

Salt Mines soundtrack. When I heard this great ambient track after the elevator touched ground, I expected (and hoped) to encounter some nameless and amorphous Mold monstrosity, Shoggoth-like thing if you will, while treading those passages. But no such luck.

[h1]Cons[/h1]

Never before have I been passionate about the gun's design until I first gazed upon Albert-01 handgun, and also heard its magnificent sound. Too bad that the replica version doesn't hold 9 ammunition in its clip nor even its laser sight... It makes sense that the replica isn't as powerful as the real one—as in Jack and/or Marguerite dying from it prematurely, but that kind of downgrade?! Such wasted potential. I would've otherwise used it alot more in future playthroughs. And they completely butchered Albert-01 in Village... Its supposed to be the super-weapon against B.O.W.'s!

The alternate (or, if you will, the bad) ending. Do I really need to elaborate? Seriously... Ethan went there to save his wife, Mia. That was his main goal even after he survived Lucas' traps. And then that moment of choice comes up. With no build-up to it from Ethan whatsoever. It just feels wrong to choose Zoe, when you realize from early on that Mia cannot control her actions, because of Eveline. That's the problem when Capcom decides to create a character in the RE universe, while simultaneously twisting him to be "the Player".

Puzzles. Shadow puzzles are one of a kind, but there could've been more of a variety, i.e. challenging ones as in the first one.

[h1]Some other things[/h1]

I may be in the minority, that I prefer Ethan Winters as a protagonist more so than Chris or Leon in the previous games. Ethan is somewhat akin to Ash Williams (in the first two Evil Dead movies). What I didn't like, is that while Capcom made Ethan as a character in that universe, they also made him - for some god-forsaken reason, you the Player. It doesn't make sense. And also the fact that they (in their infinite wisdom) won't show his face. What were they thinking? And it gets worse in the sequel, oh boy. They have some weird kind of obsession with keeping Ethan's face out of the picture, making some of the cutscenes cringe-worthy; when it would've made an impact finally seeing him.

Some people are complaining that there weren't enough Molded variations, and I have to disagree from the lore perspective. Considering the fact that Eveline was rapidly aged to look like that of a 10 years old - when she was born; who just wants a big family in a twisted way. She could've done much worse things had she been older in years. Same thing with Alma Wade—before she was locked away for the time being in a sensory deprivation tank in an induced coma (located in the Vault, deep within the Origin Facility), two days before her eight birthday by her father, Harlan Wade - more about this later. And why am I suddenly talking about F.E.A.R.? Well: As a die-hard fan of F.E.A.R. (also the second one and its Reborn DLC, which is the end of the storyline - unless they can fix it somehow back to the Monolith timeline while also making a better game which follows first one's gameplay, but I digress), I almost lost it when it became clear that they were ripping off of Alma. It's no wonder that the writer who wrote Extraction Point (which starts the TimeGate timeline and ends in Perseus Mandate) in which he doesn't understand F.E.A.R.'s story; is also the narrative designer of this game. Alma realized at the end of first F.E.A.R. what she really is = 46 years old, clinically dead but refusing to die. Meaning that she doesn't need to project the memory of her "ghostly" being from when she was locked away—not the actual almost eight years old child form what she was, but how she remembers herself. If I really have to hammer it home: Her dead body was loosened upon the world from inside the Vault, and no need to "become one" with the child form - which is very ridiculous from the story standpoint!

The game that brought the franchise back from the dead! 

Weird story, but I found myself digging the whole mold thing more than the usual Zombie tale we've all heard a thousand times. 

Also - the Circular Saw is THE way to play, I tell you.

After reaching the lowest level of quality in the franchise, in RE6 (compared to the classics) it seemed like the franchise would become something generic that would come out every year.

Even with very low expectations for the announcement of RE7. I was very surprised when the idea of ​​the game being in first person was introduced and I had some doubts. But after playing a demo, the game sold all its concepts to me, from a more immersive experience to reviving the classic gameplay of the series.

With the complete game and all its DLCs available I had the opportunity to play the campaign once again and access the extra content for a reasonable price. Firstly, I can say that the campaign is worth every penny.

The game builds tension from the first moments and I felt a lot of difference in the presentation of the game compared to the old games. An initial narrative with a more serious tone that aroused my curiosity.

The classic mechanics were very well implemented, as were the photorealistic graphics, I imagine that anyone who had the experience of playing in VR felt much more scared during some parts of the game. And even though it was a game with VR mechanics, I didn't feel that the focus was on VR but on the quality of the product. 

Enemies are introduced dynamically and distributed very well throughout the campaign. Just like all the items were separated and positioned in a smart way. Some of the puzzles are very easy, but none of them were frustrating. The map is very well organized and has its secrets.

The combat has had a drastic change, it is no longer kung fu with frantic quick time events. Not that the other games are bad, but I feel like they saturate you too soon after playing several games in the same style. In RE7 you really feel like you're having a hard time surviving and think about whether it's worth shooting or dodging the monster to save ammunition. This change alone makes the game follow a more realistic and fun direction in my opinion.

After finishing the campaign I can say that I really played with pleasure from beginning to end, the story surprised me a little and it wasn't so cliché. 

Now, while the DLCs left me excited, I felt that some ideas were very well implemented and others were a little over the top.

I really liked one of the VHS vol.1 tapes you play to escape a room. The puzzles are very well done. Now surviving in the basement of the house is simply brilliant. It's impressive to see how developers take something as simple as a piece of the map and turn it into something cool to play just by changing a few rules. 

Now I didn't really like the two story DLCs, but other people can certainly enjoy them. I just felt that they were much inferior to the main campaign!

In conclusion, after years a big change made the series successful again! And without losing its roots and game design style. I recommend it to everyone who has played the other games and even to anyone who wants to start with this one!

I had already played Resident Evil 7 on PS4 when it first came out, and even now, it still doesn’t disappoint. The game marked a bold departure from the traditional third-person perspective of previous Resident Evil titles, moving to a first-person viewpoint. While it was a big change, the game still delivers a tense and immersive horror experience. I do admit that I sometimes miss the third-person perspective, as it would have given a different feel to the exploration and combat, but the first-person view works very well for creating a sense of fear and immersion.

The difficulty is generally moderate, depending on the level you choose, but the game isn’t overly punishing. Scarcity of resources like ammo and health items adds tension, making encounters with enemies more intense without feeling unfair.

Graphically, the game is impressive. Environments are detailed, atmospheric, and hauntingly realistic, with creepy lighting, textures, and set pieces that make every moment feel intense. I did notice that some character models can look a little rough even with everything on high settings, but overall the visuals contribute greatly to the game’s mood and horror atmosphere.

The soundtrack and sound design are excellent. Creepy ambient noises, sudden spikes in music during tense moments, and realistic environmental sounds create a strong sense of dread. The voice acting is convincing, adding depth to the characters and heightening the story’s suspense.

Gameplay with a controller feels smooth and natural — there are no awkward controls that hinder your experience. Combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving all feel intuitive, and the first-person perspective makes encounters with enemies much more intense and frightening.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a masterful reinvention of the franchise. It’s atmospheric, immersive, and terrifying in all the right ways. Even years after its release, it remains one of the most memorable horror games, and I highly recommend it to fans of the series or anyone looking for a gripping survival horror experience.

A modern classic. The game that brought back elements of survival horror to the Resident Evil franchise without compromising on the action, and put things back on track, at least for a while..

The game takes place in Dulvey, Louisiana in 2017, as you take the role of Ethan Winters searching for his missing wife. He tracks her down to a remote farmhouse in the bayou, but before they can safely escape is captured by the family who lives there. He now has to brave the gauntlet in store for him and get out alive.

RE7: Biohazard (or originally Biohazard 7: Resident Evil in Japan, clever naming) is the make-or-break entry in the series after a long stretch of action titles. Not that RE4 (my beloved) is by any means a bad game, it set a trend for all Resi games after itself.. and even after this game to follow. Biohazard temporarily brings the franchise to its roots in survival horror by focusing on inventory and resource management while throwing enemies and puzzles your way. The main enemy you'll encounter are creatures created out of mold that come in all shapes and sizes, as well as the crazy family holding you hostage. The game is chock full of setpieces, and you will trek through the different areas of the Baker estate in order to make your escape. You spend most of your time on the Bakers' estate, going from the main house, to the more run-down previous location nestled in the nearby swamp, to a more urban compound created by one of the family members into a sort of SAW-like torture escape room. Crafting returns for the first time in a long while for a mainline numbered Resident Evil game (since RE3: Nemesis), letting you make throwables, ammo, and healing items. Your inventory is once again more limited and can only be expanded by finding rucksacks hidden around the residence (of evil..). The game is average length, but it's paced well and provides a fun new setting for the series and a completely new perspective (first person) that makes everything feel a bit more intimate. Biohazard also comes with several DLCs this time around, having arguably the most consistently solid set of offerings on that front compared to even the later games, ranging from narrative-driven prequel events, to arcade gamemodes and new difficulties to get your blood pumping.

As I do often these days, I also go into the presentation of the game. Much like Revelations 2, the environments here are particularly disgusting, full of rot, dirt and mold. The Baker household in Louisiana very much reflects old southern US design sentiments, with rickety old wooden halls and the muddy trails surrounding it. It wears its inspirations on its sleeve, taking notes from horror classics like the Texas Chainsaw Massacre (the original one), and Evil Dead, which makes it stand out among the other titles in the series. It is definitely the game that stays in my memory the most in the series, for better or worse.  

Great at full price, but also goes on sale during the fairly frequent Capcom publisher sales on Steam, as well as comes with a few interesting DLCs (End of Zoe being the most interesting among the paid ones), including one free mini-campaign that puts you in the shoes of an old favorite character.

What’s the deal?

First-Person Freakout: Forget third-person views; now you’re eyeball-to-eyeball with terror. It’s like your screen’s whispering, “You’re on your own, pal.” 👁️👻
Creepy Dulvey Mansion: Picture a haunted B&B run by the Texas Chainsaw Massacre family. Yep, that’s your vacation spot. 🏚️🔪
Bizarre Mystery: Your wife’s missing, and her cryptic email leads you down the rabbit hole. Spoiler alert: It’s not a cozy tea party down there. 💌🕳️

Atmosphere: The air’s thick with dread, like you’re breathing in ghost fumes. The Baker household feels lived-in (minus the cannibalism, hopefully). 🏡👀
Combat: Unpredictable! Sometimes you’re Rambo, sometimes you’re a scared kitten. Ammo’s scarce, so choose wisely: “Knife or shotgun?” 🗡️🔫
Return to Form: Capcom dusted off the classic RE vibes, sprinkled some nostalgia, and said, “Here, have nightmares.” 🌙🎮
The Not-So-Good Stuff:

Puzzles: Simpler than a toddler’s jigsaw. No riddles, just “find key, unlock door.” 🗝️🚪
Enemies: Repetitive like a broken record. “Oh, another moldy zombie? Yawn.” 🧟‍♂️😴

Its second half devolves into more action-based gameplay that is simply not on par with what came before. I really enjoyed Resident Evil 7. The game is filled with disturbing and scary moments, keeping you on edge throughout the main campaign. The fear of the unknown lurking around each corner of the Baker family house adds to the intense atmosphere. The game features a variety of engaging puzzles, both optional and mandatory, that challenge the player to think critically. Each member of the Baker family is memorable, with their own terrifying personalities and abilities that make every encounter unique and horrifying. The genuine dread I felt while sneaking around the house, trying to gather resources to progress, was palpable. I particularly loved how the game doesn't hold your hand; there are no indicators or HUD elements guiding you. Instead, you're encouraged to use your brain to solve puzzles and figure out your next steps.

I found the story of Resident Evil 7 to be exceptionally well-written. The plot twist near the end, where you discover why the Baker family acts the way they do and the true identity of the mysterious woman in the wheelchair, was particularly compelling. This revelation added a deeper layer of understanding to the horror and made the story even more engaging. Even after finishing the main game, the story isn’t truly over. The two main DLCs continue the narrative, providing closure and enriching the overall experience.

The gameplay in Resident Evil 7 was very smooth and easy to get the hang of. At no point did I feel like the controls were uncomfortable or difficult to use. Veteran Resident Evil players might need some time to adjust to the new first-person perspective, as opposed to the traditional third-person view, but aside from that change, the gameplay mechanics felt intuitive and well-designed.

The graphics in Resident Evil 7 can occasionally show their age, with some textures appearing low-resolution compared to others. However, this is a minor issue that doesn't detract from the overall immersion of the game. For the most part, the graphics are quite realistic, making me feel as if I were in a real house and environment. The visual design does an excellent job of immersing you in the game's unsettling atmosphere. Sometimes, the graphics are almost too good, as the detailed scenes of dismemberment and gore can be quite graphic and intense.

The music and sounds in Resident Evil 7 greatly enhance the immersive experience. The audio design is superb, often making you feel on edge as you sneak around the Baker family house. You frequently hear unsettling noises like banging sounds or creepy snarling, which make you glance over your shoulder, only to find nothing there. The ambient sounds, such as animals making noise outside or frogs croaking in the swamp, add to the realism. The creepiest aspect of the audio is the footsteps—you can hear not only your own but also those of the Baker family members. They often taunt Ethan, the character you play as, making the tension even more palpable as you try to sneak around and avoid detection.

I played Resident Evil 7 on Normal difficulty, so I can't speak for the Madhouse difficulty, which is the hardest setting in the game. On Normal difficulty, I found the game to be fair in terms of the amount of ammo and resources provided. The boss fights weren't overly difficult—in fact, they were relatively easy if you knew the bosses' weak points, as each one has its own specific vulnerabilities. I was able to complete the game without many issues, finishing it in about 9 hours.

I particularly enjoyed the different boss fights in Resident Evil 7. Each arena where you fought the bosses felt meaningful and carefully designed to be impactful for the player. The arenas were genuinely scary, making you feel trapped as you scavenged for enough ammo to take down the grotesque bosses. These moments made my heart pound with fear, as the bosses could inflict significant damage if I wasn't cautious while grabbing healing herbs or ammo around the arena.

Resident Evil 7 stands apart from previous Resident Evil games, which often had a more lighthearted, goofy vibe and didn't quite feel like true horror games. In contrast, Resident Evil 7 delivers an intensely scary and unsettling experience. If you're looking for a genuinely frightening game, I would 100% recommend this one. It doesn't disappoint in terms of horror. Completing the game felt like a weight was lifted off my shoulders, as it does an excellent job of making you dread what's around each corner. At certain points, I had to take breaks because the game stressed me out—in a good way.

Pros:

The game is genuinely scary.
Terrifying boss fights that are impactful.
The environment is eerie and unsettling.
Well-written story with intriguing twists.
Fun and engaging gameplay mechanics.
Graphics that still hold up well.
Perfect for Halloween or fans of horror.
Cons:

Puzzles may frustrate players who dislike them.
Depiction of the Baker family could be triggering for some due to themes of abuse.
Intensity of scares may be too much for some players to finish the game.


I would highly recommend Resident Evil 7 to others, even those who aren't typically fans of the Resident Evil franchise. This game stands out by delivering a truly scary horror experience that stands on its own merits. It's not for everyone, especially considering its depictions of dismemberment and family abuse, which can be triggering for some players. However, if you can handle these elements, you're likely to have a thrilling and immersive experience.

Soon, you come to the property that was given to you in the email and you have to search the creepy old and falling apart residence of the Baker family who are all extremely violent and dangerous.
