The character designs (if we do not count Jack Baker, who is the exception to most of what I’ll write here) are awful. The characters look like a PS2 model with more polygons, but barely better textures. Evil Mia is quite silly looking, Marguerite is straight up laughable. It’s impossible not to laugh at Marguerite’s silly face. The hostiles are just uninteresting in design. The exact same design is used in two hostiles, but one has got a pointier arm and takes more to kill so better have great attention to detail while playing in this game which also is way too dark so you will not be able to discern the two. The other two hostiles (there is one more but I barely count it) are just the first hostile in more annoying iterations. One stands on all fours and just move erratically to be annoying and the other is a big fatso who vomits on you causing Ethan to have a long animation and this can stunlock you. Fun. 

Jack’s section, which is the first section, is actually a rather decent section. Jack is a good character, there are some actually decent puzzles, there’s some tension there that could be counted to fit a horror game, even though it’s not scary it’s relatively well done. 

Marguerite’s section, the second section, is the worst section I’ve ever played. Marguerite is annoying  in writing, in dialogues, in voice, in appearance. The hostiles in this section are bugs. Flying little bugs that are just as annoying as bugs in real life. I hate this section and I wish the person who decided upon this section would get terminated (something I never wish otherwise). There’s nothing to this section. There’s nothing interesting, nothing unique and nothing engaging it’s just annoyance. F... this section. 

Third section is again quite annoying with the son Lucas, who is so uninteresting that it’s laughable. He’s a stereotypical joker character mixed with some Jigsaw in a bad way. It’s just bad, he’s badly written, the section is uninteresting, you’ve heard it before. 

[spoiler]Then you can choose to save your wife who tried to murder you throughout the game and in her moments of lucidity didn’t give a ♥♥♥♥ to say anything to help, or Zoe who actually helped you. I wanted to cure Zoe, but I read online before I made the choice that this would just mean that Zoe would still die and you’d get another boss fight (and I didn’t want to prolong this game anymore than I had to) so I chose Mia. But this is a problem for the game. What kind of horrifically bad writing does this game have? It’s so awful on every level. If you save Zoe she dies from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ magic. F--- you.[/spoiler] 

So you get to the fourth section on a boat and play as Mia and it’s still retreading old grounds. Nothing unique. Nothing interesting. You chase the big bad, Eveline, who is just your stereotypical child villain. It’s been done before. It’s been done better before. She’s not even creepy. She’s just a child who sometimes wishes you die. [spoiler] Even the jumpscare that they tried after Mia rejects Eveline’s call to be her mother is so bad that I genuinely laughed out loud because it’s so badly made.[/spoiler] 

[spoiler]The game culminated with Ethan managing to inject Eveline with the toxin that should destroy her but instead makes her huge so failure good job, writing team. Then he gets a magic gun from what turns out to be Carl Redfield (#notmychris) which magically can destroy Eveline for reasons left unsaid.[/spoiler] 

So to summarize: This is an awful game. The writing makes no sense; the characters are very annoying and written to shock with no regard for personality or feel of the game. Resident Evil 7 is, in my opinion, a very bad game. It features terrible and unoriginal writing, unrealistic and sometimes nonsensical dialogue, frustrating controls, boring and repetitive gameplay, weak characters that aren’t properly fleshed out or meaningfully differentiated from one another, a paucity of unique enemies, and a clear intention to cater to trends such as VR rather than to craft a unique and interesting experience. Perhaps one of it’s worst sins is not being scary at all, relying on kitschy jump-scares and mountains of gore rather than utilizing atmosphere and tension to build a truly frightening experience. It’s a game that brings nothing new to the table and provided no fun for me whatsoever.

The game plagiarizes the plot and gameplay of Outlast, a game that came out 4 years earlier and featured better graphics, a more original story, and way better writing, dialogue, and gameplay. In both Outlast and RE7, you play as a normal guy (not a cop/ex-military tough guy, etc.) who goes into a large creepy structure and is chased around by scary entities. The main difference is that in Outlast the player cannot attack at all, whereas in RE7 the player can attack and can occasionally kill some things, but often has to resort to the very same "run away, hide/wait, then creep by and complete objective" tactics that the player would be doing in Outlast. Also, one of the writers for this game, Richard Pearsey, also worked on two F.E.A.R. expansion packs, which is likely why the lazily written plot contains a character (Eveline) who is almost identical to Alma from F.E.A.R. The members of the Baker family don’t really have unique personalities and could have been made much more interesting if more effort was put into fleshing them out and giving them unique characteristics.

RE7 is woefully linear, which is a far cry from previous Resident Evil games, which were very non-linear and scarier as a direct result of this attribute. The gameplay largely consists of navigating through a mazey Texas Chainsaw Massacre-inspired house looking for items and keys while bizarre murderous rednecks and gooey, vaguely humanoid blob monsters chase you. The game discourages exploration in many sections, because often the player is relentlessly pursued by enemies that can’t be killed and thus must be avoided. This type of approach to gameplay begs for responsive controls and good maneuverability, but instead we get clunky controls and a player character that moves like he is wading through Jello. In addition to being incredibly frustrating, the controls are often unintuitive, such as the poorly designed real time menu. The player’s run speed is painfully slow, and often one cannot differentiate between non-interactive sequences and moments where the player is expected to try to regain control of the action. The non-boss encounters in this game are pretty boring. There are very few unique enemy types, which is a confusing decision for a franchise which always had fairly good enemy variety. The boss fights are terribly designed and janky as heck. On normal skill level I was unable to beat an early boss even after almost two hours of attempting to defeat him. This was 100% due to unresponsive controls, trash gameplay mechanics, and just an overall poorly designed boss fight that wasn't fun to play at all. It was very obvious what I was supposed to do, yet effectively executing it was so difficult because of the poor design and absolutely waterlogged controls. My deaths were not the result of a lack of skill, because I was doing exactly what the game wanted me to do. Rather, the boss' movement speed, hit detection, and even hit points seemed to fluctuate in a way that always worked in his favor. So the fight was just frustrating and tedious and sucked any fun I may have been having right out of the game. And I didn't care enough to want to keep wasting my time trying to beat an early boss in a game that I don't even like.

The dialogue in Resident Evil 7 is absolutely abysmal. By comparison, Outlast had truly haunting dialogue and used set pieces and key visuals to tell the story artfully. This game is ham-fisted and goofy at best. As an example, after the player character learns that his wife (who has been missing for 3 years) might actually be alive, we see him calling his friend as he’s driving to where his wife presumably is. However, his demeanor during this phone call does not match the gravity of the situation at hand. His attitude conveys things like "Hey buddy, just FYI my wife is actually alive...I might try to find her, but I'm good so don't bother helping me or calling the cops or anything. I'm going alone without any weapons to some place in rural Louisiana. And I'm not gonna bother telling you the address because I'll be just fine despite having no military or law enforcement training and being unarmed." Then he gets to the place and beholds mutilated cattle/farm animals and rotting meat everywhere, watches a snuff video on VHS (yes VHS, because people still use that format?) where at least two people are clearly murdered, and then wades through water inches from a dead human body and traverses rooms full of gore. But when he finally finds his wife, he reacts like someone lacking a functioning limbic cortex or hypothalamus which could allow for proper emotional responses. This Asperger syndrome sufferer keeps stopping his wife and bugging her with questions like "What happened? Are you gonna tell me what's going on? Hey wait, what did they do to you?" This is in no way realistic. Any remotely well-adjusted human being would be looking for the exit immediately, and wouldn't be interrogating their own WIFE who suffered unspeakable torment. But our protagonist literally says to his WIFE who has suffered horrible abuses for 3 years, "Just stay here, I'm gonna have a look around." Yes, that is actual dialogue, verbatim, from the game. The man found his wife who's clearly been kidnapped and brutalized for 3 years, and he decides to leave her in another room of a charnel house so he can look around. It is absolute garbage writing, and it doesn’t get any better from there. I was unable to immerse myself in the game or suspend disbelief when I was hearing such ridiculous dialogue and witnessing the player character react in ways that made no sense and didn’t fit the scenario at all. We of course know that Silent Hill was always the thinking man's survival horror game with superior psychological horror and replete with deeper meaning and symbolism, but I still expected at least passable writing from a game which is attempting to be serious and scary. Boy was I wrong.

The game also has little to do with Resident Evil, despite being touted as a return to form after RE6. Chris Redfield is shoehorned in at the very end of the game, and the Baker house has puzzles, so I guess those were the nebulous connections to the Resident Evil franchise. But to me, this felt like a wholly different game with Resident Evil written on the package.

This game is the antithesis of a fun time. It's a poorly written, hard to control, heavy-handed, hackneyed, boring experience that insults my intelligence, and the dialogue sounds like it was written by a 10-year-old autistic child. I'm glad that I only paid $8 for this pile of detritus, and despite not being eligible for a refund, I have permanently removed it from my Steam library, because I don't want to give this game the honor of existing alongside the truly great games which adorn my collection.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard: A Terrifying Reinvention

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard marks a bold and thrilling reinvention of the iconic series, delivering a chilling experience that stands out as one of the best entries in the franchise. As a longtime fan of Resident Evil, the shift to a first-person perspective in this installment was a game-changer that added a new layer of immersion and intensity.

Embracing the first-person shooter mechanics for the first time in the series, Resident Evil 7 plunges you into a visceral and harrowing journey through the decrepit halls of the Baker family estate. From the moment you step foot into the eerie plantation, every creaking floorboard and flickering light contributes to a sense of palpable dread. The decision to adopt this perspective pays off immensely, allowing for a more personal and terrifying experience as you navigate the twisted corridors and face off against grotesque creatures.

Visually, Resident Evil 7 is a marvel. The graphics are stunningly detailed, creating a hauntingly realistic environment that feels unsettlingly tangible. The dilapidated mansion and its surrounding swamplands are rendered with such atmospheric precision that they become characters in their own right, each telling a story of decay and horror. The character models, particularly the grotesque Baker family members, are disturbingly lifelike, adding to the game's unnerving atmosphere.

Sound design and music are utilized to perfection, heightening the tension and fear throughout your journey. The ambient noises of the dilapidated mansion, the distant echoes of unknown horrors, and the chilling score all contribute to a spine-tingling experience. Every sound is meticulously crafted to keep you on edge, ensuring that each encounter is as nerve-wracking as the last.

Gameplay in Resident Evil 7 strikes a delicate balance between survival horror and intense action. Exploration is key, as you scavenge for supplies and unravel the mysteries of the Baker estate. Combat is visceral and adrenaline-pumping, requiring careful management of resources and strategic use of weapons to survive the relentless onslaught of enemies. The addition of puzzles and environmental challenges further enriches the gameplay, offering a satisfying blend of cerebral challenges and pulse-pounding encounters.

Story-wise, Resident Evil 7 delivers a gripping narrative that delves deep into the dark heart of the series' lore. Playing as Ethan Winters, a civilian drawn into a nightmarish ordeal, you uncover shocking truths and confront unimaginable horrors along the way. The narrative twists and turns keep you engaged from start to finish, culminating in a thrilling and satisfying conclusion that leaves a lasting impact.

In summary, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a triumph of horror gaming, successfully reinventing the series while staying true to its roots. With its groundbreaking first-person perspective, stunning graphics, immersive sound design, and captivating gameplay, it sets a new standard for survival horror. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the franchise, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is an essential experience that exemplifies the terrifying potential of the Resident Evil series in a new era of gaming.

Resident Evil 7 is a refreshing new take on the Series that this franchise desperately needed! And what a blast I had!

RE7 changes the previous formula and does a lot of things very well while doing so. This installment brings the franchise back to its survival horror roots and creates a whole new feel. Graphically it's also in a whole new league and the level and game design is wonderfully crafted. The story can finally be taken seriously again and says goodbye to cheesy dialogues and dull, over-dramatized action and embeds the experience in a wonderfully dense and captivating atmosphere. It's really been years since a horror game was able to captivate me as much as this game did. Most recently it was Alien Isolation from which RE7 apparently took some inspiration. The game is a thrill from start to finish, combining modern technology and classic RESIDENT EVIL elements to create an incredibly entertaining game. It even managed to occasionally send shivers down my spine. I loved it to the bone :) I'm happy to have had this gaming experience, as I haven't been too impressed with what CAPCOM had done with the game series since RE4. After finishing the campaign I immediately went and got RE8 THE VILLAGE, which sufficiently satisfied my hunger for more.

I clearly recommend this game to everyone who loved RE1 to RE3 und wants to see a modern take on a winning formula from the good old days! This game is worth your while. Play it!

My history with the RE saga is complicated. I traditionally hated the first game as it got the credit for doing the same thing Alone in the Dark did a few years before (with way worse presentation, true) so it took me a lot to get to the saga. Then I loved RE4, I did not click with 5 or 6 as everyone else and I started gathering them on my backlog until one day I decided to play 7.

Well, this is the scariest game I have ever played. Of course, in my opinion and all that, but the thing is that it feels so... physical. It gets everything that horror was about in the 00s (the body horror, the torture horror) with other modern nods (found footage) and classic nods (The Hill Have Eyes, Chainsaw Massacre and all other Evil Cannibal Family stories) plus taking bits that worked really well from survival horror games that tried a different approach like Amnesia/Penumbra. And all of this, summed? Works marvels. It feels violent, claustrophobic, anxiety inducing, and the presentation of it all is wonderful. 

Incredible game.

*spoilers*

Well, I did it. It was much easier than I though apart from one DLC: End Of Zoe. The DLC is fun and all but on hardest difficulty: Joe Must Die, there was one or two really difficult sections. However, after a break I did it all first try. I had so much heals and weapons by the end that the last boss fight lasted not even a minute, and I took no damage. 

I honestly thought I wouldn't be able to 100% this due to the madhouse difficulty and the Ethan Must Die DLC. However, this was all easy. Madhouse, with a guide of course, I had no issues with. I died once for being stupid, but other than that I was absolutely stacked by the end that it was a breeze. I had collected so much yet conserved it all as if I would need it all so desperately. Therefore I literally had tons of ammunition by the end. 
Now, Ethan Must Die WAS NOT THAT HARD! I watched a vid in preparation and watched a guide. It took me around 5 attempts. My RNG was at least decent every single time. I just died twice to the game being an *sshole(turret shooting an explosive next to me, then after the exact same explosive being triggered by my knife when I was trying to knife an enemy) and me being an idiot and dying to the end boss. I don't remember any other deaths. I completed it with a 18 minute run.  This DLC was really really fun and I didn't feel too frustrated after dying those times as I knew the route and loved the RNG aspect. 

I would also like to mention another reason I thought I couldn't do this: 
the 21 DLC, especially survival/survival+. Survival mode I did first try. Survival+ took me a few tries I have to say. I took a break, and next day I did it first try. I knew the last guys cards and saved a card especially for him. I only got tortured once, and the bet was only by 1. This can be seen from a screenshot of mine. Again, this DLC, even after failing over and over on survival+ was very fun. Though, It was a little more frustrating when dying so late game. 

Overall, I love this game and its DLCs - I mean there is a reason why I'm writing this review at 04:09AM. Anyway, that's that. I have no idea what RE game to 100% next. Maybe Resident Evil 5? Or Resident Evil 1 HD Remaster, but I haven't even completed that on PC yet! I might try and get into it again, but I'm not completely sure. I may not 100% another Resident Evil for a while. Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a survival-horror game in the well known Resident Evil series, which deviates strongly from the rest of the game (at least the ones before it), among other aspects because it is now from a first-person perspective. 

Pros:
+ Plenty of tense moments that can really scare you. It is really about survival in a very scary and eerie setting (especially while on the initial complex of the houses).
+ Specific enemies are very well designed and become almost instantly memorable. 
+ Very nice graphics, music and sound effects. Their combination conveys an atmosphere of complete decadence. 
+ The part that is reminiscent of a movie series (SA*) was excellent, the highlight of the game for me.  
+ The video sessions of the game are a very clever addition that increase the duration of the game without being at all boring as they are important part of the story. 

Cons:
- My main complain is that once you leave the house complex the quality of the game drops significantly. Especially the very last act is very generic and boring. The final boss battle is also very underwhelming. 
- While this is a AAA game production thematically it feels like an interactive B movie, with all cliches of the gender so that there nothing new brought (including almost immortal enemies). Still, it is so fan being able to be the protagonist of such "movie". 
- Some scenes and instances are too gory and very unrealistic, almost hilariously so. Maybe this is done on purpose.
- One of the first boss battles has a difficulty spike that almost made me quit the game. Not only it was quite difficult but the hit boxes at instances felt very random.
- Technically no native ultra-wide support (but can be fixed through external program).

All-in-all an excellent survival horror game that deviates for the usual formula of the RE games. While perhaps my impression was not as positive as the general consensus, the eerie and tense atmosphere of the Baker house is outstanding. Definitely recommended.

Graphics: Absolutely perfect! I think they combine live action footage with computer generated imagery in the beginning of the game. I'm not sure. Either way, I'm impressed. 
Gameplay: Challenging. I haven't died so much in the game, but whenever I died, I recognized some flaw in my playing style which needed to be addressed.
Story: I often cringe at the storytelling in video games; RE7 is a pleasant surprise. I found myself engaged with the story, wanting to know more. 
Quibbles: Why in the world can't you manually turn your flashlight on or off? This would have been such a great feature in the game! It gets frustrating when you're walking in near complete darkness, but you know that the protagonist is carrying a flashlight.
Atlast, despite some minor complaints, RE7 comes highly recommended. 10/10

The regular enemies look and feel rather repetetive in style and mechanics, and there's a much smaller variety of them.
The explorable sections feel considerably smaller in scope compared to say 2 even though you can tell they went for that puzzle/keyhunt vibe.
The bosses that have a special (sometimes optional) way of taking them down, tend to wear down their novelty simply because they have too much health. A chainsaw battle is cool, but having to take down Jack three times after getting it feels a little... flat near the end. And that's a sentiment I feel is repeated throughout most of the bosses. There's cool ideas, and then they wear out their welcome.

The DLC are particularly egregious in exposing the weaker sides of the games. Not A Hero reduces the game basically to a more typical FPS. Unless you're particularly wasteful with your ammo, you'll always have ammo, so it's more a matter of not getting stupidly hit.
End of Zoe's unarmed system is interesting, but the way the fist combo's unreliably que up means that I drop a lot of my very-much-needed combo finishers. Getting the gauntlet near the end makes fighting normal enemies feel great, except when you then play on Jack Must Die and... the unlocked gauntlet feels weaker than a bare fist on Normal.

A lot of experiments were run here, and they lack a certain sense of polish. I've yet to play Village, but considering the variety of enemies alone (and what I've seen of some of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy boss fights...) it's quite possible RE8 has the polish RE7 needed. Or not. Guess I'll find out the next time it's on sale.

Huh. I can’t believe I didn’t review this game when I played it back in the day. It was one of my favorite [i]Resident Evil[/i] games at the time. I refuse to blame myself, so the excuse I’m going with is that there have just been so many great entries in the series released since then that this one has gotten lost in the fray… But that’s a good problem to have, I suppose.

Well, let me set my opinions in stone, here and now: it’s damned good.

As one of the many people who were afraid that the series was starting to lose its way after sixth (and, arguably, the fifth) installments in the series, I was happy to see Capcom step back and reevaluate their darling horror franchise. And, unlike many reboots, it was a huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ success. Not only did the seventh game signal a return to the series’ horror roots, it did so while being the first mainline entry that took place in first-person perspective. Basically, it was a win-win for everybody, whether they wanted something old or something new.

Normally, I’m not a fan of intelligent “zombies”. (It kind of defeats the purpose of the whole “zombie” thing, if you ask me. They’re supposed to be stupid.) But, the Baker family is so interesting / likeable / terrifying that I don’t mind it here. Jack Baker stalking me through the halls of the house and the subsequent confrontation with him are stand-out moments from, not only this game, but the entire series, if you ask me. The family is truly unforgettable.

Of course, like every good [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, it starts to fall flat. Just like most of the others, the bosses start to have [b]too[/b] many tentacles and there are just [b]too[/b] many head explosions for things to be scary anymore. But, again, most [i]Resident Evil[/i] games do this, so I won’t take off [b]too[/b] many points for it happening here.

Honestly, my biggest gripe about this game is that we never got the VR version that PlayStation players got. What the ♥♥♥♥, Capcom? Don’t you like money?

Okay, my memory about the game is starting to fail me. So, in conclusion, if you haven’t played this one (and especially if you played and enjoyed [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i]), you really ought to do yourself a favor and play it. You could wait for a sale, but, seeing how low the asking price is now, it’s even worth picking up when its not on sale.

TL;DR: A great return to form for survival horror lovers. If you enjoyed RE1 & 2 definitely pick this one up. Skip the DLC, though.
[hr][/hr]I had high hopes for this game going in, as it has been roundly praised by fans of this series. Fortunately Resident Evil 7 delivers on its premise of getting back to the series' survival horror roots, eschewing the action movie vibe of later titles. While I did enjoy RE4, it's globetrotting, president's-daughter-rescuing, jetski-into-the-sunset exploits are pretty far from the claustrophobic and creepy atmosphere of the first two games. Here, we're back to basics (for the most part): our new protagonist Ethan gets a message from his long-missing wife and sets out to a house in the Louisiana bayou to find her. Without spoiling anything, things don't go well for him, and the story plays out in a way that will feel familiar to returning players. Thankfully it avoids the worst of the overwritten nonsense that started to creep into the series over time without completely jettisoning established lore.

This was the first outing for Capcom's new RE Engine, and even seven years later it still looks fantastic. The environments are beautifully detailed, with everything covered in just enough grime to make it look natural to its setting. Character models and animations are near movie-quality (though Mia does give me slight uncanny valley feels). I played the game in HDR mode, and was completely in love with the art direction and color palette they employed. My one gripe visually is the implementation of the flashlight; Ethan will only turn it on automatically in specific dark areas, but there are [b]plenty[/b] of areas that are too dark to actually see into that Ethan will not illuminate. From a design perspective, I understand that this was done to maintain tension and immersion in this spooky setting, but from a seeing-what-the-hell-is-going-on perspective I was mildly annoyed fairly frequently.

A big change-up in this entry was the switch to first-person camera. I was a initially a little hesitant about this, mostly due to how much I suck at FPS games; I certainly don't miss the older games' tank controls. Happily, the first-person view not only feels completely natural, but it gives things an eerie found-footage vibe (which the story leans into in a few places). The combat and exploration both felt great (I used a controller), and the only minor complaint I had control-wise would be that some big fights would really benefit from a slightly faster strafing movement. On Normal difficulty the main story was slightly challenging with a few difficulty spikes, and careful resource management gave that welcome feeling of getting more powerful as things progressed.

Having gotten this game late and on sale, I went ahead and picked up the package that contained all the DLC as well. Having played through it all, I would recommend giving it a miss. Story-wise, they range from including a little extra info on an inconsequential character to showing you implied plot elements that anyone with an imagination could have pictured. At worst, they start introducing the stupid nonsense that I didn't enjoy about a lot of other Capcom games from the 2000s, in several cases undercutting the world-building of the main title to do so. They do change up the gameplay a little, but rarely for the better. One section is essentially an escape room. Another has you playing a deadly card game.  One switches up the focus to be much more action-heavy, while yet another introduces stealth kills and fist-fighting. They're fine, but nothing to write home about. There were a few that changed things to feel more like minigames or survival challenges. Definitely not my cup of tea, but I guess they're there if you want them.

Finally, a quick discussion about achievements. I liked this game a lot, but not quite enough to try to 100% it. Admittedly I went out of my way for some of the achievements that seemed fun, but there are far too many that look like they'd be too grueling to enjoy working toward. While I feel confident that I could do the speedrun and limited healing challenges on Easy mode, would I really feel like I'd accomplished anything getting there? I'll save the hard-mode run for if I ever feel like playing the story again, and I didn't have near enough fun with the DLC to slog through the punishment of chasing those.

Overall, I highly enjoyed the main game on offer here. It felt like a great modern take on the classic survival horror experience, presented with beautiful attention to environmental detail and storytelling restraint that I didn't think Capcom could do anymore. I can see myself replaying this someday, and I hope that RE Village lives up to the high bar that this game has set.

[h1] Back to Roots, Wrong Protagonist [/h1]  
Resident Evil 7 Biohazard successfully recaptures classic survival horror tension but stumbles hard with its lead character.

[h2] GOOD [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b] Classic Resident Evil Feel [/b]  
The game returns to tight corridors, limited resources, and constant dread that defined the series' early days. First-person perspective amplifies vulnerability while keeping the core survival horror DNA intact.  

    [*][b] Solid Content Volume [/b]  
Main campaign plus DLCs, tapes, and unlockables provide substantial playtime. Multiple difficulty options and collectibles give completionists plenty to chase without feeling padded.  

    [*][b] Strong Soundtrack [/b]  
The audio design sells the horror—creaking floors, distant banging, and Michael A. Levine's unsettling score create oppressive atmosphere. Sound becomes another enemy you can't see.  
[/list]

[h2] BAD [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b] Bland Protagonist [/b]  
Ethan Winters is painfully generic—zero personality, zero backstory, zero memorable lines. His obliviousness to obvious danger kills immersion, and passing up established characters like Alyssa Ashcroft (who gets name-dropped) feels like a massive missed opportunity. Clancy would've brought actual character depth.  

    [*][b] Annoying Molded Enemies [/b]  
The Molded are less scary, more frustrating bullet sponges that keep coming no matter how many times you shoot them. They lack the distinct terror of classic zombies or hunters, feeling like generic obstacles instead of memorable threats.  

    [*][b] Mediocre Jumpscares [/b]  
Most scares rely on loud noises and predictable enemy spawns rather than building dread. The few good moments get diluted by repetitive cheap shots that lose impact after the tenth identical surprise.  
[/list]

[h2] Final Thought [/h2]  
Resident Evil 7 nails the atmosphere and gets survival horror right again, but man Ethan drags the whole thing down hard. Dude's just boring and clueless—I'd take Clancy or even Alyssa Ashcroft any day over this blank slate. Positives outweigh the negatives, but that protagonist choice puts it right on the edge. Still worth grabbing on sale or in a bundle if you want classic RE vibes despite the weak lead.

Resident Evil 7 is a [i]big[/i] departure from earlier entries in the series, particularly from [i]recent[/i] titles: it's first-person perspective instead of the traditional third-person (or even more traditional fixed camera), there's no partner/buddy, and the atmosphere and gameplay are back to survival horror for the first mainline title since RE3.  

The characters and environments look great, although it is [i]dark[/i]. You spend most of the game in unlit indoor locations, accompanied only by the world's most useless flashlight. Like, the first time I walked inside, in the first chapter, it was so dark that I was convinced I wasn't allowed to go that way and walked out again. That aside, they use the creepy environments to great effect, creating tense exploration situations, or frantic scrambles for a key item while an enemy hunts you through previously-explored corridors.  

I appreciate that the bosses are largely "figure out the gimmick and exploit it a few times" instead of "shoot them until their bodies are 94% lead by volume". Even so, I'm pretty sure I had to retry all of them at least once.  

I did really enjoy both the story and the gameplay, despite Ethan Winters being probably the dullest Resident Evil protagonist since Chris Redfield, but it took me [i]for [b]ever[/b][/i] (in real time) to finish the game, because they went back from RE5/6/Revelations's autosave system to the traditional "you need to find a typewriter" (in this case an audio tape recorder). This works well with the type of gameplay, since you get a chance to take a breath in a "safe room", then make your next foray out, but for me personally, it meant that I had to find hour-plus blocks of uninterrupted time with no young kids looking over my shoulder to have a realistic probability of accomplishing anything.  

I really enjoyed RE7 a lot - it's probably tied with Revelations 2 as my favorite entry in the series so far.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard marks one of the boldest reinventions of the Resident Evil franchise, delivering a tense, atmospheric first-person horror experience that feels both classic and refreshingly modern. By switching to a first-person perspective, the game pulls you directly into its decaying world — from the claustrophobic corridors of the Baker estate to the grotesque rooms where nightmares feel physically present. Survival horror mechanics are front and center: ammunition is scarce, environments are designed to make every corner feel threatening, and every encounter demands careful resource management rather than reckless aggression.

The gameplay loop expertly balances exploration, puzzle solving, and survival combat. You’ll methodically search crumbling rooms for key items, piece together fragmented lore from documents and clues, and solve environmental puzzles that cleverly gate progress without becoming obtuse. Combat encounters are meaningful because you rarely have enough firepower to treat fights as routine; retreat, stealth, or clever use of explosives often feel like equally valid strategies. The tension is amplified by the game’s minimalistic save and upgrade systems — you earn enhancements slowly and must decide when to invest precious resources into weapons or healing items.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard isn’t just about jump scares — it’s about presence. It makes fear feel tangible and earned, and keeps players invested through pacing that masterfully blends dread with discovery. Whether you’re tucked into an attic with one bullet left or slowly unlocking another piece of the estate’s dark past, this is survival horror at its most immersive.

— The Ember Archives

It feels like Capcom spent a ton on a new IP, got scared, and then someone high up went "We need to make sure this sells well, slap the Resident Evil logo on it". "But sir, there's nothing in this game even remotely related to Resident Evil". "Don't you worry about that, I'll have the team make so many changes that no one will ever be able to say this isn't a Resident Evil game"...... Has the team change health items to green & red herbs as well as throw in first aid sprays. Adds Fake Chris Redfield showing up for 30 seconds at the end of the game to essentially say "Hi, I'm Fake Chris Redfield, this is now a Resident Evil game because I, Fake Chris Redfield, have shown up to say that I, Fake Chris Redfield, am rescuing you. I, Fake Chris Redfield, have to go now, my planet needs me". Fake Chris Redfield ain't going to be punching no boulders. ♥♥♥♥ off Fake Chris Redfield.

The story in this is straight up garbage. Resident Evil games aren't exactly known for their amazing stories, so this would be fine, except there isn't a single likable character in the game to make up for it. You're never going to care at all about Ethan, or Mia, or other woman, or those people, or whoever else. Ethan literally has no character. You don't care at all about Mia when things start going wrong with her so you have no investment with her. You make a choice at the mid game point. If you choose to help the person who's been helping you all game long, they immediately retcon your choice by killing her and then lock you into getting the bad ending for the game. Cool beans. I guess the best character is Ellis, or Billy, or whatever hillbilly son's name is that I can't remember.

There is something clearly wrong with the brightness in this game. It is excessively dark to a point where you can't see things. It's like they made the brightness slider and then afterwards as a joke someone went into the game files and set brightness to "/2". Make sure to have the brightness slider up way higher than the game suggests.

Do you remember all those memorable, or at least fun, enemies from actual Resident Evil games. Well wait until I tell you about the exciting enemies here in Fake Resident Evil 7. There's Goo Monster who is an actual goo monster. Goo Monster + who has a goo claw and more life than Goo Monster. Goo Monster Crawler who crawls on the floor and leaps at you. Fat Goo Monster who's fat. Big Mosquito Bugs that either sit in one spot for you to murder or fly around at unhittable supersonic speeds. Small Bug Swarms that come out of hives if you get too close to them and annoy you. Finally, there're Spiders that sit on cabinets and block you from getting the stuff inside the cabinet until you flamethrow them off the cabinet. That's it, welcome to your exciting enemy variety for your 9-12 hour stay.

There is also the Baker family who make up most of the boss battles. Outside of that, 2 of them will patrol areas and annoy you for a while until you hit certain points in the game where they no longer patrol those areas.

Once you reach the ship, the game becomes completely bland and stale. The final section of the game is in a mine and is outright bad. These two segments make up around 1/3 of the game and were clearly added for no reason other than to pad out the game length.

Boss battles vary in quality. The worst one is with Mama Baker who generates the annoying bug swarms during her fight. I put so many rounds into her that I actually had to go outside the game to look up and verify that her boss battle wasn't some sort of puzzle you have to solve and that she's actually killable. Nice in game feedback there Capcom where I can't tell if I'm actually hurting a boss.

Then lets talk about the absolute worst part of this game. Something that drove me nuts all game long..... the movement speed. Note that the word speed is being used ironically because there is no speed. You can walk, which is tiptoeing, or you can run, which is slightly faster than tiptoeing. I'm going to try to help you picture in your head how maddening the movement in this game is.

Ever watch someone pretending to run in slow motion? That's what the movement in this game feels like.

Ever have a dream where someone is chasing you or you're chasing after someone? They move at excessive speeds while you're barely moving in your dream and even thinking in dream "Why the hell am I moving so slow? Go faster". That's what the movement in this game feels like.

Ever been somewhere where there are slim rows/aisles, you walk like a normal human being who actually wants to get somewhere, and there's a person in front of you with two legs and no physical disability who keeps walking the same pathway you're going, and they're taking up the middle of that row/aisle giving you no way around them and walking like they've got nowhere to be, and they have no idea that any other person exists other than themselves and now you're stuck walking behind them and forcing yourself to walk at an incredibly awkward slow pace? That's what the movement in this game feels like. It's fu..ing infuriating. Just fu..ing move you fu..ing prick. Why the fu.k do you have no situational awareness and walk like this is the first time you've ever fu..ing walked in your fu..ing life and you're afraid of falling on your stupid fu..ing face? Just put one fu..ing foot in front of the other and walk like a normal fu..ing human being.

Just thinking about the movement speed in this game is currently very mildly annoying me.

Anyway, I think this is it for me with the Resident Evil/Fake Resident Evil series. I had Fake Resident Evil Village on my wishlist but took it off when I learned that it has the same protagonist and the same engine this game does, which means it probably has the same movement speed issue this game does, and if I have to experience this movement speed again, my brain may explode. Overall, Fake Resident Evil 7 is an above average game at best, but that's it. At least I can say it's better than Resident Evil 6..... what a bar to beat. That's the only mainline Resident Evil game it's better than. It's certainly not some horror classic and I'll never play it again. Anyone considering this game to be a classic is as big a joke as this game is.

A seriously creepy title even in the resident evil series but none the less a classic title in the franchise, the first resident evil game I played 7 holds a specific spot in my heart for the games. The graphics and sound are exactly what you expect with the Capcoms resident evil games and the story begins Ethan's and Mia's journey in the world. I loved how they balanced linear and open world as well as how Jacks AI would wander hunting for you similar to Mr X always keeping you on edge. The enemies are as creepy as you can expect and I truly hated the bugs section of the game even with the new weapons. Each of the Baker's  have their own unique style, area and attacks meaning you cannot rely on the same methods for each of them. This also meant that you would not know what is coming with each of them, further keeping you invested in the story and Ethan's journey. I found very little bugs (Bar the little critters in the game) and loved every minute of it, and the DLC made the game even better and more enjoyable enhancing the experience and providing more backstory to the game and Baker's. 

If you love even more horror in your resident evil game's and love the design, game play and sound of the game's this will without a doubt be a pickup even off sale. At this point though it is easily on sale and can be picked up for dirt cheap compared to it's already low price, without a doubt recommended.

"Resident Evil 7 Biohazard" marks a significant departure from the traditional formula of the iconic survival horror franchise. Developed and published by Capcom, this installment takes players on a terrifying journey into the depths of rural Louisiana, where they must confront grotesque horrors, solve puzzles, and uncover the dark secrets of the sinister Baker family. Released in 2017, the game received widespread acclaim for its return to the series' roots while also introducing fresh gameplay mechanics and a chilling atmosphere. At its core, "Resident Evil 7 Biohazard" is a first-person survival horror game that emphasizes exploration, resource management, and intense combat encounters. Players assume the role of Ethan Winters, who ventures into the dilapidated Baker estate in search of his missing wife, Mia. The game's perspective shift to first-person adds a heightened sense of immersion, placing players directly in the shoes of the protagonist as they navigate through the derelict surroundings. Unlike previous entries in the series, which often featured larger, interconnected environments, "Resident Evil 7" focuses on a more intimate setting, with the majority of the game taking place within the confines of the Baker mansion and its surrounding areas. This tighter design allows for more focused level design and a greater emphasis on atmospheric storytelling. The gameplay mechanics of "Resident Evil 7" revolve around exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. Players must scavenge for resources such as ammunition, healing items, and key items to progress through the game while also solving environmental puzzles and uncovering clues to unravel the mystery of the Baker family's dark past. Combat in "Resident Evil 7" is deliberately slow-paced and methodical, requiring players to carefully manage their ammunition and health resources while strategizing their approach to each encounter. The game features a variety of weapons, including handguns, shotguns, and flamethrowers, each with its own strengths and weaknesses against different types of enemies. The narrative of "Resident Evil 7 Biohazard" is steeped in mystery and intrigue, drawing players into a web of conspiracy, experimentation, and supernatural terror. As Ethan delves deeper into the twisted world of the Bakers, he uncovers horrifying secrets and encounters grotesque creatures that defy explanation. The game's atmospheric presentation is one of its greatest strengths, with haunting visuals, chilling sound design, and masterful use of lighting and shadow to create an oppressive sense of dread and tension. From the creaking floorboards of the decrepit mansion to the eerie silence of the Louisiana bayou, every location in "Resident Evil 7" oozes with atmosphere and foreboding. The characters of "Resident Evil 7 Biohazard" are brought to life with convincing performances and well-written dialogue that adds depth and personality to each encounter. From the unhinged Jack Baker to the enigmatic Mia Winters, every character in the game feels distinct and memorable, leaving a lasting impression on players long after the credits roll. The voice acting in "Resident Evil 7" is top-notch, with talented actors delivering believable performances that enhance the immersion and emotional impact of key moments in the story. Whether it's the manic laughter of Jack Baker or the desperate pleas of Ethan Winters, the voice cast captures the essence of each character with remarkable skill and authenticity.

"Resident Evil 7 Biohazard" is a triumphant return to form for the iconic survival horror franchise, delivering a harrowing and unforgettable experience that will leave players on the edge of their seats from start to finish. With its immersive first-person perspective, atmospheric storytelling, and bone-chilling encounters, it stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of the Resident Evil series and a must-play title for horror enthusiasts everywhere.

[b]TL;DR: RE7 and Soma are the best horror game experiences I've had. Combining horror with anxiety, claustrophobic spaces, delirium and immensely well written dialogue/story. Slap great animations, graphics, sound design, voice acting and lore on top of that and you're left with this absolute gem. The holy grail of horror games.[/b]

My favorite thing about this game is that you're given the tools to defend yourself. The horror doesn't revolve around you being helpless. You get plenty of weapons and ways to try and fight your way through. It's just that the fear of the Baker family doesn't get diminished by having an arsenal. On top of that the decision to switch to a first person view is much appreciated. Helps a bunch with combat and also the immersion.

It pulls on the right strings, putting the player in the exact spots it wants them to be. Inducing fear, paranoia and anxiety even when nothing is happening. The game being quiet is a good and bad thing. Depending where you are, what you're doing. Sometimes it's eerie what this game does. Goosebumps and a feeling of unrest. It keeps you on edge.

Generally it doesn't rely on jump scares to set the tone, although that doesn't mean there aren't any. When they do use them they don't feel cheap. It's good timing and some of them aren't even accompanied by a sound,  leaving you with an uneasy feeling.

Animations are unbelievably smooth. They look so natural and it adds to the overall immersion into the role of Ethan. You believe these characters and take them seriously when they threaten you. Animations aren't the only thing however. The models and textures are also a thing of beauty. Truly astonishing work here. I assume this is thanks to the new RE engine they created for this game. The best part is none of this comes at a hefty performance cost. I played all the way through with RTX on medium and everything else on high with no performance issues whatsoever. Sitting at a comfortable 80-90 FPS. The only 'bad' thing about graphics here is the hair. It's weird sometimes. Especially on Mia, but it's just a minor detail, not a big deal at all.

The only part of the game I wasn't a massive fan of is the ending. It felt a little out of place compared to the previous 80% of the game. It wasn't bad, it wasn't even mediocre, it just (in my opinion) didn't fit the general feeling of the game.

Supported with the behemoth of a lore that is Resident Evil, this game comes out really having it all.  One of, if not the best horror game out there at the moment.

Honestly as a return to form RE game, the team did great in creating a horror atmosphere. It's about as classic as they come, with spooky sounds in a old, moldy house, and a psycho family sequestered in a swamp. 

Where I think the game falters is in most other aspects. 

Puzzles are simplified in an effort to welcome back fans of the older, more puzzle-house, survival horror games, while also being careful not to frustrate a new casual audience that I think the game is chiefly concerned with. It's not RE2, it's not trying to be, and even if it's not particularly satisfying or interesting, the choices on puzzle design go well with the atmosphere and show restraint. (It bears worth mentioning that Lucas' section breaks this pattern and is highly memorable as a result. I thought that section was a lot of fun as a pallet cleanser).

Combat, on the other hand, prioritizes the horror atmosphere over anything else. The first person viewpoint in claustrophobic, dark hallways with slimy black targets make for a degree of frustration as you try to get a clear shot, and while you can tiptoe backwards while shooting, it's difficult not to get snagged on terrain while a mold monster flails all over your blood-smeared screen and you try to reload, heal or get enough headshots to get it to stop. Obnoxiously, the number of shots needed to put them down is fairly hard to count accurately BECAUSE of how unclear the visual language is. 

Now, mercifully, while you CAN reload while running, which allows you to pick your moments to shoot and kite backwards, it still feels like the "combat language" of this game isn't clear for a long time. The big key to fighting efficiently seems to be blocking before hits, something that feels pretty foreign to the horror genre and you'll have to suspend your disbelief for. With the health obfuscated, it takes time to realize how effective it is. Taking more careful, focused aim, also seems to do more damage and therefore conserves ammo.

I can say during my playthrough, I found the tension and atmosphere to be powerful tools the game uses well, but the combat felt cheesy and unintuitive, and the puzzle work in this game is a shadow of it's former self. The experience ends up feeling pretty linear and empty of quality gameplay, particularly compared to previous Resident Evils. Can't say I enjoyed it much, even if it was pretty and spooky.

RE7 is a drastic departure for the franchise, following the lead of recent first person horror games. Games like Amnesia (2010) and Outlast (2013), which were the first of its kind. RE7 does away with the action-oriented third person shooting of the last 3 mainline games in favor of running away, hiding, sneaking past, and a serious attempt at scaring the player.

	This has received resounding praise, and I can easily jump on that bandwagon. But instead of regurgitating praise (we'll save that for later), let's touch on a few mistakes.

	So from the start: the game's introduction feels extremely linear. Linear in the 'this feels like an extended cutscene' kind of way. You're in narrow hallways and only ever have one way of going most of the time. It feels like a conveyor belt where you are (figuratively) holding 'W' most of the time. And this is fine for tutorial areas, but this is the first hour of the game. In a six to eight hour game.

	In its defense, I enjoyed the tension and suspense of the first locale. But try replaying it after the 'newness' wears off. You'll realize there's not much control you have. All RE games are linear (this isn't an open-world franchise), but they usually give the player a full level and control right away.

	Like-wise, the third (and final) area is similarly about prioritizing exposition. It's not as constrictive as the first part (there are enemies to shoot here and there), but it lacks in slower exploration and puzzles. The upside is that you start getting answers to the story. More on that later.

	The second area; the middle of the game, is where it shines. The game starts in earnest, with multiple doorways, keys, puzzles, a few files, etc. It feels like RE1 all over, but in first person. Creatures start getting thrown at you to shoot. And the ammo is somewhat sparse as well! There's decisions you have to make in terms of crafting more healing items or ammo. 

	The first person perspective heightens tension, because the FOV is capped. You can't see a wide view of the entire environment, which is fine since you're usually in small rooms or corridors. But because of this, the amount of info you get about your surroundings feels limited, and just as the fixed camera angles did in 1-3 (and CV), it heightens anxiety. Coupled with the few unkillable enemies that (sometimes) patrol the environments, and it makes for a fantastic experience. The (few) jumpscares exist only to heighten tension at their possible reappearance. 

	If we left it at that the game would be near perfect. It almost is, but there's one more thing that brought the experience down for me. This next point is something I'd imagine only me and a few others feel any particular way about, and that's the plot. By the end of RE6, the lore and world was unnecessarily convoluted to the point of criticism. I figured 7 would be a reboot since it's all new characters and none of the familiar organizations are mentioned. But, and this is a minor spoiler, they come into play at the end.
	
	If 7 is a reboot something simple is expected and acceptable. Instead, the game's simplicity comes about because they don't know how to proceed with the current plot threads. What we have is a game metaphorically shackled to the existing lore. It can't do much, and in the end it has to end with 'Umbrella experiment'. It leads to an expected and basic conclusion. I was disappointed. 

	It's a shame, because the game is otherwise a fantastic one. I don't think the majority of people will subtract 'points' from this game over this, but it did bring the mood down when I got to the end. We're still solidly in the 'the war on terrorism-bio terrorism' Call of Duty world of present-day RE. 

	I've spent my time criticizing the game, but only because it's (rightfully) received praise. And rather than regurgitate that, I'd like to mention items that aren't brought up as much. Even with my reservations, I believe it's one of the best titles in the franchise. If REmake is the best RE game, then 2 and 4 are battling for 2nd place. With 7, it's either a close third, or it replaces RE4 in that battle for 2nd. I've trash talked it, but that's because I didn't want 8 paragraphs of me repeating 'this feels like RE1 in first person' for the entire review. And that's the highest compliment you can give.

I really recommend only buying this game during steep discounts. It's worth playing, but it's not worth the non-sale price imo.

First tried the DX11 branch as the DX12 ray tracing update for RE2R & RE3R wrecked performance for no actual gain, so figured it was similar here. Of course, the game decides to enable HDR on first launch, I disable it because the HDR on my monitor is awful, but for whatever reason even after restarting the game, OBS was capturing the game as if it was still in HDR, which resulted in really messed up/washed out colors on my stream. Maybe this would've went away if I restarted OBS and/or my PC, but I just wanted to play and not interrupt my livestream, so I waited 10 minutes to redownload the DX12 version of the game. Naturally, it seems only incompetent people were involved in creating the DX12 update, because every time you launch it, it switches your monitor into HDR mode regardless of what you set in the options menu. If you have it turned off in the options, it disables HDR once you reach the title screen. While this isn't the end of the world, there's simply no excuse for this other than laziness.

Now, onto the game itself:

I really like the setting of the game. I want to say that it's a decent game, but there's a lot of glaring issues, especially compared to the newer RE games (note: prior to this, I've only played RE2R, RE4 OG, RE3R, and RE4R in that order). 

Overall, the game just feels clunky and unpolished. Inventory management & UI feels super clunky compared to RE2R & newer. 

Color scheme used in the dedicated crafting screen to indicate whether you have the necessary materials to craft something is not intuitive at all (everything is grayscale, they just alter the shades of gray to indicate whether you have the materials or not). Also, the game doesn't pause when you open your inventory, which is really annoying to deal with during combat.

Combat feels *extremely* clunky compared to RE2R & newer, especially in the bossfights where it is never clear if you are actually doing damage, or the game does not make it clear *how* to deal damage...or sometimes you will spend forever shooting aimlessly after destroying all eyes on a boss & wonder why it hasn't progressed, only to realize that there was an eye on its underside, which I feel has a very low chance of being seen due to how the boss moves around you in that particular fight. You can't crouch/stand up when taking damage from bees, which is particularly annoying as you encounter them in an area where you frequently need to crouch.

The game does a really horrible job at teaching you any of the mechanics it tries to introduce. The lack of inventory space in the early game results in constantly having to cycle various items in the storage box in order to do objectives. Ammo ends up feeling annoyingly sparse in some sections of the game (I know this is a design choice and a common theme in the RE games, but I feel like RE7 was overdoing it), while other sections of the game have practically unlimited ammo.

There are some puzzles where it's not even obvious that there *is* a puzzle you should be solving to begin with, and that was despite the fact that I read the notes on the wall that indicated how to solve the puzzle (I just figured it was unrelated/not important/relevant to what was actually in the room with me lmao). [b] Summary: Just save yourself the frustration and play Resident Evil 4 -- an actual survival horror game, not a crappy linear FPS with three mandatory stealth segments. [/b]

The first half of the game (5~6 hours) is an enjoyable survival-horror experience, but once you get to the basement, the experience falls apart. 

At that point you have a pistol with approximately 30 bullets and you're tasked with retrieving something from the far end of the basement. The basement is a labyrinth of narrow hallways connected by narrow doors. Ten slime person enemies guard the hallways, and they can only be killed with three headshots each. So the net result is that you have to fight your way through a series of narrow hallways, getting 30 out of 30 headshots using all your bullets, against slime enemies that duck and weave and charge you, and if you take one too many steps backward the slime enemies disappear and then respawn again at full health. Fun!

Q: Can you kill them with the knife if you run out of ammo? 
A: Feel free to try! You'll die! They kill you with two or three hits!

Q: Can you run past them? 
A: Nope. Narrow hallways with narrow doors -- the slime enemies physically block your path.

Q: Is there any way to get more ammo? 
A: Nope! Gotta kill all ten before you can advance to the next room containing ammo.

I didn't complain about the unkillable enemy in the early game (I actually thought it was fun), and I had no problem with the boss fight, even though it was hard, but I draw the line at this dumb skill checkpoint where you have to successfully land 30 out of 30 headshots on moving targets, or reload and try again. Resident Evil 7 is supposed to be a survival horror game. If I can kill eight or nine out of ten slime enemies, it should at least be possible to sprint past the last one or two. Or sneak past them. Or finish them off with the knife. But alas, it's just about impossible to progress unless you land 30 headshots with 30 bullets -- in one go, because they heal and respawn if you retreat.

I gave up.

Apparently I didn't miss much, because even the positive reviews say that the second half of the game is lame. They say that after you get past the basement, the game starts giving you nearly-infinite ammo and grenades, and spawns infinite or nearly-infinite zombies. That is, Resident Evil 7 turns into the same zombie horde shoot-em-up as Resident Evil 5 or Resident Evil 6.  

Resident Evil 7 was supposed to be a return to the franchise's roots. I don't feel like it succeeded at that. 

Just save yourself the frustration and play Resident Evil 4 -- an actual survival horror game, not a crappy linear FPS with three mandatory stealth segments.

I'm at a loss for words to describe this game adequately—it's an absolute masterpiece! For the past seven years, it has been my favorite in the genre, and I constantly find myself returning to it for the unique feeling it evokes. Interestingly, I've spent more time watching gameplay than playing it myself, which speaks volumes about its captivating nature.

The game's atmosphere is dark, scary, and incredibly tense, creating an immersive experience that's hard to match. The animations for certain events—some of which only a fraction of players might witness—are crafted with remarkable attention to detail and thoughtfulness. Character design is another area where the game excels, with each character boasting a distinct personality, strengths, and vibe. The environment and items are created with such care that the game feels incredibly authentic and rewarding for those who take their time to explore, read notes, and solve puzzles without feeling penalized for missing something. These puzzles are seamlessly integrated into the game, with even the character acknowledging them at points. The suspense of exploring certain areas or the presence of specific enemies offers an unmatched level of excitement. The game's unpredictability enhances the horror aspect, constantly keeping me on edge and eager to see what comes next.

For those who can't get enough, the DLCs offer an amazing variety, extending that incredible experience repeatedly. Each DLC maintains the high quality of the main game and, considering their current price point, comes highly recommended.

Replayability is another strong point, as players learn more about the enemies and environment, unlocking special items for future playthroughs by completing specific challenges. Speaking of challenges, I never had more fun in a game, trying to get all the steam achievements. Only missing very few now!

If horror, suspenseful atmospheres, and a preference for more than just shooting are what you seek, this is the game for you.

Thank you for taking the time to read my review. I hope I've managed to convince you to give it a try!

RE7 is my first out of the RE franchise and quickly became one of, if not my favorite, in the genre of horror and actually piqued my interest in the other games. (Which I will probably end up writing a review for as well...) This game doesn't send you into sensory overload until you audibly gasp at something via jumpscares (not that it doesn't contain any), it will make you feel a deep and uncomfortable anxiety that you just can't shake off even throughout multiple playthroughs. And this is exactly what I'm looking for in a horror game. So naturally I had to 100% it. So here's my honest review of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard + DLCs after getting all 58 achievements.

The game's mechanics are similiar to other RE games: An array of different weapons, limited ammo, healing items and inventory space, a bunch of things that try to kill you in the most grotesque fashion ever, a rudimentary crafting system and variable itemplacement on harder difficulties also make for a classic RE experience. After clearing the game on a certain difficulty or collecting coins you can unlock more weapons and buffs that make subsequential runs much easier and establish a sense of reward for completing challenges (we'll get to that later...), which I was very thankfull for, as I had to play the base game a total of 5 times on different difficulties to get all achievements. Overall these mechanics made the game very enjoyable and created a replayability, that I didn't think possible for a game this linear. On the other hand the controls and gameplay sometimes were a tad bit clunky (especially frustrating when trying for achievements...), where enemies sometimes got stuck in doorways, or the AI otherwise bugging out.

While RE isn't known for it's gripping story, I thought it was okay. The VA was fine, if occasionally poorly executed. To not take away too much, I think they could have characterised Ethan more like other protagonists of the franchise, which makes me think they weren't planning on implementing him as a MC longterm (haven't played RE8 yet). At least the Bakers felt believable and acutually made me feel bad for them by the end. Even Mia has more personality than Ethan and she's a side character. Overall the villain setup was good and kept me interested throughout the game and the DLCs answered any questions left.

Set in a swamp in Dulvey, Louisiana it sets the tone for the entire game. Insects. rot and decay all make very prominent motifs, that the devs played with to make our stomachs churn. Brilliantly executed, the game evokes not only fear, but disgust and an unease, making you emotionally AND physically uncomfortable. This creates a unique experience, where you're constantly on edge because the environment is not only scarry, but also utterly vile. And even on multiple playthroughs, I just could not shake this feeling. 

The music and sounddesign compliment the atmosphere and adds to the uncomfortable and bleak theme of the game. Each section of the game (and boss) has a unique track, which makes those sections feel even more special. 

The general design of the game as well as the graphics overall add to the themes mentioned above and highlight the dingy atmosphere throughout the game. I especially like the cellar in the main house, as that place never failed to make me feel utterly uncomfortable. So if there's a texture that isn't that high in resolution it only adds to the feel. That being said; game looks nice, but some textures do look a bit muddy, but I'm nitpicking.

NOW, for the achievements: This game is by far one of the hardest experiences in terms of 100%ting I ever had, which is mostly fine. It was a good mix of mechanical skill and general knowledge of the game, requiring the player to really commit to the game and its quirks in order to get the achievements. HOWEVER, the clunky controls, as well as broken enemy AI at times made some achievements an absolute nightmare, the DLCs in particular (End of Zoe, I'm looking at you...). Throw in a really punishing game mode and you have a classic RE experience. The "Ethan Must Die" achievement almost made me ditch this entire run, but finally getting it with a bit of luck after DAYS of trying made it all worth it. There are four achievements for collectables, which I generally do not like in any game, as I consider fetchquests to be the laziest form of challenge. It doesn't require skill, but just the ability to not go insane while having a guide open in the steamoverlay on 50% oppacity for hours JUST to be sure you didn't miss a file. Overall I felt challenged and rewarded for trying to unlock achievements, as the game gives you more options and weapons to play with after completing a challenge and that is all I seek when I did these runs. Alas, I think I do have a few more gray hairs because of a few trophies.

That all being said RE7 is one of my favorite games in general as well as in the genre, that I would recommend to anybody looking for a unique horror experience, that doesn't shy away from a challenge.

It took me a while to come back to this game after the first time I played it.  I got tired of having to run away from the same invincible person all the time while also trying to find stuff and solve puzzles.  The AI just gets completely in the way to where sometimes it's ceases to be fun.  They don't even do you the courtesy of providing you places to hide.  There was even a point where one door opened as unrealistically slow as universally possible while someone was approaching me.  That's not suspenseful or immersive, that's just asinine.

The parts where the game allows you to fight and defend yourself, in contrast, are definitely fun.  Especially with some of the weapons you can use.

The story is nothing new.  Give paranormal superpowers to a spoiled brat and make everyone else helpless to her.  Yawn.  There's actually a bit of thickening between this and RE8 Village, so I suppose I shouldn't criticize it too much.  If you pay close attention, you can deduce a bit of a twist.

There's a no-win decision you have to make near the end that annoyed me.  Developers need to understand that enabling your players is always a good thing.  Capcom, in this case, doesn't care.  I shouldn't have to buy DLC in order to not feel like a loser.

So, I see why this game is as popular as it is, even if it was maybe half-good to me.  I know there are a lot of players who like the helplessness of a predator avoidance situation.  So, if you're one of those, you'll like this game.  The puzzles are pretty good and satisfying to solve.  There is definitely a redeeming amount of combat, but not like other RE games I've played.

If I were to compare this to Village, I'd say Village is easily ten times better.  Still, Biohazard has it's charm in some ways.  Give it a try if you like survival horror.

[h1]The Gameplay: [/h1]
The first person perspective handle at a slow suspenseful pace is a fantastic direction that RE decided to explore in. Having a block mechanic is also a nice touch along with a very accessible heal. Swapping through hotkeyed weapons is a breeze, however trying to use one that is not hot keyed is a nightmare, but I suppose that's part of the charm. Fighting the molded was a little frustrating once you start to learn that the game actively moves them away from your reticle and they stumble forward every time they take a hit, no matter how hard the hit. They would later refine this when they used this same system for zombies in RE2 where it wasn't as aggressive and had some variation. Overall with the way items, puzzles and combat rounds out 


[h1]The Story:[/h1]
The story is possibly the best part of this entry. It's twisted, full of dramatic shock and action but mostly it tells a true horror story. Seeing how a normal wholesome family could get so warped is actually kind of depressing. It tells the story well and is far from predictable, and has proper foreshadowing and character development. 

[h1]The Visuals:[/h1]
This game showcased the RE engine and it did not disappoint. Everything looks great, maybe not Mia's hair per se, but it looks real enough while still appearing to be clearly a game at the same time. The enviorments are absolutely stunning and the lighting is amazingly done in such a way to inspire the maximum dread. It is an all around great looking game.

[h1]The Sound:[/h1]
The sound of the boards creaking under your footfalls and the slight pang of metal groaning in the distance really does a lot of lifting when it comes to setting the horrific suspense this game delivered. The voice work on top of it added an extra layer of chill as Jack or Margarite Baker chase you down. The music seemed good, but the other elements honestly overpowered it. I can't really recall the music too much for this one, but it definitely didn't stand out as a bad thing.


[h1]The Experience:[/h1]
You can tell this game was a labor of love that in fact saved the RE franchise. It was a great exploration into well what the namesake of the game is. Things that are familiar like a home in an almost evil state. It perfectly portrayed that and was one of the few RE games that successfully pulled off being scary. I actually enjoyed that it did not feel the need to constantly throw action in your face. Well at least in the beginning of the game, near the end or in any of the DLC they just shovel it onto your plate, which fine. It is overall an experience I would recommend any who have dabbled with the series or any level of horror game to try out.

Resident Evil 7 is one of my favourite entry in the series and honestly it sort of revived the series. The praise that it receive is certainly well deserved and the shift to first-person perspective is an interesting choice but it works. The game leans heavily onto it's horror element instead of being a more action oriented game like it's previous entries. The game is definitely a step in the right direction by Capcom.

The gameplay is pretty identical to older Resident Evil games. It's a survival horror game with a sprinkle of FPS on it. The game features a crafting system and the resources are quite limited which makes you think before you act when encountering enemies in the game itself. The various bosses designs are beautiful and the boss fight itself isn't overly complicated or hard but resource management is definitely a key. The game ambience is also beautifully crafted, during any boss fights or enemy encounters, the soundtrack actually gives you anxiety and makes you feel uncomfortable. This definitely carries the game to another level and although the core gameplay is similar, such as looting, crafting and progressing the story. It definitely doesn't feel repetitive as it's really enjoyable. The game itself is definitely a lot scarier and the atmosphere definitely serves it well.

As for the graphics, the art style and environment is definitely one of the highlights for the game, coupled with the first person perspective which limits your vision it's definitely anxiety and fear inducing. Definitely an improvement when compared to it's predecessor. In terms of the story, it's definitely one of the better written ones however that isn't to say there isn't any flaws. The ending for me is definitely a bit underwhelming as most of the plot points went unexplained. They did however address some of the points in the follow-up DLC. Speaking of DLC, the additional content provided is definitely a blast to play through and it's really enjoyable. The Banned Footage & Not A Hero is definitely a highlight amongst the DLCs.

Resident Evil 7 is definitely a breath of fresh air when compared to it's previous entries on the series. Although the game does suffer from few minor flaws, it's negligible and I would recommend to pick it up if you're into Resident Evil franchise or horror games. It's a prime example of horror games done right and it got me hook from start till end. I would personally rate the game [b]9/10[/b] for it's polished gameplay and overall a great bargain especially during discount.

Tries and mostly fails at recapturing the claustrophobia of the early games, due to sometimes very tedious gameplay (tiresome reuse of areas and annoying/nonthreatening or bulletsponge enemies that aren't scary), puzzles that are often either braindead easy or overly obtuse in an attempt to be clever, and clunky first person action that can be tense or even thrilling at times, but more often just feels unrefined, unwieldy and occasionally unfair. Including a third-person mode in RE8 was a good decision, if only for me.

*Minor story spoilers :3*

Moments of great horror are brought down by mostly inert, handhold-y and cliche storytelling at best, along with an overuse of disgusting imagery/gratuitous gore that really desensitised me. I'm also so tired of the evil little girl trope, at least in how it's presented here (basically just F.E.A.R's Alma Wade with very little difference, beyond more of an attempt at sympathy I guess). Ethan and Mia are relatively uninteresting protagonists as well, although Mia's gameplay section towards the end is at least a nice change of pace (maybe just because she's not a stand-in white guy with a damp towel of a personality).

There are original ideas here, and great gameplay moments sprinkled throughout that do feel like a solid modern take on the RE formula, which is what makes the overall experience all the more frustrating and deflating as a series fan.

I powered through the story mainly to have greater context going into RE8, which I think I will enjoy more. Hopefully playing the two story DLCs will sweeten my palette somewhat.
