It really pains me to leave a negative review. In a lot of ways this is what in my opinion RE should have been after the second one. A slow survival game with limited ammo and small spaces blocked by a few zombies. A game that requires careful navigation and conservation of ammo rather than having unlimited ammo and facing endless bullet sponges. It doesn't have absurd dialogue and story and is very grounded for Resident Evil standards. 

It should be amazing but it fails in the details. The game has long cutscenes that you can't skip and has sequences  that lead to instant death. It isn't always clear what you must do so you will die a few times in order to understand what the game wants you to do. It ruins the horror atmosphere and make the game tedious to play. If you make a second playthrough it's even more unbearable especially if you play on hardcore where saving is limited. 

Another problem is the evil family in the house. When you get chased in RE 2 by Mr X he has a imposing figure (tall and silent)  and you can't kill him. You can only run away in opposite direction and hope a zombie wont kill you in the way. Mr X showing up creates tension you can't fight him but you can run faster than him. He can be evaded with planning and luck. In RE 7 you get chased by rednecks that talk nonsense, always get killed but come back. The worst thing is they run faster that you and it's not easy to see them or know when you're hidden. They spot you and have to fight them again or run to a safe spot for them to spawn again. It's very tedious. The fact this is a first-person shooter compounds to the problem you can't see as clearly as in the other games. 

I really tried to like this, it's huge step in the right direction. In a lot of ways it's everything RE should be but  I can't, it just isn't fun. I played till the end and almost everything I did wasn't scary or engaging and made me say "wow this is dumb".

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Finally, the residents are evil.

After such an experimental run with RE5 and RE6, they went with this, which I would call equally experimental. But this time they're back to what made the RE fans love the series in the first place - and it's arguably RE at its best. It was something the franchise needed a lot at the time, as it was slowly dying.

Mostly reminding me of RE2, this game is absolutely unforgiving, but it is also far scarier than anything else in the series. It's probably survival horror at its peak. The atmosphere is ominous and chilling and half of it lies in how unpredictable everything is. It's far more than just cheap jump scares. It's the tight corridors, the dark ambiance, the very realistic and gruesome graphics, the incredibly immersive sound design, the tiny inventory where you're always low and saving on resources - all of which make for a really nerve-wracking experience. The story is great throughout the whole game, but I think that everything about the Bakers family is phenomenal, from the characters themselves to their past, which you discover throughout the game. I love the map design, it reminded me a lot of RE2's police station, as it is pretty much a fully open experience, and all the areas are consistently great, but there's something about playing in first person that makes it all even spookier. One comment I read said "the atmosphere of the Baker mansion was so on point that I got excited every time a door was locked" and I couldn't agree more, but at the same time, ironically enough, you spend most of the time backtracking and solving puzzles just to unlock that exact door.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3109998686

The thing is that once you do find a way to unlock it, you get both a feeling of satisfaction and uneasiness. What's behind that door? Is it more loot, or am I getting completely f*cked once again? You never know. What I didn't expect playing for the first time is how big the map actually is. It just keeps getting bigger as you are exploring and unlocking new areas. Compared to the amazing mansion section, the tanker area and the salt mine are significantly weaker, but they're still good, interesting stages and they're also very important to the story. I believe this is mostly because the atmosphere is not quite matched, there are less enemies and they're much weaker than Bakers.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3110000751

Overall, the enemies are not too hard, but the Bakers' boss fights are. The mutated stages are great, both for Jack and Marguerite. But I must say that I had a good laugh at the garage sequence while fighting Jack. It's not bad, it's pretty great, but it is so goofy and so Resident Evil-esque. On the other hand, mutated Marguerite is a really good boss fight. She turns into a monstrosity, but she's still showing her vulnerabilities, so you're forced to fight your way aggressively in order to succeed.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3111024465

After two really questionable games, Capcom understood their mistakes of going for the trending ideas, which led to some really Hollywood-esque moments, and finally chose to make what the fans wanted, what this series really is. It's Resident Evil back to its roots, but modernised for even greater immersion.

I can't recommend this game enough. It's a must-try for horror fans.

- Ammo and consumables are just the right amount of frequency based on difficulty level
- The birthday puzzle was fun
The only thing I didn't like was the "run" speed.  Wish you could run just a little faster to make it worthwhile to run away from enemies if you want to conserve ammo.  I found myself just carefully aiming / shooting or blowing up enemies just because it was too much of a pain to run away.

This is by far the scariest RE game, at least in my opinion. It's one of those where even when i know whats coming it still gets me every time I experience it again, and that's a rare thing to capture with horror in general I feel. That enough should interest you, but if not I'll go into more detail.

RE:7 Biohazard works as a soft reboot of sorts to the Resident Evil franchise, everything that happened before is still canon and is occasionally referenced but you don't need to know anything about Resident Evil to jump in and understand what's going on in this game.

We are given a brand new protagonist named Ethan Winters, a man who's wife Mia has been missing for 3 years and has suddenly sent him a message with her exact location telling him to come pick her up to go home. This is the plot we're given to start with and with a brand new inexperienced protagonist RE is given the opportunity to be truly scary again, because for the first time in a long time you feel almost helpless. Ethan has never held a gun before this incident and it shows in the way he handles, but not in a way that makes the game not fun to play which is obviously an important balance...

Also with a new protagonist comes a new POV, for the first time RE is in first person like the original was going to be before they decided they could fit more on a disc with fixed camera angles, and it really works here. The new mansion (The Baker Estate) is full of claustrophobic areas and little dark nooks and crannies you can explore into.
Along with a first person perspective we have some new buttons, block and crouch! 
The enemies here are just as windy and jerky as the zombies in RE2, but are also now stretchy and lanky, meaning there are some attacks you can duck under and some attacks you might be forced to block, a welcome addition to the usual RE gameplay loop imo

The weapon variety here is pretty lacking though, aside from the first Glock you obtain from a police officer in the beginning, the only weapons you can find are about what you'd expect to be in a rundown Louisiana estate, a couple shotguns here and there, a DIY flamethrower and grenade launcher for takin care o them wasp nests, and of course theres a magnum. there are however variants of the pistol and shotgun you can find hidden in the mansion if you look around, and a couple secret weapons for completing achievements.

What REALLY shines in RE7 though are the characters, and the performances given to them. While the entire game takes place in a single estate and none of the areas look particularly different to each other, there are 3 members of a deranged family inside you have to contend with, each one of them paying homage to a different western horror film, and you can tell each one of the VAs for the villains had a fantastic time playing these characters (especially Jack).

Aside from the main story there are multiple extra modes you can play with a story concurrent to the main one, there's Not A Hero and The End of Zoe which take place after the main story ends, there's the Banned Footage DLCs which takes place at roughly the same time as the main story, as a character named Clancy who was right ahead of Ethan the whole time he was in the estate. Each of the DLCs have their own gameplay style and are very welcome especially in RE games where you'll be playing the main story over multiple times if you want all the secret weapons and items.

All in all a fantastic entry in the RE series and a VERY welcome homage to the original after the abomination to society that was RE6. Pick it up it's well worth full price.

Another damn good entry into the series that once again redefines the game's main "thing" while also capturing what makes the series Resident Evil.

Definitely worth playing. As with all the RE Games, experiencing the story for yourself is a lot better than reading a review - but rest assured, the gameplay is solid as ever.


==Banned Footage (both volumes)==
I've always been kinda neutral on the side modes each RE games has, but the ones I've tried out have been quite fun (so far, only The Mercenaries in RE 4's remake and all the ones from this game) - and they're all quite good. Not really a fan of 21, but that's mostly cuz i don't like the game IRL.

As for the little mini-stories Banned Footage adds, I quite enjoyed them (though the escape room can be unclear at times).


==Not A Hero==
I love how Chris returns in this game, and his DLC is a great bit of fun. There's new enemies, weapons, and a couple new mechanics while also carrying over the Antique Coins from the base game - however, you don't need to collect them all to open every cage this time 'round.

The actual story of exposing some organization Lucas is sort of helping feels a bit out of place (in the sense that it wasn't so much as hinted at in the base game), but it's fine.

Give it a shot. I personally love the return of punching enemies to death (great way to save on ammo!).


==End of Zoe==
I really like this expansion - but the final boss makes it rather frustrating at the end. Damn thing does too much damage... however, the rest of this is good (except the alligators).

Melee combat can feel a bit clunky at times due to limited range you're given, but once you adjust it's not bad.

I recommend giving all the DLCs a shot as they all offer something unique, and the entire game + DLCs is only ~15 hours long, so it's (thankfully) not a timesink.

Resident Evil 7 grounds itself in elements that made the original great while still indulging in a risky new shift in style that both helps and hurts the beloved formula in equal measure. But it’s also the closest a numbered sequel has come to recapturing Resident Evil’s slow, but thrilling and atmospheric adventure game roots in a while — a welcome return that I truly hope to see more of in the future.

RE7 is a fresh take on the Resident Evil series that fondly recalls the classics even as it takes a bold new direction.

Is it the greatest RE ever? Depends on who you ask. Did it revive the franchise? In many people's hearts, yes.
After RE 5 and 6, Capcom must've realised that a Resident Evil without a residence and some evil isn't very RE like. Don't get me wrong, co-op is great, but it isn't everyone's cup of tea. So back they went to the drawing board and they conjured some of the most grotesque, in your face, pure horror. 

Story: You get a call, your long lost GF just resurfaced. It's rescue time. You go to Louisiana where nothing ever goes wrong and you meet the Bakers family. While the story is pretty much Resident Evil nonsense, it is fun to be able to play different characters through DLC and to see events from different perspectives. Ethan, the main protagonist, is as detached as they come, he's a no drama and a -dafuq?- kindaguy. I don't wanna say more than the plot isn't all that interesting, but the characters are. One's groovy, one's nasty, one's crazy, and all the others are VERY annoying in their individual, special, unique ways. The main campaign lasts a solid 6-8 hours. This is an example of quality over quantity. Lots of replayability, if you enjoy unlocking weapons, that is. There is 2 endings, but only one is cannon and the other is just sh!t (they're dictated by a decision you'll have to make halfway through the game)

Gameplay: 1st person shooter with cramped spaces and in your face danger. Scarce ammo, many hidden weapons and upgrades, making players who explore be very rewarded. There's a block.. blocking? whatever... mechanic which is very helpful when enemies get too close, and learning to aim can be tricky, unless you disable to head bob, which I eventually did. Check points are a plenty and thank god for that, because if you wasted all your ammo by missing all your shots or on a part you could have just run, you WILL regret it. Because when you're low on ammo, you turn into this mode where you run from everything and and end up getting cornered and... well, die. Again, and again. 
Each DLC has a different play style (though all in FPS) that vary from playing cards, being able to follow up with melee when enemies are stunned, escaping a room and the house to plain punching everyone to death. They all tell tales of the different NPCs you've met so they are worthwhile, though also very short.

Graphics: I remember playing the crap out of this game back on release on the PS4, got platinum before any DLCs released. I remember how well it was optimised... Hoping back on this today (oct. 2023), it felt like it wasn't as well optimised. Nostalgia? My old fart memory tricking me? NEIN! After a few tweaks (disabling FXAA and TSA and only using SMA, and also turning off depth of field), it looked a lot better. Maybe only the beginning area looked iffy. Enemies also are bleargh and get redundant. 

Audio: Great. Nothing bad here. Maybe too few sound tracks but each hit when and how they're supposed to. Tense moments bring a tense ambience. The house creaks how it should and brings about a sensation that something might lurk here or there. And since a lot of things are in your face, the sounds are... well... they're what you'd hear if they were close to your face. 

It's an amazing entry in the Resident franchise. Strong in the fear factor, but weak in the action.

TL;DR RE7 is a fine game in terms of gameplay, but I personally think it doesn't feel like a Resident Evil game, and if you’re looking to get scared, I’d say look elsewhere since if you’ve seen *any* horror movie in your life, nothing here will impress you.

Had I played this without the "Resident Evil" in the title, I'd never know I had been playing an RE game, and instead would have thought I was just playing a *really* generic horror game based off of an existing film.

RE has always had a few elements that made it what it was, regardless of whether it was one of the "classic" games or the "action" games: Zombies/BOWs, Umbrella, iconic protagonists that were entertaining in their own ways, not taking itself *too* seriously, and for lack of a better word: Charm. Those games were "generic" in their own ways, sure (zombies are pretty overused), but there were elements (the ones I just mentioned) that made it feel more original, and what made the series so iconic.

7 on other hand lacks those elements. The Bakers feel like dime a dozen horror villains and the designs of the molded aren't threatening, and are thoroughly uninspired; normal molded are just watered down zombies and the four legged molded are just watered down lickers. The “virus” of this game feels less like a virus that mutates people and is more akin to [spoiler]posession [/spoiler]. It may as well be something supernatural as opposed to scientific. 

There is no Umbrella or otherwise any real antagonistic force that was behind the game’s events, and no protagonists or other past characters we already care about present [spoiler] and no Chris Redfield being shoehorned in along with a "rebranded" Umbrella doesn't count, and neither does a shoehorned antagonistic force that is named only in the Not a Hero DLC [/spoiler], and instead we get a new protagonist who is honestly pretty boring with no real personality who, despite being a faceless "everyman", takes an amount of punishment that would leave an ordinary human as severed as your suspension of disbelief watching him take those injures like they're nothing and quite literally gluing himself back together. In past classic REs, you played with the assumption that your character was never bitten or otherwise seriously injured by anything that might turn them, but here Ethan takes lethal hits and loses limbs in cutscenes and walks it off. [spoiler] I know there's a reason for it, but the reason is just as dumb if you ask me and I refuse to believe they planned that plot twist ahead of time. [/spoiler] 

And on top of all that, what makes this game really “generic” feeling for me is its liberal use of references to other works. You can only reference Saw or Texas Chainsaw Massacre so many times before the audience starts to find said references jarring or wish they were watching those instead to get their horror fix. It really makes the game feel like it’s trying too hard to oversell itself and overcorrect the series from previous “mistakes” (*ahem* RE6). Aside from the fact that people overreacted to RE6, that game’s "problem" was that it was unable to be taken seriously by everyone due to how over the top it was. But obviously, as with all the games in the series, that game wasn’t really trying to be serious. 7 most definitely is. And ironically, to me at least, 7 feels like the opposite extreme of 6 in this regard - it’s hell bent on you taking it seriously, but at the same time feels like every horror movie you’ve ever watched (or heard of) ever. 

If RE6 represents the extreme of being too goofy with too many explosions, RE7 meets it at the opposite: Trying to oversell the horror aspect and trying way too hard to be serious. RE6 may have been different, but because of it having the “charm” I mentioned previously, I still view it as an RE game. Such is not the case for 7.

All this said, I know RE isn’t a game you play for the plot, but these factors in particular make this my least favorite RE entry, and to me, it feels like the game is trying too hard to sell itself and overcorrect from the past RE6. 

Like I said at the beginning though, 7 is a fine game and one worth playing. It has good ol’ survival horror gameplay like the classic entries, and if you’re looking to get scared, you probably will be assuming you have had no exposure to the horror work it references. However, I don’t think it’s accurate to say it “saved the franchise.” Rather, to quote a friend of mine: “It turned it into something else.” It's gone from being a series you don't take too seriously that had occasional "scary" moments to one that practically begs on its hands and knees for you to be scared. And I think that’s kind of a shame. It is what it is though.

[h1]A great return to form, and one of the best RE's to date![/h1]

After the absurdity that was RE6, having what feels like a soft reboot is honestly welcome.
We go back to spooky houses/mansions, gain a first person view, play as a new protagonist, reduce the action on the combat, and bring back the need to scavenge for your ammo and upgrades.

All that aside, I think this is just a real fun horror game.
It has very few references to the rest of the series, and it really makes great use of its setting.

[h1]These Residents are Evil and there's like seven of 'em[/h1]
The Baker Family are some of the most twisted parts of the series, and are overall effectively used.
From establishing a weird setting to being some of the most persistent hunters in the series, they're a major part of why I enjoyed this game.

They consistently taunt you all throughout whatever section you're exploring, jump out unexpectedly, set traps/puzzles and consistently keep things pretty fresh and well paced as you go through the campaign.

If they weren't threatening and uncanny as is, the boss fights certainly are, turning things from unsettling to straight up absurd, with the first real boss fight acting as a fantastic introduction to actual combat and problem solving.

[h1]The Residence is also quite noteworthy[/h1]
This is some of the best level design in the series, even if it doesn't have as many noteworthy puzzles as the older games.
There's so many little hidden items to pick up and a nice amount of rewards for remembering to backtrack.
Backtracking thankfully, isn't really painful, as you usually feel a good sense of progress for clearing out sections as you progress, and shortcuts help speed things up quite a bit.

Though unrelated to level design, the sound design is really nice, so many little sounds that help make this house feel active, even without people actively hunting you. All the creaks and moans, bits of machinery, the squish of mould under your boots, it really helps contribute to the great atmosphere.

[h1]To make some negative comments[/h1]
I'll go a little deeper on that lack of noteworthy puzzles comment, most problems in this game are usually the result of something being locked off or needing a new weapon to progress further. It's usually not a problem to find these things, it's just a matter of going deeper and deeper into the house to find what you need, instead of needing to puzzle your way out of most problems. Puzzles still exist mind you, they're just not as abundant as they used to be.

On a different note, enemy variety is debatably the worst in the series.
Discounting the various Bakers, you really only have 3 - 5 consistent enemy types.
One is a generic grunt, one is a faster/slimmer version of that grunt, one is a fat guy, one is a shielded grunt and one is location specific, [spoiler]insects[/spoiler].
I wouldn't be so annoyed with this if even the first game in the series did better than this, plus the amount of weapons and ammo you can pick up in this game proportionate to the amount of threats you're facing is almost too much.

Lastly, there is a point of no return I feel could've been telegraphed a bit better, to give vague spoilers of where it happens, [spoiler]when the game wants you to deposit your items to progress, turn back to finish up any unfinished business[/spoiler].

[h1]Summing up the DLC[/h1]
Not a Hero and The End of Zoe are basically the epilogue for the game, they're roughly 1 - 2 hours each and while they don't add anything substantial to the plot, they do tie up some loose ends while bringing some fun gameplay of their own, with TEoZ being a series highlight as far as I'm concerned.

The lost footage on the other hand kinda sucks depending on who you talk to, as they're more gimmicky, featuring a survival, escape room, cards and prologue.
I'll be honest, I only did the escape room and prologue ones and I didn't like them at all.
The escape room has puzzles which make you wait, at minimum, 3 minutes, and has some rather cheaply hidden items and moments where if you mess up, you just end up wasting your time.
The prologue has barely any story, doesn't establish anything new, and has a garbage requirement for a true ending which didn't need to be there, absolute waste of time.

[h1]Despite some issues, I still think this is one of the series best entries[/h1]
Consistently well paced, plenty of memorable aspects and a great setting and atmosphere do a lot to help make this a new classic, and a very easy recommendation to series veterans or newcomers alike.
With how cheap it is nowadays by default, I have very little reason to say you shouldn't get it, it's just a fun time.

Resident Evil games have always had an element of over-the-top arcadey horror but this just takes it to another level that just... isn't scary and ends up being a chore to play. Examples of things that aren't scary and just gore (all of this is in first person):
[spoiler]Your infected wife shoving a chainsaw in your stomach and ripping it up through your head while laughing[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Your infected wife chops off your hand with a chiansaw[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Getting force fed intestines[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Getting a knife shoved in your mouth[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Watching your arm and neck get broken[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Watching someone get their head sliced in half by a shovel[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Redneck chainsaw battle where he attacks you with chainsaw scissors and you chainsaw his head in half while he laughs... repeatedly[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Shoving your hand elbow deep in to a day-old headless corpse's neck hole to get an item you need to progress[/spoiler] 
[spoiler]Playing as a secondary character and watching first person as you're set on fire and burned alive (a good 10-20 seconds)[/spoiler] 

I could keep going, that's like the first half of the game. How is any of that scary? It's not (at least not to me). That and the jump scares are just pure laziness. There's also a part about 60% in where you [spoiler]have to explore a little girl's room when your flashlight is flickering and stops working[/spoiler] that was really well done too. Other than that it's just a frustrating gorefest.

If you want to get into Resident Evil, definitely go for the Resident Evil 2 and 4 remakes, or even RE8: Village. Those are recent games that are much better entry points to the series imo. Horror franchises NEVER do soft reboots right, mostly because it's an almost Herculean task to end up not just playing it too safe and making an unnecessary, worse version of the original. Most of the time, it seems that the creators lack any insight and are unable to recreate what made the original good, but in a different enough manner to have it feel new at the same time. Resident Evil 7 is a masterpiece, not only in and of itself but also when looking at it through the lens of what it's trying to accomplish in a more meta manner, which is to be to the franchise now what Resident Evil 1 was to the franchise then, and it does the impossible, it really does. From the game design to the narrative beats, to the quiet yet resounding references, Resident Evil 7 is not ashamed of the cheesiness of the originals and is even less afraid to bring new horror inspirations to the franchise without losing itself in its own world. Although to those who became too involved with the lore of the franchise may find it hard to agree to any statement of the supreme quality of RE7, it's for those who have always enjoyed what Resident Evil set out to accomplish at first to realize that the franchise didn't lose its way, but instead realized what most people trying to soullessly recreate classics these days forget: When standing on the shoulders of giants, don't think of yourself as bigger, but instead see how tall you can be just by keeping yourself balanced.

"Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" had a lot to live up to, considering the towering legacy of its predecessors. Unfortunately, it misses the mark by a significant margin. One of the most glaring issues is the movement speed. In an era where responsive controls and dynamic character movement are the norms, RE7 feels sluggish and, frankly, outdated. Players find themselves painstakingly trudging through the Baker mansion, turning what should be tense moments into frustrating experiences.

The gameplay style, too, is a far cry from what fans of the series have come to expect. While innovation and fresh takes are always welcome, RE7's attempts at creating a different vibe are more jarring than groundbreaking. The absence of a 3rd person perspective option is a significant disappointment. It not only alienates long-time fans who've grown accustomed to that playstyle but also limits the player's spatial awareness in critical situations.

Narratively speaking, RE7 feels like an odd one out. The story doesn't seamlessly align with the overarching lore of the Resident Evil universe. The unique charm, consistency, and depth seen in previous titles are noticeably lacking here. The Baker family saga, while intriguing on its own, feels like a detour rather than a meaningful contribution to the franchise's rich tapestry.

Compared to the depth, complexity, and sheer thrill the other titles in the series provide, "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" feels like a missed opportunity. All things considered, if I were to rank all the Resident Evil games, RE7 would regrettably find itself at the bottom of the list. For newcomers to the series or veterans alike, there are far superior Resident Evil experiences to indulge in.

[h1] Resident Evil 7: A Fearful Homecoming [/h1]

For two decades, Resident Evil has been a roller coaster of gaming quality. From the terrifying vulnerability of the early games to the action-oriented pivot of Resident Evil 4, the series has seen its ups and downs. Stagnation crept in, and fans hungered for something fresh. Then came Resident Evil 7, and it's nothing short of a revival, marking the best entry in the franchise in a decade.

In Resident Evil 7, Capcom masterfully balances pacing. The story unfolds rapidly as Ethan Winters, in search of his missing wife, becomes ensnared by the Baker family in Dulvey, Louisiana. What initially seems like a Texas Chainsaw Massacre-inspired tale surprises with depth and twists that defy expectations.

While Resident Evil 7 draws from Western horror influences and shifts to a first-person perspective, it retains its unique identity. Combat is about small, tense encounters rather than hordes of monsters. You'll feel the stress of every bullet and every decision. Inventory management returns, adding a layer of strategy to item collection and combining resources.

Boss fights are thrilling, with multiple approaches and surprises. The game's storytelling, while not aiming for awards, is intriguing throughout, offering a mix of fear and levity reminiscent of the Evil Dead films.

Playing in PlayStation VR elevates the experience, despite some technical drawbacks. VR immerses you in the horror, adding genuine scares and making every encounter intense. Whether in VR or not, Resident Evil 7 is a journey worth taking, packed with secrets, unlockables, and multiple endings.

Capcom has reignited the series with Resident Evil 7, blending its roots with fresh ideas. It's a pulse-pounding, atmospheric horror experience that has me excited about the franchise's future once more.

I'd say this is one of the weaker RE games for me. I know the game gets heralded as the game that brought back the horror into the RE franchise but there were a lot of things I just didn't enjoy about the game.

- Stalker aka Jack: I get it. Having an invincible entity chasing you around the game is an easy way of making the player feel stressed out but between this, RE2 and RE3 I feel like we've had more than enough of this. At this point I feel more annoyed by it than anything else ...

- Items: Key items like cranks and door keys don't get marked if they have no more use in the game. This is annoying and has been done better in other games. The crafting system also feels like a step down compared to the other games e.g. you cannot craft specific weapon ammo. You also drown in gun powder and herbs but don't get nearly enough stuff to mix it with. Which brings me to finding items: it sucks. You have to constantly crouch and look in between tiny spaces in order to find items. There is even a drug that you can find and use which enhances your ability to find the items so the devs must have knows how annoying the item placement is ...

-Gameplay: Probably the biggest issue for me. The first person feels awkward to fight with and your narrow  view hides important information. Multiple times did they make enemies rush up behind you without you being able to see them e.g. in the testing area under one of the mines or when you get the SMG with Mia on the ship. I didn't mind the lack of enemy variety since I don't think the games need that many enemy types.

- Characters: I know it's just "Resident Evil" but I always liked the characters in the games even though they had some cheesy dialogue. Heck maybe I liked them because of it ("Jill Sandwhich"). In this game I don't like anyone at all. In fact, the MC is pretty unlikable. His reactions to the events happening in the game are also puzzling. The guy is just a regular citizen and he's barely reacting to anything that's happening. Like right from the get go his arm gets stabbed by a knife, then by screwdriver, then it gets cut off by a chainsaw and he even "kills" his wife and yet there is barely any reaction. Like what's his deal?

-Visuals: the game doesn't look bad per se but it reminds of the brown shooters from the PS3 era. The colour palette is nothing to write home about.

Resident Evil 7 - The Redemption of Survival Horror

The Resident Evil franchise has come a long way since its iconic debut in the late 90s, but with Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, it's evident that the series has made a triumphant return to its survival horror roots. Departing from the action-oriented gameplay of its recent predecessors, this installment brings the franchise back to its origins while simultaneously pushing the boundaries of terror. Resident Evil 7 Biohazard truly marks the redemption of survival horror in the gaming world.

Revisiting the Essence:
The franchise's recent titles moved away from the spine-chilling tension and puzzle-solving of the original trilogy, focusing instead on explosive action and larger-than-life scenarios. Resident Evil 7, however, returns to the series' core principles, embracing the vulnerability and helplessness that characterized the early games. This shift represents a much-needed redemption, rekindling the nostalgic feelings of unease and anxiety that fans had been longing for.

A Symphony of Terror:
The sound design in Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a masterclass in creating a haunting atmosphere. Every creak of a door, rustle of leaves, or distant whisper serves to immerse players in a world of perpetual dread. The utilization of sound as a storytelling tool is nothing short of remarkable; it's the eerie footsteps or the muffled groans that alert players to the lurking horrors. This level of detail ensures that players are in a constant state of unease, with the sound design seamlessly blending into the overall horror experience.

Engulfed in Dread:
Resident Evil 7 introduces a transformative shift to a first-person perspective, fundamentally altering the way players engage with the game world. This change amplifies the immersion, allowing players to experience the terror through the eyes of the protagonist, Ethan Winters. The gameplay encourages exploration and resource management, delivering a visceral sense of survival against grotesque foes. The return to puzzle-solving enriches the gameplay further, requiring players to use their wits to progress and fostering a sense of accomplishment.

Unveiling Nightmares;
The narrative of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a tapestry of mystery, fear, and family secrets. By following Ethan's desperate search for his missing wife, Mia, players are drawn into the twisted world of the Baker family. The pacing is deliberate, allowing for gradual reveals and shocking moments that propel the story forward. The integration of found objects, tapes, and journals into the narrative deepens the connection to the game world and heightens the player's engagement. This storytelling approach ensures that the horror is not only visual but psychological, creating a lasting impact.

Overall Rating - 10/10:
Resident Evil 7 Biohazard stands as a testament to the resurgence of survival horror. With its return to the franchise's roots, brilliant sound design, immersive first-person gameplay, and captivating storytelling, it successfully revives the genre's essence. This installment is a bold leap forward while paying homage to the franchise's history. Resident Evil 7 Biohazard earns a resounding 10/10, a score that reflects its status as a defining entry in both the series and the survival horror genre. Whether you're a long-time fan or new to the horrors of Resident Evil, this game delivers an unforgettable experience that redefines what it means to be afraid in a video game.

Resident Evil 7 was controversial for some. At the time of this interview I am not a longtime RE fan but I have played most of the games fairly recently. Many of the mainline ones REmake, OG 2 and 3, 4, 5 and this. 
This definitely is the comeback the series needed from the heavily action packed RE6. The studio had a whole shakeup with new leadership.
I played it on Normal mode. And played the Ethan must die mode. 
I think this game is great and the new game director had used his position wisely. 
It is very spooky, atmospheric and gritty. They used some sort of photogrammetry to get high resolution pictures out of real life Louisiana. The ame looks good and is moody. The house lived in and yet worn down and horrid. The game has some gross violence and bodily harm. Mold is definitely an interesting and fitting element of decay to fit the theme.
The story is simple. You play Ethan Winters a man looking for his wife Mia in the Baker house. Redfield is the only legacy character to return but his storyline from RE6 is touched upon but expanded upon in a revelation in a DLC. The dev team must have felt the series needed to move on from the character bloat and the crazy world ending nature of the stories that came before. This is more focused and the stakes not as high.  
Its important to play this before RE8. You get to be with Ethan Winters a man who is inexperienced before he becomes the badass Dad in RE8. In this game he runs extra slooooow. He slashes his knife wildly and his aim a bit shaky. You are playing a dude in a bad situation. The game took me 9-10 hours. You might be longer. The Baker houses are filled with secrets like items hidden in boards udner the house you can sue to repair guns or coins to buy new guns so be diligent exploring! There is no merchant or store, just you scavenging. But there are chests like in the original trilogy to store items.
The one criticism I have is the enemy variety ain't great. Instead of zombies you fight mold monsters. They have a variety too but are otherwise not as interesting as zombies. They are also not that crazy bad to deal with. They are slow. And when they die they completely disappear. They don't come back like crimson heads and can be dealt with surprisingly well with the knife so you can save a lot of ammo stabbing em. The boss fights aren't too bad. I found the end wasn't so bad as i had stored lots of ammo and guns I didn't what to take so just be smart. The ship section kinda loses luster as it is not as spooky and lacks Ethan. It is sort of abrupt and only after that mission you resume as Ethan and by then the game is nearly done and you are shooting your way to the end boss. There is a boss fight when you go through Lucas's SAW-like trap house that becomes a point of no return.
Overall the main game is very good. It has a found footage aesthetic and feels very inspired being in a southern setting. Heck even the safe room has no piano for once and is an old banjo to fit the setting and tone. Its a very strong reboot. I personally don't mind first person view. I like fps games and I think it is immersive. 
I woulds also recommend the DLC to get the footage modes that are unique in their own way like one being a sort of wave horde mode. 'Ethan must die' is a gauntlet of you running through the main house against monsters and traps getting items form RNG crates. It is very tough and I recommend beating it. Use what you learned to play. The Jack Birthday is amusing and can be addicting to trey and get S ranks. The Chris Redfield dlc is good if you want some fps action playing as a well armed Chris. The Joe Baker DLC especially is quite goofy fun punching your way through molded. The Chris and EoZ dlc tie up parts of the main story for certain characters which is a bit odd of a choice to leave unanswered though not really necessary to explore. These modes even have unique difficulty options to change up playthroughs and things to unlock. 
The game also has two different endings depending on who you save though one ending is realistically canon.
Also do try and collect and save up those coins!
Definitely check this game out!

Even though I only played this game in 2023, I can see why people were excited when it first came out in 2017, before the REmakes, as a return to the Resident Evil series' true spirit.

For people who don't know what Resident Evil is all about, it's a horror survival game. The gameplay is mostly about solving puzzles, looking for items to solve the puzzles, managing your supplies so you have enough to healing and ammo to keep yourself alive. This means weighing wether you should kill that monster or try to avoid it, etc.
There's not much to introduce here, to people who already know the series. It's the same recipe as Resident Evil 1, 2 and 3. It's good, and the setting is really well done. The big change here is first person, which works really well for a horror game.

In my opinion, this game really shines during the Bakers' manor sections (which is a lot/most of the game anyways). The characters are interesting and the 'creepy family' setting is very well done, and some moments are actually kind of funny depending on how you take them. I thought Evie was the least interesting character, just because we've seen the whole 'evil little girl' gimmick one too many times. The DLCs are also worth it as additions to the story, tying up some loose ends, each one offering some differences in gameplay from the main game.

Okay so my review of this game is surely going to rile up many RE fanboys, but buckle up for some brutal honesty if you have the patience to read...

As a huge fan of the Resident Evil franchise I was eager to get my hands on this but the more I played the less I enjoyed it.

The best hour of the game is the first hour you spend with it but this quickly wears off. The game is not as open as the old school games, normally anything you find would have to be kept until later on in the game, this means it forces you to make dangerous trips back and forth while managing your items carefully, however in RE7 anything you find will most likely be used in the area you're in. I've noticed the Baker family events are scripted as well and unlike Nemesis in RE3, is not random at all.

At the end of the day this is a poor man's Resident Evil and being first person does not help. I'm more shocked over the "high" reviews praising the game but it's obvious Resident Evil 6 lowered expectations so much that anything after would be better. This game isn't Resident Evil, I give it a 5 out of 10 because at least it is a decent survival... But the relation with the roots of the franchise is nonexistent.

The atmosphere doesn't fit with Resident Evil at all, I'm not saying it is bad for a horror game, but in a Resident Evil game, this doesn't fit at all, in the older games you were on mansions, castles, police stations... all those places have kind of rich and decadent look, the location on this one however is just a redneck house full of rubbish.

The camera is a point where everyone should agree, I don't like it but it's not the first camera change on the franchise, they already did it in games like RE Survivor for the PS1 or in RE4 onwards (though it wasn't a first person POV), anyway the camera change in this case is to make it more similar to modern/generic horror games and to sell more VR, in other words just a gimmick to get more people buy the game and the VR.

Also... Where are the characters? The older Resident Evil games were full of characters aside from the antagonist, you had partners, maybe they weren't well written at all (somebody wants a Jill sandwich?), but to be fair that was part of the essence, Resident Evil was like a B movie all along full of memorable characters. On this one you have your generic faceless protagonist (thank god at least he has a name), the rednecks (aka Leatherface family), your possessed girlfriend and the black guy (who like in all horror movies dies first) and that's all... 

The story is a complete mess, it isn't related to the franchise in any way, it's a mix between Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Evil Dead and F.E.A.R. , the paranormal stuff is completely out of place, I didn't care that they tried to give it an explanation, they just put that garbage that doesn't fit in a Resident Evil game and tried to get out with it with some lame excuse. It's an incomplete story with holes for DLC.. the whole game was a huge drag to play once the Wrecked Ship part comes in, also the ending is so disappointing that it will question you a full price purchase.

The ending to this game is a horrible let down for a few reasons, completely skipping out one of the main antagonists without really addressing why and then rushing straight to the end with only the occasional text file to fill in some of the many blanks.

But the two biggest let downs are the final boss and the laughable attempt to link to RE universe. The final boss fight is nothing but a scripted 2 minute fight with unsatisfactory pay off in regards to the design of the monster and the means with which you quickly kill it. The cameo of a character at the end and the arrival of umbrella is completely cringe worthy as far as how forced in it feels, especially with the character looking and sounding nothing like their self in other RE games.

This didn't need to be a Resident Evil game and it pretty much isn't, in the same way if they made a new super mario game, but you didn't play as anyone from any Mario game and the only reference to Mario in it was that you could jump, run and see the occasional picture of previous mario games on the wall. 

It's an okay horror game, worth buying on a huge sale, but it's not a Resident evil game. 5 out of 10.

Exploration is a staple of (most) Resident Evil games and it is most profound in this one. It isn’t extremely heavy on the backtracking, it just encourages thorough searching as items are hidden in sneaky spots and the map doesn’t show when an area is completely searched.
The items that you use in this game fit survival horror well, and they are properly limited. You start off with a knife and pistol. The knife is to save ammo, or if you’re out of ammo, a last resort. The pistol is the main tool, being used to take out the weaker enemies which are higher in number. You are then introduced to enhanced handgun ammo which can be used as a boss-killer but is expensive to craft. After that, you get the shotgun. Shotgun ammo is more scarce than handgun ammo, but it destroys whatever is in front of you. The flamethrower is a situational tool that you use for DoT but is never meant to kill enemies. The grenade launcher is much the same but also does heavy hitting with its two ammo types: flame and neuro. The Magnum is The Gun. It destroys but ammo is extremely rare, and unlike the shotgun, it doesn’t have a spread of pellets that can make up for a ‘lack of skill, friend.’ The SMG is only available for a short time. I am not a fan of machine guns in survival horror as they encourage spray and pray without the timing that pump-shotguns require to be effective. You also get bombs at the end. Minor healing and greater healing can be crafted alongside a wide variety of ammo types. This gives the player a choice between health and damage, and it’s what I love about this genre. Managing your very limited resources so that you survive. That’s why the slightly hidden items work so well, because you are searching diligently for more resources.
The story is very interesting, and while this may not have been the game that inspired me, this was my first Resident Evil game, as well as my first horror (unless you include FNaF which I watched Markiplier play before playing myself) so I was very scared at almost every part of the game. It got me into the series and it cemented my passion for biology. Ethan and Mia Winters are pretty bad characters to experience the story through, although the three [hostile] Bakers are excellent villains, especially Lucas.
This game has a decently-lengthen campaign that can be replayed on varying difficulties with multiple challenges. These challenges can be completing the game using a limited number of heals, finishing it under a certain time and much more. Resident Evil 7 is packed full with a glorious variety of DLC. End of Zoe and Not a Hero stray from the horrific atmosphere of the main game to being power-fantasies. Daughters is a typical defenceless horror, Bedroom is a puzzle horror, 21 is Blackjack but horror. Then you have Ethan Must Die and Jack’s 55th birthday which are fun arcade-like extras with the latter having a happy tone.

Some things I didn’t like:
• Ship section
• That there’s two endings
• Doors are annoying to open
• Unskippable cutscene which makes replaying the game very annoying
An additional point is that the opening is so long that replaying the game is dreadful. It also wasn’t a good first impression on me. I had seen my friend and YouTubers play horror games before, and before Resident Evil, I was only aware of run away and hide games like Outlast, mascot horror like FNaF, or collectathons like Slenderman. I had never heard of a resource-management, shooter horror. I probably would have quit this game as I thought it was going to be like Outlast up until you defeat Jack for the first time. Not like Outlast in the sense you are defenceless, but in that there isn’t any skill gap. I thought I was just on a roller coaster with minimal control over my items. Thankfully, my friends kept pushing me to play. So while this is a great game, I wouldn’t recommend it as an introduction to survival horror as first impressions are very important.

Resident evil 7 is one of the games I have played this summer. I don't usually play horror games, but after completing death stranding in January and completing the last of us part 1 in may on PS5, I decided I would give this one a shot. TLDR: I am glad I did and would recommend you do too.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay structure follows Ethan Winters(here on refereed to as the player) exploring an old decrepid family home and its various offshoots in an effort to find his missing wife, Mia. Puzzle solving is usually limited to: recognising the objective, exploring for the solution, finding information on the solution and finally enacting said solution ([spoiler]Usually killing some gooey mould men along the way[/spoiler]). That description only covers the puzzle solving aspect of the game, however Resident evil 7's gameplay is comprised of combat and puzzle solving -which are usually intertwined. Looking at combat, it plays out like your typical survival horror game: find weapons, manage ammo and run when ammo can be saved or when there is no ammo left to be saved. The main difference to this typical combat formula is some of its boss fights (spoilers ahead [b]and clearly covered[/b]). [spoiler]In the second fight with Jack baker, its a puzzle in the sense of trying to use your environment to your advantage while also dealing damage with the chainsaw.[/spoiler]

[h1]Story[/h1]
Resident evil 7 is not a direct continuation of 0 through 6. There is some carry-over through lore and references, but the main story can be self contained and still understood. the story presents many mysteries and not many explanations till the end allowing for an increased factor of fear. The story i also interesting to find why Mia went missing and what made her go missing. [spoiler] My favourite part of the story is where it feels like fear is removed, at the end, Ethan finds the soul of jack and Zoe baker and talks to them about what Evilyn did to them, It solves that one final mystery and brings resolution. Furthermore, the ending takes you to the same guest house you started in, showing the cyclical nature of evilyn's escape rise to power and subsequent capture.[/spoiler]

[h1]Fear[/h1]
The final segment of this review will be an analysis of how fear is shown through the game, seeing as it is a horror game after all. Fear is placed into the player the moment they say Jack Baker in the forest. That is the first seed (or spoor) planted into the players mind. From there, it blooms into creating a continuously dark and creepy atmosphere: with dead animals nailed to doors, strange organic structures coating walls, unappetising fridge contents and the very idea of mystery itself a turn off for the player. sticking to the last mentioned factor, the idea of locked door once inspiring inquisitiveness, towards the middle of the game begins to insight distrust of what one may find.

This game has left an impact on me: it has made me play a horror game for the lore and intricate story telling it presents. Due to to my enjoyment of this game, I will be taking a look at resident evil: village (8), and also the remakes. 8/10

Resident Evil 7 is, for me, a welcoming reboot of the series as a whole. It breaks away from many things that define previous RE games, while also retains some nods & gaming conventions. It’s a fresh new take that tried to appeal to new horror fans but didn’t alienate older fans.

RE7 is a first-person survival game in lieu with other modern horror titles, such as Amnesia, P.T., Outlast, Alien Isolation, etc. The pacing is quite slow and methodological that only help to tense up the horror effectively. You could feel claustrophobic at times or grossed out by what’s presented on screen. It makes for an unforgettable horror experience.

The story, surprisingly, is a self-contained one but still connected to the larger RE lores. You’ll see nods and mechanisms that hearken back to first few RE titles. Some have been translated or repurposed to fit in modern setting. It shows that even after all these years, RE can still evolve and keep up with time. It also shows the devs love and understood what players want from these games. There’s so much details in this title.

Playing trough RE7 is really enjoyable even for non-horror fans. The level difficulty, puzzles, enemies, etc. weren’t frustrating or punishing for players who want to take their time with it. The length wasn’t short either. It manages to strike a balance between a complex storyline with fun dan engaging gameplay.

Overall, it is superb.

I've been itching to write a review about the so-called savior of RE franchise for a while now. After several years since its release I think it's safe to write an honest review, when all the dust is settled.

Let's start with the positives.
+ Very graphical (at the time). 
+ Very authentic feel. At least to me, I am not a Louisiana resident. 
+ Has actual puzzles unlike 5 or 6.
+ Very fun villains (Jack is carrying the game like no one else)
And... that's it. From here on out, there are no more positives.

Let's start with the small ones first
- The plot. It's a mess even by RE standards. Chris Redfield's appearance is all proof I need to demonstrate. As is Not a Hero DLC.

- The gameplay. Look, it's just terrible. You move as slow as a snail. I get it, you are not a Leon SK or Chris Based and Redfield, but why does Ethan jog around at such a pathetic pace? After a while trying to play the game becomes a snoozefest because of how SLOW you move.  
Now, I get it, you are a horror protag and all that, but that's another problem - enemies are neither scary, nor fun to kill! Molded, molded, molded, MORE molded, Jack, Margueritte, molded, molded, MORE molded again.

- The horror. There's none. I am sorry, I cannot be scared for the life of me when a jolly man that laughs with murderous intent is trying to kill me. It's a B-movie experience, if you are utterly scared of that, you probably haven't played good horror games. 

At the end of the day, what we have is clearly a very confused (ironically just as confused as RE6 is said to be) game that has a very clear identity crisis going on. Considering this is Capcom's first game on RE engine, this game feels more like a tech demo of what their engine can do and frankly? When you play that game, you will feel like that's exactly what the game was meant to be.

Two extra points to cover: DLC and RE7's legacy. 
I will be brief. DLC carries the game. It's the only reason I have so many hours in the game, more fun to play than anything else in the entire game. 
RE7's legacy is also downright depressing. We now keep getting stalker enemies everywhere since the trend has started in 7 and we even got the RE8 and god forbid RE9 be like that. People love to blame RE6 for all that's wrong with the series, but I think RE7 somehow has had a more devastating impact. Yes, I know, I myself am shocked I am saying such things. 

TL;DR : Don't waste your money, don't be lured in by the promise of return to survival horror. Just don't. Watch it on Youtube if you must, watch some streams if you are so inclined. Worst case scenario, get it on a discount.  It's just a glorified tech demo with limited gameplay.

What more can I say about this game that hasn't been said since 2017. Resident Evil 7 is a great return to the Survival-Horror roots of the franchise, and while I did enjoy Resident Evil 6 I can understand it may have disappointed many and that this game was a nice return to form for them. While I prefer the third-person adventures a bit more than first-person I can confirm that it works perfectly here as it sucks you into the world and makes you feel trapped and helpless whilst escaping from the Baker family. This is the scariest game I've played in the franchise and that is nothing but a complement to Capcom and their amazing world/level design in this game. As someone who isn't a big horror fan this was a test of courage, cause man do some of the scares just seem unfair and out to get me specifically at times, but it was good fun all the way through. 

The one thing that I wish I could've experienced first-hand was all the puzzle solving as I have seen way to many people play this game online, so I knew what I was doing for most of the game, this in no way is against the game its mainly against myself, It's like re watching a show or movie after you've known the big twist for years, it still has impact just not as much as when you experienced it the first time.

Finally the antagonists carry this game so well as the Baker family are some of my favorite villains in gaming and in all of fiction. The story is great and doesn't connect to the greater Resident Evil world until the very end which helps let this game's story and characters hold their own. Jack Baker has some of the best lines and is a funny yet terrifying stalker enemy who constantly is taunting you throughout the game unlike the silent threat Mr. X and, the monster obsessed with S.T.A.R.S. Nemesis! 

I really did enjoy this game and you will too!

With the introduction of the RE engine with this game and the return to SURVIVAL HORROR makes this an unforgettable RE game. I 100% recommend this game to anyone and everyone and to new and old players of the Resident Evil universe alike. A fantastic play and a much needed return to its roots.

After its time as an action game, RE7 was the franchise's return to Survival Horror. While far from perfect (and imo the least good of the games of its era), it's still a great entry in the respectable franchise.

PROS:
+The introduction of the RE Engine: the textbook example on why companies should spend time on optimizing their games.
+The Baker family is an enjoyable set of antagonists, each with a different gimmick to deal with as a boss while progressing through the game.
+In particular, the constant looking-over-your-shoulder for Jack and Marguerite felt reminiscent of looking out for Mr. X in RE2R.
+However, among them, Jack Baker stands out as a scary yet fun antagonist, eagerly showing Southern hospitality before chopping you in half with a shovel.
+Somehow, Japanese writers get the American Deep South better than many American writers, Yankee, and Southerner both.
+Ethan in this game is actually a protagonist I really like. It's nice to see "the random guy in over his head" as a protagonist, and Ethan's just as good in that role as Claire was/is in RE2.
+Every weapon has a time and place where it shines. Doesn't mean that every weapon is good throughout the entire game, just that it's easier to kill wasps with a flamethrower than a shotgun.
+The music is very rarely heard in the base game, and always heightens the tension of the situation.
+The story is ultimately about those who suffered directly at the hands of Umbrella and their ilk. It's well and truly tragic, and I honestly pitied the ultimate antagonist even as I was shooting them in their face.
+Certain spoilers in RE8 can be inferred by elements of this game. The whole story is laid bare by Chris in that game, but you can figure out what's going on in this one.
+A whole bunch of fun puzzles. I enjoyed the shadow-sculpture puzzles and the Saw setup the most.
+You can gather more information by playing through flashback video tapes, which serves both as a fun framing device and a window into the lives of those slain by the Bakers.
+This was the first Resident Evil to gross me out. Kudos for that!
+At the end of the day, I really can't fault Capcom for making the new BOW-substance mold. I mean, we've had viruses, parasites, bacteria: fungi and mold were really the only two left, and The Last of Us had just done Fungi.
+The change to First-Person doesn't work everywhere, but there were some gross-out moments made grosser by using it.
+Chainsaws!
+Mods!
+(Micro-)Flamethrowers!
+DLC: Various alternate game modes. Most of them are fun, especially the escape room, Zombie Survival mode, and two additional chapters. Others are...less so.
+DLC: "Not a Hero" picks up exactly after the game, providing a satisfying coda to the main game. Worth playing!
+DLC: "End of Zoe" serves as a fantastic conclusion to the game, offering an enjoyable change in the gameplay style.
+DLC: "Nightmare" is a welcome change from other zombie survival modes like in Call of Duty and Killing Floor. It's different while being familiar, and is a definite joy to play.
+DLC: "Bedroom" is a wonderful change of pace and a challenging puzzle! I really liked it!
+DLC: "Ethan Must Die" is a pain in the ass, but beating it was satisfying. I now get why people like RogueLikes.
+DLC: "Jack's 55th Birthday" is probably my favorite RE DLC of all time. Sit down Separate Ways, Jack's hungry!
+DLC: "Daughters" is genuinely tragic and heartbreaking. It hits different to see how good the Bakers were as human beings before everything happened.
+Completing the secret in the Demo will give you a bonus to your currency in the main game!

CONS:
-Despite not being able to fault Capcom for making the enemies Mold, I dislike that the standard Molded enemy takes 2x-3x as many bullets to put down as a regular zombie, regardless of your difficulty.
-Marguerite really needs a longer dress or some pants.
-I audibly said "wtf" when I saw the organization Chris was working with during the end cutscene. The DLC "Not A Hero" explains it better, but it still feels off-kilter to me.
-Depending on the decision you make as you approach the end of the game, a character's appearance at the next location feels really illogical.

When I first heard about an FPS Resident Evil, I was very skeptical. In fact, I had just written Resident Evil off and decided to ignore 7 and then later on 8. I was one of the many RE fans that didn't really like how the series went with the success of 4. I liked 4, found 5 to be meh and I didn't play 6 because I heard from reviews that it was basically a pure action game and the survival horror bits from old were pretty much all thrown out, and those were my favorite parts from the RE series. The claustrophobic feeling, finding keys and solving puzzles, all the while killing monsters and worriedly watching your precious ammo dropping, wondering when you'll find more. Those were my favorite parts of the RE games. And they were slowing moving away from that, and with 4, started in a new direction. So I figured 6 killed the franchise since I'd heard it didn't do well and so wrote RE off. But like the zombies of old, they rose again with RE 7. At first I was excited, they were coming back to their survival horror roots, yay! They were bringing back the keys, puzzles and central locations, yay! And it was FPS... crap!
The thought of an FPS Resident Evil filled me with dread and confusion. I thought they were just jumping on the bandwagon of those survival horror games like Alien Isolation, the Amnesia series, Slenderman and all those other FPS games that pitted you against some horrible monster that you couldn't kill, or didn't even have weapons like with some games of the genre. So I wrote off 7 and 8 and just hoped for something better. Then the remakes came along and I was revitalized. With the 40th anniversary of Capcom putting all the RE games on sale, I decided to bite the bullet and fill out the rest of my collection and snap up 5, 6, 7, and 8 for the PC. 7 and 8 are very damn good. I was, quite frankly, shocked and amazed at how good they are. They are pure Resident Evil, all the keys and puzzle solving, limited ammo but enough to kill everything you run into if you aim right and make the right crafting choices. I also was ashamed of myself for not giving 7 or 8 a chance and ignoring them all these years. I might be late to the party, but I finally got here and I am completely enjoying myself.
Bottom line, if you are a fan of the game style of the older games, the puzzle solving, the keys and the claustrophobic feeling of the environment, then 7 and 8 will be welcome editions to your Resident Evil collection!

After postponing my trip to Louisiana for so long, it was time I finally shook hands with the Bakers, experiencing the game that reinvigorated the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise. And I won't beat around the bush — [b]if you fancy yourself a survival horror fan, play it now![/b]

[h3][b]The Girl Who Wasn't[/b][/h3]
Right off the bat, the setting and plot feel more grounded than anything previous [i]Resident Evil[/i] games provided me with. Sure, there are still outlandish moments. But, as a whole, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is not as over-the-top as some previous iterations. Also, I was pleasantly surprised by how invested I was in the Baker family. They weren't a perfect family, but I felt genuine sadness when the revelation of their misfortune befell me upon completing the game and all subsequent DLCs.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2970679203
As for our new main guy, Ethan, who gets entangled in this Louisiana nightmare while looking for his sexy wife, Mia, he holds his own. Doesn't punch boulders tho. But it ain't about how hard you hit. It's about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward. How much you can take and keep moving forward. That's how winning is done! And Ethan's willing to take the hits. Severed limbs? [i]'Tis but a flesh wound.[/i]

But enough about the plot. All that mysterious gooey mold on the projector screening the [i]"Baker House Incident"[/i], you should remove it yourself. So, let's instead discuss the gameplay, which underwent a massive change — [b]it's now a first-person game.[/b]

[h3][b]I AM THE DANGER![/b][/h3]
Some will like this change in perspective, others will die on the [i]old is gold[/i] hill. But [i]me gusta![/i] It amplifies the horror, gifting me a more intimate date with all the [i]wonderful[/i] beasties yearning for my very own, still beating heart. I could feel their touch and moldy breath as we exchanged blows.

And in many ways, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a homage to the first [i]Resident Evil[/i] game. A big house/mansion, survival horror put front and centre, and the plethora of hallways and interconnected paths, with many keys to find, doors to open and puzzles to solve. Perfection. The homestead was a joy to explore, with many layers and all accessible without a single loading screen. But despite it being [i]hughmungus[/i] and having copious amounts of backtracking, skedaddling around the map never became tedious. Sadly, the endgame levels weren't as good and were a bit lacklustre.

The gameplay also changed a bit. A few times [i]Capcom[/i] resorts to the (un)popular defenceless horror trope — [b]an unkillable enemy stalking you.[/b] So, you'll have to be sneaky, avoid their gaze as you complete some silly puzzles the Bakers prepared for Ethan and fight a few moldy boys along the way. Overall, the gameplay is slower, more methodical, and claustrophobic, with the accent put on resource management. [b]In other words, it plays exactly how a survival horror game should.[/b] And to help further elevate the horror element, the RE Engine delivers a masterclass in horror ambience. I was in awe, watching the shadows and light perform their sensual tango routine, effortlessly making my neck hair salute.

Now, the climax does forgo horror in favour of action, and it's the correct choice. At that point, I had plenty of ammo to feed Milunka, my trust shotty, so any attempt to arouse anxiety out of me would fail.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2990083646
So, let's talk combat.

[h3][b]Perfectly balanced, as all things should be[/b][/h3]
It's stiff but not tank-ish like the first few games, with Ethan's movements and actions still having weight. And the shift in perspective also required re-balancing the combat. It needs to be challenging but fair.

Since Ethan's not trained in the dodging arts, he can [b]block[/b] by using his steel forearms, cushioning incoming damage. But not fully. And the [b]enemy design[/b] also helps make combat less frustrating. Only one mold enemy is agile with erratic movement, making him a bit tricky to headshot. It resembles that [i]Stranger Things[/i] Demogorgon creature, walking on all fours and jumping around. But agility comes with a price, with a single headshot putting it to sleep permanently. The other moldy boys are more resistant to bullets but slower and more straightforward with their attacks. Also, just like in [i]Dead Space[/i], they can be crippled. However, them crawling on the floor doesn't make them a moldwalk — they will lunge at you. Lastly, be wary of the fat mold — [b]its plumpness hides a wet surprise.[/b]

And since Ethan's [i]sexy wife rescue operation[/i] can't be laughably easy, [i]Capcom[/i] gives the mold an edge in some ways. The obvious one is [b]level design[/b], creating that claustrophobic feeling I spoke about. Lots of tight hallways and corridors await you, so movement will be limited, with the moldy boys just marching forward, despite you gifting their head full of lead. Constantly backing up without being aware of my surroundings and the moldy boys coming out of unexpected places got me cornered a few times.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2990048907
But just letting loose until the fat mold sings isn't a sound plan as [b]resource management is a crucial aspect of the game.[/b] So, as the wise purple Bruce Willis once said, [i]"You should have gone for the head."[/i] And so, I did, often. Technically, this only applies to common enemies — bosses have weak spots and [b]they do be bullet sponges.[/b] But you get the gist — [b]I was frugal with whom my gun's barrel kissed.[/b] Even then, I often found myself with a worrying amount of bullets in my pockets. This was completely absent during the endgame, with it being more action-oriented, showering me with ammo. I didn't mind this as it felt like icing on this delicious survival horror cake, giving me a satisfying end to Ethan's stay at the Baker's estate.

There's also one more thing — [b]bringing up your inventory doesn't pause the game.[/b] I had to craft consumables and ammo on the fly, adding another layer of challenge to the combat. It was a bit troublesome during boss fights, I won't lie. How dare they not wait for me to craft and then eat my green weed juice to recover!? And as I'm not that great at multitasking, I died a few times... But the fights weren't too difficult overall. Some even had fun gimmicks. Still, most did end up being a [i]just-pump-the-boss'-weak-spot-full-of-lead-until-they're-dead[/i] fest. Ultimately, they were all fun — [b]except one![/b] [i]Capcom[/i], some things weren't meant to be seen by the human eye.

But I digress.

As for the bad, I only have one complaint — [b]abysmal enemy variety.[/b] Sure, they would pop out of lord knows where and startle me. But I was underwhelmed by the mid point, with that initial scare factor wearing off as the more I saw of them. Besides the moldy boys, there were some flying bugs during one section. I don't really consider them proper enemies. Apart from buzzing in my headphones, making me feel icky, the butter knife I had would one-shot them. At best, I would call them pests.

And, with all that being said, I hope I was clear — [b][i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was a blast to play.[/b]

It's a soft reboot of the franchise, providing homage to the first [i]Resident Evil[/i] game in more ways than just being set in a mansion-like complex — [b]it went back to survival horror, the series' roots.[/b] So, bring your weird green juice and dive head-first into this welcoming piece of Louisiana land, where the misfortunate of the Baker family and tons of mold await you.

After the more action-oriented 4, 5 and 6, this is Resident Evil's return to actual survival horror. In practice, it means that it is quite scary, that your character feels weak compared to the monsters he's facing (no punch, suplex or other head-bursting roundhouse kick), that the game doesn't throw many enemies at you and prefers to keep you on your toes from your anticipation of them rather than by their actual presence, and that the resources feel somewhat scarce.

The story in only loosely connected to the other Resident Evil games and pretty much every character is brand new.

In general, the graphical quality is quite good. It does have all the habitual problems such as all the silly options that are on by default: motion blur, depth of field, bloom, lens flare, chromatic aberration... All the usual suspects that make you glad you're playing on pc as you're able to just go and uncheck them all. The game's way of mimicking eye adaptation to light is particularly irritating and the way to turn it off is unfortunately unclear. If you set up the brightness as the game dictates you will end up with wild variations of light whenever you turn around, move a bit, look at a file etc, often forcing you to stop for something like 2 seconds every 180° turn to wait for the light adaptation to settle down so you can see hopefully see something. The game will also be far too dark, which is never a good idea, even in horror games, as it transforms any scariness that you might experience into frustration. In short: the game's handling of luminosity is truly egregious. When setting up the brightness, don't bother reading what the game tells you.

I've had two critical errors in 30 hours of playing, which isn't that good, but isn't terrible either I suppose. They were both unusually severe though, since they forced me to reinstall the game entirely to make it work again for the first one, and restart my computer for the second one.

Overall, I very much enjoyed the game despite its problems, and I'm glad to see that survival horror is back on the table in Resident Evil's main line after so many years. Not incredible, but pretty good.
