Biohazard is a very interesting and different game compared to the rest of the Resident Evil series, but honestly, it's fresh, and likely my favorite one of the series

The thing about Biohazard is that it has a focus on horror that is simply just not present in the rest of the games in this series. Sure, 1 and 2 are likely the scariest along with this one, but they also have a large focus on action along with it. 2, in my opinion, is the closest you can get to this game. Once you get to 3 and beyond, the series mostly focuses on the action compared to the other 2, with 5 and 6 really honing in on pure action with nearly no horror.

It was really hurting the franchise, and the "return to form" that the director had in mind made him reverse on the action far more than what was likely anticipated. And I for one f***ing love it. I think the pure focus on horror is really what makes this game shine, and even the gunplay comes second. Don't get me wrong, wielding a gun feels powerful and realistic in this game, rather than a simple COD game, and the limited resources (I mean, this is a survival horror game) can make things extra scary, but it's really all so that they can compliment the horror of this game. If you really liked RE 4, 5, or 6, I believe you may not appreciate this game to be part of the series, because despite the fact that they may be the same franchise, those 3 really focus on good combat, where the horror is what is focused on in this game, and the combat (which is great) is purely secondary.

The area design is also incredible. With it designed to be similar to an actual home in this setting, they easily make everything feel extremely claustrophobic and worrying if you'll get trapped at any point in time. It's definitely scary and gives me exactly what I came here for in the first place. The lighting of the areas is also just incredible, making sure you don't feel comfortable at any moment because of a warm light. Walking into a safe room makes you feel super happy and genuinely safe, and the moment you step out, you already feel like taking a step backwards. They make a strong setting that I haven't really found in many other games, and anytime I see any visuals, it makes me want to experience the game for the first time again.

The story is also quite incredible, giving you information about the different characters each individually as you prepare to face them head-on. Although not nearly as direct as the other games, it ties in with the rest of the series' story quite interestingly and it makes up for an incredible 12 hour game.

I really loved this game, and I HIGHLY recommend you check it out. I think the game is 100% worth the 20 dollars at full price, and 150% worth the price whenever this thing is on sale, which I am finding, is quite common. If you have the money to spare, I would definitely recommend shelling out the money to buy this incredible experience of the game.

There are games, like Amnesia, or Outlast, which I'll just watch videos on, because the idea of being depowered in a horror game can be frustrating. 

This game has it too, but this game's atmosphere, story, and gunplay is second to none in the genre. I wanted to find out what would happen next, how the family was doomed from the start, what scary crap was around the corner. I was gaming with the equivalent of squinting with my hands in my face. Every action was tense. I hate being chased, especially in the beginning where you have no way to fight back. But once you can and you get the layout of the land, this becomes the most exciting and tense and horrific of the series. It's a great jumping on point for people unfamiliar with the series. And if you can get through this then you can play Village and see how Ethan's story continues. 

In the end, it has it all. The DLC is all great. Every piece completes or adds on in a great way. Daughters is a good one. But my favorite has to be the End of Zoe, where it's the anti-RE 7, where you get to duke it out with the scary monsters that gave you trouble all base game long. All in all, it's a varied, amazing package and I'm glad this game exists. Play it!

[h1]The Dignity of Being Finite[/h1]

I open my eyes to find myself tethered to a chair. A guest constrained, the first sight to greet me is a banquet in a state of utter putrefaction. This nature morte—the still life of every canvas—has failed to capture eternity or immortality. It has succumbed to rot. Its perennial imprint is precisely this: the essence of being dead.

The surname of this family, as they proffer their loathsome hospitality, is a curiosity indeed. They are the Bakers—those who should fashion bread—yet there is no greater testament to their presence than this repast. I know not whether they perceive the decomposition, the fetid stench, the insects emerging from putrid carcasses through fragile apertures. For them, this is sustenance. Even Mistress Baker is roused to fury when one refuses a morsel. The food, as if unwilling to become mere waste, persists in decay—much like the soup of maggots that never leaves the aluminium pot.

This immortality is singular, and terrifying. Unlike the common notion of the immortal—so often imagined as pristine—the Bakers exhibit an eternity of putrefaction. No confirmation is more harrowing than the mutilation of the son’s arm. He offers no complaint; he merely affirms that this is not the first occurrence. The limb regrows, unseen by our eyes. It is as though immortality were a purely corporal sentence.

The body—the body alone—resists its demise. I find myself implicated in this defiance without my own knowing. Once untethered from the table and left alone, I seek an egress. Mr Baker prowls the kitchen. Unawares, I am overtaken; with his tool, he severs my leg. The curse transmits itself to my very frame. I, too, possess something of this corporal immortality. I drench myself in a fluid that causes my limb to cohere; it refuses separation. And then, following the death of another, I behold something utterly harrowing.

Though I remain whole, it becomes manifest that my limb—and indeed my entire body—follows an order over which flesh claims no true sovereignty. Mr Baker demonstrates a fragment of regeneration; his body reconstructs itself. The conclusion presses upon me: the body is immortal, yet the soul is not. How, then, can the soul be the form of a body whose nature is so utterly alien to it? It is as though one were to claim that the body is the form of the soul. The order has been grotesquely inverted.

And yet, something reveals itself.

It appears there is no soul at all—only flesh, driven by a blind impulse to persist. My singular clue emerges upon meeting Zoe: she alone among the Bakers has not undergone the transformation. How can I be certain she is not as the others, despite her desire to aid my escape? The answer lies in the strains of Go Tell Aunt Rhody, which I once attended to within my carriage. This capacity for remembrance likewise renders me distinct from them. A verse declares: “They locked me up and took my soul,” and adds, “Shame on what they made.” The Baker family has lost its soul, humiliated by the hand of another.

The same refrain declares that they are dead. Something within this place denies the body its rightful decomposition, yet binds it to that ignoble state: perpetual decay. The Bakers have forfeited their dignity. There is no more poignant testament to the loss of their identity than the squalor of their dishevelled garments.

This truth was heralded from the outset, during my passage through the moribund woodland. Death had seized the land, transmuting it into eternal decomposition. The revelation takes form: holomorphic—its very name betraying a form founded upon a formless whole. Thus do the Bakers’ bodies comport themselves. When Mistress Baker “perishes”, when her body ceases motion, she transforms into a hollow husk, fragile and pallid. Their souls were extirpated, as the walls of the house and its scattered papers attest to the kindness they once possessed, before the arrival of Eveline.

The loss of dignity lies in the desire to manipulate that which holds no affective power over another. Eveline does not perceive that controlling the body—as though it were a doll preserved in decay—cannot elicit love, nor create a family, nor found a hearth. Just as she plays at tea with dolls and “house”, these physical trifles, devoid of affection, cannot manifest what truly dwells within a home: the soul and the heart. The soul grants the capacity to love; the heart permits the creation of a home within the space we inhabit.

It terrifies me when the dead body regenerates. Unlike other creatures I have encountered, which fall inert upon losing a vital part, within this manor even the dignity of death is stolen. The Bakers perish only when Eveline so decrees—when she decides her dolls, more akin to puppets stripped of soul and reduced to husks, have served their purpose. It is as though one were to implore a doll for an embrace. I do not see playthings; I see only putrefying flesh, denied the form bestowed by the soul.

Eveline aspires to be the form of the body, yet she cannot achieve this, for she herself lacks form—and lacks, too, the understanding that the desire for the Good lies in allowing beings to endure as whole, rather than dissolving into mire.

Eveline exerts control, yet in doing so she withers the soul. Bereft of soul, there remain only remnants bearing the semblance of a body—objects she may manipulate, like adjusting the posture of dolls, or lending them a borrowed voice through a species of ventriloquism. In a manner almost ingenious, we inject Eveline with a substance that restores her to her rightful condition, revealing her miry essence: devoid of soul, that is, devoid of form.

I administer the necrotoxin. I restore to the body its true nature: mortality. It is not merely that I sever the mental bond; I grant her the necessity of death. For the ultimate terror is not dying, but the impossibility of perishing—and the ignorance of one’s own death.

To be mortal is our quiet dignity.
In knowing our finitude, we tend to ourselves and to others,
and love extends, gentle,
until our final breath.

Banned footage Vol.1 & Vol.2:
nightmare (Night Terror) – nothing really notable, just survival mini-game with its main aspect being resource management. 
Bedroom – one of my favorite DLCs, short but almost scarier than the main game, its main activity is solving puzzles which I think everyone would enjoy.
21 (survival, survival+) – I’d buy this if it was a separate game, didn’t know blackjack could be this fun with addition of trump cards and torture to its recipe.
Daughters – Short story (with two endings) that shows you beginnings of bakers infestation. No new addition to the gameplay, basically just a cutscene with one or two simple puzzles. 
Ethan must die –  at first it looked impossible, very frustrating and unfair, but once you realize there’s a trick to every deviously placed trap and enemy it becomes very enjoyable and quite easy. I definitely recommend this one if you like pushing yourself through hard challenges.
Jack’s 55th Birthday –  only DLC that I didn’t enjoy almost at all. You have to learn best paths to take with some trial and error and bring food back to jack in time. Challenge being timer and limited inventory.
End of Zoe: entirely new gameplay mechanics and weapons, easily the best DLC. Play as joe baker who is apparently the strongest human being on earth who can smash through walls and any type of mutated monsters, walk through swamps infested with molded crocodiles to save his niece.
Not A Hero: second best DLC, if you liked playing against Lucas in the Testing area. Play as Ethan with umbrellas equipment in a new area hidden in the salt mines.

The only "positive" highlight are those remotely triggered bombs, that are pretty easy to use and work really great to dispatch pretty much every one of the "standard" monsters, that all seems to be bulletsponges in other regards.

Developed by Capcom, this installment takes the series in a bold direction, immersing players in a terrifying first-person experience that successfully revitalizes the Resident Evil formula.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is its masterful use of atmosphere and tension. The game takes place in a dilapidated plantation mansion in Louisiana, exuding a sense of dread and foreboding from the very beginning. The meticulously crafted environments are hauntingly detailed, with dimly lit hallways, decaying walls, and eerie sounds that constantly keep players on edge. The shift to a first-person perspective intensifies the horror, making each encounter with the game's grotesque enemies a heart-pounding experience.

Resident Evil 7 should have been named Amnesia: Hillbillies. If I had to choose between the post RECV direction of the Resident Evil series between this an the over the top horde shooter that are RE5 and 6, I'd choose the latter. There is like one memorable puzzle moment in the game, the story has nothing to do with the previous games, the main character is dumb as hell and the other characters are not much better. I think the whole game had one single interesting room near the end, which contained all the lore dump, then it was over 10 minutes later.

[h1] Review[/h1] 
A lot of people felt that Resident Evil lost its touch. Especially with 5-6 and somewhat 4. For me each game in the mainline franchise felt so completely different, maybe aside 1 and 2, from each other that its hard to say you have to specifically do it like that. While I loved 6 and every mainline Resident Evil game so far in general: This game is a right step into the correct direction for such a game. There aren’t many high quality, bestselling proper horror games out there that aren’t walking simulators.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Capcom took a few core elements of what the main franchise mainly consists of and what people might want or wanted to see in a modern horror game. So, the game is set this time not in a mansion but a relatively large countryside house, together with a guest house and an old structure and then some. It’s a really impressive and most of all; credible place I found myself lost in quickly.

Additionally, they took the franchises puzzle nature and adapted it. I always like this, combining and using items at the correct spot or finding a key that opens up new places or shortcuts. Especially if the game makes you feel smart or gives you an endorphin rush when you find an item you need to proceed further.
Combining the place and the puzzles makes for a relatively twisted horror house scenario, with weird switches, keys and traps around. There are items to find and craft into items you currently want and need or secrets to find in every corner. Exploration is very fun, although after some time a bit tedious due to the main characters relatively low movement speed coupled together with the amount of backtracking. Which isn’t bad but the amount was slightly too much.

The games switch towards a first person perspective is a welcome one, not that I prefer any perspective over the other. I just like variety. Combat itself is fun due to the very strong enemies and very weak main character. You can also block do reduce a lot of incoming damage. Enemy variety is rather mediocre, there are in total 4 enemy types and a couple of different bosses or bossfights which are the highlight for me in this game. There are more unique bossfights than regular enemies. 

In general, the game is highly enjoyable and entertained me from start to finish. There is an infamous section on the boat, mostly because it gives you a relatively weak weapon to fight off enemies and it becomes way much more linear and combat focused compared to the beginning of the game. And the game has the perfect length. A first playthrough will take you from 7-10 hours, a second or third less than 3-5 hours. I especially like how on the unlockable madhouse difficulty not only collectible coins are replaced, but also different items are there to find. An annoying factor is that you cannot skip cutscenes.

[u]Story[/u]
Initially It has absolutely nothing to do with Resident Evil. I feared that it might be a complete reboot, completely disregarding the franchise earlier games but the ending connects it towards it while also hinting for a new game.

The basic idea is that the main characters girlfriend disappeared and he gets an anonymous letter where to find here. When being at the place it turns into a 90s horror flick, hillbilly mad people with somewhat inhumane powers. 

There is also two endings but only one is canon as the non canon one just absolutely makes no sense whatsoever.

[u]Sound[/u]
I always respect it if someone translates and dubs games in a lot of different languages. Capcom always did this and I always appreciate it. Additionally, the soundtrack is barely noticeable. Most of the time you have only environmental sounds. Even the save room theme is barely noticeable. But i liked that they didn't use a mute main protagonist which i don't really like, especially nice that Ethan is a likeable guy.

[u]Graphics[/u]
The game is overly reliant on various filter. These fit to the game especially in the baker property although I can understand why people might dislike the vignette effect that is ramped so much in this game that it became an artstyle choice almost. Atleast the colours aren’t completely undersaturated which is something I absolutely dislike. What I really love are the various small animations the game does when you use an object like cutting the chain or healing.

Character models are rather uncanny which is basically the only type of game where that makes sense to have. Additionally, the game can be tweaked a lot, making it look very great but can also run on any potato. I only disliked the general art direction of the enemies, just black humanoid blops.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
Game does everything right a horror game should do. A neat setting where the main character actually feels dread and is constantly under suspense. Graphics and style choice are great and the game runs really good. Combat is fun and especially the exploration and interconnectivity of the whole baker property is something I really love. Crafting is also a neat and welcome addition. Although I’m not really a fan of the common enemy type opposed to the really awesome boss battles. Also, during the very lategame the game turns rather linear and is more action focused.

I have never been one to enjoy horror games, partly because I don't like being stressed out and partly because some of them just kind of look boring, but Resident Evil 7 has been different. I have completely fallen in love with this game. The story, the atmosphere, the characters; it's all phenomenal. I had never played any of the original RE games (although I fully intend to now), so I came in not really knowing what to expect, but I was completely blown away by how well-developed everything in the game is, as there was not a single dull moment.

My biggest qualm with horror games is that, for the most part, a lot of them don't let you fight back, and/or anytime you seem like you're getting an upper hand on the enemy, the game strips it away, and you continue running for your life. While I understand that appeals to some people, it doesn't really appeal to me. RE7 (and the entire series, from what I understand) does not do that. Sure, for the first few hours, you might feel helpless and weak, but as the story progresses, you grow stronger and stronger until by the end of the game, you can finally get sweet revenge on the monsters that have been tormenting you throughout the game, and that is what is so great about this game. It plays the horror tropes well for awhile, and then says "alright, we've had our fun. Now you go have yours."

All the extra content is phenomenal, too. From a horde survival mode, to a high-stakes card game, to proper story DLC, I have sunk more time into this game and its DLCs than I have into any game not labeled as an RPG or a live-service, and I am not finished yet. For the price you are paying (especially during a sale), I cannot recommend playing this game enough.

Revisiting Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (hey, that's the Japanese title!) after playing the immaculate Resident Evil 4 remake, this can happily stand as an excellent, if not completely realized, entry in the RE canon. 

Atmosphere and visual design are top notch. The opening moments of the game, where Ethan wanders toward the Baker cabin as dusk immediately sets, are electric. You feel the walls closing in around you as you realize that your mission to find your girlfriend Mia is rapidly getting you into deep, deep trouble. The opening third of the game, where you scrounge for resources and flee the Baker family who just. won't. die. is immaculate. The designers have carefully constructed a small but detail-filled map that is initially disorienting, but gradually becomes more familiar as you begin to gain the upper hand over this gang of monstrous hicks. 

Later segments of the game are more streamlined, but the middle section is still my favorite. It's creepy, and signposts future sections in a way only horror games can do. On more than one occasion, I found myself thinking "oh god, I have to go in there?" It also contains one of the best examples of RE7's best trick: interactive videotapes where you experience a flashback to an area you'll go to later. It's an excellent narrative trick that can build fear or be used for puzzle solving. 

It's also one of the areas that feels like it could have been fleshed out even more. The puzzles it presents aren't very challenging at all. In other weak areas, the combat feels a bit flakey. Weapons don't seem to do much damage at all, which is intentional at first, but even later weapons fall a bit flat when you should finally feel like you're turning the tide. The flamethrower especially has some bizarre hitreg that often seems to miss an enemy at point-blank. 

Even with it's flaws, it's difficult to find a single moment where RE7 isn't engaging on some level. It's still only about a 10 hour game, but every minute of that has something scary, intense or worthwhile. It's not on the level of the classics (or those classics' remakes even) but it's still a very proud entry in the series.

I didn't believe "Resident Evil VII" could possibly be any good. When it finally came out and was flushed with acclaim, I read all the reviews and figured: OK, I was wrong, it's actually good. But it still didn't exactly seem like my thing, seemed more like a P.T.-inspired first person escape-from-unkillable-monster affair with some mediocre shooting thrown in to pretend like it's in any way related to its series. So I waited 5 years before I actually played it. The first few sections were very competent, but didn't exactly seem like my thing. But a few things kept me going: the slowly opening environment, the light puzzles, the item hunting, the increasingly complex and satisfying gameplay, the cool set pieces. By the time I reached the first boss fight (the one with the car), I was very much intrigued and determined to push on. By the time I reached the second boss fight (the one in the basement), I knew I was in for something special. By the end of the game I was in awe: of the horror, the suspense, the grotesque characters, the camp, the dark comedy, the disgusting art design, the incredible levels, the simple yet satisfying puzzles, the exploration, the item management... It felt like an evolution of the classic survival horror, not exactly the same, but equally as cool. By the time I finished it I was also already playing "Resident Evil 2" remake, hardly believing that it was, indeed, actually a pretty old school survival horror game. It's a rare experience for me to suddenly feel an excitment for something old afresh, but that's exactly what "Resident Evil VII" gave me. It's a special game, and probably one to be remembered for years to come. A little uneven, but less so than "Village", it's one of the better games in the series.

You are Ethan Winters, trying to find your wife who cut her connections with her husband three years ago. Suddenly you receive a message from her with the exact location of her and you drive off to meet the horrors that no one has ever seen. Although the events seem like unexplainable supernatural occurrences, they become more and more clear that these things are actually connected to some secret organization and there is a scientific background to it.  

The game itself is packed with action, horror-thrill and puzzles. There are two difficulty setting at first and one more to be unlocked once you finish the game on normal mode. I recommend getting the DLCs because they offer side stories and explain what had really happened before the main game. Beware though, if you are easily disturbed by jump-scares and creepy atmosphere (especially if you are claustrophobic), this game is not for you. Otherwise, go for it. The game that saved the franchise and brought Resident Evil back to its routes. I personally was very skeptical of this game at first, especially after RE6 disaster from years back, but gave it a shot years later and I was not disappointed, this game might be one of the best games in the whole series.

Game has new characters, new story and barely any mentions of any of the previous characters and locations, and it honestly felt like a breath of fresh air going into this one. I guess you could say it was a soft reboot for the franchise, stepping away from the god awful over the top action and putting us back to survival horror where I have to save my ammo and take every resource into consideration and how to properly use it etc. 

And we got to experience in the first person, which was off putting at first, but quickly got used to it. I still would've preferred the third person view though.

While the majority of the game is good, the end portion of the game was a let down, and kinda out of place. It didn't ruin the whole experience for me or anything, just felt like it was "slapped on there".

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard Review

"Come for the family dinner, stay for the PTSD."


---

Pros:

•  Terrifying Atmosphere: The Baker family mansion is so creepy it makes my childhood basement feel cozy.

•  Graphics: The level of detail is so good I can smell the moldy walls—and I don’t like it.

•  Immersive Storyline: Who wouldn’t travel to a decrepit house in the middle of nowhere because of a vague email from their missing wife? Romantic and dumb.

•  Ethan’s Hand: This man gets it sliced, diced, stapled, and somehow still uses it to reload a shotgun.


Cons:

•  Baker Family: They just really want you to stay for dinner. Permanently.

•  Jump Scares: I nearly threw my controller when Mia came at me with a chainsaw. Thanks for that.

•  Inventory Management: Deciding whether to keep bullets or healing items feels like Sophie's Choice, but bloodier.

•  Marguerite: She’s terrifying, crawls like a spider, and has an "interesting" bug collection. Enough said.



---

Personal Experience:

I spent 15 minutes trying to open a drawer because I thought the key was in a perfectly suspicious spot. Turns out it was just a shadow. Meanwhile, Jack Baker was chasing me around like it was tag, but with axes. I died because I panicked and used all my healing items on minor scratches. 10/10 survival instincts.


---

Final Verdict:

If you enjoy:

•  Screaming at doors that open too slowly,

•  Thinking mannequins are enemies,

•  And second-guessing every creak you hear in your house...


...then Resident Evil 7 is perfect for you. Just don’t play it at night unless you’re okay with sleeping with the lights on.

Resident Evil 7 is a game that's not for the faint of heart. If you're easily scared, you might want to grab a friend to hold your hand. Or a teddy bear. Or a bottle of tequila. Whatever works for you.

The game takes place in a creepy, abandoned plantation in Louisiana, where you play as Ethan, a guy who's looking for his missing wife. Now, I don't know about you, but if my wife went missing in a place like that, I'd be like "Sorry, honey, you're on your own." But Ethan's a brave soul, or maybe just stupid, so he goes in alone.

The game's graphics are so good, it's like you're actually there. Which is not always a good thing, because some of the stuff you'll see is downright disgusting. And the sound effects? Let's just say they're not going to help you sleep at night.

The game's enemies are some of the most messed up things you'll ever see. They're like a bunch of hillbillies on steroids. And don't even get me started on the boss battles. They're so intense, you'll be screaming at your TV like a lunatic.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a game that'll make you jump, scream, and laugh at yourself for being such a wimp. It's a great game to play with friends, because misery loves company. So grab a buddy, some snacks, and maybe a change of pants, and dive in. It'll be a wild ride.

[i]The Ethan Winters Torture Simulator or How I learned to love D3D Fatal Error.[/i] 

You are Ethan Winters, torture subject de jour. Ethan Winters received contact from his wife, which would be normal except she is dead. Ethan attends support groups with James Sunderland. As any sane human being would do, Ethan immediately drives to the derelict home in the middle of the Louisiana swamp where she claims to be. This unfortunately does not go well. 

The first issue is that Ethan has a serious problem with his eyes. Everything is a muddy mess of brown and gray and he forgot his glasses back home. This won't bother you too much once you are inside since everything will be too dark to see. The upside is he did bring the world's smallest flashlight. What follows is a building of tension that is quite good at setting the mood. 

That is until you run into the family staying there. Afterward involves not so frantic cat and mouse games and chases. Ethan has brittle leg syndrome and cannot move faster than an amble. Every time the enemies of the game get hold of you, you can never be sure if this is yet another scripted Ethan torture session or if you are meant to do something to defend yourself. The game certainly won't tell you. 

The game certainly wears its influence from Texas Chainsaw Massacare on its sleeve and I might have been interested to see where the story goes but that brings us to the final part of this review. The dreaded D3D Fatal Error. The game is a finicky beast and loves to crash to desktop often just to keep you on your toes. There is no better tension than being unsure if you are going to lose all your progress at any moment. 

I did all I could to fix this error but with no luck. As such, I will have to be left wondering what ever became of poor Ethan Winters and if he ever did find his glasses.

G) Seems to be on a shorter side;

I can see why RE's franchise was revived by this entry in a series, but so far I'm not really hyped while playing it. But, I am having a slightly better time than before.
However, I do like how much side content 7 got after release and that some side missions are connected with 7's story. That's good.

== DLCs ==
Two DLCs - Not a Hero and End of Zoe.
[b]Not a Hero[/b] absolutely blows despite giving us better combat; now you can stagger Molded to punch them, which allows you to kill them in one hit and you can properly ADS with weapons.
But its gameplay is trash, and sadly that killed it for me. Running like a chicken with its head cut off in a claustophobic, gas filled corridors, while avoiding turrets and fighting unlimited amounts of Molded was not fun. 
They even gave us Chris Redfield, but he's not voiced by Roger Craig Smith, he sounds pretty generic and looks nothing like RE5 Chris.

[b]End of Zoe[/b] is a second story driven DLC, where we play as Joe Baker, Jack's brother, and our task is to make sure Zoe will survive, no matter what.
Gameplay is fantastic because it's simple - you punch Molded. Seriously, you do. You beat the shii outta them with your bare hands, while doing WWE finishers on one of the bosses. Hilarious but also pretty badass.
Joe is a cool MC; typical southern government hating redneck, who will do everything for his family. 
I recommend this one.

== TL;DR == 
Tl;dr - Came back years later, have more fun but I don't see why is this such a masterpiece like a lot of people are saying it is. Downvote because neutral score doesn't exist, which is something I would choose.

Played it on the ps4 when it came out and my initial skepticism was dashed to bits within a few hours. 

Fantastic game, and even though it leans more into a first-person horror styling, it is still Resident Evil at it's core. That being said, I do have a few criticisms... 

1. The horror starts off strong and gets weaker the more you progress. 
I've never been truly scared playing the original REs(more like thrilled? white-knuckled?), but the first person perspective with gross atmosphere and almost nauseating depth of field/FOV creates a very claustrophobic, terrifying experience. I piss my pants pretty easily with scary stuff when you can't fight back, or are limited to feeling like prey at all times. So, like most RE titles, you become more and more like a walking gun locker as you progress. That, coupled with how limited enemy variety is and how the game is front-loaded with jump scares and dread, makes it so by the 3rd act there's nothing to be scared of. You're an 80s action hero and all that's left to take care of are walking blobs of black goo.

2. There are some moments I wish you could skip altogether. 
While the feral hillbilly/found footage thing works really well as an uncomfortable setting, the parts where you play out recordings on videotapes was not enjoyable at all for me. They become true cat and mouse horror segments, which my nerves just can't stand. I suppose my real criticism is that it commits hard to that type of horror game initially, then eventually not at all, making the first half something new for Resident Evil and truly scary, to eventually feeling more like something typically RE but with no fear or intrigue left. By the end of the game you're just blasting through everything, waiting for the final story beat. 

Everything else about the game gets a shining approval from me, but for the criticisms outlined above, I find it very hard to motivate a return to this game. It's most interesting, atmospheric and exciting when it's scary, but that's also when it's palpably uncomfortable to play(for me). Since I find the atmosphere genuinely icky, it doesn't hit me the way other RE games do, where I relish the art direction, level design etc, and instead of feeling scared I just feel excited, tense and nerd out over all those details. 

The game is very good, but it's probably my least favourite entry in the series(not counting RE6) since I scare too easily.

The overusing of these characters during first hours of the game makes it boring and you just want to go on with your mission instead of dealing with that.

Lighting is awful and that's the reason this game is the most "dark" atmosphere because you really can't see anything at all. Even the flashlight can't illuminate properly the things in front of you. Gameplay wise this is not okay because I don't want to turn up the brightness just to see the place. And because of this bad lighting, stealth becomes completely random since there's no way to tell whether you're in the dark spot or not. At least they solved this issue in village and RE2 remake. 

After the high tension start with family, game continuously loses its immersion and horror factor. Because it basically becomes pew pew simulator since you don't have to worry about ammo at all. And there are lots of safe zones to escape from monsters thus saving you ammo. Typically if you run from one room to another and close the door yeah you're safe. Basically when you get used to game let's say after one or two hours, scripted events is slowly starting to kill your excitement.

Story is bad and cliche even in RE standards. I wish they just go along with Mia vs Ethan since it was more thrilling and interesting to see what they will have become. Baker family just disappears after couple of hours playtime which is a real shame and game completely becomes shooter-looter with very linear level designs. Voice acting, sound effects and musics are great as usual though.

And there's almost no enemy varieties at all. Boss fights are extremely easy and poses no threat. The last 3 hours of story is just all time bottom level it can get. Not just story is downgraded, level designs, mobs, immersion are also completely fade away.

Game more feels like initially they decided to just make Baker family stuff then add whole another story into the game just to make it longer I guess. The story is not giving you a feeling as a whole, it's more like fractured random bits and pieces. The first half and second half of the game has no real connection to each other at all other than some forced writing.

Really good atmosphere and story, but tedious game play and inconsistent combat.

You'll want to remember pretty much everything you come across, because you will have to backtrack a lot if you want to move forward. If you find yourself struggling to progress somewhere, it's probably because you need something in an area you thought you cleared or didn't realize you were supposed to go back to yet. If you don't like relying on walk-throughs, the game can get very frustrating as you fail repeatedly trying to figure out what to do. That said, it's been a VERY long time since I played an RE game, but I think that tracks with what I remember from RE 1 and 2 on Playstation or wherever I played them. 

With regard to combat, the only reason to use anything other than the shotgun in most scenarios is because the ammo is so limited and the only ammo that isn't craftable. The pistols have jarringly inconsistent, but overall slow fire rates and do very little damage (magnum excluded) unless you land headshots. The damage you do is also dependent on how well you're doing, as the game dynamically scales with your performance. Sometimes you will kill a specific enemy type with 2 headshots, sometimes it takes 4. It's a cool idea in theory, but annoying as ♥♥♥♥ in practice.

Is it worth playing? The story and atmosphere are worth it, but I can't say it was the most fun I've had. Then again, the game play does seem consistent with what I remember of RE from when I was a kid, and I think I liked it back then, so maybe I'm just old and grumpy now. That said, it's probably less tedious to just watch a playthrough or something if you value your time and have a low tolerance for awkward gunplay in games.

ok i beat the game on normal and madhouse difficulty now, so i will try to make a review for this RESIDENT EVIL 7 games...

- GRAPHIC

amazing graphic, i love the atmosphere of this game.. the detail of the wood house, the detail on bakers family characters, is amazing.. all the gore feel so real, and this is maybe the most beautiful RE games for now. i love the HDR effect, so if you are staying on a full light room and after that you enter a dark room, it is really dark.

and yes, you must play the game with the reccomended brightness to really feel the game (but if you are not brave enough, just maxed out the brightness), and this is a matter of taste, the color range, the BT.709 i think better than SRGB (but many people more like the SRGB, it's just a matter of personal taste), cuz i think the BT colour offer more contrast and a pure dark color in a dim lighted area, it's more atmospheric, the SRGB on the other hand is more to a desaturation and minimal contrast but it's also have a heightened gamma so the game more bright. for the Antialiasing method i prefer TAA only, so the image is appear softer and almost eliminate the staircase effect, i personally reccomend you guys dont use FXAA+TAA because it makes the graphic too soft and it looks blurry.

And if you don't have at least a 6gb VGA card dont set the texture to max, and also the shadow count is better turned off to maximize the performance (i'm using 980Ti, and the dynamic shadows and shadow count is turned off).


- PERFORMANCE

i'm playing this game at all max and render scale on 2560x1080 using the  GTX1660Ti the game run smoothly without hiccups.

aaaand, there is an issue, if you alt+tabbing this game, when you switched to this game again, the frame rate will be droped to maybe a single digit maybe at around 9-18fps, so at this time i reccomend you not using a borderless windows setting.

-GAMEPLAY

at first, when i see the demo on youtube i feel a bit dissapointed because capcom change the perspective to a first person, why?? even after i play the demo on steam, i still a bit dissapointed because the RE i know is not a FP games. but eventually i decided to buy it, and after play it a couple of hours, i feel satisfied, THIS is The TRUE Survival Horor i feel i'm back to my childhood (i play the RE 1,2,3 around age of 10-12 years old and enjoying it), the RE4 is very phenomenal, but i'm little dissapointed on RE5 because it becomes more to an action game than a survival horror and the inventory management is gone, and the RE6 is good (but not too good) because it is becoming more more action oriented and ammo everywhere and no invent management.

so when i play the demo i checked the inventory, and feel happy to see the little inventory tab at the screen, the item box and classic safe room. WOW. the walking speed on ethan is slow (but you can upgrade it by wearing light shoes after you destroy a certain items) the run speed is not too fast too.

the reload speed is trivial, it's not a problem at all, and the main things in RE games is the inventory management, so you can spend a couple of minute to try to manage the limited item to your limited inventory to make more space for you if you found another items, the stack is not too big, the ammo is scarce so you have to carefully manage it all and use it with efficiency and it makes the game more challenging.

the gunplay is good, but nothing new, you can shot the enemy limbs example you can shot the fat mold feet when he's charging so he's fall, you can shot the head to make a big damage. the new feature is the guard system, the guard is your friend, and on madhouse difficulty guarding is vital to your survivability.


Speaking of Madhouse difficulty, the Madhouse difficulty is a True RESIDENT EVIL, when you play in that difficulty all the item location is changed (different from easy or normal), the ammo is very limited, the enemies have a bigger health and damage, and the checkpoint is limited to your save file, and even the save file is also limited by a cassette tape so you must think and cleverly survive and make a decision, it really add more tension and fear of dying, and also if you dying a lot it can be an annoying thing too, cuz you have to start all the way through again from your last save and maybe lose and hours of progress, but hey i beat the madhouse, so can you. :) :)


- SOUND and MUSIC

oh my god...!!! the ambiance sound in this game is top notch, i play it with my kraken chroma, and the ambiance sound of surrounding is often surprise me, sometime i though my own footstep is enemies walking behind me, the voice actor is good, but the best part of voice actor is a guys who voiced jack baker, the voice is too creepy and menacing, but it also have a kind sound that gone bad, kinda explain you that jack is not a really psycho, just a normal man who turned psycho by the main antagonist of this game,.

Set in Louisiana, the game follows protagonist Ethan Winters as he searches for his missing wife in a creepy and isolated plantation mansion. As Ethan explores the mansion, he uncovers a sinister plot involving a mysterious family infected with a deadly virus, forcing him to fight for his survival while trying to unravel the mystery behind their twisted existence.

One of the most impressive aspects of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is its atmosphere. The game creates a feeling of isolation and dread, with eerie sound effects and a haunting soundtrack that keep players on edge throughout the game. The mansion itself is intricately designed, with plenty of hidden secrets and puzzles to solve, making it a joy to explore.

The game's survival horror elements are also noteworthy. Players are limited in their resources, forcing them to carefully manage their inventory and choose which weapons and items to use. The enemies in the game are also challenging and formidable, requiring players to use stealth and strategy to survive.

Another standout feature of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is its use of virtual reality (VR). The game can be played entirely in VR, providing an immersive experience that makes players feel as if they are really in the mansion. However, playing in VR can be intense and may not be suitable for everyone.

One minor issue with the game is that the story can be a bit convoluted and confusing at times, with some plot points feeling rushed or underdeveloped. However, this is a minor quibble in an otherwise excellent game.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a must-play for horror fans and anyone looking for a thrilling and intense gaming experience. Its excellent atmosphere, survival horror elements, and use of VR make it one of the best entries in the franchise and a standout horror game in its own right.

While I recommend the game in general, I had to drop it myself - just not for reasons that can be applied in general, but may apply if you're one of the very few like me, since a lot of people enjoy RE7 (some even say it's the best installment)

First and foremost, I've known and played the classic RE games, but eventually stopped at RE5 back when. Recently I've picked the series up with RE6, but dropped RE6 ironically because of the opposite reasons of RE7 - or you could say the same reason: It didn't feel like RE to me.

RE6 was like when you strap a dynamite in your underwear, going down a rollercoaster that won't stop for a damn second to let you check the date on your clock unsure if you've taken your medicine recently, because if not then it all would make sense now. It's action packed, every zombie drops live ammunition like a kid in US school and there was literally 0 horror (for me).

RE7 is the extreme opposite. Instead of dropping, or even having enemies (which are rare, unless you want to count bugs as enemies...) you're forced to skim through every corner and every object inside a room (or garden...) to find anything, something, whatever. It works in older RE or even the remake RE because of the smaller passages and because you get enough ammunition/healing-items even if you're not looking explicitly (and can dodge zombies anyway). Here you are desperately finding stuff, even small hints to get you through the next objective.

But the worst offender in my opinion is the first person camera... I felt like playing Outlast. It wasn't much anymore about having an option to run through or shoot, it became instead a separation of those two things - you have to shoot your way through the few zombies, unless you want to get sandwiched.. and the family won't take a bullet for a no, so it's running time. Even more things adding to a Outlast experience, which doesn't have to be a problem per se - just for me personally it's not RE anymore.

There's a third person mod, but I felt like that was too much hassle to get it to work.
As a last note: The horror/jumpscare in this game is by far the best, but I think it has to be attributed to the first person view. The horror changes drastically when your viewpoint is narrower.

So, you have to know a couple of things about me for this to make sense:
1) I only get a couple hours a day to play games like I really want.
2) I play games for the feeling of being powerful. I don't like games that are all about "failing forward" or running away from your problems until you're able to solve them (I do enough of that in my real life).
3) RE:4 was my all-time favorite, followed by RE:5.
4) Also, I'm primarily a console player, but since I got my gaming PC I decided to try things I normally wouldn't.

This definitely qualifies for outside my norm. And I got the deluxe edition on a great deal, so it's turning out to be a great purchase. I really feel like I'll be enjoying this one, and RE:8 that I also got close to the same time.

There's a LOT of that "running from your problems"  I mentioned above; I'm used to being capable and standing your ground right from the start, but this is not that. Expect to run as your primary response to most encounters in the early hours. You will probably also die a lot, because Ethan doesn't seem to move very fast, and the tricks to surviving a lot of the encounters require great timing, and beating the foes to the punch. I can't knock the game for doing it that way, it's way scarier and perfect for the mood they're going for. And some of the actions are very well thought out, once you put together what you should be doing. Overall it's not what I prefer, but still very well done.

So far what I've seen is classic Resident Evil. Collecting items, dodging vicious enemies that can wipe the floor with you (sometimes literally), and solving puzzles that involve putting Renaissance-era statues together, all par for the course. Looks great, plays well, and is definitely a solid purchase if you're a fan of the series, or of horror games.

I plan on beating this and 8 before I get the 4 remake, but let's be honest here, I'll slug through this one hour at a time, get RE:4 Remake the day it launches, and throw it on the backlog like several dozen other games I really want to play. But in the meantime, I recommend giving this a shot.

[h1] Preface (Spoilers ahead!) [/h1]

I played this game once when it came out on another account so I recently bought it again and replayed it before getting into RE: Village (I just started RE:8 yesterday) and honestly, I'm [almost] glad I did! Why almost you say? You see, I love Resident Evil games for their action combat! I started with RE:5 and had a blast playing local co-op with my cousin. It was one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. The lack of ammo, the way you gradually find weapons, secrets, unique bosses... It was all amazing!
Now back why I "almost" liked it. Well, this game has some cool action, bosses, puzzles and you definitely gradually find your weapons. bullets are scarce and the whole RE vibe is there. Having said that, this game is scaaaaaaary! And I'm not a huge fan of horror! This game is so dark (literally), it has jump scares, it has scary atmosphere, scary story. Horror fans would love this! (The DLC is also perfect IF you like horror and there is plenty of DLC in this game!). Anyways, the extreme horror aspect not my cup of tea...

[h1] Review (Spoilers ahead!) [/h1]

This game is amazing! The story starts beautifully and develops into a mind blowing plot that you wouldn't expect! It's probably my favourite out of the RE titles I've played (RE:5, RE:6, RE:7). I loved how they ramped up the horror gradually until I couldn't play the game at night time anymore! The world building was great. I wasn't a big fan of the maps because I'm claustrophobic but they were perfectly built for a horror game.

[h1]Resident Evil 7 Biohazard[/h1]

Yeah, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is good. 

[i]I originally played this game on PS4 when it released and while I wasn't completely into it at the time, it also gave me some serious motion sickness after a few hours. I think it has to do with the wobbling camera when Ethan moves so if you play this game and can help it, just turn it off. Definitely had a better experience with my second playthrough on PC.[/i]

After 12 years of the Resident Evil action horror era, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard brought us back to the roots of Resident Evil: a survivor horror atmosphere with an emphasis on ammo/resource management and problem solving. This game delivered on that return with flying colors and even made some new additions to keep the experience fresh.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoliers)[/u]

[spoiler]Set four years after the events of Resident Evil 6, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard sets itself in southern America where the main character, Ethan Winters, travels to Dulvey, Louisiana after receiving a letter from his presumably deceased wife, Mia, to come and find her which leads him to the property of the Baker family ranch.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]While the plot itself is pretty decent on its own as Ethan delves in to the Baker plantation house and finding out more about what's happening, it adds layers by leaving behind plot points about Eveline's involvement with the family, her purpose as a BOW, and that there are other sides at play like the Organization and Blue Umbrella. The fact that Eveline (or her presence) is mentioned by the Baker family members often really puts out that you're facing an entirely different foe from other big bad enemies in past Resident Evil games and that there's more to her than just being another bioweapon. It's a great buildup that makes you more interested in how she got to the Baker plantation in the first place.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]For the characters, Ethan is treated a self-insert for the player to become immersed into the game. While he does have his own motivations, he's pretty bland for the most part and that's okay. I didn't feel like he needed to be a complex character at all; his motivation for saving Mia and getting the hell outta dodge is good enough. He's got his badass moments, but stays relatively anxious and confused about the situation he is in which I appreciate considering he's not a hardened combat expert like the past characters we're familiar with. The Baker family, as a whole, are pretty entertaining for a group of mind-controlled inhabitants. Jack is among the best of them overall, Marguerite is a great mid-tier boss, and Lucas is seven flavors of messed up (and a bastard to boot).[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

The survival horror aspect for Resident Evil 7 Biohazard goes hard as far as classic RE mechanics goes: relatively low health pool at beginning, sparse ammo, minuscule resources, stout enemies, and an emphasis on being smart about how you deal with your problems. Even on normal difficulty, most enemies can easily bring Ethan's health down quickly if you aren't careful. Because ammo can be scant at times, you need to be very precise with headshots and learn how to manage your crafting materials because the recipes do overlap with one another, not to mention that they can take up a lot of space in your inventory. Being slow in movement while limited in maneuverability and visibility due to the first person camera means you have to be even more alert so you don't get cornered by the Molded or members of the Baker family but this is at least balanced by the ability to guard enemy attacks to lessen damage.

Puzzles are plenty and can take some brain power to get past so you can progress through the map. This becomes especially more prominent in the set pieces like where you have to face Lucas or the Old House which are honestly some of the most fun puzzles I've ever done. Some placements for puzzle pieces change in Madhouse difficulty so don't get complacent if you decide to take that challenge. There is also high importance on checking your surroundings since some items will not be placed outright in front of you - certain items, like Antique Coins, will sometimes be packed in hiding spots.

Weapons vary from your typical handgun to the exotic flamethrower and more. They're all useful throughout the game and certain weapons will be recommended for some parts of the game since they are more effective on specific enemies. Although, ammo outside of handgun ammo can be rare or expensive to craft.

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

With the introduction of the RE engine, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is one of the best looking Resident Evil games in the series. The lighting and atmosphere of a decrepit and rotting plantation are perfect combinations with the emphasis on a horror atmosphere that is both eerie and immersive. Shadows are accurately refined even as far as reflecting the player's own shadow of Ethan.

The sounds are intricately defined from the powerful sound of certain gunshots to the cue of Molded enemies giving out their position. You can tell quite easily if an enemy is nearby and be able to pinpoint their location from that alone. Some of voice acting in this game is great too as a side note, with Jack's VA doing amazing work acting as the patriarch of the Baker family.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is an amazing addition to the Resident Evil franchise and holds a high image among the franchise for being that game that "saved" Resident Evil in time where it fell into decline after the stagnation of the action era games that preceded it. 

A modern title for the Resident Evil series that goes back to its 1998 roots, I would recommend Resident Evil 7 Biohazard to anyone who is a fan of the survival horror genre.

At first glance this doesn't even feel like a Resident Evil game. The classic RE characters are nowhere to be seen, and there are no zombies in sight. Without a few recycled puzzles from the previous games and an occasional reference, you would never guess you're playing Resident Evil. Despite all that, I'm gonna say this is the best Resident Evil since the PS1 era.

The environments are beautiful and disgusting all at once. Great use of light and shadows intuitively guides you through the levels, and memorable set pieces ensure you don't get lost despite the maze-like structure of the buildings. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, with great pacing and build-up leading to rather scarce but all the more powerful jump scares. The monsters are disturbing yet cool, and the sound design is simply fantastic. I also particularly appreciated the VHS mechanic that foreshadows future events. It's smart and very well done. Add to it great, responsive controls and you have one fine game on your hands.

If you're a survival horror fan, this is a must-play title for you.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a fantastic addition to the Resident Evil series, even for those who haven't played all the previous games. As someone who has dabbled in the series before, I found this game to be a refreshing change of pace while still maintaining the classic survival horror elements that make the franchise so memorable.

One of the things that immediately stood out to me was the game's setting. Taking place in rural Louisiana, the Baker family's dilapidated plantation house was a creepy and atmospheric environment that kept me on edge throughout the entire game. The Baker family themselves were also an interesting cast of characters, each with their own twisted personalities and motivations that added to the game's overall sense of dread.

The game's switch to a first-person perspective was a bold move for the series, but it paid off in spades. It made the game feel more immersive, and the use of VR only heightened the horror experience. The game's puzzles were also well-designed, and the scarce resources made every encounter with enemies feel like a life-or-death situation.

I also appreciated how the game managed to tell its own story while still tying into the larger Resident Evil universe. The game's protagonist, Ethan Winters, is a new character to the series, and his personal story of searching for his missing wife made for a compelling narrative. The game's connections to previous games in the series were also well-placed, and it was satisfying to see how everything fit together.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a must-play for fans of survival horror games, even if you haven't played all the previous games in the series. The game's atmospheric setting, well-designed puzzles, and compelling story make it one of the best games in the franchise, and a standout horror game in its own right.

RE7 - The game that fundamentally changed the franchise as we know it, while going back it's roots. Paradox? You decide.

This review only encompasses the base campaign, none of the DLC.

---

Graphics - 9/10 || RE Engine's major debut as far as I remember. Game still to this day looks absolutely gorgeous. The lighting ESP. is top-notch. This is improved upon in subsequent RE Engine titles, ESP. Village.

Performance - 10/10 || One of the best optimized games I've ever experienced on PC. Everything cranked to the absolute maximum, AMD FSR set to Ultra Quality. Game looked amazing and almost -never- buckled from the 120FPS cap I enforced.

I7-6800K 4.0 OC'd
32G DDR
1080 STRIX

Gameplay - 8/10 || Gone in this game is the standard 3RD person experience, opting instead for 1ST person to convey the intense dread the player is experiencing the entire time playing. There is gunplay, and while it's solid and works for what it is, the overall gameplay loop in this game is -heavily- influenced by the original RE trilogy. High horror, high stakes. Puzzles and back-tracking. Ammo is extremely scarce, enemies are bullet sponges and hit hard. There is a crafting mechanic to assist the player but at times that barely feels like you're getting by - by design. The way the feeling of anxiety is forced on the player in this game is masterclass, and easily the best part. No other series handles atmospheric horror the way RE does, ESP. since this installment.

As I understand it the VR version of the game on PS4 was the definitive way to experience the game when it launched. I sadly can't do this as I get violently ill. :trolldespair:

The first half of the game is some of the best survival-horror you will experience. Sadly the latter half of the game/climax flushes that all down the toilet instead opting for the more action oriented experiences introduced with RE4. It's not bad persay, but the direction in this regard taken feels... odd.

Enemy variety in this game compared to the RE titles of yore is severely lacking, but the highlight of the game is easily the boss encounters. Some truly wild stuff here.

The game is also criminally short without DLC, my playthrough coming in at shy of 6 hours. Speedruns of this game are -extremely- fast when cutscenes are skipped and you know the routing, there isn't a lot of meat here at the end of the day. Whats here however is the finest level of wagyu quality; at least the first outing.

Controls - 9/10 - The game controls like you'd expect a first-person shooter to. Aiming is precise, movement, allbeit sluggish at times, functions as it should.

Sound - 10/10 || Masterclass sound design. Begs to be experienced with high-quality audio.

Story - 9/10 || It's bewildering and utterly insane. A huge departure from Resident Evil as you know it, but eventually, things start to come full circle. CAPCOM managed to breathe new life into the narrative of this series in a very interesting and well done fashion.

Replay Value - Medium (With DLC - High) || This game begs to be purchased as the Gold/Complete edition with all the DLC for the additional experiences it has to offer, otherwise all you have at that point is to replay the campaign on higher settings which doesn't offer a lot in my opinion. As mentioned above, the base campaign length is -very- short, clocking in just shy of 6 hours of my first playthrough blind.

I've made it a point to play RE4-8 before REmake 4 drops in March. I'm ready.

RE7 is a perfect example of taking an established franchise and changing it at it's core - and while injecting new life into it, manages to retain what makes the franchise special and beloved by countless individuals all over the world.

Demands a playthrough, ESP if you can snag it with all the DLC on a heavy discount.

Yes, I can easily recommend this game for RE fans. Is it an FPS survival horror game? Yes, and its true that it differs from more classic RE titles but in so many ways its got just right what the series was all about. Puzzles and claustrophobic settings, enemies a bit on the slow side but punishing all the same, an inventory system that you have to account for item space and how much you have in resources to justify fighting. Its got all that and in a tightly designed set of areas you'll visit and travel about in the same vein you would do for more classic RE games. 

Some of the boss fights feel a bit off from what you would expect from an RE game (chainsaw duels, jigsaw-like death traps) which leads me to believe they leaned heavily into found footage and grindhouse aesthetics throughout this game, which honestly isn't so bad. The game's campaign is loosely tied RE's previous lore/story up to 6, but it honestly doesn't matter as its a nice self contained survival horror experience that doesn't really need you to understand the previous stories much at all. Gunplay feels solid, responsive, and with a variety of weapons (should you find them, its an RE game afterall) that are pretty rewarding to use when you have the ammo to spare. I can easily say most of the DLC content, minigames and additional campaigns were given about as much effort as the main content. A definite recommend.

Comparing this to RE2 remake, it falls flat in every way. 

Want to try to solve a puzzle, and not sure what to do next? Good luck inspecting items and looking for things while Jack (who is much faster than you) chases you around the tiny house. Compare that to Mr. X (who you can outrun) in the GIANT police station and you see my point.

Speaking of where to go next, the game gives you ♥♥♥♥-all in terms of subtle guidance. It's more like hitting a wall you can't pass so it forces you the other direction. One such example would exploring the dissection room in the main house. You'll hit a certain room with 3 molded (more on those later) and it's impossible to pass them with just the pistol. Well, go get the shotgun then. Would love to but I've got no idea where the pieces to that puzzle are, and the area the clues are in is currently patrolled by Jack, which as we mentioned, will just skewer me the instant he sees me. Fun. It's important to identify the distinctions here between where Mr. X chasing you in RE2 as a success, and Jack chasing you around the house as a failure. Mr. X comes in midway, while you already know your way around the station, so you have some confidence to solve puzzles and work your way around on the fly while he breaths down your neck. Jack is on you from the jump, every time you start to sink in to enjoying putting clues together, a cut-scene cues and there he is to chase you then the solution is to cower in a corner?? Fun.

Now, the molded. So they designed one enemy and thought, that's good? Let's just have multiple of them at all times. There's one point on a pier where the game spawns in (which, btw, sometimes you can literally watch the molded spawn in to existence. Seems like a pretty glaring detail in need of a patch to me. Compare that to zombies barging in the windows of the police station and scaring the ♥♥♥♥ out of you, in a good way, while maintaining your immersion) like 5-6 molded at one time just to chase you and intense music comes in. Pretty lazy if you ask me to just spawn in the same enemy you've been annoyed to deal with to give some sense of tension, especially when you can just run past them all to save-point.

In the same vein of lazy animations and coding, I don't think any characters mouth besides Lucas' and Mia's actually moves in time with their dialogue. Marguerite's mouth animations with her dialogue timing were laughable. No idea how Lucas' animations looked so good and lifelike and Marguerite looked like a fromsoft NPC when she spoke.

Boss fights. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible. The boss fights were the worst parts of RE2 as well, but these are even worse given the clunky first person perspective. I didn't enjoy a single one. You start to realize how unnecessary boss fights are for the survival horror lexicon once you've played a game like Signalis. I think that game had 3 bosses, and they weren't annoying as hell to do, and they were a very, very small part of the game. 

Let me explore, let me puzzle, let me be spooked and give me some tension and impetus to my exploring, don't ♥♥♥♥ me up with a cut scene and combat at every other turn.

Overall, it's a well put together game and is way better than many other incomplete games coming out these days with no personality whatsoever, but that's the minimum.

Mechanics are simple and straight forward, the puzzles are pretty simple if I remember from the top of my head. I enjoyed the combat and it can be somewhat satisfying at times, although in first-person it could feel slow compared to previous RE games, but it is the right direction to sacrifice action for horror, this makes sense as the main character Ethan is just a regular guy who can't punch boulders out of the way or perform a back-flip to avoid dozens of lasers. 

> Graphics: 
Nearly 6 years since its release and it still looks amazing. 

CONS:
>Boss fights: 
The first boss fight was kinda epic, the rest of the bosses I feel like there should be something more added to it (not that it's just bad), I feel like it didn't reach the height like the first boss did if you get what I mean.

Resident Evil 7 is a return to form for the franchise, going back to the survival horror components of the first games, but elevating the formula with great atmosphere, a chilling story, and intuitive gameplay. 

The nastiness of The Texas Chain-Saw Massacre mixed with a quarantine horror scenario makes for a perfect substitution of zombies and easter eggs of monosyllabic notes spread around an old mansion. The wet, slimey setting of the Louisiana bayou makes traversing the map almost cringe-inducing, but in a GOOD WAY! You find yourself stuck in a terrifying scenario with monsters marching after you, but nothing is too difficult to induce infuriation. 

The story is simple at first, but becomes progressively convoluted and complex. It isn’t bad by any means. Discovery is key to the intrigue of Resident Evil and the extent you want to know the full story is up to the player, which is refreshing cause many AAA titles want to lull you to sleep with 20 minute cutscenes. I won’t give away too much, but it’s real morbid and fascinating.

Gameplay is solid, yet challenging enough to make self-defense against the Baker family pretty damn difficult. Combat is pretty standard. Puzzles are fun and challenging. Environments allow exploration and hidden items add just enough depth to an otherwise limited open-world. Boss fights almost make you want to run away and if you’re out of ammo, you’re a goner. It’s old school Resident Evil, but accessible enough for new players, like me (I know, I know. Never playing an RE game before is very embarrassing).

In short, this is very, very good and you should play it! Just don’t let the swamp people touch you with their shrimp-stained sausage fingers.

I have already played the game on all consoles it was released and it's about the time I finished it on PC. Resident Evil 7 is obviously a great game. There are hundreds people, on Steam alone, playing it on a daily basis. For a singleplayer game, that was released almost 6 years ago, that's a great thing. Capcom has done a amazing job releasing a horror that is truly scary, BUT... there is some stuff missing. At least for me, who is a long fan of the series.

First thing that I rather dislike is the new main hero. Ethan is just like every second standard regular guy that would fit any modern horror or any other genre, whatever. He is not memorable, he is not likeable. He is plain boring. The franchise used to have a whole lot of interesting cast. Ethan for sure doesn't fit the role of main character.

The second thing that I'm not fond of is the story. Maybe newcomers who doesn't know all of the plots and stuff from other entries wouldn't mind that it's something new, once again, but I have trouble fitting this stuff into the universe of Resident Evil. Looking back, even RE6, which as everyone knows didn't had the best story even for a "B-Horror" label, did that much better and more engaging. Everything here feels like not-so-much of Resident Evil and uses its name only. Well, besided the ending, but that too didn't make much sense for me.

And finally, the boring enemies. Even compared to the enemies from the very first RE game, these looks so bad. A dark-looking monster, other the same but with the shield, a crouching one and a fatty. It feel like enemies taken from REvelations, but made looking more cheap. Heck, even the mentioned spin-off had more types of enemies. I don't count bosses, these are OK besides the last fight. It feels so unnecesary. There is nothing epic from it like it was during the last fight with Nemesis from RE3, with Wesker in RE5, or even with Simmons in RE6. Seriously, on my list, it's definitely the most boring looking boss fight.

So why I'm leaving a positive note? Well, the mansion brings a lot of nostalgia, same about the ship. The game have it's nice moments and overall I had tons of fun playing the game. For me, it's the repeating of the history when RE4 was released for the first time - I hated it as a Resident Evil game, but loved it as an action game. And that's it. I personaly would love to see another game with Jill as heroine, play a game that would tell me what happened to Wesker Junior after RE6, or maybe see a game that would focus on someone else that wasn't seen in a long time from the franchise. But sadly, at this point it might be not possible. Unless Capcom will go all out and decide for a full restart of franchise, introducing the same but new characters with a brand new story. I'm not sure if I would love or hate to see that.

Anyway, it's a must play. Being a gamer nowadays and not having a single RE game beaten would be a shame. The game goes cheap during sales, so wait for one and grab.

[h1]A really good Survival Horror game and the reboot the series needed[/h1]

Resident Evil 7 brings to the table true survival horror with deep exploration and puzzling with limited resources, just like the good old games. I think may people would be pleased to play this game especially considering that RE5 and RE6 were more focused on shooting. RE7 almost doesn't have shooting sequences, they are mostly short one on one sequences or during boss battles, not multiple zombie shooting. It's true focus is survival with puzzling.

In this game I felt like they took the violence, creepiness and the disgusting stuff to the next level never seen before in the series. Just looking at the screen and the cutscenes give an unique feeling of horror that is not jump scare neither psychological. It's just Evil from the Residents of the house welcoming you to the family.

The puzzles are good but not completely difficult. What really takes the gameplay time is the exploration to discover key items, but overall I think the game is really well balanced by giving the right amount of puzzles, shooting, exploration and story cutscenes at the right time. It never felt repetitive even when backtracking some areas because something different always happens.

The main story took me 8 hours to beat. It is certainly still a short game but longer than the Remakes so it's a full experience worth it's current price that is actually really cheap right now.

My only complaints about the game are that the combat is not ideal and can be difficult to control during boss battles especially because the reloading and healing animations are very slow. It's not bad, I just think it could've been smoother.
And the other is that even though RE7 is an excellent survival horror game by itself, I think it missed the point on what makes Resident Evil, Resident Evil. The first person camera and no real mention about the Umbrella and other things that the series is known for set this game a little bit apart from the others. It felt more like another different game carrying the Resident Evil name. Not necessarily a bad thing, but they really wanted to make something new and different.

The PC Port is also excellent and it's possible to run the game at 1440p 60fps everything maxed out on a RTX 2060 Super. It runs incredibly smooth through the entire game without a single frame rate drop. It is smooth as butter and incredibly polished. The graphics are also really good, not as good as seen in RE2 and RE3 Remakes, but it makes sense since RE7 is actually the studio's first take on the new RE Engine.

I recommend this game. It is a really good high quality Survival Horror game and essential to anyone who likes this genre.
It sets itself a little bit apart from the old Resident Evil games formula, with a new first person camera and a different definition of horror.

About the Gold Edition DLC: Not worth it to be honest. Only "Not a Hero", which is free, and "End of Zoe" are kinda worth playing because they offer post-story content to tie some loose threads, but each can be completed in just an hour. The others are basically 20-30min minigames.
Not worth paying extra. Get the Gold Edition only if the price is almost the same as the Standard or cheaper.
