Resident Evil 7 is a great game that's terrible to 100%. It's a breath of fresh air after balls to the wall ridiculous action and COD copycats. It has a strong narrative and atmosphere, including an intriguing mystery. Although I personally didn't find it scary (Silent Hill is something that I would consider scary) it made me jump a few times. It's combat is fun too and true to the classic RE games despite the shift in perspective. I also 100%'d this game so I'll talk about its DLC now.

The following 4 are under the Banned Footage Vol.1 DLC:

Nightmare-Generic horde survival with no new enemies. I'd rather play COD zombies.

Bedroom-Tense escape room puzzle, with a unique game play mechanic. Similar to the movie Misery. Pretty fun as an hour diversion.

21-The worst ♥♥♥♥ I've ever played. I didn't buy this game to play cards. The story mode is fine, but Survival+ gave me a stress induced headache. It's the perfect combination of ♥♥♥♥: cheap, tedious, very long, and luck based. Awful. I can't stress how much I hated it. It's why you shouldn't complete this game. Maybe irl with friends this would be fun but playing against the computer for an hour on end damages your mental stability.

Daughters-Interesting. Tells the story of the Baker's encounter with Eveline. But after 30 mins its over and doesn't offer anything interesting game play wise. An hour of content if you go for both endings.

_________________________________________________________________________________

Not a Hero-Play as Chris Redfield in an ok shooter. Fun to punch the Molded in the head. Leans back into an action oriented experience. Other than that, it's pretty generic and there are no memes to make Chris interesting ;(. On Professional mode it becomes better as you only start with the knife, forcing you to be creative with how you clear rooms. It's challenging but still nothing compared to 21 Survival+.

End of Zoe-Play as Joe Baker and rescue Zoe. It's a weird first person brawler with very basic level design. Joe Must Die, the game's final difficulty is very tough. It throws all the tricks at you from other game modes. The levels can be very frustrating, but the boss encounters are actually really fun and more like Dark Souls than anything else. Slightly better than average.

Jack's 55th Birthday-Corny minigame with remixed areas of the main game. You have to feed Jack food scattered around and the faster you do so, the better rank you get. Some people will find this fun, it's the replacement for Mercenaries. To me it was about a 2 hour diversion and not much else. Kind of nice as a break from all the seriousness.

Ethan Must Die-Probably the most famous DLC from this game. Play through a linear version of the Baker house with very strong enemies and a boss fight against Marguerite. There are traps everywhere and loot is randomized every play through. One death sends you back to the beginning. It's the unfair Mario of first person shooters; extreme trial and error game play. Eventually after enough attempts you can finish this. It's not as reflex oriented or long as Joe Must Die, nor as awful as 21+. All the traps in the house can be used against your enemies, making it much easier once you know where everything is. It's very high difficulty, but it also gives you a lot of opportunity. For the Hardcore, this is a balanced challenge.

$20 is a good price for this. DLC can be fun if you really liked the game, but pick and choose what you want. Overall, I recommend it very much. But I do not recommend completing it.

In 1996, a new franchise was released upon the video game world. Known as Bio-hazard in Japan, then Resident Evil for the american and European audiences. Led by the then young programmer Shinji Mikami, Resident Evil was a revolutionary take on horror adventure games that later become a new genre known a "survival horror". 
Having the roles of special unit law enforcement you traverse into a lonely mansion and uncover the it's horrific secrets. 
Played in third-person perspective you wander and shoot you way through a zombie infested mansion zombies and gathering resources and information that will lead you deeper into the mystery of Resident Evil. 

With a sense of dread and fear that permeated the game its clunky controls and limited resources, the true holy grail moment happens when you first round the corner of a long hallway not knowing what to expect as a Zombie dog jumps through the window to attacks you. Video game history was made. 

Jump  forward twenty one years later and a new Resident evil 7 graces our counsels. Shinji Makami, long gone a new generation of directors - Koshi Nakanishi and producers - Kawata Tsuyoshi, kanda and Masachika again create the Resident evil. 
But is the fear back? 

I gotta say, hell yes. 
Not just back, but back with the proverbial bang. This isn't your mom's and dad's Resident evil. This is first-person gory body horror, that's both graphic, repulsive and violent in a way that the first incarnation could never achieve.
If you were around in 1996 and remember and love the first Resident Evil, you'll love this latest survival  horror fest. 
You as play Ethan winters a hapless fellow who goes off in to the bayou swamps of Louisiana in order to find his lost girlfriend. (Silent hill two anyone) Mia Winters. 

I leave the story there for you to discover, but if you love movies franchises like Texas chainsaw you'll relish the first twenty or so minutes of the game. Afterwards it slowly but surely morphs into the Resident Evil formula that we've all grown accustomed to. 
Scattered resources, hidden keys, puzzles level progression and bits and pieces of lore and story info scattered throughout. 

In fact, arguably this game is really Resident evil 2, just in a new skin and a much scarier tyrant. 
But what really shines is the narrative tale told through the eyes of Ethan as he discovers the Baker family. The dinner scene alone was a master class of narrative storytelling. Honestly words cannot convey the genuine experience that takes me back to the first Resident Evil. Just go out and PLAY the game. 

Is it perfect? Well, no nothing is, but if I had a compliant it's that it's a Resident Evil game. What does that mean? It means the characters, story and backdrop could have been in my opinion an entirely different franchise! 
Yes, to me Resident evil is about zombies and zombie dogs. What we got here was something much different and in my opinion better. SO why slap the Resident Evil label and force a narrative that wasn't needed! 
I'm purposely obtuse in case you haven't played the game before but when you leave the bayou that should've been the ending. But it's a Resident Evil game damn it! Government conspiracies are needed!


In closing this is great work from Capcom. A new vision that's sorely needed. But I say why not just make a new franchise? Maybe I just complain too much. So go out and discover the horror of Resident Evil 7 for yourself.

I only just started getting acquainted with the Resident Evil series. It's taking me long, considering this is one of the most iconic videogame franchises of all time. You got the birth of survival horror and the foundation of third-person action shooters both in the same game series. Starting with Resident Evil VII, Capcom decided to go back to the franchise's roots, with a greater emphasis on both the survival and the horror, and a more restricted environment. 
The premise of Resident Evil VII is you're a man looking for his lost wife somewhere in a bayou in Louisiana. Once there, you find a decrepit manor belonging to the Baker family, who have not only been up to no good, but also hide something sinister in them. It is at this point (and also during the opening sequence) that you realize part of what inspired this game: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Blair Witch Project.
And that's it, you're playing. You're walking around the Baker manor trying to hide from its deranged and evil, ehem, residents. At times zombie-like enemies appear, and every time they do it's kinda terrifying, because you really need to use your ammo and heals wisely, especially during boss fights. One thing that I like about the game is the atmosphere of the manor itself. If you enjoyed the way Luigi's Mansion had you exploring the different rooms in the titular homestead, you're really going to enjoy this, since it's basically the same thing except, well, actually scary. Speaking of scares, there are some legitimate and well-earned jumpscares in this game, and they don't appear to often, which means they never overstay their welcome. 
Close, to the end, however, all of this kinda disappears. The game never ceases to be very fun, but I feel like it is a its strongest earlier on. It's also a little bit short, at between 8 and 10 hours. Those are probably the main issues I have with the game, so I recommend you try it for yourself. The highs are way too good, and it has few lows. If you play, try not to spoil yourself from the encounters and the story. It's pretty cool getting to the end and understanding what was going on. 
As evidenced by its sequel, this game as revitalized the franchise, and now that I've played it, I can't wait to see what's next for Residen Evil.

I have mixed feelings about RE7. Overall I enjoyed it, but I really wish I had played on easy instead of normal.

The acts that were more "walking simulator", where you're avoiding monsters and have minimal (or no) means to defend yourself were my favorite parts. Very tense and disturbing, and very reminiscent of Amnesia and Outlast. But the parts that were focused on combat, especially the bosses, were frustrating, tedious, and not scary (probably due to the frustration). The fights aren't intuitive at all. Spoilers for a few of the bosses:

[spoiler]The first boss makes a point of demonstrating how he's invincible, so when you first go to fight him you'd expect to have to look around the room for a means of escape or alternate solution. I hopped in the car, which he then proceeds to steal and try to run me over. I circle him dozens of times, trying to get him to crash into different things but he just keeps going. Eventually I give up and unload all my ammo into him at which point the fight finally ends.

In another section of the game, there's insect nests all over that you destroy by incinerating them with a flamethrower. The boss for that section has an identical looking nest attached to her, so naturally I think I need to light her up. But I go through all my damn fuel and then all my regular ammo and the boss is still alive. Looted everything around me so there's nothing else I can use. I end up having to frantically try to kill her and her thousands of bugs with a knife while praying that she doesn't kill me first.

Finally you fight this giant monster with very clear weakpoints. I destroyed them all (I thought) but the monster kept fighting. So I once again decide to unload most of my ammo thinking maybe it just needs to be finished off or I need to trigger some ending, but no, there's one tiny little weakpoint in a very hard to find location.[/spoiler]

The combat in general is pretty lame. Blocking is overpowered and running away (which should be the default in a horror game) is too clunky to be reliable. Aiming with a controller is a nightmare as enemies sway erratically and the aim assist is pretty lacking. Enemies' health seems to be inconsistent as you fight the same monsters yet have completely different experiences with what's able to kill them quickly. And sometimes the combat doesn't even work. I can be as close as possible to a crawling enemy and unable to hit it with the knife.

But the worst part of it all is how all the tension disappears when you realize most of the time you don't even have to fight or sneakily avoid the enemy, [spoiler]all you have to do is sprint past them and make it to a saferoom[/spoiler].

And then there's the story. Overall it was interesting enough and kept me engaged, but the biggest issue is the protagonist and his dialogue / voice acting. His responses are painfully detached from the situations he finds himself in. He ruins the immersion from the get-go with how he barely reacts to all the demented ♥♥♥♥ and doesn't even seem to care for his wife (yet still goes on to continue exploring this house despite [spoiler]getting his hand lopped off by said wife[/spoiler]). There's a supposed "main" character that has no relevance to the plot and could've just been removed from the game entirely. And finally what could be the most emotional part of the story, [spoiler]with the girl and her perspective[/spoiler], isn't fleshed out or explored enough. 

But all that said, this is my first RE game. And maybe I was just expecting something that RE isn't.

With Resident Evil 7, Capcom has proved me wrong about the Resident Evil franchise.

Resident Evil 6 was a game wildly out of touch with its own fan base; this beloved horror series has struggled for relevance since. It’s had a couple of solid HD remasters, and the Revelations spinoff series has stayed strong, but the disaster of the last mainline entry in the franchise has lingered.

Now, a little over four years since Resident Evil 6, Capcom’s new numbered game in the series is more than just a return to form. Resident Evil 7 capably demonstrates that, given the right mix of pressure and time, Capcom still has unique design and narrative space left to explore in what is by far its most popular — and commercially successful — franchise.

Resident Evil 7 features Ethan Winters, a milquetoast protagonist whose search for his missing wife leads him to the bayou of Louisiana. Once there, Ethan finds himself kidnapped and tortured by a family of murderous cannibals known as the Bakers. Both in the specifics and general tone of its seemingly stand-alone story, much of Resident Evil 7 is a departure from the zombie outbreak roots of the series at large. I won’t spoil if or how RE7 might eventually tie in to the greater Resident Evil universe, but I’ll say this much: You don’t need to be invested in the 20 years of backstory that exists to jump into this game.

While Capcom doesn’t require a degree in Resident Evil lore to jump into Resident Evil 7, there are echoes of the series’ history within it. Dulvey, Louisiana, isn’t Raccoon City, but like the original Resident Evil, RE7 takes place in and around a single large house. A huge portion of the game’s 10 to 12 hours is devoted to exploring the Baker residence — and not just exploring it, but really getting to know it. I had to scour every corner of the house for resources. I had to memorize secret passageways and figure out which doors I could hide behind, and which hallways could get me to safety fastest.

That last requirement is notable, because no Resident Evil game since the first one has done as good a job as RE7 at making me feel scared and helpless. Ethan is not a special forces agent or a police officer; he’s just a regular dude with no particular combat skills. When enemies start popping up in the Baker house — both the Bakers themselves and some other terrifying opponents — often Ethan’s best tactic is simply to run like hell. The more I memorized the layout of the house and surrounding areas, the more likely I was to dodge and juke my way past bad guys without wasting precious, rare ammo and healing items.

Of course, there is ammo, because there are guns, and combat is an option. Every weapon you acquire in RE7 feels different, and, most importantly, everything beyond the standard pistol feels powerful. When you blast a bad guy with the shotgun or fire a spray of machine gun bullets, it very clearly and visibly has an impact. Headshots, in particular, are both extremely satisfying and damn near necessary to take out most enemies without throwing away tons of bullets.

The approach to combat is fairly standard for Resident Evil — albeit more on the side of limited, difficult fights, like the early games, rather than constant combat as in Resident Evil 4 through RE6 — but RE7 features at least one major, controversial change-up for the series: It’s now in the first-person perspective. Some fans have decried this change as further evidence of Capcom losing its way, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. The shift to the first person takes Resident Evil 7 closer to its roots than the series has been in more than a decade.

While a fully controllable first-person view is quite different from the static third-person cameras of the old-school Resident Evil games, it shares a key element with them: a limited perspective. Resident Evil 7 restricts this perspective even further by making Ethan’s turning speed very slow. This adds a huge amount of tension as you explore.

In the original Resident Evil games, you might be cautious because one corner of the room was obscured, and you didn’t know if an enemy hid there. In RE7, you have to be cautious because you never know if an enemy has slid into the room behind you, or if there’s some creature shambling down the hallway to your right. If you turn to check, you might find yourself suddenly blindsided by an attack from ahead of you.

This constant tension is compounded by the game’s sparse, creepy audio. The Baker house is constantly creaking, full of strange noises that left me terrified at what might be waiting beyond the next door or around a nearby corner. Was that slamming sound just a tree branch hitting the side of the house? Or is one of the Baker family about to burst through the wall and threaten to slice my head off with a shovel? These noises blended with tiny movements viewed from the corner of my vision, shadows stretching across the wall, teasing horrors to come. It’s extremely effective stuff, aided by that first-person point of view.

Not everything is different, however. RE7 does fall prey to one of the series’ long-running weaknesses: It contains only a handful of bosses, but they’re by far the worst part of the game. These encounters break the otherwise perfect tension and pacing of the rest of the experience. You are by necessity given tons of ammo and healing items in the lead-up to each boss fight, because these bigger enemies are invariably bullet sponges, sucking dry whole clips from your gun before finally falling. Worse yet, the wonderful feedback that’s present in most of the game’s other battles doesn’t really exist here; in numerous boss fights, I found myself not totally certain if I was hurting the boss or how much, because the game doesn’t make it clear.

These frustrating moments wouldn’t be that notable, save for the fact that the rest of the game’s level design and pacing are so clever and well done. The stealth and survival elements are caught in a constant tug of war with brief phases of empowerment, where you have enough supplies saved up to go all-in and attack every enemy you come across.

This is a tenuous balance that few games manage, but Resident Evil 7 finds it and, outside of those boss fights, walks the line flawlessly. The back-and-forth between slower low-power segments and faster-paced fighting creates a sense that the game is really mixing things up every 20 or 30 minutes, which means it never allowed me to get bored.

I would have been pleasantly surprised with much less than Resident Evil 7 brings to bear. I would have settled for, been excited for “not bad.” Yet the Resident Evil series has thrived for over 20 years now in part because of a willingness to change the franchise, to mutate with the times. Resident Evil 7’s changes — especially the shift to first person — may be off-putting to some. But it’s an evolution that fits perfectly into the world and source material Capcom has created. It’s hard to know if Resident Evil 7 will stand the test of time as much as classics like the original, or RE4. Taken on its own, however, it’s an excellent game that pushes the series in worthy new directions.

I want to mention right out the gate that I'm speaking as a Cajun here. Louisiana born and raised. This game nailed it with the scenery. There are little things around the game that I was genuinely surprised to see because typically only locals know about them/do these things, so Capcom must've done their due diligence with research for this game! Seeing the water out behind the old house, the storm damage to the buildings, the textures on the docks & walkways - it really feels like home, which added so much to this game for me. And on top of that, the accents! In most media, southern accents are over exaggerated and never sound accurate. Jack and Marguerite were perfect, especially in the Daughters DLC! Textbook definition of southern parents. The only one that sounded remotely inaccurate was Zoe, and even then it fits if they're far enough south, and it's clear by the scenery that they are. Judging by voices, condition of the buildings, scenery, and all else, near as I can figure the Bakers probably weren't too far off from Dulac, though probably a bit farther south of it.

The Molded as a concept is fascinating to me. I'd have loved to see more variations of them, more twisted aberrations and mutations! The pacing through the game left a bit to be desired, and Ethan has very little personality, but it's really refreshing if I'm going to be totally honest. Ethan is a character with so little to him in a series where every character is ridiculously extra - it's nice to see a protagonist who's just a normal guy. The dinner segment of the game was weird, I'll admit, but after that things really settled into place. This game does a solid job of adding an eerie, unsettling atmosphere! When I first played this game back in 2018 I didn't get further than the trailer in the yard, decided it was boring and I didn't like it. I'm glad I came back to give it a second chance because this is an excellent return to form for the series! It left a bit to be desired, sure - but hey, it's a LOT better than the absolute dumpster fire that was Resident Evil 5, and that's all that matters. And as for Chris in this game - it just amuses me that Capcom, even after all this time, still can't decide on a set appearance for Chris Redfield. Different every game! That being said, personality-wise this was the closest he's been to his RE1 variant since Code Veronica X, so that was a pleasant surprise! 

If you're reading this as a fan of the classic games and are questioning whether to give this game a shot, I say do it, but don't go into it expecting it to be like the classic games. It's very different, but mostly in a good way! Though funnily enough, monsters aside, the most unrealistic thing in this game was the Baker family home being that big in Louisiana's economy. All in all, I give Resident Evil 7 a solid 8/10. 

Oh, and the Resident Evil Outbreak reference was perfect. <3

Resident Evil 7 is, in my opinion, the quintessential survival horror experience. It combines all aspects of terror, creepiness, and helplessness in one perfect masterpiece. I have played 5 RE games so far, and this one sits comfortably at the top.

For starters, the story in RE7 is as simple as they come, where you receive a mysterious message from your long lost wife and go on a search for her in the mysterious and surely infested Baker estate. Whereas other entries would lose me to a degree on the background of the stories, with the BSAA, Umbrella Corp, and the long histories of the main characters, RE7 unfolds its story and mysteries in a very deliberate and careful manner where you're excited to find out more about it with every step you take. The characters are all very unique and well written making all your encounters with them fresh and also intriguing.

What really puts this game above all others though is definitely the dark and dreary atmosphere. With its varying color schemes, the chilling sound design, the ever-morphing and changing environments, the first person POV, and the menacing soundtrack, not to mention the ridiculously wonderful textures and graphics , it immerses you completely in the different zones and chapters of the game. Considering most the game takes place within one large area, you always have to look over your shoulder since you can't really escape the dangers of the estate, but at the same time, you also become deeply connected and familiar with the place and characters, which plays heavily into the game's themes of family. Jack Baker pursuing you in the first area takes away any sense of safety you may try to find between your encounters with the horrific molded around the house, while Marguerite along with her bugs create a sense of total uneasiness throughout your traversal of the old house. The incredible voice acting and facial animations of these characters are definitely some of the most well done aspects of the game, driving the feelings of anxiety into the player.

The combat is also very well done, but is frankly what you would expect from a Resident Evil game, starting with pistols and shotguns, and progressing into magnums and grenade launchers, which definitely keeps the combat feeling fresh and exciting all through a playthrough. The boss fights all feel very unique and generally fun to figure out and fight. The puzzles are also quite fun and add a layer of mystery and intrigue to the environments. They're usually pretty simple and straightforward to solve but rewarding nonetheless.

As of writing this review, I have completed all achievements in this game, and it was definitely worth it. A lot of them you can try to get easily on your first playthrough, but having to complete the game on the highest difficulty once then again in under 4 hours, along with a few more feats, made me appreciate all the effort and details the devs really put into this game. If you have already finished the game once, I would highly recommend trying to get some of the other achievements, especially since the game rewards you with very fun weapons and items for completing some of them.

If you enjoy the horror genre to any degree or are simply looking for a good 7 hour campaign, I would highly recommend giving RE7 a shot, then trying some of the DLC! Most of it is very fun too.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is quite simply, absolutely stunning. It's a masterclass in survival-horror, genuine survival and genuine, terrifying, pulse-pounding horror and fear and it's almost flawless in every single aspect. 

I realize hardcore fans of the series probably weren't too happy about the new first-person perspective, but I have found third-person horror to be very rarely effective, not least in the Resident Evil games, and only Dead Space was the real exception to that rule, due to it's almost obsessive focus on immersion and atmosphere. Here, the first-person perspective worked wonders, bringing the claustrophobic environments up close and personal, the horrific creatures and mutated creations of nightmares right in your face, towering over you as they shamble in your direction. 

The art design and atmosphere is so dense and textured it's almost tangible, you can almost smell the corruption and rot as you creep along the maze-like corridors and rooms. There was also thankfully very little of the cheesy silliness that the series is almost hallmarked with, and the part that is there feels cheeky enough to be noticeable but not jarring enough to take you out of the immersion, and the story is actually really quite good, especially the Baker family, and the bayou itself, nothing ever feels like parody or stereotype, the game has such a strong identity and style that it feels genuine and unforgettable, especially with parts of the game where you suddenly see characters in a whole new light, fear and disgust giving way to sadness and sympathy, just so well executed. And I just have to mention the design of the logo real quick, bleeding Seven and Evil together has to be one of the best and most clever designs for anything ever. 

If I had to criticise something, I would say the ship chapter playing as you know who drags just a bit, especially as it all looks so similar, in stark contrast to the tightly designed and unique Baker Estate. The DLCs too, were all fantastic, but End Of Zoe stood out, playing as Joe "Sigma Gigachad" Baker was the catharsis we all needed after going through the main story terrified of every corner, and just curbstomping and headsmashing your way through it as this badass was the high point this game needed to perfectly end. I could honestly talk all day about how fantastic this game is, but suffice it to say I loved practically every minute of it, and I really hope future games in the series go back to this gritty, claustrophobic survival-horror instead of being glorified action games like Village, which is also a great game by the way, but just can't touch Resident Evil 7 in my opinion. Hopefully the 4 Remake will make us all happy. I really can't recommend this game enough, and can honestly say it's one of the best survival-horror games of all time.

Absolutely fantastic experience. After RE5 feeling like an extended edition of a co-op arcade game and the fiasco that 6 was (which I admittedly dodged), I didn't have much hope for this game. I played the demo and thought it was interesting, but not worth $60. Having finally dug it out of my backlog, I now wish I played it earlier because it's such a good game. I don't even like horror games but the atmosphere and attention to environmental detail is so entertaining that it's hard to put down. It's a real struggle to find anything negative to say about this... the intro is a bit slow (in terms of both pacing and actual movement), the last boss feels stolen from another popular survival horror game, and I don't like the Nemesis/Pursuer enemy. However, these are all either staples of the genre or the series at this point so it's hard to hate them too much.

This is also the first game I've played with native HDR support and it really added to the experience. Software-based HDR has been around for ages now (the tech demo Half-Life: Lost Coast came out in 2005), but hardware-based HDR is a completely different ball game. Your character's vision reacts realistically to bright light sources, like when spinning away from an exposed light bulb for example. The difference with a monitor that supports it is that the monitor outputs actual light differently, compared to the software-based solution of the games' shading just changing in these situations. Light sources look amazing and it honestly looks more realistic than VR in some areas. Also like VR, there's no way to demonstrate the experience through just screenshots because of the hardware involved. There's so many new graphic buzzwords flying around now, but this is something that can be experienced with just a GeForce 1050 and a decent monitor (I purchased mine for $300 this summer), and is definitely worth checking out.

The graphical quality, level design, environmental details, sound track, voice acting, and game play are all remarkably good. Resident Evil looked to be stuck in a design rut for a while but this new direction is really fantastic. You can tell the people working on it poured their everything into it. This probably would've been my GOTY for 2017 and I regret not playing it sooner. Even though it has almost nothing to do with the Resident Evil universe, this might be my new favorite game in the series. Highly recommended.

Not only was RE7 the revival of the franchise, it marks the era where this series took a whole new direction. Instead of the cheesy dialog and crazy mutated creatures from the previous games RE7 focuses on one thing, scaring the absolute ♥♥♥♥ out of it's players. Gone are the cheesy one liners and over the top fight sequences in the middle of an active volcano. Instead we have a game that feels more relatable, Ethan Winters (the protagonist) is not a highly trained super solider, instead he is a normal guy who ends up finding out his girlfriend has been the victim of the Baker family for the past 3 years. Exploring the Baker family home is unsettling and you never know what will happen next. From chainsaw duels in a dissection room, to a bugs nest growing on Marguerite's Baker crotch area, this game relies on it's claustrophobic atmosphere and grotesque visuals to make you not only feel powerless but also scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of whats to come. The gameplay is now in 1st person which makes the game naturally more scary and the lack of overpowered weapons, ammo and healing items make the safe havens feel even more rewarding. And everytime you miss a shot you really feel like an idiot for wasting precious ammo. This game has great level design from the Main House, to the Old House, to the Testing Grounds, almost all the games areas feel distinct despite keeping a somewhat small scale compared to games in the past. The sound design too, from Jack Baker referencing Evil Dead to Marguerite calling you a ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥, it all comes together in a beautiful yet disgusting way. The Baker family are some of my favourite antagonists ever. Lucas's sadistic games, Zoes need to leave the family, the Grandma who leaves you in confusion until the end, to Jack constantly following you like you're a child to an abusive father. You truly feel disgust and hatred towards a once normal family who became victims of the mold. I also love the various tapes you find around the locations that can help you solve puzzles later on at the cost of seeing someone/or multiple people facing brutal deaths, the "Happy Birthday" Tape is a prime example of this. My only issue with the game would be the boat section/ending which I felt drags on a bit too much, however the pacing before the final fight with Jack is near perfection. I certainly recommend this game to any fans of Resident Evil or horror in general.

Resident Evil 7 is a triumphant return to form that put this horror classic back on the map and back into the minds of gamers, it was brutal and scary and radically different from all that came before, we now play in a first person view and the game has (almost) no connection to the originals. 

It was controversial when announced as it seemed to be jumping on the PT bandwagon, a FPS horror game which would probably be filled with jump scares and basically just stealth, whilst those things are in this game it is undeniable old school resident evil at heart and only a few pacing issues in the second half truly bring this horror classic down. 

Pros 

A return to what makes Resident Evil good, non linear levels with many branching paths, secrets and puzzles to uncover. Tight level design and smart use of the environment is key to survival. 

Interesting story and villains, really it's the villains that carry this and Jack Baker is so iconic.

Resident Evil 7 clearly has a goal in mind from the outset: to unsettle and frighten from beginning to end, refocusing a series that, by this point, had lost its direction, eschewing horror in favor of heavier action. In this regard, RE7 easily delivers on that goal, with the combination of its first-person viewpoint, the setting, and the monster design delivering an extremely well-crafted horror experience.

First-person and third-person, are, naturally, vastly different experiences, but that difference is hugely amplified in the horror genre. You can't detach yourself from what the protagonist is seeing - you're experiencing the world straight through their eyes. The field of view is significantly narrower, meaning that you need to take more risks in looking out for enemies or objects, and that ratchets up the tension severely. Everything jumps straight out at YOU, rather than your character - an enemy getting in your face means they fill up the entire screen, amplifying the claustrophobic feeling inherent to first-person horror. 

Being what one may describe as a "big baby," this made playing through RE7 an exercise in self-torture. Fortunately, however, the bad feelings are well worth the experience. The setting is gorgeous - the dilapidated houses, wide-open swamplands, and dark, dank cave systems create variety in the experience while being equally frightening at all turns. The Bakers are excellent villains, ghouls that haunt you around every turn in the major setpieces of the game, and as the story unfolds and you discover the truth of what's going on with them, the story manages to extract a surprising amount of pathos from them, giving them depth beyond "horrible swamp people." I never felt that the narrative got in the way of the gameplay - rather, they pair nicely together, each enriching the other. Combat, meanwhile, is satisfying - on the standard difficulty, I could feel the strain of limited resources, without ever feeling like I was being unfairly punished. Some boss fights were harder than others, and of course I hate pursuit segments, but the atmosphere and tone of the game made up for those personal shortcomings.

WIth RE7, Village, RE2, and RE3 all on the RE Engine, it feels like this series offers players much more than it did in the days of RE6 and Revelations, and we have the triumph of RE7 to thank for that. When it comes to first-person horror, little can match Capcom's RE team firing on all cylinders, and RE7 is the pinnacle of that.

I did a replay of this game on Halloween this year, it's been a few years since I've touched this game and I didn't remember a lot of it so I thought it'd be a good time to play it again.

It's real weird going back to play this one after Village considering all the improvements that one made to the formula. You're a bit slower, and you can't take as much of a beating in this one so it's got a bit of a different feel to it. It definitely plays more like a classic style Resident Evil game but in first person rather than one of the later action Resident Evil games. Combat is slow, you don't have a lot of bullets and supplies and you're running around a big house unlocking doors, finding upgrades and secrets and it's just as good as it's ever been.

It's all pretty good stuff. I remember back when it first came out everyone was upset that it didn't connect with the other games that much (me included) and I also remember not really liking Ethan as a character/protagonist. Funny looking back because he's definitely shot up my list of favorites in the series after playing Village. 

As for ACTUAL issues with the game, there's a section near the end where you're on an old dilapidated ship that serves as a flashback sequence to explain the story a bit more and I really don't enjoy it. It's super dark and the boat just isn't as interesting level-design wise compared to the Baker house. There's also not much enemy variety here, there's actually only 4 enemy types in this game and they all look very similar. One of them is pretty much just a stronger version of another that does more damage.

I think where RE7 really shines is in it's atmosphere and world building. I still think this is the most immersive RE game to date. Something about the way you move and the narrow fov along with the house being built to accurate size helps you feel like you're really there. I really like all the weird stuff that happens in this game too that you wouldn't even expect from a videogame let alone a Resident Evil game. It has a lot of memorable set pieces and events and the villains are just great, especially Jack.

RE7 is flawed, yeah. But it's still good even with some of those flaws and it singlehandedly revived this franchise so that's gotta count for something.

Resident Evil 7 has easily taken its place as my favourite RE game to date, and is my favourite horror game. 
Now it may not technically be the best the series has to offer, and yes it has its flaws, but it is scary, thrilling, tense, and grounded in comparison to some of the other games may be.
I'll start by addressing complaints/negatives of the game first before talking about the stronger suits and counters to the negatives. No Spoilers ahead!
Cons:
- Let's start with the obvious one: the infamous "Third Act". Yeah, the game does fall off in the end, and loses tension as antagonists are taken out and the locations broaden up, losing the isolated feeling of the beginning. Now I do kinda like the third act for its exploration of lore for the game, but it isn't nearly as scary as it could or should be. And is filled with/ highlights another flaw of the game:
- Lack of enemy variety. There are 3.5 types of non-boss enemies called 'the molded' which are good enemies, but lose their fear factor after awhile as you power up your arsenal and you see the same creatures 30+ times just with different spawn patterns in different locations. I say 3.5 because there are *technically* 5, but 2 are just slightly changed versions of the original, so a half point is generous. Now, the DLC for the game does actually introduce quite a few new types of creatures, which expand this roster nicely, but I can't help but wish that I could have seen them in the main campaign to actually up the stakes. The bugs in the main campaign are a nice shake up though!
- First-Person Camera? This can be seen as a positive or a negative, but I myself lean on the fence towards positive. Yes, it can cause some motion sickness for some, but I don't really experience it when I play. I do dislike the blood on the screen. Yes there is an option to reduce the blood on the screen, but it still doesn't feel like enough. The first person camera takes away and limits from something the RE series is really good at, good animation and character work especially in some cut-scenes (but after trying RE6 I am NOT really complaining). But the variation is welcomed and does actually vary what can and can't be done for better or for worse, which I believe to be for the better from a horror perspective. Take Jack grabbing and spinning you around for an example, that can be a scary moment that just couldn't happen the same way in third person. As well, it directly places you in the horror, and removes a layer of suspension of disbelief. I enjoyed their revisiting of this in the RE3 remake for small horror based sections.
- Ethan. Ethan is a boring protagonist, and although it works from an objective perspective aka, he has basic but firm goals so he is driven to keep going forward to drive the story, he is a basic boy and is just one degree off of a silent protag which is just a stand-in for the player. Which does add to horror but takes away from the longevity of his usage in future uses. Re has fun, memorable protagonists that are main stays for good reason, they are: likable, clever, selfless, visually distinct, resilient, and role-modelish. Ethan has like, resilience as a stubbornness, and family-oriented as his traits.

Pros:
- Atmosphere. This game is the first ever to use the RE engine, which has gone onto being used in RE2, RE3, & RE 4 remakes, RE8, and Monster Hunter Rise, etc. The environments are phenomenal, and expertly crafted to highlight the terror of this game. Filth and muck has never looked so good than in this game. To add to the atmosphere we have the sounds of the game. Ugh, YES! The motif of "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" is just great, highlighted by character's usage to spook the player when it suddenly cuts-off when you approach. The grimy garbage has flies, the crawling bugs, and creaking floors are awesome. A footnote or two: I love the dismemberment system of the main molded which is expanded in a great way in RE2 remake. And small moments like characters bursting through a wall or cutting limbs off just to screw with you are NOT going to happen in every playthrough and still sometimes scare and surprise me. I'm still wondering what other kinds of interactions I haven't seen yet!
- Antagonists. The baker family is amazing. Intimidating figures that honestly are the best part of the entire game. They are all unique in their style of how they will hunt you down, leading to a unique feeling of danger even as you progress through the game, they will make your weapons never enough. The fights are all extremely unique in presentation and execution and are the most entertaining part of a replay as they can be very different depending on how well you play them.
- Story. This game MAJORLY grounds itself, and focuses on a smaller scale of threat which is claustrophobic and personalized to the protagonist. Because for once it isn't just "because it's my duty" or "for the greater good" which is just far too easy for a zombie game. For a long while the story does feel like it just "forgets" about the rest of the series and is disconnected, but does actually connect itself with some notes and through certain character involvement explored even further in the "Not a Hero" DLC. The heart of the story is family, through the Bakers and the Winters, and I love the continuation into RE8 whereupon this is expanded and reinforced. And... *ahem*  two endings, which may not be as incredibly distinct as they could be, but still does add replay-ability to the game which some games lack.
- There are more positives but really, do play the game for yourself and see what it can do. It is scary, challenging, and is a fantastic entry point into the series (It actually was my introduction to the series. Good enough to make me purchase 10 other games and try multiple spin offs) and doesn't need any any prior series knowledge to start playing! And watching and play really is different, even if you know every scare and trick in the book, your own ability to ward off these terror with aim and blocking and resource management as well as the enemies randomness will make every run through unique.

Quick looks at the DLC:
- "Not a Hero" is free and helps to wrap up loose ends and add connectivity to the story to previous entries. Not as scary, but tension filled and fun. Combat is enhanced but still challenging! The expanding of one of the antagonists is appreciated as I felt we definitely could have had more of them in the main game. 8/10
- "End of Zoe" confirms the canon ending of the game, and also wraps up more loose ends of the game. Not required to play RE8. This DLC has you play as the most bad ass character in the entire RE series, and is the most fun gameplay wise. Stealth kills, bare-handed destruction, and using literally anything and everything to become an unstoppable force. 10x better of a protag than ethan. 10/10
- Jack's 55th BDay. It's a mad dash for any and all food to feed the hungry bday boy. A silly yet fun side mode that's like a mercenaries replacement, I enjoy actually being the rewards for replays. 6/10
- Ethan must Die. It's as the name implies. Ethan's gonna die. A lot. It's a extremely challenging mode with randomized equipment, and 1-2 shotting enemies. Good luck getting to the end. Comes with any DLC purchase I believe. 7/10
- Banned Footage. 4 small expansions to the events of RE7 that all take place before the main game. They're kinda like minigames but are enjoyable nevertheless! Nightmare is a wave survival mode with Jack 6/10. Bedroom is an escape room with Marguerite 6/10. 21 is a game of black jack to the death with Lucas and captives. 8/10, I liked the extras in this one, I'd get this as a standalone game. Daughters puts you in Zoe's shoes and sees the haunt begin for the Bakers. 9/10, multiple endings.

I love the direction this game pointed the series in, and I am loving the modern era of Resident Evil this game kicked off.

This is the first Resident Evil game I've played and for the most part, I liked it! It's a solid horror game with an interesting narrative, thought-provoking puzzles, fleshed-out mechanics, and constant tension and dramatic moments throughout. Especially the first leg of the game, which has plenty of major scares and some big unexpected story twists right off the bat that set the stage well for the rest of the game. And, once the introductory level of the game is over, the game opens up into a big, interconnected map that has polished individual sections retaining their own atmosphere and enemies, while also letting the player explore and backtrack to some areas for collectibles and upgrades.

As much as I liked the exploration and variety offered, RE7 isn't an A-grade horror game. There are some wonky physics and animations during combat and boss battles that pulled me out of the experience from time to time... most notably the REALLY scuffed boss battle against Marguerite, where I was laughing at the boss's ridiculous animations and movement more than I was scared of the boss itself. I appreciate RE7's attempts to make big, open, dynamic boss fight arenas, but the bigger they are, the buggier they fall, and the animations and AI just aren't fine tuned enough to compensate for some of these environments. I had similar problems with a certain boathouse monster boss that I was always able to stay behind so that the boss kept rotating and could never hit me... and many of the less intimidating enemies throughout the game have that same issue, making the combat throughout the game feel more like I was trying to fight back against the game than the monsters I came up against.

Graphical issues with the game include occasional low-res textures and weird-looking shadows in well-lit areas. I normally wouldn't notice this much since I care more about general creative direction in regard to a game's visuals than pure graphics quality... but horror immersion relies somewhat on realism, and having some objects/enemies ingame look worse than everything else is counter to the overall experience.

I want to give Biohazard points for everything it's able to do right - which is to say, quite a bit! It has lots of great exploration, well-realized inventory balancing, interesting puzzles, and a tense yet entertaining story. But its lack of polish in regard to combat, animations, and enemy AI holds the game back from its full potential. 7/10

(1/1/23: This is a rewrite of my RE7 review after finishing all the mainline games to make it more in-line with the others & to express my thoughts more thoroughly.)

RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard is a great game & I think really saved the franchise after 6 came and burned the name of Resident Evil to the ground. Yes, I hated 6 that much.

RE7 introduces brand-new protagonist, Ethan Winters, alongside his wife Mia Winters who has been MIA for 3 years in the beginning of this all-new adventure!

RE7 takes you to an ominous estate where your wife Mia tells you to "Come get me.", and once you find your way in, you learn that maybe this home is owned by someone. Well, actually, you should've known that already. Why would you ever go to a home and it not be owned by someone in this franchise?

7 definitely returned RE back to it's horror roots after it's dive into the action scene with 5 & 6, which is for the better. While 5 may have done the action thing really well in my opinion and I really liked that game, 6 completely ruined the name of RE and had the franchise gone down that route I have no doubt it would've failed. Thankfully 7 came and fixed all that mess.

The new protagonist, Ethan, is alright. He's pretty quiet throughout the game & you don't get lots of personality with him. Some people kind of complain about that which I understand, but then again, if you're stuck in this hellhole of a house, are you reaaally going to be using your voice that much? Didn't think so.

Your new antagonists, the Baker family are... well, quite literally insane. Once you get in the house & see your environment, some stuff in a pot and maybe a little bit in the fridge, you should know the people here aren't exactly... okay, but once you get "welcomed to the family" by Jack Baker, you'll soon find out how insane these people are. They feed you... food? If that's what you consider food, sure. Even if you haven't played this game you probably know about the iconic dinner scene. Spooky, huh?

After playing through all the mainline games + Revelations1&2, I can confidently say that RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard is the scariest game in the franchise. This game was my first RE game and it had me wanting to ALT+F4 around every corner, and none of the others did that. This game is insanely scary. Apparently "too scary" by the Village Team's words, since they apparently "dialed Village down" after 7.

So, even though 7 holds the most scares to me, it does get less scary the farther you go. It doesn't completely wipe out the scares, but they get less & a little more cliché the farther you go. This isn't a bad thing, as the game still holds up really well even with the scares dissipating a little bit.

RE7 moves away from the whole zombie thing, and introduces you to something new. Mold. Weird, right? Yeah, kinda, but it's interesting & it works and it gives you a true meaning behind the craziness of everything within the game.

RE7 really disconnects itself from the rest of RE's events with little-to-no mention of anything that has happened. Yeah, that's right! No Umbrella Corp. No mention of past events, nothing. Which is interesting for sure, but that's not bad. That doesn't mean it's not connected of course, it definitely is, it just doesn't shove it in your face. This makes RE7 a really great starting point for the franchise if you find yourself here instead of RE1 first.

RE7 is basically a soft-reboot for the franchise, keeping it within the same continuity, but bringing it back to survival horror after 6 and bringing in the new (and great) first person view. This new perspective really brings in a new element of horror to the franchise and keeps your senses alert at all times. This perspective along with the amazing RE Engine makes it feel extremely REAL and immerses you very well, keeping you on-guard 24/7. Drop your guard and you'll probably scream.

Overall, RE7 was a really great game and it saved the franchise in my opinion, and the new perspective breathes a new life of horror into the beloved franchise. I loved my time with it & I am so glad it was made the way it was. Amazing game.

You can't skip cutscenes and the checkpoint system is frustrating. A boss battle usually begins with an unskippable cutscene and, if you die, you have to trigger the cutscene and sit through it all over again before you can make another attempt. It brings the game to a frustrating standstill. 

While the game is in the house, it's a near masterpiece. Jack's section is incredible. Marguerite's section is just annoying. Lucas's section is pretty fun. However, the game takes a huge dip in quality during the boat section, salt mines and finale. The final half of the game matches more late-era RE titles and it's pretty disappointing. It's heavy on action, low on scares and painfully easy. 

Overall, the game is still worth a playthrough and is genuinely great in parts. Your first time through will have you nervously turning corners in dread of what's waiting for you ahead. It's also a welcome return-to-form and the best RE title since RE4.

Experienced in Vive VR courtesy of Praydog.

I held out until VR mods for Resident Evil VII were in a good place. And they are thanks to Praydog and a related motion sickness mod you can find on Discord--just search Praydog for all of that. Is VR essential for this game? No. It's so good I would say, absolutely not. VR gives some more weight to the grossness, tension, and definitely makes you more vulnerable to well used jump scares and enemies just around the corner or sneaking up behind you. Great for me! REVII in VR may be too much for others. You'll know if that's you because the idea alone will seem like too much, ha.

VR aside, the base game itself is fantastic. They really embraced the first person perspective well for gameplay and narrative. I loved the optional VHS tapes [Why would you not play them?!] as added story pieces giving variety and essentially placing you in found footage horror shorts. VR isn't essential but playing those tapes in VR reminded me of Duck Season--great immersion! Overall, this is a tightly designed experience that felt good all the way through without any sections I felt dragged or were tiring. The narrative is strong. The characters and villains are engaging. Most importantly, this is the closest the Resident Evil series has been to its roots in a long time!

The survival horror is here and this time it's darker, uglier, and more twisted than ever before. While it's well rooted in the RE universe, they pulled from some great places for influence. There's so much Evil Dead in this game and Resident Evil VII proudly wears that inspiration on its sleeves and dismembered limbs. Toss in a splash of Texas Chainsaw Massacre for the gross, a bit of ick reminiscent of RE:0, plus some of the Japanese body-horror we've seen in past RE titles, and you have a game that delivers for horror fans.

I just finished the main story, and I'm looking forward to playing through all the DLC. Going off the base presentation and style of REVII, I'm very optimistic about the DLC.

It's easily the scariest of the games thus far (having played 1-7, and the Revelations games) and it knows how to keep supplies low to keep things tense.... until it doesn't. The last sprint to the ending is easily the weakest part where it remembers Resident Evil likes to lean into action. The final encounter was also probably one of the easier fights in the game, despite me not realizing what I was walking into and as a result I didn't even gear up for it. Despite a weaker last ~10% of the game, overall it is a solid time.

---The DLC---
It seems fair to split out the DLC into it's own section. I'm generally less compelled to do the types of content in the "Banned Footage" DLC, being more intended to be replayed for high score/low time chasing so I didn't do much of it. I DID play through 21, and that was enjoyable.

 The free "Not a Hero" DLC is in a lot of ways a better ending and embracing the action side of the series makes sense here with the change in character to someone that SHOULD be well armed. It's overall alright, and is worth a play as a free addition. If you were looking for a final boss that puts up a big in-game fight, you'll get that here. 

The "End of Zoe" DLC was.... a really fun time, but really weird in gameplay compared to the rest. Going from "oh I need to be concerned when enemies are around" in the main game, to "I should try to conserve ammo, but generally I'm well armed" in Not a Hero, to "Imma give this moldy boy the ol' 1-2 and show 'em how we do things 'round 'ere" is quite a jump. It's a lot of fun boxing out the enemies, it's stupid how strong punching is, but I can't deny it's a delight to have special punching combos and just hammering away with a barrage of jabs. I have fallen in love with the Resident Evil series, and it started with this game for me. I am not much at all into psychological horror games - NOT because I do not like them, but simply because of anxiety, fear, etc. This game is a survival horror, action-adventure, first person shooter type. For people who are die hard fans of this game since its release, they seem to be critical of every new release. For instance, in the older RE: 1,2,3, etc. you play in 3rd person (Where you view your character as an onlooker instead of controlling the game from their view directly) - This one, and Village is 1st person (Which I personally like better). It also introduces a new protagonist, the person you are playing as: Ethan Winters (Pretty much all new characters, story, and some new plot/backstory revolving around the old).

The beginning plot to the game.
[spoiler]It's mid-2017, and you're Ethan Winters. You received a worrisome video in an email from your missing wife, Mia, who has been missing for 3 years, warning to "Stay away" at the end of the video. You end up driving to an old derelict home in the small town Dulvey, Louisiana, USA. Where a lot of real-life ghost sightings have been. You start the game off in front of the house, eager to find your wife.[/spoiler]

This game is like a playable horror movie at times (Although, I say that about a lot of games now-days). With rich and interesting characters, a very interesting plot that is tied together with science, mistakes, and corrupt government agencies - learning more about "what happened" as you go, via reading documents, looking at photos - and trying to stay alive through the many challenges to find it all out.

The game may be unattractive and unforgiving to people who aren't steady on their toes, really ready to solve puzzles and points that seem impossible to get past (I guess you could use a walk-through, takes away that mystery and fun with this series, though), conserving supplies, and ready to possible die to something at anytime. It can be frustrating. As this is a 1st person, survival, psychological horror game. I personally even held off playing/beating this game after I first bought it, only making it [Spoiler]to the Main Hall with only 2 of the dog-heads[/spoiler]. There are hidden secrets, items, collectibles, and more for people who really want to dig for them. You can go back to areas at times, to look for things you may have missed - but not after certain points.

The graphics are beautiful. The game plays amazing for me (Using Capcom's RE Engine). The sounds are amazing (Even in times of backtracking through "safe" places, you hear that random "crack" in the wood as if something was there). And if you are into scary games, this could be a "must have". Even if you aren't, the story-line, and game are so good - that it just can't be passed up in my opinion. At-least give it a try, like I did.

Also, the DLC is pretty good as well. As of writing this comment, I haven't tried all of the DLC - As I wanted to jump into Village next. The "Bedroom" part of the "Banned Footage Vol. 1" was fun.

This was the game that got me into the Resident Evil Series so this may be a bit biased. In short this was the game that revived the series and is worthy of a 10/10 score for the base game.

The setting, characters, and lore have made it a masterpiece in video games. You are faced with these human looking enemies as your main obstacles throughout the game. I ran out of ammo and resorted to knife fighting. People said online "just walk past them". I didn't pay $40 to walk in circles, keeping an eye on 5 monsters, while I am looking for my next clue. I will rant about this game(mostly because of hype by others), but first things first. I highly recommend this game, definitely worth owning and playing, a few times. People who keep saying this title is entirely  different from other Resident Evil titles are both right and wrong. It's more atmospheric than other titles, but it still has ridiculous giant blob monsters that have orange pustules that need shooting. Just because there is less convoluted story and monsters, doesn't mean it's THAT different, just less of those things. A story about people that didn't want to hurt anyone, but had to because a virus or mold made them, that's COMPLETELY different! The game clearly states that there is a SMALL window to cure people, but Mia and this poor family has this mold-virus for three stinkin' years, yet only Mia and Zoe are curable and everyone else dies from the cure? There is a lot of running and hiding in this game, THAT'S what is different. It's not a bad story, but it's not the game changer a lot of people say it is. In my opinion, the RE series was never really scary, but intense(there is a difference). Just my opinion, but I can see why others deem it kinda scary. This game IS more intense than other titles because the player is running from the same people zombie monsters over and over again. That's why the replay value of the story is not that enticing to me. The same spooky cut scenes over and over with very little action just isn't my thing. It's awesome the first time, but the intensity is gone after that having to run and hide until it's boss fight time. I prefer the zombie shooting action, which IS all other titles. The more I look it up, the more I find out many fans keep re-playing the 4-6 games. Why? IMO, it's because of choice. The player has the choice to run or fight(a variety of baddies with a variety of weapons). People keep saying the stories of those games are messy, but this title no is no different, just less of a mess. Trying to make the players feel sympathetic towards the family that held your girlfriend hostage was a mistake. The family was FORCED to act like serial killer jerks that enjoyed killing and torturing people for three years? That's...unfortunately dumb. Let me be clear: This game IS great, dripping with atmosphere, and the bonus mini games are fun. I really THOUGHT that the game was doing something almost unprecedented is the RE universe. When I first started playing this one, I dropped my jaw because I thought the story was heading to the idea that a sadistic mass murdering Texas chainsaw massacre-like family that ended up with a mold(it's not a virus, it's a mold that spreads) that made them immortal monsters! It turns out they were just a normal family that were forced to be monsters because of a monster virus-like mold. WOW! That's not different from other RE titles at all! All I'm saying(that's not fair, this is a rant). All my boo-whoing ranting brain is saying is that, it's not THAT different from other titles. It's less action and more horror which makes it unique in the RE universe, but in the end, it's STILL a RE game with all of the checkbox's marked. The game raised so many questions about how the story was put together that I couldn't possibly have asked them here without sounding even more insane and ranty than I already am. Plus, I DON'T want this game to LOOK bad. It IS highly recommended that you buy and play this game! There are elements of Blair Witch, haunted house's, killer families, etc! My rant doesn't change that this game is top-notch AND a unique experience in the RE universe. Just don't expect to be blown away by the same story line told with just a few zombies, rather than a whole town or city. Please continue to encourage the creators of these games to keep making them by buying them and enjoying them in your own way!

RE7 is okay. It's very alright all around, with problems here and there I'll probably write down. What's more important, to me at
least, is that it has been advertised since the beginning of production as "going back to Resident Evil's roots", and to that I
say that it does not go back to it's roots, just moving forward like RE4 moved away from the first 3. To me, it comes off as a
watered down variation of the first Resident Evil, and a lot of the design choices that were made now I feel were purposely 
avoided before.

The most blatant difference, the camera perspective, shows a lot of the issues that Resident Evil avoided for a reason. Initially,
RE1 had a phase as a first person game, but was quickly scrapped. The camera angle used in RE1 is of multiple fixed cameras that 
are juxtaposed onto pre-rendered backgrounds. In order to get the character moving in a fashion around corridors and such without
it being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chore and terribly unresponsive it had to be controlled via tank controls (as in, hitting up makes the
character walk forward whichever direction he is currently facing, and the same for the rest of the directions). The tank controls
were neccessary for the camera chosen, and it can also be said that when tension rises with the player, the controls being awkward
almost fit being flustered or nervous, which is bound to happen in a zombie infested freak show you've accidently stumbled upon.
It also limits the players vision while also giving him an advantage, you can see whatever the game wants you to see at the point
as a design choice, and leaves offscreen threats to appear quickly to scare the player (basically a jumpscare).

RE7 instead uses a first person camera, giving the player a personal view of the surroundings. While it makes threats and the such
more realistic, it also takes away a lot in order to surprise the player. RE7 took an approach of making everything in the game
REALLY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dark, and needing to inspect everything to make sure you didn't miss anything important. RE1 was well lit, and
everything you needed was more or less obvious to you. You didn't need to flounder about in the dark looking for ♥♥♥♥ on the
ground because the game decided that making everything dark is "scary".

"Scary" is subjective, which makes defining a game as scary difficult. However I find it's easier to just break down scariness
into different categories to differentiate horror from horror. RE1 got it's horror from atmosphere and confusion mostly. The only
real threat were the zombies, and everything was for the most part well lit and identifiable. What became scary though, was the
scenario. You are alone in a mansion with things that make zero sense and are left to just explore it to figure something out.
Every hallway (there are a lot of hallways) has many twists and turns that leave it almost like a maze. It's scares came from
jumpscares mind you, with hunter/dogs jumping through windows causing sound cues, but it wasn't the only thing.

RE7 uses scary much differently. It uses the unknown as horror, rather than what is actually there. Rooms are dark and messy so
anything could be in there and searching may lead to horrendous findings. Jumpscares are more prominent, but each enemy is
occampinied by a musical score in order to tell the player that a threat was nearby (RE1 only did so with jumpscares) which can
also be seen as a way to help players see pass their blind spots, due to the 1st person camera.

The "scares" portrayed are also neutered due to the 1st person camera in RE7. Because you can only see infront of you, and every
setting is two steps from pitch-black, the developers also made the enemies you encounter incredibly dark. The enemies in RE7 are
really no different from the first game. There are like, four variants of enemies in each game. RE1, however, gives each enemy 
some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ color and variation in design. You can quickly tell a zombie from a dog from a hunter. In RE7 everythings a weird 
black blob that walks at you and swings at you. One kind is on the floor sometimes but the other ones sometimes go on the floor
too. RE7's distinction comes from the Baker family instead, each sporting different abilitites due to their illness. While these
add variety to the game a bit, it also means that the map design had to change.


RE1 had enemies in like, every room. Sure, most if not all were zombies who barely moved or did anything besides walk in circles,
but the issue didn't come from the enemies, but rather the location. The game was designed around narrow-ass corridors that you
could either attempt to dodge the zombies, or blow through them with whatever leftover ammo you have to make it easier. RE7 has
instances of this, but many hallways are wide and make dodging a breeze (Jack literally will do no damage to you if you just run
at him and walk through him kinda). Enemies are also lessened, with a whole floor holding 2/3 zombies at most. Rooms are also huge
in occasions, leaving enemies to run amok aimlessly and be almost a sight rather than an obstacle. The reason behind the enemies
being so few and far inbetween more then likely has to due with the way doors work.

Now doors in the classic RE games were more or less loading screens. However, these were definitley not needed because of power
limitations (the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DS version could skip them). These were in place in order to give the player some sort of location in
the house and to give each zombie a location. Having loading screens for each room made it so zombies did not have to leave rooms
and wander aimlessly once off they're given A.I track. RE7 has smarter A.I, mind you, but it also makes it so enemies generally 
don't enter rooms they are not spawned in. If a door is shut behind them, they will just slam their heads into the door, kinda 
clipping through it and waiting until the door is open. This also leaves the locations much more blurry, and unreconizable. Having
everything be connected makes rooms feel too joined together and cohecent, which sounds good, but makes it so the player cannot
pick and choose what is the best/worst route and try and pick according to their situation. Instead it makes the location feel
like one big room that is just broken up into running around slowly.

Really nitpicky, but healing in RE7 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blows. I get that making it seemless from healing to gameplay looks nice, but control
wise it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blows. I've accidently wasted multiple first-aid kits because for some reason the PC controls are retarded and
CTRL is healing rather then crouching (which is C),

Now, is it not being "Classic" resident evil bad? No. 4-6 are not at all like classic RE but I like those still, because they're 
their own thing. I feel like, if you look at RE7 as the beginning of a trilogy, rather then continuation, it'd stand much better.
As 1-3 are B-tier horror movies, and 4-6 are B-tier action movies, I feel as if 7-9 should just be similar to the SAW series.
First person and intense gore (which, this game has quite a bit of) fit well and making a horror that is more "unsettling and
uncomfortable" rather than the exciting and atmospheric kind of horror 1-3 is more known for.

Also just to add on, RE7 had the worst ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss battles ever. None of Resident Evil's are too good, to be fair, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
these are some the most clunky and most anti-fun ♥♥♥♥ I've dealt with.

Absolutely an amazing revamp (not remake) of the Resident Evil franchise, which was needed in all honestly as I didn't enjoy any RE game that came after RE4.

Best way to describe it would be; Resident Evil meets Silent HIlls P.T. with some creepy horror mixed with it.

I would probably had less of a frustrating playthrough if I didn't play RE Village before this one. You can see where the changes in Village where really really needed. 

For example, the inventory management and crafting are just horrible. You end up carrying so much crap around that you're running to an item box every 5 mins cause who wants to not pick up healing items and ammo when you have no clue what will happen next. 

Not being able to equip non-keybinded weapons straight from the inventory is just tedious as the inventory screen doesn't pause the game (makes sense tbh). But to then have to drag that weapon into the keybind slot, be hit by enemies while it sometimes doesn't register is just plain annoying. Luckily you'll most likely run with the same 4 weapons the whole game anyways.

Another minor complaint is how useless the magnum felt, picked it up early hoping it's own ass on the bosses but you run out of ammo halfway through the game (think in total I found like 10 bullets in total) which made it totally not worth buying compared to extra health/faster reload speed. And do you ever need faster reloads, that shotgun reload animation looks like it's be slow motioned by 50%.

What really does sell this game and made me love it is the story. You go from not having a clue to slowly unraveling the events of RE7. Although the game only has one type on enemy (mold boi), it doesn't matter as the Baker family are the stars of the show (along with Eveline, but you won't see her much till endgame).

The atmosphere is just creepy af, the creeks, wind, moans, you feel like at any point some mold freak will come out of nowhere and slash your face off. You're not really hauling half a gun store around so using ammo  when it's actually really needed (or pop off headshots) will keep you not having to swing your little potato knife around.

All in all, it's a very good game but with some quality of life options missing that were added in RE Village. If you plan on playing both, start with RE7 then Village and you'll have a slightly better experience.

Still loved the game and can deffo recommend you pick it up. There's also quite a lot of added DLC (haven't played as it's not free so might pick it up on sale) so there's deffo some content. Game took me about 8 hours to finish on Normal (I wasn't in a rush), will probably do Madhouse difficulty at some point which will probably take longer.

Minus the last act, it's a full-fledged resident evil game with a little camaraderie. Capcom has made a unique decision to distance itself from the characters and the main storyline of the series; Something that turned out to be a better experience and just what this series needed.

- Great recreation of the best elements of classic resident evil and horror/survival genre
- The wonderful combination of subcutaneous tensions and bloody actions
- Baker family house design
-Members of the Baker family!
- New system of VHS tapes
- The amount of details used in the visual and audio design of the game
- weak points
- The secondary enemies lose their fearsomeness very quickly
- The last act of the game is in everything a significant drop compared to the events of the Bakers' house
- Dissatisfying ending in the mood of Resident Evil 6
- Lack of challenging puzzles
