Resident Evil 7 came out at a time when the Resident Evil series was at the precipice of irrelevancy. Following a string of mediocre, poorly reviewed, and outright commercial failures in the early 2010s, Capcom needed to do something drastic to get the series back on track. I noticed the series decline starting with Resident Evil 6- a bloated, stiff, obnoxious game that most fans prefer to forget. Following 6, more games failed to capture the interest of anyone outside of hardcore fans- titles such as "Operation Raccoon City," and "Umbrella Corps." Even decent titles such as Revelations and Revelations 2 were largely ignored- the brand had been tarnished, and it was hard to take any game in the series seriously anymore. 

Then Resident Evil 7 was released in early 2017. Controversial at first due to its switch to first person, it was a breath of fresh air for the series as it went away from the more quirky, reference-heavy, and frankly corny schtick of the late 00's/early 10's to a more serious tone that harkens back to the original PS1 games (bad voice acting aside.) The most production value was put into the atmosphere of the game- it is stunning. I imagine it is because it was designed with VR in mind- but even playing it standard you can see details that immerse you in the creepy and horrifying world of the Baker family compound. Mold growing on everything, detritus from household neglect, and general grime and scum covering most of the game's surfaces make you believe you are in a dilapidated swamp compound. Many of the boss encounters mirror those from popular and influential films- The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, House of 1000 Corpses/Devil's Rejects, Saw, and the Evil Dead series. The character that creeps me out the most, I would say, is the son Lucas as it is shown through exposition that he showed symptoms of psychopathy as a youth- and was exacerbated by the influx of mold. He's a blend of the Toy Box and BTK killers, and the Unabomber (hoodie included.) The sound, graphics, and story are all of top-notch quality- which partially makes up for several of the game's issues. 

...and here is the part where I am going to be a wet blanket. Upon release, RE7 was highly praised almost universally. I understand why- considering the series' decline, it was a tremendous improvement and a good sign that the series was going back to normal (with RE2 and RE3 remakes coming out over the next few years due to RE7's success.) I played the game about two years after release...and was not impressed. The first half of the game holds a ton of promise and is very much a great romp- slowly exploring the compound and reading all the documents while defending yourself from the Baker family and their minions. But let's get some of the issues out of the way- first of all, the vast majority of the cutscenes are unskippable. For 2017, that is unacceptable. Maybe if you interacted with them (outside of just shaking the camera and trying to not fall asleep as you hear a long-winded tirade,) that would make sense. But it doesn't- especially for speed runs and replays, it completely destroys any replayability. This is the issue with VR-focused games- instead of focusing on making a concise, fun game, they focus on more superficial elements like someone grabbing you by the throat and raving about murdering you. 

Combat in this game ranges from enjoyable- the boring parts on the ship in the latter half of the game are an example of such, to insufferable. A perfect example is the chainsaw fight with Jack in the basement- your item management system runs in real-time, which means that you cannot pause the game and then figure out your inventory. If you are not expecting a major boss fight- you may fill up your inventory and then get caught by an auto-save trap where you have to quickly juggle your items. Since likely you will die a couple times trying to figure out the boss' move set- you have to reset everything which is incredibly frustrating. I had to toss a couple of items in order to make room for the chainsaw that is required to beat Jack and unlock the door to escape- all the while trying to make sure I don't get cut in half. I don't rage often at video games, but I was definitely feeling the anger bubble up as I was helplessly being slaughtered just trying to do a basic maneuver. 

That's a major problem with this game- in order to build suspense, it creates arbitrary and quite frankly, annoying, obstacles that are one-hit deaths. Things that you wouldn't know are an issue unless you've played the game before- but like I said, since the game doesn't feel replayable, likely you'll just suffer and then be done with it. My only other major criticism is that the main character, Ethan, is incredibly bland and has some of the worst dialogue written for a video game. Just a lot of "what's going on?" "huh?" type things- they greatly improved his character for RE8 where he is at least semi-likeable. Also, his fiancee Mia is insufferable and most of the time I just hoped she would die and the game would end with Ethan walking away from all the madness. 

Anyway, do I recommend the game? Barely. I would rate it a 3.25 out of 5- if you are a Resident Evil or horror fan and can get the game on sale, please do. You'll likely be able to put up with the game's quirks- but honestly, it hasn't aged well and RE8 is far, far, far, far superior in so many ways. But I'm a sucker for Resident Evil and even at the game's worst, it's still better than 6.

A seriously unique blend of West and East which came at a time when the franchise had lost its way and had to find new footing.

Rather than play it straight and return to roots, they did the thing where they (again) change the camera perspective and introduce entirely new ways of engaging the environment and engaging the enemies. Old tech and conventions get replaced with unexpected analogues, while retaining trademark Resident Evil ideas that still work in the new style. Atmosphere, pacing, and level design are all top notch.

If you're under the impression it's "not Resident Evil because it's first person" -- [i]please[/i] get that idea out of your head. It's nonsense. Puzzles still feel RE, shooting still feels RE, even driving Ethan around the twisting hallways of the Baker residence feels RE. And if it sheds any light, be aware the first game was never meant to be third person or fixed camera, as both conventions were a direct result of technical limitations. 5 years later, it's more obvious than ever RE7 is a worthwhile entry in the series. Whether you were more into the fixed camera or over-shoulder games, this one is assuredly worth your attention.

I was uninterested in this game for a very, very long time. Horror games were never my genre, and out of all of them, the slow moving, low field of view horror where anything or anyone could be standing right next to me without me knowing is propably the type of horror I never wanted to experience or spend money on.

However, I got into Resident Evil with the RE2 Remake, which (with the exception of being terrified of the Tyrant) was a huge hit for me, and RE3 followed closely after. I thought, what the hell, RE7 is like 6 euros now, I'll give it a shot: sat down with my wife because I was not going to play this alone lol, and we had a BLAST playing through it. The game is scary and creepy as hell especially early on, when you don't really know what to expect in the dark, and yes there are some thankfully very short episodes where you have to hide from an invincible enemy and get from A to B, but once you are a few hours in and get a little sense of control about what you are up against (there are really 2 types of enemies, and rarely a 3rd miniboss, and all of them are few are far in between) you are good to go. The game manages to stay high pressure all the time though because this time you are not up against zombies, these guys can crawl out of literally NOTHING so enemy spawns make the dark always tense, because you just don't know when and where they'll be, and that's good for a horror game. The semi-open world of RE2 is present, lots of puzzles and riddles to solve, and what surprised me the most is that unlike RE2 and RE3, the game has a shockingly good story that will make you rethink your initial impressions a lot, and manages to keep a lot mystery to think about throughout the whole time, and even answers all of them AND connects to the main Resident Evil storyline in a cool way, and all of this information is given to you at a very good pacing. 

What I did not like though were some, if not most of the bossfights. Most of your bosses have an insane amount of regeneration (in the story, not mechanically) so it's always unclear if you should be running, finding an escape and shooting them with everything you have is a colossal pointless waste of ammo, or you should be looking for a specific item somewhere in the boss arena because that is the only thing that will hurt it, or if this item is only revealed later on in the fight when something opens or breaks, and it's overall a very frustrating experience when boss fights are designed in a way that you DON'T KNOW if you should be fighting or looking for a way out, and there are both type of situations quite a lot in this game, especially early on, when sometimes you should be running, sometimes shooting DESPITE knowing there is no way you should be killing that person at all or this early on. Compared to other bosses in the series (and some of them are present in this game too!) that clearly communicate weak points such as glowing eyes you should be shooting at, this was very frustrating and caused me to die and reload a lot.

Difficulty-wise I felt right at home with the likes of the first three classic RE games. Normal feels fine for a first playthrough but Madhouse is where it's at. Madhouse doesn't just make enemies stronger and faster but changes their placement. It also changes some item placements and some boss encounters, which was a huge surprise to me the first time through. Madhouse is much harder and therefore is also vastly rewarding. Boss fights are mostly intense and thrilling.

There are upgrades you can obtained to increase your reload speed and your max health, ala RE4 to a degree, and you're gonna need them in Madhouse. Collectible coins are scattered and well hidden, which can be used to unlock different powerups and weapons. It really works well and will make you check every nook and cranny trying to find all 33 of them.

While the gameplay is obviously the main attraction here, the plot leaves a lot to be desired. I won't spoil anything but the second half of the game takes a drastic nosedive. I still enjoy it, but the areas after the Baker property aren't interesting or nearly as fun to navigate. It seems like Capcom lost steam or ran out of time near the end which is unfortunate considering how perfect the first half is. It is straight up, classic survival horror with great inventory management, then kinda turns into exposition for a long time.

All in all, if you're doubtful of RE7, give it a shot. It's easily in my top 5 RE games.

[i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] is a survival horror game. Fight for your life in the derelict mansion of the demented Baker family, utilizing combat skills, stealth, and your smarts to solve puzzles. This title is a phenomenal return to form for the mainline [i]Resident Evil[/i] titles, and is a must-play for survival horror fans. With a modern classic setting through the midgame and some unforgettable sequences, come immerse yourself in the horror as soon as possible.

You play as Ethan Winters, a man searching for his wife Mia who was last seen three years prior. After receiving a message saying that Mia's in Dulvey, Louisiana, Ethan travels to the rural town in search of her. He winds up at the expansive backwoods property of the Baker family - and almost immediately all hell breaks loose. Struggle for your survival in this house of horrors as you search for an exit, fight different kinds of twisted monsters, and try to discover a solution to the mysterious force that started all the terror - before it escapes and threatens the world.

The [i]Resident Evil[/i] series was in a lull at the time of [i]7[/i]'s release. Verging ever closer to action gameplay while losing its horror roots, the widely-panned [i]Resident Evil 6[/i] left fans pining for more. Cue [i]Resident Evil 7[/i], which represents a return to series form. The core of this game is its haunted house experience - the Baker Manor is an instantly iconic location dripping with dread, rot, and tons of scares. Players will peer around every corner, never being quite sure where the next enemy will emerge from. The game keeps players on their toes for the entirety of the roughly six hour campaign.

While the horror and atmosphere take precedence, there is no lack of combat in [i]RE7[/i]. Ethan is outfitted with melee weapons and guns increasing in lethality throughout the run. Granted, the selection is smaller than the more action-oriented [i]Resident Evil[/i] games' inventories, but it feels appropriate to the more scaled-down scope of this game. Ammo scarcity is also not as harsh as in other titles; players can opt to play anywhere between full combat and full enemy avoidance, with there being just about enough ammo to support killing every enemy (assuming the player has good aim). Learning enemy attack patterns and how/when to block will be key skills for all players, though, especially at higher difficulties.

Some puzzle elements also return in this entry, though they are very scaled down. Fortunately, they help to keep the realism of the setting: unlike in other entries where, say, a police station requiring antiques to open basic hallways feels very videogamey, most [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] puzzles boiling down to finding keys for doors feels natural and unobtrusive. These puzzles are also very simple to remember solutions to, which helps facilitate repeat playthroughs. And there is some replay value here to boot, in the form of unlockable weapons and items that change the types of viable strategies in future runs, not to mention the crushingly difficult Madhouse mode. [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is certainly the kind of game a horror fan might want to come back to every so often, like a cozy book or a seasonal film.

While a great game, it does have a weak point. [i]RE7[/i] took inspiration from [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]'s area structure, namely in how the later areas grow less atmospheric and more action-driven. This game's later areas are some of the least inspired in the series, unfortunately. It's something of a blessing that the areas are so short, though it does raise the question that if the game's main selling point is its thoughtful, effective haunted house - why not set everything in there?

Overall, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a much-needed reboot for the original survival horror franchise. The ideas introduced in this excel at adding character and tension to the Baker family and the mansion they inhabit. Moreover, the reduced role of combat and puzzles let the scares shine while still keeping gameplay engaging. Though not of even quality throughout, there is enough solid game here to warrant multiple runs. [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] gets an A.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[a] is a 2017 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. The player controls Ethan Winters as he searches for his long-missing wife in a derelict plantation occupied by an infected family, solving puzzles and fighting enemies. Resident Evil 7 diverges from the more action-oriented Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6, returning to the franchise's survival horror roots, emphasizing exploration. It is the first main Resident Evil game to use a first-person view.

Resident Evil 7 is the first full-length game to use Capcom's in-house RE Engine. The development was led by Koshi Nakanishi, director of the 2012 Nintendo 3DS game Resident Evil: Revelations. A year prior to its announcement at E3 2016, it was presented as a virtual reality demo called Kitchen. The team took inspiration from the 1981 film The Evil Dead, scaled back the game to one location, and used a first-person perspective to immerse players. Two downloadable content scenarios were released, Not a Hero and End of Zoe.

You play as Ethan Winters, an American systems engineer tasked with finding his wife who is missing for the last three years. You then find yourself at at a creepy farmhouse where she is located. The atmosphere in this game sends tingles down your spine with it's impressive visuals and audio design that make for a very immersive atmosphere. The RE engine is absolutely amazing at rendering the environment & character models. You'll find yourself taking your time exploring the house because of the many interesting rooms, items and enemies to discover. The Baker family had their strengths as well with each of them their own unique and special character traits providing you with a good old scare. Boss fights were fun and challenging and the soundtrack was pleasant to listen to, especially the Go Tell Aunt Rhody tune. Expect this game to give you the spooks. There is also many cheat codes in the game that you can unlock after completing the game which can increase the overall replayablitly My recommendation is to also try the Madhouse mode for veterans of the RE series. It is a totally different experience and is a lot more terrifying. I can't recommend this enough to any fan of the horror genre or fans of the Resident Evil games respectively

I'm not really sure how to estimate the games' value for time. I did one pass through on the main game and most of the DLC. I'd say the main game is a fair price for what you get. Definitely a great addition to the franchise and worth playing.

Resident Evil 7 was my first experience with the RE franchise. I'd seen footage of Resident Evil 4 before, but I hadn't played any entries into the series. Coming out of it, I felt spoiled. RE7 was a fantastic intro to the series that emphasized survival horror, inventory management, and tense action sequences. It didn't excessively rely on the lore of previous games - it stood on its own merits while subtly advancing the franchise's plot along. I thoroughly enjoyed it as an FPS fan and a person who occasionally likes horror games.

Resident Evil 7 centers on Ethan Winters, an ordinary IT specialist whose wife went missing three years before the game's opening. After finding footage of her being alive and asking him to go to Louisiana, he heads south and makes contact with her in a dilapidated guest house. His rescue attempt goes poorly, and he ends up trapped in the plantation with the Bakers, a mad family of cannibals with unnatural abilities. Cut off from the outside world, Ethan is forced to fight tooth and nail to stay alive while the Bakers and their "Molded" monsters hunt him down.

You are not some well-trained cop or ex-soldier in RE7, and it shows in the gameplay. Ethan fumbles new shells into shotguns and struggles to quickly reload pistols. He is a slow shot and can only carry so much on him at once. It's a logical choice for his character that makes the fights that much more tense. It is extremely important to manage your ammo/herbs and scrounge up what you can, especially because some enemies can only be temporarily wounded instead of killed. Some of the most intense action occurs early on, when Ethan is defenseless and forced to hide from Jack Baker, the family's patriarch. Close calls and intense chases will make your initial encounters with him extremely memorable. 

The game is set in a first-person perspective, putting you face-to-face with the Bakers and the horrors lurking in their plantation. RE7 is surprisingly scarce on jumpscares (they still happen, though). Most of its frightening sequences come from the tension of escaping some unstoppable threat or fighting something with inhuman endurance. There is plenty of blood and gore to go around, both for your enemies and for your own potential death sequences. Some bits are more nauseating than scary, but they add to the unnerving atmosphere around the Baker House. You'll be relieved when you finally come across the game's limited Safe Rooms.

Your limited inventory space can be used to carry around weapons, ammo, health items, and other craftable materials. You often have to make choices about what to use your items on. Should you combine items together to make a strong healing solution, or would it be safer to craft some high-power pistol ammunition? Excessive items can be stored in a locker that carries over between Safe Rooms, so you can at least set aside some materials for later. Managing your inventory is a major element of RE7's dynamic, and it feels like the game gives you just enough storage to avoid being excessive or too limiting.

Most of the game's pacing is good. The intro and efforts to escape the main plantation house were the highlights for me. The subsequent sections in the plantation yard, greenhouse, and barn are still good despite being a step down. There is a late-game section that isn't quite as polished or as fitting as the other parts. Going into details about it would spoil major parts of the story, so I will leave it vague. I still enjoyed this penultimate part of the game, but it was a major tonal shift that might not be for everyone.

Resident Evil 7 should take you a decent amount of time to complete, especially if you like to scrounge for secrets and items. You can replay the game to complete challenges and unlock bonus weapons. It also comes with a free DLC called "Not A Hero" that ties up some loose ends of the story and puts you in the boots of an actual soldier. The difference is almost immediate, with heavier weapons and deadlier counterattacks at your disposal. It can be cathartic to stomp the Molded in every sense of the word after you spent so much time scraping by as Ethan.

Resident Evil 7 won me over with its chilling setting, great horror setpieces, tense action, and memorable characters. I would highly recommend buying it if you are a fan of horror games or story-driven FPS games. It's worth the price at $19.99, especially if you're a completionist who likes replaying games. The paid DLCs for it are not worth the money,  barring "End of Zoe." Grab that one whenever it goes on sale, as it is actually good and concludes the few remaining plot points in a satisfying way.

The perfect amount of scary and horror mixed together. For some, you might find that is not true, but for me, that was just the case. As someone who typically tried to avoid horror games (my experience with them being limited but not spectacular), I decided to give this one a shot after all of the hype surrounding Resident Evil Village. I had a blast with this game. The puzzles felt difficult, but not unfair or beyond my grasp of being able to solve, the horror was present, but didn't make me too scared to play the game (a problem other horror games have had for me in the past), and the gameplay and exploration felt great. Finding things in hidden areas or using the environment to help eliminate threats, such as getting an enemy to trigger a tripwire meant for you, was refreshing and fun. I was worried coming into this game that it would be too challenging, as I had tried the Resident Evil Remaster, and found difficulty with it, but it seems that the developers have gotten in their groove and have ironed out a lot of the creases. This game makes me want to play Resident Evil Village, and other future games under this franchise. Who knows, maybe I'll even give RE1 a shot again. I'd say that justifies a good game. It stayed long enough to tell a story, but didn't stay too long to make me sit and chew it forever. I would recommend this to anyone who isn't afraid of spiders.

let's just go chronologically a bit. First up is the guest house portion of the game. Well done atmosphere and introduction. You get a full-on creepy vibe from the property and the house that follows throughout this portion as you are being introduced to gameplay aspects. This portion of the game is great!

Main house: Great game of cat and mouse in portions, with a nice difficulty depending on how you are playing. Puzzles are fun but not to difficult and this portion of the game molds (ha) well from the guest house. Scare factor is still there and is enjoyable

next up is the old house. This portion loss some steam for me. At this point I was learned up on the gameplay mechanics and was just enjoyed by this stage's boss more than anything. The creep factor was lost a bit during this time until the end. overall, pretty good

Testing area: again the scare or creep factor, whatever I'm calling it, was lost more in this portion. I was well armed and ready for most of the challenges thrown in my way. still fun but loosing itself along the way.

Boat House: fun boss fight but like much of this game I felt that as the boss fights went on the easier, they got.  Great point in the game though to add a choice with potentially large consequences. 

Wrecked ship: Alright this is where most people and I seem to disagree. The game throws you through a loop and how I played it then had to play an entire level playing cat and mouse again looking for supplies and trying to survive. This made the game feel challenging again which increased the scare factor and fun factor for me. Great part.

Salt Mine. No real scare factor, more action game than anything. By this point you should be so armed that anything the game throws at you is easy to deal with. least enjoyable part

ending was fine, boss was too easy for the buildup.

And sure, it may be a visceral and frequently shooty horror game, but the gory action takes a backseat to decently challenging puzzles, built up with a wide toolbox in ever-changing circumstances that masterfully ramp pressure up and down to keep things permanently interesting. I wasn't enamoured enough to bother playing any of the DLC - exhausted by the same enemy type being used in almost every encounter, of which there are many - but the nine-ish hour campaign was satisfying and worth a go for horror fans of all stripes thanks to this being more of a series reboot despite its numbered title, good enough to overcome the heavily clichéd plot that will surprise nobody who's played a previous entry in the series, although I do wish the game was maybe two thirds its length, as there's really not enough depth here to justify the running time. The ingenious puzzles and navigational challenges are the stars of the show, and with the villainously campy cast often woven in to introduce new challenges, they never fail to be entertaining. Resident Evil 7 knows when to be stupid and when to be clever, and even though the combat's not interesting enough and the game far outstays its welcome, it earns my respect and a solid recommendation.

Despite the disappointing lack of puzzles, RE7 is a great innovation on the traditional RE games, bringing it back to its roots with much more horror than the previous installments. This game resurrected the franchise (no pun intended) by incorporating a new custom-made game engine, "RE Engine," and throwing the player into the first person POV (for better or worse). 

Almost all of the characters in the game are new to the universe, leaving little connection to everything that has happened prior. However, the story does tie into the rest of the game franchise. Starting with a new cast allows for more freedom with the plot and provides more mystery and uniqueness for the player.

The lack of 3rd person POV minimizes how much the player cares for and sympathizes with the main character and leaves a lack of character depth and character arc; however, playing in the first person is welcoming to a broader player base while also feeling more personal and horrific. Incorporating a 1st person POV provides a more immersive experience at the cost of a more personal main character.

Pros:
More horror oriented gameplay
Beautiful graphics and environment
Familiar FPS control scheme
Much more similar to RE1 than the previous three installments
Each section incorporates a different variety of horror
Exceptional voice acting and character movement due to motion capture technology
Cons:
Lack of variety when it comes to enemies
Restricted range of FOV (≤ 90°, I believe)
Last quarter of the game kind of drags on
Lacks 3rd person POV
Slightly clunky movement

Because of the newly developed "RE Engine" and more efficient game development techniques, Capcom was able to produce the RE2 remake, RE3 remake, and RE Village (a direct sequel to RE7 and spiritual sequel to RE4) all within three years of RE7s release.

[h1]Resident Evil 7 Biohazard[/h1]
Behold, [b]Capcom[/b] surprised at E3 2016, revealing [b]Resident Evil 7[/b] and already kicking in the door with an incredible demo. Gradually, it became clear that the saga indeed seemed to return to its origins in terror, even betting on virtual reality to bring immersion and fear. But, at the same time, the game turned around and what started to be talked about is that he got too far away because of the first-person camera and the many similarities with other games of the genre.

[h1]It's Resident Evil, yes. And a lot.[/h1]
“Oh, but this looks like Outlast!”
“Wow, they copied P.T. (Silent Hills) in the face!”
"Sounds good, too bad this isn't Resident Evil!"
These were just some of the comments from part of the community during the game's announcements. So, having played the full title, I need to make one thing clear: not only is it still Resident Evil, it's also a great Resident Evil.

[b]Yes, the first-person perspective is reminiscent of Outlast, Amnesia and other similar titles.[/b]
But who said this is bad? Of course, there is a strangeness, since the franchise has never experienced this feature in the main series, but overall the title is of great quality and maintains a series of trademarks of the series - including rescuing others after a long time. Experiments have happened before — some lasted, some were abandoned — and Capcom deserves praise for its courage.

[h1]This family is very close...[/h1]
The game's plot is pretty basic: you're a boy named Ethan Winters and you receive a message from your missing companion, Mia, asking you to pick her up at a farmhouse in upstate Louisiana. Arriving there, you begin to encounter oddities and dangers that make you question everything you thought you knew — and your own sanity. Did you feel the tone of Silent Hill 2 there?

[h1]“Fear returns home”[/h1]
The sentence above is on the back of the game's box and fits perfectly into the proposal of Resident Evil 7. The atmosphere of terror is present in several aspects: the sound, the graphics, the camera game and the script contribute to creating a game that will make you tense for several moments, jump on the couch and get your heart racing after meeting an enemy in a narrow hallway.

[h1]The face of horror[/h1]
Along with sound, visuals are equally important in designing a horror game. In the case of Resident Evil 7, you can't say that Capcom got it right, but the company is far from having done a bad job.

The game presents very varied scenarios, even having a small place where the story takes place. The Baker mansion is amazing, full of macabre details, and the makeup of the other properties is just as interesting.

[h1]First person: love it or hate it[/h1]
Undoubtedly, Resident Evil 7's biggest disagreement will be the first-person perspective, which is constant and even makes the title almost lack cutscenes, since almost the entire game takes place in real time and from the perspective of a character. The approval of the sudden change will not be unanimous, it is no use insisting: it is a matter of taste to prefer one style to the other and you will feel the strangeness of, after 20 years, playing a main chapter of the franchise with this camera.

[h1]Is it worth it?[/h1]
No doubt! Resident Evil 7 is an extremely risky game in many ways and, in the end, Capcom got it right by stepping out of their comfort zone once again. It is effective as a new chapter in the franchise, manages to insert itself in the horror genre and brings more than interesting perspectives for the future of the series.

[h1]Positive Points:[/h1]
- It's very Resident Evil, it's very horror
- The atmosphere of tension was very well built
- The Baker family is amazing and steals the show
- Brings new and classic elements in the right measure
- High quality sound effects and graphics that don't compromise

[h1]Negative Points:[/h1]
- The main character could be better developed
- Gameplay is still limited
- Questionable script decisions in the second half

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard – A Revolutionary Horror Experience

Released in January 2017, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard marked a bold departure from the series' roots. As the first game in the franchise to feature a first-person perspective, it was a return to the series' survival-horror origins, while introducing new gameplay mechanics that elevated the experience. The game was a critical success, praised for its return to suspense, terrifying atmosphere, and a fresh perspective that revitalized the franchise.

Story and Setting
The game introduces players to Ethan Winters, a regular man searching for his wife, Mia, who has gone missing for three years. His journey leads him to the dilapidated Baker family estate in rural Louisiana, where he uncovers the horrific secrets of the mansion and the twisted family members living within it. The plot feels like a blend of classic horror films and the deep, strange narrative Resident Evil fans are accustomed to. The story excels in creating an unsettling atmosphere, and the pacing is perfect, keeping you on edge with a mix of narrative-driven scares and survival moments.

Atmosphere and Visuals
The atmosphere is one of the standout features of Resident Evil 7. The game’s visuals are a dramatic leap forward compared to previous titles in the franchise, offering detailed, photorealistic environments. The lighting, sound design, and level of environmental detail contribute to a palpable sense of dread. Whether exploring the eerie Baker house or encountering terrifying enemies, the game constantly pushes the player into a state of nervous tension. The first-person perspective amplifies the fear factor, with you feeling more immersed in the creepy surroundings, as if you’re truly in Ethan’s shoes.

Gameplay and Mechanics
Resident Evil 7 returns to the slow-paced, survival-focused mechanics of older Resident Evil games. The player is required to conserve ammo, manage inventory, and solve puzzles in order to progress. The game also introduces an effective blend of exploration and combat. One of the most notable gameplay elements is the use of limited resources to make every encounter feel more impactful. The sense of vulnerability is heightened by the limited ammo and health supplies, which forces players to make tense decisions about when to fight and when to run.

The puzzles, though straightforward, are well-integrated into the story and environment. The first-person perspective also allows for new interactions, such as picking up objects and inspecting them in a more immersive way, giving the game a tactile feel that enhances the realism.

Horror and Terror
The horror in Resident Evil 7 is relentless. It combines traditional survival-horror with new scares, such as the gruesome enemies you encounter and the way the house itself seems to warp around you. While the game delivers the expected jump scares, it also builds psychological tension through its disturbing ambiance and bizarre scenarios, making it truly frightening. The Baker family members, with their twisted personalities and erratic behavior, add another layer of horror, making each encounter feel dangerous and unpredictable.

The game excels at building tension with disturbing visuals and grotesque creatures, but it never veers too far into gore. It’s a careful balance of horror, psychology, and grotesque imagery. The presence of the family, especially the relentless Jack Baker, creates a sense of being hunted that is amplified by the restricted movement and limited resources.

VR Mode
One of the most immersive features of Resident Evil 7 is its compatibility with PlayStation VR. The VR mode elevates the horror experience even further, creating a level of immersion that has rarely been seen in the survival-horror genre. For those who can stomach it, the VR mode adds an entirely new layer of terror, as you are trapped in the world of the game with nowhere to look but into the darkness ahead.

Sound and Music
The sound design in Resident Evil 7 is a key element in building the atmosphere. The game makes excellent use of silence and ambient sounds to keep players on edge, with creaks, whispers, and distant noises that contribute to a constantly uneasy environment. The music is subtle, but the occasional score will intensify moments of dread, enhancing the tension of critical moments.

Final Thoughts
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard stands as one of the best entries in the franchise, effectively mixing old-school survival horror with modern innovations. The terrifying atmosphere, immersive gameplay, and gripping narrative make it a must-play for fans of horror games. By successfully reinventing the franchise while retaining its core elements, it sets a high bar for survival-horror games and proves that the series can evolve without losing its roots. Whether playing in traditional third-person mode or in the terrifying world of VR, Resident Evil 7 delivers a heart-pounding, unforgettable experience.

Gun to my head? 7/10. Biohazard was a strong step forward for the resident evil franchise. Moving away from campy action aspects of the series and embracing immersive first person horror and puzzle elements was the right choice. After all, things can only really be scary if you can somewhat suspend your disbelief. RE7 made a good effort to scare me and succeeded at points. Graphics are good and I think RE7 mostly succeeds in balancing horror and  game elements. The puzzles are interesting and, well, made me feel clever. 

I have three criticisms. The first being that it sometimes feels like you aren't given agency for things that could raise tension. An example of this is that you have a head lamp that just turns on and off by itself depending on where you are. I think having the ability to control when it's on and having a consequence like being more discoverable by monsters when it's on would have raised tension more. Another example of this is in some of the boss fights. There is usually a specific thing you have to do and if you don't trigger that sequence you simply fail. I think giving more plausible solutions and making the player choose which one they think would work best would have made those sequences more tense. 

My second criticism is that the game overstays its welcome by the ship level in my opinion. Fear of the unknown is an important aspect of horrors but RE7 goes to great lengths in the closing hours to explain everything and tie it to the rest of the franchise in a neat bow including absolution for some characters actions. This is totally unnecessary and I think it shoots the sense of mystery in the foot.

Last on the list are just some of the "gamey" aspects that could have been done better in aiding immersion. Antique coins are a good example. You collect these throughout the game to then trade in on coin slot locks that open bird cages with items in them. I can think of at least 3 other ways you could do the same thing without having the arbitrary inclusion of birdcage slots. Yes, this is a picky one, it just stands out to me because the rest of the game works so hard to be immersive. 

It seems that horror games currently trend toward multiplayer or "experiences" rather than being horror single player games. The reason is obvious, It's pretty difficult to get it right. Though I do believe RE7 gets a bit of grace for being an RE game, it doesn't take away from the fact that they nailed it and I hope they recapture it and iterate on it because it's good stuff. Resident Evil 7 launched back in 2017 and despite it's overwhelmingly positive reviews across the globe I just recently came around and finally played it in 2022. 

Let's get the obvious out of the way first. Yes, it's a good game. Yes, it's Resident Evil to the core. Yes, it's in 1st person perspective but even as a RE purist I have to admit that it was a great design choice. Yes, everybody even slightly interested in survival horror genre should play it. And no, you don't have to be familiar with Resident Evil's lore to enjoy this title.

Now that being said, let's talk about some things I wasn't so hyped about.
I said it's Resident Evil to the core which also means that there are plot holes, silly writing, two boss battles are beyond frustrating and there is downright stupid design choices especially near the end. Like Capcom rushed RE7 out or something. 2/3 in the game and it becomes a power fantasy. You get so many resources, bullets, guns and healing items leading up to the point where all suspension is gone because you can just run'n'gun everything in sight with ease. I have yet to try RE7 on the hardest difficulty, but what I've heard and read so far is that the end game plays pretty muchly the same. What a shame because first 2/3 of RE7 is like a beautiful mixture of everything that made the original Resident Evil trilogy so great. However these are just minor annoyances otherwise in a solid survival horror package, so take my words with a grain of salt.

RE7 may turn little stale towards the end, but overall it's fantastic "reboot" for the franchise after RE5 and 6. Resident Evil 7 is absolutely pure "Resident Evil experience" mostly in it's good sense and it delivers some great survival horror regardless of player being already familiar with the franchise or not.

Just beat RE7 for the first time so now I want to get out this casual review. RE7 is an extremely well made first-person survival horror game. I believe at the time in the early to mid 2010s people were wondering if Resident Evil as a franchise was done seeing how 5 & 6 really strayed far from their horror roots. However RE7 for me felt like a return to form with a modern re-imagining of the original formula of puzzles and claustrophobic exploration. RE7 also took a lot of western horror inspiration with the grimey 80s Slasher motifs reminiscent of the original "Texas Chainsaw Massacre". You could also throw in some elements of classic "Evil Dead" & the "F.E.A.R." franchise as well. It in many ways feels like a scary art house film. 


The mood and atmosphere is oppressive, and you can't help but feel chills rounding corners hoping something won't jump at you. If you're wondering about the resource balance, the game gives you just enough if not a little more (If you're careful with your shooting and not taking a lot of damage) to progress without taking away the tension and suspense. Towards the end I found myself with more than enough to finish the game, but personally I'm pretty stingy with using resources unless I feel I have to use them. Can't speak on how it is for 'Madhouse' mode though which is the hardest difficulty (You unlock this after beating the game once on normal).


Overall while in many respects RE7 is its own thing, I think it took the best parts of classic Resident Evil and brought it forward with this new style the team is now going for. It's a tight adventure with little fluff clocking around 7-ish hours give or take depending on how much you take your time and explore the various "zones". Seeing as this came out in 2017 the visuals look just slightly dated, but are very nice still aesthetically for the type of immersion the team was going for at the time. 


I believe Capcom is going to release an update soon with some slight visual updates, and ray-tracing (free for everyone who already owns the game), which should add more to the atmosphere of the game. Also if I'm remembering this correctly RE7 is the first game using Capcom's now relatively new RE Engine, RE an abbreviation for "Reach for the Moon". And it's an amazing game engine that Capcom should continue to push to it's limits. (Would later be used for Devil May Cry 5, the remakes of RE2 & 3 and Monster Hunter Rise to name a few)


I'm glad I finally got around to playing this classic, and it was definitely worth it. Not sure why it took me so long to experience this, but it's better late than never. I got ending 2 so I'll probably at the very least get the canon ending then maybe dive into the DLC at some point. But there's a lot of replayability here for speedrunners, and achievement hunters. If you enjoy horror games or have previously given up on Resident Evil, you really owe it to yourself to play this. It's fairly short (In a good way, no bloat), and easily beatable in a sitting or two so there's no excuse especially if you can get this on sale. Resident Evil 7 is truly something to behold. Coming off the heels of the very mixed Resident Evil 6, RE7 decides to take it back to it's horror/puzzle roots with a newly added 1st person mode. With the amount of dedication towards the project and the scope of it from the Beginning Hour and Kitchen demos to the main areas of the game, there is real passion coming out of CAPCOM here and started the streak of good Resident Evil games to come such as RE 2 & 3 remake along with 2021's Resident Evil Village. 

Gameplay wise, the inventory management and design of the HUD for our main character Ethan Winters is compact and minimal (not as tight as RE2 remake's inventory space but closer in scope), creating quite a challenge as you try to escape the Baker house. Each of the guns through the game serve good purposes and I appreciate how each can be tied to a specific area of the game. Using antique coins as collectibles that can help the player get useful boosters like steroids and a magnum is pretty genius as well.

For the story, a majority of it is written pretty well. Each area of the house is designated to one of the Bakers and each centering around a new type of horror. While it is clear that Jack's area gets the most attention (a trend similar within Resident Evil Village), I appreciate that some characters get additional screentime through one free and one cheap expansion. Some of the story itself is pretty underexplained without the context of Village after this game but I mean, how else are you gonna make a trilogy?

My only complaints with this game come with a slump gameplay wise near the end of the game as we move into it's final act. The game strips you of everything you had just to have you get a little exposition and wrap the game up. It doesn't really go out with a BANG that I thought it could have. Also, the enemy variation within this game is quite nonexistent. Each type of the "Molded" as they are called differ only slightly and are enemies that can be seen within other games (like COD Zombies; see crawlers). 

All in all, Resident Evil 7 is an excellent addition to the franchise and a soft reboot of course which is good for people who lack Resident Evil knowledge (myself included). If you want a scary game that is able to keep you engaged with puzzles and action, this is your game. 

P.S: I would recommend buying the package with all DLC for this game because the banned footage is REALLY GOOD along with the two expansions, Not A Hero and End of Zoe.

It's surely the most modern feeling and looking resident evil so far in the series, while also having SOME classic elements.
That doesn't mean it's a perfect "return to form", nor does it mean that it has the perfect "modern immersion" that it was hyped up to have.

As we have come to expect, here we have nice connecting areas with clever as always yet, more realistic than ever architecture, but sadly, that is really only the first half of the game.
The first half  feels very organic, but that declines over your hours of gameplay, which each new section of the game feeling less atmospheric and more rushed. 

Honestly not much new to happens in this game, not that that is bad. 
We still have crafting, inventory management, only a few guns but each one is unique, the ability to run out of items, puzzle solving, navigating small corridors unaware of what's next.

It seems this game focused on just polishing the ol' coin, which they kinda did a good job of, but it still suffers from inconsistency with its pacing and design.

I don't even entirely mind that we really only get the mold as our only enemy type, and I dont mind that we go from seeing them, to running from them, to killing one at a time, to facing a while hoard. You can argue that it devalues them, but I think we get alot of progression out of them and have lots of variety with the baker family themselves.

No I am talking about pacing in level design. The puzzles and the layout of areas, the story telling. The game play is always engaging and fun, but it can lose you sometimes too. There was a few times, in the last half where I had to push myself to start the game up, because I stopped caring. The story drops off and exploration gets MUCH more linear.

I did enjoy the idea of some of the twists in the game, but the execution is flawed.
Even after the many twists, I still don't care about Mia, she is too inconsistent.
eh the story is the least interesting part, has plenty of holes, and is honestly not worth talking about. Basically the game would've been better without the ship or the mine part. Quality over quantity.

Don't get tricked into thinking it's super immersive or that your choices matter, just accept the game as what it is and try to have fun, I think you can.

If you have never played a re game, play re2 instead if you want a good horror survival game or play re4 if you want a good horror action game.

I've beaten all the main line RE games (except for 3 & 8); and I have to say 7 certainly reminds me of the series' roots. I'm not very uptight about what I expect from the RE series, I even enjoyed 6 to some extent. So it's given that I really liked 7. I recommend it to fans of the series. However, it does have a more serious tone—it might be difficult for some players to see all the violence or hear all the cursing and shouting. The constant use of gore and profanity can be a bit exhausting.

My favorite part about the game was the Baker family and the big house you get to explore. I wasn't the biggest fan of all the in-game cut-scenes, but I do remark how unique it is that they don't always occur the same way or in the same sequence. For example, some player probably don't know that you can get your leg chopped off by Jack. Or that you don't have to get in the car during one of the Jack fights. So, even if some of these moments are intrusive, it does make the events feel organic somehow. Some scenes are conditional too.

I've seen some people complain that you can't save anywhere you like; to that I say: it's Resident Evil, I don't recall too many of the games (if any) ever allowing for quick saves, etc.

Game-play wise it's bit of a slog, you don't move very fast: obviously they wanted the mechanics to contribute to player vulnerability (and it works) but you might not like it. Funny enough the bosses are kind of easy once you know how to fight them, so speed doesn't seem to matter. The game eventually starts throwing a lot of monsters at you in the latter half of the game. Some people don't like how "samey" the monsters look. I disagree—each monster fits the them of the game, and since the game is pretty short, they don't over stay their welcome. People also dislike how short the game is; personally I think it's the perfect length. Maybe some folks feel that the price tag should equate to a longer experience. But honestly, looking at how beautiful the game is, it probably cost a boat-load to pay designers to build. You can kind of tell Capcom was trying to get the most for their millage by reusing areas, such as in the "tapes" and by swapping  between certain characters. It seems like every location can be visited at least twice.

I'm not a mega-RE fan, but this was a very memorable experience. Some bad things in between, but overall an enjoyable journey and likable characters.

Ah, traversing the treacherous terrain of Resident Evil 7 requires a delicate waltz with those molded adversaries. Swift attacks are not their forte; it's a choreographed ballet of survival horror, my friend.

Now, when delving into the gameplay, it's no leisurely stroll through the park, oh no. Resources are scant, foes hot on your heels, emanating those classic RE vibes. Choose between evasive maneuvers and a Rambo-esque display of pinpoint shooting, armed with nothing but a dependable knife—a true savior in a world bereft of abundance.

The design, exquisite as ever, embraces the art of classic RE backtracking. As for aesthetics, a parade of terrifying foes and a dash of uncanny valley with the fairer gender—it's all part of the spectacle.

And the scare factor? A rollercoaster of emotions—atmosphere, dread, B-movie gore, and just a sprinkle of absurdity. They play mind games for sheer amusement. When darkness descends, it plunges into profound obscurity. The narrative weaves it all together seamlessly, arguably the pinnacle of the RE saga.

In terms of performance, it's a marvel of optimization. But here's the twist—the playtime. Surpassing thirteen hours on Madhouse difficulty, deaths aplenty. Steam may proclaim 13, but in reality, it's more like 9.22. Exploration, secrets, decisions—a mixed bag. Hasten, and it's a brief sojourn. Linger, and it's an extended odyssey. Madhouse? A dance with danger, reminiscent of the good old days.

Now, those autosaves? Scarce, oddly positioned, yet cunningly deceptive. The challenge remains unscathed, a ride worthy of undertaking. So, in the grand winter sale of life, seize these games, embrace the terror, and relish every passing minute. It's a heist, my friend, a heist.

RE7 plays much differently, with a much larger approach to horror and atmosphere rather than combat, although combat is still an element of the game. the story starts very simple, about a man who's searching for his missing girlfriend at an address she's presumed to be at. like most horror games, it's better to walk in blind about the threats/atmosphere of the game in order to be fully immersed. the graphics are great, sound design is wonderful, puzzles aren't too cryptic like many of the past RE games. the gameplay certainly doesn't hold your hand, but is also not quite as unforgiving as prior entries. similar to other horror games, it seems to jump the shark a bit by the halfway mark, plot wise. not super into [spoiler] paranormal sci-fi-esque [/spoiler] stuff but resident evil has always been known for having far-out plots. i suppose i just wish there were more horror games out there with simple stories. seems like a lot of them go for this [spoiler] paranormal, sci- fi-esque [/spoiler] feel by the end that just feels like it simply didn't need to be there. not enough horror games that are grounded in reality. it's still a good game, plays well, albeit controls sluggishly at times. for people calling it an "outlast clone", i disagree entirely. this game has better gameplay, but outlast controls better. this game for me was MUCH scarier than outlast for the first playthrough as well.

Presentation: 4.5/5 : In a horror game, presentation is everything and while graphically this game is a couple of years behind high-budget games of its time, the darkness, settings, atmosphere, and enemy design keep things terrifying despite the slightly outdated graphics (that are most noticeable at the beginning during daylight). Sound design is excellent and helps with the feeling of unease, especially during the first half of the game. There is a virtual reality option that I'm sure improves the experience.

Story/Dialogue 3/5 : Decent and limited on cutscenes. It does its job to complement the game without causing a distraction. Voice acting is pretty good and enemies that speak do not sound goofy and can sometimes add to the terror.

Gameplay 4/5 : Initially you are helpless though dangers are mainly story-based boss fights, but these fights are gruesome with a clear element of danger (and they stay that way throughout the game). A bit later in the game, once the 'molded' are introduced and you have limited ammo and weaponry, game is at its most terrifying with you checking every corner and being alert as you explore. Weaponry feels intentionally a bit cumbersome, as you control a character without experience with firearms. This is a good game design that keeps Resident Evil 7 from becoming a plain shooter game. The later parts of the game do get a bit closer to shooter game territory but not overly so.

[h1]PROs:[/h1]
✅ Incredible, tense atmosphere from start to finish.
✅ Features a fantastic and truly memorable cast of "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy" antagonists.
✅ "Open-ended" exploration / locked door progression
✅ An excellent story full of mystery and satisfying, unexpected twists.
✅ Fun boss fights and unique "tape flashback" gameplay sections.
✅ Great character models, animations, and overall sound design.

[h1]CONs:[/h1]
❌ The Field of View (FOV) is uncomfortably tight, even at the maximum setting.
❌ Some scripted events are awkward, with enemies seemingly warping into view.
❌ Some environmental textures and facial animations look noticeably dated.
❌ Scarce ammunition can lead to tedious "poke and run" combat if you're not a fan of that style.

[h1]Comments:[/h1]
This is probably my second favorite Resident Evil game, right behind the RE2 Remake. It’s a fantastic return to the series' horror roots, driven by an incredible atmosphere and one of the best families in gaming. The "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy" Baker family members are the absolute blast. The tense, claustrophobic setting is amazingly designed. The level design is great, and the unique "tape" flashback sequences were a lot of fun.

The gameplay is pure survival horror, which means ammo is intentionally scarce. Personally, I don't have the patience for the "poke and run" gameplay that this encourages. I found myself constantly running out of ammo even with careful headshots, so I eventually switched to an infinite ammo unlock to keep the pace moving and enjoy the action.

The game isn't without its jank, however. My biggest complaint is the damn FOV, which feels incredibly tight and claustrophobic even when maxed out. I also ran into some awkward scripted moments where enemies would just warp in out of nowhere. While the character models are great, some of the environmental textures and facial expressions look pretty rough, especially when compared to the newer RE Engine games.

A quick word on the DLC - just get the Gold Edition. It includes all the worthwhile content. 
The "Banned Footage" packs add fun puzzle/challenge rooms, 
"Not A Hero" is a great free action-focused chapter,
"End of Zoe" is a hilarious adventure where you play as a badass redneck punching his way through monsters. 

All of them are worthwhile.

Despite some technical flaws, the amazing atmosphere, unforgettable characters, and great story make this an absolute must-play.

As if we needed one, Resident Evil 7 provides yet another reason to stay as far away from the deep south as possible. It also happens to be a decent game, even if almost manages to blow itself up at the end.

RE7 is a lot of fun most of the time. It feels like Resident Evil again. Tight hallways, dark rooms, nasty creatures, gratuitous violence, recursive gameplay, safe rooms--the works. This iteration may be in first person, but the vibe is right--especially when you factor in the fantastic visual design and graphical detail.

For the most part, the fact that RE7 feels like RE is a good thing. But it does have some downsides. For one, inventory management continues to be an irritation. I know many RE diehards will argue that the inventory issue is "part of the game," but I continue to believe that it's annoying, outdated, and serves no purpose other than to artificially pad the game's length and difficulty by forcing players to traipse back and forth to a stupid stash box on a regular basis. 

I don't want worry about how many green herbs I can stuff in my pocket with some old coins and body parts. I just want to play the game.

Another downside of the RE7's return to its roots is the clunky control scheme. It may have been okay for characters to control like school buses when these games were third-person adventures, but that lack of mobility feels really bad in first person. That's doubly true because the game insists on forcing you into action-y sequences on a pretty regular basis. Having to precisely target some giant monster's eyeball with a pistol that your character handles like a drunk dude in a full-body cast is not a great experience.

By far the biggest issue with RE7, though, is its poorly done and absurdly drawn out ending sequence(s). Apparently having run out of interesting things for the player character to do and realizing that its dark hallways aren't all that scary anymore when you have a grenade launcher, RE7 invokes the ol' take-away-all-your-stuff-and-make-you-play-as-someone-else malarkey about two-thirds of the way through the story. 

Basically, you get to spend most of the game's final hours in a different area trying to scramble for resources and weapons again like you just started out. Talk about a mood killer...

Oh, and that new area? It's really not even fun. Well, unless you enjoy climbing up and down ladders a million times to get the stuff you need to advance. In that case, you'll love it. 

Seriously, developers... Why have players spend so much time and energy collecting items, saving ammo, and preparing for the final battle only to take it away from them at the last minute? And why destroy the otherwise solid pacing of the game by gating the answers we've been waiting for behind hours more tedious gameplay in a new zone that is inferior to the main map in every conceivable way?

Honestly, the last three hours of RE7 feel like one of those pranks where someone teases a dog by pulling a treat away every time he goes for it. I almost stopped playing a couple of times. By the time I finally made it to the (real) ending, I couldn't wait to be done so I could go to bed. 

Those final hours are so irritating that they almost manage to sink the entire experience, but RE7 is good enough otherwise to still earn a recommendation. It's still a decent horror experience and an okay way to spend 8-10 hours of gaming time. If you like RE, you'll probably like RE7. Just don't be surprised when the last third of the game makes you want to reenact certain chainsaw scenes.

I've beaten this game roughly 15 times, on console and PC, and I can safely say it was the best horror/fun experience I've ever had.. up until halfway through the game. Upon beating the third boss, the game doesn't completely die down in enjoyment, but the mediocrity soars like you would not believe. It's still a fun game all throughout, but oh my god it really seems like the writers ran out of ideas and decided to wrap things up in a crunched time period. 

At the beginning of the game, you're presented with this amazing environment. It is brought up in this southern american redneck property and it's weird, it's creepy, it's almost like you can get a whiff of how bad it smells and I love it. You can easily tell something terrible has happened since the place is a wreck and it just makes you want to dive on into the lore of the game. The antagonists are presented perfectly with this type of environment, as a screwed up family that you want nothing more than to get away from. 

Near two thirds of the way in, as I have mentioned earlier, you might find yourself asking what the f**k happened to the game and why is it so lame compared to what I was enjoying an hour ago. I'm obviously going to keep spoilers out of this, but this needs to be said, it gets extremely repetitive by fighting the same waves of enemies over and over again. The shock value and edge the game originally had? Gone. The ending is tied together by a cliche and you're just left with this "oh.. well okay" aftertaste. 

It's still a great game though, and I'd recommend it. It's fun to speedrun on Madhouse (the hardest difficulty), and it's fun getting all the collectibles too.

This review doesn't contain any spoilers:

One of the greatest horror games I've played in my life. I had seen the game streamed before and loved the art direction and gameplay, but playing it is something even better. One of my friends once told me that a certain vegan chicken dish tasted "like chicken, if chicken were actually good." I think a good way to describe this game would be "Outlast, if Outlast were actually good" but with the frame and mindset of the first two Resident Evil games.

There are tons of references to classic horror media like Evil Dead, the Texas Chainsaw Massacre, and the Hills Have Eyes. The entire section taking place in the Baker Estate works mechanically like Resident Evil 1's mansion or Resident Evil 2's police station, with the outline of a rural slasher film.

The only reason I rank this as the second greatest Resident Evil game is that it goes from "amazing" to "good" after the midway point or so, which is typically where I throw on a podcast and mindlessly shoot at things. Most Resident Evil games suffer a drop in quality in the second half, but this one's is far worse than the others. It's maybe worth waiting on a sale for that reason alone, but the second half of the game is still far above the quality of most horror games, so don't let that dissuade you.

Amazing game. The first half of it is easily an 8-9/10 experience. It's paced very well, from the first moments you set foot in the game it does its best to keep you on the edge of your seat. The characters all have personalities, and each feel very distinct. Every twist is foreshadowed very well, and nothing feels like it came out of nowhere. The boss fights are all fairly unique. The first half is survival horror at its peak.
The second half of the game is closer to a 5-7/10 experience. It's still good, but a good portion of it feels rushed. The mechanics are good, and it does feel like a natural progression of sorts, especially for a Resident Evil game. The twists, once again, are handled very well. The characters do all still retain good personalities, but the pacing is definitely off. The last leg of the game is much better, with the pacing going back to the quality of the first half, and it really does feel natural.
The free DLC, Not A Hero, is pretty good, solidly 6-7/10. The pacing is good, it handles characters fairly well, the enemies are intimidating in a different way. It's definitely not the survival horror aspect of the original story, but it does maintain some aspects of it throughout.
The game has a good degree of replay-ability, whether it be a harder game mode, or Madhouse, you can return to it plenty of times. The atmosphere is almost always on point, especially in the original story. I would definitely recommend the game to anyone who enjoys the survival horror aspect of games, and the atmosphere of horror

Resident Evil 7 is good value on sale and arguably at full price excluding DLC if you're a die-hard fan of the series or of horror games in general.

The game has decent graphics and audio, an atmospheric setting with interesting level and enemy designs, fun boss fights and occasional moments of tension.  

Puzzles are present but most of them are little more than DOOM-style searches for the "keycard" item that lets you move on to the next area.

Combat is basic and antiquated.  The game introduces the series to FPS controls yet doesn't have iron sights for your guns.  Enemies are not too bullet-spongey on the standard difficulty, and do stagger and show reaction animations to being shot, which isn't always a given with action FPS games.

Character development is weak to nonexistent.  Your primary protagonist is some guy trying to find someone and displays little in the way of personality or development through the game.  Most of the villains are (warning - light spoilers) your textbook creepy swamp rednecks straight out of a B movie, with a Resident Evil twist.  Having come in to this game after finishing Yakuza 0, an equally inexpensive game on sale with a *phenomenal* story and characters, it felt lacklustre. 

Resident Evil 7 uses save points and emphasises smart inventory management and ammo conservation, as is typical of the series.  

The game is short, as many AAA games are.  It offers about ten hours of play for the average gamer.  The free DLC will add extra to that.  I did not play the paid DLC, which didn't sound interesting to me.

Overall a solid diversion when you have a free day or weekend.

The Resident Evil series goes back to it's roots in this seventh outing, and it's all the better for it - making it one of the best in the franchise.

Essentially the first Resident Evil was a dressed up "haunted mansion adventure", with many key-opens-door and other logical puzzles and booby-traps. In RE:7, this adventure-style gameplay makes a huge comeback, and includes some really tight level design with unforgettable set pieces. The house gradually opens up for exploration. This means you'll have to revisiting areas to solve puzzles and get things you saw tantalizingly just out of reach, but couldn't interact with earlier. The haunted mansion in this game looks like it's been heavily inspired by Leatherface's home in "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre", and probably a few episodes of "Hoarders" as well.

There's some amazing graphical fidelity with the RE engine to give you jumpscares and a real sense of horror as well. This is especially evident with the hulking villian whose thunderous footsteps can heard coming down the hallway, increasing your heart-rate as he hunts you down. Your only chance of survival is to try to hide in darkness to avoid confrontations, lest you expend ammo trying to hurt this tank of a monster. You'll have to think quickly on your feet to survive many confrontations, as slow reactions without a plan will get you repeatedly murdered. 

There is some great voice acting and story, but the game is let down a bit by some comically violent deaths, lack of exposition, and how people seem to lose limbs as if it doesn't bother them much. It breaks the fourth wall a bit and pulls the player out of the immersion. This weirdness gets explained later on but it's a bit jarring when first encountered as it suspends belief of the new player and impacts the serious tone of the story.

All the same though, this is a great game that will keep you hooked until you finish it.
Even when you finish it, there's a good amount of DLC available with loads of replay value. It's great.

This is the first Resident Evil game I have ever finished and it was really good I don't have too many complaints about this game so we'll kick off with the good stuff.

The horror aspect of this game is pretty good, I'm not often scared by games or movies but there are definitely times here that had me shook especially very early on when the game isn't just throwing guns and ammo at you so you have to think more about how and when you will use your resources. The game does lose this towards the end as despite the large influx of enemies you have so much ammo and powerful guns that your not worried about running out it's just a bit of a shooting range. The game also has a very tight field of view that can be changed slightly but this really creates a claustrophobic feel that just adds to the tension not being able to see everything around you. It allows the game to play some pretty cool tricks as it has more room to place enemies around you.

Gameplay is pretty good overall, the only real issue is the very long animations for everything. On one hand this makes the game very tense as Ethan moves very slow and climbing up ladders when running away can be one annoying and scary. Then on the other hand this can cause moments when you are stuck in an animation for 5 seconds just being pounded by an enemy with absolutely nothing you can do, this is fairly uncommon though so it doesn't detract from the game too much. The best thing that comes out of these long animations is that the entire game feels like a movie or someone playing for an E3 preview as everything feels so meticulously built and purposeful. The graphics also help with this as the depth of field effect the game has is very well done as in most games with an effect like this bug out and I can't see certain things but it works so well here and just makes the game feel and look amazing. One last thing on the gameplay is how slow using guns is I know this has been in previous Resident Evil games that when you're ads you can't move and you can move a bit here but its so little you really feel vulnerable even when holding a 12 gauge.

Boss fights in this game are pretty good I really like the 2nd one it's in such a tight enclosed space with very little light and it's the best one by far in my opinion. Non of the boss fights do anything too complex the trickiest it gets is "shoot the big glowing things" like well yeah obviously. It's bit of a shame that the last one which you can't really even call a boss fight is so lacklustre even though it's the one the entire game builds up to it just feels like a glorified quick time event.

Finally the story, now I won't spoil anything but the story in this game overall is good it has a good twist and the concept is fun some parts are a tad cliche but I'm not gonna start crying about it. My main issue is the stories pacing it felt both too long and too short as the last 30 mins feel so incredibly rushed but the 2 hours before that I felt the game was going on for too long so I just think the pacing towards the end of the game is all over the place but I do love the start it's so so good just kinda feels like they didn't have a plan of what to do after the 3rd boss fight.

Overall this is a good game not much more to it. If you're looking for a horror experience there are definitely better games out there but RE7 has a great mix of gameplay whilst having ,for the most part, a focus story and I would recommend it to pretty much anyone if it is on sale for around £10.

A unique entry to the series that unfortunately overstays its welcome.

As many have already said: the game looks phenomenal & utilizes its great setting throughout - wood looks old & rotted, insects skitter among trash & gunk, foliage sways in the breeze, rooms in the house look lived-in but also un-cared for. The Baker Family (the main antagonists) is distinct, with their own dialects, body language, & more - even if I didn't personally care for any of them, the detail & focus on them is admirable. For the most part, the first-person experience is immersive, with a strong showcase of moving about & reflecting the world simultaneously: blocking attacks or being struck conveys weight as the player character's vision sways & blurs, they brush their arms from various wounds & hazards, weapons bounce from direction to direction as the player turns. Unfortunately, that's the game's biggest strength. Once such novelty wears off, odd gameplay mechanics & various shortcomings grow increasingly obvious.

I wasn't expecting Shakespeare, but with how the story is framed & how it progresses, it goes from suspenseful thriller to dollar-store indie horror pretty quickly. Other than the Bakers themselves (who are crazy but believable & "committed to the role"), almost the entire cast flip-flops from panicked bystander, to cool & collected hero, to sensitive & emotional. As if they were intentionally trying to check off every cliche they could think of. The [spoiler]law enforcement officer[/spoiler] is /just/ incompetent enough to get himself killed. The [spoiler]missing spouse[/spoiler], who is the cause for the game taking place at all, is more affectionate in the opening cinematic than the rest of the game put together, while also being just as inept as our "average joe" protagonist, despite them being [spoiler]Special Forces[/spoiler] apparently, in the epilogue. The almost-nameless bystander becomes a de facto hero in half of the DLCs - so is he really hapless & dead, as the story goes, or not? Let alone the out-of-place, laughable "jumpscares" that The Real Villain™ features with late in the game.

I also realize that the game emphasizes exploration & puzzles moreso than combat, but the player character has two speeds: shamble or power walk. I can appreciate taking things slowly & trying to convey the weakness of the character, but it's annoying to travel from one end of the house to other at a snail's pace on multiple occasions. It's also immersion-breaking to be able to sidestep-strafe the boss & just spam the melee attack until they die.
Having said that, however, I do have to praise the locations & some of the puzzles. They're creative &, as overly elaborate as they are, feel as "rusty" & "gunked up" as the house that they're in (a few comical & ridiculous ones aside).

Unfortunately, the majority of my enjoyment of the game were 2 action-oriented DLCs. One, where you play as [spoiler]Redfield[/spoiler], a professional soldier - the combat was fun & I applaud how different it plays from the main game. Unfortunately, the writing was just as awful, so I lost interest somewhat quickly. The other, a wave defense spin-off, where you still play as a weak, untrained civilian. Nonsensical fun - but it doesn't try to be anything more than that, which is roughly half my playtime in itself.

Personally, I wouldn't recommend this title. If it looks interesting & you like exploration, you may enjoy it if you find it on sale & you're patient. I would really only make a case of recommending the action DLCs, but those are not included with the base game. As for the overall experience, you'd likely enjoy it more watching a Let's Play with the more boring & annoying moments cut &/or the streamer going through the trouble for you. If you want Horror / Suspense & Atmosphere, I'd recommend Layers of Fear, instead - Amnesia: The Dark Descent for more gameplay & puzzles. Or If you're looking for a more Action-oriented first-person adventure, I'd go for Dying Light. For both Action & Horror at the same time, you may enjoy UNLOVED or Cry of Fear.
