Overall:
A fantastic return to form for the classic survival horror series, that has been going from strength to strength since its release. It pulls off a magic trick, by being simultaneously true to the original formula, while modernizing it and subverting it, managing to appeal to both new fans and veterans.

9.5/10

The good:

Boy, this is going to be a long list. Starting off with the technical stuff, the game looks and sounds great, with the RE Engine's great lighting and gore being the highlights, along with the game's stellar sound design. The game is also optimized quite well, so performance should be good for most everyone out there. One of RE7's greatest strengths is its ability to combine elements from previous entries in the series, as well as take inspiration from modern horror games, and use these elements to craft a very well paced experience. During the first hour of the game it becomes clear that you are very underpowered to deal with the situation you're in, and the best course of action is running and hiding, with the gameplay being pretty similar to Outlast. Slowly but surely, as you explore more of the environment, finding supplies, solving puzzles, and putting the story together, your weapons arsenal gets bigger, earning you that feeling of empowerment from overcoming tough challenges. Towards the end, the game shifts into a focus on action, much like RE4, which feels like a great payoff for all the running and hiding you were doing in the early game, surviving encounters by the skin of your teeth. The level design is great, and it allows for lots of environmental storytelling, and a great sense of atmosphere, just like RE1. The story starts off pretty standard, but gets more and more interesting as the mystery behind the Bakers unravels, and we get to see how it ties into the series lore. Though the game is about 10 hours long for your first playthrough, it offers lots of content through DLC, as well as a harder difficulty which changes a lot about the experience, making the game very replayable.

The bad:

While the game is great overall, I did have a couple of minor complaints. Firstly, the enemy variety is pretty small, and as a result, the combat can get a little repetitive, especially towards the endgame, when you're fighting more and more enemies. The second complaint refers to exactly that, the final bit of the game. The slow buildup of power, granting the player and the protagonist more agency in their situation reaches a sort of climax towards the beginning of the game's third arc. What should have been a short, yet action packed victory run, seems to go on a little too long, which results in some of the impact being lost. After a great action sequence where [spoiler] we control Mia, trying to save Ethan in an abandoned ship, starting off without weapons and ending with a machine gun, Die Hard style [/spoiler] the game goes on for a completely forgettable and pointless final stretch, before (quite underwhelming) the final boss and ending.

The meh:

While there is a lot of cool stuff on the DLC, like a Survival mode similar to Mercenaries from RE4, and some extra bits of story, other additions are quite superfluous and pretty much skippable, at least for most players.

I don't know what it is about this one but I just can't get into it. A return to form for the franchise. I loved classic PS1 era Resident Evil, as well as Code Veronica. RE 4 was a necessary progression as technology advanced, and by most accounts a good game, but for me that was when RE lost its identity. The claustrophobic camera angles were no more. Psychologically it was hard to be fearful when the heroes are all hardened veterans with mountains of monstrous corpses under their belts. I can barely even remember the story to RE 5 and 6, something about Wesker and a helicopter and a volcano... cool action games I guess but a million miles from the survival horror roots.

Well technology has moved on again, and Resident Evil 7 is here with a soft reset to the franchise and it's great. It does seem to be set in the same continuity as the other games but that is not evident from the start and doesn't play a major role even once certain facts come to light later in the game. It's a brand new story and you are playing as just an ordinary man who has come to a creepy looking estate to find his missing wife. The claustrophobia is back, not with the awkward pre rendered camera angles of yesteryear but rather with a first person perspective inside a rich enclosed environment. The ammo is sparse in the early stages and the enemies feel intimidated. There is a real sense that you are being hunted, you are not the hardened veteran taking it to the enemy, but a normal man way out of his depth fighting to survive. And that's what it's all about: survival... and horror. Resident Evil is back!

Meu primeiro jogo da franquia. Comprei por estar numa fase de jogos de terror, após zerar Outlast resolvi dar uma chance a esse jogo, e ele não decepcionou. 

             O conceito de survival horror em primeira pessoa é muito bom, você se sente dentro do personagem e todos os eventos se tornam mais impactantes por você estar vendo eles com os seus olhos. Apesar dos recursos serem poucos, eles são suficientes para vencer os desafios, já que na maioria das vezes você pode só ignorar os inimigos e salvar munições e itens de cura para uma ocasião mais importante. 

             Sobre o level design do jogo, ele é excelente! Você caminha na maior parte do jogo na "Mansão" dos Bakers, essa tem portas e passagens que são revisitadas a toda hora, mesmo passando pelos mesmos cenários sempre há algo de diferente a se fazer, com novas chaves, novos itens que liberam novos cômodos e áreas. A ambientação do jogo também é muito boa, sempre passando a sensação que há algo errado e nojento nesse local. 

             Os inimigos são pouco variados, tendo praticamente os mofados como inimigos padrão e algum integrante da família como um boss, não que isso seja um problema, mas poderia ser algo melhor no jogo. Em relação aos quesitos técnicos o jogo também se destaca, tendo gráficos muito bonitos, dando destaque aos personagens, que possuem uma movimentação e expressões faciais impressionantes, além disso o jogo também tem uma trilha sonora muito boa que dá um impacto para cenas e aumenta a tensão enquanto explorando o mapa.

             Outro ponto positivo do jogo é a história, no começo ela parece ser algo mais intimista, apenas um homem procurando sua esposa desaparecida, porém ao passar do jogo a história começa a crescer e se conectar com os eventos dos outros jogos (não que eu tenha jogado, mas eu tenho uma ideia de como é a história da franquia). Tendo também algumas reviravoltas no fim.

              No momento eu acabei a minha primeira gameplay, apesar do jogo ser curto, ele possui um fator de rejogabilidade muito grande, tendo mais de um final e alguns desbloqueáveis e coletáveis que estimulam a jogar o jogo mais de uma vez. Enfim, o jogo é muito bom vale muito a pena ser jogado.

Plot
Set deep in the heart of the Louisiana Bayou, Resident Evil 7 casts players in the role of Ethan Winters, a newcomer in the series who is searching for his wife Mia who has been missing and presumed dead for the past three years. On receiving a video recording from an obviously distraught Mia, Ethan heads out to a seemingly abandoned estate deep in the swamp in search for her. This leads him to the Baker estate, a sizeable property consisting of various houses and outdoor locations.

Turns out the Baker family estate isn’t so derelict as Ethan is quickly captured by Jack, the imposing patriarch of the Baker family, and forced to partake in a gruesome family dinner in which is arguably the most iconic scene in the game (and a tribute to The Texas Chainsaw Massacre). Most of the Baker family seem to be utterly insane, intent on murdering Ethan, and are infected with some sort of virus that allows their bodies to sustain injuries that would kill a normal human. It becomes evident early on that the Baker family have been abducting, experimenting on, and killing people for some time as Ethan finds journals alluding to kidnappings and bodies strewn about the Baker house.

Along with Jack, there is also Marguerite (my favourite character), his foul-mouthed wife with a fondness for creepy-crawlies, their son Lucas, a scheming ‘jigsaw’ type character who designs murderous traps and games for his victims, Granny Baker, who unnervingly shows up throughout the game despite being catatonic and confined to a wheelchair, and Zoe, Jack and Marguerite’s daughter who is unlike her insane family and works with Ethan throughout the game to find a means of escape.

Review
The graphics and general aesthetic of the game is phenomenal. The Baker house really feels ‘lived-in’ and has an interesting art-deco and rustic style combination to it. The house is littered with clutter from laundry to leftovers and you can spend a considerable amount of time just looking among all the nooks and crannies that are crammed full of intricate little details.

*I also recommend checking out the Horror Night Reshade preset by kyOuZz_- if you’re on PC, it gives the game a much better horror atmosphere by making it darker and more claustrophobic.

The Baker family make for an excellent supporting cast and are easily the stars of the show. They aren’t over-the-top villains with grand plans (here’s looking at the lovable Wesker) and there is just something about them being an otherwise normal family that plays very well into the immersion factor. Jack and Marguerite Baker are delightfully chaotic while Lucas provides a more methodical take on madness and the game has you spend adequate time dealing with each of them.

There is a permeating sense of disconnect between the events of the game and Ethan. Ethan himself is a pretty bland character whom we get no background on other than he’s Mia’s Husband and he undergoes no character development whatsoever throughout the duration of the game. This is especially noticeable in cutscenes and scripted events early in the game where he has little to no reaction to injury or events happening and ultimately works against the initial horror atmosphere it tries to portray.

In addition to the Baker family you’ll also have to deal with the moulded - giant fungal-like monsters covered with black tendrils and razor-sharp teeth and claws. The monster design here is pretty generic and kind of goofy at times as all the moulded are missing from being ridiculous is a giant pair of googly eyes.

The first 2/3rds of the game is pretty engaging. During this time you are constantly moving forward discovering the secrets of the Baker home and surrounding areas, often while being hunted by Jack or Marguerite. It is during this portion of the game where it’s at its best and most tense as you are introduced to the Baker family and struck by the amount of attention to detail the developers have put into the design of the Baker Estate.

Unfortunately the game really starts to fall apart around the time we get to the infamous tanker section. Here the game ditches any horror aspect it had going in favour of action as you mow down the moulded creatures with a machine gun and remote explosives as you make your way through a bland and uninspired boat level (which has been done quite a few times in the Resident Evil series at this point, Revelations handling it much better). The focus shifts much more towards the story at this point, which, when laid out bare, can be summed up in two or three sentences and really isn’t worth remembering, it also leaves some basic questions unanswered that I won’t spoil here.

Gameplay
You’ll spend time in part exploring, fighting, and hiding as you are chased by members of the deranged Baker family and the moulded monsters. In the early stages of the game you’ll discover that Jack and Marguerite cannot be outright killed, rather they can be stunned allowing you to escape to a hiding spot.

Available weapons for Ethan to utilize range from knives, handguns, shotguns, explosives, and a makeshift flamethrower, if you’ve played a Resident Evil game in the past you’ll be familiar with the arsenal. The weapons feel great to use, however you’ll have to conserve ammo wisely as it’s limited especially in the early game. Absent from this game is the weapon upgrading system that was present in Resident Evil 4 & 5, although there wouldn’t be much point in such a system as the majority of the game has you exploring rather than shooting, you can however craft enhanced ammo should you need the extra firepower.

Inventory management and resource crafting play a major part in the gameplay as Ethan has a limited number of storage spots available meaning you can’t just carry everything that isn’t nailed down with you. Throughout the game you’ll find chem fluid which can be combined with gunpowder, herbs, and other items to make bullets, first-aid kits, and various other consumables to help Ethan survive.

The series’ puzzles make a return in this instalment of the franchise, however they are rather simplistic and far and few between, with most taking the form of a ‘match the shape’ minigame.

Conclusion
Resident Evil 7 provides a welcome change to the series’ usual format (action-shooter at the time) while still keeping its survival-horror elements and atmosphere. The first half of the game alone is well worth the experience as you explore the insanely detailed Baker house and try to piece together the mystery of what has happened to the family and how you are going to escape. Unfortunately the grand reveal is underwhelming and introduces more questions than answers that you probably won’t bother with as the main characters, Ethan and Mia, are completely forgettable by the ending. 

Despite the lack of an engaging story and some repetition towards the end, Resident Evil 7 offers a solid survival-horror experience and some beautifully creepy aesthetics to ogle. A thorough knowledge of the events of previous games in the series isn’t required to dive into this entry and as such I can easily recommend it for newcomers and survival-horror fans alike.

Capcom shifting one of my favorite franchise from Third person Action Survival Horror to First person Survival Horror with bits of action, was a decision that I wasn't expecting would turn out to be as good as it did. 

The horror elements are on point. 
Even if you've seen some videos of the game on youtube, the impact of jumpscares will be there.
The chilling atmosphere of the remotely based house;
Whether you have jack baker on your trail with a freaking chainsaw or zombies made of mold squirming in the vent right above you ready to drop, everything feels impactful.
The sound in this game is underrated and not much talked about but it really delivers the tone of the moment. 
Hearing jack chasing after me made me feel like running irl.
Gameplay is slow and unique to fit you in the shoes of Ethan Winters who's NOT a combat vet with classic inventory management but this time it's tougher because you can carry like 1/5th of the stuff that Leon or Chris could which makes sense because it's Ethan. 
Graphics are a new generation of resident evil altogether from the previous entries. 
Makes you feel the gore and disgust with more clarity than ever. 
Another not talked about point is the intelligent AI that can spot you even through small window panels and isn't that dumb to be easily fooled, making the challenge of "survival horror" really interesting. 
The story although towards the end becoming as convoluted as your typical Resident Evil games, is pretty engaging for the time it stays through. 
Another plus point was the optimisation. 
RE engine is awesome. 
I ran this game on a weak cpu and a 1050ti and it looked beautiful even on medium settings (I was able to play on high with no problems as well) 
the hair textures looked a bit off at times but no frame drops made me overlook everything else.

Now the cons that aren't really "cons" but just minor convenience problems 
I wish they added a skip cutscene option at least once you've completed the main game.
Even when you die and continue, some cutscenes are not skippable and it wastes a lot of time. 
Another problem that the game has (or maybe this was intentional) is the "HUD" for items. 
you need to absolutely submerge yourself into the proximity of an item for it to be visible. 
this overrides other RE games HUD for example RE 4 where a bright red light would indicate the items which although cheesy for 2017, was very convenient back in the day. 
The story towards the end becomes less indulging because it abandons the antagonists who deliver the best horror elements and focuses on another character who feels like a knock off from the F.E.A.R franchise.


Be sure to play the DLC's "End of Zoe" and "Not a hero" for closure on 2 side characters that the main story leaves on cliffhanger along with a bit more lore around the Bakers and even Chris Redfield. 

there's also other challenging dlc's for enthusiasts and achievement hunters bringing the total average hours of the game to around 16-17 hours for an average player which is pretty decent for a timeline where speedrunning horror games in less than 1 hour is possible and content is getting lesser. 

TLDR - Capcom shifts the tone and delivers on all fronts that this game advertises itself to be. Nothing more. 

Get it on sale for around less than $10 for best value that the game has to offer in terms of hours and entertainment.

Resident Evil is one of the great franchises of gaming. But it is no secret the later numbered entries to the series had lost something of the magic of the original trilogy. The most obvious reason for that was an increasing focus on action and a break from its survival horror roots. First clearly evident with Resident Evil 4 and getting progressively more pronounced with each sequel. Resident Evil 7 was hailed as a return to form. Less action and more scares as you try to escape yet another house of horrors. Promising, but does it deliver?

You play Ethan Winters, who suddenly receives word from his long lost wife Mia that she is alive and needs his help. This brings Ethan to a dilapidated house somewhere in a Louisianan bayou. If that house looks a bit like a haunted house, that's because it kinda is. Ethan is a typical everyman, or at least a typical American Deep South everyman, judging by his skill with firearms. Unlike previous Resident Evil protagonists he is not a professional, nor related to previous protagonists, nor particularly much of a character anyway. He is just a random guy in the wrong place at the wrong time. This is a deliberate choice. The game goes for a more intimate, a more personal experience. In a similar vein, the game plays this time in first person. This enhances immersion further, while making Ethan feel even more like a vessel than a character.

The game takes a much more low key approach to the biowarfare element of the series. The primary opponents, the Baker family, are full-fledged characters rather that mindless zombies. Initially at least, there is nary a hint of anything biological there. Instead the game plays more like a paranormal horror story, as if what you are facing is supernatural. For the longest part the big bad is little more than a ghost. In fact, there is a drastic change in style as a whole from the classic trilogy. Gone are the opulent mansions and police precincts, gone the shiny underground labs and colourful city streets. This is a grimy swampland, dominated by rot and decay. The Bakers seem stuck in the 80s with old school TVs and cabled phones. Only the son of the family, Lucas, resident tech-junkie and Batman supervillain wannabe, has a mobile phone.

Granted, the atmosphere of the game is truly incredible. All these factors help create a powerful experience. Throughout your journey around the Baker estate, the atmosphere will cow you into submission and force you to think twice before rushing to the next area. The game plays great too. Combat can be fun and intense, though the random mooks do feel a bit limited. Black sludge guy, or black arachno guy being the only real flavours. The game encourages exploration and taking things slow. There is a ton of hidden items all over the map, items that can really make the difference between survival and many frustrating deaths, so keep your eyes open. I recommend this game. However, the experience is a bit uneven. It's not as perfect as RE4, but it's an exciting new direction and stays very true to its roots.

VISUALS:
It's astonishing. On highest settings, it verges on truly photoreal frequently, and has perhaps the best lighting and materials i've ever seen in a video game (I have not played RE VIII yet). Performance was great, as well. The engine is clearly powerful and the game seems well optimized. Character faces fall into the uncanny-valley a big unfortunately, but otherwise it's a 10/10 on graphics and aesthetics.

STORY:
Without going into spoilers, the game does a good job of feeling like a RE game without trying to hard to incorporate/expand the already-obtuse and bloated canon. It's a small story, no saving the world, focusing on basically a single local and a few key characters. The way the story is told is compelling, and you're left wondering how it will be explained throughout most of the game. For a while, this was a little irritating because I wanted to know what was going on, but the game eventually spells it out and I'm happy to have been in the dark because it allowed my imagination to try and understand what might be going on behind the scenes. The characters are pretty well-acted, and I don't think I found myself rolling my eyes much/at all.

GAMEPLAY:
RE7 has plenty of survival/horror, action, and story/boss encounters. However, I'd say the game has a hard time striking that balance throughout. The beginning is very much about story-driven/boss encounters and navigating the levels to avoid confrontation is key. However, the rules of engagement are not well-defined to begin with, and this is made more difficult due to the mechanic/plot point of characters "regenerating" and not dying. In the first act, it often felt futile to even attack enemies, given that it was unclear what success looks like, and how little you're given in terms of weaponry/ammo. The first few hours sort of feel like an interactive cutscene, and I debated stopping the game there. 

I'm very glad I didn't, because once things get going and you're into the second act (after you find the trailer), I found myself really enjoying the game. There is more variety in encounters, and the game gives you just enough ammo and tools to survive. Everything sort of gels. The environments are all well-designed and put to good use for the different moments and mechanics. Exploring them and finding loot, combining items, finding secrets, and taking it all in is really a delight. The game moves at a slow pace and you're meant to soak in every detail.

Then, you get into the last portion of the game, (the ship and through til the end) and it becomes clear what the main flaw of the game is: aside from a few key bosses, there are really only 2 or 3 meaningfully different enemies in the game. This is a huge problem because the general "mobs" of the game are there to lend tension and fun to the portion of the game where the story isn't really unfolding. Simply put, the average enemy encounter is actually sort of lame, not especially fun, and feels the same every time. It's rather telling that one of the better sequences of the game doesn't have a single enemy (the SAW homage). The game takes its realism a little too far in the controls department, and the character is sluggish to move around with many irritating animations, which becomes infuriating during major boss fights. The game also begins to overload you with ammo in the last few hours, diffusing the tension that was hanging in the air for the majority of the playtime.

To end on a few positive notes, the UI is minimal but is handled very well. The atmosphere is incredibly satisfying, and this is definitely a scary entry in the RE series. The scale of the game is small, and it benefits greatly from it; each part of the environment seamlessly blends into another and every space you find yourself in is meaningful and beautifully detailed. The small scale also makes the amount of backtracking that you'll do palatable. It does a great job of blending the old and the new, and the move to the first person camera is done with great respect to what Resident Evil has always been about. This is a flawed, but very good game.

Resident Evil 7 is a decent 'reboot' to an incredibly stale series of video games, though a few major issues prevent me from recommending it. 

One of the main issues in the game is the length; it takes forever to get anything done due to the incredibly slow pace of both your character's movements and the level design. Prepare to backtrack into the same rooms hundreds of times to unlock a single new room or find an item. This has always been a problem with the series, and it's no different here.

Another issue is the resource system. It's incredibly cumbersome trying to find items, combine them, and organize your stash. Seriously, the inventory in this game is normally what you see in bad, loot-based RPGs.

I didn't think I'd have to complain about this next flaw, but it needs to be said - the game is ridiculously dark. In great games like Outlast, the rooms range from well-lit to pitch black. In either setting, you have a camera light that you can activate whenever you need it. In RE7, your flashlight only turns on in scripted portions of events, meaning you'll be wandering through practically pitch black sections of levels without any way to illuminate an area. Raising the brightness only makes a slight improvement.

Finally, the game suffers from balancing issues. In the beginning of the game, you have no weapons, meaning stealth is vital to survival. I found myself immersed into the atmosphere of the first few hours of the game because my character was defenseless. The further you get, however, the easier the game becomes. Similarly, the focus on survival horror is later undone when the game becomes a mediocre FPS.

It's a shame, too, because the story and characters are very interesting here. Some gameplay segments allow you to play as different characters through the form of VHS tapes, which is just as cool as it is inventive (rather than a generic cutscene). The graphics are solid, the sound effects are realistic, and the atmosphere is incredibly tense compared to ANY of the previous Resident Evil titles. But while the game takes many steps in the right direction, it's still inferior to many of the best survival horror games.

[b]A very different mainline Resident Evil game, even compared to the originals.[/b]

Just like almost any Resident Evil game, there's practically no story connection to the previous game. And just like any of those games, the story isn't really anything noteworthy outside of a few moments: some guy looks for his wife in an abandoned house, horror stuff happens, now you have to survive. 
For whatever reason, almost every cutscene can't be skipped, making immediate replays kind of annoying if you really don't want to listen to the same stuff you already knew again. The ones that can be skipped though can't be paused despite a whole menu being brought up asking whether or not you want to skip it.
It's also so different from previous games that it's a wonder why they even bothered attaching the Resident Evil name on it at all as the only connections to those games are some unrelated references here & there as well as the appearance of one familiar character at the end. Doesn't help that all of a sudden they use the scary-little-girl trope, which seems like the most out-of-place horror element in this franchise.

The game's true to its survival horror nature in terms of its gameplay and general atmosphere.
It's an incredibly dark game half the time with some fun jumpscares here & there. You have a flashlight, but for whatever reason you can't turn it on outside of specific locations, which is annoying for when you're trying to find items in little dark spots without having to turn the game's brightness up.
The survival aspect of the game is a return to classic Resident Evil games in terms of being slow-paced and having limited resources to work with as well as a small inventory. However, despite all that, it's way too forgiving in the end provided you actually take your time to aim your attacks properly. Where in the older games, ignoring zombies was highly encouraged for ammo conservation, you can just about kill every single enemy in this game and still have loads of ammo left in storage; even knifing enemies is easier here, regardless of difficulty setting.

The difficulty setting you unlock after you beat the game once though is a lot more like a classic Resident Evil game: resources are extremely limited, enemies are no longer forgiving, and even your saves are limited as well. Enemy encounters have been changed up too so you can't just always rely on a strat you found in the lower difficulty settings.
Due to the tanky nature of the enemies here combined with ammo being way more limited, actual strategies like ignoring monsters or baiting them or locking them into rooms becomes way more encouraged.

It's a great survival horror that probably should have been a spin-off title at the very least.

So, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard. Where to start? This game is an absolute masterpiece of the horror genre and actually is a scary game, unlike other RE games. It revived the RE franchise after not-so-great previous entries and yet it did even more than that. It created a sort of template on which every next installment of the franchise is expanded upon.

The game features a thrilling and truly terrifying atmosphere and story. It makes you feel unsafe in every single location you visit. The silence and music create an eerie mood that makes you shiver. It's horrific, that's what defines horror.

The story at the first glance might seem simple and kind of like any other horror plotline but it greatly evolves over time and makes it really interesting. It also quite nicely ties up with the overall RE lore. Generally, as said previously, the story is scary and memorable, it's awesome.

The gameplay is perfect. It was a bold move for Capcom to change to a first-person perspective but in the end, it paid off. I can't imagine it being in the third-person, it just wouldn't be as creepy as it is. Gunplay is fun. Resource management is really important. Overall gameplay is engaging.

The puzzles are well thought out. Lucas' ones are especially prominent and creative and of course, you feel a lot of pressure doing them because of the horror nature of the game.

I can totally recommend this game to literally anyone. Even if you're not a big fan of the RE series. This game is just so well-put-together that you don't have to understand or like the franchise to enjoy it and that's what makes it excellent. 10/10

PS. I just wish other RE games had the same eery atmosphere. Really, it's probably one of the scariest games right next to Outlast.

During a time Resident Evil stopped being a horror game and leaned more towards over the top action with Resident Evil 4-6, and while those games can be fun in their own right, it stopped being a survival horror game. Resident Evil 7, brought the series back to where it belongs, as a survival horror. You play as Ethan Winters, traveling to a presumed abandoned house looking for his long lost wife Mia, What makes Resident Evil 7 different though is the perspective is changed from 3rd person to 1st person, which allows for new mechanics and ways to search for items. However while it's in first person it's important to stress the game does not play like a first person shooter. The shooting slow and clunky like it is in past games, where you have to rely on wits and positioning to successfully kill monsters, while also aiming carefully to avoid wasting ammo as every bullet counts with how scarce ammo is.

It's worth mentioning, although the game has a 7 on it, no you don't need to play any of the other Resident Evil games to know what's going on as RE7 is it's own standalone thing. It does take place after the events of the other games, but none of that matters as Ethan's story is it's own thing. There are references to the older games though hidden as readable text logs, and there's a bonus good feeling of playing the other games. If you want to try another Resident Evil game before jumping into 7, play Resident Evil 2 Remake.

So yeah, grab it. It's a fantastic horror masterpiece and will leave you satisfied, and scared of any random ambient noise you hear afterwards. Enjoy!

Obviously these are survival horror games and are meant to be stressful so I don't mean that as an objective complaint - just a personal gripe.  RE: 7 takes place at night in an old abandoned house and it just has more of a suspenseful vibe to it as well as lots of jump scares.  Also unlike RE: Village, ammo and resources are scarce and there are a handful of sections where the player is forced to think quickly and run instead of fight - similar to the earlier RE games.  Tons of people love this style of game and I totally see why, but personally it's not my cup of tea.  I thought RE Village did a great job of blending the survival horror and FPS elements of RE: 7 with a slightly more action-oriented style in a slightly less eerie setting.

Overall, it's a great game and it's objectively a thumbs up score from me.  However, if you're looking to backtrack after Village and expect more of the same, be warned that it is a bit different in terms of balance and setting, even if the core principles of the game are the same.

This was given to me as a gift because I could never afford it, even when it went on sale. I played the demo, and it was interesting, but now that I've actually played the final release of the game, with the patches and updates... This really isn't Resident Evil.

My biggest issue was the human AI of the Baker family, and that it might be a bit broken. I couldn't escape the dinner scene, and I thought I might just be stupid, so I broke down and looked up a walkthrough. The game I was playing played out nothing like what the text and video walkthroughs were Showing. Jack Baker never walked in the paths described / shown in the walkthroughs, and always seemed omniscient, knowing exactly where I was at all times. After about 7 deaths- including bleeding out with a hand cut off, and the game refusing to allow me to follow the prompts it was giving me- I turned the game off, and uninstalled it.

The human AI is too smart, right up their with Mortal Kombat II reading your button inputs, and reacting before your character animations can even begin. That feels like an apt comparison, because no matter what I did, no matter where I chose to hide, no matter when I decided to make a break for the next area, Jack Baker knew exactly where I was at all times, and simply did not allow me to progress through the game, even when I had my hand held by the community, telling me exactly what I'm supposed to do.

The shift to first-person was also controversial. I hear people point out that the OG RE was intended to be a first-person experience, but the fact is that it never happened, unless you count the ultra-abridge, Wii-exclusive Umbrella Chronicles which condensed the entirety of RE1 into a 12-minute on-rails light gun shooter. Personally, it always felt like a pissing contest with Konami and their Silent Hills Playable Teaser (P.T.), but considering that got the axe, it feels jarring at best, and out of place at worst. The shift from fixed camera angles to over-the-shoulder third-person was at least transitional as RE4 still had tank controls, and RE5 still forced you to stand still if you wanted to attack.

This just isn't Resident Evil, and I probably won't be playing RE8 either. RE0 is still my favorite in the franchise. I've got easily 60+ playthroughs on GameCube, and almost a dozen on PC. Compare that to all versions of RE1 that I've played (Windows 95, GameCube Remake, Wii port, Umbrella Chronicles, and PC HD Remaster) with only a combined 7 or 8 playthroughs, and it's obvious which one I prefer. RE2, I never beat, and only played on GameCube, RE3, I rented on GameCube once and never beat it, Code Veronica X, I beat once on PS2, RE4, I cleared 6 times on GameCube- and unlocked all of the content- 4 times on PS2, 1 time on Wii, 2 times on Xbox 360, and 4 times on PC, totaling 17 times, paling in comparison to RE0. RE5, you can't really track full repeat playthroughs due to the chapter and checkpoint systems, but I'd say I've played a couple dozen times, mostly just replaying the same handful of chapters because they're either fun, or easy to grind for money and supplies. RE6 has a similar issue in tracking repeat progress, but I'd say I played through it all at least 8 times. Revelations 1 and 2, I've beaten 1 time a piece. Outbreak, I beat on a fundamental level 1 time, and Outbreak File #2, I beat maybe 4 times. RE2 Remake, I've basically unlocked everything over about 15 playthroughs; same with RE3 Remake.

If you're new to Resident Evil, I guess this might not be the worst game to come in on, but I can't recommend it. It's just not really a Resident Evil game.

I expected to like this game. What I did not expect was for it to become one of my favorites. While I think it's still too soon to tell whether this game will stay as one of my favorite games of all time, I have no doubts that it will be one that I remember for quite a while.

To start, I'm going to talk about my experience with Resident Evil 7.

It felt like (at least for most of the game) it was very focused. It didn't feel to me like there was a lot of padding or annoying segments. There were some, but they were pretty infrequent and didn't really detract from the rest of the experience. It was a game that was fun all the way through.

One of the things that stuck out to me the most was that after finishing the game, I immediately wanted to start another playthrough. I was happy to finish the game, but I still wanted more. After beating the game, (gameplay spoilers) you unlock the game's hard mode. I expected it to be simply the same game, but enemies dealt more damage. Maybe a few items would be missing compared to the normal mode, but nothing major. I was proven wrong. While Madhouse mode isn't that different from normal, it changes enough up to keep the game fresh on a second playthrough. The enemy placement, for example, is different. Some enemies are added, while a few are actually removed. Combined with the added difficulty, the changes help to keep the tension intact and make the horror elements stick out that much more.

The gameplay mostly consists of exploration and combat. The exploration is less guided than some games, but it is still pretty linear. You aren't really allowed to go wherever you want like the old games. You're still bound to wherever the game wants you to be at that moment. But because you usually go to new parts of areas you've already been to, the feeling of backtracking is still there.

The combat is less action focused than previous games. Pretty much all you can do in the main game is aim and shoot. This is definitely not a bad thing, however. It helps to keep the survival horror elements of the game present. Ammo is limited. Meaning that you really need to be careful with how you place your shots and which gun you use with each enemy. In addition to the ammo that you find lying around, you can also craft ammo using chem fluid. The catch is that chem fluid is also used to craft healing items. This creates an interesting situation. You can choose to craft ammo so that you can defend yourself better, or you can choose to craft first aid meds so that if you get hit, you have the ability to heal yourself. It also rewards skill. Because if you're better at combat, you won't get damaged as much, and thus, you can spend more chem fluid on ammo rather than first aid meds.

The story is the last thing I'm going to cover. Throughout the game, there are many things that don't make sense. A character may say something strange that seems to just be meaningless. It isn't until your second playthrough that you understand what they were saying, and things start to make a lot more sense. It adds another layer of replayability to the game that I really appreciate. The scale of the narrative doesn't necessarily reach the heights of the previous games, but I don't think that's a bad thing. They didn't need to have villains that were plotting to take over the world. And Capcom knew that. It felt like if you were on the other side of the world, you wouldn't know anything about what was happening in Dulvey, Louisiana. And I think that's just the way it needed to be.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 turned out to be an amazing game and experience that I can't stop thinking about. Even when I'm trying to go to sleep.

Sometimes that makes for an interesting backdrop, especially as you begin to trace the residents of the Dulvey Mansion’s descent into savagery and uncover the way it’s manifested in their domestic life. Traces of humanity aren’t hard to find behind all the locked doors: old photographs, trophies for academic achievement, a discarded football helmet. Compared to the cold, medieval interior of the still-beloved Spencer Mansion, the Baker household actually feels like a lived-in space rather than a grandiose maze of traps and hidden laboratories, which is an interesting and more intimate change of scenery that focuses on something that the series has never fully explored before.

Other times, Resident Evil 7’s roots in “hillbilly horror” relies too heavily on overplayed tropes about rural America and begins to border on the cartoonish. The Bakers are disgusting, dysfunctional, and at times pretty laughable, but most of this is at least explained later on, which — without spoilers — satisfactorily avoids putting the blame entirely on their rural upbringing. But even with its faults, Resident Evil 7’s change in style and setting never fails to deliver a strong sense of place that makes frequent exploration and backtracking through the dingy Dulvey property and its secret underground lairs work without wearing out its welcome.
The Baker family, like unstoppable tyrants with unpleasant personalities, are among the first enemies you’ll encounter, and they’re by far the most interesting. The first fight with Jack Baker had me both laughing hysterically and scrambling frantically for a way to defend myself, a winning combination that made the unpredictable encounter one of Resident Evil 7’s highlights. Jack’s patrolling of the mansion — at one point even bursting through a wall, Mr. X-style — actually felt like a real threat, even after I was armed with more than a knife. To survive, I needed to either flee or fend him off by unloading my handgun on him, which is a decision that can come back to haunt you.
Despite the shift to first-person, Resident Evil 7 feels more like an adventure game than a first-person shooter, which is a welcome return to what the series was in the ‘90s. Thanks to a compelling pace that ensured I always knew what I needed to do next, most of my time wandering hallways, collecting keys, and unlocking secret passageways and shortcuts around the Dulvey property felt well spent, especially as the central mystery unraveled around me with each file and phone call I received.
Resident Evil 7 grounds itself in elements that made the original great while still indulging in a risky new shift in style that both helps and hurts the beloved formula in equal measure. But it’s also the closest a numbered sequel has come to recapturing Resident Evil’s slow, but thrilling and atmospheric adventure game roots in a while — a welcome return that I truly hope to see more of in the future.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard can be seen as a new chapter in the series, serving as both an experiment for the developers and a true challenge for fans. The switch to a first-person perspective brought a fresh feel and added intensity to the game's atmosphere.

The game immediately takes the player into a world of anxiety and uncertainty. Instead of the usual zombies and infected, we encounter a creepy "Addams Family." The game's atmosphere is more about creating a constant sense of unease rather than outright fear. This is especially felt in moments when you have to hide from Jack or "kill" him, only for him to return again and again. It's reminiscent of films like "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre," but with an immortal main enemy. The addition of various grotesque elements (decay, insects, slime) further enhances this feeling.

The storyline provides satisfactory explanations for the unfolding horror but leaves some questions unanswered. For example, what is Mia's job, and what did she mean by saying "you were right"? These gaps slightly mar the overall impression of the plot.

Despite being a numbered, main entry in the Resident Evil franchie, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard plays and feels very different from the other main RE titles, and feels more like a spin-off game compared to the Revelations games. First of all, the game is in first-person, where other RE games are in third-person. Secondly, it returns to the survival horror feel of older RE titles, unlike the action horror oriented RE 4-6. You play as Ethan Winters, a man searching for his missing wife in a plantation occupied by the creepy Baker family. You also won't meet any iconic RE franchise characters such as Leon, Jill, Ada, and others, with the exception of one in the very end. There are quite some references to RE events in some documents and objects, though.

Inventory management is a thing again, as you have a limited inventory, but can be expanded, although not by much. Ammo and enemies are also quite scarce, and your main focus is usually exploration and finding items to progress further. Some areas are free-roam, while "transition" areas are linear like in RE2 Remake. Sadly the lack of enemies also means there's poor enemy variation. Other than some bosses, all the enemies are just variations of one design, plus some big bugs. The boss fights are pretty fun, but the final boss is sadly disappointing and feels more like a QTE event. I stocked up items for nothing.

RE7 is probably the scariest RE game I ever played. The combination of realistic graphics, first-person view, scarce ammo, strong enemies, and the overall decaying plantation look makes for a really great horror experience. Especially during the early levels, you will feel really helpless. As you progress you will find more weapons and feel "safer". My only complain about this game is about how demanding this game is, stutters quite often and sometimes so bad, the audio lags during cutscenes.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a great horror game, but for me it doesn't feel like a RE game. I think because I never played the original games and I'm more familiar with the action horror era. It feels more like Outlast with combat for me. If you're a fan of other RE games, you might enjoy the new horror era brought by RE7 and 8. If you're not a RE fan but a horror fan, you most likely will enjoy this game, and have a new franchise to love.

Resident Evil VII is, in my opinion, one of the best horror titles of the last decade. It is a complete package with everything a horror fan might want and need. 

Without spoiling anything, RE7 is set in Dulvey, Louisiana, a swampy backwater town with little to no connection with the outside world. The game's protagonist receives a message from his wife, who's been missing for three years, and travels to the said derelict plantation in hopes of saving her. However, what he finds is beyond anything he could have expected, a part of a much, much bigger plot. 

This installation introduced a new engine and a first-person perspective, which brings the immersion to a new level. The VR version is something else, but no comments here since I don't own one. 

As a newcomer to the series, I have nothing to compare RE7 to, but I did find the interface convenient and the resource management system easy to use. The player can also manipulate objects, like in the Amnesia series. The shooting feels very responsive, and popping heads is probably as satisfying as it gets. Difficulty spikes throughout the game felt minor, and the puzzle-solving will hardly make you scratch your head. One thing to appreciate here is the replay value. When choosing the 'Madhouse' difficulty, the items are randomized on the map, and the resources become even more scarce, which should keep most players from getting OP and losing all interest in the game.  It's a small thing, but definetatley a nice-to-have. 

The graphics, lighting, music, voice acting are all top-notch. The game ran smoothly for the most part, but I remember experiencing some crashes. 

To wrap it up, I'd say RE7 is a perfect introduction to the series if you haven't played an RE game before and a worthy sequel for the fans to play. It will scare and disgust the sh*t out of you while looking great and feeling fresh. I fully recommend this one!

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
From start to end, RE7 delivers an oppressive, tense atmosphere that conveys the feeling of imminent danger behind every corner or door. The "chase" sequences prove to be the highlight, as they really make the tension mount, unfortunately there are few. Visuals, acting, sound direction are all of excellent make: together they deliver a beautiful experience.

[b]2.[/b]
Making every bullet count is the mantra of survival horrors, and it proves true also here. Either being extremely accurate or only fighting the mandatory enemies are viable strategies, what counts is saving enough resources for the next boss fight, because YES, it's possible to run out of ammo, and that means almost certain death even on lower difficulties.

[b]3.[/b]
The Baker estate is huge, each room filled with hidden goods in every corner, behind furniture, under beds and so on. Some great hoards of supplies, unique weapons or special items are often barred behind optional backtracking that well-rewards the extra effort.

[b]4.[/b]
All the actual boss fights feel significantly different, and often have nuances, mechanics or alternative ways to deal with them. These terrifying foes really feel like a significant challenge, much more so on Madhouse setting, and a test for all the effort players made thus far.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
The usual, pointless choice of barring the highest difficulty behind beating the game continues to baffle me, since the RE games of old. If players want the highest challenge straight off the bat, let them have it I say. I see no point in this design choice, other than creating content bloating.

[b]2.[/b]
That's right. The final boss, for which Ethan will hoard tons of ammo and healing items, will be nothing more than an interactive cutscene with no challenge, where equipment won't matter. Utterly disappointing and cheap.

[b]3.[/b]
Four enemies, that is the grand total excluding bosses. Even for a nine hour campaign, that is not enough variety. About halfway through, enemies start to become repetitive, boring and quite a chore to fight against, as they bring no novelty anymore compared to Ethan's increasing loadout power.

[b]4.[/b]
The last 30% of the adventure features an almost always overpowered Ethan facing more and more filler, with way too much ammo and resources around for his own good. This simply removes the whole survival horror feeling, and is disappointing.

[h1]Gameplay Breakdown[/h1]

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed on foot, with a map of each area becoming available either as Ethan explores it, or by finding a complete map item on the premises. Some exploration segments have a pursuer chasing Ethan in order to kill him, and act more like a stealth survival horror type rather than action; these segments are however few. Most of the time, players will be focused in looking everywhere to scrounge as many ammo, resources and items as possible, as every bullet and herb counts - many are hidden very well in the most remote corners and holes. The Baker Estate also houses many secrets, treasures and unique items that can lead to better weapons or significant advantages. Enemies come in finite amounts and do not respawn under normal circumstances.

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out in a FPS fashion, with players able to carry up to four weapons simultaneously. All enemies, including bosses, have weak spots, that deliver significantly more damage if hit: for efficiency's sake and given the rather low amount of ammo present until late game, this is the way to go. Enemies drop nothing and it's not mandatory to kill all of them, as it may be wiser to evade them when possible, especially on Madhouse difficulty, to save resources. Ethan is able to block, a vital skill that greatly reduces damage taken from most attacks, and may even enable counters during specific fights. Notably, some boss fights have more than one way to be dealt with. Even on Normal, most enemies hit hard if not blocked, some even able to 1-shot Ethan if not at full health. The knife has unlimited uses, but is very weak and only is good as a last resort: it is definitely possible to not have enough ammo for a boss, so saving as much as possible is the meta, as it should be in survival horrors.

[b]Inventory Management[/b]
Is performed with a panel initially composed of 12 tiles, that can be further expanded by finding backpacks. Most items occupy one slot, while more cumbersome weapons, two. Items can't be dropped, but only permanently discarded or stored in the Item Box, present in most Safe Rooms. Especially during the first half of the game, deciding what to take and what to leave behind is a rather common occurrence - one can always come back later to get what is left, though. Several items can be combined together to form new ones, such as heals or ammunition. Unlike other RE chapters, there isn't a trader or any currency, only Antique Coins are present, usable in a specific location to gain upgrades and a special weapon.

[h1] This. This is the one that got me into Resident Evil. [/h1]
I know that upsets some people, the same bunch who claim this to be an OuTlAsT ClOnE.
Boi, if Outlast had guns, it wouldn't be nearly as scary. You'd just shoot the big pig man and that would be the end of it.

Similarly, while RE7 has a pretty decrepit and freaky atmosphere, it fails as a horror game for me.
But I don't think that that's what it set out to do. And what it did do? I immensely enjoyed.

I've replayed this game over 10 times, because it's what I like to define as "short and sweet".
The intro, while a little bit long, basically gives you a little sneak peak and does so with immense cinematic value.
And after that? The game... begins.

[b] [Gun- and Gameplay] [/b]
The Baker family is brutal and without good equipment, you won't be getting anywhere.
Luckily, their Household provides that in plenty and boy, do they feel excellent.

I remember when I first shot the gun and I saw smoke come out the end of it. It blew me away.
The weapons in this game feel fantastic and every upgrade you find feels meaningful.
It's probably the best gunplay in any RE games up to that point. It's fantastic.

Sadly the game lacks in Enemy variety, as aside from the Bakers, Zombies have been replaced with goo monsters that come in 4 fun-sized, similar-looking versions. It's probably the first in the series to lack in that aspect.

However, the Bakers are split up in a way where they're not really too far between each other. The goos usually serve as a bit of downtime until the next bombastic encounter between you and one of the Bakers ensues.

Overall, you'll spend up to 6-7 Hours on your first run through the most blockbuster RE campaign to date (Yea, I'm looking at you RE6).

[b] [Graphics and Sound] [/b]
When I first played this, the graphics blew me away. 4 Years later, you tend to notice some crispiness here and there. Regardless though, the RE Engine manages to render some fantastic looking environments and it runs really great too.

The sound is eerie, in a good way. Walking through the Baker Mansion and hearing the wooden floors crackle beneath and above you is haunting. It sounds weird, but its legitimately the most realistic sounding House I've ever heard in a video game.

I can't remember much from the soundtrack, other than the menu music (which perfectly fits the games atmosphere), the save room music and Go Tell Aunt Rhody (which are both bangers).

[b] [Story] [/b]
While it has a bit of that japanese writer cheese to it, RE7 tells the most coherent yet vague story in comparison to its predecessors. 
Ride Wife, Life Good
Wife Gone, Ethan cry
Ethan gets text. Save Wife?

Over his time in Lousiana, Ethan comes in contact with good old southern hospitality and tries to figure out what makes them such good-hearted people, and leave with his wife before bedtime. 

Ethan is your go-to generic "WhATS GOIN ON HERE?? AIRPLANE FOOD??" protagonist, which balances out the craziness of everyone around him. Also Mia either has alzheimers or schizophrenia, like your grandma. You love your grandma, right?

Only the bakers remain, which is where most of the quality writing went. They're such entertaining, violent goofballs that the moment you see em you can't help but give out a worried laugh as you try to find the nearest fire exit.

Doesn't that all sound pretty simple yet convoluted?

[b] [Conclusion] [/b]

RE7 is simply put a blockbuster. It's a game that I could replay time and time again and have fun with it everytime.
While it doesn't give a good impression of what the rest of the series is like, it works in getting you invested and wanting to find out more behind the things that caused the Baker Incident to begin with. I absolutely recommend this game to anyone intrigued by its premise. It's on sale pretty regularly as well, which makes it a no-brainer at that point. 
At least give it a try, there's a lot of fun to be had.

[b]Resident Evil 7[/b] is, after RE4, the second game in the main series of the RE franchise to turn a full 180 on gameplay and mechanics. Did it have the same effect as RE4 had back in 2004? No. Is it a f**king great game? Oh boy for sure!

In RE7 we take control of Ethan Winters, who tries to find his believed dead wife in the lost swamps of Louisana. While all REs before this one are "classic" third-person-shooters, RE7 is the first first-person-shooter in the mainseries. With this big chance many classic elements changed as well. Sure, things like the save mechanism, inventory management and also the puzzles still remain but the first-person-view makes room for a whole new kind, a more "close" horror. It's obvious they got inspired by the massive success of Outlast. Furthermore the "gunplay" feels really statisfying, especially compared to the  prequels. It's been a reaaaally long time that i got scared in a game for real as i played many horrorgames in the past. But particularly the first half of the game was f**king terrifying!

For fans of the franchise i have to say that the link to the prequels is more or less hidden and not really important. Similiar to RE4 it stands alone and can also be enjoyed without having played any RE before. But as nearly always i do recommend to have at least played one prequel before this one, for RE7 it's RE5, to enjoy the connections and characters.

I highly recommend playing the DLCs! Nearly all are great fun and particularly "Not a hero" is a fan favorite! (But recommend the season pass on sale as the DLCs are quite short)

[h1]Texas Chainsaw massacre + Saw  = Resident evil 7[/h1]  

[u]What I liked about the game [/u] 
[list]
[*]	I liked the idea of a resident evil game being in first-person. 

[*]	I thought the horror atmosphere was really good. The game reminded me lot of the films Texas Chain saw Massacre and Saw. The game has quite a few jump-scares and moments where you just feel generally uncomfortable. The first half is definitely the best, but after that it becomes more action orientated.  

[*]	The game has some good puzzles to solve.  

[*]	The game had some really memorable moments, especially the boss fight with Jack Baker. 

[*]	I liked how they changed things around in the madhouse difficulty mode. 

[*]	You get awarded items, if you find all of the collectables or complete the game. 

[*]	The game had a nice selection of weapons to use. I liked the idea of when you play as a different character you get a different selection of weapons. I also liked the idea of being able to use unique weapons during boss fights. 

[*]	The baker family (excluding Zoe) and Eveline were great antagonists, and were quite terrifying. I felt sorry for the baker family towards the end. The protagonists were likeable characters as well, like Mia and Ethan. 

[*]	The Not a Hero DLC comes free with the game which ties up one loose end. The campaign is only short, but you get to play as Chris Redfield, and you also have some new content, like new weapons and unlockables.   

[*]	I liked how you can interact with things in the environment, for example, picking up a tin and examining it and finding out how to unlock it. 

[u]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/u]
 
[*]	I didn’t like the idea of having to use chem fluid to make items. I would have preferred just combining two lots of gunpowder to make bullets. 

[*]	I didn’t like the animation of the character administrating the medicine; I thought it looked a bit silly; Ethan just pouring medicine all over his hands.  

[*]	 I thought the developers could have done a better job with the design of the Molded. 

[*]	I wish the game was a bit longer.

[*]	I would have been nice to be able to craft over ammunition types like shotgun shells and sub-machinegun bullets. 

[*]	I wish you were able to unload weapons.  

[u]Conclusion[/u] 
Overall I enjoyed Resident Evil 7. Compared to the previous games though, I still prefer the over-the-shoulder perspective, like in Resident evil 4. I like how this time round they focused more on the horror aspect rather than the action.  The boss fights were awesome, but I was a bit disappointed with the design of the molded. The first half of the game was the strongest for me and then it slightly goes off after that. If you enjoyed the original resident evil games then I highly recommend you give this game a go.

Even though I consider myself a horror fan, I had never played any of the RE games, not only because I have always been able to find creepy games to keep me busy, but also because to be honest I never found them that scary to begin with. I started by playing Alone in the Dark and Phantasmagoria way back in the day, and then slowly made my way through the years of Silent Hill, Project Zero, Doom 3, FEAR, Dead Space, Amnesia, Alien Isolation etc. Amidst all those I never even considered that I would be missing out by not playing the RE franchise, as it didn’t seem to offer anything particularly frightening. With all the recent remakes and the newly released RE, I decided to pick up RE7 on Game Pass just to see what the fuss was about because, since there was seemingly no connection between the story in Biohazard and the other games, this seemed like a good place to start. And I have to say I am now very tempted to pick up not only 8 but also the 1, 2 and 3 remakes.

I was quite impressed with the tense atmosphere they were able to create throughout most of the game, even if there seemed to be a couple of missed opportunities. I love it when a game doesn’t overly rely on jump scares, because they somehow think cheap tricks that force a natural flinching reaction are the same as a genuine sense of dread. Biohazard walks an almost perfect line between these moments, especially at early stages when you aren’t certain what to expect or what the story is about. I do have to admit that, as my playthrough progressed, my reaction towards the game became looser precisely because the fear of the unknown wasn’t there anymore, but that was to be expected as you start to understand the story a bit better. And even then, the game does a good job at making you question whether you’re equipped enough to progress through the challenges you’re still going to be facing (fairly often I was left wondering whether my ammo was going to be enough at that particular point). I also found the story to be pretty interesting, though not having played the ones before I assume it might be a fairly standard narrative throughout the franchise. Finally, I do think the 1st person perspective is what completely sells the game as it feels custom made for it. And if I’m honest, that makes me wonder how I’ll feel about the 3rd person titles.

As for the negatives, to me the main issues were that the movement felt a bit sluggish and the inventory management seemed more convoluted than it needed to be. Additionally, I have mixed feelings about the enemy you most frequently come across, which to me didn’t seem particularly interesting. But these criticisms are minor compared to the rest that RE7 has to offer.

Bonus tip-   Ultimately, if we measure a survival horror game by how effectively it can provoke in the player a sense of tension and, at least, something close to fear, I’d say this game is definitely able to bring that to the table, even if not on a consistent basis. In my opinion, Biohazard is a 4 out of 5 and a great game to consider if, like me, you’re a Resident Evil ‘virgin’ wanting to explore the franchise.

Resident Evil 7 takes a brand new spin on the Resident Evil franchise by not only introducing a new protagonist and point of view, but by reconstructing the Umbrella Corporation's ties to a new disaster and bioweapon, Eveline. I found this game to be delightfully horrifying, each twist and turn agonizing with anticipation for the next jumpscare or boss encounter. Even when the lights are on and you seem safe, you are constantly on edge because you know you are never fully safe from traps, mold spores, mold monsters, or even Old Woman Eveline waiting for you. That, and Jack Baker likes to crash through walls just when you think you managed to shake him off of you. If you want a truly terrifying first person horror experience, you have come to the right place. You don't need any knowledge of the decades old lore of the RE franchise, though some parts may be a fun little easter egg or reference should you be familiar with past characters and plot points. RE7 introduces a deep plot that will not fully make sense until you've played through the whole story and can piece it all together, and the plot twists you never expected come into full view when the huge web of conspiracies and disappearances meet in the middle. RE7 brings the series back to the true meaning of the survival horror genre that the original RE made such a name for. If you want something that will keep you up at night, then this is truly the game for you.

It's one of the best things that happened to RE franchise.

Pros.:
- Fantastic development overall.
- Gameplay. The game evolved into FPS but with survival horror, System Shock, Bioshock-like elements. There are familiar save spots (audio recorders and boxes). You progress through the locations and open them more and more. You may come back and find forgotten secrets or items. You still may kill, but should keep an eye on the inventory. All from the past and best of RE games. 
- Story. Even though the story AGAIN is about a "small little girl with superpowers" (F.E.A.R., movies like "Ring", etc.) it is explained through the virus and experimentation. The virus resembles Uroboros. Still, Evelyn is a vulnerable kid with family issues. Her behavior and dramatic consequences are the result of the mistakes of the adults actually. 
- Characters. Amazing characters of the Baker family, especially Jack ("Howdy") and Lucas. Fantastic development, animation, interactions. Horrifying in several episodes.
- DLCs are finally worth its money. All DLCs are cool, especially 21, The Room, Sisters. Didn't feel I finished the game without finishing DLCs, especially Nightmare (it was hell of an experience).

Cons.:
- Not enough upgrades. Inventory could be more flexible and comfortable to surf.
- Need more background story about Evelyn and Blue Umbrella.
- Redesign of Chris. Ugh... When will they stop redesigning well established characters?..

Forgot to mention. Evelyn's family issues are the direct reference to the Twilight Zone episode about a boy with the same desire who dragged random people to his house and made them hostage, forcing them to pretend to be his family members.

Still, fantastic game. Must buy!

It took a couple of false-starts for me to properly set my mind to sitting down and indulging the relentless fear and slower pace, but once I did RE 7 was the game that finally made my mind click over to understanding what the series is. I was right in the target demographic when RE 2 was originally released in 1998 - it took me this long to 'get it'. But I got it.

It's no one feature of the game responsible - it's the game as the sum of its parts. The first-person view properly rectifies the series-long issues with tank controls and clunky over-the-shoulder cameras while still retaining the restricted field of view so essential to the player's sense of vulnerability. The visuals are, without hyperbole, utterly incredible. The way the game sets the tone and its steady increase in threat is masterful - opening the door to the house and seeing that pitch-black hallway for the first time as the sun begins to set was genuinely distressing in a completely unique and thrilling way. And after I got the hang of the rhythm of sneaking around and escaping the creatures - once I properly comprehended that the obstacles the game presents are meant to be surmounted - it clicked. 

It's a masterpiece of design and execution. There is no point - even after finishing the game multiple times - that it stops being terrifying, and its absolutely worth a buy.

Resident evil 7 is a action horror game which recently made the transition from third to first person. This has only elevated the “immersion” faction making this an excellent example of a linear story game.

I was expecting this game to be an exclusively horror focused experience but found after a while that it didn’t resort to any cheap tricks to spook players, instead the game makes the player feel as claustrophobic and tense as possible. The camera angle is very narrow forcing the player to be aware of there surroundings without looking. Ammo is sparse, you can afford to kill most enemy types, but you have to ensure you have enough resources for the next area. All of the boss fight are real highlights for gameplay and narrative I will remember them all.

The game world isn’t very big consisting of 3 houses and some connecting areas and yet each is so spectacularly detailed that you never get tired of each location. It also helps that the game is so well paced always keeping you moving forward and unlocking new areas/abilities.

The story is pretty solid and has many freaky moments which will unsettle you but never so much as to keep you awake at night. However I did find the last section of the game to be a bit drawn out as most of the plotline had been concluded yet the game went on. 

Overall, this is a great game and definitely worth playing even if you aren’t a fan of horror games.

Finished all the core game achievements and I deeply enjoyed it.  I would still recommend the remakes over this, but if you want to try this out, it's worth the cost.  This game returns the series to the survival horror genre instead of the action genre and the storytelling and exploration are fantastic.  

You play as Ethan Winters in this one, who is searching for his fiancee, who he assumed had been dead for 3 years.  She turned up in Dulvey Parish, Louisiana at the Baker estate and you are tasked with going thorough this large plot of land with 2 houses to figure out what happened.  This is probably one of the first resident evil games where the antagonists play a huge role and you will care about them and what happens to them just as much as you will care about the main protagonists.  It's an amazing balance.  

The first person perspective mostly works.  I will say that Resident Evil 7 did to the Resident Evil series is what Metroid Prime did to the Metroid series.  It works well enough and gets you engaged and immersed enough for it to be worthwhile.  I still prefer the behind the back style that 4, 2R, and 3R gave, but this would be a worthy alternative.  

There are some issues, but none of them really make it so the game is broken and unplayable.

- You can't skip cut scenes.  This is either someones wonky vision or a grave oversight.  There's only one movie that can be skipped near the end of the game and that's it.  Thus, speed running this game is a huge drag.  

- You have to watch Ethan heal himself with first aid medicine instead of it just being instant.  This is a bit of a novelty in the beginning, but it quickly becomes annoying as you have to run away and heal yourself in the middle of a fight.  The control for this is a bit bonkers too, as it doesn't always activate and you have to mash the heal button sometimes to get it to start.  I would rather just be able to click it in my inventory and heal up right there.  Not as immersive, but if I had to pick between that and what this does, I'll pick the inventory heal up every time.  I would say that this is the biggest issue the game has for me.

- The exploration is great; the combat...not so much.  Mostly that happens around the first person controls, which can be oddly unresponsive at times and doesn't feel polished.  It's good enough and doesn't ruin the game, but if you were expecting COD like combat, explosive action, and heavily polished controls, this is not where you're going to find it. Most players overlook this since the majority of the game is exploration and puzzle solving anyway.

- There's very little enemy variation.  You don't have zombies, dogs, hunters, or any unique monsters; you have what's called the molded.  You get the basic molded, the 4 legged molded, the fat molded, and the basic molded with a big knife on the arm.....that's pretty much it.  It's all variations of the same creature that are just 1-1 mappings of past creatures.  It's not a big deal, but it's just a bit boring seeing the same skins over and over again. 

- This game has too much DLC.  Some of it is fun, others not so much.  If you're chasing a 100% achievement score, expect to get milked unless you get it on sale.  Just get the season pass if you want it all.  That'll be the best deal.  But honestly, this game for a full 100% in the core game ranks in at about 30 hours.  If you get all the DLC and expect to finish that too, then expect another 20-30 hours just in that content.  I would recommend breaking it up and coming back to the DLC as separate games.

While it has it's issues, it's still enjoyable and I would recommend the core game at least.

The Resident Evil games never seemed very scary to me. Suspenseful, yes. Tense, sure. Yet when it came to actual horror there wasn't much besides the occasional jump scare. That's why I had some trouble wrapping my head around why people would criticize the later games for not being scary anymore, and when RE7 was heralded as a "successful return to its roots as a horror game", I simply shrugged it off without much thought.
And so I waltzed blissfully ignorant right into what would be the probably most scary experience I have ever had in interactive media. The beginning is such a masterpiece that builds layer upon layer of finely crafted (horrible) experiences, that everybody with a taste for horror should definately give it a shot. It is quite fascinating how much it does right, and in what ways. Take Jack for example, who has stepped up to continue the proud legacy of Mr. X and Nemesis, and dethrones them effortlessly. The creators could have made him bigger, badder, more powerful than his predecessors. What they did instead was - to make him more human. More relateable. In fact, all major enemies including the final boss are humans first and monsters second. There is always something tragic lurking under the terrible surface, and this is where the real horror begins.
They could be us. We could be them.
