[h1] The ultimate review of RE7: Biohazard [/h1]

[b] Overview [/b]
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard has done something incredible. It made the ultimate scary survival/horror experience come to life in the eyes of Ethan Winters. Capcom successfully created a game that utilizes different game machanics, horror elements and an engaging story that also stays true to the "Resident Evil roots". This is a huge step forward after the disappointing release of RE6.

[b] Gameplay [/b]
This game is everything i want it to be in a gameplay perspective. Everything is well thought-out and executed. There are a great variety of enemy encounters that will keep you on your toes and forcing you to think about how you should tackle each and everyone of them. Each weapon feels unique in it's own way which keeps the gameplay fresh through out the game. With limited resources and ammo, you will have to think a little harder and be more careful with how you handle things. One misstep can cost your life.

A new fantastic addition to the game is the new blocking mechanic that will help you reduce incoming damage from enemies. Sadly the dodging ability didn't make it into this game. But it's okay from my end, since you don't fight a lot of enemies at the same time. RE7 focus more on survival/horror than action this time which is something that i really appreciate, but of course the game do have their "action moments".

There are a variety of dangerous threats that will sometimes make you jump out of your chair. Crazy family members, molded creatures and bugs. The bosses are very different from each other. Each having their weaknesses and should be approached accordingly. They often come out of nowhere as well which really adds more tense to the game. The bossfights feels satisfying and rewarding. I'm still in chock becuase of how good each and every family member are written. Each having their own personality and backstory.

[b] Length and Replayability [/b]
I've only played it through once which took around 12 hours to complete since i am a person who likes to take my time to explore. I'm normally almost never in a hurry except if the game makes me to. They created a really interesting setting which i wanted to see every nook-and-cranny of. The game-world is full of files and environmental storytelling. If you would have played the game and skip all side content, it would probably take around 8 hours to complete. Capcom did actually add an additional second ending to the game but according to me I think the endings are too similar for a second playthrough just for a different ending cutscene alone. I would wait a couple of months before play it again.

[b] Performance and Issues [/b]
GPU: RTX 3080 Strix
CPU: Intel i9 9900k
RAM: 32 GB 3200 mhz
COOLING: custom watercooled
MONITOR: 1440p 165hz

The game ran consistently smooth with very few to no suttering issues at all. I had almost always around 150fps or more. From my experience alone, I didn't encounter any bugs or at least none that i noticed. But of course, there have been a couple of years to address any issues since launch.

[b] Conclusion [/b]
Overall, i think Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a wonderful addition to the RE universe and i'm beyond excited to continue on Ethan's story in Resident Evil 8: Village. I give this game 10/10!

[i]Resident Evil 7 doesn't rush to place itself within the familiar world of the franchise—an intricate universe that's been built over two decades, which might feel a bit overwhelming for players new to the series. Personally, until the moment I sat down to play this game, I hadn’t experienced any of the previous titles.

But in a beautiful return to its roots, Resident Evil has embraced simplicity in the best way possible. After traveling across the globe and exploring the unknown, it brings the focus back to a single, intimate setting. The fear feels more personal now, grounded in classic gameplay, deeply relatable characters, and a captivating story that unfolds with care and attention. The camera perspective shifts to a first-person view, but it never loses that sense of intimacy.

[b]For me, Resident Evil 7 marks the closing of one chapter for the series—and in that same breath, [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3cR89qOunY8]it feels like the start of something beautiful and new.[/url][/b]

The game gently takes its time to draw you in, encouraging you to explore every corner of the house, uncover hidden treasures, and piece together the story through documents and photographs. This lingering sense of mystery continues to envelop the experience, urging you to search high and low for clues that will ultimately reveal the deeper layers of the narrative.

This sense of discovery isn’t just limited to the main game, either; even the demo beautifully teased the charm of cassette recordings and collectibles. The first-person perspective adds a new layer of depth, making it easier to uncover secrets tucked away in unexpected places, some of which require you to look up or down to find. It’s as if the environment itself becomes another character, telling its own story alongside the others.

The first-person view also makes combat feel a bit more natural and fluid. As someone who finds comfort in using a joystick over a keyboard, it felt easy to adapt to, offering a simpler mechanic than the more complicated third-person approach. But there’s an undeniable tension in trying to escape from enemies, especially when you’re running for your life, with the thrill of trying to make your way to safety while keeping an eye on what’s behind you.

Graphically, Resident Evil 7 generally impresses, with stunning lighting and shadows that create the perfect atmosphere of suspense. While there are some occasional low-resolution textures, especially on older systems like the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One, the lighting is still rich and effective, enhancing the dark, dangerous feel of the environment. The characters, too, are rendered with such realism that it’s almost impossible not to feel disturbed by the madness of the family or the grotesque forms of the creatures lurking around.

Every detail in the scenery invites a reaction, from the insects scuttling across walls (or even crawling over you!) to the unnerving sight of blood splattering after a brutal blow. It’s the little things that make the world feel so alive and intense.

Resident Evil 7 is the gift fans have been waiting for, and I truly recommend it with all my heart to anyone who loves a good, spine-tingling adventure. If you’re a horror fan looking for six hours of edge-of-your-seat excitement, this is definitely for you.[/i]

2026 Mar 24 -> Just played this game tonight. I have to say that this game is already outdated in terms of overall game design. Re2R, which came out 2 years after this game, still holds well while this game ages like milk. The control scheme is the most clunky one in all the resident evil games in the RE Engine era. This game is structured like a movie while treating half of the gameplay as filler. There's a lot of gimmicky gameplay mechanics and segments in this game. There's only one way of doing things and one sequence of doing things.

Nakanishi's game design philosophy -> Nakanishi's game design philosophy is to micro-manage players to experience the set pieces the exact ways he wants. It works great for the first playthrough. But for the subsequent playthroughs, this approach starts to show its flaws because the game doesn't leave enough room for variations you can explore on your subsequent playthroughs.

All the set pieces and gimmicky gameplay mechanics becomes so shallow to the point where I start to think that, "Why do I even bother to play this game again?" There's no meaningful variations you can do to make the subsequent runs stand apart from your first run. You play the exact same ways like before.

So, to remedy the situation, Nakanishi introduces the self-inflicted challenge run difficulty, the "madhouse" difficulty. Some items get shuffled around; Some scripted events changed a little bit; The damage enemies can deal to you drastically increased.  

You actually need to think out-of-box to play on this difficulty. The tips and tricks, or techniques that you learned from the lower difficulties will set you up for failure on this difficulty. 

One of the fundamental gameplay mechanics is blocking enemies attacks. But, if you actually do that on the madhouse difficulty very often, you die faster than ever before. The correct way is to duck half of the time when the enemies attack you. 

There's no tutorial messages for "crouch to avoid attacks", or the need to duck to avoid attacks if you play on the lower difficulties. This is where you need to think out-of-box a little bit. As long as the attack is not a slam attack, you should duck instead of blocking. The whole point of blocking on the madhouse difficulty is to give you a second chance to run away because blocking stops your character's health status from being dropped to danger immediately. But it won't do much for you the second time you get attacked before you heal. You are gonna die or be in danger status. Since your character runs the slowest when his health status is in danger, you are gonna die soon after. So you either avoid attacks by looping around objects you didn't even think you can do when you play on the lower difficulties, or hope it's not a slam attack so you can duck when enemies attack you.

If you leave the tutorial message on when you play madhouse difficulty, the game still tells you when enemy attacks you, you should block. WHAT? The game literally teaches you how to die faster. Clearly the game was never made for this difficulty. The more I play, the more I feel like it's just a mod that I downloaded from fluffy mod manager after I installed REframework.
 
Playing on this difficulty is not fun because I need to learn everything from scratch again in a most stressful and frustrating way possible just to play on this difficulty. [/h1]

[h2]Resident Evil 7 Biohazard[/h2]
 
 [h1] Introduction [/h1]
 
 Whenever someone mentions “Resident Evil”, it reminds me of Zombies due to the movies. But Resident Evil 7 doesn’t actually feature zombies. Capcom took a serious risk while making this game completely different from the previous titles in this franchise. The usual third-person perspective has been replaced with a fresh & well-implemented First-Person perspective. This not only adds to the fear factor but also makes the game a bit more realistic. 
 
 [h1]Information on the Game[/h1]
 
 [h3][b][u]Storyline[/u][/b][/h3]
 
 The game takes place immediately after Resident Evil 6. You play as Ethan Winters who receives a video mail from his presumably dead wife, Mia. He is drawn to a derelict plantation in Dulvey, Louisiana by this video in search of his wife. Will he be able to save his wife from the horrors & challenges that await him? 
 
 [h3][b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b][/h3]
 
 I haven’t played a lot of Horror games but Resident Evil 7 was a completely different experience. The game makes you expect something but it doesn’t happen. It has the ability to make you brace yourself for moments when nothing would happen but throw scares when you least expect it. The perfect formula for a horror game. There’s always this eerie feeling that lingers around you due to the multiple elements of surprise present in this game. There several moments which made me jump off my seat. I swear this game gave me too many heart attacks. 
 
 The basic movements are perfectly okay. But you can’t jump! But the key meant for jumping is bound to blocking. Blocking is very vital during fights as it minimizes the damage you take which can otherwise be fatal. 
 
 Moving onto weaponry. There are a total of 17 weapons in Resident Evil 7, out of which 6 are Melee weapons (including the Chainsaw & Circular Saw), 1 is a bomb (Remote Bomb to be exact) then the rest are Guns (including the Grenade Launcher & the Burner). The weapon mechanics are on point. The recoil is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it makes sense as the character you are playing as is overwhelmed with fear & is fighting for their dear life. The worst thing is that the enemies are literally bullet sponges. Ammunition is scarce but one enemy can eat a whole magazine.
 
 Apart from scaring you & pushing you into a corner, the game also tests you with a series of puzzles. To be honest, the puzzles aren’t that hard to solve as the solutions are right in front of you. The Light Shape Puzzle thingies were the ones that annoyed me the most as it took a while to get the right shape. 
 
  Items, ranging from medical supplies to ammunition, are very rare to come by. They give you the ability to craft items to compensate for this. You can find the necessary materials then combine them to get the desired item. This is very useful as you run out of Medkits & ammunition very fast. Inventory management is vital as you have limited inv space. You need to carry the items that you think might come in handy. 
 
 Almost every decision you take will haunt you later. For instance, in the fight against Jack Baker, you have three options: Empty your handgun on him, try killing him with your knife or just flee. Each of these options has a huge drawback that will bite your back later on. There’s one thing you need to remember in this game, death is only temporary. You will understand what I mean once you play the game. 
 
 The one thing I did not like about this game is the doors. You will never know what to expect behind a door. Firstly, when you open the door, it doesn’t open fully. You have to push it open after opening it a bit. This adds to my anxiety & scares me. On top of that, after you enter a room, the door automatically shuts. I have no clue why they did this. It just makes the game harder as escaping from some enemy will be a pain. 
 
 [h3][b][u]Graphics & Audios[/u][/b][/h3]
 
 Graphically, the game is as realistic as a 2017 game can get. They nailed the eerie & disgusting surroundings. The disgusting parts almost made me barf. This game stands as a prime example of how a horror game should be like. The details they added are wonderful. Everything is detailed, even non-interactable objects. Graphically, this game is perfect.
 
 Sounds play a vital role in a horror game. The right soundtracks set the desired mood. RE7 was excellent in choosing the perfect sounds & also the placements of the sounds. Sometimes, the build-up sound plays but nothing happens. This is a clever way to trick the player to expect something but give them nothing. A perfectly executed tactic for a horror game. 
 
 [h1]Pros [/h1]
 [list]
 [*] A prime example of how Horror Games should be. It instills actual fear in the players.
 [*] The graphics is as realistic as it can get for a 2017 game. They set the perfect mood to scare the players. 
 [*] The game loves playing with you with a lot of unexpected surprise elements.
 [*] A perfectly woven storyline. 
 [/list]
 
 [h1] Cons [/h1]
 [list]
 [*] The puzzles aren’t much of a challenge. Could’ve made it a teeny bit harder to crack. 
 [*] Ammo is a bit too scarce in my opinion. I always ran out of bullets.
 [/list]
 
 [h1] Conclusion [/h1]
 
 If you really want to get scared off your chair, then you’ve got the right game. RE7 has a lot of content to offer accompanied by a perfectly blended horror experience. The scariest game I have played so far. I recommend grabbing it on sales. The DLCs, I do not recommend getting them as they come with a heavy price tag.

Resident Evil 7

Am I recommending this game?
Yes.
Should you get it based on my recommendation?
Questionable.
But why?
Well, first of all for some reason that not even I know, I got really attached to this game. I love the story, the atmosphere, and the characters too much. I was genuinely sad when it was over and was sad to see the story wrap up.
 
The game has it's stealth and combat elements. There are parts when you are faced with an immortal enemy roaming around the house which is a big threat until you defeat it in a fight, so at some point there is the feeling of the defencelessness even tho you have guns in your hand. And when that part is gone, there are the common enemies and boss fights where you can have some action yourself. On normal difficulty the game is challenging enough that I had to retry a few times (less than 10) even on my second run, so it's not cakewalk, you aren't Doomguy after all. 

The combat isn't easy. Even common simple enemies can make it hard for you to deal with them. They wobble around as you shoot at them making continuous shooting more difficult, or block their weak spot until they are close enough for an attack. This can make every single enemy take down you make feel like a mini victory. Especially if you did it with the minimal amount of ammunition. Which is important since.

Ammunition. Depending on the difficulty and mode you play it can be plenty or barely enough, maybe even less. You have to go around the house, searching for ammo and items you can use to craft more ammo and healing. If you play on normal, you have a decent amount of ammunition throughout the entirety of the story, and towards the end you probably have too much ammo. 

Inventory space can be, small. You progressively get more space in your inventory as you find backpacks. But even with the largest inventory, you probably run out of space quickly if you want to bring everything. Not even mentioning that you can only bind 4 weapons to your quick slots, which can be annoying if you have more than 4 weapons, since the game doesn't pause if you go to your inventory, so it is a bad idea to move stuff around in a middle of a fight.

The story is good. It builds up nicely with hints along the way, and makes sense in the game's universe. I don't have much to say here besides, damn. I love Lucas's part in this game. I find him funny while threatening, he is also creative when it comes to trapping and killing his victims. Someone watched me play through this game and they were really disturbed and felt unsettled by him which is great in my opinion. 

DLC's 
Not a Hero - You are facing threats bigger than in the main story with some new mechanics. And learn more about the story.
End of Zoe - Boxing simulator. Not much story but it can be fun if beating everything you see to death is your cup of tea. (except gators, those will kill you)
Banned Footage Vol 1 and 2 - It is nice. 
Nightmare is a survival mode, if you just want to test your fighting skills and how long you last. 
Bedroom is an escape room puzzle, where you also have to avoid being caught trying to escape and have to escape before you die. 
21, it is the same as the card game 21, except with an unique way of betting, and tokens that you can use to help yourself or make it harder for your opponent to win.
Daughters is a little bit more backstory of Zoe while also being a puzzle, since you have to do the right things to the get the true ending while avoiding danger.
Ethan must die is just a really difficult mode, if I have to be honest you probably won't touch this much. I know I didn't but maybe I'm just too bad at the game. 
Jack's 55th Birthday is a fun little game mode, and good challenge if you aim for a high score. Basically you retrieve food on the level back to Jack in the shortest amount of time possible while avoiding or killing enemies.

Aaaaand, that's all....I guess.

A very immersive survival horror experience and a step in the right direction after mainline RE started struggling with its identity. Despite being in first person, it's the closest RE has got since 3 to recreating the classic formula; you start with a handgun and a knife and you're thrown in a huge interconnected location where weird ♥♥♥♥ is happening, ammo is scarce, you progress by solving puzzles (albeit not that complicated), collecting strange keys and backtracking while something is following you for the entirety of the game.

Capcom's RE Engine which debuted with this game is a pleasure to the eyes and still holds up 4 years later, sound design is fantastically atmospheric and voice acting is some of the best in gaming, especially for the Baker family. Story is typical RE silliness and without going into spoilers too much, it's enjoyable enough, especially in the first half. Boss battles are amazing and I won't say anything for anyone who still didn't play it yet. Well, outside of the final boss, that one was a dissapointment.

The problems i have with the game is mainly the main character, Ethan, who manages to be the first bland RE protagonist after many times Capcom struck gold with RE main characters. It feels more like he's the vessel for the player instead of an actual character, but then he opens his mouth and says something mindnumbingly stupid (and not in the B-movie one liner Leon Kennedy fun way) and you're just like "eh...". He should've been a silent protagonist from the start. Other problems include the lack of enemy variety (seriously, outside the "main" monsters there are THREE types of enemies.), game falling off in the second half with a frustrating location which for me kills the replay value and an utter trash cinematic final boss which you fight by left clicking your mouse. 

Despite the said issues, it still manages to be a very solid game and probably the scariest RE so far in terms of horror alone (let's face it, RE was never scary). Atmosphere is really its strongest selling point and a return to the classic formula with a twist makes me optimistic for future games and happy that RE reclaimed its identity. As I started making this review I realized I was specifically making it for people who love RE4 and are unsure about getting their hands on this entry, because that's basically the boat I was in for a long time. RE4 is one of my favorite games ever and I was a bit unsure about trying RE7 because of how different the two looked. Although at the end of the day there are many different things between the two there's also enough similarities so that I think a person that enjoyed RE4 could easily get into this one.

In many ways RE7 takes all the best things its predecessors had to offer and distills them into a tight little package without much in the way of filler. It has an obvious emphasis on survival horror but the first person view and the very effective gunplay, as well as the boss encounters, make it so that there is still plenty of action. 

There are never any large hordes of enemies but every individual encounter still keeps you on the edge of your seat. Not to mention that the game does a great job of making you think that there could be an enemy around every corner. That classic inventory management is still here and it still tricks you into being overly careful and stingy with your bullets even though if you do so you'll eventually find yourself as ammoed up and overpowered as you would in a game like RE4.

Similarly this game starts you off feeling like a wimp with some very great horror moments but as the game progresses you realize Ethan isn't really all that frail which again takes a bit of that horror edge off and allows you to focus more on the game's action, the game even gives a pretty heavy action portion near so you can use all that ammo you were saving up.

This game is also spot on pasing and story wise. I always felt like I loved RE4's story despite it's cheesiness and over the topness but not because of it, and this game certainly proves that point. This is a much more contained and grounded story and it is all the better for it. The first two acts do a great job of getting across that pure horror vibe before the third act takes us into more of that Resident Evil territory but keeping just restrained enough so that it doesn't turn into an anime like other RE games. I think this is where the game's length also helps it. It's a pretty short game but this means there's no need to add 5 different plot twists with overly long areas that make you wish the game was coming to an end. Definitely my favorite RE story so far.

Overall everything in this game works beautifully. Besides a couple of audio glitches here and there there are only really two things that I think could have been improved: The first is the final boss fight which honestly felt more like an interactive cutscene than a boss fight, this is however solved by the DLC in my opinion, but I still think they could have handled it better. That being said, underwhelming final boss fights seem to be pretty common in RE games, even RE4 is pretty weak in this department. 

My last complaint is the enemy variety, most of the "molded" you encounter come in two basic varieties that don't really distinguish themselves and then you eventually get another two types that are a bit different to handle but don't really pop up enough. There's a couple variations of these same enemies in the dlc but it's too little too late at this point.

So my final verdict is that as an RE4 fan I really enjoyed this game. If I'm being honest I find it better in most aspects, but my nostalgia won't let me say this is my new favorite RE game just yet. I'll give them both a replay eventually and maybe I'll be more confident about that, but for now I 100% recommend it.

I originally ended up refunding this game as it was jarring on my retinas. But, given the praise of 7, recently finished 8, and being a fan of the series from the original in 1996, I wanted to give this game some proper time playing it. And it was the most miserable I've been playing a game in a long time. The game is filled with sensory anxiety. Gore, scat, and body horror are about all you'll find and I was too overwhelmed to actually feel any form of "survival", unless that's included with the dry heaving.

The game is scary by working on overloading aversions and senses while giving you a first-person field-of-view that induces tension headaches, basically making the game too hard to look at to be aware things are happening until it's too late. It actually ends up giving me the opposite effect, forcing me to disconnect entirely just to actually play the game. "Back to it's roots" and scares that aren't "cheap" as claims to it's fame make me thoroughly hate the entire internet right now. So many times all I can expect from a situation is to see a face engulfing my entire screen and poop. Just, poop, everywhere...

The first few hours I played were boss rushes that were too hard not to predict. I had watched some of the game so I do remember how a lot of the early major cutscenes played out. But I had not realized how much of the game was lacking entirely between those segments. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (also known as Biohazard 7: Resident Evil in Japan) was released in 2017 and serves as a soft-reboot and a fresh start for the long-running series. Transition of RE to action was a big success and RE5 is the most selling game in the entire series, but we can't deny that with RE6 the game had a bit of it's identity and almost abandoned everything that made it appealling in the first place. With RE7 the series tries to go back to it's roots of survival horror. But RE had also to reinvent itself for a new generation, and with the success of such horror titles like Amnesia and Outlast, Capcom decicded to take this opportunity and bring RE into the first-person view. Armed with references to such classics as Evil Dead, old slasher movies, body horror and even modern torture flicks like SAW, RE is back as a terrifying nightmare.

The story of RE7 follows Ethan Winters, who gets a message from his wife to find her somewhere in Louisiana after three years of her disappearence. Little Ethan knows, this is going to be the biggest mistake of his life, as he gets trapped in the walls of Baker residence, which serves as a home to the lovely family of cannibals and murderers, that seemingly posses supernatural abilities. Now Ethan must simply survive this nightmare and save his wife if it's possible. 
The story of RE7 is okay on the surface. What holds it back is absolute lack of any character in Ethan, which reacts to the crasiest stuff he's seen in his life with mild confusion and annoyance at most. Also, there are moments in the story that can lead to some plot-holees if you think about them long enough. The game tries to explain everything in details in various files and documents scattered around, but if you don't pay attantion to any of it won't make much sense and some of my conclusions still feel like headcannon to me. Still, you will be distracted by those details only if you explicitly look for it.

The graphics of the game are really good. The RE Engine really pushes itself to photorealism as much as possible. The characters look really detailed with impressive facial animations, although some shots will still give the effect of uncanny valley. The environments look stellar, with immense attention to detail.  Almost every element was thought of when desingning locations here. And all of it is really well optimised for how good it looks. On my PC it easily broke 100 FPS with max settings. The only problem I had was with really narrow FOV, but for survival-horror game that seems kind of intentional, you are not going to bunny-hop with 180 FOV here. 

The gameplay of RE7 is one thing that ties it to it's roots the most. As someone who experienced almost all of the RE evolution in one month I can comfortably say, that this is a decent attempt at adapting classic RE formula in current time. You walk around searching for keys and solving puzzles to progress, in between bits of progress you have to engage in combat, or avoid it if possible. Add to that also big element of inventory and resource management with weapons ammo and healing items, and you get pretty much classic RE. the main difference is in perspective. First person camera really puts you face-to-face with horrors of Baker Estate. Add to that the fact that, unlike many protagonists in the past, Ethan is just a normal guy, that is just very determined and stubborn for his own good. He doesn't have superior training of a S.T.A.R.S. operative or even a basic weapons training. Although he seems to be infected with the same virus as Bakers, which gave him pretty good resilience and extreme regeneration. 
Now, the weakest point of the gameplay is easily the combat. The guns sound and feel nice to shoot, so that's a good start. But the enemies in molded don't really do them justice. They all look like the same thing with different slight variations, regular monster, fat one, fast and annoying one, despite depicting different archetypes just look too similar to each other. And they don't react to shots very well until they are dead. There is also the problem that the main way of defending youself is a new guard mechanic, that IS effective, but really feels counter-intuitive. i don't really get how Ethan can shrug off a lot of damage by simply getting his hands up, but then again, virus superpowers maybe.
And while Baker family is a very charismatic bunch of villains, their bossfights feel underwhelming. They look cool, especially fights with Jack, the father of the family, but the mechanics in them basically boil down to either shooting all of your bullets until they are dead, or interacting with janky, half-baked mechanics that don't feel as good as they should.

But overall, I think RE7 was a big success in what it tried to do. Unfortunately, the stigma surrounding first-person horror games put off some of the fans of the series, that prefer third-person, or even return to the classic fixed cameras. But this is a great project that put RE back on track and there is plenty of potential with this new formula. And there are great discounts to this game frequently, even with complete edition, that adds a bunch of additional content, including two smaller campaigns with new mechanics and characters. This is a really good value project, that really deserves all of the support and praise it's getting. Strongly recommend.

A solid campaign and a good return to form for Resident Evil in terms of delivering solid jump scares and less action popcorn blockbuster flick sequences. The story is engaging and interesting, slowly unraveling over time to where it doesn't give too much away at once and instead keeps you dangling. You definitely have to suspend your disbelief on a lot of things (like, y'know a severed hand that somehow gets stapled back on and it works normal?), but the game makes sure you can't dwell on it because you've got too much to keep track of. 

Combat feels satisfying, for most of the game you're forced to straddle the line between ammo conservation and fighting. There were moments where I'd find myself having very little ammo and trying to count how many shots it would take to kill each enemy based on headshots, and then there were other times where I went into places like Rambo. 

Exploration is fun and rewarding -- I HIGHLY recommend looking through every room you can and looking for any items you can. There are some things that might not make sense right away, but when you figure it out they're worth the effort. Part of me was frustrated with everything that I missed in game, but what I did find made the game all the more enjoyable.

I would highly recommend playing this before Resident Evil: Village to get a feel for the direction the games are taking as well as a comprehensive story for Ethan and Mia. Plus it's worth the money! :)

Plot start:
The RE7 story begins with a new protagonist, Ethan Winters. Three years ago, his wife, Mia, went missing, but suddenly a letter comes from her name: she says that she is alive and asks to take her home. This time, the old Baker mansion in the middle of the endless swamps of Louisiana acts as a "special meeting place". On the same day, Ethan takes off on the road and goes to the aid of his beloved - after all, such stories always end well, right?

Atmosphere of the game:
The first hours pass unforgettably, the old house in the swamps draws in its atmosphere, frightens with rustles and inhabitants, and the number of problems and threats continues to grow. Grandfather Jack, who has gone, will chase you around the house until you kill him. The house itself has a very narrow space, which creates a feeling of fear, which is very pleasing. There is also a basement in the house, in which there are creatures that suddenly come out and scare. After we run away from Jack's house, we get to the mother-insect, who will be tougher than his grandfather. grandmother's whole house is teeming with flies and spiders that will bother you in every possible way, and the house itself is very creepy. And the last of the Baker family is Lucas. His house is full of traps, and he himself offers to solve riddles. Unlike previous locations, Lucas' house is not so scary. In the second part of the game, the action takes place on a destroyed ship, in which the biological weapon "Evelina" is hidden. The ship is teeming with monsters and mysteries, and the atmosphere is no worse than the Baker house.

Characters:
Jack Baker - The head of the Baker family, a sadist and generally a very cruel person who wore a manic smile most of the time and is ready to attack anyone who makes him angry. He often and violently swears with his son, Lucas, even cutting off his hand. Upon encountering Jack's original personality in the Hive Cell, he regrets his actions and says that he would never harm him if not for Evelina's influence.

Margaret Baker - Almost nothing is known about Margaret's past, except that she married Jack Baker and gave birth to a son from him - Lucas. Despite the fact that their family was considered quiet, Lucas was called "bad blood." In 2014, their family mysteriously disappears. Some time later, local residents began to see ghosts near the abandoned house.

Mia Winters (Main Character) is a former Connection employee who worked on a covert project to create Evelina, acting as her guardian, hiding her real job from her husband Ethan. After she was presumed dead in 2014, the Baker family found Mia, who lived with them in isolation until she was found again in mid-2017.

Ethan Winters (Main Character) is a former American systems engineer and biological weapon. Winters was infected with a pathogen called Mold during the 2017 Dalvey incident. He and his wife Mia were rescued by Blue Umbrella soldiers, but were in danger and isolated in B.S.A.A.

Zoe Baker - Zoe lived with her family on a plantation in Dulvey, Louisiana. She was exposed to Evelina's "gift", but somehow learned of a neurotoxin cure. Unlike the rest of the Bakers, Zoe was unable to gain control of Evelyn's mind despite being infected. She refused to participate in the murderous activities of the family, choosing instead to isolate herself from them in her trailer in the yard. Zoe tried to heal herself and flee several times, helping the victims abducted by her family, but none of them survived.

Lucas Baker - Referring to Andre's words, Lucas was "bad blood" in the family. But despite his rebelliousness and terrible nature, he was still a very capable inventor, for which he received awards that can be seen in his room. It was also mentioned that he received a 259-piece mosaic from his mother for agreeing to undergo a head scan. As indicated in Lucas's diary, it is likely that he was already mentally unstable long before he met Evelyn.

Evelina - A ten-year-old girl who, due to rapid aging, began to look like an elderly woman in a wheelchair. She is wearing a white suit and a red scarf. He doesn't contact the character in any way, but uses his abilities directly to control infected people, forcing them to see hallucinations in the form of ten-year-old Evelina, infect new people and create a "family" out of them.

For this being my first Resident Evil game, i must say that this was a great introduction to the series for me.
The Story follows Ethan Winters, a normal individual who had just received a message about his missing wife Mia and goes to look for her, when in fact he is lured into the Baker household and must fight against the monstrosities that lurk within. The characters a well voice acted and have their own unique personality traits that make them stand out. For example, Jack Baker is the "twisted family man" and is the brute force of the family while Lucas plays with the psychological side of the game. The story itself is decent and keeps the game moving at a steady pace. 
The setting of the Baker estate is really immersive as a twisted labyrinth with many secrets that lie within and the many enemies that lurk around each corner. My personal favourite area was the main house as there were loads of places to look around such as the basement that held a mortuary and gives you the introduction to the Molded, to the what should be baron but warm interiors of the living room and the pool room. It gave the impression that the devs really care for this area especially. The courtyard of the establishment serves as a great intermediary between the different locations that the player must go through. The lake house really feels infested with all sorts of creatures and captures that essence of Marguerite in its entirety with bugs nests laid all across the area and it being dimly lit in a disgusting yellow undertone. The Guest House work really well at easing the player into the themes of the game before it really kicks off, but i feel that it was unnecessary for it to be returned to the last part of the game. For some the boat area is their least favourite, however i quite enjoyed it as it gave the player the openness of the many floors to venture while having the claustrophobic feel of the tight corridors, especially when enemies were within them. My least favourite places would have to be the Lucas section and the Mines as they are very short experiences and were not really given any character like the areas that had came before it. 
Graphically, this game looks amazing with the settings, weapons, and characters looking really realistic as possible. However, the animation for the characters talking could have been worked upon as dialog would not sync with their mouth movement. The atmosphere is spot on and really make the player feel like their in an unknown, disgusting territory and are on edge for what might come next. 
Sounds in this game work really well as guns, objects and something as simple as walking on different terrain feel authentic. The audio for the grievers was really well done, giving them this low snarl that fits well with their character. I think for me the gun sounds were just satisfying from the reloads to aiming down sights. 
In terms of gameplay, it really captures the idea of being a survival horror game. With player being in the role of Ethan who has had no experience with guns, aiming in itself is hard at the start but the more and more you progress through the game, the better you become at aiming and i really liked this ideas as it felt that Ethan himself was getting better at shooting. When it comes to items, you really have to be careful on what you carry in your inventory and how much ammo you will use as everything counts. There have been many times where i would use up bullets when i could have saved them for either another area of even a boss fight. It really make the player think about what the best strategy is and enforces the survival horror motif, however it losses this essence towards the end of the game as the player is essentially fed ammo and consumables, becoming a cake walk rather than an intense experience. In terms of enemies, the Molded are the main type with their being 4 different Molded with there being the standard, Molded with shield, 4 legged Molded and the Big, Chunky Molded. While there is variety within the Molded themselves, it had gotten really repetitive seeing the same masses coming at me one by one. The Bakers are great with the inability to kill them until their boss battles. The only way to survive against them is by shooting them in the head and staggering them to give the player enough time to try and escape, making the player feel insignificant in stopping the tyrants that are the Bakers. The boss fights are great pieces from the chainsaw fight with Jack, to the abandoned house fight with Marguerite. However, the final fight with Eveline is really underwhelming. There is a great variety when it comes to weapons and resources that the player can use to their disposal while keeping in mind of how scarce they might be. The inventory system is well done with the players having to consider what is essential and what they can either discard or leave in the box. The collectables of the antique coins and the Mr everywhere's give the player more reason to look around every nook and cranny. Finally, the crafting system is ok as there is not really a lot to craft, however it is a really useful feature when it comes to really intense moments. 
Overall, Resident Evil 7 really captures the true essence of what a survival horror game should be and i would highly recommend this entry in the series to both veterans and newcomers.

[b][u]The Good[/u][/b]
• A much more serious story compared the really silly stories of the previous games.

• Graphics are really impressive, particularly for how well the game runs on lower-end hardware.

• Map design and creepy atmosphere are really well done.

• The game does a pretty good job of making you feel anxious/uneasy at many points throughout the story.

• HDR lighting is really good if you have everything set up correctly. One of the few games that isn't afraid to have the game be really dark.

• Madhouse difficulty is really fun. It's just the right difficulty and gives you just enough ammo to get through it. It also changes the way to progress through the game enough to make a second play-through fun and interesting.


[b][u]The Bad[/u][/b]
• For most of the game's bosses it is unclear what you need to do to defeat them. It is often a matter of trial-and-error, just dying several times to figure out what the game wants you to do.

• The game has an adaptive difficulty which makes the game easier every time you die. This can very easily destroy your save game by making the game completely trivial as you die several times trying to figure out the method of solving a puzzle or defeating a boss. There is no way to disable this terrible, game-ruining feature.

• As with all Resident Evil games, your inventory is extremely limited which results in about half of your play time just being you running back to an item box constantly to store items you've picked up or retreive items that you had no way of knowing you'd need. There is absolutely no logical reason for the inventory to be so ridiculously limited.

• The "scary" elements of the game are typically nothing more than cheap "jump scares" and scenes that are so ridiculous to the point that it's just impossible to be immersed into the game at all.

• Cutscenes cannot be skipped. Cutscenes related to boss fights need to be watched through entirely every time you attempt to fight them.

• As with all of the recent Resident Evil games, there is an awful black vignette around the outside of the screen that is intented to make the game look darker/scarier, but it fails to do that and instead just makes the game look uglier. Third-party tools are required to remove it.

I played on an xbox controller. The controls are smooth and intuitive. The story is engaging the whole way through. I found Ethan to be a more interesting protagonist than previous RE games, specifically because he wasn't a combat trained military/law enforcement veteran. His dialogue is usually confused and freaked out. There's no tough guy one-liners or stoic heroism. When I as a player do something stupid, or run away to the nearest safe zone, it seems like something a guy in over his head would do.

The Bakers are absolutely the stars of the show. They're the best RE villains in the franchise so far (yes, even better than the Giant Vamp Mommy Dom from Village). Locked in the house and escaping from Jack is brilliantly done. Escaping from Mom Baker is probably the weakest sequence, but it was still full of creepy ambiance and body horror. 

The game loses some steam at the end. It feels like it's trying to go for a big action movie finish, but the controls and environment don't really support that. It felt more like slow paced a hunting simulator (the way I played it). The final boss is mostly just pulling the trigger and waiting through cut scenes. 

Critiques of the end aside, the entire Baker compound is a masterclass of environment design. They really nailed the run down swamp house feel. Just walking around the environment is creepy and unsettling. They also managed to make all the RE weirdness (like special keys, and weapons stashed all over the place) make perfect sense. 

For anyone new to the franchise, you don't need to know anything about the previous games to understand this one. It's a great point to jump into the series.

RE7 is a great example of a survival horror done right. With appealing grafic and great atmosphere it is a great comeback to the franchises roots of survival horror genre.

[h1]The atmosphere and map design[/h1]
The game takes place at an old family estate in Louisiana which is in swamp area. The game shows the estate as abandoned, rundown that is full of bugs. This estetic of the old estate will be present through the whole game while bugs flooded areas will still exist there that replace them in some areas (equally as disgusting ;) ) to keep the game immersion of  a complete rundown. The areas are designed in a way that there are 3 areas connected with a hub (in this case yard). In order to get to another area you need to get a key item to open doors or you need to solve various puzzles in order to progress from one area to another. There is a bit of backtracking (most notable being getting 2 keycards) but its mostly fine since it adds a twist to it and is not overused. My only complaint about the map design is a boat section because of how confusing it is at first and the amount of backtracking in it is a bit overdone. Overall the atomsphere does good job at keeping you immersed, while I would not say that the game is scary, it caught me off guard a few times what I do like.

[h1]Gameplay loop, combat and puzzles[/h1]
Gamplay and combat are heavily focused on avoiding enemy attacks and conserving ammo (especially on Madhouse difficulty) in addition to searching areas for all resources you can find because resources are limited. Aiming for the crit spots is a key. You can also melle your enemies with a pocket knife (but i did not find it to be necessary at any point during any of my playtroughs because resources are not that limited). In addition to resources there are notes, upgrades, 18 antique coints and collectables hidden trough game. Antique coints serve as currency to buy upgrades in hub area and magnum (Upgrades to more max hp and faster reloading and weapon handling). Puzzles are interesting and can be tricky at first but overall they are rather simple, which is also a shame, and one of my complaints about the game, because I would like some bigger variety of puzzles outside of Projector shadow ones. Only notable puzzle is Lucas escape room. The majority of the game you fight bosses in which each fight is unique (most notable one being Margaret) with several "normal" enemies that are called The Molded. Molded are black creatures created out of E-type virus mold. There are several types of Molded to keep gameplay and combat diverse, most common and the easiest to avoid and kill being Normal molded. They have 2 attacks and both can be dodged or blocked (if you block you still do take damage which is reduced) with relatives ease. The 4 legged ones should just be killed asap (1 pistol headshot and they are dead) and for fat ones you use all that you have to kill them before you get cornered by them (grenade laucher, shotgun combo do the trick). While Molded are not bad addition as an obstacles you ecnounter in order to progress through the game, the boat section of the game where you fight only them is pretty meh overall. That is because you lose all your saved resources saved through the game by this point and cannont acces them until a later point in the game. Also becasue you fight a lot of enemies in sections that you have already been through, in addition this sections hallways are narrow so it forces you to fight enemies which can become a slog and not even Madhouses fixes this area repetitive nature. Salt mine doesnt have this issues as bad as boat considering that in salt mines you are constantyl going forward widout backtracking. Also the last boss of the game really does suck when compared to the ones you fought before, actually I legit think the whole fight is scripted so even if you dont shoot a single bullet until you get Albert with anti bioweapon rounds that you wont die. 

[h1]Invetory managment, weapon variety, QoL and replayability[/h1]
Managing your invetory plays a key part in this game considering that at beginign its very limited and only way to upgrade it is to progress through game. Thankfully, there is a stash in safe areas which lets you depoist items that you dont need in it. You can also always return to area where you forgot to pick up something or had to leave it because your invenotry is full. Crafting system is simple and fine, and also helps you manage your resources better. There are 2 types of pistol (3 if you beated game once) which has 2 types of bullets (1 is stronger then other), 2 shotguns, home made flamehtrower, grenade launcher with 2 greande types, SMG and the Magnum (if you collect enough antique coints to buy it). While different Shotguns and pistols have some diffrences in stats (for example, startign pistol has bigger mag then Colt, but does less dmg, while Albert has higest dmg per shot it only has 3 bullets in mag and slow rate of fire which makes it less appealing for bosses). Idea of each weapon having some advantage over other there is very clear destinction of which weapon is supperior to its counterpart (Double barreled shotgun is in every situation better then pump-action one, flamethrower is uselles on Molds because it takes too much ammo to kill them etc.). Now to talk a bit about game performance and bugs, overall in my 3 main game playthroughts I did not run in any performance issues (was on max settings outside of shadow quality) outside of 1 bug that i manage to find fix on forums that your FPS gets capped and 13 for some reason. During the game itself only bug I encountered is double damage bug which sometimes occurs if you play the game on above 30 FPS (basically you get attacked once but it counts as you were attacked twice). Overall bugs did not ruin my overall experience of the game since they were easily fixable but they were kinda annoying. To wrap up this section Ill talk about replayability and how game encourages it. Basically once you beat the game on any difficulty for the first time you unlock several items to help you on your next playtrough. You also unlock specific item for your next playtrough if you find all hidden collectables and then there is also one if you finish game under 4h. All those items are permanent unlocks that you can get for finishing game and use them on any playthrough (only thing you must be able to do is survie until 1st stash in game). They will also help you greatly in your Madhouse playthrought (if you finish game on Madhouse you unlock infinite ammo).

[h1]Madhouse difficulty[/h1]
In this section I will specifically focus on Madhouse difficulty changes compared to normal game (which are not simply just you take more dmg and enemies and bosses have more hp). Firstly, most obovious change is that you need cassette tapes to save the games which are limited (also you get only few auto saves). Secondly, you have 33 Antique coints and none of them shares a place with 18 from normal mode. Also you can now buy 6 items with coints instead of 3. You also can not buy all items. Furthermore, in order to progress the game at all from 1st area (Bakers house) you need to find at least 3 coints. Furthermore, enemie placements are different (so you cant just speed through the game). Lastly, most weapons, repair kits and objective items are hidden at different places so you cant just go take them at the place from previous playthrough. For example I managed to save a huge stockpile of ammo for Margaret and thinking I was well off with my resources only to end up killing her with 20 normal pistol bullets left. Jack is also much faster now (if he spots you, unless you hide, he will catch you because you can not outrun him. Overall, Madhouse was very enjoyable experience for me and the game felt fresh despite it being my 3rd playthrough.


To wrap things up I absolutely recomment this game to anyone who likes horror games and peopel who enjoy a good challenge.

I wasn't sure if I felt this was a Resident Evil game or not until I realized it has the quintessential RE fault.
A stellar first half, and a just passable second half. Yup, it's Resident Evil.
Thankfully the DLC gave us a bit more to chew on, and it was enough to sate me.

Still, I am glad Capcom moved away from it in Village and the Remakes.
This game has great atmosphere, and probably one of the more interesting (and almost totally self-contained) stories in the series. However, in terms of gameplay... 

It doesn't have the interesting puzzles of the classics, and only very minor concerns about surviving, and it doesn't have the fun gunplay of the post RE4 entries, either.

I guess Capcom really just wanted to tell the story this time and take a few notes from stuff like Amnesia and Alien: Isolation in terms of using the first-person perspective to induce a sense of dread, and fair enough, it kinda worked, though it was inferior to either of those games to me.

Amnesia had better puzzles, Alien had better survival (and a god-tier atmosphere).

RE7 was... an interesting, but IMO ultimately very flawed attempt.

I still had fun with it and enjoyed the extra modes quite a bit.

Best Resident Evil game I've played so far with the contenders being 0, 4, 5 and 6. 

The narrative for the first two thirds is compelling and even with a few letdowns it ends up being a generally cool tale. The last third is weak because of the forced "Resident Evil(tm)" crap. I genuinely can't imagine people caring about fake, badly written biological mumbo-jumbo of how the virus totally interacts with the patient's nanocells. However, the Baker family are generally great with the father of the household being the most memorable. The non-canonical ending that I got was completely non-sensical however and literally none of the story is built for that ending. It's weird that they even tried to include a second ending when they had no plans of making it even decent. 

This game managed to be compelling with its scares, surprisingly enough. Getting punished with actual gameplay consequences through mainly resource management was great to see after the boring punishment of "Play the game more" from Alien: Isolation. Also the familiar setting of a decrepit and aging house is relatively relatable probably to most people. Same goes with the weird family. You'll have seen someone unsettling, some place that's just creepy. It works. Then of course the Resident Evil(tm) part comes in and kind of just ruins it, but it could be worse. 

Graphically this game's great and also a bit of a mess. The game looks like a found footage movie without actually doing the formula and it feels just insanely grimy and dirty. However if you're planning to stream the game, just beware that the game really screws with the brightness of the game to such an extent that you'd think that your screen is turned into a sheet of white paper when looking at the Steam Overlay or the actual stream footage. Window Capture worked to fix it, but it's insane to see how unusable this method of brightness makes anything you're trying to use on the side. 

Action-wise it's also very solid. Everyone's beatable and you'll never be in a situation where the enemy's unknowingly invincible while you're supposed to escape or something. It's just too damn appreciated in a game about resource management. Taking control of the fear is one thing, but also taking control of the logical mechanics of the game is also a must here. I'm glad it's the way it is. One small issue I have is the fact that it feels like your attacks have little impact other than preset stagger animations. Resident Evil 6 had great headshot damage visuals compared to this and it's just very disappointing to see they didn't keep it going. Regardless that's a minor issue and a nitpick mainly.

So far, Resident Evil 7 is the closest it can get to a grounded, immersive, scary and atmospheric survival horror experience, when we talk about modern RE games (if we do not include Resident Evil 2 Remake).

I, from a personal taste, was not a big fan of the environment and the general geographical area RE7 took place in, however, that's just my personal taste and, for what it was, it was extremely well done. Also, didn't really enjoy the story much and the main protagonist, but the story was never the main selling point of Resident Evil, so, do not let that hinder you by any stretch of the imagination. If you can look past some of the cliche, corny and cheesy horror segments, you will be left with an almost excellent, grounded, atmospheric survival horror experience.
 
I do not recommend standard difficulty, however, as I found it to be too easy and, if possible, start with the madhouse difficulty, you will struggle at the start, but the experience is worth it. 

One other thing to consider: Outside of the main story and one free DLC, there is basically no content at all and after you finish the game on madhouse difficulty, there really isn't much desire or incentive to replay the game (unless you are a very hardcore RE fan). I haven't bought other DLCs, therefore, I cannot say if I recommend them or not.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is not an excellent, but almost excellent representation of what RE was all about and what RE should be in the future - grounded, atmospheric, scary, immersive, dark and beautiful survival horror experience. It would have been great, if the game stayed away from some of the cliche, corny and cheesy horror movie story elements and didn't have lame protagonist (in my opinion), but again, story was never the main selling point of Resident Evil. 

A very solid 8.5/10. Absolutely buy it and enjoy it! I only subtract 1,5 points because: What I mentioned about some story elements above; Standard difficulty is not balanced (too easy, resources are scattered everywhere, etc. This can really mess up that survival experience on the first playthrough, when you first experience the game); Could use some more content and scale that comes with the base game (for example, more fun unlockables, extra free game modes like mercenaries, unlockable character models, weapon models, concept arts, etc.). As a side note, puzzles needed balance as well, as they were astonishingly and unsuitably easy.

P.S. I wish Resident Evil Village deepened the survival horror gameplay, aspects and general tendency of Resident Evil 7 and not go into over the top, unsuitable and ridiculous territory in almost every aspect, but it already happened.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a great horror game and an excellent return to form for the Resident Evil series. All right it's time we talk about the story. 

Ethan Winters is just a regular man not a soldier, not a mercenary just a good old-fashioned Joe. But his life is going to be thrown into chaos when he received an email from his wife Mia who disappeared three years ago telling him to come to Louisiana, so now Ethan must find her but doing so maybe more than this regular guy bargained for.

Now the likes, the story is pretty good with plenty of nice twists and great scary moments in it, the game also has lots of references to Classic works of hard like Texas Chainsaw Massacre and The Hills Have Eyes. The atmosphere in the game is pretty good definitely spooky as you wander around the creepy house and Beyond it. The DLCs are also pretty good and fun but I'll talk more in depth in the review for them.

The graphics/levels are very good definitely both beautiful and disturbingly creepy and gross. The enemies/bosses are pretty interesting; while the molded are not exactly the most creative monsters in the series they're still somewhat interesting.

The bosses are pretty interesting like Jack he was pretty tough, plus I love how it's not advised to fight him you have to run away and hide but you can still fight him in a pinch if you have too, reminds me a bit of Clock Tower.

The characters were also very interesting like Ethan I found him a nice protagonist and some of his dialogue is fun to listen to but I do have to wonder why he didn't just call the police when he first saw scary stuff, I also like Lucius that guy is such a magnificent and fun bastard with very funny dialogue.

The games puzzles are good nothing too hard they were pretty fair. The music in the game is pretty good especially the ending song.

Now the dislikes, well the one thing I really dislike is that when you open your inventory the game doesn't pause, the game still goes on even with an enemy trying to attack you. I found that really annoying.

Now with that said Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a great horror game and an excellent return to form for the Resident Evil series. With a pretty good story with great references to other works of Horror, very good graphics/levels and good puzzles.

So if you were disappointed in Resident Evil 5 and 6 don't worry this game is a great return to horror.

Disclaimer: While I do play a fair share of horror games, I am by no means a longtime Resident Evil fan. I started with 5, jumped to 6, then RE2R, then to 4, and only now have I played 7. Ergo, take everything I'm about to say with a grain of salt. 

Both my partner and my best friend decry this game's switch to a first person perspective. Speaking personally, I can't say I really agree. REVII's main goal, in my mind, is to instill a feeling of intense discomfort and fear in you, and primarily achieves this through an expert use of claustrophobia and incredible sound design, two facets that would be harmed if the game was portrayed in third person. Crawling through moldy ducts, wading in swamps with rotten floorboards overhead, and most especially getting up close and personal with the list of enemies you'll be taking out along the way, are all made severely more impactful due to you never leaving your player character's head. I haven't played VIII, so I can't say how first-person works there, but in VII's fantastic return to horror, I feel like the change in perspective was a stroke of genius. 

Unfortunately, VII does put its best foot forward first, and never quite manages to recapture that quality. The first two hours of this game are absolutely platinum in terms of spook factor, yet the more you arm yourself and, in my case, hoard resources, the less threatening the game becomes, and as such, the less scared you are. Even so, VII does its best to keep a strong grip on the flavor of terror by inventive uses of hallucinations and boss battles that never overstay their welcome, and provide both momentary reprieves from the sensation of power beyond reproach, and from the hordes of same-looking mobs. 

VII stumbles in two key ways, the lackluster enemy roster being the most prominent. In the entire game, you will encounter only four enemy types, only one of which acts in any truly distinguishable way from the rest. While this is far from irredeemable for so short a game, it is nonetheless baffling, considering how truly incredible the enemy variety was in RE4, 5, and 6. While it might be silly to ask for Spanish knight zombies to run around with shields in a Louisiana household, a bit more inspiration should've gone into sprucing up the enemy encounters to help them uplift the game rather than drag it down.

The second flaw is the final encounter. While every other boss fight is memorable and engaging, the last one is nothing short of hilarious in how on-rails it is. The opportunity and form was there for a large-scale encounter, a fireworks display to bring in the credits, but instead, you are lead along a singular trying thread that doesn't let the game shine as brightly as it did half an hour prior. 

With both those flaws having been described, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to any fan of horror. Go in blind, if you can. It's short, unsettling, and completely fresh. Absolutely worth the asking price, even in launch, Resident Evil VII is the origin of Capcom's redemption arc, and it was a dawn well worth waiting for.

[h1]Resident Evil[/h1]
RE7 understands on a fundamental level why the first Resident Evil worked so well. Many people get lost in the minutia of the fixed camera angles and specific gameplay elements. Resident Evil 1 was so good because it took control away from the player and kept putting the player in near "no win" situations. All items in the game were limited and enemies didn't drop anything. If you killed a zombie you used up some of your finite supply of bullets to only temporarily remove a threat. The first Resident Evil game was survival horror to a Tee.  

Resident Evil 7 understands this and is a phenomenal survival horror experience. Both making the player feel terror while also letting them grow and progress so they don't always feel helpless. Resident Evil 7 understands what it wants to be and does a splendid job of it. They made a lot of changes in this game, most obvious among them being the first person camera, but they were all done in service to that vision. Survival Horror. 

This may be the best Survival Horror experience on the market.

NOTE: I played it after Resident Evil Village.
----------------------------------------------------------------
Honestly, I can't recommend it, it just plays like the worst version of Village in terms of everything.

It starts intriguing, but falls short towards the end and becomes a chore that you just want to finish already.

It seems to follow the same formula as Village:

- You play as Ethan Winters.

- You're going to search after your lost wife (Like the lost daughter, in the village)

- You get into a creepy unknown forest.

- You find out that the people in this location have gone crazy and are cut from any sense of normalcy.

- You get trapped in a house, you need to find a way out (like the castle in the village)

- You start by killing all the main antagonists, one by one, to gain individual parts of a mutated body separated into pieces they hold on to each, to create a serum (Like Rose's parts)

- An antagonist (Lucas) plays games for entertainment on your behalf, talking to you through big speakers, unleashing enemies at you, and so on. (Like Heisenberg's games)

- You question whether your wife is bad, for performing questionable acts, she dies for a short while (like in village)

- The main antagonist (Eveline) takes a form of a side character (The grandma) which follows you around the entire game (Like the old hag, as Miranda)

- You realize your wife is good again, it wasn't her fault, external influences gave you this negative expression up until now, she is still your sweet wife.

- You go through a very action-based part where most of what you do is shoot repetitive enemies with high-end weapons, to give the player a sense of overcoming the threat and satisfaction or whatnot

- You have a final boss fight where everything becomes chaotic and out of control, you somehow win.

- Chris is your savior once again after doing everything alone, to give you a sense that the nightmare is over and is under control and the entire world is aware of the horrors you went through

For me, only the start was worth it, found the Baker's house pretty intriguing, but as the game goes, the quality just drops and drops until it is not even fun or anything anymore.

In my opinion, the story is pretty damn shallow as well, and it doesn't develop further than:

"Blank Slate protagonist, wife lost, must find wife, creepy location, crazy family, wife bad? escape location, wife infected, find parts for a vaccine, wife good, a creepy girl is the cause for the craziness, the creepy girl just wanted a family and is misunderstood, good solider savior saves the day

I did not find the OST or audio design to be anything special.

Art around the house is pretty impressive but the rest is just gloomy black smeared textures and boring grey industrial settings, the more "wild" parts that are supposed to show some nature are very blurry and uninspired, full of 2D sprites and lacking details overall.

Can't recommend it at full price, especially after playing the sequel, also the main story is very very short. (more so than village, which some people complained about)

I'd say It is a worthwhile experience if you come without expectations in advance, perhaps it will have a more fresh feel to it.

Edit: Changed To Positive, Thinking back, It at least grabbed me enough to the end, I've also played most of the extra DLCs which added a little more value, grab in a sale if you're interested.

Resident Evil 7 changes direction from previous games. It goes back to its survival horror foundations: puzzle solving, exploration and avoiding enemies instead of confronting them. 

From the sickly yellowed colour pallet, the American gothic seclusion, the idols made from bones and animal parts all the way to the decrepit family members who are wheeled around like vicarious, unsettling sentinels, it’s all in there. The Baker family dinner scene in the opening portion of the game was borrowed almost entirely from the film,"The Texas Chainsaw Massacre"(1974) and is used to introduce you to the warped menaces you’d be charged with escaping.

In Resident Evil 7, your first persistent menace is Jack Baker, the inhumanly-strong, seemingly unstoppable, wall-smashing patriarch of the Baker family. As he stalks you he calls out, dimly aware of your location and revelling with childish glee as you cower in the corner. His transformation to Leatherface is complete when, surrounded by the butchered remains of his victims, he fires up a chainsaw and you go head-to-head in a makeshift morgue.

If you’ve never played Resident Evil games before and you’re a fan of the horror genre, go out and buy RE7 immediately. Either way you’re a winner; I really can’t recommend it any more highly. Grab a Jill sandwich, some green herbs, and show off your master unlocking skills… Survival horror is back.

I love how it is simultaneously a Resident Evil sequel that still has story elements from previous games, and yet it feels complete as its own game separate from the franchise - both in story and in gameplay. My first playthrough had me gripped from start to finish, even in the second half of the game where it is arguably weaker than the first half. The horror in this game can be truly terrifying at times, yet campy and fun enough to not give you nightmares afterwards. The perspective change made this game far more immersive than other Resident Evil games I've played, and I can only imagine how intense it must be on a first playthrough in VR (please Sony...)

I don't want to give away too many specifics about what this game entails, much of it is said in other reviews and videos about the game anyways (and its been out for 4 years now so most of the cats are out of the bag). And I feel that the less you know going in, the more tense the game is and that combination of tension from the horror and action is what makes this game so engaging for me. Mechanically, its strong and feels great to play. I always felt powerful enough to fight back yet under-powered enough to always play carefully to avoid death - especially on Madhouse. Madhouse has some surprises for you though, so all I'll say about that is that its a wonderfully stressful challenge that can bring back some of the horror that's lost on subsequent playthroughs.

Through my on-going horror kick, this has easily become one of my favorite survival horror games, and on to be one of my favorite games of all time. Its tight design and mechanics, great horror atmosphere and homages, and its compelling story make this a fantastic game. You won't regret it!

05-10-2021:
I'm about 13 hours or so into Resident Evil 7 (Steam) and think it's awesome.

RE7 feels like like it has 3 real parts to it: old-school survival-horror game; walking sim; and 1st person perspective game.

It feels like it's part old-school survival-horror game, just like the old Silent Hill games and RE games...where you need to conserve ammo; more methodical & slow-paced in the actual combat when aiming, shooting, and moving; solve some puzzles; and more psychological in the horror here.

Also feels like this game's also part walking sim here, too...as you will need to look at items you pick-up in the game-world up close; rotate them read what's on the Lore; open it or crack it open; etc etc.

All of this, while in the new 1st person perspective; I'm really enjoying it all in 1st person perspective, as it feels more intense & up-close and personal here, too.

05-12-2021:
Finished-up the Campaign for RE7 (base-game). Some thoughts, after spending around 15.3 hours with it in total, according to Steam.

While I didn't mention performance before, I really should mention both performance & graphics quality here. This game was easily running at 1080p at 240fps, which I didn't need - so I capped it and was running maxed-out at 120fps. It never budged below 120fps, running like an absolute top. And this was all meanwhile it was looking as great & awesome as it does, both artistically and technically...without even having Ray-Tracing support here.

This is one of the more terrifying & memorable games in not just RE history, but also gaming history - yes, in all of its grotesque & explicit violence and horror, this evokes things of often disgust & shock. It was a feeling to me that was unlike many horror games here, as this was often giving me vibes of Deliverance, Hannibal, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, and Wrong Turn; sick & chilling vibes that I'd often feel more so in movies of that sort than in game. Pretty much, it doesn't get much more psychological, sicker and disgusting than this, when it comes to game - and this game can & will deliver more shocks, chills & thrills than most games ever have.

For the story here: Ethan Winters - who is who the player plays as, during most of this game and experience - goes to Louisiana. Winters does go down to the Bayou, to find his wife Mia. She went missing and he's to go find her, running into a House and a lot of swamp-land, where a family known as The Baker Family resides. Of course, all of that is really just part of the story, as that's only part & sum of the 1st 3/4ths of the base-game.

Onto the final parts of the game, the game takes a drastic turn, into the last section of the game. Most of the game is survival-horror and whatnot, namely in its 1st 3/4ths - but it becomes more action-y in the end and explains more as to why what happened & caused the first 3/4ths of the game, its story, and characters to...well, go the way that it did. 

With a lot of Lore in the game-world having plot, story, and whatnot...especially in the last 1/4th of the game, where it all really ties its bigger picture and more of a grand scenario into the very personal & horrific story for the 1st 3/4ths - of course, it's all loaded with some twists, turns, revelations & whatnot. While the 1st 3/4ths is fantastic for both the rebirth & evolution of survival-horror, the last 1/4th brings & re-welcomes us to that action that we've seen in the last few RE games (i.e. RE 4, 5 & 6; and even some parts of RE: Revelations 1 & 2) all while in 1st person.

Nothing short of awesome & out-standing, RE7 delivers in all fronts, delivering one of the best survival-horror games & most personal of the RE games in the 1st 3/4ths of the game and also one of the best conclusions & tie-ins with a much bigger picture & grander scale with the last 1/4th of the game, going out with an absolute bang...and then some.

When first person shooters came out, there was a sort of immersiveness about them that wasn’t found in many other games. They felt like a sneak preview of virtual reality. The more I’ve played, though, the more I’ve gotten used to the feeling and it isn’t so special anymore. Playing this game recaptured that feeling of what made FPS games immersive while also managing to reignite my old survival horror flame (a passion that died out around RE3 or so). 

If you don’t enjoy the fear, desperation, and scarcity of the survival horror genre, then this game and its shift to first-person won’t change that. However, if you enjoyed games like Alien: Isolation, System Shock 1 or 2, or Sir, You are Being Hunted, then this might be a good choice.
