Ethan himself is a bit of a generic protagonist out to rescue his sweet heart, but his self-aware dialogue makes him likeable (in particular, I got a solid laugh out of one character quoting Evil Dead 2 and Ethan disagreeing with the assessment.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I would probably 100% it if I wasn’t about to play the next game in the series. If you liked the previous Resident Evil games, you’ll probably enjoy this new take on the formula if you don’t mind the first-person switch (which I love!). If you haven’t traditionally been a big RE fan, then this one might just be the one that changes your mind.

Let me say first that I am a pretty decent fan of Resident Evil, I own every major release, and a lot of the games I own on almost every system they are available, so I have a lot of ground covered when it comes to this series. That being said, Resident Evil 7 is a game I put off playing for a while, and put finishing off even longer. Before I bought it I was still hurt by Resident Evil Survivor on PS1, and although *MOST* of the Resident Evil Light-gun games were decent, I didn't have much hope for this, not only because of that but also because Capcom isn't known for FPS games. Not only do they not have many successful FPS titles under their belt, but most shooters they come out with end up having bad gun-play and weird control schemes for FPS games. But gosh darn, they did it. They finally made a FPS game that isn't so mediocre or bad that I want to stop halfway through (However, I DID stop halfway through! Why, you ask? BECAUSE I WAS SPOOKED!).

Resident Evil 7 is a NON LINEAR Survival Horror game that tries to call back to the older style of Resident Evil games. This game distances itself away from the more linear style of Survival Horror Shooters we had been getting with games like Resident Evil 4 and Dead Space, and tries to focus more on the non linear large map based designs of old school survival horror games. You won't be walking down straight corridors all the time in a linear fashion. Instead you will be exploring a open but limited environment trying to find keys for doors to unlock new rooms and areas, while also solving puzzles.

So, you play as a guy named Ethan looking for his wife on the Baker Family plantation. Who are the Baker Family? They are a family of southerners who have been infected by something of unknown origin and have been driven mad, yet they also now possess superhuman strength and regenerative abilities. Don't expect to be chased by every family member, but that doesn't mean most of them don't get enough to do.

While exploring and puzzle solving you will have to fight strange creatures. They have a few variable types but overall for a resident evil game the enemy types are SEVERELY lacking. In fact, I would say that's the biggest problem with this game. Resident Evil is a series known for great enemy variation. In fact, OG survival horror as a genre is known for that. But this game only has about 5 types of enemies besides the baker family the entire game, and most of them are way too samey.

Now, back to what I said earlier about now trusting this game previously on the basis its a FPS:

The controls are good, both with controller and mouse and keyboard. However, you can really tell this game is not developed by FPS veteran developers. Movement and controls as a Survival Horror game is fine, but as a FPS it's clunky and weird. The movement is far too clunky and slow for quick decision making, especially since enemies come from different angles like spawning behind or above you. It's still better than all past Capcom efforts on the FPS genre, yet it still doesn't feel "good". I'd say its passable. Speaking of shooting, I felt the weapon variety on a first playthrough was just a smidge lacking. Luckily the enemies are programmed to be slower, and the faster ones are built to have wait stances to give you time to adjust your position before they attack. It makes the combat fair, although it's still not fluid.

The puzzles for the most part were simple. This will be a plus for some and a negative for others. There were a few times I got stumped due to my own stupidity but I doubt the average player would have the same issue. Overall, puzzles are not up to par to OG RE standards.

Regarding graphic content, this games actually one of the goriest and most violent in the series. It oozes grossness and the atmosphere of movies like Texas Chainsaw Massacre 1. 
Speaking of which, this game is heavily inspired by that film, along with the whole Killer Hillbilly sub-genre of slasher films, which genre staples include the Texas Chainsaw series, the Wrong Turn series (Recently butchered by a horrid non hillbilly remake), and the Hills Have Eyes series. So it's very graphic and gross out like it's inspirations. Also, who the ♥♥♥♥ writes the dialogue for the new resident evil games!? I always loved that the only resident evil games had barely any F bombs. It made it feel far more cheesy and the heroes far more likable and heroic and less edgy. Like the kind of heroes you saw on a Saturday morning cartoon. Now with this game, RE8, and REmake 1 and 2 every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ character in letting out ♥♥♥♥ this and holy ♥♥♥♥ that, I came here to see cheese, not get hit with edge. The writing of dialogue as a whole as seemed very off ever since 6 came out. Even revelations 2 was affected by this while Revelations 1 wasn't (Get Moira Burton and her "Moist barrel of ♥♥♥♥♥" line OUTTA HERE. I don't care that she's a fan favorite.)

Also, this game only has 1 mini-boss that is repeated 3 times throughout the game. That is BLASPHEMY after 4 and 5's mini-bosses. 

Voice acting is okay at best for almost everyone, but was especially great from the bakers (Minus the daughters voice actor).

Also, they spoil a major twist for you in a document late game. When I read the document I guessed what was coming very easily. It pissed me off. I wish I hadn't read the damn thing so I could be surprised.

However, no matter how much I praised this game, I do think the whole First Person View for this game was needless and pointless, and was obviously a change late in development to cash in on the hype for Silent Hill P.T.'s demo. I don't care for first person horror as a whole, and I certainly don't want it for the future of Resident Evil. People argue that it's a good change that Resident Evil needed to progress. They are totally wrong, and probably weren't playing the series before now, and if they did, most of them probably started with 4 or 5. I hate how with tons of franchises nowadays the new fans are coming in to tell the old fans how the franchise should be going forward, and although the game is still good regardless, this camera ain't it, son.

Here comes my biggest gripe with the game. The one that makes me hesitant to recommend this to true Resident Evil fans: There are NO established Resident Evil characters in the story! We fans want to play as characters we've known and loved for years, but instead of that you give us a group of psychos, and emotionaless twatty wooden board of a protaganist, and NO ESTABLISHED CHARACTERS AS SIDE CHARACTERS?! What the hell man?! (I know Chris is in the DLC, though it might as well not be since they replaced his face and voice actor (NOT MY CHRIS) and see how well that went since with RE8 they got the old guy back.)

Overall it's a great little sorta self contained legitimately scary modernized throw back to old school survival horror. I'll be back for more, I'll tell ya what.

(EDIT: For clarification since making this review I have grown to absolutely LOVE first person horror games, because of games like Fobia, Nightmare Of Decay, Dead Beacon, Night At The Gates Of Hell, Demntium 1 and 2, and developers like Puppet Combo, Henry Hoar, and Chilla's Art, however I still think that changing Resident Evil to a first person perspective in a non spinoff entry is very needless.)

[h1]Actual evil residents, this time around[/h1]

Well, it was a long time coming since I hadn't bought nor played RE7 on release and it is only because RE8 just came out that I remembered that it might be time to actually play and finish RE7 if I ever plan to get to the 8th game.

And given that the game has been out for years by now and that the hype has died down, I can safely say this : RE7 is a new kind of Resident Evil experience with a new viewpoint to better convey the horror aspects of the game and returning to the root of what made Resident Evil special while suffering from a few issues that, I believe, come from the game having a VR version on PS4.


[h2]The Good[/h2]

The game has stunning visuals and running at a steady 144 FPS made every moment very tense as the barrier between the "show" (witnessing the game) and the "game" (actually playing the game) is so small that moving from one moment to the other felt very natural.

On top of that, the audio work kept me on my toes where I often wondered if a sound I heard was due to a monster creeing around or if it was just ambient noises. It got to the point where I turned around just to make sure an enemy didn't just spawn in my back. I rarely have that reaction in other horror games and RE7 does it very well.

Ressource management-wise, once I figured out I could use my knife to deal with the most common kind of molded reliably, I managed to keep a decent amount of ammunition for my weapons from the second third of the game onward. Inventory managed was thankfully lenient given that it eventually expands. Crafting with the herbs and gunpowder gave you the choice to risk either running low on ammo or running low on healing ressources and thus bank on either your skill or a decent padding in case things go wrong.


[h2]The Bad[/h2]

Like I mentionned originaly, I believe that the issues I've personally had with the game comes from the fact that it's gameplay was tailor made for PSVR and certain design decisions affected the game in such a way as to give a negative experience.

For one, Ethan's full 'sprint' speed is about as fast as a very light power walk; in fact, I feel his "sprint" speed should have been his default walk speed. But I understand the reason might be twofold : for one, for the PSVR experience, having too rapid movement might incur motion sickness in the player; for the other, having the player move too quickly might invalidate the threat of enemies. But here's the thing : a lot of areas are thin corridors where enemies will spawn either behind or ahead of you. And that means that it forces a confrontation as the enemies will likely be large enough to block your way or at least, make it very difficult to run past them or even away as they might just catch up to you.

Weapons using a crosshair 'dot' for aiming instead of ironsights. I have seen some PSVR gameplay and given that they didn't actually implement weapon handling in VR, this means that your shooting experience is based off of where you look instead. I feel that if I am playing a game in first person and that I am asked to 'aim', I should at least have the perspective of aiming said weapon instead of shoulder firing every one of them.

Related to weapons, the damage model for enemies is inconsistent. I would have 2 run of the mill Molded face me; I could decap the first one with one shotgun blast to the head while the other could tank 3 of them to the face, get knocked down, getting back up and then taking a last shot to actually finish it off. Now I don't mind having enemies of the same time have some variance to their stats... but when that means having 4 times the toughness, that's a bit ridiculous.


[h2]The Verdict[/h2]

RE7 was one of those games that registers in my brain as "It has been finished, now time to move on to something else" as by the time I was in the last leg of the campaign, I wanted to be done with it. It is not to say that it is a bad game by any means; it is excellent but it does seem that some design choices for the VR version kind of impeded on the overall experience if you were playing the standard version. 

Add to that the VR version never officially came to PC despite having been planned originally is a shame as surely the experience would have been far more intense while completely immersed in the world of Resident Evil 7.

I do recommend the game on the basis that it is truly a different experience than the previous titles and a kind of throwback to the old style of Resident Evil (1 and 2) where ressource management and a constant feeling of unease and dread lingers from the beginning to the end was what the design intended and properly achieved.

Resident Evil 7 is in many ways a throwback to the older games.  Exploring a spooky mansion for keys and items to proceed, all while trying to evade and deal with deadly enemies with limited resources. Solving puzzles along the way and being pursued by invincible and terrifying enemies.  It certainly evokes the same tense and claustrophobic feelings, but Resident Evil 7 finds its own identity in a far more personal story and also being [in my opinion] the only truly scary Resident Evil game.  

While most Resident Evil games detail a viral outbreak in a large city, town or otherwise.  7 takes place in a large house (much akin to the original game).  It's plot is built around a husband working to rescue his wife from the clutches of the horrifying murder family, all while slowly piecing together the plot of something greater and more insidious.  In the narrative sense, 7 is Resident Evil at its best.  While it keeps some of the goofy charm the series is known for, it is an intimate and unnerving experience brought to life by brilliant atmosphere, music and A+ level design.

Resident Evil 7 isnt without some shortcomings, it is, despite having a focus around exploration. A far more linear game than the original.  You can't do to many things out of sequence. And while speedrunning is obviously possible, there are many scripted cinematic moments that must be done before open gameplay is allowed.  This makes repeat playthroughs frustrating for some, as the first 30 minutes is very much on rails.  As well, like many Resident Evils, drops somewhat in its brilliant quality somewhere after the halfway mark. Definitely one of the stronger games in the Resident Evil series, 7 changes the formula in many creative ways while also having a few hiccups in the later half. It modernises a few things while keeping a few traditions and the blend of both (for the most part) makes something really enjoyable. 

The first half is focused on horror and is where the game really shines, it's intense, stressful, and scary. You can really see the inspirations here such as Outlast and the Shining. It's almost humbling how much 7 pays homage to the horror genre and it's impressive.  

The second half of the game focuses less on horror and more on action. It's the weaker part of the game for sure, but it's still good thanks to the variety of weapons and puzzles. The second half unfortunately has the story stray away from the Bakers (the psycho family) which is a shame because they're the most interesting thing about 7 in my opinion. DLC does clarify a few things but it should have been there at launch and for free.

The game moving to a first person perspective bar a few issues with FOV and mouse sensitivity, is a net positive. It was a good choice for the first half of the game which is filled with jumpscares and creepy scenery to justify the more immersive perspective. The second half however feels less focused on making the FPS gameplay work because the focus is on action something that 7 isn't the best at, Resi 4 this ain't.

There's also some great smaller additions such as the new upgrade system, the VHS tapes, and more. These are also what make 7 so great as it makes the game feel more polished, and you can see that especially in the first half.

Overall Resident Evil 7 is a great game with a second half that some may find a little dull, not bad but not as enjoyable as the first half. But there's enough here for any fan of Resi, horror games or even action games to enjoy. I'd recommend this one.

Resident Evil 7 is a successful transition of the series formula into a first-person perspective, and a game much belied by its pre-release trailers and even its demo which in particular I think did a disservice to the experience of the full release. I wasn't even really interested in the game at first until I heard about what the Eighth game was going to be like, and how it was similar to 7, in contrast to how I perceived it. 

I was startled by 7's  smoothness of gameplay and impressed by its aesthetic and atmosphere. It has reminded other reviewers of Outlast, P.T., Silent Hill and even the F.E.A.R. games, but I was actually most reminded of a recent film adaptation of HP Lovecraft's The Color out of Space, also a story of a family of ordinary farmers destroyed utterly by an outside-context force beyond their control. Ironically, I noted later with amusement a document in the free "Not a Hero" DLC called "Operation: Lurking Fear".

A key issue I have with many eastern games is ease of control. To this day I have not played any through the entirety of any Resident Evil game prior to 4, which was my introduction to the series. The "tank controls" beloved by series purists have never appealed to me in the slightest, and in my experience, many other games by Capcom and other eastern developers have varying degrees of jank, ranging from only slightly as found in Devil May Cry 3, Metal Gear Solid V or Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night,, to being nearly unplayable, with the game fighting me at every turn, as in the early Monster Hunter games, the first Dark Souls, or Godhand, most other titles falling somewhere in between.

RE7 casts you as series newcomer Ethan Winters, who after the mysterious disappearance of his wife Mia three years earlier, has just received a cryptic message from her to come and find her, somewhere in the Louisiana bayou, at the homestead of the Baker family. This being the sort of game it is, he very quickly finds himself in well over his head and fighting for his life. The gist of the story is a lesson I know well, and I've seen it played out in a lot of other stories, both horror ones like F.E.A.R. and also military stories like Rambo: If you try to make a person into a weapon, you can expect consequences you did not want.

Whatever the Bakers were before (psycho loner Lucas not withstanding), they are most certainly something different now. What begins has something more akin to the "helpless protagonist" horror games of recent years like Outlast or Amnesia quickly unfolds into an experience much more similar to Resident Evil 4 or the 2 remake, with you creeping about the halls and marshes of the Baker estate and its environs, almost always well-armed, but almost never really safe, outside the series' signature save rooms, cassette recorders taking the place of the classic typewriters. It is both a familiar experience and evolutionary step forward in the franchise, though not without the occasional hiccup.

At least on normal difficulty, health, ammo and the resources to make more are in generous enough supply, provided you move and fight carefully, and enemies are few, but individually quite dangerous, and often encountered in very confined areas. As an FPS veteran I had little trouble with most combat encounters. The game is tense but never feels outright unfair, with my few actual deaths attributable to the aforementioned eastern jank, especially in the first real boss fight. Moving, shooting, switching weapons and healing on the go are fluid and intuitive, but the mouse interface for the inventory is oddly "sticky", making it hard to move items around when you need to do so in a hurry. I used a guide to find collectibles but almost never found myself needing one for puzzles or progression. 

Many of the series' core mechanics and gameplay quirks are present and accounted for, including some that have been notably absent since the earliest entries of the series. There is still a quick-turn button, very useful for when you need to run down a hallway to get some distance on an enemy before about-facing to shoot them. Item crafting returns, allowing you to mix herbs, gunpowder, bagged chemicals and pills to make what you need when you need it- usually. Unfortunately, an older style of inventory system also returns, with key items notably taking up space in your inventory that could be used for precious healing items or ammo, and there are precious few inventory expansions. The linked item boxes return however, allowing you to stash items you don't immediately need and retrieve them from any such box later. Some of these key items are also familiar- animal-themed keys that open different doors in the Baker house, for example, contrasting the card-suite keys of RE2. 7 feels more grounded thematically then previous titles in addition to handling better, but every so often you get a little reminder that you're playing Resident Evil- for better or worse, depending. I felt like the running speed could have been a bit faster, for example, and melee combat is awkward, so it strikes me as odd that one of the DLCs focuses on the latter.

There was also an issue I had with FOV at first, as it defaults to an unacceptably low 75, which I was at least able to change to 90. I also had framerate issues until I capped it to 60 and shutdown a number of background processes. To the game's credit, it runs mostly smoothly at 60 fps with only occasional texture pop-in and dropped frames. I have seen far worse even in western releases in this regard. It's a good-looking game, especially the 
 light sources, interiors of buildings, and inanimate objects, but It falters elsewhere, usually with close-ups of characters' faces: Mia and Jack Baker in particular.

Resident Evil 7 is an extremely solid survival-horror title, and a very decent first-person game, and I think is worth playing even if you're not a Resident Evil fan in particular.

And the game manages to do all of this without feeling like a piece of crap to play (like the first Resident Evil). It's horror feels grounded more in the game, and less in the roadblocks technical limitations built into it. But as great as these things are, the longer the game goes on the more you start to see it's problems. The mold-men are extermely boring to fight and only have 3 or 4 variations. At first this is fine because they're not a big part of the game, but as the game starts to run out of scary ideas they throw more and more of them at you until this comes to it's logical conclusion of you fighting hordes of them.

It's hard for me to give this game a number rating because the parts of it that are good are really good, but the difference between those parts and the parts that are on the lower end are so vast, that it holds this game back from achieving it's full potential. Despite that I think there is a lot to be said of how important this game was for not only Resident Evil, but the entire survivor horror genre, so you have to respect that.

One thing why beating at that gamemode is worth tho is that you get the achievement, which i hunt (i like to get them), and second motivation was that you gain access to infinity ammo, like in RE2 (if you beat it with S rank). Basically I'd say it's an ok but dull affair that I got for £6 and was worth it, but any higher than that and I would say stay away.

Resident Evil 7 is the first in the series to use the first person view for the entire game. I recently replayed the game + dlc’s “No Hero” & “End of Zoe” just in time before the launch of Resident Evil Village. You play as Ethan Winters who received a video message from his wife Mia who was missing for years and now suddenly reappeared, telling him not come to Louisiana and stay away. Of course we ignore her wishes and make our way to rescue her. Soon after arriving at this creepy looking house in the swamp we meet the Baker Family and they are very eager to kill us in the most horrific way possible. A masterpiece of story telling that brings back the classic Resident Evil formula in a new suit, featuring : (Item management, ammo preserving, exploring, puzzle solving) and being chased around by a member of the Baker family (similar to the Nemesis in RE3) which can not be killed for good until you fight them in a Boss battle later on. Soon you will discover more about Evie (Eveline) and the mysteries that surround her character. From the Baker Property in the Louisiana bayou, including murky cellars and dark tunnels to a stranded oil tanker and a salt mine, your journey of terror leads through a variety of cool locations and provides enough opportunity to fight some disturbing creatures or run for your life. If you have never played any Resident Evil game before, maybe it’s a good time to jump in here and continue the story of Ethan Winters on may 7th 2021 when Resident Evil Village is released. 10/10

Unexpected experience!

I'll be straight - I haven't played many Resident Evil titles. With that said, Resident Evil 4 (RE4) is one of my all time favourite titles. Knowing that the game is played in first person view, I thought it would detract from the experience I know of RE.

However, I was proven wrong. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (RE7) is now one of my all time favourite, horror games. Right up there with Amenisa: Dark Descent. The return to survival horror, where every enemy poses a challenge, is welcome and refreshing.

What makes RE7 stand out is the atmosphere. The setting, the characters, and the claustrophobia all helps push the narrative to help you (the player) remain engrossed.

Without spoiling, there are times where the pacing falls flat when, during your first play through, you feel more than well equipped for the challenges. Additionally at this point, the characters that were once present, driving the atmosphere, are absent. 

On a positive note, after you beat RE7, You'll unlock "New Game +", a higher difficulty which randomizes item placement, new items and other reasons to play the game again. As well the game comes with two DLC's that expand upon the main campaign and provide additional context and replayability.

Highly recommend!

Edit: Following up a year later on a new playthrough (Madhouse difficulty) and still having a blast. Coming back to this title after playing Resident Evil Village (RE8) and it still holds up as my favourite RE title.

The boss fights also have a great presentation but the gameplay around them is - with two exceptions - very, very barebones. They are basically nothing more than trigger events. After Resident 4-6 all of this felt like a massive downgrade regarding the gameplay. And I hate the fact that just outrunning enemies is more efficient and "the way to play" than fighting them. I hated that in the old Resident Evil games and I still hate it.

I can see why people prefer this style of survival horror, but after Dead Space and Resident Evil 4, I just can't go back to the clunkiness of all of this. The brain-dead AI doesn't make the whole thing very menacing as well. You literally just have to close a door before an enemy and he won't pursue you most of the time.

There is also some major backtracking problems in this game and some segments like the second house felt like running back and forth at least 5 times, just to pick up another item.

Another problem is that the game kinda falls apart in the last third. I didn't even hate the ship level, I kinda liked the more action-focused gameplay. But the finale was weak, with a bad boss fight and despite some cool twists, the story ended up being just your usual Resident Evil bollocks.

I decided to replay this game to get ready for RE8 and it is still a great game. They took all the great elements from the old games horror theme trilogy (1,2, and 3) and very successfully translated them to first person. The Baker house has some Spencer mansion vibes to it for sure. Ethan does move extremely slow, I imagine to give that horror feel of not being able to get away super quick but it definately feels clunky for better or worse. There is a wide variety of weapons and encounters that keep things fresh. There is also a nice upgrade system that rewards searching around for collectibles from the environments (and things are surprisingly well hidden you'll find after using psychosimulants an item that reveals items for a short time). The Bakers are great villains without spoiling to much, each has there own brand of horror and encounters that are very interesting. The optional video tape mechanic is a cool addition to play other perspectives in the story. I'd also recommend the "Not a Hero" and "End of Zoe" dlc as they shed some more light on story aspects that may carry into RE8. "Daughters" Banned footage is a  interesting prologue dlc as well the others are less story important in my opinion but may be good horror experiences (I only tired one a while ago on PS4).

Pros:
-Great return to survival horror and translation to an fps
-Wide variety of encounters and enemy types/bosses
-Rewards exploration to try to keep you in the horror of the environments
-Interesting new story to the RE franchise (perhaps the start of the fps trilogy)
-Good villains, maybe some of the best in the franchise (Lucas in particular is my favorite villain, he's great at being a huge jerk)
-The bigger dlcs are very fun (Not a Hero is probably the best)
-Higher difficulties offer most items and challenges
-has some nice call backs to older games that if you've been a fan of the franchise you'll have fun with
-A good ammount of puzzles which for me is a RE staple so glad to see those back! :)

Cons:
-Controls can be clunky and slow (probably intentionally but something to be aware of)
-Some sections towards the end provided a long gap in between saves (was mostly an issue since I was trying to stop for the night and it seemed like I was at a good spot but it was probably like a 2 hour gap before I could save more of a personal issue)
-Lack of official VR support on PC if you are looking for that (seems to be Playstation exclusive)
-ran into slight technical issues using HBAO+ on my rig which is very beefy dropped my frames from my usual locked 60fps to 20fps with it on and everything else maxed and 4K(use SSAO instead) (I also lock my games to 60fps since my display is a tv and doesn't support super high frame rates)

If you are a fan of the older horror elements of RE and want to try that experience in First Person this is a must buy. However, if you are looking for the game to tied in older characters or develop things in that way you will be disappointed outside of the dlc, even then I wouldn't get your hopes too high. They are trying to build a new story line and freshen up the franchise with new characters, which I think is a welcome addition and I think a good way to mix it up which is why I'm not marking it as a con. I'd recommend this to anyone that likes survival horror where you are able to fight back and horror fans in general, and I think a must play in the RE franchise.

[quote=]
[h3]Common criticisms I've heard:[/h3]
[b]"Not a Resident Evil game, just a P.T./Outlast knockoff."[/b]
Play the game for more than 20 minutes. You'll know you can fight back. Finish the game, and you'll see how it ties to the RE universe.

[b]"I hate the new protagonist! Give me my fav RE character."[/b]
"Fear of the unknown" was probably a theme Capcom was going for, along with player immersion. They borrow from the previous REs, horror movies, and even horror games like Silent Hill to provide something fresh here, while feeling familiar.

[b]"Why is this in first person? RE is best in 3rd person."[/b]
Agree, and disagree. While 3rd person perspective is still awesome, Capcom makes 1st person work in RE. The claustrophobia, and interacting with the world has never felt so personal. Well, RE1 is still an amazing game, and a terrifying experience, given it's neither in 3rd nor 1st person.

[b]"The common enemy variety sucks!"[/b]
Well, my friend, I'm glad we align on something. See Negative(s) section.
[/quote]

[h3]Positives:[/h3]
+ The Baker Estate is my favorite main setting in the series, next to the Spencer mansion.
+ The visuals, powered by spectacular lighting, helps bring the creepy atmosphere to life.
+ The Bakers are memorable characters, resulting in engaging boss fights.
+ The game tries to invoke fear by going for phobias. Can get disturbing.
+ Time-honored gameplay mechanics with modern tweaks result in constant tension.
+ Excellent level design, with impressive level of detail, plus well-hidden items.
+ Surprisingly deep, and well-written story for a Resident Evil game.
+ Masterful sound design. Silence is used very well.
+ Shooting's not bad at all! All the firearms sound and feel just right.
+ Madhouse difficulty is a brilliant campaign remix. Challenging, and well thought-out.

[h3] Negative(s):[/h3]
- Lack of common enemy variety. The game's tight pacing suffers towards the end because of it. Should've had at least 2 more unique types. It doesn't get any better with the DLCs either! The couple additional types aren't too different from the existing, FFS.

[h3] Mild annoyances: [/h3]
= Photo-realistic visuals of the game is a smart effect that works from afar. Get close, and behold the low-resolution texture greatness. Not too off-putting, but noticeable.
= Some weird hair and facial animations.
= [spoiler]Why no RL to dispose of the main baddie, Capcom? You're ruining the tradition![/spoiler]

[h3] Note: [/h3]
⚠️I typically call out modern Capcom for their scummy business practices. This one surprisingly has nothing predatory in particular, just a few (albeit a bit overpriced) DLCs. It was a time when everyone was calling Capcom out, so they should've had a different master plan. After completing RE7, RE2 Remake, and RE3 Remake, I can say, with confidence that Capcom's milking the living f**k out of the RE engine. I get that competent game engines should enable shared assets, scalability, faster time to market etc. The scale of reuse across these three games is mind-boggling - bolt cutters, firearms, shooting mechanics, set pieces, boss battles...the list goes on and on!

With RE: Village, Capcom should now have most of the game assets to do quick remakes of RE4, and RE: Code Veronica. Maybe even remake RE1 once again, because why not? Capcom's making millions with these remakes. Don't think they're gonna stop anytime soon. I only wish they put in more effort into these remakes, while keeping them faithful to the originals.

A lot of RE purists will not like this opinion, but I'll honestly say that this RE was the second best RE ever made.

RE7 took the same concept of "Virus/parasite make people go bad" but refined it with a bunch of likeable 'villains' and an... at least kind of more complex combat system. Instead of just running and walking, you can now also duck and block.

Pros:
I really like the setting of it. I was always a fan of forest/swamp settings, and RE7 delivered that beautifully with a big house in a forest swamp. I am really thinking of an area that I did not like visually, but I actually cant think of any.

The 'villains' are likeable as I already said. They may be chasing you around or luring you into traps, but at least they all still have a personality and are funny.

You feel squishy, you aren't, but you feel like it. This is in my opinion a big point, in RE5 and 6 you were just kind of an immortal badass and it felt meh. In RE7 you actually feel like you're a human. You get your limbs cut off, you get thrown around, you stumble when you get hit by something. But I said that you aren't actually squishy, and I will talk about that in the cons.

The DLC's are all pretty good. This might sound weird, but I think my favorite part out of all the DLC's is the little 21 card game. But yeah, I think they all add something to the game and I think that the End of Zoe DLC is one that everyone should play after finishing the main game, because it gives you a nice closure.

Cons:
Game is straight up too easy. I have the habit of sounding like an elitist, but I actually feel like this game was way too easy. Blocking and ducking is way too OP imo. I went into Madhouse difficulty, expecting to get frustrated as hell and losing hours of progress constantly due to not having enough tapes for saving my game. But I did not get any of that. I'd still say that Madhouse was a better experience than normal difficulty, but I am kind of disappointed. Ducking got kind of nerfed on Madhouse, but blocking is even more OP than before thanks to 2-3 items that buff your block. Normal difficulty was so easy that you could just straight up walk up to enemies and knife them to death and if you knew how to duck and block you lost barely any HP if at all. 

The bossfights were really meh imo. The first one was kind of cool and the second one too, but the third one was basically just a bunch of running around and finding the boss who would constantly just run away from you. The fourth one was also pretty meh, because you just had to dodge/block some slow af attacks while shooting the bosses weakpoints. The last boss felt like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ playable cutscene, you just kind of shot it until it died, without actually being able to do much else except for that.

The inventory system. This is a point where again, most RE purists will probably put me on the cross for. But I honestly think that RE's inventory system is an outdated way of artificially making the game harder. Except it doesn't make the game harder. This may have worked in 1996 - 2005, but not in 2009 - 2021. Its just kind of meh having to run back to a chest just because you don't have a key item you need just to put it back in afterwards to find out you need it once again. I'm not just gonna rant about this system tho, if I criticize an entire system, I will also talk about a solution. A lot of people will probably argue that it would make the game too easy because you could just run around with practically infinite bullets and infinite healing item. But I am gonna present a simple solution: item limits. 3 small healing items, 3 big healing items. 120 pistol bullets, 600 SMG bullets, 25 magnum rounds, 30 shotgun shells. And you get infinite space for key items. This will completely eliminate this outdated inventory system and will overall make the game more fun imo.

Game is too short. This game is actually incredibly short, it is so short in fact, that there is an actual achievement that wants you to beat the game in under 4 hours. And those under 4 hours still give you a ton of breathing room. I went for this achievement and it literally only took me 2 hours and 31 minutes. Now, of course you may argue that this wasn't my first playthrough, and you'd be right, it was my third one. But my first one wasn't much better and still only took me 7 hours and 40 minutes. Now if we compare this to RE4, a game from 2005, the average completion time of that game is 16 hours. A 2005 game is twice as long as a 2017 one. This cant be right imo.

Enemy variety was pretty much non existent. You had 4 enemy types, if you don't count the Baker Family, and they all were pretty much just kind of a reskin of the standard Molded. One was just kind of crawling around on all 4's and did unholy amounts of damage on Madhouse difficulty. One was literally the standard Molded but with a weird mold blade on its arm. And one was just kind of fat and shot vomit at you. All the other RE's weren't much different, where you had the zombie, the zombie and of course the zombie, but at least there a lot of them looked different. In RE7 every enemy just kind of looks the same. Tall, with black skin that kind of looks like its melting and a big mouth with big teeth.

Overall I think this was a great game with its only flaws being the length, the difficulty and the enemy variety. I give it a 8.5/10 and hope that Village, which I will buy on release, will be even better. (It wasn't. RE8 was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ disappointment. Bravo Capcom)

I am currently playing through Resident Evil 7 again in anticipation of RE Village releasing. I beat this game on PS4 when it first released. I have played every Resident Evil game, and this one is my favorite. I loved the switch to first person, as I feel it really enhances the horror aspect of the series through player perspective. The graphics have a very gritty and realistic feel to them. I love the design of the mansion, and all of the classic survival horror elements are present and utilized in such a way that you feel consistently challenged and on edge playing through the story, but you always have just enough supplies to survive.

Such a fantastic game. I beat it twice in the little over ten hours I have logged on this game on my pc. 1rst play was on normal to enjoy the game as it was intended to be played. Then once more on easy to get the "get me out of here" achievement for beating the game within a 4 hour time limit. I did it back to back in one sitting... Even my first go through the game wasn't entirely challenging. No insane puzzles offered and the combat sections were pretty easy on the normal mode. I plan on returning one more time to play the game on mad house difficulty. Just to see how things scale up as far as combat and the awareness of the patrolling family members. I thought the pacing of RE:7 was really fluid and smooth. Exploring and opening up more areas as you collect keys and figure things out along the way felt very classic RE. I thought the added outlast style patrolling Baker family really brought a nice touch to the over all atmosphere of the game. Having people you were helpless against (until the scripted fights with them) really kept me on edge as I was exploring through the main areas of the map. I thought the blend of survival horror and FPS action paired really nicely. I felt in control of my character the whole time but not so much that I felt I had a total advantage in first person. There is a lot to collect and explore and the game offers plenty of reasons to play it 2-3 times. With RE:8 coming soon and this game being the beginning to a trilogy through 7,8,and 9. I highly recommend picking this one up. its worth full price, even better on sale. My experience as far as the technical performance of the game was also surprisingly pleasing considering I have quite an old rig. I was able to get 60fps with everything on high. I really didn't notice any bugs or glitches. I have been know to miss things like that but nothing stuck out in this game as broken or buggy. It's a very well put together game and I think it's a great addition to the RE franchise.

Edit: I added an extra two hours to the game to check out madhouse difficulty because I enjoy a good challenge. After playing through the first couple of hours I decided to hang it up. Resident Evil 7 is a lean, mean slasher movie of a game

Resident Evil 7 is probably most famous for being the Resident Evil game that made the jump from third to first person perspective, and for being the title that redeemed the franchise after the disaster that was RE6. For both things, it is, I think, rightly praised. 

But there is plenty more cause for admiration here.  

When the game starts, you are Ethan Winters, on a mission to find your long lost wife, who apparently turned up in a dilapidated mansion in the Louisiana swamp after three years of being missing. That’s all you’ll learn of his back story, and that’s all you need to know. Ethan is the protagonist, but he is not the star of the show. 

The main gameplay loop is familiar: you explore the various properties of the Baker family, scavenging for weapons, ammunition and items, all the while being in danger from the murderous denizens of the location, which you have to evade or fight off. Occasionally, the game throws an environmental puzzle at you, to spice things up. 

Combat is a sluggish, uncomfortable affair. Aiming your various guns feels slow and imprecise. Ethan is so slow on his feet that evading your enemies’ attacks is almost impossible. Melee attacks are possible but almost completely ineffective. This is not a detriment to the experience. RE7 is a horror tale, the protagonist is not expected to come out of the mayhem unscathed, and while there is plenty of harm inflicted upon Ethan during cutscenes, it’s quite hard not to get bled during the regular engagements, as well. There is never enough ammunition to actually feel confident during engagements, but usually there is enough to never actually run out. The whole system is balanced really well: It engenders terror, but never frustration. Full marks. 

Exploration is also great, and this is mostly a credit to the art direction. I usually take a lot of screenshots to memorize the beautiful moments within a game, but while playing RE7, I rarely ever felt the need to make a screenshot. This is a compliment: The locations here are so lovingly crafted examples of irredeemable rot and dirt and dilapidation that I felt the constant urge to wipe my monitor instead. Every surface feels soiled and moist. The soundscape wraps you in squelches and screams and blubbering and so many other disturbing noises.The environment is so scary and oppressive that I breathed a sigh of relief every time I entered a safe room. Those are just as expertly crafted to feel comforting as the rest of the game is to terrorize you, without them feeling out of place. 

The puzzles are fine. There are no real head scratchers, nothing to get stuck on. They serve to structure the route Ethan takes through the game, and although some of them stretch the limits of suspension of disbelief, none of them broke it for me. 

The plot is great, I think. A lean tale, mostly unburdened by the convoluted Resident Evil mythos, laser focussed on the struggle between a murderous family of degenerates and their would be victims. The characters are great for what they are. None of them feel really developed, but they don’t have to be: they are great implementations of their tropes, the enemies feel menacing. The few allies you have you build a connection with simply by being in the same horrible situation, and they are likable enough that you feel it when horrible things happen to them. The main villain has a somewhat sympathetic back story, but I hated her with a passion anyway, which made the truly bonkers final confrontation quite cathartic for me. 

The game is also very well paced. The locations are spacious, but not overly so. There is no filler, every room has a purpose, both within the game world and with regards to the story. You get just enough time within each location to get familiar with them, but before that familiarity can breed feelings of security, you move on. 

Since we are in an imperfect world, there are a few marks against the game. While the main antagonists are unique and memorable and well designed, at some point the game introduces a couple of rank and file monsters, and those designs, while memorable when first encountered, are very samey. There are three main types, which is too few, and they look very similar. Also, the most impactful moments of the story are front-loaded, so the engagement levels drop a bit during the middle chapters, until the revelations of the final third of the game ratchet things up again. 

Finally, a word about the DLC: There’s, like, a ton of it, and I only played the story-based one’s but those are excellent additions to the game. They give you more time with the Baker family and, at their best, equal the first hours of the main game in excellence. Well worth your time and money. 

TLDR: If you ever wanted to to the protagonist of a really good horror movie that still manages to be scary even if you avoid all the idiotic decisions the people in the movies keep making, spend your time and money here.

Starting with RE7, someone at Capcom must've remembered they published God Hand all those years ago, and decided that every Resident Evil game from 7 onward should feature a similar difficulty system that dynamically alters some aspect of the game depending on how well you play. Check [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1754350187]this link[/url] for more specific info (from people way smarter than me) on what I'm whining about in regards to this game.

My complaints with this system essentially boil down to the fact that the better you play, the less damage you will do to enemies, and the worse you play, the more damage you will do. Perhaps I'm alone in being bothered by this, but if I encounter an enemy that gives me some trouble, I want to improve in order to defeat it. With this system, improving means I'm just making things harder for myself up to a certain point, and if I fail the game is going to baby me and make it easier (again, up to a certain point) until I start doing better once more.

Maybe I'm being overly critical and the system is better than I am giving it credit for. It doesn't really matter to me because being punished for doing well and being babied for doing poorly annoy the hell out of me. Resident Evil 7/Biohazard is a great game; survival horror at its finest. The first ~2 hours were genuinely terrifying as Ethan (and the player) try to figure out what is going on: What happened to your wife? Why are these creepy hillbillies trying to murder you? How the hell do you get out of this mess?

The presentation is what really makes this game. Although there are times when the graphics get a bit rough up close, for the most part it looks great and the art team really did an amazing job of creating a creepy and weird world. The Baker's house(s) of horrors, the abandoned shipwreck and the final area that fills in (most) plot holes - each area is painfully detailed and really makes it easy to immerse yourself in this world. There are tons of little details which shows how much effort and passion was put into making these areas and the secrets - although not the most challenging - I found to be fun to puzzle out. Some people might dislike the backtracking, but I enjoyed exploring the environments so much that going back and forth a couple of times to make sure I got as much as I could for the upcoming fights really didn't bother me. 

Apart from the art and level design, the audio work for this game really deserves to be complimented as well. The first time I entered the Bakers' house I constantly had a chill down my spine as there were always sounds of another person (or thing) moving around inside the house. This made me rush everything I was doing as no ways did I want to be caught by whatever was living in this hell hole. Eventually you do get to meet the residents and they really are a (terrifying) delight. The voice acting is really good for all of the main characters, but the Bakers really steal the show here with their insane babbling making instilling both laughter and fear throughout their screen time. Ethan - the protagonist - is arguably the worst of the bunch, but I found his lack of emotion to be quite endearing. Instead of being a whiny crybaby, he is pretty chill about everything and manages to keep a (relatively) level head which really helped sell me on the fact that he's the kind of person that could get through this situation. As you would expect from a Japanese developer, the music is of course on point here. It is eerie, haunting, frantic and heroic when it needs to be and if I had to rate this game on sound design alone I would give it a 10/10 (the voice actors must have had an absolute blast recording some of the creepier parts and it shows). 

Finally we get to the meat and potatoes: the game play. it's old school RE with a first person twist and it really works. The first person perspective really helps to sell that Ethan isn't a badass like Chris or Leon, but rather just a normal dude in a messed up situation. It makes the horror elements of RE creepier than ever and I really liked the change. At first you will be mostly running away from enemies and defeating them by slamming a door in their face (95% of this game's enemies are too stupid to open a door), but by the end you will be going full Rambo on them and mowing them down with your machine gun, shotgun, grenade launcher and remote bombs. The power creep is well paced and rewarding and it felt great to really start kicking ass after running away for most of the early game (this does however begin to take a lot of the "scariness" away). The absolute highlight of the game play is hands down the boss battles. Each of the Baker's has their own unique personality and quirks and they result in some of the most creative and fun boss battles I have ever played. They are challenging, they are scary, they are cool and you feel like an absolute beast when you take each psychopath down after they had been tormenting you for so long. 

I don't want to discuss the story too much because this is the type of game best played blind, but I will say it's there and it's very good. It won't give you a life-changing existential crises or anything, but it's well written, well acted and kept me engaged throughout.

I have 2 big criticisms for RE:7 however. 

1.) It's short. I finished the story in about 8 hours (and I was taking things slow). It was a very enjoyable 8 hours, but there is little replay value apart from try-harding for achievements as I feel a lot of what makes this game so good will be lost after you experience it the first time (the eternal curse of the horror genre I suppose). 

2.) As with most Japanese games, it is far too expensive. I bought it on sale so I don't feel like I wasted my money, but if I paid full price I certainly would have felt a bit cheated. The DLC also are not on special and while they are good, they are certainly not worth what CAPCOM is asking. This criticism is not unique to RE:7, but it still should be pointed out. 

All in all, RE:7 is a strong contender for my all-time favourite horror game. There were times when I was genuinely scared and I absolutely adore how well they executed the house of horrors with the Bakers. It does dip a bit after the half-way mark, but those first ~5 hours were so good that I can't not reccommend this game to anyone who wants to give themselves that all too familiar adrenaline rush that us horror fans crave.

This game is really, REALLY good. I'm not a huge horror game guy but I'm a casual fan of the genre and no game has ever scared me like this before. This game actually made me paranoid to open doors IRL, thats how bad it got. That said, I love the feeling of being terrified in a video game and this game had many moments where I was too scared to even move around.

The game is mostly scary through the atmosphere, sound design, and darkness. There are jump scares, but they are not the main way that the game tries to scare you. There are just enough however to make you paranoid of them, which only adds to the dread of traversing the game. I have not played it in VR but if you do, don't be surprised if it's overwhelming. The best way to play is to let yourself be immersed in the game, it's easy to not be scared if you tell yourself that it's not real, but the true experience is to believe that it is real and be scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The game is incredibly immersive, especially so now that Capcom switched to a first person perspective, which leads me into my next point:

The game looks GOOD. Like, really good. Even now, I'm reviewing this game 4 years after release and I am still impressed with how good everything looks. The graphics are extremely realistic, especially on the enemies, which adds to the terror. Best of all, the game is optimized beautifully and runs exceptionally well. Even older midrange systems (5+ years old) should be able to run it without issue. If you have a modern system, the game can pump out some high framerates so enjoy the added smoothness. There are definitely some bugs with the performance that I encountered, mostly having to do with alt-tabbing and HDR, so prepare for some jank if that's your thing, but you can expect to hit >144 fps on max settings if you have a good rig. 

The gunplay is overall enjoyable and satisfying. Guns feel good to shoot, but the lack of ammo and the difficulty of landing headshots keeps you from feeling too strong. Similar to other games in the series, you can only take 2-3 hits before you die, so any enemy that manages to get up in your face becomes extremely dangerous. The only defensive option you have, besides just running away or trying to run past an enemy, is to block with your arms. This will reduce the damage you take from an attack, but only by about half, and as such is not a reliable way to stay alive. Capcom injected a bit of Street Fighter into this game because if you block at just the right time (usually referred to as a "just guard" or "just block"), you can perform a "parry", which reduces damage even further and can even stagger some enemies. Learning these timings will let you get away relatively unscathed from a bad situation, and is essentially required on higher difficulties.

As for the story, I very much enjoyed it. I had a great time uncovering the truth of what was really going on, and the way the game reveals it to you is very impactful and definitely enhances the experience. Definitely read all the files and logs that you find. There aren't that many of them and they are all very short, it will be worth it in the end. I think the story is even better on the second playthrough because you immediately recognize all the clues that you totally missed in the beginning of your first playthrough that literally spell out what is happening, you just didn't have enough context at the time to put them together.

The puzzles are just what they are in other Resident Evil games: gates. The "puzzles" are not designed to be challenging to figure out, but rather to limit your progress until you solve them, forcing you to explore and backtrack until you have all the pieces. I'm totally fine with this method of progression, I think it works well and the pacing is such that it never becomes overly repetitive. 

The pacing of the game is something I'm a bit mixed on. In my experience, the game starts off leaning hard towards the horror side of the action/horror spectrum. As you progress through the game, it starts to lean more and more in the action direction. This makes sense, as you gain more guns and items as the game goes on, but the scariness level that the game achieves in its first act is never matched again. The action sequences are enjoyable, but there is very little enemy variety and after a while it feels like the game is throwing enemies at you just to eat through your ammo. I wish the game stayed scarier for longer, but I was also relieved to have a break from being extremely on edge at all times.

My one complaint about the game is how slow your character (Ethan) is. Ethan really must not be in a hurry because everything he does is SLOOOOOW. He walks slow, he even runs slow, and he reloads guns with the urgency of a guy who kinda needs to pee but is too lazy to get up (none at all). Like, I get that he's "just a guy" and not a cop like Leon or part of a paramilitary group like Chris, but I think they took it a touch too far. At some points I was questioning if I could reload a gun faster in real life. You can eventually unlock an item that increases your walking speed, but you need to complete the game first. There are items called stabilizers that will increase your reload speed, but it just seems like an excuse to put more items in the game and I would have preferred if your reload speed was just quicker from the start. Expect to move slow throughout the game, and don't count on walking backwards and shooting to defend yourself. Enemies will catch up to you pretty much right away if you do that, it is better to turn around and run. 

Overall this game is fantastic and a new high for the Resident Evil series. I'm on my 3rd playthrough and I plan to do more after that, so I definitely got my moneys worth. I have most of the game memorized at this point and it STILL manages to be scary, which is a testament to the fantastic atmosphere, graphics, and sound. I have no trouble recommending this game to anyone, not just horror fans. I don't want to come off as too pretentious, but this definitely feels like one of those games that you would call an "experience", not just a game. I don't generally like to use number rating systems, but this game gets a strong 9/10. My complaints are minor and the game absolutely nails just about everything.

First off, I don't want to make anyone who had fun with the game feel as though they're wrong for enjoying it. If within the first 2-3 hours you find this to be your cup of tea, by ALL means pick this up, especially when on sale.

Look, this game has all the pieces set up: The chilling ambiance, the immersive sound, the graphics - I personally believe - hold up really well (once you get past that Fugly forest in the beginning), The F a m i l y is a very idiosyncratic and interesting dynamic for your main antagonists in the game. Overall: if there were a movie of this household and the Mold, I'd 100% watch it.

But what should have been a movie was made as a game. . . And when reading up on the Wiki forums about the Lore, is more entertaining and enthralling than the ACTUAL GAME, you have a problem. They set up all the pieces perfect for knocking down, just to completely miss their shot.

To make my point: I, for one, am a HUGE fan of the RE2 Remaster. It was cinematic yet the gameplay was tight. Great audio, Great optimized graphics, the guns are absolutely fun to use (even if unloading smg ammo into an un-phased zambie's cranium is a little bit questionable), the tension was there, the sense of dread from the unknown when you first play, the desire to play with as little saves and as fast as possible when you play more times, Mr. T all-around was an imposing, terrifying threat of an enemy, who's stomping through the police station put fear into my soul when he would walk right where I needed to be. Overall: I 200% recommend RE2 to anybody.

Was the shift from 3rd to 1st person the problem? Not really. Was the diverting storyline that is a little more separate from the T/G Virus the problem? Not at all. For me: it was the p a c i n g. 
They took a terrifying family unit and - outside of the well-choreographed cutscenes - made them dull and b o r i n g. Before you get hit by shovel: hold space to swing your hands in the air for less damage. Boringly wait for Pops to finally leave the area as he is scripted to walk in. Slowly walk from Set A to Set B and wait for the director to say "aaaand ACTION!" - Shamefully predicable jump-scares that completely disgrace the amazing ambiance of the game that they worked so hard to fine-tune. Stupidly traversing a well-designed and fleshed out Southern mansion... just for there to be c l e a r l y  b r e a k a b l e  w i n d o w s  f o r  y o u  t o  e s c a p e  f r o m , B u t  y o u  c a n ' t . At least in RE2, raccoon city is FLOODED with zambies, Lickers, and dogs, making it unrealistic to just run out willy-nilly instead of finding some sort of shelter (police station) first, then "oh well would you look at that, equipment in the station, And an escape route, and oh hey asian lady? You're not ominous and will be the Mcguffin of letting me escape." etc. In just the first 2hrs of me playing Biohazard, I always felt like my immediate instinct to escape and call 911 is hindered by G a m e  L o g i c . 

Your first 1-2 hours should be your selling point of the game, if by the 1st hour I'm dreadfully bored, take a long near-month to even pick it back up, and am STILL bored after your main "OH MY GOD MY GF WAS INFECTED" and "WELCOME TO THE FAMILY BOI EAT YER SUPPER" (okay that was actually cool, but that's exactly my point, MORE OF THAT, PLEASE, LESS BORING HALF-ASSED STEALTH MECHANICS AND FIGHTING) then what you have was a flopped game that missed out on a loooot of potential. Like I said, Give me the movie of this game, because frankly: The Baker family, The mold, the kitchen-area with the crow inside the microwave and roach stew, the Cow-effigy outside, and overall the general dismay of the entire residence was what fascinated me. The gameplay? I could stomach Marguerite's supper like fine dining before I could stomach this boring game. 

But don't just take my word for it: try it out for yourself while it's only 10 bucks, and if you agree with me, just refund it and read/watch Lore about the game. You will have a more enthralled time doing that while your imagination can fill the blanks, than playing a game that completely misses the pins they set up to be knocked down.

Resident Evil 7 brings the franchise back to its Survival Horror roots with an incredibly creepy atmosphere and item management. The game also takes a new perspective in first person that adds to the immersion of the game. Music composed by Akiyuki Morimoto, Miwako Chinone, and Satoshi Hori that adds subtle goosebumps to the background of the game. The music adds so much to the atmosphere that you should try turning off the music and see how much is lost because you will not actually notice it until the music is gone and that to me is just incredible work from these composers.

They also brought back the safe rooms and the iconic safe room music that also provides you with a sense of relaxation and safety till you get the nerve to go back out and explore this Louisiana estate. The sound design of each gun clanking around while you run around is also a very nice touch to the overall experience.

The next thing that I personally love about this game is the Baker Family. My personal favorite "Villians" of the Resident Evil Franchise. Jack Baker (Daddy) has this incredibly large personality that toys with you and keeps you on your toes as you go through the first third of the game. He will mock you as he chases you and it shows how little of a threat you are to him. He is easily the best baker of the bunch and was named after Jack Torrance from the Shining and provides that slasher horror in the game. Next from the Bakers who takes up ACT 2 is Marguerite Baker and she provides the body horror of the game and has an interesting personality that just loves bugs. She is not as fleshed out as Jack which in the bedroom DLC kind of gives her more character that you get to see from her but in the main game she is definitely the best boss fight in terms of mechanics and boss "arena" which allows you to move around and play cat and mouse with her. Then you have Lucas Baker who was clearly inspired by saw and takes up Act 3 of the game. He is the genius of the family and likes to play games with his victims. He provides more of the puzzles in the game which are pretty satisfying. Then you have Zoe Baker and she helps you along the way throughout the game. I do not have much to say about her honestly but she be doing her best. 

The characters and the atmosphere of the game make this game worth playing for anyone that loves Survival Horror or just Resident Evil in general. ACT 4 (Final) is where the game falls off a bit for me personally because of the ship sequence and Evie is an ok Villian that doesn't really bring me in like the bakers family does. I know that there is a lack of enemy variety in the game and that is a very valid reason to shy away from the game but I honestly believe that the Bakers make up for that in design and personality. The game has its flaws but I strongly recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of the horror genre. I would put this at my favorite Resident Evil game in the series. Capcom is on the right path.

I liked a lot of the RE games, loved RE4 and the remakes of 1 and 2 were great.  This was definitely not their best work.  
Story - So many plot holes and stuff that just didn't make much narrative sense.  There were so many weird choices that just took me out of it.  If someone just read me the synopsis, I'd think it was cool but this was just delivered poorly.  
Graphics - The remakes looked so much better than this.  Considering when this game was made, I expected much better.  Maybe it's because they had to make this for VR too...either way still not great.
Gameplay - the first person thing was neat and felt good for just moving around the world.  You still get the joy of finding the right key to the right door, managing your inventory and exploring a creepy environment.  I hated the boss fights which were frustrating and not very interesting both from a story perspective and from gameplay aspect.  The creatures didn't have much variety or good reaction to getting shot.  There is a lot of backtracking and I didn't get as much of that tension that you want out of a game like this when exploring, wondering what will be around the corner.  And the blocking mechanic was just terrible.  
Sound - Nothing bad to say here.  The sound was really good and added a lot to the experience.  

Overall - I didn't pay much for this since I got it on sale, but if I could go back in time and tell myself not to buy it I would.  I'd rather just watch a video or read a summary to get the story and hopefully the next RE game will have learned lessons from this game.

If you're a die hard fan, my review probably won't change your mind. But if you have an open mind... here it goes.  **EDIT**: Just read all the negative reviews and thank goodness I was not the only one that felt this way! I do think it does a lot of things well and is worth getting on sale, but my gripes still stand.

I understand that the franchise was getting too 'action movie-ish' and Capcom wanted to return to their survival horror roots. I think because of this, reviewers and gamers alike were quick to give this 9 out of 10 because they wanted to reward Capcom for listening to their fans. 

But here we are a few years later. I picked it up and beat it for the first time. Obviously, this game broke ground with graphics and gameplay thanks to their new (at the time) RE Engine. 

My main gripe here is 1 - the pace of the game, 2 - lack of enemy and difficulty, and 3 - the story. 

1) This is such an odd game with the flow of fighting, hiding, and running away. Essentially, you spend most the game running around from one boss fight to another with little action in between. Fight Jack... go look around this section, fight Jack again, go look around new section, fight Marguerite, go fiddle around this section. It follows this flow (with the exception of Lucas who you don't fight) right up to the final boss of the game. 

2) The Molded and bees are the only main non-boss enemies in the entire game. You could say the same for other RE games with zombies, but they have so much more variation than the same 1 of 3 Molded you see. I guess there is also the barfing one. But that's really all you get. And for a game that is supposed to leave you with scarce items..... well..... they didnt. I mean, the Molded take one shotgun bullet to the head and they never re-spawn. The last boss took maybe 5 grenade launcher bullets after I had horded much more thinking I would need it all. Theres just too many items to ever be afraid of what is around the corner. I was always over prepared for a fight.

3) I wish there was more background on the Bakers. Especially since the game reveals that the son was already a murderer before the infection. This after a cured Jack Baker says I would never hurt a person, neither would my wife, neither would my son. I understand the need for mystery, but by the time you get to the end of the game, you think they would clarify. And... I know they want to tie it all in. But what is the point of returning to survival horror and a new story when all you are gonna do is go to a lab at the end and find out it is all because of Umbrella? This was their chance to break away from the mold, but they kind of stuck with the tradition. 

Anyway, this is the first RE main-series game I didnt love. Still, a good game and worth your money and the play, but not as perfect as people would have you believe.

Resident Evil 7 is a very simple video game. Capcom decided for some reason to 'get back to basics' with Resident Evil, by simplifying the plot, cutting out all the familiar characters you know and love, the like eight different protagonists of Resident Evil 6, and altogether cutting the game back down to the simplest possible premise: a guy goes to a house and Weird Stuff happens.

The change in perspective does absolutely nothing to change the 'Resident Evil formula' so to speak. I don't think it's a problem but to move to first person didn't actually change any element of gameplay. Your guy is still limited to walking about as fast as you'd expect Leon or Chris to sprint in third person, and your overall speed is much lower than previous games to compensate for your capacity to strafe and generally move in any direction you like. 'Grazing' enemy hitboxes and such with your face has never been so visceral and traumatic! So, it's hard to say whether it's an improvement. More of a sidegrade, I guess, either camera suits the series fine.

This is all of course because... the shooting is actually pretty much exactly like every other Resident Evil. You may have expected to get Call of Duty style ADS mechanics in Resident Evil this time around but, no! No. Unfortunately... well, it's not really that big a deal, the game draws a dot in the centre of the screen when you aim and that dot is where the bullet you fire will go, just like the laser in RE4 or the crosshairs in RE5. Additionally, Chris (in his free DLC) is the only character that actually uses the sights, Ethan eyeballs where his bullets are going to go, which I kind of like. It's just a change in viewmodel and nothing else but it's neat.

So with all that out of the way of the description of the 'newer' mechanics, it's a Resident Evil game through and through. It takes a good half hour to and hour to get going before you get the chance to walk around and start exploring of your own volition, but the lead-in is fairly cute. After that, it's just like Resident Evil 1 where you walk around a scary house and find cool things and avoid scary people, which is reminiscent of Haunting Ground. You get keys to open specific doors to progress so you can find other keys so you can find new stuff so you can get to new areas so you can progress, etc.

Overall the tone of the game is worth mentioning, I think undoubtedly there will be people who struggle with the 'scary' elements of this one, but to be honest aside from a few spooky setpieces RE7 is not a terribly frightening game and it's much closer to like a darkly comedic, dry horror game where often the absurdity of situations is enough to get you to laugh. All of the Resident Evil games are generally a little bit funny, but RE7 is one of the few where I spent most of the game chuckling or outright laughing at all the things in it, be it the dialogue or the characters or just the situations you're confronted with.

One of the only criticisms I have is, there aren't very many locations, and eventually you kind of get a little bit sick of running through endless corridors, which sort of sums up most of the game. It even sort of makes me nostalgic for Resident Evil 4 and its absurdly eclectic collection of areas. That said, RE7 is much shorter, it's only like a 7-8 hour game all up, so the endless decrepit corridors only overstay their welcome a little bit.

The enemy variety too, I suppose, is a bit lacking. While there's a couple of minute differences between the standard 'walkers' in practical terms there's no difference. The 'crawlers' too are just awful to deal with and not particularly fun to fight, especially on PC where they die in only a headshot or two anyway. When comparing this game (and it's inevitable) to previous entries, it does kind of make me feel like they could have added another enemy type or two to freshen things up at certain points.

Anyway, overall Resident Evil 7 is a very very good game. It has some great bosses, the story has a few nice twists and turns, and several plot points and elements stolen from the F.E.A.R. series, especially F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is pretty much survival horror done perfectly! This is the first first person Resident Evil game and it's done really, really well. Everything is incredibly confronting and even running feels too slow in this game, that's a good thing though, it makes the game much more intense when running from enemies.

You play as Ethan Winters which received an email from his wife Mia, who has been missing for 3 years with no contact at all. Ethan being the dumbass he is, he goes to Lousiana to go looking for his wife. We arrive and not shortly after we are greeted with the Baker family, they have been infected with some sort of virus which basically makes them completely insane serial killers. Just 15 minutes into the game and you get one of the most creepy starts of a horror game (at least in my opinion)

The game is really intensive for the most part, but you do have some safe rooms when you're lucky. Here you can use an item chest (which is basically an ender chest from Minecraft because the items get teleported over in every chest scattered through the game). In old school Resident Evil fashion, there are amazing boss fights and ammo is scarce, you also get a lot of puzzles which are not too difficult to solve but may leave you thinking for a while. It feels great when you finally did the puzzle all by yourself though.
Ammo is scarce in this game as I said, but it's not to the point where I felt like I didn't have enough. It was just enough for most situations. Heck, I even saved so much ammo and gear for the final battle, and found out I didn't even need most of it.

Tip: when fighting the molded (common enemy in this game), just run past them if you can.. it's not worth the waste of ammo. When you are fighting bosses while not in the 'actual' boss fight, also don't bother wasting ammo on them. It's not worth it.

In conclusion. This game is truly amazing. I really loved the original Outlast, but this definitely tops it! The story is amazing and it ties in a little bit with the other RE games (you don't need to play the other RE games to understand the story btw). The intense situations this game puts you in are really good, the jumpscares are not cheap and predictable, and the psycological horror is done really well too!

I definitely recommend every horror loving fan to play this game. It's really a masterpiece.
