[h1]Summary:[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 is a masterpiece in both monster and atmospheric horror. While the resolution of the story is a little lackluster and the UI and inventory management can be frustrating, these annoyances pale in comparison to the phenomenal world building, atmosphere, and visual presentation.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
   [*] The setting is phenomenal. I for one am a sucker for stuff set in the American south, particularly in the Bayou sections of that territory. There is something inherently eerie about being in a swamp out in the boondocks that makes just the location alone generate tension. All the different locations on the Baker ranch have their own vibe and are not only terrifying, but a joy to play in.
   [*] Biohazard's story is insanely compelling, both the over arching narrative and the characters that fill it. Everyone from the protagonist to the family holding you hostage is exploding with personality. The Bakers make great villains and the mystery surrounding them keeps you going through their house of horrors. Not to mention how well the game is paced. No sequence, location, or character overstay's their welcome and the game ends about right when it's supposed to. Part of crafting a good story is also doing a good job of selling the world in which it takes place. The game is rife with notes, newspaper clippings, or playable videotapes that establish the Bakers as a threat, or give you a small glimpse behind the curtain to the bigger picture. An even bigger boon to the overarching narrative of Biohazard is that its seemingly devoid of the overly convoluted narrative RE fans have come to know. It is mostly self contained, with a few surprises here or there that old fans of the series will appreciate, but don't get in the way of letting Resident Evil 7 shine on its own.
    [*] There are many ways to generate horror: jump scares, unsettling mood building, scarcity of resources, and this game does them all well. The jump scares are frightening but not frequent enough to be cheap. The soundscape constantly puts you in a state of anxiety. Often as you walk through the house you will hear creaking floors, window shutters battering back and forth with the wind, or bumps where there shouldn't be. When you aren't being chased by something, the rotting carcasses, creepy iconography, and the creatures of the bayou will make sure you rarely feel at ease. Resources are plentiful enough as not to be frustrating, but scarce enough that every shot counts. Each wasted pull of the trigger means you are less prepared for whatever horrors lie ahead. 
    [*] While RE7 isn't an outright shooter like Bioshock, the guns are surprisingly good. My worry for this game was that the guns would feel like an afterthought. But they all feel weighty and fun to use.
    [*] Biohazard's greatest success is in the pacing of its gameplay and how it makes you feel safe in the status quo, only to turn it on its head. There are short spurts of solace in stocking up at a safe room, or an area devoid of the things you have come to fear while you solve a puzzle. The game lets you become comfortable with these moments and find some much needed relief amidst running from the more aggressive members of the Baker family, or crawling through the dredges of their house. Only to take that comfort away when you least expect it. This sets a tone later in the game that you truly are never safe, the rustling of the grass in a previously quiet courtyard might not be so harmless after all and the black ooze that you have become accustomed to might just be more than an eerie sounding set piece.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*] A hallmark of games coming out of the east seems to be frustratingly clunky user interfaces and unfortunately that is true for Biohazard as well. While there isn't much UI in the game, what is there is often frustrating to use. The mouse control seems floaty outside of first person view and the way you interact with your inventory is beyond frustrating.
    [*] Inventory tetris is a staple of the RE franchise, and you will find it here as well, for better or worse. It does create some interesting decisions since there is a limit on what you can carry, but often times it becomes an annoying as you are ferrying items back and forth from your safe room storage or moving things back and forth for crafting. There isn't a lot to gain from the inventory constraints here, and what is there feels more like a chore than a feature.
    [*] Despite my earlier praise for the setting, I couldn't help but feel let down at Biohazard's lack of wildlife as enemies. We see pieces of it, but that is lurking below the swamp is sometimes scarier that what is above and I can't help but feel there was a bit of a missed opportunity here.
    [*] While RE7 feels more grounded than the more recent entries in the series, that unfortunately gets thrown out the window in the latter portions of the game. The grandiose final encounter and the introduction of some of the bigger players feel like they come in opposition to the tone of the rest of the game. It also casts doubt on Capcom's ability to keep the newer entries smaller and more character focused going forward, but time will tell.
   [*] While mostly bug free, there were a few issues where alt tabbing would permanently tank the fps and require a restart. There was also some issues with sounds bugging out and replaying past their context.
[/list]

[h1]Rating: 10/10[/h1]
Overall RE7 is a horror masterpiece that any fan of the horror genre (RE or otherwise) will greatly enjoy.

Graphics, story and game play are all top notch with this one. As more of a casual gamer, I'm always amazed at the level of background detail whenever I get a new AAA game. I don't buy many, which always makes the next one a leap forward for me.

RE 7 does a great job of gradually building tension. I like that in any horror story, and the same holds true for horror games. The farmhouse succeeds at being incredibly creepy all on its own, and you're given an opportunity to explore a little before all hell breaks loose. It's like exploring an abandoned building in real life: You know you really shouldn't be there and you never know what you'll encounter. Now add the fact that you're dodging crazies who want to messily kill you and seemingly can't die. They may be right around the corner or all the way on the other side of the house. Either way, you can bet they're looking for you, carrying whatever nasty implement they can find to ruin your WHOLE day.

The other thing I like about RE 7 is how the story progresses and moves you forward. I hate games that leave you stranded with no intuitive way to move the plot forward. RE 7 doesn't do that. You find items along the way and it's usually pretty clear how you can use them to proceed, at least in my experience. That makes game play entertaining, as it should be. There's nothing worse than buying a game and having it turn into more of a chore than a treat. RE 7 is more of the latter.

So far there are two downsides for me. First, my eyes aren't that great so it's tough to spot things in dim areas that other people may pick up more easily. I know, I know: "It's a HORROR game! It's supposed to be dark and creepy! What do you expect, you stale soft pretzel?" This is an issue with my eyes, and I'm just being honest here. Second, the cut-scenes are incredible, but it's sometimes hard to tell when they start or leave off, so I'm a little unsure of when to just watch vs. when to take action. Not a big thing, but definitely noticeable in some places.

Overall, I'm not sorry I bought this one. I'm only part way through it, but I'm loving it so far. I totally recommend it for mature gamers.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 7[/b] is something special, a horror game that attempts to introduce something interesting and unique in its own aspect to break from the mold. The series up to this point has given us a character to play with an assortment of combat skills making it easy to adapt to whatever situation arises.  However, this time we play as [b]Ethan[/b] who only has a few select options of skills that he can use to protect himself with. At the same time, we still get things that are familiar and usually found horror movies/games, such as the creepy old house in the middle of nowhere. Even with these traditional choices, the game still succeeds in being an experience worth checking out.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]A great story that's maybe cliché, but still interesting
[*]Very limited running space, makes you feel that there is nowhere to hide from enemies 
[*]Fun gunplay with useful weapons to unlock and use
[*]Fantastic graphics that look impressive and creepy
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Ethan is a bland protagonist
[*]The game’s horror dies down too early before reaching the end
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is set in the middle of 2017 somewhere in the [b]Southern United States[/b].  [b]Ethan Winters[/b] has been looking for his missing wife [b]Mia[/b] for three years who is thought to be dead. One day he receives a sudden call from [b]Mia[/b] begging him to come and find her. [b]Ethan[/b], not taking the time to question the validity of the call, travels to [b]Louisiana[/b] eventually finding himself in the middle of a forest coming across a farmhouse in his search for [b]Mia[/b]. Upon investigating, he runs into [b]Jack Baker[/b], the patriarch of [b]The Baker Family[/b], and finds out that they are more than just eccentric people and realizes that he has to find a way to escape.

[b]Resident Evil 7[/b] gives us the classic horror movie/game tropes that we all know and love. Examples can include, a creepy house in the middle of a forest, a crazy family that eats some really messed up stuff, a creepy little girl that is silent most of the time, a cop that does not listen to a single word of the main character, and guns and ammo being in random locations for no reason, it has it all.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2406902297

This may look a little cliché with everything it throws at us, but it manages to do its job by making the story interesting and worthwhile. I found quite a lot of enjoyment out of how they gave us enough familiar content to to know that we are playing a horror game, but still throwing in a few new twists here and there to remind us that we are playing a new title in the series.

I really loved how the [b]Baker Family[/b] was handled and loved their personalities. Each one of them has something unique and creepy about them fitting the theme of horror perfectly. 

The only issue I had with the story was with [b]Ethan[/b] himself. He is mainly a bland character that lacks an interesting personality and unfortunately shows no character development throughout the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
What we have here is a fun game to play and I really enjoyed the survival horror elements that it has. This time, instead of getting a collection of weapons that you can carry around to defend yourself with, you have a limited amount of items that you can carry throughout the game forcing you to make tough choices on what to pick up, and what to leave behind.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2406903335

There are a few puzzle solving elements, but not many, mostly you find yourself going from point A to point B. When the puzzles did show up, I really appreciated how they were done and they felt nice to complete, each having something unique about them. 

There is also a crafting system built into the game. You will not find much to craft all in all, but what you can craft helps you out in combat situations such as getting healing bottles or better ammo for your guns that you can use.

Everything feels very claustrophobic with limited space for you to run.  This is something that I loved as it felt as though I was actually trapped inside this house with nowhere to escape constantly feeling as though some sort of danger was approaching.

Gunplay is another area done right. The weapons I was given felt nice to use, however, despite this I did not feel overly powerful leaving me with a constant sense of vulnerability. Ammo is scarce so you will need to be cautious when using it as the alternative is to try to run or hide. You will mostly find ammo for the handgun throughout the house, but you can craft ammo for everything except for the shotgun and magnum.

The only issue I had with the horror is the fact that it sort of died down in the later parts of the story. In games like [b]Outlast[/b], I felt scared when something was chasing me. However, that was not the case in this game as nothing really new was there in terms of horror. I found that I could simply fight anything that showed up leaving me with a lack of fear of what could be around the corner.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
The graphics for [b]Resident Evil 7[/b] are beautiful. Every area in the game looks alive with this creepy vibe going for it. I really love this about the game giving me a feeling of dread and unknown while exploring through the house.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2406903150

I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM. I experienced no issues while playing and it ran at 60 FPS. I should note, however, that you will need a decent computer to run this title.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
If you were disappointed with how [b]Resident Evil 6[/b] was handled then I recommend you go and play this new addition to the series. It may not be like your typical [b]Resident Evil[/b] game like [b]Resident Evil 2[/b], but it should provide you with a good experience and I bet the fans would like the return of the survival horror aspect. 

Also for those that are looking for a nice horror experience then I would say [b]Resident Evil 7[/b] is worth trying out, despite the horror dying down in the later parts of the game. This was my first [b]Resident Evil[/b] game that I played fully and I am happy with what I received and I look forward to what the future games have to offer for the survival horror genre.

I've played RE4 on the Wii (It was one of the best Wii games in the history of the console), for probably around 100+ hours.
And I've played RE1 & 2 for a couple of hours each (and didn't like it much).
So I might not be an expert in the subject of how Resident Evil games should be...

But the first few hours of RE7 (around 20% - 25% of the game) feel like the least Resident Evil game I've ever played.
It reminds me much more of games like Outlast (which I can't stand), where you're chased by monsters, and your only option is to run and hide.
This is nothing like the Resident Evil games I've had the chance to play up until now.
In the first few hours, I never would have guessed it to be a Resident Evil game.

I must admit that afterwards the game becomes much more Resident Evil-y in it's gameplay, and much more enjoyable to me.
Although quite short.
I managed to finish the main plot and the free DLC in around 10 hours. And I'm a person who likes to take his time and explore games (rather than rushing to finish them).

The paid DLCs are quite numerous, and quite expensive.
Most of their reviews are negative because they either should have been in the game in the first place, or should have been much cheaper.

Also the controller implementation in the game is quite bad, and makes playing the game x10 more difficult than playing with a mouse/keyboard combination.
I wouldn't recommend it.

Another thing I didn't like is the inability to save game normally.
Even consoles have been releasing with hard drives for the past 10 years.
There is no reason whatsoever that a modern game doesn't allow you to save your game.
I've just finished playing Wolfenstein II - which allows you to save where you want, and as much as you want.
Before that, I played ELEX - which allows you to save where you want, and as much as you want.
Before that I was playing RDR2 - same.
There really is not reason to use 2001 game mechanics in a 2017 game.

Pros:

1) RE7 focuses more on atmosphere building and horror unlike RE6 and RE5. This is a welcome change and is sure to please fans of the first three games in the franchise.

2) The graphics are really good and help enhance the spooky, dingy, disgusting sandbox you find yourself in.

3) There is a good story being told here. The tale might seem a tad generic and flat in the beginning, but the lore gets richer as you keep progressing further and finding out more (Be sure to read the notes and documents you pick up as well. They often add to the story).

Cons:

1) Your character feels slow and clunky. I understand that Ethan handles the way he does to make the game more VR friendly (Yes, the PS4 got a VR version), but it can get a little annoying at times since you aren't playing VR.

2) While the rest of the characters have a great amount of backstory and exposition, the character you play as, Ethan, is a boring, blank slate.

3) The antagonists show up a little too conveniently at times. I understand that this is done for jumpscare/shock value, but it does break the immersion a little bit.

Survival Horror is back, and boy oh boy, you are in for a world of tense horror gripping experience. 

Some key points that this game offers:

1.	Terrifying horror experience
2.	VR Mode
3.	Photorealistic visuals
4.	Updated Mechanics and gameplay

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers Ahead:

I knew it was going to be totally wild, but not to this extent. The survival horror atmosphere had me on edge the entire playthrough. They went above and beyond to bring Resident Evil back to its original roots. The game does an absolutely marvelous job of creating the horrific atmosphere and then sustaining it throughout the campaign. You never feel safe, and you never know when the seemingly unkillable monsters will appear next. 

The deeper in you go, the stranger it gets. The fact that they used a brand new character who has no past dealings with anything zombie in nature makes this so much more memorable… We have this run of the mill guy in search of his long-missing wife, and when he finds her, he finds so much more than he could possibly have imagined. It is a constant struggle and fight for survival against things that don’t die or stay dead…

The dread that is RE7 on VR is indescribable, The sheer dread of exploring that haunted house with Jack patrolling the hallways is out of this world. It's utterly enhanced by the beauty and realism that VR creates around you, but that just makes the scary that much scarier… I enjoyed the puzzles; they were fun and some were quite the challenge too. This is as close and perfect as you can get to bringing Resident Evil back to its horror roots. Now that it's here they can only up the fear factor for future titles. 

Weapon variety is not in abundance as before, but there is still enough to help you get the job done, and more creative flair was added here. There are no hi tech military weapons lying about, instead, you will find yourself a makeshift rocket launcher and then some… They went the distance to capture every element and ensure that it adds to the overall delivery of the game… Boss fights are out of this world and you will love every second of it, whilst dreading it as well… 

A terrific and utterly realistic horror infested experience you will never forget and this they did perfectly… Topping it off so that it takes place in the current timeline of where the story is within the RE universe to boot. They did an absolute marvel of a job here.

I remember being concerned upon hearing about Resident Evil 7's reinvention of the franchise, completely altering the aesthetic and perspective of the classic series. However, RE7 is a classic return to the survival horror that was gradually fading from the franchise after the first 3 games. RE7 proves itself to be an outstanding & unique experience in the survival horror scene, as well as one of the best entries in the series.

What really stood out to me was the murky Louisiana swamp being used as an amazing setting. The Baker Estate is unlike anything the series has shown us so far and I absolutely loved it. The house is especially eerie, seeing what should such a normal location being so intensely distorted made for a unsettling vibe throughout the game. It all looks very great graphically too, environments are overloaded with little details and lore that tell you more about the story, it makes hunting for every secret or useful item very enticing. Each area you progress through really has it's own compelling identity through visuals and gameplay, they all feel so unique from one another and draw a lot of inspiration from various horror movies, I imagine you'll have a lot of fun if you are a fan of the genre. Unlike most titles in the series, there weren't any general low points because every environment was relatively short and fully utilised the aspects that made them stand out, each area greatly complimenting the character progression across the game. All of these areas were great, but they are so distinctly different and spaced out that they can feel a too isolated from one another at times, I wish everything tied together just a bit nicer. This is especially apparent in the video tape sections, (none of which are mandatory, but do contain vital information for the player), which are very disconnected mini levels that felt very restrictive and boring to play. The disconnection doesn't stop the setting from being a blast to run through, making for a really unique and intense location for a battle of survival.

Something I've always appreciated about Resident Evil is the empowerment of the main character as you go from running from any visible threat to becoming capable of confronting them. RE7 does a great job of maintaining this formula, but with the added twist of a first person perspective, it manages to completely change the horror. The perspective limits your  vision and weaponry quite heavily, when combined with the tight environments, it makes enemy encounters far more horrifying when you feel so powerless. Yet, I'm amazed at how quickly this feeling manages to turn around, gradually understanding the household feels extremely rewarding when you're eventually being faced with more and more challenges, and they keep throwing curve balls that really shake up encounters. I'd say the only mechanic I don't love with the new perspective was the focus on guarding over evasion. It's a completely understandable change, but guarding felt a bit too ridiculously powerful in it's implementation, and I kind of just preferred having to keep away from threats in general. Of course, the greatest enemies within RE7 are the Bakers themselves, and they are thrillingly chaotic to experience. Every family member gets their own time to shine within the story, and much like the environments they inhabit, they are overwhelmingly filled with charm and scares. They're surprisingly funny too, there's a lot of humorous dialogue I wasn't expecting, watching Ethan, the most normal character in the franchise, play off of the absurdity and freakishness of his predicament was great, it was especially fun when they were able to take the piss out the series in general. The boss fights are when the Bakers are at their best in their insanity, but unfortunately these fights often fall into the general RE trap of having simple mechanics and merely serving as a bullet sponge. RE7 really delivers on what makes the series both terrifying and fun, refining the qualities while adding enough changes to bring a fresh experience to the table.

Commendation is warranted for just how well RE7 handles replays too, the series has always  thrived on this due to their typically short playtime,  but I think 7 handles it especially well. RE's formula has always had distinct mechanics that can be played around with in repeat playthroughs. Attempted  speedruns can be a lot of fun after knowing what's in store for you, shaving hours off of your original time, or a no item box run makes you completely reevaluate the value of every item in the game. There are also plenty of secrets to uncover throughout the game which can be fun to return to, and all of these activities can be rewarded with permanent gamebreaking unlocks, so they do have value outside of personal challenge. It's especially notable just how excellently RE7 handles it's hardest difficulty. On top of generally making the game more dangerous, the inclusion of the classic "limited saves" mechanic makes the game far more tense to traverse. On top of that, a lot of elements of the game are rearranged to surprise the player once more, I won't spoil any of them but I'll firmly state that I don't think I've ever seen a game so intensely recapture the experience of my first playthrough once more. The only major problem is unskippable cutscenes, they are so lengthy and annoying in the early stage of the game on repeat playthroughs. It's amazing to me this wasn't reconsidered, it really made me space out my playthroughs due to how annoying this was. RE7 is an amazing experience, but more than anything it's also a game that's worth returning too.

Resident Evil 7 Biohazard was the definite return to form for the series (reaching a stride it has kept going with the masterful Re2 and good yet short Re3).  Both presentation and atmosphere of this game are outstanding, rivalled only by the very best games of its generation (like Alien Isolation). Its sound design and soundtrack are incredible. Obviously the game's narrative falls within the stablished Resident evil cannon, however, and even though in most games its narrative is not its strongest point (despite of the rich lore built around the franchise). I would say the narrative aspect of this game it's one if its biggest strengths, thanks to a few twists and interesting and compelling character decisions. My only real complaints would be the lack of enemy variety, (although boss fights are incredible, one in special), the lack of an upgrade system for the weapons and the overly priced season pass (which I bought as well). At least the "Not a hero" DLC is free. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to both horror fans and new comers to the Resident Evil franchise (and veterans as well of course).

After RE lost its way and release the infamous RE6, they revamped their franchise mainline and release RE7.
At first I was doubting the game a lot, because I can't imagine RE7 game in first-person perspective, but they did it amazingly.

Pros:
+ The first-person is amazing. It amplifies the immersion, the scares, and suits really well for 'survival-horror' genre.
+ Balanced and well mixed recipe of combat and horror elements.
+ The 'smaller' scale in terms of quantity of enemies and characters somehow makes the game feel more personal, and make the antagonists characters to stand out even more.
+ Brand new, fresh story with different protagonist. One of the best thing about the game is players are going in blind and not sure what to expect, even for a long-time RE fan.
+ Classical puzzles are still in place, typical of RE franchise.
+ Well implemented sound design. Hearing the footsteps of enemies walking around looking for you, or when they are chasing right behind you are scarily amazing.
+ On the tech side, the game is well-optimized, running well and stable performance.

Cons:
- The controls and aiming might take some time to get used to for some players, especially for controller users. The implementation of looking speed acceleration as a default is a weird choice.
- HDR mode is hard to be optimized. Lots of times it's too dark, and adding up brightness will only make the ambient lighting too white.
- Item management for those who used mouse might struggle with it. You need to click twice to select an item, and for items that took more than 1 slot sometimes the click has to be precise. Easy solution is to use controller or keyboard.
- Item manipulation on some puzzle might not be natural or intuitive if using keyboard + mouse, because players tends to missed the fact that they can use keyboard as well to rotate the object (players will intuitively using the mouse only while examining the item).

DLC contents not only gave you a full circle of the story, a closure, but also a lot of fun features and game modes, funny one, scary one, challenging one, all there. The only complaint I got for the DLC would be the steep pricing. Buying RE7 complete edition with the DLC is more economical and worth the price, especially if you are getting it on sale.

Resident Evil 7 is a pretty damn good game. While it's not as good as Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's still a really good game and laid the groundwork for RE2R. The game takes a much grittier and more serious approach to the story, setting, and characters (particularly in comparison to Re4, Re5, and Re6.).  You play as Ethan Winters, an average guy whose wife disappeared 3 years ago. When Ethan gets a message from her telling him to meet up with her at a derelict plantation in Louisiana, which he decides to go to. The story (like all good resident evil stories) is carried by the characters. In this case, it's the villains who carry the game. Ethan's a bit of a wet towel, especially when compared to characters from past re games. He's not very interesting and his reactions to everything seem odd (I'll touch on this later). On the other hand, the bakers are really cool villains. Jack Baker is the patriarch of the family and a total bad ass. The guy is basically a terminator, no matter how you kill him or how many times you kill him, he always seems to come back. Marguerite Baker is the wife and is a little obsessed with bugs. She's definitely the weakest member of the family in terms of her character, but she's still pretty cool. Lucas Baker is basically just a younger, more fidgety version of jigsaw (with the only difference being his motive for torturing people in his elaborate death traps). 

The boss fights against the bakers are really well done, beating out RE2R's boss fights by quite a bit in my opinion. RE7 is unique in the fact that it's the first mainline Resident Evil to be in first person. Combined with the RE Engine, this really makes the game's atmosphere pop. Just be sure to keep your brightness low (the game looks like ♥♥♥♥ if the brightness is too high). The game takes heavy influence from films and tv shows like Deliverance, True Detective (season 1), and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre. The game's setting is by far one of its greatest strengths. The game's puzzles are also really well done, especially when compared to a game like Resident Evil 3 Remake...

With that being said, the game is by no means perfect and definitely suffers from some issues. The biggest one that comes to mind is the fact that the enemies that you fight in the game, the molded, are really bland and just unfun to fight. They're basically just walking blobs that go down with a couple of head shots. For the most part, they look extremely similar and just aren't as interesting to fight as the zombies or bows from either of the remakes. They were particularly annoying to fight in the ship section which is by far the worst part of the game. The other big issue with the game is its tone. RE7 still has moments of pure Resident Evil cheese, which would be fine if the game wasn't going for a more gritty tone. Some of the things that happen in this game really break immersion and make you wonder "did that really just happen?". The first person perspective also ends up taking away from Ethan's character. Since you never get a good look at his face, you never get to really connect with him. This, combined a lack of insight to who he is as a character, leads to him just coming off as a generic horror movie protagonist, which for all intensive purposes, he is. 

One department Resident Evil 7 does significantly better in than Resident Evil 2 Remake is DLC. RE7's DLCs are really fun to play. Not a Hero is a fun if short romp that ties up a loose end. End of Zoe is an extremely entertaining slug fest where you go around beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of molded. Jack's birthday is a really fun mini game that sees you going around trying to keep jack fed by killing different molded. Ethan must die is an extremely difficult challenge mode where everything kills you in one hit. The banned footage DLCs are a series of minigame DLCs that are extremely fun to play through. 21 is just blackjack but saw. Room is basically an escape room where you have to not get murdered by Marguerite. Sisters is just a prequel to RE7. Nightmare is just a survival mode, kind of similar to call of duty zombies. 

Overall, RE7 is a really enticing package and a fun time. I'd recommend picking the game up if you're a fan of survival horror games or if you like Resident Evil.

[i]Something's wrong with her[/i]

Ethan Winters has a problem. His wife Mia, missing and presumed dead, has popped up again after four years. Apparently she’s deep in a Louisiana bayou—a lead which Ethan pursues in the hope of reuniting with her.

He finds a creepy house on a plantation, some unsettling totems, and a dilapidated van formerly belonging to a group of hack “haunted house” filmmakers. There’s nothing about this setup that bodes well, but with all the gumption of a man who definitely didn’t watch the first season of [i]True Detective[/i], Ethan enters the creepy house.

It goes downhill from there.

One of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] series’ most impressive attributes is its ability to experiment with form. It’s undergone many permutations since 1996—from survival horror to white-knuckle third-person action—reinventing itself whenever the formula became too staid. It hasn’t always been successful (for instance, I don’t much rate the light-gun entries), but it definitely commands respect.

[i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] was one such deviation from the norm—or at least what had become the norm. Swerving away from the action-oriented third-person format of the post-[i]Resident Evil 4[/i] phase (a game each subsequent installment failed to live up to), [i]Resident Evil[/i] went first-person for the first time since that light-gun game I didn’t much rate.

But it went further than that: it restored the series’ survival horror roots, which hadn’t really been seen in the mainstream since the remake of the original [i]Resident Evil[/i] (2002).

I don’t begrudge what [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] brought to the franchise—it’s one of the best games ever made, so, y'know—but the gradual depletion of horror was nevertheless disappointing, especially when [i]Remake[/i] was firing on all cylinders. I suppose it was inevitable that Capcom would look to change gears after [i]Resident Evil: Zero[/i] disappointed... The series has often suffered from a "one step forward, two steps back" curse.

[i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] brings most of that horror back, chiefly by making players vulnerable again and putting them at the mercy of a limited inventory.

The first-person perspective is an immersive tool used to sink us into the Bakers’ (the family who have kidnapped Mia) plantation and impede our movement. We’re slower here, incapable of kicking down doors and punching enemies, and our main mode of defending ourselves for the first part of the game is holding up our arms to block enemy attacks.

When the shooting does start it’s important to conserve ammunition and health, although that’s arguably much easier than it used to be. If you’re familiar with old school [i]Resident Evil[/i] you shouldn’t have any real trouble here, but there’s still plenty of decent scares—the plantation is an impressive setting and a mighty addition to [i]Resident Evil's[/i] unpleasant geography.

It helps that the game is absolutely gorgeous too, even when it’s dripping blood and ooze and, um, mould.

One of its issues is that it has a protagonist problem. Ethan Winters is straight out of a persistently mediocre horror film that’s been thrown onto Netflix to die. He’s totally boring in comparison to the two female leads, Mia and Zoe (the latter is the Bakers’ daughter, who provides help throughout the game).

The plot would’ve been much improved if it had exercised Ethan entirely and focused solely on Mia, whose backstory and relationship to the key antagonist is at least thematically relevant.

What of the plot, then? It’s okay, for the most part. It’ll keep you engaged, if not wholly compelled, for the game’s duration. It’s a plot that attempts to meld the [i]Texas Chainsaw Massacre[/i], the creepy little girl trope, and [i]Resident Evil's[/i] love of bio-weapons together, and it is not successful in that attempt. None of these elements cohere.

Worse is that it unfortunately traffics in some ugly clichés of the America south. Whilst there is an attempt to subvert these clichés by making the Bakers victims of a strange infection, they indulge Southern tropes even in their possessed state, like derogatorily commenting on Mia’s sexuality. It's so weird, in part because the approach is scattershot; it doesn't resemble anything rooted in reality.

But even if the game fails to come up with a successful narrative, it fulfills much of the criteria to work as a successful piece of video game horror. And once the campaign’s done there’s two pieces of DCL that offer quite different slices of gameplay to the main game, meaning there’s a decent amount of content on offer for its asking price.

In a few months [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i] will serve as a direct follow-up to this one. Once again you’re Ethan Winters, which doesn’t inspire much confidence, but it recently revealed the voluptuous vampire Lady Dimitrescu, whose figure and hat set the internet ablaze. She on the other hand inspires quite a bit of confidence…

I'm really, really hoping that [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i] doesn't fall prey to the series' unfortunate tendency to take a couple of steps back after a triumphant fresh reinvention. I wouldn't be too surprised if it did, but just like [i]Resident Evil: Remake[/i] and [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] before it, [i]7's[/i] fine reputation will remain intact, come what may.

Survival horror is a genre that can be described best as "experimental". Over the years many studios have come along to add their own little twist on the genre whether it was the cramped cosmic horrors of Dead Space, the Japanese horrors of Fatal Frame, the deep psychological torment of the Silent Hill series, they all owe their existence in part to Alone in the Dark and of course the topic of this review, Resident Evil. Resident Evil for the past 20 something years has had quite the rollercoaster in regard to how they tackled survival horror, whether it was with the eerie Spencer Mansion, the Raccoon City outbreak, or the more action packed adventures taking place in Spain, Resident Evil was not afraid to do something different, so much so that this constant ramping in change sort of killed the franchise for a while thanks to its action-centric Resident Evil 6. However, after laying dormant for 5 years, Capcom went back to basic, and I mean BACK to basics. Resident Evil 7 was the first Resident Evil to scare me in a long time, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was it good. 

Resident Evil 7 takes place somewhere in the backwoods of Louisiana. You take the role of series newcomer Ethan Winters, a man searching for his missing wife, Mia. However, once you arrive at the now notorious Baker residence you can tell that Capcom took a lot of inspiration from films like Evil Dead, Last House on the Left, and The Blair Witch Project and as a Marylander I don't know why that makes me happy. Ethan isn't some special operative or cop, he's a civil engineer, he is the most boring and normal person you can play as and that's not an insult because it's perfect. In previous games, you played as someone with some semblance of military expertise Ethan might be hot ♥♥♥♥ at drawing some blueprints but he sure as hell does not know how to use a gun. Playing as a regular guy in a secluded house in the middle of hillbilly land is scary, and it's made even more terrifying thanks to how isolated you feel, you feel like you're trapped in a box that never lets up and thanks to the inclusion of near-invincible stalker enemies it just makes you feel even more trapped because this is THEIR playground, and you're simply a guest for their sick games. Granted you will be armed throughout the game but even early on just shooting these bastards merely tickles them and the RE Engine does a great job at rendering brutal injuries, it makes the gore in this game not just some technical marvel but also uses it to great effect as set dressing. You will see some straight-up gross ♥♥♥♥ in this game, you will do some gross ♥♥♥♥ in this game, and it is really unsettling for first time players.

All in all this a great return to form, and sadly I wish the successor Village could have reached the same level of quality, but it's whatever I guess. But all I can say is if you like feeling uncomfortable, definitely play Resident Evil 7.

Now, I'm not a Resident Evil kind of guy, nor of anything similar, like Silent Hill. The most I've indulged in of the series is two playthroughs of Resident Evil 2 (remake), half of Resident Evil 1 (remake), a playthrough of 3 (remake), and clips of 4 (very few clips). Not much, as far as what can be experienced. But out of all of that, Resident Evil 7 is my favorite by miles. I watched a playthrough of it when it came out back in 2017, but only just recently did I take to playing it myself. And even now, after all of this time, this game is still amazing. A game like this is unique in the horror genre, for a few reasons. 1, it is a return to form for a series which had been thought dead, 2, it is one of the most immersive experiences ever, and 3, it balances its horror with a poignant story. Resident Evil 7, the first of its franchise to be first person, follows Ethan Winters as he travels to Louisiana in search of his lost girlfriend, Mia, who left him one last disturbing message. Ultimately, his journey leads him to the Baker family home, a ruin left in the swamps of Louisiana. When he makes his way inside, what at first seemed an eerie locale soon became the place where his life or death would be decided. He finds Mia, but not as he thought he would. She is infected, changed by some mysterious entity. Soon, Ethan is thrown into a whirlwind of horror and gore as he begins to meet each member of this ruined family. Where most horror games would resort to ending the game with some massive, horrible boss fight, Resident Evil 7 manages to say true to that formula while also presenting the player with a heart-wrenching story of an innocent family torn from normalcy. But between the moments of quiet, be it the safe room or certain cutscenes, there are these pieces of terror and grotesque imagery which remain burned in the mind long after they're over (I still remembered Marguerite, even after four years). The first person perspective allows for a greater immersive unlike the previous installments, and combined with the amazing graphics it really does feel like you are Ethan, inside that tortured house filled with secret doors and items. Oh, yeah, there's plenty of that, too. This is a true Resident Evil game, filled with the same item examination, hidden items, secrets, mechanics, everything. The guns are well crafted and the scarcity of ammo allows for a certain tension to persist throughout the entire game, and for moments of ammo surplus to feel powerful and deserved. Even the DLC is good, with the Banned Footage filling in the gaps of certain side narratives, Not A Hero following Chris Redfield after the events of the main game, and The End of Zoe closing Zoe's story with a short, 2 hour campaign that is one of the most unique parts of the whole experience. Overall, Resident Evil 7 earns its place among the best that horror has to offer, reinstating the legacy of this beaten down franchise. Carried by good horror, a beautiful and haunting score, and a beautiful story which I have remembered for years, this is a worthy addition to any horror enthusiast's collection. 8/10, THE GRAVE WILL OUT THE TRUTH

The Good:

[b]Graphics/Art[/b]: The game looks very good, the atmosphere they create is the best the series has ever seen and the art direction is top notch. The gross out factor for a lot of what you go through is what more RE games need.

[b]First person[/b] view doesn't ruin the series, it fits and doesn't feel out of place oddly enough. It does up the tension a little by not being able to see whats behind your or around the corner before you get to actually look around the corner.

[b]Gun mechanics[/b] are solid. You're not a soldier and you don't wield your weapon like one so there are times where you have to be careful to line up a head shot because you're low on ammo and you have 3 monsters bearing down on you ready to eat your face. Other times you just need to pop a few shots off to throw them off balance so you can run past them and get out of there.

[b]Story[/b]. Story isn't perfect, there are some issues with the main character acting ambivalent to whats going on around him, but overall its a nice compact story that doesn't throw in too many side stories and unnecessary bloat. Gone are the cheesy action dialog moments from other games in the series, and aside from the main character the characters are well written and natural (aside from one frustratingly stupid interaction with a cop). The game drives you forward at a good pace with a story just intriguing enough to want to find out whats going on.

[b]Puzzles[/b]: Not so much that the puzzles are super great, but im very happy they're not some convoluted overly complicated key fetching. Why on earth does a police station have so many hidden doors and stupid statues that need gems? RE7 simplifies everything for the better. Yes, they could be more complicated but at least they're not annoying.

[b]Its not open world. Seriously, I'm getting burnt out on every game needing to be open world.[/b]

The Bad.

[b]Main character dialog/acting[/b]: Writing and acting are an odd thing to criticize in a video game but this guy has some of the puzzling reactions to everything going on around him it would often throw me out of the game when he would interact with other characters. (side note about the story [spoiler]the whole creepy little girl bit is over done at this point[/spoiler])

[b]Creepyness fades[/b] The game looks incredible and has a great atmosphere but I quickly grew comfortable with each environment that it wasn't long before I started sprinting everywhere not worried about what was around the next corner.

[b]Boss fight game[/b] The boss fights are fun, but that's essentially what the game is. A series of boss fights with some exploration and puzzle solving in between. There are other "grunts" that you encounter but the variety is small and they're not always the most interesting to fight.

This game isn't simply a classic, it is a truly classic entry in a franchise which has produced some of the most beloved games in the survival horror genre. It manages to capture every element that one should expect from a Resident Evil game. It is dripping with atmosphere, quite literally in places; the game's environments are quite simply gross in the best possible sense and watching the already decrepit walls of the Baker's home grow black with slime as you descend the next set of stairs inspires dread in a way which so many horror games simply fail to do.
The game's combat and encounter design have real depth no matter how the player chooses to approach them. Whether you are creeping around each corner gun in hand or sprinting from room to room knifing monsters in the knees as you go, the game rewards strategy, encourages the mindful and punishes the cocky. And no matter how bad things might look, your health meter low, your inventory empty, the game always presents a way forward with both its "flexible" approach to enemy and player damage or through sneaky boss mechanics.
The writing is a well balanced combination of hammy b-movie nonsense and cryptic drama. The mystery surrounding the games new protagonist(s?) and their connection to the franchise's existing lore is well constructed, never giving so much that it overloads and bores the player, but giving just enough that fans of the series will have no trouble building intricate theories as they delve deeper into the game's gruesome environments.
While the game's visual presentation is a triumph, it is the combination of the new first person perspective and truly visceral audio design that brings the world of Resident Evil 7 to life. The rotten boards creak ominously as you traverse them, you can feel the fetid swamp water slosh about as you wade through it and you can hear the monster's groan and retch as they slough off the mould caked walls. This is a game which demands the use of good quality headphones to experience it correctly.
The game itself may not have a particularly long run time; with a casual approach the game can be beaten in about 5 or 6 hours. However the density of the environments and the way the survival elements encourage exploration makes repeat playthroughs very appealing. It is very unlikely that a first time player will see everything this game has to offer in a single run, and with the games higher difficulties and the completion unlocks available that becomes impossible.
When considering the elements from previous games that RE:7 absolutely nails and the ways it manages to refresh the franchise and propel the genre as a whole, it is an easy recommendation for horror fans new to the series, and an even easier one for veterans.

Playing through steam will be my second play through of Resident Evil 7: Bio hazard as I've played through 80% of it on the PS4. As a huge fan of horror I can say that this game has unsettled me and truly creeped me out more than any horror movie in recent memory. Most of that is probably because of the interactive nature of video games but this game still gave me quite a scare multiple times.

Story:
The story is actually pretty solid. Having not played any previous RE games I was worried I'd have trouble understanding the larger story and aside from deep cuts to previous entries and the final act RE7's story is very self contained. The story is simple. Ethan Winters receives a message from his presumed dead(3 years) wife to come get her in some swamp in Louisiana. While the main character Ethan doesn't have much characterization or really any character arc for that matter the game still keeps you intrigued as you learn more about the crazy family and the backstory behind the Baker family. The story keeps you engaged throughout its entirety and makes you want to find Mia and take down the Baker family.

Gameplay:
The gameplay is honestly great. The combat is fairly simple which is honestly super appropriate for this time of game. Ethan isn't some super solider who can barrel through enemies like it's nothing. Enemies are smart, scary and often can take some though in how to approach them. ]
This game also focuses a lot on puzzles. The entire mansion feels like one big escape room and finding all the little secrets and piecing all the pieces together is really satisfying.

Graphics:
The graphics are pretty good by 2017 standards. Textures can sometimes look a little weird(it's especially noticeable when it comes to hair or skin), but its not anywhere close enough to distract you from your enjoyment. The scenery and atmosphere of the game are insane. The ambient noises and background audio gives you chills as you walk through the house. I play this with a pretty good quality headset and I'm constantly tense and jumpy from the audio.

Score:
Overall this game is genuinely one of the greats. It's creepy atmosphere combined with the engaging story and thought provoking survival horror elements make it a must have for an horror game fan. Because this game goes on sale like once every month i'd recommend picking it up when it's a little cheaper, but if you're dying to play it full price is well worth your money. Overall i'd give this game an 8/10

Took me this long to finish RE7 but with the hype building around RE 8 and enjoying RE 2 Remake, I'm all in for the series now. I've only played RE 3 wayyy back in the day and never touched the series until 7 came out since hearing that the Resi games from 5 onwards were a bit too actiony, it didn't sit right with me but glad that it's gone back to it's survival horror roots.

RE7 and RE2 seem to play out a similar pattern : You come across a big mansion/building , you find out crazy things are going on, you get chased by some crazy guy, you go through some horror bits, then some actiony bits and back and forth. Then towards the end it all unravels into something very different and starts to tie in to some corporation mingling with test tubes and causing havoc because they're idiots. I noticed this  parallel after playing both games but I like the formula as it keeps each act fresh and interesting, and makes you want to go on and find out more.

RE7 starts off as Texas Chainsaw Massacre, with you pitted against a deranged family infected with the black plague. It then slowly unravels itself as a traditional Resident Evil game when you start to play Inventory Manager and running back and forth picking up stuff, dropping them off into your inventory box in the safe room and looking for more goodies. And the good old "shoot it in the head because its the best place to shoot" otherwise you're gonna waste a lot of bullets.

I'd say RE7 is more of a "Boo!" type of scare than a psychological one. Once you know what happens, the surprise is gone as you realise events are scripted but for good measure. Being chased by Jack Baker, the crazed madman with an axe,  was a nice touch as it was reminiscent of Alien Isolation's alien hunting you down as you figure out where the heck the alien is. Same works for Jack, you wonder where he's gonna go and need to creep your way around, sometimes you just have to run past him, shoot him in the face and hide.

Like RE2, RE7 gets a bit more actiony in the final act as you begin to gain access to some cool toys to use on enemies.

The one downside of RE7 however is that there's not much replayability compared to RE2 Remake. There's no incentive to replay the game once you know where the jumpscares and peekaboos are at and you'll probably cheese the game easily on your 2nd run. Still, it's a good atmospheric experience but I'd say Alien Isolation is a more superior horror game as I felt more dread in that game than i did in RE7.

A very well done Resident Evil game that has loads of spooky atmosphere, fun exploration and puzzle solving. The first person view fits very well and serves to heighten your anxiety when playing (especially in the basement). The game looks beautiful and runs without any issues, the RE Engine is nothing short of incredible. Combat is fine mostly, you are mostly defenseless which makes you even nervous and the scarcity of resources also contributes to that. The Bakers are hilarious and menacing at the same time and exploring the Baker residence is peak Resident Evil stuff imo. Other characters are ok mostly. Ethan Winters is pretty dull and his voice delivery is highly questionable, although it does lead to moments of hilarity. The story was pretty interesting and I was fully invested the entire time as well. I also didn't find the ship part to be as bad as everyone was saying? I mean don't get me wrong, the first 2/3 of the game is definitely better but I think this section gets too much hate, it's linear sure but I found it enjoyable anyways. Difficulty is about what I expected, and Madhouse with randomized item locations and making blocking a necessity definitely makes the game a lot more interesting. 

There are some negatives I have with this game however; the boss fights are very clunky and all of the bosses are way too tanky, I didn't enjoy any of the boss fights in the game and found it a chore. Intro takes way too long and makes repeat playthroughs a slog. The lack of enemy variety is a bit disappointing, was hoping for more stuff to fight and run away from, and the Fat Molded's projectile vomit has a jank hitbox which is completely unfair. 

The DLCs are pretty great; the one with Chris is fun enough but End of Zoe is absolutely incredible. Playing as giga Chad Joe Baker that can fight these mutants with his bare fists and spear alligators was hilarious. 

Overall, this is a game that does a lot more right than it does wrong, and it's easily the best RE game since 4. I would definitely recommend getting this game with the DLC.

Having played every game in the series, Resident Evil 7 is probably my favorite, beating out even the original because of its amazing atmosphere and innovative design. The game takes classic resident evil tropes like the save rooms, big mansions, underground labs, backtracking, and zombies of course, but makes it all first person in a brand new setting. 

This is definitely the scariest resident evil yet because of how realistic everything is. Gone is the campy acting and story of the older games and it is replaced with a gritty realistic style that makes it much scarier throughout. I know some people love the camp of the old games, I do too, but I personally really like the move to make it more serious. It makes this entry feel fresh. The first person perspective is also a huge change, and I really like it. The limited view reminds me of the old games with fixed angles where you can't see everything at once and can be easily ambushed, it really ups the tension.

Graphics and sound are amazing as well in this game, everything looks great and the spacial audio makes it so you can hear things before you can see them. Sometimes and empty room with some sounds coming next door is the scariest part of this game.

The game offers a decent amount of replayability with the madhouse difficulty, I just came back to this game about 2 years later to play it and had a blast playing through the campaign again. It remixes all the item locations, makes enemies tougher, and adds manual saves like the old save ribbons in classic RE games. There is also a free DLC that in my opinion is better than most of the season pass content. It is a must play after the campaign. If you just play the campaign and free DLC it will be a 10-15 hour experience, but with replays and season pass content it can go up to 30 hours easily. I would say the season pass is worth it, I like the extra modes it adds, about half of them are new story content, half are minigames and time trial type content.

The one huge missing thing from this game is the VR support, I am so disappointed that Capcom still refuses to add it. Being stuck in PSVR is a huge shame because that platform is dead now while PCVR allows the game to be playable on practically all future headsets. I would even pay for a VR DLC for this game just to add that support in, it would be one of the best games on the platform if they did add it.

Overall, RE7 is a must play for horror games and in my opinion one of the finest games in the genre. The free DLC is a can't miss too, well worth playing. The season pass content is a nice extra but I would not pay more than $10 for it.

Ever since Resident Evil 4, Capcom had been unsure of what direction to take the franchise. Resident Evil 5 thought it would be enough to simply ape the core gameplay from Resident Evil 4 without realising it was also the pacing, intrigue and set-pieces that made that game great. Resident Evil 6 was simply an abomination for far too many reasons to list here. The Revelations spin-offs were decent games in their own right, but ultimately nothing more than a footnote in the series’ history. Hell, great though it was, even 4 should never have had the Resident Evil name stamped on it.

Finally, with Resident Evil 7, Capcom seemed confident and convicted with what they were doing. Resident Evil was finally scary again for the first time in 15 years; terrifying in the first few hours, in fact. Resource management was finally a thing again, and it was a nice surprise to see the gunpowder mechanic finally make a comeback from Resident Evil 3, albeit in simplified form. Resident Evil had finally woken up to what made it great in the 90s and early 2000s and managed to integrate those components into a fresh, modern concoction. (Yes, it clearly plagiarises The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, but that’s one of the greatest horror movies ever made so I’m willing to give it a pass!)

Resident Evil 7 does lose some of its impact in the final third of the game, flirting a bit too heavily with the action side of things and threatening to generally go off the rails. But while it shines, (which is for most of the game) it shines brightly. Not brightly enough, it seems, considering the rather lukewarm commercial response the game got and the worrying direction Capcom seem to be going with Resident Evil 8: Village.

At first glance, this game looks closer in DNA to Bloober Team's atmospheric haunted house series Layers of Fear than Resident Evil, but ultimately it's still stuffed with RE series staples - from puzzle-hunting to limited resources to inventory Tetris, there's plenty of mainstays that make 7 feel like a Resident Evil game despite the enormous shift to first person. In addition to the holdovers from past entries, 7 adds all sorts of new and entertaining elements to the series, most notably through its VCR system. The VCR is a clever substitute for traditional cutscenes, communicating valuable information to the player via playable interludes. The story here is... fine. Ethan isn't a particularly compelling protagonist, and the Bakers, while scary, aren't extremely well-developed in the base game (though I've heard good things about the DLC). The real appeal, though, is the scare factor, and the game certainly delivers there. RE has never been scarier, and the game maintains its momentum through to the very end. Overall, it's an excellent experience for anyone who enjoys Resident Evil, or any horror games at all.

Don't let the first-person perspective and Texas-Chainsaw-Massacre inspired atmosphere scare you, this is one of the very best RE games out there. Which also means this is one of the very best horror games out there.

Resident Evil 7 is a respectable entry into the series. It's paced much like the first game. I'm someone who's been critical off the series after "Resident Evil 4." Resident Evil 7 isn't a bad game and is worth picking up on a sale if you're a fan of the series.

This game earns all the praise it got for re-inventing a twice deceased franchise. It's pretty appropriate that a series about zombies and other un-dead drives their concepts to they ground with ridiculous ideas a then it pulls them back to un-life with fresh takes on the basics.

It's worth noting that you don't need to have played previous Resident Evil games to understand the events in this game (Ethan Winters goes to find his wife and what happens next). You will only miss out on some underlying context of what is actually going. If you are not the type to stop and read newspapers and notes left behind you will not suffer this at all. Also you will have no idea of who the guy in the "Not a Hero" DLC is or what he is talking about but again, not completely necessary to understand the events of the DLC.

[b]Things to like:[/b]
- The first person camera fits Resident Evil like a glove. It's as intimate and claustrophobic as the Original Trilogy's fixed cameras were intended to be without the god-awful clunkiness that came with them. 
- The controls are just good enough that you feel in control, and limited enough that you feel as the game intends you to. You are just a guy in over his head trying your best.
- The pacing is constant and the plot will hook you in one way or another.
- This game gets to the point. You have a goal and anything you do revolves around getting it done. It's weird to mention this as a "recommendation argument" but it is refreshing to have a game that doesn't waste your time after telling you how important it is to do what you need to do. Looking at you, Witcher 3.

[b]Things to dislike:[/b]
- For all its understanding of subtlety and change RE:7 can't entirely let go of the past. The need to offer a challenge(TM) at some specific points will frustrate you more than anything and it will break you from an otherwise perfect constant flow of tension/relief. 
- No spoilers, but If you are very intimate with certain movies and games the nods/references to them might take you out of the "zone". These references are just original enough to not register if you are not paying attention, but they lack the depth that made the originals work and if you notice them it will hurt you suspension of disbelief.
- Somewhat weak ending in comparison to the rest of the game. This is just to say that it is "decent" instead of "great". It keeps the momentum just enough to stick the landing and it doesn't overstay it's welcome.

Overall it's a short but very sweet experience. I recommend playing at the very least the "Not a Hero" DLC. It's basically just a couple of hours of pure catharsis after playing the entire base game as poor, in-over-his-head Ethan Winters.

Resident Evil VII is a great game marred by a bland and disappointing ending. 

Astoundingly good atmosphere for 75% of the game, you're just underpowered enough to feel weak and endangered but still feel like you're progressing and gaining power. Part of this is to do with the world layout of the Baker estate; as the game goes on you'll unlock more parts of the house and outbuildings, with a comfortable home base/safe area and masterfully disturbing enemies in the deranged and infected Baker family. For this part of the game, you will always feel tense and on edge, and the way the map folds out in a pseudo-metroidvania fashion as you acquire new keys and exploration tools felt truly great. On top of that the early gunplay was perfectly balanced for a game of its type, really reinforcing the feeling of tension.

This all comes with a caveat though. The last quarter of the game sucks. Big time. After making a decision that seems important, everything suddenly changes, and becomes a series of linear corridors full of the exact same enemies, which were scary and threatening the first time you see them, but by this point in the game are boring and begin to seem almost cartoonish rather than genuinely disturbing. This is clearly not what the gunplay was designed for and as a result it just feels like you're playing a really badly made ripoff CoD zombies game or something. The first handful of bosses are great, but I think it's the fourth(?) boss where they just become ridiculously huge masses of generic writhing black stuff. These parts of the game do add to the story, and help to elucidate just what happened to the Bakers, but would have done better to be included as video tapes or something.

Overall, get this game. Especially on the current sale, but either way it isn't very expensive. Most of it is some of the best video game horror I've experienced.

[h1] A Return to Form [/h1]
After the action-oriented focus of Resident Evil 5 and 6, Resident Evil 7 takes the series back to its roots. Yet, even though RE7 goes back to the old formula, it still manages to feel fresh and new. With one of the most intense atmospheres in any game I've played and great level design, there is a lot to like about RE7. In fact, I'd say the first half of the game is near perfect. However, around seventy-five percent of the way through the game, RE7 starts to make some missteps; most notably with its atmosphere. For instance, during the first few hours, I was always on edge; but after those first few hours, I never found myself on the edge of my seat. Now, that doesn't mean that the latter half of the game doesn't have its moments, it certainly does, but it's definitely toned down compared to the beginning. Along with this, RE7 is really short, like less than six hours for a first playthrough. Yet, besides the length and a few missteps, RE7 is an extremely good game. If you enjoyed the old RE games and want to experience an amazing atmosphere, I'd suggest you give this a try.

As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil series, I approached this game with high hopes and expectations. Unfortunately, those expectations were met with disappointment due to Japan's baffling censorship policies regarding gore.

I initially purchased the game, confident that I would be diving into the same intense experience that everyone else was enjoying. Little did I know, the gore had been significantly toned down to an almost comical extent. It felt as if the blood was replaced with candy sprinkles, and the swear words had been sanitized to a point where they might as well have been replaced with innocent playground chatter.

In an effort to salvage some semblance of the Resident Evil experience, I purchased the "grotesque version," hoping for at least a fraction of the gore that defines the series. While it was marginally better, it still fell short of expectations and was a far cry from the visceral thrill that I crave.

This game, in its uncensored form, is undoubtedly a masterpiece. However, the heavy-handed censorship in Japan leaves much to be desired. As a Japanese resident, I can only advise against purchasing the local versions if you're seeking the true Resident Evil experience.

In the end, I found myself with not one, but two versions: the "Candyland edition" and the "somewhat teen version"—both of which left me feeling unsatisfied and regretful. This could have been a great game, but sadly, the overzealous censorship has stripped it of its essence.

This game is one of the worst in the series if not the absolute worst. The game is set up as a survival horror but misses the mark by as large a margin as is possible on the horror department. Instead of crafting any real scary moments they use gross-out, gore, and torture porn at attempts at horror, which really gets worn out before you finish the tutorial.

The character you control plays as the general unbelievable idiot in other games and movies. Big-ass ax, sitting out in the open, easily accessible for usage? Nah, just use the tiny 3 inch pocket knife to kill the towering lazily designed moss creatures. Reasonably fit main character fighting for his life, needs to get away to stay alive, what does he do? Run away? Not at all. The most he can do is walk at a pace slower than an infant crawling, fresh out the womb. Seriously, he moves so slowly, that to outspeed the slowest creature, you have to be on easy mode, which over halves the speed of enemies (with one exception).

You have 4 enemies you will be facing through the game. Two of which are almost carbon copies of one another, just dealing more damage. I don't have a problem with limited enemy design. Some games can really put it to good use. However, I do not believe this can fit among those games. Their danger lies in the fact they do an incredible amount of damage per attack and their attacks actually have a fair bit of coverage. Shouldn't be a bad thing right? It wouldn't be if the entire game wasn't a hallway following another hallway following another hallway following another hallway following.... you get my point.  Truth be told, even this wouldn't be quite so absurdly annoying if there was anyway to avoid the damage. What's that? There is blocking?

Thats right, the character can block in order to receive ~40% less damage from an attack. Which still causes you to die in a frighteningly small number of hits, even on Easy mode. Good thing the game gives you plenty of heals right? Well, sure. I can't really say no. Except I am. Remember how the game was touted as Survival Horror? One of the ways the developers decided to make it fit the "Survival" tag was turn provide you with very limited resources, as could be expected. This wouldn't be so bad, if there were any way to deal with the hundreds of enemies littering the game without being made to use up resources. You can use the knife. Slash at the enemies heads for maximum damage and - now you are significantly damaged and now you heal or die. Or you can run past th- nope. Can't do that, they block the hallways with their overgrown bodies. Add that in with the bullet sponges they call bosses and you can see how this really doesn't deserve the praise given to it. The tried to make a Survival game, with no thoughts on balancing the difficulty, just on the game alone. Outside of the Easy difficulty they modeled the game around the character using all the special items  you get from beating certain challenges and achievement milestones. The fact that Hardcore is locked behind beating the game once should serve to illustrate that point well enough.

Even then, the difficulty developers decided to apparently say ♥♥♥♥ it to all the defensive measures they put in place for the game (Guarding, guard boosting items) by making all enemy attacks on hardcore, in addition to already being strong enough to two shot the main character from full health, hit twice per attack. The guard works like this; hold down a button and Ethan holds up his hands in a 'defensive' position. If the enemy's attack connects with the hands on screen (most of the time) the character will take reduced damage and will break his guard for a second. If Ethan is surrounded and blocks one hit, and gets hit before moving his hands in front of his face again, he will take full damage from the attack. It works the same across all difficulties, but on hardcore (and i will admit this might just be a bug, but it happens to consistently to just shrug off) enemies attacks will hit Ethan twice in the same frame, breaking his guard and dealing full damage at the same time.

This might be a glitch for most of the molded, but it cant be anything but intentional for the four-legged crawling molded found everywhere, which will consistently, reliably hit twice on every difficulty with their jumping attack. I've even been hit what I think is three times with one attack. I say, I think, because this could be an issue with the game altering the amount of damage the enemies can take and give based on... something i cant figure out. I can take out a crawling molded with a single headshot with any weapon most times, and then other times they suddenly become Superman until they kill me. Again, happens way too often for me to consider it a mere bug or glitch. 

Speaking of how much damage enemies can give or take, its real annoying having 1 enhanced bullet headshot take out a molded, and the next time having it survive 3. Add that to the fact that enemies don't show any hint of taking damage until they die and you either spend an inordinate amount of time killing enemies you feel you must, or taking the risk of taking damage to shorten the time.  An all those combat issues are cranked to 11 with the boss fights. Each and every boss attack from melee range and all move faster than, and are all placed either in rooms smaller than a cup or a building of hallways where the boss can stay out of damaging range and take out half your health in one hit from complete safety, or even all your health with their myriad of attacks that lock you into a death animation. 

One of the final gripes is the fact that Jack teleports to always stay with you or to catch up, no matter what the scenario is. Earlier in the game there is a point at which Jack breaks through the wall, Kool-Aid man style (oh so horrifying) and continues chasing you. By using clever movements you can actually prevent him from doing this at all leaving him to do so later in the game. The issue with this is this happens whenever you cross a threshold while the game registers Jack as chasing you. He can break through the wall in front of you, even if he was two inches behind you or if you were already looking into his eyes as he comes walking towards you. It can even happen after he has been "permanently killed" and he shouldn't appear at all. He will just break through the wall, say something, and despawn. With this being a triple-A game, this is nothing short of unacceptable lazziness. This is a subpar Indie fangame with a AAA budget worth less than the disc they were printed on. 

Considering this game has been out for 3 years at this point and none of the glitches at least have been fixed just goes to show that they don't care about making a good game, they just care about making a quick buck off a once respected title. Don't get this game for anything more than 10$ including all the DLC's. This game and studio just aren't worth anymore that that. 

CAPCOM, you were once such a respected publisher, what the hell happened in the past few years?

Resident Evil 7 is a good game with some minor annoyances, as well as some story-related events I don't understand. Make sure you have a good computer. While I played through the game, I seemed to have sort of lag, particularly with turning. It made aiming a bit difficult at times. I messed around with the settings a bit, but fluidity did not seem to improve. At times (and still) I wondered if this "slowness" was an intentional gameplay element. I say this because there is genuine slowness in the game such as when Ethan (the main character) backs up and moves in general. There are almost times where he will fall to the ground and attempt to fight off creatures. The developers even added the ability to block, a first in the Resident Evil series. These decisions -- and the game as a whole -- was designed to feel as realistic as possible. This is helped with the incredible graphics and creepy atmosphere. The environments are so creepy at times I would draw my gun in areas I'd been through numerous times because I felt as if I was about to be attacked. Further, the family in this game is humanized and made to feel like a real family.

Probably the biggest improvement I would suggest if it were possible to go back and tweak the game would be the stealth portions of the game. At certain parts of the game you are expected to be stealthy. When I first encountered this, I was confused about what my full abilities were. This is because there really are none, and hiding basically consists of running to the next room and ducking in a corner. I imagine the developers didn't want to add more options for players because they didn't want this game to actually be a stealth game and were unsure of how to best go about implementing this feature.

That said, RE7 feels like a throwback to RE1. Having the game be located in Louisiana was a good choice. I got to experience a part of the country I haven't before.
