I'm torn -- on the one hand, Resident Evil 7 disappointed me; on the other hand, I thought Resident Evil 7 was astoundingly good. 

I'll explain. 

I've decided to give RE7 a solid thumbs up because for 80% of the game I was so absorbed in its atmosphere; so captivated by its puzzles, and so gutted by its absurdly gruesome gore and maniacal horror that I was constantly in awe. Games are unique in that things happen directly to you -- the player. This is where immense potential exists for scaring the living piss out of people. You're not watching things happen to other people on a screen -- those things are happening to YOU as you play. I'm a pretty big fan of horror with some of my favorite films being The Shining, Psycho, Silence of the Lambs, Halloween, Get Out, It Follows, etc. I've also played a number of horror games like Amnesia, SOMA, Dead Space, Layers of Fear, F.E.A.R., Eternal Darkness, and Bioshock. Let me tell you -- Resident Evil 7 WILL SCARE YOU. It is, quite simply, terrifying, and in more ways than one. It honestly is really impressive just how many ways Capcom is able to invoke fear in an individual -- from eerie music, tense sound effects, dastardly and vulgar dialog, disgusting gore, and peek-a-boo jump scares. 

I haven't had that much experience with the Resident Evil series. I've played a few hours of 4, though never finished it, completed 5, and now 7. I wanted to mention this since I firmly believe that RE7 is a great title even for those relatively unbeknownst with the franchise. Many people who have been longtime fans are praising the game, but I see few perspectives from those who aren't veteran t-virus zombie hunters. It really is a game that is highly enjoyable for anyone interested in horror games. However, fair warning -- don't gingerly step into this game thinking, "I've never played a horror game before, I want to see what it's all about!" My friend, you are not ready. You are not ready for just how ungodly disturbing this game is. 

What about the remaining 20%? Well, that 20% happens to be the final two segments of the game, which I really did not enjoy at all. After being forced to make a choice that would seemingly have a huge impact on the outcome (which ended up not being the case), setting things up for a well-timed resolution once you have escaped the madhouse, Capcom decided to instead say, "just kidding! Game's not over yet! There's a whole big segment you have to do at a different place that feels disconnected from what you just did!" These final two segments are nowhere near the same atmosphere or design of the rest of the game, and the experienced is tarnished because of it. These two segments are not scary -- they feel gimmicky, confusing, and like a distraction from the conclusion you were looking for. There are some things in these segments that fit into the overall story, however they should have been designed differently and placed a bit earlier on in the narrative. They should have been cut down to only focus on how those moments tie into the Baker family. The enemies in these segments are boring blundering infected bodies that hulk and crawl around, as opposed to the still mostly human, demented members of the family (which were much more interesting). The final boss fight, despite coming after an interesting reveal, is regrettably underwhelming, and the conclusion is the least bit satisfying with that choice you had to make having very little impact. 

As I look back on my experience, I can't ignore the sour taste that the final two hours left, which is rather unfortunate since prior to that I was in the midst of an enthralling, dark, and twisted adventure. Hopefully, as I reflect on the game into the future, and continue to discuss it with people, I'll focus more on everything that I enjoyed. Those facets of the game were truly incredible, and I find it such a shame that it lost some of what made it so great before it was over.

About this game:
Resident Evil 7 biohazard is the next major entry in the renowned Resident Evil series and sets a new course for the franchise as it leverages its roots and opens the door to a truly terrifying horror experience. A dramatic new shift for the series to first person view in a photorealistic style powered by Capcom’s new RE Engine, Resident Evil 7 delivers an unprecedented level of immersion that brings the thrilling horror up close and personal.

Set in modern day rural America and taking place after the dramatic events of Resident Evil® 6, players experience the terror directly from the first person perspective. Resident Evil 7 embodies the series’ signature gameplay elements of exploration and tense atmosphere that first coined “survival horror” some twenty years ago; meanwhile, a complete refresh of gameplay systems simultaneously propels the survival horror experience to the next level.
Yeah, man. I'm into it.

Simply amazing experience. 

I was a bit late to the party on this one, being that I had fallen out of love with the series after the 4th in the series (Code Veronica nearly threw me off the brand completely but I endured for Leon’s best outing in my opinion). 

Resievil 7 BH is a very different title to that most seasoned RE fans would expect, it is a first-person perspective horror driven title with less emphasis on action (especially in the first 3 quarters of the playthrough) and more terror and evasion than I remember even in the originals (amplified further in VR so I have been told).
 
The story centralises on the disappearance of Mia, the main protagonists Wife who went missing a few years ago. Ethan (You) receives a message from Mia saying, “Stay away” and of course, like any good husband, he ignores this completely and goes looking for her immediately. You reach the location this message leads you too, the delightful and honestly massive Baker family residence, where things appear to be become very twisted and dangerous as you search for you spouse, uncover the secrets of the house and survive the encounters you have with its inhabitants. 

The graphics hold up well at the point of writing once I got the settings right. The V-sync wrecked my initial 30 mins as all textures were blurry and the hair animations were pixelated but I soon fixed this by switching it off. This is one title you definitely want darker on brightness, very dark, unless of course you are not interested in simulating the true horror this can achieve, which would be a darn shame. 

The soundtrack and SFX are spot on, they are all very chilling and often lead you to think that something is about to come and kill you when in fact all is well, providing a constant oppression that never lets up. The voice acting is okay, you will probably feel that some of the facial animation that accompanies it seems a little off at times, but this is forgivable and does not steal from the immersion. 

Handling wise, it is better on game pad for sure, I had a lot more fumble moments using KB and Mouse then I did on my Xbox pad when using the item interface and the dexterity in combat was much easier to master. 

Replayability is there to a degree, you can ramp up the difficulty and use your first play through experience to make a mockery of the higher difficulties. Once you understand the mechanics of the games and its denizens, you are in control near fully, just mind out for the ‘Molded’! 

Overall a very positive experience and honestly I had to take a few breaks to muster the courage the continue in certain sections of the game, not for lack of quality but I genuinely couldn't face what was lurking ahead at certain points. This added heavily to the feeling of achievement once I progressed through the parts of found particularly terrifying. All being said RE7 BH is not the hardest game I’ve played in recent months being that I initially completed it on Easy and have ripped my way through my hard play through extremely fast but definitely the most terrifying game I've had the pleasure of trying in quite some time.

Resident Evil is back, baby, and in first person! This game is awesome. It is a big shift from previous RE titles, especially recent ones, and that's not a bad thing. This game gives me hope again for the future of the series. 

You play as Ethan, mostly, some random dude who sets off to find his long missing wife (presumed dead) when he receives a message from her. Apparently she has been held hostage by some crazy family. He is pretty much a totally flat and boring character, although I guess that is not out of line for RE. However, it's not that big of a deal as the game is pretty immersive. Going from third to first person, you will feel more like YOU are there and you don't really care about Ethan that much. 

It brings back the "survival" in survival horror in a major way. In recent titles, ammo has not been much of an issue. You are either a badass fighter and don't need much ammo, or the game gives you more than you need, or both. But in this game, you are not a badass fighter, and the game rarely gives you more ammo than you need. Oftentimes you will have to run and hide rather than fighting at all. This is a refreshing change and really helps make the game terrifying, especially in the beginning. I will say that there are a few cheap jumpscares. Normally I am not a big fan of those, not because I can't handle it, but because usually it is a way to make a game scary without actually putting effort into true horror, the kind that makes your skin crawl. Well this game does both. And it pays off, this may be the scariest RE ever made. So I'll forgive the jumpscares. 

The storyline is pretty cool. There are a few twists that you won't see coming. The characters are really well designed. Well, at least the Baker family (the main antagonists). They each have their own creepy abilities and personalities and the boss fights are a thrill to play. Jack is the scariest of all, mainly because he is so aggressive and it seems he is impossible to kill. Lucas' segments are tons of fun to play through. There is one particular puzzle sequence that is really well done and satisfying to beat. 

The DLC is fantastic as well. I would definitely recommend buying the whole bundle. There are a lot of cool little games you can play, each interesting and creative in its own way. The only one I wasn't a fan of was "Ethan Must DIe". Normally, a super hard game mode sounds fun to me. But this is over the top. You die in one hit a lot of the time and get almost nothing that can be used as a weapon. I saw someone beat it online, and realized I probably could do it if I really wanted to, but, honestly, it didn't seem worth the effort. But every other DLC is worth playing IMO. There are some really cool minigames, and the actual expansions where you play as Chris Redfield and Jack's brother are well done. I forget the brother's name, but he is such a badass!! He is like some kind of survival expert and he just goes around beating the crap out of zombies with his bare fists! Awesome! The best part is when you have to face off against the swamp monster in an epic boxing match! So yeah, get the DLC.

The only complaints I have is that some of the faces in the game look weird, and as I alluded to before, some of the main protagonists are a bit boring. In fact, I didn't even feel like saving Mia the first time through, but I did anyway as I felt that is what the game wanted me to do. But all in all, I would put this as possibly the best RE game, or at least up there with RE4, and definitely one of the best horror games to come out in the past few years. Can't wait for the next one!

Resident Evil 7 pivot’s the franchise into a new direction, taking the player from the city-wide zombie outbreaks to an intimate hillbilly house in Louisiana where you are hunted by a redneck family as you search for you missing wife.

The game takes True Detective season 1’s deep south mystery and mashes it together with Resident Evil’s virus outbreak theme which I loved. Players get to experience puzzles, shootouts and horrific boss fights from the 1st person perspective this time round which worked great to emphasize the horror.

I did think that the redneck horror theme ran out of steam by the final act as the expected Resident Evil revelations were made. Until that point the game was fairly unnerving and tense, but it stepped aside for more action and fast paced scares by the end.

Overall, I had a great time playing Resident Evil 7. This is a great revitalisation of the franchise and I look forward to seeing how the game slots in with the series moving forwards, or if becomes a separate branch.

A deliciously creepy but unnecessarily uneven game, RE7 makes for good scary fun, especially the first part.

Roughly the first half of the game provides pure survival horror. The guest house, main house, and old house/greenhouse chapters place the player in a cat-and-mouse game with precious few resources and a slew of creepy characters. The opening twists and the brutal visuals came as a complete surprise to me, and left me terrified as I rounded each corner.

The game complements these superb chapters with exceptionally realistic world-building. You can feel the stench and ruin of this house. The sound design seeps into the marrow of your bones, and the weapons feel strange and appropriate. 

Unfortunately, RE7 finds it hard to sustain this atmosphere and tension. The second half begins with a Jigsaw wannabe, but he never really lives up to the ambition. The "traps" are uninspired and pedestrian, especially after watching the relevant VHS tape that previews the main trap. Subsequent chapters dispense with creepy survival horror in favor of classic Resident Evil action and plotlines. None of it really makes any sense, and it in some ways undermines the terror of the early chapters.

Still, there are some good moments, even towards the end, and it doesn't take away from how much the first few chapters are worth experiencing for their own sake. It's not SOMA or Outlast, but it's a powerful addition to the digital arts horror canon.

Resident Evil 7 makes a departure from the traditional 3rd person view of the older games to first-person which presents the player with a terrifying new perspective on the Resident Evil formula. What originally started out as a tech demo for Sony’s PlayStation VR, ended up becoming a full-fledged entry into the Resident Evil franchise.

You start out as Ethan Winters, just a guy who’s just looking for his long-lost girlfriend, Mia, whom he finds her last known whereabouts in Dulvey, Louisiana. Fate takes a turn for the worst for Ethan when his search takes him to the Baker mansion deep in the Louisiana bayou.

The game’s grimy, oppressive feeling along with the sound effects and soundtrack, gives it a terrifying ambiance. The game’s enemies are quite unsettling, along with the main antagonists, the Bakers (Jack, Marguerite, and Lukas) all looking to tear you apart in some way or another.

Gameplay-wise, RE7 includes all of the standard survival horror gameplay elements: inventory management, save rooms, creepy enemies, puzzles, survival, limited weapons and ammo, etc. with each section of the game filling out the rest of the story giving you an idea of what the hell happened there.

The game is somewhat short, but I feel that its atmosphere, story, and gameplay more than make up for it. The DLC consists of various challenging mini games and scenarios that delves further into the game’s story or put your skills to the test. I find that the mini game “Ethan Must Die” interesting because all of the items you find are randomized, but at the same time you don’t really need any of them.

I find that 7 is a satisfying and a much welcome return to Resident Evil’s survival horror roots and to the genre itself. At the time of this review, you can find this game and DLC pretty cheap when on sale, but I will also say that even at full price it’s still worth it. Two thumbs up, bravo Capcom.

[h1]A good restart[/h1]

Resident Evil 7 presented itself to the world as a kind of reboot, or restart, for the whole franchise. After the disastrous Resident Evil 6, this one bets again for a more survival horror experience. We can discuss the results if we divide the game in two halves.

The first half of the game is very, very good. You will feel kind of weak, you will not have a lot of resources and the map (or, in this case, the house) is full of details. The characters displayed are interesting too, and some minor puzzles that you will have to solve keep the rhythm of the game fresh. You will really want to keep on playing, discovering what is behind every door and keeping an eye on the enemies that may spawn. In my opinion, a lot of effort during the development of the game was put on this phase of the game, and the result is very good. However, the game length of this phase is not that huge (around 4 to 5 hours), and I believe that the developers felt that they had to “add something more”. That is how we get to the second half of the game, which is way weaker. Here the locations are not that interesting, and the game turns into a first-person shooter more than a survival horror. Do not misunderstand my words, the game is good even in this part, but it lacks the excellency of the beginning. Kind of sad because the whole result could have turned to be a flagship for the survival horror genre and finally it is only a good game.

Other aspects of the game such graphics or music are good.

In the end, if you see this game for a good price, you should give it a chance. The overall experience will be quite satisfying.

Resident Evil 7, (or if you prefer it's much more fitting Japanese name Bio Hazard 7,) is the 7th main installment in the survival horror franchise. This game aimed to return the series back to it's survival horror roots, and did so perfectly already becoming many fans favorite installment despite it only releasing a few short years ago. This was not my first time playing the game as I had owned it on PS4 previously. The story follows our main protagonist Ethan Winters as he supposedly receives a message from his wife who had gone missing 3 years prior, telling him that she is at an old farm house in Dulvey Louisiana. As you arrive at your destination you realize the gate is locked and the ringer is out of commission, in fact the entire house is completely run down. You are only let with the option of taking a side path into the swamp with a mysterious abandoned news van, and a fence with a sign that has says the words "Accept her gift!" written on it. Resident Evil 7 as I'm sure you are aware is a survival horror game. That mean there's a lot of resource management, only using stuff when absolutely necessary. If you like horror then you'll like the Texas Chain saw massacre atmosphere that the insane Baker family gives off, as well as the many molded creatures you'll encounter in your fight for survival. This game almost feels like a soft remake of the original game playing it, one of the many reasons it was so successful. Also it's just a really fun and thrilling game in it's own right that has held up pretty well since 2017.

To begin with, I was skeptical about Resident Evil VII at first, cause, you know, RE game with 1-person view? Nonsense, you say. But hell no! I can’t say is it for the best or worse, but the fact is – it’s still resident evil, andi will tell you why.

The levels layout is very similar to the classic RE games – big locations, that are connected between themselves and you are to move around and explore them, progressing through the game by obtaining certain items (like keys) to open new rooms/routes. The saferooms are still here too! With nice new music theme. It is really fun to explore the world of the game, just like it used to be in previous games, like the first RE or the recent RE2 remake. The aesthetics of the game is eerie and the atmosphere is rather creepy that is really great. There are a lot of items to search for, secret areas to find. Weapons, ammo, heal items, even permanent upgrades for the main character. The story is nice, in my opinion it is better than most of previous games in the series. It is far more personal with introducing new character Ethan and evolving around him and his seemingly lost fiancé. Ethan is not some superhero (like good old chris redfield, yeah), but an ordinary man. Which results in the total absence of knowledge (for him) about all the umbrella and virus sh!t and makes the experience much more fresh. 

I have some problems with Ethan though, in terms of character writing and voice acting (other characters are OK). He seems too indifferent considering all of the circumstances and events happening around him.

As for the drawbacks - the first hour and the last chapter of the game are too linear and scripted. Another big mistake of a gamedesign is, in my opinion, the visible autosaves at some moments, that spoil you that you’re gonna have some hard time, which results in you being prepared to it and not to be scared at all. Boss battles are so-so. Some of them are fun, others very scripted and boring. Also some of the weapons are completely useless (yes, burner, I’m looking at you). For some reason the ammo cannot be unloaded from the guns in the inventory, that is very inconvenient.

All the DLC’s are okay, it was nice to get some extra time with the game and to know how the story ended for some of the side characters of the game. There are also quite a few “arcade” modes, that are also fun to play or to pose a challenge for yourself.

Overall, solid survival horror experience, nice story, a lot of content for hardcore players, everything RE fan loves is in this game. Definitely recommend to try it.

As someone who's been a fan of the RE series since the very first game was released on PS1 (a game I still love to this day, despite it being horrendously dated), RE7 is a solid game. It's definitely a serious departure (in many respects) from the older titles in the series, and while I would hardly consider this to be among the best RE that Capcom has ever released, it's far from being the worst either. In short, any RE fans who won't mind a different sort of experience from the one they've (probably) grown used to will likely enjoy this game.

The most obvious departure from the older REs is that RE7 utilizes a first person point of view. Which means controls, navigation, and combat mechanics are quite different, and it's hard to overstate just how serious of a change this is to the overall RE experience. Whether the change is good or bad is, in many respects, a matter of personal taste. I prefer the over-the-shoulder perspective of REs 4,5, 6 and the 2 and 3 Remakes, but suffice it to type that while the first person execution is hardly flawless in 7, it nonetheless works well enough to be a generally enjoyable experience. All but the most nit-picky of players will likely agree.

In other respects, RE7 is actually standard RE fare. The familiar horror themes, story, atmosphere, puzzle elements, unspeakably deformed monsters out to kill you, etc. are all here. And that's mostly a good thing.

That's not to say that I don't have my gripes with this game, because I do. The story is, quite frankly, not terribly original. And while there are good aspects to it, it's fundamentally based on a tired trope that anybody who's played any other REs will not only be familiar with by this point, but quite possibly downright sick of. But given that Capcom decided to stick with said trope, they did about as well as they could with it.
The combat is, in my opinion, disappointingly limited in the main game and not especially well paced. There are remarkably few "normal" enemies early on, and the focus seems more on evasion and avoidance. Yet toward the very end, you'll out of nowhere start encountering hitherto unseen amounts of these same "normal" enemies. In between, you'll encounter a handful of boss enemies, all of which I judge as being on the acceptable end of overly difficult. Hence, RE7 seems to take the mentality of later games in the series: to have generally fewer enemies and less combat overall, but to make each enemy and each encounter considerably more difficult than it was in earlier RE games. Again, I prefer the older RE enemy philosophy, but also understand the appeal of this new (and evolving) philosophy. Preferences aside, the combat is still generally good and enjoyable; challenging, frustrating at times, and occasionally even demanding on patience...but fun, nonetheless.

The main game is a bit shorter than I would have cared for, but it will still take several hours for a typical gamer to complete. For practical intents, its length is sufficient for a full-priced RE game.
The content outside the main game is far inferior, in my view. While the post-game campaign addresses my complaint about somewhat stingy combat during the main game, the combat is neither especially fun nor memorable. Its not atrociously bad by any means. But it just doesn't enhance the overall game package much. All but the most serious RE fans can safely skip it and not really miss out on much.

CONCLUSION: RE7 is a good game that all but the most casual of RE fans should probably play at some point. It's hardly a masterpiece, nor is it what I'd consider to be even close to the best RE game in the franchise. But for those willing to try a different type of RE game, it's still a fun if often quite challenging experience. Some will inevitably hate the new first person mode, while others will love it. My view is something between these two extremes, as I believe anyone who's open-minded, and not completely wedded to old and in some cases outdated gaming mechanics will treat this first person game for what it is: hardly flawless, but good enough to derive a satisfying survival horror experience from.

TLDR: Whether you’re new to the Resident Evil [i](RE)[/i] franchise or not, if you’re after a First Person [i](FP)[/i] survival horror game with some action thrown in then this is easy to recommend.

I’ve played the majority of the main RE games from RE0 to RE5 plus Code Veronica.  The RE franchise has changed a lot since the early days and with the reception RE6 had upon release I’m not surprised that Capcom have, in a way, gone back to the Survival horror roots.  Even if they have left a lot of the RE lore behind with this instalment.

Story wise, which I’ll try to keep as spoiler free as possible, you are Ethan Winters.  A new protagonist in the RE franchise.  Your wife, Mia, went missing 3 years ago but has contacted you saying she’s in Dulvey, Louisiana at the Baker’s residence.  The game opens up with you driving to Dulvey while on the phone to a friend saying you’ve found Mia and you’re going to get her.

From there you find Mia, who seems to have somewhat of a split personality, and the Baker family.  Jack, Marguerite, Lucas & Eveline are the main antagonists of the game, while Zoe is the only member of the family who isn’t out to kill you.  Instead not only does she want to help, she wants to escape along with Ethan.

From here you explore the huge Baker residence as well as few other areas late game, slowly uncovering what is happening and what caused all of this.

I’d say this game leans far more on character interaction than previous RE games.  You learn a lot more about the Baker Family either through direct dialogue, documents scattered around the area or from what others say.  The Baker family are well written and acted characters who you’ll have a lot of interaction with.  I think this is at its best late game when you have a kind of hallucination/dream like talk with a character who feels like they are having a real heart to heart with Ethan and explaining that they are the victims and why this is all happening.  Also I couldn’t help feel a slight hint of sadness about everything.  It’s difficult to explain without spoiling the plot but just pay attention to the motives and documents you get to read.

There are some typical RE plot-holes and questions along the way but I feel this are par for the course with RE games.  Also some things happen for plot-convenience rather than anything but these are few and far between.

As I said in the TLDR, you don’t really need to know a lot or anything about any of the previous RE games to pick up RE7.  There’s only a couple of minor mentions to previous games, most of which take place after you’ve completed the game.  This does make it more open and welcoming to people new to the RE franchise but I’ve seen more than a few people say this is a RE game in name alone.  While I somewhat disagree I do see their point.


Gameplay, to get the obvious out of the way this if the first main RE game to take place from a FP perspective.  It also relies a lot more on horror, suspense and a couple of jump scares compared to the previous 2 RE games.  For me this is a good thing.  I didn’t really enjoy RE 5 and 6 looked way too action heavy for an RE game.  RE7 is a lot slower paced with an empathies on atmosphere and ambient sounds/music over action.  Although you will be doing some fighting along the way, this is a lot more simplistic where you fight 1 to 3 enemies at a time rather than countless hordes.  Along with the mandatory boss fights.  Ethan is not a trained solider and you get that impression while playing, at least to start with.

RE7 has also gone back to how the first 2 RE games played in that you have a limited supply of items to fight/heal with.  You also have a central “hub” area, this being the Baker main house/basement, which you start in and come back to a few times after visiting a few other areas.  The hub area changing slightly as the game progress.

When you start off you’ll find doors or passages locked or blocked off by an item you need to find such as a specific type of key or item.  You’ll find this as you progress allowing you to go back to previous areas and use them.  This can be story related but also includes optional areas where you can find certain items.

Inventory management is again a key part of RE7 as you’ll find far more than you can carry and will have to store your excess items in boxes that are scattered [i](and connected)[/i] throughout the game.  You will also find numerous items that you can combine to create either healing items, ammo or other consumables.

The gameplay itself is solid and if you’ve played a FPS before you should know what you’re doing.  The guns in the game are varied and feel weighty to use.  There are helpful tutorial messages along the way which give you tips about what to do.  These are helpful without being too intrusive/annoying.  These can also be turned off from the start if you prefer.

I didn’t have any technical difficulties.  The only thing I noticed is that there was a slight pause, maybe a second or two, when I was moving from one area to another.  I assume this was because the area was being loaded.  This only happened a couple of times in a particular area for me but apart from that I didn’t have any problems.

On your first play-through you are probably looking at somewhere between 5-7 hours but once you get the hang of the game, know what you’re doing and know where everything is you can finish RE7 in about 3 and half hours.  There are unlockables and achievements that encourage multiple playthroughs as well as MadHouse difficulty once you complete the game.  All in all I spent nearly 80hrs on this game but that does include all the DLC which I won’t cover here.

Personally I really enjoyed RE7 and during my very last play-through I did feel a bit sad it was all coming to an end.  I’m glad the RE franchise has moved away from the action-heavy RE5 & RE6 and gone back to survival horror.  I know it’s probably the most removed RE game in terms of lore but I’d still recommend this to RE fans and new people to the franchise.  It is and enjoyable, solid survival horror game.

This game is a masterpiece. 

Cons first.
-The boat section is miserable at times (but super juicy lore-wise!).
-Eveline is really ugly.

Pros now.
+Brilliant atmosphere. Super spooky. Very icky. Even after my tenth playthrough, a few sections still get my heart pumping (although at this point it's because I'm being chased, many of the scares are only scares on the first playthrough).
+Excellent voice acting. Solid all around. Yes, I include Ethan in this statement.
+Ethan Winters' character is polarizing but I personally like him a lot. His improbable pain tolerance, skill, stone cold reactions to horrifying things, it all just makes him endearing in my eyes. He's a great blank slate/everyman for the player to enter the game with.
+The action is tense, and at times infuriating. 
+The post game unlockables and challenges are fun to use and complete. The game really is extremely replayable in my opinion.
+Stellar DLC. Just...mwah. From absurd minigames to incredible sources of lore, it all works so well.
+Solid length. Not too long, not too short. If you play your first game on Normal, which I suggest you do, you should be able to do it in about 8 hours. The fastest anyone has ever completed the game is 1hr27min. As a non-speedrunner, I managed to beat it in 1hr47min. Like I said, very replayable.
+The story is AMAZING. The action and lore come together to make a wonderful game.

Rating: 9/10
Genre: First Person Survival Horror

The Good: 
+ The game oozes atmosphere in every possible way. Every location, setting, area is well detailed and looks amazing. The production values are very impressive. 

+ I applaud Capcom for taking Re7 back to its traditional horror roots. Compared to the last few entries in the series, this game focuses almost entirely on exploration and stealth over action. Re7 feels slower paced and more methodical (at least in the first half of the game). Re7 seems to be closer to Re1 in terms of pacing, design and structure.

+ Manage your ammo and inventory space wisely, often times you have to make tough decisions in what to keep or what to get rid of. 

+ Hard mode changes items around, adds new enemies in unsuspecting places, and adds a few more additions providing a good reason to replay this difficulty. 

+ I recommend the season pass as it adds a lot of great content. The content ranges from additional story levels, puzzles, mini games, survival mode etc. 

+ Great boss battles and characters 

+ Does not require any previous knowledge of other RE games so newcomers won’t feel lost. 

The Average:

I'm just going to admit it - I'm fan of the classic Resi games in the classic styles, my favourite being 1, very closely followed by Zero. I played Resident Evil 4 and 'enjoyed' it at the time, but my heart is most definitely with the classic style of game, to the point I just couldn't finish Resident Evil 4 when it was re-released because of how arcadey it plays, and how weightless the shooting was.

In terms of the 'other' styles of Resi games, though, there is absolutely no doubt in my mind that R7 is my favourite so far. 

Meaning it is for me the third best Resident game released to date.

The atmosphere it is able to generate (above all else in the first 1/3, confined to the house) is nothing short of ingenious, thanks in part to the best sound design yet encountered in a Resi game since the original all those years ago. In terms of apprehension and terror, it is without question unrivalled in the series. The second location is good, rather than great, and unfortunately it isn't quite able to sustain itself for the final third. But, thumbs up for the most part.

The shooting and combat feels cumbersome enough to be real and yet effective, along with the combat. The boss battles (until about halfway) are fantastically designed set pieces - the chainsaw - is again a series highlight. Considering how I hated the QTE route long since introduced previously, I thought I would hate all the boss battles in this game. Most of them are excellent.

As for problems, well, there isn't a great detail of enemy variety all told, and actually the designs of the ones that are there are somewhat lacklustre, though that is very much in keeping with how everything 'slimey' has become in recent games.

Oh, and whilst admitting I enjoyed at least half the boss battles, the other half were frankly pants - The absolutely worse thing that R4 introduced onwards was the 'giant eye' or 'very clear shiny weakpoint usually an eye' and that rears it's ugly... eye. More than once. Such a shame, but I guess that has become part of the lore now.

As for what's next, time will tell. But I hope this is a sign of things to come with a return to horror, that very clearly is influenced by horror films such as Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Saw, instead of recent efforts, R4, 5 and 6 being like Hollywood B Movies. 

Hearty, solid (but not spectacular) DLC rounds everything off as an easy enough recommendation.

[b]Intro[/b]
Having finished both RE2 Remake, RE5 and having played a good chunk of RE4 and RE1 HD lately, all for the first time, I decided to give this one a shot. Gotta say I was pretty excited for it as, although both the third-person and 'camera in room' camera angles work fine for me, I've always preferred the first-person
perspective in games, so this sounded right up my alley... spoiler alert - it's my favourite Resident Evil so far.
Note: There are some actual spoilers in this review.

[b]The Great:[/b]
++I'm not a die-hard RE fan who's been playing them since childhood... I don't know the ins and outs of these games, but to me this game seems like a pretty flawless transition to the first-person perspective whilst maintaining the original Resident Evil gameplay concepts. I get why people were nervous about this
release a few years ago, especially after the PT/Outlast-esque gameplay demo, but I certainly think this game stays true to its' roots.
++Which is to say, thank God for that, because Resident Evil's basic gameplay formula is so damn enjoyable, replayable and unique that to change it in any substantial way would be a big disappointment
++The game looks great and runs well too. I especially love the swampy, delapidated setting that occassionally feels like a homage to RE4.
++The antagonists are very memorable and are just great

[b]The Good:[/b]
+The audio design is very decent... just make sure you turn off binaural audio. It doesn't work nearly as well here as in other games. All it does is make things sound tinny and distant even when they're right in front of you, such as your own footsteps.
+The soundtrack is pretty good. Especially the save/safe room song, which is equally as good as RE1's legendary one.
+The free DLC, Not a Hero, is a brief (I finished it right on the 1 hour mark first/last playthrough on Normal) romp through some additional nonsense that really plays like Call of Duty: Resident Evil Edition more than the main game. Fun, though, and free, which is quite nice.
+Voice-acting's great
+Despite my criticism below where I think the game's unintentionally hilarious at the beginning, I do appreciate the obviously intentional jokes here and there, usually from your character's responses. Rare, but funny stuff.
+The playable VHS tapes are a great addition
+There's quite a few weapons available in this game, even if some aren't terribly helpful
+The boss fights are terrific and very... imaginative. You'll probably not believe your eyes at one of them.
+The story is a little cliche but overall I enjoyed it quite a bit
+The enemies in the game are fairly varied beyond their generic appearances and feel great to kill, as they always have in RE games (those headshots!)
+The puzzles are great, if suitably (by RE tradition) nonsensical from time to time

[b]The Okay/Not Too Big of a Deal:[/b]
+-The three items available for purchase with coins you find throughout the game should have been expanded upon. It's a cool system, but the choices are very limited.
-+Some of the weapons are next to useless or are very situational
+-This game's never scary beyond a few jumpscares sprinkled thin throughout. Whether that's an issue or not is up to you. Still, the gross out bits and confronting enemies make this the game in the series most likely to get ya freaked out if you're prone to being a wuss (I kid, I kid...)

[b]The Bad:[/b]
-The beginning of this game slowly becomes funnier and funnier as it progresses until it's an outright comedy. The over the top gore, the silly, absurd set pieces, the total lack of genuine reaction to big moments... (getting your arm chopped off and walking around as it spurts doesn't even get a passing mention
by the voiced protagonist beyond a few mild groans right after it happens, neither does believing you just killed your girlfriend, nor seeing her for the first time in 3 years) this initially makes Ethan unlikeable and unrelatable. I legitimately laughed out loud multiple times when I felt like I should've been 
on the edge of my seat
-Unlike as in previous games, there's not a whole lot of reason to replay this
-At 8 hours and 55 minutes on a first playthrough, the game's not overly lengthy, which is disappointing given how quickly the best bits pass (half an hour of that was stuck on one fairly simple puzzle because I'm stupid)

[b]The Horrible:[/b]
--The last third slightly drags and becomes more linear with less environmental exploration. Not to say that these bits are bad or unenjoyable in the slightest because they really aren't, but Resident Evil's at its best when it chucks you in a place with locked doors and areas that you gain access to naturally as
you complete puzzles and explore, so to ditch that concept, or make it more brief, makes the game less enjoyable beyond any brief segments. This issue seems to be a running theme with the games I've played so far, so while it's not at a massive detriment to the gameplay, this is why I'm putting it in the 'horrible'
category.

Sound: 8.5/10
Graphics: 8.5/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Content/Replayability: 4.5/10 
Overall: 8.5/10

[b]Conclusion[/b]
For the first time in a while, I'm actually excited for a new video game release with RE8 coming next year. Bring it on. This game's awesome (can't believe IGN gave it a 7.7) and everybody should play it - as long as extreme gore doesn't bother you.

Overall a really strong chapter in the series, have recommended already and would recommend again!

--------------------------------------------
Short introduction:
--------------------------------------------
Resident Evil 7 is a return to good old classic survival horror roots about solving puzzles, managing your inventory, ammo, health, item boxes, combining items together, fighting monsters, exploration with addition of enjoying your time with the Baker family.

It's a really, REALLY good game with perfect (not too long, not too short) length
of around 11 hours. 
The game can be speedrunned in 4 hours (or less, similiar to older Resident Evil games) which rewards you with achievement. 
There is also tons of different fun achievements related to replaying the game in different ways.

Resident Evil fan or not - buy this game and it's season pass. 
You won't regret it!



--------------------------------------------
About Item Box::
--------------------------------------------
I am really glad that Capcom decided to go back to idea of Resident Evil 1 style Item Box but here is a small issue with it:
They copied it way TOO GOOD and by that I mean they didn't tried to improve the system.
Your item box is a giant scroll list just like in Resident Evil 1 but there is no manual sorting or category tabs that would improve use of it immensely. There is "sort all" button but thats about it.

You can manually organize your inventory but you cannot do that with Item Box even tho you could in Resident Evil 1 for some reason.

Also when moving items there is always a pop up windows asking if you want to move one object or whole stack - wouldn't be better to have option to chose how much you want to move or have 2 different buttons on "move one" and "move all" instead?

Why I can't just simple press X button (whihc is for moving items in the inventory) and move it around betwen item box and inventory item 

Why items do not stack in the item box.... Just why?  
Yeah, it's so fun to scroll even more through a giant list full of items when you have 30 unstackable items and 10 times 30 stacks of pistol bullets and bunch of healing drinks.



--------------------------------------------
About inventory:
--------------------------------------------
Inventory system in this game is really well designed. 
Still, did found couple of issues with it:

Why not combining it with a map screen and files screen with stats screen?
Using map or files screen or nventory doesn pause the game so combining those into a one menu in which you switch tabs with LB/RB would make sense and player wouldn't need 3 separate buttons for that (Start, Select, Y).

Why when using inventory you have to stand still?
Why not allow player to use Left stick for movement and Right stick for inventory management instead?
It would feel less cheap to get hit by enemy chasing you while trying to find a specific item in your inventory.

Why inserting items like Stabiler, steroids or First Aid on quick use button doesn't allows you to ....well, quick use them? 
Sadly, it works only for weapons.



--------------------------------------------
About "the choice":
--------------------------------------------
At one point in the game you will have to do a choice between two characters which affects next cutscene after that and a bit ending cutscene of the game and ...... thats really it.
Everything else is the same.

Kinda a let down because difference between those two endings are not even that big.

Would be better if there was way more into that to encourage replayability.

Why even bother with designing the choice if its pointless?

The game would end up better if it didn't exist to not confuse players into thinking that it even matter.

Also I found bad ending way better just because ending is thematicly better for Resident Evil game (in my honest opinion) and it gives you one extra boss fight (not a good one tho).



--------------------------------------------
About other stuff:
--------------------------------------------
1) No controller layout 
This is not the first time I see a PC port that straight replaces controller layout window with keyboard+mouse keybinds window. 
What's up with that?
Why not have both?



2) Enemy variety
There is a lot different weapons to use but not many enemies to shoot.
From normal enemy types there are only Molded, Molded with spiky arm, crawling Molded, big insect, only one mini-boss: fat Molded and 3 boss fights.

Thats really not a lot considering that this is a First Person Shooter game from 2017 and that older Resident Evil games had quite a lot more different types of enemies and bosses.

It would be great if Resident Evil 7 had like 3-4 more variety of enemies and at least one or two more of mini-bosses.

Gladly in DLC's you can find 6 new enemy types and 2 boss fights to spice up variety.



3) Unskippable cutscenes
They was annoying in 2010, they was annoying in 2017 when the game was released 
and shocking - those are still annoying now.

B button on the controller is used only to cancel stuff such as menus.
Why I cannot press it skip cutscenes - both pre-rendered and in-game?
Cmon! 
Resident Evil 7 is all about replayability - unskippable cutscenes feels like unnecessary punishment for trying to enjoy more of a video game those days.



4) Puzzles
I really like those that are Resident Evil 7 but I feel that there could be more of them and a bit harder. 
Puzzles related to shadows and rotating objects are my favourite.
I wish there was just more of those.

It's kinda funny that Resident Evil 1 HD and original Resident Evil 2 had still to this day the best overall puzzles while being also very fair and challenging in design.



--------------------------------------------
About other downloadable content:
--------------------------------------------
Each one of DLC's is something different bringing a lot of variety and fun stuff to the main game and to be perfectly honest - its a way better idea for DLC's than what Outlast developers did with Whistleblower which was just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ more of the same for 3 hours without bringing nothing new to the table.

Short spoiler free description for each DLC:

1) Not A Hero
Takes place at the same time as final hours of the main game.
Different protagonist, new area, new weapons, punching mechanics, new enemies and new boss fight.

2) End of Zoe
Takes place at the same time as final hours of the main game.
Different protagonist, new area, a melee combat system, new enemies and new boss fight.

3) Nightmare
An interesting spin on classic mercenary mode. 
Kill enemies, collect scrap, buy upgrades, unlock new perks

4) Bedroom
Escape Room style collection of fun puzzles

5) Ethan Must Die
Basically Resident Evil 7 but as challenging roguelike

6) 21
Blackjack mixed with random trump cards and unlockable rewards

7) Daughters
A prologue to the main game that shows Baker Family fall into madness.
Its short and simple with 2 different endings. The main challenge is to figure out on your own how to get good ending

8) Jack's 55th Birthday
Imagine classic mercenary mode but addition of collecting and crafting food for Jack to earn bonuses to reach best possible score



Overall DLC content for this game is awesome and definitely worth playing!

I am truly surprised with this game.
At first, I was skeptical because I am a huge fan of the Resident Evil franchise, and this did not seem like RE at all (especially because of its First-Person perspective, but also because there is only one playable character from the original games, and it's a DLC).
But the new camera angle is refreshing. The first three RE games had a fixed-camera angle. The other three (4, 5, 6) had an over-the-shoulder view. So I understand Capcom wanted to changed things up, and show us different ways to enjoy survival horror, and this is truly the scariest RE game I've ever played (and the camera angle influences this greatly).

The new characters, but specially the protagonist (Ethan) truly give us new content to this world, but I did find him a bit boring. I reckon this makes all other characters more interesting, so I'm good with that.
Also, I did find many nods to previous games, including the bathtub (from RE1) and Alyssa Ashcroft (from the Outbreak games). The puzzles are great. Not so hard, yet not so simple. Just what I expect from Resident Evil.
I haven't finished the game yet, so I'll probably find some more, and I will be sure to update this review if I think it is needed.

I wish we had zombies, lickers, hunters... But hey, I don't blame Capcom for trying something different. That's great. And I'm not a petty fan, screaming "please me, please me".
I appreciate their creative and innovative thinking.

Resident Evil 7 is the revival title for the Resident Evil series after a long and messy history. This series is home to some of the greatest games ever made and the early series entries helped to popularise and set the standard for survival horror. Unfortunately, after the massive success of Resident Evil 4, a more action focused title, the series had a total downfall. Resident Evil 5 was a complete retread of Resident Evil 4's gameplay, but without any of that games character and featuring an over emphasis on co-op that massively hindered the singleplayer aspect. Resident Evil 6 was an abomination of Michael Bay style action, incredibly generic and uninteresting writing and an unnecessary episodic structure. Resident Evil 6's failure led to the main series going into a hiatus for a long while. Thankfully, Resident Evil 7 shows that they truly learned from their previous mistakes and it takes the series back to ground level where it belongs.

The story follows Ethan Winters, a new protagonist who goes to Dulvey searching for his wife Mia, who he previously believed to be dead after years missing. Soon after arriving however, things quickly unravel and he finds himself fighting for his life as he his hunted by the crazed Baker family. Your goal is to figure out what is going on and to escape with your life. Without spoiling anything, its a very solid plot that holds your attention the whole way. Ethan as a character is pretty hollow, but by thinking of him as an extension of the player, it didn't bother me too much. Thankfully the other characters in the story are far better. The Baker family is intimidating and endearing. There is far more to them and their predicament than meets the eye and as the puzzle pieces fall into place, not only does it all make sense, but you discover how it ties into Resident Evil as a whole.

Visually, the game is really great. Initially I noticed some strange lighting problems in the beginning, but with some simple setting changes, this cleared up straight away. In addition to looking good, the pc version is also runs very well without any performance issues. I was able to run the game at 144 frames maxed out the entire way with no problems. The lighting effects and environmental detail do a lot to generate atmosphere and there was never a moment where I felt pulled from the game. I was immersed the whole way through.

The sound design is also really good. The creaks and random sounds of the old Baker property sound perfect as you scurry about. The weapons all sound very solid and feel great to use when fighting the various enemies throughout. With the exception of Ethan's frequently bland delivery, the voice acting is top notch. Jack Baker in particular is a huge standout and every moment he appears on screen is a treat.

The gameplay of Resident Evil 7 goes back to basics. Its a linear experience, taking place across the various areas of the Baker Property. By dealing with the bakers and exploring new rooms, you will find keys, unique items and puzzles that will aid you in opening up more of the property. There are numerous unique weapons for you to use against your enemies, ammo doesn't grow on tree's and you have a small inventory that must be managed. Saving the game requires save rooms, giving you a save point and also a storage box for any spare items you find. It is in all essence, Resident Evil, with the only difference being that it is in first person. 

It is also important to note just how important knowledge is in this game. Knowing who you can fight, where you need to go and where all the items are can not only massively shorten the games length, but also make things way easier on you. This marked probably my 4th play through, as I had beaten the game once prior on pc and twice on xbox years ago. Playing through it again on normal, I was able to blast through the game in just over 4 hours and still having hundreds of bullets and items spare.

Your first time beating it would probably take you more 7 to 8 hours, but this all depends on your knowledge determination.

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a great game and I would easily recommend it for any horror fan. Some may not care for the character direction it took, or the first person view. People need to understand however, that without this game, Resident Evil would have either gotten worse, or stayed dead.

I purposely swayed away from this game for quite some time, as all I constantly heard is "boo it's not resident evil at all", but now I've finally got around to try it out for myself and well I'm actually very pleasantly surprised. Idk where a bunch of those people are coming from but aside from the first person camera perspective, it still holds all of those key resident evil elements we all love in their games (well unless someone loves tank controls and fixed angles). It has the inventory management, item hunting, heavy emphasis on exploration, cute puzzles and bizarre big disgusting bioweapons. I don't see what you're missing here. If you still disagree then tell me what makes a resident evil game and what from that is missing from this game aside from the changed approach.

Yeah the world isn't with your classic Leon, Claire or Jill, but that's not exactly bad, we can't just be stuck with the same stuff over and over, you gotta have something new and fresh, and sure, Ethan and Mia aren't quite anything really. Ethan is a pretty basic protagonist, which I don't necessarily hate though, I don't really mind character-less protagonists in games. Mia is kinda bland aswell, just your "I'm not gonna tell you anything" side character you're hunting for the entire game.

Speaking of the game, well the pacing is a little bit off, the first half or two thirds are really really strong, but when you get to those finisher areas (ship and mines) it wears down quite a bit. The mines are "ok", they're just kind of a straight run to the exit through a bunch of enemies, but the ship sucks man, it's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring. Atleast it unravels some of the story elements. 

I wonder if there was some inspiration from Texas Chainsaw Massacre, as the setting and circumstances are quite reminiscent of it (crazy family, old big house, trees?). And btw yeah, you get to have a chainsaw too, don't worry. 

There isn't really much I could hate, story is nice, graphics aren't the most high quality, but the way the detail and atmosphere is done brings it all together to make a very good rusty-feeling vibe and photorealism. Soundtrack is whatever, nothing memorable really. Enemy variety is small but it's whatever aswell. The jumpscares are pretty wacky, but they're nothing too crazy and are fairly far between. What I didn't like at all is this FEAR-esque antagonist (the Eveline girl), that was just kinda goofy to me, never found little supernatural girls too scary.

Aside from that, I also didn't like the crafting much, it's basically a "universal item + whatever = something". So as long as you don't have the universal item, you're just sitting on a bunch of gunpowders and herbs, but then again, atleast you're not wasting as much inventory space with a bunch of crafting materials (usually). And that brings me to the fact that if you face it, this is pretty much the RESIDENT EVIL 2 Remake but from first-person gameplay-wise. You can break crates with your knife, gather supplies, use the save rooms with the storage chest, and while on that you also evade some invincible enemies, kill some lesser enemies and solve little puzzles. 

I don't see what's so different here and now I understand why this game actually has a pretty high score despite the initial backlash. I'd say it's a strong recommendation if you're looking for some classic survival horror experience and don't mind the first-person camera.

[h1]What I loved:[/h1]
I have played a lot of horror games and this is one of the few that managed to startle me at times. It manages to do a great job at making you feel trapped with a bunch of family members out for your blood just like real life. The move to first-person may annoy some people but boy does it work amazingly with the type of gameplay and atmosphere present in RE7 as it goes back to Resident Evil's roots of being a true horror survival game. Also, the characters and the story are very well written, which is something previous few RE games have struggled with.

[h1]What I didn't like:[/h1]
Close to the actual end of the game, you will be asked to make a choice. Now my gripe isn't with the fact that you are expected to make an RPG-esque decision in an RE game, or the fact that [spoiler]Zoe[/spoiler] ending is pointless af for  [spoiler]Zoe[/spoiler] ; No. My gripe is that regardless of the choice you make, you will follow the exact same gameplay sequence and be forced to play through the weakest part of the game[spoiler](The Abandoned Ship)[/spoiler] in both endings, just because [i]Capcom wasn't ballsy enough to deprive players of exposition if they made the alternate choice(bad ending)[/i].
 As for why I  am not a fan of this segment? It's because this is the part where RE7 turns from a horror-survival game into an arcade zombie shooter. The creepy atmosphere, the mystery of exploration and the sense of vulnerability is given up in favour of arena styled linear level designs where you go forward mowing down Infected with your SMG and explosives as if you are a descendant of freakin John Wick and Doom Slayer. Fortunately though, this part is quite short ranging from 1-2 hours depending on your speed but you will have to go through it twice to get both endings(and the difference is nothing more than a different cutscene). 

Even with that minor issue I have with this game, it doesn't stop it from being one of the best horror game I have ever played. Really Excited for RE VIII 😍

TL;DR: If you can stand playing under constant high tension caused by darkness, eerie sound and creepy music and the constant fear of running out of ammo, then this is a game for you. Otherwise, stay away.

I played Biohazard after a short excursion into Resident Evil 5, which is just horrible, completely ruined by its bad controls. I was relieved that the developer opted for a standard WASD control scheme. It works great without even remapping keys, which is rather rare today. The other technical aspects of the game are also very competently done. In 2020 the graphics, animations and the sound design are still superb. Only the textures and models of the faces and extremities of *normal* people look waxen, like that of dead or very sick humans. Especially Mias first, un-mutated appearance in the intro sequence looks quite uncanny.

Most of the game happens inside the horror movie staple, dilapidated farm house of the Baker family. You are vulnerable, badly armed and lowly supplied. This and the dreadful atmosphere created by gloom, shadows, creaking and pattering noises, the ominous and, in times of imminent danger, pounding music score, will keep your adrenaline level high all the time.

Monsters require head-shots unless you want to waste your precious bullets on them. But they have the annoying habit of suddenly bobbing their head around or protecting it with their arms. This can get you pretty fast cornered or out of ammo. And for me that meant reloading. In certain passages this can be quite frustrating. On the other hand, foes will not respawn once you've dealt with them. This and ability to save the game as often as you like on any tape recorder you find (i.e. not requiring tapes as in earlier installments of the series) take a lot of the edge off.

But still, the constant stress is the weakest point of the game. There is nothing joyful in it. It kept myself asking, why am I playing this? And I was severely annoyed when after ten hours of this ordeal and after what I thought to be the final boss fight in the Baker's family home, the game kept going on for another four hours. It was actually too long. I wish there were more relaxing sequences where you could explore what lead to this horror.

TL;DR: RE7 is a good game. It's not incredibly great, but it's good.

The visual style of the game is great, with incredibly detailed environments, a fresh look into a not-usually-explored setting, and good animations for everything too. The faces can be somewhat uncanny valley material, but this IS a horror game, so that actually fits. The hair, on the other hand, just never looks good, regardless of graphics settings. The first problem this game has is also related to this: the settings are apparently a little broken and you need cards released after the game to be able to play it with some settings on High. Still, pretty much everything looks fine even with some stuff on Medium, aside from one scene right at the very end where a bunch of blocks kills immersion.

I've talked animations, but the voice acting in this game is also pretty good for a videogame. It's cheesy, for sure, but Resident Evil knows what it's doing, and wears its heart on its sleeve. Jack and Lucas' actors are particularly good in this regard, with really good performances anytime they show up. 

As a horror, RE7 manages to have a creepy atmosphere at several points (though it does fade away with you getting more and more used to the game's tells), has disgusting visuals at several other points (whether that's scary or not is up for debate), and does have the occasional monster-jumps-in-your-face moment to startle you, but those are few, and often used well. The monsters themselves, including bosses, on the other hand, are the opposite of scary, several times looking almost comedic. Horrifying, still, but in a comedic sense. RE knows it goes over the top here and there, and it's not afraid to lean on that, which I respect, but a huge face with 10 eyes as weak points in front of me gets me to giggle instead of making me afraid.

As a shooter, it's mostly competent. You're not supposed to be guns blazing, and the game gives you enough resources that if you manage well you can be extremely safe through the whole playthrough, but you'll still have moments with a shortage of ammo or health. This sometimes makes the bosses in particular feel too long. There's some weapon variety, but I found the Burner in particular to be extremely underwhelming, being useful for exactly two enemies, and never again.

As an exploration/puzzle game, I loved it. Scouring through these maps and figuring out the madman's way of locking off areas of the house in order to make intruders unable to get anywhere, and even going through some pretty wildly weird and video-gamey puzzles was fun. It's never too ridiculous, and the story has a perfectly acceptable fallback in Lucas' particular case of psychosis, which leans us into the story.

The story is mostly fine. The game sort of presents backstory by giving you tapes that people have filmed on some sort of portable cam recorder (that are fire proof, still produce a tape even after it's been dumped in water, and well, produces a tape to begin with) which doesn't really work a lot of the time, but that's a gimmick that can be forgiven. The actual story of Mia and the Bakers itself is passable, and figuring out the mystery of why everything's going to hell is fun, but it's nothing remarkable in any sense. What makes it specially disappointing is that at one point in the game you're given a choice of ending, but one of the choices is just... wrong. So much so that the game just invalidates your choice entirely not one minute after and all you get is one more unexciting boss fight. It feels cheap, and the choice is before the final chapter of the game, so if you want to get that achievement you're forced to play that whole segment again, for no additional look into the story or characters whatsoever.

I don't know if RE7 is a good Resident Evil game having not played others, but it sure as hell is a good game. Its bad parts are either easy to forgive or just annoying for achievement collection/completionists, it's competent in all regards with a [i]maybe not[/i] on story at most, and definitely gets you immersed in this weird swamp house and its crazy meat family.

I played standard edition of this game. A good and spooki adventure. I recommend [b]but only on a big discount[/b] due to what I believe is low playtime/replayability compared to other games I'm into.

[h1] The (Mostly) Good [/h1]

Definitely a compelling horror game, at least for the first two thirds. Lots of tense sequences where you gotta sneak around or the big bad man will get you, other sequences where you just gotta run for your life, etc. Something I haven't heard anyone talk about in this game is there's a whole separate location after the farm, so I was expecting it to be a short game and thought it was about to finish when suddenly there was a whole other section of the game to get through, so that was a nice surprise. However at this point it becomes more of a shooter than a horror. That's okay and gives some variety (You don't want to spend the entire time crapping your pants) plus gives you excuse to use up all the weapons you acquire, but in my opinion it's just not as good as the first third of the game.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

The demo I played before buying this raised my expectations. In that demo really small choices you make determine what happens next and what items spawn where, etc. The demo even has three endings! I thought these principles would apply to the real game, so I thought certain things that happened in the game could be done differently (like the screwdriver in the hand sequence in which your character moves if you hit the right buttons) and I reloaded my game to get a different result... only to discover everything is completely scripted and they've just given you the [i]illusion[/i] of being able to affect the outcome. Don't fall for that trap, folks, you'll just wait your time replaying annoying bits for nothing. There's just too many scripted events in this game for my liking, to the point it started getting stupid. They specifically give you a choice of characters to make 2/3rds into the game, and if you make the less obvious choice, then it doesn't matter because the person you're [i]expected[/i] to choose magically teleports to you despite not having a vehicle to get to you. They make zero attempt to explain this at all. And other stuff like one of the bad ladies was on the other side of an inaccessible area, I then sped across using a passage and she teleported in front of me. Because I knew where she was coming during replay I aimed my camera there and yeah she literally materialised out of thin air... no one in this game is meant to have teleportation.

So yeah, mainly just overuse of scripted events (Also the tank-like nature of recurring bosses), and the lack of actual choices in this game compared to the demo. Those lack of choices mean that to me the game is not worth replaying; their encouragement of you to replay is by giving you an even harder difficulty and go "oh no everything's still the same but we moved a couple items around, and now it's even harder", that just doesn't interest me at all.

[h1] Free DLC [/h1]

No matter which version you buy, you get the "Not A Hero" DLC, and apart from the first 8 minutes it uses completely new maps, so that's nice. However this is quite obviously just an action game now, no real horror, just shoot everything that pops up. It kept me busy for just under 2 hours all up I think. I wasn't particularly impressed with any aspects of the DLC, just exploring a map that you don't go to in the main game (But it's a pretty average map... a bunch of caves). This DLC has zero choices, compared to the main game which at least gives you little choices even though they don't affect the overall outcome. If you haven't played the "First Hour" Demo for RE7, play that, it's better than this DLC. No reason to replay this DLC, it just gives you a bonus item and harder difficulty if you do.

[h1] Summary [/h1]

I bought this game off Fanatical for $12.20AUD, and for me it was definitely worth it, I got my money's worth. It's a good game and I glad I played it, but I was expecting it to be better, and I felt slightly misled by the demo which had a focus on multiple endings and all sorts of different choices and paths to uncover.  Still though, good game if you're not paying full price for it

When I first played RE7 I wasn't sure at first. But after playing through most of it I really enjoyed it. It was a solid horror experience.

Game isn't quite as typical when it comes to the Resident Evil gameplay style we've all grown to know, this one takes it from 3rd person to 1st person and adds a crouching mechanic as well as a guard one that reduces damage taken if done right. Overall my biggest interest in the game was the new concepts they implemented and how surprisingly well they worked out given how many times they used the old 3rd person mechanic. It plays fluidly and has a great story with a generously catered to backstory to appeal to those who thrive on immersing themselves into the storyline alone. The game even has an after-ending campaign you can play that takes you into a new persons mission, a familiar (yet physically unfamiliar) face now working for the one and only Umbrella corporation re-established by some of the original employees and some new, dedicated to fixing their predecessors wrongs, or so it seems, you play as Chris Redfield, an agent enlisted by Umbrella to help contain this new outbreak before it gets out of control, the gameplay in this mode is also just as enjoyable if not more so(more goodies to play around with and experiment using) although not as lengthy as the main campaign, its still a good enough and reasonable length considering its an epilogue to the main story where you take down the last remaining enemy whom I shant name here as to not spoil too much for those who are reading this before buying. Better than average boss fights all throughout and when it comes to the newer generation of games these days this definitely is a 4.5/5 star game if not a full 5 stars. A must buy for those who love the franchise and even more so for those who felt disappointed with Resident Evil 6, this one definitely makes up for that and then some. 110% recommend this for veterans and newcomers alike.

Alright, after an initial negative impression and review, I have to make things right and correct some statements. So it took me quite some time to get into this game, because it failed to catch me. The first 3 hours took me about 5 days with short sessions to play. Even though mechanics like finding keys to open doors and little puzzles here and there are main elements of the Resident Evil series, the overall setting just didn't felt right. There were no Zombies, no connection to the previous parts of the series. This basically was "just" a good horror game, which I wasn't looking for. I felt betrayed, because this game seemed like it changed way too much of the successful formular. 

So I eventually forced myself back into the game after a long time. The game loosely can be broken down into 3 parts. The first 1/3 of this game is as I described at the top. We get a unique setting in a house full of crazy people, looking for your missing girlfriend. It becomes quickly clear, this is more a horror game than Resident Evil. The character is weak and basically just running and hiding a lot. Ethan, the player character isn't Military or Police or something unlike most of the other RE characters. The most annoying part here I think was that characters suddenly can appear out of nowhere and take control of your camera in 1st person. I think that is what I hated the most, because I want to stay in control and not get stuck in so many 1st person cutscenes all the time, which basically are nothing more than jump scares.

But then the game changes. The 2/3 of the game you can see how Ethan evoles as he further explores the house and unveils it's secrets. Basically the moment you exit the house into the backyard and the trailer. That's where things get more Resident Evil appropriate. You will encounter some Zombie-like enemies, other than just the Baker Family. Also your weapon arsenal slowly gets better, which takes away the horror and turns into "payback time" situation.

The last part of the game 3/3 is a little hard to describe, as it might would spoiler a little too much, so I'll keep it short. The last part turns into a full Resident Evil experience, with all the elements I was expecting from this game at the first place. It has some weaknesses here and there, but overall the last part is the most enjoyable and the story finally managed to hook me.

So to summ things up: The game has a slow and rough start, which is quite untypical for any of the RE games. But it surely deserves a chance, because what follows gets better and turns into quite an enjoyable experience. It also creates some connections to the series, even though I was hoping for more. Protip: don't skip any log files, since they make out most of the story... The game leaves some unanswered questions at the end though, which some DLCs further explain, what a coincidence ;)

If you also felt betrayed like me from the first 3-4 hours of the game, then definitely give this game another try!

RE7 is a return to form for the series, and is, in a lot of ways, the game that RE1 (the original, '96 release) was meant to be. 

This game is a claustrophobic first-person experience with a slow pace, heavy horror themes (lots of homage and reference to Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Blair Witch Project, The Grudge, The Ring, Sweet Home (the NES game that laid the groundwork for the development of the original RE) and of course Resident Evil itself (namely the original game)). If you're a 'second-generation' Resident Evil fan that originally encountered the series around or after RE4, the gameplay will feel slow and off-putting. If you're a 'first-generation' RE fan that encountered the series in the mid and late 90's, then this game is right up your alley. 

If you know anything about the plans for the original Resident Evil, you'll know they originally wanted a first-person horror experience, and were hoping to make another 'Sweet Home' game (following a team of film-makers trapped in a haunted house). This game takes some of those original ideas and brings them to life, now that they have the technology. The Bakers' mansion is also a huge call-back to the original RE (similar layout, themed keys to collect, even a shotgun booby-trap). So it's just really neat playing the game the RE devs were dreaming up back in '95, but couldn't develop because the tech wasn't there yet. I'd say that alone is worth the price of admission if you're an old-school RE fan.

Aside from that, I'd also highly recommend this if you're a horror-gamer in general. Like most narrative-driven horror games, after your first play-through you know where the scares are, so it's less tense, but the AI of the pursuit bosses (Jack and Marge) can still surprise you at times. The harder difficulties and extra modes in the DLC add replay value if you like challenging yourself, doing speed-runs, or scratching your completionist itch.
