A lot of people say this was Capcom coming back to true form for the RE series. Although I can definitely see why people would say that, by the end of RE7, it felt, to me, like they went right back into their old RE 5/6 ways. A lot of ammo, and the fear factor pretty much non existent. For me, the first half of this game brings so much enjoyment I know Ill play again. The Bakers and their mansion is a wild ride, and the slower moving character along with the sound of ever enclosing foot steps right behind you, while trying to bust down a door that likes to be caressed apparently before opening, will absolutely get the heart racing! To finally finding your first gun, and Ethan says, "alright, you want to fight, lets fight" (most likely butchered what Ethan said, but still) and you can actually feel this emotion! Although finding the first gun doesn't take too long, in comparison to a typical RE game, its truly different. 

One thing I have to give credit for, is the main character, Ethan. Capcom does not give him a standing ovation of acting, or plot development. However, they do incorporate his lack of skills and you can sense his fear in the beginning of RE7. One thing you do notice though, is every fight, he seems to harden up a bit, and become more of a fighter, then a confused guy looking for his wife in the back woods of Louisiana bayou. Going from frantically running and hiding, to saying lines like, "STAY DEAD!". For me, I enjoyed this part, because as the player, I felt these emotions throughout the game as well. However, there should be a balance here, which sadly, Capcom did not do.  

If you haven't heard, the standing ovation goes to the Baker family. Everyone does their part, from the alpha dog, Jack. To the wise cracking, young buck, Lucas.  The survivalist, Zoe, and to top it off, the freakiest, Marguerite.  I had a blast finding my way through the mansion. Although I think the puzzles in the entire game, could use some work. First time through, I think you are more star struck on how good the game looks, and the horror vibe its going for an nails, keeps you from seeing the cracks in the walls. But the second / third time through, even if its more then a year later, you will easily remember the answers or what to do. That being said, up until the last quarter of the game, the mansion, old house, and Lucas SAW (the movie) like inspired barn are a sight to behold and designed very well. Which in turn helps the jokingly easy puzzles through out RE7. The last few locations were quite boring, in my opinion, and like I said, mix that with zero terror and pretty much all the ammo you want, and you just kind of feel confused on who took over the reigns randomly while developing this game. Granted, one location, is story driven, and makes sense, I just wasn't the biggest fan of it after the the original locations. 

One things I have to give MUCH credit for is the score! Wow! If you play RE7, look at the map until you see the 'kids play room', or something along those lines and listen to the track as you go back through the halls! It does exactly what it needs to. Although the filler enemies in this game are lack luster, after seeing and fighting them. But mix the enemies, with the beautifully, creepy, aesthetic, and of course, score, it kept me on the edge of my seat the entire time. And you most likely know, and cannot forget the main track, Go Tell Aunt Rosie (in the game trailers). You actually hear this hummed by an NPC actually, which I did not realize this my first play through, and it is the end credits track, which tops it off very nicely. So as far as the score, phenomenal job! 

The gun models look great! I cannot really complain about any. However, one HUGE drawback, and, to me, every RE suffers from, is they do not feel different. More then that, do not sound too intimidating. I REALLY hope Capcom corrects this in RE8. Although I doubt this because I do not see too many people bring this up, I really hope they take it upon themselves to try and push their own boundaries. Also, the way Ethan holds a pistol is WAY off. At first I thought, Ethan is not well versed with weapons, so I can let that go. However even Chris, in the Not A Hero DLC (which is FREE with purchase of RE7), holds his pistol wrong. I know this is small, but this is 2020, and little details go a long way in my opinion. All I could think of, when seeing how Ethan and the gang hold their pistols is, "You want recoil!? Because that is how you get recoil!". These are small details, and of course do not alter my decision on the game itself, but again, I do hope are corrected in the next installment. 

So, from characters, to surroundings, score and all! This game has it. Although a weaker ending and, I hate to say, terrible DLC (the one I played, Not A Hero, which is worse then the ending of RE7 ammo count). So, there are faults here. What started as a wild, scary, heart pounding night, ended with Leon from RE6 giving a high five to Ethan. But I know Ill want to revisit the Bakers again one day! Run from Jack, while being completely freaked out by Marguerite! Great job Capcom! I hope RE8 is even better!

Which brings me to my final point: it feels like 90% of this game is either wandering around or doing chores, while 10% is the actual fun, difficult part.

As many reviews have noted, RE7 is a reversal from the action movie style of previous RE games and is much, much slower paced.  Both in the literal sense of your character's movement speed, and in the number and frequency of enemies thrown at you.  This isn't really a bad thing, it's just different.

The shift to first-person works well and makes the game feel more claustrophobic.  I definitely recommend playing with headphones.  The overall horror atmosphere can be pretty intense, and I imagine VR is amazing.

Controls are fluid and responsive, and really easy to pick up and learn.  Pretty similar to past RE games, you won't be overwhelmed with a billion moves and button combos and need 500 tutorials to figure out crafting and leveling and blah blah blah.  These have always been really accessible games, and this one is no different.  That said, if you play with a controller it suffers the same problem of every FPS game ever played with a controller in that turning and aiming and sluggish and tank-like.  Enemies are way, way obviously designed around this.  It's pretty funny, you'll notice how enemies lurch and sway at just the right moments while you're trying to sloppily aim for a headshot.  I didn't try playing with a mouse and keyboard for some reason, so I don't know how much different / easier the game is that way.

The game is a lot shorter than other REs.  Other REs would clock in at 15-20 hours on the first playthrough, and this one I finished in a little over 9.   The areas are much smaller, and there aren't a lot of obtuse puzzles or the need to carry around puzzle items in your inventory or stash until you discover what they're for later.  You'll get a key or an item and pretty much immediately know what's it for and be able to run straight to that area and use it, and then either the item leaves your inventory or you can just dump it in your stash for good.

As I mentioned earlier, there's far fewer enemies than a typical RE game.  There's also very few respawns, so most of the time you can backtrack through entire areas unimpeded to search for missed items or unlock previously locked doors.  If you're a decent shot and fairly thorough in searching, you'll finish the game with an abundance of ammo.

The enemy design is probably the most uninspired in the entire series, and maybe even the entire horror genre.  It's really bad.  Everything is a generic-looking black humanoid mass ("molded").  Not a memorable thing about them.  I don't know if they just settled with the most boring design ever or if they were trying to contrast them with the Baker family who are well-modeled, animated, and acted, but I really hope they do better in the future.  There's about 1 good boss fight, and the  rest are pretty lame.  I'm similarly bored to death of "tangled mass with 30 eyeballs" that's been in like every game in the series.

The story is....acceptable, I guess.  The setup is sort of stupid.  Your wife disappears after going away for a "babysitting" job,  which you learn from watching a video where she's way obviously standing on the deck of a ship in the ocean.  Is she babysitting for a Saudi Prince?  Who travels long distances to babysit?   I get they probably didn't care  and just wanted any kind of reason to get you to a haunted house in Louisiana, but still.  The story plays out in a mystery fashion, and a lot of details you encounter early in the game don't fall into place until near the end which works well.  There's a lot of "OOOOOOOOH, that's what that referred to" moments.  I do appreciate that you actually play through the videotapes you find instead of just passively watching a video.  That was a good idea.  There is, however, a moment in the game where you get to make what appears to be a pretty heavy choice, and it turns out to be the most disappointing thing ever, probably one of the most in any game I've ever played.  The choice turns out to be completely meaningless, it's undermined probably about 1 minute after you make it, and the rest of the game plays out exactly the same no matter what, except for an extra (trivial) fight and literally about 10 seconds of footage in the ending movie.  Oh, and you get an achievement for completing the game with a different ending.  I played through twice just for that, but it wasn't worth it.  They should have just taken it out altogether.  

Speaking of things I hate and am bored of in RE games, it seems like the first half or 3/4ths of every RE game is in a location that's really interesting and novel and fun to play through.  Then by the end you're stuck in an environment where everything is made of ugly grey metal, like the high-tech labs and research facilities that are a staple of earlier games.  This one is no different.  The haunted house is great, everything after that not so much.  If you want me to understand these viruses are made in a lab, just show me pictures or mention it in found files.  Don't make me slog through miles of gun metal grey corridors.

Overall, I'd recommend it.  It's a well-made game.  Flawed, definitely not the best in the series, but good.  Oh, and the game supports ultra-wide monitors just fine now.  I guess it didn't for quite a while after it launched, but I guess that got added recently.  I had no problem setting it in the options menu, at least.

While I wouldn’t call myself an uber fan, I have followed the Resi series over the years.  I remember playing 1 and 3 when they came out (jeez I’m a dinosaur) and then 4 a couple of years ago, which was probably my fav… until now.

While the older Resi games were hammier than a pork farm in south Wiltshire, 7 ditches the camp, the shlock, the b-movie meets anime schtick and instead, for the first time ever, knuckles down on the ‘horror’ part of survival-horror, and as such provides probably the only video game in history that’s actually had me in danger of soiling myself.  While not being a terribly hard game, it’s tense, moody, atmospheric and full of genuinely creepy and disturbing moments.  The first person camera is incredibly immersive, bolstered by some fantastic sound design and surprising well done voice-acting -  no Jill sandwiches here -  and throughout my playthrough I was constantly cheered by the many Easter eggs and references to classic horror films like Evil Dead, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, the Thing, The Ring and more.  The game also benefits hugely from having a small setting with bucket loads of personality and probably the best villain in the series to date in old Mr Baker.  And when combat does happen, there was the most satisfying pop and heft to the gunplay I think the series has ever had.

Yet, at its heart, its still a Resi game, and the bones of the series do begin to shine through as you play – safe rooms, keys, environmental puzzles, and frustrating walks back to the item box every 5 minutes because your inventory is smaller than a vacuum-packed purse dog.   

Its not all good though. Like older games, the backtracking can get tedious, and soe of the puzzle solutions are a bit silly.  There could have been a lot more enemy variety too.  Also, why does Ethan seem to be blowing his wad every time he walks up a ladder?  

I know the Resi 2 and 3 remakes have been more popular than sliced bread, but I really hope Capcom will keep doing Resi games like 7, as, IMHO, it’s the best kinda reboot imaginable.

Resident Evil 7 is a return to the horror genre from the survival action games that the previous three games had been. Presented in a first person perspective, you play as Ethan, a man who is trying to find his missing wife, who sent him a mysterious message, first telling him not to look for her, then where to find her.

The game starts off very promising – the house is suitably creepy, and when you run into the Baker family for the first time, they’re proper horror game enemies. Completely impossible to kill, they are implacable and unstoppable, and all you can do is slow them down and then run and hide. Horrible things happen to the main character, and there is something fundamentally wrong with his wife, Mia. Zoe, who seems to be related to the Bakers in some way, helps you out over the phone, and the whole thing seems to be unfolding rather nicely, as you try to explore a house while being stalked by a man who can’t be stopped and can’t be killed.

There are even boss fights against these enemies, where you use powerful environmental objects to seemingly cause them severe damage and even “kill” them, but just minutes later they pop back up again and start throwing you around.

The problem is, the game has to move on, and after that point, the game stops really working.

The reason for this is fairly simple – when you’re early on in the game, you are weak and helpless. The house is creepy, the enemies are implacable, and you don’t know what’s going on. The few “lesser” enemies you face are really tough to take down and take a ton of shots from the pistol to the head to kill.

To finally break out of the house, you get a shotgun and you manage to take down one of the Bakers before you break out. The fight is suitably dramatic – after multiple prior encounters where no matter what you did, your foe kept on coming back, here, you can finally do a good number on him, and there isn’t the same sense that he’s just going to pop back up again.

But at this point, the Bakers are no longer invulnerable, and you are better armed and can actually meaningfully fight back. And this pretty much makes the game fall apart, because now, you know what’s going to happen – you’re going to creep around for a bit, there’s going to be a boss fight, and you’re going to kill them, and then they’ll come back and you’ll kill them again.

So what was originally a really cool horror game turns into a more action oriented game. The enemies are still not something you want to waste ammo on, but the fact that you know you CAN just take them down makes them feel a lot less menacing – something that stays until a brief section towards the end of the game, where you are temporarily disarmed again (well, sort of. It’s complicated). The feeling of helplessness is gone.

Worse, after searching the first house, the next two areas just feel like rehashes, where you’re just going up against a different member of the Baker family. The third area does mix up the formula a bit, but it still ends up following the same structure, which makes the game feel too predictable, which undermines the horror.

And frankly, the other two members of the Baker family just aren’t as good at being intimidating as Jack is.

The result is something like letting air out of a balloon, as the game feels like it just gradually deflates, transitioning more and more into a FPS game as enemies become less and less of a threat – but it still feels a bit janky, because it was originally a horror game.

All in all, by the end of it, I was armed to the gills and ready for anything, and while this served as a bit of catharsis, it ultimately felt like the game was too long even at only 10 hours in length.

It doesn’t help that the protagonists of the game – Ethan and his wife, Mia – are frankly not very interesting characters. Ethan feels kind of generic, and often seems to be kind of useless, and Mia’s character is very vaguely defined for most of the game, until you get to nearly the end of it. And while Jack Baker is a cool foe, the other two members of the family aren’t as interesting, even if a late-game twist tries to fix that.

So what are my overall feelings on this game?

On the one hand, the start of the game was really good, and delivered the horror, “don’t get caught” feel very well. On the other hand, the game just kind of goes downhill after you escape the first “real” area of the game.

So I’m not sure I can really recommend this. It was interesting to play through for a bit, but at the end, I wasn’t terribly invested.

See, here's the thing. I'm a decent Resident Evil / Survival Horror fan, but every time I looked at RE7, I was pretty indifferent about it. I saw multiple gameplay videos on YouTube and didn't experience any "shock" factor. I wasn't particularly impressed by anything, and a lot of things in the game felt too generic for a horror based game. Because the overall first impressions didn't entice me, I didn't bother to try and understand the overall gameplay or mechanics of the game, because if I did, I would have realized that it works pretty much exactly how a classic Resident Evil would, except in First Person.

Recently, my friend steamshared the game to me and said he'd watch me play it, and because I've been bored for many weeks now due to Covid lockdown, I told him I'd give it a shot. I downloaded the game and started playing, with my discord streaming enabled. The immediate beginning of the game was paced slow, but that was fine, because very quickly, the game ramped up with some gritty scenes that were obviously designed to tell you that this is a gritty, unforgiving game where you won't know what to expect. That is the impression the game gives you in the first 10-15 minutes. I already knew about all of this however because I spoiled myself from videos years ago, but I pressed on.

I passed the famous dinner scene where the Baker family is sitting with you, forcing you to eat their disgusting food, and I also knew about this from watching videos on the past. It wasn't until I entered into the main center hall of the Baker's residence where something in my brain just popped. I discovered a new room I've never seen before in any YouTube video, and it looks amazing. There's so many objects to interact with and so many things to see, both big and small. Wow, what is this, a puzzle? What's this, a locked door that I can't enter?

As I played on through the game, my map grew bigger and bigger, I was discovering new areas, encountering new threats, and the overall story of the game was getting larger. I actually started loving the game, because the pacing was perfect. The game never held your hand too much, you were left on your own to find out what you're supposed to do or where you're supposed to go, but they got the pacing right.

I got to a point in the game where I beat the "final boss", and after that, I thought I beat the game. I was wrong, there was still so much more after that, expanding the lore, and the gameplay, along with new areas to discover. The game literally blew me away.

And the fact the game was in first person didn't bother me a bit. I liked it, it worked with the setting of the game and the gameplay it established. The puzzles in RE7 were great too, better than anything I've played before.

Once I beat the game, I unlocked a new difficulty mode and am planning to replay the game again due to the gameplay being different. Also, the new DLC content they added to the game is also worth playing. It adds to the overall story and you get some great new gameplay and puzzles in them as well as some minigames.

One very minor complaint I had with RE7 was that enemy variety can get stale because it felt like there weren't much major enemy threats, but this is still extremely minor. The overall gameplay, atmosphere, visuals, sounds, puzzles, they are way too good to pass up.

I am glad Capcom went back to the roots of classic Resident Evil and making it a true survival horror / puzzle based series with resource management and a bit of action. RE7 is the perfect blend of all of that, despite it being in first person.

Now, thanks to this recommendation from my friend, I can't wait to see RE8. Let's hope it's not a disappointment.

The intrigue presented by the story is strong, and the premise, I think, is great; it provides a good setup for the continuation present in Resident Evil 8: Village. 
The acting in 7 is some of the best the series has to offer. I thought the actors/actresses that played Mia, Jack and Lucas did an especially good job. The way Ethan's dialogue is delivered is middling. It's [i]fine[/i] but nothing seriously mindblowing. 
The music, though minimal throughout the game, can be a heart-pumper in tense or stressful situations.
The game is still very pretty, though most games from 2017 of course still hold up graphically in 2022 (and I have no doubt RE7 will look even better after the next-gen update supposedly arrives on PC later this year). I found that indoor areas looked especially good and detail-ridden. However, outdoor areas suffered from muddy textures in my experience (on Max graphics settings).
The gameplay is reminiscent of classic Resident Evil games, and is a perfect fit. I find looking for items and combat a lot of fun on repeat playthroughs. Resident Evil 7 returns to the structure of the first two games with a focus on exploring an interconnected space, slowly opening it up with every unlocked door and solved puzzle. Where this installment diverges from the classic entries is in the combat and camera: the game is played from a first person perspective, which means that you can actually aim your guns effectively. In this way Resident Evil 7 merges the old exploration based and newer action based games into a superbly polished hybrid, similar to the Resident Evil 2 and 3 remakes.

If you fancy watching horror movies, then this game is a must. It's visual graphics compacted with excellent lighting, and enemies will try to induce you in phobias like you've never had before.

Headline:
You've just got a message that your wife Mia has sent you an email telling you not to look for her. Being the curious cat you are, you venture out to the Baker family's residence to uncover the truth of what happened.

Gameplay:
You'll often find your heart beating faster than an engine when staying in lit areas and making subtle sounds for the fear you'll be killed the next moment. Sometimes you'll question when trying to traverse dark areas whether there will be someone or something.. that jumps at you and grabs you by the neck. In this situation, your only emotional support are your guns, medic items and "key's" that will help provide you more assets to combat the unknown. As well as save points to let yourself be at ease.

Along the way you'll learn the truth of the Baker residence and the victims who tragically fell to their demise, only to be served on a silver platter for you and "your family" to eat. Yummy.. The bosses you'll encounter and defeat are everyone that's sitting with you at the supper table, including your wife Mia.

For what feels like the hundredth time in Resident Evil, this entry feels like yet another completely different franchise. These games just can't stick to one approach.

Between the first-person view, the primary focus being on scares, and the unlock door puzzles, RE7 is very similar to Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Outlast. There is combat, though it's used sparingly in the main campaign as it retains the classic survival gameplay of scrounging for what little ammo and supplies there are. The Baker estate, while huge, does not feel unrealistically big the way video game maps so often have to be for the sake of game length, yet the game manages to be quite lengthy anyways through great level design and clever reuse of areas in ways that keep it from feeling tedious. The Bakers themselves have so SO much personality, the backstory on what's going on is interesting, and the setting is a surreal scary environment. This is a very good entry.

Get the DLCs, not only to complete the story, but also for some very different quality activities that should not be missed out on.

Heart warming tale of a family accepting a new comer and his wife into their home. Cute southern family in a rustic country side house and a natural landscape. The story follows the wacky antics of each member of the family and how they interact with the newcomer, Ethan.

This Resident Evil is a different story from ones before, but it's safe to say that the beloved characters we knew over the years have completed their stories. This new spin on the series delivers the same feel as the older games. 
I felt dread the entire game, literally not one moment of peace. At first, I hated feeling like I was always going to be in danger in every area other than the save rooms. But then that jogged some old memories from earlier in the franchise. It is exactly what RE always did with monsters reappearing in rooms and monsters bashing through walls at any given moment. I would argue the scale of terror is different, that RE7 turned up the notch 200%. After playing well over half of the game I finally started to get brave. I started to hate the Family trying to kill me [Ethan]. I would yell back at them insults and petnames like "Margie" for Margeurette like I was Ash Williams "Show your ugly face, Margie! I know you're gonna pop out, COME AT ME!" I would yell at the screen, trying to ease myself and muster up courage. It was kind of a cool experience, to feel so many emotions towards something that is in a game.

This game has gotten a lot of backlash from the fans without warrant. Those fans seemed to have forgotten the terror we all felt during the famous cutscene from RE1 when you walk into one of the first rooms of the Mansion to be greeted by a decaying zombie turning its head slowly to peer back at you. RE 1, 2, and 3 were all one of a kind in their time and there were no games to match. There are grievances from fans that no zombies are present in this game, but let's not forget what RE is all about. RE was never about zombies; RE was about the mutation of humans from bio-terrorism. The main and most intelligent villains in the games are mutated monsters and powerful individuals who caused the apocalypse.

Because of being spoiled by other games that provide lots of down time, I wanted the game to end [practically] the whole time I was playing it. At the same time I was addicted to the fight-or-flight feeling. Yes, your heart races very fast and you will sweat a little. I personally hate being chased, like it's the worst feeling for me. I was chased the whole game so that was a huge jab at my fears. I am never likely to be taken by crazies like Ethan was, but because of the first person view I was able to really be in Ethan's perspective and empathized with his situation so much that it felt like it was happening to me.  I felt everything Ethan felt, as much as one can in a chair comfortable and not actually in any apparent danger. All throughout the game I was feeling pure terror and that is what I want to feel when I play a horror game or watch a horror film. Horror in its purest form something primal made of three ingredients: dread, terror, fight-or-flight. Resident Evil 7 touches on all three.

After the commercial failure of Resident Evil 6, Capcom returned to its roots and released a Resident Evil title fully focused on survival horror. I do not say that lightly, the setting is consistently unsettling throughout the entire game, and enemies are true bullet sponges, leading to classic Resident Evil moments where ammunition is scarce and panic sets in as you struggle to reach the next save room.

The game also shifts to a first-person perspective, which was a necessary and effective change. Rather than controlling a character in a demanding survival horror experience, you are the character. This perspective significantly reduces awareness of your surroundings, adding an almost claustrophobic tension to the gameplay. Overall, Resident Evil 7 represents the revival the series desperately needed, and Capcom delivered without missing the mark.

[h1] Gross-Out Horror: The Video Game [/h1]

       I am a HUGE Resi fan, I love the games to a great extent, have played almost all mainline games, some spinoffs, and I consider Resi 1 to be one of the greatest horror experiences ever, period. So knowing the legacy this game holds, I figured it's about time I give it a shot!

       ...Just disappointing for me. The AI is unbelievably simplistic. Their sight triggers are often late and if say, Jack walks in a room looking for you, and sees you, you'll watch his ENTIRE animation of him looking around the room BEFORE his trigger activates to chase you. Mia, similarly, in a very VERY early fight, can be stunned by headshotting her, waiting for her animation to finish, and headshotting her again. There's almost no point in shooting her during this, since as a player, you pick up that she's not affected as much until after you let her stun animation play.

       The entire first 70 minutes consisted of maybe one genuinely good scare, in my opinion as a massive horror fan. Every other scare was either: 
[b] "HEY! GROSS BUGS GROSS FOOD OH LOOK HOW GROSS THE KNIFE IS GOING THROUGH YOUR HAND AREN'T YOU SCARED YET OH CHAINSAW OFF YOUR HAND LOOK AT YOUR STUB SO GROSS AREN'T YOU SCARED YET??" [/b] ...or if it wasn't overly forced gross-out, it was a predictable, drawn out cutscene that anyone could see coming from a mile away. 

       [i] Taking control away from the player in these sequences results in us being pulled out of the moment. We are disconnected from what the protagonist is supposed to be feeling. [/i]

       This creates this awkward middle ground that YES, you're playing a "horror game" but...I'm not horrified...at all. The AI seems ripped out right from early 3d games twenty years ago, the characters look pudgy and unrealistic as all heck, which, in a hyperrealistic art style, pulls us as the player out of the world, which is something that should almost never happen in a successful horror tale. This, and knowing the enemy types in this game are very slim, made me pack my bags and go back to my "Resi 1 was the peak of the franchise" camp that I'll probably sit on until I die (lol). 

       If you don't engage in horror or games or both often, then this will probably scare you. For me, I just couldn't enjoy it no matter how much I wanted to. 

       Closing statement? What a shame. Here's hoping "VIllage" isn't the shlock of 4 mixed with this game's lack of tension.

Alright, overall I love this game to death. 
Though it is definitely not a perfect game, this is easily my favorite resident evil installment.

(Btw this is mostly spoiler free and I am only talking about the base game as I have not finished all of the DLC yet)

The GOOD.
This game is made to be the most immersive resident evil game in the series thus far, and I believe it achieves this goal. This is created through it's first person perspective, amazing writing, and constantly looming dread that plagues the Baker property. The Baker family are a terrifyingly quotable bunch that are the best part of the game besides Ethan himself, and the brief time you get in the shoes of Clancy Javis. And no, I did not forget about Mia, we will get to that.

The combat and weapons of RE7 are all very interesting and have their own purposes, whether they be combat tactics, interaction with environment, or the balanced ammo management (especially on madhouse). The variety of weapons you can choose to use or not use between playthroughs will change your approach to combat greatly, and often the most overpowered weapons will take the most work and strategy to use consistently (excluding the broken shotgun as it lives up to the name with how common the ammo is for it, I honestly recommend playing on the harder difficulties without it for a more balanced and difficult experience).

This game has only two cut scenes in the entire experience. The developers opted to have pretty much all of the character interactions to be in engine, having the POV rarely interrupted. These choices lead to a very, very immersive experience and were likely influenced by the developers' opportunity to make this for VR. There are plenty of moments in the game that reflect that idea, and I am sure they get better reactions from players like myself on the proper platform. Regardless, these interactions are what really make you love the personalities of the Baker family.

The characters, where do I start? The Baker family are written to have a modern "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" vibe and it works perfectly. Lucas Baker, the son of the family and a southern John Kramer personality without the moral backbone. He creates many jury-rigged torture devices and is always up for playing with his food. Always having another game to play, Lucas Baker is a weasel, joking boy who will likely grow on you through the game with his serial killer charm and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-ish traps he lays out for Ethan in his journey.

Marguerite Baker is the keeper of the old house, and the queen of the bugs. She will undoubtedly scare you on your first playthrough with her spastic jumpscares, her horrifyingly contorting body, and her endless swarms of hornets and locusts. She was constantly able to keep my attention with one of the dirtiest mouths you will ever hear and her lurking presence. Marguerite undoubtedly holds the best part of the game with her husband. Speaking of which,

Jack, Freakin, Baker. I can't imagine someone not loving this character. Jack is immediately presented as the alpha of the rabid Baker tribe. He serves as the chasing threat that Mr. X or Nemesis was in previous installments in the beginning of the game and boy is it a lot more thrilling with Jack berating you with his threats as you panic down the hallway, hoping to lose the almost invincible, dominating figure. Every, single, line Jack gives you is great and I can't help but constantly quote him when I do another playthrough. You have the most encounters with Jack than any other Baker family member and all I can do is love every minute of it. 

The not so good.

I believe this game had a shift in budget or production in the last third of the game. Though it is not the worst writing I have seen in a resident evil game, it is almost incomparable to the game before you leave the Baker property. Mia's section obviously has a purpose in the story of the game, and I recognize that. To kind of shed some light on why Mia got caught up in all the mess in the first place. Though it drags on for way to long. The interior of the ship is full of the same textures and drabness for the entirety of the segment and that is why I believe it has something to do with budget. The developers also included a mandatory, and also the most lengthy and boring tape in the game that has a very poorly executed performance of the character Alan which the player has no choice but to deal with every time they play the game because it is unskippable unlike every other tape. Having the ability to skip this tape would obviously cut the overall game time but would make the section of the game a lot more tolerable. The gauntlet of the Salt mines with the return of Ethan as the final section of the game could be made a lot more interesting as well, but it is leaps ahead in quality when compared to the ship section of the game. 

With that elephant out of the room, lets talk about the other one.
The enemy variety. The concept of the molded is undeniably interesting, and I think the models for them are very high quality. Though they are undeniably boring. Every single type of molded are almost identical except the physical trait that influences their combat behavior. For god's sake even the names of them sound like they kept the model template names from the beta. Molded, Crawler Molded, Fat Molded, Blade molded? (Of course I'm not including the DLC molded which only continue the list of adjective, molded and maybe a crocodile to jazz things up). 

If it wasn't for the good parts of this game, this would be a very mediocre Resident Evil title. Though luckily, it does have them and it is here for anyone to greatly enjoy it just like I have. Even with it's flaws I cannot recommend this title enough, I guarantee it will be a roller coaster for anyone willing to try and unconventional Resident Evil Title.

[i]Resident Evil 7: biohazard[/i] was looked down upon at first: after many a questionable choice that led to the hot mess that is RE6, fans were understandably skeptical of the new installment. Couple that with a new perspective and a story that is seemingly detached from the narrative centered around zombies and morally bankrupt corporations and you have an extremely hard audience to please. And RE7 does just that.

The story in this game revolves around Ethan Winters, a systems engineer from Texas, going to the Dulvey parish, Louisiana, after he receives a message from his missing wife Mia. However, things quickly go south as Mia warns Ethan of his mistake upon the latter's arrival, and soon after that the unlucky hero gets captured by the Baker family, who have been holding Mia captive for the last three years. The southern gothic horror story doesn't start out the way you would expect a Resident Evil game to, but it quickly reminds players of its roots: the crazed Baker family members stalking you a-la Mr X from RE2, the familiar setting of a decrepit monster-infested mansion with many a puzzle to solve and a constant sense of dread and despair that accompanies you through your journey as you scavenge for what little supplies there are. At the same time, you don't need to know the lore of the previous 6+ games to immerse yourself in this one - the most that you're going to miss is a couple of throwbacks and nods to previous titles.

The gameplay is yet another callback to the early titles in the franchise: Ethan moves slowly and wields his weapons like a rookie would, needing to pause in between shots to achieve good accuracy. The switch to first-person mode allows the game to shine in a new light, hiding items in places that fixed camera angles or behind-the-shoulder view wouldn't allow as well as introducing perspective- and light-based puzzles, on top of making the horror much more intimate and personal. Doesn't matter if you get stabbed in the abdomen with a shovel or pushed down the hallway with the force of a revving truck, you [i]will[/i] feel it.

The pacing in the game is, for the most part, well done. You slowly begin accustoming yourself to the mad house that is the Baker estate after defeating foes and solving mysteries and puzzles, gradually feeling more and more powerful, yet still vulnerable to the many dangers that lurk around you. The beginning section is great for establishing the world of RE7 to first-time players, but can drag on for longer than welcome on repeat playthroughs, and the combat-heavy gauntlet closer to the end of the game feels heavily rushed. Other than that, playing this game is a satisfyingly brutal challenge.

In conclusion, [i]Resident Evil 7: biohazard[/i] is a welcome addition to the collection of any survival horror fan, no matter if you're a veteran or a newcomer. The controls might feel a bit clunky and unresponsive at first, but you quickly get used to it.

[b]TL;DR[/b]: A satisfying, if slightly flawed return to the roots of Resident Evil.

[h1] [b]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard – A Terrifying Return to Survival Horror[/b] [/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/b] is a bold reinvention of the iconic survival horror franchise, taking the series back to its roots while introducing new ideas that redefine fear. With its shift to a first-person perspective and a chillingly atmospheric narrative, Capcom delivers an experience that’s as terrifying as it is unforgettable.
[h3] [b]A Gripping and Intimate Story[/b] [/h3]
Set in the eerie, decaying halls of the Baker family estate, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] weaves a tale of survival, desperation, and unspeakable horrors. You play as Ethan Winters, a man searching for his missing wife, Mia, in the swamps of Louisiana. What begins as a simple rescue mission spirals into a nightmarish descent, confronting players with grotesque creatures, shocking twists, and the chilling menace of the Baker family.

The storytelling is intimate and grounded, making every encounter feel personal. The Bakers—especially the unhinged Jack and Marguerite—are terrifyingly memorable villains, their presence looming over the game even when they’re not onscreen.
[h3] [b]Atmosphere and Immersion[/b] [/h3]
The shift to a first-person perspective heightens the tension, immersing you in every creaking floorboard, flickering light, and grotesque detail. The Baker mansion and its surroundings are masterfully designed, blending claustrophobic hallways, grotesque body horror, and moments of quiet dread that keep you on edge.

The use of lighting, sound design, and environmental storytelling is exceptional. Every corner of the house feels alive, with unsettling noises and subtle visual cues that build an oppressive sense of dread.
[h3] [b]Gameplay: Tense and Rewarding[/b] [/h3]
[i]Resident Evil 7[/i] emphasizes survival, resource management, and puzzle-solving, much like the classic entries in the series. Ammo is scarce, and healing items are precious, forcing players to think carefully about every shot and decision. This scarcity amplifies the tension, making each encounter with enemies a nail-biting ordeal.

Combat is deliberate and visceral, with enemies that are grotesque and relentless. The Molded creatures are grotesque manifestations of horror, each encounter feeling like a fight for survival. Boss battles, especially with the Bakers, are intense and creatively designed, pushing players to adapt and stay sharp.
[h3] [b]A Modern Twist on Classic Survival Horror[/b] [/h3]
While [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] captures the essence of classic survival horror, it also incorporates modern gameplay mechanics that enhance the experience. The inventory system strikes a balance between challenge and usability, and save points create a sense of relief without breaking the tension.

The game’s VR compatibility (on PlayStation VR) takes immersion to an entirely new level, making it one of the most terrifying gaming experiences available.
[h3] [b]Visuals and Performance[/b] [/h3]
Powered by the RE Engine, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is stunningly detailed. The grotesque environments and character models bring the horror to life, while the fluid performance ensures the game remains smooth and responsive even during the most intense moments.
[h3] [b]Room for Improvement[/b] [/h3]
The back half of the game shifts away from the intimate horror of the Baker mansion to a more action-oriented tone, which may feel jarring to some players. Additionally, while the story ties into the broader [i]Resident Evil[/i] lore, newcomers may find some of the connections to the series' overarching narrative unclear.
[h3] [b]Verdict[/b] [/h3]
[i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] is a masterclass in survival horror, blending the series' classic elements with bold, innovative design. It’s a harrowing, edge-of-your-seat experience that reinvigorates the franchise and sets a high bar for horror games. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer, this game is an essential journey into terror.

Tremendously well done. I am a huge fan of horror games (Silent Hill series super-fan) and I try my best to save myself the time and money weeding through jump scare and gore shock-value games who's only unique quality is how overwhelmingly unoriginal they can be. And then there is RE 7..

Pros:
1) Sound! Blast them speakers. In the settings you can actually adjust the type of sound environment you have (speakers/headphones, close/far, etc.). Thought it might have been a gimmick. It's not... Also, excellent voice acting. It's often overlooked (heard?), but it deserves credit, and especially here. 

2) The environment is not completely static. You will scare the hell out of yourself knocking over whatever was in front of you but were too freaked out to even notice. There is no noticeable cycle of noises as you explore and, even if you did just walk down that hallway and everything was peaches, don't expect it on your way back. Lastly: VHS tapes. That's all i'm going to say.

3) Lore. You will get lost in the story that feeds you NOTHING. You have to put pieces together yourself or you'll be on the outside looking in. You'll have an idea of what is going on, but you'll need to immerse yourself. This is not a run-and-gun. I've been playing horror games for most of my gaming life. And that's why I barely play them anymore. The genre is getting worn out in movies, shows and games. It happens. But this brings that feeling back. It's a story i'm invested in and I have no idea wtf is about to go down and that's wonderful. Not knowing is fear incarnate. 

Cons
1) Triggers. There's a good number of noticeable triggers. Nothing's perfect. It happens. And besides, it's RE. Can't not have a boss battle right after finishing that lengthy objective now can you? Ironically, it's the comfort of knowing a trigger has been hit that I dislike in horror games. I paid to be in misery ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!

2) Loot. You'll find it, sure, but once you realize how much is overlooked after you find that ammo box behind a crate in that forgetable hallway and, oh look, that small consumable item you could really use is in an outlet behind a door. The idea is to incentivize the player to really explore. But sometimes you'll find yourself spinning around a room ducking under everything like a maniac for some ammo. 

Pro/Con
1) Puzzles. Most are really awesome and you really have to be perceptive of your environment to figure them out or to save you a lot of time. But others are just meh. A socket shaped like some animal? But, it's RE. They are pushing to new frontiers but they always with the medievel quest items..

Resident Evil 7 is my first time beating a game in the RE series (tried RE4 years back and got stuck very early), and I thought it made for a great entry point for a first-time player. The first-person perspective really works here to reinforce the gun-play, add to the immersion, and really sell the claustrophobia and horror aspects of the game. This is the kind of game that you kind of dread, but it's very hard to put down once you start. I had a great time playing though it.

While the game is definitely scary and twisted, I actually found it fairly forgiving in terms of item/ammo management and such. While you start off with just a few bullets and try to make every one count, you'll find that as you go on you'll stockpile a fairly large trove of supplies, meaning that even if you miss half your shots and don't save scum, you still have a pretty decent chance to win in the end. I definitely used the save system a fair bit to get optimal results in encounters. Of course, if you want a serious challenge once you beat the game, there's Madhouse difficulty which kicks everything up a few notches and limits your saving capabilities. For me, Normal was enough to make me feel vulnerable without it being ridiculous. I never had to try a boss more than twice. Guns feel solid and responsive, which is a good thing because accuracy is very important here. I'd recommend playing with M+KB instead of a gamepad for best results with aiming.

In terms of story, I very much enjoyed it all around. There's plenty of mystery around the situation you find yourself in, and really crazy stuff happens without much initial explanation. By the end, things fall into place in a satisfying way, with little room for ambiguity. The evil family is fun to hate; the banter and dialog is both serious and pretty funny in a lot of cases. This is a game that knows how absurd it is and revels in it; it's just having a good time, scaring the pants off of you.

Visually it's also very impressive, with real contrast between the oppressive darkness and your flickering flashlight beam, environments that feel lived-in and true to life, and just some all-around creepy-as-hell set dressings. I did notice a few textures that were pretty low detail, but as long as you're not going up to every tree and looking for pixels, you're going to find it's very impressive to look at. The lighting especially is a standout and really drives the impressiveness of the visuals. I also liked the music, which is mostly ambient but there's a really comforting track that plays when you're in a safe room that you'll come to love. The game ran smoothly for me on a GTX 1080 GPU with an i5-9600K processor (stock speed), usually hovering around 120+ fps at 1440p resolution. No crashes were observed in my playthrough.

RE7 is an absolutely exceptional example of what survival horror can and should be. It's scary, it's fun, and it looks great. This will probably get me to try some of the other titles in the RE series, and I'm excited to see what RE8 ends up being. Also be sure to check out the free DLC "Not a Hero", which completes the story from the main game. This is a must-play for horror fans, highly recommended!

TLDR: Alien: Isolation except with more swamps. 

SUMMARY
Another shining example of what happens when a struggling franchise kicks itself in the head and, for a brief moment, pierces the veil of modern gaming mediocrity and remembers what it used to be. Resident Evil 7, in addition to being a terrifyingly effective survival horror game in its own right, represents a return to all things classic Resident Evil. Well, mostly. The horrid writing and voice acting is missing, but what we got in return is, I think, more than worth it. 

LIKES
- Pacing
If there’s one thing that stuck out the most, it was the game’s fantastic creation of organic tension and, more importantly, how it doled it out to always keep it fresh and discarded it when it had stayed its welcome. So the first hours of the game are textbook survival/stealth horror. I creeped around an appropriately creepy house, stalked by an even creepier antagonist. Trepidation mounted as I desperately searched for the next step forward, but just as it felt like I couldn’t take any more the game eased off, granting a new weapon, clue, or saferoom. A temporary, but welcome, respite, just enough for me to build up enough courage to venture forth again. This loop continued, my confidence slowly growing before the thrill of felling the first boss.
By the time the second boss fell, though, the fear and suspense had evolved into cautious confidence as my arsenal and game knowledge grew. The developers seemed to understand this and, rather than force more tension as in Alien Isolation, deliberately built the rest of the game to slowly morph from stealth to a puzzle/action blend to full on action by the finale to keep pace. To give you an idea of the full transformation, the finale starts in essentially an open field with more Molded than the entire first half of the game combined. Did I run away or sneak around? Nope. To quote Danny Devito, I started blasting. And by Barry Burton’s beard after a game of crawling around pissing myself at every little sound the catharsis was incredible. 
- Tutorials
In addition to the standard issue random documents, RE7 includes a number of video tapes explaining lore or fleshing out missing details. Far from simply cutscenes, these are fully interactable and serve as tutorials or deliver hints as to the immediate or future surroundings. Indeed, one level even requires you to recall the steps taken in one of these video tapes in order to bypass part of a puzzle and avoid a painful death. 
- Writing
Believe it or not, yes. I’d argue this is one the better, if not the best, written RE game in the series, though the bar’s not exactly very high. RE7 pulls a RE4 and is almost entirely removed from the mainline RE ‘story’. Rather than campy action, though, RE7 goes for a more heartfelt, tragic route and it works for the most part. By keeping the overall tone muted, RE7’s more bombastic scenes hit all the harder. 
- Sound Design
No small part of the game’s success in genuinely unnerving me was its excellent sound design. The protagonist’s shaky breath, the creaks, groans, and dings of the aging house, and the tentative footsteps all contribute to an undercurrent of dread. This in turn makes each punctuation, be it a monster’s screech or misleading clang, all the more effective. 
- Streamlined Crafting
A small note, but a mainstay of the RE series has been combining herbs to make better healing items. Here it’s replaced by a system of combining herbs and gunpowder with two qualities of chemicals. This results in heal juice and pistol bullets with regular chemicals and more powerful heal juice and pistol bullets with the higher quality chemicals. The method used is quite streamlined with minimal menu navigating, though not so streamlined that you can just throw together more bullets and meds mid-combat. 

GRIPES
- Meager Enemy Variety
Even the original Resident Evil had more variety. Here the variety of non-boss enemies numbers just 4, each being a slight variation in both form and function of the basic type. All have basically the same strategy of ‘shoot until it stops moving’. It would have been nice to introduce something that required a bit more strategy to defeat, but what’s present works well enough. 
- Shallow Mechanics
The whole is greater than the parts, in this case. None of the game’s mechanics are all that involved. The stealth is a case of ‘wait until the big thumpy thing goes away’, the puzzles are too easy, and the gunplay is similarly basic. This was only in retrospect, though. In the moment the game’s strengths made these mechanical shortcomings hard to notice. 
- Key Persistence
A very minor gripe, but it would have been nice if once a key had exhausted all its uses it was automatically discarded. Keys take up an entire inventory slot on their own and knowing when one could safely be stashed away would have been nice. As it were, the inventory upgrades and safe room item boxes were more than enough to sustain inventory space.

After beating the game and really enjoying it I played the DLC and that is what changed my mind. Banned Footage Vol. 1 and Vol. 2 are fun little distractions and the horde mode Nightmare stole like four to five hours from me, daughters is also great and has tons of replay value with two endings. But the really great DLC is Jack's 55th Birthday, End of Zoe, and Not a Hero which makes the game more action focused and really made me appreciate the combat even more. While I still think that Resident Evil 2 this game was incredible and I have already started a madhouse game to grind out. Resident Evil 7 did something I was starting to think would never happen. It made horror fun again. The story is engaging, and the design and pacing can be called nothing short of masterful. The game, at heart, delivers a story that reasonably turns the confused, helpless protagonist into a juggernaut just as experienced and sick of the s*** as the player becomes. Immersion is an accomplished focus of RE7, yet the game manages to gracefully retain many discombobulating aspects of the RE franchise that, by now, define it. The voice acting is superb, character animations are passable, environments are largely realistic, and the game, at least through its first half, can be intensely frightening.

I'm not terribly fond of the final section of the game, it being more action-oriented than the rest, although it does successfully complete the character-player transformation, and it provides a mediocre but satisfactory end to the plot.

Do I recommend this game? To fans of terror, horror, adrenaline, the RE franchise, and game design, yes, I do. A million times over. I also recommend picking it up during a sale, as that seems to happen often, though Resident Evil 7 is definitely worth its full retail value.

After the boredom known as Resident Evil 6, Resident Evil as a franchise was in the doldrums. Then this game came out, and in one great experience, the survival horror Goliath was brought back. This game took itself incredibly seriously, and didn't use Umbrella as a plot device for the thousandth time, and gave us a new threat. Not saying that Umbrella is terrible, but having a new group made for a more interesting experience and lent itself to a brand new story. The first-person adventure through a crazy house in Dulvey, Louisiana, and the insane infected family was a wild ride from start to finish. From the opening, I was impressed by how much this game went back to the Resident Evil formula of "tight inventory, heavy spooks". The references to the old games are also nice,[spoiler]like a renovation note in the attic of the house that mentions Trevor & Chamberlain, the company that built Spencer Mansion in Resident Evil.[/spoiler] The enemies in this game are not mindless zombies, but instead these scary eyeless monsters that actually use their limbs to block your shots. The Baker family is also insane to deal with and are also infected with this new bio-weapon. You get more than enough to handle them, as you get a bunch of weapons to help your chances of survival out. The game has a wide variety of collectibles to find, and a bunch of achievements to unlock at your pleasure.

In all, RESIDENT EVIL 7: BIOHAZARD is a great addition to the Resident Evil family of games. I honestly would love to have the next Resident Evil game be in first-person just like this game. This is a major upgrade over Resident Evil 6, and I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to get into Resident Evil or is a fan of the old games.

A powerful return to form by Capcom, Resident Evil 7 is a survival horror game through and through, breaking away from the heavier action focus of Resident Evils 4, 5 and 6. Now of course RE4 is a 10/10 title but 5 and 6 had mixed receptions, to say the least. RE7 assures you that the horror comes first with a good game that stands on its own merits in gameplay and story. For the most part, as RE7 does falter near the end. Still, who can complain about an 8/10 horror title?

Resident Evil 7 stars generic everyman Ethan, receiving a mysterious message from his missing wife to go house hunting in the American South, ignoring all warnings of frequent hurricane seasons and flood damages. He soon runs afoul of insurance agents and a homeowners association. I believe RE7 is at its absolute best on your first blind playthrough so I very much don't want to give away almost anything about the story. You're thrust into dark, terrifying situations, literally and narratively, stumbling around foreboding run down and battered locations, excellent sound design working your last nerve as the wind and various bumps suggest something is closer than you'd like it to be. You have some reliable weapons that produce visceral effects for visceral enemies, the core of exploration-resource gathering-intimidating foes challenging you to make the most of what you do find and weigh the best way to proceed. This is very much a slower paced first person shooter, where you must choose engagements well, watch your ammo, running can be a big commitment and it's more important to aim well than to strafe(especially as you can't!)

The well-known stalkers of the game have each section of the story separated neatly, giving you an introduction and a fresh need to be wary of them, hiding while trying to earn progress, often driven to combat. The vibrant personality put into each enemy is wonderful, even down to the standard enemies who have very disturbing designs and mannerisms. There is sheer delight in interacting with the primary stalkers and cold terror in evading the black mold zombies, segments like the processing mortuary making me uncomfortable even on repeat playthroughs. It is difficult to sing the praises of the main encounters without spoiling them so I'll settle for saying the first half of the game always makes me grin ear to ear when I get to them, laughing at stalker lines and feeling tense yet pumped, always on my toes and eager to deliver that final blow so it can all be over until the next time.

What sells RE7 so well is the atmosphere. Of course the developers were free to look up house designs online but the sheer charm in each individual room suggests they must have flown out and did a tour of quite a few actual old southern homes. Entering the main hall of the Baker house and seeing the casual card game spread fills my head with memories of my own rural Maryland family homes, calling to mind smells and cool night air sensations with crystal clear clarity. So much of this game is crafted with a masters touch and attention to detail, so many little pieces in every individual room are there to be found by the curious explorer even if they serve no purpose other than to help paint this vivid picture. The graphical strength extends to the high detail of characters and the polish on the spooky bits. Use of darkness and closed interior heightens fear wonderfully and the ambient black mold fills me with the same disgust as if I were seeing it in real life.  It is next gen polish, at least for when the game released.

I'll delve into spoilers for my next points so maybe this is all you need to know for now. RE7 is a strong game. If you want to play a horror game, try it. If you want to get into the Resident Evil series, try it, it is stand alone with an original story that takes place in the same universe without need to know 6+ games worth of connections. If you want to play a slower paced first person shooter with some scares, try it. Any fan of any of the genres at play or the RE series owes it to themselves to try this great experiment. That first blind playthrough is gold and after that the game holds up, challenging you to replay it on harder difficulties, to clear it quickly, to consider the DLC. Not a Hero is free and a decent conclusion with a good gameplay shift to emphasize your new protagonists strengths, End of Zoe is another quality addition in the same vein, the rest add more if you can't get enough but are "More Gameplay" instead of "More Story."

*SPOILERS* I love this game, really. I laugh frequently in the first third because I love Jack, I love fighting him, I love his goofy and sadistic mixed personality. I like the clear differences between him, Marguerite and Lucas, all are strong but Jack really steals the show. The game is solid overall, I even enjoyed the transition to the Boat section which shakes you up a bit by disarming you and forcing you to be very aware of your surroundings in time to take in a load of fresh story and new atmosphere. The only real disappointments I have with the game are that the more you play it the more you can see the strings, but that is true of almost every horror game. The Mine is a poor finale in gameplay, murdering any interest the molded had left to offer by making them pure dull fodder, including teleporting in behind you at times. And call it a personal thing but the starting pistol feels a bit too weak, sure, it adds to the terror to wonder if you can actually stop this molded as your headshots don't do much, but still an unsatisfying sensation. At least it adds greater value to using better weapons like the shotgun early on. The story is pretty good, it has a few plot holes or parts that are stretched thin but there's nothing hamstringing the experience aside from the butchering of the Zoe/Mia choice which just punishes you if you choose Zoe, the end, no moral. Really the biggest flaw in the game, but thankfully not fatally so. *END SPOILERS*

RE7 isn't perfect but it is very fine, very fine indeed. Horror fans, FPS fans, Resident Evil fans, give it a try.

Level design, sound design, graphics, gameplay, character animations, voice acting, lighting effects, inventory management - I am at a loss of where to start with this Mona Lisa of survival horror. And if survival horror is not your cup of slimy goo then I would say you should DEFINITELY play it as the perfect game to get you hooked into the genre. Be warned though, most of what will come after this stellar achievement by Capcom will feel like a lesser game (though there are some really good one out there).

Let me first start by complimenting the studio Capcom for going in the direction they did with RE7; this game would not have achieved what it did on an artistic, technical or atmospheric scale, without the first person perspective. With the other elements such as sound and light complimenting each other so well, the FPS aspect really makes the horror close in on you with the hopeless claustrophobia of terror within the Baker mansion. You always feel like you are in some place you REALLY shouldn't be.

As Ethan you are not a super soldier, not a badass gunslinger but simple a man looking for his wife. There is a sense of relatability to this and further adds to the desperate weakness of the protagonist against seemingly insurmountable enemies. The way he walks, runs, talks and generally navigates is well set against the overwhelming odds against him once again complementing the game with a balance that even zen masters can't achieve. Your missing wife, who told you specifically not to try to find her, and yet there you are (Silent Hill much?) at a place which is both of this world and inhumanely horrifying. So there you are at the Bakers' place and somehow get whacked in the head finding yourself sitting across the table from what looks like the world's worst family Christmas dinner. And when you find Mia (your wife you lucky dog) then that's another story about subversion of expectations of this tale of blood, guts and entrails.

The Bakers, oh the Bakers. God could not have conceptualized a more perfect gamut of deplorables for RE7. So much care and painstaking work has been put into these errr people(?) and it shows. You witness them well into their descent into horrifying madness and nothing will feel safe after your first meeting with those sickened beings. Though the horror is omnipresent and persistent, I wouldn't call it Lovecraftian but that's ok since RE7 doesn't deal with subtlety and many times the terror is staring right back at you uncomfortably close, like kiss your face close.  Jack, Marguerite and Lucas are friggin insane man! Though Marguerite just reminded me of my mother whenever I would get terrible grades in school (please God dont make my mother read this review). But seriously, these guys are nuts - like cut off limbs on the dinner table for shiggles NUTS. I am just mortified of the sight of Southern families from the USA now - please don't dismember me or feed me you damn hillbillies, I will never trust your kind again. These guys behave like runaway mental patients on crack and speed.

And you would think that a mansion will be a drab and repetitive location to fight an unvanquishable evil in. But it's not. The mansion is beautiful like a perfectly still dead body and has personality leaking out from every room, like a black sludge, that you take your tentative steps into. I especially liked my encounter with Marguerite Baker on her side of the Baker mansion though they are all great to be honest. Come to think of it, Lucas' part was my fav. Actually I also loved where and how I had to navigate around Jack Baker too. See? You can't choose one good thing about this game, it is the amalgamation of it all - this is a good problem to have in a video game. Each frame of RE7 is greater than the sum of its parts, truly elevating video games as an experience just like how the original RE did back in the day.

The game is genius. It's perennial tension. A love letter to ANYONE who enjoys being pulled into a new world and the story isn't bad either. You think all those guns and bullets will make you feel safe? HELL to the NO. You are always scared and escape looks unachievable right till the very summit of the game when you actually do escape and your real life begins to suck again.

Please stop being an idiot and buy this game. You don't need a sale for this, you need 15 hours of crapping your pants and you need it now. There is literally NOTHING to complaint of here.

[b]Resident Evil does Southern Gothic in grand style![/b]  

Instead of the customary S.T.A.R.S. or BSAA member, you're merely Ethan Winters, untrained everyman.  After receiving a mysterious video message from your three-years vanished fiancé, you're led to search for her in an abandoned farmhouse on the edge of a gator-haunted Louisiana swamp.  This decrepit old house, however, isn't as empty as it first appears; the Bakers still call it home, and they're jacked out of their ever-lovin' minds on a funky kind of fungus that only thrives in RE's pulp-horror universe.   

Immediately, it struck me that while environments in RE7 may be small, they're even more finely detailed than those in the lavish new remakes.  It's a startling degree of craftsmanship, one you might associate with a professional miniature-maker before a game artist.  The deliberate first-person gameplay (a gamble in itself) works perfectly with this cramped, cluttered, and hyper-defined world to give a deeper feeling of immersion than RE has yet seen.  These spaces are real, [i]lived-in[/i].  You're surrounded by the relics of a once-normal family life turned to madness and decay by forces beyond the Bakers' control; you can still [i]feel[/i] the tragedy of it while Pappy Jack is trying to take the top of your head off with a long-handled shovel . . . even when Mama Marguerite is wall-running on all fours and squeezing out mutant wasps.  These were once good, wholesome people (well, except maybe Lucas), not the tired Southern stereotypes they too easily could have been.

If there's one thing RE7 could have used more of, it's enemy variety.  Other than the mutated Bakers and several sub-species of anthropomorphic mold monster, there's not too much for Ethan to battle; this is something RE8, which will once again feature Ethan as protagonist, should look to improve on.  However, taken in total with the rich experience offered by this new and rather experimental installment, a limited bestiary is a small gripe indeed. 

(The DLCs "Not a Hero" and "End of Zoe" are such integral parts of the story that you [i]have[/i] to play them if you like the main game at all.  In the latter, you're a swamp-dwelling recluse who bashes monsters with his bare fists while sh*t talkin' like a true Southern badass.  Joe Baker would have done Manly Wade Wellman proud!)

I liked this game, but it definitely does not really feel like a Resident Evil game. It feels like it is an entirely different game from a series that decided to have a very loose Resident Evil theme. I say this for a few reasons.

*************************
Some Spoilers  Ahead
*************************

First off, this is the first Resident Evil that focused on gross out horror in the vein of the Saw movies. I know they were really pushing for the VR experience on the PS4 (which they still don't have officially on the PC version, probably because of exclusivity contracts) and it is very well done for what it is, but this was never a focus of the RE games. It really feels out of place in a franchise that is known for campy dialogue and slightly gross monsters. 

Second, the monsters are not scary and not aesthetically pleasing. I know it's weird to say that the zombie monsters are not aesthetically pleasing, after all they're supposed to be grotesque, but these new monsters all basically look like the same black blob monster just in different sizes and with a few different modifications. I know it's weird to talk about the aesthetics of zombie type monsters, but what they did to the licker in this game is downright criminal. The licker is one of my favorite monsters of all time, it's such a cool design, but their equivalent mold monster in this game just looks so boring and lame. Worst of all, it's super weak and easy to kill! That was the biggest let down of the game for me.

Third, scary supernatural child that can do magic as the main villain have no place in RE games. They tried it in the movies, and look how well that worked out. They made her too powerful and never really explained why she can kill anyone at any moment she chooses, (even when they literally just took a drug that was supposed to make them immune to her abilities) and yet she can't kill Ethan when he approaches her with the neuro-toxin. There are a number of theories out there as to why Ethan seemed somewhat immune, but from a narrative perspective in this game it just felt really disjointed and they never even attempt to explain it. Even if they have a really interesting big twist in RE8 where they explain who Ethan is and how he fits into the grander story, it's still a major failure in this game.

Fourth, Ethan is just plain boring and unbelievable as a human being. Time after time crazy freaky stuff happens to him, and the only really human moment he has is with the police officer, excuse me "Deputy", in the beginning of the game. The guy has his hand cut off and stapled back on and doesn't seem to bat an eyelash. He doesn't look at it and go:

"What the hell is wrong with these people, why would they staple my hand back on...I need to get to a hospital...wait a minute, how the hell can I move my hand again?...oh god oh god oh god...what is happening!?"

He just breaks out of his restraints and goes about business as usual. No PTSD, no trauma, no explanations at all. He also doesn't freak out at seeing grotesque BOWs, but nearly jumps out of his pants when a dead body suddenly appears out of the muck under the house. He's just so inconsistent.

Overall the game was decent for what it was, but it did not feel like a Resident Evil game to me.

Sh*t your pants scary, clever, creative and just a little silly; this game is beyond fantastic. Sorry RE3, I'll be saving my cash for RE8.
