TL;DR - Resident evil 7 is worth buying if you’re at all a fan of the series or the survival horror genre as a whole. While imperfect, this game feels like a fresh and focused take on the Resident Evil formula, and actually managed to excite me for the next mainline game in the series. Most importantly, especially for people who don’t like most horror games, Resident Evil 7 is simply a fun game to experience. Given that this game is a few years old now, it can easily be gotten for $20 or less on sale, and also has some pretty fun DLC to go along with it.

________________________________________________________________________________
Review:

Resident Evil  is a narsty place full of even narstier people.

That’s not a bad thing though. While the Bakers’ home is a steaming pile of literal mutant cow dung, Resident Evil 7 itself is a wonderful twist on an aging series and a return to form of the Resident Evil series. Rejuvenating a game series over 20 years old is no easy feat. Instead of following the same path as the past several titles in the series, which has been a 3rd person shooter since 2005’s Resident Evil 4, Resident Evil 7 reinvented it into a disgusting and unsettling first person shooter in backwoods Louisiana. That change has unexpectedly returned this series to its horror roots, and it does so with a very strong showing. 

Premise and Storytelling

In Resident Evil 7, you play as an Average Joe named Ethan Winters, who is looking for his long missing wife, Mia. After years of silence and withering hope, Ethan receives a message from Mia that sends his investigations to a secluded house falling apart in Dulvey, Louisiana. Unfortunately for Ethan (and you), the inhabitants of this house have every intention to do you harm. And harm you, they do!

As you discover the mystery of this home and the family living in it, and what has happened to Mia, you’ll find a plot that is just as wacky as it is spooky. However, it does not take itself so seriously as to let the creepiness factor to override the fun ride that people expect out of Resident Evil stories. As the game progresses, it leans more into the bizarre humor of Ethan’s situation. This helped them create a tastefully spooky and delightfully funny horror game. As opposed to one that filled me with dread - a la 2019’s Resident Evil 2.

That being said, the pacing of the game’s story has some flaws. The first hour of the game is effectively very tense and slow paced, and the two thirds of the game move along at a really solid pace that did a great job of keeping me engaged. This changed in the third act, which slows everything to a halt. Some people might love the shift in the third act of the game, as it takes a slower pace and returns you to the feeling of hopelessness that the first hour of the game had. From my perspective it put too much of a halt on the fun factor and is where the game began to enter Chore to Play territory.

Gameplay and Graphics
Graphically speaking, Resident Evil 7 is the title where Capcom first revealed their RE Engine, and it’s quite the looker. From the characters to the environment, the visuals are detailed and designed to look subtly realistic. While some of the textures can be a bit smudgy at a closer glance, the majority of the time it succeeds in feeling like you’re stuck in a very real, very gross place. The visuals truly shine in the indoor environments, particularly the Baker’s residence - where you will spend the majority of your time playing this game. The magic is in the details, and you can tell that Capcom put a lot of work in designing the Baker household to feel like the home of a loving family that had something go terribly wrong. There are affectionate pictures all over the place along with other family memorabilia, and it feels very lived in. When you combine this home with the layer of grime, blood and mysterious black goop that Capcom added on top of it all, it creates an unsettling juxtaposition for the player.

While the human characters in the game have an appropriate amount of detail and are distinguishable from one another, the undead enemies are unfortunately very bland and forgettable. They’re satisfying to kill in a fight, but far from the star of the show.

While this game’s first hour of gameplay is a haunting affair, full of building tension and a sense of you being in over your head, this quickly changes for the majority of the game. After the first hour, the game begins to give you the necessary tools to defend yourself. A knife. Guns. Grenades. A frickin’ flamethrower (eventually). Before I knew it, I was stockpiling ammo and supplies to defend myself, and felt confident about most encounters. While I felt that the game occasionally was too generous with ammo and resources, this ultimately made the game more fun to play for me. While I can appreciate games that focus on the Survival part of Survival Horror, I prefer being given sufficient means to defend myself. This game handled this well, as most of the tension was in the environment as opposed to how well I used my resources. 

Being able to defend yourself in a game wouldn’t be worth talking about if it wasn’t fun to do so - and fortunately, it’s a solidly fun time to rip through the enemies in this game. The gunplay is a little bit clunky, but it’s a good time and is enhanced by the yummy gore that happens when the occasional head blows up. Ethan has quite a bit of weight to him, and feels like someone who has no experience in battling biohazards. The exploration and puzzles in between the fights are fantastic, as the Baker home (and surrounding environments) are a joy to explore and uncover the mysteries of. This is a title where simply unlocking doors and finding new paths in the environment is exciting, and it ultimately leads to you feeling like a master of the enemy’s domain. Backtracking is usually my least favorite aspect of this series, but this game hit a sweet spot for me.

Unfortunately, there are some downsides in the game design, and that comes in the form of the boss fights. While the combat in Resident Evil translates solidly to a first person shooter when it comes to the standard enemies, it’s quite a bit less fun in the bullet sponge boss fights. It isn’t terrible, and they aren’t the most challenging, but they were ultimately my least favorite aspect of the game.

Sound and Voice
While a memorable musical score can define a game and bolster its atmosphere and tone, it is a different art form entirely to know how to use silence to create tension. While there are tension building musical/sound cues in Resident Evil 7 that can create unease for the player, silence is much more prominent. As you navigate the game, you’ll hear wood creeking, scurrying in the upcoming hallway, or the wind howling through holes in the wall. This created a natural tension in me that was more fitting than musical cues for the grounded-yet-surreal style of horror this game went for.

The gameplay sound design is a bit of a mixed bag. While the enemies each have their own excellent and distinct sound quality, I was less impressed with Ethan’s weapon effects. Particularly for the pistols in the game, which I spent plenty of time with as they were my primary backup weapon when my favorites ran dry. It was more of a peashooter than a handgun. On the more impactful end of the weaponry were the sounds from the shotgun and flamethrower, which had the appropriate amounts of boom and sizzle respectively. While the weapon sound effects weren’t always spot on, I did love the way my weapons interacted with enemies. The enemy noises as they approached, and honestly as they died, are very wonderfully designed. I can firmly say that in some of the larger fights you will have plenty of flesh-popping noises to look forward to.

RE7 brings the franchise back to its survival horror roots with a game that's a lot less action-oriented and more focused on the horror elements. The main change is that this game plays in first person, but still maintains many core gameplay elements like inventory management. The story is played from a new perspective, instead of being based on well known characters from the franchise, and it's a welcome change of pace as you play the unexperienced Ethan who tries to help his missing wife, after he gets a message from her 3 years after her disappearance.

The game has a great start that sets the mood and shows how dangerous the Baker family is. It hits a bit of a stumble once the basic enemies start to show up - the limited ammo and enemies that wobble around too much and take multiple headshots to die are supposed to show what it feels like to be an unexperienced person having to deal with monsters like these, but it ends up being a source of frustration when you're trying to get a much needed headshot and the enemies just keep moving all over the place. However, it picks up the pace again not long after that and the game works well for most of the campaign. The Baker family makes for some truly great villains and the game has some really amazing and horrifying moments throughout the campaign.

The DLC campaigns and extra modes are also greatly worth it, for the most part. Banned Footage has some interesting moments that tell more about the stories from 2 characters, with Daughters being the best of them. Not a Hero brings back Chris Redfield and does so in a great way, including a few gameplay changes and more story. End of Zoe is also great and plays quite differently in terms of combat. Both Not a Hero and End of Zoe also include their own unlockables for further replayability. Jack's 55th Birthday is a fun little addition to the game that also has some interesting unlockables. The only mode I truly did not like at all was Ethan Must Die, which is basically just a mode that's meant to be extremely hard and most enemies kill you in a single hit. While I know that it's doable, I just found it to be a terrible idea overall and not fun in the slightest.

Easy recommendation. And here's hoping that future games of the franchise continue to follow what RE7 did.

Resident Evil 7 forces the player to think outside of the box. I spent most of the game wandering around looking for objects to help me progress and/or figuring out how to solve certain puzzles. The game doesn't hold your hand by giving you the solution either, you have to figure out everything yourself and some of the solutions to the puzzles require serious thinking. Sometimes you are better off looking at a guide if you are truly stumped imho, which has happened to me plenty of times during my first playthrough.

Resident Evil 7 has fantastic level design and amazing story-telling, you really feel as if you are facing a life or death situation playing as Ethan Winters trying to escape the clutches of a psychotic family. There are many creepy and scary moments throughout the game that tend to keep you on your toes, so watch yourself. The game rarely employs the use of cheap jumpscares, the atmosphere and aesthetic alone are enough to keep you on edge as you creep around the Baker estate.

The DLC's take a slightly different approach and become more action-packed as you take control of Chris Redfield in the Not A Hero DLC, while fighting for your life as you try to clean up the molded infestation while also trying to hunt down and capture Lucas Baker. With the End of Zoe DLC having you literally punch your way through enemies with your bare fists as Joe Baker, Zoe's uncle.

Overall, I highly recommend if you are a fan of the Resident Evil series, or just like horror games in general. It's a really good game.

Resident Evil 7. I’ll be honest, I did not expect to like Resident Evil 7. I was prepared to put it aside quickly. I dislike horror in general, I just am not a fan of the genre, I abhor Amnesia, which is just an absolutely terrifying game. I somehow beat Resident Evil 7 and had a great time with it.

As I played Resident Evil 7, I thought one thing, this is effective horror. Those words have been in my head almost the entire time of Resident Evil 7, and I’ve considered doing a video on what I mean. Essentially there are only 7 enemies I’d count in Resident Evil 7. Maybe that’s why it’s called Resident Evil 7. The thing is, those are all the major enemies including all the bosses, but those 7 enemies are so skilled at harassing the player that they become better than what you expect.

Resident Evil 7 made me impressed by how well it does horror and how you don’t need horrific monsters or scenes to drive home this horror. Spending the majority of the game low on ammo made the game feel intense without relying on constant combat. Resident Evil 7 focuses on the deeply unsettling nature of a situation that a player doesn’t want to be in.

I’d give Resident Evil 7 a top score. If you like Horror, you’re going to enjoy this, and if you’re like me and avoid the genre, this might be your exception also. I already have the Resident Evil 2 Remake, I’ll probably also play Resident Evil 3 before long as well, and if they drop Resident Evil 4 as a remake, why not. Resident Evil is a great horror action franchise , but as we know, it’s just had a few missteps in the past. 5 and 6.

I can't recommend this game to fans of the Playstation to GameCube era of Resident Evil games. On some fronts, there was a clear effort to bring the series back to its roots and please longtime fans: the initial setting inside a large house for you to explore, the inventory and save system, and hunting down decorative keys to pass through locked doors all make you think you're playing a real Resident Evil game. But after a few hours, the veneer wears off and you begin to see that more recent horror games were more influential to RE7 than the RE series' legacy.

The Outlast comparison is unavoidable. From the first-person perspective, VHS tape sequences, and invincible enemies for you to sneak around, it seems likely that the developers saw the popularity of Outlast and tried to emulate certain elements. While this may appeal to fans of Outlast or Amnesia, it is not consistent with RE. 

The inclusion of VR in the PS4 version may be a negative to some players of the non-VR PC version, as much of the game's horror relies on cheap "in your face" jump-scares. During the mid-game, ammo and healing is plentiful, but the handgun and flamethrower are so ineffective against the game's core enemies (uninteresting goopy black mold monsters are the zombie stand-in), you'll find yourself just using the shotgun to dispatch them in a single headshot. For this reason, there is no horror derived from the enemies for the bulk of the game. Along the way, you are funnelled from a large RE-esque house into a handful of smaller and very linear buildings where you will either be one-hitting fodder while looking for a McGuffin, hiding behind corners from an invincible enemy while looking for a McGuffin, or avoiding traps while you look for a McGuffin. There is an interesting puzzle sequence reminiscent of an escape room, but you may end up solving it twice if you watch the VHS tape you find shortly before the sequence in the main game. It's as if they were aware this was one of the game's stronger moments, and milked it for all that they could.

The final act of the game sees a bit of a switch in the setting and gameplay. Without spoiling anything, there's a point where you are granted an automatic weapon and lots of ammo, then walk up and down a series of corridors and shoot bullet-spongey mold monsters as they spawn in front of you until, presumably, you use the last McGuffin you inexplicably have in your inventory and the game ends (I had had enough by this point). It would have been nice if the weapon they gave was fun to use--or even better, if you could access the arsenal you had amassed over the course of the game, but alas, you spend the game's final hour doing the following:

1) Encounter a small group of mold monsters
2) Firing at them with your full automatic pea shooter
3) Watching them not so much as flinch until they move into their attack range
4) Turning around 180 degrees and running back up the narrow hallway
5) Turning around again to face the monsters 
6) Repeat step 2 until there are no more monsters blocking the hallway, and you can proceed to the next group of monsters or exposition dump.

I avidly followed the period between demo and release, back in 2016. Resident Evil 7 was possibly one of the largest topics back then, with speculation about the contents of the game being commonplace, and dissatisfaction with the more supernatural take of Beginning Hour and the dummy finger. Back in those days, we had no reason to expect that the ghost girl in the tape was Mia, and we had no reason to believe that the Molded in the basement was the result of Eveline, causing some confusion when RE7 finally dropped due to all of the misdirection in the demo.

The Guest House in RE7 is one of the shortest segments in the game, but it's a nostalgic segment. After spending so much time watching Beginning Hour reviews and playthroughs, it was interesting seeing more of the basement firsthand and how it connects to the Baker family residence. It would've been nice to have more emphasis on the residence in place of the Mines, but all in all both segments - in total - were around 4 hours each with exploration. From Antique Coins to Madhouse, there's plenty of reasons to replay the game, so length is not an issue here.

That said, it's not a perfect game by any means. Quickturn feels sluggish and plenty of the colors are similar, and being set at night in rural Louisiana, it's very difficult to see things at times; dialogue is awkward and cheesy at its lowest point; it's not a particularly long game, and I was able to beat it in six hours. None of this detracts from the experience, of course - especially the length, as quality is better than quantity.

TL;DR: Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a well-made, well-rounded albeit imperfect game from Capcom that deserves all of the praise it deserves.

[h1]A fresh, masterful execution of a horror game, Resident Evil VII proves that there is still plenty of new ground for the genre to tread[/h1]

You play as Ethan Winters, a bloke who one day receives an email from his wife, who went missing three years prior to the game's events. Risking it all, he journeys into swampy Louisiana to the address provided to him, venturing into a decrepit old house where he manages to find her still breathing. Events unravel in spectacularly quick fashion and you soon find yourself hostage to the estate's owning family: the Bakers, a wretched family of mutated psycopaths -Jack Baker, Marguerite Baker and their son Lucas, along with an elderly matriarch- bent on pursuing you across the house and murdering you as you traverse the estate's various structures looking for your wife and a way out. In the course of your odyssey you come across a fourth Baker: Zoe, Jack and Marguerite's daughter and thus Lucas' sister who, despite being infected, has yet to fall in the depths of irreversible madness that her family finds itself in. Thus, a sypmhony of characters and intertwined stories unravels as our character delves deeper into the morass of whatever happened in this secluded and sinister ranch, all the while fighting another type of creature: the molded, viscous beings that materialise out of a black, muddy substance which - resembling some of the series' mutants seen in previous iterations - are the first ties we have to the main saga, for the game up until the later segments seemingly shows little to no connection to Umbrella, Nemesis and everything we love about the cult series. 

But despite the FPS camera and the seemingly Outlast mechanics, the game is a Resident Evil game through and through: from the riddle-filled house evoking the Spencer Mansion, to safe rooms, storage lockers and green herbs, everything reeks of our beloved franchise. Careful item (and bullet!) management makes a comeback -though not to be used as sparingly as, say, Resident Evil 1, nor as freely as 5- as well as the series' landmark, bizarre puzzles; everything is there to remind us that despite everything, even if on the surface it should look as something else entirely, this is a Resident Evil game to the core and if anything this game proves that not only a Resident Evil game can be done right with a FPS camera but rather, it feels so instinctly part of the game that it is actually difficult to think that we used to play other games in the saga from a different angle.

On the technical department the game is simply flawless: let us start with the graphics, which even some 2 years and a half after the game was released look spectacular. The whole game feels as it is some kind of movie. By getting rid of lousy HUDs or other distracting visual queues, the game makes you feel absolutely immersed in the events taking place before your eyes. The game [i]feels[/i]  alive in a way few other can accomplish. Then, there are the sound effects, which manage to capture the tension of the moment: be it eerie momentum-building shrills to distant rumbles or creaking planks, the game has you constantly on your guard fearing that sooner or later you will turn around to find one of the Bakers' distorted visages peeking at you with their sadistic scowl. The game has an impressive musical score, yet the main theme (Go Tell Aunt Rhody) wins the day being one of the most memorable in recent years; I still sing it repeteadly days after having finished the game.

Finally, as befits a Resident Evil game, the story might be a tad cheesy at times. The whole biological terrorism, mutations and whatnot end up being a bit over-the-top, but [i]how[/i] this story is conveyed is a whole other matter, as the execution is downright [i]masterful[/i]. I reckon it just boils down to a matter of taste, but a portrayal this good coupled with a slightly more believable story would have been just perfect. But the game, in a way, already is: the pace, the tone, the graphics, the music and even the length -not too short nor too long- is just about right. It sets the bar way higher for future horror games and reminds us what a sheer joy playing a good, beautifully-crafted game can be.

An afterword on DLC: there are five DLC that compound Ethan's story. The first one, "Banned Footage", chronicles the trials and tribulations that Clancy, a previous hostage of the Bakers' had to endure during his captivity. There are four different segments to this DLC: one, "Nightmare", has Clancy survive waves of attacks from the molded and Jack Baker while collecting scrap, the DLC's currency which in turn allows you to buy more and better weapons and upgrades. Then, there is "Bedroom", a level which chronicles Clancy's escape from a room in which he is manacled to a bed while being tended to by Marguerite Baker. There is also "21", a sadistic take on Blackjack that pits Clancy against another captive in a high-stakes match of the fabled card game that -in true Saw fashion- may end up in amputation of fingers, electrical shocks or even... decapitation, presided, as might be expected, by Lucas Baker himself. Finally, the last portion of this multi-tiered DLC is "Daughters": a heart-wrenching chronicle of the final hours of the Baker's sanity as they make the discovery that will change their lives forever, paving the way for the events of Resident Evil VII.

The second DLC, "Not a hero", takes place immediately after the events of the main game. Just after its bombastic finale and as the credits are rolling for the main character, the DLC chronicles the journey of none other than our beloved hero - Chris Redfield - as he sets out to tie up one last loose end before it is all over. While this one still resembles the base game to some degree, it is still way more action-packed, as Chris -as expected- brings a veritable arsenal of weapons to the fray. The DLC felt awesome to play, especially as we get to play with such an iconic character as Chris -if anyone had any doubts as to the game's relation to the franchise, then this is it.

There is also the third DLC, End of Zoe, which picks up after the events of "Not a hero". This particular DLC  follows Joe Baker, Jack's brother, on his quest to save Zoe and try to salvage whatever remains of his family. Joe's fighting style is a remarkable departure from Ethan's hapless sneaking in the base game: that is not to say that he is unable to do some stealth of his own, for he can even pull off stealth kills on unsuspecting enemies. Yet he is in his element rushing headlong with his bare fists to beat the hell out of anything that stands in his way. Not only it is an extermely fun DLC to play, but also this last quest for redemption fits the game's wrap up perfectly.

Finally, there are two DLCs that serve as a compensating comic relief for the game's despairing nature. In one of them it is Jack's birthday and you have to feed him before time runs out. You have to go on scavenging runs through the house as you battle your way against spawning birthday caps-wearing molded, which, coupled with a lively tune, accompanying sound goofy effects, and a fitting HUD, make the game hilarious to play. The last DLC, titled "Ethan must die", has the protagonist, as one would expect, constantly die as he tries to survive a level populated with spawning molded which can one-hit our protagonist. This is probably the weakest, feeling rather dull and repetitive. 

Yet ultimately the game can be more than excused for that, for it is one of those games that leave a mark on you, that somehow after you put them down you are still thinking about them, still humming to their tune, still thinking about their story, still hearing their characters' voices. Still under the sway of its magic, you will be yearning to return to swampy Louisiana long after you beat it. To experience what the beauty of a perfectly-crafted story entails.

It is one of those games you will remember forever.

I really liked the initial premise. James Sunderla--Ooops, Ethan Winters gets a message from his missing wife and goes to find her. The opening hour of this game is truly unrivaled by any other game of the genera. Obviously inspired by The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Evil Dead (remake) films. It creeps along eerily, building tension and suspense. Sprinkling in some creepy imagery and inducing paranoia through misdirection. 

A truly masterful set-up, one that allows the player to ignore the fact that the protagonist is a husk devoid of personality (aside from his seemingly unbreakable balls of steel...seriously, nothing phases him) but that's the point. Ethan isn't so much a character as he is a vehicle for the player. This works out excellently...for the first 2/3 of the game...then you realize that he's not a very nice ride...he's more of a beater that reliably breaks-down when you're a mile from your destination.

Let me explain.

When the game is at it's best, it's easy to ignore the fact that Ethan has less personality than a bag of bags. When you are making your way through the Baker estate being pursued by...spoilers...one of the Bakers. It's easy to get absorbed in the horror. It feels uncomfortably real almost in spite of the fantasies it keeps on display.

Then the game remembers it's a part of the Resident Evil franchise and throws all nuance and subtlety out the window. Then the character and narrative flaws hog the spotlight.

About 2/3 of the way through, the narrative decides you (the player) are too stupid to piece the connections to the greater-franchise together yourself, and skulking about a creepy manor won't cut it. You require (relative) hoards of enemies, and a super heavy connection to the rest of the series. All of this culminates in a ridiculous final "boss" fight, proceeded by a jarring and baffling gameplay shift. I don't want to spoil the story because it is still fairly interesting -- but if you've played it, you know the moment the game shifts to something more akin to a FPS....the quality drops dramatically. The tension, the creep factor, the unsettling realness of being hunted -- all gone. It is during this shift that you become acutely aware of how boring Ethan is, because you no longer feel like you are the character.

Restraint is what made the first couple of thirds so special. Restraint is what made the first  handful of hours worth admission. Unshackling the game during the home-stretch made it all feel so anti-climactic. Though, with an admittedly cool cameo. 

Pros:
RE-Engine, baby!
Amazing opening
Super-tense moments
Uncomfortable atmosphere

Cons:
Just that last couple of hours, so terribly close to greatness....

Still worth a play. There's more good hours than bad.

For some weird reason I suddenly decided to pick up my half finished playthrough (not finished simply because I had a lot of games to get through) of this just as RE3 is dropping. And tbh, I am glad I came back.

This game has a lot of really great elements. Brilliant graphics. Well planned and paced storyline. Strategy and puzzle elements, balanced with the intense boss fights. Really good voice acting too, was a big fan of both Jack and Lucas in particular. 

For people who dont really know what this game is, it is a horror game, in which the main protagonist (Ethan) is contacted by a long lost spouse whom he had assumed was dead. However travelling to the old buildings in amongst the swamp has Ethan meeting folk who are...unique. To say the least. And creatures that quite freakish in their own right...

But in general, the main highlight of this game for me is replayability. If you look at the steam achievements, You'll notice challenges to, amongst other things, complete the game in 4 hours, complete the game without healing and complete the game without using storage crates. As well as making second and subsequent playthroughs more interesting, the completion of some of these challenges reward in-game items that can drastically change how you play, adding to the fun. 

Finally are the DLCs. I am not going to pretend like I have finished all of them yet, but the work put in to make a diverse range of DLCs has paid off a lot. From the survival game of Nightmare, the strategy game of 21 and the puzzle game that is Bedroom, I think the DLCs were more than worth it.

Anyway to summarise this long ramble, this game gets a big 'thumbs up' from me! ESPECIALLY if you are able to get it on sale with the DLC.

Without a doubt the biggest departure from the mainline Resident Evil entries in tone, plot and gameplay. RE7 is a first person shooter in claustrophobic environements with a definite Slasher movies inspiration (Texas Chainsaw Massacre for example) complete with derelict houses and found footage. The link to other Resident Evil games is there but kept tenuous until near the end.
As a standalone game it is pretty fun to play with the first couple of hours amazing with tension and horror and slowly steers towards more action as you're getting close to the ending. The antagonists and boss fights I found were the high point of the game, my favourite being Jack just for his almost comic-relief lines that still manage to blend perfectly with the tone of the game.

As a Resident Evil game you won't find much that's familiar besides the puzzles: the bestiary is completely forgettable and regarding gameplay, to fans of RE0-3 it isn't enough of a survival horror and to fans of RE4-6 there isn't any variation to defeating enemies. Both DLCs (Not a Hero and End of Zoe) play closer to the more action type games of the series, for example Not a Hero has melee takedowns for staggered enemies and End of Zoe has you punching your way through the story. I enjoyed both as they played differently from the main story.

I recommend it simply because it's a good game but just keep in mind that if coming from another Resident Evil game you won't find exactly what you're looking for.

RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard / BIOHAZARD 7 resident evil (that's how it used to be called on the store page) single-handedly pulled me back into the series after a long hiatus, so I owe it everything. It's an obscene, vile, gross, depraved, hardcore homage to the 1970s-1980s exploitation and body horror. Of course, it's not only about cinema, the game also pays respects to its roots with universal item boxes, overall resource scarcity and a myriad of other subtle little things. It's Splatterhouse to the core, at least the premise is kinda similar on a surface level, and it's also all about visceral terror, sinking grotesquely oversized fangs and claws into your face at every opportunity. If you're looking for nasty bugs, gore, mutilation, cruel contraptions and freaky old people nesting in ultra-realistic, ultra-violent setting, look no further - RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard / BIOHAZARD 7 resident evil got you covered from head to toe. This might be the grossest, scariest game in the series, also my personal favourite story-wise. It probably won't make you cry, but there's more to it than meets the eye. Don't read anything, don't watch the streams (I know I'm a little late with this advice), walk into the house blind, sniff up the mold, soak in the rot, then meet the Bakers.

I came pretty late to this party, but I'll cut right to the chase: this game is GOOD. Especially compared to the dumpster fire that was Resident Evil VI! I played Resident Evil 2: Remake before playing this, and I don't think RE2 would have been nearly as good if this game hadn't come first, if only because this game pioneered the new graphics engine and a lot of the gameplay. Both are excellent games, but let's just talk about VII. 

What VII really, really well is a return to old-school survival horror. What really impressed me is how this game changed the setting of the games to Louisiana, gave us all new characters, and entirely new threat, and yet... DAMN! It is DEFINTELY Resident Evil! This is a breath of fresh air for the fans of the series, because all the roots that made the original games so great are still there, even if you're not fighting zombies. In some ways, VII feels a bit like IV, in that the biohazard at play is strange and unfamiliar, but the fight to survive is not. 

REVII really impressed me. The atmosphere great, and the design is incredible! Creeping around the Baker House, the Old House, The Guest House... these places are completely a wreck, and really adds to the overall tension and creep factor. 

Oh man, and the Bakers? They're pretty creepy, but what really impressed me is how they are almost immortal, especially to your puny weapons. Jack Baker in particular is like the damn Terminator... nothing stops him! 

I digress... this game keeps the overall count of enemies you face pretty low, but makes each enemy a true threat. If you get hit, it HURTS. If you're not careful with ammo, you will run out. And sometimes, it is just way better to run than to stand and fight. 

My biggest issue was inventory management. It takes a long time in the main game before you expand your inventory capacity. It's meant to make you backtrack and make careful choices, but really, it just felt like it was padding the game time. Thankfully, Once an area is a cleared, it's pretty much cleared, with the exception of a few scripted returns to previous area where some molded had shown up. I felt like that was kind of cheap, but I was partially expecting it due to the devs using the same trick in RE2 Remake. 

Ethan is really one of my only complaints. He's just... well, I guess it's easier to just say he's no Leon, Claire, Jill, or Chris. Ethan is kind of bland as a person... I think that's to help make you see yourself in the role. Overall, he's supposed to freak out a little but hold himself together enough to survive the horrors, so I guess it makes sense that he's so muted. Lord knows if it was me in there I'd be cussin' up a storm, but... well, more power to him, I guess. 

The only thing I didn't like was the unresolved story hooks in the main game; it turns out, those hooks are picked up in the DLC's. I'd rather we addressed those in the main game and do something different for the DLC's, but it's a choice I respect and it still works. Chris picks up the trail on Lucas Baker and has a VERY intense combat DLC... (if I never have to go through the gas filled area of the mine again, I'll be grateful). I didn't play the Zoe DLC so I can't comment. 

Overall, the game is tense, exciting, and danger lurks around every corner. The Baker House is filled with surprises, and I really liked the 'Slasher Flick' inspirations for this outing. I personally didn't find it as terrifying as Zombies, but that's because Zombies are my personal kryptonite: they scare the hell out of me so badly that I had nightmares about being in front of the RPD fighting off hordes of infected dead before I even bought RE2: Remake. That's how psyched out they make me! 

For REVII, it aims to be more disturbing and more mysterious. I liked that! I enjoyed having a mystery about the family and the molded to piece together, I thought the Baker's were really unique to each other and disturbing in their own ways, the setting was awesome, and this game gets a 10/10 on tone! I actually stood in one part of the Tanker near the end and just stared out through a blasted wall for a while looking out into the swamp... this game just nailed the new setting and tone so well that it's gonna stick with me for a long time!

If you enjoy Resident Evil, and you want test your mettle against some really difficult opponents, I recommend this game A LOT. 

My tips: 

1) Watch the VCR tapes on the first run - clues about new areas and puzzles are found within. The one skippabe VCR tape is "Mia", which has a BS sneaking section that isn't the worth the time sink. 

2) Run from Jack. You don't have the ammo to bring him down most times. 

3) Once you have the right key, run back to the main house and grab the grenade launcher ASAP. It's a great weapon, even if there's not much ammo. 

4) In the Old House and Greenhouse, watch your ass. Margurite loves to attack from odd angles. 

5) NeuroToxin Ammo looks graphically like Acid Rounds in RE2: Remake. But they don't melt anything. They will however, hit with the force of a magnum round and stun your opponent in place. These are great to make near the end run! 

6) Never trust Lucas Baker. Don't trust ANYTHING revolving around Lucas. Don't trust breakable crates, don't trust his games, don't trust his word. If I haven't made myself clear, he's out to get you. 

7) You came to find and save Mia. Keep that in mind if you want the best ending. 

8) Magnum rounds are exceedingly scarce. You're better off using ancient coins on the other cages. 

9) Once you beat the game on any difficulty, you get a free gun for anyother playthrough, including old saves. It's always in the item crate in save rooms. This gun is AMAZING... but it does have limits. Still, I consider it better than the magnum by leaps and bounds... so I'd recommend blasting through the game to get this instead of trying to get the Magnum I mentioned in point 8. 

10) Bosses are made to soak up your bullets and ammo. Line up your shots well, otherwise you could be in really big trouble down the road. If it doesn't kill your sensibilities, look up some guides online on what to do ahead of time if you're not looking for a huge headache.

I have no qualms with funneling, I did it from time to time to beat Dark Souls, but having to try 5 times in a row to funnel because you only have ammo to miss 3 shots on your save file is insanely frustrating. After that, I was treated to a horrible boss fight. From the previous fight, I had learned too look in your surroundings for things that might help, and clearly saw the chainsaw. I tried picking it up, walking to the back corner to see if there was a lever of some kind, and letting jack swing at me to see if he could knock it down for me. None of these work. Up until this point in the boss fight, I had felt like the movement mechanics were really clunky, but was willing to give it a pass because it added to the horror aspect of the game, but after I slashed Jack with the chainsaw, the chainsaw dying,  the movement mechanics really showed their flaws, I couldn't turn to run away from jack because my character is far to slow, so I tried to block, but alas, Jack did some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ instant kill attack on me, forcing me to start the bossfight over yet again. How, as a player, am I supposed to strategically take down a boss if I don't know the obstacles in my way.[/spoiler] Its really a shame the first 2 hours of the game really felt like survival horror. TL;DR - An impeccable return to form that brings horror and novelty back to the series as well as the impressive RE Engine, but with a limited amount of longevity.

At Length - Resident Evil 7 is a text book example of doing everything in a survival horror game correctly. It creates a genuinely disturbing atmosphere that it thrusts the player in only to force them to confront demented psychopaths and terrors in the middle of the night before assaulting their sanity and sense of perception. But like the earlier games in the series, and unlike many of the First-Person horror game imitators that came later, it keeps the strategic resource management elements and slow build of character progression (through stronger weapons and more ammo) to eventually empower the player so that they're allowed to confront the evils they encounter in order to overcome that fear and relieve the tension it builds in a very satisfying way. 

I genuinely felt the tension and got effectively creeped out playing this game, which is the highest compliment you can really give a horror game. The tale of the Baker Family and their madness hits a lot of emotions, even -surprisingly- notes of tragedy, sadness and regret. I was expecting a family of Leatherfaces but got one of Lisa Trevors instead.

But there's one real caveat here; at least when it comes to the main game you need to do this all quickly. The game really works best on your first play through, done in one or maybe two sittings in the middle of the night with the volume up. It's totally feasible and how I experienced it. It's important because once you spend enough time getting acclimated to the monsters and the mechanics just like every RE that came before it, the effect of unnerved caution you'll feel will fade and you're going to be playing a Spookum Shooter yet again. Only this time it's an FPS rather than in 3rd Person. 

Luckily, by the time that occurs there's a bunch of DLC to play through which takes advantage of this acclimation effect to give you remixes and reinventions of the main gameplay. As well as 2 short follow-up chapters to the main game, one FreeLC, one Paid DLC. All of the additional content is good, but it's a question of whether or not it will be worth the price to you, and that'll depend on how much the main game captures your imagination. 

I think for those that don't like this game, it will be because they take too long through the main game or come in with too much information after playing a lot of the demo or watching stuff online. If you get acclimated to the horror effect too soon, the last half of this game becomes a bit of a slog and you're not going to want to finish it, let alone try out anything post-game.

But it all worked for me and I'm immensely impressed that the crew at Capcom found a way to reinvent the wheel yet again for this franchise so late in it. Hopefully the intent, if not the exact implementation, of RE 7 will be the mold they follow for successive numbered follow-ups for a while, and they keep the Horror strong in the series like they did here.

This game made me feel scared, trapped, desperate, and all together wondering why all of those feelings were exactly why I kept playing. This is Resident Evil with your perspective as close to the action as humanely possible, and the developers use this shift in perspective to assault your senses. Frequently I grimaced in disgust and shock at what RE7 had in store during its 10 hour campaign (on normal difficulty). 

This is like scuba diving in the most disgusting lake imaginable. I'm not sure there's a prize at the end, but damned if I just feel like taking one more dive while I still have my sanity.

Main Game:

RE7 is an absolute beast of a game, the main mode is highly story rich and put together really well. For those who enjoy the horror types of games then RE7 is a must for you as it was both very jumpy as well as disturbing. I can’t complain about the length of the main mode as there is plenty going on, the story itself leads on well through the game with no crappy parts that put you off. The level of gore at times is high, some of it is very twisted as well which adds to the whole experience. RE7 is definitely one of the goriest games I’ve played to date. 

I’d suggest taking it slowly in this game, there is speed run of about 2 hours but doing that will just waste the purchase. There is a lot to explore in this game so take it easy. I think I completed the main mode in sub 20 hours. 

The characters are well designed, Jack is awesome and Lucas is damn right hateable. Zoe is also a great character along with Mia; who you are primarily there for.  

The skill level of the game isn’t easy, I’d say on normal difficulty it at times can be a challenge, however there is further skill levels which are worth doing if you find it easy, achievements and trophies etc. 

The DLCs:

I purchased all of the available DLCs once I’d completed the main game, and I can say they’re definitely worth the extra money. The games themselves further explain what happened to the characters before and after the events in the main game. There is also some additional missions in the DLCs which are “just for fun”. 

The skill level for the DLCs is way beyond that of the main game. Two of them in particular are Ethan Must Die and 21 Survival+. Ethan Must Die was HARD! I think it tops my count of repeated attempts at something like 70… You can check the skill level required in the steam achievements or whatever platform you play to see the percentage of people who have completed them.

Ah, yes. Resident Evil 7. The game that for me, personally, started it all. Granted, I was scared out of my mind on my first playthrough, but if it hadn't been for me sitting down and committing to playing "A spooky game for October", I would've missed out on what is hands down, one of my favorite Capcom franchises of all time. The Resident Evil devs sat down and pretty much said "We need to scare our fans again". And boy did they deliver.

The experience playing Resident Evil 7 is quite surreal and very enjoyable. It offers a truly horrifying look into the events that occurred before the other games, I assume an attempt to fix the somewhat convoluted story line that Resident Evil offers. The graphics are intense, game play is smooth, buttery, I mean I don't lag at all and I don't have the most advanced computer in the world. The combat is interesting, the models beautiful, the environment is scary and gorgeous at the same time. The story is well written and no matter who you are, at times your heart is going to race playing through this game.

You get to witness multiple perspectives during your time, the main character "Ethan" being the primary player, albeit a little stupid but definitely committed to his family. You get to cycle through a decent variety of weapons and fight some pretty creative creatures and bosses (Although I will say the repetition of some of these bosses is a bit annoying). There's really not many cons I have with this game.

Pros:

Beautiful scenery and models. Intense graphics to the point you almost never tire of looking at the game.
User friendly UIs and features that offer a variety to the game.
Creative story writing

Cons:

A little lackluster in the weapons department, in my opinion.
There isn't much of a variety in the enemies and bosses though this is to be expected with the game's direction.
It can feel a little tedious at times due to slow paced events.

[h1]Triple AAA Disappointment[/h1]
10 hours!? That's it? I would be so mad if I bought this game at release price. I'm irritated that it got so much acclaim, because it's absolutely mediocre. Gorgeous graphics, but that's all. And the beautiful graphics are actually kinda creepy considering the mouths don't move quite right and everyone looks like talking mannequins. I think they should have simply used real actors with that level of detail.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
Boring, linear, obvious. Anyone who pays attention to details instead of just being dragged along by the plain storyline will see the "shocking" revelation from the first moments of the game. I think they knew the storyline was terrible, which is why the game ends with an in-your-face "WTF?" moment that doesn't make any sense in the Resident Evil universe, just so people would theorize and talk about it. A cheap gimmick to cover a bad, unsatisfying story.

Also, much as I used to love Resident Evil when I was kid, aren't we a bit past the idea of a Reverse-Escape Room? Why do these crazies go through all the trouble of crafting these maze-like situations for people trapped in the house? Surely they didn't decide it would be fun for themselves to hide keys in random places or have to track down puzzle pieces just to go into the back yard...

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]
Quite possibly the most inept playable character I've ever played. I can't stand "realism" that clearly doesn't have any clue what real life is like. Wobbly door? Kick that thing open! If you don't want me to get through it until I find the right key, you'd better make it solid. Glass window beside the door with a gun right behind it? Better search the house for the key instead of just grabbing a chair and smashing the window.

I'm pretty sure old ladies at the mall powerwalk faster than Ethan "runs". He can't jump, can't kick open a flimsy wooden door, can't move the simplest obstacles blocking his path, and does this really irritating "stop" when you try to break off from a run. It's like he's taking a quick step backward, and it's much more irritating than my explanation makes it seem. And backing up is so slow that I kept thinking there was something behind me. Good thing that...

[h1]The Combat[/h1]
...sucks. Enemies have extremely repetitive, wide-arcing attacks that are necessary because Ethan moves so slowly that anything else would be impossible to dodge. And you have to dodge. Or block...block a giant monster's crab-like arm with your flimsy little forearms that can't even move a box out of the way. Or block a chainsaw with a folding knife...who designed this combat?

[h1]Final Words[/h1]

After having to suffer through Michael Bay-esque action movies with Resident Evil 5, 6, and Umbrella Corps, Resident Evil 7 is a welcome return to form and just the shot in the arm that this series needed for years

The game excels in establishing a sense of place and atmosphere in its world. The environments are intricately detailed and reward a good eye and willingness to search every nook and cranny for items. And while the story itself may not be much to write home about, it serves its purpose of segueing the player from point A to B. Also the Bakers are incredibly fun antagonists to fight against, with each having their own unique theme to the environments they inhabit

Now the game isn't perfect by any means, and I wouldn't even say that it's one of the best Resident Evil games. Despite how varied and engaging the Bakers are as antagonists, the Molded enemies aren't nearly as interesting, with there being so few types to fight against. Also Ethan is one of the blandest protagonists out there, utterly lacking in the charm or charisma that characters like Leon or Jill from past games had.

My biggest flaw with the game however has to be how the lead up to the finale is paced. At a certain point, all of the tension is thrown completely out the window and the game devolves into a shallow repetitive shooting gallery, with the Molded not really posing much of a threat since you get showered in healing items and ammo. The ending itself is worth the payoff, but it does leave a damper on the experience since the game does a fantastic job of building tension and fear all the way before

All in all, RE7 is still a great game despite its flaws, and is 100% worth playing if you're a fan of survival horror or games with a great sense of exploration. And between this, the remakes of RE2 and 3, and the inevitable Resident Evil 8, the future is looking bright for this series.

If you're a Resident Evil fan, then this is a great continuation of the series. Resident Evil 4 is still my favorite, but this game has some memorable moments for sure. You'll start out a bit confused in the beginning, but as the game progresses you'll figure out what is going on and the pace will pick up quite a bit with a lot more variety in enemies and weapons later on.

Resident Evil 7 is a drastically different RE game. It is the first RE game that is an FPS. It has other several unique gameplay features that makes it completely different from not only RE games, but horror games as well. There are also some gameplay elements borrowed from other horror games.

One of those elements is hiding and running away from invincible enemies who chase you as in Outlast games, however, those sections are only limited to early parts of the game where you can't defend yourself because the enemy that is chasing you in the location you explore is invincible. Where and how often he appears depends on difficulty settings you choose to play at. After you face him in a boss fight, you are free to explore locations for the rest of the game just like in other RE games.

All enemies you are going to face in main game have attacks that can be blocked by your arms which greatly reduces damage you take. This block feature is very useful, however it is not always necessary as you can run away from your enemies and shoot them from a distance. Though there are some enemies and bosses that are very fast so you will often have to use this feature. 

I'm feeling very unsatisfied when using the word 'enemies' because in main game enemy variety, compared to other RE games, is incredibly mundane. You will be fighting only three types of enemies. I know it sounds crazy, considering RE games having a large variety of enemies in the series. You also won't find any enemy that you fought in other series - all enemies are brand new. 

Your character isn't a STARS or BSAA member or a police officer this time - just a normal guy travelling to a dangerous place to find his missing wife and trying to survive the nightmare. This make the game a more disturbing experience.

The lore is also different, but I am not going to spoil it - game is crystal clear about this new type of bioweapon however I'll only say that what you will be facing this time won't only be a mutated monster. It is different, if you play you will see it. 

However, it is still a RE game. You start with limited resources, struggle to find ammo, get through areas to pick key items and solve puzzles to explore more areas. And as you progress further you get to receive more weapons, ammo, healing items. Pretty simple power creep as in other RE games where you end up with a lot of supplies when you finish the game - even on the hardest difficulty setting, unless you are aiming blindly. 

This game offers a lot of unlockable gameplay mechanics such as items and challenge modes that drastically changes the game. Also, there is a great difference between normal and hard difficulty settings, in hard mode (called Madhouse) all items are in different locations, randomized, enemies appear in different places and their AI improves greatly, puzzles are changed - so CAPCOM didn't simply change numbers this time, they put a lot of effort into this game.

In my opinion, you should own all DLC's (except perhaps those coins that gives your character a slight boost) as they offer long hours of enjoyment. Of course, though, they are short if you are simply going to play them for just once, but they have great replay value. There are no Mercenaries DLC, but there is a mini game similar to mercenaries where your character has to survive until morning, but most simiar one is Jack's 55'th birthday - but it has a twist.

This is a very enjoyable RE game, you will get to feel like playing another game at first, but after a while you will feel like it is still a RE game. Highly recommended.

It doesn't take more than an hour before I'm sold on the concept. It has been more than ten years since the fourth part of Capcom's acclaimed series revolutionized the gaming industry, the horror genre and changed the Resident Evil brand forever. Or yes, changed to today at least. With Resident Evil 7, Capcom has finally chosen to listen to the millions of fans who sighed, prayed and asked for a return to all the elements and values that once defined the entire genre. And fortunately, Capcom chose to listen, responsively. The evil that grabs me when I set foot in Baker's family home completely binds me and doesn't let go of me until the journey is over about nine hours later. It is then that the sun's rays search their way through the swampy marshlands of Louisiana - and further into my own blinds. That's when I summarize this as a fantastic game that every horror fan simply has to experience.

In short, my points:

+Perfect balance between horror and action, nasty and violent, 
+Minimalist but effective presentation 
+Exciting exploration, varying horror. 
+Fantastic atmosphere and mood
-Some questionable actor contributions, and forgettable soundtrack.


Resident Evil, the series that has long been in desperate need of a fresh start, has finally returned to its terrifying roots but with better puzzles, less backtracking, frugal supplies and open spaces. It is clear that Capcom has been looking at our current generation of horror heroes like Outlast and PT, but they have been no more than been inspired by the titles, Resident Evil 7 stands firmly on its own. For the first time in the history of the series, we get to experience with our own eyes, in the first-person view all the shivery that is hiding in the family of the Baker's deceased mansion and the new perspective really works amazingly.

The game starts off incredibly well and brings the thoughts to the first part of the series but loses focus somewhat enormously towards the end. However, despite the lost focus and sprawling story, this is the right steps in the right direction for Resident Evil and just what the series needed.

I played this alone, at night, in the dark, without guides or YouTube videos because I’m not a casual. I had no idea what to expect from the game - except that the Steam user reviews were consistent in saying how good it was - and I wasn’t disappointed!

I felt genuinely scared on my first play through and fell victim to basically every jump scare in the game. Early on I had to broadcast the game and seek confidence from the chat to continue into a pitch black basement with just my trusty rusty knife.

The games story is a simple one. Your wife goes missing and a few years later sends you a message to rescue her. The game is set within a large, seemingly abandoned, estate and it’s surrounding buildings. Known locally as being a haunted house. The environments were believable and detailed. The house itself looks lived in and has all the rooms you’d expect. It wasn’t just a series of interconnected, poorly lit rooms full of wooden crates because of reasons.

I liked that many of the items tied to your survival; such as ammunition and first aid were hidden behind and under objects - encouraging the player to dig around in each room to find its secrets!

The resources in the game are sparse, as is your inventory space. Making each decision on what to carry and why, much more meaningful. It really enhanced the survival element and makes you feel as if you really are an interloper in someone else’s grim home!

The gaming trope of loading you up with health and ammo before a ‘Boss battle room’ remains consistent. A necessary evil I suppose.

The textures are inconsistent at moments, I was running this on a very high end machine and some parts looked excellent - then I’d see a tree or rock that looked like it was from a pixel point and click adventure game.

The enemies don’t respawn once an area is cleared, so there are brief moments of respite to explore and scavenge until you advance the story or leave. I found gaining the shotgun quite emboldening and it did actually remove a lot of the earlier trepidation, but it didn’t fully spoil the tension for me.

The puzzles were pretty simple, which I was fine with. I think the real difficulty comes from dodging the enemies chasing you while solving them.

The boss battles are almost always in tight rooms or similar close quarter environments which could annoy some people and there’s a few logical things such a breaking down doors with axes or guns that should happen but doesn’t - however ultimately it’s a game and some suspension of disbelief is always necessary.

This is one of those games that actually enhances your second play through with permanent item unlocks and challenging game changing achievements; such as completing the game without healing or not using the storage chests etc. Items change locations based of the difficulty too which adds a nice twist. Need that handgun ammo you remembered was under the stairs? Too bad, it’s moved!

I’m not familiar with the Resident Evil franchise and lore overall so I can’t offer any comments on how it fits into that, or if a hardcore fan of the franchise will be satisfied. There were a few moments and references that I didn’t understand, so these were likely there for the fans of the franchise.

I didn’t experience any bugs in my two play throughs and the game is well polished.

I’d strongly recommend this game to any horror survival enthusiast.

[h1]RESIDENT EVIL 7.[/h1]
[i]Go tell Aunt Rhody…[/i]

[b][u]Introduction[/u][/b]
Resident Evil 7 is a slow-paced, story-driven, survival-horror FPS game released in early 2017. Heralded as a soft-reboot for the franchise, RE7 appears a perfect starting point to jump into the series. I’ve never personally played a game in the Resident Evil franchise before, so RE7 was a pleasant surprise for me. The game is about as elegant and well designed as a horror title can get, with only a few missteps. I’ll say now that if you’re a fan of the genre, Resident Evil 7 is a must play.

[b][u]Plot[/u][/b]
In Resident Evil 7 you enter the life of Ethan Winters, an undeveloped protagonist outside of the fact that his wife, Mia, has been missing for three years. She disappeared on a mysterious job she was working, but then at the start of RE7 contacts Ethan, telling him to come to Dulvey, Louisiana to find her at the Baker Family Ranch. Suspicious but overjoyed to discover that his wife is alive, Ethan makes for Louisiana and enters the swamplands of the Baker estate. What he finds there beggars belief.

[b][u]Presentation[/u][/b]
One of the most important elements of any horror experience is the presentation. Luckily, Resident Evil 7 delivers beautifully on this front. The art style is uncut realism, featuring extremely lifelike environments, models, and effects. Textures, atmosphere, and post processing are all of A-grade quality for 2017, and hold up perfectly well three years on. The lighting and faces are particularly impressive though. RE7’s lighting is dynamic, moody, and claustrophobically dark, while the realism of the faces can produce grotesque spectacles. The only visual defect can be found in the somewhat janky movement animations. As for the sound, I have no complaints. Audio is consistently good, with terrifying ambiance and a fitting OST. Performance is also damn-near perfection, with hardly any bugs and comprehensive PC optimization. When it comes to presentation, RE7 has no true shortcomings.

[b][u]Level Design[/u][/b]
The level design in RE7 is an aspect that is part presentation, part gameplay. The decrepit Baker Family Ranch is eerie and hideous, contributing to the atmospheric unease. Various environmental details tell the story of what has occurred there, but I’ll leave that for you to discover. From a gameplay perspective, the level design is broadly “linear,” but this is not entirely the case. You can return to almost all of the areas you’ve been to previously, however as you make progress throughout the campaign there is usually only one way of doing things. Due to the linearity and this being a game that thrives on the player’s fear, some moments are distressing when the single path forward is unclear and you become trapped by enemies. Whether this is a failing or an intentional feature of the design, I’ll leave up to you.

[b][u]Gameplay Mechanics[/u][/b]
Looking at what you actually do in the game, it’s a mix of classical survival-horror and FPS mechanics. Your movement speed is painfully slow, so running away from danger is usually a poor option – you’re meant to sneak around or stand your ground. When it comes to standing your ground, there are various weapons and tools you’ll collect throughout the game. The guns vary wildly in effectiveness; for instance, the pistol is basically a water gun, and the shotgun functions like you’re shooting a damn freight train. RE7 also has the same obligatory loot and crafting system of all survival-horror games these days, enabling you to create first aid meds, pistol bullets, etc. The fun side of this crafting system is that resources are actually extremely limited. Every encounter with an enemy will cost you, making the non-boss fights feel like mini wars of attrition. And when it comes to the bosses, each battle is simultaneously frightening and challenging, keeping you engaged in frantic attempts to destroy your adversary as you pour more and more resources into combat. This core gameplay loop is so surprisingly good, but what’s better is that it’s only the second best item on the menu of what RE7 is serving.

[b][u]Scare Factor[/u][/b]
At Resident Evil 7’s opening, the game is absolutely terrorizing. Like, muscles-tensed-up-and-fight-or-flight-reflexes-engaged-in-real-life kind of terrorizing. This level of intensity fades after about 2 hours, but the sensation of angst and anxiety as you approach every corner never fades entirely during the 8-10 hour campaign. I believe the sickening setting of the Baker estate, the possessed inhabitants themselves, the resiliency of the enemies, the graphics, the audio, and the uncertainty of what the hell is going on in the narrative all have a hand in producing the most palpably “horror-ific” atmosphere of any game I’ve ever played. RE7 has the classical horror theme down to an absolute science.

[b][u]Narrative[/u][/b]
Ending on a bit of an anticlimax, the story itself is a bit of an anticlimax. This isn’t to say the writing is particularly bad, but for a game that spends a decent amount of time emphasizing its story, there really should have been more here. The main narrative beat is about what has possessed the Baker Family that is holding your wife Mia captive, and figuring out why they are functionally immortal. You accomplish this through encounters with each family member individually, as each member of the Baker Family has a stage of the game where they are the primary antagonist. This is an interesting enough mystery to solve, but the reasons behind their possession are never explained too well, and none of the characters in RE7 are compelling or relatable. In essence, the writing is very bare bones. The splendid gameplay and great atmosphere certainly make up for this one deficiency, but it holds Resident Evil 7 back from the dizzying heights it was so close to.

[b][u]Conclusion[/u][/b]
Resident Evil 7 is a refreshingly clear cut, good game in a genre full of mediocrity. It executes on its core design principles flawlessly, resulting in an experience that should be regarded as a shining example of how to do horror right. Its level of polish is something I’ve only hinted at so far, but I believe it’s what makes RE7 as outstanding as it is. Other than the underdeveloped story, there is absolutely nothing about the game that I can point to as a big shortcoming. Add in the high points of its frenetic boss battles and the crippling anxiety its scary side produces, and you have an instant classic on your hands. If you have any level of interest in playing Resident Evil 7, do not hesitate.

[h1]Personal Rating: 9/10 – Absolutely Outstanding[/h1]

*Note: RE7 has one short free DLC, “Not a Hero,” which I have played. It introduces a few new gameplay mechanics and expands upon the story in the aftermath of the main game. It’s a solid addition if you enjoyed RE7, however it’s less survival-horror and a lot more FPS-horror.

Resident evil is one of the franchises i did not play growing up mainly because i liked action adventure better than horror survival.And the other reason that the games were too scattered among different platforms and i could not play them easily.I am glad that i started with this one.From what i saw and read from other reviewers is that this game was a breath of fresh air for the franshise.A new engine,new protagonist,new setting and a first person character view.These were a great combination to create one of the greatest horror experiences i have ever had.

[b]Graphics[/b]
I really do think that the resident evil engine is one of the best on the market right now solely because it creates some of the most believable settings and character models i have ever seen.It is just gorgeous to look at.And while someone could argue that this beauty may limit the animations then i am glad to report that this engine also provides really fluid animations that tend to be even more impressive during gore moments.

[b]Story[/b]
Now if you are a horror movie viewer then this story won't surprise you much.I think it has been covered many many times before.Relative goes crazy,Guy gets trapped in a place while looking for a missing person,little kid gets possesed etc.You know how it goes.The game puts you in the shoes of Ethan.The most brave man i have ever seen in a horror story.And i am saying that because while in many movies the protagonists get trapped,there is usally no way to escape until the villian is dealt with or help arrives.But no Ethan walked into this mess by his own will determined to find his missing wife Mia and even after witnessing the horrors of this place he still stayed and fought.And that deserves a praise or maybe some therapy for stupid decisions.Take your pick.

[b]Characters[/b]
Now the characters are the strongest part of this game.It's what drives it forward with great momentum.With the exception of Ethan that i meantioned above Mia and the Baker family were amazing.Each and every one of them.We have Daddy Jack who was my favourite of the bunch,creepy wife Marguerite,crazy son Lucas,strange daughter Zoe and even a mysterious grandma.Each one with their own section to hide and escape from and latter fight on.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is what you expect from a game like this.You need to hide,you need to fight and you need to survive.It's what outlast would be if they added guns.But don't let that fool you.Even though you have guns it is still a great horror experience and the guns won't always help you.There is also inventory management in the game where you have to carefully take the things you need like quest and healing items and stash them in order to make room for new ones and also prepare yourself for the battles that follow by taking guns bullets and first aids.The whole setting at the Baker Estate was truly an immersive spectacle even more so if you try this game on VR.It has some great puzzle segments that you needed to solve in order to progress,find some tools to unlock previously locked areas while trying to escape from the hands of the Bakers.

The only thing i did not like was a choice that is forced upon you near the end of the game that makes no sense at all.This was adressed with a DLC that pretty much covered the hole.Some people also did not like the ship segment.I think it was fine.It gave some backstory to the events prior to the game's and was neede in order to give an ending to this game.

I also suggest to check out the 2 DLC: NOT A HERO AND END OF ZOE.Both give a proper ending to the rest of the Bakers.They are short but enjoyable.I also enjoyed the Daughters episode that gave a bit of a backtory to the Baker family before their fall.

Overall i think this game was amazing and it deserved the praise it got.I would rate this with a 9/10.

Resident Evil 7 biohazard (or BIOHAZARD 7 resident evil in Japan, guess we've come full circle haven't we?) is a fantastic homage to the schlocky horror b-movies we remember laughing with drunk friends at midnight, only this time it's actually terrifying as ♥♥♥♥.

RE7 instantly shot up to becoming my favorite horror game near instantly. It manages to tightrope across a line of being campy garbage while also staying serious enough to be engaging and terrifying. I love stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I also love a good story, and RE7 has both in spades. It has plenty of self-aware moments for a good laugh and indulges in some insane over the top setpieces while bringing you back down to Earth and hitting you with surprisingly in-depth and tragic backstories.

What really sells RE7 though is the approach it takes to survival horror, blending its classic Resident Evil roots into the modern survival horror mold. As much as I love Alien: Isolation, SOMA, Silent Hill & the such, I have to admit that the gameplay loop didn't evolve much from "hide when the unkillable monster is near and proceed when it goes away". RE7 has that too, but it's much more than that. The Bakers are permanently unkillable, but it is possible to temporarily kill them. Suddenly, a wealth of options opens up where you have to play a balancing act of ammo, time, health, resources and the such.

Unlike Alien: Isolation or SOMA or Shattered Memories, where your only option is to hide, it is possible to become genuinely good at Resident Evil 7 and come up with frantic, desperate strategies as you try to get the hell out. You are absolutely not in power; with how tough a single basic enemy is let alone the Bakers should make that obvious fast, but you never feel helpless because of the weapons you have. This just makes it all the more sweeter as you slowly learn more and more about how the enemies work and you get access to more and more powerful weapons.

RE7 was my first Resident Evil game and it is a stellar introduction. Almost every aspect of this game has been carefully managed to make a fantastic survival horror game. From the graphics that perfectly show the washed out aesthetic of an abandoned country house to the self-aware campy tone that still tells a phenomenal story for those who seek it, the sound design that makes me twinge in my seat and especially the gameplay that demands your focus only to make you lose it in a flurried panic...

Resident Evil 7 is a game that you should gladly welcome into the family of Resident Evil, and especially survival horror.
