The Worst Resident Evil Franchise Game Ever

It's no secret that Resident Evil 7 is my all time favorite horror game of the last decade but what is it exactly that makes this game so good? In this review I'm going to attempt to explain why I consider Resident Evil 7 to be a nearly perfect game. First of all, the setting through out the majority of the base game is absolutely stunning, it pays respects to a lot of old school horror classics that I grew up liking like The Texas Chainsaw Massacre for example. The Baker estate is massive! There's the main house which is basically a homage to the Spencer mansion from the first game filled with puzzles and secrets to discover while still being a dreadful hellhole. There's about 3-4 other buildings present in the game as well that's also part of the Baker estate but I won't go too much into detail regarding their purposes since I'd have to go into spoilers. The baker family members are all very intimidating and at times hilarious antagonists that'll chase you around the houses till you get to that eventual boss fight. In total there are 7 boss fights (8 if you count a mini boss) in the base game that all feel very unique with 1 fight, in particular, being quite challenging depending on your difficulty settings. What really sets RE7 apart from its predecessors is that the entire game is in first person, this might annoy some old school RE fans but it works so well that if the game was done in third person it would've taken away a lot of the tension throughout the game. One issue I need to point out is that the only enemies in the game besides members of the Baker family are these weird-looking creatures called "The Molded" Now these guys will jumpscare you at certain points due to their clever positioning around corners and genius hiding spots in dark rooms. In total there's 4 types of Molded, there's the basic molded, the 4 legged molded, the fat molded, and the enhanced molded (There's more types of molded in the DLCs). At first, these creatures can be very intimidating due to their fast movement and aggressive nature, but once you learn how to toy with them and exploit their weaknesses they turn into nothing but small obstacles. There's a few other enemy types (2 to be exact) that does appear in a few sections but they're not real enemies, it's like the crows in RE 1 that just annoys you but can be avoided. Madhouse mode which is the hardest difficulty can be a rather challenging experience, however, there's plenty of ways to cheese Madhouse mode to the point of it becoming kind of a joke. There are no ink ribbons on any difficulties except for madhouse, in fact, when you're playing on Madhouse it feels like the game's giving you too many ink ribbons (Or in this game it's cassette tapes you're getting) The crafting system is simple yet very cool, combat feels great since every gunshot you fire feels real! You can feel the weight of the bullet piercing through the enemy's skull! The game's filled with alot of gore, body horror, swearing, vomit, and all kinds of weird ♥♥♥♥, what I'm trying to say is you'll see some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up ♥♥♥♥ throughout this game. In terms of collectables, there's a ton of ♥♥♥♥ to collect! If you go out of your way to find the hidden secrets and you're clever with your use of certain items then you can obtain around 3-4 optional weapons! See this is something I'm all about and I've based the route that I take around a certain weapon for when I speedrun the game. Besides weapons, you can find hidden coins which allow you to buy 1 specific weapon, steroids, and adrenaline, these consumables can be used to increase your maximum health and the time which it takes to reload your weapons. You can also shoot some bubbleheads hidden throughout the many different locations present in the game, destroying all of them will get you a nice little unlockable for future playthroughs. Now the game sadly ain't perfect, in fact, the last fourth of the game is so incredibly boring that it felt like a chore to complete. Eventually, you will leave the Baker estate and when that happens you'll be sent to a ship and a mine which doesn't really fit into the story even though they tried to link it all together. Every time I play through the game I'm having fun all the way up till this part of the game, at this point, I just wanna start over and replay the good part which is 75% of the game! Resident Evil 7 is a solid 9/10 for me. If it wasn't for the last 25% of the game then I'd give it a 10/10.

[h1] RESIDENT EVIL 7: BIOHAZARD [/h1]

Resident Evil 7 was a much-needed return to form for the franchise. No more Michael Bay explosions, only straight-up classic survival horror at its finest. RE7 took the series in a new direction by introducing a first-person perspective for our new main protagonist, Ethan Winters, which I think is incredibly bold and necessary. Many old fans might be put off by the fact that they're not playing as one of the four classics: Jill, Chris, Leon, and Claire; But, I think it's time that we get some new blood into the family and start expanding the roster of main characters.

[u] What Resident Evil 7 got right [/u]

I was a bit concerned about how the first-person perspective might affect the game, considering I was so used to always playing in the third person. Still, I was reasonably happy to find that it greatly benefited the experience in profound ways. It increases the tensions in a much more natural way, unlike the fixed camera angles of old, which does nothing but to annoy the ever-living ♥♥♥♥ out of you; This, however, does an incredible job at immersing you in the world and make the game that much scarier to play.

The story is also another unexpected highlight of RE7 that I never thought I'd love so much. Seriously, the Baker family has to be one of the best villains to come out of Resident Evil in a long time. They are creepy as hell in all the best ways possible: Intimidating, unpredictable, exciting, psychopathic, and funny. Running away from them as they throw insults and taunt you is simply one of the best parts of the game; You do feel a sense of dread and unease every time you encounter them, and it's just as fun fighting them as it is running away from them. 

Here's a rapid list of things that I love about Resident Evil 7:

1. The atmosphere: Lighting, music, sound design, excellent graphic, and great acting all go into making this RE game one of the best in the franchise.

2. The gameplay loop of exploring, puzzle-solving, and combat made a triumphant return. Almost everything is well-paced together, making the overall experience very fun to play. 

3. Being able to go back in time by watching VHS tape and replaying the horror that went down in the Baker family ranch through the eyes of other victims was something I thought was very cool and creative. 

4. Level design has always been a high point for almost every Resident Evil game, and RE7 is no exception.

[u] Where Resident Evil 7 fell short [/u]

At some point in the game, it presents you with what seems like two critical choices that should have had real consequences by the end, depending on what you choose. Spoiler alert: They don't matter in any significant way. The gameplay and story are still 99% the same regardless of what choice you picked. So yeah, it's incredibly disappointing. 

The enemy design is boring. They're called the molded, and they're quite uninspiring. They all look relatively the same; They all behave relatively the same, and the way you deal with all of them is relatively the same: Go for the head. Despite having four enemy variations, they all feel the same. Resident Evil is known for its iconic monsters throughout its many games, but RE7 drew the short end of the stick.  

The final boss fight posed no challenge and too short. Overall, it was kind of disappointing. While it was fun to watch, I think a lot of people who played this game can look back and agree that the last boss can undoubtedly be improved upon to make the gameplay more engaging, challenging, and memorable. RE7 has some of the best boss fights in the franchise, and it makes this problem stand out like a sore thumb. 

When you get to a particular portion of the game much later in the story, it starts to slow down and drag the overall flow of the game. I won't spoil what it is, but you'll know what I'm talking about when you get there; I can guarantee you that. The only upside to this is it's also the part where much of the questions you've been having will finally get answered. 

There are a few inconsistencies in the story and the lore; It doesn't detract from it in any considerable way, but it deserves mention. These issues can quickly get addressed in the sequel should they ever want to continue the story. For that reason, I think the average player is going to have an easier time overlooking this problem. 

The lack of an option to skip cutscenes is also one that can be quite troublesome if you're the type of person that likes to replay Resident Evil games multiple times as I do. Sitting through the same scene over and over is a chore, and I don't understand why skipping it isn't an option.

The DLCs for the game is quite disappointing. From what I've seen from gameplay, the extra contents are not worth getting. Maybe wait until there's a discount.

[u] In conclusion [/u]

Resident Evil 7 is a freaking beast. Even if you haven't played any of the previous games in the franchise, nothing is stopping you from enjoying this one. This game rightfully deserves a spot in your library.

This game has a lot of good things running for it. I think this is the first horror game i've picked up in a long time that felt genuinely scary. You can tell the devs know how to do the horror genre justice instead of relying on cheap jump-scares and branding it a 'horror game'. RE7 absolutely nails the atmosphere from start to finish and does a great job of pacing itself the entire way.  The gameplay i had a lot of mixed feelings about. I really hated the fact the main character, Ethan, walks around like he has cement bricks tied to his ankles. [just a personal quirk but i feel like it really just makes the game slow to a crawl unnecessarily. I would've really preferred if the sprint option was an actual run opposed to a ''walk marginally faster'']. I think the game when played on normal has a bit of a tougher power spike at the beginning that just falls completely flat in the mid to endgame as more powerful weapons become available and the enemies themselves don't really change or become harder to accommodate that. A couple of the puzzle pieces felt not very obvious, but a quick google search can fix that but i felt it was worth mentioning. As for the story. I think this game tells a decent narrative. giving no spoilers i think it's an interesting time that'll hold your interest as you progress through it but I felt like there were a lot of times where the game does things and doesn't really explain them well because the devs couldn't think of a reasonable way to incorporate the story into the game itself. I had quite a few moments where the reasons for things happening simply made no sense at all which really turned me off of this game as a whole. What really holds this game back for me though is that a lot of the characters simply don't feel like that have enough depth to them. The characters themselves are very memorable, but I would've liked to see more interaction and story relating to the Jack,Marge or Zoe. Overall, I wouldn't say this was a *bad* game. I think overall it does a number of things well, but I personally didn't find a lot of the game to be enjoyable enough to really validate recommending it. Do I think the average person would like this? yeah, probably.  Do i think this is a game that you should absolutely pick up though? No. I think this game is a great demonstration of how to do horror in video games, but with the personal quirks with the gameplay, the loose ends in the story and the insufficient depth of certain core characters,  I can't recommend this game.

This time you're not an elite police officer mowing down hordes of zombies, just a normal dude looking for his wife in a creepy part of louisiana. They absolutely nailed the horror. I was shocked at how hard the game comes at you early, and even if it gives you tools as you progress, the atmosphere really belongs to the classic horror movie style, from the tapes you finf that you have to put in old school VHS machines to get the flashbacks, to the sound design and tropes that immerse you into the setting. 10/10 for me, ballsy changes like these  are more than welcome, it does breathe fresh air on the series.

It's intense, fun, and challenging. It feels like a more natural progression of the first game, than what ended up happening with RE4. There's a lot of moments where I'd be walking down a quite hallway, stop, turn around out of a gut feeling, and see something coming my way, only to panic and start running away as fast as I can. The atmosphere is really spooky. Eventually around halfway through the game you get use to it, but the first couple of hours, I was pretty on edge, wondering what was going to happen next. And one of my favorite things is that fights with enemies could take a completely different turn, depending on how things turn out. For instance, there's one fight early in the game with a set piece that as you try to interact with it, either you're successful, and can end the fight with it, or you're pulled away, only for the boss to take control, and turn things around in another direction.

However, I wish there was more RE1 elements. I guess they were going for a more realistic feel with the mansion this time, which does help to feel more immersive, but it's smaller than I anticipated. There are a few RE1-esc puzzles, but not as much as you'd expect. And I thought I'd spend more time sneaking around the house avoiding Jack as he patrols, but it's only for one segment. On Madhouse mode, it is done a little bit better. In fact, there was a lot of things I liked in Madhouse difficulty, a lot of things were changed. But everything was more balanced for Normal, and often times Madhouse felt frustratingly hard with out unlockables. Though, that could be just my fault, since I suck at any FPS that doesn't have you runing like a roided up Kenyan, and you have pinpoint accuracy at all times.

All in all, it's a fun horror experience that fans of Resident Evil, or new comers to the franchise would love.

Resident Evil 7 represents a crowning achievement in the modern AAA gaming sphere - a developer in charge of a much beloved franchise that was steadily declining in quality actually listening to the fans, revisiting what made the franchise so loved, and moving forward with that in mind.

If you're a fan of the survival horror genre or scary games as a whole, or someone (like myself) that poured most of their childhood into the Resident Evil series, this game is an incredible success. The combat is sparing and, while certainly not perfect, well-designed enough to be fluid. The bulk of the game is a focus on exploration, solving puzzles, and slowly unraveling the mystery while - you got it - surviving. The environments are beautiful and detailed, the pacing is excellent, 
and the overall tone is consistently eerie - the game does an excellent job keeping the player on edge. The story itself is compelling and relatively original, the writing is above average (though not exceptional), and the mediums the game uses for storytelling are unique and interesting. RE7 feels more like a Resident Evil game than anything released since RE4. While short and not as replayable as some of the other entries in the series, every minute is utilized to it's fullest, and I enjoyed them all immensely.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard. A game developed and published by CAPCOM.

Resident Evil has been a staple of the horror genre since we were graced with the release of the first back in 1996. Ever since then the series has exploded, Sequel games, Books and even a collection of movies to sum up a totality of lore and story that defines the genre. In my own opinion the series took a drastic decline with the release of 4, losing a lot of its horror and zombie themes for more of a genetic evolution stand point on the virus, The games became a lot more action based and less horror themed and overall became a more adaptive type of game for the general gamer. That is until now, Resident Evil is now scary again and i will explain why shortly.
I break my reviews down into 4 categories, Story, Gameplay, Graphics and Audio followed by an Overall section that summarises the game in totality. If you are against the idea of reading long reviews please feel free to scroll to the bottom.

Story:
Resident Evil began its genre following a very systematic outbreak of a virus that causes the dead to reanimate. Ever since that fateful day in 1996 when the first game was released, the series has become more and more of a cinematic experience rather than that of a horror game. That's not to say these games aren't scary or at least intense in their play but they don't share the same feel as the original. Resident Evil 7 aims to change that, Bringing you back to an "abandoned" house in search of your wife "Mia" who has apparently been taken to an old house atop a Bayou in Louisiana. From there you begin the game, and start to see how deep you really are. You eventually meet the Bakers, the protagonist family that systematically begin to ruin you day from start to finish of the game. The story unfolds and you begin to understand the concept and reasoning behind everything that is happening and has happened including some rather spine tingling twists and intriguing plot points that help push you through the story and keep it interesting.

Gameplay:
This is a weird one because it does everything really well, in a very nostalgic Resident Evil kind of way, but doesn't really revolutionise anything. Nothing will suprise you, and nothing will really be the next big "Every horror game needs that!".
The game feels very much like Outlast right off the bat, you are a relatively normal person, coming to unknown territory, unarmed against an unknown enemy. You spend the first portion of the game really just running, hiding and crawling your way through the Baker house until you ultimately are gifted with your first weapon, A pocket knife. Not a lot but when you are panicking and hiding, any weapon is a good weapon. The hiding mechanic is almost non existent here, although the house is quite dark, you more have to stay out of an enemies Line of Sight to avoid detection, This can take some getting used to especially if you are used to the hiding mechanic of Outlast and Alien Isolation (A little different i know but has quite an interesting hiding mechanic). Unfortunately a vast majority of the enemies in this game can't actually open doors and don't move very fast making avoiding them or just running past and closing a door your best way of taking care of them. A bit sad because i think the idea of being pursued a great motivator for horror games. The "I'm never safe" mentality is a good motivator to keep moving.
The gun play here is phenomenal, I don't recollect every shooting at an enemy and wondering if i did anything. The damage is evident as you begin to unload lead, whether it leaves visual bullet holes or completely removes limbs you are feeling that every bullet makes a difference. 
There are no maps straight off the bat here, you need to find them scattered around the house and property. I think this greatly takes away from the games atmosphere but offers a lot of accessibility to a vast majority of gamer types. You could just avoid using it and have a more authentic horror and "lost" experience.
The boss fights, a tricky one because like i already mentioned the game doesn't really reinvent anything here. The bigger bosses here are fairly generic, big eyes or evident "critical hit" spots. Although the earlier boss fights offer an element of suprise to the game which you don't often see, you will find that they aren't just bullet sponge fights, but really require you to think outside the box.
Lastly, I think the game does extremely well, being a horror game you need a place of respite. A room where you can manage your inventory, save and just take a breather before setting off into the world again. RE7 does a great job of this, not overly saturating the game with safe zones but adequately enough to offer you a safe haven amidst the darkness.

Graphics:
Resident Evil 7. having been released in 2017 is fairly far from cutting edge by any stretch of the imagination. It does however offer a beautifully horrific experience the entire way through, A mark of the attention to detail the developers have implemented here. The game ran impeccably smooth on my mid to high range PC sitting comfortable above the 60 FPS range on Ultra settings. Quick loading and saving transitions as well help compliment the experience here allowing you to hit the action relatively quickly.

Audio: 
I found that most horror games do an excellent job on the audio, RE7 is no exception. It brilliantly orchestrates emotion and intensity throughout the game by just subtly integrating music into the scene or by just offering the ominous silence that follows most scares. The house creaks and shudders, windows rattle and water puddles splash as you and enemies walk through them. This provides a very realistic atmosphere and demonstrates another amazing attention to detail. Especially in the earlier parts of the game where you have no weapons and are basically hiding to survive, your ability to hear your enemies is your only tool. Brilliant effort here and a sensational audio experience.

Overall:
Although Resident Evil 7 is a fairly late game of a mostly dying genre/series and doesn't really offer much in terms of new sensations, It brings back an extremely satisfying nostalgic feel, while also entirely making you uncomfortable the entire way through not just through its horror theme. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, it more offers you a different style of it. Bringing you to terms with horror in a very real way, but in the same time offering you a gratifying combat system with enemies and antagonists that are very down to earth and that give you a sense of being completely screwed for the entire play through. Nothing new here which is unfortunate, but what is here is ultimately captivating and worth a play for any fan of the horror genre even if Resident Evil isn't your thing anymore.

After the train wreck that was Resident Evil 6, Capcom needed to bring their A game. After playing through, I can without a doubt say they did, and this definitely feels like a return to form. A true modernized take on the classic Resident Evil gameplay, with actual human characters as opposed to lantern jaw super human reflexes beefcakes or female special ops forces with not a hint of muscle definition.

At least for a large portion of the game…You play as Ethan Winters, who is looking for his loving wife after she was missing for a few years due to an accident that occurred at her work. You go looking through rural Louisiana where her boat has seemed to crash. You begin searching through some houses that were situated in the area and meet up with your wife…and a few dead bodies along the wife. Instead of a loving embrace and getting the heck out of dodge, your wife seems to have other plans...
After losing contact with your wife, you are now trapped in the home of the Baker family, a family of crazed, super powered republicans who just want to live as a “Normal family”. Ethan has to find a way out of this madhouse, along with finding “what” has happened with his wife…and what other “evil” that lurk in the background.

Gameplay is solid. A modernized take on the classic RE gameplay. As opposed to a third person view, you take a first person view which I always tend to prefer especially for horror games. Over the course of the game you find a host of weapons and items to defend yourself as the game starts as a Survival horror game like Outlast and ends more in line with action survivor horror like the latter RE titles. Puzzles are also present, though nothing too obtuse like in the classic games. The game is balanced properly, controls very well, and the spirit of the older games are represented very well with none of the drawbacks of the era, such as the convoluted and childish writing and voice acting, and confusing nonsensical puzzles. 
I am trying to keep this review as spoiler free as possible (My slight synopsis earlier in the review is literally the first 30 minutes or so.), so in terms of criticisms I should say that the game doesn’t have much enemy variety, however the creativity of the Baker family boss fights makes up for it. It also doesn’t overstay it’s welcome as it is a medium length (About 6-10 hours). The only part of the game I felt was a little bit padded was the “Ship” section (Which is an opinion I have found is shared by many).

But all in all, a solid game that worthy of your time, and I am sure I will replay in the future. The BEST DLC, Not a Hero, deals with the aftermath of the story and is especially in the vein of the newer RE games (though I found it enjoyable) and stars a quite prominent figure in RE canon is also really good. The rest of the DLCs I found to not be worth it (outside of End of Zoe, but that’s like an hour so your time is better spent watching it on YouTube).

- - - DTR review RE7 - - -

*Spoiler warning!
The video and review contain spoilers, if possible play the game blind first.

For those who have played the game already and want something cool to watch as a reminder of why this game is loved by so many people or those who just want to see why i love this game without having to read the review then click the video below:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YE2Pkh0bsKI

Personally i have never enjoyed horror games but RE7 is rather special and certainly stands out from other horror games and other RE titles.
You don't have cheap jump scares and the quality of the writing and characters is truly outstanding, the Bakers who by the end you really sympathise with even after the many brutal fights with them, Eveline as an entity is honestly scary what with the fear many people have of losing control of their brain being the main fear factor behind her, and by the end you grow to really hate Eveline due to her taking over what were kind loving people and turning them into absolute blood thirsty monsters.

The best part of the game for me was the feeling of terror whilst sneaking around the Baker's home constantly worrying about bumping into one of the residents along with the hallucinations and mental mind games played on you by Eveline later in the game, note i would have loved the game to focus more on the Eveline mind play aspect within the house itself rather than moving later levels to the ship which pulled me away from the intense horror setting of the house, i find it more appealing to revolve the game around a home which many great horror movies tend to do as the scary feeling of walking in your own home after playing and checking the stairs and shadows for Eveline or the Bakers leaps from what was confined to the game, now follows the player into reality which i have never had from any horror game, only the best horror movies have succeeded in doing this, RE7 has managed this but if the later levels were in the house with more mind games it really could have maximised the scary factor.

Overall RE7 has no real replay value but the quality of the characters and the experiences i had in the Bakers home will stay with me for the rest of my life, as a game it really is special, yes it is not perfect as it diverts from the core and turns into a shooter game in later chapters which personally i found way less enjoyable than the early chapters, the moulded are probably the most boring characterless enemies i have fought in any game for a long time, yes i am aware the shooty aspect is down to RE's heritage but i am not a RE fan or a shooter genre fan, story for me is more important.

DLC note: The Zoe aspect of the story really should have been in the main game, it would have made the decision of who you save much harder and would have filled in the gaps in the main game, it really feels as if it was cut from the game to be sold as DLC. Naughty Capcom, very naughty.

Closing thoughts...
Please make more games like this, i think this genre has so much room for more experiences such as RE7, the horror game genre is filled with cookie cutter cheaply made throw away jump scare zombie games and RE7 has showed us a well crafted story, characters and setting can make for a truly memorable and frightening experience.

8.5/10 Points off for DLC naughtyness and wondering from the house setting in later chapters.

What was once the game that inspired a whole genre, now itself is getting inspiration from the latest (back then) craze of 1st person horror games and perhaps a reaction from the controversial cancellation of Silent Hills. But does that mean that RE is a copycat shadow of said games, a mere walking jumpscare simulator or is it a succesful re-invention and a much needed rejuvenative injection (of the T-Virus!?) to a derailed franchise?

Gamplay-wise I was very surprised to discover that despite the camera switch from third to first person, RE7 is still the classic survival game you know and love from the era of the PS1 classics. You have the map with the interconnected rooms in a maze-like mansion. Item & inventory management. [spoiler]all the classic weapons, from the humble knife to the all powerful magnum and grenade launcher [/spoiler]   The need to look for special keys to open new areas. Solving puzzles, combine items and herbs. And hearing the calm music, reaffirming that you reached a safe room. It's quite an amazing feat and in all honesty, the whole structure of this game and it's pacing is eerily similar to that of the very first Resident Evil from 1996, but from a certain point of view "soft-rebooted" for a modern audience. 
This means of course a few quality of life, modern improvements, like modern smooth controls and being able to save unlimited times and using a very generous amount of auto-checkpoints. But if hearing this makes your survival horror soul scream in disappointment don't be afraid! By finishing the game once, you unlock the Madhouse difficulty which sees the return of even more staples of the genre, the need to use a limited number tapes to save at specific points and many other surprises that make the game more intense on second playthrough, by subverting the expectations of the players already familiar with the main campaign.
(thus the need to play this after the default normal playthrough - think of it like the Arrange mode in RE1-Director's Cut!)

It is important to note that the change of camera view makes the game also feel more tense as it forces the player to be even more aware of his surroundings, searching every nook and cranny. Make sure to check out drawers, ceilings, dark corners while ducking. It will make the difference between survival or death, in your constant search for health and ammunition.

The overall presenation also deserves high praise. The atmosphere of the game is unparalleled in its delivery of isolation and dread. The first hour of the game was one of themost gut-wrenching moments I had in recent gaming. Walking around the dilapidated Baker house, searching through dark corridors and hearing all kinds of creaks on the wooden floor, not knowing if it's just you, the wind, or your pursuer closing by trying to kill you (or worse) makes for a terrifying experience. [spoiler] The Baker family also makes for some of the most intense and imaginative boss encounters in the entire series offering plenty of intense head-to-head battles, always bringing something new, from simply a stealth survival chase of cat and mouse, to a full blown chaisaw duel or worse! [/spoiler]
The story of the game is also one of the most interesting and well presented in the franchise, with a wonderful cast of heroes and villains, with some of the best voice acting it has offered so far and being not only a tribute to the classic RE series (especially the first game) but also a love letter to fans of horror in general, with countless nods and references to tropes and horror films of the past. 
Although, truth be told, the last part of the story is perhaps a little weak compared to the rest, losing some of its charm, but still enjoyable.

Special mention has to be madefor the DLC especially the FREE DLC "Not a Hero" that I absolutely recommend trying out after finishing the main campaign. For a free dlc, the quality is quite high, offering roughly 2 hours of gameplay and expanding some of the story threads of the main game and perhaps correcting a couple of "mistakes" some fans had with the last part of the story.

The RE ENGINE used to create this game is wonderful and I think the technology used to create the models of the characters is very nice. Featuring a crazed hillbilly family was definitely a good way to showcase the strengths of this technology, showing some very detailed and almost life-like expessions adding a sense of realism that immerses the player more into the horror that happens around him.
It also seems to run pretty well on the PC and offering plenty of graphical options to tinker with. Unfortunately I noticed a small problem with my humble PC, apparently a memory leak problem (?) causing some freezing and framedropping every time I entered a new area and slowly dropping performance. Thankfully it was solved by simply reducing the texture quality to Medium settings, without losing any significant graphical fidelity or detail. I was quite impressed by how well the game not only runs but how it looks on a slightly weaker machine as mine, with most of the settings still set to the Higher end. 

During this time, Capcom has been experiencing a renaissance in the horror/RE franchise, releasing the highly succesful RE2. One now has to wonder how this will affect the future of the franchise, but it will be very interested to see what path will the next installment (if or when it happens) will take.

[h1][i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a western approach to the series, and a really welcome one[/h1]

For years since [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] revolutionized the third person shooters, the franchise stalled into the genre with [i]Resident Evil 5-6[/i]'s cheap structure of action movies, focusing on online multiplayer design features – completely forgetting about the good mix of the action/horror presented in the earlier singleplayer games.
[i]Resident Evil 7[/i], on the other hand, feels almost like a reboot: first person perspective, singleplayer only, no known characters from the series, not a single mention of the ABCXWhatever-Virus, Umbrella or affiliates... it seems like a generic horror game at first, but then you start playing more and more, always with tense muscles and dilated pupils: the atmosphere is incredible, the pacing is perfect, and every single enemy encounter is meaningful and horrifying. It will feel familiar at times so, somehow, it all works inside the [i]RE[/i]'s universe. A [b]horror[/b] game, after a decade of cheesy non-stop action. 
The gameplay, combined with the creepy visuals/audio design and good crafted storytelling – not the [i]forte[/i] of the franchise until then – makes this odd and surprising western design approach to [i]RE[/i] probably the best game, quality wise, ever presented by [i]CAPCOM[/i].

Now, the game does fit into the survival horror genera and they include some game mechanics that make it partially control as a Resident Evil Remake “like” game, but it is truly has much more in common with Silent Hill, but with me, I still somehow prefer an actual Silent Hill game. 

The game starts off by completely cutting and pasting the classic Silent Hill plot point with the main character that you play as driving off into the middle of nowhere to find his missing wife and putting himself into perilous danger...  It's opening feels very much Silent Hilly and like one of the older Silent Hill titles and the infamously canceled Silent Hills (P.T) this game is only in the First Person perspective and really feels (screams) like it was heavily influenced by that canceled Konami Silent Hills P.T. demo.  Now prior to this title, all previous numbered titles in the Resident Evil series, had all been in the Third Person and all have a different feel from this, as they had all before at least in some form or other had continued to add onto what had come before it (with it's previous numbered titles, continuing with characters that where introduced and the series lore).  More over all titles had multiple methods/modes to bring in replayability, with the later titles also adding multiplayer as an option, but one could still play through everything by ones self. 

Resident Evil 7 ignores all of that, and instead it focuses on it's new character and it's new world that despite taking place after the events of Resident Evil 6, ultimately has nothing to with the Resident Evil series (outside of a later tacked on inclusion of one of the character from the past games, who even then, you need to be told who it is as the character actually bears no actual likeness to said character, nor sounds like… trying to keep this spoiler free). The game is also much smaller in scope then previous titles (also less of a story) and after a bit, it begins feels repetitive as you keep having to fend from the same threats over and over… the opening of the game is the exception to this as this feels very solid and well thought out and I think ultimately this game was really meant to primarily be a VR experience, but sadly, this was something that was only available (and still in 2019) only available to people who play the game on a Playstation 4 console and with the optional VR accessories...


     Lastly, besides this game being much smaller in scope, it has zero replay value, unlike all prior Resident Evil titles before it.  As a direct result of these changes made to this series, this was the first time I opted out of getting the additional dlc content for a Resident Evil and the first time I found myself not wanting to revisit it for a second, third, forth or fifth time.

   Final caveat, If you want to play another Survival Horror title, and or you can separate this from the Resident Evil series if you are familiar with it, I could recommend it…  and if they ever implement VR for the PC, that recommendation would be even stronger… It is a shame that they never had the option to add that back into the PC version; it would instantly make this title a contender for one of the best VR experiences.

[h1]Welcome to the Baker Family[/h1]

[i]Fear and isolation seep through the walls of an abandoned southern farmhouse. "7" marks a new beginning for survival horror with the “Isolated View” of the visceral new first-person perspective.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Resident Evil 7 follows Ethan Winters as he searches for his missing wife, Mia, at a derelict plantation in Louisiana. He finds her held by the mutated and violent Baker family, who are infected by a fungal bioweapon called the Mold. Ethan fights to survive, uncover the Bakers’ dark secrets, and escape, while discovering that a shadowy organization is behind the creation of these bio-organic weapons.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a first-person survival horror game. It’s the second game in the series and the first main line game to use such a perspective. Your arsenal ranges from melee weapons like knives and chainsaws, to stronger firearms such as handguns, shotguns, and a makeshift flamethrower.

You start with eight inventory slots, plus four quick-access slots (tied to the D-pad for controller) for weapon assignment, but can expand your inventory by finding backpacks. Safe rooms scattered throughout the game serve as enemy-free zones containing item boxes for storage and tape recorders for saving progress.

Items in your inventory can be examined to reveal hidden details, discarded, or combined to craft useful supplies like first aid solution, ammo, or psychostimulants, which temporarily highlight nearby collectible items. You also have a flashlight, but it automatically turns on and off when in darker areas.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The most common enemies you’ll encounter are the Molded—grotesque, humanoid creatures that relentlessly close the distance to attack. Firearms feel noticeably weaker compared to the more action-focused entries in the series, making combat more tense and deliberate. These enemies are tougher, capable of sidestepping and blocking attacks, and they rarely stay down for long. This encourages you to rely on stealth, evasion, or quick escapes rather than direct confrontation.

Throughout the game, you’ll also face various members of the Baker family. Initially, they act as roaming pursuers, creating constant tension as you try to avoid them. Eventually, each family member becomes the focus of a larger boss encounter, where success depends on carefully targeting their weak points while dodging or guarding against their attacks.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The environment is mostly linear but cleverly interconnected, with locked doors and paths that can be opened later by finding key items. Locations include the guest house, Baker residence, greenhouse, wrecked ship, swamp, and more. Maps can be found for each area to help with navigation by marking locked doors and item boxes.

Exploration plays a major role, as solving puzzles opens new routes, reveals key items, and advances the story—some requiring specific tools to complete. VHS tapes found around the estate let you play short segments as other characters, offering story insights and puzzle hints, similar to the “Zapping System” from Resident Evil 2. You can also search your surroundings for useful items like weapons, ammo, and healing supplies.

The atmosphere is eerie and the horror comes from dark areas with dim lighting and stressful encounters with intimidating enemies. The first encounter with the Molded emerging from the wall was unexpected and beautifully made. It really made me think “Oh, wtf is that?!” Marguerite in the greenhouse is especially unsettling and memorable. The derelict ship towards the end is darker, but not as scary, completely infested by the molded.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The Baker family is filthy, insane, and disturbingly human in their madness. Their old Louisiana home shows the same decay—dirty, falling apart, and filled with rotting food, human remains, and stacks of unwashed dishes. Some rooms are covered in a thick black slime left behind by the Molded, terrifying creatures made of fungus and tar-like goo. These monsters have long claws and sharp teeth, and every time you shoot them, blood and pus spray out.

Your health and damage are shown both on-screen and in the game itself. The screen gets covered in more blood as you’re hurt, and you can check a wrist device in your inventory to see how badly you’re injured.

Sound plays a huge part in the tension—especially when you’re inside the old house and Marguerite is stalking you. You can hear her footsteps, her muttering, and her unstable voice echoing through the halls, keeping you constantly tense. The Bakers’ twisted behavior and disturbing personalities perfectly show how sick they’ve become—both in body and mind.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
I wish the game had more map features—like marking items you couldn’t pick up, so you could return for them later.

It would also be nice to get a notification when certain items, like keys that have already unlocked all their doors, are no longer needed and can be safely discarded.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Overall, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is one of my favorite survival horror games and stands out as one of the best entries in the series. The weapons feel great to use—every shot has weight, thanks to the powerful sound effects and sharp feedback. The visuals make combat even more satisfying, especially when you land a clean headshot on a Molded, with all the gruesome detail and realistic gore that adds to the horror atmosphere.

The story is one of the best in the series, with memorable characters and a tense, creepy vibe that keeps you hooked from start to finish. The boss fights are exciting and well-designed, with the battle against Marguerite being a standout moment. Her sudden appearances and unpredictable movements around the greenhouse—especially when she peeks down a hole in the ceiling—make for one of the scariest moments in the game.

Although the horror reaches its peak around the middle of the story, it still stays scary—just a bit more focused on action afterward. The pacing never slows down, keeping the tension and excitement strong right up to the end.

There’s a staggering irony to [i]Resident Evil 7: biohazard[/i]. Despite being arguably the least original mainline entry in its often-ground-breaking series, it may actually be the best of the bunch. It’s all about revival rather than reinvention (to a much deeper level than just reverting the genre), but it does so with significant modernization that makes it compulsively playable while reintroducing horror more intensely than ever. The first-person perspective immediately makes it the best-controlled [i]Resident Evil[/i] in existence, and outsourcing the narrative to western writers drains away its usual uncomfortable campiness. The plot is unfortunately full of holes and incomplete threads, which certainly puts a damper on things, but it’s also presented in a variety of clever ways that make it worthwhile.

With the series’ two most common issues ironed out, the game can now focus on what it does best: level design and scaring the ♥♥♥♥ out of me. The former is like playing [i]Gone Home[/i] with traditional gameplay instead of the genre bait-and-switch – a compact but thoroughly detailed environment that greatly assists with narrative immersion. As for the latter, [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] excels at predicting player behaviour, so its jump scares are woven organically and unexpectedly into the gameplay. The audio design also ratchets up the paranoia by always giving a sense that there’s [i]something else[/i] nearby even when you’re alone. The voice acting and writing are still fairly mediocre, however.

Quick Description:
-Resident Evil 7 is a departure from the action focused formula of RE 5 and 6.  It's arguably the creepiest and most intense Resident Evil ever made.  I really enjoyed my first 5-6 hrs exploring a vile and disgusting Bakers house, trying my best to survive.  Unfortunately, the next 10+ hrs of the game offer extremely dull, repetitive gameplay and nonsensical storytelling that ruins what could have been one of the best entries in the RE series.

What's Good:
-I think that the change to a first person perspective and a focus on methodical, intense moment to moment gameplay was a great choice.  The best moments in this series created a balanced blend of scares, action combat, progression, and inventory management.  The early stages of this game do a great job at bringing the game back to it's roots.  These fundamental core changes were a step in the right direction imo.
-Visually, Resident Evil has never looked better.  I personally prefer a first person camera angle regardless of whether the game is action focused, horror focused, or a blend of both.  The setting of the Bakers dilapidated house creates a very suspenseful, intense atmosphere.  It's especially terrifying to slowly go down to the basement and see what awaits in the dark.  Shooting animations and the blood splattering upon impact have never looked better in the series.
-Some of the boss battles are really fun and intense, even if they aren't the most challenging ever.  Facing off against a Leatherfacelike creature is badass and scary as hell.  I wish that the boss battles were a bit more varied, but they are fun and work well enough.
-Inventory management, progression, and combining items has been brought back.  This was less of a focus in RE 5 and 6.  These are core mechanics of the series, but also fit the combat horror genre really well.  

Could Use Some Changes:
-Resident Evil has always had an issue w/ pacing.  Almost every game imo, starts off really strong and struggles to carry that momentum to the finish line.  However, RE 7 stumbles greatly in the later stages of the game.  The weird Sawlike components of the mid game, to the annoying spiders, to the incredibly dull and boring ship final stage all combine to ruin a game that I had such high hopes for.  
-There are far too many tedious scripted moments in this game.  I figured out really early that there was no point in wasting bullets on certain enemies that could never die.  You could eventually get them to leave the screen for a while, but it was a massive waste of ammo b/c you could just run away instead and it would do the same thing.  This is a massive issue w/ some of the bosses.  For every one really fun boss, there is another boss that is close to nothing but scripted moments.  
-There just isn't nearly enough diversity in enemy types of attack patterns.  There are way too many variations of the weird black mudlike creatures that slowly walk towards you.  It's strange that these creatures are a part of early game, mid game, and even late game.  
-There are basically no puzzles, the game is exceptionally linear, and the game holds your hand most of the way through.  Nothing is all that challenging especially once you get past the few first hrs.  

Thoughts:
-Resident Evil 1-4 were some of my fav games growing up.  I have a special place in my heart for 1 and 2 especially bc they scared the ♥♥♥♥ out of me and they were so fun.  I also really loved the Resident Evil 2 remake.  Unfortunately, I can't recommend RE 7 to anyone b/c I just didn't find it very fun.

Consensus:
-Bottom Shelf Gaming (Tier 5 and makes up 10% of my reviews).  I'd recommend the Resident Evil 2 remake or Darkwood over this in a heartbeat.  Those are both great games.  Although this game took some steps in the right direction, it also took several steps backwards.  If you absolutely love this series, then you probably owe it to yourself to try it, but moderate your expectations.  I was really disappointed.

One of the best Resident Evil games to date.

Despite taking place in the first person perspective, it manages to retain the horror and difficulty from the earlier third-person fixed-camera games prior to Resident Evil 4, and never turns into a glorified shooter like Resident Evil 6.

Speaking of the shooting, it's much more methodical as you can't rapidly fire without losing significant accuracy.
Movement is sort-of tank control, which older survival horror fans will be at home with.
The enemies are pretty spooky. Although the enemy variety is lacking in comparison to older titles, the enemy placement is  on point, and prove a challenge in the game's more claustrophobic areas. The bosses are also creepy, and manage to put up a great challenge.
The story, while all right for a Resident Evil game, has plenty of idiot-ball moments from both the protagonist and the characters he comes across. [spoiler] The deputy is possibly the biggest violator here, not only story-wise, but police conduct-wise. How this guy managed to get into the position of deputy without getting shot and killed on the job is a mystery in of itself. [/spoiler] 
There's plenty of collectibles to find in the game, such as coins that you can redeem for power ups and unlockable weapons. These are almost necessary as the bosses will dunk on you if you haven't bothered to do so.

Overall, a pretty good survival horror game that I've spent countless hours in, beating its hard as nails Madhouse Difficulty and generally speedrunning it.

[h1]P R O S :[/h1]

- RE7 Satisfies your thrill-seeking appetite with gradual exploration through a mysterious Louisiana mansion.  Excellent story and dead on pacing.  If you enjoyed the Outlast games, even Alien Isolation, you'll love this one.

- One of the most intriguing hooks to a game, it reels you in within the first 30 mins of gameplay and then you have the urge to discover the mysteries at hand.

- The actual game design of delving into the mansion and progressively unlocking new areas on the map feels very Resident Evil.


- The visuals are absolutely stunning, it feels as if you are in an epic horror movie.  The use of photogrammetry and lighting gives this game a polished, cinematic level of quality.


- The soundtrack, especially towards the end of the story gets you pumped up to win which is pretty satisfying.  The new saferoom theme is perfectly serene and geographically appropriate, a subtle touch but it shows the attention to detail these developers have for this universe.

- The characters were memorable and each uniquely different from one another.  They each even had humorous moments at times which made them that much more captivating and creepy at the same time.  Excellent voice acting, I can still hear Jack Baker's voice in my mind: [i] "Ethan, Ethan, Eeeethan!" [/i]



[h1]C O N S :[/h1]

- I didn't feel a major need to use the hand-block feature for a good majority of the game.  It still looked really awesome.

- The inventory click & drag system operated somewhat finicky at times dragging an item to an unintended slot, however just a nitpick.

Although, this game does not rely on the tropes of modern horror games and balances its fear and anxiety inducing adventure and puzzle gameplay with exhilerating and adrenaline fueled boss fights. The gunplay of the games is non inherently unique but well executed leading to your character not feeling too powerful, yet somewhat capable of defending himself, cleverly used during boss fights as well. The story of the game is well done for a horror game, yet does leave some room for improvement. However, the story does still hold its own very well.

All in all, Resident Evil 7 is a game any fan of horror games should definitely buy at its current price.

Resident Evil 7 gets off to a great, if hackneyed start, piling on atmosphere, gruesome details and a sense of vulnerability that unfortunately starts to give way once the combat becomes established, weapons and ammunition become increasingly plentiful (comically so in the third act, with the addition of a rapid fire weapon with hundreds of rounds just lying around). The game's strengths, if not in it's unremarkable writing (so far, so Resident Evil, in that regard) are in the sparsity but intensity of the encounters in the first half of the game, largely revolving around a few distinct characters (or at least two of them - with a tanker-ship sized plot hole simply leaving one antagonist floating somewhere in the ether, never to be discussed ever again). The relatively small variety of creatures to deal with, all of which are less than challenging to dispatch, are also fairly similar, and familiar, and after the initial shock encounters lead into repetitive headshot after headshot, the tension dissipates rapidly. Boss encounters are also a mixed bag, the first two being staggered and increasingly weird affairs, eventually becoming trad-Resident Evil Giant Monster Eye Target Practice. It's so badly in contrast with the claustrophobic, minimalist approach at the beginning of the game that it yanks you out of the experience. 

All this being said, though, I had fun, even if it wasn't as consistently thrilling and genuinely uncomfortable as Alien: Isolation. The first half of the game plays brilliantly, full of tension and every corner of the Baker residence is a curiosity, lovingly rendered in explicit, grimy, mouldy detail. The environmental design throughout is exceptional, bar for the closing chapters which revolve around bland metal corridors and caves. If this wasn't a Resident Evil franchise entry, however, I suspect the developers could have gone in more interesting directions, instead of falling back upon overly familiar tropes as fan service.

For the past 20 or so years I've been more or less indifferent in regards to Resident Evil as a game series. I've clocked in some play time over the years, but the overarching story lines and plot have never awoken my interest. That said, I'm very glad I decided to give RE7 a try and am happy to say it has awoken my interest in the series and I will be making at least some selective backtracking through the previous entries in the series.

RE7 is superb first-person survival-horror. Think along the lines of Outlast, but with guns (no it doesn't ruin the premise, I swear it won't), puzzles and weird bio-weapons experiments with a supernatural twist. The atmosphere is very immersive, the characters and antagonists are interesting, the story keeps on moving and there's a lot of replay value thanks to collectibles, new difficulty modes and a ton of DLC for those who get absolutely hooked on this game. The soundscape of the game really warrants the usage of hi-fi headsets and if you can stomach it, the game hits its stride in VR without a doubt. There are not all that many jumpscares and most of the horror in this title comes from the settings, atmosphere and various sounds and the soundtrack that keep you company throughout your playthrough.  

The puzzles aren't too hard and although the game does have you backtrack through a lot of areas, there are usually a ton of dynamic events, story progression and objectives to keep you busy enough to a point where it won't bother you. Even if you have to backtrack a bit, you are usually discovering new areas and items as well as mission objectives within those previously passed through areas. 

[b][u]I can easily recommend this game[/u] [/b] for any fan of horror games and the survival horror genre as well as those who might've been turned off of Resident Evil as a series by the content of their more "action-oriented releases" in the series. This is survival-horror in almost its purest form and a great return to the roots of the series. Totally worth checking out if you have even an inkling of a thought that this kind of game might be right up your alley.

In RE7 you're playing ( mostly ) as Ethan, an asthmatic guy with a peg leg who can't run to save his life. The beginning of the game is quite good, the atmosphere is awesome, the sound design too, and there are a few jump scares but I think they're used well and not overdone. There is a good balance between calm but stressful exploration, and combat/avoiding enemies, until they throw everything out the window in the last part.

Graphically however the game is clearly lacking, maybe due to the new engine, which clearly was improved for the RE2 remake. Even on the highest settings the textures look like PS3-era at best ( and Mia's hair is terrible, which constrasts a lot with the "realistic" photo-scanned character models... ), sometimes they are so low-res I don't even know what they're supposed to represent, it's just blurry pixels. And don't tell me it's because of the console port, a lot of console games look better than that. It's even worse here because RE7 is mainly made of small rooms and corridors, they should have been able to pack it with details since it's really not heavy to render ( look at Alien Isolation for a good exemple ), but nope. It almost feels like the game was supposed to use a far away 3rd person camera like the old REs, but then they switched to a first person perspective and now you have your nose right on those ugly textures.

On top of that the game manages to drop to 40-50 fps here and there depending on where you look at, but it's not constant so it's not that bad.

Anyway, the game is good and the story intriguing for the most part. It's divided in 3 parts, and unfortunately the quality varies a lot :
- the Baker's house/farm is the longest and most interesting
- then there is the boat, where you play as Mia and learn how she's involved in all of this and where the contamination came from
- and the last part is the salt mine, with a really small lab ( because having a lab in a RE game is mandatory ) inside and then you go back to the farmland for the final boss.

The last part is really disappointing and the game just falls appart here. The salt mine is a grey corridor with no exploration where the game just throws enemies at you, and they often spawn and depsawn right in front of you, or in your back. It feels like they ran out of time and money.

In the middle of this mine you find some kind of lab with two documents explaining the whole plot in a few lines ( again this feels rushed ) and then you exit the mine and you're back to where you've begun, with flashback hallucinations and you finally fight the boss, which is, without spoiling, one of the worst boss I've seen in any video game, ever.

Speaking about bosses, they're probably one of the worst part of the game. Early on you never know if you have to fight, run, hide, or if it's scripted to make you "lose" just to activate a cinematic making the story progress further. It's incredibly frustrating to waste ammo on bosses without knowing if they actually take damage or if they're invulnerable until a script activates to give you a solution about how to beat it, and even then you can be hitting the boss over and over without knowing if it actually does something.

There are also passages where you can't fight them and have to hide, but when you do so THEY DON'T GO AWAY and will patrol the same tiny area until you finally reach a scripted point and then they disappear.

During the last boss you can't even move, the boss grabs you and throws you around and all you can do is shoot, again with no feedback showing that the boss actually takes damage, until a special weapon ( not a rocket launcher, but again they tried to imitate the old REs ) drops from an helicopter and you can use it to kill the boss.

And then the game kinda ends on a cliffhanger with Chris Redfield ( whom doesn't look at all like Chris, just a random dude in combat gear ) rescuing you in a frigging UMBRELLA HELICOPTER, which is just a bait for the DLCs.

Ooooh the DLCs, let's talk about them, shall we ? The paid DLCs are mostly mini-games, a really short story ( 10-15 minutes ) about how the Bakers turned into monsters, a puzzle game where you try to escape a room ( couldn't finish it due to a bug ), and The End of Zoe, a joke DLC where you play as Uncle Joe going full Russel Crowe in South Park and killing monster WITH HIS FISTS, which could really be just a reference to Chris punching a boulder in RE5. It's fun but feels out of place, and I was ROFLing all the time especially when I found the super punch gauntlet and when Joe just goes German Supplex on the boss.

The last DLC is free ( Not a Hero ) and, for some reason, the longest and most "interesting" of the lot. Why did they choose to make you pay for the ♥♥♥♥ ones and give the good one for free is a mystery, but hey that's Capcom. If you wondered why Chris is working for Umbrella, you get the answer righ off the bat when reading a document that Chris carries : Umbrella wants to make amends for the ♥♥♥♥ they've done in the past and they've hired the BSAA ( Bull S hit Anti Aliasing I guess ) to fight bio-terrorism. So you play as Chris and have to capture Lucas, last member of the Baker family still alive ( except for Zoe ), in the most boring area of the main game : THE SALT MINE. Yup, we definitely needed more of that. Pointless to mention that it's mostly a shooting gallery focusing on action and it feels more like RE5 or 6 than anything else.

Firstly, this game in VR would be down-right frightening; I'm quite sad I don't own a VR headset--but it's probably for the best (and my sanity). Secondly, I bought this game a year ago, played it, become frightened instantly (I'm a scaredy-cat), and only just returned to it. I'm glad I did as this is a quality game. 

Resident Evil 7 comes packed with the usual design choices of the earlier Resident Evil games: intentionally clunky controls to remove a sense of power from the gamer, zombie-like monsters (technically Bio Organic Weapons (BOWs)), death-by-inventory-management item management, and Metroidvania-style puzzles; however--as you most likely already know--its camera swapped from third-person to first-person. And let me tell you hwhat (queue Hank Hill)... it's quite immersive. Paired with an audio engine that knows how to make you double guess sounds and their direction, it's quite an experience. I legitimately found myself shaking my mouse frantically from left-to-right while backed into a corner--certain zombies were closing in on me. Please play this game solo, with the lights turned off, and with a headset.

All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Resident Evil 7. After you complete the campaign, you should play the free Not a Hero DLC. You'll gain a glimpse of what the future of the Resident Evil series may bring. Afterward, if you find yourself wanting more, consider buying the Season Pass as it offers ~10 new mini-content (5 of which are worthwhile, in my opinion).

Three words to describe this game: back to basics.

I didn't think the series could be salvaged after the messy RE5 and the farce that is RE6, but thankfully this game got the RE franchise turned in the correct direction.  

The Good:
The environments are creepy. I LOVE the Texas Chainsaw Massacre vibe that this game embraces. The enemies aren't numerous, but are strong enough to make basic encounters stressful. Differences in difficulty are more than just scaling up enemy damage and health (though that is very much the case) and include new puzzle locations and collectibles. Resources can be scarce or plentiful, fully dependent on the player's skill level. The game clocks in for a casual player in the 4 to 6 hour range, which is great for replayability. 

The Bad:
The ADR ranges from passable to awful. The inability to skip most cutscenes is annoying after the first playthrough. A branching narrative "decision" in the game has a definitive good and bad answer for the player, making just something that a first time player would make on accident. Some design choices for Madhouse difficulty enemy encounters and boss fights are a bit unfair, in my opinion. 

The Weird:
Does anyone else think that the little girls face looks just like Eddie from Silent Hill 2?

The Verdict:
A fantastic return to the roots of the series. Tense encounters, resource management, memorable environments. A few blemishes, but definitely still worth it. I actually have hope for RE8, once Capcom gets done with a victory lap doing quality remakes/remasters of previous series entries.

Resident Evil 7 is a brand new start of this franchise. It is the first FPS title of the series, in order to create a more immersive experience and a more spooky atmosphere. This time you are not those overpowered characters from previous games that survive from tons of bullets, explosions, zombies, monsters and vehicle crashes. Standing at the angle of a normal human being, players will play as a new character Ethan Winter to experience a small-scale but horrifying bio leak in a country house in Lousiana. 

By doing this, Resident Evil 7 returns to its survival horror root. With limited supplies and inventory slots, you must carefully manage your resources and fight your way out of the haunted house. The survival part is not as tough as some classic Resident Evil like Resident Evil 1 (and it is a good thing), but the horrifying atmosphere surpasses all the previous works. It has fewer zombies, yet it is even scarier. 

I like this change, and it is fine to put aside all previous characters and tell a new story. Still, I hope I can see the return of these beloved characters in the future Resident Evil.

The main game is around 10 to 11 hours, DLCs should provide another 10 hours of playtime. 

Not a Hero DLC tells the story of Chris Redfield, who came to the infected zone to clean up the aftermath. It extends the story background and gives some information on how things go after Resident Evil 6. The main game reveals these a bit, but more details are in this DLC. This DLC plays very similarly to the main game, except Chris is much stronger with more powerful gears and faces much more zombies. 

End of Zoe DLC is the follow-up story of the side character Zoe. This DLC plays like Street Fighter in the first-person perspective and you beat up zombies instead of persons. It does not really match the more realistic tone of the main game, as you beat the sh*it out of these scary monsters and blast their head with your bare hands. I also don't think this story is very believable since the Bakers has been infected three years ago and the news of people around went missing is already widespread. It is unit this moment that Jack’s brother jumps out of nowhere and claims to protect his family. Where was this family man during these years, not even a visit? Additionally, if you decide to fight your way through only with your fists without any weapons for achievement, good luck, it is a hardship.

Banned footage contains a mode like the raid mode of Resident Evil Revelations, a room escape, a walking simulator and a card game. The card game 21 is very fun. 

There are two more additional modes in DLC I didn’t play much. 

+ The plots are solid and more convincing and realistic than all previous stories, offering a very different horror experience. 
+ Very spooky atmosphere and immersive experience. 
+ Some very successful environment design, particularly the basement session really gives me a spook. 
+ DLCs are well-made and worthy, with various contents. 
+ Great voice acting with the South American accents (the Bakers). 

No obvious drawback in my opinion, though I can find some tiny nitpicks. 
 
This is Capcom’s first FPS game, and it seems to have minor issues on aiming and accuracy. 
Moving is painfully slow. 
You have no control of the flashlight. It should be on in some dark environments like the basement, to provide a better vision for aiming.

[b]RESIDENT EVIL 7[/b] is the latest installment in Resident Evil series, unlike the previous games this one uses first person perspective and features a bit of stealth moments. The game tries to bring back a lot of stuff from the first Resident Evil games, like exploration of a mansion, solving puzzles, crafting ammo and boring shooting mechanics. Unlike previous game, where you could skip shooting most of the time, this game's hero is very slow and corridors are usually very tight, so you can't just run past enemies. 

The story is more grounded than in previous games. You play as a guy, who's wife went missing 3 years ago, but he receives a strange message from her,  asking him to come to some abandoned house in Lousiana. In the best horror traditions he comes alone, doesn't take any weapons and opens every basement door without hesitation. The game is pretty scary at the start, because of the lack of ammo and weapons to deal with enemies, so you have to sneak around or run. Though when you find the right path the game becomes easy, because there are lots of ammo and crafting elements lying around. At the end of the game you become a walking arsenal, but that's common in Resident Evil games, when you play them on normal difficulty.

The other feature that they brought in from older Resident Evils is multiple endings. In the last part of the game you have a choice to make, I won't go into detail as to not spoil anything. But one of the options is considered wrong by developers, so no matter what you choose, it won't affect your playthrough. It will only change some cutscenes and that's all. It feels like it was thrown in at the last moment. In my opinion the game would have been better if there wasn't a choice at all. 

Best parts of this game are its atmosphere and graphics. Everything looks so detailed and realistic. The game is very immersive and makes you want to buy VR just to walk around the mansion and look at stuff. Voice actors do a good job at bringing their characters to live and the soundtrack makes you feel uneasy.
