[i]Resident Evil 7 (RE7)[/i] is a survival horror game. Nearly all of the action elements that made the series what it has been in the last decade are absent. That was a bold choice by CAPCOM, and the result is quite polarizing. 

People who grew up playing the Resident Evil games of the last 10 years, i.e. RE5, RE6 and both Resident Evil: Revelations (RER) games and who have derived from those games certain expectations about what they think a Resident Evil game should be like, may be sorely disappointed with RE7. 

But there are two groups of people who are pretty much guaranteed to love RE7:
1. People who grew up playing the Resident Evil games from before RE5 and found the installments of the last decade severely lacking in the survival horror aspect;
2. People who are into quality survival horror games. 

The fact that someone can both love quality survival horror games AND love the action-focused gameplay of RE5, RE6 and RER 1 & 2 means it's entirely possible you'll have a love-hate relationship with RE7, like I do. I'll try to explain both sides of my feelings about RE7, but in the end the 'love' part surpasses the 'hate' part by a lot, so I recommend RE7, just not to people who are only looking for the (gun) action-focused gameplay of the Resident Evil games of the last decade.


[h1]Story[/h1]

You play Ethan, whose wife Mia went missing three years ago during a long-term babysitting job. Out of the blue, Ethan received a brief message from Mia asking to come pick her up in Dulvey, Louisiana. Not sure what to expect when he pulls up to the southern farmhouse where he was supposed to be greeted by Mia, Ethan will soon find out that even his worst nightmares were sunshine, lollipops and rainbows compared to the horrors this place has in store for him.


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

I think it's best to start with the 'hate' part of my love-hate experience with RE7, as that feeling was most apparent during the first half of the game, after which I learned to appreciate RE7 for what it is, and I became more inclined towards the 'love' part.

As I said in the introduction, RE7's gameplay is very different from its last few predecessors which played more like shooters or at least action games, intertwined with some elements that referred to their roots in survival horror. In RE7, the survival horror takes the foreground. Almost completely. And therein lies my first gripe with RE7. Going 'back to basics' and 'back to the roots' is fine for many people, myself included (I can appreciate both genres the Resident Evil series has dabbled in), but I think it's too bad they threw out literally everything that made the last few Resident Evil games, as if absolutely nothing about them was good or fun. 

For example, none of the beloved characters of the series make an appearance and the whole Resident Evil lore isn't referenced at all until the very end of the game. It made me think of [i]Bioshock Infinite[/i], which had nothing to do with the previous Bioshock games besides a quick reference to those previous games at the very end. 

There are no weapon upgrades like in RE4, RE5, RER & RER2, no more chapters or missions that offered interim scores and rewards and opportunities to replay those sections in order to improve your performance, keeping the gear and such you had gathered.

A lot of the longtime fans wanted less of an action / shooter game and more of an adventure / survival horror game, and they were catered to. For the first part of the game, RE7 plays like an adventure game where you move from one 'event' to the next, while player input is extremely limited. You witness B-horror movie type things happening to you and to others, rather than being an active participant. 

The family who occupy the farmhouse are literally immortal opponents and you need to avoid them, until eventually a scripted fight occurs where you can disable them temporarily or definitively. 

RE7 has the least variety of enemies in any triple-A game ever. Apart from the two family members you'll fight as 'bosses', there is one more type of enemy. One. Yeah sure, it comes in three or so varieties, but so did zombies and the likes in previous games. But in previous games, zombies or basic mutants (Majini, J'Avo, …) were only one of at least a dozen different types of enemies.

I find it mindboggling that there is no information on weapon damage AT ALL, not in the game and not anywhere on the internet. And as is typical for the internet, it's full of contradictory information on which weapons are better suited for which situation, so you pretty much need to experiment and guess a bit.

This is the point in the review where I go from talking about my gripes with RE7 to what I felt were good things about the game.

There are fewer types of weapons, and ammo is a lot more scarce. Finding a new type of weapon isn't something that happens all the time and it really feels like it makes a difference. 

There are some puzzles to solve and a number of secrets to find or unlock, something especially RE6 was lacking.

The fact that the first part of RE7 plays like an interactive movie with little player input, also fits the list of good things about the game. In the long run I realized how important that part of the game was, both to set the atmosphere which is meant to make you feel powerless, lost and scared to death, and to make it clear this is [b]not[/b] a shooter game like the previous installments were.

The tense atmosphere at the start of the game gets even tenser as things progress. I don't think a game can actually make me feel scared anymore (save jumpscares, but those are just a cheap mechanism to mask the fact that the game is essentially [i]not[/i] scary), but RE7 did make me feel tense and immersed to an extent few other games have ever managed.

The first-person view of RE7 is new to the series and was a risky choice, but it works. Man, does it work! It adds to the immersion and the tension, and brings them to a level the previous Resident Evil games could only ever dream of reaching.

So all in all, I had a wonderful, exciting, tense but fulfilling experience playing RE7, even though I can't call it a perfect game and its style and gameplay took some getting used to after playing RE5, RE6, RER & RER2. 


[h1]Graphics and sound[/h1]

RE7 was developed with CAPCOM's very own 'RE Engine'. It produces graphics that can be called decent to nice, but no superlatives like great, excellent or beautiful come to mind. For example, people's hair consists of only a few thick strands of hair that wave around as if the strands are alive, instead of bunch of thin strands or even individual hairs like we've seen in recent triple-A games. Faces look plastic-y and waxy, and facial expressions don't look very realistic or convincing.

Actually, I often thought the RE engine made RE7's graphics look a lot like a Unity-based game. You can pick up a lot of items (photos, notes, etc.) that are shown in the middle of your screen,  where you can rotate them a bit and put them back, exactly like in any Unity-based game.

The soundtrack is amazing. I mean, the score and ambient noises add so much to the creepy, scary atmosphere of the game I think the people responsible for the soundtrack should be showered with awards.

RE7's voice acting is very good. Our protagonist Ethan doesn't talk a lot, so his personality is established more by the horrors he keeps overcoming during his adventures, but all the other characters are brought to live largely due to top-notch voice acting.


[h1]On Steam's extra features[/h1]

RE7 has 9 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 5 while running the game.

The 58 Steam Achievements are varied. RE7 is a game that's very hard to 100%. Some achievements are tough as nails and many can only be unlocked through playing all of the DLC, some of which aren't very good and all of which are fairly expensive for what you get.

TLDR;
9/10

I'm very passionate about Resident Evil, and I hate FPS horror games like Outlast and Penumbra, and their reliance on taking away player movement and start to kind of feel like a haunted mansion. So when I heard Resident Evil 7 was going to be a first person game, saw the godawful trailer with that stupid soundtrack, and the amount of advertising towards Twitch streamers, I reckoned I just didn't want to play this game and took it off of my list. 
Later I did pick it back up again for a fair price, figuring I could at least give it the change people told me I should give it, and to my surprise actually enjoyed this game a fair bit.
But what's more, I was freaking terrified playing this game and was purposefully stalling every minute just to not have to open the next door, I wasn't this terrified of a Resident Evil game since being a child, terrified even by just the boxart of Resident Evil 2 alone.
The amount of hours I've spend playing this game are a testimony to how scary I found this game, because I finished it in about 6 hours on a single playthrough, and spent the rest of time stalling time, waiting for people to come home so I wasn't alone, and watching cheery videos.

The graphics of this game are great even 2 years later, the voice acting is fantastic, the design and the overall structure of everything is a bit tropey and I would've liked a stronger Japanese twist to everything, but it's serviceable and doesn't take away from anything.
The engine makes everything look like its own thing, and I can't really think of any other game that looks quite like it, it really serves to make enemies look gross, dirty, and creepy, and everything works as a solid whole without ever feeling like the engine is running out of possibilities.
 
The story is pretty standard, and never really does anything too great with it, especially near the ending, but even then it's fine and easy to overlook. The story is best when it's in the backseat, when the game is driven on its broody atmosphere, never making you feel safe without forcing you too hard towards a disadvantage, and the cracking and slamming sound effects alone.

I wish I could've just kept it at praise while accepting some of Resident Evil's standard quirks, but the game does have some issues of itself that will probably never make me want to play it again. First there is the lack of enemy variety, something you'll read all over the internet, and while this might not be entirely fair considering there is some variety to them, they all look and feel very similar and can all be approached in similar fashion. Molded simply don't have the strength behind them to carry the game alone, and once you realize that fighting slight variations of the molded is all you're going to do, it starts to wear quickly and loses its creepy atmosphere, and your fear of the unexpected. A second gripe is that the game feels like it's trying to come up with reasons to keep you trapped in a single location, while that location isn't as big to begin with. Yet we're finding items, running after people, all the while it doesn't feel like we're trapped in a house, more like we're running some errands around the house while taking plenty of detours. Thirdly the game doesn't manage to remain consistent in quality of places to explore and things to tackle, there's an entire ship sequence that feels incredibly tedious to play, and entire puzzles that feel like they're part of the game because it's Resident Evil, rather than being part of a certain flow that fits the game.
This doesn't just count for the areas, tasks, and puzzles, but also the boss fights that after a certain lady simply become bigger blobs that need to be hit in certain spots to go down, and certainly go down easily without trial and error. 

I wouldn't get the DLC if I were you however, it's like the ending of the actual game, but worse, even more action oriented and even less about atmosphere and horror elements.

So this is a true to its roots Resident Evil sequel. The inventory management is back and it's fantastic, the puzzles feel great and the progression mechanics of being forced to backtrack through areas that you know have danger brought back the tension that was lost in previous releases. Previously, and even in RE4, you just were constantly going forwards in the environments and that cuts the fear factor in half in my opinion. Fearing what could pop out at you as you go is one form for sure, and that's present in this game and the others, but the fear of KNOWING what is going to be there because you already experienced it and have to go back through in order to progress because you needed something in one place to open up something somewhere else creates a dread that is what Resident Evil used to really have mastered. Glad to see it's back. 

The first person perspective brings it into the modern era as well, and if there were as many enemies as there are in previous entries, this would have been exhausting to play, but by replacing a large quantity of enemies with a small amount of high powered ones, this definitely translates to FP well. The molded are a bit of a pain, they have the resource-draining design where they just kinda twitch all over the place so that you will waste ammo missing what would have been a headshot because they just spazzed out for no other reason than to create an excuse to reduce your inventory. And items are limited, not insanely, but definitely will have you second guessing which to use at what time. 

The ending was pretty bland from a gameplay perspective, but story-wise it was alright for an RE game. Lots of people were annoyed by the Chris Redfield redesign, but honestly I hated the redesign he got for RE5, and he looks like what the Chris from the RE1 Remake would look like after some years of both life and console generations. RE5/6 Chris was a cartoon and I'm glad he's back to being a human again.

Some of the DLC is pretty good. Jack's 55th Birthday is super annoying, but the free Not A Hero was a fun diversion from the tension of the main story. End of Zoe had some annoying bits to it, like a final bossfight with ridiculous hitboxes, but it was still worth playing. Banned Footage had a bunch of different games to play through and they all had their own cool styles. Each was a completely different experience, minus Daughters which was actually something I think complemented the main game the best of the whole lot. I'm glad it wasn't before the game though because it would have ruined the main game's reveals, but it was a great prequel to play afterwards. 

All in all, yeah this was great. I was waiting for a VR version to be available on PC, but it's been long enough after the PSVR exclusivity ended for me to know it's never going to happen.

RESIDENT EVIL 7 takes the series back to its survival horror roots while also bringing in some new elements that have never really been touched upon in the franchise. Moving from third-person over the shoulder view to an intimate first-person perspective, the game follows everyman Ethan Winters as he journeys to the swampy backwoods of Dulvey, Louisiana to search for his missing wife.

Similarly to the original Resident Evil game, RE7 takes place (mostly) in a single location; the decrepit residence of the Baker Family. Fans of the series will notice the similarities; you'll need to solve item puzzles to progress, find keys to the right doors, and avoid enemies to conserve ammo. Altogether, it feels like exactly what the series needed in order to get back on track with what made the original games so good. It's probably one of my favourite horror games from this generation.

Yes!  This is a great horror story, backed up by good solid survival gameplay.

I enjoyed the new first-person camera perspective and the much more intimate story than we've previously seen in the series.  More than any other Resident Evil game, this story is really about the protagonist.  Ethan Winters, searching for his missing wife, gets caught up in a terrifying situation with a crazy family miles from civilization, and everything happening in the story logically progresses from that.  It was very easy to continue feeling motivated to solve Ethan's problems and get him out of there.

This intimacy also extends to the game's antagonists.  This is not a game about wandering through levels fighting a thousand zombies; it's about a man trapped with a few very persistent and frightening adversaries.  There are some expendable monsters as well, but they are window dressing; the focus is firmly on Ethan and his struggle with the major villains.

Despite the obvious departures, this still feels very much like a Resident Evil game, thanks to a few design hooks and thematic callbacks.  Setting tropes like assembling multi-part keys, manipulating mythological statuary, and triggering improbable mechanical doors all remind one of the RE universe, and the weapons available, the magical "item box" that makes your equipment accessible from multiple map areas, and the tape recorder rooms very much reflect the gameplay we're used to.

I'll say briefly that the art and level design of the game are nothing short of brilliant.  The old house and the surrounding areas are scary, period.  Getting chased through this place makes one feel constantly vulnerable (except when hearing the reassuring "tape recorder room theme" which means you can relax and take a breath!).

Scarcity is also handled very well.  Balancing weapons, ammo, healing items etc. feels just right.  I was always worried about running out of ammo, yet didn't feel the need to reload the game if I missed a few shots ... and when you're in a state of panic, sometimes you miss a few shots!

If you play this game with the lights on and try to "beat" it like a perfectionistic pro, you're going to miss out on what makes it so great.  Don't do that!  Don't reload to correct your mistakes, really turn the gamma down low so loot items are hard to find, and absolutely do not read walkthroughs or hints & tips unless you're truly stuck.

For a special challenge, the game allows you to disable the HUD entirely, making loot much harder to find.  I played this way from beginning to end for greater immersion and it made the experience amazing.

The only ding I might make against the game is that some of the boss fights are a bit too unforgiving, especially as you aren't trained to use all available abilities.  For example, one fight is made much easier if you remember that crouching can help you dodge attacks ... yet crouching to dodge is not suggested or useful at any prior point in the game, so there's no reason you would think of it now.  Another boss' weak point is the stomach, with no feedback to make you guess that, as up to that point headshots are most effective against every enemy.  A good boss fight is a "final quiz" of skills the game has taught you; here, each new chapter fight throws the old rules out the window.  This is not an insurmountable problem for the player but I feel it could have been handled better.

I got the game on sale for a bit under $20 and playing the main game took just under 15 hours.  I definitely got my money and time's worth and look forward to enjoying the free bonus "side stories".  Even without the extra content I would be completely satisfied with my purchase.  Well done CAPCOM!

[h1]My first time with the Resident Evil series and I'm quite surprised that I liked it but there are few things I would like to point out about the game and mainly, about the Season Pass.[/h1]

[b]Gameplay[/b]

[list][*]The game itself is not that long, you will finish in 8-10 hours. It depends how much time you spend on exploring the areas for extra loot, collectibles, and files to read. Thanks to the dynamic story I think that the game time for this game is ok because the part of the game on a wrecked ship near the end of the game was way too boring to play after the amazing mansion which you explored earlier. 
[*]You will have to sneak/run or shoot your way forward to your goal and unfortunately the game itself is not really hard because you have only two difficulty options - easy and normal. After you finish the game, you will unlock the Madhouse difficulty, which is probably the best experience for the game but it requires that you have a knowledge of the situations and events which will happen in your playthrough (Or you can buy the difficulty via microtransactions which are just stupid).
[*]I was disappointed that puzzles were not really hard. The one with the "birthday cake" was probably the most enjoyable. 
[*]Crafting system is ok, it suits the pace of the game. It's the same with the weapons - shotguns are great, it feels good to shoot with them.  Unfortunately, the game gives you even on the normal difficulty a lot of resources and especially ammunition. Of course, you can play the Madhouse difficulty which will reduce it but you have to finish the game first or pay for it and I know that many people don't have the need to replay games.
[*]AI is quite stupid, you can easily outsmart them (and the regular enemies don't know how to open a door). Yet, their design, moves, and attacks are good. Boss fights are ok but a bit clunky.[/list]

[b]Story and characters[/b]
[list][*]I think that the story of the main game is overall good. It borrows a lot from various horror movies (as every RE game). The weakest part of the story is definitely the main antagonist [spoiler] Eveline. Although she itself as a part of the story and reason behind all of the situations which are happening isn't bad, it's her character which is just boring random wanna be creepy spooky little kid and that's why I didn't like the ship scene, she is just too boring. [/spoiler]
[*]On the other hand, all members of the Baker family are amazingly written and voiced. Daddy Baker with his son, Lucas, is really good and entertaining. 
[*]It seems to me that the main character, Ethan, is at least half-retarded. He proves it with his idiotic behavior to environment many times and with the cake [spoiler]which explodes - BUT YOU HAVE SEEN IT ON VIDEOTAPE BEFORE, BUT HE IS STILL STANDING HERE AND WATCHING IT EXPLODE TO HIS FACE[/spoiler] it was the final proof that he is half-retarded.[/list]

[b]Graphics and sounds[/b]
[list][*]The game looks good, but there is the weird blur or something which was random during my playthrough. Also, at least in the first 2 hours, my game HAD to run 60 or 30 fps steadily or there would be a weird voice inconsistency with the motion of the mouth. I guess that this can really be a problem for you if you don't have a recommended specs for this game.
[*]The voice acting, sounds of monsters and every other sounds are great. It probably adds to the atmosphere of the game most.[/list]

[b]Season Pass[/b]

[list][*][b]Not A Hero[/b] is the only free addition for the game and it continues the story after the events of the game. It's about 2 hours long and it offers new weapons, enemies and items. The story is ok. But it is kinda sad (well, it's good for the DLC), that this is the longest and most enjoyable DLC (for me) which this game offers but it is free.
[*][b]End of Zoe[/b] This is the first and final main story DLC for which you have to pay. It is not as long as the previous DLC and not as entertaining. It's just like angry redneck punching everything which is fun but for that price? I don't think so...
[*][b]Banned Footage Vol. 1 and 2[/b] offers a few minigames and videotapes which are just not good enough. They have nothing to do with the atmosphere of the main game (and main DLCs). There is a survival mode, rogue-lite mode, blackjack mode and more. It's a nice addition, but I would expect that this would be free.
[*]So overall I don't think that the Season Pass is worth the price for you if you want more of the main game - you will not get it there. If you like these challenges and minigames - than it is for you.[/list]

While I am in the minority of loving Resident Evil 6, I like everyone else saw that Resident Evil was in desperate need of rebooting. Changing the formula is what the series thrives on, from the larger scope of 2, the new camera in 4, and the emphasis of action in post-5, I welcome change as a Resident Evil fan. That being said, when the trailer dropped for Resident Evil VII: Biohazard, I did not know what to think. Maybe it was TOO different. But I always had a strong curiosity for the direction it took. I'm a huge Tobe Hooper and Sam Raimi fan, and I loved how the game spliced Texas Chainsaw and Evil Dead together. I finally played and beat RE VII this year, and even if I don't think it compares to the franchise's best, it is still a very strong and always captivating video game.

The game takes full advantage of its new camera system just as RE4 did over a decade ago. Even without VR (I almost do not want to imagine how terrifying it would be to use it) this is still an extremely immersive game. That goes beyond just the camera; the attention to detail in level design, graphics, and soundscape really sell this uncomfortable world. Also with is are the vocal performances, which dare I say for a Resident Evil game, are actually really great? Seriously, everyone is fantastic. All the members of the Baker family are so iconic in every way, from their lines, designs, fights, character, everything. They're some of the best group of baddies Capcom ever put out. Ethan is a step down from other RE protagonists simply because he exists more as an avatar for the player, but even then he has his moments ("Who builds this ♥♥♥♥?!"). The real star is Clancy, the unseen previous victim of the Bakers explored in videotape flashbacks. Every one of his scenes are among the most revolting and he hardly speaks a word. I really do wish the whole game was around him.

Like every other Resident Evil, it has its fair share of criticisms. My biggest one is that there is practically zero enemy variety, even in the DLC. The design for the grunts, called Molded, are totally uninspired and visually uninteresting, and all of them are practically the same. Like many other RE games, it loses its tone in the finale, becoming a streamlined action game. The difficulty curve is all over the place, beginning really stupidly hard before quickly becoming easy and easily exploitable, until you get to the ship and it once again because hard until you find the big stash of one hit kill explosives. Everything from then on is a glorified QTE, especially the final boss which, while interesting in design, is one of the most monotonous final bosses of recent memory. While the rest of the bosses are pretty good, one fought in a barn was a real disappointing bait and switch that's easily exploitable. But hey, chainsaw dueling Jack makes up for it.

Everything up until the finale is near perfection, however. The game banks heavily on the first RE in terms of design and atmosphere but still goes out and makes its own thing. It's strange to see a RE game played so straight, but it works amazingly well here, and even then it still is not afraid to show off some camp. The story is a genuinely interesting one full of intrigue while also succeeding at that small scale "anything can go wrong really fast and no one will know" paranoia that makes 70s horror so great to me. Controls are surprisingly good for a first time mainline FPS entry, though leaning mechanics would have helped out a lot in a certain part of the game, and making inventory selection real time feels like a mistake when the interface is still as clunky as ever. Little new things, like the Madhouse difficulty which totally changes things up like making you find secret coins to unlock key items as well as the trademark perfect RE balance of brevity and content make this an extremely replayable game, and I cannot wait for my second and even third playthrough despite its flaws.

RE VII shines in its concept, design, characters, and story, doing a great job at rebooting the series from over the top camp to something more believable while losing nothing that RE is known for. Even if it ultimately doesn't reinvent the wheel, it's a must play for fans, and even a good entry point for newcommers since it's so narratively separated from the others.

Resident Evil 7 is a good game with a good balance of horror, gameplay, and story. I like horror, but I've never been into Resident Evil, so this was my first dive into the series (save for playing 30 minutes of Code Veronica). 

As far as the horror aspect goes, Resident Evil 7 is scary, but there are scarier games. I'm not saying that's a bad thing. Lots of people are turned off by playing a really terrifying game. Personally, I think having weapons in a horror game makes it a lot less scary, so it's nice that Resident Evil 7 can still give you the creeps, but it can also scratch a bit of that FPS itch. 

The difficulty in the gameplay comes from many sources. You will need to go in guns blazing sometimes, sneak around sometimes, and solve puzzles others. There's also a bit of resource management. Resident Evil 7 makes you decide if you want to craft more bullets or health potions for example. I really liked that there are several times in the game where you're like "Oh, it's still going!" There were times were I thought I was dead and the game was like "Nope, you're still fighting with that flesh wound there." 

The story was okay, but personally I thought it was the weakest point. As you can tell from the trailer, you are basically in the house of the demented Baker family and you have to figure out how to escape. The story was easy to follow for the first 75% of the game, but then they did the thing where they just throw in several plot twists at the end and it starts to not be clear anymore. Spoilers below about what specific plot holes I had a problem with. 

[spoiler] There were two parts of the story in particular that I didn't understand. If you can tell me what I missed, please go ahead and comment. So number 1: I chose to save Mia so I gave her the syrum and she's supposed to be cured of the Mold Virus thing. But then at the end of chapter 6 / beginning of chapter 7, she pushes you out the door to save you and says she can't resist Evie much longer. Isn't she cured? And then she's just fine in the final cutscene? I didn't get that whole progression. And number 2: In the main story you fight Lucas at the end of chapter 5 I believe (maybe 4). Correct me if I'm wrong, but you do kill him right? I was confused why Lucas is back in the "Not a Hero" extras mission that takes place after the main story. [/spoiler]

Overall I'd still say I enjoyed Resident Evil 7 a lot. Like I said before, it's a good balanced game that doesn't make you feel bogged down in any one style of gameplay. Final note, legitimately one of the most impressive things I found in the game is how they made the bad guys' heads sway so it is actually a bit challenging to cash in on headshots, even on slow moving targets.

Resident Evil 7 is, as expected, mundane. If the other games in the series hook you for their themes, gameplay, or puzzles; then the best point of Biohazard is its status as being nearly a film. Everything about the game is cinematic, but that fails to make up for its mediocre gunplay, absence of puzzles, and atrocious story. Honestly, if it WAS a movie, I likely would have turned it off after half an hour and never returned. If you're a fan of horror, and you can power through a god-awful hour or so at the start, it slowly settles into typical RE themes any player should be familiar with, but you are not missing a lot.

The hardest point to discuss is likely the visuals. RE7 is appealing in some ways, and disgusting in others. Not because of its insects or gore, but because of the sheer choppiness of its display. Unless it's on its ultra settings, the visuals are vomit-inducing, constantly appearing as though you're looking through a bad camera feed than human eyes; and every single texture is jagged and blurry. But the price of its realistic visuals is the tax on your machine. A game like SOMA can be visually pleasing with minimal cost to performance, but RE7 is so demanding that it will buffer while turning corners. Rather than have lengthy loading screens, it instead will generate only what you can see, and you'll find the gameplay pausing to catch up and unimmersing you from the experience. On an average level, it's no more impressive to view than Resident Evil 4, and its setting leaves a lot to be desired compared to the mansion in RE1. At times the graphics will look almost photogenic, and then they can hardly render a believable human face. 

There's nothing special about the music or sound, other than to say that the southern accents ham up the cheesiness of the Resident Evil franchise, and it's impossible to take anyone with a Louisiana accent seriously as a villain. The acting is piss-poor and almost makes you think it's some dumb satire, with perhaps one of the worst child-actors to ever appear in any media ever made. Even the sound of insect wings doesn't irritate me, because of how unremarkable the experience is.

The gameplay is where you'd look for a saving grace, and you can at least thank god that this isn't just a walking simulator horror game, but it's close to it. You have your typical inventory, ammo management, and collectibles, but you're cut down a lot by a lack of interesting enemies and varied weapons. The short length of the game lends a bit to this flaw, but it's still depressing how unimaginative and simple it is compared to other horror-action games. And, like always, the gunplay is a bore. Enemies are bullet-sponges, and bosses are even worse when they aren't just a "ATTACK THE CRAB'S WEAKSPOT FOR MASSIVE DAMAGE" encounter. You can sprint, but the flashlight comes up automatically. You can't really jump or platform at all, and you tend to push doors open automatically. There's no real hiding, since there's nothing to hide with, but not enough ammo to fight every creature. As such, I found myself running past a lot of enemies, just hoping that the game was ending soon. I was never stuck with a puzzle, and found nothing interesting or memorable; there was only keys to acquire which had obvious uses. 

Unlike some of the other games, RE7 is both generic in its repetition and frighteningly dull. It has your typical parasite plot, your residential setting, your government cover-ups, and some "undead." This game felt like some kind of Spider-man: Venom comic, as the entire theme here was "black ooze," which was alive and could control people and increase their abilities. You had your family cast as bosses, who were all boring to meet and play against, as they were all essentially immortal, but then they just settle into the commonality of the series by becoming giant monsters in their final encounters. The only other enemies in the ENTIRE game are black-ooze creatures that act like Regeneradors. They're undefined, not frightening, and will "glop" out of walls or the ceiling to "surprise" you. They bite at you, walk slowly, and have a few subtle variations where they have a longer tentacled arm, or they scurry on the ground. You just blow up their heads or tear off all their limbs. It's somehow even less interesting than zombies, and they never do anything horrifying. They aren't even undead, since they're just created by the ooze, and you'll be bored of them after the initial encounter. And, like most experiences in Resident Evil, the game just goes on too long. It ends, and then they tack on another two hours and a few crappy boss-fights, and one finds themselves asking, "Do I even care? When will this end?" But there's nothing to work for, and no real achievement or challenge to find. There's no reason to be satisfied with a resolution to a bad narrative, and there's surprisingly no real enemity or connection to be felt with any of the characters. They put you into situations that seem like they're begging for you to have an emotional reaction, but they fill up their world with cardboard cut-outs. 

I say give it a pass. If you've played one, you've played 'em all. And if you've never touched this series, you'd be better off exploring an earlier installment. RE7 is just a soulless flick in a series that was stale fifteen years ago.

I'm perfectly ok with the idea of a First Person Resident Evil game, however the combat system is just so dull and janky I can't wrap my head around it. In Fixed Camera Resident Evil games you would never miss a shot as long as you were facing the direction of the enemy. In 3rd Person Resident Evil games you would take a risk reward shot on enemies heads, there was plenty of room to move around so they would stagger back and forth while you were aiming. THis game runs a lot of close quarter combat early on so you are forced to run around the enemy causing them to stagger a lot, messing up your aim.

The game's response to you running out of ammo is to have you combat the enemy with a knife, there is no system in place to stagger the enemy with the knife so you are going to get hit a lot. Since you are going to get hit a lot, the game provides you with a surplus of healing items. For me, this raises the question on why wouldn't they just provide you with ammo instead of an insane amount of healing items. More ammo would prevent the player from finding out how non-threatening the AI actually is when they are close to you, creating this greater tension on how scary the AI actually is.

Once you find out that the AI are a bunch of Teddy Bears, you really start questioning how scary this game actually is compared to how annoying it is trying to defend yourself. Rather than trying to conserve my ammo and going for headshots, like in a traditional Resident Evil game, I find myself counting down how many bullets i'm shooting into an enemies chest, as I await to ultimately run up and start slashing at them as they wail on me.

I'm pretty sure Dr. Salvador or a regular Hunter would have a proper response to me slashing them with a knife. Not raising their hand at me, like a parent trying to threaten a child.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Edit for the DLC, Not a Hero: It's nice to see the "Stagger and Melee" mechanic return alongside Chris Redfield, but it just has me scraching my head, wondering why this hasn't been incorporated into the main game. Now the DLC is free and ties into the main game, but paying $60 on release for 4 hours worth of content in the main game doesn't seem right to me. 

The new $30 price tag is fair, but if your expecting a Resident Evil title and not some indie horror developer's wet dream, stay clear until you already know what your getting into.

Okay, but really, this was my first time playing a Resident Evil game myself (I've watched Let's Plays of the others because I'm a scaredy cat buuut I love the stories and lore), and honestly, with Resident Evil 7, I was just lured in by the beautiful graphics. Horror games just aren't my thing, I thought, but I found myself loading it up one night with the lights off and the brightness turned all the way down. If I was going to play my first horror game, I was going to do it right. 

And I'm so, so soooo glad I did. 

Resident Evil 7 absolutely nails the atmosphere from its opening moments as you (Ethan Winters) drive to the Baker's home in Dulvey, Louisiana, going only off a message you receive from your wife Mia, who has been presumed dead for three years. In typical horror fashion, Ethan sees all the signs of something being not quite right in the Baker residence, but of course, in typical horror fashion, continues his search for his wife regardless. What starts out as a search for your wife ends up becoming a lovely vacation with the Bakers. Just sit back, relax, and enjoy all the atmosphere of their loving home and hospitality!

That palpable eerie atmosphere of the game that is so consistent throughout, is undoubtedly due to Capcom's own beautiful RE Engine. Running the game on an i5 6600k and a GTX 1070, I had absolutely no issues with framerate or stutters, enjoying smooth gameplay all the way through my 17 hour (Like I said, I'm a scaredy cat. You horror veterans can probably get through it much more quickly!) playthrough. Light, darkness, dynamic shadows and volumetric lighting all worked together amazingly to create a truly tangible horror experience. Textures are a bit muddy in spots, but it's really nothing to complain about. The attention to detail, specifically with the audio of the game, is just superb. I thought that the first-person perspective, a first for the Resident Evil series, was implemented perfectly, and I never had any awkward moments in gameplay, whether I was falling through floorboards, combing the entire house in search of those elusive coins, or running from... well, you'll see. While I can't truly compare the gameplay to other Resident Evil games, having only watched them, from what I observed, the return to the survival aspect of horror is absolutely welcome here. I had so many "oh s**t, I'm low on ammo, now what?" moments that made my time with the Bakers so much more tense, and eventually, rewarding, than it would have been otherwise. And the first-person perspective only heightened that sweet, sweet tension. 

The characters were mostly well written (I found Ethan to be such a dull, typical protagonist in the beginning, but by the end of the game I was just as done with everything as he was-), but the Bakers really steal the show here. And there are some brilliantly written nuances to a certain character that I don't want to spoil, but they really cemented the game for me!

I didn't mind the boss battles, but I didn't love them either, save for one (which I won't spoil), but thankfully they are few and far between, and playing on Normal difficulty, you have plenty of resources to take the boss down. I promise you too, will soon be wondering why the f**k they won't just die already!

As of writing this review, I've only completed Ending 1 of the game, and I'm already excited to go back and complete Ending 2 when I have an itch to visit the Bakers again! I truly believe that the ending felt earned, and you might even actually breathe a sigh of relief when its all finally over. 

Resident Evil 7 has somehow made a horror lover out of this previously "avoid scary games at all costs" gal, and if that isn't a high enough recommendation to experience this game, I don't know what is. If you usually avoid horror games like me, I should warn you that there are some jump scares (but they aren't overused or cheap), and some genuinely terrifying and gruesome moments, but they are absolutely worth playing this game! If I can do it, kicking and screaming the whole way through, you can too!

Admittedly I've played this twice, on the same difficulty because I love it so much. I might play Madhouse difficulty some day.

Story:
The story is awesome in this. It really brings the Resident Evil lore forward. I like that they've moved away from the action hero stars like Jill, Claire, Leon and Chris, and now you're a nobody with no previous experience with the virus. So you're experiencing the game from the perspective of a nobody, and not some professional operative like most of the Resident Evil game.

I also like that the antagonist in this game is not related to Umbrella or the Weskers. It really feels fresh. If you play the game without reading the log books scattered around, you're really missing out. I remember playing it the first time round and I ignored most of the log books, only realising at the end of the game, I have no idea what the wee girl was all about and how the protagonist's wife is related to the wee girl. Only after playing it the 2nd time around, reading the log books that I understood how everything ties together. Don't want to spoil it, but all I can say is that this game has quite a deep story. It's not your typical, "I gotta go save the president's daughter and get the f out of here" or as convulated as "we have to travel to 3 different countries to stop this virus, OMG big boney dinosaur man has just appeared. Quick use quick attack on it". There is a key player in the game that is working in the background as you go through the experience and the supposedly "antagonists" (the Baker family) are not what they seem.

I even thought the DLC story was good. Playing as a Baker family member is fun and hilarious sometimes (in a good way). Also the DLC truly completes your Resident Evil 7 experience.

Gameplay:
Moving away from you being able to view your character in third person, you're now in first person and this really bumps up the immersion into the world of Resident Evil 7. You experience it as if you are there and it gives a nice personal touch. YOU want to stay away from Jack Baker, not Ethan, but YOU. Open a door and bam! There's Jack Baker throwing you on the floor, giving you a head start at running away from him. Running away feels tense as Jack chases you around the house with your safe havens being able to reach the save room or the more fun and adventurous way - hiding till he goes away. 

The shooting is fun too. And conserving ammo is so important in this, especially the Shotgun ammo as there are only limited supplies scattered around the estate. You definitely want to land those headshots when you can. Or even better, run from enemies! Enemies do not drop items, so killing them is only a means to get to where you want to go or wasting bullets.

Puzzles in this game is quite fun too. You may get stuck in some areas like the part with the dog head and the grandfather clock. Took me a long while to figure that out on my first playthrough. All on all, for the main game, if you do not use guides and walkthroughs, you can easily spend 10 to 12 hours playing the main game as you explore every nook and cranny, collecting items, ammo, running away, etc. On my second playthrough, because I know how the puzzles work, it still took me between 6 to 8 hours to finish. You'll also get some special rewards if you finish the game in under 5 hours.

What I don't like is that you never truly know how your character actually looked like. It would be nice if in Chris' campaign, they show you Ethan's face, but I guess the game wants Ethan to be you, to make it more personal.

This game is a very good buy. I'd highly recommend the DLC, so you get to conclude the story properly. I hate that companies do that but they do these days.

While I liked Rev 1 and think RE6 had a great Mercenaries mode at the very least I would definitely agree that RE7 is still overall a great return to form for the franchise. Rev 2 felt like a jumbled mess of a game where it really felt Capcom couldn’t decide whether it should be action-horror or survival horror and it really suffered for it I feel, so much so that I just stopped playing barely half-way through. RE7, on the other hand, has real confidence in what it is and does a great job at it; striking a good balance between combat, stealth, and just running the hell away.

RE7 is a great modernization of the pre-RE4 games in a first person perspective, it allows you to fight back but monsters can be tough so it’s not always the best option. There is a good amount of exploration that rewards you with stuff like permanent health upgrades and weapons. There is also that old RE mainstay of solving puzzles to get weird keys. The game does peter out a bit when you leave the Baker estate but it doesn’t drag the whole game down at all. 

Speaking of the Bakers, they are fantastic antagonists and the real stars of the show.  They are a great mix of darkly humorous and genuinely threatening, like even more effective versions of Nemesis and Mr. X. The first fight with Jack is also fantastic. The later boss fights are also overall pretty solid too. The main character, Ethan, is just kinda there though, just your bog standard white dude video game protag here to save his wife, Mia. Mia’s got more going on for her at least. Overall the plot is solid for RE, mainly in the fact that’s it’s got some nice foreshadowing.

The game’s atmosphere is fantastic; it’s got this really grimy and run-down aesthetic, even more than any of the other games in the series had. 7’s aesthetic feels kind of like a grindhouse horror movie on a grainy VHS especially what with its use of VHSes as a game mechanic.

[h1]Resident Evil [b][i] returns to its roots [/i][/b] with a fresh first-person perspective, a new family of enemies, and a gritty and intense atmosphere. RE7 is essentially Resident Evil 1, 2, 3, and Code Veronica with a modern first-person twist. It captures the essence of Resident Evil gameplay, puzzles, and singular environmental design.[/h1]

The Good
+ First-person perspective with classic Resident Evil feel
+ Gripping, intense, gritty, dark, and atmospheric
+ Searching every nook and cranny for ammo and items is conducive to gameplay
+ Attention to detail
+ Scarce ammo and items
+ [b]No cheap scares[/b]
+ Inventory is limited which adds to survival-horror feel, but very manageable
+ Homage to classic elements such as special doors, tight corridors, and singular environment
+ Great set pieces
+ Excellent pacing 
+ Save rooms (are placed fairly)
+ Excellent voice acting and delivery of lines
+ Controls feel just right - there is sprint, but you will only need to use it when combating enemies
+ Walking does not feel sluggish like other people have complained about - take it from someone who hates sluggish movement in walk simulators. 
+ 10-12 hour campaign - RE2 and 3 were about 8-12 hours and Resident Evil 4 was roughly 16-20 hours long. This is about right for RE7's story and premise.
+ Combat feels like classic Resident Evil in first-person - masterfully executed
+ Enemies are like the Hills Have Eyes, The People Under the Stairs type. New take on how enemies should look like in a Resident Evil game.
+ Right amount of backtracking
+ Excellent optimization - 60+ fps without a hitch @ 3440x1440p (Read specs below and "The Bad" section for mod support)

The Neutral
+/- Fighting the same boss in different scenarios throughout the game
+/- Story 
+/- Premise
+/- Bosses and boss types
+/- Enemy types
+/- Lite-puzzles
+/- Parts that required stealth

The Bad
- Lack of strong worldbuilding makes ending confusing for newcomers and those that have not played every single Resident Evil videogame
- Ethan Winters (protagonist) - He does not embody what a Resident Evil character should be, although the voice actor who plays Ethan delivers a good performance. 
- Lack of emotion and connection between Ethan and Mia (more so on Ethan's end) 
- No 21:9 Ultra-wide support but can be modded - follow instructions in this link: [url=http://www.wsgf.org/dr/resident-evil-7-biohazard/en]Play Resident Evil 7 in Ultra-wide![/url]

It never felt like you were some super trained badass, which I really liked. Im sure if the game had a third person camera it would have still been a great game, but going first person really allowed me to (at most times) feel the panic of being just some joe shmoe stuck in a horrible situation having to use only what was natural available to me.. sound and a very limited arsenal of tools to survive with to get me through 'hell'.

 I had a lot of fight or flight moments compared to RE4 - 6. They were great games if you wanted a more action oriented shooter. In those iterations I knew I was going to kick whatever monsters ass because.. well, you played a trained-experienced force to be reckoned with with awesome weapons and tools to destroy what got in your way. Didnt really need to run away from any fights in those games unless it was to reload and get back into the fight. But with RE7, that was hardly the case at all. The enemies were interesting, and (for my first playthrough) unpredictable/unexpected, and creeped the hell out of me because of it. I had a lot of deaths due to "trial and error" fighting. I found myself having to run from a fight because it was literally suicide to try and fight the horrors you run into.

 As far as graphics, controls, and stability goes I never experienced a single bug or glitch, which is extremely rare in this day and age (sad when you think about it). I used a Xbox One controller so I cant say about the KB & mouse, but the controls felt great after turning off that aweful "Camera Acceleration" option. Maxed out settings in 4k ran at a beautiful 60fps with only a few dips in a very few areas. My only real complaint is sometimes the lighting when a light source is used (like a flashlight) upon entering a well lit area wouldnt register and throw the lighting (colors, shadows, etc) off but that only happened maybe 3 to 4 times in the entire playthrough.

Overall it was a fun adventure, and cant wait to play RE2's remake on this engine.

Fighting is not always the best option in this game; you will certainly have to choose when to pick a fight. The decision to break away from the forumla they had been using was a very smart move. Some time ago I watched as Dead Space 3 brought downfall upon one of my favorite series with it's "new, modern ideas", glad that against my expectations after RE6 that this game did not fell into this trap.

It brought a lot of fresh air into play mainly with first person view this time that actualy works pretty well along with great visuals. I also don't mind new playable character instead of all the canon crew, fact that seem to have put a lot of fans into haywire for some reason. 
In parallel with new we have also well implemented return of old stuff like classic save rooms, a lot of backtracking and overall scarciness of resources. It all seem to click with each other just right making RE7 a game that even without zombies is a pretty good RE game but not nececary as good as the 1,2 or 4 to which I go back quite recently.

There is no rose without thorns and here are ones I stumbled upon. Firstly the game is in my opinion quite challenging on normal and above due to mentioned earlier lack of resources mainly bullets. 
That may be just me or time spent getting use to other modern, easier titles but I really struggled at times often running away or pass enemies, some times locking them up in rooms because my ammo count was 0. Making enemies more beefy and resources more scarce is in my opinion as bad difficulty modifier as they get if thats the only thing that changes.

Bosses could use a bit of mechanical touch if you know what I mean, tactic "simply lay into them all you've got" is not that impressive anymore, specially when you ain't got much to lay in the first place when you manage to reach there.

I'm not a fan of nemesis type enemies and while I have nothing against Jack I do think that lesser enemies respawing in the areas up to few times in a row is cr@p, specially if you don't get squat for killing them and that's what happens often.

Finally there is no new game plus scenario which saddens me greatly. I always adored game with that function and I think here similarly to RE4 it could have worked quite good. Since it's not here I see no reason to keep on playing longer than 3-4 clears to check all the dificulties and get all achievements, unless you're speedrunnin' fiend but nature of that is something I will never understand :-)

I hadn't play this game too long, but there is something this game shoved down my throat that I had to spit out to get rid of the foul taste in my mouth. 

As a long term RE/Biohazard player, I've been following the game since RE 1, and got greatly disappointed by the action play style of RE4, 5 and 6. This time, RE 7 is said to return to its root of survival horror, so I was thrilled and purchased this game when I saw it on sale, and anxiously start playing...

But it is not what I expected!

What I hate most about this game is, the enemies never dies, at least not until the devs decided you have too much overdose of the Bakers and felt that it's time to move on to the next boss, so that you can reach the end of game.

In the older games, all you have to do is put a bullet in the zombies' head and BAM! It's dead and stay dead. Until after a relatively long time will it be respawned. In this game, there is no zombies anymore, just the immortal Bakers who kept coming back alive and pestering you again and again. Things get tired soon. At least I am.

A RE/Biohazard game without zombies, T-Virus, Umbrella Corps and Albert Wesker? Nope, Capcom, you have strayed even further away from the roots of the RE/Biohazard series. (Alrighty, the last one is a jab, I can gladly accept a new RE game without Albert Wesker.) Yeah, the puzzles and less actiony play style is great, but the immortal enemies just aren't what I expected. One step forward, two steps back, Capcom.

So far, I'm disappointed.

Edit: Now that I have finished the game, I can talk more about game related issues, but be warned, mild spoiler ahead.

1) Too little diversity in terms of enemies. Mia, Jack Baker, Marguerite Baker, Molded (with varients), Bugs, Hives, Swarms, Eveline (Travis not counted, since he is just a stronger varient of the Molded). That's all. No wonder the devs have to make the Bakers immortal, or else they don't have enough resources to build a full game. I'm also very discontent about not getting a chance to kill the biggest A-hole in the game: Lucas Baker. This, IMHO, is really making this game very imperfect.

2) Extremely slow movement. Yeah, this, paired with most of the time you just can't fight back, is how they introduce the "horror" element in this game. Just like Alan Wake, where the fear stems from extremely sluggish movement and getting gang-banged, the fear is not from the setting and atmosphere of the game but because you are severely in disadvantages and will die most of the time, you're just afraid of dying and have to redo all the chores again and again. I think this is the cheapest way to inject fear into players' feeling, beside cheap jumpscares.

3) Jumpscares, that's the cheapest way of "horror" elements. Yeah, I got surprised a few times, and all these jumpscares have done to me is some cheap scares and followed by some curse and swears towards the devs, nothing else has been done to my mental state. In other words, they only induced anger instead of fear to me.

4) So I have only 1 serum left and must choose between Mia and Zoe. BUT HOW ABOUT ETHAN (aka the player)?! Had he mystically inmmune to Eveline's infection? He did gained the ability to heal and re-connect to amputated limbs, so that means he DID get infected, no?  The game never offers any explaination in this matter. Maybe it's in the extra contents, but I'm just not so interested in playing more "VHS Adventure" anymore.

Edit-edit:
5) After playing through with both path (Mia or Zoe), more unsolved mystery emerged: If you choose to save Zoe, she got eff'ed by Eveline near the wreckage, then the next moment, you (the real life player) will magically became Mia at the shipwreck. The shipwrect!!!! How the h3ll did she end up there from being left to die at the boat house of the Bakers??? No explaination. RE/Biohazard just never need any explaination at all, I guess.

6) Ill-intentional weapon design. Hand guns are all sheetie (except for the Magnum maybe) that don't do squat to enemies (especially against Jack Baker). The first shot gun packs some punch, but has only 4 ammo capacity, and reloading it is slow as molasses, you'll get banged by Jack Baker if you use it during the battle of the 'red dog key'. The second shot gun packs more punch, like, it can cut the ammo consumption by half killing enemies (Jack Baker not included, he is un-killable by any weapon, just put to temporary comma, even with Albert 01 replica), but also only carry half the ammo rounds, so even more slow reload time, if you are caught needing to reload (the gun, that is.) at the most awkward moment, prepare to reload (the game, that is.). The granade launcher is even worse (I didn't even bothered to pick it up on my 2nd playthrough), the worst weapon in the game that only carries one round of ammo and is slower than molasses-ses to reload. Albert 01 Replica (I guess this is how they say "Hey, Albert Wesker is INDEED in this game!") is knida powerful, but 3 ammo capacity is just making it less than useful compared to the initial hand gun that  the poor deputy dropped. The Magnum, while being very powerful and has 7 ammo capcity, is the best weapon in the game only if its ammo isn't so scarece. I estimated that I've never found over 20 ammo for this gun throughout the whole game.

Do you see the pattern now? Most powerful weapons are being limited their usefulness with extremely low ammo capacity and reloading speed in the game, even fully upgraded, still makes you scream and curse when you need to reload, often. The people working at Capcom, especially the RE7 team must have been suffering some psychology imbalance and need medical mental help immediately. They just don't want you to have fun, they wan you to suffer, since they hate their job so much.

Points (4) and (5) shows that RE7 has really sheetie script writting and is rushed and unfinished --  they even have to leave the execution of the greatest A-hole (Lucas Baker) to be done in the DLC extra content!! Also, for someone who never played the game and will waste time in exploring, can finish the game in about 8 hours. According to their "unlockable" requirement, you should be able to finish the game in normal difficulty in less than 4 hours. That's how short and unfinished this game is.

The devs behind RE7 are masters of their craft, the kung-fu masters of horror and fear. 

The build up, the camera angle, the sound, they have perfected this craft and they are hitting you with everything they've got. Its like they did in-depth studies of classic Western movies like 'The Thing', 'Texas Chainsaw Massacre', 'Evil Dead' - and combined that with in-depth studies of their Asian counterparts, and used their veterancy in the developing of horror games to make their Resident Evil magnum opus.  

The RE series, as you know, was often a puzzle adventure in a horror scenario. Those classic RE puzzle elements work just as well in first person, and somehow that is where the real RE nostalgia kicked in for me. This is a true, honorable RE game, even though it is first person. It works, and it works to such an extent that I'm kind of sad that the RE2 remake won't be in first person.

Never before have I experienced those slasher flicks from a PoV view. To be the one dragged through the corridor by some psychopaths is refreshing and horrific. The graphics and environments are so realistic, there was a time where I shot the pistol by accident, spooked myself, and I was so immersed that I could smell the gunsmoke. Multimedia wise, there's nothing like it. There were moments where I had to stop what I was doing and take a moment to honor the graphics and respect the game. I remember playing RE1 on the PS1, and now look at this. How masterfully this game is crafted. Wtf.

About the Season Pass, I got more than I expected from it: worthy epilogue's to the story, a stand-alone Stephen King's 'Misery' inspired type of ordeal, some more or less arcadish type of games, and thankfully nothing related to unlocking (cosmetics). I feel like they made this content with as much passion as they had for the original game. The arcade tongue-in-cheek stuff is a welcome, humane, change to the serious horror they produce. 

A worthy rebirth of RE, recommended, 10/10, a horror masterpiece.

A glorious return to survival horror. While Resident Evil 4 was a very good and successful game, it also spearheaded the downfall of the serie. After the disaster of RE6, terrible spinoff games and movies, Capcom has finally got its act together and delivered a great game. 

The first act is pure survival horror. You have little to no means of defending yourself and you must play a cat and mouse game against stronger enemies. The second act is closer to classic Resident Evil gameplay and the last act (the weakest one) felt more action oriented like the bad RE games.

The game comes with some very good DLCs. There's a little bit for everyone; more story, action, horror, survial mini game...

+ Resident Evil is back to horror (for how long?)
+ Looks and sounds great
+ No QTEs. Not one.
+ Exploring the Baker estate was a lot of fun.
+ Reaslistic item search. Nothing is shiny and obvious. You need to properly look under furniture, between boxes and down containers.
+ The inventory is a good middleground between the Classic RE, RE4 and RE5 systems.

+\- Borrows heavily from other horror games and cinema.

- You have a flashlight, but the game decides for you when you need it, which is annoying.
- It's impossible to unload weapons, so if you find a better pistol, you still need to shoot the old one to empty it.
- Some enemies are boring and unimaginative.
- Coins and bobbleheads are hard to collect without a guide. (like the emblems from RE4 and RE5)
- I had to fiddle a lot with the graphic settings to get the best possible image quality and framerate.  With the default settings, the game was a blurry pixelated mess.

Some will be stymied by the gameplay; but altogether I'd say this is a worthwhile horror experience, with some nice touches and pretty cool ideas.

It starts out strong with the Baker family mystery, then tries to connect with the RE universe. And this is where the game starts to lose some of it's momentum but then towards the end, starts to pick up again a bit. Very nice survival horror game with good atmospheric graphics and plenty of disgusting gore and tense atmosphere. A lot of inspiration drawn from Hills have eyes and Evil Dead films. The only major gripe I have with this game is the extremely uneven texture work. You can have quite decent textures but then you can have textures that look like PS1 era resolution. When the overall texture quality is decent, it really breaks some of the immersion when suddenly some textures look like wet diarrhea smeared onto surfaces. It can be difficult to even see what is the texture supposed to be like when it's zoomed so hard on the screen. Would be great if we got a PC texture pack but that's most likely not going to happen.

I ran this game on full settings on a gtx970m which is roughly the equivalent of a geforce 600 series chip and at 1080p game ran smooth for me. Supersampling was off, everything else turned max. I have seen claims that say turning supersampling on high would make those muddy and poor resolution textures look sharp, but these are trolls who don't understand how that works. Supersampling can only help in aliasing, not in texture resolution as the texture size remains what it is and just get supersampled onto the screen. This makes absolutely no impact on blurring of textures except on very far away surfaces where the supersampling can help make textures look a bit more detailed. Considering the performance impact, it makes no sense turning this setting on and if you have a strong computer, just run the game on DSR 4k from Nvidia control panel.

I would rate this game a 7.5/10 due to the fact that we don't have many quality survival horror games and the parts that are strong, are actually quite strong and able to carry over the weaker parts of the game. This is a console port so controlling on a mouse feels awful, but it does not matter as this is not a fast moving action game where you need to have good shooting mechanics. Definitely a recommended from me.

As a true Resident Evil fan, firstly I want to say that I wasn't expecting much from this game because of the changes they made in this episode. All the episodes in the series before 7th episode was either in OTS or fixed camera angle, so I thought after they ruined the series with 6th, now they're trying to change the original concept of the game. But I was wrong. Actually, they went back to roots and playthrough is a lot of like the original episodes if you exclude FPS camera perspective. It's not a bad thing they changed the camera perspective, but I still prefer OTS or fixed angle.

**This is my second review of RE7. My first was written when I was 6 or 7 hours in and was negative. I have deleted that and am switching to positive but with some serious caveats. Also this review is for the base game only and does not deal with the "Not a Hero" DLC or any of the season pass DLC.**

To summarize why I initially gave RE7 a negative review:
 
Most of the combat in the first several hours involved boss characters, specifically the various members of the family inhabiting the series of buildings in which the beginning part was set. I did not enjoy these parts of the game. You see, in RE7 the main antagonists are somehow able to reassemble themselves after serious injuries. I mean extreme mutilation and loss of limb, not mere bullet wounds or broken bones.  It was frustrating for me to think I had defeated a boss only for them to return later, even more powerful than they were before.
 
I nearly lost all patience with the second boss  who required an obscene amount of firepower to defeat. I swear I unloaded four or five tanks of flamethrower fuel, multiple shotgun shells and 44 magnum rounds, everything I brought with me PLUS what I could find in the area where the battle took place. Still, this was not enough. I ended up having to go back to an earlier area and unlock the grenade launcher, which enabled me to deal sufficient damage and overcome that boss.

In addition, the early parts of RE7 did not run very well on my system. With a GTX 970, 16GB RAM and an i5 4690k I should not have experienced frequent drops in the framerate, especially considering I had several settings either turned off or set to low. However, later parts performed much better, probably due to the fact that the environment became darker, less intricately detailed, and more confined.
 
It wasn't just the performance that improved after about 7 hours. I also found the gameplay and story much more enjoyable. RE7 really found it's footing in the final third, starting with the boat section and up to the ending. I felt that on the boat I was experiencing high quality survival horror gameplay. The game gave me just enough resources to squeak my way through and required a good deal of planning before making my next move. Eventually I found a machine gun and remote bombs and got to feel powerful for a little while before that part of the game came to an end. My only complaint regarding the boat section is that it was arguably the least visually interesting of all the environments RE7 offered.

I would describe the rest of RE7 as competent and generally enjoyable. After the boat there was a brief section in a mine which lasted only for about an hour. I don't have much to say about that part except that it had some intense moments of combat with multiple enemies attacking at once.
 
The final part of RE7 was even shorter than the mine. There was no combat outside of the final boss battle, which I did not find very compelling. First I had to chase them back and forth across the game's beginning stage, a rather tedious affair. Once I finally confronted them I only had to shoot them in the face a dozen times or so and that was all. I only died once and felt very little satisfaction when I defeated them. There was a nice little plot twist involving this final boss, though, so at least it had that going for it.
 
To quickly conclude my review I will say that RE7 certainly had its moments of well-executed survival horror and is in my opinion the best game in the series since 4. It's unfortunate that it took several hours to get to those moments, and that most of them occured in the most visually boring setting of the entire game. If you're willing to look past the flaws I've pointed out then this game could be worth giving a chance, especially if you can get it on sale like I did.

[h1]Back to the roots[/h1]

Latest entry in Resident evil series. In my opinion Resident evil went downhill starting with Resident evil 4. Then the fifth game was meh, they tried to do an action game with old controls which don’t work well together, although I must say it was pretty fun game if played in coop. I don’t even have anything to say about Resident evil 6, it’s just bad. But Resident evil 7 goes back to the roots. But it also comes with the drawbacks of old games.

The game is good old Resident evil. Scary house the size of a factory with a bunch of rooms and some of them being locked. You must find items and keys to open the locked doors and progress through the plot. There’s a lot of backtracking and hidden items. Speaking of story i like it very much. If old games were all about zombies, this game is about crazy family. The family members will try to kill you and chase you. When you reach a certain point in the game you fight one family member as a boss.
Another difference is of course first person view. I personally prefer third person view but I must agree first person view works really good in this game. It adds some immersion and makes the game more scary.

Graphically Resident evil 7 looks amazing. Character models are very well done, cut-scenes look great and most importantly lighting is very good. Lighting is one of the most important aspects in horror games, it creates the atmosphere and this is done right in this game.
Environments look really good too. Dark rooms, scary gardens, child’s room or extremely terrifying tunnels. It has everything.

Sound design is another aspect these developers done right. Voice acting is great and special sound effects send the shivers through your spine.

I don’t like few things in this game. First is inventory management. Yeah I get all that “back to the roots” thing, but seriously it’s annoying and doesn’t make sense. Why the hell a key, a simple keys takes one slot in the inventory? I get it that shotgun takes more space than a handgun, but why two keys and a coin takes the same amount of space as shotgun?
Now another thing I don’t like is much is all that invincible enemy chasing you. Yes it’s thrilling and fun for some time. But if he kills you and you try again there’s no thrill anymore, it’s just tedious and annoying. I prefer taking my time to explore, to walk freely.
I also dislike those black monsters, not because they’re hard to kill or anything, but I dislike the design choice. Just give regular zombies, slow walking moaning zombies instead of some black mass from the Venom comics.
And i'll throw in a technical issue some people are having. For some strange reason it's not possible to take screenshots in this game and steam overlay is very bright. I haven't found a solution to fix this. It may have something to do with an HDR TV connected to my PC but i'm not going to unplug it. Every other game works perfectly fine.

Overall a really nice horror game every horror fan should play. And if you’re a fan of old Resident evil games this is a must have. Scary atmosphere, great character design and good sound makes this one of the best modern horror game.

Terrific return to horror and a very atmospheric game with tight design that creates great pacing and tension, and I say that as someone who's enjoyed their more typical (and usually much dumber) outings like RE6 and Revelations 2. 9/10. 

Criticisms: 
- Some very "gamey" elements. I don't mind the "Resident Evil" bits like herbs that heal you and tape recorders for saving, but stuff like the collectible coins you can pick up to unlock special boxes with powerups are just immersion breaking. 
- You have to unlock the hard mode, which from what I've heard does things that would actually improve the experience like having limited saves. 
- Normal enemies that are just thrown in there for you to fight are kind of lame even if they make sense plotwise. 
- The ending starts getting weak, both gameplay (it becomes more combat oriented and you start tripping over supplies, where before supply management was part of what made the game so effective) and story wise (even if it does make sense, Capcom starts tying it into the Resident Evil lore a bit too much, which doesn't fit in well here)
- It's a little short. 

Finally, almost none of the DLC is worth playing. 
- Nightmare, Ethan Must Die, and Jack's 55th birthday are just minigames that I didn't bother with, but maybe you would enjoy them. 
- Bedroom is a decent puzzle game but pretty short and has some poorly written "gamey" elements (wish I had another word to describe this). 
- 21 is literally just Blackjack with some torture porn. 
- Daughters is horrible and the only one I recommend actively avoiding because what it does ruins the experience you had with the actual game (seriously). 
The only two with any substance are Not a Hero and End of Zoe, which are respectively:
- A very typical Resident Evil outing with Chris Redfield with strong Call of Duty vibes that does neither of those things well, partly because of the (intentionally) rough combat mechanics of the game that don't fit, and partly because of the bad writing and lame setpieces. They seem to have went back and had the typical Capcom team do their usual thing (but more lazily), which again makes no sense given this new type of Resident Evil game and actually makes it disappointing that they spent resources making new maps and everything for this. 
- An interesting idea for a DLC that mixes up the formula within this new engine, but doesn't have enough stuff in it to keep it from getting boring quickly and is also badly written (not to mention doesn't make sense given the canon of the game). 

This kind of ♥♥♥♥♥ with me a little, because I loved the base game and would like to throw more money at Capcom for it, but buying the DLC would give them the wrong signals. 

Nonetheless, to reiterate, yes, buy the base game.
