[b]Terror In First-Person[/b]

I hated Resident Evil 6. As much as I loved 5 (I completed it with a friend at least 3 times including the highest difficulty setting) I was not very fond of the 6th instalment of this franchise. Actually, I gave up on it. I was not interested in the Revelations titles nor in the upcoming HD remake of RE 2. In general, this is how I approach Capcom these days. I played Street Fighter 4 a lot but I do not intend to play the latest episode and as much as I had fun slashing zombies in Dead Rising 3 I am not going to do the same in Dead Rising 4.

But I know something changed back in 2017. The idea of moving from third-person to first-person in Resident Evil felt appealing, therefore, I decided to give this episode (not the series) a chance. It was easy to make this decision considering the many horror games released in this genre (special mention goes to the excellent Outlast titles).

[b]Dinner At The Baker's[/b]

Our protagonist, Ethan, goes to Louisiana to look for his long-disappeared girlfriend, Mia. As all clues point to a farmhouse it is there where we encounter the Baker family that consists of lunatics or simply just cannibals. Horror fans will appreciate the dinner scene which (along with other scenes) emits a certain vibe that reminded me of Texas Chainsaw Massacre. Another thing is how challenging it will be to deal with the Bakers - every encounter is a boss battle and requires great patience on your end. 

Most of the scenes and action will take place in or around the house. There is a lot of emphasis on exploration so much so that you may return to a key area hours later just because you obtained a lock pick which can finally open that drawer in the corner of a room almost forgotten. This often makes you smile as by checking the map that says the only unexplored dark area is called "storage" you know you'll find items to your liking there.

[b]The All Too Familiar RE Things[/b]

It wouldn't be Resident Evil if you were not able to find a lot of herbs and combine them with special fluid to create the means to heal yourself. We also have limited inventory and saving is only possible in certain areas (though we do not have limits on regular difficulty settings when it comes to the number of saves). 

Monsters will often appear almost out of nowhere and you have to make do with scenarios where you will be hurt. In fact, the game gives you the option to raise your arms and by doing so protect yourself - you will still be damaged, though. This is an interesting and at the same time a terrifying idea - the sense of fear that you cannot escape from being grabbed by monsters. While running is an option I invested time in learning how to time my "guard" stance perfectly beside properly aiming for the head.

Some of the things you experience during gameplay (including the above) can be annoying but then again this is a survival horror game, after all. Limited ammunition and healing items will make you learn how to tread carefully. In fact, not everything is limited that much - you just need to check every corner. Really! You may find a useful item on a bookshelf next to the last book in the row.

[b]Fright In Photorealism[/b]

The game looks tremendously beautiful. You will notice it immediately as Ethan gets out of his car upon arrival. It looks so realistic that you might just end up throwing up if you happen to play right after dinner. Case in point is the fridge which is full of already expired food and a lot of worms. You also have to rummage through the toilet and even a bathtub full of disgusting black liquid. 

I also liked the opportunity of seeing Ethan's legs when looking down or how he raises his hand when approaching a door so that he can push it open. Same goes for hitting the wall. Minor things only but they can greatly help with the immersion. There are a lot of items we can pick up and by rotating and carefully examining them we can find more clues or items to continue the story. 

[b]Ethan's Ladder[/b]

To see through Ethan (and Mia's) journey RE 7 requires us to invest at least 10-12 hours. Completing the game and collecting all the files, antique coins and finding and destroying all the hidden bobbleheads will grant us some great rewards that await us in the game's so-called item box which we have to regularly check during the story if we want to store items instead of dismissing them.

With extra firepower and other gear available to make our struggle with the Bakers easier we can pick the Madhouse difficulty to face RE 7's ultimate challenge. I say ultimate as not only does everybody do greater damage but the creators changed enemy placement and even limited the number of saves possible. I, personally, was satisfied with two walkthroughs on "normal" only which was good as the game offers 2 endings anyway.

[b]Résumé[/b]

Resident Evil 7 is a terrifyingly (pun intended) good horror game. I picked it not because I was the fan of the franchise (as explained at the beginning I am actually not) but because I simply love the combination of horror and FPS. So, if this was enough for me to complete it I believe there is no need to justify my recommendation for Resident Evil fans.

It spooked me
It's by Capcom
It's Resident Evil
I'm happy.

I have to say that I am mildly disappointed by the game. I played the introductory demo version first and really liked it because it did not seem to be a regular RE game (collecting thrash, moon logic) but it turned out to be one. That said, I liked a lot of things about it. I liked the atmosphere, characters and story. I don't think I will play this game again. I definitely would not say it was bad but it was not for me.

I can't say that it kept me interested. There were a lot of things that felt like you've experienced them before. What I am glad about is that the game is not heavy on jumpscares and goes more for the lingering unease. The molded enemies were just easy to avoid instead of fighting in the late game and overall stakes just did not seem too high. The boss fights were just bad, with exception of the last, climactic one and the garage one.

Would I recommend it? Yes, to someone who is into the series, yes to someone who is into narrative over gameplay. No to someone who is not a big adventure games enthusiast.

If your like me and prefer FPS, here's your chance to get into the excellent Resident Evil franchise without having to rewire your brain for weird controller/camera controls.

To say that the Resident Evil series went a bit off the rails in the last 10 years could be considered an understatement. What started out as a tense fight for survival inside a zombie infested mansion in 1996 turned into a convoluted universe of shadowy organizations, terrorists, and virus-based bioweapons which the player cut their way through in something more akin to an action-horror third person shooter more than anything else.

Resident Evil 7 clearly sought to reboot the series and return it to its roots: slowing down the pace, shrinking the scale, and focusing on creating an atmosphere that's tense and incredibly eerie as protagonist Ethan tries to survive a literal house of horrors in the Louisiana swamp - hunted by the infected family members who aren't too hospitable to outsiders.

The game does the aforementioned incredibly well and has some seriously skin-crawling and tense moments throughout - emphasized by great lightning effects, unsettling art direction, and the adoption of the first-person camera but Resident Evil 7 isn't without its flaws to be sure.

A surprisingly short completion time (perhaps 7 or 8 hours) and some areas that can become frustratingly difficult to get through hold the game back from being perfect but thankfully neither completely ruins the experience. The DLC offered is also a bit underwhelming as much of the Banned Footage offerings are mini-games, survival/horde modes, and a very brief story-related bit while the Not a Hero and End of Zoe portions ultimately feel tacked on but do provide some closure into what happens after Ethan's trek through the Baker estate.

All-in-all the return of the franchise to survival-horror is a welcome change and one that I hope Capcom continues with going forward.

[h1]Short version: 75% (89% with DLCs)[/h1]
Resident Evil 7 tries to bring a new kind of action-suspension horror into the palette of this colourful series, but its schizophrenic nature also means that every player will find almost as many irritating elements in it as excellent ones.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is another attempt from Capcom to reinvent this long-running series. While its first-person viewpoint is hardly new in the franchise, many other additions in its gameplay are—granted, they are hardly innovations; RE7 mostly just integrates successful elements from other popular horror titles.

Initially, it feels akin to Outlast; we play as an everyman looking for his missing wife in a grimy, old, dirty abandoned building in rural Louisiana, running from one scripted torture scene to the other.
This is a façade though, since the meat of the game is reminiscent of classic Resident Evils, where we explore a large and a smaller maze-like house, looking for key items, ammo, or crafting material, while dodging or killing monsters created by a freakish scientific experiment.
The endgame evokes F.E.A.R., surprisingly, with a similar final antagonist and gameplay closer to classic action-packed first-person shooting than any kind of horror.

The result is something where everyone can find something to enjoy, but they are unlikely to like all parts equally. Moreover, some annoyances are difficult to get past: things like slow and uncancellable player animations, painfully low enemy variety, or an astonishing amount of glaring plot holes—even for a franchise known for its cheesy low-grade writing.

Still, the game as a whole is immensely enjoyable and—thanks to its unlockables, Madhouse mode, and achievements—it has a high replay value. Additionally, the DLCs considerably increase the entertainment factor, but not to the point where we can forget or forgive the game’s flaws.

If you want to play as a complete idiot, have limitied control of your actions, and have to solve stupid fetch puzzles, then this game is for you. If you want an intelligent , enjoyable game look elsewhere.

I actually played this game in both non-VR and then VR. I wish this game had native VR, but I don't think that will happen. I will not be focusing on the review of the game per se, but the experience in VR using Vorpx versus the non-VR experience. My personal opinion is that this was a good game, a good rebound for the Resident Evil series, but it's not a great game. I would rate it a 7/10 personally. Nice story cinematics, some interesting mechanics, but at the end of the day you are either okay with sluggish gameplay or not and I just don't like the sluggish movements / actions, which I think has held the series back from greatness.

Anyways, VR with Vorpx is not great with this game. You really need to look at YouTube videos on setting up this game with Vorpx to get it to even look okay. Out of the box, it barely works. So after spending a good amount of time watching videos and tinkering with the settings, the game will work ... sort of. You will have to downgrade the visuals. Maybe if you have a 1080 TI you will have a different opinion, but on my 1060 it just never looked great.

The 3D effects were nice, it is full VR with geometry settings. However, the FOV will be greatly reduced. Weapons will never look placed correctly. You really need to see as much on the screen as you can with this game and there's so many times you'll be looking at menu, so you'll have to go in and out with the Vorpx shortcut keys so the menu HUD is visible. 

It really takes away from the enjoyment of the game. I think I enjoyed this game in Non-VR more than VR. It just looked nicer. 3D effects are great, but not at the expense of frame rates dipping and the world looking lower resolution. I don't mind some degradation, but in this game it really was noticeable. 

VR Rating 5/10. Really not worth it unless you're curious. Even then I would recommend you have at least a 1080.

I'm glad that Capcom decided to take a leap of faith and try something new with the dying Resident Evil franchise after the Resident Evil 6 flopped, because it actually paid off for them.

Resident Evil 7 goes back to the survival horror roots with the addition of a new claustrophobic 1st person view. It's because of this 1st person view that why the game was compared to the Outlast when it was first announced, but after playing it through myself I can agree with other that these two games are totally different from another. In Outlast you can only run and hide, while in RE7 you can run, avoid or fight back. It's all up to you how you want to approach the enemies. Usually avoiding them is the best solution to preserve ammo for the bosses.

The story is also quite interesting. You're playing as Ethan Winters, an engineer who's following the traces of his wife, Mia, who went missing 3 years ago. Everyone thought that Mia has been dead for the past 3 years, but one day Ethan got an email from her saying that she needs help and she even provided an adress where she's being held. Ethan follows the trace to that address to this run down hillbilly manor and so the game begins.

I'm not gonna go any deeper with the story, because I don't want to give you any spoilers, but I'll say that its well worth to go through it.

A word of warning though, as I mentioned before we have a new protagonist this time, meaning that the old familiar Resident Evil characters like Jill and Chris are replaced with new set of characters. At first I thought that this is too big of a change from the past, but after actually playing the game I don't really mind it anymore. Sometimes the change is needed if you want to spice things up. You can find some hidden documents that links the game to the Resident Evil universe, but I'm not gonna spoil them for you any further.

Gameplay is absolutely horrifying with the new 1st person view mdoe. Again, some people might hate this change, but sometimes the change is needed in order to spice things up. Lets not forget how the Resident Evil 4 was also criticized for how it turned from fixed camera angles to 3rd person view, but people became fond of it.

Overall, I was a little sceptical for how much the game had changed from its predecessors, but after playing it through I'm loving the outcome. Resident Evil is back baby !

Cons:

- Too short, you can clear it in ~10 hours
- Can't play on hardest difficulty without first playing through it at least once on easy or normal difficulty
- Resources such as healing items and ammo are slightly too common to find

Do I recommend?
Absolutely yes if you're into survival horror games. If you can put aside the fact that the familiar characters are replaced with new ones and that the game is now in 1st person view, then you're into one hell of a ride.
I hear that the game is even better on the VR, but I don't have a VR headset so I couldn't test it out myself.

Verdict: 9 / 10 - Would be 10/10 if the game didn't lose some its traction towards the end.

Replayed the game recently after 8 years, and I'm still in awe of how this entry revitalized the series. From the co-op action shooter that was RE6 to coming back to the roots of the survival horror genre but bringing in the first-person perspective on a new engine. Haven't touched the Resident Evil series in a while but wanted to replay this before the release of Requiem. They even added ray tracing to this game, which, to be fair, breaks the lighting if you turn it off. If you're using an older GPU, you should go for the older version in the public beta branch. If you have a card that can handle ray tracing, the performance hit isn't very big. I comfortably ran the game in 1440p with all the highest settings on RX6700xt in ~70-110 FPS. All the mechanics, including combat, crafting system, inventory management, puzzles, and level design, complement each other. Although the game is linear, exploration is rewarding, and the level design makes backtracking very easy. Shooting heads is really satisfying, though it can be a bit tricky with the enemies erratic behavior after getting damaged. If you're licking every wall and exploring every crack, you'll get enough resources to get through the game (at least on normal difficulty). The game is still worth every penny even at full price, although with how often you can find it on discount, it's wiser to wait for one.

Hmmm - this is a rewrite of my original review, having finished it now. And...well, it's still a negative (obviously!)

1) The game runs like dookie, with freezing and stuttering happening far too often. It's far from the most visually amazing game, and there isn't all that much going on in terms of enemy numbers onscreen, so quite why it has performance issues I don't know. 

I could be in an area running through it, and it will be fine. And then that same area will be jerky later on, and nothing has changed.

2) It's a rather lacklustre experience. Since I've completed it it can't be too bad, but it's pretty underwhelming in every way. I paid £12 for it, and it was passable, occasionally ever so slightly exciting. But if it wasn't on sale I'd have been pee'd off with it, and that's why it gets a downvote from me.

>> The enemies aren't interesting in any way - either to look at, or to fight. And the game never manages to build up any tension whenever they're present. That's a pretty big failing in a title that wants to be in your face horror (quite literally, given that it's in first person). 

It's only the satisfying weapons that make combat enjoyable. The change in perspective might have felt like a way to freshen up a series that was in need of rejuvenating, but they just lack the ability to make it thrilling. 

Most fps survival horror titles (these days) don't give you any means to fight back, and with RE 7 it's apparent why that is. When you have limited ammo it's frustrating and tedious. When you have enough to let rip with your guns it's constrained by the lack of intensity - small environments, few enemies and pedestrian combat.

>> Boss battles are all dull affairs in terms of the gameplay mechanics, and one of them is the most ridiculously stupid looking thing ever seen in a Resident Evil game. Which, considering it's often been pretty badly designed, is quite an achievement. 

>> It's not scary, which is another big failing in a horror game. Many of it's supposed "scares" are poorly done, with them being unable to hide how they are cheating to achieve the effect. Like: looking around a corner briefly, and seeing that it's not large enough for someone to hide in (and also happens to clearly be empty!). And then someone magically pops out of there anyway, just a little bit too late on the timing to really be effective.

It''s understandable with one of the characters, as there is a reason for them being able to appear and disappear, but with the rest it's just cheap and lazy attempts to spook you. One other example is: someone you're following goes ahead, and to stop you witnessing the moment where they get "abducted" the game simply throws up an invisible barrier to halt your progress. 10 seconds later you can suddenly move forward, and they've vanished. An utterly pathetic way to facilitate this! 

This isn't a bad game, but for the price it's just so mediocre that I can't recommend it.

Resident Evil 7 is a first person survival horror. You must navigate an "abandonned" farmhouse is search of your wife Mia who disappeared 3 years ago. Classic tropes from the first RE trilogy make a comeback with strict inventory management, neat puzzles, claustrophobic enviroment and memorable cast of characters. Along the way, you can find base material and combine them togheter to make health bottles or ammo.

The art and graphics are as awesome as you'd expect from a triple-A company like Capcom. Every square inch of every room have been polished very well. I've tried very hard to look for an overlooked detail/missing texture/etc. There's none of that here. There's no copy&paste job here. The graphics and overall map design is probably this game's strongest point. Last but not least are the character's faces and facial animation. Stellar work right there. Every emotions displayed by characters feels believable and doesn't feel overdone or cheesy. It's just right. The art and graphics alone get an A+.

The ambient sounds too are very well done. You will often hear banging and floorboard cracking in the distance, making you doubt your safety. Gun sounds are great too. I liked running around with a shotgun and hear the metal clanking of the weapon. Again, this shows the amount of polish this game went through. However, something that kinda annoyed me was the constant panting from the character you're playing. You're just walking around and your character is panting and weezing like it just jogged a 100km marathon. Mia's panting is huh... a bit too sexy for an horror game, especially that part in the tanker, jeez... I had to lower the sound to, you know, concentrate on the game... :D Lastly, I think the theme song from the intro/credit video is cringe-worthy. What is this dubstep/trap bs that sounds like Enya on steroid? Really, really cringe-worthy.

Now let's dive into other details of RE7 that I more or less disliked.

First is the enemy variety. The Family by itself is very good and each of their encounters are well tailored, no doubt about that. However, it's what's in between that quite lackluster and kinda boring. You fight these things called "Molded" which looks like some of the enemies you fought in previous RE titles (looking at Regeneradors from RE4). There are only 3 types of these Molded: the regular one, the one with the blade arm and the spider one. There are 2 other enemy types but they are fixed to a location or are special encounters. If you're acustomed to the enemy variety of previous RE's, RE7 will disappoint you.

Second is the gunplay. Animations and sound are cool, but guns don't feel powerfull except Shotgun. This calls back to the first issues, the enemies. They are litteral bullet sponges, requiring many bullets to the head before dying. It's annoying to Quick Turn every 5 seconds to get some distance from the enemies. Even the Grenade Launcher is underwhelming and very costly to craft bullets. Had there been more enemy variety, the gunplay and the difference in power would have been felt. Here, you just shoot-shoot-quickturn-run-quickturn-shoot-shoot and repeat until it's dead. A side-dodging mechanic could have been cool, but what's the point with so little enemy type?

Third is the lenght of the game. There's a handfull of locations to explore and they're not that big. They are well designed and polished, yet by the time the credit rolls in, you just wish there was more. Backtracking in previous RE's was thing. Re-exploring previous locations to open that one door you couldn't open. Remember in RE1 when you go back in the mansion and then the Hunters started spawning? This is the kind of thing that made re-exploring fun; you just didn't know what to expect around the corner, even in familiar territory. RE7 does this thing, but very, VERY breifly with no new enemy, allowing you to go back to the farmhouse to open animal key doors.

Lastly, 2 little technical details. You cannot skip cutscenes, so if you die, you'll have to endure the previous cutscene again. This makes replaying through the game a bit annoying. 

Then there's sloppy controller support. You can see the keyboard button layout and customize it fully, but there's none of that controllers. You can't see the layout and you can't customize anything, except for inverting Joystick click (lol what the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥?). And guess what, my ultimate gaming pet peeve sin's in there: Sprinting is bound to Left Joystick click... YOU WILL BURN IN THE FIRES OF HELL, I HATE YOU. STOP DOING THAT ♥♥♥♥, GAME DEVS.

People keeps saying this is a return to form for RE. That must be because RE6 was so bad. But this, this is just an okay-ish horror game that borrowed a big name it didn't deserve.

With this game, RE finally got back on track to being a survival horror game with puzzle elements and an immersive story, but retains some of the action elements that fans liked from the installments that followed in the wake of the original game without going quite as overboard as some of the later installments did. 

The Bad: 
- Certain Story Elements are confusing and may initially be mistaken as poor game design. They begin to make sense as you play the game. 
- The entire story can't be fully grasped without playing the DLC. 
- The DLC elements will 100% spoil the main story, but the main story is difficult to understand without the DLC content. 
- As usual with RE games, guns are basically nonsensical. The G17 uses the same ammo as the 1911 (which isn't impossible, but just somewhat implausible given the latter deals more damage). The G17 only holds 10 rounds, when the gun was literally named after its ammo capacity - and so on. 
- Regular difficulty is already fairly easy - Easy Mode is a total breeze. The game difficulties were made with console players in mind, and the 1st person design is much easier to work with on PC, so the difficulty levels are somewhat unbalanced for PC. I recommend playing on hard mode if you are used to 1st person shooters. 


The Good: 
- Best voice acting and screen play of any RE game I have played to date. 
- Minimal over-the-top action sequences that make you think you're playing an anime. 
- The story starts out feeling more like a Stephen King novel and doesn't really lose that vibe until towards the end. 
- Believable characters that act in a way humans would - with some exceptions that are largely explained by the story as you go on, but initially, somewhat, breaks your immersion, but the later start to make sense and gives you a great feeling of the "story coming together". 
- There's less obvious "Japanese tropes" and odd '90ies tropes inserted into the story - the game feels like an American horror-story until the end of the story when it sort of ties into the actual Resident Evil franchise - you don't have those moments where you squint and wonder exactly what the writers were thinking that made other resident evil games kinda laughable at times. 

The DLC is amazing. 
The DLC that features the character "Zoe" functions as a prequel to the actual main story, explaining exactly what happened prior to the game starting. 
The DLC that features Chris Redfield uses the same game mechanics but plays out as a tactical action packed little wrap-up story, which is a great way to work out your frustrations from having been, more or less, helpless for most of the main story. 
The DLC that features the Baker Uncle is my personal favorite - you go from being the prey to being the hunter - amazingly hilarious and nearly impossible to take seriously, but such a great way to end the game, relieving all of that tension you've built up.

Capcom is finally back in their element, and I hope they'll continue to expand and bolster this formula going forward.

Just as a disclaimer, it took me THREE atempts and two months to change my opinion that RE7 is not a total piece of crap which has nothing in common with the actual franchise. Three. Having stopped twice at about the same location (at the main hall after the garage fight) I was more than reluctant to give this game a third chance. In the end it was a good decision because the game does get better. 
All the talk you hear from Capcom and RE7-fanboys about "going back to its roots" is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though. Except for the one fact that we have evil residents in this installment.

-----------------------

Story: 6.5/10 
[i]Ethan Winters is drawn to a derelict plantation in Dulvey, Louisiana, by a message from his wife, Mia, who has been presumed dead for three years. He finds Mia imprisoned in the basement of a seemingly abandoned house...[/i]
The core story is nothing too special, heck it's a weaker version of Silent Hill 2's plot. However, it is something you can work with and not shabby at all.

Sound: 4.5/10
Let's be honest, sound-wise Resident Evil was never near the top, there were one or two good and/or memorable songs in there (usually the save room track). But other than that they were always rather uninspiring. 
I've played through the game four times now and am not confident enough trying to recognize if a song is from Resident Evil 7 or not. 
      
Graphics: 9/10
I give you that Capcom, the game looks damn fine. Locations look creepy, monsters look scary for the most part. So yes, good one.
           
Presentation: 7/10
The game's atmosphere is actually well done. Fitting locations, narrow corridors, you never know what is behind the next door. The suspension and the need to know how this all happened. No complaints in that regard.
But let's look at the facts here, it was promised to go back to the roots. What did we, the players, get in the end? Half baked atempts to copy things we saw recently (P.T.) and an approach to the Outlast/Amnesia/whatever crowd. 
Then we get to see cutscenes which could come straight out of the movie "Texas Chainsaw Massacre". 
And let's not forget the main antagonist and the whole mind controlling, a trope out of RE4 and the newer titles. Gosh, I hope when RE8 is coming close to its release, they won't spout so much crap as they did before RE7, and RE6, and RE5...
But other than that the actual presentation really IS good, just not for a RE game.
      
Gameplay: 6.5/10
Gameplay is like you remembered it from the older titles. Tank controls, no masses of ammunition and puzzles you have to solve here and there. Sluggish but fun to play, you get used to it pretty fast.
I can't get over the fact though that they had to include a first person perspective. In WHAT way has this anything to do with the back to the roots claim? In the end the only thing Capcom wanted to achieve with that was to appease to the Outlast and P.T. crowd plus showcase that annoying VR gimmick (which you can't even use as a PC player). 
"More immersion than the other games" you wish, all it did, was to make the gameplay more annying.  

Replayability: MEDIUM 
Achievement-wise you will need a few playthroughs to get everything. And while you go through the same game more than once you realize nothing shocks you anymore. Monsters are where you remembered them, cutscenes are scripted and the jump scares don't make you flinch in the least.
But there's a twist. Go with the "Madhouse" difficulty to get a fresh RE7 experience with new enemy placements, items at different locations and so on. It's worth it.    
--------------------
[b]Final rating: 67/100[/b]

In the end I do recommend the game under a different brand/name. But even then, it's not the gaming revolution some people claim it to be. All the game mechanics you can find in here, we've seen better in other games.

But when the solution is to steal plots of american horror movies (Texas Chainsaw Massacre, SAW,...) or to mimic gameplay methods which are cool right now with the crowd (runaway simulators, P.T.), then just stop. Stop bastardizing the franchise any further and just give it a new name. Everyone will be happy.
And in that regard I just cannot recommend it as what it had to be: A Resident Evil game.

I do have high hopes though for the remake of Resident Evil 2. The new RE engine in itself is pretty good, RE7 showcased that. I'll be interested how the final product WITHOUT the first person perspective will be, in my opinion it can only be better.

As a fan of the series and someone who has played all of the mainline games before it (1-6), I would say that this is the game that most faithfully captures the essence of the original game, while still taking a fresh take on it.

All of the core elements of the first three games in series are there. Finding keys to unlock previously locked areas, solving puzzles, backtracking, inventory management, save rooms, etc. 

The biggest difference is that the fixed camera and tank controls have been replaced with a first person perspective, fixing some of the frustrations. As a result of this change, rooms and corridors are more confined and darker, while some interesting stuff is done with what can and cannot be seen on the screen in order to induce the fear of not knowing what might be hiding behind the corner. The sound design also helps with achieving that horror aspect, with squeaky doors, stuff falling on the floor and environmental effects keeping the tension high.  

My only two complains are that the main plot of the game is weak, and the lack of replayability. Completing the main game will unlock the Not A Hero campaign, which lasts for about 2-3 hours and is more action packed, but other than that the lack of a mercenaries mode and the few unlockables means that there little reason to get back to the game after you have finished it, unless you want to do some speedruns.

On a more technical note, the new RE Engine is absolutely fantastic. Graphics look great and the game runs smoothly on my GTX 1060 / i7 laptop at the highest settings without any hinges. 

Overall, I would say that I really enjoyed this game and I would definitely recommend it to anyone, series veterans and newcomers alike, as this is the most accessible instalment to date.

The phrase "Back to the roots" has been thoroughly and completely run into the ground.  But it's actually true in this case, as someone who has been a long time fan of the series, Resident Evil 7 is the closest we've gotten to a proper sequel since 3/Code Veronica were released oh so long ago.  This is not a big dumb action game, it's a big dumb Resident Evil survival horror game.  

It's an incredibly well-executed blend of old and new elements, adding a pinch of modern horror while elevating the classic RE combat and item management in a way that is not always perfect, but is never annoying, unlike in other contemporary horror titles like Outlast you are very rarely shoehorned into a passive role where sneaking is your ONLY option.  While combat may not be the BEST decision when dealing with the Bakers, it's nice to play a spooky horror game with a near-immortal opponent that doesn't result in insta-death upon being spotted and doesn't make you a complete puss who can't fight back.  

The plot also bears special mention, as it's basically a well told version of a classic RE game, with antagonists who have motivations that make sense and characters who progress and develop over the course of the narrative.  You get to slowly peel back the sordid mystery of the Baker's homestead, and it's all very engaging.  Despite being rather separated from the RE lore, it remains connected and uses the tropes established through it's predecessors to great effect, keeping what works and twisting what doesn't so it remains fresh and well executed.  

For all the praise the game does get for returning to the classic roots, the one thing I think that they could have done without emulating is the short length.  I managed to complete my first playthrough on 'normal' with a few deaths and thorough exploration in roughly 6 hours, and that felt criminally short.  But 'I want more of it' is hardly a damning complaint, and I really can't recommend the game enough to both new and old time fans.  Here's hoping Capcom keeps going with this direction, I'd be very excited to see a sequel develop this style more.

[h1]A new Resident Evil after RE4![/h1]

After playing RE5, I didn't even touch RE6 because the game felt more and more like an action game.
But this, this is different. If you're in doubt because you didn't quite like the last two iterations of the franchise, just go ahead and buy this one because you won't be disappointed!

The game starts off with what I think is the scariest part of the game: you've just entered the house and you start exploring in order to figure out what's going on. The amount of moments and feelings that get under your skin during this first section is amazing! And the thing is that there's not even much to be scared of; it's just the whole atmosphere and how the game portrays it; and the fact that you have nothing to defend yourself with!

After only playing through the first section, you start getting the feeling that this might be a true Resident Evil, and Capcom won't let you down! All of the things that make a Resident Evil a Resident Evil are all there: scarcity of ammo, scarcity of inventory slots, puzzles and creepy enemies!
In my opinion, the game becomes a bit less scary as you progress and start collecting ammo and weapons but it remains still very good nonetheless.

There are a few things I didn't like much about the game, the main one being the lack of references with the story (there are a few but they're very subtle with the most evident of them only in the end). Also the puzzles, they're not that many and they're not very difficult; none of them will make you squeeze your brain to find the solution. They're basically pretty simple and linear for the most part. My third point, but I admit that this is sort of nitpicking, the lack of enemy variety: besides the members of the Baker family, [spoiler]the crawling molded spiders[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the molded[/spoiler], that's pretty much it. You kinda get used to them by the end.

In conclusion, this is a very great game. Buy it if you're a fan of the franchise and feel nostalgic about what the old REs were. It's a solid 8.5/10 for me.

[h1]LONG VERSION[/h1]
As a Resident Evil veteran, I was very wary of this game.  Some people were turned off by the first person perspective, but what made me uneasy was the fact that it just didn't look like a "Resident Evil".  It felt like they were trying to slap the franchise name into a new, entirely different kind of game.  Even after playing the demo I remained unconvinced.  Luckily, the game was on sale for cheap, so I plunged in and tried it.  And you know what?  [i]This game is pure Resident Evil[/i].

First let me preface by saying that by "Resident Evil veteran" it means I've played all but two of the existent RE games (I never got to play Survivor 2 for the PS2, and I'm certainly not going to touch Umbrella Corps).  I've been a fan of the series ever since I played my first RE a couple decades ago.  I love the lore, I like even some of the less liked games in the series, like Gaiden and 6 (though I certainly don't LOVE those), and it remains one of my favorite videogame franchises to date.

RE games are all over the place in the way of gameplay.  From puzzle-focused survival horror to co-op action, to first person shooters and even multiplayer tactical shooters (though that particular one gets a very well deserved bad rep) the reason for this game to feel so [i]unlike[/i] RE was that the previews made it look more like a "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" rip-off.  And, while there are some elements of that at first, it's clear that the goal of the game is to pay homage to classic horror franchises (besides TCM, there's a bit of "Friday the 13th", "Halloween", "Nightmare on Elm Street", "Saw, "The Shining" and other works by Stephen King) while at the same time remaining steadily set in this franchise.

What makes a "true" Resident Evil game is almost entirely subjective, that's why games so entirely different as RE2 and RE5 can still be considered part of the same franchise.  This game is, like I mentioned, more in line with the classics (1, 2, 3, 0 and Code: Veronica): it's focused on puzzles, you're more encouraged to run from enemies than to fight them, there's a [i]major[/i] feeling of isolation and quite a bit of claustrophobia.  Don't expect to turn into a gun-totting badass who can shoot his way out of everything.  This is exacerbated by the fact that certain enemies are entirely unkillable by conventional weapons.

What makes this game scary is the atmosphere.  Small corridors, dilapidated scenery, lighting that's low enough to keep things interesting but not low enough that you feel frustrated, creepy ambient sound, and the constant dread of running into enemies who you can't see coming.

Not everything is great, though.  I have to mention that a couple of story-related decisions are underwhelming at best, and as soon as you lose control of your character for a cutscene he's likely to start acting like an idiot.  The worst part is that the PC version of this game has [i]major[/i] optimization issues.  Even if your PC exceeds the requirements you're likely to run into stuttering and short freezes that can become prevalent enough to make the game near unplayable.  There are some solutions to this, though.  Lowering certain settings is the obvious one, but I only got to make the game work properly by downloading a third-party software that limits the game's use of CPU cycles.  The game now works great, but unfortunately no thanks to the developer.

In any case, you can always try the game and get a refund if you don't get it to work.  The game only gets resource-heavy at around the hour mark (once you reach the mansion), which is below the alloted time for a refund.  I'll have you know that while this game has a demo, and playing it to completion can net you an item that can make things easier for you in the first half of the game, that demo is [i]not[/i] any good as a performance test, due to it using a much smaller map (incidentally, the one you play in the first hour of the actual game), so it doesn't use nearly as many resources.

If the game works properly for you, then keep it, because it's definitely worth it, and you're likely to get more than just one playthrough (btw, your first run through the game will last between 9-10 hours, pretty standard for a RE game).

This is not a survival horror game. This is a point-and-click adventure game on a rail, with occasional instances of ResEvil gameplay.
The threat of harm is scary. Harm itself is not. This game is crippled by an over-reliance on gore to be scary. This kills atmosphere and immersion. Before the first bossfight, you literally get your hand chopped off by a chainsaw-- and yet you don't die, don't bleed out, and can somehow still reload your handgun? That's not scary. It's stupid.
The game has several "tyrants": invulnerable enemies who occasionally pop out to chase you. This itself isn't a bad idea, but in this game they serve as forced stealth sections. Which is a TERRIBLE idea. Add to that the fact that these invulnerable enemies are also the game's bosses and you have a catastrophe: They are invulnerable. Except when they are not. They are not scary. They are confusing and annoying.
The "bossfights" are nothing but gimmicky puzzles with poorly implemented and undefined solutions. I honestly feel some fights cannot be beaten without either looking up a walkthrough, or dieing enough times for the game's loading screen to tell you how (and even then, it is often incorrect). 
That is terrible game design.

Some of the game's weapons are cumbersome to the point of being a liability in combat-- the flamethrower in particular makes no sense in how it works; if you ignite an enemy, do they continue to take damage? How long do you have to keep a stream on an enemy before they take damage at all?

But...
In between the Bakers, in the rare moments where you are let off the leash, you get to explore the game. And you get some generic enemies. And you don't have enough ammo to kill them all. And you have to choose, whenever you see one: Do you fight, or run? You have to keep juggling that choice, along with careful item management to avoid filling your pockets too much, and along with having to scavenge for supplies.
And THAT is what a Resident Evil game is supposed to be. That is survival horror.

This game is not fun. But Capcom is remembering what makes ResEvil games fun. I think I can support buying the sequel to this game, if not this game itself. And that gives me hope for the series' future.

The original Resident Evil was an intense experience. It was also difficult, mostly due to some cumbersome controls that made you accidently run toward the undead when you were trying to high tail it out of there. The premise of the game was simple; solve various puzzles while conserving key resources (healing items, ammo, and ribbons that allowed for the saving of the game). It was intense because you had to make every bullet count (and to make sure to always have one bullet saved for yourself in the end just in case, well not really but I’m a romantic for this kind of mindset). All while trying to not get hurt as to not waste healing items, and progress as much as you could before using one of the rare ribbons. All with a limited number of inventory spaces.

Fast forward to Resident Evil 4, and the series made a transformation similar to Alien to Aliens, which is to say more emphasis on action, and less backtracking to solve puzzles. 

Resident Evil 7 goes back to the style of the original. The new first person perspective and much better controls are very welcome. This also has the consequence of removing the artificial difficulty due to bad controls, so overall the game tends to be much easier than the original. At least on the normal difficulty. 

Michael Levine did an excellent job with the “Go Tell Aunt Rhody” and it really sets the mood right at the start. There is a haunted (guest) house, and an evil bigger haunted house, and some other locations that eventually lead to (surprise) a secret underground laboratory, and then back to the haunted house! The game channels Jack from “The Shining” as the crazed father (also named Jack).  But you soon realize that Jack is haunted by more than writer’s block. And not much longer, you’re hunted by Jack. 

Having Jack actively search for you is at first unnerving, but soon you realize that you can run around the house and lose him. One can almost imagine “Yakety Sax” playing during these times. Still, being caught off guard with Jack lurching toward you can be quite startling. Once Jack is out of the picture, zombies “the molded” take his place. The good controls make headshotting them not too difficult but one soon realizes that you can run away from them and use their greatest weakness against them. Their inability to open doors. 

The next part of the game deals with Jack’s wife who throws insults (and insects) toward the player. Then it’s on to dealing with Jack’s slack jawed son, with his traps and tricks, and finally on to the wicked ship, and back to the haunted house after a quick stop at the salt mines and the aforementioned secret underground laboratories. 

The end is a bit predictable and the final boss isn’t the most satisfying boss fight, but it checks all the boxes. There’s a certain satisfaction to being an ammo miser for most of the game and then unloading everything on the baddies at the very end. In the end, while not perfect, Resident Evil is a big step in the right direction for the series. 

Good
-	Good controls and first person perspective
-	Eerie and atmospheric settings
-	Minor changes in the environment lend to the feeling that something ominous is afoot
-	Background story of various characters in the way of interactive VHS movies
-	Weapons pack a punch, enemies are generally not bullet sponges (outside of boss fights)

Bad 
-	No way to drop items when you need some inventory space just temporarily. Instead have to go back to item box.
-	Boss fights are tedious and not very interesting
-	Easy to outrun most threats, you can make the “molded” literally disappear in front of you if you give them the run around sufficiently.

[h1]This is how you bring a franchise back![/h1]
[list]
[*]The graphics are stunning and have that well thought out design that the Resident Evil remake had, except with dynamic lights and sharp shadows and, of course, a full on 3D environment.

[*]The sound design is really awesome. I played through the whole game with a 5.1 system and it was freaking great. The voice acting is good and the quality of the sound effects is really great to the point where it can get hard to distinguish the game from reality.

[*]Thankfully, Capcom knew that you can't make an RE game without some form of combat. This game pulls it of really admirably. It's not like RE4 where you have tons of ammo and you barely ever need to worry about running out of ammo.
It just feels like a perfect balance of FPS and the original RE games.

[*]One thing I usually dislike with both horror games and movies is the over reliance on trying to market it as the "SCARIEST GAME/MOVIE EVER!". This, however, feels like the scares are used somewhat sparingly. It did get me a couple of times, but usually it's scary in the way a survival horror game should be. I just loved the way they used the grandma to freak you out on occasion.
[/list]

Obviously, I kinda loved this game. BUT there are a few flaws.
[list]
[*]This game is somewhat on the short side by todays standards. The best parts of any RE game for me are the metroidvania-esque levels where you explore big areas room by room looking for secrets and solving puzzles. This had that, but only for about half the game. As a result it felt much more linear than the old RE games. 
[*]Most of the puzzles were just shadow puzzles ripped straight from Silent Hill Shattered Memories. Having to do that same puzzle 3-4 times is a bit disappointing.
[*]I did not like the item combination system in this at all. It felt like a crutch for the designers because of how little ammo or items can be placed throughout the game. Instead of just having different herbs there are 2 chemicals that are mixed with herbs, gunpowder, supplements and so on to create items like ammo and first aid kits. I almost never made anything but regular pistol ammo or first aid kits. It just didn't feel very well thought out.
[/list]
So overall it feels like they skimped out on the meatyness of the older RE games. 
What is here shows alot of promise, though. If they ever make a RE 8, I'm gonna be pretty excited, but I am hoping for a lengthier or at least a meatier experience with more vast and complex level design.

If there is anything more undead than Resident Evil’s enemies it is its twenty-year continuity and its adherence to its traditions. As with RE1 and 4, RE7 strives to reinvent its identity through a literal perspective change. Whether this change was inspired by modern horror trends or the impetus for a VR game, RE7 brings the series to first-person survival horror. In these regards, RE7 is a revolutionary milestone for the franchise, though as a newfound standard of survival horror it carries too many previous pitfalls. As with the other two landmark games, these games can be great despite their shortcomings; however, in the case of RE7, the problems highlight how much greater the game could have been beyond the confines of the series’ name. 

None of what I have said should devalue RE7’s positive reception as it brings back direction to a franchise in dire need of self-evaluation. RE7 is certainly a game that looks itself in the mirror questioning where and how it went to stray before falling back to sleep to repeat its mistakes the next morning. Some may argue it is a return to Resident Evil's roots, though in reality these connections are tenuous at best—and it’s precisely this need to limit the franchise that keeps RE7 from truly becoming a masterpiece on its own. Instead of retracing past glories, RE7 reinterprets the series’ most effective elements that holds the potential to make a new name for itself. 

[h1]The New Resident on the Block[/h1]

Of all the critical praise, the most jarring idea is the constant mantra that RE7 is a return to the series’ roots, and I couldn’t disagree more—especially not that these callbacks made the game better. Reviews mention qualities not necessarily associated with Resident Evil such as the one location/mansion design, the slower paced combat, etc. Without playing the game, it can be easy to see how reviewers came to this conclusion either from other reviewers’ influences or misunderstanding the innate qualities of Resident Evil. After a few hours of playing it for yourself, there is very little in common with its past.

Why does this aspect deserve special attention? It’s precisely because people gloss over the bad qualities inherited from the past that tarnishes the many good callbacks. Aside from the mansion layout, which is debatable if that is inherent to RE, RE7 takes the subtle Spencer family storyline of RE1 and makes an entire game based around that narrative with the Bakers. This aspect is what resonated with me the most, but it’s not an innate quality. The flaws, however, are more easily familiar such as the nonsensical puzzles given unbelievably elaborate mechanisms, the campier elements meant to excuse plotholes, the action-focused nature towards the end, and the intentionally hampered (first-person) tank controls. Even if you would argue these problems are tied to what makes RE its own game, they feel even more out of place in RE7.

Unlike other RE games, RE7’s gameplay issues become magnified thanks to the first-person perspective. Believability is critical to the immersion of first-person horror, which has always been the hallmark of classics like Amnesia, Outlast and Alien: Isolation, and it’s precisely the campier elements of RE7’s plot and puzzles that feel out of place. Questions about the world and characters are the quickest way to draw the player out of tension as well as make light of the situation, a problem inherent with Ethan who reacts unrealistically to a situation. On a more fundamental level, however, the gameplay itself breaks the immersion the most.  As I previously described, tank controls are the only appropriate way to describe how movement works as you swerve around enemies while moving forward; backing up or turning slows you down, and there is a 180-degree button to help. This feels more like a concession with VR, and until you get accept these limitations you may find yourself taking more damage than you should. In addition to these issues, the body count the player accumulates quickly takes the tension out of future situations from overuse. Thankfully, by the time the player reaches the end after a mid-game return to the intro feeling helpless, the power-fantasy will stay only long enough to bring closure to the game.
   
[h1]Be Kind to Your Expectations and Rewind[/h1]

Another glaring oversight by reviewers is the emphasis on how much Madhouse difficulty impacts the experience, which is true up until the player leaves the confines of the Baker residence. The big appeal is that item placements are restructured, incentivizing more frugal usage of weaponry and a refreshingly new experience after finishing the game, as well as there are more rewards to unlock with the Antique Coins to change how you explore the house. These include unlocking keys or items to puzzle solutions for early and/or new weapons and buffs. Unfortunately, these changes begin to become less noticeable when you arrive at the Ship and the Mines, and the difficulty spikes aren’t worth the hassle due to the game requiring a plethora of ammo and/or unlockable weapons for boss fights. Instead of making the gameplay more compelling or immersive, Madhouse mode feels severely underdeveloped. 

As previously mentioned in my review of the demo, the biggest disappointment with RE7 is how safe it plays with its NG+ options, which could have incorporated these rewards to be more engaging, yet more gamey, by utilizing the VHS tapes to unlock secrets. This change would have made the campier elements easier to accept if the game adopted the unique idea from the demo of influencing future events with prior knowledge such as the Fuse solution. Instead of gaining powerful weapons by meeting milestones on the next playthrough automatically, players could access this content seamlessly if they knew how to find them from the get-go, which would enrich gaining those rewards. The VHS tapes where you control alternative characters is a brilliant idea for optional yet immersive navigation, foreshadowing as well as hiding away hidden rewards, and it’s a shame RE7 falls short of the latter category. This concept could have been further expanded on with the Madhouse difficulty mode changes as players tinker with the game as they uncovered more and more rewards like mindlessly fumbling with a Rubik’s Cube.

Again, the purpose behind stressing this missed opportunity is the demo made it the incentive to replay the prologue multiple times not only to obtain new items but also a PT-esque puzzle only the hive-mind of the Internet could have solved collectively. Nothing in the base game or the DLC of RE7 ever reaches the pinnacle of that idea teased in the demo, and it further cements how safe the developers were to create a Resident Evil game with all the greatness and the follies associated with the name. Even ignoring how the prologue set expectations, the drawbacks of Madhouse mode keep it from becoming something worthwhile beyond initial impressions, especially with the difficulty spikes it introduces from the start. Like with many ideas of RE7, the potential remains while the execution feels halfway between the death of the idea and the reanimation of it.

[h1]And So, Ash Seeketh Embers… Oh, Wait, Wrong Game[/h1]

Considering how much impact RE7 will have in the future as one of the few AAA survival horror series left as well as the legacy it will leave behind as one of the VR’s most fully realized titles, it is perhaps one of the most promising disappointment I’ve ever played. Sequels will always have the potential to iron out the many flaws of something new rather than fall victim to its shortcomings (a.k.a. RE5 and 6). Whether Capcom will make something new rather than reiterative remains to be seen. However, if you take the game on its own merits, then RE7 manages to do the impossible by rekindling fondness for a series after its legacy seemingly rotted away all it once meant before it had run its name into the ground.

From its very inception the Resident Evil games have been an attempt by Japanese game developers to gamify the appeal of western horror films with varying levels of success. Having just finished Resident Evil 7: Biohazard I think it nailed it. From the first few hours feeling like a direct game adaptation of Evil Dead and Texas Chainsaw Massacre to the explosively Hollywood finale it felt like I was playing the lead in a FANTASTICALLY well produced B Horror film. And the game's theme (a take on Go Tell Aunt Rhody) is eerie and captures the feel of the game fantastically. It even manages to subvert the evil rural canibal family trope. It truly is damn near a masterpiece amongst modern horror games. 

It also plays beautifully. It empowers the player just enough without compramizing horror. You are given weapons but little ammo as expected but due to the first person perspective and excellently executed locational damage your skill in combat can actually give you an edge in an organic way. A bullet to a monster's head is far more valuable than a bullet to the gut which feeds in really nicely to limited ammunition. The game does get a bit action heavy near the end, but given the fact that most horror games outstay their welcome and lose their effectivness by about the 3-4th hour or so the change of pace was, for me at least, welcome. The more action focused ending also doesn't feel tonally out of place for Resident Evil given its desire to emulate american horror.

Overall the game is absolutely FANTASTIC and is the greatest horror game since Silent Hill 2.

This game is a mixed bag, I won't lie. It's great, and kinda meh at the same time.

The main antagonists of the story are fantastic. Without divulging too much information for those who actually don't want to be spoiled, the primary baddies are GREAT. You get a good sense of dread from them, the boss fights are actually well done, and they're staggered apart pretty nicely. It's a good old RE formula that they didn't really need to mess with, and they played to their strengths and did it well.

The environments are creepy and really well done, and there's definitely a handful of downright uncomfortable areas for some people. Despite it being first person, it was a great horror game, and felt more like an RE game than RE6 (or honestly, RE5).

The downside is apart from the main bosses, the bad guy variety is garbage. Don't expect lurkers and hunters and all that jazz. Expect a generic "zombie" (if you will) and get used to that, and only that. It's not even particularly scary or intimidating, and it gets old REALLY quickly. While other RE games had the excuse of zombies, and then other predatory monsters to keep you on your toes, RE7 really fails to throw anything extra at you in terms of monster variety, which bummed me out.

The only other complaint I had was the final "act", involving the location change. That entire chapter was just boring, and unenjoyable. The fast pace of the homestead was far more enjoyable, and the location change really just threw the game balance off IMO, and for me, I lost interest in what was going on. A bummer, because the rest of the game was SO GOOD.

Regardless! The game was still fantastic, highly recommend it, AND all the extra content is A+, super fun. If they keep this sort of thing up with their games, then I'll be buying more RE games in the future, instead of when they're in the bargain bin anymore.

The past several Resident Evil games have been very action focused. Capcom took a punt with this in 2017 which is the same year that many developers and publishers took their franchises back to their roots. They stripped the game back to it's roots and made the player focus a lot more on survival, horror, inventory management and exploration. It paid off. I would go as far as saying this is the best Resident Evil game to date.

Spoiler free, the game drops you straight into a mysterious setting in an unearthly woods. You are controlling a character called Ethan Winters in first person mode throughout the game. You are looking for your wife who went missing and her last location was in the woods at the Baker house. A house filled with death, horror and terrifying characters. You are tasked to find her and either brave what faces you ahead, or simply Run. Hide. Repeat.

There are several different difficulty levels. You are able to pick up and upgrade various weapons including handguns, shotguns, flamethrowers, explosives and chainsaws and you forced to manage your inventory with precision as it is a grid based system with limited slots until you are able to upgrade. The game mechanics are perfect and everything is extremely responsive, including the good addition of the 180 degree turn. The upgrading system is fair and you are forced to explore in order to fully upgrade as you have to collect different coins and keys all over the game. There are just the right amount before the collecting becomes a chore. The soundtrack is amazing, the atmosphere throughout the game is terrifying and the sound effects of the guns, monsters and general environment is unbelievably euphonious to the ears.

The DLC's are as good as the game and require some skill to get the 100%. For achievement hunters, this game is not too brutal but will take some time. There are many missables and there are also difficulty based achievements which are quite challenging, but doable. I don't like permadeath games, i'm pleased to say that this isn't one and removes the unnecessary stress added with those modes. It makes this game perfectly enjoyable and although it is scary, it is also very fun to explore.

I would pay full price for this game. No need to wait for a sale, whatever the price it is well worth it.

I admit I saw a large percentage of RE7 through Twitch streamers to satisfy my curiosity from a safe distance on its release. Even after owning and finishing it myself, it strikes a good number of elements of survival horror very well - surprising in this day and age. Even from the shift to first-person, the game maintains some of the combat difficulty of prior games, with a good amount of survival tension. Adding the ability to block attacks to mitigate part of their damage keeps the combat close to the intent of a good horror game, and avoids some frustration.

Level design is very effective, with hidden items galore, maps that loop back on themselves, and often just enough to let you survive. Enemies are designed to never give you items, meaning that while good aim or even knife hits might let you win a fight without spending much health/ammo, another option is often to rush past enemies in classic Amnesia: TDD fashion. The game's story progression also includes moments of resetting your inventory (to be returned later) so that the survival aspects can be fresh once again.

I don't often play horror games, but the standouts to me are Amnesia and Fatal Frame. Even after knowing a lot of the cutscenes ahead of time, RE7 ranks right up there - often making me a bit too anxious to actually play. Thankfully, at just the time scares and survival tension get repetitive or unenjoyable, the game does give you a chance to start expending the ammo you've amassed against an endgame onslaught. The only downside to this portion is that enemy variety is a bit low.

I also played the Not A Hero DLC and it had an appropriate change in tone, but was also quite fun and involved crisscrossing paths.

It has been quite some time since I've looked forward to a new Resident Evil game. But there was something about 7 which had caught my eye. Perhaps it was the sudden shift in tone and viewpoint, or maybe the quirkiness of its villains. But one thing that I had definitely noticed was a comeback to the world of survival horror.

Resident Evil 7, in my honest opinion, is a much needed breath of fresh air for the franchise, after having living in the shadow of it's fourth installment. Gone are bombastic action sequences which would potentially make Michael Bay envious. Gone are the quick time events which had become so prevalent in the series. Instead, we are provided with the filthy horrors which lurk within the Baker Plantation.

The shift in view point has proven to be quite divisive amongst fans of the franchise. Some scoff at it with pure hatred, and others praise it for bringing something new to the table. I have to say I'm in the middle of the spectrum. I am interested as to what Capcom has planned for the next main installment, and hope they refine the first person controls (if they continue on with it.).

Gameplay is ripped straight out of classic Resident Evil titles, with numerous puzzles and some enemy encounters which will make one quite tense. Ammo is scarce, and you have to pick your battles wisely, or wind up some creatures next meal. Save rooms return, as do item boxes and an upgrade system. These provide a moment to catch your breath and decide what your next move should be.

Replayability is an issue I see sprouting up frequently. The game has three difficulty modes one can go through, with the third being unlockable. Trophies are there for whoever wants them. Hidden figurines populate the plantation, which beckon to be destroyed. There are bonuses for beating the game under certain requirements, such as new weaponry and infinite ammo. 

The story for the game doesn't bring anything new to the table. Rather, it chooses to play it simple and safe. After Resident Evil 5 & 6, this was a great pallet cleanser. The story isn't bogged down by lore set by its predecessors, making 7 an excellent entry point for new comers. However, that isn't to say there aren't certain things sprinkled in to cater to veteran fans of the series.

All in all, Resident Evil 7 is a gem of a game. Fans of old school Resident Evil will feel right at home, and newer players will be able to jump right in. It is not without its faults, such as questionable sound design for some circumstances, and lack of extra modes. However, there is plenty to enjoy in the molding corridors of the Baker Estate.

After the recent fiascos that were some of the late Resident Evil games, the whole series seemed like it was going under for good, due to Capcom having the series deviating further from the actual horror that made Resident Evil what it used to be, with titles like Resident Evil 6, Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City and even Umbrella Corps. But thankfully, I'm not here to talk about those games, today.
I wanna start by saying that, when it's said that Resident Evil 7 Biohazard took the series back to its roots, it's no joke. And it's certainly not a sarcastic statement. A game like this is what the series has been needing for a long time. And while I may be a little late to the party, considering this game came out in 2017, I think it's still worth sharing my thoughts on the game.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Let's start with the story. It's not the "There's been a viral outbreak, send an ultra badass protag into the scene, performing roundhouse kicks and punching boulders towards saving the day" sort of thing, like in past Resident Evil games. The game starts with a mysterious video from Mia, the wife of the game's protagonist, Ethan. She admits that she did lie to him about something that apparently has gone wrong and asks him to stay away. Going against her wishes, Ethan sets out to Dulvey, Louisiana, thanks to an e-mail he got from Mia, who was presumed dead between 2014 and 2017. The e-mail contained the address to a derelict residence. Exploring the seemingly abandoned house, Ethan finds Mia in the basement, who attacks him while posessed by an unknown force. With no other choice but to defend himself, Ethan ends up fighting Mia and forcibly killing her in the process. After their fight, Ethan is contacted by a female named Zoe, who tells him he needs to get out of the house and suggests him to head to the attic. After the phone call, Mia's body disappears, leaving no sort of trace behind. As Ethan was on his way to the attic, Mia appears again, attacking him by piercing his hand with a screwdriver, leaving it as if like nailed against the wall while she grabs a chainsaw. Ethan manages to pull out the screwdriver, but Mia manages to slice his hand off and walks away up to the attic. After getting back on his feet, Ethan heads to the attic, after Mia, finding a handgun up there and fights her, killing his wife once again. Soon after, he is knocked out cold by Jack, the patriarch of the owners of the house and plantation around it, the Baker family.
Sometime later, Ethan wakes up in front of a dining table and apparently with his hand attached to his body again. He soon finds himself in the presence of the Bakers. Jack, his wife Marguerite, their son Lucas and an old woman on a wheelchair. He finds himself restrained on his chair, while Jack, Marguerite and Lucas torture him as he's refusing to eat what they're eating. After the three of them walk away from the dining room (minus the old lady as she looks half-dead), Ethan manages to escape his restraints and explore the house, looking for Mia and for a way out, while being constantly stalked and confronted by Jack and, one by one, the other members of the family, who demonstrate the ability to heal fatal wounds like gunshots, burns and even dismemberments. Particularly Jack.
This is pretty much how it starts, as I'd like to leave the rest for those of you who haven't played/watched it yet to see for yourselves.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Among the changes Capcom made in Resident Evil 7, I'd have to say the gameplay was the one that was changed the most. For starters, the game engine. Something that not only allowed graphical improvement (which I will talk about later), but also allowed to go for a different kind of experience, gameplay-wise. Throwing the MT Framework engine out the window, Capcom developed the RE Engine specifically for this game, allowing the most noticeable change of them all, which is the first person perspective. The RE Engine was also made especially for the game to be experienced in VR (so far, only on the Playstation 4), give you have the headset for it. And it works wonderfully, from what I've seen. That aside, the way the games were supposed to be played back then makes a return, as you have a limited inventory (which you can get small upgrades for if you find them) and you have to conserve your ammo. The puzzles are also back and they're pretty fun to do. I especially loved doing the shadow plinths, which in order to complete, you have to use a specific object that is somewhere around the house to create a shadow that matches the shape on a painting. Do these and you gain access to new areas of the house. The game also introduces a new kind of item you can find throughout the game, called the Chem Fluid. Which is a crucial item to find as soon as possible as it has plenty of different uses in the game. It'll always come down to combining it with something, but you can combine it with herbs to make first aid meds or with gunpowder to make handgun bullets. And these are just two of its uses.
Resident Evil 7 also introduces a new kind of enemy to the game. These monsters covered in a strange black substance, called the Molded, which have different variations that you see throughout the game. There aren't that many variations, but at least it's not always the same one type of monster in the whole game. And while you can fight them, I suggest running away whenever possible. It'll help you saving ammo.
There are also collectibles you can find throughout the game, such as the antique coins. These special coins are extremely useful for the player to unlock special items that are locked behind cages. Each item requires a specific number of coins, in order to be unlocked. And these coins become extremely important, if you play the game on the Madhouse difficulty, which you unlock after beating the game for the first time. As certain key items can also be found locked inside these cages.

[h1] Graphics [/h1]
This is honestly the best looking Resident Evil game I've seen, so far. As I mentioned before, the RE Engine allowed for great graphical improvement, over the past games. Thanks to the new engine, Capcom went with a more photorealistic look for the game, with photorealistic rendering and realistic shading. The RE Engine also allowed other new graphical and rendering techniques, such as dynamic shadows, subsurface scatters which is a shader method for producing highly realistic human skin, the ability to output 4K and even a VR mode, which as I said before, it's only on the Playstation 4, right now.
To put it simply, the new RE Engine allowed Capcom to give Resident Evil a new and extreme makeover. The only thing bothering me is the texture pop in. Which seems to happen even on console.

Overall, if you're into Resident Evil and have been rather disappointed with the latest titles, then trust me. This game is worth your money. The final score I give to Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is a 9/10. A must own. Now while the base game is great, it's some of the DLC content (which I wasn't able to talk about in detail due to character limit) that ends up being a bit disappointing. But that still doesn't stop RE7 from being an amazing experience. If you can, go even for the Gold Edition. If possible, look up the Beginning Hour playable teaser and check it out beforehand. It's free and it's still on Steam!

While this is definitely a step forward in the right direction for the Resident Evil series, I can't say that this game is the best of it's genre, let alone the whole RE series.

Looking back at it, it felt more of a one-shot, glorified tech demo of an indie game, that blatantly wore Silent Hill PT's influence on it's sleeve, like the trillion other indie horror games did. 
Which is somewhat alright if this tiring 'Infinite Hallway' gimmick was used sparingly, but man did it get old and unoriginal fast.

Back to the game, it managed to do a few things quite well, like it's semi-realistic art-style and gritted ambient; the surrounding environment looked mostly abandoned and decayed, which is the game's best quality for me, RE7 is still, if not, one of the best looking Resident Evil titles, since the first game's remake. Most of the weapons were fairly solid, believable and not out of place, since the available weapons are limited to you, because you were basically stuck in the middle of a swamp, even though there happens to be magical healing liquid in the same game. The DLCs were actually one of the best a triple A game could offer on Steam and are well worth their price.

I also like that the whole thing is in first person, it's so much more immersive that way and it is much better than having the camera pointed toward the back of your head throughout the entire game. Just stop it with this stupid third-person gimmick please.

However, everything else in this game was more or less of a genre-clustered mess; As if it couldn't decide on what type of horror game it should be - we got guns so Action Horror, no? Okay how about a Walking simulator? There are a bunch items lying around, so is it a Survival Horror or a Psychological Horror? I mean, just pick one already! 

Resident Evil 7 also has the worst enemy variation in the series, we only have three or four types of Molded, a bunch of Bugs and a Hillbilly family, like is that it? I would've been fine with the Hillbilly family taking the 'persistent pursuer' role, even though that is nothing new, but my god is the Molded such an uninteresting and uninspired type of zombie. Excluding the additions from the DLCs, couldn't the game's surprisingly deep pool of creativity muster up a few more enemies before giving up?

The story had honestly felt nothing special - Trapped in large house, monsters, use gun, escape. Haven't seen that one before. The Horror aspect in RE7 is comparable to that of a 2016 Popcorn Horror movie, it's predictable, unoriginal and all amounts to nothing, the little girl horror cliche is done to death. Mia, the main character's malnourished girlfriend... Oho I can't begin to tell you how laughably lame and predictable the beginning horror sequence with her was, all you need to know is that it happens so fast, that you'll forget about it in the next five minutes of the game like I have.

I could go on and on, but the Resident Evil franchise is slowly, but surely getting there. Since the bar has been set pretty low, this game is still a decent reboot for a Resident Evil game, but it's incredibly weak for a standalone horror game, I bet RE7 would have never been made, if PT didn't happen in the first place and if that were to be true, then that would show even more of this game's complete lack of originality. I would still prefer this over the remake of Resident Evil 3 and almost everything else post-Resident Evil 5.
