This game is great. It mixes the feeling of the original games with a completely new style. Capcom really stepped up for long time fans, bringing back the horror and hopelessness of the RE1 and 2, moving away from the action/sci-fi shooters that the last handful of games morphed into. Resident Evil 7 really shines after beating the standard game, with the unlocking of madhouse difficulty, where saving is item based again, and the enemy are far more intimidating. No singular fight is a given win and any individual monster could end the game, requiring a change in strategy and harsher item management, regardless of powerful unlocks from previous playthrough.

The graphics are fantastic, looking much closer to photo realism than any other game in my library. It's properly optimized as well, allowing for ultra settings on mid range GPU's. I've played the game on a 1050ti, rx580, and finally an RX Vega 64, and at the highest settings, never dropped below 60/90 frames at 1080 on the first two, and 150 frames 1440 on the Vega. Oddly enough, this is the only game I know of that runs and looks better with motion blur on. The environments are incredibly detailed and alive throughout the game, enough so that I spent a good amount of time just admiring mold on the exposed boards behind walls, or the piles of rotten food in old refrigerators. The facial animation on Lucas Baker are stunning in there own right.

The voice acting is on point as well. With maybe two parts of the game requiring a little forgiveness, nothing comes off as cheesy or unbelievable. Jack Baker is fantastic; every line he offers in this game is absolute gold. Each character has their own identifiable quirks and personality traits, and are seamlessly brought to life through character interactions and idle dialogue.

The story line is hectic and gripping, with each chapter working together to make one cohesive experience. Each member of the Baker family is a solid representation of a different kind of horror, changing the gameplay to help keep it interesting throughout. Jack is a homage to classic slasher films, as an unstoppable madman constantly pursuing you with whatever random tool he has laying around. Marguerite is more reminiscent of extreme body horror, trying to feed you repulsive materials in some places, and giving birth to the mutated insects infesting her body in others. Lucas represents psychological horror akin to the saw movies, making complex puzzles and filling his portion of the game with traps. Eveline is more along the lines of classic ghost stories, with hints of more modern japanese horror. The late game brings back a familiar feeling from the original series, exploring complex laboratories to find documents explaining the science of what's been happening.

The DLC  for RE7 adds a lot of fun to the game, along with more backstory on some characters from the main game. Some of the DLC also brings bits of the ridiculousness of more recent resident evil games, but in a way that adds more playtime without harming the main game itself.

Altogether, Resident Evil 7 has become one of my favorite games, and in my opinion, the best game in the series since the remake of the original for GameCube.

For me it was quite active times, when I was playing with my friends online and coop games all the time, so they were kinda mad at me, because I dropped them for a few days while I was playing RE7.   

I really enjoyed the game. Mainly, because I enjoyed the script a lot and the way the developers tell us the story. The way how the manage to make you to become a part of this terrifying creepy story. And what's really important, the whole game is not focused to scare you so you would die because of a heart attack. No, it's more about telling you an immersive story with a charismatic insane family.

Unlike previous games, which were focused a lot on combat and non-stop actions, this time we will deal with a first person survival horror game. Basically, the whole game play is set in one place only and this is a big house with its wild territory. You come here, deep in American rural to find your missing wife. In this chapter, you are not a soldier tough guy anymore, you are just a simple guy without special combat skills Ethan. During your exploration you will encounter an insane family with a shocking story and after all the madness you will see the only thing you'll care about will be leaving this hell. However, it won't be that easy. Especially, if you are playing on the hardest difficulty.  

The whole gameplay is about exploring the mansion, searching supplies and stuff to help you to survive and get out of that place. From time to time you will solve some easy puzzles and encounter some boss fights. It's hard to say, that you will have a wide arsenal of weapons, but more than enough to escape that creepy place. I really appreciated, that they didn't add stupid QTE elements to the game and focused more on actions scenes, where you really play by yourself. Mostly, game's main goal is to create an atmosphere of fear, desperate and claustrophobia. And they managed to execute this idea perfectly. However, lots of players wasn't so happy about this game, saying that it feels more like Silent Hills rather than Resident Evil.

From my own perspective, as a person who is not an expert in a games of this genre, I can say, that Resident Evil 7 is a pretty amazing quality product, with an interesting story and atmosphere you will never forget. Some scenes in this game will be damn shocking for you and unforgettable. If you are more a casual player and you just wanna experience the story and this whole game feel, you can set the easiest difficulty and just run through the game in few hours. Well, you will definitely not feel that survival thing, the way how was the game was designed to be played, but if you don't care about it, then you will be fine.

Ok, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Love horror games 
+ Atmospheric games are your thing
+ Are a fan of games with survival elements
+ Enjoy creepy stories about insane families
+ Louisiana swamps vibe!
+ Looking for a game with a great graphics
+ Eager to see memorable characters, villains and surrounding

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Sensitive nature (it's a horror game, after all) 
- An experienced horror games player. As far as I can see, this game can be a disappointment for people who like to compare RE7 to some other more classical games.

Enjoy!

Resident evil 7 is an amazing game overall and definitely a step in the right direction. But its not quite on par with the best and classic RE titles yet. After the more recent action focused titles in the series, RE7 shifts back a few gears for a more traditional, slower paced survival horror experience. 

Story:
The story is about Ethan Winters, a guy who lost his wife a few years back, but then receives a message to meet her at some plantation, somewhere in Duley, Louisana. Anybody who played the brilliant Silent Hill 2 knows that there are so many ways this could go wrong, but Ethan sets off to find her anyway. Without going to much into spoiler territory, the Baker family undoubtly steals the show here. They are frantic, loud and intimidating. There's also another character that i liked alot, though im still not sure how well she actually fits the game.

Controls and Camera:
This is a hot topic with every Resident Evil game, the controls and camera. Earlier RE games used static camera's and tank controls, while the more recent titles featured an over the shoulder perspective with slow controls. The first thing you'l notice is that RE7 is played from a first person perspective. I had my doubts about it at first, but it works good for the most part. The control is smooth and despite looking like a FPS, it still controls clunky enough to be considered horror. The game mechanics are also pretty good. But there is one gripe i have. A common complaint in early RE games is that you cant see the enemies well because of the fixed camera angles. "Thats over now because this game is in first person, right?" Thats true for the most part but capcom never needs an excuse anyway: so now some enemies wil literally pop up right in your face! In the early RE games, you might not see them, but you could still notice and track them by sound. In RE7 theres times where there are little to no hints on when the enemy decides to visit you. (apart from some areas with "substances") Either they spook you by grabbing you from behind or from around a corner, or they just dont give a ♥♥♥♥ at all and just materialize right in front of you. It feels cheap and some of it seems to be catered for the whole cheapscare in VR hype. It doesnt ruin the game, and most of the time you can see and aim for yourself. But if you had this problem in previous games, then expect to run into something similair.

Gameplay:
The gameplay is what gives me mixed feelings. The setting and atmosphere is really good throughout the whole game, but surprisingly, this game feels like it has more different playstyles then RE6 was supposed to have. Some are really good, while others not so much, so il line them up. Cheers!: 

Modern Horrorfare:
Some parts feel like those run away simulators that first person horror games mostly do these days. While i can appreciate games like Amnesia and Outlast at times, it doesnt feel like RE. Now this doesnt actually have to be a bad thing per se, but the way it's implemented is just very barebones. Sometimes, you'l have to run away from pursuers, and the only thing you can do is run, block, slam doors in their faces and hide. Ethan runs pretty slow for a man in panic, slower then your pursuers. Blocking attacks works okay but of course, you can take damage either way. Slamming doors is helpful, but only buys a little time. So that means you'l have to use every move you have! The thing that ruins this is the actual hiding. When you break line of sight, you'd think Ethan could use a number of hiding places, like closets, underneath beds, bushes/haystacks and darkness. Maybe even barricade doors, like in 4 and 5, or creating distractions by sound would be nice but the only real stealth elements you have is line of sight and sound of footsteps. Sometimes they clearly see you, but they just dont give a ♥♥♥♥, and then there are even some spots that enemies just wont bother checking at all, even if they obviously saw you going there (apart from saverooms ofc). The area's dont offer much room or options, and you pursuers must be able to pinpoint your smell because they will almost always look for you in the same room. It's not that bad, but this element is not really great either. Overall, it doesnt improve the game and it doesnt really fit in with classic RE.

"Now where do you think you're going?!?!"
The chases get downright cheap and broken on Madhouse difficulty. I'm not sure if this was difficulty-bound but I had one very cheap moment with Jack on Madhouse: I was hiding in the shotgun puzzle room while Jack was searching the rest of the main hall. After a while, i saw him going through the double doors on the left side of the 1st floor room. I took my chance and quietly snuck up the second floor, and stopped at the door to my left. I heard him cursing me from the room underneath me, behind the double doors downstairs: Thats good! He's still down there, il quietly check the second floor now then. I snuck through the doors, look to the left and BAM!!! Jack grabs me from the right, as if he was hiding behind the rightside door all along... This is not even scripted to happen for the storyprogression or even explainable by lore so... CHEAP is all i could say and think (ok, along with a cascade of cursing that steam doesnt want to hear) while i dissapointedly marked the end of my madhouse playthrough.

A fimilair feeling:
But later on, theres more of the fimilair RE style of gameplay. You'l find a handgun, get your hands on a shotgun and even harder hitting weapons. You'l need to use them with some restraint because ammo is scarce. You have to explore the area for ammo, keys and other items while finding the best routes to avoid slow creatures. This is easily the best part and what makes RE7 great. Once again, inventory space is limited, so you think about what you bring along, and leave the rest in the fimiliar item boxes. Theres also abit of upgrading, but nothing crazy. Combat is a mixture of modern and classic RE. Hitting different body parts result in different reactions: Head does most damage, arms will limit their attack and range, feet will make them stumble or trip over, etc. But you can no longer use melee moves, except whittling away at them with a knife that is. These creatures (is that you Revelations?) dont offer as much variety as the old games, but it works. The Boss fights are also pretty fun and challenging. A certain section later in the game also offers room for exploration and this sort of gameplay is all really good.

Back for more?:
And then there are sections that remind me of the more recent RE action games *cough 6 cough*. It's mostly just a gauntlet of enemies and traps with little options but push right through it. But unlike 6, theres still no melee or fancy moves that accomodate this kind of gameplay, so its pretty average. It can still be entertaining and frantic, but it feels rushed and nowhere near as interesting as the open parts of the game.

DLC:
The DLC is also mixed package. End of Zoe and Not a Hero add story and new mechanics to the game, while the others are certainly fun but mightve well been VHS tapes within the main game itself. A RE2/3 mercs style minigame is sorely missing though!!! To sum it up:

Pro's
+ Looks amazing
+ Nice controls and solid mechanics
+ Exploration (in some parts) and survival horror!
+ Baker family very interesting and well done (but in a sick and intimidating way)

Cons
- Chase sequences are barebones and sometimes downright frustrating
- Some parts are lineair gauntlets and traps
- Some enemies are not the best in design, and theres little variation
- Pop up encounters are cheap

[h1]A Horror Masterpiece[/h1] 

Resident Evil VII needs no introduction.

Its memorable marketing campaign ("Welcome to the Family!"), flood of positive critic reviews, and endless coverage on Youtube during it's release catapulted an already iconic franchise into the stratosphere. Gamers who had been burnt by P.T.'s unexpected cancellation finally had a reason to celebrate, and to bury the hatchet on one of modern gaming's most persistent issues: A true lack of single-player AAA horror experiences in the wake of a multiplayer-obsessed culture. But one question still remains: Was RE7's positive reception justified; or was it a case of settling for less after a survival horror draught? 

The story begins simply enough--our main character Ethan recieves an alarming message from his wife, Mia, who's been presumed dead for the last 3 years, and Ethan goes to investigate the old Louisiana plantation where she was last sighted. Things quickly go to hell, and Ethan finds himself at war with the Baker family, and a far more sinister supernatural force. The set-up to all of this is done fantastically; slowly introducing a feeling of dread as you draw closer and closer to the game's climactic moments. Before you "meet" other members of the Baker family, you'll find horrifiying tidbits about them along the way from letters, notes, and videotapes scattered around the house. 

Ammunition is scarce, and it can be intimidating if you aren't used to playing games that punish you for not preparing for encounters in advance. You might go into an area with a gun and 7 bullets, there will be 4 monsters to take out, and each monster takes at least 5 shots to the head before it goes down. In situations like these, you need to creative by shooting off their limbs and making a run for it while they're incapacitated, or just being ballsy and running towards the next checkpoint and praying they don't hit you with their wide, sweeping attacks. 

Even if you scrounge for ammo, and make an active effort to hoard your items, the game doesn't let up. Sometimes you'll be given precisely the amount of ammo you need to advance past the next area, and nothing more. You'll also quickly discover that most enemies are bullet sponges, so in a lot of cases, the best decision is to avoid enemies altogether (which is way easier said than done). 

There are also puzzles. While some can be kind of cryptic, most of them can be figured out if you pay attention to the environment and the notes you pick up along the way. It's satisfying when you're rewarded with extra ammo and inventory slots for going out of your way to complete them.

The main game takes around 10-12 hours to complete on Normal difficulty if you're taking your time and scrounging for loot. You can probably beat the game much faster than that if you know what you're doing, and there's even an achievement for beating the game in under 4 hours. You unlock "Madhouse" difficulty after beating the main game too, which adds some replayability if you really want to put your skills to the test (it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard).

I can't speak on any of the DLC's aside from "Not A Hero" which is free to download. It lasted about 2 hours, but it was extremely fun, and far better than I expected it to be. It also provides closure to a plot thread that was left unaddressed in the main game.

Although I generally enjoyed REVII, there were a few nagging issues that lingered on my mind after the closing credits. 

Before I started playing, I noticed a good number of people complaining about not having the urge to replay REVII again after beating it. I didn't really understand what they meant until I did. The unavoidable fact is...

[i]REVII's map is very small.[/i] 

It's much easier to remember where every item is located on a second playthrough, to the point where it stops being fun. The environments are so different, varied, and crucial to observe, that they will inevitably be etched into your memory. It truly is a one-and-done kind of experience. Once you know all of the jumpscare and item locations, the game just isn't the same. Enjoy the ♥♥♥♥ out of your first playthrough, because you won't get another opportunity to recreate the same exhilirating, adrenaline high ever again.

The second issue I encountered was purely performance-based. My PC is about 3 years old, so it's not going to be able to handle every new AAA without a few graphical downgrades, but no matter how much I tweaked the settings, I would get constant framedrops whenever I moved to a different area. I'm talking 60-1FPS, which lasted a few seconds everytime the game tried to transition into a new environment. [b]SO[/b] annoying, and it really broke my immersion. According the the Steam  forums, a lot of other players have this issue as well, so proceed with caution before you buy the PC version.

All in all though, Resident Evil VII [i]delivers[/i]. I can't imagine any horror fan walking away from this game dissapointed. The incredible visuals, tight gameplay, and gripping story deserve to be experienced. Your mileage may vary after the main game is completed, but this is a gaming milestone you don't want to miss out on.

Not really sure why this has such amazing reviews. I've played Resident Evil 1, 2 and 3 so you could say I'm a classic resi player. However, that been said reviewing this as a standalone game reveals it's many weaknesses. 

First off, I play in 21:9 and it really pisses me off when dev's don't accommodate for it, some games fully program for it (Shadow of War) others just simply extend the screen from 16:9 (GTA V) and some turds just simply put black bars at the edge (this crap) and whilst some games do this for gameplay and balancing reasons (Helldivers) there is no excuse here except they couldn’t be bothered.

Other evidence of half arsed programming is the fact that the shortcuts for your weapons only appear in the HUD as the direction control on the Xbox controller, and entering numbers on keypads can't be done with a keyboard number pad.

Anyway, once we move past that, the game itself doesn’t really know whether to stick to the past or move forward, For example you have save points, but the game auto-saves as well. Make up your mind and have one or the other, there is no need for both. The key antagonist is the 'creepy little girl' that was done to death in the movies with 'The Ring' and 'The Grudge' and bested already with the excellent FEAR game, they all did it better, and more importantly 10 years ago.

Now for the biggest negative of all, the boss battles are just plain ♥♥♥♥♥. Deus Ex was torn to bits for it's boss battles, and they even had to re-program the bloody game, but for some reason this bucket of ♥♥♥♥ get's applauded for them! They are terrible, with no clear direction on what to do, and, broken in some cases. For example, want to fight Jack in the pit? Good luck if you don't have enough room to pick up the chainsaw BEFORE the fight, cos you can't do it during whilst he's battering you! I simply did not enjoy a single boss battle, they were infuriating.

Throw into the mix that you have the traditional and terrible 'lose all your weapons' bit, the 'character swapping bit' it all feels a little cliché. I also tried my bloody hardest to kill my wife, christ she was so bloody irritating! I think I killed her about 4 times and the tart kept coming back even right at the end! I'm sure you're meant to care about her as a key character but I really couldn’t give a toss, I just wanted rid of her.

The good? Some scares, had me jump a few times, the house was great, which was just even more puzzling when they move you on to another location that didn’t have the same atmosphere, it should have stayed at the house. The old lady was a creepy addition, always popping up around, shooting was alright, some nice puzzles but overall, it's just alright.

In summary, pick it up for a fiver, but, if you want to play this style of game (Suspenseful, Horror). Forget this steaming ♥♥♥♥♥, go and buy Alien Isolation, it's the same type of game and is longer, better, more polished, terrifying and accommodates for 21:9. Only mindless Resi fans need apply for Resi 7. True gamers will play Alien Isolation and realise Creative Assembly stole the mantle of horror game on their first go, and, more shockingly, when their speciality is RTS. This is the seventh game in Resident Evil and they still couldn’t get it right.

I never really was a Resident Evil fan and even was pis sed and wishing that 7th installment should have been canceled instead of Silent Hills. When I saw the gameplays and finally played RE7 now...my mind changed. It's an absolute masterpiece! I played a bit of RE1 and 4, but they didn't grow on me like RE7 did. Everything was absolutely amazing: The visuals, atmosphere, tension, gameplay, the characters, the enemies, the story, the soundtrack and much more. When you have to deal with Jack Baker for the first time, it legit feels like you're a mouse being chased by an overly aggressive cat. Hiding is even hard, because often the enemies spot you unlike in other survival games and that's what makes this game so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ scary. Not to mention there are not many places to hide and you gotta rely on the safe rooms, which are pretty rare and only in certain spots. Some moments where you're performing an action and an enemy shows up make you tense up a lot too. As for characters, every character is written and performed in a unique own way. As well this is one of the rare games where the girlfriend/young wife character isn't an annoying useless brat. Well Mia was useless kinda, but she probably had to hide things from Ethan due to the situation she was in for his own safety and that gives you a reason not be annoyed at her for being useless. The game mechanics are okay, but this is where I take the rating a bit down. What I didn't like is the limited space for items and how you had to store the items in the boxes which weren't everywhere either. Sometimes I would end up putting an item into the box to then later realize I needed it and then backtrack to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ box just for the one item. After using it I thought I could put it back and replace it with something more useful, just to find out I needed the same item for more tasks and having to carry it around and taking space for more useful stuff. Also the game giving you more space just at the end of the game where you didn't need many items anymore sort of was kind of a d ick move from Capcom. Well maybe it's just me, but that's my opinion. The variety of enemies kinda disappointed me a bit. I know that the baker family were having mutation stages, but I wanted to actually see non human mutants like the regenerators for example or any special, advanced mutation from the molded, because if you can aim well and conserve the right ammo for the right molded type, then they're an easy target, even the fat ones. This is probably the reason why it didn't feel like a Resident Evil game in fact. You didn't get someone who works for a company or military organisation to investigate what's going on. You got a simple average young guy who had no weapons or whatsoever to defend himself until he found an axe and a gun in the attic in the house. As well the lack of various enemies took that feeling of a traditional RE game, but you know what I say about this? I love this! I am dead serious! This is what made this game unique and outstanding. You were not fighting some zombies or brainwashed villagers, you were fighting an infected family who still had personalities and certain character traits. I guess the new mutations/zombies were the molded, but they were not that special to me. Also their designs didn't stand out much. Overall with all the nitpicks I give this game a glorious 9/10! Even if you are not a Resident Evil but a more a survival game fan like me, then this game is definitely worth checking out!

Capcom goes back to its roots to bring us the old formula: an old mansion, a mistery that goes nowhere and no sane person cares about, forgettable heroes, some great villains, absurd gore, awful aiming and tank controls. All of this crammed into a first-person dungeon crawler that quickly evolves into a slow corridor shooter in the last few hours (just like every classic RE, to be honest). It's not innovative, but it feels good.
The original Resident Evil format was, at least in my experience, never scary. Sure, it was opressive, tense, and sometimes nerve-wrecking, but I ain't afraid of no undead (or, rather, the goofy putty patrollers that come out of the wallpaper). To me, a truly frightening game would be something like Alien: Isolation or the first hours of the REmake. I'd dare say the demo was more subtle and disturbing than the final product on the whole.
RE7 is silly fun (F-U-N, fun). You can even unlock wacky challenges and minigames to waste your precious time revisiting the same mansion by the bayou over and over again (with rearranged furniture and a convoluted chronology within the narrative, but who cares, right?). Lately developers and publishers have been talking of 'games as services', a trend that the RE7 team seem to adhere to with the inclusion of all these game modes that are just desperately screaming for my attention. I spent 30 hours playing RE7 and I think that's enough for now. We must part, my summer love. You go your way and I'll go mine. Uninstalled 'til less busy times.

The risk was totally worth it for Capcom. They've created something that stinks of moldy classic game design with a pinch of some new ideas to adapt to the demand of unpopular sensitivities. And that's all right.

[h1]Review: RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard / BIOHAZARD 7 resident evil [/h1]
[list]
[*]Graphics / Audio:
Developed with the RE Engine ( Probably a Resident Evil Only Engine ). The Game looks mindblowing, facial scans are impressively well made showing perfectly emotions etc. Textures are perfectly sharp almost photorealistic, lighting is top notch too. The way everything is created has as result an amazing creepy atmosphere which is perfect for a Resident Evil game. Simply put, this is one of the best looking games out there currently. The Audio and Voiceacting is High Quality too.

[ 10 out of 10 ]

[*]Gameplay:
Gameplay is solid. It is a First Person Shooter but thankfully they didn't try to make this a ''Shooter'' as the mechanics are different compared to other mainstream FPS titles. Its main Focus is on Survival and they did that great. You need to be efficient and accurate when dealing with enemies as Ammo supplies and Health pickups are limited. The Game has a couple Boss fights which add a little challange and each Boss fight is different which doesn't make the game 'boring'.
Puzzles and Map Design are as always very good and makes you think in order to reach your target.

[ 9 out of 10 ]

There will be no spoilers, or not any major ones atleast!
I grew up with Resident Evil 4 which was more of an adventure title than a Horror one.

I am fan of franchise for 20 years. During this time the franchise have good, average and bad games. In recent years the CAPCOM moved from survival horror to action shooter. But fortunately here we have excellent successor of original resident evil from 1996.
First of all the game is good product. Triple "A" game with normal optimization on day one without microtransactions not common in those days. Only problem (for some people) is Denuvo but game's performance don't impact by it.
With new entry we have new game engine. Graphics look great, especially NPC characters. Game world full of details that make environment real. Dark colors create tension and feeling of dread. The game know how to use lights and shadows to enhance game experience. Levels design also very good. In first half the game big creepy house with additional structure and later multi level ship. Each location handle with care.
As for audio. Voice acting extremely good. Characters very believable. You feel connected to their emotions and thoughts. The game have some high quality soundtracks but nothing unique. Sample for audio like wind, water, creak and ect. good and capable to improve game experience.
Story never was the strongest part of resident evil games. This game have new set of characters and new stand alone story. You play as Ethan, man that looking for his missing wife. And he found himself in wrong time in wrong place. In beginning it's feel not connected to lore and even not about bio weapon at all, but eventually everything start connecting. Step by step you discover what happened in this place. Should you choose to play I strongly recommend to read all files since the game don't have any audio log. The story is typical for resident evil (bad people create bio weapon) but interesting enough to continue. This time events more personal and don't require to save the world like it was in previous titles. However the story have some inconsistents but nothing super critical.
The gameplay really good. The closest thing to classic titles. Explore environment, backtracking, save rooms, crafting ammo and health items, fighting and/or run from monster, big bosses, item management - all those activities here. Also some puzzles but unfortunately it's same type. Really enjoyable. Slow paced survival horror that put you in excellent created world and keep you edge to the end. 
The game have some replayability. Two ending, some unlockables and challenge achievements . Also I want to mention madhouse difficulty. It's not just hard mode but more like arrange mode from resident evil directory's cut. Items (including weapons and story relevant keys) in different places, enemies appear in another location and more deadly. It's feel relevanty fresh for during second playthrough. 
The title have some problems. Enemies variety is low, idea for the not canon story good but implementation not so much. Second part of the game weaker compare to first but overall it's very enjoyable experience. But despite all issues this game is big step in right direction - survival horror. Can't wait for next installment.

Back then, the Resident Evil series had grown long in the tooth and the standard gameplay mechanics were at odds with how far games had evolved. RE4 changed all that by radically changing up the formula, and in the process bringing back the scares of the original series.

Fast forward to 2017, and we see the RE series in desperate need of redirection. The difference this time is that the wild success of RE4 had somehow convinced the folks at Capcom that people really wanted an action adventure. The result was eight games of dubious quality that strayed further and further from what made the series great. The abysmal performance of RE6 (which jumped the shark even by RE standards) forced a drastic reworking of the series. This brings us to RE7. 

The most obvious change that comes to mind with this entry is that it is all told from a first-person perspective. However, the whole RE: Gun Survivor series had been doing that for seventeen years at this point. No, the real change that Capcom put into this entry was the pacing. This game plays much more similarly to the original Resident Evil than any other RE game since RE Zero. The first-person perspective enhances the creepy atmosphere of the Baker estate, and the slow movement of your character (even when running, it feels like your are in molasses) really adds to the fear. These are areas where the game shines.

Unlike previous editions of Resident Evil, there are fewer enemy types this time around. The enemies can essentially be broken down into members of the Baker family, and the molded. The Bakers feel like souped up versions of the Las Plagas from RE4 and RE5, whereas the molded give off a more classic Resident Evil vibe. Each of the two enemy variants requires different techniques to dispatch, with the Bakers acting more like tyrant fights, whereas the molded stand in for the zombies and other bullet fodder. 

As with previous entries in the main series (barring RE5 and RE6), items are sparingly populated in the environment, thus requiring a frugal use of weapons and healing items. This is nothing new for any RE veteran. During my play through, there were numerous moments in the game where I had to make multiple trips back to item chests because my inventory kept filling up. By the time I reached the final section of the game I was never hurting for ammo. All that said, if you do find yourself scrambling to keep bullets or herbs in your inventory, the game does have a crafting mechanic that allows you to create most of these items. 

The RE Engine is a beautiful thing that really gives the title a next generation feel to it. However, despite gorgeous character models, the lip syncing never quite felt right, making character mouth animations appear remarkably stiff. There are also some monster models that just don't look as good and seem a bit at odd with the atmosphere the game is pushing. These small gripes aside, the game itself is gorgeous and well worth playing on a high-end machine.

RE7 harkens back to previous RE titles with its convoluted puzzles, hefty backtracking, and a storyline that feels just a little bit over the top. This made the game feel very true to the series and I very much enjoyed it. However, if this type of slow-paced horror is not your thing, then RE7 won't win you over.

Story-wise, this entry has only tenuous relationships to the overall plot of the series. The incident at the Baker estate does ultimate have ties to the series persistent villain, The Umbrella Corporation, but the way in which it all plays out feels more like an isolated incident. Overall, I think this approach is more effective for the game and I hope to see the series continue down this more intimate path, as opposed to the world-ending craziness that had diluted the series over the past decade.

In the end, Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic edition to the Resident Evil franchise, and one that has blazed a new trail for the series to explore. The game is well worth the full price tag, but if you can get it a deal with the DLC bundled in, I would jump at the chance. The extra content helps really round out the story.

Resident Evil VII:Biohazard known in Japan as Biohazard 7:Resident Evil (smart sons of glitches) is a First Person Perspective (shocking) survival horror game released in 2017 by Capcom. The game was meant to be revolutionary but does it fit Resident Evil "family" just as fans wanted?

Ethan Winters is a typical no one, his wife has gone missing three years before but receives a message from her to meet in Dulvey, Luisiana.  There he is obducted by psychotic Baker family who started his worst nightmare (...and I am not talking about Resident Evil Gaiden! Seriously, the worst game I have ever seen). Suprisingly for once the plot was not written by someone from Japan and it really works.
Gameplay, or should I call it an unexpected change of perspective? Our "hero" can use guns as good as previous protagonist but shooting feels much less confident, thanks to new view every encounter with enemy is terrifying (in postive sense, not many games can do that). Quite big location on swamp terrains serves as our quasi-open worpd where we can return to some locations anytime we want, collect some items we have missed (props for developers for hiding them creatively) or simply to save game on VHS reader (on Madhouse we need to use casette tapes which are limited). Our endurance and perception can be upgraded by finding hidden steroids, but still we are weaklings in all this mess. Some items are locked in bird cages so we can get them by using a number of coins scattered through the game. Just as in previous Resident Evil games we have a lot of unlockable content acquirable by destroying all figures, beating the game under 4 hours (took me 8 in first run) or by beating madhouse difficulty (quite a dissapointment that nobody gives us Rocket Launcher, it was a tradition of the franchise).
I have mentioned madhouse before, well, it is the highest difficulty in the game and it is insane: enemies are more frequent, they deal more damage, bosses haunt you longer and locations of items are changed. But what would Resident Evil not do to unlock Infinite Ammo...
The game has no multiplayer at all, so you will not find Mercenaries here (WHYYYYY CAPCOM !? WHYYYYYYYYYY!?!?)
About enemies, they are not various at all, we have normal molded, agile molded, fat molded, bugs and the best thing - Bosses (There are 5 in total, the final kinda dissapoints but it is nothing really important), in any case they are preety smart, come out of nowhere and are hard to kill.
Graphics even on lowest settings are decent, and the whole game will support VR when exclusivity on PS VR ends (someday in this year).
Do not expect to find many bugs here, except those meant to be in the game, glitches are also hard to find though.
Bit suprising is that my PC can launch it in fluent 45 frames on medium (praise the optimalisation!).
Eventually you can extend the game with preety expensive season pass (Just buy Gold Edition insteand) adding some canon (Bedroom,Daughters,End of Zoe,21) and non-canon (Jack's 55th Birthday, Ethan Must Die, Nightmare) chapters to story.

I`m not a fan of horror games, but I guess I was in the mood of something evil to try and fight and bring righteous Light to...

Have you ever watched Carpenter`s The Thing? Well this game reminds me of that, especially later on.

You are some bloke looking for his lost wife. You discover  she`s in a creepy house deep in the countryside which you, alone, like an idiot, decide to enter, instead of calling the cops for a woman that`s been missing for 3 years. Sure why not, what can possibly go wrong?

The atmosphere at the start is suitably dark, oppressive and claustrophobic. Seriously, everywhere in this house is horribly cold, lonely and just not somewhere you want to be, especially alone.  Incidental noises keep you constantly aware. I never play with music, it`s creepy enough as it is. You expect anything to happen from anywhere... And it does. 

It`s enough to make you shut down the pc and go do something else, but if you shoulder bravely (or stupidly) on, you`ll eventually get a knife... then a gun... and some ammo. There`s even prospects for a shot gun, even a flame thrower. Things start looking up.

The game is in 1st person which I much prefer over 3rd person. It`s much more immersive and I don`t have myself in my way. I can deal with whatever face-to-face.

However, while you can aim with your gun, you can`t look down the ironsights- Why? Is it to make it harder to headshot enemies? Because it certainly does that, even if you use a Mouse. Also, you run like a waddling duck, you can barely keep ahead of anything and what you really have to do is use obstacles to keep you and horrible things at a distance while you reload your gun or panic.

You`ll never really have enough ammo for your gun, so get used to using your penknife while back-forthing  and blocking (you can kill things this way as long as they`re alone). You save the game and stuff at tape recorders, do it whenever you can. Grab herbs and combine for health. Finding stuff helps to gain access to places and ammo.

Also some things happen that don`t make total sense and purely just to keep the game going. For example, you are basically forced to go places where in reality you just would not because you KNOW something very bad is going to happen. There are `escape routes` which you can`t escape through as you would if it was real. Your character is stupid because he just doesn`t get out once he sees what`s he`s up against and get the cops. Nope, you`re just forced to blindly carry on with your penkinife and one bullet in your useless gun even if the worst Thing itself is going to appear and kill you.

There`s a stupid girl who knows where you are at all times by phone and tells you to do stuff without telling you the important dangers... Even my character told her off for not telling him about them and she`s like, "Oh, sorry! Now go on this other task because I say so!" 

Expect jump scares that you can`t really avoid (which is annoying) and creatures that find the concept of dying from serious head wounds hard to understand.

However, it`s pretty good, very creepily atmospheric. And, I suppose, enjoyable. Just wish I had ironsights and could run just a bit more swiftly.

A lavish survival horror game, Resident Evil 7 is remarkably well-assembled.  The game has stylish, amazingly well-realized graphics (nigh-photorealistic at times), coupled with superb voice acting and great sound design.  Despite the phenomenal aesthetics, the game runs well, even on budget systems and is quite stable, rarely crashing or glitching (I'm looking at you PubG/Dead by Daylight!).  The plot is convoluted nonsense but the occasional scares, tongue-in-cheek humor and fantastic atmosphere more than make up for it.  While the game can be completed in six to eight hours, the demo (Beginning Hour) and free DLC (Not a Hero) should add one to two hours more.  The game has limited replayability, despite branching paths in the gameplay and there is no multiplayer.

Still, the game can be had on sale for about 20 USD.  The ten to twelve hours of frightful entertainment that RE 7 produces are more than worth the asking price.

Recommended.

As a fan of the series from way back, this was a refreshing return to form. Having loved every entry from the original through 4 (I even enjoyed 5, albeit not as a Resident Evil game but as a fun co-op experience), I skipped out on 6 due to its lukewarm reception. Having wikipedia'd the plot and seen a Let's Play, I don't feel like I missed much. 

So, it was with some curiosity that I gave the demo "Beginning Hour" a try. It did a great job whetting the appetite and I pre-ordered the game immediately. Having tried it on both PC and my XBOX One I opted for the XBONE version initially because it didn't seem to run well on my PC for some reason. I had a blast-and almost one year after getting 100% on the initial release version I bought it on PC and am happy to say that they seem to have patched/optimized the game since the initial demo. I consistently get 144+ FPS on my 980, i5 system. The only major FPS drops I experience are in the seamless loadtimes when transitioning between areas and they aren't really that bad, to be honest.

This is a return to the close-quarters, claustraphobic horror of the very first game in the series. Gone is the third person camera, replaced with a first person one, which as a series purist I felt some trepedation about. However, compared to the run-n-gun third person camera of Resident Evils 4-6, I much prefer the first person camera. Also, another important note is that this is possibly the tightest the series has been in regards to controls, with your character responding as they should based on inputs and no feelings of controlling a walking tank like in the earlier fixed camera entries. 

The story is remarkably subdued as well, relying on small-scale horror with large scale implications if you've been following the series from the beginning. It's nice to see the global pandemic-threat of some of the wilder entries scaled down into a smaller horror setting, as a kind of "what if one of those bioweapons ended up in the middle of nowhere without one of the series heroes to help out?" Even if you haven't played the other games the story does a good job of presenting itself in a way new players will understand, while also leaving enough breadcrumbs to connect this entry with the series as a whole.

The scavenging aspect of this survival-horror entry is top notch as well. The developers take maximum advantage of the first person perspective to hide health items, ammo, lockpicks, and in-game collectibles (used to purchase upgrades) in all sorts of nooks and crannies. If you find yourself low on ammo, health, etc. check behind desks, cabinets, and so on---there's bound to be something useful somewhere.

Another point worthy of mentioning is that this game features two radically different modes. Easy and Normal play out almost identically, but there's a third "Hard" difficulty called "Madhouse" that rearranges most of the game. Items, enemies, and weapon placements will be different in addition to enemies hitting harder and having more health. There will also be less ammo, health items, and so on. Beating the game on normal then going to Madhouse feels like a fresh experience, and while you can use powerups you unlocked when beating the game, if you're a hardcore survival horror lover like me I reccommend you don't. I save the uber weapons and unlocks for achievement/speed runs, but that's all a matter of personal preference.

Now for the DLC: I hadn't played the DLC on XBONE but they came as part of a discounted package on the Steam summer sale. I'm not a huge fan of frivolous DLC, so I did embark on playing them with some trepidation. The fact I got them at a discount might be coloring my opinion of them, but I thought all of them were great fun. The Banned Footage selections are short vignettes of sorts, featuring a puzzle escape scenario in "Bedroom", a prequel of sorts in "Daughters" (which has 2 distinct endings), a violent twist on Blackjack in "21", and a Mercenaries (fans of RE3 and beyond will know what I mean) like mode called Nightmare/Night Terror. My least favorite of these was probably 21, which IMO is a bit too long and RNG dependent to beat on the Survival + mode. Even then, I managed to beat that in 3 or so attempts, however those attempts took upwards of an hour+.

Beyond Banned Footage there are a few addendum DLCs as well. Jack's Birthday Party is another mini-game with a mercenaries like feel, albeit with a festive twist as you fetch food to feed to Jack while fending off enemies for a time bonus to gather more food and try to achieve a high score. I had fun with this mode and the big challenge was maximizing your time bonuses using powerups and kill-chains. Then there's Ethan Must Die mode, a short and brutally difficult challenge mode featuring random loot where you try to clear an area of the game, get a key, then go beat a boss. There are a few cheap one hit kills that I don't feel right about, but other than that this was a good mode for people who like hardcore "rogue-like" experiences (there are no saves/checkpoints in this mode, but there is a Dark Souls-esque mechanic where you can reclaim a random piece of gear if you can get back to where you died and smash the tombstone that marks that location). Finally, there are story add-ons Not a Hero (which was a free release), and The End of Zoe (which clarifies the fate of one of the characters from the main story). Not a Hero was a bit short, imo, but fun-and since it was free the fun is the only part that matters. It features 3 difficulty modes like the main game-Easy, Normal, and Professional-with Professional being it's own spin on Madhouse. I have yet to play End of Zoe but it seems to have a positive reception, so I'm looking forward to that!

All in all, as a series fan, and a fan of the survival horror genre it helped define, I definitely recommend this game and its DLC.

First of all, this is the first game I've completed in 2 over years.

I've had an on/off relationship with Resident Evil. While the first 4-5 games looked extremely intriguing, as a kid I was just too scared and incompetent to play the games. With RE5 I decided it's finally time to get my feet wet, and it's still one of my very favorite games. RE6 and Revelations had some issues sure, but I'm still in the minority that had a ton of fun with them. I also liked the movie series a lot, and it's one of my favorite sagas. Recently many game series turned out so disappointing that I have been thinking about giving up with games altogether. Resident Evil has been the very last franchise I'm interested in following storywise. So Resident Evil 7 had big shoes to fill, and it worried me to the extreme that while the game is rated pretty well it also very much sounds like a soft reboot, which would make all the past history I love gone. But still, this is one game that I just had to try eventually, even if just to know that it's time to find a new hobby.

I liked the PC demo of RE7, and thankfully all of that is still here. The game starts with the usual path tutorial that leads me toward my impending doom. I notice I've kind of grown out of these as I was constantly just thinking "I really wouldn't go to this place. Does it count as winning if I quit the game now and pretend I never went in?". But then as I pushed myself further and inside the halls I was greeted with the extreme detail familiar from the demo. The paintings, the pictures, the floorboards, the wallpapers, the faces, the murky furniture and everything just scream quality and attention to detail. The graphics are excellent, the dialogue and sound effects are really good and there are tons of drawers, boxes and notes to explore. The cast is also brilliant, particularly Jack Baker is perfectly psychotic, funny and menacing. The dynamics of Mia, Zoe and Eveline are another high point of the narrative. Also the untold stories of the other victims are an essential part of the experience.

After the demo I was curious how would a full game play out. Fortunately for the most part it flows great. RE5-kind of inventory is back and there's a nicely balanced mix of secrets, puzzles, inventory management, action, hiding, reading and just creepy strolling in Metroidvania-like environment. It hasn't been this easy to be committed and push forward in a game in a long time. It's not flawless though as the stealth AI turns out to be not so awesome, with some handily places hiding spots from which you can deduce that the patrol pattern is pretty mechanical and makes the otherwise so believable people seem like robots. Also the game starts with so much gore that it kind of numbs me right from the start. If I can have my hand chopped off and walk around as usual, it just makes the later instances of gore seem like not big deal. Perhaps this is partially the cause, but also I never really felt that this is actual survival horror. Very quickly I mastered headshots, knowing when to run, how to find the things needed and so on, which kind of made me feel like some sort of chosen one - which one of the characters also somewhat hints at. I found the usage of steroid upgrades to be a pretty funny (intentional?) joke, as I always thought it made sense Chris started to take all sorts of enchantments after confronting the first monsters and that's why he's almost superheroic later on. So Ethan pretty fast starts to go in that direction, and I didn't ever feel like I want to get out of the plantation. Instead I'm the one who will liberate this place. I pretty much only died because of the magnetic finishing moves that some enemies have. It's not really a bad thing, just an observation. The harder difficulties probably make me break controllers and use the phones to call mom, but they weren't available when I encountered the horrors for the surprising first time.

The game showcases a couple of pretty unfortunate modern quirks. First of all I had to download the 20GBs of game, then some various updates, then I was greeted by black screens that turned into static loading screens that lasted for like 20 minutes. In the end I decided something was wrong and played around, finally somehow getting the game to show up. So from the moment I wanted to play the game, it took about 12 hours before I actually got into the game. Furthermore I almost completely avoided all trailers and videos, but having played the demo and watching just a few minutes of internet footage, the amount of deja vu I had was surprising. Originally I thought that the demo would be a separate case not present in the full version in any way, but it's mostly here. Playing through the game I felt like I have precognitive capabilities because every location gave me a flashback of an old video and I almost knew what was going to happen. As I was avoiding spoilers, I'm interested in how much worse it is for those who actually watched every trailer and sneak peek beforehand. Another thing in my mind was naturally the grander connection to Resident Evil universe. It's a new incident which seems pretty tame and down-to-earth in comparison to the events of Raccoon City and there's almost no connections. But the small hints like a a newspaper article by Ashford and the fact that the molded goo has some resemblance to Uroboros made me cautiously optimistic. Then in the end there's no doubt this is the same universe, which cemented my liking of the game.

Summary:
I really liked even Resident Evil 6, and the new direction of Resident Evil 7 worried me a lot, though based on the demo I was confident that at least this will be an alright standalone game. The audiovisual design, quality, attention to detail and composition is really solid, coherent and of great quality. The game has an entertaining balance of suspense created by action, escaping, hiding, puzzles, exploration and decisions about inventory content. Capcom is cherry picking a lot of things from other games: Deus Ex inventory is about the best on the market, parts of the game are pure Arkham Asylum, Amnesia's and Outlast's hide and seek gameplay has been the thing about recent horror games and so on, but Capcom managed to make a game that stands mostly on it's own. The gameplay is even more than the sum of the components because of good story and delivery. The plot is a good mix of wicked hillbilly murder cult and classic Resident Evil elements. The narrative switches from tension to tragedy to humor to solace without ever being jarring. There isn't one character that I "didn't buy". When the end credits rolled I noticed I was loving the theme song, thinking how will Ethan and all the events connect with the Raccoon City survivors and had chills running through my spine. It's not the very best game ever, but the only annoyance is how they changed Chris again and even he isn't that bad. I wasn't even caring that the game doesn't have anything to replace Mercenaries, which was a good way to pad longevity but one that I never player for more than couple of hours in total. Capcom frightened a lot of people when they revealed Resident Evil 4 - a game that ended up revitalizing the whole game industry. I feel they did the same thing again here. This is the way to do "reboots". Resident Evil is still alive in my books, unlike Halo, Mass Effect, Splinter Cell, Tomb Raider and a bunch of newer series that have been wrecked with nearly irreversible mistakes. My must-buy list now has two games: Elder Scrolls VI and Resident Evil 8.

It seems the "revolution" in Resident Evil happened mostly in the Capcom press release. While the game introduces first person camera for a fresh experience, it cuts down on pretty much everything else. Hardly inspired storyline draws deeply from cult pop horror elements and prefers jumpscares to deliver emotion. Dialog is often bland or illogical, and the otherwise high quality audio tends to be overused for random house creaks, with some truly outlandish sounds for footsteps and environmental objects. Compared to the complexity of previous installments, the game is almost linear with barely any depth to the environment or actors aside the visuals. It still feels like Resident Evil and you will be swapping shotguns on a piedestal, but the experience leaves you expecting more game and less F.E.A.R./Silent Hill meets Evil Dead B-movie.

After a painful lack of quality in the series, Resident Evil 7 finally brings back some former glory.  Taking ques from Rob Zombie classics such as The Devils Rejects and House of 1000 Corpses, Resident Evil 7 creates its own unique take on southern gothic horror. Reinventing itself as an FPS, RE7 maintains  old-school aspects of the series such as  competent puzzles, resource management and (intentional) clunky movement . This is also blended in with  modern horror aspects  such as cat and mouse gameplay  similair to  Amnesia and Alien Isolation , creating  that atmosphere of vulnerability.  However  RE7 it is not without flaws. Outside of the fantastic Baker family cast the enemy variety is awfully lacking, leaving some diversity to be desired. Also the game begins to run out steam making the last quarter a slog to get through. But considering the massive jump in quality from previous installments, Resident Evil 7 gives the series a much needed push in the right direction.

After two disappointing installments in this franchise, RE has (finally) bounced back. It’s almost as if they read my reviews of RE5 and RE6. They are finally trying something new without any linkage to previous games. “New”, is a curious way to to describe this game though. Sure, the first-person gameplay is new to the RE franchise (unless you are including Resident Evil Survivor or Dead Aim, I’m NOT!!), but Capcom is definitely capitalizing on the successes of the Outlast, Amnesia and Alien Isolation franchises. That’s all perfectly fine. It works in this environment and the story they tell. 

The gameplay is well done; players use a combination of running and hiding, shooting and puzzling solving (just like the original games). There’s very little cut scenes, which means the player is playing more and there’s a few throw backs to some of the original mansion puzzles. Remember the crank? 

The game succeeds by making ammo scarce, with the exception of the game’s finale, which forces players to choose wisely when to spend that last bullet. The eeriness of the house’s layout adds to the ambiance in addition to the stellar sounds effects and music queues. 

Sure, there’s some jump scares. And this element of the game I found most depressing. There’s no need to have enemies teleport near the player for a cheap jumps care. This happens on two or three occasions involving two of the game’s antagonists Marguerite and Jack.  
The boss battles are clever, and the ending Boss battle is reminiscent of Dead Space.

The action elements that were present in RE 4, 5, and 6 have been significantly toned down, there will be some jump scares, most of which are encounters with the main characters, but the other enemies are often foreseeable and can be ran from. [h1]STORY[/h1]
Having never played a Resident Evil game before, I can say that the story may require some sort of background knowledge.  The events and what's going on around and in the house, however, do not require any sort of prior knowledge.  The only thing that will require this background knowledge is actually the background.  The game refers to companies and bio-weapons that I had no knowledge of such as "Umbrella" and "The Connections."  The game's story and events have absolutely no foot in reality and I wouldn't expect them to either.  Just don't expect to have an immersive realistic experience.  The story of the game, however, is pretty laughable but the game certainly makes up for it with fun gameplay and set-pieces.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
This game for me has absolutely been a blast to play and try to complete.  If you want to see what I've done so far you can check my achievements.  Right now, I'm trying out Madhouse mode which I'll get into later.  The game has many different elements and some choices in what you do.  You can run from enemies, kill enemies, or hide from them.  There are two main types of enemies that divulge into other types; molded, and infected.  The molded are monsters made from the mold of the bioweapon.  They divulge into other types that are presented so well it would be a spoiler to tell you.  Next is the infected, by infected I just mean the humans (Baker family) that roam and have fights.  These guys help to give the game some tension when they appear.  The game also has a loot system that works really well.  Your inventory is limited and at times you'll have to choose whether to bring your items back to the box (an infinite storage box in your safehouse that carries that are universal in the items they carry) or save time and scrap them.  The game slowly builds your inventory as you get new weapons that way you can carry them and the new ammo.

[h1]FEAR FACTOR[/h1]
This has to be said for this game since it is technically a HORROR game.  The scare factor in this game is honestly laughable.  Jump scares are painfully obvious when the camera fades to black so something can pop in your face.  Next, we have chases, these can be tense but when the AI for them is pitifully stupid in any mode besides Madhouse it becomes easy to just abuse them.  The molded honestly can provide the most in terms of scares as you hear them approach or spawn and frantically look for them.  The most HORROR in this game comes from its atmosphere.  The atmosphere is down very well.  As you wander around and hear the environment, hearing the wind blow with curtains flying and other things really adds to the atmosphere of just a rotted rundown house.

[h1]Optimization[/h1]
First I'll start with my core build:
GTX 970
I5-4570 @3.2 GHz
8GB Ram
The game runs well enough to be playable.  The game has settings though that outright make it ugly or stuttery.  First is Rendering mode; keep it on normal unless you want to watch your game go from good to potato.  Next, Shadow Caching; just turn it off, it takes destroys the performance of the game way too much to even consider it.  For me, I ran all my settings at Medium at 1080P and it ran smoothly besides occasional freezing when loading new areas.  The final thing I should mention, VRAM.  This game took so much VRAM that it honestly made me wonder what was using so much of it.  The graphics shouldn't require the amount it took as they were good at best.  My best guess why VRAM usage was so high is so that the game keeps everything rendered as there are no loading screens unless you going into or out of a cut-scene.

[h1]REPLAYABILITY[/h1]
This game for me has actually been super replayable and that's been for two reasons.  First, the reward system.  The game rewards you for completing the game doing different tasks during your playthrough.  These rewards really help to entice you to replay the game and try it again.  I will leave the rewards below in spoiler text in case you don't want to see them.  Next is Madhouse mode.  This mode changes EVERYTHING.  After I felt I had already figured out what to do in every case, Madhouse changed it all.  Guns are given at different times, enemies are placed differently, and the biggest thing of all, you need cassette tapes in order to save.  This makes choosing when to save stressful since you want to save a lot of time in case you die but you don't want to waste a cassette.  Madhouse truly is a different game entirely.

[b]Rewards[/b]
[spoiler]Madhouse: Complete the game / pre-order / DLC
The Albert Pistol: Complete the game
The Secrets of Defense: Complete the game on normal
The Essence of Defense: Destroy all Mr. Everywhere statues
Walking Shoes: Destroy all Mr. Everywhere statues
X-Ray Glasses: Complete the game in under 4 hours
Circular Saw: Complete the game in under 4 hours[/spoiler]

[h1]LENGTH[/h1]
The game can be long if you are looking to find everything and loot to the fullest effect.  I completed my first playthrough on normal in about 6 hours and 20 minutes.  My second playthrough going for the "Get Me Out Of Here Achievement" (complete the game in under 4 hours) on easy took me 2 hours and 50 minutes.  Knowing what to do substantially decreases this timer and this knowledge will help you in the long run.

[h1]OVERALL[/h1]
This game was well worth the money in my opinion.  I bought this over the holiday sale and it has taken just about every bit of time that I have had.  I have had so much fun just playing this game over and over as I try to complete it.  I think I'm going to 100% this one.  I highly recommend you pick this up and play it for yourself.

A genuinely fantastic game and a genuinely fantastic Resident Evil game. With some very dark and subtle psychological themes constantly hinted at and packaged in this beautifully paced and presented adventure that's as creepy as it is fun - clearly combining the best of REmake and Resident Evil 4 + a whole lot of unique innovations into one complete and quality package - I'm happy to say that Resident Evil is finally back. The transition isn't always perfect, with the classic and very contrasted shifts in tones being sometimes way too saturated with very ridicolous moments that's sometimes paced out rather awkwardly and unfocused during the middle part of the game especially. However, during the first and third final part of the game the pacing and shift in tones is specifically what makes it and the entire series so special. Especially if you get the ending I got that ends in such a genuine and legitimately happy way that's a perfect reflection of what this game and the series really is. It's genuine. No matter how dark or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up it can get especially with its very human and deep hints at family and dysfunctionality etc. everything's alright by the end. It's all okay. That's what Resident Evil has always been about to me and that's exactly what this game is. Which in a lot of ways is in itself a great reflection of the journey this series has gone through. It's had some very very dark moments (*ahem* RE6) but now with this release everything is really alright. 

Now I could go on about how incredible the first person presentation is as well as it's animations and how it weaves into the very responsive and fun combat and story that seemlessly goes from all out horror and fear into fun tight action. The great voice acting and plot that, albeit is inconsistent and can get really ridicolous and sometimes awkward really does equally reach some incredible peaks that feel as unique as they are quality. And I can go into detail about how good the graphics are and how well optimized it is (1060 3GB, Ryzen 5 1600 - easily plays at 1440p high settings at about 80+ FPS at all times). Or how this really is, much like Breath of The Wild - a sort of celebration of the past but also a closing of it and an opening and appreciation of the future and innovation. Just like Ethan says - one door closes, another one opens. 

But at the end of the day for me it really does come down to just what a warm, genuine and fun game it really is which is exactly what I think Resident Evil is all about - hence why it's an absolutely fantastic game, and an absolutely fantastic Resident Evil game. Don't get me wrong, this game has plenty of flaws and for many of it's unique and fantastic qualities it can still be rather inconsistently delivered. But it's unmistakable and genuine Resident Evil heart really does overcome all that it gets wrong and I'd really consider it perfectly imperfect. I love it, and I couldn't be happier with it.

The list above shows my top three FPS horror games of all time and RE7 absolutely has earned it's right in that list.  An absolute horror masterpiece that shows that you can stay true to a franchise while overhauling the design, feel, and game mechanics of an already established horror staple.

First off - The atmosphere.  Anxiety, dread, and apprehension wash over you in the beginning of this title.  The suspense and tone make you want to shrivel up and not push on.  The lack of an intrusive UI allows you to get a full frame environmental experience that will put you face first into the disgusting, grimy world that the level designers have created.  What seem like impossible to navigate, mazelike corridors soon become familiar as you find trinkets and hidden messages that allow you to press forward.  Very immersive.

The story was original and as disturbing as any of the other RE tales have been.  The voice acting is convincing enough, and the scenarios you experience first hand will give you something to remember after you shut the game off.

Although the combat and inventory management is clunky at times, it stays true to the inventory system of the earlier games in the franchise and force you to resource manage instead of horde everything.  Swapping weapons and crafting makeshift first aid meds shouldn't be easy for your average joe character, so fumbling for another item in your inventory while something lurches towards you feels appropriate.

All the hallmark puzzles and little easter eggs appear as they did in previous RE games, but for them to incorporate them into the first person experience really makes you feel like you're still in that Umbrella Corporation universe we all know and love.

An absolute must buy for any Resident Evil or horror game fans out there.  A one of a kind experience.

A brilliant return to form for a series that desperately needed it. Much like Resident Evil 4, Capcom have taken the series and turned it on it's head, while maintaining many of the small details that make a Resident Evil game FEEL like a Resident Evil game. The best writing the series has had (which isn't saying much, admitedly, but the story is actually geniunely enjoyable), a spooky atmosphere to rival even the scariest of "pure horror" games, and boss characters that are incredibly memorable combine to make RE7 one of the best in the series. 

It's not perfect, the last third of the game is pretty lackluster and forgettable, and the presence of the regular zombies honestly detracts from the awesome atmosphere the first part of the game set up, as they tend to show up in areas where you're expecting something more significant. RE7 maintains some of the "action-horror" aspects of the earlier RE games, but it is absolutely not a FPS that you play for the gunplay or weapon variety. 

Overall, RE7 is a great horror game, a great Resident Evil game, and an okay action game.

Welcome to the family, son!

After the abysmal reception and sales of Resident Evil 6 in 2012, Capcom changed the course of the beloved horror franchise for the better. Resident Evil 7 is a reboot and the return to form which RE aficionados and horror fans have been waiting for years. 

Resident Evil 7 opens up with a man named Ethan who is looking for his long-lost wife, Mia. After 3 years a mysterious video clip emerges in which Mia asks her husband not to look for her. Mia's traces lead to Dulvey, Louisiana where a towering mansion rests deep in the bayou. Once inside, Ethan is captured and forced to fight for his life against the Baker family who would make Leatherface himself feel right at home. Ethan needs to manage dwindling resources, tight inventory management, and keep a keen eye at all times to survive the trip.

The game is played from the first person perspective which works surprisingly well. The gameplay compliments this new addition to the series by giving players more freedom to search every nook and cranny, but also to take in the horribly beautiful visuals. The game looks absolutely gorgeous even on lower settings with a lot of attention to detail and environment. The Baker household looks like someone has actually lived there with shuffled piles of papers and books, refridgerators full of maggots and intestines, and wear and tear on surfaces and furniture. The ambient sound design and voice acting are great, as well, and deserve a special mention in how they serve the purpose of utmost immersion.

During the course of the game Ethan finds your typical RE arsenal of weapons, including handguns, shotguns, a grenade launcher, and a machinegun. On normal difficulty munitions and herbs are plentiful enough. On RE 7 you won't find gold lying around, but instead antique coins which are well hidden. With enough coins, Ethan can upgrade his abilities or acquire better weapons. Weapons themselves cannot be upgraded. After the first playthrough, a set of unlockables is granted, with them a new difficulty setting. There is no mercenaries mode or any other extra content available after the main campaign. The free extra-dlc "Not a Hero" is available to everyone who have purchased the game, but needs to be downloaded separately.

RE 7 hits the rights targets on many things, but certain foibles still exist. Enemy variety is one of such ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Sadly, there are only few enemy types in the game, and since this is Resident Evil, one would expect an armada of different types of monsters. The "Molded" which make an appearance early in the game lose their scary-factor quite fast as the game progresses. Another thing is the sheer lenght. For the full asking price, RE 7 is NOT worth the price of admission. The content on the base game is around 8-9 hours (+ Not a Hero). Consider buying the game during a sale.

Resident Evil 7 is an entertaining haunted house simulator, but do consider picking it up during a sale.
