[h1] Information English [/h1]

RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard is a first-person horror game and the long-awaited sequel to the series, which was developed by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. was developed.

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

This time you don't play a special agent on steroids. This time you are a simple plain guy named "Ethan" whose wife "Mia" disappeared 3 years ago. After 3 years he gets a video message from her and an email with the address where he can find her ... Bakers Farm, Louisiana. He sets out to find her ....

It plays like a real Resident Evil part again and feels like it. To compare the former part Resident Evil 1. You just have to imagine the first part from the first person perspective and that with a really damn good story, as well as very good graphics and great sound effects. Everything we have missed in recent years is simply there again: limited inventory, items that can be combined (for the production of medicines, ammunition, etc.), safe rooms with the inventory boxes known at the time for stowing and storage options. There is an auto save function, but this is usually only at key points in the game. Otherwise you always have to go to the safe room to save on a dictation machine, similar to what was the case last time with Alien: Isolation. There are puzzles to solve again and lots of keys to get for the doors. Of course it did some "backtracking" again but in this case it was really great. Because just because you have already been to a place does not mean that nothing new is waiting for you there.

[h1] atmosphere [/h1]

What a terrific horror atmosphere. When it comes to survival horror, Resident Evil 7 sets completely new standards. You always have that certain uncomfortable feeling when you have to turn around. You constantly have the great need to close the door behind you. I'm a big horror fan of all kinds of horror, but rarely has a game completely captivated me in 45 minutes

h1] graphics /sound [/h1]

The graphics are just great and are presented in great detail. Not only the presentation, but also the level design. With the very gloomy soundscape, you feel like you are in the action. Everything is simply harmonized with one another.

[h1] Combat system [/h1]

There are different types of weapons such as Knives, pistols, rifles, shotguns, grenade launchers and flamethrowers. Some can be found in the course of the game and for others you need keys or solve puzzles. There is the right weapon for every type of enemy. Ammunition is rather in short supply, but it all depends on the level of difficulty, as this varies. Later you will be happy about every available shot in your pocket.

[h1] Pro [/h1]

+ oppressive, exciting story
+ after part 5-6 again a good Resident Evil
+ exciting boss fights
+ gloomy atmosphere fueled by the darkness
+ Moments of shock
+ Goosebumps
+ very detailed graphics
+ scary, beautiful sound
+ good AI
+ Documents, coins to collect and destructible figures
+ unlockable after playing through
+ Achievements and trading cards

[h1] Contra [/h1]

- History can also be confusing if you don't understand it
- very few different opponents
- 3 to 6 hours of gameplay for the campaign

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Resident Evil 7 embodies the unmistakable gameplay elements of exploration in a tense atmosphere, which shaped the "survival horror" genre about twenty years ago. I just say back to the roots. Clear purchase recommendation for fans of the series or those who like this genre.



[h1] Information German [/h1]

RESIDENT EVIL 7 biohazard ist ein  First-Person Horror Spiel und der lang ersehnte Nachfolger der Serie, welches von CAPCOM Co., Ltd. entwickelt wurde.

[h1] Gameplay/Story [/h1]

Dieses Mal spielt man keinen Special-Agent auf steroiden. Dieses Mal ist man ein einfacher schlichter Typ namens "Ethan" dessen Frau "Mia" 3 jahre zuvor verschwunden ist. Nach 3 Jahren bekommt er eine Videonachricht von ihr und eine Email mit der Adresse wo er sie finden kann....Bakers Farm, Louisiana. Er macht sich auf sie zu finden....

Es spielt sich mal wieder wie ein echter Resident Evil Teil und fühlt sich auch so an.  Zum Vergleich der damalige Teil Resident Evil 1. Man muss sich den ersten Teil einfach nur aus der Ego-Perspektive vorstellen und das einfach noch mit einer wirklich verdammt guten Story, sowie einer sehr guten Grafik und klasse Soundeffekten. Es ist einfach wieder alles dabei was wir die letzten Jahre vermisst haben: Begrenztes Inventar, kombinierbare Sachen (zur Herstellung von Heilmitteln, Munition o.Ä.), Safe-Rooms mit den von damals bekannten Inventarboxen zur Verstauung und Speichermöglichkeiten. Es gibt zwar eine Autospeicherfunktion, diese ist aber meist nur an Schlüsselstellen des Spiels. Ansonsten muss man immer den Safe-Room aufsuchen um dort an einem Diktiergerät zu speichern, ähnlich wie es zu letzt bei Alien: Isolation der Fall war. Es gibt wieder Rätsel zu lösen und jede Menge Schlüssel für die Türen zu besorgen. Hat natürlich wieder etwas "Backtracking" aber in diesem Fall wirklich super umgesetzt. Denn nur weil man schon mal an einem Ort gewesen ist, heisst das noch lange nicht das dort nichts neues auf einen wartet. 

[h1] Atmosphäre [/h1]

Was für eine grandiose Horror-Atmosphäre. In Sachen Survival-Horror setzt Resident Evil 7 komplett neue Maßstäbe. Permanent hat man dieses gewisse unwohle Gefühl wenn man sich umdrehen muss. Andauernd hat man das große Bedürfniss die Tür hinter sich zu schliessen. Ich bin ein großer Horrorfan von allen möglichen Arten des Horrors, aber selten hat ein Spiel es geschafft mich in innerhalb von 45 Minuten komplett in den Bann zu ziehen.

[h1] Grafik/Sound [/h1]

Die Grafik ist einfach großartig und wird sehr detailliert dargestellt. Nicht nur die Darstellung, sondern auch das Leveldesign. Bei der sehr düsteren Soundkulisse fühlt man sich wie im Geschehen. Alles ist einfach stimmig aufeinander angepasst.

[h1] Kampfsystem [/h1]

Es gibt verschiedene Waffenarten wie z.B. Messer,  Pistolen, Gewehre, Flinten, Granatwerfer und Flammenwerfer. Manche findet man so im Spielverlauf und für andere benötigt man Schlüssel oder muss Rätsel lösen. Es gibt für jeden Gegnertyp die richtige Waffe. Munition ist eher Mangelware, allerdings kommt es ganz auf den Schwierigkeitsgrad an, da dies variiert. Man wird später über jeden zur Verfügung stehenden Schuss in der Tasche froh sein.

[h1] Pro [/h1]

+ beklemmend, spannende Geschichte
+ nach Teil 5-6 wieder ein gutes Resident Evil
+ spannende Bosskämpfe
+ düstere Atmosphäre, die durch die Dunkelheit angetrieben wird
+ Schock-Momente
+ Gänsehaut
+ sehr detaillierte Grafik
+ schaurig, schöner Sound
+ gute KI
+ Dokumente, Münzen zum sammeln und zerstörbare Figuren
+ freischaltbares nach dem Durchspielen
+ Errungenschaften und Trading Cards 

 [h1] Kontra [/h1]

- Geschichte kann auch verwirrend sein kann, wenn man sie nicht versteht
- sehr wenig verschiedene Gegner
- 3 bis 6 Stunden Spielzeit für die Kampange

[h1] Fazit [/h1]

Resident Evil 7 verkörpert die unverkennbaren Gameplay-Elemente von Erkundung in angespannter Atmosphäre, die vor etwa zwanzig Jahren das Genre „Survival Horror“ prägten. Ich sag nur Back to the roots. Klare Kaufempfehlung für Fans der Serie oder wer dieses Genre mag.

Yeah, I'm one of those dinos that's been playing the series throughout, back when we were all coping with static backdrops, tank controls, and hilariously fumbled dialogue. And so for me this is a welcome return to the ammo-counting days of the early games. But thankfully, it takes everything we've learned about survival horror and horror games in general, and applies them. And it works really well. I don't know if I'd call it a revelation, but it's an extremely polished entry in both a series and genre that's been massively underserved. Don't get me wrong - there have been plenty of good horror games - but those lean more towards fleeing and hiding, where this is a game where you get to shoot the bads. But shooting them doesn't give a feeling of safety, and that's part of RE7's strength.

Wisely, the game dials things back from the "save the world!" bioterror plots of recent entries, mainly focusing on saving yourself instead. While the monsters tend to be a little generic, they by no means come across as unthreatening, their unsteady gait making getting headshots a tense and dicey experience. The villains have more personality than almost any other horror game in my memory, and though it definitely leans towards the B-movie side of things, the boss sequences were some of the most surprising and memorable moments I've had all year. Just when I thought I had the number of a boss, it'll often pull the rug out from under you. However, some of the later bosses still fall into less interesting "shoot the flashy wobbly bit" sequences series veterans will know well, at the same time I felt harrowed throughout.

To digress a little, one of the dillemmas with horror games as time goes on is the simple matter of controls. Early survival horror games like the original Resident Evil built tension with their flaws - things like limited camera angles and an inability to aim well made things very tense, compared to more recent games where you have full ability to run, aim, and look wherever you like. Resident Evil 7 works with that by using the first-person perspective to limit your view, and generally makes your character sluggish while aiming and vulnerable while running - a good compromise between full FPS shooter controls and the clunky survival horror controls of old.

The full story, when it becomes more obvious, is where the cracks start to appear. When everything is a mystery, it's more frightening, but as the familiar bioterror elements emerge, things fall more comfortably into series tropes, and more obvious plot holes emerge. Still, it's worth the ride, and constantly keeps the tension up throughout, even though the horror starts to fall off as the game goes on.

Still, if you like survival horror, or just want to jump in and see the series at the strongest it's been at in a decade, this is a good place to pick up. You don't have to know much about the series' history or lore to appreciate it, and there are mercifully few callbacks to the larger plot and setting of the series. This one stands on its own, and stands well.

A Terrifyingly Fun Experience

WARNING: This article contains spoilers for Resident Evil 7 (sort of).

After over 7 years, I finally played a new Resident Evil game I enjoyed, Resident Evil 7. I can’t really make any comment that hasn’t been made before; the game goes back to its roots with survival horror instead of action, and the first person perspective is a significant change but it works really well. What I can comment on is my own experience playing the game.

First thing first, I played the game on Easy difficulty and have no plans on playing it on Normal or Madhouse. The reason I chose this was because I wanted to enjoy the game for its atmosphere rather than have it be a frustrating challenge that I give up on half way through. I felt very uneasy during the first half of the game, and could only play for 15-20 minutes at a time. After each iteration I had to take a break for at least 2 hours, which meant that I usually played it once a night (on weeknights). The game starts you off with limited ammo, so I only took a shot when it was absolutely necessary. Several reviews I read suggested that in order to preserve ammo it might be better to shoot the Molded in the leg and run, but I preferred to take them on one at a time and defensively stab them to death. This allowed me to roam the cleared areas freely, thanks to no re-spawns. I didn’t even use the Chem Fluids, herbs, and gunpowder until I was completely out of handgun bullets or First Aid Meds. Half way through the game I found that I was doing pretty good on resources, and started to get a bit freer with them. However, I rarely used the Flamethrower and the Grenade Launcher. When I picked up the shotgun I didn’t feel as helpless anymore and thus the game was less unsettling. The shotgun has been my favourite weapon in all of the previous Resident Evil games I played. By the time I got near the end game, I had a lot of resources stashed in the trunk. I could have been fairly liberal with the resources throughout the whole game. I never fired the magnum, I wish I did.

The one place I felt that the game was lacking was regarding the puzzles. The previous Resident Evil games had some interesting puzzles, but there were only the shadow puzzles here, which were fairly easy to solve.

The scariest part of the game was the Grandma. She kept showing up in random places, and always watching you. She doesn’t say anything, she doesn’t move, but she keeps showing up where you have to go.

All in all, I enjoyed this game very much. I beat the game in a little over 8 hours so it felt pretty short, however it is still a complete game. I’m happy I played through it.

Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic throwback to the survival horror of RE1 and RE2. It has the soul of those games with the exterior of a modern AAA title. The shift to first-person perspective is brilliantly executed, accentuating the tension and abject terror of the game as well as its very tight gunplay. The various locales are nicely detailed and thick in atmosphere – this game just exudes anxiety, and item management & ammo conservation add to the survival horror feel. There are many cinematic set pieces that would feel right at home in a great horror film, and despite a relatively weak third act, RE7 is well-written, featuring memorable characters and a story shrouded in dark mystery and moody intrigue. While it often borrows a little too much from previous Resident Evil titles (two sections in particular are very similar in layout to RE1’s mansion and RE5’s boat), it separates itself from them with its largely self-contained story, variety of cinematic influences (including The Blair Witch Project, Deliverance, Ringu, and particularly  Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Saw), and new first-person POV and gameplay mechanics. I was skeptical about Capcom’s ability to pull off a good sequel to the abysmal RE6, but they really surprised me – this is a true Resident Evil game for the current generation and one of my favorite games of the year. This is worth picking up not only for the excellent, highly replayable campaign, but for the free Not A Hero DLC which takes place after the events of the campaign and ties it into the Resident Evil universe. I was stoked to learn that RE7 was returning the franchise back to its horror roots, as the series had, in my humble opinion, devolved into an interactive action/adventure movie with the random quick time event.  The gameplay itself had become sporadic and stale, the storyline mundane, the characters were steadily losing their charm.

RE7 is the breath of fresh air the series desperately needed.

It is legitimately scary, featuring deliciously unsettling sfx ambience and a thoroughly creepy atmosphere; and while jumpscares abound it doesn't depend on them to the point of feeling cheap.  The storyline is somewhat predictable (It's RE afterall) but it differs enough from previous installments to keep you alert and interested.  The boss battles are fun and intense,  and the Baker family proved to be superbly sinister and unhinged.  

RE7 sits comfortably on my list of favorite horror games, although the early Silent Hill installments still reign supreme.  (I'm still upset over PT getting axed.) 

Now, that all being said, I do have a bit of a grievance with it: the dlc - specifically "Not a Hero".  The previous dlcs were released fairly quickly and while there was some silliness (Jack's 55th Birthday for example), there were also some heart racing minigames as well (such as Bedroom and Nightmare).  Overall, those dlcs were enjoyable and fleshed out the base game's backstory quite well.

Now here's where it gets a little bit spoilery:

[spoiler] At the end of RE7 we're treated to the return of one of the series' most beloved characters - Chris Redfield- with a not so subtle hint that he'd be the focus of an upcoming dlc.[/spoiler]

The hype was real.  I think RE fans, in general, were excited about this revelation.  The dlc was coming soon!  No wait,  it's coming later, the devs said.  Much later. They want to give it the attention it deserves so that it lives up to the quality of the base game.  Okay, fair enough.  

Well, it's nearly a year later and that dlc [i]finally[/i] dropped.  I just finished it.  I have to wonder if I let the hype train speed me along to the land of unreasonable expectations because I feel as though the dlc did [i]not[/i] live up to the quality of the base game.  It felt generic and lackluster.  There was a smidgen of storyline and a wee plot twist, but it didn't feel as if it were some masterfully handcrafted dlc that had taken almost a full year to produce.

**Edited to add that the dlc in question "Not a Hero" is FREE and while that in itself is a bit of a redeeming quality, I still stand by my original assessment that it fails to live up to the hype surrounding it.**

That little disappointment aside, RE7 is a solid game that stands on its own within the horror genre and the series itself.  With its financial success and almost universal praise from the playerbase,  I hope the devs continue to guide the series along its current path.

Yep, I have learned to wait for a sale, but I'm glad I did, so my review is based on Value as much as anything 
While It is still unclear whether this is actually a complete reboot or not, and the debate Rages on through a Thousand forums in all it's Geeky Fury, I personally feel that RE7 retcon's the series cutting out the events of RE 5 & 6, which are not bad games in and of themselves, but the series had become far too silly to  recover and seriously be considered "Scary" again.  In the late stage of the game you find a note about "Raccoon City Sixteen Years Later " in an area that has been abandoned for a least three years which would place this game around 2004 - 2005.   Personally I think it was a wise move to remove 5 & 6 from the Cannon - in much the same way it was wise to remove Fate's Carnival and Sacred Grove from the Mystery Case Files Cannon - so this seemingly takes place either shortly before or alongside the events of RE 4.  

WHAT IT DOES WELL -  

The main game is divided into Two very separate and distinct halves including Two optional mini games via video tapes Two mandatory Video Tapes and a really good "SAW" level at the half way point. 
As mentioned above the first half plays, and feels, very much like a Hillbilly version of Alien Isolation but is still completely recognizable as Resident Evil with the crazy Jack Baker playing the part of the Alien or perhaps a Nemesis type character that stalks around attacking you on sight.  There is very little to do here other than run, hide and try to escape the house.  As also with Alien Isolation there are secondary enemies in the basement that act in the same way as the Working Joe did which can either be fought or avoided to survive.  Make no mistake this does bring back the scares and the tension, perhaps not on the same level as Amnesia or Outlast, but still a very worthy return to form after the series went from it's Campy Beginnings to full horror to complete farce.  Evidently the recent Campaign from a very rich and very Orange Man with Small Hands and a Bad Wig to "MAKE RESIDENT EVIL SCARY AGAIN" has definitely paid off.......or am I thinking of something else? 
After escaping the house the Tone of the game changes drastically and becomes a lot more action based, very much like Doom or Dead Space.  Fans should know though that this offering does not place much importance of Boss Fights as there are only Two "Bosses" really (three if you count the SAW TRAP), that being, Jack Baker, Margaret Baker with the final battle with ALMA....ahem....I mean...."Eveline" being more of a Set Piece rather than an actual Fight.   BTW it's pretty easy to figure out which member of the Baker Family ALMA really is in the early stages (no, it's not Zoe). 
 
Playing this on very high settings (both with and without the Depth option) this can't really be called "Photo realistic" as is claimed by Capcom because there are many really bad textures and patchwork backgrounds, in fact the Graphics were actually better on the Demo "Beginning Hour" for some strange reason.  Nevertheless this is very well optimized and by toning down the brightness, combined with the Washed-Out look of the color pallet this will make the visuals perfect for this game rendering the graphical shortcomings largely unnoticeable.  I can play this through my NVIDIA 870m at maximum settings perfectly smoothly with the only shortcoming being a time lag between the voiceover and the speech animations. Also for people with low to mid range rigs setting the frame rate at 30-fps is perfectly adequate (yes I also tried it on my older Rig and was surprised at how well it performed). 
 
 
THE "NOT EXACTLY BAD BUT SLIGHTLY ANNOYING" -  

Your character "Ethan" is rather wishy-washy and bland, often speaking dialog that is meant to be camp and humorous but is completely out of sync with the dark atmosphere of the game.  (Why are so many heroes in  Video Games always called "Ethan" anyway?!)

Escaping the House and completing the first half was somewhat of a let down as the Vaccine you have been risking your life for doesn't work anyway, even playing both of the "Choice" options (again feeling like one of the pointless tasks in Alien Isolation).

This I will admit after waiting all these years annoyed me a little but as I got the sale price I can accept that. 
 
The DLC 
 
Just when I thought that CAPCOM had completely redeemed themselves they go and pull a stunt like this and I am rudely reminded why so many people tend to hate on them!  Suffice it to say that most of the DLC content has clearly been cut out of the main game forcing us to  "Buy it at a High Price" and it just isn't worth it.  The best offering is the room escape which is will please fans of HO Mystery Case Files type games (or fans of "The Room" series).  In fact CAPCOM are so greedy for money that they actually Retcon their own game with the "Daughters" DLC which completely contradicts the story of RE7.  I'm sorry if this annoys people but to Retcon it's own story is such an obvious cash grab and is completely unacceptable. 
 
Despite this I the game pulls through with no need for the DLC as completion unlocks the "MADHOUSE" mode which is much more enjoyable and challenging making it's short duration worth the effort.

Resident Evil 7 / Biohazard 7   

Release Date: January 24, 2017 

Strengths: 
-Pure Horror (The most chilling RE title yet)  
-Originality (Yes, it is not at all like previous RE games. FPS, more horrific, better graphics etc. etc.)  
-Good graphics (Pretty solid special effects and rendering)  
-Great story and direction (Feels like playing a role in a top rated horror movie)  


Limitations:
-Graphic content (Sudden shocks, dark corners, scary scenes. Can be too scary for certain players.)
-High violence (Cutting, slicing, decapitation, amputation, gore is common. Stay away from this game if you have a  problem with that.)
-Main game is pretty short (Can be completed in around 6-9 hrs)


Conclusion:

Simply superb, if you are into story driven and horror class games. RE-7 gives a new touch to the earlier games by bringing in a completely new story, first person perspective (which adds to better horror experience) and new characters. Rather than being part of some elite force like previous RE characters, this game's protagonist is an ordinary man looking for his missing wife. The gameplay progresses just like a horror movie : you start in a car, go to a jungle, reach an abandoned looking house, watch pre-recorded tapes to find out what's happened etc. It may get boring at the start, but the action/fun starts pretty quick as soon as you get the first handgun. Weapon system and combat is very realistic and enjoyable (if not scary ;)). In spite of the differences, the game still preserves the touch of previous RE games with features like having a special room for saving games, item boxes, puzzles, combining items, making custom ammunition etc. I'd like to add that this game is tough. You'd die probably more than any other RE game in the Hard Mode especially in Boss fights. If perseverance is one of your qualities then the game would not bother you that much ;).  I'd not say that this is the best RE game till date but nevertheless definitely recommend buying it as it is clearly one of the scariest/atmospheric games I've ever played.

Not only is this a good game, it's a good Resident Evil game. It's full of ridiculous situations, nonsensical puzzles and magical shadow paintings. If Resident Evil didn't exist and the first one came out today it'd be this. 

The biggest difference from the rest of the series and what I loved the most was the reliance on atmosphere as opposed to obnoxious jump scares in order to build tension. This Blair Witch-type of scary is true horror and it isn't used nearly as much as it should in games. Not knowing what might be in the house with you heightens the feeling of danger as you play the game and its pacing of building tension, cutting it with a jump scare or a fake out only to start building it up again is how I feel horror games should be like. In Resident Evil 6 I struggled to play for 10 minutes without getting bored of all the action and loud noises. With Resident Evil 7 I got so hooked I forgot to go to sleep.

While the first hour is very atmospheric and scary the game never manages to capture that mood again because as you progress you get more and more powerful and enemies become less intimidating. It reminds me of Doom 3 in that way because that started out as a survival horror game but slowly progressed into a full-fledged action fantasy. Granted, there is a section later on where you don't have all your weapons for a while but I feel that the lack of enemy variety undercuts the tension that section was supposed to create. A fear of the unknown is a cardinal rule of the horror genre and I think they missed the mark with The Molded being the only enemy type in the game.

But the worst part of Resident Evil 7 by far is that there's no achievement for popping all of the balloons during Lucas' party! I was really bummed. There isn't much about the game that's original but there isn't much about it that's bad either. Resident Evil 7 takes after some of the biggest trendsetters in the genre of the past few years and that's by no means a bad thing. It takes the best parts of those games and makes them its own and it proved to be a solid return for the franchise I love.

After coming off the completely lackluster and, frankly, disasterously banal "Revelation" additions in the Resident Evil game lineup, 7 has proven, to me at least, that CAPCOM is trying their best to come back down to Earth and make RE games not only enjoyable again but actually have some kernal of believability in something that's already dealing with the fantastical. 

Sure, there are still bosses that are grotesquely monsterous, horridly deformed, and downright disgusting to look at so you may think it's not that far a depature from the imbecilic T-Rex in 6 but you'd be wrong. While that T-Rex was definitely an interesting boss it was, perhaps, a complete reach in trying to maintain "bigger, badder, more challenging" aspect of the RE games which has had quite the problem with trying to one up itself each and every game and, for the most part, especially after 4, has been just making their enemies larger rather than actually giving them something that actually makes them unique and challenging...and let me just say that having a character suddenly gain the basely boring ability to "shapeshift" into several different creatures doesn't actually make them that interesting, especially since it REEKS of "haha this isn't even my final form" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that, quiet frankly, got old by the end of Oct of 2011 when that particular meme hit its peak. 

RE 7 brings with it a breath of fresh air and a familiarity as its muderously monsterous molded motherhunchers bring back  a feeling of nostalgia from the first games where the things you're trying to fight while frightening, in some aspects, aren't completely beyond the realm of believability. Yes, still fantastical but less of a stretch to the imagination, especially when it makes one think back to the Hunters which were similar in size, if a bit smaller, and just as terrifying to fight against if you weren't prepared. And the bosses in RE 7? Amazingly designed, challenging in their own right, and not plagued with the oneupmanship "bigger is better" mindset that's saturated the last few RE games. 

Of course, this is all a very personalized opinion and some people won't agree or will argue aspects of this review until the cows come home but, really, the fact remains that RE 7 is a departure from the droll entries that we've seen in the last few years from CAPCOM in regards to the RE franchise and I'm 100% for it to become the new trend because CAPCOM is actually THINKING and making Resident Evil actually interesting again.

[h1]Best Homecoming Simulator 2017[/h1]

Before this game was launched there were ads going on with the phrase "Welcome Home." It was a message for those who played the original Resident Evil (1996) and following sequels. What it also means is that developers decided to look back and analyze what made those first games so succesful and beloved, and then make this game on the base of that research. Far as I see they succesfully managed to bring out once again all the fun aspects of 'survival horror' game.

Story begins with a mystery and main protagonist(s) have a reason to begin investigate that, somewhere along the way it turns out everything is not what it seems and turning back is no longer an option. Usually this is the point where the player can start to roam around freely and explore the surroundings for keys and helpful items. As you progress your story you'll witness bizarre things, question your sanity, solve puzzles and wonder why on earth you want to even continue. Careful searching is rewarding and provides the player with extra ammunitions, health and even background knowledge what is going on. At the end of the day your ultimate goal is simple; just "survive the horrors" and possibly try to save other people that are trapped with you too.

This game gives also subtle references how it is connected to the rest of the "Resident Evil" world, in the form of newspapers, books, paintings etc. (distantly in storywise too.) But mainly this is refreshing settings with previously unknown characters. Main protagonist (Ethan) is "faceless" most of the time and personally I think it was for the reason to be more easily approachable as a player's character. Whatever the real reasons would be, it was a good counter balance for the over character dramatizations that has been influencing Resident Evil series for awhile. There was a time when Resident Evil was no longer considered as a 'Survival Horror' but rather as a 'Character Drama.'

Then the difficulty setting was one of the most enjoyable I've seen lately. Normally after you complete the game, you'll unlock the top difficulty. This (Madhouse) is whole new setting where items have changed places and even some encounters have been altered. Also even some enemies can run instead of walking. It's whole new layer of fear, and this is something that was true to the original games also. It's not just changing some values to make you headbutt wall more, but instead change your comfort of knowing.

I was initially skeptical of RE7 when it was unveiled. I thought it was just going to ape the slew of other first person horror games on the market nowadays. Thankfully, what I just played was by far the best Resi game since RE4 and, honestly, the scariest one in the franchise.

If you're a classic survival horror fan and Resi games after RE4 - or even including RE4 - have left you cold, do yourself a favour and get this game. You won't regret it. It's a true return to survival horror. You feel limited and powerless, but combat is satisfying, and you are rewarded for playing a bit conservatively, e.g. saving items for boss fights to make them more bearable, and also for exploring potentially dangerous areas for helpful items.

The story is well presented, the characters/villains are very likable (but terrifying), the world around you is rich with detail and a thick, creepy atmosphere, and the game knows exactly the best ways to scare you; it employs a lot of subversive tactics that will keep you on your toes. It's borderline heart attack inducing in a few instances. It's also really well paced; there's hardly any babying the player at the beginning, and the game knows when to give you respite, when to give you puzzles or send you on exploratory missions, and when to drag you through pure hell.

I do have a handful of minor critcisms that I'll just whittle through here. Inventory management is fine and meant to be restrictive, I get that; however, I wish you had the option of temporary extra inventory space ala RE4 when picking up one item too many so you are given the chance to combine it with something you already have and thus not have to discard something else in order to make room for it.

I also wish you could map more than 4 weapons for the weapon hotkeys, or at the very, very least allow the player to equip a weapon not mapped to a hotkey. You have to swap out a weapon on the top row for a 5th one in order to equip it. This is just clumsy and makes things needlessly complicated in terms of extra button presses as opposed to being a reasonable restriction for a survival horror game.

There's a lack of enemy variety. About 2/3 through the game you've pretty much seen all the monsters in the game, and the Molded start getting overused quite heavily as the only mooks you face. They are scary and all and continue to be nearly all the way through but it would be more interesting if at least a couple more enemy types were thrown in by this point.

The final half an hour or so is much easier than I was expecting as you're overloaded with ammo and remote bombs and enemies can be easily run past. This wouldn't be too bad if this didn't culminate in a pretty pathetic final boss that feels more like an interactive cutscene more than a proper fight, which is a shame because most of the bosses in the game are awesome.

Finally, no Mercenaries mode :( Obviously it wouldn't be as deep as the last few games due to the more limited controls but I think they're solid enough for Mercenaries or at least some sort of decent arcade-y mode resembling it.

Other than these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game is a masterfully crafted experience. Count me in if RE8 is anything like this.

Played almost all Resident Evil's to date. Honestly i was expecting to be put off by the radical ''FPS'' change. My expectations were not met. Welcome to the family.

Gameplay : 

Resident Evil has not been this good since 4 . While it's still quite different to the original RE games , 7 still feels like the classics . This is by far the creepiest and most Horror like Resident Evil game yet . 7 takes you back to the series survival horror roots and you will want to conserve everything you have very carefully , I even found myself having to do this on Easy mode . 

The atmosphere is on point throughout the game , accompanied by great music , and you're always looking over your shoulder wondering what's next . In classic Resident Evil style ,  there are a number of puzzles / item searches throughout the game , and while they can be confusing , they're not frustrating , there was no point were I was struggling or feeling like I wasn't enjoying the game , as challenging as some parts were . 

Graphics : 

This game looks amazing , it has all the modern graphics settings , plus a resolution scaling option that can make the game look even better , providing your PC can handle it .  there is major attention to detail  also . 

The PC version feels unoptimized and needs some fixing though ,  as I did experience frame drops on a number of occasions , at one point near the garage I experienced lag so bad that I had to restart my game . My PC is very capable of handing this game , and I know other people have had similar issues . 
For those wondering about the Anti Aliasing options , I found FXAA + TAA gave me the best results personally .

[h1]This Game Is Brutal![/h1]

TLDR Version:

[b]THE best iteration of Resident Evil to ever grace our gaming fingertips[/b]

Pros +
- Insanely detailed graphics so you can see the gore and brutality up close and personal
- VR integration makes for a wicked experience
- Constant fear of being caught grips you throughout the entire story
- Brilliant story to follow
- Gameplay mechanics are entertaining and boss battles pack heaps of thrill
- Puzzles are back!

Cons -
- A bit tricky to get your graphics settings configured for optimum detail

Full Review

As I sat there rocking my 10 week old baby boy to sleep in his bouncer, I thought I had a few minutes to spend trying out Resident Evil 7: Biohazard. Those few minutes eventually turned into hours and thanks to my little boy, he stayed asleep for that whole time! Plus, if it weren’t for the comfort of having him nearby, I probably would have exited the game very quickly because I was so freaked out by it.

Resident Evil is back and better than ever! With the stigma associated with RE:6, a lot of gamers seemed to be backing away from the genre-defining series. RE:6 had a lot of problems that I myself would have to agree with, such as the Mercenaries mode lacking the same excitement and satisfaction it did with other RE games, especially the 3DS game Resident Evil: The Mercenaries 3D.

Taking things in a completely different direction, the team at CAPCOM have redefined the horror survival genre. Sure, P.T. seemed to do it first, but with the cancellation of such a promising game, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard picks up the broken pieces of what would have been Silent Hills and puts it’s own twist on the concept. A twist I find completely distances itself from what P.T. set out to accomplish.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard HouseThe Resident Evil series doesn’t feel like it’s been the same since RE:4 in my opinion. After that, the series seemed to go down an action genre road, mixed with mutated monstrosities. The feeling of fear associated with RE:1 through to the RE:4 was lost. RE:5 and RE:6 just felt like action games set in the world of Resident Evil.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is still set in that familiar world but it moves completely away from the paths of Leon Kennedy, Jill Valentine, Robert Wesker et al. This time you play as someone we’ve never met before called Ethan. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is supposedly set after the events of RE:6.

Ethan receives a mysterious email from his wife who had disappeared three years previously. The email is very vague and only says, “Dulvey, Louisiana. Baker farm. Come get me.” Of course wanting to know what happened to his wife, Ethan sets off straight away and eventually find himself in a bayou outside a run-down Southern manor.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard CharactersThis is where everything begins. As soon as you enter that house, your gaming experience will be filled with fear, exhilaration, disgust, wonder and many other feelings that will altogether heighten your new Resident Evil experience. I don’t want to spoil too much of the story but this house you’re in has some pretty messed up individuals residing in it. I can however, tell you there are multiple endings to achieve!

The game is played entirely from a first-person point of view, something that has never been done by a Resident Evil game. Playing the whole game from this aspect adds so much more fear to the experience, especially when you’re sprinting down a hallway knowing you have a crazed man wielding a massive sledgehammer on your tail.

It’s these feelings of fight or flight that fill you with adrenaline, and not being able to see the area around you as easily as a third-person view would allow really puts you on edge. I can imagine playing Resident Evil 7: Biohazard with a VR device would seriously cause some pretty nasty nightmares.

One such part of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard that I found quite interesting was playing through the eyes of other characters. As you explore the game, you’ll come across video tapes to watch. When you watch them, you get to control the person who’s filming. This doesn’t just provide a bit more game to play, but also fills in gaps of the story.

Gameplay mechanics we are familiar with in RE games make an appearance such as hunting down herbs to craft into healing agents, saving your scarcely found ammunition, solving those oh-so-missed puzzles we used to love and setting up those all important headshots. Also in amongst Resident Evil 7: Biohazard are secrets to be found. Everyone loves secrets and these come in the form of antique coins scattered about the place and bobbleheads to shoot.

Boss fights are as well thought out as they have ever been, giving you an environment to use to your advantage. One such fight lets you wield a chainsaw against an opponent who also has a chainsaw/scissor hybrid weapon. These boss fights are pretty damn intense!

Some new mechanics also enter the fray such as hiding in shadows to avoid being caught by crazed lunatics. It’s no longer about churning through zombies and clearing the area so you can progress, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard truly defines the meaning of horror survival. You need to do what you can to survive.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard GoryApart from that, I am particularly impressed with how CAPCOM haven’t held back one bit with the gore and brutality. Playing through the eyes of Ethan you see every attack coming your way. As a knife slices it’s way through the air toward your body, you get to watch Ethan raise his arm in defense, causing the knife to cut right through the flesh of his forearm. The next attack from the knife results in Ethan grabbing the blade in desperation. It’s all so teeth-grittingly realistic but so fascinating and detailed that you can’t look away.

[b]Aesthetic Charm[/b]

Seriously, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard takes graphics to a new level. With a whole new gaming engine built solely for this game called RE Engine, the attention to detail with everything is superb. There’s a particular scene right at the beginning where you see Ethan driving his car past a body of water. This scene looks so photo-realistic you would not be able to tell the difference if you saw it in a magazine.

Motion capture makes characters move so seamlessly, however there still seem to be some discrepancies with mouth movements when a character is speaking. It’s a small qualm but not everything is perfect.

Music and sound effects add to the atmosphere of the game so perfectly and footsteps, creaking of floorboards, slamming doors etc. will have you jumping out of your skin!
Final Thoughts

With it only being January of 2017, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard has already set the bar for gaming so high. I really can’t imagine how any other releases this year could top what CAPCOM have pulled off.

Personally this is the game I’ve been waiting for. Something that packs a story fascinating enough to pull you in and not stop exploring, something with insanely good graphics, something that includes gunplay and melee combat so as to not leave the protagonist as someone who can’t fight back, and something that doesn’t censor itself but instead reveals the true nature a merciless monster would present a human.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a must-play for everyone. Obviously not for children or those who are squeamish around blood, but everyone else will find something about this game that they’ll remember for the rest of their lives.

While it may not carry some features found in the classic trilogy up to the same standard in terms of number of locked rooms, interactive puzzles and complexity of the map design (though it does bring them back which is very welcome nonetheless), it makes up for it with its simple yet harrowing atmosphere as well as far more robust shooting mechanics with faster enemies to take advantage of the new system. It even brings more elements to the table (at least only compared to the classic trilogy) that are unique to this entry, such as secret items that are hidden much better than in previous entries to the point that they're very missable, some new intimidating villains which actively persue and harass the protagonist, and secretive optional puzzles that won't be that obvious unless you pay very close attention. The opposition is now far more conniving and malignant when compared to those of the classics' as well, alongside some of my favorite boss fights in the series (how many games let you [spoiler]have a chainsaw vs giant scissors melee fight with an angry zombiesh hilly billy?[/spoiler] Yeah. Not a lot).

In terms of visuals, the game nails it with almost life-like character designs and animations. The more quasirealistic contributes to the game's unnerving and eerie atmosphere. Unfortunately, there are times where certain models feel less realistic and more cartoonish-looking, though the gore and viscera at display helps to distract you from it just a little bit. The game doesn't shy away from taking risks, with special segments that can be triggered in-game that only contribute to building up the Baker family as this malicious force even further. The game will surprise you with genuinely-unexpected moments, by remixing the enemies you run into as you move around the house. A crafting system is available in the same way one was available in Resident Evil 3, but unlike then where it felt like it easily broke the game, this time around the new crafting system here manages to keep things balanced to a fairly large degree, without detracting much from the main experience.

It breaks my heart, but there are some very apparent flaws with this game that need to be addressed. The new Molded enemies do leave a lot to be desired even if they do manage to do an okay job at filling in whenever the Baker family isn't after your buns. The tone of the game also takes an odd turn and has a more action-focused not-really-all-that-scary atmosphere somewhere around the third act, with the very last hour of the game especially feeling more like a drag rather than an actually-entertaining lead-up to the final showdown. Also, what's up with all the remote bombs in this game's third act? It keeps throwing so much at you in place of actual ammunition, so even if you decide not to use them, you've pretty much got your hands tied behind your back.

Four last minor gripes: cutscenes are unskippable due to how they're integrated into the game so speedrunning is going to be a bit problematic; the limited saves via this game's version of the ribbon ink is limited to the highest difficulty in the game, which is something I absolutely despise as it was a feature that added additional weight to the player's actions; there are only sixteen save slots for some reason, which is odd considering how Resident Evil 4 has a total of 20; this one is more related to the PC port itself and it's the CPU-throttling which causes various degrees of stuttering, depending on your hardware, through various points in the game which could render it unplayable (turning textures down to medium seems to solve this issue, and oddly enough the game's textures on characters look just as fine on medium as they do on ultra, most probably due to all the other effects, which I'm not entirely sure of, masking the textures' clarity).

Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a welcome return to form that returns to the original formula while also maintaining an identity of its own. It's certainly no Resident Evil Remake (or whichever one's your favorite), but it manages to do a wonderful job at delivering an experience reminiscent of the original survival horror classic it started out as. It's absolutely worth giving a try (unless you dislike first-person shooters) and hopefully a sign that Capcom is on the right track again with this franchise.

In Resident Evil 7, the player controls a new character, Ethan, who has travelled to a spooky house deep in the swamps of Louisiana in search of his missing girlfriend, Mia.

It won’t surprise you to learn that there are things living inside the house that aren’t friendly, and that want to kill you, although it clearly surprised Ethan, because he didn’t bring any weapons with him. Fortunately there are plenty of weapons to find including 2 varieties of knife, 3 different 9mm handguns, a magnum, a shotgun, a machinegun, a flamethrower, a grenade launcher and some remotely detonated bombs.

I like that most of these weapons are hidden behind puzzles, not exactly complicated to solve, but they reward exploration. Its entirely possible that some players could complete the game without finding everything.

RE7 has changed to a first person perspective, after the other main games were mostly third person. This is definitely a massive improvement, as the environments are more immersive and the combat is more enjoyable. Most of the weapons are fun to use, the only one that I didn’t really like was the flamethrower. Outside of one boss encounter, it seemed to be quite weak.

Its good that most of the weapons are strong, because Ethan moves really slowly, kinda like Isaac Clarke in Dead Space. I guess its designed to make the player feel vulnerable, but when you also factor in the level design, which is often quite narrow and cramped, especially inside the house, you won’t be running away from many enemies. There’s a lot of backtracking through previously cleared areas too, so in the long run its better to kill whatever you see.

Thankfully I was never really in danger of running out of ammo. There’s a useful crafting system, where you can combine chemicals with either herbs to make healing items, or gunpowder to make ammo. You can also take some drugs that temporarily allow you to see hidden items. Plus, playing on PC with mouse aim, I didn’t waste many bullets (although there is this one annoying enemy who has a habit of jerking its head from side to side just as you’re about to fire).

The enemies are the weakest part of the game in my opinion. While trying to avoid spoilers, there are Human bosses, where Ethan’s slow movement speed mean you’ll inevitably get hit even when you’ve learned the attack pattern of the boss (you can block to reduce damage). There are four types of “molded”, that are basically monsters made of a black ooze, and some flying insects. Their visual designs and their attack patterns (run towards player and attempt to melee) are all too similar. The game really needed more enemy variety.

The story is probably the best of any Resident Evil game. Plenty of the usual elements are present – [spoiler]bioweapons, shadowy organisations[/spoiler] – but its told in a way that feels more believable and easy to understand. The game is good from a technical point of view – I didn’t crash at all, and I could easily maintain a consistent 60 fps. Controls are fully rebindable.

I’d probably rank this as my third favourite Resident Evil, behind RE1 and Revelations 2, so if you’re a fan of the series, RE7 is definitely worth playing. It would also be a good place to start if you’ve never played a Resident Evil before, as the story doesn’t link to any of the other games. However it only took me 11 hours to finish the game, so the standard purchase price is excessive, and I’d recommend waiting for a 50% sale.

Okay, there's no easy way to say this, but I kind of hate this game.

On a technical and graphical level, RE7 is pretty great: the entire game ran smooth as butter at 4K on some pretty high settings for me and will no doubt scale well for less powerful PCs. If nothing else, I can safely say that visually, the game is pretty damn incredible, and if the idea of a traditional Resident Evil experience that looks utterly gorgeous is enough to get you interested, then I predict you're going to have a good time.

Unfortunately, it seems I don't like the very fabric that makes the series tick.

The first and possibly worst element of the whole game is the awful movement and combat. Were this a more Outlast-style experience without any kind of weapons, then perhaps the game would be better, or by contrast, if the developers put more effort into making the gunplay meatier, then maybe I wouldn't have felt nothing but frustration throughout my playthrough.
As it is, however, basic control of the game feels like a nightmarish frankenmonster composed of World of Tanks and Cuphead.

Which is to say, you move around with all the speed and manoeuvrability of a Panzer, and your guns are about as effective as Cuphead's finger guns.

This results in a feeling that every single encounter in the game takes place at the pace of a leisurely stroll and that using your weapons is just an inconvenience for all involved. To be clear, it is entirely possible to have an effective horror experience and satisfying combat: Condemned managed it by giving you a surprisingly deep and effective melee combat system and made the guns you encounter both incredibly scarce and suitably effective, Alan Wake - in spite of its weird controls - managed to mete out supplies and weapons at a pace that made sure you were never helpless, but never felt truly confident, and FEAR even managed to serve up some quality scares whilst giving you assault rifles and bullet time.
And then, of course, there’s Dead space. All hail Dead Space and its pitch perfect juggling of firepower and vulnerability.
By comparison though, RE7 seems to try to attain that same feeling by simply nerfing all but the .44 Magnum and the shotgun into oblivion, which makes a whole lot of the early gameplay super frustrating because there’s a constant feeling that the game isn’t actually pitting you against horrific, all-powerful foes, but instead that it’s just being really, really cheap.
Oh, and then there’s melee combat… lord help you if you ever have to use that.

The game's story sadly also failed to do anything for me: perhaps had I not played Outlast 2 before this, I would have found the experience scarier, but as it is, everything in the game just feels like I've seen it all before.
Because after a literal room of dead children, there’s really not much this game can offer to match that in terms of sheer shock factor.
And that’s possibly the biggest problem with the scares RE7 tries to throw at you; where SOMA will stay with me for years to come for its harrowing and excruciatingly in-depth exploration of human consciousness and the very nature of being alive, RE7 will probably stay with me for as long as it takes me to get these gripes out of my system, because the scenarios I was faced with during my playthrough all seemed merely hum-drum.
It’s not like the game doesn’t try to do what it does well, and as many have pointed out, the Baker family are all a wonderful bunch of crazies, but unfortunately, none of them seem to be actually all that scary in and of themselves and the story behind them is woefully uninspiring.
Moreover, the game commits horror sin number one for me, which is that it gives you plenty of easy opportunities to AVOID THE HORROR yet forces you to go towards the obvious horror because a videogame has to happen.
Perhaps the most vexatious of these instances is really early, when the game has you rescue your wife from a basement dungeon (not as kinky as it sounds) then expects you NOT to want to go back the way you came, irrespective of the damaged - but still probably climbable - ladder, which is the only thing standing between you and getting away scot-free.
Or maybe the worst instance is the numerous completely working telephones in the house which the player character doesn’t use because… apparently Ethan can’t remember that 9-1-1 dials the emergency services?
Or could the worst offence be the fact I couldn’t shoot the big baddie until the very end of the game, despite the fact I knew that character would be trouble later and that I had a perfectly good shotgun right there?

And then of course, there’s the final nail in the coffin for me: the inventory system, and by extension, resources in the game in general.
While it’s nowhere near as complicated as previous games, RE7’s stripped-down inventory system still manages to make inventory Tetris a central and infuriating part of the experience.
Inventory Tetris isn’t fun. Inventory Tetris has never been fun. Inventory Tetris is to fun what the AK-47 is to world peace.
Where other games get by just fine without one or employ an inventory in some other less restrictive way, RE7 clings to the archaic combine-and-conquer inventory system that the series has always had and the flow of gameplay suffers for it.
The limited amount of inventory slots makes the earlier gameplay in particular extra frustrating because ammo, weapons and health items all take up vital inventory slots, leaving you with no choice but to get rid of important stuff on-the-fly, or trudge back to a magical teleport crate because the thing you need to progress takes up an inventory slot.
And - coming back to that melee bit I mentioned earlier - should you ever find yourself short on ammo or health items, the game never gives you any way to replenish those resources, meaning that the entire game can become literally impossible to beat because you simply don’t have enough ammunition to ever finish the fight, and never will have, because you either can’t possibly access it or used it all earlier.

It gives me no pleasure to say I don’t like this game. I tried my best to like it, I really did, but in the end I just found that there wasn’t an awful lot in the game that didn’t rub me the wrong way. Fans of the series may find this is the jolt they needed after the reportedly awful RE6, but I just can’t see the appeal here.
I’d heard so many great things about this; that it was crazy bonkers scary, that it was the series back on form, that it’s an absolute masterpiece, but instead I found a game that was neither satisfying to play, nor offered anything particularly scary or new for me. I only regret that I stuck with it in the hopes that it would get better long past the two-hour window, and didn’t refund it after the first hour or so.

I cannot stress this enough that if this is your first game you're playing as you dive into the Resident Evil Saga, please understand that this game (VII) in no way shape or form reflects the plot and/or theme of the original series. Unfortunatley at the end they name drop one of the main protagonist from the series (SPOILER) Chris Redfield and the big bad company behind everything Umbrella. Aside from that, I am going to get into a detailed review about Resident Evil VIII.

Let's look at the good, the bad and the wrong.

The good - 

* Storyline (Stand alone game) is great! Really enjoyable however once you realize you're unable to develop a further understanding without purchasing DLC, well... That hurts.

* Gameplay is smooth, crisp and response time is very well done. There are times where the character feels a bit sluggish, but it needs to be remembered that this is a survival horror, not a FPS. Realistcally some actions take delay, which is why this is a + on the gameplay.

* Graphically - Holy SH*T. From shading, lighting and the interactive qualities of the enviroment. This is some premium work!

* Unforgiving - Leave it to Havok. Make sure, as you play, to conserve and prepare. I actually found myself on the final boss, out of ammo for my primary weapons, and was basillcay SOL. RE7 does make an effort to prepare you for the battle, but its up to you to explore and find obtain said equipment.

* Video Taps (SPOILER) - While immserive breaking, they're very cool in assisting players not waste precious resources by implementing an almost demo bit to attempt a certain area.

The bad - 

* Tool Tips/Loading Tips. This will give you near literal itteration on how to defeat anything you're having problems with. Why? It takes the learning portion of our survival out of it. 

* Document Control. Unlike other RE's, you're unable to store (at least copies) of the articles, lab reports, newarticles, etc. that you find through the game. Perhaps it isn't very important due to the Tool Tips tell you all the answers...and...

* Grocery Questing. This is a horrible implementation for any game. By looking at the map screen you can see all the things YOU need to do. Boring! This really defeats the limited open world aspect of RE. This limits the player to think on their own and develop a crutch on the mini-map rathat than their ability to navigate and solve puzzles. 


The wrong

* DLC for Story? This is for real. Additional content, further plot and story understanding can only be found via the DLC. That's a real shame considering the game is $60. That leaves a real nasty taste in my mouth. 

* NOT Resident Evil. As it goes, this game is more of a Rob Zombie flick. The story, for the most part, is really enjoyable, Due to it being Capcom and having a Reisdent Evil title, you'll continue to try and wrap your mind around how exactly it fits into the genre. It's almost like a Terminator-Time-Line inception. And I am here to tell you, it doesn't make sense. The characters are all new, the plot deviates from Reisdent Evil (more on this...)

* Boss Battles (SPOILER). These are kind of lack luster. Almost kind of easy, but the problem is, there are 3 primary residences, but we only fight Jack and Marguerete (SP). I didn't recall exactly if we fought the 'son.' The concepts behind the 3 boss FIGHTS are interesting, but they're more offensive mechanics rather than structures way to defeat them. Pretty much unload enough ammo onto anything and it should die at some point. 

* Bugs, Molds, Pukers. Again, not a Resident Evil game that I familiar with. I am grateful for the minor boss mutations, but where are the zombies? lickers? Ivys? There was a perfect oppertunity in the game for them to introduce a familiar monster, but instead I am left pumping a countless amount of ammo into the boss.

* Immersion Breaking (SPOILER). Are these guys all outfitted with GoPros? And who is rendering their digital footage into VHS Low Def? Maybe that's what Lucas is spending all of his time doing at the end of the game?

OVERALL - 

Solid game, shouldn't belong in the RE series unless it is reintroduced a stand alone portion. Great graphics, enjoyable story, always use a Headset, and turned up, at night. alone.

It's Horror Movie, The Game!

Resident Evil 7 manages to take the best tropes and cliches of the horror industry without making it feel forced, cringy, or overdone in a way that actually fits well with their already existing story. Taking inspiration from games like Outlast and Alien: Isolation, you'll find yourself running and hiding a lot from some of the overpowered baddies.

However, not all the villains are overpowered, because your standard "zombie types" still exist here, and the game retains it's action elements despite all the reviewers saying it doesn't. Only once did I not have enough ammo to deal with the zombies that faced me, and I only just ran past them without a care in the world. Having at least a little sense of conserving ammo and health should be enough to get you through this game without worry. This didn't bother me, but it may bother some who truly don't like this part about the Resident Evil series. 

Also, the overpowered invincible enemies that chases you also has problems too. They don't run very fast and have very short term memory. Which means if you got a firm grasp of the level design, you can often outrun them. But they can sneak up on you if you're not careful. My biggest criticism is that there are clearly rooms that Jack and some baddies won't chase you to. It breaks the immersion and the terror. 

Nitpicking aside, this is truly the best Resident Evil since RE4, and I hope Capcom doesn't ♥♥♥♥ it up in future titles.

Context: I grew up playing RE.  I remember when RE opened and Chris Redfield was smoking a cigarette.  The 90s were awesome.  RE remake, RE0 and RE4 were my favourites, played them over and over and over again, on the hardest difficulties.

Details: the protagonist, who I presume to be a mild mannered guy who doesn't like to offend anyone and has a tendency for misplacing things, is looking for his wife, who 3 years ago decided to work for some family in the middle of nowhere, and who he abandoned after not hearing from her for a time, despite knowing the location of her workplace. Why did the wife go work in the middle of nowhere for some random family?  Was she a babysitter, a chef, a housemaid, the gardiner?  We don't know.  Why didn't the husband give her a call, go to her workplace or phone the police when he stopped hearing from her?  Not sure, but right out of the gate the plot is hollow and you know you are playing as a guy who is a loser.  Many of the responses I have received is that this is all explained in the game and the guy is actually the coolest RE protagonist ever.  I doubt it, but even if we accept that...

Having received an email one day containing two new videos from his wife (one of which should have prompted him to phone the police and FBI), he decides to visit her workplace alone and unarmed (despite the contents of the video which, I repeat, should have prompted him to phone the police and FBI).  On the car ride there he's on the phone with a friend and tells the friend he doesn't know if it's actually her.  It's a very odd phone call to be making, makes no sense, and cannot be attributed to being "lost in translation" from Japanese to English.  But whatever, let's just play this game.

Within minutes of the protagonist's arrival at the workplace: there she is, in some random guy's dungeon.  The couple have the most unrealistic exchange you would expect between a husband and wife in such circumstances, and the immersion in the game is immediately lost.  Then the crazy begins.

It's clear the protagonist's wife has suffered some mental ilness/RE infection during her stay in captivity and is suffering from Stockholm syndrome; not to be unexpected. Crazy wife decides she's going to help the protagonist escape the dungeon she's been living in for 3 years... by throwing him through walls and doors with the strength of the incredible hulk and attacking him with a knife. Also not unexpected.  I get how zombies(RE1+)/infected townsfolk(RE4)/Africans (RE5)/abandoned wives (RE7) behave.

What was unexpected however, given that in previous RE games the protagonist dies when attacked, if he/she cannot fight off the attacker is that: he survives a knife attack from his wife, in which he is repeatedly stabbed all over his body with deep wounds, has his palm pierced by the knife, which is healed by pouring alcohol over it.  As if this hand hasn't seen enough, it's stabbed through the palm again by a screwdriver, such that it is stuck to a wall.  The protagnost tries hard to pull the screwdriver out of the wall only to have has hand cut off by a chainsaw.  I figured the "You Are Dead" screen would appear, or he would pass out and find himself attached to medical equipment.

Remember when RE4 scared the hell out of you because you were going to be chased by a chainsaw?  Well, RE7 brings back the chainsaw, except this time being cut by a chainsaw will be about as fatal as being hit by a lightsaber in the new Disney Star Wars movies, i.e. it'll just leave a scratch. Unless it's part of a scripted part of the combat (press A, press A, press A), in which case you lose your hand.

His left hand chainsawed off and bleeding all over the place for several minutes, the protagonist conveniently finds a handgun and 3 clips of 9 mm bullets (which he loads into the gun despite missing his left hand).  These bullets are insufficient to drop his wife, despite hitting her directly in the head and knee caps, so he resorts to a trusty handaxe that spawned out of thin air after his wife threw him through a door previously barricaded by layers of wood and nails.

Having survived this ordeal by pouring alcohol on himself, the protagonist finds himself chased around a similarly enclosed space by the dungeonmaster and his cliched deep south incestous family, has his foot cut off by a shovel, then manages to put it back on.  So the protagonist has lost his hand and his foot, but both of them are put back on, and I am supposed to keep enjoying this.  I tried.

He watches a black police officer have his head cut off by a shovel - not at the neck, but mid-face, it just doesn't make any sense.  (Where are BLM and the SJWs on that one?)  Meanwhile your protagonist is unloading more 9 mm into deep south dungeon keeper to no avail.

You can't drop him.  I mean, you're swinging a knife into his neck, head, hamstrings, back, chest, eyes, but he's undroppable.  You shoot him all over the place and he doesn't drop.  I know RE bosses are semi invincible, but it just doesn't make sense this early in the game.  He cuts off your foot again, because apparently that's what this guy does. He stabs you in the gut with his shovel, lifts you into the air.

How does his shovel do these things?  How is it you can fight back with guns and axes, but not your fists?  In the earlier combat with the wife you had the "mash A, mash A, mash A" prompt to fight her off, but not with deep south dungeon master.

Why can't you run away when you hold shift?  Don't ask me. What I do know: apparently you can still live, even though you've lost your limbs, are in immese pain, and have lost enough blood to feed a vampire colony for weeks.  Finally, if you do drop him, do you really care to keep playing?  I don't.

Sorry for upsetting so many players.  I wanted to be one of you.

I've been a pretty big Resident Evil fan ever since I played the Wii edition of RE4 almost a decade ago (I know, I'm a real heathen). I've played through a lot of the classics (though I've yet to play 2 or 3) and the only game in the series I'm pretty indifferent towards is 5. I even liked 6 in a weird, sick way. All that to say, there are some common elements throughout the series I love, horror being one of them.

Resident Evil 7 is far and away the biggest departure for the series, and I'm happy to say it's a good time. However, some of its changes are fairly serious misteps, in my humble opinion. While many would assume the camera change to first person was the most signifcant change, I would disagree. The series switched from isometric fixed camera angles to over the shoulder camera angles before. Far and away the most significant (and worst change) is the tone. No longer is there the charming and vibrant cast that pushes you forward, or the cheesy one-liners that makes you crack a grin. It's a much more serious affair, with the only offbeat moments being some ridiculously over-the-top (read: great) boss encounters. Ethan is a dry character, plain and simple, and so are all the other non-antagonist personalities that show up. Give me Leon, Claire, or hell, even Steve over Ethan, his wife, Alma, or not-Chris any day of the week. I'm a fan of the core RE characters. I love 'em. Thankfully we got the stellar CG movies like Vendetta to give me my fix, but I hope we get a return of some great personalities to the main series.

...Now with that out of the way, the core of the game. The overall structure is certainly a throwback to RE1, with the exploration of a spooky manor and backtracking to previous areas. Visually it's pretty stunning, though I did get a fair bit of screen tearing in my play through (that's honestly probably on me for not knowing how to properly optimize my recently bought gaming rig). I really appreciated the amount of environmental detail in it, they really nailed the vibe of a trash house. The overall game story was fine, though nothing to write home about. The villains certainly provided plenty of memorable moments, but the core "man searches for his wife" horror story didn't do much for me. Again, this kinda fell on some limp characters.

Onto the meat of the game; the mechanics, exploration and horror. It definitely feels different from prior REs for me. The weapon upgrade and treasure system from RE4 doesn't make a return, which is a shame as I thought those systems were incredibly rewarding and engaging. Instead, improvements are few and far between, and they are either gotten through searching the environment, buying them with antique coins hidden about, or solving a puzzle to get them. I appreciate this approach as well, and I think it served the game well. Capcom stuffed coins in places you wouldn't expect, such as underneath dressers or in small corners of the room, basically invisible even when looking straight at them. This may sound like a negative, but I love games that give purpose to taking in your surroundings, and this certainly was one of those games. Exploration never felt confusing like in some of the previous games, but it also never felt to linear like 6, so I think they really nailed it here. As an aside, I loved the optional VHS mechanic as well, particularly the Birthday Party segment. The horror was a little more mixed for me. There were plenty of tense and skin-crawling moments throughout the game, but I wasn't a fan of the heavier emphasis on visceral gross-out scares. Granted, there's still plenty of spooky moments for people who like the more Fatal-Frame style ambience. As far as tense moments go, I still think the Verdugo scene from RE4 reigns supreme, but there are some pretty solid onese here for sure.

Anyways, a bit of a long review, I apologize. Definitely one of the best horror games in years, and one that I could actually class as a game. Whole heartedly recommend if you like horror or exploring detailed and spooky environments! Recommend less so if you only really cared for the amazing cast, lovable cheese factor, and warm heart of the earlier games.
