So, let me get started by saying, due to the season, I was in the mood for some horror games.  I went from the Evil Within to this.  I did the Evil Within first because I assumed this to be a better game.  I really loved that game, ultimately.  This one... not so much.

Get the good out the way:

The graphics were generally really great here.  The faces had that slightly odd too realistic look to them which only added to that creepy factor here.  The color pallette was bland, but it fit the game perfectly.  Not too many chances of popping color when most of the game takes place in dark enclosed areas that are poorly lit.

Overall, the creep factor here was really high, though I wasn't expecting so many jump scares at the beginning, but they teetered out pretty quick and then it evened out. At points it really did feel like a haunted house experience which is what I was really going for.

Also, the game is optimized really great at this point.  I didn't play it on release and I never heard anything bad, but everything here was butter smooth.  Not single FPS issue the entire game.

Some of the bad:

I have a few criticisms here that are highly person.  The first is the overall size of each area.  The areas in this game are tiny.  I wasn't expecting huge open areas or anything, but each area is really miniscule.  I also feel the areas you go to are kind of derivative at this point.  You start in a tiny abandoned house.  You go to bigger (but not by much) house, then a boat house, then a boat, then a min....  The boat which is probably bigger than all of them and it felt noticeably bigger.  One of the reasons it feels that much bigger though is the enemy count.  You have to take it slow, check each room, watch out for enemies.  But once everything is dead and you take a run through, you find out that the areas can be almost entirely explored in about a minute and half when you aren't searching for items or being attacked.   

One of the ways they extend these areas is the use of tapes, which at first I really liked.  You get to play as another character going through an area with slightly different events happening.  But then I realized that all they really did was utilize an area you were about to go through as Ethan.  In one section, they have you solve the puzzle on a tape, only to have Ethan run through and know the solution already.  

Gunplay is terrible.  I wasn't expecting to come here and play a shooter, to be clear.  I wasn't looking for a first person shooter.  But, when you put guns in a game they should feel right or you should not have them.  First, no matter what I did, it always felt like there was a noticeable delay between me clicking my mouse and the gun shooting.  I would also like to point out that I was running the game just fine, I wasn't suffering from any FPS issues anywhere in the game, as previously mentioned.  Also, I have no idea what is going on with the enemies hit boxes.  I used my beginnig handgun on a mold, 4 shots to the head and it was done, bang, head exploded.  I thought, it makes ammo tight, but I can handle that.  Well, they must have decided later that 4 wasn't enough and left players with too much ammo to keep the suspense high.  So soon, it's taking no less than 7 headshots with that gun for the same enemy.  And by that I mean with actual hits, not shots I wasted that went wide because of the delayed feeling in the mouse click to gunshot ingame.  I get a shotgun, but I'm told that you can one shot these guys with a close shotgun blast. Alright, ammo is even tighter here since you can't craft any shotgun shells in the game, so I lure them in close.  BANG!  I see splurge come out, the mold goes down, I'm happy... then it starts to move and get up.  I had shot it basically point blank in the face, the animation where it covers it's face with it's arm wasn't happening, and yet I blew it's arm off.  So, now, the weird hitboxes and what I assume is how they change the second an animation likely begins is costing me ammo. 

Next up is the fact that you are spending this entire game as if it takes place in a giant pool of molasses.  You are so slow, which is one of the ways I assume they also use to try and make areas seem bigger than they are.  But that translates to you aiming your gun.  More than one of my deaths was due to me essentially getting stun locked by a crawling mold.  These guys are fast.  You can outrun all the other kinds, but these guys will run you down quick.  I learned that early on, so I would purposely save shotgun ammo for them.  But on several occasions I would wait for them to get close with my shotgun aimed, I click, they somehow attack me first, my shotgun doesn't shoot, and ethan has to recover from being hit before he can aim his gun again, but the enemy now has me stun locked between recovery and pulling out my gun, the mold recovers faster.  Sometimes I could get it off, but it was nearly impossible not to waste ammo like this.  Some enemies feel like they were placed to simply make you waste ammo and take unavoidable damage.

I read in several places, "sometimes it's best to avoid combat and just run".  That is great, I like the idea that maybe I can run away and recover or get my bearings.  Only, the vast majority of locations in this game are constructed in such a way that you can't just run around enemies or avoid them.  For instance, there is a part in the main house that you have to go through a series of basement corridors and molds spawn in the corridors.  Sure, you can run back the way you came, but the molds follow eventually disappearing, meaning you can't kite them to larger areas where they can be avoided.  Then, when you continue down the corridor again, they spawn again.  I found very few sections of the game where I was not stuck in unavoidable combat.  I expect that from boss fights, but from basic shambling enemies it was more annoying and frustrating, which was then compounded by the fact that you spend the entire game in molasses.

I beat the game, but it felt more like a personal financial obligation by the end.  You start the game underpowered, then 3/4 of the way through you are stacked to the teeth with guns and ways to kill enemies.  It felt very uneven.  At one point I found myself confidently striding down hallways not afraid of what might come.  I had gotten my hands on a bunch of these remote bombs that I could place, run back and set off to kill groups of molded.  And if I ran out my inventory was full of other weapons.

Inventory management was back, but often I found myself weighed down with things that I never found a use for.  For example, I never used the psychostimulants once.  When you take them it makes it easier to find items laying around, which might have been useful for more Magnum ammo, which I had about 10 rounds of the entire game, which I didn't use till the last boss.  But it was never worth useing them I thought because I could thoroughly search rooms myself.  But, the caveat here is I couldn't really just leave them where I found them.  You don't have the option of picking an item up when you hit the action button, you pick it up.  Sometimes due to the frantic nature of the game I was running around trying to avoid enemies where I could and picking up everything I could see with little time think on it.  So your inventory fills up with things that you may not find useful and you may not have easy access to your storage container without a molasses run to the trailer.

For me, this game was more of an exercise in frustration.  The shooting mechanics were bad.  A good portion of my deaths felt cheap like the game had cheated me somehow.  One time I got caught between enemies when I hit two with my shotgun at close range, one fell to my side, but I got trapped between a wall and two fallen still alive molds.  The game plagued with moments like this.  The overall world was tiny.  I got it on sale, but it still kind of feels like money wasted.

As a long time Resident Evil fan I was initially very skeptic of this new approach to the series being first person but somehow Capcom managed to make a competent game out of it, which mostly doesn't fall victim to many modern horror game tropes that many other modern games fall into. RE7 mixes both classic and modern RE formula as one package, at times leaning towards one bias more than the other and vice versa, which creates both really good and really bad moments.

Let's talk about the bad moments because these are the most jarring moments of my playthrough and most of them are either easily fixable and/or avoidable. The first, major and most occurring flaw in this game is its unfair difficulty spikes both in and out of combat. It seems the game's only way to kill me in combat is to either outnumber and/or overpower me with sudden and unexpected strikes. In previous RE games, enemies that come within boundaries of you will slow down and walk towards you to give you time to react, but in this game the times that they relentlessly strike at you they not only stunlock you but they do it at the same time making for an almost instant kill at full health. Outside of combat, the puzzle room where you're trapped in with Lucas results in a forced death right after solving all those puzzles - that's your reward - a death and having to reload. Capcom thought it was a good idea to force "optional" content in order for you to solve that puzzle.

That's another weakness of RE7, the VHS tapes and the story/pacing. The "optional" VHS tapes really are garbage and don't add much to the already weak and dumb story. The one involving Mia is just avoid the scripted trigger box, the Happy Birthday tape is some crappy backstory for Mr. Nobody who has little to do with anything, and the only tape that's worth something is the one you're forced to play with Eveline. The story though, while it isn't bad or garbage, it's dumb and just not the game's driving force for me. The limb detachment mechanic is incredibly dumb, even for suspension of disbelief purposes, and the game attempts to explain this away by some white cell regeneration crap that conveniently only applies to Ethan and Jack. What Capcom could have done to improve the story is make the other characters as fun and interesting as Jack and Lucas, more related backstory, more logs to read, more iconic encounters with unique bosses and to do make the Baker's story more fleshed out in cutscenes. The moment when Ethan was talking to Jack about Eveline's virus disaster was probably the best moment in the story, the game needs more of that!

Other weak areas include the pacing of the game is too quick, the game is too short and it feels like the game doesn't want you to stay in one area for too long - despite the backtracking. You're being constantly pushed forward, sometimes literally, and there aren't enough moments where you can just explore some creepy locations and do some time wasting puzzle solving. It seems all the "puzzles" in this game are fairly straight forward A + B = C, with little room for me to use my imagination on how to find a solution. The only time I became stuck was trying to find more Corrosives in the Ship, but finally remembered about the 2F safe, which was guarded by a puzzle easier than singing the ABC song.

So what're RE7's strengths? Thankfully, they are gameplay and presentation related. The limited inventory, save room with transferable item boxes, RE1/4 style of presentation throughout the game and the variety and surprises that each scenario presents is surprisingly refreshing. The bosses were fun albeit with obvious weaknesses, except for the pit fight, which I really hated because of the stunlock crap. Jack is probably my favourite character and it was good to see him persistently used as the sort of "comeback stalker". During the early encounters, he scared me once when I saw him charging at me with an axe down the corridor, but he breaks out into some genuinely funny dialogue that helps break up the seriousness of the situation.

So I mean yeah, the combat is fine, headshots are satisfying, the variety in guns is okay, there're secrets, collectables and  extra game modes. No Mercenaries Mode sucks hard but the DLC has variety in them. I clocked in 7 hours first try on Normal mode, which is half as long as I expected the game to be. Playing as Mia was cool, I wish it was longer because the Ship segments are probably my favourite in the game, and she has more personality and reasoning for being in the story than the literal faceless Ethan.

Overall, I actually like RE7, I think it's the best RE game since 4 but that isn't saying much since the modern RE games are all garbage anyway. Capcom can do even better by making a longer game, more fleshed out story, revise their design decisions in terms of difficulty, make more challenging puzzles and keep the classic RE systems in. I don't think I'll be replaying the story again but the DLC content should keep me abay for a few more hours.

TLDR: Whether or not you're a fan of Resident Evil or not, you WILL enjoy this game. Solid gameplay, well optimized yet graphically impressive, good level design and easy flowing progression.

Story: The first part of the game doesn't quite feel like a Resident Evil game, despite traditional formula of scarce ammo and healing items. It feels like a spiritual successor to P.T. in many ways, including level design. After getting further in the story you eventually feel the Resident Evil formula of puzzles and combat begin to set in, which still doesn't feel overdone. The references and easter eggs found throughout the story serve as a clever connector to the main series. The main character is a little unlikeable for a few reasons. He seems underwhelmed by the supernatual horrors unfolding before him. At one scene in the game literally seeing a glimpse of a severly deformed humanoid creature and responding with all the enthusiasm of "oh, neat." However the nitpicks with the main character don't take anything away from the overall experience. 

Graphics: Despite this game being very well optimized and running at a very consistant framerate, it is VERY graphically impressive. Playing on max settings results in incredible lighting and shadow effects that in some scenes are nearly photorealistic. Throughout the entire game, despite being chased through some of it, I found myself stopping to appreciate the very well placed partical effects and crisp textures. Playing this on ultra with a mobile gtx 1070 resulted in a consistant 120 frames per second. Attempting Medium settings on a gtx 870m resulted in a very smooth experience as well. WIth a few tweaks this game may even run on a machine that doesn't quite meet the minimum specs.

Gameplay: The gunplay in game wont blow you away by any means, but certainly won't hinder your experience. Despite the ammunition scarcity typical of a RE game, your patience and aim will make sure your bullets hit home and never leave you without ammo for too long. Encounters never feel unfairly difficult, despite some being a tiny bit frustrating. The puzzles are fairly challenging but giving every environment a modest search will result in several clues to help should you get stuck on a puzzle. I found only one or two times I had to use a guide for solutions that turned out to simply be something I overlooked due to impatience.

Conclusion: If you just like horror games, this is a solid title in the horror genre. If you enjoy the Resident Evil series, this one will be no exception. All in all this game is a good example of a well executed AAA game. Even if you buy at the AAA price, this game will be a good purchase.

The Good:

If you know what Resident Evil used/was supposed to be, then yes, this is in fact a great RE game [u]for the most part[/u]. I won't say this is the flawless return to roots nor the most amazing Survival Horror experience I've ever played, because it's not, but the elements of a proper RE experience are in fact right here in this game: We got exploration, backtracking, item management, key hunting, puzzle solving, and [i]some[/i] combat in a tense and horrifying situation.

That's how RE used to be before it turned into casual horde shooter with piñata enemies, badass indestructible agents, merchants, and QTEs and explosions everywhere. In RE7 you do have access to a variety of guns to fight back, but combat is not the main aspect of the game, this is not a typical shooter that throws dozens of enemies at you one after the other so you can just gun down everything in your path because "it's cool and fun".

The Bad:

It lacks enemy variety and has quite a drop in quality towards the last section of the game, when it suddenly turns into a corridor shooter with a terribly scripted final boss battle and a shoehorned fan-service ending. So basically you'll realize there's pretty much nothing new or interesting to see once you reach the last third of the game. The free DLC Not a Hero somehow fixed this by giving the game a more inspired final section, which was probably intended for the main game but cut due to deadlines, it's easy to see that when you look at how dull the Salt mines are in the base game.

Should you buy it?

If you're looking for a Survival Horror experience (adapted to modern gaming conventions that is, don't expect literal old school survival), definitely yes. Now if you just want an horror-themed "zombie" shooter, then better think twice, this might not be a game for you.

For a survival horror fan this is a step in the right direction for sure, and a good game overall, but it has some flaws and stuff that feels rushed towards the end.
Recommended! DLC material is also very worth its price.

[h1] Resident Evil VII. The horror game we didn't knew we need it.

Wow... just Wow. [/h1] 

This is the best Survival Horror game that I've played in a while, the graphics are gorgeous, the attention to details is overwhelming, the narrative is engaging and the mechanics are amazing.

Resident Evil VII manage to rescue the main elements from most classic horror movies, and put them in a cohesive story line. You'll have bits from The Exorcist, The Evil Dead, The Shining, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, The Ring, Blair Witch Project, Saw and even Se7en, all set up in a "beautiful" Louisiana environment that resembles the first season of True Detective in the most elegant and respectful way.

The First Person Perspective has been refined from previous games of the genre like Outlast or Alien Isolation, to put you right in the shoes of the main character, making the jump scares and the psychological terrors even more intense. This game have some of the most memorable moments in the history of the genre, moments that will accompany you and haunt your dreams, long after beating the game (Mia and Eveline are giving me a hard time sleeping).

The combat mechanics are by far the best of the series and manage to keep you by the edge of your sit at every moment and the boss fights are creative are ever changing (My fight with Jack in the garage was completely different the second time around), same for the stealth sections of the game.

The story surrounding your missing wife Mia and the insane Baker Family is fascinating to say the least and the pay off is extremely well constructed and satisfying, opening the door for a new chapter within the Resident Evil mythos and at the same time paying homage to the old premise.

[b] Conclusion: [/b]

For the last couple of years, the horror survival genre has been driven by the indie industry (Outlast, Amnesia, Slender Man) with a few exceptions, but Capcom just proved that the AAA companies still have a say in the matter. After the cancellation of Silent Hills (way to go Konami), Resident Evil VII is something that all the enthusiasts of the genre desperately need it without knowing and manages to deliver beyond my wildest dreams in every single aspect.

I can't wait to see where the franchise is gonna go after this, and I hope Capcom don't forget about us PC Gamers.

Finally, Capcom returns Resident Evil to it's former Survival Horror roots. This game plays exactly how a modern Resident Evil game should. It has all the hallmarks of a classic Resident Evil game but streamlined to make it a bit less frustrating or confusing for new players. 

Everything here is high quality, from the voice acting to the locations in the game, the music and the graphics, the combat and the bosses. Everything just works well here and fits together nicely. Emphasis has been taken away from the action and focused more on it's horror elements. This is immediately noticable with the decision to go 1st person which I think is for the best. 1st person allows for a more immersive experience versus the cinematic experience of the last few RE titles. Additionally, there are few cutscenes that take control away from the player, no QTEs and no co-op so there is nothing to take you out of the zone in this game.

In terms of pacing it nails it down perfectly as well. A good horror game knows when to get silent and let the player explore a new spooky area. Tension rises as the player becomes skeptical of the safety of the area until finally revealing the enemies. However my only complaint here would be the enemy variety, I wish just a few more were added into the mix. Especially considering the weapon arsenal is larger than necessary.

Difficulty is another important aspect of a good survival horror game. I only played on Normal so far so I can only comment on that. I think the balance was just right for a first-time playthrough on Normal. If you are very careful, thorough and accurate as well as avoid taking damage as much as you can, you will find more than enough to get by but not so much that it feels too easy. So in other words, you will always worry about your supplies but never exactly run completely out of them so long as you have some level of competency. Take this comment with a grain of salt though considering I have been playing Resident Evil games since 1996.

I will be playing the game again on the harder difficulty and will update my review if anything unexpected should arise. Overall, I think Resident Evil 7 is a great comeback for the series and a step in the right direction for survival horror as a whole. I would love to see more games like this and to see Capcom continue in this direction while thinking of new ways to innovate the genre. For classic RE fans or horror fans in general, this is a must buy.

Extremely surprised at how good the game was. I’m really specific in which survival horror games I choose to play. I generally only like survival horror games that are similar to the first Silent Hill games.  RE7 turned out to be a pretty honest game to be specified as survival horror, considering that most games labeled survival horror nowadays are just a first-person game in a spooky setting with nothing but jump scares. RE7 has survival horror roots such as limited ammo, the option to run or fight from enemies, and “stiff” controls (not in a bad way, but in a way that makes certain points of the game more intense). While the game has good original survival horror elements, it also takes place in First-Person view which is a change from the RE games, but it’s not used as a gimmick so much as it makes the game very atmospheric, and a good combo of classic survival horror with a more modern twist. RE7 also has a very good inventory system similar to RE4 making item management something important, and makes it feel slightly more realistic as your character can't hold every weapon given to them throughout the game. Overall this game is very good and has replay value, and I hope can inspire other game developers to make survival horror games more like RE7.

Is it perfect? No, not at all. Weapons like the Burner suck, the game itself is relatively short, and the final parts of the game starting from the ship have a noticeable drop in quality compared to the first section of the game.

Don't buy if you're looking for a dollar to hour ratio (I mean, you shouldn't buy horror games period if you want a dollar to hour ratio, they're a genre that inherently benefits from being short and sweet), but do buy if you want a decent, but not necessarily classic, Resident Evil game. Here's hoping the free DLC is good, and that the best influence this game had is on Capcom's business philosophy, though looking at sales compared to Resi 6, prospects of Resident Evil returning to actual decent games as opposed to blockbuster Michael Bay-esque garbage seems bleak. At the least, we can enjoy it while it lasts.

A True Resident Evil

[b]Introduction[/b]

After recent degredations of Resident Evil, Capcom has brought Resident Evil back to life with a fresh approach to Resident Evil, along with going back to Resident Evil's roots by including elements of problem solving, written lore left to be discovered, and true horror. Capcom has also made Resident Evil now a first-person video game, before I played the game I believed this would increase the suspense of horror, but I thought it would feel more like a first-person shooter than a Resident Evil game - I was completely wrong. This feels like more of a Resident Evil game than anything after the original Resident Evil games in the series.

[b]Going Further[/b]

The first-person element in particular in my perspective makes the game somewhat harder, as you have a smaller field of view while playing, and you must look around very carefully. Capcom however did add arrows above items you can interact with if you are close enough to it, this helps to alleviate looking at every single thing very closely in the game, which would have been very tedious; if I'm not mistaken the demo didn't have this in it.

Another notable feature of this Resident Evil is Capcom's use of video tapes to give the player a deeper understanding of the world they're in. These video tapes allow you to play as different characters within the story, after the tape is over you return back to the character who's watching the video tape. I don't want to spoil the game, but in some points of the game, the video tapes are very important.

There are key elements from the original Resident Evil present, including: a tape player (type writer in the original Resident Evil, doesn't require any items to save however on [b]Normal[/b] difficulty, however it does on [b]Madhouse[/b]), combination system (I will expand on the different elements of this combination system later), item box, key system, etc.

The Combination System: In This Resident Evil you can't combine two herbs, like in the past. You must however find fluids to mix with herbs and different ingredients (you'll see what those are when you play). You can combine different things such as: gun powder (you can create stronger versions of ammunition or standard versions, both easily switchable between while playing), different types of ammunition for different weapons, combine two items needed to advance further into the story, and other things can be combined that you will see. This combination system is easier than the original Resident Evil, since there's a tab that says Combine which shows different things that can be combined together, and it highlights what you can combine if you have the ingredients present.

Well, that's all I have to say about this game. It's an excellent game, and if you like Resident Evil or horror games in general, I recommend this game highly. Also, *There is no arachnophobic alert, and if you're wondering how long this game might last, I beat the game in 8.1 hours.

It's challenging enough to the point where you don't get bored easily, but not extremely difficult to the point where you just want to say "f*** it, I quit".

The classic horror franchise is getting a new perspective in this sequel/ soft reboot. Hopefully the game turned out as well as the fans hoped and provided some horrific tension to experience. I will be reviewing Resident Evil 7 with a pro/ con style and finish it off with my conclusion.

Pro:
      The game has amazing music. The game has so much music and how it influences mood and atmosphere. One of my favorite has to the be saferoom music. The other songs are splendid to listen to.

       The new perspective allows to new opportunity of experience. Yes lets get it out of the way that Resident Evil 7 is also on VR and how it is natural to play a vr game in first person but there can be a deeper meaning that adds a level of fear to the game. The idea that you as the player are Ethan. You see the experience through his eyes and its a bit easier to become immersed in the world. Soon as the player the enemies feel like they are not attack Ethan the but you as the player.

        Welcome back old mechanics. Long have i missed the time of item boxes from the earlier Resident evil titles like 1 and 2 and it is nice to see them come back for this title. Item management was a pretty big deal back then so it was great to see that come back with the idea of limited item space. It always makes the player worry about picking up an item and using the space and later learning there was medic supplies a little further down. So there will be the struggle of do i need more health items or ammo or need the space to have my shotgun or other key items.

          There is a new difficulty. The new difficulty ironically named "Madhouse" is in all sense of the word madhouse. It is very challenging since enemies are obviously more bullet spongey and supplies are limited but there is a new twist added to it. Items are moved around to different locations than their normal difficulty counter parts, enemies are in relitively newer locations than they were in previous difficulties such as now an area has 2 fat guys than 1 or now there is 3 crawlers than 1. It provides a definite challenge to those who seek it but a newer and unique experience than their previous experience.

           The story is very nice. The story is held together with cliche's from other horror icons like texas chainsaw, fear, saw, ect. Learning how the bakers were before the infection was nice.

Jokes aside, the atmosphere created is amazing with how old and unkept the areas are and the cliche of a backwater family in the middle of the woods raising horror on intruders is something that was in a few movies but this game lets you experience it as the character. Truely a horric experience.

con:
      Late game gets very challenging when you play as mia and the first area you get to explore has those annoying 4 legged crawlers and a handgun that give you just 2 bullets. I get that challenge is important in a game but that is just annoying. It could have been better but it came off as slow and annoying.

You get to make a choice to see who live and dies when if you chose the one other than mia she dies regardless which makes no sense since you cure her infection and Mia gets angery at you which is rightfully so since she is your wife for 3 years but on the flip side if you choose to save Mia the other girl gets angery because you didnt save her even though you dont really know her that well so her expecations that you would choose to save her over your wife of 3 years. This story elements felt kind of forced and really if time was taken could have fixed it so it doesnt feel like some teenage drama than anything rational.

Conclusion:

The game play was very classic but with the new twist of first person which was always a welcomed change in my book. I am a massive fan of the Resident Evil series and it was good to see how the tides of how crappy the franchise became after 4 are now back to its normal enjoyable experience. Given Capcom's more recent entries in the franchise being more heavily oriented toward action gameplay I have to say that RE7 was a very pleasant surprise. It's hard to disclose everything positive about the game without treading into spoiler territory so here's my attempt at doing so and explaining my reasoning behind my recomendation of the game.

The biggest factor for me was the return of the atmosphere. I was skeptical at first about the perspective change to first-person as it was clearly done this way to make it VR compatible and I don't subscribe to the belief that VR is a worthwhile investment in its current iteration. However upon actually playing the game I found that the shift in perspective was actually pretty well executed in terms of the gameplay and horror aspects of the game.

Walking down hallways and turning corners is suspenseful, the audio plays a huge part in this like it did with the older entries of the series. Like any good horror game the audio is key in predicting what you're up against and isn't just a tool to add cheap jumpscares into the mix. There were a lot of genuine moments in my first playthrough where I would hear footsteps or moans that indicated an upcoming threat which gave me the freedom to choose how I engaged the situation.

Because of that last point I soon realised that not only did the atmosphere contribute to my enjoyment, but the freedom to choose between fight or flight did too. A large part of why I bought this game in the first place is that I had heard about it paying homage to the older games in that regard. I simply adore the first three games and Code Veronica because of that aspect, in many situations you don't even need to fight if you know how to avoid the enemies.

I will say though that the variety in threats does feel a little underwhelming compared to the originals and that does somewhat detract from the scare factor. That said, my first encounters were all still just as memorable to me as they were in the older games. I wouldn't necessarily say this is an entirely bad point though, the first game also suffered a similar flaw afterall.

In terms of combat I feel that they did a fantastic job of blending the old inventory management aspects of using items and weapons extremely well with the hotkeys and action aspects of more recent titles. Your inventory space is very limited like the old games, but you can hotkey your weapons and there is a dedicated heal button that removes the need to navigate the menu mid combat. Admittedly I have mistakenly hit the heal button without meaning to which has caused me to waste items, but that's my own silly fault.

That about sums up my thoughts on the game in terms of spoiler-free critique. There's a lot that I love about the game that I feel should really be experienced blind though. I love this game and I recommend it because of that, though the DLC options leave a lot to be desired. 

Here's hoping the upcoming free DLC will be just as engaging and thematically fitting to the source material.

Though with a quick glance, RE7 may look like just a cheap Outlast rip-off with the Biohazard logo smacked on the cover due to the new first person view, but beneath the new perspective, it's very much like the older classic Resident Evil titles from PS1 era, especially on the madhouse difficulty. Unlike the former ''modern'' RE games such as RE4, RE5 or RE6, Capcom has truly kept their promise of bringing the series back to its roots even though they often like to f*ck with and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ their fans to a degree.

The Premise

No longer are you gunning and meleeing through hordes of villageers or ♥♥♥*ers or anything at all, this time RE has really gone back to the slow and vulnerable style of the classic games and you're not even playing as someone with any sort of military/combat experience like Chris or Leon, this time you're Ethan, just an average guy who finds himself in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ life endangering situation and... well to be honest, the protagonist is f*cking horrible and has as much as personality as Gordon Freeman for example and you won't be hearing much else than ''f*ck that'' and ''f*ck this'' from him...

The graphics and atmosphere are top-notch and the performance is great. I believe Capcom tried to go for some sort of ''90s Camera Recorder'' aesthetics when they were designing the visuals. Enemy Variety

Absolute horsesh*t! Basically, there are only 2 kinds of common enemy types, the molded zombies and some f*cking bugs. Aside from the Baker family which belong to the boss category, there are no other enemies and you'll be fighting the same black slimy zombies and bugs till the end of the game. Late to the party writing this review, but it's still good for people wondering about whether this game is worth it.

**TL;DR: It abso-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-lutely is.**

Not gonna give spoilers, but your experience may vary depending on whether or not you're fine with or know of all the cliche tropes in most games nowadays ("lol plot armor", "lol good guy evades danger 2752767891 times"; best example I can give is the ♥♥♥♥ that happens in, like, Dead Space 3). I'm not using the term "cliche tropes" in a negative light at all.

DO NOT PLAY ON EASY FOR YOUR FIRST RUN. Even if you do have a different version of the game that gives you the option to play on Madhouse, I still wouldn't really recommend Madhouse for a 1st run. I think I got more out of this game on a Normal run than I would have had I picked Madhouse.

Gonna break this game down in halves, again doing my best to not spoil. That said, I love this game so much that I'm probably going to sound like I'm overhyping it. Leave any and all expectations you may have on the ground floor when you first play this game.

1st half: 12/10

Ho-ly ♥♥♥♥. In my opinion, RE7 has probably the best first half of any video game I can ever think of. First off, this half made me feel something I rarely feel in video games: fear. A lot of the ♥♥♥♥ that happens enabled me to establish a new-found respect for any horror movie protagonist I've ever thought was a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for doing something exceptionally dumb (or not doing something at all) when faced with the bad guys (more on them in a bit).

There is another thing I haven't seen other games do as well as this half did: create an actually compelling, immersive environment (though I could still argue this somewhat tapers off towards the finish of this half). Obviously, the environment is scary, and is still done exceptionally well, but I would have probably gotten bored with it if it was strictly just scary. The timing of adding interesting dynamics to the environment was absolutely PERFECT. Each time I would have  probably started to get bored/numbed/jaded about my surroundings, they throw in something that enabled me to sort of restart or recycle my ability to really be able to take in the environment and feel compelling fear once more. My favorite part of this is that many of these instances have absolutely NOTHING AT ALL to do with the story, and were so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great I didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ it didn't play into the story because I was at least entertained. I felt extremely rewarded for actually taking the time to pay attention to details, keeping otherwise trivial parts of dialogue in mind, and exploring.

As an aside, another thing this game was great with in terms of timing was finding the inventory upgrades. Every single time I felt like I would be absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ by a lack of inventory space, the next room had a backpack.

I feel the first few encounters with the more "common" enemies added to the atmosphere of this game, and were fairly symbolic of the struggles of the game, but this kinda runs out of gas as you progress and figure out how to block. The first few can kinda give you a swift kick in the balls in some not-immediately obvious ways, but once you're done with the sort of feeling out process in how to deal with (or, more specifically, fight) them, they're not too bad. Still, at any point in the game, getting hit just once by one of them, even if it was a fluke, usually opens the floodgates that lead you to the "YOU DIED" screen.

Last but not least...

The boss fights. Oh my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ God these boss fights. I loved these boss fights so much, I feel I need to break these down in parts, too. Again, I'll try to not give too much away.

1st fight - Remember when I said I have a new found respect for dumb horror movie protagonists? And the tropes? It starts here, both in their unique way. I found it easy to forget certain things when faced with such a threat as this boss, and it was "only" the first one. Normally, I'd probably class this as an average tutorial-like boss fight with typical hit and run strats,  Great opening fight.

2nd - THIS. MOTHER. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. FIGHT. This is among my all-time favorite boss fights, especially the first time I tried it because I could not believe I made another dumb horror film character mistake, and it was probably the dumbest one of all time, and I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loved it. I was entertained. This fight is possibly also the craziest and most entertaining boss fight I've played in a long, long time. That is, until...

3rd - ANOTHER AWESOME FIGHT. I generally preferred the fight before this one, but I know many others who preffer this, and for damn good reason. It was this fight where I knew I was in for something special with RE7.

4th - I honestly don't know whether this was a good fight or a bad one, or a middle-of-the-road fight and am still debating it with myself to this day. Quality aside, I'll just say I will forget the other fights way before I forget about this one.

5th - Still pretty crazy, still pretty good, but is probably the weakest of the bunch so far in terms of actual combat. Perhaps also the least remarkable of the boss fights, but it certainly fits in. Works great for a conclusion of the first half.

And it's downhill from here. Not a sharp decline, but I don't think they could have topped the first half.

2nd half: 7.5/10

Early parts of this half retained some of its fear factor, but quickly turns from a horror game into much more of a shooter, and the game seems more confused in doing so. Many of the subtleties that brings everything together for the first half is pretty much gone, and tries TOO hard to get jumpscares, as opposed to radiating a feeling of fear or impending doom, again, as found in the first half. By this point, you know how to deal with enemies, and no new ones appear for the rest of the game, with the exception of a variant of an enemy after a long gauntlet-type pushing uphill fight, and you will have the most OP weapon in the game (not the magnum, if you could believe it) at your disposal, but is/was still at least a reward for exploring thoroughly.

A couple decent ambushes kinda save it, but it's just generic shooter 3436257 at this point. A certain revelation could have been done far, FAR better, but is still uplifting enough to not really get considered offensive as far as the characters go, and gives you motivation so you can soldier through the rest of the game.

In true RE fashion, the final boss is an absolute pushover. No real creativity, just a dump your mag, lolcutscene, gg sort of boss taken from Dead Space 1, but without needing to contend with wacky aim or small weak spots. It didn't help that the path to said final boss is probably the most annoying sequence in the game.

Overall: 9/10. Definitely take a shot with this game.

I’ve had this one in the backlog for a while now and only recently got around to playing it. Resident Evil 7 is the 7th main entry to the popular survival horror franchise. After receiving a lot of negative feedback for the past few Resident Evil games, Capcom decided to reinvent the franchise and switched the game’s perspective from the traditional 3rd person action gameplay to a 1st person game with a larger emphasis on horror. But were the changes enough to save this classic franchise? 

Well… yes and no. Resident evil 7 does bring back the survival horror aspects from the original games along with the tight inventory management and puzzle solving, but the new 1st person perspective brings its own issues, and fans of the past few resident evil games may not appreciate the slower pace. 
The game’s story starts off with our main protagonist, Ethan driving out to some swamp looking for his girlfriend. It’s not very clear how Ethan managed to figure out the exact location of Mia but whatever. Once you reach the old rundown house, you’ll immediately start encountering cliché scary things like balls rolling across the hallway and little girls appearing down hallways. Within the first hour, you’ll meet the family and the game’s main antagonists throughout the story. There’s Jack, the deranged redneck father who will continuously pop up when you least expect it. Then there’s his wife, Margerine, a crazy insect lady, and then there’s their son who isn’t really a scary character at all, but does make it possible for the developers to throw in a clever “Escape Room” segment later on. The game’s broken up into a few distinct chapters defined by these characters and each character has their own boss encounter. Towards the end of the game, the game’s setting will change drastically and the story will start to piece itself together, but it feels shoehorned in and I can’t help but remember the final half of Metal Gear Solid 2 where you take control of a different character and the story and gameplay starts to get ridiculous. 
Resident Evil 7’s gameplay is much more focused on puzzle solving and horror. You’re given weapons, but ammo is extremely limited and I never felt like I was prepared for encounters. The weapons themselves all feel incredibly weak and most of the enemies in the game can’t even be killed. Because of this, running and shutting doors behind you is often the best tactic for escaping conflict. The game’s enemies will occasionally roam around the narrow corridors of the house requiring the player to sneak around, but the map design never really lends itself to this type of hide-and-seek gameplay and you often just need to wait for the enemy to walk from one spot to the other before you can move to the next segment. If the enemy spots you, you can awkwardly slow jog down the hall away from them and close the door behind you to slow them down. Once they lose sight of you, they start roaming their same scripted path again. After a few encounters, you’ll start to have a better understanding of how the game’s designed and the horror aspect of the game doesn’t have as strong of an impact as it does in the opening hour. You’ll realize that you just need to bypass the person hunting you, find the key to a door, turn around and go back, then crawl through a small confined space that the enemy can’t follow you into until they inevitably jump out at you in a scripted scene that sets up a boss fight. 
The game’s boss fights really highlight the weaknesses in the game’s core control scheme. Trying to fight Jack in a tiny arena was incredibly frustrating because of the slow player movement and painfully slow turning speed. The game requires that you make precision shots often and they’re difficult to pull off in such small areas. Couple that with the game’s incredibly slow reloading mechanic and stupid slow sprint speed and it’s easy to see the flaw in the game’s controls. 
The game also features some basic inventory management, but it felt like more of a hastle than it needed to be. You not only need to manage ammo and weapons, but you also need to make sure you have enough space to pick up important quest items like keys. There were several instances throughout the game where I was stuck backtracking to pickup a key I had placed in storage to make room for ammo. I never felt like this inventory management added to the experience, you could always just carry a large amount of ammo for each weapon and kill all of the enemies in the area, then backtrack to pick up all your keys from the storage container and walk around opening locked doors without any threats. 

And finally, let’s talk about visuals and performance. Resident Evil 7 runs great completely maxed out with framerates ranging anywhere between 100 to 160 fps at any time. The game’s visuals look phenomenal but I did feel that some of the character’s speaking animations felt off and didn’t look that convincing. Aside from that, textures, lighting, and sound design are all top notch and the best this series has to offer. 

And that’s all there really is to say about this game. Resident Evil 7 abandons the action oriented design of the past few games and instead borrows elements from the original Resident Evil while also taking elements from modern horror games like Outlast and Alien Isolation. But unfortunetly, it doesn’t seem to be better than any of those titles. The redneck family simply isn’t that scary, even when they jump out at you, and the game’s awkward slow paced controls that try to make you feel vulnerable just don’t feel believable and it makes for more of a frustrating experience than a scary one. The story is decent enough, but I couldn’t help but notice that it borrows a lot of elements from FEAR which came out over a decade ago. Thankfully the graphics and performance are excellent and the overall product feels very polished. The game by itself is a great experience with a few scares here and there, and a decent story (albeit incredibly copy-paste). 

I recommend picking this one up, but at a good discount. There's better games in this franchise, but this is a step in the right direction for Capcom and hopefully they'll learn from mistakes made in this game for their inevitable Resident Evil 8.

As someone who has played nearly every Resident Evil game (even Resident Evil Gaiden), I think that RE7 is not only a great game on its own, but also a step in the right direction for the series. Of course, many fans of the series probably will not like the transition to first-person, but for me that isn't too much of a problem. For me, it's not the camera angle that makes a Resident Evil game good, but the horror elements and enemy designs, which RE7 delivers on.

Here's a basic list of my experience

Pros:
+Shooting is made tense by the limited ammo combined with enemy movement patterns.
+Baker family is full of personality, and make each cutscene fun to watch.
+Exploring the Baker Mansion is a blast, and you never get the feeling that there's a useless or boring room.
+Boss fights are very well-designed (with the exception of the final one). No two boss fights are the same.
+Tons of graphical options, including some I've never even seen before. Whether you play the game on a toaster or a quantum computer, you should be able to find the settings that are right for you.
+Tons of inspiration from horror movies, especially Evil Dead
+DLC is actually well-designed, and pretty fun
+Decent new game+ rewards for completing certain tasks

Cons:
-Tons of unskippable events where nothing really happens. This isn't much of a problem for the first playthrough, but when you're going through your 3rd or 4th run they will eat up almost half of your game time. These are especially bad in the Guest House area.
-As mentioned earlier, the final boss sucked, and barely even qualifies as a boss.
-Not much enemy variety. Excluding the Baker family, there's only 3 types of enemies (4 if you include the normal molded with bigger claws)
-Some of the DLC should have just been part of the base game. Minigames are basically standard in the Resident Evil series, so it's kind of unfair that they didn't include at least one in the base game.
-No unlockable costumes, which has been a staple in the series (to be fair, this doesn't matter as much in first-person, but it would have been nice)

Neutrals (either good or bad depending on the player):
=Game is short, but doesn't have any filler. Some people may prefer longer games, even if it means more filler.
=Like many other games in the series, this starts off as a horror game with limited resources and weak weapons, and ends as an action game with tons of weapons (including a grenade launcher)
=The game isn't very connected to previous games in the series. You don't need to have played the previous games in order to understand the story in this one (though there are a few references newcomers will miss).

One final note: If your favorite game in the series is either 4, 5, 6, or the Revelations games, you may be disappointed. Unlike those games, this game does not focus that much on combat. There is no ammo or currency dropped when you kill an enemy. The inventory is much more restricted. And you are much more vulnerable in this game.
If you loved the classic Resident Evils, and you don't mind the change to first-person (which Capcom had been experimenting with since Resident Evil Survivor), you'll probably like this game.
If you have never played Resident Evil, but you love horror games, you'll probably like this.

If you are the sort of person you likes nothing better than to search the house from top to bottom for missing car keys this is for you. Apart from the run of the mill boss fights this game consists of endlessly searching for different types of keys and other itimes to open a particular door or raise a bridge. Its the exact same format that was being used in early computer in the 1990. Its very old fashioned and very boring.

It's a very enjoyable "immersive experience" that successfully injects some classic RE mechanics into the first person horror genre, such as inventory management and combat. However, it's a very brief experience that also runs out of steam very early on. For those who have yet to play it, the most iconic setting, imagery and character which this game's marketing puts forth as the central experience is over within the first few hours. The rest of the game remains serviceable but rarely provides as interesting levels or scenarios.

The majority of my play time comes from the DLC content which I bought up front in a sale. Most of this content is fairly well made albeit gimmicky and once you've had your fill of each "minigame" you'll likely never want to play it again. My favorite is Jack's 55th Birthday Party, which goofy aesthetics aside I find to be the most mechanically deep game this package offers. It requires you to manage your inventory under a time pressure and balance your backpack with items important to scoring points with your ammo,guns and health items, which all take up the same slots.

The only problem is that without these DLCs RE7 is criminally lacking in content, and feels like they should have been in the game by default. They're asking for nearly half the price of the main game for these gimmicky mini games, and they haven't even followed through with the other DLC content they promised to finish. As of present RE7 is practically an unfinished product and they're asking for $60+$25-30 for its presently incomplete state.

My final verdict is that RE7 is an impressive demonstration of the RE engine that is worth experiencing at least once. But as of present RE7 is a barebones product that is asking a steep price for its minimal content. My recommendation is to wait for the complete edition or if that never comes then to buy this game at a deep discount, because impressive visuals aside it isn't worth more than any one of the other first person horror romps floating around on steam.

edit: I gave a negative review a long while ago saying that Re7 was a good showcase of the RE engine but being sort of lacking in its content for what it asked for for 60$ at the point of review. Now that the total game has been out for a long time and revising my attitude towards highly polished concise experiences, especially at this price. I can easily say that this game is worth the price it asks and probably one of the best of the first person horror games that you can play on all of steam. You couldn't go wrong with this even if it was still asking for $60.

[h1]A Preface of Cringey Hesitation Thanks to RE6[/h1]
After Resident Evil 6, I didn't buy 7 at launch, having lost a significant bit of faith in the franchise. 6 was the inevitable result of the developer taking 5's too-heavy action leanings (I love 5 but acknowledge it's a poor direction for the series), and turning everything up to 11 until it's just an ear-bleeding din of too many playable characters, no horror, and a giant boss that just felt desperate how big it was, and another that was just a face-palmingly non-sensical Transformer. It took me 3 different attempts at getting through all of RE 6 before I finally forced myself to finish, and I honestly never plan on touching it again, so 7 was something I just wasn't interested in...man, I'm glad I took the plunge and finally gave 7 a go.

[h1]Graphics/Art Design[/h1]
Graphically, if you don't have a video card that meets the recommended specs, certain things in the game will look a little weird, like hair, and certain things will be a little blurry (even without motion blur), but the game looked good enough on my GeForce 770 for me to get by. Artistically, however, my video card didn't hold things back at all. The visual design itself of the game was great, with characters who looked more like real people and less like someone went down an anime character trope checklist like the series seemed to be going for previously. I would dare say only one character was a massive trope, and there's a very cool late-game twist that I didn't see coming until a few minutes before the reveal. The decrepit southern home and other locales were disturbingly creepy to be in from a visual standpoint, though there's more to these things than just how it looks...

[h1]Sound/Voice Acting[/h1]
Working in concert with the look of the game, the sound effects are excellent, and they round out the spookiness of the environment. The look and sound of the locations had me nervous as I went along, inching forward, listening carefully for sounds that might signal impending danger. The voice-acting was handled well. I'm from the American south, and the voices sounded believable and not like silly cartoon versions of southerners, which is nice for immersion.

[h1]Story[/h1]
RE7's plot has more twists than I've ever seen before in an RE game, which i found to be very fun. There are some nice clues that typically don't give too much away, but might help you figure something out and be surprised at your own revelation a few minutes before the reveal, or the surprise will completely blind-side you. Both of these happened to me, and I loved it each time. I only have 3 complaints about the story: 1. You are viewing what your main character views, but the game cuts out an entire scene which he has no excuse for forgetting, and it vastly changes how you should feel about certain characters. 2. There is a choice you have to make which determines your ending, and I think it was handled poorly because you aren't given enough information to make a good decision and doing the most selfless thing gives what most consider the "bad" ending. 3. Regardless of your choice, one character just drops out of the game completely, despite being quite important. I'm hoping upcoming DLC or a sequel will address it, because that character is probably my favorite character in RE7. These are pretty minor complaints, though. Over all, I think this is my favorite RE plot to date.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
This is the meat of the game. People sneer at first person shooters, but it's an excellent perspective for immersion, and your own character doesn't block the view.  This means tank controls are gone, though it's compensated sufficiently by having your movement speed cut down while you're aiming guns, and ammo, though not terribly scarce, is in short enough supply that I found myself resorting to the knife in most fights (though I wish I hadn't in retrospect...there really is enough ammo). You get a new knife late-game, and it's glorious, allowing for easy kills, but the early-game knife is just terrible. My favorite weapons were the shotguns, and they feel quite powerful when you land a perfect headshot up close.

The opening hour of the game (your first run if you're not going fast) might be kind of a drag. It has little to no Resident Evil gameplay (weird puzzles, gunplay against slow-moving monsters, inventory management, etc., and mostly consists of wandering around a creepy environment designed to milk jump scares out of you. I found myself getting drowsy until nearly the climax of the opening, at which things get good and stay really good until you complete the game, so I definitely suggest sticking with it if the very opening is dull and doesn't feel very Resident-Evil-y for you.

RE7 features sneaking, which is only in very specific locations and very, very, very few enemies will not notice you immediately, meaning you will be running away or fighting almost everything in the game. If you hear "RE7 has sneaking," don't go thinking that this is a stealth game, because it's not, and the stealth is just kinda okay.

Puzzles are back, baby, and so are the locked doors you'll get themed keys to unlock. Nothing is terribly complicated, though one puzzle was rather awesome and I think Jigsaw would approve. You can watch an interactive video tape and use what you learn from that to change the outcome of your own dealings with that puzzle, which felt incredibly satisfying for me.

This game had less bosses than some RE games, but that's a good thing. RE6 had piles of boss fights and more combat than you could shake a stick at. This game is a return to form for Resident Evil, feeling closer to something between RE1 and RE4, with 1's map design and puzzles, and 4's sensible combat without going full-on action game.

Some folks take issue with the game being short. There's an achievement for finishing in under 4 hours, though it took me over 14. Granted, I did only heal 3 times because I was such an item tightwad, and kept getting killed. I honestly prefer shorter games that last a handful of hours to an experience that drags on for the sake of padding out run-time, so RE7 has won my appreciation in that regard, having great content without stretching it out and diminishing the well-paced structure of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Not everyone will love the game, but I really enjoyed it and I feel like Resident Evil is back and fun again. As an entry in the series, I recommend it alongside great stuff like the REmake, 2, and 4. It feels a little weird, especially during that first hour which just feels like a horror game with jump scares and nothing more, but when the Resident Evil locked doors and map exploration starts up, things got [i]really[/i] fun for me, and I hope it will for you as well.

If for you Resident Evil is all about zombies, Wesker and T-Virus... just avoid this game, if for you RE is about survival horror, exploration and avoiding enemies, solve puzzles, be in an state of tension every single time you need to come back all the way with a new item on your inventory... this game is a must have.

The game takes successful elements from contemporary horror games and mix it with the classical elementes of the saga. If you don't like RE maybe you find some things odd but if not, this is RE, every bit of the game. [h1]Excellent Blend of Old & New[/h1]

Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic new entry into the franchise, which, let's be honest, has gone very stale in the past years. The developers did something really impressive: They took a step back from the previous games and tried to find a completely new approach for this one, without disregarding everything that made the older games good in the first place. They combined elements of different games  in the genre to create a fresh and interesting blend. 

[i]Take some Outlast, mix it with a bit of F.E.A.R. and top it all of with a nice dose of good ol' Resident Evil Horror[/i]

[u]Story[/u]
Read the story synapse on the store page, there is not much to be add. The Bakers are very interesting villains, but don't be fooled by the promo material and trailers: There is so much more going on and the game offers surprises all along the way. It caught me off-guard how much twists and turns they put into this.

[u]Atmosphere & Setting[/u]
The Atmosphere in this game is brilliant. They have balanced out suspense, action and exploration rather well and there are definitive peaks along the way. There are passages that are downright frightening and suspenseful, followed by some intense action (thank god not as much as in the previous two games), followed by some calmer exploration and puzzle-solving. The constant change helps the game to not get boring and to always feel fresh and interesting. 
The redneck-Setting is also a welcome change. The Bakers are interesting villains with unique traits to each of them. One warning though: This game is bloody and in some scenes downright disturbing. So if you are kinda sensitive to violence, gore and Horror in general, you might want to reconsider playing it. Also: Jump Scares. Not too many, but they are there, and they are well done. I jumped.. more than once.

The great thing is, the game never relies on cheap jump scares. There is so much subtle horror spread in as well, and especially these subtle elements made this game frightening (That freaking old woman in the wheelchair, I swear...).

[u]Gameplay[/u]
The Gameplay might have switched massive in terms of perspective, changing from shoulder perspective to first person, but the core is still the same, as you might know from older entries in the series: Explore a complex, but somewhat open area, try to solve riddles and collect items to open up new ways. The inventory management can get a bit tedious, but I think they deliberately made it that way to recreate the way, the older games worked. 
The shooting works fine, although the enemy-types get somewhat stale after a few hours, especially since the main enemies aren't all that interesting to begin with. Excluded from this are the bossfight, of which there are plenty. Every single Boss fight has some sort of gimmick and creative idea and all in all they are plain fun.

[u]Presentation[/u]
This is where things get a bit rough. The graphics are fine, but nothing to write home about. The Lighting is very atmospheric and the use of color is clever in most places, but whenever you stop to look at details, washed out textures and rough edges, combined with some horrible smoothening effects will make your eyes hurt. The physics are also almost laughably bad, especially when it comes to the movement of hair. I don't know, if its because of the havok physics engine, but other technologies, like in Rise of the Tomb Raider do a far better job.
But when it comes to sound, Resident Evil 7 steals the show. The music is subtle in most places, but always fitting while the sound effects are the main reason you almost crap your pants every five seconds. The whole house is creaking, every object in the envoirement that would emit some sort of sound has a realistic sound made for it. The world feels alive and the immersion is therefore fantastic.

[u]Replayability & Content[/u]
The game is not too short and not too long. It took me about 8 hours to complete for the first time which is nice and dandy, since it started to drag a bit in the end. Interestingly, there are different endings and since you have to settle on one ending way before the game actually ends, I am keen to replay it again right now to find out how the last third of game pans out with  a different choice.
Can't say much about the DLCs, havent bought them, yet. But for the main game, it is worth it's price tag.

[u]TL;DR[/u]
PROS
[list]
[*] Atmosphere is great
[*] Gameplay is fun
[*] Very surprising twists and turns along the way
[*] Interesting setting and villains
[*] Replayability
[/list]

CONS
[list]
[*] Technical fidelity is kinda meh
[*] Riddles are a bit too easy
[*] Last half hour drags a bit too much
[/list]

Summary: 
This game is good and I do think it is worth picking up on sale. This game does many things right, but many things wrong as well. I am a big Resident Evil fan and to give you an idea of how I like the previouse games in the series I would rate them as such: 4,CXV, 2, 1, 0, 3, 7, 5, revs2,6,revs1,ORC. 

Story: 
The story was overall weak in this game. It does not really deliver anything new and the pacing is pretty rushed near the end. Most of the twists you can see coming a mile away. None of this would matter if it kept the B-Movie action-horror vibes of previous games like 1 and 4 but it doesnt. The way the story is presented in the first half of the game is very good though. The game goes back to the earlier form of resident evil story telling. You go to an isolated place, messed up things are happening, get to the bottom of it. It does these things very well. The characters are pretty bland overall with the exception of Jack. Jack is a great character, so much so that I let him chase me around just to hear his dialogue. Lucas is pretty interesting as well. The rest are just bland or annoying. This game lacks the comedic aspects to Resident Evil that always foiled with tense atmosphere to create greater horror. Ethan is probably the blandest RE protagonist to date.

Gameplay: 
This game plays okay. The first person camera did not bother me as much as I thought it would, but it did have some negative effects. The first person camera alloweds you to explore the corridor like areas of the house without having to worry about the third person camera getting caught on terrain. It also allows for interesting hiding places for various items. On the negative side however this made the game much easier because the controls in this game or too smooth. This may sound odd but clunky controls add to the tension and challenge. Look at RE4 that game is super fun to play but the controls are somewhat clunky. you cant move while shooting the position of your gun always starts off a default point making you have large amounts of tension as enemies approach this game has none of that. Also Leon in RE4 with elite training does not have perfect aim yet Ethans hands dont move at all when aiming his gun and he doesnt have any training at all as far as you know. This makes the very small enemy roster even more apparent. Outside of the games 3 real boss fights(arguably 4) you only fight 4 enemies total one of which is a tiny variation that does more damage. All of these enemies look very similar and are largly uninteresting and unthreatening as they move very predictably and slow(except the crawler who is ver easy to kill). This game is also very short. Considering how rushed the second half feels it seems as if the game was shortened to meet a deadline or something. The game also lacks replayablity outside of difficulties and achievments. Compare to RE 1 with 2 playable characters, or RE4 with the very long story, and the extra ada story, and the mercenaries, and the unlocklable special weapons and the amount of content just seems very short for a RE game. The level design is very inconsistent. The first house was great and the boat was good, however the mine was horrible, and the boat house wasnt good either. Nothing comes close to any of the classic RE level desig, doesnt even come close to 4s level design. To me the game was not scary at all. I did not even feel tense like I usually do in the fights, even 5 made me feel tense in the big battles. Its simply because the enemies are not scary, some like Jack are interesting, but not scary. The game does feel very polished and the inventory management is great which means the game is fun. I enjoyed trying to save every last bullet and use my knife as much as possible(I didnt need to tho) and the shotgun was a very fun weapon. Lots of secrets to find as well if your into that like I am.
 
Conclusion: I think this is a bit of a mixed bag as a RE game however as a game of itself I think it is very good. This is a great starting point for new fans who like first person horror games though I would heavily suggest 4 or 1 first or after if you have not played them yet.

I guess Capcom got tired of the series having two different titles in Japan and America so they combined the two names into one. Unimaginative name aside, this game is a return to form - Capcom recognized their mistake in turning the series into co-cop action games and returned to a single player horror experience, this time with a fresh first person camera perspective. While this is easily the third best game in the series after REmake and RE4, it's also one of the most frustrating entries thanks to some unfulfilled potential.

In a break from RE tradition, this game introduces a new main character, Ethan Winters. The basic setup is very similar to Silent Hill 2 - he receives a message from his wife who has been missing for 3 years, summoning him to meet up with her - but it quickly diverges from that template. This message brings him yet another mansion, only this time the mansion is a run down estate in Louisiana owned by the Bakers, a truly deranged southern family. They spend the first 2/3 of the game stalking you through the estate's many houses and outbuildings, the scope of which silently conjures a familial history of slave ownership.

The opening sequence in the guest house immediately shows you how serious they were about returning to horror here - this is BY FAR the scariest game in the series. I didn't this the RE series would ever go this far - this may be the first time a horror game has ever had me freaked out in the daytime. The claustrophobia induced by the odd camera angles from the early games has been wonderfully updated in first person with tight spaces and a flashlight which gives you a tiny field of view. The house is downright disgusting, and a lot of what you have to do to traverse it is quite nauseating (naturally including draining a mold-filled bathtub in a tribute to the original). The visuals are wonderful, and the music is used sply but effectively. The monster designs are great, and while there are a few reprised ideas, they feel more like a cute nod to previous entries than lazy recycling.

Mechanically, this game is a return to the core principles of old RE. Magically interconnected item boxes are back. Typewriter save spots are back in the form of cassette recorders (though you only get a limited number of saves in the form of cassettes in the 'Madhouse' hard mode that's unlocked after beating the game - otherwise it works like the RE4 typewriters). The core of the game is once again a key hunt in a big house. It's difficult even on normal, and you will run out of ammo frequently, putting you in hairy situations. Health and ammo crafting systems have been combined and streamlined - you can combine a green herb, gunpowder or solid fuel with a chem pack or strong chem pack to craft 6 different items. This isn't quite as much of a return to old-school design as the teaser implied - it holds your hand a bit more in the form of frequent autosaves and an objective list - but it feels like a nice compromise between the cruelty of those old games and the excessive handholding of modern ones. It hits a nice sweet spot.

Most of the game feels like it could have been a new IP or offshoot, thanks to a much more intimate story with a new main character, a new camera perspective, and a very different kind of horror. Unfortunately, it becomes much more uninspired once it starts trying to be a Resident Evil game again in the final act. Several plot twists feel like forced attempts to tie this unrelated story into the main series, transforming the story into an addled and incoherent mess of smashed-together tropes. This is primarily frustrating because for the first time ever, the plot of a Resident Evil game was almost good. It was probably silly of me to expect it to remain that way.

To make matters worse. the gameplay also declines in the final act. The Bakers aren't the only enemies in the game - there are also new zombielike creatures called the Molded. These creatures are quite scary and hard to defeat early on in the game, but once the game forgets about the Bakers and gives you stronger firepower, it devolves into another dull zombie shooter. Granted, it doesn't swarm you with enemies in a fast-paced manner filled with quicktime events (of which there are close to none), so it's still a step above the previous entries, but it's a big step down for this game. It doesn't help that the environments become rather mundane once you leave the estate - the salt mines in the final stage are particularly dull.

After the lengthy action trilogy, this game returned to being brief and tight - my clear time was around 7.5hrs. I feel like this is an optimal length for a horror game (though it seems a bit scant if you're paying full price, as there are no extra modes), but seeing as even this brief game had filler towards the end once they ran out of ideas, I would have preferred that it was even shorter and they'd just made the Bakers the entire focus. I can only imagine what the game would have been like if they'd brought in the history of the deep south a bit more. I haven't bought any of the DLC, so I can't comment on that, but not all of it has been released yet anyway.

The PC port is great - I can't remember the last time I could get away with running a new game on native resolution, let alone without turning everything down! It took quite a bit of tweaking to get to that point, but my GPU isn't supposed to be powerful enough to run this game at all and I managed to run it on high settings - while the initial release evidently had some optimization issues, they seem to have cleared them up incredibly well with patches.

For survival horror games, I do think this is inarguably a return to form. Modern survival games are largely either secretly action games ([i]The Evil Within[/i]), or just totally boring and not in the slightest scary ([i]Amnesia[/i]). However, I think that there's a serious point to be made about the fact that the game throws all of its "wow" moments at you pretty much before the end of the first hour. Most of the games moments are heavily scripted, and as a result, there's not much to get out of the game on additional playthroughs.

Other than this, possibly the most significant issue with the game is the fact that it features lots of unavoidable, or otherwise extremely hard to avoid, combat. What this means is that the game is entirely inclined to constantly hand out health and ammo drops (or otherwise, the materials to create those items), which means that there's no real tension in combat. Combat itself is rather tedious, and is not aided by the fact that the standard grunt monsters are overused and underdesigned.

Back in 2005, Resident Evil switched from a survival-horror to more of a third-person shooter with elements of Resident Evil's entries. the games had switched the set camera angles for an "over-the-shoulder" view. most of the puzzle solving had been outed, and it had more fighting in it. Resident Evil 7 was liked and disliked by the Resident Evil fanbase. it traded away the gigantic arsenal of weapons for more realistic weapon handling. most of the enemy variation has been traded off for a more intense survival-horror feel much like the classic Resident Evil games, and the over-the-shoulder camera was switched for something never done in any Resident Evil game: a first-person camera. this, the slower pace, and the puzzle solving were beloved by fans of the classic RE entries, and of course, who wouldn't love the lovely cast of The Baker Family? of course, you have haters sadly. alot of people called it a ripoff of Outlast and Silent Hill. it's a survival horror with a stalker figure, other horror games did it too. anyway, when Not A Hero first came out, people called it a DOOM clone.
