Resident Evil 7 is one of the better and more definitive titles in the series.  It took a series that, in my opinion, had strayed from its roots, and brought the very things we want in a Resident Evil game back front and center.  From the visuals, to the gameplay mechanics, to the sounds and musical score, to the storyline, everything about Resident Evil 7 looks modern, polished, and fixes everything you may not have liked about the series in its more recent action oriented titles.

First the visuals.  Resident Evil 7 adopts a new "RE Engine" with photo-realistic graphics, lighting, etc.  When I say photo-realistic, I MEAN photo-realistic, not just high resolution, photo-realistic.  The people, the walls, the lighting, the water, even the way your flashlight refracts off your weapons, it all looks absolutely incredible.  There are plenty of moments when you first enter a dark room with nothing but your very dim flashlight, and it FEELS like you really are in a room that dark.  There's none of that artificial light that's just bright enough for you to see an item like in a lot of other games.  If the lights are out, it gets DARK, and when there is light, it looks incredibly natural, especially against the photo-realistic people and textures.

The audio is just as awesome as the visuals.  The soundtrack is usually very quiet and subtle, but is present enough to set the mood.  The music is high quality in terms of audio fidelity, and it's not loud or abrasive enough for you to "notice" it, which is a very good thing in a game where you want to be engrossed in a moment and not distracted by the musical instruments playing in the background.  The voice acting and sound effects are well done, and there's lots of audio cues to help you stay alert of what's going on around you.  The virtual surround sound worked really well with my headphones.  If something was behind me and on the other side of a wall, it actually sounded correct; I could tell the direction, and its presence behind the wall, because of the quality of sound.  Paired with the great visuals, the quality audio work does a really good job, especially if you're wearing headphones, of making you feel like you're actually there in that moment.

The gameplay is another area where this game has done a lot of things right, and even made some positive changes.  You don't feel like you're playing Gears of War with zombies.  Ammunition is rare enough that you find yourself fighting with your knife, or avoiding fights altogether when you can in order to conserve it.  It keeps some staples of the series like the "safe room" with a storage box, save point, etc.  For the first time I am aware of in the series, the game is first person, which really helps put you in the game when paired with the photo-realistic visuals and quality audio work.  You don't feel like you're controlling somebody else, you feel like you are there.  Movement was fluid and responsive with no noticeable input lag even with VSync enabled.  Combined with the realistic and often sparse lighting, the first person view also lends aid to the occasional jump scare where you may enter a room and there's something hiding in the dark just outside your field of vision, waiting to jump right up in your face in the light of your flashlight; something that's harder to accomplish when playing in over the shoulder 3rd person mode.  Inventory management is improved over older titles as well.  You no longer have to manually move items around in order to make sure two spaces are next to each other so you can hold a larger weapon.  If you have enough spaces for an item, it will automatically move things around if necessary to accommodate that item.  You can craft ammo, potions, etc., or you can even break them down into their base components again using another special item if you really want to.  There's plenty of puzzles to exercise your brain, but none that are too difficult to reasonably accomplish, and thank goodness there are NO SLIDING PICTURE PUZZLES! (I hate that kind)  You might have to find a lockpick, or a special key, or fit some insignias together into a door, etc., but most of the puzzles can be solved simply by paying attention to details in your surroundings as you play.  The puzzles are enough to keep things interesting and give you objectives, without being too difficult to be enjoyable.

The story in this game is a unique and interesting tale.  It does a good job misleading you, making you doubt your own decisions and assumptions, and expands on the story of some well known icons in the Resident Evil series.  As soon as you think you know what's going on, something happens to make you doubt yourself just a little bit, and things that may at first seem harmless or inconsequential, may turn out to be the complete opposite.  One of the weirdest parts about this story is that I finished the game sort of feeling sorry for even the villain.

In summary, Resident Evil 7 has done what it was supposed to, it brought Resident Evil back to its survival horror roots.  From the amazing visuals and audio, to the first person perspective with realistic lighting and sparse ammo, to the intriguing story line, Resident Evil 7 was an enjoyable game that legitimately scared the daylights out of me at times, and left me with some new questions regarding the role of certain players in the Resident Evil drama.  For those who are a fan of the series and thought some of the newer games felt a little too much like 3rd person shoot-em-ups with zombies, Resident Evil 7 is the perfect example of how to return to your roots when you've lost your way.  I highly recommend this game not just for fans of Resident Evil specifically, but for fans of the survival horror genre as a whole.

I pretty much have this game alone to thank for getting me into survival horror. And now, years after first playing it, I've finally put in the nightmarishly frustrating effort of getting 100% achievements, and can safely say that I'm done with the game once and for all after god-knows-how-many playthroughs.

To very briefly summarize, this is by far my favorite Resident Evil game, maybe my favorite horror game, and has the potential to be my favorite game ever period. The issue is that, while the first 2/3rds or 3/4ths of the game have nearly [b]FLAWLESS[/b] pacing, story, mystery, level design, survival horror gameplay balance, and constant introduction of fresh scares and unique environments and challenges, it all kind of falls apart in the last chunk, where the game gets a little too heavy on the actiony side, overgenerous with supplies, and the story loses its luster since it lacks the first half's compelling villains.

If the last quarter of the game was as up to the quality standard set by the first three quarters, then it would easily be my favorite game. As it is, most of my replays of it stop once I reach the boat section cause I can't be bothered to slog through it again lol.

So I still really, really, REALLY recommend it if you want some of the most elegantly designed survival horror you'll ever play, with a compelling plot and dumb-but-fun side content, but only if you're okay with the knowledge that the last quarter kinda fails to stick the landing.

After completing this game, there's only one verdict I can possibly come to. About time Capcom! Resident Evil was a pioneer of the survival horror genre. While RE5 and RE6 were indeed fun to play, clearly those two entries lacked horror. However, this is not just a return to horror. This is the next stage of evolution for the series. Bringing back familiar gameplay features we remember from the good old days, while uplifting the franchise to a whole new level. The first person perspective has made this entry far more intense than it's predecessors. It felt like I was a part of a horror film, while retaining the well developed RE universe. A new story and a new kind of protagonist. Yet ultimately still connecting to the rest of this well crafted horror universe. From beginning to end, I had no complaints about this one. In fact, I'm looking forward to what's coming next. I would go as far to say that the first person viewpoint should be used from this moment forward. At least until Capcom revolutionizes the survival horror genre yet again. Knowing Capcom, I wouldn't be surprised if they do years down the road. But for now, we have much to look forward to.

Final Verdict: Resident Evil 7: Biohazard not only goes back to the survival horror roots, this groundbreaking entry into the series seems to be just the beginning of a brighter future for the Resident Evil franchise. Or due to the circumstances, a terrifying one. Either way, the previous mistakes made by Capcom have clearly proven to be nothing but the past. With Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, Capcom has achieved redemption. Well done!

Game itself reminds me the first game in the RE franchise, especially with the inventory management, safe rooms and cassette recorders, since its the only way you can save the game. On madhouse difficulty it's a way different game, which makes replaying way more efficient. Enemies not only hit harder, they are more tough, they walk faster, you can meet them at different places, or vice-versa, they are missing somewhere, for example basement fridge. Generally I don't write reviews, because I'm not very good at them but this time I felt compelled to do it. Resident Evil 7 was an unexpected surprise for me. The first time I heard about it and watched the very first reveal trailer I thought: Jesus dudes, what are you doing? What's wrong with you? We've been asking for a traditional-style Resident Evil game since the fourth... and what are we going to get instead? I think this was a feeling shared by every RES fan. But in the end, a couple of weeks ago I decided to buy it, just because Capcom deserved the benefit of the doubt... Well I can say now that it was the best choice I could have made. Resident Evil 7 is absolutely revolutionary. It has everything we all needed from a RES game, plus the innovative gameplay which some had turned their noses up to – however, I can tell you that this is its strength and it will surely make you feel like a part of the game. 

I’ve watched every video that I could find on the internet about the creation process of the game and I was amazed by Capcom's hard work, especially the work on sound design - which, honestly, is outstanding. They‘ve put considerable effort into it and they‘ve recreated every sound and noise paying great attention to detail. The voice acting is amazing too. All of characters are very well dubbed and characterized, and last but not least, the soundtrack, which corroborates every aspect of the gamesound and gameplay. 

Now, let's talk about the graphics... (I apologize in advance for my "nontechnical" opinions :] ) The "RE Engine" does an excellent job. It's not very demanding, so you will be able to easily play the game without resorting to too many compromises. The atmosphere and locations are very well designed thanks to their layouts and great textures, but I warn you that you will rarely encounter very low res textures, however, if you do they're not that big of a deal - as in they won‘t compromise your experience. I really loved the lighting effects and I think you will appreciate them as well. Physics are good too but sometimes, like for the textures, you will find some effects that are not perfectly made , but they're not a biggie either. I don't want to talk about the story, you need to discover that by yourself and I promise... you won't be disappointed :). 

As for the gameplay... Resident Evil 7 is a survival horror adventure with all the typical elements of RES games. The innovation is the "first person perspective" which has never been used in any of the previous games in the serie (the only exception were the arcade style first person shooter games called "Resident Evil: Survivor" which were specifically designed to be played with a light gun). This is driven by the concept of Resident Evil 7, which is a "return to horror". I want to quote Capcom developer team's words about this:<< At this particular time in games, it was determined that first-person was the most advantageous way to present horror to the player. When confronting the enemies, there are no barriers between you and them. This also applies to exploration and gimmicks and traps and things like that. We felt that it really gets you up close and personal with everything, which adds to the game the horror element we need.>>. I can tell you that it really feels like this. Every aspect of the game and especially this one makes you really feel like an integral part of the game. You will feel the terror and anxiety rising up in you. 

In conclusion I can say that this was the best choice that they could make to bring Resident Evil back to its roots, while being innovative at the same time. But remember; this is not a "Survival horror walking simulator" where you just need to run, run and run over and over to reach the end of the game. Here you’ve gotta kill, solve puzzles, explore, craft, face and survive the horrors that the whole game and especially the Baker's house will offer you. I don't think I need to say anything else, also because I don't think it’s necessary to go into detail. I guess you will like to discover the game by yourself :). I hope that you all will enjoy this review and I wanted to thank you for taking time to read it. I just wanted to share the intro of the game, because I think it really deserves to be appreciated. It looks like a trailer for a big-budget movie or TV serie and it's very well done. There is no a better presentation than this intro :).  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0OR_fse21IY  Welcome to the Family, Son!!

After beating Resident Evil 7 twice now, I can assure any doubters that it is the perfect modernization of the original game's themes and concepts. It's not RE4, which was a masterpiece in its own right, but its still fits into the current plethora of horror games.  Instead of taking the action focus of the last two release and puts it back in the background.  Avoidance and preservation are going to be big focuses of your play time.  The pistol is very weak and it takes quite a few shots to down most of the enemies with it and its the weapon your going to find most the ammo for.  The shotgun on the other hand feels like a tank, when you shoot it, you can expect something to tobble.  Ammo is on the low side for it and the other speciality guns you run across, so you will get used to just running around the enemies you can. 

As far as graphics go, I thought most of the game is breathtaking.  The textures are all really good and by narrowing the focus of the game to just a few areas, I feel like they were able to invest more heavily in making sure each one works. This of course goes with the overall tone and theme, which is another thing the game gets right.  It feels dark and harrowing in the mansion and around it.  As you repeat the same areas with new spins, you will be able to navigate it like your own house.  There are so many little details that make it feel fully realized as a place (photographs, small things like lighting being in realistic places, etc.), it was a joy to see how each new area would look and feel. Disclaimers: Completed the playthrough in 9 hours, medium settings. Haven't played any of the previous Resident Evil games. Not a follower of the Resident Evil movies. Lets get to the review!

[h1] Gameplay 4/5 [/h1]
First person perspective in a survival-horror setting. The gameplay mechanics are not vast or complex but they are done right. Conserving ammo and health potions is a must. You can craft items in game and they it is smartly implemented. Some items share components, so you always have to see which item you need more at that time. There are some puzzles to be solved in between, which I really liked. 

[h1] Story 5/5 [/h1]
For this type of game, the story is more than half of the reason why it can fail or succeed. Here, the story delivers. From the trailer you can see the main character is in search of his wife and he ends up in a remote house in the middle of a forest. And the horror entails. The best part of the story is that there is no expedition or motage of events shown to tell the story. It is all done through video tapes and memories, which you basically see from 2 characters. The whole story does not unfold till the very end and it keeps you gripped the whole time.

[h1] Level Design 5/5 [/h1]
In a horror game, the scare does not work if you don't build up the tension. In this game, as soon as you take your first step, they start building the tension and it piles up till they give you a scare which makes it really effective. Another great thing about the level design that even though it is not vast, but made available in bits and pieces so even after going through the same area after 4 or 5 times you can get into new stuff.

[h1] Characters 5/5 [/h1]
The main character is Ethan. He starts the game with the main objective of finding his wife, but then as he finds out new things, his objective changes. This makes for a good character development. There are only a bunch of characters in this secluded house, but all of them really takes the spotlight when it is their show. The voice acting is great and the animation is well done. 

[h1] Replayability 2/5 [/h1]
The game do have two different endings. But apart from that, the scare only works for the first time. When you know, when or how something is coming at you, the surprise factor is not really great which lessens the experience.

[h1] Overall 4/5 [/h1]

So, I have played every RE to date and I have almost every horror game on Steam. RE7 has its good qualities and its bad qualities. Lets start with the good;

- First person is actually somewhat refreshing in this series and enhances the horror aspect.

- The mechanics are pretty solid. Combining items, puzzle solving, ammo conservation etc etc. These are all still present, as they should be. 

- The Bakers are pretty damn scary especially Jack. He makes the early part of the game the most memorable.

- Decent graphics.

- Fantastic soundtrack.

- Keeps you on your toes from early to mid-game. 


Alright. Thats the good. Lets get to the bad;

- Very small game area. RE series has always had this but I really feel that this is even more the case in RE7 and first person actually enhances this negative aspect.

- Short. *So* short. I mean I get it. Its a new engine but come on.

- The Bakers make the *early* part of the game the most memorable. Then they take a backseat to the mould which is just insane to me. They clearly should have been persistent threats like Nemesis seen as they were the most flaunted aspect of the game.

- The mould are *not* scary past the first time you see them. They're brown sludge. Are you frightened by brown sludge? No. Me neither. Its not even as though they couldn't have gone a different way with it. If you have a monster that converts biomass into more of itself you could have something like John Carpenters "The Thing". (The original, not the remake.) Now *that* was scary and it could masquerade as people you knew.

- Theres a choice you're given before you get on a boat. Its a pointless choice with results that make little sense. Its pretty obvious which choice is canon and which isn't. If you're not going to make that choice matter just don't offer it to us, its not like people look to RE for this stuff anyway.

- The second half of the game is considerably weaker and turns into an FPS rather than a horror game.

- The final fight with Eveline is basically a cutscene. Why? I mean isn't she meant to be the big bad? Also, why turn her into just a big monstrosity? Wasn't part of what made her scary the fact she could insidiously ♥♥♥♥ with peoples minds? It feels like an opportunity was missed here and I just don't get why.


Conclusion; I want to recommend this game and you know what? I would have but the rose-tinted glasses are off now and I look back and for the life of me the only parts I can remember fondly are the earliest parts of the game. Because that was the most similar to what I was sold in the trailer; a horror game. The rest just felt like "oh look, uroboros again" as if that was a part of the RE series we wanted to revisit. It isn't.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a thrilling and chilling return to the survival horror roots that revitalizes the beloved franchise. With its first-person perspective, the game offers an immersive and terrifying experience that keeps players on edge from start to finish.

The story is gripping and atmospheric, taking place in a decaying plantation mansion filled with horrifying secrets and grotesque enemies. The tense exploration, resource management, and puzzle-solving all contribute to a sense of vulnerability and dread that defines classic survival horror.

One of the game’s standout features is its incredible attention to detail — the environments feel lived-in and hauntingly real, adding layers to the storytelling without relying heavily on exposition. The sound design is exceptional, using subtle audio cues and ambient noises to build tension and fear.

Resident Evil 7 also introduces a perfect balance between action and horror, with intense combat sequences interspersed with moments of quiet suspense. The inclusion of VR support takes the immersion to another level, making the scares even more visceral.

Overall, Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a masterclass in horror game design. It respects the series’ legacy while innovating in gameplay and atmosphere, delivering a memorable and spine-chilling experience that both longtime fans and newcomers will appreciate.

Basically original Resident Evil is multi-layered puzzle game with arcade gameplay mixed with exploration, ammo conservation and movement planning set in horror-flick themed setting.
Resident Evil 7 is exactly the same game at it's core. It still a multi-layered puzzle game with arcade gameplay mixed with exploration, ammo conservation and movement planning set in horror-flick themed setting. The difference is in it's form, not function. Functionally it is still the same game as first. Capcom used all modern tech and design doctrines to recreate the core Resident Evil experience into new generation. They used it to create the most immersive, scary and polished package in recent gaming. It is what PT (Silent Hills) was to Silent Hill: reimagination in new era of gamedesign while keeping the essence of series. And while Silent Hills was canned, Resident Evil 7 got to release in absolutely glorious form. Not to mention that PC version is the definitive one with great visuals and optimisation.
Also proper story DLCs are free, and paid DLCs are not required at all - they are all experimental and standalone mini-games for fans, they don't affect core story and game. It's DLC done right - they pushed away content that is not required, but won't work standalone. So you get complete package even without buying DLCs.

The king is back baby. And now it's finally scary.

PSA: One thing: the game requires a lot of high speed vram to be played on high settings since whole engine was designed around current gen hardware with a lot of high speed vram. For high settings your GPU need to have proper 6Gb of vram and for medium GPU needs proper 256bit bus. Otherwise it'll stutter. So, sadly, Nvidia folks with their midrange 128bit cards and 3.5Gb 970 got shafted. But that's not exactly the problem of the game itself tho

Resident Evil 7 is a welcome change after the fiasco that was known as Resident Evil 6 (aka. The Evil Giraffe BJ.) RE7 strips away a lot of the over the top action compared to previous games, and returns to claustrophobic close quarters horror with some intense item management reminiscent of the first three RE games.

In the beginning, you are completely defenseless, which means you'll have to sneak or run from enemy encounters. You'll eventually get a knife and even firearms, but you'll have to spare ammo and juggle using your weapons depending on the situation. Health also doesn't regenerate, so every hit you take is something you have to live with.

At around midpoint the game starts to have some annoyingly bullet spongy bosses, and towards the very end the game started feeling almost more like Doom than RE, but luckily the game didn't delve too deep into the shooter territory. The survival horror elements could be felt throughout the game.

Technically the game seemed quite solid, but as always, your mileage may vary. Not once did the game crash on me or corrupt my data. My potato (1st gen i7, GTX 960) runs this game at 60 fps at fairly high settings on a 1080p resolution. Only towards the end did I start to occasionally dip below 60fps, but that was mostly because of larger events happening. Loading times on SSD were barely noticeable. 

While I have my minor gripes, RE7 is definitely a damn good game, and a long needed renewal of the RE series.

Though the game was a little short, it successfully returned the RE series to its roots as as a pure survival horror experience instead of simply an action game.  While perhaps not as revolutionary as RE 2 or 4, it nonetheless excels in the most significant aspects of the genre, namely that of tension building and overall atmosphere.  It accomplishes this through clever use of lighting and most importantly in the use of music and sound. While not quite matching the quality of the series' zenith in 2002-2003, RE7 is a confident stride in the right direction. This is a good entry point for those new to the series, and a shining glimmer of light for seasoned fans. It plays very well and is pleasing to the senses, but suffers from a weak story, is far too easy, and not particularly scary.
GAMEPLAY:
RE7 used typical FPS controls, with some welcome returns from previous series entries. Your inventory is limited, so you will need to choose what to carry on your person, storing excess items in item chests. It aids in the horror element, and is a nice return. There's also a crafting system, allowing players to create their own supplies and repair damaged items. There's a bigger focus on stealth than previous entries in the series, though it doesn't quite go as far as, say, Outlast. You are encouraged to sneak around recurring enemies, which is a nice change of pace and contrasts nicely with boss fights and typical enemy encounters. When you do fight enemies, they've found a way to include an element of the clunkiness of the early games - which is a huge plus. Reload times are slow, it takes a second to fine aim, and there's a small amount of bullet spread, meaning that shots can miss if not carefully aimed. Combined with a lack of on-screen hud, enemy encounters are immersive and require some thought (though not exactly a lot of effort) to overcome. Otherwise, you will primarily spend your time going from A to B, fetching items to unlock doors. Unfortunately, puzzles are sparse, and when present are far too easy - almost to the point of insulting the player's intelligence. RE7's lack of difficulty is perhaps its biggest flaw (see the "horror" section for more detail).
A big point in this games' favour is its optional content. There's a lot - for example, upgrades for purchase, and hidden VHS tapes that add short side segments, which are a nice diversion from the main story - especially when they change the gameplay style, for instance having the player escape from a locked room by solving puzzles. What's nice about all of these is that they're integrated into the game world - there is no end-of-level upgrade menu, or merchant selling you weapons. They've found ways to subtly place these things into the game world, which does a huge service to the players' immersion. 

VISUALS:
The game looks great, with lots of nice attention to detail - though it's lacking in a few areas. On-screen button prompts detract from player immersion, especially when there's no HUD present, and the facial animations look very robotic at times, getting into uncanny valley terrirtory at times, and some of the hair animations have a strange floating quality to them - though the character models are wonderfully animated. One of my favourite touches is the healing animation - rather than just saying "you've been healed", Eathan will apply his medicine in a way that's relevant to his injuries. There are some low-quality textures upon close inspection, and the game misses an opportunity to create atmosphere through lighting (partially due to the afrorementioned lack of control over the flashlight) and I think it suffers for it - there are few opportunities to create the shadows that are very nicely animated. Moreover, the latter quarter of the game opts to send the player to some very bland environments, shunning the excellent detail of the mansion.

AUDIO:
The voice acting is excellent and packed with all types of emotion - particularly noteworthy are the Bakers, whose performances make every scene that they're in. The rest of the cast is acted almost as superbly - it's certainly a far cry from the early games! 
The game doesn't do much in the way of music - except for the return of the save room themes which, though a bit of a weak tune, is a nice touch. When present, the music is so subtle as to be almost unnoticable, which can be good for creating an unsettling atmosphere. RE7 is generally pretty quiet except for environmental sound effects - props to the footstep sounds, which actually gave me a spook once or twice. Another interesting note is the presence of a vocalized theme song, which suits the game nicely, and somewhat signifies a change for the series.

STORY:
I have issues with the way the story is presented - the player is rushed into action very quickly, provided with very little to go on for most of the game, and then given a large surge of information at the end. I found myself not knowing much about the characters or why the events were happening, so I found myself not really caring much about the game beyond its mechanics - in short, I was not immersed. When the game did try to do something emotional, or especially frightening, I raised an eyebrow and wondered why I was supposed to care. When it all comes together at the end, it feels like a much to do about nothing, and the primary antagonist is incredibly weak, even cheesy - and not in an intentionally campy way. The story definitely does well with the progrssion of Eathan's character, but he's a little too much of a blank slate for me to feel invested. I think the story could have benefited from some more even pacing towards the mid-section, and some more screen time for the Zoe.

HORROR:
RE7 does some things very well with its horror, and some things not so very well. The game start off very tense, giving the player little in the way of weaponry, thus forcing them to hide or run from enemies - this creates some very tense moments, especially when certain enemies begin to stalk you throughout the area. Unfortunately, this sense of horror virtually disappears once some weaponry is amassed. In RE7, I never was wanting for anything, as previously mentioned.  The crafting system made this even easier, in that I was not just given items, but that I could make what I wanted. This meant that I could stroll through the game with hardly a concern - there were heavy weapons that I didn't even use outside of testing them out for fun on some basic enemies. There are two causes for this - one with an easy fix, and one with a more difficult solution.
1) The first, as I've iterated, is the difficulty. Yes, I unlocked "madhouse" difficulty after completing the game, but I'm a busy guy, and I'm not so sure I want to replay RE7. Another difficulty level from the start, perhaps with an advisory of "for experienced horror players" or something along those lines, would have given me a much more satisfying experience.
2) The second problem is more inherent to first-person shooting - with the precision of fine aiming, the quality of shots varies wildly. In traditional third-person horror, barring a few tricks, one can shoot one of three levels (up, down, or across) and the hits generally register the same way - either you hit or you don't. In short, there's much less variability, and thus fewer ways to waste ammo. The game can then carefully control your ammo supply. Games with fine aiming need to compensate for this, and players who are more skilled will end up landing most of their shots, and thus have huge stockpiles of ammo. I'm not quite sure what the solution to this is, but I wonder if a smaller reliance on firearms is a good remedy, like Condemned: Criminal Origins has.
Otherwise, I found the campy humour, though entertaining, to detract from the horror (a particular one-liner had me thinking of Duke Nukem). Perhaps it's just me, but I can't find myself able to feel afraid if I'm laughing - humour and fear are opposite emotions in my eyes. The enemies get very repetitive as well - RE7 has what is probably the smallest enemy roster in the series, and familiarity with your enemy isn't conducive to fear. Perhaps this says more about my inurement  to horror games at this point, but there were very few times that I felt any tension. 

Overall, this game is very good. With a few tweaks to this style, I think the next entry could end up being a masterpiece of the series.

This is one of the very few survival horror games where I actually found myself put in a fight or flight situation, rather than having it be so polarized, where the game would either feel like an episode out of Road Runner or just straight up Call of Duty. The fact that they included a supernatural aspect to the horror also made it so much more terrifying.

Initially, I felt like the psychostimulants were useless and were made for people who weren't used to the style of RE, where items are hidden in very unexpected locations. However, Capcom made use of things such as lighting and enemy positioning to hide various useful items, forcing me to use the psychostimulants occasionally. 

Also, there was a decent amount of backtracking, and I found myself opening doors that were "Locked from the other side" or required a key item that I didn't have, adding to the complexity of the mansion which I liked. I also liked how you play as the characters in the tapes you view, and how they incorporated the character's knowledge about certain areas that he would use if placed in the same situation, like the Birthday part.

Overall, I think this game represents what the Survival Horror genre is lacking nowadays, to be honest. It's hard to incorporate a sense of fear and dread, while giving the user a choice to fight and not making it feel like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

[b]Now that's how you make a Resident Evil game.[/b] It combines the creepy mansion aspect of RE1 with the unrelenting tension of a monster that keeps coming back to life of RE3, and the good controls of... well... a game that isn't Resident Evil. There's also a decent amount of things that remind you of the eerie unreleased Resident Evil 3.5. If you prefer Resident Evil 4, 5 and 6, you won't like this game. However if you like 1,2 and 3, it might just be for you. Its gameplay is almost identical to the first game with the only difference being the perspective.

Rig:
-Windows 7 Pro 64-bit
-Intel Core-i5 4670K @ 3.9GHz
-Nvidia GeForce GTX 760 (4GB)
-8GB RAM
-AOC G2460F 144Hz @ 1280x720 (Yeah I wanted a better framerate)

The expected:
►Fully rebindable controls
►Field of view can be adjusted. Capped at 90°
►Very few quicktime events, and with sensible controls

The good:
▲Good amount of graphical options to balance performance with visuals
▲Supports high framerates with no problems
▲Separate sensitivity options for looking and aiming
▲Interlaced rendering mode gives massive performance boost with little visual impact
▲Combat, exploration and mechanics are virtually identical to Resident Evil 1...
▲...however it doesn't suffer from RE1's bad controls. So best of both worlds
▲Flow of levels and variety in environments follows the same formula as RE1. Mansion, old house, suddenly something entirely different
▲First person perspective allows secrets to be hidden in any little nook. Players can't just run into bushes mashing the "activate" -button hoping to vacuum in some extra items
▲Good use of immortal enemies that the player must avoid or flee from
▲Very well balanced resource scarcity. You never have an abundance of anything
▲Difficulty setting changes everything, from item placements to enemy encounters and save mechanics
▲Aiming is just difficult enough so you'll have to make every shot count, but not so hard that it could be described as bad controls
▲Nearly all of RE1's weapons return in some form, changed to fit the setting so the more exotic ones aren't out of place
▲The ridiculous puzzles that the series is known for are for the first time justified in the story
▲Story features a new biohazard that manages to actually be interesting despite including some overused tropes
▲Every location is gorgeous and intricately detailed, with extremely realistic-looking materials and beautiful lighting. And I'm not even playing on high settings
▲Exposition via interactive videotapes is an interesting concept that the game uses very effectively
▲Best map system in the series so far
▲Very beefy weapon sounds. Good sound design overall
▲None of those stupid arcade modes like Mercenaries or Raid.
▲Apparently there's going to be a free expansion DLC. Huh.

The bad:
▼Mandatory antialiasing. FXAA is the lowest setting.
▼Enemies have boring visual design
▼Worst "save room" music in the series
▼Can't open doors towards yourself. This results in enemies being able to block doors from the other side
▼Long unskippable cutscenes
▼Relies too much on body horror and repulsive content, expecting players to be disturbed by it
▼Scripted jumpscares
▼Repetitive simple puzzles
▼Resident Evil still doesn't seem to be able to let go of some kind of an economy system where the player must "buy" things with a currency of some kind
▼Explosive-trapped item crates in set locations. You can waste ammo to avoid damage by shooting them instead, or you could just memorize them. If the idea was to force players to spend valuable ammo, the traps should have been randomized
▼Some pretty bad plot holes
▼Absurd binary choice that affects the ending. One of the choices is never justified in any way, even though it very easily could have been
▼Almost feels like some sections of levels rely on the player exploiting enemy spawning and despawning
▼Mechanically terrible end boss fight
▼Some glitches in lipsynching
▼That is NOT a Louisiana accent, Zoe. Nobody on the planet has that accent. Stop it.
▼First game in the series to not feature any of those unrealistically attractive waifus :(

A fantastic return to a more creepy and scary Resident Evil game! 

I'll give some brief pros and cons first and follow up with a more detailed write up so some people can read it quickly and those looking for a more thorough opinion have a reason to read too!

Pros:
[b]+ Scares:[/b] Turn your brightness down, use headphones and play in the dark. Wear adult diapers.
[b]+ Length (for an RE game)[/b]: My first run was 19 hours. A bit of time was spent hiding.
[b]+ Graphics / Performance[/b]: The game looks and runs great on my older system.
[b]+ Audio[/b]: The game has superb audio, some gun sounds are weak though.
[b]+ Immersion[/b]: The graphics + audio combined make a fantastic atmosphere. It's intense.
[b]+ Story[/b]: The story is not perfect, but it's interesting and made me wanting to know more!
[b]+ Controls[/b]: Controls surprisingly well using keyboard and mouse.
[b]+++Saved the series[/b]: This game has put the failing series on a new path in a new direction with scares and fright as the focus. I can't wait for what comes next!+++

[b]Cons:[/b]
[b]- Variety of enemies[/b]: There are simply not that many different enemies in the game.
[b]- Linear game[/b]: Could consider this a positive since it provides a better story and experience, but the game gives you little choice.
[b]- Little weapon variety / no upgrades[/b]: I felt there were too few weapons throughout the game and no customization of weapons.
[b]- No post game modes / lack of Mercenaries[/b]: No Mercenaries or any modes. Where are they, Capcom?! Madhouse is a difficulty, not mode!
    

[b]A more detailed write up:[/b]

I see a lot of people upset about this game simply because it's not Resident Evil 1, 2 or 3, or whatever game they prefer best. If this game was titled anything other than "Resident Evil", I'm sure it would receive even better reviews from those same critical people.

I'm one of the fans who's played Resident Evil since it's original release on PS1. RE 2 and REmake 1 are my favorites in the series.I absolutely love 4, I think 5 was fantastic (though I was worried with the decline into more shootery and *punchy* gameplay) especially when played cooperatively. 6 was 'good' at it's very best, overall  it was decent. This may help you align yourself to my opinions and ideas.

What I love and what I think this game does great is how it gives you a sense of powerlessness at first and then slowly gives you some power to fight back, but then takes that away. I started the game unarmed and afraid. Having played the demo's previously, I knew a bit of the guest house area somewhat intimately so I was expecting things to jump out at me at certain spots, but thankfully they changed it around from the demo so my expectations were being played upon. 

When I obtained my first weapon I received a very strong burst of confidence and I had a level of comfort thinking I could fight back, but I was wrong.  Even when you get gun, most weapons are only good at slowing down the family members who are hunting you, so save your ammo for the other things lurking around the home. By the end of the game, I pulled myself to the end of the game, conserving ammo as much as I could, avoiding enemies when ever possibly. I had a lot of ammo stored up, armed to the teeth expecting the worst, only to fight quite possibly the easiest enemy in the game. Queue the muted trombone.
 
The duration of the game was great for an RE game. It took me around 19.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough on normal, though I was very thorough and spent quite a lot of time hiding and trying to find ways around enemies. My second playthrough on Madhouse took me around 11 hours. FYI: Madhouse changes the placement of items around and could be considered as a different game mode, in a sense. Think Leon A / Claire B vs Claire A / Leon B from RE2.

[b]The guns:[/b] Feel great and powerful; if you line up a headshot you'll do exceptional damage and stagger enemies more often than not. Close range shotgun blasts are as beautiful as ever. For some criticism on the weapons, I felt there weren't enough weapons in the game, the sounds are a bit weak and there's no customization or upgrading which has been a standard in the series since RE2.

[b]All in all[ (TL;DR)[/b] I thought this game was fantastic. I was afraid it was going to be a last ditch effort for the series where it would copy more modern horror games, and while it did take queues from some of the more popular, modern horror games, I think it ended up like nothing we've seen before, and I hope it kickstarts the series back into gear, into a more "survival horror" genre instead of the boulder punching action shooter it had been!

I don't think it's hard to say that Resident Evil 7 is one of the best games in the series. The first few hours of the game were an absolute blast for me. The atmosphere and presentation are excellent, and the gameplay and area/puzzle design are pretty solid too. It also manages to be pretty scary without really abusing jump scares or just being gross. 

By the end my starry-eyed wonder faded a bit, but I think the slightly disappointing ending bits are mostly only very negative in comparison to the perfect beginning bits. Some irritating enemy types are introduced, the later areas are smaller and more linear than the main house, there's a bigger focus on boss fights and shooting and the Bakers start to lose their scary intrigue and become less of the focus. Also I guess for some reason the beginning led me to believe the story would resolve with some unepected revelation or explanation for everything, but it's really pretty standard Resident Evil stuff in the end.

That said, this game's worst parts are a lesser game's best parts, and I didn't reach the end feeling unsatisfied. I think this game came out a bit like a cross between the best "classic" Resident Evill and the best "modern" one, and that is a good direction to take the series in my opinion. Not just a callback, but not simply carrying on the status quo either.

I've just competed Resident Evil 7 on easy mode. It took me 18.8 hours, a length of time that I'm sure many gamers may consider extensive. First, before I begin my review, let me say that I have been a fan of Resident Evil since the first iteration. Also, I should state that, while I enjoy being challenged enough to become emotionally involved, I am not the most talented gamer in the world, and that is fine with me. I tend to play games with a narrative. I prefer to play a game wherein I feel I am a protagonist in a story, and I am usually at least as interested in the story as I am in the gameplay aspects of the experience.
Having said this, Resident Evil VII was the most immersive game I have ever played. Every aspect of this game is brilliant, from the story to the music, to the artistry of the environment and the characters. I love the intemate, almost clostrophobic, cabin-fever inducing combination of the first-person perspective with such enclosed, dilapodated environments. I actually felt afraid! It takes a lot to get an emotional reaction of fear out of me... hesitation about what is around the next corner... tension in response to the unknown... The well-crafted sounds of the environment and of my movements over the floors and his/her breathing, etc., added greatly to this, just as did the visually stunning, artfully crafted environments and immersive story.
In addition to the visual, auditory, and narrative aspects of this game, the pacing was closer to perfect than I have ever experienced in a horror game. I love the shorter length of the game, too, as I feel that it adds to the horror focus of the experience. One problem with many horror games is that they go on for so long that I feel I am losing track of my immersion in the story... This usually arises from there being too many conflicts, objectives, and fights that seem to be simply for the sake of challenging gaming prowess at the expense of the narrative and the immersion therein. For this reason, the relatively shorter format of Resident Evil VII is a move in the right direction. Quality vs. empty quantity.
Finally, in re the Resident Evil series and RE VII's place amongst them, RE VII brings the Resident Evil series back to the intions and ambience of the first few games. When Resident Evil began, the overarching intent was to immerse players in a horror environment... elliciting fear was the main goal, not challenging battles with monsters, as the 4th, 5th, and 6th iterations drifted to in focus. Resident Evil VII is a return to Resident Evil's roots, using current game design technology to achieve that goal, and yes, first-person perspective is a part of this goal as well.
I applaud everyone who worked so artfully, mindfully, and creatively, to bring such a wonderfully unnerving, utterly immersive experience to us in the gamming community. Thank you, Resident Evil VII team, for this wonderful return to the essence of what Resident Evil is meant to be.
If there were one dischordant thing I could say, as a recommendation for the next game by this wonderful team, I would suggest doing away with the over-the-top monster bosses encountered as the 2nd and final "boss" encounters, and replacing them with character-centered bosses more similar to Jack in the garage scene... These were the two moments in the game wherein I fell out of immersion in the story and felt I was, again, back in the usual "fight some bosses for the sake of gaming-prowess-testing tradition"... remove moements like these, and you could be approaching the perfect, horror survival game.
...as a side note, I LOVE the introductory sequence that plays whenever the game starts. This is the first game, wherein I enjoyed the introductory sequence (animation and music) so much that I never once skipped through it in restless haste to begin playing the game...

Resident Evil games have never been that good. The idea behind them was kinda cool but the games themselves are often only held up high due to nostalgia. I loved Resident Evil 1 and 2 as a kid growing up but even then I found Resi 1 very clunky and never completed it and often found more time for Resi Evil 2 as it felt like the better game with plenty to do. At the time they were special as it was mature (ish) content and blowing the heads off zombies wasn't common at all. Zombies at this time were barely utilised in the media...

The main attraction then was shooting zombies and getting scared. The puzzles were OK but for most people it was the exploring and discovering that kept us all going. As much as killing zombies was cool you never had enough ammo to waste and aiming was no easy task. BUT...we all remember the days we spent playing Resi Evil...it made an impact.

Now we have Resident Evil 7 and although it "looks" new it still suffers from the same issues that previous games in the series have fallen victim to. The game play is focused on picking up items and finding where to put them. 

The action is sparse and can be like taking part in a lottery in most encounters. Facing up to a "small" enemy means trying to hit a head that is constantly wobbling all over the place! Sometimes it's two shots for a headshot and then others it might be 3 shots! Boss fights suck as they give the boss unfair advantages to make it scary and stressful instead of designing a better interaction. Putting you in a small room with a dude that can walk like grease lightning isn't fun or fair. Stressing out the player with unfair buffs to the boss is pretty cheap in my book. And then there's flying enemies...still just as rubbish as it was in previous Resi Evil games...trying to hit flying enemies is no fun at all with them flapping about all over the place whilst you swing your knife about like an idiot!

Puzzles are straight forward with only a single solution. You are "pushed" down a narrow, linear path where there is only ever one way forward. 

A huge amount of the environment is covered in darkness but the developers gave you a torch without the ability to actually use it whenever you want!?!?! The torch only comes on when they want it on...this really annoys me!! Dark games require torches...why?? Because if you don't then you are expecting your players to go in and out of the menu's changing the brightness setting which is absolute BS!! Let us turn on the torch!! What harm can it really do???

I hate to say it but once you've played through this game once there is almost no reason to go back and play it. It is the best walking simulator out there as it has stuff to do but this is no video game...it's an experience that can only really be enjoyed once! Going back and playing again only highlights this downfall as everything feels familiar and...pointless...once you know where the scripted events are.

And that's all this game has to offer...a once in a lifetime chance to experience being chased by the Dad, mum and brother. However, this mechanic was just lifted from Alien Isolation which does it so much better and is a better game overall in almost every single way!! 

If you feel the need to "experience" this game then go ahead but just don't expect a video game. You will play this once and then move on. It constantly holds your hand, it has very little to discover and it can be very immature at times.

Would have been cool to have a classic Resi Evil game with zombies in a huge house to explore. You could have barricading mechanics to stop them coming in through doors. Multiple ways in and out of rooms and the ability to make climbing tools like bed sheets tied together and use them to climb out of windows. With graphics and sound this good you really don't need much more...I feel Resi Evil 7 really is nothing more than a shell of a game. There is so little to it...the majority of what you look at are static props and NONE of the gameplay is original. Even one of the early puzzles is ripped straight from the first Resident Evil!!

5/10 - Looks great and sounds nice but the game, which is why we're all here, is almost non-existent. If only we had PT (Silent Hills) to enjoy we'd realise that games like this can be made well with interesting game mechanics. BUT, as we only have Resi Evil 7 then all we have is the same ol' ♥♥♥♥ tarted up in a nice dress...basic puzzles, basic combat...SEEN IT ALL BEFORE!!! 
P.S. Massive respect to the sound design team though...

[h1]A superb recovery for RESIDENT EVIL[/h1]

Wow, really wow CAPCOM, this is how you do RESIDENT EVIL, this is what RESIDENT EVIL looks more like, you don't need action (though this game does have a little bit, but it's extremely minor), you don't need over the top scenes of action. No this is what you do to make a RESIDENT EVIL game, a survival horror game, where you feel contained, you feel weak but gain strength over time, you feel like the enemies you're fighting are actually a force to be reckoned with, this game is near perfect, and is the right direction for the series.

The gameplay is superb, it is smooth and feels real, the gunplay is really well done, the guns feel smooth, everything is right about it, nothing feels weak, and nothing feels too overpowered for what it is, the pistols are somewhat powerful, but have little ammo and don't shoot automatically, the shotguns feel powerful but are extremely limited on ammo, and you'll find yourself to use it little unless you are in a big situation. The machine guns are late game, but shoot fast and have loads of bullets in a magazine, but the damage is the lowest. No guns need to be overpowered or underpowered and this game shows it perfectly. The controls are smooth though just a warning the crouch button is "C" and to quick heal is "Ctrl", I had on many occasions accidently quick healed instead of crouch, but this is more of a own issue than the games, they are also remappable though, so as said it's only a personal issue for never changing the controls.

The graphics are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing, CAPCOM using a graphic style of photogrammetric was perfect, it really brings the fear to life, it makes you feel more uneasy as everything looks more real around you, you pick into the littlest details making sure everything is right later game, and listen out for audio and shadows for the new enemy type "molded", this enemy type feels scary but a bit lacking compared to actual zombies, but the story to them makes sense.
And the audio in the game is near perfect, and it had to be, this game needed superb audio, and CAPCOM damn right made the audio near perfect, the atmosphere from the audio is superb and realistic and adds to the tension.

The story in the game sounds simple, after 3 years you recieve an email from your missing wife called "Mia Winters", she tells you to go save her, the protagonist - Ethan Winters - goes to the house, and then the game starts, that sounds innocent well, the game is by far not normal, you meet the Bakers family and well it just goes downhill from there for Ethan. I can't say much for the story without spoiling it because the one thing that is negative for the game, is that it's too short, the game can be done in about 6-10 hours, and really the story is so contained it keeps a flow and from that you can't really go into details about the game without spoiling it. But those 6-10 hours are really really great, and the game does luckily have a good level of replayability to the level of other games like this, such as Outlast.

Sadly outside of the story there's nothing, seriously it's just the game's story, no horde mode just like RESIDENT EVIL 5/6/Revelations 1and2, and though it does make sense due to it's nature, it would've been nice to have a extra mode. There are modes that act as minigames in the DLC... it's a DLC thing, and it's not really great that you have to pay for those.


TL;DR

+ Amazing story
+ Really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tense, thanks to the atmosphere and well placed jumpscares
+ The Bakers' Family
+ Smooth Gameplay
+ Great Audio
+ Brilliant Graphics

= Short story, but replayable.

- Nothing outside of the story

Overall a 9/10.

As a person who has barely played Resident Evil before and who is completely immune to horror, this is my basic view of the game. [spoiler] I have only finished by saving Mia. [/spoiler]

I focus more on the negetives of games. That doesn't mean the game is bad, just that it isn't perfect.

Positives:
 - Great graphics
 - You can view extra story parts through VCR tapes (In the main campaign, not just the banned footage).
 - Boss fights had variety, and were quite fun. Unfortunately they did sometimes just feel like a way to get rid of your ammo though.
 - Characters were interesting, and had depth.
 - Well optimised, with no lag spikes. I did have one or two freezes but that can be attributed to my dying hardware.

Negetives:
 - Weapon scroll can be a bit sticky, and it's led to me wasting ammo on crates by accident.
 - Gameplay consistency (There's a single point where you make a choice, when there are several points beforehhand I would've chosen differently compared to what the protagonist chose. Hell, I would've actually preferred no choices at all and a longer game.)
 - Quite short (my normal difficulty playthrough while also exploring was 8 1/2 hours long).
 - No ability to lean around corners (when you want to stealth through an area or check for enemies).
 - Story was predictable after the game actually bothers to tell you anything at all

Overall, I would describe this game as the first Resident Evil and Alien: Isolation trying to emulate PT (at least for the mansion bit). This game was enjoyable to the point that I am considering buying the DLC and replaying for the achievements. If you are interested in survival horror games and like Resident Evil, then I recommend this game. If you're looking for just a survival horror game, then get Alien: Isolation, then this if you want more content (because A:I is cheaper, longer and has a better story).

I'm a horror game enthusiast that grew up playing classic Resident Evil more than any other games and they remain my favourites to this day.  After being told Resident Evil would be going back to its roots as part of the marketing for RE6, Revelations, and Revelations 2, I had literally no expectations for this game on that front.  But my dear friends bought it for me as a gift, and I played it.  From that perspective, let's review it.

My overall impression was that I thought it was excellent but that it didn't feel like Resident Evil.  I hadn't expected a first-person game to feel like Resident Evil, so I wasn't disappointed.  I was just glad it was good.


Gameplay:
The gameplay mechanics are intentionally sluggish.  I'm personally biased against first-person games because I never feel as in tune with my character ironically (I feel third-person compensates visually for the other senses and perceptions that physically being somewhere would yield for you).  Other people may not have this problem but sometimes the sluggishness felt off and I didn't know exactly where I was in relation to some other nearby object, or my timing was off as a result of a sluggish animation.  Again, could just be me and my first-person problem (FPP).

None the less, the sluggishness is usually a really good thing and feels just right.  And the enemies seem designed well to move in ways that complement the sluggishness of the player character.

The game is primarily designed with atmosphere in mind and it's fantastic atmosphere.  The enemies are in my opinion not always great, but for once they're not exactly the focus.  The atmosphere is.  And the enemies frequently synergise well with that atmosphere.

The main antagonists of the game were interesting.  They were extremely well acted and there was a lot of diversity from one to the next.  They were often derivative of modern horror films and that sort of annoyed me at times, but at least I can say I don't really think I've seen it done in games before, not like this at least.

A great thing about this game is that your actions are often capable of driving the situation in an utterly different direction, depending on how quickly you work sometihing out or if you choose something totally different to what would be the obvious choice.  There are glaring exceptions to this here and there, but overall it's impressive how well developed the various scenarios sometimes are, and their quantity.

I enjoyed the save rooms.  I didn't enjoy having infinite saves but I did like that I had to be in a specific location and save my game manually (with some exceptions for surprise boss fights and the like).  On Madhouse difficulty, it appears this is rectified.  Brilliant.  In my opinion, limited saves are crucial for good horror.  Perma-death is usually a bit too much I think, but if saves are limited in a well balanced way you can hit the sweet spot between the torture of perma-death and the hedonism of auto-saves every time you enter a new room.

All the boss fights were well done I think.  Rarely frustrating but rarely very challenging, and each one was highly individual and unique.

On the one hand, I'm impressed that there's not only loads of DLC but that one of them is free, and on the other hand, I'm essentially against DLC in general.  I miss the good old days when everything was unlockable and on the disc you'd purchased, and it was there as soon as it was released.  But no-one forced them to make one of them free, whether or not we need to wait a while, so that's nice.


Story:
The story is compelling.  It's not high art but it does make you want to go on.  The acting is great and the writing is great.  A lot of stuff is left unexplained but there's reason to expect most of it will be handled by the DLC.

My biggest complaint is a minor spoiler, so I won't reveal it here.  Fortunately, by the end of the game things change and my fears are unfounded, but I feel that overall the design came first and the story used a sort of afterthought to make an excuse for the design, and I feel that the baggage of being a Resident Evil title conflicted with their ideal design in this respect, which was the cause of the awkward situating of a few of the relevant plot points.

My other biggest complaint is that the game's story punishes you to some degree if you're a critical thinker or if youdon't agree with their simplistic view of the situation they've presented.  I'm avoiding spoilers so that's essentially what you're getting here.

Actually, following from that, I can complain that the characterisation in general was pretty poor.  The villains were done well enough but anyone that isn't trying to kill you is just such a barely explored character.


Audio:
I was thoroughly impressed with everything in this regard.  Great voices, great music, great spatialisation, and great detail afforded to the sound effects.  The music was refreshingly traditional overall.  The footsteps were just slightly overdone in my opinion, as there were too many instances when I heard my own footsteps but was barely moving and I thought it must be another entity.  Even so, the footstep sounds were still well done, despite being unrealistically loud at times.


Graphics:
The graphics are middling.  I've heard great praise but I just don't see it.  I think the lighting was rather nice, but the textures just don't appear to be as well done as my PC's workload would imply.  A lot of jagged edges and swimming texture artefacts.  The trouble is diminished on high-end GPUs for sure, but I've seen these problems remain on YouTube videos made specifically to showcase specific higher-end GPUs' optimal settings for this game.

After a good deal of tinkering I did get the game running extremely fluidly without looking poor on my GTX 750 Ti.


Length:
If this is important to you, the main game was about sixteen hours for me, and I like to look around a lot.  Madhouse difficulty is from what I hear worth playing.  It's said to change the game considerably.


As a Resident Evil game:
I like the game very much but I don't see this one.  A lot of great homages are present but you could say that about Last of Us or Evil Within.  This game reminds me far more of Outlast but I personally found Outlast scarier.  By miles.  In fact, I didn't find this game scary at-all.  I've read that Madhouse difficulty is more frightening, so I'm willing to have a go with that.

I do see that there's a bit of resource management, that there are some great keys and doors, and that the franchise is horror for the first time in ages.  But I find the gameplay mechanics entirely antithetical to the classic games, the inventory space not limited enough, saves not limited enough, the characters and story not similar enough to the calssics, the enemies not similar enough to the classics, and the atmosphere quite different to that of the classics.

The atmosphere in this game is more about showing you things you wouldn't want to see, whereas the classic games were about juxtaposing abandoned opulence with a sense of threat and the occasional evidence of death.  It was more about mystery than making your skin crawl.

Another point is that the story is finally successful as an American story, and the game no longer seems as Japanese as its predecessors.  They finally got everything right.  I personally miss that Japanese signature but I imagine a lot of people prefer this.  It's certainly easier to take it seriously (besides a couple of really ridiculous points I won't spoil).  The acting and dialogue are very well done.


Overall:
To evaluate this game without expecting any Resident Evil qualities, I'd say it's really a great game.  But I'm not sure it's worth its asking price.  I'd probably give it a 7 out of 10.

Having played Resident Evil 4 and enjoyed that game, I decided to buy the newest installment in the Resident Evil series even though I'm not a hardcore fan of the series.

The game takes place in Louisiana, USA, and the atmosphere is creepy and bleak. If you've seen some American horror movies, you can notice the references to them throughout, particularly The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (1974). The American references are mixed with Japanese elements, as the game's developed by Capcom. I loved the return of one of the monsters from RE 4. RE 7 often relies on jump-scares throughout, but also creates tension through the use of foreboding music and disturbing surroundings. There were several sections in the game when I was stressed and entertained, but the scariness wanes a bit halfway through.

Personally it took a couple of hours for me to get used to the feel of the game, particularly how to use the environment in the boss battles, and how to stay alive without much firepower at hand. The game's also hard, even on normal difficulty, and I felt that having to repeat some sections and boss-battles repeatedly was tedious. However, many boss fights later in the game are enjoyable and challenging. 

RE 7 is the first Resident Evil game in first-person. Even though the gun-handling and inventory system is great, the player movement is frustratingly slow. Yes, it's meant to be that way, creating more tension, but it doesn't feel realistic. No-one in real life standing face to face with a monster would run as slow as the protagonist. I can usually handle logical inconsistencies in games and movies, but it's not hard to notice several of them in RE 7.

I would've appreciated a more black-humoured feel to the game (like the SAW-like puzzle sequence), as it gets pretty depressing and brutal at times, but overall Resident Evil 7 is a great horror game with a memorable story. Finished it in 10 hours.

Play this game with the right brightness setting, the atmosphere is really important; and with the right brightness settings it will scare the life out of you. The horror aspect of this game is incredible; 9/10. The story line is solid, and although I have not played previous resident evil titles, I did feel like the game tried to make a connection to them at the end. At least there was a hint to the first Resident Evil movie.

The gameplay mechanics are well thought out except for the heal animation (I wish there were more animations then just pouring down antiseptic liquid with cellular regenration promotion properties on your hand). Ammo conservation is required to some extent. The inventory managment system is good and easy to get a grip on even during fights. I see that a lot of people are complaining about Ethans running speed. The fact of the matter is that its quite close to realistic. We as gamers have gotten accustomed to fast walk and run speeds which makes us feel like this one is slow. But given the distance covered per unit time in terms of visuals (a hallway, a yard, a room) the run speed can only said to be as slightly slower than real life. Which I approve of anyways since the game intends to give you a feeling of helplessness.

Finally the graphics. The good thing going on here is that the textures are really good. The lighting is exceptional and so are the shadows. However, the game does suffer from some optimization issues as far as shadows are concerned. I personally have a GTX 980 Matrix from Asus and I can max out everything at 1080p except shadows. Shadows at only high give me +60 fps. Very high shadows start to give me frequent and random fps drops. Hopefully this will be fixed in any patches they release.

Finally the worst aspect of the game that I encountered is (some, not all mind you) AI characteristics. AI seems to be fairly smart during combat and does present a challenge. However, there are times when they are supposed to be looking for you and your job is to complete your objective and (optimally) not run into them while doing so to avoid greivances. Their field of vision is unrealistically narrow and they seem to be deaf to the sounds you make completely. Although fixing this issue to the realistic point would make the game massivley difficult, some improvment could be used here (i.e. slightly improved periphal vision plus some radius in which they investigate sound disturbances).

Summary:

Unlike a lot of games released this year and late last year, the developers have taken their time to produce an excellent game albeit some fixing required which is not something that should degrade the game. Hopefully the issues I mentioned above will be fixed soon. There is some replayability factor. Once you end the game and start it again, some item locations seem to be changed which is good because it discourages walk through consultation.

Resident Evil goes back to it's roots.

As a longtime Resident Evil fan, I was dissapointed by where the franchise started to go when Resident Evil 4 was released. Although a good game in its own right, the only thing that it shared with the original RE was it's name. The franchise switched from survival horror to full on shoot-em-up.

Resident Evil 7 brings the series back to its survival horror roots. You can no longer buy ammunition but instead have to pick and choose your battles. The decision to make this a first person game is excellent and the fact that you are and were so vulnerable increases the fear factor. This is the most disturbing game I've ever played. I've never played a game where the characters make such brutally vulgar threats towards you while you run away in panic: it scares the ♥♥♥♥ out of you. 

The graphics are extremely well done. I often took time just to look at the small details in the scenery. The shower curtain with drops of water on it, how the light shines off of concrete bricks in a basement - it's extremely well done and runs well.  The real winner here is the sound. Every ambient creak and crack made my hair stand up as it made me expect another monster ambush. 

The only downside is it is *relatively* short. Capcom plans to release a free DLC as Chris Redfield so hopefully that will add to the replay value. I look forward to the next installment of this game and hope the series stays with this format.

-----------------------
The first thing I have to say is this game was not what I expected but I had to high of expectations for it anyway. I have played the original RE to RE Revelations 2, and I can say this is a great return to the RE series with a new engine and a new view on the world! The gameplay is good, nothing special your average shooter. Brings back the classic weapons such as the shotgun, grenade launcher, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ knife, and a classic weapon that you all will love. There are not a lot of enemies to fight against, only because you're in a farmhouse, but the interactions with the Baker family are nothing less than scary. The story starts out strong and works its way up to a disappointing ending with a choice that makes no difference at all, the voice acting is great (No Troy Baker, and Nolan North). The story does not tie in with the canon until the end and there will be a free DLC coming in spring to really tie in the RE universe. The Port of this game is very well done, really good FPS with a GTX 970 and a AMD FX-8320 above 100+ fps most of the time. No widescreen support or FPS slider to have a noticeable difference, something with the engine I guess. The DLC I can say is not worth $30.00, the most time you will get out of both VOL 1 and 2 is about 1 1/2-2 hours of gameplay they are very short, well done, but short and is not worth the full $30.00 price tag it holds.

Fantastic game, well worth the price and easily one of the (if not the) best horror/survival games I've played.

Gamplay: 9/10.
Well paced, with great boss fights that are a challenge wihtout being cheap. I died a handful of times, but was able to learn from my mistakes and make steady progress each time. Health/ammo/item placement is spaced out enough to make the first 2/3 of the game tense and require careful use without being impossible, although this changes quite a lot in the last 1-2 hours, where ammo and medical supplies start raining from the sky. Most of the game had me sneaking around at a crouch jumping at shadows and unexpected noises. Think Alien: Isolation but replace the alien with a deep south hillbilly axe murderer. The level of atmosphere and that genuine feeling of survival is just superbly done. The only two complaints that I could level at this game is that a handful of times walking past a certain point obviously triggered the game to spawn a Molded directly behind me, which came over as a bit of a tacky 'monster closet' moment, even if it only happened 2-3 times in the entire game, and that the hit detection for the giant fat guy things vomit attack had a bad habit of hitting me through solid objects and stunlocking me. Overall though these are *very* minor complaints and I felt like the game was a masterpiece from start to finish.

Graphics and performance: 10/10.
None of the issues that so many releases have these days with consolitis making it's way into PC versions. Full graphical options, full mouse/keyboard and controller support, and it ran flawlessly at 2560*1440 on my GTX970 with most settings on high. Not a single crash or bug in my entire playthrough. Graphically this is also one of the best looking games I've seen, rivalling the likes of Doom for level of detail and effects. The attention to detail in small things like foliage and the surrounding environment give parts of the game a borderline photo realistic look.

Take the best parts of the franchise over the years, ie good and engaging horror/survival with a belieavable setting and remove the worst parts, ie retarded tank controls and horrible over the shoulder camera angles, stupid corny 3rd action gameplay, and you have this. Exceptional all round. Buy it.

Claustrophobic hallways, limited view (albeit first person); we're stuck in a mansion again, plenty of puzzles, special keys to find and go back through to find matching doors. Resident Evil 7 is as good as a horror game can get. From splatter to gore to psychological horror and the very Asian ending - some chapters may be more fun than others but ultimately it all comes together to a satisfying whole. There are two aspects that remain stuck in memory long after playing: family and plot.

The Bakers initially so unpredictable and repulsive sooner than later become somewhat comprehensible human beings. Especially in the end the player empathises with the abused and corrupted family, Lucas being the exception. The depiction of the three antagonists of the first two-thirds of the game seems surprisingly authentic presenting compelling characters. They are the ones providing comic relief in the most tight situations.

The story, first only hinted at through scattered statements by the family, gains in importance during the last third of the game. Right as the horror of the splatterfest wanes the game makes a turn unfolding what's the cause of all this mess. Gathering information and discovering all the bits and pieces that lead to where the player is now is enlightening but also results in an unsatisfying ending as it doesn't offer closure.

Regarding gameplay, the player is put in the shoes of an impotent protagonist. The slow and ponderous movements require high frustration tolerance at the beginning. Most of the time though the excellent level design paired with the indulgent enemy AI provide just enough space for navigation. Overcoming the initial hindrances and eventually beating the boss fights have an incredibly cathartic effect.

There are instances where the levels connect, the enemies make sense or you find items in impossible places. Needless to say those moments are pleasant to experience and top off the overall quality of Resident Evil 7.

There's no reason not to play it.
