[h1] Resident Evil 7 - A Retro Delight [/h1]

Let me start off by saying, if you are a fan of the original Resident Evil games, then Resident Evil 7 is an absolute must-play. The game is a true throwback to the classic survival horror genre that started it all. The camera style has changed, but let me assure you, it doesn't detract from the feel of the game. If anything, it adds to the tension and suspense that we all love.

[h1] Graphics [/h1]

Now, let's talk about the graphics. They are simply breathtaking. The level of detail that has gone into every corner of the game is remarkable. The closed environment of the game has allowed the developers to focus on making everything look so dirty and grimy, which is incredibly realistic. From the shadows that are cast across the rooms to the clutter that fills every space, no room feels empty. And let's not forget the lighting! It's just amazing. I wish I had HDR, but even without it, the game looks stunning.

[h1] Story [/h1]

The story of Resident Evil 7 is top-notch. Your wife goes missing, and years later, you receive an email from her stating that she is in Louisiana. This leads you to investigate the Baker family residence, where your journey begins. The script is undoubtedly the best ever written for a Resident Evil game, and I believe they could make an incredible movie out of this game. The voice acting is phenomenal, and the Baker family is some of the most convincing voice acting I have ever seen or heard in a game.

[h1] Game play [/h1]

If you're looking for an OG Resident Evil experience, then Resident Evil 7 is the game for you. The gameplay is much slower-paced than the newer games, and it consists of a mix of puzzles and encounters with the Baker family, with a healthy amount of monsters sprinkled in-between. You can play the game at your own pace, taking your time to explore each room and appreciate the effort that has gone into creating the house.

Herbs, ammo, maps, and cassette recorders for saving the game are all here, just as you would expect in a classic Resident Evil game. The experience of being stalked by the Baker family is very familiar to being stalked by Nemesis in Resident Evil 3. And let's not forget the classic Resident Evil lines, such as "JOOOSEPH" and "That was too close! You were almost a Jill sandwich!"

[h1] Final Words [/h1]

In conclusion, if you're a long-time fan of Resident Evil, then Resident Evil 7 is a must-play. I had high expectations for this game, and I can confidently say that I was not let down. The franchise has been resurrected with this game, and it's a beautiful thing to see. As far as I'm concerned, the original Resident Evil has been brought back to life. And let's not forget the iconic line, "Victims were apparently... eaten." I still can't get enough of this game, even after six months.

A wonderful return to its survival horror roots, a little on the short side if you know what to do, but if you take your time and explore on your first play-through the experience could last around 8 hours.  It also has some replay value, with Madhouse mode, and the DLC that's been coming out.
This is the best Resident Evil game since Resident Evil 4.

Of all the developers, I never expected Capcom to actually listen to their fans. RE7 takes the franchise to its roots with an original twist. There are so many things here that scream with Resident Evil nostalgia. I haven't finished the game yet, but every minute I've played it (I dare to say) it almost feels like playing the first three games including Zero. 

Bravo, Capcom! After two very weak releases continuing RE4, plus the horribly un optimized RE HD, I had given up on one of my favorite franchises. But I decided to try the demo and that just won me back. Been playing the full game, and I can feel the oldschool passion once again. It's almost like what Doom 2016 did.

Technical wise, the game is very good as well. Maxed out. System played on:

i5 6600k @4.2ghz
GTX 1070
20GB ram
Asus 144hz 1ms gaming monitor

Graphics are not the best out there even maxed out, but it has its own unique atmosphere to it. Nonetheless it is a very good looking game. Very smooth textures and character designs. Breathtaking light effects. Some shadows do have a very grainy filter applied that was not present in the demo. It is not very pleasing.

Sound is a bit muffled, but it is a trend RE has shown since RE4. Most of the classic sound effects are there which is a real treat for die-hard fans. Music and ambience sounds will make you look behind you at all times.

Controls are responsive. Very well optimized for keyboard and mouse, even though you can tell it was made for controller at times.

Overal gameplay is not as extreme as it seems in the demo, or at the beginning. The game does slow down a lot and other than a couple of monsters in a basement, some of your classic mutated insects and some invulnerable enemy stalking you constantly a la Nemesis or Mr. X, the game doesn't feel that clustrophobic, unpredictable or extremely scary. Which is fine, because it makes you enjoy it a bit better rather than becoming a nerve-wrecking chore. Classic puzzles are back, classic map and backtracking are back, safe rooms with trunks are back. Overall, you find yourself playing a genuine RE that ballances a bit of suspense-horror, a very few jumpscares, uncertainty when you walk into a new area, but at end you feel you are in control at all times.

Best RE in decades. I hope RE8 is bigger, brings classic characters, but at the same time keeps the same engine and gameplay formula than this game.

I'm a long time fan of the Resident Evil series, and I'll say first and foremost that I was not one of the people looking forward to this "new direction" for the series. I'm not particularly fond of First Person Horror games, and I disliked the Texas Chainsaw Massacre vibe (I still don't really like it after finishing the game twice). That being said, I think this is the best Resident Evil game since Resident Evil 4. 

So, I'll say a few thinkg about what I liked and disliked.

First off, the new engine delivers some great graphics. Especially where the skin textures are concerned, this is one of the better looking games on the market. However, you should be wary of playing this game on lower end systems. The VRAM requirements are pretty insane, going over 10GB's frequently. I play it currently on a system with an EVGA GTX 950 (which is a very good low-mid range card) with 2GB's of VRAM, an Intel i3 6100, and 16GB's of DDR4 RAM and get decent framerates for the majorty of the time (60-90fps) but experience very frequent stutter. With some settings tweaked, it's playable, but still stutters quite a bit. 

Other than this though, the game looks and plays great. The shooting/combat mechanics get the job done and done well, but could have been improved in my opinion. They're a little stiff, but that could have also been a bit of a design decision. Also, I really hope Capcom or whoever decides to keep the healing system they came up with. The animations for wounds healing right in front of you is pretty awesome, and I hope they expand on it with different types of injuries and their subsequent healing animations.

This game is violent. Very much so, which I appreciate. I won't spoil, but some of the early game injuries are pretty shocking your first time through. The level designs are very good, with a lot of meaningful backtracking, puzzles, and environmental storytelling. The Baker Estate was a surprisingly good area to play through and explore.

And, since I brought it up; Let's get on the topic of the story:

I thought this game had a very interesting story, (even though the main concept is almost straight ripped from Silent Hill 2) with some VERY interesting characters... except the main character. I found Ethan Winter likeable enough, but a lot of what he says and does (plus his reactions to things going on) do not fit well with the tone of the story they're trying to tell. It doesn't make much sense for Ethan to keep on trucking through all this crazy s*** just to find his wife. That being said, the game gives you just enough threads of story to keep you interested and invested until you hit about halfway to three quarters of the way through. Especially with the very last few hours (let's say 2), the narrative just kinda drops off and everything falls into place a little too neatly. There are two "endings" triggered by a choice you make close to the end, but really there's not much of a difference between the two and the obvious choice is the one that you're better off going with. The ending left me intrigued, as it has some very interesting implications for long time fans who have followed the story like I have. 

The only other real complaint I have is that the game is a bit on the short side, taking about 6-9 hours during a normal playthrough.

I want to see where they're taking the series, and hope to see the old characters make their returns.

I honestly had low expectations for this game. The demo didn't really win me over as I hope it would and it also did not feel like a resi title to me. I have always wanted resident evil to be a first person shooter. Always thought it would be more creepier if horror is right in your face. in the end, the final game surprised me. It took elements from games and movies such as FEAR, Silent Hill, the Texas chainsaw massacre (original), SAW movies and obviously the very first Resident Evil game. 

As we remember the original resi title; you are in a house full of monsters with tide corridors, limited amount to carry stuff, back tracking, puzzles, healing plants, limited ammo and manual savings. Only instead of typewriters we use cassette recorders. At least for them you don't have to find tapes. 
You play as Ethan, some ordinary guy, who got a message from his wife, Mia, who was believed to be dead. As in Silent Hill; our hero goes to the location she has send the message from. Only to be sucked in by the Texas chainsaw...I mean Baker family, who will hunt you down. You have the "beat up first, talk later" father, an insect control freak mother and the son who is a younger version of Jigsaw. 

The monster you occasionally encounter look like oil covered version of Ooze from Resident Evil Revelations 1. They move exactly like them. Then you have a much fatter version of them who easily remind you of the Boomer from Left 4 Dead. Because they vomit on you. And obviously the family who are boss battles when the time comes. Otherwise they just hunt you, were escaping is wiser than wasting ammo on them. 

The locations are a house, swamps and a derelict ship. A lot them are dark and at times creepy and do not give you much room to maneuver. Exploration is still required to find the right items and the much needed ammo.

What I disliked was that you never see the protagonists face. Also the small variety of enemies and how slowly Ethan does things. From reloading to running.  
What I did like were the tide and narrow corridors, sometimes the graphic can look photo realistic, only few enemies, the aim for atmosphere instead of pure action and that you can play as Mia. 

So overall, it was a good game. It still does not completely feel like a RE title to me, but that is just me, but the direction they have taken is very good and I hope in future, they stick to it.

But for me RE7 did a Condemned 2; started off as a 10/10 game, 180'd on its strongest elements and took a disappointing dive in quality until coming to an awkward and seemingly rushed ending that goes beyond unsatisfying.  

The first 30 minutes of Resident Evil 7 are extremely promising. Opening strong with the abandoned house from the demo (this time with some context) the game goes heavy on the psychological elements which I really liked. It was all pretty visceral and immersive, reminicent of Outlast, up until the end of the first scripted fight. After a brutal setup and first confontation the game abandons its realism; adopting a 'voice in the sky' character and an uncessesary HP meter with no sensible explanation or setup. While I did enjoy the "house" the most comparatively, it quickly became one blatantly easy and often nonsensical puzzle after another. Solutions were always right next to the puzzle or flat out explained via VHS tapes. With really only 2 distinct enemies, the occasional, easily avoided, roaming 'boss' character and with very few player inputs in general, the game is largely a walking simulator following along a linear path, you aquire items, then use them immediately to proceed. 

Visually the game is great, animations look good, flesh is particularly realistic and the atmosphere is consistent and there's a lot of nice, putrid little details which I expect will be extra tasty in VR (Not that I cant play it on my Vive thanks to Sony's awesome exclusive deal). However, while mostly the game's visuals are gritty and realistic there are numerous assets (almost always puzzle related) that looked glaringly out of place. While it wouldn't bother most players and could even be considered a convention of the Resident Evil series it still came across as poor design to include so many outright ridiculous looking puzzles and mechanisms. In an otherwise creepy and immersive world I often wondered why the ♥♥♥♥ thing's couldn't have just been simpler, to add to the atmosphere instead of pulling me out of it. 

Gameplay wise RE7 is as basic as you can get; you only have to walk, shoot and press F when the game  tells you to. You always have a map of the entire area, everything loops around, and there's a large abundance of safe 'save' rooms. While I've only completed the game on normal, I never felt particularly vulnerable after the first 30 minutes or so as the game is extremely generous with supplies and weapons and while inventory management is initally frustrating (you can't just use or swap out an item, even when its required to win a boss fight for example, unless you have space) it becomes entirely arbitrary later on. Why the game abandons stealth horror completely in favor of action but keeps a few diluted survival horror elements still confuses me, as they're more annoying than challenging and add very little to the experience.

Boss wise it again starts of strong, you get to know and get tormented by a family of characters and each has a particular flavor when it comes to fighting them. Boss 'zones' are nicely themed and the 'father' character, who brutally stalks you throughout the early stages of the house, has a great setup and a series of fights creating a high expectation for the rest of the game. Unfortunately this too is abandoned as subsequent fights follow in the footsteps of previous Resident Evil games; large enemies and very little player input, glowing weak spots and scripted events, these disappointing encounters pave the way for a terrible and short final third of the game and a climax that is essentially a quick time event followed by some fan service. 

Resident Evil 7 shows so many glimpses of a game that could have been an absolute horror classic. While its infinitely better than the steaming ♥♥♥♥ pile that was Resident Evil 6, it makes some dumb design choices and comes across as lazy after such a strong opening. You'll probably love at least 1/3 of this game, which is more than can be said for most.

Mixed feelings on RE7- the game tries very hard to be a reboot of the franchise which is a good and bad thing. It's probably better to list the pros and cons about the game and try explain my feelings towards it.

Positive: 
- Survival horror returns in a new way via first person with limited means of surviving including limited weapons, ammo, healing items and inventory management (ESPECIALLY in the first few hours of the game) 
- Atmosphere is well executed bringing back the horror element through dark claustrophobic environments, disturbing lethal enemies and a psychologically twisted plot
- Gameplay is pretty intense for most of the game as you struggle to fight, run and survive against the terrors found around the baker home which is huge and reminiscent of the classic mansion in RE1/REmake while at the same time being vastly different due to its country setting/style
- Well designed puzzles mentally challenge you and are a good comeback to the series 
- The story and characters are pretty interesting and as you find out what happens as you progress you'll become more intrigued reading files of the victums, history, circumstances e.t.c
- There are a few nods to the storyline of previous resident evil games (mainly 1,2 & 3) and some classic RE meme-style references e.g "master of unlocking" 

Negative:
- It doesn't feel like a Resident Evil game, which is ironic considering the series identity issues since RE4 but what makes this even more apparent is the lack of any returning character/story and the new first person perspective which can be considered as a slightly cheap way for jump scares. They have clearly tried to make the core mechanics "classic Resident Evil" (limited ammo/weps, herbs, tense claustrophobic atmosphere, inventory management) but you can easily forget that the game your playing is supposed to be the 7th mainline game in the Resident Evil series.
- As mentioned above you play as an entirely new protagonist and all other characters are completely new aswell- this is refreshing but also disheartning as it is the first game since RE2 (excluding obscure sideline RE titles- RE survivor, outbreaks, OP RC) where you aren't playing as a familar face in the RE universe. Don't get me wrong I'm glad to not be playing as Chris Redfield AGAIN (or leon) in the main game but there are still characters who are long overdue to be the main playable protagonist who I and many oher fans would love to play again e.g Jill, Rebecca, Wesker. There isn't even the classic mercenaries mini-game which gave you the opportunity to play as old and new RE characters.
- The boss fights are average with the exception of maybe 1 as they follow a "find the weak-spots and unleash your ammo" style which many other games follow aswell. Not to mention the final fight is SO disappointing as you are motionless while unleashing all the ammo they practically throw at you in the last 20 minutes and then the scripted "finish em' off" part leads for a poor finale. 
- The game is entirely single player, which is GOOD for the main game but it would have been nice to see a mercenaries game mode where you can play with 1 other person or even the nightmare dlc could have had an option for local & online co op mode where enemies & difficulty increase with an extra person while having to share supplies and weapons. 

Overall Resident Evil 7 is enjoyable and definently welcomes back a style of survival horror incredibly different from the action packed games in the franchise like Resident Evil 6 and fans of the old resi games will at least moderately enjoy it. Saying that I don't necessarily think this should be a staple for all newer Resident Evil games to follow but its a step in the right direction. My personal score is 7/10 for RE7

I was surprised by Resident Evil 7. Not just because of the whole "going back to its horror roots" (and they didn't just go back to its horror roots - they outdid it by far!), but also because they managed to balance it so well alongside small tidbits of action, as well as keeping the story within the established universe.

Resident Evil has a very rich lore universe. There's so many characters in the series (both playable, NPCs and those you just read about in files and what not) that it's impossible to keep track of them all. That's not a bad thing in itself. I mean, you can have a field day visiting RE-oriented wikipedias and fan sites to read up on whatever tidbits of lore you didn't even know existed (mainly due to it not being a part of the main series). And while I agree that Resident Evil needed to reinvent itself, I did not want to see the established universe disappear either. And boy, was I in for a treat!

The game does its horror very well. Right from the get go you are introduced to a very dangerous world. One you have to thread alone as you uncover the truth of everything, and fight to survive and ever darker plot. It's got atmosphere. It's got creep factor. It's got terrifying enemies. And it still manages to balance that horror with some action. At first I thought to myself "This reminds me an awful lot of Outlast". Don't get me wrong, Outlast is a fine horror game. But we didn't need Resident Evil to go down that road. We already have Outlast for that. But that soon changed up. Resident Evil is experimenting with a variety of different themes, and they're nailing it. The whole game is really well done, and they amount of details they've put in is astonoshing. This is a must play in my book. Top notch here from the developers.

Looking forward to seeing what the future holds for the franchise now. This is an excellent game.

So, I'm traditionally not a fan of horror games. This game, however, did horror really, really well. Most horror media nowadays relies purely on cheap jumpscares. Resident Evil 7, however, does not have many. I counted maybe four jumpscares in an eight hour playthrough. The fear comes from the atmosphere and proper suspense. You never really know what's going to happen next, but watching it unfold slowly is just very unsettling and done very well. There's a section late game where you climb slowly up an elevator shaft, and I was expecting a jumpscare that never came. I reached the top and had no idea to what to expect as I was trying to recover from a non-existentant jumpscare, which kept me in an air of suspense.

On to the lore! I won't spoil it, but the characters are neat. Ethan, the protagonist for the majority of the game, is my favorite. His attitude is "♥♥♥♥ off". Not in the douche way, but in the sense that he wants to stop fighting monsters and go home. One particularly hilarious exchange was a character was introducing a mini-boss, and Ethan just goes "No....and ♥♥♥♥ you too!". There are also clues starting as early as the prologue to a reveal in the final few moments of the game, and if you catch them all, the "a-ha" moment just mere minutes before the end of the game is so satisfying. The final boss, however, doesn't fit the tone of the game. It's more like something from DMC

On to the gameplay! The resource management works for and against the game. It's generally fun to make the choices and you feel pretty clever when the choices you make eventually pay off. However, the reason you feel clever about those is kind of poor. Objective items require the same inventory space as actual items like medicine, guns, or crafting ingredients. On one occasion, I had to leave ammo, a rare commodity, behind to have enough space to carry the objective forward to progress the story. That lack of ammo caused me to lose a fight that I was entered into by that objective. Besides that, the shooting is fun. The shotgun specifically is gloriously satisfying with the kicks and the famous click as the new shell is racked.

Minor nitpicks: Some weapons have a few animation issues which bother me as somebody who uses firearms as a hobby. Both the shotgun and smg (which is erraneously reffered to as a full machine gun) both chamber a new round after reload, meaning you theoretically should have ejected one. There's also one late-game segment which requires a bit of backtracking.

Graphics: Amazing. Even on medium, it's one of the better looking games I"ve ever seen for the most part. 

Overall: 8/10. I highly recommend the game, and when I ain't broke I intend to get the season pass.

I guess I haven't really finished doing EVERYTHING in this game yet. I think I have a good enough jist of the game though to give my impressions.

Resident Evil 7 is a good game. I'll say that it's one of the better Resident Evils that's come in years since RE4. The RE Engine does a really good job with giving the game a dark eerie feel, some of it feeling the the "found footage" movies us horror fans have already watched such as Blair Witch, V/H/S, and my personal favorite, REC 1. It really does do a good job into putting you into other characters shoes and making you feel immersed, almost as if you're in their situation.

For people that are old resident evil fans, there are elements that do come back to this game. You've got keys, puzzles, safeboxes, limited inventory, and well, although they're not completely zombies, encountering molded for the first time does make make you tactfully think how you should handle enemies. "Should I take them out? If so, how? Where am I going to stand? Can I afford to use this ammo? Should I make a break for it?" This is how the first game felt when it came to taking out zombies, and what made it stand out, giving it birth to the survival horror genre. Note the keyword is "survival" here because a game that has survival as part of its genre is supposed to make you feel like you're struggling against all odds, and I think they did a pretty good job of that in this game.

Now, one thing I'll say. I think that, comparing to the other resident evil games, the enemies feel that they are lacking a little bit. There also isn't much enemy variety. I know a lot of people want to see different enemies like dogs, hunters etc. I do want to see more enemy variety too, but I also think that the first person perspective and the way that the character handles was part of the reason why they didnt have much enemies to begin with. When I played Ethan in this game and got his gun, I felt like his movement and aim was kind of slow, and not really suited to deal with faster enemies. Truth be told, I think Ethan would be killed rather quickly by the RE dogs or crimson heads. Any creatures who shoot at him too would probably be well....to be put kindly, not really fit into place here. I can imagine a lot of players calling those enemies cheap, getting shot at while not knowing who's shooting at you. And in madhouse, that can prove fatal, especially when two to three hits in madhouse can kill you. Truthfully though, even though there isn't much variety, I do agree that the difficulty in this game is balanced.  Almost everytime I ever got killed by an enemy, I never really thought it was cheap. And whenever I got killed, I strategized a new way into my head how to approach the situation differently and never be killed that way again. Every enemy can be dealt with in this game with taking a strategic angle, even in Madhouse. 

There's also issues with puzzles too. I found that the majority of the puzzles were very much the same. Almost all of the puzzles in the game were shadow puzzles, which were matching the silhouettes with pictures on the wall. There are three other puzzles off the top of my head which werent silhouette puzzles, and only one of them actually required thought (the happy birthday puzzle). The other ones were very easy to solve, especially the picture puzzle on the ship. I found the picture puzzle to a little insulting actually because if you look at the right wall across from the puzzle, the game practically already gives you the answer. I mean, come on.....this is the best you can do? They really could have done better here in the puzzle department.

If I have to say the lowest points that hit the games score for me, it would be the ship and the final boss.The ship feels like it goes on forever the first time you play it. I understand why they made that area the way is, because they didn't want you blowing through everything by the time you get there, but I still believe that it could have been handled better. By the time you reach the ship, you already have a wide arsenal. You can technically still use that arsenal, but here, I would actually bring in more tougher enemies and more tense situations, not end up losing your arsenal for 15-20 minutes until you get to the next area. For the final boss well...to say the least, there really should have been more strategy here, not just shooting at a wall for 10 seconds. That's probably the biggest disappointment that I have with this game.  I believe if Capcom just tried a little bit more, they could have made this fight a little more creative.

All in all, there are a decent amount of flaws in this game, but it IS trying to go in the right direction, and a lot of the things that resident evil 7 does, it does fairly well, hence why I said it's a good game. However, it's not an amazing one like REmake. If you are a new Resident Evil fan, I suggest buying that game first. I paid around $40 for the full game including season pass, and I believe I got my money's worth on that end. I've yet to play the DLC, and from my front, I am a hardcore RE fan, which is why you see that I have this many hours. I'm trying to platinum this game currently. 

If you are a normal-casual gamer, you will probably get around 20 hours out of this. If you are a hardcore game/hardcore RE fan/ or an achievement hunter, expect to put at least 35+ hours maingame, probably more if you end up screwing up a run. My estimated value would be $30 for normal/casual gamers, while for hardcore RE fans and the like, I would suggest $40. My final score would be a 7.5/10 for those who are playing this game for a casual/normal experience. For me personally, I really enjoyed madhouse, which is why I would say for those who are hardcore RE fans/survival horror game fans, I would give it an 8.5 for madhouse alone.

After Resident Evil 6 shat the bed for the series, Capcom needed to do something drastic to save it. That, apparently, was to do what everyone else had been doing for over 4 years now. Make a first person, horror focused game involving seemingly unkillable stalker enemies... at least for the most part. And it worked... again, at least for the most part. The game tries to at least go back to a horror element that was starting to be abandoned in RE5, but uses a few outdated tropes that stop the game from achieving pure greatness.

The pros, firstly. The Baker Family are great as antagonists. Daddy Baker, Jack, does come across as someone who will wreck you if he catches you, while trying to contain a giggling insanity within him. The first actual fight being, in my mind, the most memorable. Mommy Baker, Marguerite, invokes images of old-style witches, gurning at you, swinging a lantern, face contorted into a ugly looking smile and hiding something under it that you really don't want to know about. But the son, Lucas, is possibly my favourite. You rarely interact with him directly, as he tends to put you through the 'SAW' like sections of the game. Most of his conversations are done through cameras, monitors and speakers. And each of these spouts of dialogue and visual interactions are just golden. I honestly think the developers put a lot of time into his face motion capture, as he gives off the impression of total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ before he even speaks a word.

The first person perspective works with the games setting, a collection of houses and buildings on an old plantation, just as the restrictive camera angle worked in RE1-3 and it's tight hallways. You are relying a lot on audio cues for incoming threats not in your field of vision, adding to the tense feeling. Music is used correctly, only as a warning while in combat or similar situations, not drowing you out to some crap 'tension building' faux rock song while nothing is happening. The parts when nothing is happening, it's oddly quiet, apart from the afore mentioned audio cues.

The middle bits. Combat is ok. It's good that capcom didn't go for a 'Anything not nailed down is a weapon' approach that games such as Condemned did, as a big part of the gameplay is about scavenging for items, ammo and healing goop. Running out of ammo while fending off Jack and having to switch to your knife requires you make every shot count, and this is true in the first two thirds of the game. Also, get good at using that block button. It might not be a defend against all move, but it will save your life. And it is amazing how easily you can forget you have it in RE7.

The story is okay. It's nothing special, but does the job very well for the game. Clues are dropped about everywhere to push the story and various plot threads along, but it does shine when the game starts to show the emotional toll such events in the RE universe have on the innocent bystanders that get caught up in these bio weapon outbreaks. No other RE game, aside from probably the first two maybe, have shown on an individual level what making these BOWs does, with everything post 3 showing en mass infections of people and the immediate fallout. It's not until the latter third where the story just throws its subtlety out the window and starts pushing back down roads familiar to RE4-6.

Which brings onto the bad. That last third. It relys HEAVILLY on the 'Little girl with creepy super power' trope that was overdone when F.E.A.R did it. While it was present through the rest of the game, it was swept behind the overarching need to escape the Bakers. And Evelline, as an antagonist, is boring and predictable, creating jump scares and basically a waypoint for the player to go to, nothing more. [spoiler] The last hour, however, gets better as it's revealed who she actually is and what was done to her. And while it doesn't excuse her forcing the Bakers to be her family and creating the molded, when you realise she's the Grandmother character from the beginning and she breaks down crying infront of you as you inject her with the anti-BOW serum, you can't help but feel a little sorry for her [/spoiler]

The only other threat in the game is The Molded, who will be serving as your zombies for the evening. Basically, think RE4's regenerators, not as tough, a bit faster and more twitchy. While the initial shock of them appearing, and the first encounter with their varients are also initially shocking, they quickly become plain annoying. Headshots are the best way to deal with them, but the game is very inconsistant as determining how many it will take from the same gun for each individual Molded. Sometimes one-two does it, other times you could fire an entire clip into them before they pop. And, again, in the last third of the game, RE7 starts throwing them at you like cannon fodder, while also offsetting this by throwing ammo and supplies at you in a similar manner, turning the last area of the game into a first person shooter with sluggish controls.

RE7 was marketed and sold as a return to Survival Horror roots, where it brought back the feel of the classic games but with a new perspective. 

That's not what the game is, though. It's a horror game where some older RE mechanics are tacked on. 
Sure, there are safe rooms with a manual save system, but the tension that made them impactful before is removed since the game regularly autosaves for you. 

There is limited inventory with a return to backtracking as a way to progress, but it offers no challenge or room for strategy since the game makes sure to give you items only when you’re right next to where you need to use them and goes to pains making sure you know exactly what to do at all times.  There is no mystery to anything in this game.  The demo, on the other hand, teased depth and mystery by having strange items with unapparent uses and three different endings that suited different playstyles; the most extensive of which being so strange that the community had to work together online to figure out its mysteries.

Puzzles make a return, but they are ridiculously, and in some cases offensively simplistic and repetitive.  Why bother putting them in this game outside of nostalgia?

The original RE games were fun and replayable because these mechanics all had purpose and worked well together.  If you look at RE7 just as a horror game, it’s not bad.  It even has more depth than your average horror title because of these mechanics.  But as a core RE game that promises to recapture these elements, it’s really disappointing.

Even the things they do that are new aren’t really handled well.  I was excited about the use of the VHS tapes and imagined all sorts of scenarios where they could show you interesting events with very different tones and locations that could not only be a bit of a break from the campaign, but serve to give you little details about the characters, the virus or other figures involved.  What did they do with them, though?  They allow you to play an area at a different time, giving you a clue how to proceed when you access it in the present.  Then you go through the area all over again in the present.  It felt lazy and pointless.  Even the best example, the birthday room, was dull.  I’d rather die a few times trying to figure a puzzle out than figure it out once from the safety of a tape, then do it all over again, instantly and easily fooling Lucas.
It also gives away practically all of its uniqueness by borrowing from so many other IPs.  I don’t mind that it does this in general (the Evil Dead-like fun of Mia cutting off Ethan’s hand only for it to be stapled back on is awesome!), but it does it so bluntly and frequently that it doesn’t really feel like its own story.  The game takes elements from The Blair Witch Project, The Evil Dead, FEAR, The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Saw, just to name the most obvious examples.  I think the reason that people tend to be so impressed with the scene where Jack asks you to save his family is because it’s one of the few moments that is unique to the game and not distractingly influenced by something else.

If you’re a big fan of horror games and don’t follow or care about previous RE games, you may enjoy this, but I’d only recommend it if it’s $30 or less.  The base game just doesn’t offer $60 worth of content, in my opinion.

Puzzle solving, spooky house, limited ammo, unforgiving enemies, inventory management, tense stressful boss encounters. Even the storage box is back. Gameplaywise, it's thrown way back in time, whereas the newer Resident Evil games (4,5,6) are more or less quick time events and action oriented rather than survival horror. You're surprisingly in first person perspective, which at first I was a little taken aback, but Capcom really knew what they were doing when they threw this at me. I'm going to preface this review by saying that I've never played any other of the Resident Evil games, and if you think that means my opinion is irrelevant, okay.  This review will be basing it off what it was like to me playing a standalone horror game.

I don't play many horror games besides some of the indie ones that have come out in the past like the old Slenderman games that we've all played, and I never gave Outlast a shot, so I can't say I'm a huge horror game buff.  However, if you allow yourself to become immersed in the world of Resident Evil 7, I think that you will enjoy it.  
The game looks beautiful, and for me at least, ran smoothly.  The ridiculous amount of visual options it gives you allows you to play it to full effect.  There weren’t really any visual glitches that I can remember, and I never really found an area within the gameplay world that lacked detail.  If you’re somebody like me and you enjoy stories and immersion, then the graphical style of the game will be enough to satisfy you.

  The gameplay is a different subject altogether though, and here I risk losing some people who have been fans of the RE series their whole lives.  Though I enjoyed some aspects of the combat, the uselessness that one feels when they fight some of the enemies in the game doesn’t make me think that it’s a difficult challenge, it just feels like filler.  The enemies (outside of any of the Bakers) to me just feel like bullet sponges whose entire purpose are to make you dispense ammunition.  It becomes a dull chore after a while and instead of feeling frightened and challenged by these enemies monotony begins to creep in.  The linear aspect of the game makes it so you will know where and how many enemies will spawn, thus adding to the feeling of monotony over challenge.  As someone who is currently on their second playthrough on a harder difficulty (I beat it on normal, now I’m playing again on madhouse) the addition of new spawn points for enemies are still fresh, but I fear once I beat it again I will have no reason to step foot back down this path.  On the contrary, there are some points in the game where the combat is fun while challenging.  The whole end sequence on the boat where you, at first, have no idea where the enemies will be coming from is awesome.  The boss battles are interesting ideas, and while they too are always the same, that’s usually the case.  I enjoyed the craziness that occurred with every subsequent boss fight, and the surprises were well worth it.  One of the biggest problems I have with the game is that not enough time is spent on puzzles and searching for clues, because these are the parts where I had the most fun.  Nothing says atmosphere like creeping around a house with immortal Jack Baker looking for you, and to me those moments were the best parts of the game.

This all begs the question: is it worth the price?  I think so, considering $60 now is the standard AAA game cost.  I think the season pass is over kill especially at an additional $30.  You are pretty much paying $60 to play an interactive horror movie, but the horror movie is less like The Boy and more like The Witch.  If you appreciate horror, especially horror films, I think you will enjoy this game.  And if you have a VR headset that would probably make it more enjoyable.

TLDR: I enjoyed the game, it was fun experience, and the second playthrough on madhouse will be a fun challenge.  The game feels far too linear however, most confrontations happen in the exact same spot regardless of difficulty and begin to feel monotonous after a while.  The story is good, probably worth the price of the game, but the season pass is no way worth an extra $30 and should have been included either with the original $60 purchase or at an expense of like $5-$10.

Resident Evil 7 is absolutely nothing like the past few Resident Evil games, but in that sense it makes it that much better at being a Resident Evil game because it's returned to its survival horror roots. The game is heavy on immersion and immaculate details, which help to drive our feelings of dread and demonstrate that we, too, have the ability to scream at the top of our lungs (while Ethan, surprisingly, is pretty unfazed with getting gut punched by pretty much everybody).

The strength in this game really does lie in the horror elements, not because these elements are present, but for the fact they take these elements and add small subtle changes that make them interesting. For example, depending on Jack's location he can very easily intercept you and break everything in his way to get to you. Or, he can also taunt you as you're within an inch of your life crawling towards a first aid bottle. I won't mention anything with the boss fights, but let's just say some of them can play out very differently if you don't do a specific action first. These details make the game enjoyable for both replayability but also differs the horror experience for every individual.

I wouldn't say the game is pretty  (Have you seen those disgusting bugs and rotted wood and wallpaper?) but I do believe this is one of the best looking games to come out this year in terms of graphical fidelity. I understand that might be a little too early to say considering 2017 just started, but the level of detail is astounding, and it adds to the macabre and grim nature of the game. The sound design is also top notch, as the ambience it adds makes every step questionable as you move forward and makes playing with headphones an absolute must if you want to hear every faint creak in the house. Also, the game as sections that get very small and cramped so if you have claustrophobia it's going to be kind of tough.

The pacing in the game was very good and was neither too slow nor too rushed. It's got enough action to move the plot forward without ever dragging anything down, and the scattered lore throughout the game reveals a lot about what happened in the Baker household, making it a very rich story to add onto RE's already extensive lore. However, the game is fairly short despite being well paced, so it can be very easy to finish this game quickly (assuming you haven't been so scared you shut it off already).

Despite what is already a pretty damn good game, it does have its flaws, and I think the biggest one comes from the choice you have to make about 3/4 of the way into the game. This choice does alter some things, like the ending you get, but I believe the execution of this choice was fairly poor and skews heavily to one singular choice. I mean, I get why the best choice is the right one in a narrative sense, but the outcome of the bad choice changes very, very little over the course of the last half of the game. It felt incredibly rushed, and honestly felt like it shouldn't have been a choice in the first place.

I highly recommend this game if you're into survival horror, or are an old RE fan turned off by the newer installments. Even if you're just casually interested because you think it'll be a good scare, I say play it. as the experiences you'll get will be worth it. Baker-Certified, I daresay.

Resident Evil 7 took me by surprise. Not just because it was actually good, but because it managed to evoke that traditional feeling of survival horror like the first three Biohazard titles did. At first, I was pretty sceptical about the change in perspective. However, longtime fans of Resident Evil shouldn't be dissuaded by this. Make no mistake, this is classic survival horror, just in a new perspective.

What does that mean? Well, Resident Evil 7 follows a somewhat similar structure as the older games, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis in particular. Items are hand-placed and scarce in quality. Unlike the newer games since Resident Evil 4, no enemies will drop items for you. That means that almost every fight (save for bosses) can be avoided. The flip side to this is, if you clear out an area, it will only repopulate after a story trigger. Unlike older games where combat was often expected, here it's discouraged. You'll have to decide for yourself when to fight or flight. 

Don't expect a lot of combat or different enemy types, however. Zombies are gone, having been replaced by the molded enemy types we saw in the teaser. In total, there are about 4 generic enemy types that can be killed or avoided. In addition, there are very powerful sub-bosses that will pursue you relentlessly a la Nemesis. This is also where RE7 incorporates elements of newer horror games such as Amnesia. Stealth isn't just possible here, it's a necessity in many cases.

Resident Evil 7 takes elements of survival horror both old and new to create something that feels at once new and nostalgic. Fans who enjoyed the old PSX games will definitely appreciate this return to form, but overall there's a lot to enjoy here. The story isn't fantastic, but it's serviceable and inoffensive. There's plenty to come back to, and like the Biohazard games of old, it can be played and replayed many times whilst still offering different challenges and spooks each time.

Whether you're looking for a decent horror game to scare you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or just pining for some good old-fashioned survival horror, Resident Evil 7 is for you.

Having been a fan of the series through the good & the not so good, I was interested in this game but wasn't going to get at  launch. Having watched a few small videos & hearing some good things about the game I caved in & purchased. 

The 3rd person view point is gone & so are the major characters of the previous games, this means that you play a unknown who is caught in a messed up situation. The game has the item management of the early games as well as finding that good old safe room in order to save your progress throughout the house. A number of hardcore fans were disappointed at the change in view point & that it didn't really real like a RE game, however the further you get into the game the more it feels like one & I can say that imo I it felt like a pure RE game more so than some of the previous instalments. 

You recieve a tape & end up going to check out the address, from here your messed up journey begins, you meet a family where something just feels off & that is proven quickly to be true. There are four enemies that you will mostly be encountering all with unique ways of testing your survival skills wether it is the head of the Baker family with his slow meandering & weapons to the son who would rather let you do his work for him, all have unique elements about them. You will also encounter a very small amount of other enemies until the later stages of the game where these become more frequent & less & less is about the family. 

This game takes elements from many horror films that have been terrorising people's minds for years. This being said I only really had 3 to 4 jump scares & most of these for me personally were at the very early stages of the game, although that moment in the old house which let to a showdown in the greenhouse was up there. I do feel that Alien Isolation however at least in the early stages of the game, which has a similar hide & do not try to take head on was more scary, but this does it pretty well. 

The atmosphere in this game is unreal, it feels closed in & it makes you feel tense & on edge even when it seems that nothing is there. The house feels big in design but isn't too overwhelming meaning you will quickly get used to the surroundings. The later parts of the game bring you to new areas some better than others but the house is where the main fear is. 

I did come to a part in the game where it just didn't fit that well & that was involving Lucas, it was cool but it never really led anywhere where as the other family characters you meet ends in some kind of showdown, with Lucas you are more left with the feeling of but what about him etc. A few of the boss fights were a bit of a let down & had the same feel of bosses of previous instalments. Also about 3/4 of the way through you are put on the spot out of no where really which I guess it effects which of the two endings you get that for me came too soon, meaning in order to see both endings you would have to keep a save file near that point & finish the last quarter again. 

The game ran really smooth for me & this added to the enjoyment, however although my character dialogue was on max the speech was really too low & spent the whole time reading subtitles. Not sure if that is a setting my end or a fault in porting the game from console versions.

The setting & characters are nice but for me the game needed to make use of these better at the later stages of the game. The boss fights could have been more interesting as well considering the family members you come up against, again I mean the later bosses, the earliar encounters were interesting & felt different. The game makes you play on normal or easy at the start & for me normal was way too easy although I did die a number of times. In the later stages of the game I had an inventory with way too much ammo & health which made you feel that you were unstoppable at that point. Overall I would give this game an 8/10 & would recommend it for fans of the earlier RE games, as well as for survival horror games, for a higher score I would like to have seen a little bit more to some elements of the story, if this is however the 1st in a new line of RE games that bring the game back too survival I feel it is a good starting point.

Unlike a lot of people I am not such a huge fan of Resident Evil that I can say the now very cliched tagline "It's a return to form for the Resident Evil series" because if I'm being honest I skipped the terribly controlled survival horror infancy and was introduced to the franchise well into its over the top action phase but I can say with certainty that this is a welcomed departure from what we've come to expect out of the franchise in recent years.

Pros:
- The atmosphere is dripping with the sick and macabre.
- Very little space is wasted, it feels like there's something to explore in every nook and cranny of the mansion whether it's story related or helpful items to add to your inventory.
- The cramped environment leads to more methodical action which makes the encounters far more intense.
- The limited inventory forces you to make a decision to fight or flee making every situation life or death.
- Inventory management plays a sizable role which means there is a bit of strategy into picking things up and putting them where you need them at the right time.

Cons:
- The romance between Mia and Ethan is uninteresting. I didn't feel compelled to save her at all because there was no real storytelling involved between them and not a lot of chemistry there. You weren't given nearly enough time with her for any kind of attachment to blossom. I felt more attached to Zoe because at least there's some interaction with her. It would have been a nice dynamic to see more of her and have more touching moments between the two only to be ruined by Eveline's possesion.
- Sometimes Ethan's movements feel purposely/ synthetically slow to build tension and often times it gets him hurt or killed. I don't know of any human being that would react as slowly as Ethan does to opening a door or shooting especially when his life depends on it.
- It is incredibly linear.  While I know they made it clear that the demo wouldn't have much to do with the game itself I still would have liked to see differing paths instead of having one singular moment that only slightly changes the outcome. It's not a huge deal, I enjoy the story for what it is but I would have loved to see multiple endings and branching paths.
- Paltry run time at a little over 10 hours to complete your first run of the game. Not really a deal breaker for me but I can understand why someone would be hesitant to buy a $60 game that takes less than a day to complete.


In my opinion this jaunt into the backwoods chaw chomping Louisianna sludge is worth the purchase price . I can only imagine what people with VR feel but personally I often found myself having to shut the game off after an hour or so of gameplay because it's so intense and claustrophobic that it feels stressful but it's the good kind of stressful. The kind of stressful that makes you want to keep coming back, the kind of stressful that says "I can get past this area, I know I can figure this out, I just have to take it at my own pace" It's the kind of frustrating that a game should be, frustrating enough to get you momentarily stumped but not so frustrating that you want to break something. This game touches a few different types of horror throughout the campaign: there's a bit of Texas Chainsaw Massacre, a bit of F.E.A.R, a bit of SAW, etc., and it handles those types of horror masterfully. From beginning to end, there's a palpable sense of dread and unease that will make part of you really not want to progress, though this is overwhelmingly overshadowed by the desire to push through this fun and intense experience.

Graphically, it's interesting. The design itself is great, with some photorealism and artistic liberties thrown in here and there to keep the game feeling... fantastical. It's a great looking game, especially from a distance, but getting too close to some textures will definitely show off a sort of lack of depth to the objects. The characters all look disturbing and great, and the environments ooze atmosphere from the design itself.

The sound design is on point. The entire game will keep you on edge from simple noises you can hear 2 rooms down, and everything in the game has a sense of perminence and weight that really stems from the sounds they make-- footsteps, scrapes against the walls and floors, the way screams echo down the hallway.

The story (no spoilers) will please most people, including long-time fans. There's an air of mystery throughout the entire experience, and it doen't fully pay off until the last maybe half-hour in this 10-ish hour game. The action is well paced alongside the narrative, and you'll be constantly weaving in and out of action, intensity, and story which keeps things fresh and pushes you along in a comfortable (or uncomfortable, depending on how you look at it) pace.

I couldn't be happier with this game, and will gladly recommend it to everyone. If this is what's in store for us in the Resident Evil series, sign my ass up.

Resident Evil/Biohazard 7 (RE7) incites a familiar feeling to the series by bringing it back to it's roots of survival horror. That being said, it's not without some flaw. 

RE7 takes place on the Baker Property in Dulvey, LA. A swamp with an engrossingly eerie atmosphere, even in daylight. You take control of Ethan Winters, a man in search for his wife (Mia Winters) who has been missing for three years. Upon arriving, things already feel out of place, getting progressivly worse upon entering the Baker Guest House.

I felt a great sense of dread wandering the halls of the Baker Residence. Will a "molded" appear around this corner? How many will there be? Do I have enough ammo (usually not)? I felt helpless at times. The atmosphere, made possible by the photo-realistic RE Engine, is so on par, it could be compared to a photo of an abandoned house. 

Slowly strolling along, I heard creaks in the floorboard, crows cawing in the distance, thunder from storms outside. All this melded with the desolate imagry of the home. Photo's of the Baker's were neatly displayed, their personal items available for discovery. This "was" their home. 

The personality of the Baker Residence is truly the star of RE7. It's almost immaculate. That feeling of dread stayed with me through my playthrough (10hrs 11mins/Normal). Sadly though, after the Baker's Residence, I felt tense rather than terrified. The later area's of the game, while presented perfectly, lost that sense of personality that made the Baker's Residence such a dismal delight to wander though. (No Spoilers) 

This is all anyone who is looking to buy the game should know about the general exposition. Swamp. Creepy House with multiple additions and f****d up monsters. This isn't a story summary, it's a review. 

Gameplay:

-RE7 takes place in first person, a first for the series. This adds tremendously to immersing yourself in the atmosphere and actually feeling frightened. 
-The gun-play has a great solid feel to it (when I missed a headshot, I knew it was my fault). Guns have "oompf" to both firing and the audio associated with it. 
-Ethan moves pretty slow, but not to a level where it feels unfair. 
-RE7 really isn't puzzle intensive. Find key with corresponding lock, match object shadow to match photo. I did, however, enjoy hidden items such as the toy axe (misplaced, seeming to have no purpose, but opens a lock).
-The pacing is set nicely by incremental breaks made possible by Safe Rooms, where you can save and do inventory management. 
-Upgrades are optional by buying them in the trailer via "Antique Coins," adding more reason to explore. (Some can be found in the world.)

Story:

The only aspect of the game that keeps it from a perfect score. It's well written and never loses it's self up until the end, but, I felt that the last hour was rushed. Tied up in a bow even. For long time gamers, it's like Halo 2, great up until that final encounter where it felt like they ran out of ideas and just ended it. I wanted a more, not dramatic, but more impactful resolution (for both endings, I got ending 1). It was good, but not great, nothing like it deserved. 

Pros:

-Amazing Atmosphere
-Incites Fear
-General Gameply works great
-The Baker's are iconic

Cons:

-Lackluster ending
-Felt "shooty" in later stages
-Some texture pop-ins

Verdict:

9/10- Awesome and worth the purchase.

Resident Evil 7 is easily the best game in the franchise released during the last decade, underneath it's Texas Chainsaw Massacre style exterior is a pure RE title that brings back a lot of the lore and mechanics that made the franchise so memorable. 

Outside of boss fights there is really no need to fight enemies and for the majority of enemy encounters it is really recommended to save your ammo and hightail it. Space is used to a level of pure genious, with compact locations having multiple paths for you to make your way around. Boss fights are for the most part really well put together with the exception of the fight in the butcher room which isn't designed as well as it should of been and the final boss encounter which is pretty much a scripted event, which is somewhat saddening since tha final boss encounter could of been used for a pretty intense fight, something that is a staple in the RE franchise.

I also found puzzle solving to be child levels of easy and the lack of varietty of molded enemies ends up beeing pretty noticable after a few hours, if i am not mistaken there are only 4 differnt types. Although these arent really any major issues and doesn't break you from the immersion it still something that long time fans of the classics will notice. Scares are used sparecely and well placed, they are mostly used during the first few hours of the game since this time frame is where the player is still gettting used to the prespective and feel of the game however some of earlier scares are plainfully obvious meant to enhance the VR experience, during the last hour or two the scares are almost non existent since the game picks up it's pace and takes more of an action oriented approach. 

One of the features where this title stands out among other games is in it's pacing, it is hard for me to even think of a game that rivals this one in this aspect. Encounters dont go on for too long nor are they too short, when you need breathing space the game will give it to you and when tension needs to be high the game will make sure they are, this is probably one of the reasons that the game comes out as being called short by some players and one thing that needs to be understood is that length does not equal quality. I never found myself being bored and was constantly on the edge of my seat and excited to see what would happen once I turned the next corner.

Overall RE7 is a game I would recommend to anyone, the shift in perspective and the lack of returning characters will put off a few of the more hardheaded fans however I believe that a new instalment in a game doesn't need returning cast nor a reboot to continue (I am looking at you God of War reboot). I can only urge anyone to stick with the game to the end and make your decision once you beat it.

Resident Evil 7 is a subtle yet effective change for the franchise. The first person survival horror adventure takes place in Louisiana near a seemingly-abandoned backwater plantation house. You are searching for somebody previously thought dead, and while you find them almost immediately, things go awry.  The Baker family—residents of the house—seek your death and torture for reasons unknown. What follows over the next eight hours will be a memorable horror experience.

The pacing, particularly in the first half, is excellent. The gameplay is mixture of action, stealth, puzzle-solving, exploration, and resource management. Stealth is rudimentary and finding safe areas is clunky but this emphasizes vulnerability.  Managing your inventory is mostly trouble free, although not being able to drop items is annoying, and the magical interconnected storage containers take away from the experience. There is quite a bit of backtracking, but circumstances change and new foes appear. Encounters with the Baker family are always a treat, with tense cut scenes that bring you face to face with terror. It also takes players to new areas on a regular basis (e.g. from the guest house to the main house) and makes efficient use of all locations.

The last third of the game is more action intensive. Players are taken to a different locale and, despite a few good moments of stealth, it behaves almost like a first person shooter. While the story reveals more during this half, the gameplay is not quite as agreeable because it lacks the variety and tension. Nevertheless Resident Evil 7 comes highly recommended, whether you are a fan of the series or not.

I've put some hours into the game so far, and I'll be continuing to do so. Quite frankly I'm pretty pumped for the future DLC's that will be coming our direction....but anyway, let's get on with the review shall we? I won't be putting any major spoilers in this review.

[b]Resident Evil 7 takes place a few years after Resident Evil 6, but taking things to a new, though at the same time a very familiar situation, that being survival horror instead of way overdone sci-fi action that was ruining the series in my opinion. Albeit, this is not the typical survival horror you'll be all too familiar with, no, no zombies, but a different kind of chaos that erupts when the main protagonist, Ethan, gets a call from his wife...to come get her. Instead, what you walk into is a twisted family. But what is wrong with them? Why are they psychotic? Jump into their madhouse, and seek the answers.

The games core represents the turn the series should have made a LONG time ago. From having to manage your inventory carefully, to now having to actually rely on being conservative with your ammo, to a tense atomosphere that will make you tense about what's going to be around that next corner and most importantly, keeping your wits about you to not get slaughtered. The horror elements in the game is well scripted and the voice acting is done well, I had my fair share of jumpscares with this game on my first playthrough. This is what Resident Evil is all about. The game focuses on making you tesne, and it does its job with the inspiration of some other titles that no doubt influenced some of the situations you get yourself into. But let's get on to the good stuff, a game like this doesn't need its plot spoiled too much.[/b]


-------------------------------------------------

[b]Pros[/b]


[list]
    [*]The graphics are well made, the game is a beauty wrapped in darkness.

    [*]The voice acting is superb and was well executed. The personalities of the actors they chose couldn't have done a better job.

    [*]Fans of the older RE games will have the familiar feels of things of what they now have back in their grasp.

    [*]The atmosphere of the game is what really nailed it. What little lighting is in the game is what makes everything tense. Trust me, use the recommended brightness setting, you'll see what I mean.

    [*]Unlockables! Yes, Capcom has kept it old school for us.

    [*]Survival Horror: Need I say more? 

    [*] Despite a couple crashes, this game runs flawless despite a few areas. With a GTX 1060 6GB paired with an FX-8320 CPU, I can lock the game at 60FPS with no issues, everything cranked to its highest. 

    [*] The first-person perspective is excellent and I just wished they'd remake the first RE in this exact style.
[/list]

----

[b]Cons[/b]


[list]
    [*]Your FOV is limited to a 90 cap, but obviously this was a design choice, though would have been nice to have something further of our choice.

    [*]It varies, but in my case there's a few spots where stuttering gets so bad, the game will crash. However, this has not been a regular occurance, but it is frustrating at times, espeically when needing to run.

    [*]There could have been more about Ethan that would have been nice to know. Not to mention for him to have had more dialogue, but it's nothing that should be a deal breaker to anyone.
[/list]


-------------------------------------------------

[b]Honestly, I can not think of many cons to this game. For me, personally, it's everything I wanted it to be since the demo. Capcom revied the series with this masterpiece, and I sincerely hope they continue to do what they are doing, and most importantly, I hope that this review, though may not be worded as appealing compared to others will entice past fans of the old RE series and enjoy what Capcom has made for us. It's worth every penny.

[h1]Resident Evil 7 is the Resident Evil 2 of modern gaming.[/h1]

For ages, this franchise has been lacking horror. RE 4 was, IMO, the last pure-horror RE game. Of course, this isn't to imply that the future games weren't good, no, but they were catered to those who loved action and only a little bit of horror. I enjoyed those games, but they didn't have the same effect on me that the other games (Especially 2, hence the title) had on me.

[b]First of all, Capcom have nailed the tension aspect of this game[/b], throughout the experience (Because RE 7 is not a game, but an experience), I was finding myself looking behind my shoulder to check if Jack was running at me with his massive axe/scissor/sword thingy, I love that, this game will make you feel unsafe 100% of the time.

I didn't even feel safe in the save rooms.

[b]The graphics are stunning[/b], and yet, the game is extremely well-built, even on an entry-level gaming laptop, I was able to run the game on very-high, with a solid 30fps (Which I didn't mind). I feel as though the first-person view really helps emphasise the finer details of the game and help players immerse themselves into the environment. Furthermore, the first-person perspective also brings a new dimension (In terms of RE) to the horror that we all grew up loving.

[b]The game has replay value[/b], and I cannot stress this enough, [u]play the game on madhouse after you finish your first play-through[/u] and you'll be meeted with a fresh, more scary, more difficult variation of the already-difficult game. And for those who played the older games, you'll notice that madehouse mode introduces ink-ribb..... sorry, cassette tapes, which you acquire throughout the game, you use these exactly like ink-ribbons.

[b]The story is rich[/b], not going to spoil the story, but I liked the many twists and "explanations" throughout, I was always learning more about the experiments and the Baker family themselves.

And man, that ending...

[b]So yes, I absolutely recommend this game[/b], because finally, we have a RE that has returned to it's roots.

[h1][b]A return to the original game's roots, and possibly the best horror game of 2017.[/b][/h1]

[b]Overview:[/b]
Resident Evil 7 is a great survival horror game which returns to its' roots of what made Resident Evil scary. It is packed with frightening and tenseful moments, together with sufficient action. It's more of a horror game than a survival horror game, and often you will find yourself feeling stressed due to the narrow corridors, huge map, and threatening enemies. In fact, you will want [b]less[/b] enemies than more, as ammo is limited. The environments vary [i]a lot[/i] and are different enough to keep the game unpredictable. I've never been more tense when playing a game in my entire life, and always checking corners for monsters.

Resident Evil 7 also features inventory management once again, but unlike other Resident Evil games, it is more akin to 4's where your inventory space is limited, and you have to manually reposition items and/or discard them to make space. There is a good variety of weapons in Resident Evil 7 which you can use to protect yourself from the enemies and stun the recurring bosses, ranging from melee weapons to long-ranged weapons. Moreover, there is now a crafting menu in the inventory, where you can craft herbs, ammo, and a bunch of other stuff which I won't spoil.

The boss fights in Resident Evil 7 are not monotonous, and are the thing you will dread [i]the most[/i], due to how terrifying some of them can be. They are generally all set in different and unique environments, and on harder difficulties they can be excruciatingly frustrating. Resident Evil 7 also features an auto-save and savepoint system, together with cassete type/ink ribbon style saving if you're playing on a harder difficulty. The story is a mystery, but you gradually discover what happened to the Bakers, and the conclusion is [b]extremely[/b] satisfying and well done. There are notes and collectibles around, for story and achievement's sake, and there is also loot scattered around the environments, some of which are cleverly hidden. On the hardest difficulty, many of the known loot places and bosses are changed and moved, making it an unfamilar and difficult experience even for those who have beaten the game.

Beating the game and/or complete several challenges gives you access to some neat unlockables which can help on a second playthrough. The game's story, while linear (as it's a story-based game), is [i]highly[/i] replayable due to the random behaviour of the enemies and secrets.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
Overall, the game is extremely fun and tense, and has to be one of [b]the scariest and frightening games I've ever played[/b]. Given that I'm generally afraid of playing horror games, moreover beating them, Resident Evil 7 managed to keep me addicted [i]to the extent[/i] where I overcame my fears just to beat the game. There were several terrifying moments where I had to sit down and take a break, and unlike other games, the game does not use cheap jumpscares to scare you, and instead takes advantage of the atmosphere and the unknown. On my first playthrough, I didn't know what to expect, and that's where Resident Evil 7 succeeded in, creating a tense atmosphere where the player is always looking around and expecting something, or someone.  The game has a branching story and even multiple endings, based on your choice.

The enemies in the game are great and intelligent and will give you nightmares, the inventory management is challenging, crafting is a breeze, story is extremely well-written, and the overall mechanics and gameplay feel are simple to understand and use. Looting in the game works fantastically as well, and the game had me on the edge of my seat every second. Last but not least, the graphics in the game are top-notch and are some of the best I've seen, especially for a first-person horror game. Resident Evil 7 is the definitive horror experience that all other horror games should follow, as even with combat, it's still equally terrifying, knowing that you are helpless to some extent. It is the scariest game I've ever played, and I highly recommend it to any Resident Evil and/or Horror fan. Even if you're not a fan of either, you should give the demo a try, as that's how the game generally plays, with the exception of combat, story and a wide range of environments.

[b]Score:[/b]
[h1]9.5/10[/h1] (It's not 10/10 because of PC stuttering issues, which have yet to be fixed, but aside from that, it's the best horror game I've ever played, and I intend to play it more.)

[h1][b]I highly recommend this game to anyone who hasn't tried it yet, you're in for one of the most thrilling and terrifying rides of your life, and you won't regret it.[/b][/h1]

[b] Target Audience: [/b] [I] Survival Horror fans, or fans who love Tension [/i]

[b] Summary: [/b]  
The rebirth of a franchise that it desperately needed. I was one of the biggest critics of Resident Evil Revelations 2, as the tone and gameplay that it set was so inconsistent to its own themes that it literally drove me insane at times. So to see the series that I loved in games like Resident Evil 4 and the original trilogy be driven to such a gameplay mess, it was disheartening. 

But Resident Evil 7 has been reborn into a more slow paced survival horror game, and its transformation is fantastic. The series has brought back natural tension: focusing on the smaller elements that can unnerve a player rather then giant T-rex bio monsters, and it's a welcome change. The game feels designed to put you into the situations: not force you into “panic” situations by shoving you into them: but actually guiding you into them and make you feel the unrest and the unease of the environment around you.  Enemies feel like a threat thanks to a reduction of speed and a good lack of control over firing at times, and the Bakers provide antagonists that actually make your skin crawl at times. It's backed up with a presentation that makes you see all the warts and veins on character models, and wonder what the hell happened to this family that made them this way. And you will panic at times: where you'll waste ammo and realize that: oh ♥♥♥♥, I need to fight this thing with a knife.

See, what really makes this game better then a lot of the recent RE games is simple: it feels like the mechanics work together. The presentation enhances the gameplay and emphasizes its strengths, rather then the inconsistent tones set in RER2. The controls feels like they were made for this game, as opposed to just being there, and trying to force them to work. For once, Capcom seems to have actually designed a game, rather then throw a bunch of elements together: which is something that is WELCOMED AT THIS POINT THANK YOU CAPCOM.

The game still has flaws: the last 1/3 of the game feels rather different from the first in a bad way, with an over reliance on repetitive enemies, and just a shift in tone in general. Our main protagonists really can't carry the story on their own due to them being....well boring, and there's little hiccups in crashes that happened while playing. 

But the game is most assuredly worth playing, especially for the Madhouse mode after you beat the game the first time. I felt fear in a Resident Evil game for the first time since Revelations 1: and that's a good thing.
