Title: Resident Evil 7 Biohazard
Platform: Windows, Playstation 4, Xbox One
Rating: M
Developer: Capcom
Publisher: Capcom
Price: $60 USD
Release Date: 24th Jan 2017

Being my first Resident Evil game and my first true survival horror game, I was skeptical about jumping into Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, but fortunately I was given a solid game with only some problems to stop the great game from being amazing.

You play as Ethan, a man that can come straight out of a cliche horror movie with the generic motive of finding his missing wife: Mia, as he is lead by a video into the Baker Farm where he assumes she’ll be. But what Ethan doesn’t realise is he’ll have to survive in this giant house by gathering resources and fighting monsters and hillbillies. The gameplay of using your limited ammo or not and managing your small inventory is quite simple but it is really satisfying and rewarding. The crafting system is thankfully also simple with all the huds and menus being extremely streamlined and accessible. 

Another good thing is that the game gives you just the right amount of enemies, and while there are only about 3 or 4 types of these common mobs, you have the ability to kill them and if you can’t then it is because you don’t have enough ammo or you want to save it. You’ll never feel like you’re versing some kind of god monster where you have to constantly hide or you’re being overwhelmed as the overall gameplay is definitely more about survival than it is shooting.

But the most fun thing to do in this game is exploring the Baker Farm with this spectacular game design the developers have created. Every room feels different and that there was a real purpose in it being there. Each room is also packed to the brink of detail and while Resident Evil 7 may not be the most graphical game out there, some interiors just look absolutely incredible thanks to the lighting and attention to detail with all this adding to the creepy and on the edge of your seat atmosphere that has been created.

Another thing that adds to the creepy atmosphere is just how brutal this game is. You’ll see in the environments and in the Baker Family themselves who act as the enemy bosses, that something has gone terribly wrong. Unfortunately the common mobs don’t feel as threatening design-wise because of how slow they move, although this is probably fixed in the higher difficulties.

Unfortunately this atmosphere and game design seems to be lacking in one of the later levels of the game with it instead turning into a labyrinth of corridor after corridor of exploration instead of the small and detailed exploration that I had come to love in the Baker Farm. 

But wherever you’re going you’ll never feel lost thanks to the handy map that notes all locked areas and rooms you haven't visited, so you’ll never have to remember it mentally. And I really liked this map because in other survival horror games you just had to aimlessly find a way to go but with this, I felt like I was always being pushed into the right direction without being forced into a linear path, thanks to its mostly stellar game design.

The story was really good, which was surprising as it doesn’t start too well with it being quite generic. But as soon as you are lead into the farm and introduced to the Baker Family. Everything starts to open up with actual character development for Ethan and his wife, and even the enemies themselves feeling natural and not just adding to the story but the game world itself. The story stayed intriguing throughout the whole game offering plot twists that I never saw coming and pushed the simple gameplay forwards with the help of the game design, especially when this element became lacking at the end. 

Also, the game does offer a choice that gives a good or bad ending, and while it is quite minor in turns of actual gameplay as you’ll do the same thing both choices, it still does give replay value for anyone that is big on the story and wants to see the differences first hand.

While the brutalness does add to the atmosphere quite well, it will never add up to how amazingly well done the sound is in this game. The soundtrack itself is suspenseful and adds to the few jump scares and many creepy moments. The actual sound effects though, reign king, in giving us a constant creepy ambience in making us feel like this world still lives, and that adds so much more freight than any jumpscare or blood bath.

Of course I can’t avoid mentioning the voice acting which is done so well into making the performances of the characters feel more real, especially the Baker Family who give absolutely terrifying performances.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 7 Biohazard was a game I had an absolute blast with thanks to its spectacular level and game design for the most part, intriguing story, satisfying gameplay and incredible sound, although the common enemies can fall flat in giving a terrifying experience and that spectacular level design seen at the start is almost non-existent in the end. Also, you can’t deny that since we completed this game in 9 hours, that is not enough for a full priced game, even if free dlc is being released later. 

But Resident Evil 7 Biohazard is still a great game and is showing us a great start for the triple A games of 2017. 

That’s why I give this game a 4/5.

The seventh numbered entry into the series isn’t bad, but it isn’t necessarily good either. I believe that the series has become stale. I don’t believe this game is a return to their roots. I was never genuinely scared for about ninety-five percent of the game,  because most of the time I was a walking battle tank for most of the game. If you had a good eye you was armed to the freakin’ teeth with ammo. I’ll start with the graphics. 

Graphics

Probably one of the most saving graces of the game. The graphics are solid. Several times I’d be walking down a hallway and see a shadow thinking it was someone behind me, and it was my own shadow. If you have the computer to play this on the very highest setting the game looks phenomenal. I can’t speak for how well the game looks on the PS4 or X1, as I have only played the PC version. Sometimes it was hard to discern if it was real or still a game you was playing. The facial animations of the characters, and what I assume to motion capture was top notch. The way Mia’s hair swayed whenever she was talking to you or when she was slinging you across the room was incredible. Another feature I’d like to touch on is in the boss the fights when Ethan shot them it would show visible damage, and stay there the rest of the fight. Made the game a bit more realistic. I could go on, and on about the graphics but I’m going to stop there. 

Audio

The audio was great. I didn’t have the opportunity to play the game on a surround sound system, and could only imagine what it was like. Walking down hallways or corridors, you’d turn around to a creak or the sound of furniture being tossed. The first hour or so that kept you on your toes but after a while the sounds started being repeated, and it lost its luster for me after that. 

Gameplay

This is where the game really lost its shine for me. Items were plentiful from beginning to end. I was never at a point to where I was scared that I was going to run out of bullets. As I stated in my brief introduction if you looked hard enough you’d have plenty of ammo for the boss fights. I didn’t find the boss fights fun or entertaining in the least bit. They were more annoying and tedious to me. Get the baddest gun you have, feel them full of lead, run around a bit, shoot’em, get hit by an attack that should’ve been avoidable, on the flip side, avoid an attack that should’ve knocked you across the room. You could avoid almost all the molded encounters. I was never scared because I knew everywhere a molded was going to pop out. Also, the game conveniently saved for you when a big encounter was coming up. Nothing was ever a surprise. I wished the developers had used a checkpoint system instead of an auto save. It seems that Capcom leaned toward the VR audience with this title as well. I think this title was made with VR in mind. 

Story 
		
The story was extremely overused. The creepy little girl story is something that has been used numerous times, and not just in video games but in movies as well. If you connect the dots the plot is fairly predictable. Grandma appearing all over the house with no apparent reason, and the little girl dressed in clothes that was popular around the 1920s. The story is very weak and has all the cliches of your typical horror game or movie. You had Jack and his wife, Marguerite, fitting the role of the creepy husband and wife. Lucas, who is dumber than a box of rocks, fitting the role of the family idiot. Mia and Zoe fitting the role of the normal ones of the bunch. Then the old lady who is clearly more than she seems (which she is). For the length of the story this game is severely overpriced. I was able to get this half off, and I’m glad I did. If you’re more into the story, like myself, then there is little replay value. The Mia or Zoe has little ramifications on the ending. Could’ve left both of them and had the exact same ending.    

Overall

	This game is not worth the premium price that it’s asking. For God sakes, there’s
an achievement to beat the game in four hours. It took Capcom four years to make a game this long? I was expecting at least ten to fifteen hours. This’ll be the last RE title I’ll buy. I had no problem with the first person view, actually enjoyed that part, gave it a more cinematic feel to it. I believed the hype that was behind it and pre ordered it, wished I hadn’t and waited for the Let’s Play videos first. The nostalgic feeling was never there for me. I feel like this is a series that is becoming a copy paste game and is need of a reboot or to be ended.

Ethan Winters receives a concerning message from his wife, Mia Winters, who has been presumed dead for the last three years. According to her email and video attachment, her location is somewhere deep in the twisting woods and murky bogs of Dulvey, Louisiana. Despite Mia’s warning to “stay away”, Ethan’s quest for answers to his wife’s disappearance drown out her desperate plea. Driving along a stretch of road that extends its reach through calming waters and swaying cypress trees that bask in golden sunlight, you come upon a long driveway overtaken by foliage. Slowly you make your way through the properties eerie woods and stumble upon the backdoor of a sizable home that offers no evidence of present tenants.

It’s within the next ten minutes of gameplay that flaunt an atmosphere so uninviting, uninstalling is still a justifiable option. The Dulvey House is littered with garbage, crumbling furniture, and a foundation that looks older than the dirt it was built on.  Beneath it’s rotting floorboards, between tight corridors and passages lies darker horrors than imaginable. Scalpels stained crimson with blood and other tools of unspeakable punishment are caked in bodily fluid. Jars containing human remains and newspaper clippings of missing persons litter the basements damp rocky walls and shelves. All these grotesque visuals are just the tip of the iceberg for what gruesome horrors await in the following eight to ten hours of gameplay.

What stood out most in my entire experience was not just the incredible atmosphere Biohazard builds, but the realistic nature of the Bakery property inhabitants. Note that I won’t go into detail on the characters as I feel like they are better encountered for oneself firsthand. However, the animation and modeling work put into their movements and appearance is so life-like that your monitor or TV will feel more like a window than a panel with thousands of tiny lights. Enemies feel grounded to their surfaces, subject to gravity and shifting of their weight, aware of their surroundings and intelligent in their ambush techniques. They see you when you peek around corners, hear you when you make a believable amount of noise and harass you with shouting when hiding. Facial animations could use some work but despite some oddly synced audio and mouth animations and extremely rare cases of clipping, they display enough emotion to immerse you deeper in this house of horror.

As you explore your surroundings, useful items can be used or crafted to increase their power or potency, or dismantled to craft entirely different items altogether. Weapon pickups are paced appropriately and ammunition is a precious commodity. Dispensing it is a battle in itself as the scarcity factor weighs on your mind, and it’s overall effectiveness comes into question. With a limited number of item slots, you’ll have to decide for yourself if backtracking to the closest bank-like chest is worthwhile, or discarding items to acquire new ones is more important. Inventory and ammo management is executed perfectly in Biohazard and its importance grows even heavier when playing on Madhouse Difficulty. 

The prevalent reminder of intelligent nearby enemies and the tense fight or flight based resource control are not Biohazards only shining achievements. Outside-of or following combat, the Baker house alone is a force to be reckoned with. It’s tight narrow hallways and passages are not so easily discoverable, and require specific keys and items that are scattered throughout all floors of the home to unlock or make your way through. While they pose as puzzles, they more-so resemble obstacles as their functions alone give you a clear sense of what needs to be done to solve them. Granted they throw a good deal of hurdles in your direction and are intelligently designed, they don’t require a lot of critical thinking to solve. 

With that being said, I applaud Biohazard for its clever use of backtracking. Nobody really enjoys visiting the same area time and time again, but in this case I never felt any sense of boredom or casual strolling back and forth. Terror lurked around every corner and it’s quality jump scares were accompanied with some very tense and hair raising moments that weren’t scripted or ‘triggered’ by player interaction. Biohazard’s scenery followed suit to others in it’s genre from time to time, meaning yes, there’s spooky dolls and eerie carvings, but it wasn’t the cornerstone for it’s frightening demeanor. Furthermore, there was rarely any noticeable cheap spike in volume and all the scares were justified by their realistic approach.

In terms of audio quality I would argue it’s fine-tuned and precise. The Baker family's vocabulary was outlandish and fitting, and their variety of dialogue while hiding or fighting was surprisingly engaging. From excited bursts of anger to taunts and teasing. Crouched down behind pallets and broken furniture, enemies would shout your name like some sick twisted game of Marco Polo. Grow delighted upon detecting you, furious in your abilities of juking past them, and laugh at your attempts of doing damage. Paired with the aforementioned animation, the superb voice acting only builds to the already immersive experience.

There’s a lot to be said about first impressions, and at first glance the graphics appear very crude in textures and lacking in overall polish. This drawback is counterbalanced by some very realistic lighting and (more often than not) ‘graphic’ visual effects. Cutscene-like sequences tie in very nicely with the gameplay itself, making for a very fluid experience all the way through. The environment itself is detailed in terms of clutter whether it’s foliage, household items, or tar-like material made by The Molded, all work together throughout the game to distract from the already mentioned above-average textures.

Enemies are horrifically detailed and their appearance was given a great deal of attention, however, they lack in variety and abilities. The Molded (and the Baker family) are your most recurring obstacles throughout the game, and while they present a very real and threatening presence, they range from: small/fast, tall/damaging, slow/resilient. This shallow range of enemies is not a massive blow to the experience itself but it doesn’t add much complexity to the later half of the game.

Lastly, and regrettably, somewhere along the way Resident Evil 7 loses it’s charm. Particularly noticeable in the later half or (arguably) last quarter. It’s narrative remains strong all throughout, however the gameplay takes a turn in a direction that is outside the tone it spent a great deal of time constructing. This could be caused by a sense of security behind a modest arsenal, or a lack of challenging enemy variants. Regardless, it carries out a wonderful story that is both engaging and intriguing. 

When it’s all said and done, Madhouse Difficulty unlocks and is another mountain in itself to climb. Saving which was previously done by interacting with a tape recorder, now requires actual cassette tapes that can be found scattered throughout the game. Item locations are re-arranged from their previous location. Enemies appear more frequently and are even more intelligent and determined in halting your progress, while ammunition and item abundance is more scarce than before. TLDR: The game is excelent and returns resident evil to its roots and possibly more.

Outstanding Pros: 

+ The Horror: I'm not a guy who scares easily. I know its a bit cliche but I really don't mean it from a toughguy (did I just assume my gender?) standpoint. Jump scares rarely work on me and most horror games don't cause me to flinch once. That being said. There are two elements to horror: the feeling and the jump scares. The feeling is incredibly tense, even playing the second time knowing whats going to happen. I beleive it comes mostly from the difficulty of some monsters (played on normal first) and how (unfortunately) annoying some of them can be. That definately doesn't rule out the excelent use of doors and other elements that add to the feeling. The jump scares are on point though. Good lord.

+ Voice Acting and Animation: Surprising that after horror this is the next thing that comes to mind. Capcom did a really good job of making the characters look, feel, and sound believable. You find yourself feeling sympathy even against those who harmed you.

Cons:

- Performance issues. This will likely be resolved with a few patches, but there were some oddities here. With settings on max and the hardware to match it, the game would run at 60 fps no problem but certain doors and areas would cause the framerate to drop beneath 1. This is a widespread enough issue that it is pretty well documented online. The good news is, that if you change a few settings: shadow cache off and textures to medium (you won't really notice) it works fine from there. I did have another issue with alt-tabbing that after a few times doing it, the game would run in windowed mode instead of fullscreen. 

- Length. This isn't a total con. By now, I'm sure you know that the game isn't the longest. At the time of writing this review I've played it for 16 hours and beaten it twice. That being said. I actually think its a good length. It isn't needlessly long and leave you wanting to replay it a few times. With additional content coming (some even free) it should round it out.

Other Points:

+/- Graphics: The game does look very nice. Though it can be a bit blurry and has made some motion sick even without VR. It didn't bother me personally.

+/- Story: The self contained story was pretty good. How it matches up with the whole time line isn't entirely clear, it takes place some years after the events of 6 but there are more questions than answers. There were some interesting details that were missed at first that make more sense in subsequent playthroughs. A twist that was hinted at enough for me to guess before it happened. And a few parts that still don't make any sense to me after two playthroughs. But all for all pretty good.

Closing:

Capcom nailed it. The gameplay won't blow you away, neither will the graphics, story, or length. But it has that origional resident evil feel and flavor (with a bit of silent hill thrown in). The reason I say that it nails it is that it really takes me back to the first time I experianced resident evil. It made me feel like that eight year old, hiding under the bed sheets watching his uncle play because he was way too scared to ever try himself. And I honestly can't recall any other game that has made me reminisce so much while still feeling like its own thing. I definately recomend that you purchase this game, though I may suggest waiting a bit, if only to get the forthcoming dlc's to add a bit more length to the game. I hope this review was helpful.

After completing the game I can confidently say that RE7 is up there with the greats of the series like RE1. The actual gameplay of the game is quite similar to the style of Resident Evil 1 where you need to find specific keys for locked doors like the "snake key", "Scorpion key" and "Crow key" etc. There is an inventory management system in the game like RE1 where you have to manage your inventory with a crate which is located in the safe zones and store items which you no longer need. Resident Evil 7 is one of the most enjoyable horror gaming experiences to date. The visual jump scares seldom feel cheap in part due to the masterful sound design. Making people jump isn’t a difficult task. However, making people terrified to progress the plot is a daunting task to pull off. Resident Evil 7 absolutely succeeds in pulling off what developer/publisher Capcom set out to accomplish. After the failure of RE6, the need for the series to return to the survival horror genre became clear. Horror is all about maintaining an atmosphere. Walking down a corridor, Ethan Winter (the surrogate for the player) might hear some variety of crash off in the next room or in the room above. The mansion is lived in (a slightly inaccurate phrase) and a sense of foreboding never escapes the player except for around the ending. The sound design mixed in with phenomenal limited lighting merge in encouraging the player never be overconfident in a given environment. Unlike previous entries, the locations are realistically scaled down. The Baker homestead never features a room or ground that feels out of place. In other words, the property is very much one might find in reality. Conversely, the game’s need to feature a puzzle at every turn suspends belief every once in awhile. In the end, the limited environmental scope aids in augmenting the horror. The developers painstakingly created the home to a disturbing degree. Every nook and cranny of the home serve a purpose in telling the Baker family’s story. The player is rewarded at great cost for exploring the environment. In addition, the exploration feeds into a very enjoyable item management system. All of the items encountered are useful. In order to make backpack space, the player has to really decide what is the most useful item in a given situation. Looking through your inventory doesn’t stop the game time. You could be looking at the very low ammo of a given gun and suddenly come under attack. In most fights, the best solution is often to run away until a more advantageous moment. The narrative lasts little more than ten hours. The duration of the experience ensures the plot never drags or overstays its welcome. The mysteries of the circumstances surrounding Ethan Walker are more than enough to ensure the player fights their fear. The player won’t be able to stop themselves from enjoying their twisted adventure with the Baker family.

This time around you are not playing as a Chris Redfield pumped up on steroids that can single-handedly destroy boulders, or an apocolypse veteran president's-daughter-saving police officer Leon Kennedy.  You are an average guy placed in an unpredictable environment looking for his wife who he hasn't seen in 3 years.

The game's combat is fun and satisfying.  Inventory management made a return, thank you.  There is an emphasis on exploration and back-tracking to find everything the game offers you.  You have the freedom throughout most of the game to wander around and search for collectibles, well-hidden items, and to just soak in the environment. This makes the game feel a lot less linear, which I think is almost always a positive.  Additionally, there are a number of puzzles, although they are quite simplistic and present little challenge in solving.

Not everything is excellent however.  Enemy diversity is seriously lacking.  There just does not seem to be much variety here.  Sound design, on the whole is excellent, but the musicality throughout is absent. Where is the memorable music when you enter a Save Room? It almost feels non-existent. 

Another unfortunate issue is the lack of 21:9 support. Playing with black bars on the side at first was maddening but you get used to it soon enough. You can remove the bars but it stretches the game so badly that you would rather deal with them. 

My final gripe with the game is that I could not save my progress with the good old fashioned typewriter.  Why could THAT not have made a return as well?  That was almost a dealbreaker for me. Just kidding

On a serious note, 7 is amazing and without a doubt captures the meaning of survival horror that the masses have been awaiting. For awhile there, I nearly thought the franchise was screwed but it has been revitalized following this release.

After what could only be described as a complete disaster after Resident Evil 5 and 6, it seems Capcom are starting to not only reinvent the Resident Evil franchise to a more modern horror based game, but also at the same time bring back the old school eeriness that the old games had back in the 90's which made the franchise so popular.

I was sceptical about the game being in first person and thought that it would just give them an excuse to fill the game with jump scares like Outlast, but this isn't the case at all, in fact I have come across very little jump scares. What the first person mode does instead is rekindle that edginess you had in the originals, where you would run down a narrow corridor with fixed camera angles that would prevent you from seeing what was waiting for you ahead, or around the corner, whereas now with first person mode you only see what is ahead, sometimes finding yourself inexplicably looking behind you at all times, side to side and even above you (can never be too careful of giant spiders).

Atmosphere wise I'd say the game is spot on.... but why only 4 out of 5 then you probably wonder? Well because I feel that this game could have gotten away without being a resident evil game, I feel Capcom felt as though they cheated their fans with Res 5 and 6, so felt the need to give something back. It may be something very trivial to lose a star, but I can't help but think that Capcom have used the Resident Evil name as a marketing ploy as well, would this game have sold as many copies without Resident Evil in the title? Who knows!

Horror is a dead franchise in the video game and movie business and now it's evolved into a physiological horror, where horror isn't based on blood and gore, but putting the viewer/player in a exasperating, punishing and daunting situation, so to take a game like Resident Evil that has been based on blood and gore with elements of fear in it, and to turn it into what Resident Evil 7 is (and successfully so) I think Capcom are onto a winning streak if they follow suit and stick to this kind of foundation.

A definite purchase for any Resident Evil fan, or any fan of Horror in general.

Resident Evil's been a roller coaster of quality for twenty years now. The first handful of games terrified players by making them exceedingly vulnerable in a world where a biological weapon turned living beings into various nasties that wanted nothing more than to kill you in horrendous ways. Stagnancy raised its head eventually, and Capcom knew that it needed to inject the series' ol' corpse with some much-needed life, and we received Resident Evil 4. Depending on your perspective, that game was either a great reboot that transmuted the series into something more akin to an action horror shooter, or the death knell of the fear that Resident Evil was once associated with.

Though 5 and 6 had a few redeeming qualities, stagnancy was flooding in once again. These games were Resident Evil 4 but bigger, less focused on horror, and you could play them with a friend. The spirit of creativity that Capcom had shown in the past was fading. With the surprise announcement and subsequent demo release for Resident Evil 7, Capcom has been coy about what we should expect. Slower, fearful encounters would make a return, as would a more intimate setting, but it would be seen from a new first-person perspective, and PlayStation VR would be a major component.

I was hesitant to see if Capcom could make Resident Evil a series worth anticipating again. At best, I expected an enjoyable horror shooter with small references to past, fondly-remembered games, and at worst, a slog through a cliché-ridden hillbilly cannibal story. Instead, we have the best Resident Evil game in ten years.

The lack of ammunition and health (you'll have to sacrifice one for the other in many decisions) and the limited space in your inventory really adds pressure to item management, really going back to the original Resident Evil's survival horror. Furthermore, the ammo-sponge enemies are back, so you'll have to choose between wasting ammo to create a safe space, or running as fast as you can past enemies to get to the next safe space. Some problems with the game are the lack of variety in boss fights as they are only shoot-and-run. Also, the end of the game devolves into a shoot-fest where it'll be all killing enemies rather than sneakily going past them.

Overall, this game is one of the best I've played that is actually scary without many jump scares, so I'll give this game a 9/10 for what it tried to do. I don't want to take away points due to it being part of the Resident Evil franchise but not being part of the storyline. (Although it kind of fits well into the bio-weapon aspect of Umbrella Corp, not the zombie aspect)

Resident Evil is back!  In a market flooded with action shooters and zombie games, the developers did the best thing they could do for this game: They returned to a true survival horror formula.  If you are looking for a fast paced action horror, you will not find that here.  This game rewards patience and being thorough.

Pros:
- First Person Perspective.  YES, I do consider this a pro for this genre.  I was initally quite sceptical of this major change for the series, but it truly works.  I feel that 1st person increases the tension because rather than see things happen to a character, you ARE that character.  That being said, this still feels like Resident evil (prior to 5 and 6 that is.)
- The inventory management doesn't take away from the experience, in fact it adds to it.  Proper management of resources always has been a part of a good survival horror game, and they did great with that here.  I enjoyed finding herbs and ammo tucked away behind boxes and in corners.  
- Voice Acting.  Prior games of the series had some corny lines that were more comical than frightening or tense.  The voice acting in this game is spot on for the genre.  I was truly convinced of the characters being believable (not in term of their abilities, but the psychotic nature of the family is so well done!)
-The Story.  Hands down, this story alone gets a 10/10 from me.  Well written with many plot twists, the story is engaging and constantly pushes you to continue through the game.  I'd go as far to say as movie directors in the horror genre should learn a thing or two from this game.
-Graphics.  I'm running a gtx 1080 on a 144hz 1440p monitor, and the level of detail is incredible.  Some of the enemies really come to life here.  

Cons:
Limited number of modes.  In fact, really there is only 1 at this time.  That being said, I never felt that this wasn't worth my $60.  I took my time with the first playthrough and got 15 hours out of it.  After that, the unlocked "madhouse" difficulty not only increases damage by enemies, but moves item locations around a bit to mix things up. 

Other Thoughts:
I'm actually glad that a cooperative mode wasn't incorporated here... it just wouldn't work.  I've seen too many "survival horror" series get ruined by forcing a cooperative mode in them.  Take these three titles for example: Resident Evil 5,6, and Dead Space 3.

Where my opinions come from:
I'm a big fan of the older Resident Evil (RE) games (0, 1, 2). The resources were scarce and the combat was difficult enough that it got your adrenalin pumping and made the jump-scare moments more effective. I even enjoyed the fixed camera angle, because it added an element of creepiness when you were unable to see all around your character while hearing things coming to get you. I was somewhat disappointed with the trend that RE4 started because the game felt like it shifted from an original horror survival concept with excellent puzzles to a more common shooter with mediocre puzzles.

Overall Throughs:
I am very pleased with the direction RE7 went. The game felt like it reconnected with it's horror roots and was more exciting than the last few releases by Capcom. If you loved the older RE games, I would recommend this!

Pros:
- Limited resources for the first half of the game added to the tension of getting acquinted with the horror backdrop where the story takes place
- Lightweight crafting with no vendors further contributed to the feeling of scarcity
- Interesting combat with enemies where weapon selection and attack/defense tactics somewhat mattered
- Engaging storyline with just the right amount of mystery and ambiguity to leave your mind guessing without making the plot confusing to the point of feeling lost and/or disinterested

Cons:
- Resources became more plentiful in the second half of the game. Although the enemies became more difficult/numerous, it felt like the resource to enemy ratio wasn't balanced as well as the first half.
- Progression through locations in the game felt somewhat linear. There were definitely some areas where I felt I had significant control over where to go, but majority of the game felt like I was being directed from place to place.
- Maybe I just felt like the puzzles were better in the old games because I was much younger, but I felt like the puzzles in RE7 were very quick, easy and obvious for the most part. I think difficult puzzles add value to the game. It adds playtime and keep the mind engaged, and in the case of RE it adds opportunity for jump-scare moments after you 'think' you've cleared the area and are 100% focused on solving the puzzle.
- At nearly $90 for the game + season pass, the cost is a bit high. I was able to beat it in under 10 hours with a completionist playstyle (read all the documents, tried to collect everything I could find, etc). I wish Capcom had lowered the price by $10-20 for the bundle and allowed us to play on a higher difficulty than Normal for the first playthrough. Hopefully the Season Pass content is worth the price tag.

RE7 was hyped up as a departure from the series in every sense, a complete refresh of the story and a new direction. That seriously put me off. I know this opinion will be unpopular but I don't care about the Baker family, or a new mansion, and new location - I am a RE fan and I want Leon, Tricell, Chris, Jill, Umbrella - I've spent 20 years loving these guys, and the idea of 'all new' didn't appeal to me. Sorry, but it didn't.

So when Steam told me this game DID feature RE lore, tropes, content and familiarity, I took the risk on it. It's a risk which just didn't pay off. For a start the game's SLI support is flaky at best and non-existent at worst - it has it but it doesn't fully work properly, and for a AAA title that's not acceptable. Secondly the game was plagued by other technical issues such as stuttering, flickering, slideshow and all manner of things which made sessions just not fun.

But the game side? It just didn't interest me. I've seen torture horror done elsewhere much better than this, and it's hard to take seriously a game which is allowing me to regrow my sawn-off arm or throwing RE-style black blobs at me when it is trying too hard to not be RE. It's like a b*stard hybrid of modern survival horror and RE which for me works on no level.

It's not scary, which is depressing, because RE is not supposed to be scary, it's supposed to be camp and gripping, but this isn't trying to be RE, so that doesn't work.

But my biggest ire with this game is I just didn't care about Ethan, I didn't care about the Baker family, I didn't care about Mia, and it felt like a cr*ppy attempt at bringing a beloved franchise into a world it doesn't belong.

RE is NOT TORTURE HORROR. It's mutants, zombies, Jill, Chris and Leon - by forcing this to be RE Capcom have made a game which doesn't belong, for me. If it had been called something else and had no RE tropes in it (herbs, storage boxes) I would actually have been ok with it. I might have adored it. But apparently Umbrella do appear later, it's another virus, and you get given a machine gun in the worst elements of the 6th game. And all the waiting for it to be RE is just a waste of time.

I wanted to adore this game, believe me, but it didn't connect with me on any level and I wish Capcom hadn't bothered with it. I know it's been popular with most fans and that's fine, but I am just sad I don't share their enthusiasm.

If you thought Resident Evil 5 and 6 were scary, you should A: Not play RE7 because you'll ♥♥♥♥ yourself and B: You are 9, where the ♥♥♥♥ are your parents? Anyway, let's discuss details:

PROS:
+This is the first real survival AND horror game in the series and damn it does the job well. The atmopshere, ranging from the use of proper light to ambient sound, is perfect. The first person view benefits greatly adds to the horror since, unlike third person view, you feel more paranoid about what is around you.
+Now the PC version has a FOV slider ranging from 70 to 90. I'm used to 100 in my games, but I'm perfectly fine with just 90 since it is high enough that it doesn't look like I'm staring down a toilet roll while moving.
+Graphics settomgs are details. Very detailed. Not DOOM detailed, but detailed enough that you can tweak to your heart's content. 
+Art direction is spot on, complimenting the horror and characters well.
+Speaking of characters, this is the first Resident Evil game where the characters actual sound like they have real voice actors who give a rip. Dialog sounds like a native English speaker wrote it instead of horribly translated Japanese.
+And characyers is about it when it comes to story. Your main dude has a reason to be there and it's very simple. Now, it isn't a negative since the characters steal the show and the flavor text left in notes is great at adding to the atmopshere.
+No FNAF jumpscares. There are some, but none of them are out of nowhere and IN YOUR FACE! HA! GOT YOU because that isn't scary. It's annoying.
+LOOK AROUND! Seriously, look around and search! There are important items not underneath a spotlight.

MIXED
+/-Even though it's a first person shooter now, the movement still feels a little like Resident Evil. You can only sprint directly in front or at a slight angle, and walking backward is slower than forward. You'll notice this more when one of the bosses shows it's ugly head around. I think it's great since it forces you to look away, thus adding more uncertainty, yet I can understand why it might turn some people off.
+/1There's a mechanic where an immortal enemy will show up that you need to either sprint for deal life or stun in some sort of way. Again, like above, I like this since it's obvious that's what the game is trying to do, but to some it may turn you off. However, it is NOTHING and I mean NOTHING like Resident Evil 6's bosses that never died and took a billion bullets.
+/-Okay, this is probably another personal preference but the difficulty presents at the start are... EASY and NORMAL. NORMAL does have a difficulty ramp up at one point, but it still pretty easy if you're level headed and a good shot.  Typically using all your ammo on a boss is how most of the inventory is cleaned out. The MADHOUSE difficulty really makes the game come alive, thankfully, so at least there's some redeeming quality to how hard the game can be.

CONS:
-If you went through all that hard work (I didn't) to get that coin in the demo, congrats! It barely benefits you.

CONCLUSION:
It's a great game and anyone who hates it either doesn't like survival horror or is a jackass. If you're a fan of horror, you'll love this game a lot.

So where I am coming from:
I have played all the Resident Evil games in the main series, and honestly... I think RE4 jumped the shark... Yea, I said it, RE4 was the downfall of the series with its over-the-top boss battles, boulders, riding off in a jet ski into the sunset, and unnecessary QTE's. After that, RE5 and RE6 just went off the RE4 formula, yet, to the extreme (But I do really love mulitplayer co-op!) 

So enough of that, does this game bring back memories of my first time I had a panic attack after the first encounter of a zombie in Resident Evil 1? Yeah it did! The jump scares are really well done and keep you on your toes just when you think you have everything under control.

First-person is a excellent point-of-view for this game, and while it isn't a typical view for Resident Evil games, I really like how this is done! Also, it prevents camera problems... (::cough:: RE4 - RE6)

Survival horror is indeed back with scouring for ammo and consumable items whenever you can. Yet, the survival part is where it gets kinda frustrating and it seems a lot of people forgive this... I for one cannot.

The game purposefully hurts you and there is no way to avoid damage!!!

This truly is not a good part in game design IMO. I understand its suppose to prove your human, but what makes it frustrating as you cannot avoid damage in certain scenes. Example: (small spoilers) you have to walk in a room with bugs in it, as you walk in, you get hurt. No way to avoid this!  So using healing items that are somewhat difficult to come by is a must and your skills at evading is irrelevant in this scene. This is one of many examples that made me frustrated with this game.

Honestly, that is the only problem with this game. 

In conclusion, if you can ignore that one negative this game is amazing! It's fun, scary and PC optimized! It left me with questions about where the series is going in terms of story and feel, and hopefully Capcom continues down this path of excellence. Now if they did a co-op survival horror Resident Evil, now we are talking!

Make no mistake, Resident Evil 7 is a pure survival-horror experience from start to finish, complete with breathtaking graphics, perfectly creepy audio, and a story that keeps you engaged while still connecting to the Resident Evil mythos. There are some minor flaws, but the game as a whole is unforgettable and I urge you to experience it for yourself rather than watch a let's play or stream. 

[b]GRAPHICS:[/b] To be blunt, the game is disgusting (in a good way). You are locked in a Louisiana mansion with mutated cannibals and that brings with it exactly the kind of gross, revolting stuff you would expect. Lighting and shadows are beautiful, as are the visual effects (such as the bloom and really well done depth of field); textures are similarly great, but I had to knock them down to "Medium" on 1080p due to some stuttering issues. RE7 is definitely one of the best looking first person games I've seen in quite a while.

[b]GAMEPLAY:[/b] RE7 is a horror game first and foremost. The action-packed gameplay of previous Resident Evil titles is gone; you still have access to guns, but they are used more like tools than actual weapons capable of killing anything. You'll primarily be relying on running and hiding in a similar vein to Outlast or Alien: Isolation, both of which are used flawlessly throughout the game. Like some of the earlier Resident Evil games, there are several puzzles that have to be completed and collectibles littering the environments, so keep an eye peeled.

[b]PERFORMANCE:[/b] Generally speaking, RE7 performs well on my i7 GTX 970 8 GB RAM system. A major technical issue was the constant stuttering I was experiencing with textures set to "High"; this was fixed by knocking them down to "Medium", as mentioned above, and the difference in visual quality is negligible. Do note that you need a fairly decent rig to run the game at 60 FPS; it's definitely next-gen and can't be played on weak machines even with tweaking. 

[b]CONCLUSION: 9/10[/b]

Resident Evil 7, when announced, left a lot of fans feeling wary from the burn of previous entries to the franchise. Since the fourth entry in this hallowed series, the games sense have lacked the scares, puzzles, and charm to which fans grew accustomed. The turn left a sour taste in the mouths of many gamers as the fifth and sixth entries leaned toward a more action-oriented approach. For the past several years, Resident Evil was not a survival-horror franchise, but merely generic action titles in their exhibition. In short, they sucked, and with the seventh entry closing towards release, I know I was one of many who remained skeptical.

Thankfully, with the seventh entry, many skepticisms may be left at the back-door of the Baker mansion, as Resident Evil has finally returned to form. Everything that made the series a smash hit are here: Item and resource management, key puzzles, back-tracking, etc, just to name a few. While the game transitioned to a first-person view, departing from the series' known third-person/over-the-shoulder perspective, I feel that this change alone(thank you Outlast/Condemned/Amnesia for the influences) is what makes the game click. With a limited view and the inability to see behind the protagonist as you creep through the Baker mansion, the change to first-person really sells the horror schtick this series is best known for. 

The game was relatively short, and I finished in just under seven hours. While normally, I would dock games points and give harsh criticisms for even allowing a full-priced game such a short playthrough, I feel that if this game were any longer, it would have suffered from being stretched too thin. The story has just enough meat for the gameplay and it's a top-notch thrill ride throughout. I am alright with the price I paid for the game, but I can see how this would detract people from purchase upon release. While I went in from launch, perhaps this is something worth waiting for on-sale.

Pros:

- Series returns to its roots.
- Puzzles.
- Limited item space leads to interesting decisions on how to take each section.
- Resident Evil is scary again.
- First-person view sells the atmosphere.
- Weapons feel great.


Cons: 

- Boss fights are simple.
- Scares(at least for me), fall off due to the silliness past the first boss.
- Third act is typical Resident Evil weird. It's interesting, just not my thing.
- Short(although this wasn't a problem for me, but may for some).

8/10

Resident Evil is back, baby!

People seem worried that this game won't be "Resident Evil" because it's not Third-Person. Well I can say that if you gave this game tank controls and static camera angles, this would fit in EXTREMELY nicely with the classic series.

The first hour or so of the game is where it's the most different, with the Bakers featured very prominently and a bit of hiding at the start, but it very quickly becomes the Resident Evil many know and love.

The gameplay is fluid, and easily grasped. It was extremely satisfying to dodge attacks not with I-frames or a quick time event, but by crouching the very same way I used to explore the environment. Every action felt smooth and buttery to perform, nothing felt janky in the slightest. Puzzles are back although some are optional and only one is as complex as most in the original game, but they are still enjoyable conclusions that feel rewarding to solve.
What helps all of that is that you get extra rewards for completing the game, and even more for completing it on Madhouse [the Ultra Hard difficulty] or in under 4 hours. 

The story is also quite nice, with an ending that I personally found extremely satisfying and ultimately the game's pretty self-contained despite many clever winks to the series. If you're looking for an RE to get into, this is great, though you may miss out on some nostalgia winks.

In terms of downsides, I can only think of three. The soundtrack, which more accurately is just decent; Some good tracks but ultimately it's better as an addition to the playing experience rather than stuff you can listen to and love outside of the game [save for some tracks, it's not all mediocre.] 

The length is another, however it's very subjective. In fact I don't have an issue with the length, but I know some people will so I'm listing it here. However, I feel like it's a very nice length for a horror game, and it's accurate with the older RE titles. In fact the game tends to lose a little steam [despite still being very enjoyable] in its last 3rd, so it's good it doesn't overstay its welcome.

Just finished Resident Evil VII. Hot damn that was an excellent experience! 
The Baker family was developed and written so well that I got truly excited every time I found a clue that went further into their history. The pacing of the entire game was spot on and no segment of gameplay ever truly out stayed it's welcome. The boss battles were imaginative and challenging, they felt like the perfect balance of horrifying and comic book crazy.
The return to a fully single player, isolated and suspenseful story is an excellent shot in the arm to what could have been a deteriorating i.p. The change to a first person camera was a choice that made me skeptical at first glance but it immediately lended itself to the horror experience by making the player movement slow as to not make the game a twitch fps.
The tradition of constant inventory management and careful supply of ammunition in the early game make for a excellent balance of being the mouse and the lion. Just like a Resident Evil game from the late 90s felt.
On the negative side my only true complaint is that, aside from the excellent Baker family, you have some enemies that get a bit stale. The 'grunt' enemies of the game are called "the Molded" and they are a faceless mass of black goo turned humanoid that, after you've met them once, become little more than a nuisance that hinder your progress and make you waste ammo. The story does a good job of explaining the reasoning for the single enemy type (with multiple forms that all essentially serve to sponge away your ammo stockpile) but I do wish we had more variety in creepy things trying to kill us.
Overall Resident Evil VII is a welcome new entry into the franchise and I can't wait to see what comes next from this excellent series. The experience summed up is Texas Chainsaw meets Evil Dead with a touch of Japanese horror. Mwua!

When I first saw heard that RE7 was going to be first person I had my doubts about the game. I thought it'd be a Call Of Duty meets Outlast experience that would offer nothing exciting or interesting. When I played the demo I was surprised, it actually felt like a survival horror game. Now that I have finished the full release I am happy to say that my judgements were wrong, this is truly a great addition to the Resident Evil series.

The game has managed to capture the feeling I once had when playing the originals, the feeling that danger was lurking around every corner and that I was never truly safe. Discovering a new area gave me that feeling of uncertainty, that every door I opened had something or someone behind it. The level design is excellent, it creates a tense atmosphere whilst at the same time makes you want to explore as much as possible. The lack of music allows you to hear creaks and bumps that put you on edge. The game is great at creating a frightening aura.

The survival horror elements are back; limited item capacity, scattered ammo and health pickups, save points and backtracking are all present. Boss fights require item management and are not a case of just standing still and shooting, there is some strategy involved in defeating them. The Baker family appear throught the game at points that give the option of standing and fighting or running and hiding, akin to Nemesis in Res 3. Don't be fooled by the fact it is first person, this is no Call of Duty.

The Baker family are fantastic enemies to fight, they have that feeling of an unstoppable force that no matter how hard you fight they just won't back down. The voice acting is good too which is surprising for a Resident Evil game. The plot is not Oscar worthy and still has that B-movie feel to it like the originals, if you're looking for a scrpit on the level of The Godfather, look elsewhere.

I will admit that the enemy variety is small, most of the regular enemies outside of the Baker family are very similar. Some extra enemy types to fight would have been appreciated. Also I managed to finish the game in just over 7 hours which isn't too short but it did leave me wanting more. In its defence though I would rather have 7 hours of good quality gameplay over 30 hours of mediocrity that you get with a lot of AAA games nowadays. Also the original games are no longer to complete, survival horror games tend not to known for their longevity.

I am happy that my skepticism was proven wrong, Res 7 has been an enjoyable experience for me and I highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of the series or anyone who is looking for a fun horror game. I look forward to seeing where Capcom goes with this in the future.

PROS: 

-Nice new FPS style storytelling method that keeps your heart racing and feels more like a horror title than a typical RE franchise game.

-Nice variety of weapons and plenty of opportunities to use them.

-Interesting crafting mechanic that makes you choose between basic/advanced ammo and healing items.

-Great characters with their own unique but terrifying quirks.

-Awesome boss fights, the first few were absolutely terrifying.

-Interesting enemies though not much variety (see CONS). 

-A handy autosave function in between regular saves keeps you from having to majorly backtrack at particuarly annoying parts. Also, the Madhouse diffuculty inclusion of "save cassettes" to limit saves was a nice throwback to the ink ribbons from earlier RE games.

CONS:

-The puzzles are incredibly easy, they feel more like an excuse to recycle content you've already explored by having you run around the same areas with maybe a new enemy or two on the way. 

-The game is pretty short for an RE title and thus gamers are hit with another DLC bait and switch instead of a full game, though what is there is a good experience.

-The lack of VR support for PC (I don't know if PS4 version suffers from this as well) was pretty disappointing. This game could have been much more terrifying in VR.

-The inclusion of collectable bobbleheads that only give you 2 achievements. No new content from these at all, you might as well ignore them. They are so out of place, why even put them there?

-The lack of enemy diversity is pretty bad. There are really only 3 types of "normal" enemies, not counting one type that may or may not have missing limbs which changes its encounter slightly.

-I don't see there being much replay value here, once you've beaten the game there isn't much else to do. I guess I'll sit around and wait for some DLC but I can't imagine Capcom is going to be able to recreate that terror I felt at the start of the game as it wore off about halfway through. There are some end game addons like Madhouse difficulty and a few items/weapons you can start over with, but that just isn't enough to make me want to replay it again.

Resident Evil 7: biohazard marks a return to Resident Evil's horror elements and amplifies the tension by bringing the player into the shoes of the protagonist.

Story: Overall it's passably campy. I appreciate that you learn more about the story from both progressing, and taking the time to read diaries / journal enties, and watch VCR tapes. It's a simple setup, but it has some twists to keep players on their toes. The game also manages to sneak in some great humor, without becoming completely over the top (like Resident Evil 4).

Gameplay: Despite being a first person shooter, Resident Evil 7 remembers it's a survival horror game (limited ammo, health packs, etc.) , players have to make their shots count and have to aim for the head. 

Music: It's atmospheric and suits the game. Obviously (much like the 99.9% of horror games) you won't find any track to be particularly memorable, but it's not a problem.

Length and Replayability: This game took me 9 hours to beat on normal (recommended for the first time playing, since you will be able to appreciate alterations made in Madhouse). If you feel like playing the game again, there are challenges / achievements you can do, which will unlock weapons and items to use the next time you play the game. These challenges range from beating the game within a time limit of 4 hours, destroying hidden bottle-heads, etc. This game has some great incentives to get back to playing it again.

As a huge fan of Resident Evil, I have to say that Capcom did an incredible job bringing back the series to it's survival horror roots. While I am only 4 hours through the game, I will separate what I love from what I hated, and update the review further as I progress. 

*Pros 

- The game gives you the illusion of safety through high ammo counts, but as soon as Jack or the molded enemies appear, you go through ammo so fast without even realizing it, leading you to helplessly run or stand your ground, pull out your knife, and do it the old fashioned way. 

- Puzzles are back, and although most are not nearly as complex as previous examples, they are always satisfying to solve and never make you feel dumb or frustrated. 

- Jack, the "daddy" of the family, is one scary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He's relentless, and doesn't let up unless you cap him in the head a few times, or in the body multiple times. His dialogue is great, and sometimes even lessens the tension with his humor, before he smacks you with his shovel to get you serious again. He's unpredictable, and isn't just out to kill you, but taunt and toy with you as well. 

- Detail inside of the house is beautifully horrifying, from it's hallways covered in mold to it's dinner tables covered in entrails, the Baker house is always keeping you on the edge of your seat. 

- Plenty of collectibles to find during your journey, and some of them reward you greatly if you can find enough! Also, lockpicks are a big part in this game, but are very limited. So you need to pick and choose what you decide to unlock. You usually end up in a situation where there are 3 things you need to unlock, but you only have one lockpick. 

- PC optimization is great! Plenty of graphics options, uncapped framerate, Gsync support for the real enlightened PC gamers out there, as well as resolutions up to 4K and HBAO+ AO for Nvidia users. 

*Cons 

- Some character models kind of look odd. Something about Marguerite Baker in particular just looks out of place. Her face looks like shes had 500 plastic surgeries done and it's just ugly to look at. I'm not sure if that's what they were going for, but I wish it was a little better. 

- Sometimes it's just TOO ♥♥♥♥ing dark. Like I want to play on the recommended brightness, but it makes item discovery 10x harder when you can barely see. I don't know why the flashlight is something only the game can turn on instead of something you can turn on and off whenever you please. 

- There are some textures that really look awful. I thought the PC version would alleviate this, but a PC can only put as much effort in as the developers did. Still better on PC with high refresh rates, game runs like butter. 

Overall, I am totally LOVING this game so far. I think it's absolutely phenomenal and worth every penny. Please don't hold out and risk getting spoiled! If you're interested, buy it now.

First Thing to State: At the 60 dollar price tag, I would not recommend purchasing this game due to it's extremely short length, linearity, and very shallow boss fights and lacking content. Wait for Sales on Steam or Steam Game Sellers such as Humble Bundle and pay 30-40 maximum for the game. 

The rest I'll Simply into a list:

Story:  This is no longer about a massive infection, but rather an isolated mansion following the style of Resident Evil 1 in a way. The story itself is fairly decent, however fairly forgettable as there is no moment where an ingenius twist is takes place nor does it break any ground. 

Gameplay: First Person as with a few other resident evil games such as Survivor back on PS1 up to the Outbreaks, however a large improvement over those titles with a solid design. Classic Health bars are back, with a twist of being on a smartwatch. Rather then typewriters for saving, there is tape recorders which does give the classic feel of RE, however due to autosave situations and retries these tape recorders don't serve a major purpose as a whole. The game gives you a baby-steps style if you die at any point letting you reload/retry right before the area that you died in. Meanwhile enemies do not respawn and this detracts from the classic style of fearing an enemy could come from around the corner. You only have four different types of Molded enemies(Fat, skinny, axe like, jumper) and the baker family that you must deal with no random unique enemies and generally easy to avoid situations for each enemy. Meanwhile Boss Fights leave a bad taste in your mouth due to the overly basic design, they are forgettable fights with very underwhelming results.

Aesthetic/Graphics: The game graphically isn't the greatest looking, which is nothing necessarily unexpected giving that this was developed with consoles in mind first, rather then PC's in mind first. There are varied settings that are not functional as of the current moment including HDR, but the atmosphere of the game and it's settings are what truly drive the title rather then it's graphical fidelity.

Replay: Overall not much except for achievement hunting to be said here. The game's linearity results in very minimal exploration or secret hunting. Due to the lack of respawning enemies mentioned in the gameplay, all the events you played in the first playthrough will remain the same. No suprises will occur.

The game does a great job at it's aesthetic and throwback to more classic resident evil with a first person twist however it's length, gameplay, content, and replay leave much to be desired. At the 60 dollar price tag this game should be avoided over other titles and obtained during a sale.

My two biggest complaints about this game are the shallow puzzles and the excess of ammo and healing items. I was never, at any point in the game, almost out of ammo or first aid. I killed every enemy I came across and also missed a fair amount of shots since I suck at shooters, but still I had more ammo than I could use. About halfway through the game I was rolling with 40 Shotgun shells and blasting the head off every enemy I encountered. They ceased to be threatening very early into the game. The enemy AI is very bad and easily exploited as well. I was never afraid to die because, worst case scenario, I would be redoing 30 seconds of progress. The checkpoints are a bit too common.

The only two puzzles that I can remember off the top of my head were unbelievably easy and didn't take more than a moment of thought to solve. Half the time, they straight up tell you the solution. Items were almost always used very close by where you picked them up. It was always glaringly obvious where to use an item and just a matter of back-tracking. The game is also incredibly linear with no opportunities to mix up the order in which things are done.

The enemy types aren't nearly varied enough. That was a huge let-down for me. WHERE ARE THE DOGS!? There's even a family portrait of a dog sitting next to the Bakers! Huge missed opportunity.

The final boss was unbelievably bad. It gets built up so much and then essentially plays like a QTE. It left a very sour taste in my mouth. The ending you receive afterwards also does a very poor job of giving the game closure and tying up the story.

It didn't do everything wrong, though. I liked the characters quite a bit. The voice acting and atmosphere were phenomenal. Lots of cool animations. The video tapes were a neat little mechanic and I liked the way they implemented a shop system, even if I never did buy any of the upgrades as I didn't want to make an easy game even easier. It's definitely the best entry in the series since RE4, but after that killer demo and Dummy Finger puzzle, I was expecting a bit more. I first played Resident Evil 1 back in the 3rd grade. After being scared ♥♥♥♥-less watching my dad play it, I eventually came around to trying it out myself. I've been a fan ever since. Well, a fan of 1, 2, 3, 0, and Code Veronica. 4 was fun but way too action heavy, 5 was even farther down this path and its once revolutionary controls felt dated once Dead Space came out, 6 was so bad that I returned my rental of it after 2 hours of play, and we'll just ignore all spin-offs that weren't Outbreak.

19 years after I started my roller coaster of Resident Evil experiences, Resident Evil 7 comes out.

While flawed, this is a great step towards getting the Resident Evil franchise back towards its roots. RE4, 5 and 6 flat out didn't feel like Resident Evil games. This feels like it's at least trying to be one even if it's design direction isn't always clear. Buy it on sale unless you're a die-hard fan.

I beat the game on normal difficulty in 7 hours and 22 minutes.

Pros
-------------------------------
+The focus is on horror instead of action AND they didn't go the popular defenseless protagonist route popularized by games like Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Gods be praised! You can fight back and it's still genuinely creepy.
+I was skeptical but the first person perspective works well.
+No loading times when exploring the environment.
+The tension when fighting a B.O.W (Bio Organic Weapon) is definitely there. You have the horror of the early games and the precision shooting of the later games without the over-the-top action movie roundhouses and dives. The gun mechanics feel a little bit clunky at times but overall, the combat hits a good balance of being able to fight back in a skillful way while still keeping the player scared.
+Barring a few on rails fights, the majority of boss fights are fun and very memorable.
+The story and overall feel of the game has me eager to play Resident Evil 8.

Cons
-------------------------------
-Not counting bosses or very slight variations of enemies, there are only 4 common enemies in the game. Keep in mind that Resident Evil 1 had 8. The gameplay is much less interesting when you know what to expect. This game has a focus on the Baker family as bosses over fighting more B.O.W.'s like the other games. This can work with enemies like Resident Evil 3's Nemesis but the Baker's lack of presence and quality AI make them feel like mild annoyances on a fixed patrol route instead of constant threats.
-Leaving some rooms will make enemies respawn with full health and leaving others will not. It's not clear which doors will cause this to happen but when it does, you'll accidentally waste ammunition. Leaving some rooms also removed all enemies from them upon re-entering.
-The merchant system in this is half-assed. I really don't think Resident Evil needs this in the first place but I'm very confused why they bothered to include it in it's current state. I've left a very minor spoiler/purchase strategy in spoiler tags that I wish someone would have told me: [spoiler]You'll find antique coins when you're playing that you can use to buy up a total of 3 possible items. You will never find new items options. When you find your first "shop", make sure you keep in mind these options are all that's available to buy in this game. If you manage to find every last coin, you can buy everything. I only found 12 of the 18 coins though.[/spoiler]
-Inventory Management. Oh boy. This is really baffling from a design standpoint. Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6 all worked under the system that non-health/weapon items like keys and crests didn't take up inventory space. This makes it so you can progress the game without useless backtracking while still having a limited inventory space to keep the player from walking around with every gun/bullet in the game in their player inventory. This was absolutely an upgrade that RE4 introduced to the series and I have no idea why they changed it. Backtracking with no enemies to worry about isn't fun and trying to comprehend that a shotgun somehow takes up the same space as two keys makes me want to have a seizure. Oh and after you use up a key, you no longer get a prompt about discarding it. You can't even manually discard it. It's just stuck in your inventory until you put it in storage. Resident Evil 1 had better inventory management.
-This is the most on rails the series has ever been. This comes with the gain of some really memorable cut-scenes but you are frequently given long stretches of walking down set hallways before actually doing anything and a handful of boss fights are forced into stationary shootouts. You can tell that this game was made with VR as a first priority.  There are a handful of sections that flat-out feel like they're set up like a VR tech demo that aren't engaging when you're playing without VR. It's the VR gaming equivalent of the early, tech demos of 3D in movies. Instead of some engaging gameplay [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h7JQBPYB2gs]you're stuck with some jackass with a yo-yo.[/url]
-Hints in the loading screens can't be turned off and they will give you hints on enemies and bosses when you die. This takes out the fun in figuring out what you need to do to beat a boss. If you're like me and you hate how much modern games hold your hand, you'll have to just squint through loading screens after you die.
-You get one bigger story choice in the game and it is very poorly executed. Even Resident Evil 1 had story choices that were done better than this.
-The last boss is very disappointing.
-There are some plot-holes but I'll absolutely take this over Leon trying to save the President of the United States' daughter all by himself from a gang of evil parasitic Spaniards.

Because the game does not support ultra-wide resolutions, I've played the game on my tv and connected a ps4 controller to the computer, which was working pretty good since it was showing as a xbox controller in the game. The game is very good and very immersive.

Too bad there is no support for 21:9, but still a good game after afterall.

I want to preface my review of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard with a short backstory on how I approached the release of the game. 

I first saw the trailer for RE7 around the time after it was announced for 2017 at E3 last year. My initial thoughts were that this could just be another cash-grab for Capcom to ride on the hype surrounding VR in games. Boy was I wrong. I'm not one to give in to hype (even before No Man's Sky) and I thought to myself that perhaps I should wait before I buy this game. I eventually could not resist any longer and decided to get it. Resident Evil 7 delivered more than what I expected and gave me an immersive experience that I won't soon forget.

I have always been a huge fan of horror games, and survival horror games in particular. Games that require careful resource management and strategic use of weapons in combat. The Resident Evil series has catered for this need in the past but with the last few installments all the atmospheric nuances were ditched for a more 3rd person shooter feel - one that I personally think let down many long-time fans of the series. So, for the past few years only a handful of games helped to satiate the craving for true horror and grit, games such as Dead Space, Amnesia: The Dark Descent and SOMA. Very few other games have managed to capture the atmosphere and eerie nature of older Resident Evil games, mixed with the more slow-paced, handpicked combat sequences that make me praise the coming of Resident Evil 7. This game is a worthy addition to the franchise and one that I believe will garner fans who have never tried a Resident Evil game before. 

The game has you playing as Ethan Winters, a man who's backstory is unfortunately not explored that much in the game.  He receives a message from his wife who has been missing for over 3 years, giving her location and asking him to come get her. He starts his search at a remote house near a stream in Dulvey, Louisiana.  After a little bit of inspection things begin unraveling and Ethan becomes caught up in a quest to save his wife from the family who have been keeping her hostage and indoctrinating her with grandiose ideas of starting her own 'family' there at the house.

The graphics and visual effects are quite breathtaking, and the lighting is expertly used as a tool to serve as your guide for seeing the shadows of monsters approaching around a corner, or whether or not a certain spot is dark enough to hide in. As with any good horror game, the soundtrack is done remarkably well and made my heart beat a little faster even when I was consciously trying to avoid it. Bundle that with masterful audio work that lets you hear and feel the sinister surroundings of the Baker family's yard and you will either turn away in fear or embrace the darkness of this spectacular atmphosheric game.

The game should take no more than 10 hours to complete even if you are an avid treasure hunter  like me. Albeit, the game offers some good replayability in the fact that you have to complete it at least twice to get all the achievements because Madhouse diffculty is only unlocked once you complete it on Normal. And then there is still the challenge to complete it in under 4 hours... indeed, good luck.

If you've never played a RE game, you can rest assured that you will enjoy this game without missing too much of the overarching  story and how this game ties in with the others.

(aparently steam claims I recieved this game for free but I didn't, not sure why it's doing that for this review~)

Anyway, I'm mostly indifferent with my overall opinion with this game but if I had to give it a choice for how it is so far, i'd be leaning more towards the negative. It's not because it's a bad game, in fact it's a pretty damn good game, but if a game starts off great but eventually leaves be with a less than satisfied feeling with it, then I can't really say I had a strong positive feeling for it. Right now I believe I'm currently at the final stretch of the game and I've already long crossed the point at the point where I just want the game to end because I feel like it has nothing of quality left to deliver and it's just dragging on and on...

I loved the first 1/3 of this game (pretty much up until the fight with Marguerite). There were some interesting puzzle, Interesting and tense environments to explore and very charismatic villains that will have you itching to found out just what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on here.

But after all of that fun, it quickly begins to show that all the depth in the games design was shovelled into the first couple hours of the game. If you've played pretty much any resident evil game before, then you already have a good idea on what the last 1-3 hours of the game design is like. The enviroments become very bland and with little to no thought put into the map design to make it interesting or fun to explore.

Like I said, I'm still fairly indifferent and your opinions may very well differ. You can either pick it up now or pick it up in a sale or bundle. Either way you'll get something out of this game.

Having played all of the main Resident Evil games in the series (excluding CODE:Veronica) I can honestly say that this game has been a blast from start to finish. It feels like they really hit all the high notes from both the new and old games; it evokes so much of the atmosphere and dread of the original tank control style games (RE0 - C:V), while having a satsifying combat system that is on par with the over-the-shoulder RE4 - RE6 games. You won't be doing b.s. spin kicks and boulder breaking power punches, but guns are satisfying to use and you always feel like you can work your way out of a situation.

My only gripes are a smaller than normal variety of enemies, at least for a RE game, and a short campaign. To be fair though, the smaller number of enemies means you will be very familiar with how to deal with them, and the game length isn't too much different than previous RE games. Plus, much like every other RE, you are meant to play a run more than once with whatever rewards you gain upon completion.

Overall, this has been a very fun and worthy addition to the RE family tree, and one that I hope will be expanded upon with the coming DLC.
